title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
description:
Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB.

The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly.

Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions. The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images.

Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion.

See the documentation for the full setup.

title: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection
description:
Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets.

Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in.

These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

title: BernBRS: Certified Backward Reachability for Deep Bernstein Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.22083v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

title: AWS Transform now accelerates migration deals for Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) benefits
description:
AWS Partners can now expedite Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) deals, from qualification to incentive payout, with an end-to-end agentic workflow in AWS Transform. Partners can manage the full MAP lifecycle without leaving AWS Transform, including deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, migration planning and execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement.

Previously, Partners had to switch between separate systems for opportunity discovery, assessments, deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. This fragmentation, along with manual handoffs between steps, led to longer qualification cycles.

Now, with the agentic MAP experience in AWS Transform, Partners connect their AWS Partner Central account and invite customers into the same engagement. Partners start by scoping customer environments with the built-in agentic discovery tool, or by importing data from RVTools or AWS-validated ISV tools listed in AWS Marketplace. AWS Transform then combines this discovery data with opportunity details from APN Customer Engagements (ACE) to automatically qualify Partner-initiated opportunities in a guided flow, so Partners get eligibility decisions sooner and close deals faster. As the migration progresses, MAP resource tags are applied automatically, and Partner cash and customer credits are disbursed based on actual usage data. Throughout, customers get shared, real-time visibility into migration projects alongside their Partner.

AWS Transform with integrated MAP is now available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) page. Partners can get started with the AWS Partner Central user guide (login required) or by contacting their Partner Development Manager. Customers can contact their AWS account team or AWS Partner.

title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home

title: The Error That Escaped Without A Collar
description:
One exit for every error of every transport: a mapped code instead of Unknown, a fixed message instead of internal text, and a panic that becomes Internal instead of taking the process with it.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The exit guard is built into the shared library and is on by default in its gRPC server chain; its tests, benchmarks and leak checks were run as targeted runs with the race detector. How often the old leak happened in production I did not measure, and I do not claim a number.

This is part 3 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Every animal that leaves an enclosure in our zoo wears a collar. The collar says whose animal it is and where it belongs. Keepers put it on at the gate, every time, by hand.

One morning Nora finds Biscuit, our dog, trotting along the main path with no collar at all. "Whose dog is this?!" Biscuit, very pleased with himself, answers the only thing he can: "Unknown! Woof!"

It gets worse. A dog without a collar does not know what not to say. Biscuit happily tells every visitor what he saw behind the scenes: "Table seven, row forty-two!" Miso hisses "Shh! Nobody asked you" - but by then the visitors have heard it.

The zoo's fix is not "keepers, please remember the collar". The fix is a keeper at the one gate everybody leaves through. Nobody leaves without a collar - even Biscuit. And when somebody faints at the gate, the gate keeper does not panic either: the animal is carried out with a plain tag that says "internal", and the zoo stays open.

The mapper you had to remember

In our services, a handler turns a domain error into an answer for the caller. For gRPC that is a status code with a reason; for HTTP a status and a body; for a consumer a decision to drop the message or try again. The library has a builder for exactly that mapping, and for a long time each handler called it itself.

That is the keeper who has to remember the collar. The library's changelog describes what happened when one did not: the forgotten call handed the caller Unknown with the internal text of the error, and a panic in a consumer flew into the goroutine of the resource that ran it. Two failures, one cause: the last step of every error was optional.

One gate for three transports

The library now has one exit for errors, with three doors on it. In the shape of the code - names shortened, the meaning is what matters:

// one exit for every transport - a form
guard.Answer(ctx, err)        // gRPC / HTTP: a mapped status, never raw text
guard.Recover(ctx, p)         // a panic -> Internal, a fixed message, the span marked
guard.Settle(ctx, msg, err)   // a consumer: drop the message, or retry it

Answer is the collar. Whatever error a handler returns, it goes through the mapping on the way out, so a forgotten mapper is no longer a leak - the gate maps it.

Recover is the keeper at the gate when someone faints. A panic in a handler becomes Internal with a fixed message, the trace span is marked, and the process keeps serving everyone else.

Settle is the consumer's door. A message whose error code is in the drop list - by default InvalidArgument and its neighbours, errors that will not get better by trying again - is dropped; anything else is retried. Before, that decision was another thing each consumer had to remember.

The guard is on by default in the chain of the library's gRPC server. A service does not import it to get it - which is why the count of services that import it directly is zero, and the count that run it is every service on that server.

Door Before After
gRPC the handler maps, or the caller gets Unknown with internal text the gate maps every error
HTTP the same, by hand per handler the same gate, the same mapping
consumer a panic flies into the resource goroutine Internal, span marked, process alive
consumer decision each consumer decides drop or retry one rule: drop codes are dropped, the rest retried

What the caller sees

The difference is easiest to see from the outside. The same failure, as a caller received it before and after the gate - shapes only, with the internal text replaced by a placeholder:

before:  code = Unknown
         message = "<internal error text: query, table, row>"

after:   code = <the mapped code, e.g. NotFound / FailedPrecondition>
         reason = <a reason code the caller can branch on>

panic:   code = Internal
         message = "<a fixed panic message>"     # the span is marked, the process lives

The caller of the first answer can do nothing but log it and give up, and the text in it belongs to the service, not to the caller. The caller of the second can branch on the reason. The third answer is the important quiet one: a single broken request no longer takes the process down with it.

Tested at the gate

A gate is only worth something if it holds under load and under races. The tests, benchmarks and goroutine-leak checks for the guard were written in a pass over several prompt sets and run as targeted runs with the race detector.

What went wrong

Two real leaks, both from the same design: the last step of an error was the handler's job. A forgotten mapper sent Unknown with internal text to a caller - the dog without a collar, telling visitors about table seven. A panic in a consumer escaped into the goroutine of the resource that ran it - the animal fainting in the middle of the path instead of at the gate.

The lesson is the one this whole series keeps repeating. A rule that every handler must remember is not a rule; it is a hope. The fix was not a review checklist or a linter warning but a gate in the one place every error passes, on by default.

What I do not claim

  • Not how often the leak hit callers before the gate. I did not count it.
  • Not that every service already runs the newest guard. It is on by default for services on the library's server.
  • Not that the drop list fits every consumer. It is the default.
  • Not a full load test. The guard has benchmarks and race runs, not a production measurement.

What of this is method

  • The last step of every error lives at one gate. Not in each handler.
  • A panic is an answer, not an exit. Internal, a fixed message, the span marked, the process alive.
  • Drop or retry is decided once. By the error's code, in one place.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 3. Next: One Ticket, Punched Once.

If your handlers map their own errors, how would you find the one that forgot? If you recover panics, where - per handler, or at one gate? If your consumers decide drop or retry, is that decision written once or many times? What did your last error without a collar say to a caller?

title: One button sent people to the wrong page. We checked all 41, and 14 didn't go where they said.
description:
On Tuesday morning I opened the page a small clothing shop was about to get from us: a short video of one of their products, and under it a single button that said "Make one with your own character."

It was a product, not a character. And the button didn't open anything that makes a video. It opened the page where you build a new character from scratch.

This post is about that one button, the 40 others we checked because of it, and the rule we wrote so it stops happening.

TL;DR
We audited all 41 calls to action on our site and in our emails. 14 didn't go where their words said. We fixed 7 the same day, 7 sit on pages we froze on purpose, and a test now fails the build if a button drifts.

The words said one thing and the link did another

I build RefVid, a small tool where you upload a few photos of a product or a character once, then make short videos that keep it looking the same in every shot. Every finished video gets a public share page, and that page has one job: let whoever watches it make their own.

The share page picked its words from a fallback. When a video wasn't made from a template, the page assumed it was about a character, wrote "Keep your own character the same in every shot", and pointed the button at the character builder (we call saved characters and products "elements").

So a shop owner watching a video of their own product would read "character" and land on a form asking them to create one. Nothing on that page says "video".

My first fix sent it to a second wrong page

The obvious patch: read the subject's type. If the clip shows a product, say "Make one with your own product". That went in at 11:15 UTC.

Then I looked at where it actually led. With no template recorded, the new button opened our marketing page for product videos. The words were right now. The destination was a page that explains the thing instead of starting it.

That fix lasted 22 minutes. The second one, at 11:37, is what this post is really about, because by then the question had changed from "why is this button wrong?" to "how many buttons are wrong?"

So we listed every button on the site: 41 of them

We went through every page type and every email we send, and wrote down each call to action as a row: the file, the words, where it goes for a signed-in visitor, and where it should go.

41 rows. 27 were fine. 14 were not. These are the 7 we fixed that day:

Words on the button Where it lives Went to Now goes to
Make one with your own character Share page, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make one with your own product Share page, product clip, no template Marketing page New video
Make one with your own subject Gallery, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make your own series Series index, episodes, making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
Try it in the studio Prompt blocks on making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
(sign in) Invite welcome sheet, no template Character builder New video
Make another "Your video is ready" email That subject's page New video, same subject

The part that surprised me: the same action, "start a new video", was written four different ways in the code. One helper went to the builder, one component opened a photo picker first, one link went to the marketing page, and the email linked to the subject's own page. Every one of them made sense on the day it was written. Together they meant a visitor couldn't predict where "make one" would take them.

Not one label changed in the fix. The words were already right in all 7 languages we ship. Only the destinations moved.

The rule: one label, one destination, defined once

We wrote it down as four rows, and every button on the site now has to be one of them:

The button means Example words Goes to
Make one like this (template known) "Use this template" New video with that template filled in
Start a new video (no template) "Make one with your own…", "Try it", "Make another" New video, nothing preset
Create a character or product Only words that say so: "New element" The builder
Go to the studio "Studio", "Open the studio" The studio home

And each row is built by exactly one function. "Start a new video" is one helper call; nothing else in the codebase is allowed to assemble that link by hand. If you want to see the "make one like this" row working, any card in our template gallery goes straight into a new video with that template filled.

The same bug, in an email, cost a user 124 credits

The same morning a support email arrived. A user had signed up on their phone, added their own photo, and somehow never started a video. Our follow-up email said, more or less: the photo you added is already saved; open the link and press Generate.

The link carried their saved photo in the URL:

/studio/t/product-black-friday?subject=<their photo>

They opened it in their mail app, signed out. Our middleware redirected them to sign in and rebuilt the destination from the path only:

/login?intent=template:product-black-friday

The subject was gone. After sign-in, the template page did what it does when you have no photo: it loaded the template's sample product, a perfume bottle. They pressed Generate, exactly as the email told them, and 124 of their 129 signup credits went into a sample perfume ad they never asked for.

We refunded the credits and added extra, and fixed the redirect so the intent keeps everything it was given:

template:<slug>[:fresh][:subject-<id>]

In the 30 days before, 72 people got that exact "your photo is already saved" email. One of them hit this. That's a small number, and it is also every credit that person had.

It's the same mistake as the button, one layer down: the words promised a destination, and something between the click and the page threw part of it away.

Tests now fail the build if a button drifts

A rule I have to remember will fail again. So the rule is a test. cta-one-destination.test.ts reads the source and fails when:

  • any file outside a short allow-list sends someone to the builder (each allowed file has a one-line reason next to it),
  • a start link is assembled by hand instead of through the one helper,
  • the share page points at a marketing page,
  • a share button says "product" and opens the builder, or says "character" and opens a product page, checked in all 7 languages.

A second test follows the email link as a signed-out visitor through the sign-in redirect and checks that the saved photo is still in the URL where sign-in lands.

What we haven't fixed yet

7 of the 14 wrong buttons are still wrong, on purpose, for now.

They sit on pages we froze on 8 November: our home page, our pricing page and our cartoon series hub. Those are the pages an AI assistant had started sending visitors to, and we decided not to touch them at all while we watched whether that traffic held. We are now unfreezing pages one at a time, each change measured against its own before-numbers. These three haven't had their turn.

Words on the button Page Goes to today Should go to
Make one with your own subject Home, gallery Character builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, header Photo picker, then builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, closing block Photo picker, then builder New video
Generate (own photos, no template) Home, composer Builder with the photos New video with the photos
Make this (an ad format) Home, ad strip The sample subject's page New video with that prompt
Start free Pricing Studio home New video
One clip Pricing Studio home New video

The guard test knows about the three that open the builder: their files sit on its allow-list, each marked "frozen page". When a page thaws, its line comes off the list and the test forces the fix; the other four are on the audit list waiting for the same day. Until then, if you land on our home page and press one of those, you'll see the old behaviour.

A question for you

If you searched your own app today for every button that says "start", "try" or "make one", how many different places would they lead, and would you be able to say which one is right?

title: What is GhostMap that Aqua Security detected in IronWorm and Atomic Arch?
description:
Aqua Security details GhostMap, a concealment component identified in IronWorm malware samples distributed via compromised software packages.

Learn how the stealth tool hides selected processes and network connections.

GhostMap does the hiding; it's not the entire malware. Aqua examined IronWorm, which was distributed via compromised software packages. Previous research had reported that IronWorm targeted developer secrets, such as login credentials and digital access keys.

How GhostMap was installed

The researchers examined the file included in the package [email protected]When they ran it with administrator privileges, the file copied itself elsewhere on the system and created a service that remained installed. The service launched GhostMap.

The test did not show that the program could obtain administrator privileges on its own or start without them.

What could he be hiding?

In tests, some programs didn't appear in a regular list of what was running. However, researchers were able to find them from other parts of the system. They reappeared in the lists when GhostMap was stopped.

The connection used by IronWorm did not appear in any of the connection lists in all three tests. However, another check still showed it, without revealing which program had opened it.

Aqua also found program names and internal structures in the Atomic Arch sample that matched GhostMap. This does not prove that the two campaigns were run by the same operator. The detailed testing of what it could hide and how it could be detected was on the IronWorm sample that Aqua tested.

What did Aqua's tool detect?

Aqua's Tracee tool detected three programs that could change data in the memory of other applications. In the test, it recorded all 48 calls involving reading directories. This suggests that it was able to detect the activity, not prevent it.

Aqua confirmed that IronWorm stored test data on the system itself. It did not observe any successful sending of data outside the system, nor did it confirm successful execution of remotely authenticated commands.

For systems that may have been exposed, Aqua suggests comparing the lists of programs seen with preserved executables and known paths. /proc/PIDIt also suggests checking for unrecognized services and programs associated with eBPF. Before removing a suspicious file, administrators should keep its information and any additional information stored with it.

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
description:
arXiv:2611.22188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.

title: Build a "Start Here" Index for Your Community with 30 Lines of Python
description:
Every online community hits the same wall. Members ask questions that were already answered, because the answers are buried in a date-sorted feed. The fix is to organize by problem instead of by date, and you can automate most of that cleanup with a small script.

Here's how I'd build it.

The idea

  1. Export or copy your past questions (title + link) into a JSON file.
  2. Map each question to a "problem" bucket using simple keyword rules.
  3. Generate a Markdown "start here" post grouped by problem.
  4. Pin it, and re-run the script whenever new answers pile up.

No AI required for version one. Keyword rules are boring, predictable, and easy to debug, which is exactly what you want from a first automation.

The input

A file called questions.json:

[
  {"title": "How do I follow up with new leads automatically?", "url": "https://example.com/post/1"},
  {"title": "Best way to start a newsletter for my SaaS?", "url": "https://example.com/post/2"},
  {"title": "Can I turn my spreadsheet into a weekly report?", "url": "https://example.com/post/3"}
]

The script 

import json

PROBLEMS = {
    "lead follow-up": ["lead", "follow up", "crm", "booking"],
    "email and newsletters": ["email", "newsletter", "inbox"],
    "data and reporting": ["spreadsheet", "report", "dashboard"],
    "getting started": ["start", "first", "beginner"],
}

def categorize(title):
    text = title.lower()
    for problem, keywords in PROBLEMS.items():
        if any(k in text for k in keywords):
            return problem
    return "uncategorized"

def build_index(questions):
    index = {}
    for q in questions:
        index.setdefault(categorize(q["title"]), []).append(q)
    return index

def to_markdown(index):
    lines = ["# Start here: find your problem", ""]
    for problem in sorted(index):
        lines.append(f"## {problem.title()}")
        for q in index[problem]:
            lines.append(f"- [{q['title']}]({q['url']})")
        lines.append("")
    return "\n".join(lines)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("questions.json") as f:
        questions = json.load(f)
    print(to_markdown(build_index(questions)))

Run it with python build_index.py > start_here.md and paste the output into a pinned post.

How it works

PROBLEMS is your whole configuration. Each key is a problem in your members' words; each value is a list of keywords. categorize() returns the first bucket whose keyword appears in the title, so order matters: put the most specific problems first.

build_index() groups questions into buckets, and to_markdown() turns those buckets into headings and links.

Anything that lands in "uncategorized" is a signal. Either you need a new keyword, or you've found a new problem your members care about.

Making it better

  • Schedule it. Run it weekly with cron or a GitHub Action and diff the output so you only update the pinned post when something changes.
  • Add an LLM fallback. For uncategorized titles only, ask a model to pick one of your existing buckets. Keep the keyword rules as the first pass so results stay predictable and cheap.
  • Track gaps. Count questions per bucket. The bucket with the most questions and the fewest good answers is your next lesson.

Why bother

A problem-sorted index gives new members a quick win, cuts repeat questions, and shows you what to create next. It's a tiny automation with an outsized payoff.

I'm building my own community, Automation Entrepreneur, around exactly this kind of practical automation. Join us here: https://www.skool.com/automation-enterenpeur-7666

title: Bad Apples in the Kitchen: How LLM Teams Detect, Correct, and Calibrate Against Their Misaligned Members
description:
arXiv:2611.22342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: What protects an LLM team when one teammate quietly goes wrong? Most multi-agent LLM work assumes cooperative partners and inspects chat between turns before acting. Real-time embodied cooperation does not allow this pause: chat runs alongside action, so a teammate whose words stay cooperative while behavior diverges can cause damage faster than the team can name what is happening. We study this case by injecting three theory-grounded misaligned agents into a custom four-player Overcooked environment, each stressing a different joint-action layer (speech-action mismatch, role invasion, and aggregate-progress disruption), and decompose robustness into three sequential gates of detection, correction, and calibration through a 3x4x2 design (n=720 episodes). Nearly all trolls are eventually named, but recovery follows only when attribution and situational diagnosis appear in the same utterance; direct source-attribution prompting improves the hardest case only by degrading the troll-free baseline by 37.5%. Robustness, then, depends less on detection alone than on whether team chat combines attribution with diagnosis in a single utterance, suggesting that sensitivity to misalignment should be targeted rather than uniformly raised.

title: When DDD Is the Wrong Tool for the Job
description:
A pure CRUD application scores zero.

That's not a critic of domain-driven design talking. It's Vaughn Vernon, in the first chapter of Implementing Domain-Driven Design, the book half the industry calls "the red book." He gives you a scorecard for deciding whether your project deserves DDD, and the lowest row is for an application that is "completely data centric and truly qualifies for a pure CRUD solution." Points for that row: 0. You need 7 before he says you should seriously consider DDD.

Here's the part that surprises people. Every major voice in the DDD world has said some version of this. Eric Evans, Martin Fowler, Udi Dahan, Microsoft's own reference architecture. The warning is right there in the source material. It just doesn't survive the trip into conference talks and starter templates, where "we do DDD here" turns into five layers wrapped around a table with six columns.

This article is about the cases where that ceremony isn't worth it, why, and the harder question: how to tell when a service that was fine as CRUD has quietly grown into something that needs a real model. It's the flip side of the modeling pieces on this site. If you want the case for the patterns, Aggregate Design and Modeling a Credentialing Workflow as a Domain make it. This one is about when to leave them in the drawer.

Note
A quick honesty note. The idea for this piece started as "real cases where DDD wasn't worth it." The scenarios below are hypotheticals built from the published guidance, not war stories, and every quote and example is from a source you can check.

The people who wrote the book already said no

Start with the sources, because they're more blunt than their reputation.

Eric Evans, 2003. The original Domain-Driven Design book describes an approach it calls the Smart UI, where business logic lives directly in the screens and the database is the integration point. Evans labels it an "anti-pattern," but with obvious irony, because he then lists its advantages: "Productivity is high and immediate for simple applications," and "Less capable developers can work this way with little training." He says it fits projects that are simple, "dominated by data entry and display, with few business rules." He calls it "an alternate, mutually exclusive fork in the road." Not a failure. A different road.

Eric Evans, 2009. At QCon London, in a talk titled "What I've learned about DDD since the book," Evans said the building blocks, meaning value objects, entities, factories, repositories, and services, were "over emphasised." He also said: "Not all of a large system will be well designed, but parts of the system can be properly designed." The job is picking which parts.

Martin Fowler, 2003. In Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, Fowler compares Transaction Script and Domain Model and gives the rule of thumb people still quote: if you have "simple not-null checks and a couple of sums to calculate," a Transaction Script "is a better bet."

Udi Dahan, 2009. In an MSDN Magazine piece called "Employing the Domain Model Pattern," Dahan names "the No. 1 most common fallacy": "Any persistent object model is a domain model." He also says flatly that "one reason not to make use of the domain model pattern is if the business your software is automating does not change much."

Microsoft's reference app. The eShopOnContainers sample, which Microsoft built specifically to teach microservices on .NET, uses DDD patterns in its ordering service and deliberately does not use them in its catalog service. The accompanying architecture guide says: "if your microservice or Bounded Context is very simple (a CRUD service), the anemic domain model in the form of entity objects with just data properties might be good enough, and it might not be worth implementing more complex DDD patterns."

So the premise that DDD is a universal best practice isn't a position any of its main authors actually hold. They all describe it as a tool for complex, changing business logic, and they all tell you to do something simpler everywhere else.

Vernon's scorecard, paraphrased from chapter 1, is the most concrete version of the test:

If your project looks like... Points
Completely data-centric, every operation is a simple create, read, update, or delete 0
30 or fewer business operations, with little logic in them 1
Around 30 to 40 user stories or use case flows 2
Hints of moderate complexity that might grow 3
Features that will keep changing frequently over years 4
A new domain nobody on the team fully understands yet 5

The threshold is 7. Notice what the rows measure: volume of behavior, rate of change, and how much you don't know yet. Not team size, not traffic, not how "enterprise" the codebase feels. His other test is even shorter: if you could build the thing quickly in Rails or Grails "and not feel the pain of lacking power and control over complexity and change," you probably don't need DDD.

What the ceremony looks like on a service that doesn't need it

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a venue directory service. Staff add venues, edit their address and capacity, archive the ones that close. Other services read the list. That's it. No pricing, no approvals, no workflow, no state machine.

Now imagine it was built "properly," because the team template says every service gets the full DDD treatment. In NestJS with @nestjs/cqrs, the update path might look like this:

src/venues/domain/venue.ts

export class Venue {
  private constructor(
    private readonly _id: string,
    private _name: string,
    private _address: string,
    private _capacity: number,
    private _archived: boolean,
  ) {}

  static rehydrate(props: VenueProps): Venue {
    return new Venue(props.id, props.name, props.address, props.capacity, props.archived);
  }

  rename(name: string) { this._name = name; }
  relocate(address: string) { this._address = address; }
  changeCapacity(capacity: number) { this._capacity = capacity; }

  get id() { return this._id; }
  get name() { return this._name; }
  get address() { return this._address; }
  get capacity() { return this._capacity; }
  get archived() { return this._archived; }
}

src/venues/application/update-venue.handler.ts

@CommandHandler(UpdateVenueCommand)
export class UpdateVenueHandler implements ICommandHandler<UpdateVenueCommand> {
  constructor(@Inject(VENUE_REPOSITORY) private readonly venues: VenueRepository) {}

  async execute(cmd: UpdateVenueCommand): Promise<void> {
    const venue = await this.venues.findById(cmd.id);
    if (!venue) throw new NotFoundException();
    venue.rename(cmd.name);
    venue.relocate(cmd.address);
    venue.changeCapacity(cmd.capacity);
    await this.venues.save(venue);
  }
}

Plus a VenueRepository interface, a Postgres implementation of it, a VenueMapper that converts rows to Venue and back, an UpdateVenueCommand class, the controller, and the module wiring. Call it eight files to change three columns.

Look at what each layer is defending. The entity's methods are setters with nicer names. rename doesn't check anything. changeCapacity doesn't know what a valid capacity is. The repository abstracts over one database you'll never swap. The mapper copies fields in a circle.

This is exactly what Fowler described in his "AnemicDomainModel" bliki entry in November 2003: objects "named after the nouns in the domain space," with "hardly any behavior on these objects, making them little more than bags of getters and setters." His verdict on it is the line worth remembering: an anemic model incurs "all of the costs of a domain model, without yielding any of the benefits."

That's the real failure mode. Not "we didn't use DDD." It's "we paid for DDD and got a transaction script anyway, spread across eight files." Every new field is now a five-file change. Every new engineer has to learn the layering before they can add a column. And nothing in those layers is protecting a rule, because there aren't any rules.

The same service, as a transaction script

Here's the version Fowler and Dahan are pointing you toward. One module, plain SQL, the database doing the work it's good at:

src/venues/venues.service.ts

import { Pool } from 'pg';

export interface VenueInput {
  name: string;
  address: string;
  capacity: number;
}

export class VenuesService {
  constructor(private readonly pool: Pool) {}

  async update(id: string, input: VenueInput) {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      `UPDATE venues
          SET name = $2, address = $3, capacity = $4, updated_at = now()
        WHERE id = $1 AND archived = false
        RETURNING id, name, address, capacity`,
      [id, input.name, input.address, input.capacity],
    );
    return rows[0] ?? null; // null -> controller returns 404
  }

  async archive(id: string) {
    const { rowCount } = await this.pool.query(
      `UPDATE venues SET archived = true WHERE id = $1 AND archived = false`,
      [id],
    );
    return rowCount === 1;
  }
}

And the "rules" live where they're cheapest to enforce and hardest to bypass:

migrations/001_venues.sql

CREATE TABLE venues (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name       text NOT NULL CHECK (length(name) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  address    text NOT NULL,
  capacity   integer NOT NULL CHECK (capacity > 0),
  archived   boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Input validation still happens at the edge, with whatever you already use for DTOs. But notice that this version actually enforces more than the eight-file one did. The capacity rule exists. It's in a CHECK constraint that every writer hits, including the migration script someone runs by hand at 11pm, which never goes through your aggregate.

This is the Transaction Script pattern, and Khononov's Learning Domain-Driven Design (O'Reilly, 2021) is worth reading on it, because he presents it as a legitimate DDD-era choice, not a lapse. His design heuristics include a decision tree for picking a business logic pattern, and mapped onto subdomain types it roughly goes:

  • Supporting or generic subdomain, simple data: Transaction Script.
  • Supporting or generic subdomain, complex data structures: Active Record.
  • Core subdomain with complex business logic: Domain Model.
  • Core subdomain where you need money tracking, an audit log, or deep history analysis: Event-sourced Domain Model.

That's a paraphrase of a tree that has a few more branches for architecture style, but the shape is the point. Choosing Transaction Script for a venue directory is DDD's own strategic advice applied correctly: spend modeling effort where the business is complicated, and nowhere else.

The invariant that belongs in the database, not the aggregate

One gotcha catches nearly every team that models everything. Dahan uses it in his 2009 article, and it's the cleanest example there is: a user's email address must be unique.

It feels like a domain rule. It's written in the requirements. So it goes in the domain layer:

src/users/application/register-user.handler.ts

async execute(cmd: RegisterUserCommand) {
  const existing = await this.users.findByEmail(cmd.email);
  if (existing) throw new ConflictException('Email already registered');

  const user = User.register(cmd.email, cmd.name);
  await this.users.save(user);
}

This compiles. It passes every unit test you'll write for it. And it's broken, because it's a check-then-act race. Two registration requests for the same address arrive a few milliseconds apart. Both run findByEmail, both get nothing back, both insert. Postgres runs at READ COMMITTED by default, so neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted row. You now have two users with the same email and a domain model that swears it prevented this.

Dahan's reasoning about why this doesn't belong in the model is the more interesting part. The domain model, in his framing, exists to capture business behavior "subject to change." Email uniqueness will almost certainly never change. Putting it in the part of the system built for volatile rules "makes little sense, may be difficult to implement, and might not perform that well." His conclusion: "A unique constraint in the database would suffice."

It does more than suffice. It's the only version that's actually correct under concurrency without taking heavier locks:

migrations/002_users_email_unique.sql

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique ON users (lower(email));

src/users/users.service.ts

const UNIQUE_VIOLATION = '23505'; // Postgres SQLSTATE unique_violation

async register(email: string, name: string) {
  try {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      `INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id`,
      [email, name],
    );
    return rows[0];
  } catch (err: unknown) {
    if ((err as { code?: string }).code === UNIQUE_VIOLATION) {
      throw new ConflictException('Email already registered');
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

The index on lower(email) also handles the case the in-memory check usually forgets, Ann@example.com versus ann@example.com. The general lesson reaches well past emails: a lot of what gets modeled as aggregate invariants on simple services is really uniqueness, referential integrity, non-null, or a range check. Databases have enforced those for decades, atomically, for every writer. An aggregate that re-implements them in application code is slower, racier, and easier to bypass.

This is also the honest answer to "but where does the business logic go?" in a CRUD service. Some of it is constraints. Some of it is validation at the edge. And if there's genuinely nothing left after that, you don't have a domain model problem. You have a table.

Four shapes of service where the model isn't worth it

These are hypotheticals, but each one maps onto a specific piece of the guidance above.

1. Reference data and back-office editors

Country lists, product categories, venue directories, feature flag admin screens, CMS-style content. This is Vernon's zero-point row and Evans's "data entry and display, with few business rules." The users are editing records, and the records are the product. A generated admin, a thin REST layer, or a transaction script per endpoint is the right amount of design.

2. Anything that wraps somebody else's domain

A service whose job is to call Stripe, send email through a provider, or sync with an identity platform. The real rules live in the vendor. In DDD's own vocabulary this is a generic subdomain: needed, but nothing special to your business. Modeling Stripe's concepts as your own aggregates just gives you a second, worse copy of their model to keep in sync. What you want at that boundary is a translation layer, which is still a DDD idea (an anti-corruption layer), not a rich model behind it.

3. The read side of almost anything

Dahan makes this point in the same 2009 article: "Showing user information involves no business behavior and is all about opening up that data." Search screens, dashboards, list views, and exports don't need to go through entities at all. Query the tables, or a view, and shape the result for the screen. You don't need full CQRS to take this advice; the trade-offs of going further are in CQRS in NestJS: When It's Worth the Complexity.

4. Code you're planning to throw away

A proof of concept, an experiment, a service with a known expiry date. Microsoft's CRUD microservice guide explicitly allows for this: "Perhaps the problem to solve is simple, or perhaps the implementation is only a proof of concept." Tactical DDD is an investment in making future change cheap. If there isn't meant to be a future, don't pay for one. Sacrificial Architecture covers how to build that kind of service so it actually gets deleted.

The trap on the other side: Evans's one-way door

Here's where the "just do CRUD" crowd gets it wrong, and it's in the same chapter where Evans defends the Smart UI. Right after listing its advantages, he gives the catch: "you can't migrate to another design approach except by replacing entire applications." He also warns that with Smart UI, "Complexity buries you quickly, so the growth path is strictly toward additional simple applications."

So there are two kinds of "no DDD," and they're not equal:

  • Smart UI style: logic smeared across controllers, templates, and stored procedures, business rules duplicated in every screen that needs them. Fast today, and a rewrite the day the rules show up.
  • Transaction script behind a clean service boundary: one function per operation, one place per operation, the database enforcing what it can, and nothing leaking into the transport layer. Just as fast today, and refactorable later.

The second one is what Fowler means when he says Transaction Script is the "better bet" for simple logic. It's simple, but it's not scattered. Each operation is a readable procedure, so when real rules arrive you can find every place that needs to change. That's the whole difference between a deliberate choice and a hole you'll have to climb out of.

My position: default to the transaction script for anything that scores low, and put your design energy into keeping it in one place rather than into layers. Layers you add before there's logic to protect aren't future-proofing. They're a tax on every change that you pay until the logic arrives, and the logic might never arrive.

The signals that it's time to upgrade

A CRUD service rarely stays exactly CRUD. The trick is noticing the moment it stops. Dahan's article has the best example of what the first real rule looks like: "a customer may have no more than $1,000 in unpaid orders." He points out what makes it different from the email rule: it "involves multiple entities and would need to be evaluated in a variety of use cases." Then he adds that an account manager can override it, so rules start overriding other rules.

That gives you a practical checklist. Start reaching for a model when you see:

  1. The same if in more than one handler. The unpaid-orders check appears in checkout, in the admin order editor, and in the bulk import. That duplication is one of the Smart UI disadvantages Evans lists: the same rules copied into every operation that needs them.
  2. A rule that spans rows the database can't constrain together. A CHECK constraint sees one row. "Total unpaid across all of this customer's orders" doesn't fit in one.
  3. Rules with exceptions and exceptions to the exceptions. Once domain experts start saying "unless," you're past validation and into policy.
  4. Rules that keep changing. Vernon's 4-point row, and the reason Dahan says the domain model exists at all: to make volatile business behavior cheap to change.
  5. Vocabulary drift. The business says "hold," "release," and "lapse," and your code says status = 3. That gap is exactly what ubiquitous language is for.

And when the signals fire, upgrade the part that fired, not the whole service. Pull the one rule into one small, pure piece of code that every operation calls:

src/orders/credit-policy.ts

export const UNPAID_LIMIT_CENTS = 100_000; // $1,000

export function canPlaceOrder(input: {
  unpaidCents: number;
  orderCents: number;
  placedByAccountManager: boolean;
}): boolean {
  if (input.placedByAccountManager) return true;
  return input.unpaidCents + input.orderCents <= UNPAID_LIMIT_CENTS;
}

That's a policy with no framework, no repository, and no mapper, and it's already doing the job the eight-file venue service pretended to do. If more rules gather around the same concept, they'll pull toward each other, and at that point you'll have a real reason to introduce an entity with behavior and to think about where its consistency boundary goes. That's when the aggregate design questions start earning their keep, not before.

Skip the tactics, keep the strategy

One last distinction, because "DDD is the wrong tool" is usually only half true. Evans's 2009 complaint was that the tactical building blocks got too much attention. What he called essential was different: "Creative collaboration of domain experts and software experts."

The strategic side of DDD is almost free, even on the venue directory. Talking to the people who use it costs an afternoon. Naming things the way they name them costs nothing. Knowing that "venue" in the directory and "venue" in the booking system mean different things, and keeping them from sharing a table, is a bounded-context decision that saves you real pain later, CRUD or not. Bounded Contexts in a Real Codebase goes into where those seams actually go.

What's expensive is the tactical kit: aggregates, repositories per aggregate, domain events, mappers, command buses. Those pay off where rules are complex and changing, which is Evans's core domain. On a table with six columns, they're the surgeon's tray next to a box that needs tape.

So the next time a template hands you eight files for three columns, run Vernon's scorecard honestly. If it comes out near zero, write the transaction script, put the invariants in the schema, keep each operation in one place, and watch for the first rule that shows up in two handlers. That's not skipping DDD. It's the part of DDD most people skip.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: Estados de email accesibles en React
description:
Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Crear cuenta”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada: enviar el email, esperar la respuesta, mostrar el resultado y permitir que la persona continúe sin adivinar qué ocurrió.

En proyectos React he encontrado que este flujo se trata aveces como un detalle visual. Un spinner aparece, el botón se desactiva y, si todo va bien, llega un mensaje verde. Ese enfoque falla cuando el correo tarda, cuando el usuario navega con teclado o cuando un lector de pantalla no recibe el cambio. La interfaz necesita un modelo de estados explícito, no solo una animación.

El problema: verificar no es solo mostrar un spinner

Un estado de email tiene al menos cinco momentos útiles:

  1. Inicial: todavía no se ha enviado nada.
  2. Enviando: la petición está en curso y no debe duplicarse.
  3. Esperando: el servidor aceptó la solicitud, pero el mensaje aún no ha sido confirmado.
  4. Verificado: el enlace fue aceptado y el flujo puede continuar.
  5. Error: la persona necesita una explicación y una acción posible.

Separar “enviando” de “esperando” mejora la experiencia. El primer estado responde a la petición HTTP; el segundo describe una espera real del usuario. Mezclarlos en un único loading hace más dificil decidir qué texto anunciar, cuándo habilitar un reenvío y qué parte del formulario debe conservar el foco.

Para probar el flujo sin tocar buzones personales, un generador de correo temporal puede servir como fixture de desarrollo o QA. La regla importante es aislar cada prueba y no usar esos datos para cuentas reales.

Un pequeño modelo de estados para React

Un useState con varios booleanos suele producir combinaciones imposibles: isSending y isVerified activos a la vez, o un error visible después de un reenvío exitoso. Prefiero un único estado discriminado:

type EmailState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "waiting"; address: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

const [emailState, setEmailState] = useState<EmailState>({ kind: "idle" });

El render puede decidir qué mostrar a partir de kind, sin depender de una colección de flags que se contradicen. También facilita las pruebas: cada acción tiene una transición visible y es más facil comprobar que un reintento no aparece antes de tiempo.

Para un reenvío, conservaría un contador local o una marca de tiempo de la última petición. El objetivo no es castigar al usuario, sino evitar que varios clics creen mensajes difíciles de distinguir. Si el servidor responde con un error temporal, el mensaje debe explicar qué puede hacer la persona ahora, por que el siguiente intento está disponible y si el email anterior sigue siendo válido.

Accesibilidad: foco, mensajes y semántica

El texto de estado debe existir en el DOM, no solo cambiar el color del botón. Un contenedor role="status" con aria-live="polite" puede anunciar que el mensaje fue enviado sin interrumpir una tarea actual. Para un fallo que requiere atención inmediata, role="alert" es más apropiado, pero no conviene usarlo para cada cambio pequeño.

Cuando aparece un error debajo del campo, relaciónalo con el input mediante aria-describedby. Si la validación impide avanzar, el foco debe ir al primer control con un problema, no a un banner lejano. La validación y el foco visual debe mantenerse consistente tanto con teclado como con ratón.

El estado de espera necesita una salida clara. Un enlace “Cambiar dirección” o “Reenviar email” debe tener un nombre comprensible fuera de contexto. “Haz clic aquí” no explica nada en una lista de enlaces de un lector de pantalla.

También revisaría el contraste, el indicador de foco y el movimiento. prefers-reduced-motion permite eliminar una animación innecesaria, mientras que un icono no debe ser la única señal de éxito. Un pequeño checklist de calidad antes del email ayuda a revisar estos detalles junto con el resto del onboarding.

CSS y rendimiento sin perder claridad

Los estados visuales no necesitan una biblioteca grande. Una clase por estado, una transición corta y una estructura estable suelen bastar:

.email-status {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
}

.email-status[data-state="error"] {
  color: var(--color-error);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .email-status,
  .email-status * {
    transition: none;
    animation: none;
  }
}

Mantener una altura mínima evita que el formulario salte cuando entra el mensaje. Ese cambio pequeño reduce ruido visual y hace que el foco no parezca moverse. Para medir el resultado, observaría el tiempo hasta el primer mensaje útil, los reintentos duplicados y los errores de validación, no solo el tiempo de carga inicial.

En la práctica, el frontend también debe tolerar respuestas lentas. Una señal como “Estamos esperando el email” es mejor que un spinner infinito. Si el backend finalmente deja de reintentar, la interfaz debe reflejar la misma decisión; este principio de decidir cuándo dejar de reintentar un email evita prometer una recuperación que ya no existe.

Checklist para revisar el flujo

  • ¿Cada transición tiene un texto visible y entendible?
  • ¿El botón evita peticiones duplicadas mientras se envía?
  • ¿El lector de pantalla recibe los cambios mediante una región viva?
  • ¿El foco llega al campo correcto cuando hay un error?
  • ¿El color no es la única diferencia entre éxito, espera y fallo?
  • ¿Existe una acción para corregir la dirección o reenviar el email?
  • ¿La prueba usa un buzón aislado, como tamp mail com, y limpia sus datos después?
  • ¿Los estados funcionan sin animación y con una conexión lenta?

Diseñar esta frontera con cuidado produce una interfaz más tranquila y más fácil de probar. React aporta la estructura, CSS comunica el estado y las reglas de accesibilidad convierten una espera incierta en una secuencia que el usuario puede entender.

title: Text-Guided Modality Correction for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.22126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) is essential for detecting objects beyond the categories seen during training. Establishing vision-language associations is crucial for recognizing unseen categories, while integrating complementary visual features across levels supports detection at different scales. However, existing methods often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment strategies, and underuse complementary features across levels, limiting their ability to detect unseen categories and objects of varying scales. To address these limitations, we propose a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network (TMCNet) that incorporates textual guidance into region feature extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding to strengthen region-category semantic correspondence and promote complementary feature fusion across levels. First, a text-guided modality encoder incorporates textual semantics into queries to guide regional feature aggregation, reducing semantic ambiguity in object representations. Second, a cross-modal alignment module strengthens the correspondence between region representations and category semantics through interactions between visual and textual features. Finally, a progressive text correction decoder combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to progressively fuse text-guided deep semantic features with shallow visual features at the corresponding scales, preserving both semantic information and spatial detail for objects of different sizes. Experiments on two public datasets, COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, demonstrate that TMCNet achieves strong performance in open-vocabulary object detection using simple text queries as guidance. Extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields performance gains, demonstrating its cross-task applicability and extensibility.

title: World-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Pollution-Aware Bird Movement Modeling Using a Multi-Instance DQN Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.21895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.
