title: A Link You Can Just Open
description:
This essay was first published on the Zyaku blog.

Here is a small scene I keep imagining.

It's late in the evening and the power has been out for an hour. In a family group on someone's phone, a cousin forwards a link: a local reporter's post about which roads are under water and which bridge is closed. The phone has one bar. The person holding it taps the link.

A page loads, slowly. It doesn't show the post. It shows a form. Email. Password. Confirm password. A code is on its way to your inbox. The bar flickers, and the code never comes. They close the tab, go back to the group and ask, "What does it say?" Then they wait for someone with better signal to type it out.

Nothing in that scene is broken. Every part works the way somebody designed it. That's what bothers me about it.

This week we changed it on Zyaku. When someone shares a public post with you, you can now read it without signing up. Zyaku asks you to join only when you want to do more than read: like, comment, follow or save. And anyone, with an account or without one, can report a post.


A forwarded link should open to the words, not to a form.

The wall in front of the words


Most links lead to a gate before they lead to anything else.

Most apps put the sign-up wall right in front of the content, and I understand why. Every visitor who turns into an account is something a team can point to at the next meeting. A link someone opens, reads and closes counts for nothing. So the wall goes up early, and its cost lands on the person who only wanted to read one thing.

I've stood on the wrong side of that wall more times than I can remember. Usually it costs me a minute. On a bad connection, in a bad hour, it can cost the whole point of the link. A shared post is often a message from someone you trust: I think you should see this. Turning that into a registration form is a strange way to treat a recommendation.

So now the post comes first. You see who wrote it, their words and pictures, and the labels Zyaku puts on posts: whether something was made with AI, whether media was altered, whether a claim is disputed, and how sure Zyaku is about the post itself. If you want to join the conversation, Zyaku asks you then, and after you sign up it brings you straight back to the post you were reading.

For people who do join, there's a small new welcome too. New accounts now get a Start here card on Home for their first couple of weeks, with one first step that fits what they said they do. Creators can practise posting with no signal: write something, switch the connection off and on, and watch what Zyaku would show while a real post waits. The practice post is never sent. I like that a first lesson can be a rehearsal with nothing at stake.

Ask at the counter


Anyone can read the rates on the wall. The paperwork waits for the counter.

Before I built software, I spent years in finance. One habit from that world took me a long time to see clearly. You ask for someone's papers when money is about to move, not when they walk through the door.

Anyone can stand in a bank and read the rates on the board. The identity checks, the forms and the signatures come at the counter, when there's something real to protect. Ask too early and you don't make anything safer. You make people leave, and you end up holding information you had no reason to collect.

That's how a shared post works now. Reading asks for nothing. Doing something that touches other people, like a comment or a follow, asks you to be someone.

We took the idea one step further than I first expected to. When you open a shared post without an account, Zyaku sets no cookie, keeps nothing in your browser and doesn't count your visit. We also ask search engines not to list these previews, so a post shared with a few people doesn't quietly become a page for the whole web.

That last part has a cost, and I'd rather name it. We won't know how many people opened a link and left. Somebody building a growth chart would love that number. I decided I'd rather not have it than take it from people who never agreed to anything.

Some doors stay shut


Opening one door made us decide which ones stay closed.

Opening the door for reading made us think hard about what should never sit behind it.

Not every post opens without an account. Emergency and crisis messages don't, and neither do posts tied to a place during a crisis. A message someone wrote in a frightening moment, saying where they are, wasn't written for strangers, and a forwarded link can travel much further than its author ever meant it to. Posts by anyone under eighteen don't open this way either. Nor do followers-only posts, mature posts or paid work. A comic chapter is still something readers pay for, and creators still get paid for the chapter they unlock.

Anything outside those rules gets the same short answer as a post that doesn't exist: this post can't be shown here. It doesn't explain why, on purpose. Sometimes the reason itself gives something away.

And while I'm on safety, the line I repeat in every one of these essays: Zyaku is not an emergency service. If you're in danger, call your local emergency number first.

In the language you read in


An open door helps more when you can read what's behind it.

An open door doesn't help much if what's behind it is in a language you can't read. So the other half of this week was about language.

Any journalism article on Zyaku can now be read in any of the languages Zyaku offers, and your choice is remembered for next time. Posts on your screen are now translated together, so they show up in your language much sooner. The shared-post preview, the Start here card and the Zyaku AI screen now appear in every language we support, not only in English.

When Zyaku translates a post, it says so. You can see that the translation was made by AI and what language it came from, and the original is one tap away. I care about that label as much as the translation. A reader deserves to know when the words in front of them aren't the words the writer chose.

This one is personal. I think in a mix of Hindi and English, like a lot of people I grew up with, and most software has treated that as a mistake to correct. A report written in one language by a reporter in one town should be able to reach a reader somewhere else without either of them doing anything special. That's the whole job.

What isn't finished


Some of this is done. Some of it is still on the bench.

Plenty.

Only ordinary posts, pictures, videos and clips open without an account for now. Comics and paid pieces still ask you to sign in, and some of that is deliberate rather than unfinished.

Reports from people without an account can be misused. We limit how often they can come from one place, and they go into the same queue as every other report. I don't think that's the final answer, and I'll keep watching it.

The phone apps aren't public yet, so everything here is about a link opened in a browser. And signing up on one bar of signal is still heavier than it should be. Letting people read first fixes the first minute. It doesn't fix every minute after that.

Underneath all of this, the offline core keeps moving too. HoldSend, our open-source library for writing offline and publishing exactly once, is public under the Apache license, and an early version is now on npm for anyone to try. Its interface may still change, and its own README says plainly that it isn't ready for production.

The first thing we ask


Read first. Decide later.

The first thing a product asks of a stranger says a lot about it. For a long time the answer across most of the internet has been: tell us who you are. I'd like Zyaku's answer to be: nothing yet.

Back in that dark room, the link opens. The post is there. The person reads which bridge is closed, types it into the family group, and goes back to waiting for the lights. Nobody had to make an account to be useful to each other.

So here's my question for you. What's the last link you gave up on because it wanted an account before it would show you anything? I'm curious what you were trying to read, and whether you ever found it another way.

Rohit Kashyap

Founder & CEO, Zyaku · Founder, TAMVEL

title: Why Your 300ms Cubic-Bezier Feels Dead (And What Springs Do Differently)
description:
Every product has one. transition: all 300ms ease-in-out. It is the reason a lot of interfaces feel like they are made of cardboard.

This is not a taste argument. There is a mechanical reason a fixed-duration curve feels wrong for interaction, and a specific set of cases where it is still exactly right.

A curve is a script; a spring is a physics system

A cubic-bezier transition says: over exactly 300ms, move from A to B following this shape. It is a script with a fixed ending.

The problem appears when the user interrupts it. Click a toggle, then click it back at 150ms. What should happen?

With a fixed transition, the browser usually restarts the curve from wherever it is, with a full 300ms duration again. The object visibly hesitates. If you interrupt repeatedly, you get a stuttering object that is clearly not obeying anything.

A spring has no duration. It has a target and a state — position and velocity. When the target changes mid-flight, the object keeps its current velocity and accelerates toward the new target. Reversing direction feels like reversing a physical object because that is what is being simulated.

That is the whole difference, and it is why springs feel "alive" and fixed tweens feel like slides.

The math, without the ceremony

A damped spring is a second-order system:

m·x'' + c·x' + k·x = 0

where m is mass, c is damping, k is stiffness, and x is displacement from the target. The behaviour is governed by the damping ratio:

ζ = c / (2·√(k·m))
  • ζ < 1 — underdamped, overshoots and settles. This is "bouncy".
  • ζ = 1 — critically damped, fastest approach with no overshoot.
  • ζ > 1 — overdamped, sluggish, no overshoot.

A concrete implementation, if you want to feel the difference in a CodePen:

function stepSpring(
  state: { x: number; v: number },
  target: number,
  { stiffness: k, damping: c, mass: m, dt }: Params
) {
  const force = -k * (state.x - target) - c * state.v;
  const accel = force / m;
  const v = state.v + accel * dt;
  return { x: state.x + v * dt, v };
}

Integrate at a fixed timestep, not per frame, or the motion changes with the refresh rate. That detail is where most hand-rolled springs go wrong.

Tuning it like a human

Numbers that produce good UI, in the units most spring libraries use:

Feel Stiffness Damping Mass
Snappy button / badge 240 22 1.0
Card or modal entrance 120 18 1.2
Playful metric reveal 180 14 1.0
Heavy panel, no bounce 90 26 1.4

These are in the same family as the values in React Spring and Framer Motion, which is a useful sanity check if you are porting a component.

The practical rule: more damping for things that carry information, less for things that celebrate. A price change should not bounce twice; a success checkmark can.

Where curves win

I am not going to pretend springs are universally correct. There are three cases where a curve is better.

1. Choreographed sequences. A 12-step launch animation with precise holds and overlaps needs a timeline. A spring cannot express "hold for 400ms then move". Use curves and keyframes.

2. Exit animations tied to a deadline. If a toast must be gone in 200ms because a modal is opening under it, a fixed duration is a feature, not a limitation.

3. Non-spatial property changes. Opacity, colour and blur do not have momentum. A spring on opacity looks like a bug. Use a short curve — 120–180ms, ease-out — and be done.

There is also the accessibility case: prefers-reduced-motion should replace spatial springs with instant or short fades. Springs make that easy if the runtime supports it, but you have to actually wire it up.

Why design tools struggle with this

Here is the part that connects to tooling.

A spring is not a keyframe. There is no "end time" to place on a timeline, because the end depends on the physics. Tools built around timelines therefore tend to approximate springs — they bake a 500ms curve that looks like a spring for one specific distance, then ship it. Move the object twice as far and the easing is wrong, because a real spring's duration scales with distance.

That is why "we support springs" in a design tool often means "we have a spring-shaped bezier preset". It is fine for playback. It falls apart the moment the object travels a different distance, or gets interrupted.

An environment that stores stiffness/damping/mass as values, and integrates them at runtime, does not have that problem. The design file and the shipped behaviour are the same simulation. That is the argument for a physics-first format, and it is testable: interrupt the animation on the canvas and in the exported component and see whether they behave the same.

A 30-second audit of your own UI

Open your product. Do these three things:

  1. Rapidly toggle a switch five times. Does it keep its momentum, or hesitate?
  2. Open and close a modal before it finishes appearing. Does it reverse smoothly?
  3. Slow your network to 3G and trigger a state change. Does the motion still make sense when it arrives late?

If any of those feel wrong, the issue is almost never the easing curve. It is that the motion was scripted instead of simulated.

The one-line summary

Use springs for anything the user can interrupt. Use curves for anything that is choreographed, non-spatial, or on a deadline. Never use transition: all — that is not a motion decision, it is an accident.

UX Baba writes about interaction design. Exode stores springs as physics parameters rather than baked curves; the free tier at exodeui.com is enough to feel the difference.

title: OpenTelemetry Collector to Loki Without Losing Trace Context
description:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

The scenario

A checkout request fails, you find the error in Grafana, and the log line has no trace link. The trace exists in Tempo, but nothing connects the two, so you copy IDs by hand. This is a common outcome when you ship logs from the OpenTelemetry Collector to Loki through a path that flattens the log record into a plain string and drops its trace fields.

The timing is good for a cleanup. Grafana 13.3 is the current release cycle (October 2026). Read its what's new page before you upgrade, because log and trace correlation lives in the Loki data source and Explore. The configuration below uses documented provisioning fields, not features specific to 13.3.

Short answer: use Loki's native OTLP endpoint (/otlp) with the Collector's otlphttp exporter, not the deprecated loki exporter, which has been removed from current contrib builds. Keep trace_id and span_id as structured metadata, never as labels. Then add a derived field in the Loki data source that points at Tempo. This applies when you run Loki 3.x and want one pipeline for logs, metrics and traces. It does not pay off if you only grep logs and never open traces.

Prerequisites

Check these before you change anything:

  • Loki 3.x with a TSDB index and schema v13. Loki keeps trace IDs in structured metadata, and structured metadata requires both. Verify your schema_config and the allow_structured_metadata limit in the Loki OTLP documentation.
  • An OpenTelemetry Collector contrib distribution. The filelog receiver and k8sattributes processor ship in contrib, not in the minimal core build. See the Collector docs.
  • A Tempo data source in Grafana (13.3.x here) and applications that already emit traces.
  • Network access from the Collector to Loki, for example a loki Service on port 3100. If Loki is multi-tenant, you also need the tenant ID.

Accept one cost up front: structured metadata adds storage and query-time work per log line. For high-volume debug logs, sample or filter them in the Collector before they reach Loki.

Step 1: Preserve trace context at the source

Trace context survives only if it reaches the Collector as fields on the log record, not as text inside the body. There are two paths.

Path A (preferred): the application uses an OpenTelemetry SDK log bridge or appender and sends OTLP to the Collector. When a log is emitted inside an active span, the SDK attaches that span's trace and span IDs to the record. You change nothing in the pipeline.

Path B: the application writes JSON lines to stdout that include trace_id and span_id, and the Collector tails the files. The Collector then has to promote those values into the record's real trace fields. The trace_parser operator in the filelog receiver does that. Without it, the IDs stay as ordinary attributes and the correlation features never see them.

Watch the ID formats. The documented expectation is a 32-hex-character trace ID and a 16-hex-character span ID. If your logger prints a different format, the parser cannot turn it into a valid trace context, so normalize it in the application's logger.

Step 2: Configure the Collector pipeline

This config covers both paths: OTLP in, plus Kubernetes container logs with trace parsing. It exports to Loki over native OTLP. Adjust paths, namespaces and the Loki address to your environment.

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317     # recent releases default to localhost only
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
  filelog:
    include: [/var/log/pods/*/*/*.log]
    # exclude the Collector's own pods to avoid a feedback loop, e.g.:
    # exclude: [/var/log/pods/observability_otel-collector-*/*/*.log]
    include_file_path: true
    operators:
      - type: container            # parses the CRI/containerd line format
      - type: json_parser          # only for JSON bodies
        parse_from: body
        if: 'body matches "^\\{"'
      - type: trace_parser         # promotes IDs into real trace fields
        trace_id:
          parse_from: attributes.trace_id
        span_id:
          parse_from: attributes.span_id

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
  k8sattributes: {}                # adds k8s.namespace.name, k8s.pod.name, ...
  batch: {}

exporters:
  otlphttp/loki:
    endpoint: http://loki:3100/otlp   # the exporter appends /v1/logs itself
    # headers:
    #   X-Scope-OrgID: team-a         # only if auth_enabled: true in Loki

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp, filelog]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/loki]

Gotcha: do not append /v1/logs to the endpoint. The exporter adds it, and a doubled path produces 404 errors that look like a Loki outage. Keep batch after memory_limiter and k8sattributes so you batch the final, enriched records. Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes the receivers on the pod network, so restrict access with a NetworkPolicy if needed.

The container operator and its options have changed across Collector releases. Confirm the field names against the filelog receiver README for the version you deploy.

Step 3: Decide what becomes a label

Loki's OTLP ingestion converts a documented default list of resource attributes into index labels, such as service.name, k8s.namespace.name and k8s.pod.name. Dots become underscores, so you query service_name. Everything else, including trace_id and span_id, is stored as structured metadata. That is the behavior you want.

Avoid the cardinality trap: never promote trace_id to a label. Every request would create a new stream, and Loki's performance and cost would degrade quickly. If you need different index labels than the defaults, set them on the Loki side. ignore_defaults: true makes your list replace the defaults instead of adding to them:

# loki.yaml (excerpt)
limits_config:
  allow_structured_metadata: true     # required for trace_id/span_id storage
  otlp_config:
    resource_attributes:
      ignore_defaults: true           # use only the list below as index labels
      attributes_config:
        - action: index_label         # keep this list short and low-cardinality
          attributes:
            - service.name
            - k8s.namespace.name

Check the exact key layout against the Loki version you run, because otlp_config options are version-dependent.

Step 4: Link logs to traces in Grafana

Provision a derived field on the Loki data source so each log line with a trace ID gets a link into Tempo. Provisioning from files keeps this reviewable, and the same idea applies to any other dashboards-as-code setup you keep in Git.

# provisioning/datasources/loki.yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Loki
    type: loki
    uid: loki
    url: http://loki:3100
    jsonData:
      derivedFields:
        - name: TraceID
          matcherType: label          # read from structured metadata, not a regex on the line
          matcherRegex: trace_id
          url: '$${__value.raw}'      # $$ escapes env expansion in provisioning files
          datasourceUid: tempo        # UID of your Tempo data source

If your Grafana version does not offer matcherType: label, fall back to a regex derived field that matches the ID in the line. Check the Loki data source docs for the supported options.

On the Tempo side, a "logs for this span" link needs the Loki data source configured under Tempo's trace-to-logs settings. Keep the filter on service_name and k8s_namespace_name, and avoid tag mappings that don't exist in your labels.

Verify and test

First, send a synthetic OTLP log with a known trace ID straight to the Collector's HTTP port:

curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/logs \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"resourceLogs":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"otlp-smoke"}}]},
  "scopeLogs":[{"logRecords":[{"timeUnixNano":"'"$(date +%s)"'000000000",
  "severityText":"ERROR","body":{"stringValue":"smoke test"},
  "traceId":"5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c","spanId":"eee19b7ec3c1b174"}]}]}]}'

# then query Loki: label for the stream, structured metadata filter for the ID
# add --org-id=<tenant-id> if Loki runs with auth_enabled: true
logcli query --addr=http://loki:3100 \
  '{service_name="otlp-smoke"} | trace_id="5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c"' --since=10m

A healthy result is one log line returned for that filter. A bare 200 from the Collector only means it accepted the record, so the Loki query is the real check. In Grafana Explore, the same line should show trace_id under structured metadata and a TraceID link that opens Tempo.

Next, watch the Collector's own metrics:

  • otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records should climb.
  • otelcol_exporter_send_failed_log_records should stay flat.

Recent Collector versions expose these with a _total suffix on the Prometheus endpoint, and names can differ by version. Confirm them on the Collector's internal telemetry endpoint.

If lines arrive but links are missing, check these in order:

  1. The log record had a trace ID when it left the Collector. Path B usually fails here.
  2. allow_structured_metadata is on.
  3. The derived field points at the right Tempo UID.

Where this leaves you

The reliable pattern has four parts: native OTLP into Loki, trace and span IDs kept as structured metadata, a short list of low-cardinality labels, and one derived field into Tempo. Do not adopt it if your logs are unstructured and uninstrumented. There is no trace context to preserve, and the extra storage buys you nothing. Start with one service on Path A, confirm the smoke test above, and only then roll the filelog pipeline out cluster-wide.

Related

  • Grafana dashboards as code: provisioning without the UI
  • AWS Cost Anomaly Alerts: Route to Owners with Tag Context
  • PostgreSQL 18 Asynchronous I/O: Settings Worth Testing

title: Zero-Dimensional Attention Topology for Linguistic Acceptability
description:
arXiv:2611.22312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Topological summaries of Transformer attention provide sentence representations for linguistic acceptability classification. We examine a zero-dimensional persistent-homology ($H_0$) representation that summarizes minimum-spanning-tree merge values from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs into 1,440 features. The retrospective evaluation uses 8,517 downstream training sentences and 521 in-domain and 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering. The recorded out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT. Attention-feature results are retained aggregate measurements; BERT predictions are rescored and length controls are refitted from the accompanying records. Analytical results show that the representation retains token-count information and discards a class of directional attention differences. Source resampling of BERT predictions also demonstrates the sensitivity of uncertainty estimates to the sampling unit. The reported results do not demonstrate a predictive advantage for this fixed topological representation over simpler attention summaries. They identify representation properties and evaluation controls relevant to subsequent studies of attention topology.

title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

title: Your Service Has Stopped Responding and You Have Never Taken a Thread Dump
description:
The service is still running. The process is there, the memory looks normal, and the CPU is almost idle. But every request hangs until it times out, and the logs stopped twenty minutes ago without a single error. Someone suggests restarting it. Before you do, spend one minute capturing what every thread inside it is doing right now. That snapshot is called a thread dump, and once you have read one, you will never want to restart a stuck service blind again.

On the Java virtual machine there are three common ways to take one. Run jstack followed by the process id. Or run jcmd with the process id and Thread.print. Or send the process a quit signal with kill -3, which makes the JVM write the dump to its own standard output, so in a container it appears in the logs. Take three dumps about ten seconds apart. A thread that is in the same place in all three is stuck, not busy.

Each thread appears with a name, a state and a stack trace. The state tells you a lot. RUNNABLE means it is doing work, or waiting on the network. BLOCKED means it is waiting to enter a synchronized section that another thread holds. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING mean it is parked until something wakes it.

Now look for patterns rather than reading every line. Are two hundred request threads all waiting at the same line, inside the method that borrows a database connection from the pool? Then the pool is empty, and the interesting question is who is holding the connections. Are several threads BLOCKED on the same lock, with one thread holding it while it waits on a slow external call? There is your problem. If two threads are each waiting for a lock the other holds, jstack will often say so plainly, with a line saying it found a Java level deadlock.

Other runtimes have the same idea. For Python, py-spy dump with a process id prints the stack of every thread without stopping the program.

Practise on a calm day. Take a dump of a healthy service, find your own code in it, and learn what normal looks like. Then, during the next incident, capture first and restart second. The restart fixes today. The dump tells you how to stop it happening again.

– Asael Shinder

title: Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM
description:
Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM

CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. I covered the background in a separate post. This one is the runbook: how to find the JVMs that matter, what to run, what to change and how to prove it worked.

I have not run this against a vulnerable machine. The commands come from the Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs and Equixly write-ups, and I only checked that the shell and Java snippets parse. Test in staging first.

TL;DR

Step Goal Time
1. Inventory Find the real runtime behind every Java process minutes per host
2. Hardware check Split hosts by AVX-512 VBMI seconds
3. Patch Move to a vendor build that carries the fix your restart window
4. Mitigate Apply a JVM flag where you cannot patch one restart
5. Verify Prove the flag or build is live in the running process seconds
6. Watch Alert on crash and decode patterns ongoing

1. Inventory the JVM that actually runs

Your shell's java tells you very little. Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak and Elasticsearch ship or select their own runtime. Equixly and Endor Labs both call this out. Ask the process.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# jvm-inventory.sh: one line per running JVM with its real binary and version
set -u
for pid in $(pgrep -f '[j]ava'); do
  exe=$(readlink -f "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
  ver=$(jcmd "$pid" VM.version 2>/dev/null | grep -m1 -E 'JDK|OpenJDK' || echo "jcmd unavailable")
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$pid" "$exe" "$ver"
done

jcmd must run as the same user as the target JVM. If it prints "jcmd unavailable", the process may be a minimal runtime without the JDK tools. Fall back to "$exe" -version.

Version triage, using the ranges Qualys and Upwind list.

Line Affected Fixed Oracle build
17 17.0.6 and later, before the fix 17.0.21.1
21 up to 21.0.13 21.0.13.1
25 up to 25.0.5 25.0.5.1
27 up to 27.0.1 27.0.1.1
8 Oracle Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf 8u513-perf
11, 17.0.0 to 17.0.5, standard 8 not affected none needed

A version number is not proof. Endor Labs warns that an LTS build with a matching number may still lack the commit, because the fix is tracked as JDK-8393212. Treat the vendor advisory as the source of truth, and note that Qualys lists Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 as released.

2. Check the hardware

Only x86-64 hosts with AVX-512 VBMI reach the vulnerable routine. Run this on each host or container node.

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' | sort

Per Qualys, you are on the hardware side of the risk only when all four flags appear. Intel Ice Lake and later server parts and AMD Zen 4 and later qualify. ARM64, including Graviton and Apple silicon, does not.

In Kubernetes, pods inherit the node's CPU, so check the node and not the image.

# Which nodes would run the vulnerable path
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
  pod="cpucheck-${node#node/}"
  kubectl debug "$node" -q --image=busybox --profile=general -- \
    sh -c "grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -c avx512vbmi" 2>/dev/null \
    | sed "s|^|$node  avx512vbmi=|"
done

Remember Qualys's caution: a resize or an instance family change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later. A host that passes today is not a permanent pass.

3. Patch

Patching is the only complete fix, and the vendors say so. The steps that bite people are all about the running process.

  • Rebuild container images from a base that carries the fixed JDK, then redeploy. Replacing files on disk does not change a JVM that is already running.
  • Restart every Java process. Without a restart you have patched a file, not a process.
  • For bundled runtimes, take the application vendor's update, not a hand-swapped JDK, unless the vendor documents it.
  • For Temurin, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat and distro packages, confirm the fixed build in the vendor advisory. Equixly could not confirm those on November 17.

4. Mitigate where you cannot patch yet

Both Qualys and Upwind recommend one flag first.

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

It turns off the fast decoder on any architecture. Qualys warns that large Base64 workloads may slow down, and Upwind reports it stopped the overflow on every affected version they tested. In a container, set it through the environment.

ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

Two alternatives appear in the write-ups, and each has a trap.

Flag Trap
-XX:UseAVX=2 Disables all AVX-512, so it can slow unrelated work. On ARM the JVM refuses to start.
-XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock Without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions the JVM will not start. Pushed through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, Upwind calls it a fleet-wide outage.

A reverse proxy is not a control. Qualys says so plainly, and CISA's size-limit advice does not stop this bug on its own.

5. Verify in the running process

Setting a flag in a manifest proves nothing until you ask the process.

# Flag state inside a live JVM
jcmd <pid> VM.flags | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX'

# Or ask a fresh JVM what it would do with your options
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics'

You want UseBASE64Intrinsics = false in the process. Remove the flag after the patch lands, because it costs speed.

6. A guard in your own code

If you decode untrusted Base64 with java.util.Base64, you can reject the malformed shape before the decoder sees it. Upwind's detection heuristic is a Base64-alphabet token of 32 or more characters that ends in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4. Well-formed padded Base64 always has a length divisible by 4.

import java.util.Base64;

public final class SafeBase64 {
    private SafeBase64() {}

    /** Rejects padded input whose length cannot be valid Base64 before decoding. */
    public static byte[] decode(String input) {
        if (input.endsWith("=") && input.length() % 4 != 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed base64 padding");
        }
        return Base64.getDecoder().decode(input);
    }
}

This is defense in depth. It narrows the input, and it does not replace the patch. I have not tested it against Calif's chains, which are unpublished.

7. Detection

Endor Labs and Equixly suggest the same few signals.

  • Authorization headers or request fields where Base64 ends in = or == and the length is not a multiple of 4. Equixly offers a WAF rule for the header: ^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$. I have not validated it.
  • Bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in request handlers, because every trigger throws after the write.
  • New hs_err_pid*.log files. Equixly warns the log will not name Base64, because the crash comes later when the garbage collector reads the damaged object. Endor Labs describes a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine with a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame, clustered by source IP.
  • Java processes that start a shell or open new outbound connections, which Qualys lists as a monitoring signal. 
# Quick sweep for recent JVM crash logs and their crash frame
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

8. Priorities

Qualys orders the work like this: internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. The first group is first because Calif's pre-auth claims name them.

The bottom line

The slow part of this incident will not be the patch. It will be learning which of your processes are Java and which JDK they use. Run the inventory script once, keep its output, and you will have the answer ready for the next runtime bug too.

How many of your JVMs would the script find that nobody on your team knew about?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

You cannot patch a runtime you have not inventoried.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, CISA alert.

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
description:
arXiv:2611.21852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
description:
arXiv:2611.21880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

title: YouTube's transcript panel gives you the full transcript — I scrolled three videos to prove it
description:
I built a YouTube transcript exporter, and one design question kept coming back: when the timedtext endpoint won't cooperate, is the on-page transcript panel a real fallback — or does it only hold the rows currently on screen?

On 2026-11-15 I measured that YouTube's timedtext endpoint returns empty bodies from datacenter IPs (curl: HTTP 200 with 0 bytes, then 429; real browser: json3 through srv3 all empty, no challenge page). Real users on residential IPs should be fine, but my test environment could not verify that path. So the panel became the question that mattered. I originally wrote that the panel "only gives the currently rendered rows, not the full transcript." That was an untested assumption. I tested it properly this week, at three scales.

How I measured it

Headless Chrome 154 with a local CONNECT relay, loading the real youtube.com watch page. For each video I opened the transcript panel, counted the rows, then scrolled the panel container to the bottom twice and counted again. I also ran my extension's own YTE_GET_TRANSCRIPT (source: panel) before and after scrolling, so the panel DOM and the extension's reading of it were checked against each other.

Results

Video Length Rows before scrolling Rows after 2 scrolls Cues (extension) Characters
Rick Astley — Never Gonna Give You Up (dQw4w9WgXcQ) 3:33 24 24 24 2,066
TED — Do schools kill creativity? (iG9CE55wbtY) 20:03 163 163 163 17,412
Randy Pausch — The Last Lecture (ji5_MqicxSo) 76:27 713 713 713 65,510

First cue to last cue covered the whole video in each case (0:01–3:23, 0:27–19:19, 0:17–1:15:26). The panel container's scrollHeight was far larger than its clientHeight (e.g. 39,870 vs 299 on the 76-minute video), so there was real scrolling to do — the row count simply did not change. The extension's transcript was identical before and after scrolling in all three runs.

What changed in my design

The panel is now the default full-transcript source (verified up to 76 minutes / 713 cues). timedtext is demoted to a backup for when the panel is unavailable. The panel DOM itself also changed recently: the old ytd-transcript-segment-renderer selector returns zero rows now; the current rendering uses <transcript-segment-view-model> with timestamps in .ytwTranscriptSegmentViewModelTimestamp and text in span[role="text"]. My reader tries the new DOM first and falls back to the old one.

Honest caveats

  • I have not tested 2-hour-plus videos or 1,000+ cue transcripts. If a virtualization threshold exists, it can only be at a larger scale than 713 cues.
  • My DOM probe truncated each row to 80 characters, so its character totals (1,776 / 11,471 / 49,505) are lower than the extension's (2,066 / 17,412 / 65,510). That is a probe-method difference, not a data difference.
  • The 2026-11-15 claim that "the panel only gives the currently rendered rows" is overturned at all three scales tested. It was wrong because I had not scrolled before writing it.

Status

YouTube Transcript Export v0.1.0 is in review on Microsoft Edge Add-ons and cannot be installed yet. The Pro tier (planned ¥19.90 one-time, Afdian activation code) is not on sale. Privacy page: https://alapha888.github.io/yt-transcript-export-privacy/

title: MAI Realtime 1: el primer modelo de voz a voz de Microsoft, con IA de voz desde $0.01 por minuto de audio
description:
MAI Realtime 1, lanzado por Microsoft el 17 de noviembre de 2026, es su primer modelo de voz a voz en vivo, desde $0.01 por minuto de audio; las evaluaciones de Microsoft dicen que supera a GPT-Realtime 2.1, y puedes probarlo en MAI Labs mientras el acceso sigue restringido por un formulario de registro de interés.

Qué cambió con MAI Realtime 1

Microsoft anunció MAI Realtime 1 el 17 de noviembre de 2026, en Ignite: su primer modelo de voz a voz en vivo, creado para conversaciones naturales de baja latencia en aplicaciones empresariales reales. Gestiona interrupciones, sigue los reconocimientos rápidos y sabe cuándo esperar a que alguien termine de hablar; entiende peticiones con ruido de fondo y otras personas hablando; se conecta a sistemas y herramientas empresariales para actuar sobre las peticiones, no solo responder preguntas; y adapta su tono, estilo y personaje mediante prompts. También es compatible con la API Realtime de OpenAI, así que puedes probarlo frente a tus aplicaciones de voz actuales. Microsoft lo llevará a Dynamics 365 Contact Center y a Dragon Copilot, donde apoyará conversaciones simuladas con pacientes que ayudan a las enfermeras a practicar interacciones clínicas.

El uso básico de voz a voz cuesta desde $0.01 por minuto de audio, y el razonamiento se factura aparte a $5 por millón de tokens de salida. En las evaluaciones de la propia Microsoft, MAI Realtime 1 superó a GPT-Realtime 2.1 en calidad, velocidad y precio en benchmarks públicos — Big Bench Audio para razonamiento de voz y τ-Voice para completar tareas agénticas — junto con evaluaciones de Dynamics 365 Contact Center. El acceso sigue restringido: puedes probarlo en MAI Labs o mediante una vista previa de acceso limitado en Microsoft Foundry registrándote primero, y los clientes de la vista previa no pagan hasta que empiece la vista previa pública. Al 17 de noviembre de 2026, Artificial Analysis aún no publicaba una página del modelo.

MAI Realtime 1 en cifras

  • Precio de voz a voz por minuto de audio (desde): $0.01 (al 17 nov 2026)

Por qué MAI Realtime 1 importa para los negocios

Por qué importa: los agentes de voz se pagan por minuto, así que un modelo de voz a voz desde un centavo por minuto de audio cambia las cuentas de las líneas de atención al cliente, las llamadas de reserva y los seguimientos que eran demasiado caros para automatizar. Si tu empresa ya funciona con herramientas de Microsoft, MAI Realtime 1 llegará al Dynamics 365 Contact Center que quizá ya tienes licenciado, y su compatibilidad con la API Realtime de OpenAI significa que tu equipo puede probarlo frente a tu stack de voz actual antes de comprometerse: regístrate en la vista previa ahora para estar listo cuando se abra el acceso.

title: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer: Why Supabase Breaks Your Pool
description:
A FastAPI service works locally, then fails in production with asyncpg.exceptions.DuplicatePreparedStatementError: prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_1__" already exists, or with ConnectionFailureError: connection is closed mid-request. The database is Supabase or PgBouncer, the connection string came from the dashboard, and no application code changed.

Neither error is about your SQL. Both come from using a client-side statement cache against a pooler that does not keep a session.

Why the statement collides

asyncpg prepares statements and caches them per connection, keyed by SQL text, up to statement_cache_size (100 by default). Each prepared statement gets a server-side name like __asyncpg_stmt_1__.

Under a direct connection that name is unique per session, so the cache is a pure win. Under transaction pooling, PgBouncer hands every transaction a possibly different server connection: the cache no longer describes anything real, and two clients that both prepared __asyncpg_stmt_1__ can land on the same server session, where the second prepare fails with SQLSTATE 42P05.

import asyncpg

# correct for the Supabase transaction pooler (port 6543) and PgBouncer transaction mode
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(
    dsn,
    min_size=1,
    max_size=5,              # small: the pooler multiplies, not the app
    statement_cache_size=0,  # no server-side prepared statements
    max_cached_statement_lifetime=0,
    command_timeout=30,
    server_settings={"application_name": "api"},
)

With SQLAlchemy, set it at the dialect level too, because SQLAlchemy builds the asyncpg pool itself:

create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host:6543/postgres",
    poolclass=NullPool,                     # let the pooler pool
    connect_args={
        "statement_cache_size": 0,
        "prepared_statement_cache_size": 0, # SQLAlchemy's own layer
        "server_settings": {"application_name": "api"},
    },
)

Both knobs exist because there are two caches: asyncpg's, and SQLAlchemy's prepared-statement cache on top of the same driver. Setting only one is the most common half-fix.

Which endpoint you are actually on

Endpoint Port Prepared statements App pool size Use for
Direct connection 5432 supported, cache them your real budget migrations, LISTEN/NOTIFY
Session pooler 5432 supported per session small long sessions, ORMs without pooling
Transaction pooler 6543 not supported across transactions 1–5 per worker most web traffic
Transaction pooler + cache 6543 collisions any never

When you see DuplicatePreparedStatementError the cache met a transaction pooler; TooManyConnectionsError means the app pool is larger than the pooler budget; InvalidPasswordError usually means the username is postgres instead of postgres.<project-ref>.

Reproduce it instead of guessing

A single-worker test never reproduces the collision. Run the same query from many coroutines against the pooler — if it passes with statement_cache_size=0 and fails without it, the diagnosis is confirmed. Do not "fix" it by catching DuplicatePreparedStatementError and retrying: the retry prepares the same name on another server connection and the error moves instead of disappearing.

ConnectionFailureError is not a bug in your query

The pooler recycles server connections aggressively — Supabase's transaction pooler closes idle ones long before a typical web worker notices. asyncpg keeps the client object and only learns the socket is gone when it writes. Retry only on ConnectionFailureError and InterfaceError, never on a query error: replaying an INSERT that failed before commit is fine, replaying one that timed out after commit is not.

async def fetch_one(pool, sql, *args):
    for attempt in range(2):
        try:
            async with pool.acquire() as conn:
                return await conn.fetchrow(sql, *args)
        except asyncpg.ConnectionFailureError:
            if attempt:
                raise

pool_pre_ping narrows the window after an idle close but does not remove the need to retry. Keeping min_size=1 and running an occasional SELECT 1 from a background task keeps a warm client, so the first request after a quiet period does not fail.

Transaction pooling also gives one server connection per transaction — exactly what async with conn.transaction() needs, and exactly what a bare SET does not survive. Use SET LOCAL for statement_timeout or search_path, and keep advisory locks, LISTEN, temporary tables, cursors and Alembic migrations on port 5432, where a session exists.

Two traps specific to Supabase

The direct host is IPv6-only. db.<project-ref>.supabase.co resolves to IPv6 unless the IPv4 add-on is enabled, so a container or CI runner without IPv6 gets socket.gaierror: [Errno -9] Address family for the host is not supported. It looks like DNS and is not; use a pooler host, and note the pooler username is postgres.<project-ref>.

Your pool size is multiplied by the pooler. Four uvicorn workers with max_size=20 demand 80 server connections from a pooler that may allow far fewer, and the failure only appears under load. Keep a handful per worker (max_size = 5) and let the pooler queue; NullPool is the simplest correct choice for serverless.

Checklist before you file a bug

  • Both cache switches set to 0.
  • Port 6543 only for traffic that does not need a session.
  • max_size small, per worker.
  • Retry on ConnectionFailureError / InterfaceError only.

Format the failing statement with the SQL formatter before hunting a syntax difference, diff two connection strings character by character with the text diff tool, and split a copied postgres:// URL into its parts with the URL parser.

The longer version, with the pool sizing table and the keepalive snippet, is on my site: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer and Supabase.

title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
description:
arXiv:2611.22133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition.

Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before.

Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide.

title: Token Pass credit now applies automatically across AI Gateway
description:
Token Pass credit now applies automatically to included model usage through AI Gateway, whether a request authenticates with an API key, OIDC token, or fx login. No dedicated Token Pass API key is required, though you can still create one from the dashboard or the CLI for keys scoped only to featured models and providers.

When Token Pass credit runs out for the billing period, requests from a standard key or OIDC token fall back to your team's AI Gateway credits. Token Pass keys still stop until the next billing period.

Requests served through the Token Pass provider remain Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Fallback requests follow your team's setting. With team-wide ZDR enabled, they route only to ZDR providers.

Available now for Token Pass subscribers on Pro teams. If you created a Token Pass key during setup, switch to a standard API key or OIDC token to get fallback. Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.

title: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery
description:
Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery (PITR), so you can restore the user data in a user pool to an earlier time. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices. Previously, you had to build and maintain your own export and restore process, and restored users received new identifiers and had to reset their passwords.

With PITR, you choose a recovery point, preview how many users, groups, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys the recovery will create, update, or delete, and then start or cancel the recovery. Recovered users keep their identifiers, passwords, MFA settings, and passkeys, so they can sign in without resetting their credentials. For example, if a script deletes or modifies users by mistake, you can restore the user data to the moment before it ran.

PITR is enabled automatically for user pools on the Essentials and Plus feature plans at no additional charge. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. You can initiate and manage a recovery using the AWS Management Console, the Amazon Cognito API, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. PITR is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Point-in-time recovery in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

title: Object Storage Service for Storing User Documents with Go Backup Pipelines
description:
A practical decision rule: use Amazon S3 when backup durability, lifecycle depth, and ecosystem coverage dominate; use Cloudflare R2 when an S3-compatible edge-oriented design fits; use Azure Blob when the rest of the estate is already Azure; consider Infrai when the main cost is integrating several backend capabilities and a plain, discoverable REST surface matters. For a fintech tenant-document system, keep every object private, make restore a separate workflow, and treat a large-file transfer as a throughput problem rather than a pricing headline.

The backup invariant is simple: a tenant snapshot is immutable to the restore workflow, a retry cannot create a second logical snapshot, and the restore target is selected explicitly. The storage provider is only one part of that contract. A cheap GB-month does not compensate for an unsafe overwrite or a restore path that cannot explain what happened.

Keep it boring.

What fails first in a tenant backup runbook?

The dangerous signal is not always an outage. It is often a successful-looking job that uploaded some objects, timed out, and ran again. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. Large files make this sharper: a retry can spend time and bandwidth on an upload whose first attempt may already exist. Keep the logical snapshot ID in the database, derive object keys from tenant ID and snapshot ID, and record the checksum and completion state before advertising the snapshot to a restore operator.

I would separate the control plane from the bytes. The control plane owns tenant authorization, snapshot selection, retention decisions, and restore state. The object store owns private bytes and transfer mechanics. That boundary gives the on-call engineer something concrete to verify: database state, object existence, object size, checksum, then restore completion.

Do not use a public ACL for user documents. A private object plus a short-lived presigned URL is the safer delivery shape, and the application must not forward its storage-service Authorization header to the returned URL. This also keeps browser delivery subject to an explicit CORS design; CORS is a browser permission mechanism, not an access-control substitute.

Which object storage service should handle storing user documents?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a direct provider architecture. The application uses S3, R2, or Azure Blob primitives directly, usually with the provider SDK, multipart upload, provider lifecycle rules, and the provider's replication and recovery features. Its invariant is provider-native correctness: the SDK and the provider agree on upload completion, conditional writes, retention, and restore semantics. This is the strongest choice when the backup path is the product and the team is willing to own provider-specific operations.

The second is a unified REST architecture. A service such as Infrai presents storage behind one REST surface, while its discovery endpoint exposes the available capability, request schema, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when the same team is also wiring queues, schedules, or other backend services and does not want each integration to introduce another SDK and credential model. The invariant changes: the application must pin the capability contract it uses, preserve provider-neutral object keys, and keep an exit path through ordinary object-store formats.

Here is the comparison I would put in a design review:

Option Strong fit Boundary to test before adoption
Amazon S3 Broad ecosystem, mature lifecycle and multipart patterns Provider-specific features and configuration become part of the runbook
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible access for workloads already centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required replication, lifecycle, and recovery behavior for the region and compliance model
Azure Blob Storage Teams already operating identities, policy, and monitoring in Azure Validate the translation between Blob semantics and an S3-shaped application layer
Infrai storage A discoverable REST integration and one credential model matter across backend capabilities No public ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration; browser upload CORS is not self-service

For a US/EU fintech project, I would choose the direct provider architecture when the document archive needs WORM controls, provider-native replication, or a migration program with bulk tooling. I would choose the unified shape for a private document workflow whose main engineering constraint is integration surface, provided an external database or compliance store supplies the missing immutability and coordination guarantees.

The live platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth is not a storage guarantee. A storage decision still turns on the bytes, the restore contract, and the controls the archive must prove during an audit.

How should the worker upload and restore safely?

Start with a durable record such as (tenant_id, snapshot_id, state, object_key, checksum, size). The worker claims one pending snapshot, writes to a deterministic private key, and records completion only after the object check passes. A retry reads that record and either resumes the transfer or verifies the already-complete object. It does not invent a new key because the network was uncertain.

For large files, use multipart transfer where the selected provider supports it. Bound concurrency so a restore does not starve ordinary document reads. Treat an incomplete multipart upload as an operational object that needs inspection: a one-day minimum lifecycle may be too coarse for a cleanup policy, and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule in the unified storage option described above.

Infrai's storage surface includes a private object put operation and presigning, and its API is self-describing: discovery is public, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in Go as well as other languages. That makes a new integration easier to inspect before implementation. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the broader platform exposes one key and a common REST convention across its capabilities, including documented idempotency conventions for applicable writes.

This is the smallest useful upload shape for a private object. It keeps the key outside the request body, uses a deterministic idempotency value, checks status codes, and backs off on a rate limit. The exact request schema should still be confirmed from discovery before production rollout.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        panic("usage: put-object <bucket> <key> <file>")
    }
    key, err := os.Open(os.Args[3])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer key.Close()

    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(endpointTemplate, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    endpoint = strings.ReplaceAll(endpoint, "{key}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[2]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, key)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "tenant-snapshot-2026-10-24")
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
                body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
                res.Body.Close()
                panic(fmt.Sprintf("upload failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body))
            }
            res.Body.Close()
            return
        }
        wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
        }
        res.Body.Close()
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
    panic("upload rate-limited after retries")
}

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the application-facing private document transfer and backup orchestration when discovering and wiring one REST capability is more valuable than provider-native storage controls. Keep the snapshot ledger outside it, and choose S3 or Azure Blob instead when object lock, native replication, or a provider-specific compliance control is a hard requirement. That is a real limitation, not a footnote: Infrai is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, WORM retention, or a workflow that needs automatic cross-region copies.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a short runbook, not a dashboard slogan. After an upload, compare the recorded size and checksum with the object metadata, then run a restore into a quarantine namespace for a representative tenant. Check authorization at the application boundary and confirm that the delivered URL is signed and time-limited. Record the request ID and outcome so a duplicate delivery can be distinguished from a second logical snapshot.

Rollback means stopping new snapshot publication, leaving the original private objects untouched, and reverting the control-plane state to the last verified snapshot. Do not promise recovery from an accidental overwrite if the selected service has no object versioning or object lock. For strict concurrent writes, coordinate through the database or a queue because the unified storage option does not provide an If-Match conditional write.

A final trap: lifecycle rules are not a substitute for a retention policy. The unified option has a one-day minimum lifecycle and prefix-only object listing; metadata is not server-side searchable. If operators need legal holds, exact metadata queries, or automatic cross-region copies, that requirement belongs in the architecture decision, not in a late configuration ticket.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the private document storage guide and verify the capability contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Infrai storage documentation

title: Refactoring Vue 3 Unit Tests: Moving from Mutable beforeEach State to Functional Factory Helpers in TypeScript
description:
When migrating large Vue codebases to TypeScript, static typing often exposes patterns in our test suites that are brittle or unnecessary. One common pattern in older Vue Test Utils specs is storing a mutable let wrapper variable in the test scope and initializing it inside beforeEach().

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3204), I converted the Labelathon page's DetailsSection component to TypeScript and refactored its unit test suite to use functional factory helpers.

Here is a look at why this refactoring improves test clarity, type inference, and test isolation.

The Component: DetailsSection.vue

The DetailsSection component renders instructions and event guidelines using accordion components from bootstrap-vue-next alongside a custom MarkdownRenderer:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { BAccordion, BAccordionItem } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import MarkdownRenderer from '~/common/components/MarkdownRenderer.vue';
</script>

<template>
  <BAccordion class="mt-4">
    <BAccordionItem title="Rules & Guidelines">
      <MarkdownRenderer :markdown="guidelines" />
    </BAccordionItem>
    <!-- Additional accordion items -->
  </BAccordion>
</template>

Adding lang="ts" ensures strict compilation of imported third-party components and child component props.

The Spec: Mutable beforeEach vs. Pure createWrapper

The Old Pattern (JavaScript)

Previously, the spec relied on an outer mutable reference:

// Before (DetailsSection.spec.js)
describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  let wrapper;

  beforeEach(() => {
    wrapper = shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });
  });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(wrapper.html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why avoid this pattern in TypeScript?

  1. Unnecessary State Mutation: A global let wrapper introduces shared state across tests. Tests should be isolated and idempotent.
  2. Type Ambiguity: In TypeScript, declaring let wrapper; defaults to any unless explicitly typed (VueWrapper<InstanceType<typeof DetailsSection>>), which adds boilerplate.
  3. Execution Overhead: If some test cases only test static exports or helpers, beforeEach still mounts the component unnecessarily.

The Modern Pattern (TypeScript)

In DetailsSection.spec.ts, we eliminated beforeEach and the mutable variable in favor of a concise factory helper:

// After (DetailsSection.spec.ts)
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import DetailsSection from './DetailsSection.vue';

describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  const createWrapper = () =>
    shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why this is better:

  • Automatic Type Inference: createWrapper() naturally returns a typed VueWrapper, avoiding manual type annotations.
  • Pure & Self-Contained: Each test explicitly invokes createWrapper() with optional prop overrides when needed, preventing test leakage.
  • Seamless Snapshot Migration: The Vitest snapshot was smoothly renamed from DetailsSection.spec.js.snap to DetailsSection.spec.ts.snap without breaking snapshot verification.

Key Takeaways

  1. Favor Factory Functions over beforeEach: Pure createWrapper = (props = {}) => ... functions result in cleaner, more readable specs compared to mutating a shared let wrapper variable.
  2. Leverage Type Inference in Tests: By using inline factory functions, Vue Test Utils and Vitest automatically infer wrapper types without verbose casting.
  3. Clean Codebases One Slice at a Time: Converting small presentation components and their specs in focused merge requests keeps review cycles fast and eliminates maintenance debt.
