title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
description:
arXiv:2611.21921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

title: Decoupling HTTP Clients in Vue 3: Extracting API Modules and Converting PendingSubmissionsPill to TypeScript
description:
A common anti-pattern in frontend development is calling HTTP client libraries (like axios or native fetch) directly inside Vue UI components. When components perform raw network calls, testing becomes cumbersome, endpoints cannot be reused, and frontend code is coupled to specific networking libraries.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3201, closing Issue #880), I migrated the PendingSubmissionsPill navigation component to TypeScript and extracted its API interactions into a dedicated, typed client module.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of decoupling HTTP interactions from components and testing them cleanly in Vitest.

1. The Anti-Pattern: Direct Axios Calls Inside Components

In the navigation bar, PendingSubmissionsPill.vue displays a badge showing how many community submissions (blog posts, talks, events) are pending reviewer approval.

Previously, the component called axios directly:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
import axios from 'axios';
import { ref } from 'vue';

const count = ref(0);

const fetchCount = async () => {
  try {
    const { data } = await axios.get('/api/v1/submissions/count');
    count.value = data.count;
  } catch {
    error.value = true;
  }
};
</script>

Why this is problematic:

  1. Coupling: The UI component is tightly coupled to Axios. Migrating to another client or adding global interceptors requires touching multiple Vue SFCs.
  2. Brittle Mocking: Unit tests had to mock global axios.get calls using URLs as magic strings ('/api/v1/submissions/count'), making tests fragile when endpoints evolve.
  3. No Contract Validation: Response data was untyped, leaving data.count unchecked by the compiler.

2. Step 1: Extracting a Typed API Service Layer

We created a dedicated client module in ~/api/submissions.ts, leveraging generated OpenAPI response types:

// app/javascript/api/submissions.ts
import axios from 'axios';
import type { GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse } from '~/api/generated';

export async function fetchSubmissionsCount(): Promise<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse> {
  const { data } = await axios.get<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse>(
    '/api/v1/submissions/count'
  );

  return data;
}

We accompanied this with an isolated unit test in api/submissions.spec.ts:

import axios from 'axios';
import { PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE } from '~/spec/mockFactories';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from './submissions';

describe('fetchSubmissionsCount', () => {
  it('gets and returns data from the submissions count endpoint', async () => {
    const get = vi.spyOn(axios, 'get').mockResolvedValue(PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE);

    const result = await fetchSubmissionsCount();

    expect(get).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/api/v1/submissions/count');
    expect(result).toBe(PLACEHOLDER_AXIOS_RESPONSE.data);
  });
});

3. Step 2: Refactoring the Vue Component

With the network layer isolated, PendingSubmissionsPill.vue became a pure presentation component focused exclusively on UI state and browser lifecycle events:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BBadge, BNavItem } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import { computed, onMounted, onUnmounted, ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from '~/api/submissions';
import { useSubmissionsRefresh } from '~/common/useSubmissionsRefresh';
import { useVueData } from '~/common/useVueData';

const { pendingSubmissionsCount } = useVueData();
const count = ref(pendingSubmissionsCount);
const error = ref(false);

const fetchCount = async () => {
  try {
    const data = await fetchSubmissionsCount();
    count.value = data.count;
    error.value = false;
  } catch {
    error.value = true;
  }
};

// Re-fetch when user switches back to the tab
const onVisibilityChange = () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'visible') {
    void fetchCount();
  }
};

onMounted(() => {
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', onVisibilityChange);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  document.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', onVisibilityChange);
});
</script>

Notice void fetchCount();: explicitly voiding the floating promise in event handlers keeps @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises satisfied.

4. Cleaner, High-Level Testing in Vitest

Because axios is no longer imported by the component, PendingSubmissionsPill.spec.ts mocks the domain function fetchSubmissionsCount directly using vi.mocked():

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { flushPromises, shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { fetchSubmissionsCount } from '~/api/submissions';
import { useSubmissionsRefresh } from '~/common/useSubmissionsRefresh';
import { createAxiosError, createVueData } from '~/spec/mockFactories';
import PendingSubmissionsPill from './PendingSubmissionsPill.vue';

vi.mock('~/api/submissions');

describe('when tab becomes visible again', () => {
  it('refetches the latest count', async () => {
    createWrapper(3);
    vi.mocked(fetchSubmissionsCount).mockResolvedValue({ count: 7 });

    // Trigger window visibility event
    document.dispatchEvent(new Event('visibilitychange'));
    await flushPromises();

    expect(fetchSubmissionsCount).toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(wrapper.text()).toContain('7');
  });
});

Tests are no longer concerned with HTTP verbs or URLs—they verify application behavior and user outcomes directly.

Key Takeaways

  1. Extract Network Calls to API Services: Never call axios.get directly in Vue components. Keep components focused on rendering and UI state.
  2. Type API Responses with OpenAPI Contracts: Typing service functions with generated contracts (Promise<GetApiV1SubmissionsCountResponse>) prevents subtle property mismatches.
  3. Mock Domain Functions, Not HTTP Clients: Mocking fetchSubmissionsCount() rather than axios.get('/api/...') makes unit tests clearer, more resilient, and easier to maintain.

title: JSON-LD that cannot lie: schema markup generated from the same data as the page
description:
Most writing about schema markup is a list of types to add. The problems developers actually run into are different, and none of them is a missing type. Markup drifts out of step with the page it describes. Markup gets injected by a script that half the crawlers never run. And markup gets added for rich results that Google stopped showing years ago, because the checklist was written before it did.

This is the developer-side version of a guide we wrote for site owners. It covers what still earns anything in Google in 2026, and then the three engineering decisions that matter more than which types you pick: where the markup comes from, where it is rendered, and how you find out when it disagrees with the page.

What is still worth marking up

The list of rich results has been shrinking for three years. In August 2023 Google limited FAQ rich results to well-known government and health sites, and in September 2023 it stopped showing HowTo results entirely. In January 2025 breadcrumbs disappeared from mobile results, which now show only the domain; the markup is still supported on desktop. In June 2025 Google began phasing out seven types it called rarely used, among them Course info, Claim review and Estimated salary, and practice problems followed in January 2026. Then on 7 May 2026 FAQ rich results stopped appearing for everyone, and in June the documentation went too. For years FAQ schema was the easiest way to take up more room on a results page. In Google it now does nothing visible.

What survives is markup that describes something a searcher can act on: a product to buy, an event to attend, a job to apply for, a video to watch. Google's Search Gallery lists 25 features as of its June 2026 update. Product with an Offer still earns price, availability and shipping details. Event, JobPosting and VideoObject still earn their own results. Organization, LocalBusiness and Article are still read, even where there is no visible enhancement, because they tell Google which company owns a page and which page is an article about what.

Two practical consequences for whoever owns the templates. Markup Google no longer uses does no harm, by Google's own statement, so there is no need to rip out old FAQPage blocks. And a rich result is never guaranteed: Google's guidelines say structured data makes a page eligible, and Google decides page by page and query by query whether to show anything.

Decision one: generate it, never write it

The single most common way schema goes wrong is not a wrong type. It is markup that was correct on the day someone pasted it in, and has been wrong since the first time someone changed the visible page. The price on the page went up; the price in the JSON-LD did not. A sale ended; priceValidUntil still says last month, and the product's rich result disappears without a single error anywhere.

The fix is structural rather than procedural: the markup is built from the same object that renders the page, in the same template, so the two cannot disagree. In a Next.js App Router page it looks like this:

// app/products/[slug]/page.tsx
import { getProduct } from '@/lib/products'
import { Price } from '@/components/Price'

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) {
  const { slug } = await params
  const product = await getProduct(slug)

  const jsonLd = {
    '@context': 'https://schema.org',
    '@type': 'Product',
    name: product.name,
    image: product.images,
    description: product.summary,
    sku: product.sku,
    offers: {
      '@type': 'Offer',
      url: `https://example.com/products/${slug}`,
      price: product.price.toFixed(2),
      priceCurrency: product.currency,
      availability: product.inStock ? 'https://schema.org/InStock' : 'https://schema.org/OutOfStock',
      // Only while a sale runs, and straight from the same field the sale banner reads.
      ...(product.saleEndsAt ? { priceValidUntil: product.saleEndsAt.slice(0, 10) } : {}),
    },
  }

  return (
    <>
      <script
        type="application/ld+json"
        // Escape "<" so a product name can never close the script tag early.
        dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd).replace(/</g, '\\u003c') }}
      />
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <Price value={product.price} currency={product.currency} />
    </>
  )
}

There is nothing clever in it, which is the point. The product object that feeds the <Price> component also feeds offers.price, so a price change in the CMS changes both. The replace on the serialised JSON is the escaping Next.js recommends in its own JSON-LD guide: without it, a string containing </script> in a product name or a review would end the tag early.

Our own site works this way. Every guide carries Article and BreadcrumbList markup built from the guide's data, every package on our price list is a Service and Product with an Offer whose priceValidUntil is computed rather than typed, and the FAQ markup on each guide is generated from the same question-and-answer array the reader sees at the bottom of the page.

The bug that taught us to strip formatting

Generating from the same data has one trap, and we walked into it. Our FAQ answers are authored with a little inline Markdown, links as [text](/path) and bold as **text**, which a renderer turns into HTML for the page. The FAQPage builder took the same strings and put them straight into acceptedAnswer.text. The page looked perfect. The structured data carried literal asterisks and bracket syntax in every answer that used emphasis, until we noticed in September 2026.

Schema text properties are plain text, so anything authored for a renderer has to be reduced to plain text before it goes into the markup. A minimal version of what our builders now call:

// "[text](/path)" -> "text", "**bold**" -> "bold", "*italic*" -> "italic"
export const stripInlineMarkup = (s: string) =>
  s
    .replace(/\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]+\)/g, '$1')
    .replace(/\*\*([^*]+)\*\*/g, '$1')
    .replace(/\*([^*]+)\*/g, '$1')

const faqJsonLd = {
  '@context': 'https://schema.org',
  '@type': 'FAQPage',
  mainEntity: faqs.map(f => ({
    '@type': 'Question',
    name: f.q,
    acceptedAnswer: { '@type': 'Answer', text: stripInlineMarkup(f.a) },
  })),
}

The general rule: the markup should carry the same facts as the page, in the plain form the vocabulary expects, and any transformation between the two belongs in one shared function, not in each builder. We had ten FAQPage builders when we found it, and the fix was one function called from all ten.

We kept the FAQPage markup after Google stopped showing FAQ results in May. It costs nothing, Google says unused markup causes no problems, and other systems that read pages may still use it.

Decision two: render it on the server

Google renders JavaScript, so JSON-LD added in the browser by a tag manager or a client component usually reaches Google eventually. Most other readers never see it. Vercel's analysis of AI crawler traffic, published in December 2024, found that none of the major AI crawlers, including GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot, execute JavaScript; they fetch script files and do nothing with them.

That makes the test for whether your markup exists very simple: request the page the way a crawler does and look for it.

curl -s https://example.com/products/blue-mug | grep -c 'application/ld+json'

If that prints 0 while the browser's DevTools show the script tag, the markup is being added client-side, and only the systems that run JavaScript will ever see it. In a server-rendered or statically generated page, as in the example above, the tag is in the HTML the server sends, and every reader gets it.

Decision three: test that markup and page agree

Google's Rich Results Test answers "which Google features is this page eligible for", and the Schema Markup Validator, run by schema.org, checks the markup against the full vocabulary, including types Google ignores. Both check one URL at a time and neither compares the markup with what is visible on the page, which is the failure that actually happens.

That comparison is cheap to automate against a built site. Pull the JSON-LD out of the HTML, then assert that the facts it states appear in the visible text:

const html = await (await fetch(url)).text()
const blocks = [...html.matchAll(/<script type="application\/ld\+json">([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/g)]
  .map(m => JSON.parse(m[1]))

const product = blocks.find(b => b['@type'] === 'Product')
const visible = html.replace(/<script[\s\S]*?<\/script>/g, '').replace(/<[^>]+>/g, ' ')

if (product && !visible.includes(product.offers.price.replace('.', ','))
            && !visible.includes(product.offers.price)) {
  throw new Error(`${url}: markup price ${product.offers.price} is not on the page`)
}

It is crude, it needs adjusting for how your site formats prices, and it catches the drift that no validator will. After launch, Search Console's enhancement reports show markup errors across the whole site, and URL Inspection confirms whether Google saw the markup on a given page.

The rules that cost you more than a missing rich result

Google treats markup that describes content not visible on the page as spam, and its guidelines say a structured data issue can lead to a manual action, which removes your rich results until it is fixed. Hidden FAQ answers, ratings that appear nowhere on the page and prices that differ from the visible ones all qualify. Generating markup from the page's data makes this mistake hard to make by accident, which is another argument for doing it.

Review stars are the other trap. If the business being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, its pages using LocalBusiness or Organization markup are not eligible for star ratings at all. Testimonials on your own site are fine to show; marking them up for stars will not work. And two plugins each emitting their own Organization block, with different names or logos, give every reader two conflicting answers about who owns the site. Check what your platform already outputs before adding anything.

What AI search does with it

Google's documentation for AI Overviews and AI Mode says there is no special structured data needed to appear in them, and asks only that structured data match the visible text. Microsoft has been more direct: Bing's Fabrice Canel said at SMX Munich in March 2025 that schema markup helps Microsoft's language models understand content. Whether the other model providers use it has not been confirmed by them.

Our reading is that schema will not make an AI system cite a page, but it removes ambiguity about the facts it might cite: the price, the opening hours, the author, stated as labelled data rather than inferred from layout. That only helps if the markup is in the HTML the crawler receives and says the same thing as the page, which brings it back to the two decisions above.

Read the full version

This is the developer-side cut. The full guide has the table of every major schema type and its status in Google as of October 2026, which types a shop, a local business and a service company need, Google's own click-through case studies, and the full markup on our home page and price list.

Schema markup explained: what still earns rich results in 2026

This copy is a snapshot from the day it was posted, and it will not be updated here. The original on our site is the version we keep current: when a study publishes new figures, a price changes or a tool is renamed, that is where the correction lands. If you want the up-to-date version, follow the link above.

Sources

The FAQ removal on 7 May 2026 and the documentation removal in June are in Google's Search Central documentation updates, the 2023 FAQ and HowTo changes in Changes to HowTo and FAQ rich results, the mobile breadcrumb change in Simplifying the visible URL element, and the June 2025 phase-out in Simplifying the search results page. The 25 supported features are listed in the Search Gallery. The no-guarantee rule, the ban on marking up invisible content and the manual actions are in the General structured data guidelines, and the self-serving review rule in the Review snippet documentation. Google's position on AI features is in AI features and your website; Microsoft's is reported by Search Engine Land. The crawler finding is from Vercel's The rise of the AI crawler, and the script escaping from the Next.js JSON-LD guide. The product page and the agreement test are illustrative examples; the FAQ formatting bug is our own.

Which has bitten you more often: markup the crawlers never saw, or markup that said something different from the page?

title: Designing a Reliable Database for an E-Commerce Application
description:
Every successful e-commerce application depends on more than an attractive user interface and smooth shopping experience. Behind the scenes, a well-designed database plays an important role in managing customers, products, orders, payments, and reviews efficiently.

Database design is the process of organizing information into structured tables and defining relationships between them. A good database structure helps maintain data accuracy, minimize duplication, and retrieve information efficiently.

Understanding Relational Database Design

While working on an E-Commerce Management System database using MySQL 5.7, I learned how different types of application data can be organized into separate but connected tables.

The database consisted of seven main tables:

Users: Stores customer account information.

Categories: Organizes products into different categories.

Products: Stores product names, prices, and SKU details.

Orders: Maintains customer order information.

Order Items: Connects products with their respective orders.

Payments: Stores payment-related information.

Reviews: Maintains customer ratings and feedback.

Instead of storing all information in a single table, dividing data into related tables makes the database easier to maintain and manage.

Why Database Relationships Matter

Relationships are essential in relational database management systems.

For example, one customer can place multiple orders, and one product can receive multiple reviews. Similarly, a single order can contain multiple products.

The relationship between orders and products is many-to-many. An intermediate table called order_items handles this relationship by storing the product reference, order reference, quantity, and unit price.

Primary keys uniquely identify records, while foreign keys connect related tables and help maintain referential integrity.

The Importance of Database Normalization

Normalization is another important concept in database design. It helps reduce unnecessary data duplication and maintain consistency.

During this project, I explored three important normal forms:

1NF: Ensures that each column contains atomic values and repeating groups are avoided.

2NF: Ensures that non-key attributes depend on the complete candidate key.

3NF: Removes transitive dependencies so non-key attributes depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Applying normalization principles helps create a structured and maintainable database.

Working with SQL JOIN Queries

After creating the tables and inserting sample records, I practised SQL JOIN operations to retrieve information from multiple tables.

I successfully executed queries to combine users with orders, products with categories, order items with orders and products, and reviews with users and products.

These operations demonstrated how related information can be retrieved without storing duplicate data across multiple tables.

Tools and Practical Learning

I used MySQL 5.7 for database implementation, MySQL Workbench for executing SQL queries, and dbdiagram.io for designing the Entity Relationship Diagram.

This project helped me understand how database planning, normalization, constraints, indexes, and relationships contribute to reliable application development.

Conclusion

Database design is a fundamental part of building scalable and maintainable software applications. Through this E-Commerce Management System project, I gained practical experience in relational database design and improved my understanding of MySQL.

title: Learning to Edit IFC Building Models: Verifiable Checkers as the Training Signal for Dependency-Aware Editing Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable code and four checkers verify validity relative to the input model, intent, dependency and preservation against a task specification. Their conjunction is strict success. IfcEdit distils verified teacher episodes into a Qwen3.5-9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with strict success as the reward. On IfcEditBench, 1,990 editing tasks on 13 held-out real projects, the final student reaches 86.78% strict success, from 79.15% after SFT. The paired confidence interval for the difference from its teacher includes zero; the same recipe on a 27B model reaches 91.76% and exceeds the teacher. On the public benchmarks BIM-Edit and BIBIMBAP the final student scores 55.19 and 54.50. On IfcEditBench, the students outperform all prompted models except the teacher under matched tool access; both evaluated frameworks also score lower. Rewarding all four checkers yields 4.83 points more strict success than rewarding intent and validity alone.

title: The Software Development Bottleneck: Why Faster Coding Doesn't Mean Faster Delivery
description:
The Coding Revolution Has Created a New Engineering Problem

What if developers could write code twice as fast, but their organizations still couldn't release software any faster?

That is the paradox modern software engineering is facing.

AI coding assistants have changed how developers write, understand, and improve code. Tasks that once required hours of manual effort can now be completed much faster. Code generation, debugging assistance, documentation, and code suggestions are becoming increasingly automated.

But faster coding does not automatically translate into faster software delivery.

A software release involves much more than writing code. It requires architecture planning, requirement validation, dependency management, code reviews, testing, security checks, deployment approvals, and production monitoring. When these activities remain disconnected, improvements in coding speed simply move the bottleneck to another stage.

The real challenge is no longer how quickly developers can produce code. It is how efficiently an organization can move software from an initial requirement to a reliable production release.

Why Faster Coding Is Not Solving the Delivery Problem

Modern engineering teams work across multiple platforms, repositories, CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, monitoring systems, and project management tools.

Each system manages a different part of the development lifecycle. However, understanding how these systems influence one another often requires manual investigation and coordination.

Consider a simple enterprise software release. A developer completes a feature quickly, but the code review identifies a dependency risk. Testing then discovers an integration failure. The engineering team investigates logs, checks previous deployments, reviews configuration changes, and coordinates with other teams before the release can continue.

The coding task may have taken hours, but resolving everything around it can take considerably longer.

This creates a critical distinction:

Coding speed measures how quickly software is written. Delivery speed measures how efficiently the entire engineering ecosystem works together.

According to the challenges described in EzInsights AI SDLC Intelligence, fragmented engineering signals, slow root cause analysis, test coverage gaps, and manual compliance activities are important sources of enterprise engineering friction.

The Five Hidden Bottlenecks Slowing Software Delivery

The biggest delivery delays are often hidden between development activities rather than inside the coding process itself.

1. Fragmented Engineering Workflows

Engineering information is distributed across source code repositories, architecture documents, Jira tickets, CI/CD pipelines, logs, and monitoring platforms.

When these systems operate independently, engineers must manually connect information to understand the complete situation. This creates unnecessary coordination and investigation time.

2. Code Reviews and Dependency Management

Generating code faster can increase the volume of changes that need to be reviewed. Without sufficient architectural context, identifying breaking changes, dependency conflicts, and potential risks becomes difficult.

The result is a growing review workload that can slow down otherwise productive development teams.

3. Testing Cannot Keep Pace With Development

Software quality depends on testing more than just the newly written code. Teams must validate integration points, existing functionality, edge cases, APIs, and dependencies.

When testing remains heavily manual or disconnected from development context, faster coding can create larger testing backlogs.

4. Slow Root Cause Analysis

A failed deployment or production incident rarely has just one possible explanation. Engineers may need to investigate logs, recent commits, infrastructure changes, dependencies, and previous incidents.

Without connected engineering intelligence, identifying the actual cause becomes a time-consuming process.

5. Deployment and Compliance Delays

Security validation, governance requirements, approval workflows, and audit evidence are essential for enterprise software.

However, manually coordinating these activities across disconnected systems can delay releases even after development and testing are complete.

The Real Problem: Engineering Tools Understand Tasks, Not the Entire Lifecycle

Traditional DevOps transformed software delivery through automation, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure management, and monitoring.

These capabilities remain essential. However, modern enterprise environments require more than individual tools performing isolated activities.

A CI/CD platform understands pipeline execution. An observability platform understands metrics and logs. A project management system tracks tickets and tasks. An AI coding assistant helps developers generate and understand code.

But how do these systems collectively understand why a deployment failed, which services might be affected, which tests should be executed, and what needs to happen before a release becomes safe?

This is where engineering intelligence becomes important.

The future of software delivery requires connected information, contextual reasoning, and coordinated automation across the entire Software Development Lifecycle.

As explained in Why AI-Driven SDLC Platforms Are Replacing Traditional DevOps Tools, the next evolution is moving beyond execution automation toward intelligent systems that understand relationships across engineering workflows.

How AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence Changes the Equation

Instead of accelerating only code generation, AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence focuses on improving the complete software development lifecycle.

It connects design, development, testing, migration, documentation, deployment, and engineering knowledge into a unified intelligence ecosystem.

This approach helps engineering teams identify bottlenecks earlier, reduce repetitive work, and make better decisions using connected engineering context.

An important foundation of this approach is the Engineering Knowledge Graph (EKG).

An Engineering Knowledge Graph connects different engineering entities and their relationships, including:

Requirements and architecture documentation.

Source code and application dependencies.

APIs, services, and repositories.

Test cases and validation results.

CI/CD pipelines and deployment history.

Logs, incidents, and production changes.

Security policies and compliance requirements.

Instead of treating these as separate information sources, the knowledge graph creates connected engineering context.

For example, when a deployment fails, AI can use relationships between code changes, affected services, pipeline events, test results, and production logs to support a more informed investigation.

This moves engineering teams beyond searching through disconnected systems toward understanding how different engineering events are connected.

Multi-Agent AI: Moving Beyond Individual Coding Assistants

A single AI coding assistant can help generate code, explain functions, or suggest improvements. However, enterprise software delivery requires coordination across multiple specialized engineering responsibilities.

Multi-Agent AI introduces a different approach.

Instead of expecting one AI assistant to manage every engineering activity, specialized agents collaborate using shared engineering context.

An intelligent SDLC ecosystem can include:

Code Intelligence Agent: Reviews code, identifies risks, and analyzes dependencies.

QA Automation Agent: Generates unit, integration, and end-to-end test cases.

CI/CD Agent: Investigates pipeline failures and dependency mismatches.

SRE/RCA Agent: Connects logs, services, incidents, and code changes.

Compliance Agent: Identifies governance gaps and maps controls to evidence.

Architecture Agent: Analyzes system dependencies and architectural changes.

These agents can work together to create a more connected engineering workflow.

For example, when a developer introduces a significant code change, the system can help identify affected dependencies, highlight missing test coverage, support code review, and provide relevant deployment risk information.

The objective is not simply to automate individual tasks. It is to reduce the delays between engineering activities.

How EzInsights AI Is Addressing the Software Delivery Bottleneck

EzInsights AI introduces an AI-Powered SDLC Intelligence framework designed to connect engineering workflows through multi-agent automation and an Engineering Knowledge Graph.

Its approach focuses on bringing engineering signals together instead of allowing code, tests, pipelines, incidents, and architecture information to remain isolated.

Through its SDLC Intelligence Platform, organizations can explore capabilities such as:

Intelligent code review and dependency analysis.

Automated unit, integration, and end-to-end test generation.

CI/CD failure diagnosis.

AI-powered root cause analysis.

Architecture and dependency intelligence.

Security and compliance evidence automation.

Engineering knowledge and documentation intelligence.

The platform describes six specialized agents working through a shared Engineering Knowledge Graph to support engineering automation and contextual reasoning.

This creates a continuous intelligence flow:

Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Operations → Continuous Improvement

Every stage can provide useful information to the next, helping organizations reduce fragmented workflows and improve delivery visibility.

The Future of Software Delivery Is Not About Writing More Code

The next competitive advantage in software engineering will not come simply from organizations generating the largest amount of code.

It will come from organizations that can move from requirements to production with fewer delays, better quality, stronger engineering context, and more predictable releases.

AI coding tools are an important step forward, but they address only one part of a much larger engineering challenge.

Enterprises need connected intelligence that understands the relationships between development, testing, architecture, deployment, and operations.

Final Thought

The software development industry has spent years trying to make developers write code faster. AI is now making that possible.

But the next challenge is much bigger.

Can organizations eliminate the hidden delays between writing, reviewing, testing, deploying, and maintaining software?

Because the real measure of engineering productivity is not how much code a team produces.

It is how reliably and efficiently that code becomes valuable software in production.

The future of software development will not be defined by faster coding alone. It will be defined by intelligent software delivery.

Explore how EzInsights AI is bringing intelligence across the entire Software Development Lifecycle.

title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
description:
arXiv:2611.21891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.22301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
description:
arXiv:2611.21879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.

title: Every despill formula bets on colours your subject isn't wearing
description:
A despill step is usually one line of maths, picked from whichever tutorial came first. To see what the three common lines cost, the comparison here uses a self-made 1280×720 test card with a green screen at RGB(20,175,65) and ten patches: hair strands, a white shirt, a light-blue shirt, light and dark skin, a yellow object and a grey veil at α=0.45. Clean foreground and alpha are known. The spill is not real light; it was added with a model that peaks at the outline, so the numbers describe this card only. Results are composited on grey (110,110,110) with the true alpha and compared to the clean version as ΔE76, hue as the HSV angle. One Apple-silicon Mac, Python and NumPy, FFmpeg for one cross-check, single run.

Spill sits on the outline more than inside

Uncorrected, the hair strands carried 30.7 of extra green, ΔE 24.0. The veil at α=0.45 came out with G about 41 above R and B, ΔE 28.8. The white shirt read ΔE 16.6 on its 6-pixel edge and 7.8 inside. Light skin was the worst case: its edge moved from hue 23° to 70°, ΔE 34.5, against 11.7 in the interior. Per pixel, a despill formula has to decide whether this green came from the screen or the object. It can't know, so it assumes.

Average-limit assumes nothing is greener than its neighbours

G = min(G, (R+B)/2) was the cleanest on almost everything: hair ΔE 6.2, veil 6.5, light-blue shirt 2.7. Its bet is that no real colour in the shot has green above the mean of red and blue, which yellow breaks by definition. The yellow patch, clean at (245,205,30), went from (248,228,39) with spill to (248,143,39) after the formula, hue 49° to 30°, ΔE 39.4. Untouched it was 12.1. Yellow-greens and pale cyans sit on the same side of the line. FFmpeg's despill filter at its defaults (mix 0.5, expand 0) matched this formula within 1 per pixel on this card. Its source wasn't read for this, so the claim stops at "almost the same on this card".

Max-limit assumes spill always pushes green to the top

G = min(G, max(R,B)) is the cautious one: yellow and skin interiors were not touched at all. That's its failure too. The light-blue shirt, clean at (196,214,236), picked up spill to (198,237,244). Green rose by 23, but it stayed under blue at 244, so the formula saw nothing to remove and left ΔE 12.3 exactly as it was. The light-skin edge stayed at (227,227,168), hue 60°, ΔE 27.6. The hidden bet is that spill only exists once green becomes the largest channel, and on pale blue or warm skin it can add a lot without winning.

Complement-fill assumes the lost energy belongs to magenta

The third family gives some of the removed green back to red and blue so the pixel doesn't darken. The variant used here takes s = max(0, G − (R+B)/2), subtracts s from green and adds s/2 to each of red and blue. Brightness held up, but the refill overshot. The light-skin edge came out (246,197,188), hue 23° to 9°, pink. The veil and the white shirt edge drifted toward purple, hues between 256° and 286°. Yellow was the worst result in the whole table, ΔE 50.8 inside and 54.3 on its edge. The refill ratio wasn't swept, so whether some split keeps skin warm without hurting yellow is still open.

One drift sits outside the formulas: after average-limit, half-transparent areas such as the hair strands landed on a blue-grey near hue 210°, because the screen has B=65 and R=20 and removing its green leaves the blue behind. That's a missing step, subtracting the screen colour first, not an assumption of any formula.

Choose the formula per shot as a policy

Formula What it assumes What broke on this card
Average-limit Nothing real is greener than (R+B)/2 Yellow 49° to 30°, ΔE 39.4
Max-limit Spill always makes green the top channel Light-blue shirt untouched, ΔE 12.3; skin edge ΔE 27.6
Complement-fill (s/2 to R and B) Removed green should return as magenta Skin edge 23° to 9°; yellow ΔE 50.8

Three years on codecs taught me to read every rounding rule as a choice of which error to ship, and this table reads the same way. Yellow props mean average-limit, and FFmpeg's default with it, will damage them, so max-limit or a mask is safer. Pale blue clothes or light skin under heavy spill mean max-limit leaves the green alone. Complement-fill trades skin tone for brightness. I'd record the choice per shot next to the key settings rather than bake one line into the pipeline.

The step belongs after alpha and before compositing; run before the key, it turned the screen dark blue-grey and the keyer stopped seeing it. AI matting doesn't remove the decision either. A real green-screen clip went through the video matting Beta of ImgIng https://imging.ai/ in a desktop Chromium-based browser, with the model running locally. Composited over grey at frame 45, its transparent WebM still had green-leaning pixels at the hair tips and on the hand, from 2.7% to 14.8% depending on region and on which of its two models produced the matte; average-limit took every one of those counts to zero. That module isn't mine. My reading is that the model returns transparency and the colour usually comes from the source frame, so the assumption is still yours to pick. Credit for the real clip goes to VOA Learning English via Wikimedia Commons (public domain; trimmed and re-encoded here). The test card is self-made, with spill added by a model.

title: Your Claude Code skills are going blank. Three settings that fix it.
description:
Last week I wrote about measuring what my Claude Code setup costs on every request. The short version: 68.5k tokens before I typed a word, and 220 of my 283 skills listed with no description at all.

The obvious follow-up question was: what do you actually do about it? Uninstalling everything you didn't use this week is a blunt answer. It turns out Claude Code has settings for exactly this, and I hadn't heard of any of them.

Why skills lose their descriptions

Every session starts with a listing of your skills: a name and a description for each. Claude reads the descriptions to decide when a skill applies.

That listing has a budget. According to the docs it scales at 1% of the model's context window. On a 1M-token model that came out at 29,997 characters in my transcripts. When the listing overflows, Claude Code keeps every name but drops descriptions, starting with the skills you invoke least.

That matches what I saw. All 13 skills I'd used in the last month kept their descriptions. The 220 that went blank were all skills I hadn't touched. The catch is that a skill you just installed has zero invocations too, so it's first in line to go blank, and Claude can't reach for it on its own because all it sees is a name.

The three settings

skillOverrides

Decides how each skill shows up:

{
  "skillOverrides": {
    "old-report-skill": "user-invocable-only",
    "deploy": "name-only"
  }
}
value Claude sees in the / menu
"on" (default) name + description yes
"name-only" name only yes
"user-invocable-only" nothing yes
"off" nothing no

user-invocable-only is the useful one. The skill disappears from what the model sees, but you can still run it yourself with /name. For a skill you haven't used in a month, that's usually what you want.

One catch: plugin skills aren't affected by skillOverrides. For those, the only option is disabling the plugin.

skillListingBudgetFraction

This is the 1% itself. 0.02 doubles the room. It isn't free, though: my listing is about 30k characters, so doubling it can cost up to ~8k more tokens on every request once it fills up. Hiding the skills you don't use is the cheaper way to get room back.

disableClaudeAiConnectors

If you've connected services on claude.ai, Claude Code loads their tool names and instructions in every session. Setting this to true stops Claude Code from fetching them. They stay connected on claude.ai. If you use some connectors but not others, toggle the unused ones off in /mcp instead (that's stored per project).

Doing it from your actual usage

Choosing what to hide by hand isn't fun with 283 skills, so I added it to deadweight, the tool from the last post. It already reads the transcripts in ~/.claude/projects to see what you used in the last 30 days. Version 0.3.0 uses the settings above:

cargo install deadweight
deadweight fix --dry-run

Disable these plugins (settings.json → enabledPlugins: false)
  ...
Hide these skills from Claude (settings.json → skillOverrides: "user-invocable-only"; /name still works)
  ...
Turn off claude.ai connectors in Claude Code (settings.json → disableClaudeAiConnectors: true)
  ...
Saves ~5.3k tokens per request. Undo any time with deadweight undo.

On my machine that's 17 unused plugins, 30 unused skills and one connector. The previous version moved skill folders into a backup. Now nothing on disk moves: it's a few keys in settings.json, and deadweight undo puts back exactly what was there before, including overrides you had already set yourself. --park-skills keeps the old behaviour if you prefer it.

When descriptions are being dropped, the report also does the budget math for you:

✗ 220 of 283 skills are listed without a description: the skill listing is full
    (~30.0k characters). Claude sees only their names, so it can't tell when to use them.
    Make room: hide what you don't use (deadweight fix), or set "skillListingBudgetFraction": 0.02 in settings.json
    (default 0.01; the extra room costs up to ~8.3k tokens per request).

What I'd still check by hand

  • Plugins that run hooks. deadweight won't disable them unless you pass --include-hooked, because a hook can do useful work that never shows up as a tool call. On my machine that's a memory plugin I'd rather keep.
  • Skills you use rarely. Claude Code deletes transcripts after 30 days by default (cleanupPeriodDays), so a skill you use once a quarter looks unused. --keep NAME protects it.
  • Servers you never signed in to. I had 36 of them still listing authenticate tools in every session. They all came from plugins, so disabling the plugin is what removes them.

A lot of this was worked out by people measuring their own listings in anthropics/claude-code#81081. It's worth a read if you want the details of the drop order.

If deadweight gets something wrong on your setup, run deadweight --json and open an issue. Those reports are the most useful thing anyone can send me.

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
description:
arXiv:2611.22179v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

The Limitations of Off-the-Shelf Templates

Off-the-shelf templates, while convenient, often fall short in meeting the unique requirements of modern websites. Here are the key reasons why they fail:

  1. Lack of Customization: These templates are designed for general use, making it difficult to tailor them to specific brand identities or user experiences. This generic approach can result in a website that feels impersonal and fails to resonate with the target audience.

title: Introducing Vercel X
description:
Today we’re launching Vercel X, a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages.

Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers.

The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners.

Applications are now open through November 29, 2026. The program runs from January 19 to March 2, 2027.

Vercel has worked with more than 100 early-stage teams from around the world across three accelerator cohorts. Alumni include Rex, Alloy Robotics, Interfaze, Cervo, and Hacktron. Interfaze and Rex are backed by Y Combinator, and Cervo was acquired by Altana Technologies.

Why Vercel X?

If you’re applying to Vercel X, you probably have an idea or project you haven’t been able to stop thinking about. The next stretch is figuring out exactly what you’re building and who it’s for.

We think you get through that stretch the Vercel way: by deeply understanding your customers, shipping quickly, and iterating to greatness.

The program includes:

  • Technical mentorship: Hands-on workshops and product feedback from Vercel’s design, product, and engineering teams.

  • Partner credits: Put credits toward hosting, compute, and model API usage as you build and test your product.

  • Founder community: A cohort of AI founders at the same stage, with weekly fireside chats featuring industry leaders.

  • Investor access: Mentorship from VC partners and the opportunity to present your company to investors, ecosystem partners, and the Vercel community at Demo Day.

Winning teams receive funding from Vercel Ventures and prizes from program partners.

Who should apply

We’re looking for technical builders with ambitious ideas and insatiable curiosity.

You don’t need a finished product or traction. Tell us what you want to build, who needs it, what AI makes possible, and why you’re the right person or team for the job.

Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below.

title: Web Scraping with Scrapy: Building a Spider from Scratch
description:
A requests and BeautifulSoup script is the right way to start scraping. But as soon as a job grows, you find yourself writing the same plumbing again and again: a loop over pages, retries, delays, de-duplication, saving results. Soon your 30-line script is 300 lines and mostly not about the data.

Scrapy is a framework that supplies that plumbing. You describe what to extract in a small class called a spider, and Scrapy handles requests, concurrency, retries, throttling, robots.txt, logging, and exporting results.

In this guide you'll build a complete Scrapy project from scratch. It will crawl every page of a bookstore, follow each book to its detail page, clean the data in a pipeline, and export it to JSON or CSV, politely.

Version note: this guide targets Scrapy 2.20 (released November 2026), which requires Python 3.11 or newer. Scrapy has changed a lot recently, and many tutorials online are out of date. The biggest example: the old start_requests() method was removed in Scrapy 2.16, and spiders now use async def start(). If you copy a spider from an older tutorial and it crawls nothing, that's probably why.

Why Scrapy?

Here's what you get without writing it yourself:

Need In a script In Scrapy
Many requests at once Threads or asyncio by hand Built-in concurrency
Retrying failures Your own loop Built-in retry middleware
Being polite time.sleep() Download delay and AutoThrottle
Obeying robots.txt Extra code One setting, on by default
Skipping repeated URLs A set() you maintain Automatic de-duplication
Cleaning and saving data Mixed into the scraping code Item pipelines and feed exports
Knowing what happened print() Logs and crawl statistics

When not to use it. For a single page or a quick one-off, requests and BeautifulSoup are simpler. For sites that build their content with JavaScript, you need a browser: see our guide to scraping JavaScript-heavy sites with Playwright. Scrapy shines when you need to crawl many pages reliably.

Setting Up

Check that you have Python 3.11 or newer, then create a virtual environment and install Scrapy:

python --version                 # 3.11 or newer
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate         # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install scrapy
scrapy version

Now create a project:

scrapy startproject bookscraper
cd bookscraper

You get this layout:

bookscraper/
├── scrapy.cfg                # project marker (run commands from this folder)
└── bookscraper/
    ├── items.py              # the shape of the data you extract
    ├── middlewares.py        # hooks into the request/response flow
    ├── pipelines.py          # clean, validate and store items
    ├── settings.py           # all configuration
    └── spiders/              # your spiders live here

Two things in the generated settings.py are worth noticing right away: ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True, so Scrapy respects robots.txt by default, and a DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second with one request at a time per domain. New projects start out polite.

Explore the Page with the Scrapy Shell

Before writing any spider, experiment on the live page. The shell downloads a URL and gives you a response object to play with:

scrapy shell "https://books.toscrape.com/"

We'll use the sandbox site books.toscrape.com, which exists for practicing scraping. Inside the shell, try:

>>> response.css("article.product_pod h3 a::attr(title)").get()
'A Light in the Attic'
>>> response.css("p.price_color::text").getall()[:3]
['£51.77', '£53.74', '£50.10']
>>> response.xpath("//li[@class='next']/a/@href").get()
'catalogue/page-2.html'

A few things to learn from this:

  • response.css() takes CSS selectors, extended with ::text (the text of an element) and ::attr(name) (an attribute's value).

  • response.xpath() does the same job with XPath, which is handy for odd cases.

  • .get() returns the first match, or None if there isn't one. .getall() returns a list of every match.

The shell is the fastest way to get selectors right, so use it constantly. Type exit() to leave.

Your First Spider

A spider is a class with a name, a place to start, and a parse method that turns a response into data. You can generate a skeleton with scrapy genspider books books.toscrape.com, but it's short enough to write by hand. Create bookscraper/spiders/books.py:

import scrapy

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            yield {
                "title": card.css("h3 a::attr(title)").get(),
                "price": card.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
                "url": response.urljoin(card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get()),
            }

How it works:

  • name is how you run the spider.

  • allowed_domains stops the spider from wandering off to other sites.

  • start_urls lists the first pages to download. Scrapy requests each one and passes the response to parse.

  • yield hands each result back to Scrapy. A spider doesn't return a list: it yields items one at a time, and Scrapy streams them to wherever they're going.

Run it and export to a file:

scrapy crawl books -O books.json

-O (capital) overwrites the output file, so you always start fresh. Open books.json and you'll have the first page of books.

Watch out for -o. In projects created with Scrapy 2.20, the generated settings include FEED_MODE = "create". If the file already exists, lowercase -o then logs an error (Not writing ... because it already exists) and throws that run's items away, yet the command still exits normally, so it's easy to miss. In older setups, and outside a project, -o appends, and appending a second run to a JSON file leaves you with a corrupted file. Use -O while you're developing, or pick the behavior explicitly with the FEED_MODE setting.

If you just want to try a spider quickly without creating a project, scrapy runspider books.py -O books.json runs a single file.

About start_urls and start()

start_urls is the simplest way to say where to begin. When you need more control, such as generating a list of URLs or adding headers, write an async def start() method instead:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]

    async def start(self):
        for page in range(1, 4):
            url = f"https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-{page}.html"
            yield scrapy.Request(url, callback=self.parse)

This replaces start_requests() from older tutorials. Note that async def and yield together make it an asynchronous generator, which Scrapy knows how to run. A leftover start_requests() isn't an error: the spider simply starts, reports Crawled 0 pages, and finishes without a word of complaint.

Following Pagination

Scraping one page isn't much of a crawler. Add this to the end of parse to follow the "Next" link:

next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

response.follow() creates a new request for the link and sends its response back to parse. It handles relative URLs for you (no urljoin needed), and Scrapy automatically skips any URL it has already requested. When there's no Next link on the last page, get() returns None and the crawl ends.

Following Links to Detail Pages

The listing doesn't have everything: the description and product code live on each book's own page. So the spider needs two callbacks: one for listing pages and one for book pages. It will also pass the star rating (which we only read from the listing) along to the second callback.

First, define the shape of your data in bookscraper/items.py. Recent Scrapy templates use a plain dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str | None = None
    price: str | float | None = None
    rating: str | int | None = None
    availability: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    upc: str | None = None
    url: str | None = None

Now rewrite the spider:

import scrapy

from bookscraper.items import Book

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        """Listing page: follow every book, then the Next link."""
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            rating = card.css("p.star-rating::attr(class)").get().split()[-1]   # "star-rating Three" -> "Three"
            yield response.follow(
                card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get(),
                callback=self.parse_book,
                cb_kwargs={"rating": rating},
            )

        next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

    def parse_book(self, response, rating):
        """Book page: build the item."""
        availability = "".join(response.css("p.availability::text").getall())
        yield Book(
            title=response.css("h1::text").get(),
            price=response.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
            rating=rating,
            availability=" ".join(availability.split()),
            description=response.css("#product_description ~ p::text").get(),
            upc=response.css("table tr:first-child td::text").get(),
            url=response.url,
        )

Notes on what's new:

  • Callbacks chain the crawl. parse yields requests for book pages, and each response goes to parse_book, which yields items. A callback can yield both requests and items.

  • cb_kwargs passes extra data to the next callback as keyword arguments. That's how rating travels from the listing page to the book page.

  • Whitespace cleanup. The availability text has line breaks and padding around it, so we collapse it with " ".join(text.split()).

  • Missing data. Some pages will lack a field, a description for instance. .get() returns None instead of crashing, and the dataclass defaults to None.

Cleaning Data with Pipelines

Right now price is a string like £51.77 and rating is a word like Three. Item pipelines are the right place to clean and validate items, keeping that logic out of the spider. Each pipeline is a class with a process_item method. Open bookscraper/pipelines.py:

import re

from itemadapter import ItemAdapter
from scrapy.exceptions import DropItem

RATINGS = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

class ValidateAndCleanPipeline:
    def process_item(self, item):
        adapter = ItemAdapter(item)

        if not adapter.get("title") or not adapter.get("price"):
            raise DropItem(f"Missing title or price: {adapter.get('url')}")

        adapter["price"] = float(re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", adapter["price"]))   # "£51.77" -> 51.77
        adapter["rating"] = RATINGS.get(adapter["rating"])                   # "Three" -> 3
        return item

class DuplicatesPipeline:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seen = set()

    def process_item(self, item):
        upc = ItemAdapter(item)["upc"]
        if upc in self.seen:
            raise DropItem(f"Duplicate book: {upc}")
        self.seen.add(upc)
        return item

Key ideas:

  • ItemAdapter lets one pipeline work with dictionaries, dataclasses, or scrapy.Item objects through the same interface.

  • Return the item to pass it along, or raise DropItem to discard it. Dropped items are logged and counted but never exported.

  • The first pipeline drops incomplete items and converts the price and rating to numbers. The second drops repeats using the UPC, a unique product code, because the same book can appear under more than one URL.

  • Older tutorials write process_item(self, item, spider). That still runs in 2.20 but prints a deprecation warning, so drop the spider argument in new code.

Pipelines are off until you switch them on in settings.py. The numbers set the order, and lower runs first:

ITEM_PIPELINES = {
    "bookscraper.pipelines.ValidateAndCleanPipeline": 300,
    "bookscraper.pipelines.DuplicatesPipeline": 400,
}

Crawling Politely: Settings

Scrapy is fast, which is exactly why you must configure it carefully. Add these to settings.py:

# Tell site owners who you are and how to reach you
USER_AGENT = "BookScraperBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; contact@example.com)"

# Adapt the delay to how quickly the server responds
AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = True
AUTOTHROTTLE_START_DELAY = 1
AUTOTHROTTLE_MAX_DELAY = 10
AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY = 1.0

# Retry temporary failures a couple of times
RETRY_TIMES = 2

# During development only: cache responses on disk so repeat runs don't hit the site
HTTPCACHE_ENABLED = True

# Export automatically, without command-line flags
FEEDS = {
    "output/books.json": {"format": "json", "mode": "overwrite", "indent": 2},
}

What each does:

  • USER_AGENT replaces Scrapy's default. An honest, descriptive agent with contact details lets site owners reach you instead of blocking you.

  • AutoThrottle adjusts the delay between requests based on how fast the server responds, backing off when the site slows down. It never goes below the project's DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second, so it can only make the crawl gentler than the default.

  • HTTPCACHE_ENABLED stores every response on disk. Re-running the spider while you tweak your selectors then costs the site nothing. Turn it off for real runs, or you'll scrape stale data.

  • FEEDS defines the output in settings, with "mode": "overwrite" replacing the file on each run.

Two more settings are handy while testing: CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT and CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT stop the crawl after roughly that many pages or items (requests already in flight still finish). You can pass any setting on the command line with -s:

scrapy crawl books -s CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT=10 -O sample.json

One catch: -O adds a second output on top of FEEDS, so this sample run also overwrites output/books.json with the partial result. Comment out FEEDS while you experiment if that bothers you.

The sandbox has 50 listing pages of 20 books each, so a full crawl is about 1,050 requests. With a delay of at least one second each, expect 20 minutes or more, so test with a small sample first.

Spider arguments

You can also pass arguments to a spider with -a. For example, to crawl one category instead of the whole site, accept a start URL:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def __init__(self, start_url=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if start_url:
            self.start_urls = [start_url]

scrapy crawl books -a start_url=https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html -O travel.json

Reading the Results

When a crawl finishes, Scrapy prints a statistics summary. These lines tell you most of what you need:

Stat Meaning
item_scraped_count Items that made it through the pipelines
item_dropped_count Items discarded with DropItem
downloader/response_status_count/200 Successful responses (look for 403, 404, 429 here too)
dupefilter/filtered Requests skipped because the URL had been seen
robotstxt/forbidden Requests blocked by robots.txt
finish_reason finished for a normal end, or the reason it stopped early

A stat that never happened isn't printed at all, so no robotstxt/forbidden line means nothing was blocked. Check these after every run. A crawl that "worked" but dropped half its items, or got a pile of 403 responses, is telling you something.

Running a Spider from a Script

Sometimes you want to run a crawl from your own Python code, for example from a scheduler. Put this in a file at the project root:

from scrapy.crawler import AsyncCrawlerProcess
from scrapy.utils.project import get_project_settings

process = AsyncCrawlerProcess(get_project_settings())
process.crawl("books")
process.start()          # blocks until the crawl is finished

Run it from the same folder as scrapy.cfg, so Scrapy finds your project settings.

Responsible Scraping with Scrapy

Because Scrapy can send many requests quickly, a few habits matter more here than in a script:

  • Leave ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True. Turning it off to get at pages a site has asked crawlers to avoid is the wrong fix for a "Forbidden by robots.txt" message.

  • Keep the delay and the concurrency low. The generated defaults are conservative, and AutoThrottle helps. Don't raise concurrency against a small site.

  • Identify yourself with USER_AGENT, and respect 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After by slowing down, not by retrying harder.

  • Read the terms of service, and avoid personal data unless you have a lawful reason to collect it. Our guide "Is Web Scraping Legal?" covers this in depth.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause What to try
Spider runs but crawls nothing (Crawled 0 pages) Code from an older tutorial defines start_requests(), which was removed in 2.16 Use start_urls or async def start()
Not writing ... already exists and an empty export -o on an existing file; projects from 2.20 set FEED_MODE = "create" Use -O, or set FEED_MODE explicitly
Empty or None fields Selector doesn't match Test it in scrapy shell
Filtered offsite request in the log The link is outside allowed_domains Check the domain, or leave it if it's intended
Forbidden by robots.txt The site disallows that path Respect it; don't disable ROBOTSTXT_OBEY
ModuleNotFoundError: bookscraper You're not in the project folder Run from the folder containing scrapy.cfg
Lots of 403 or 429 responses You're going too fast, or the site refuses your traffic Slow down; check the site's rules
Fewer items than expected Pipelines dropped some, or the duplicate filter skipped URLs Check item_dropped_count and dupefilter/filtered

For more detail while debugging, run with -s LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.

Where to Go from Here

You now have the core of a real crawler: a spider, items, pipelines, polite settings, and exports. Natural next steps:

  • CrawlSpider rules let you describe which links to follow declaratively instead of writing the pagination code yourself.

  • JavaScript sites need a browser. Plugins such as scrapy-playwright connect Scrapy to Playwright, so you keep the framework's crawling and pipelines.

  • Storing results in a database is a matter of writing another pipeline, for example one that inserts into SQLite or PostgreSQL.

  • Scheduling a nightly crawl is easy once your spider runs from a script or a command.

The mental model to remember: spiders extract, pipelines clean, settings decide how politely you crawl, and Scrapy runs the machinery. Once you've written your first spider, the second takes minutes.

Happy scraping, and please do it politely!

title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.21849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.
