title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2611.21950v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for spacecraft trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions
description:
arXiv:2611.21933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.

title: How AI Voice Models Are Trained: A Technical Overview
description:
The Building Blocks of Modern TTS

If you’ve ever asked a smart speaker to read a news article, you’ve already interacted with a text‑to‑speech (TTS) system powered by deep learning. At a high level, a TTS pipeline does three things:

  1. Transforms raw audio into a compact, learnable representation (usually a spectrogram).
  2. Learns a mapping from text (or phonemes) to that representation using a neural network.
  3. Converts the predicted spectrogram back into waveforms with a vocoder.

The magic happens during the training phase, where the model learns to predict realistic speech from arbitrary strings of characters. Let’s walk through the technical steps you’ll encounter when building or fine‑tuning a voice model.

1. Collecting & Curating the Dataset

Why data matters

A high‑quality voice model needs clean, well‑aligned audio paired with accurate transcripts. The most common public corpora are:

Corpus Language Approx. Hours License
LJSpeech English 24 Open
VCTK English (multiple speakers) 44 Open
Common Voice Multilingual 2,000+ Open

If you’re building a voice clone for a specific person, you’ll need a few minutes of studio‑recorded speech (the more, the better). Aim for:

  • Consistent sampling rate (usually 24 kHz or 48 kHz).
  • Uniform loudness (≈‑23 LUFS).
  • Minimal background noise (record in a treated room or use a high‑quality mic).

Pre‑processing steps 

import librosa, numpy as np

def load_and_normalize(path, sr=24000):
    # Load audio, resample if needed
    wav, _ = librosa.load(path, sr=sr)
    # Peak‑normalize to -1..1
    wav = wav / np.max(np.abs(wav))
    # Trim leading/trailing silence
    wav, _ = librosa.effects.trim(wav, top_db=20)
    return wav

After loading, you’ll typically extract a mel‑spectrogram:

def wav_to_mel(wav, sr=24000, n_fft=1024, hop_length=256, n_mels=80):
    mel = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(
        wav,
        sr=sr,
        n_fft=n_fft,
        hop_length=hop_length,
        n_mels=n_mels,
        fmin=0,
        fmax=sr/2
    )
    # Convert to log scale
    mel = np.log10(np.clip(mel, a_min=1e-5, a_max=None))
    return mel.T  # shape: (time, mel_bins)

Store the spectrograms (often in .npz or .hdf5 files) alongside the cleaned transcripts for fast loading during training.

2. Choosing the Model Architecture

From Tacotron‑2 to VITS

  • Tacotron‑2: Two‑stage model (text → mel → waveform). The first stage is an encoder‑decoder with attention; the second stage uses a WaveNet‑style vocoder. Works well but requires a separate vocoder training step.

  • FastSpeech / FastSpeech‑2: Removes the autoregressive decoder, enabling parallel generation. Great for low‑latency services.

  • VITS (Variational Inference with adversarial learning for end‑to‑end TTS): A single‑stage model that directly predicts waveforms from text, using a flow‑based decoder and a GAN‑style loss. It’s currently one of the most efficient choices for production.

For most developers, VITS offers the best trade‑off between quality and speed, especially when you plan to host the model on a GPU‑enabled serverless function.

3. The Training Loop

Below is a minimal PyTorch‑style training loop for a VITS‑like model. The code assumes you already have a VITSMultiScale class and a DataLoader that yields (text_tensor, mel_tensor) pairs.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
model = VITSMultiScale().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-4)
criterion = nn.L1Loss()

def train_one_epoch(loader):
    model.train()
    total_loss = 0
    for text, mel in loader:
        text, mel = text.to(device), mel.to(device)

        # Forward pass
        wav_pred, mel_pred, kl_loss = model(text, mel)

        # Spectrogram loss + KL divergence
        spec_loss = criterion(mel_pred, mel)
        loss = spec_loss + kl_loss * 0.01   # weighting term

        # Backprop
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
    return total_loss / len(loader)

# Example usage
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=16, shuffle=True, num_workers=4)
for epoch in range(1, 51):
    avg_loss = train_one_epoch(train_loader)
    print(f'Epoch {epoch:02d} – loss: {avg_loss:.4f}')

Key points to watch:

  • Learning rate scheduling – a cosine annealing schedule often yields smoother convergence.
  • Mixed‑precision training – torch.cuda.amp can cut memory usage by ~30 % without sacrificing quality.
  • Checkpointing – save both model weights and optimizer state every few epochs to resume training if needed.

4. Voice Cloning: From Generic to Personal

Voice cloning is essentially fine‑tuning a pre‑trained multi‑speaker model on a small speaker‑specific corpus. The steps are:

  1. Load the base model (e.g., a VITS trained on VCTK).
  2. Freeze the majority of layers (encoder and decoder) and only train the speaker embedding layer and a few adapter modules.
  3. Use a higher learning rate for the unfrozen parameters (e.g., 1e‑3) while keeping the rest at 1e‑5. 
# Freeze everything except speaker embedding
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    param.requires_grad = 'speaker_embedding' in name

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, model.parameters()),
                              lr=1e-3)

Even with 5‑10 minutes of clean audio, you can achieve a convincing clone that preserves the target’s timbre while retaining the base model’s prosody and pronunciation robustness.

5. Evaluating Quality

  • Objective metrics:

    • Mel Cepstral Distortion (MCD) – lower is better.
    • Word Error Rate (WER) – run an ASR model on synthesized speech.

  • Subjective listening tests:

    • Mean Opinion Score (MOS) – ask real users to rate naturalness on a 1‑5 scale.
    • ABX tests – compare the clone against the original voice.

A good rule of thumb: aim for MOS ≥ 4.0 before shipping.

6. Deploying the Model

Once you’re happy with the model, export it to ONNX or TorchScript for fast inference:

dummy_text = torch.randint(0, 100, (1, 100)).to(device)  # example token ids
torch.onnx.export(
    model,
    dummy_text,
    "tts_vits.onnx",
    input_names=['text'],
    output_names=['audio'],
    dynamic_axes={'text': {0: 'batch', 1: 'seq_len'},
                  'audio': {0: 'batch', 1: 'samples'}},
    opset_version=13
)

Host the ONNX model behind a lightweight Flask or FastAPI endpoint, or push it to a serverless platform like AWS Lambda (with GPU layers) for on‑demand synthesis.

7. Why ElevenLabs Makes Life Easier

If you’d rather skip the heavy‑lifting of dataset collection, model training, and GPU provisioning, ElevenLabs offers a production‑grade API that abstracts all of the above. Their service provides:

  • Instant voice cloning from as little as a 30‑second sample.
  • High‑fidelity, low‑latency synthesis powered by proprietary VITS‑style models.
  • Built‑in language support (over 30 languages) and fine‑grained control over prosody, speed, and emotion.

You can call the API directly from Python or via curl. Here’s a quick example that turns a string into speech using the ElevenLabs endpoint:

import requests

API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
VOICE_ID = "your-voice-id"  # obtain from the dashboard

def synthesize(text: str, output_path: str = "output.wav"):
    url = f"https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{VOICE_ID}"
    headers = {
        "xi-api-key": API_KEY,
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
    }
    payload = {
        "text": text,
        "voice_settings": {
            "stability": 0.75,
            "similarity_boost": 0.85
        }
    }
    response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers)
    response.raise_for_status()
    with open(output_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(response.content)

synthesize("Hello, Dev.to! This is a quick demo of ElevenLabs.")

Or a one‑liner with curl:

curl -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/your-voice-id" \
  -H "xi-api-key: $ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"text":"Your text goes here","voice_settings":{"stability":0.75,"similarity_boost":0.85}}' \
  --output speech.wav

Because the heavy neural‑network work is handled by ElevenLabs, you can focus on product features, UX, and integration rather than GPU management.

8. Putting It All Together

Whether you choose to train a model from scratch or leverage a managed service, the core concepts remain the same:

  1. High‑quality, aligned data is the foundation.
  2. Modern architectures like VITS deliver real‑time, natural‑sounding speech.
  3. Fine‑tuning enables voice cloning with surprisingly little data.
  4. Evaluation should combine objective metrics and human listening tests.
  5. Deployment benefits from export formats (ONNX/TorchScript) and scalable inference servers.

If you’re looking for a fast path to production‑ready voice synthesis—especially for voice cloning—ElevenLabs is a solid choice. Their API abstracts the training pipeline while still giving you enough knobs to customize tone, speed, and emotion.

Ready to give your app a voice? Sign up through the link above, grab an API key, and start generating speech in minutes. Happy coding!

title: I used to read TV audiences live. Now I read app reviews the same way.
description:
In 2013 I worked as an applied anthropologist at a market research firm in Mexico City. One of my jobs: when a TV network premiered a telenovela, I watched the audience, not the show.

While each episode aired, I followed what people wrote on social media in real time. How they felt about the characters and the story, and how that changed from scene to scene. The network learned how people felt while it was still happening, not weeks later in a survey.

That method has a name: netnography, ethnography of online communities. Thirteen years later, now as a frontend engineer, I used it again for a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier. No TV this time: 55 public comments from app stores and a Facebook community.

It turned out to be the most useful research I did in the whole project. And any developer can do it this Friday afternoon.

Why it works

Surveys ask people questions. Reviews and community posts are people talking without anyone asking. Nobody writes a one-star review to be polite. They write it at the exact moment something failed, in their own words, often with details you'd never think to ask about.

That's what I learned in focus groups too: what people say when you ask them is not always what they do. Unprompted conversation gets closer to what they actually do.

How to do it, step by step

1. Pick where people already talk. App Store and Google Play reviews, public Facebook groups, Reddit, your own support tickets. Start with public reviews: they're the easiest and raise the fewest ethical questions.

2. Collect 50 to 100 recent comments. Six months back is enough. Copy them into a spreadsheet, one per row.

3. Paraphrase, don't copy. Write what each person says in your own words, without names. That protects them, and it forces you to understand the comment before you classify it.

4. Code each comment by theme. Start with no categories; let them appear as you read. After 15 or 20 comments, patterns show up. In my case: "the app hides the basics", "I paid but it doesn't work", "support never answers", "I don't trust this".

5. Count. Counting turns impressions into evidence. "Users struggle with login" is an opinion. "In 6 of 55 comments, the registration banner hid the login button" is a finding a product manager can act on.

6. Stop at saturation. When new comments stop producing new themes, you have enough. For me that happened around comment 45.

7. Go see it yourself. Every theme is a hypothesis. Open the app and try to reproduce it. When I did, the registration banner was there, asking me to register a line I had already registered.

What I found

Here's what 55 comments looked like once coded:

Theme Comments
The app hides the basics (balance, usage, login) 12
Paid or completed, but not working 8
Support: slow, bots, no human 7
Trust and security 5
Unclear plan conditions 5

The biggest theme wasn't a bug. It was information hierarchy: promotions came first, and what people opened the app to do came second. No crash report would ever show you that.

The limits (say them out loud)

  • Reviews skew negative. Happy people rarely write. Netnography shows you where it hurts, not how many people hurt.
  • It's not a replacement for talking to users. It tells you what to ask them.
  • Private groups need permission. If a community is closed, ask the admins or stay with public sources.
  • Never publish anything that identifies someone: no names, no screenshots with faces, no exact quotes that can be searched back to a person.

The real lesson

In 2013 I read audiences so a TV network could adjust a story. In 2026 I read reviews to figure out why people couldn't find their balance. The method didn't change. What changed is that now I can also fix what I find.

That's the case I'd make to any developer: you don't need a research team to start listening. You need a spreadsheet, an afternoon, and the discipline to count before you conclude.

You can read the full case study, with the redesign and prototypes, on my site: Activated doesn't mean working.

title: Why H2H Over API? Understanding the Difference in Banking Integrations
description:
1. Introduction: What is an API?
An API (Application Programming Interface) is an interface that allows two different software applications to communicate with each other and exchange information.

For example, suppose XYZ Company wants to make a payment from its bank account using ABC platform.

The process works like this:

1.XYZ Company initiates a payment through ABC.

2.ABC sends an API request to the bank.

3.The bank receives and processes the request.

4.The bank sends a response to ABC.

5.ABC displays the payment response or status

This communication generally happens through individual API requests and responses.

Example:

XYZ Company wants to pay ₹50,000 to a vendor.

1.ABC sends the payment request to the bank.

2.The bank processes the request.

3.The bank responds with a success, failure or pending status.

The same process can be repeated for other payments. Alternatively, a bank may provide APIs that support bulk payment submissions.

2. What is H2H (Host-to-Host)?
H2H stands for Host-to-Host. It is a method of establishing direct and secure communication between two systems, such as a company's software and a bank's system.

Unlike a typical individual API request, H2H commonly uses file-based communication to exchange information in bulk.

Let's understand with the same XYZ Company example.

Suppose XYZ Company needs to make 500 vendor payments.

Instead of sending 500 individual payment requests, the company can:

Prepare a payment file containing details of all 500 transactions.

Place the file in a designated secure folder or transfer it through SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol).

The bank receives the file.

The bank validates and processes the transactions according to its rules and approval requirements.

The bank shares a response or status file containing the results of the transactions.

This allows the company to submit multiple transactions together rather than initiating each one separately.

title: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes, giving platform teams centralized control over runtime contents and updates
description:
AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes for Lambda Event Functions (formerly Lambda functions). Customer-managed runtimes are a standalone resource type that fully decouples runtime management from function deployment. Platform teams gain centralized control over the runtime contents, updates, access, and lifecycle, including the ability to push updates to shared components without per-function redeployments. Application teams consume the runtime from their functions in the same way as a Lambda-managed runtime, preserving their familiar developer experience.

Many organizations require every function to include approved components, such as SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring tools. Previously, sharing these through Lambda Layers or container images meant redeploying every function to pick up a change. With customer-managed runtimes, platform teams manage these components in a central runtime, packaged as OCI container images in Amazon ECR and compatible with existing Docker and CI/CD tooling. Functions pick up updates automatically as Lambda recycles execution environments, so there's no need to redeploy each function or coordinate rollouts. Updates can be scheduled and staged to match change control policies, with centralized health metrics and rapid rollback. With this launch, the existing custom runtimes feature is renamed "bring your own language."

AWS Lambda customer-managed runtimes is now generally available in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional charge for customer-managed runtimes; functions are billed at standard Lambda rates and standard Amazon ECR pricing applies to runtime images.

To get started, build your runtime as a container image in Amazon ECR, starting from a Lambda base image or from scratch, then create a runtime, a version, and an alias. Application teams reference the runtime alias in their function configuration and keep deploying their code as .zip files. Share runtimes with other accounts or an AWS Organization by using a resource-based policy. You can create and manage customer-managed runtimes using the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, CloudFormation, or AWS CDK. To learn more, see the customer-managed runtimes documentation and launch blog post.

최근에 SNS에 오늘의 면접질문 컨텐츠를 연재하고 있었는데, 인프런에도 해당 컨텐츠를 업로드 해달라는 요청들이 있었어요.

오늘부터 주기적으로 이곳에도 5분내로 읽을 수 있는 면접질문을 하나씩 업로드하려고 해요.
재미있게 읽어주시면 감사하겠습니다 🙇

오늘의 백엔드 질문
결제 API에 동일한 요청이 두 번 들어왔을 때, 중복 결제를 어떻게 막으시겠어요?

이력서/포트폴리오에 결제나 주문, 쿠폰 발급이 있으면 나올 수 있는 질문이에요.
실제로 이런 일이 발생할 수 있을까? 싶기도 하지만, 실무에서 종종 발생하는 이슈에요.

이 질문은 결제 요청이 한 번만 온다는 전제로 코드를 짰는지,
혹은 결제 요청이 여러번 전송되어도 한 번만 처리되도록 로직을 작성했는지 검증하는 질문이에요.

답변 키포인트
멱등키(Idempotency-Key)를 누가 만들고 어디에 저장할지
멱등키에 DB 유니크 제약을 걸어 최종 방어선을 설정했는지
처리중과 완료 상태를 구분해 저장하고, 완료면 이전 응답을 그대로 돌려주는 것
재시도와 원요청이 동시에 처리될 때의 경합
외부 PG 응답이 유실됐을 때의 대사(reconciliation)

"버튼 비활성화"처리 만으로는 아쉬운 이유
중복 결제를 이야기할 때 "프론트에서 버튼을 비활성화한다"에서 끝나면 아쉬운 답변이에요.
버튼은 언제든 클라이언트에 의해 조작될 수 있어서, 실제 방어 로직은 서버와 DB에 있어야 하거든요.

같은 키로 들어온 두 번째 요청을 새 결제가 아니라 이미 처리한 요청의 조회로 취급하는 구조인지, 두 요청이 동시에 들어와도 유니크 제약이 하나를 확실히 막아주는지를 같이 설명할 수 있게 준비하는 게 좋아요.

면접에서는
면접에서 이 질문을 받았다면 "재시도 자체를 없앨 수는 없으니, 요청이 여러 번 들어와도 결과는 한 번만 처리한다"라는 식으로 답변을 시작하면 좋아요.

그다음에는 아래 순서로 이어서 설명하면 돼요.

주문마다 멱등키를 만들고, 그 키에 유니크 제약을 건다.
두 번째 요청은 새로 처리하지 않고 저장된 결과를 반환한다.
PG 응답 유실처럼 서버가 통제할 수 없는 경우에는, 주기적인 대사 과정으로 데이터를 보정한다.
이러한 중복 요청 처리 방안은 결제 외에도 다양한 적용할 수 있어요.
쿠폰 발급, 포인트 적립, Kafka의 at-least-once 소비 이슈 모두 연관된 질문으로 나올 수 있어요.

꼬리질문
다음의 꼬리질문도 생각해보세요.

멱등키는 클라이언트와 서버 중 어디에서 생성하는 것이 좋을까요?
DB에서 주문을 조회 후 없으면 insert 하는 방식에는 어떤 문제가 있나요?
같은 멱등키의 요청 두 개가 동시에 들어오면 두 번째 요청에는 어떤 응답을 주시겠어요?
첫 요청이 아직 처리 중일 때 들어온 재시도는 대기시키는 것과 에러를 반환하는 것 중 어느 쪽이 낫나요?
PG에는 결제가 성공했는데 우리 서버가 응답을 받지 못했다면 어떻게 복구하나요?

AI 모의면접으로
나의 면접 스킬을 체크해보세요
프론트엔드,백엔드,FDE 기술면접부터 문화면접까지,
개발자 면접 준비를 실전처럼 연습해 보세요.

title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
description:
arXiv:2611.22235v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

title: I shipped an Android app for electricians: Google Play's 12-tester rule, and a promo video made in code
description:
I'm a systems engineer in building automation. Fazor is a side project: eleven electrical calculators for electricians in one offline Android app. It went live on Google Play on 18 November. Here is what the launch looked like, with the parts that surprised me.

The product

Cable size, voltage drop, breaker and RCD selection, motor starting current, power factor correction and a few more. IEC or NEC, the formula and the standard reference shown under every result.

Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, single activity, Hilt, Room and DataStore. No backend, no account, no analytics. The calculation code is plain Kotlin kept apart from the Android framework, so it runs under ordinary JVM unit tests: 397 of them, with 98.5% line coverage on the calculation logic. Rules that touch life safety, such as RCD selection, are written as explicit tables with one test per rule.

Five calculators are free with a banner ad; a one-time US$2.99 unlocks the rest and removes ads.

The 12 testers x 14 days rule

New personal developer accounts must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 continuous days before they can apply for production access.

  • Finding 12 testers took one day: my own network plus free tester communities.
  • The 14 days were quiet. I got no written feedback from testers at all, even after sending a five-question survey on day 13.
  • I expected that to sink the application, since "insufficient tester engagement" is one of the two stated rejection reasons. I answered the form honestly: no tester reported a wrong result or a crash, and the app has no analytics, so I cannot see what they used.
  • Production access was granted the same day I applied. The production release was approved and live the same day too.

So the rule cost me 14 days of waiting, not 14 days of work. If you are about to start: put the feedback questions in the invitation on day one, not day 13.

One practical trap: the Play Console form limits each free-text answer to 300 characters, which the help page does not mention. Draft short.

What I did during the wait

No new features. The decision was to ship exactly what testers had, and to release an update only if someone reported a bug. Nobody did. Instead I measured test coverage and made the promo video.

A promo video made in code

I had no budget for video and the AI video tools I tried were locked behind paid plans. So the video is a web page.

  • A 1080x1920 stage in plain HTML and CSS. Every motion is a CSS animation with animation-play-state: paused.
  • A seek(ms) function sets currentTime on every entry of document.getAnimations(), so any frame can be drawn on demand.
  • Puppeteer drives an installed Chrome, takes a screenshot per frame at 30 fps and pipes the PNGs into ffmpeg.
  • A small Python script synthesises the motion sound effects, places the text-to-speech narration, stretches each scene to fit its line and writes the timing file the page is built from. Scene length follows the voice, not the other way round.
  • Turkish and English versions come from one content file.

The result is deterministic: the same inputs give the same video, and changing a caption is a one-line edit followed by a re-render.

It took a few iterations. The first cut was boring, the synthesized music was bad and was replaced by a licensed free track, and a decorative rotating background got cut after one viewing.

Numbers so far

Launched this week, so there is nothing worth reporting yet. I will post an update once there is a month of data.

What I would do differently

  • Ask testers for feedback from the first day.
  • Check that my own product page did not still say "coming soon" on launch day. It did, for a day.
  • Create the brand accounts before launch instead of on launch day.

Happy to answer questions about the Play Console process, since most of what I found online about the tester rule was guesswork.

Product page: https://kalkansoftware.com/fazor/

title: The Best Cloud Platforms for Day Two Operations (2026): Who Patches, Upgrades, Scales, and Fails Over on Each Platform
description:
The best cloud platform for Day 2 operations is the one that takes the most recurring tasks off your team for the workloads you actually run, which means comparing who patches, upgrades, scales, renews certificates, backs up, fails over, and keeps audit evidence. Hyperscaler suites cover one cloud well, layer tools cover one operational slice across clouds, and workload platforms such as Control Plane run the workloads and handle autoscaling, observability, and security across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Day 2 operations are the recurring work that keeps production workloads patched, scaled, observable, and recoverable after deployment, and the platform you choose decides how much of that work stays on your team.

  • Hyperscaler native suites are strongest inside one cloud. AWS Systems Manager with CloudWatch and AWS Config, Azure Arc with Azure Monitor and Azure Update Manager, and GKE Autopilot with Google Cloud Observability each go deep on their own provider.
  • Layer tools each cover one slice across clouds. Ansible automates configuration and patching, HCP Terraform manages infrastructure state, Datadog handles observability, and ServiceNow ITOM ties incidents to change management.
  • Managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE Standard) upgrades the control plane (on EKS, when your team starts it) and can patch node images through auto-upgrade channels, but add-on lifecycle and scaling policy tuning stay on your team.
  • Serverless containers take the most node work off your plate but restrict persistent storage and custom networking, and Fargate offers no GPUs.
  • Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads across four clouds with no Kubernetes cluster for you to build, patch, or upgrade, plus VM workloads and your own servers through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s) and clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK).

What are the best cloud platforms for day two operations?

The answer depends on which platform category matches your workloads, clouds, and team size, and on which Day 2 tasks each one actually takes off your team.

The 10 best multi-cloud management platforms compares multi-cloud management tools more broadly.

Who does each Day 2 task on each type of platform?

Each recurring Day 2 task falls into one of three buckets on each platform: the platform does it, you configure it once, or your team handles it on an ongoing basis.

Day 2 task Self-managed Kubernetes or VMs Managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE Standard) GKE Autopilot or EKS Auto Mode Serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate with ECS, Azure Container Apps) Control Plane
OS and node patching Your team, ongoing. You apply OS patches and image updates on every node. You configure once. EKS managed node groups update to new AMIs when you start the update; AKS node OS auto-upgrade channels patch in your maintenance window; GKE Standard release channels auto-upgrade nodes by default. Platform does it. GKE Autopilot patches nodes through release channels; EKS Auto Mode applies AMI updates and replaces nodes on a maximum lifetime. Platform does it. No nodes are exposed; the provider patches the hosts. Platform does it. No nodes to patch on Control Plane-managed locations.
Kubernetes control plane upgrades Your team, ongoing. You run the upgrade, test compatibility, and handle rollback. Varies. GKE upgrades the control plane automatically within your maintenance window; AKS does so with a cluster auto-upgrade channel enabled; on EKS you start each upgrade and AWS executes it. Varies. GKE Autopilot upgrades follow the release channel automatically; on EKS Auto Mode you start the control plane upgrade and Auto Mode then replaces nodes to match. Not applicable. No Kubernetes control plane is exposed. Platform does it on Control Plane-managed locations.
Node and add-on upgrades Your team, ongoing. You upgrade kubelets, CNI plugins, CoreDNS, and other add-ons. Varies. GKE Standard auto-upgrades nodes by default, AKS offers node image auto-upgrade channels, and EKS managed node group upgrades are started by you; EKS add-ons such as the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, and kube-proxy require your action, and add-ons you install yourself stay yours on all three. You configure once. GKE Autopilot upgrades nodes and managed components; EKS Auto Mode runs the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, Karpenter, EBS CSI driver, and load balancing for ALB and NLB as built-in functions. Add-ons you install yourself remain yours. Not applicable. Platform does it on Control Plane-managed locations, where Control Plane runs and upgrades the underlying runtime.
Autoscaling replicas Your team, ongoing. You deploy and tune HPA, VPA, or custom controllers. You configure once. You define HPA or KEDA policies and the platform executes them. You configure once. Node scaling is automatic; you still set HPA for pods. Platform does it. The provider scales instances on request volume within your limits. You configure once. You set min and max replicas, and Control Plane autoscales, including scale to zero for serverless workloads and for standard and stateful workloads through KEDA.
Right-sizing CPU and memory Your team, ongoing. You analyze usage and adjust requests. Your team, ongoing. You review VPA recommendations and update manifests. Your team, ongoing. You set requests; Autopilot applies defaults and raises requests to its minimums and ratios but does not right-size from usage. Your team, ongoing. Cloud Run, Fargate, and Azure Container Apps all take fixed CPU and memory settings per container or task. Platform does it. Capacity AI sets CPU and memory reservations within your min and max from historical usage. Capacity AI is not available for GPU workloads or for workloads using CPU-metric or multi-metric autoscaling.
TLS certificate issuance and renewal Your team, ongoing. You install and renew certificates or run cert-manager. You configure once. You set up cert-manager or provider-managed certificates (ACM, GKE managed certificates), which renew automatically. You configure once. Same as managed Kubernetes. You configure once. Azure Container Apps issues free managed certificates for custom domains; Cloud Run uses Google-managed certificates on a global external Application Load Balancer (domain mapping is still in preview); Fargate with an ALB uses ACM. Platform does it. Control Plane creates and renews TLS certificates for its default endpoints and custom domains.
Secret storage and rotation Your team, ongoing. You integrate a secrets manager and write rotation logic. You configure once. You integrate AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or Google Secret Manager; rotation schedules are yours. You configure once. Same provider integrations as managed Kubernetes. You configure once. Same provider integrations. You configure once. Secrets are stored encrypted in Control Plane and granted through identity-based policies; your team sets the rotation schedule, and updated values reach workloads on redeploy (a dictionary secret mounted as a directory refreshes in place). Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) issues short-lived credentials at runtime, so there are no long-lived AWS, GCP, or Azure keys to rotate.
Backups and restore tests Your team, ongoing. You configure Velero or equivalent and schedule restore drills. Your team, ongoing. The provider backs up etcd; application data backups and restore tests are yours. Your team, ongoing. Same as managed Kubernetes for application data. Your team, ongoing. Data in external databases needs your backup strategy. You configure once. Volume sets take scheduled snapshots with a retention period and restore from them, and Template Catalog databases such as PostgreSQL offer scheduled backups to S3 or GCS. Restore testing stays with your team.
Multi-region or multi-cloud failover Your team, ongoing. You architect, deploy, and test failover. Your team, ongoing. You configure multi-region clusters, DNS routing, and health checks. Your team, ongoing. Clusters are regional; you build cross-region failover. Varies. Cloud Run runs multi-region behind a global load balancer you configure; Fargate and Azure Container Apps need your routing setup. Platform does it for stateless workloads once you choose the locations in Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC). Each workload runs active-active in every GVC location, and its global endpoint geo-routes clients to the nearest healthy location. Stateful data fails over only when it is replicated.
Logs, metrics, and traces Your team, ongoing. You deploy and maintain an observability stack. You configure once. Provider tools collect infrastructure metrics; you instrument applications. You configure once. Integrated logging and monitoring; you add application instrumentation. You configure once. The provider collects logs and basic metrics; you add tracing. Platform does it. Logs and metrics are collected automatically and explored in a built-in Grafana; traces use Control Plane’s OpenTelemetry tracing provider once you set a sampling rate.
Network policy and mTLS between services Your team, ongoing. You deploy a CNI with policy support and a service mesh for mTLS. Your team, ongoing. You configure network policies and optionally a service mesh. You configure once. GKE Autopilot and EKS Auto Mode enforce network policy; mTLS requires a service mesh. Varies. Azure Container Apps offers opt-in peer-to-peer TLS encryption with platform-managed certificates; Cloud Run and Fargate need a service mesh for mTLS. Platform does it. A deny-by-default internal firewall and mTLS between workloads are defaults.
Audit trail Your team, ongoing. You aggregate and protect audit logs. You configure once. CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, or Cloud Audit Logs capture API calls; you retain them. You configure once. Same as managed Kubernetes. You configure once. Provider audit logs cover the control plane; application audit trails are yours. Platform does it. A tamper-proof audit trail is a default.
Cost visibility Your team, ongoing. You tag resources, aggregate billing, and build reports. Your team, ongoing. Provider cost tools show cluster spend; you map it to workload owners. Your team, ongoing. Autopilot simplifies node cost attribution. You configure once. Per-request or per-vCPU-second billing simplifies attribution. You configure once. Control Plane’s Cost & Usage view shows spend per org and per resource with a projected total; you map resources to cost owners.

What do you still own after picking a platform?

Each platform leaves some operational work on your team, and each gap has a way to shrink it.

Platform type Still on your team How to reduce it
Hyperscaler native suites (AWS Systems Manager, Azure Arc, Google Cloud Observability) Multi-cloud coordination, cross-cloud failover, Kubernetes add-on lifecycle, application dependency patching, cost correlation across providers Add a multi-cloud management layer or workload platform; standardize tagging and policy across clouds
Kubernetes platforms (OpenShift, Rancher, managed Kubernetes) Starting or scheduling upgrades, add-on upgrades, autoscaling policy tuning, backup and restore testing, multi-cloud failover Enable auto-upgrade channels where available; adopt GitOps for add-on lifecycle; use a service mesh for mTLS
Automation and IaC layers (Ansible, HCP Terraform, Spacelift) Runtime operations including scaling, observability, failover, and certificate management Pair with a managed runtime; use IaC for provisioning and a platform for operations
Observability platforms (Datadog, Dynatrace) Patching, upgrades, scaling, failover, certificate rotation, secret management Connect alerts to runbook automation; use provider-managed patching and upgrade channels
Cloud management platforms (HPE Morpheus, CloudBolt) Kubernetes operations, container scaling, observability instrumentation, failover orchestration Layer a Kubernetes platform or serverless containers under the governance layer; integrate observability tools
Serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate with ECS, Azure Container Apps) Application dependency updates, image rebuilds, database backups, cross-cloud failover, advanced networking, GPU workloads on Fargate Automate image builds in CI/CD; use managed databases with built-in backups; accept workload type limits
Workload platforms such as Control Plane Application dependency updates, image rebuilds, replication for stateful data, restore testing Automate image scanning and rebuilds in CI/CD; deploy replicated templates such as Postgres Multi-Location, pgEdge, or Redis Multi-Location, or replicate at the application layer

How do you measure Day 2 load before you choose?

Audit the recurring work your team does today, then map each task to the responsibility matrix in this guide to see how many hours each platform would take off your team.

  • Count recurring Day 2 tasks per month, grouped by infrastructure, Kubernetes, application, and compliance.
  • Measure total hours spent on Kubernetes and node upgrades per quarter.
  • Track pages and alerts per week, separating infrastructure causes from application causes.
  • Record restore tests completed per quarter and the share of critical data stores they cover.
  • Log auditor evidence requests and the time to fulfill each one.

A platform that removes node patching but leaves certificate renewal, backup testing, and failover on your team may save less time than one that handles the tasks behind most on-call hours. Teams without dedicated platform engineers should weight tasks that need deep Kubernetes expertise most heavily.

How does Control Plane handle Day 2 operations?

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

Workloads run on Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions with no Kubernetes cluster for you to build, patch, or upgrade. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations, and a workload runs in every location of its GVC, active-active across regions and clouds, behind a built-in global endpoint that geo-routes to the nearest healthy location.

Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory from historical usage, separately from autoscaling and scale to zero. Security defaults include a deny-by-default internal firewall, mTLS between workloads, and a tamper-proof audit trail, and UCI lets workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Control Plane’s Template Catalog deploys open-source services such as PostgreSQL and Redis from templates. Replicated templates, including PostgreSQL Highly Available, Postgres Multi-Location, pgEdge, Redis Multi-Location, and Redis Cluster, replicate data across replicas or locations. The Control Plane MCP server lets AI assistants deploy, diagnose, scale, and roll back workloads through the Control Plane API.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant, and it offers a 99.999% SLA for workloads that run at least two replicas in at least two locations.

Kubernetes clusters you already run can join through BYOK, and your own servers through MK8s; on those, you keep responsibility for the underlying nodes. Data in volume sets is not replicated between locations, so stateful services that need cross-location failover run on the replicated templates or replicate at the application layer.

FAQ

Short answers on Day 2 operations and who owns each task.

What are the best cloud platforms for day two operations?

The best platforms take the most recurring tasks off your team for the workloads you run. Workload platforms such as Control Plane handle autoscaling, observability, failover routing, and security across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud, while hyperscaler suites go deepest inside a single cloud.

What are day two operations in cloud computing?

Day 2 operations are the recurring tasks that keep production workloads running after deployment. They include OS and node patching, Kubernetes upgrades, autoscaling, TLS certificate renewal, secret rotation, backup and restore testing, multi-region failover, observability, network policy, audit evidence, and cost visibility.

What is the difference between Day 0, Day 1, and Day 2?

Day 0 is design: selecting clouds, defining network topology, choosing tools, and writing infrastructure as code. Day 1 is initial deployment: provisioning infrastructure, deploying applications, configuring DNS, and validating that everything works. Day 2 is everything after go-live: patching, upgrading, scaling, monitoring, failing over, rotating credentials, backing up data, and responding to incidents.

Does managed Kubernetes handle Day 2 operations?

Partly. Managed Kubernetes services execute control plane upgrades (automatically on GKE and on AKS with an auto-upgrade channel; started by you on EKS) and can automate node image patching through auto-upgrade channels. Add-on lifecycle, autoscaling policy tuning, TLS certificate rotation for application ingress, secret management, restore testing, multi-region failover, and cross-cloud cost governance stay with your team.

Is GKE Autopilot or EKS Auto Mode enough for Day 2?

They cover node-level work, and the rest of Day 2 stays with your team. Both manage node provisioning, patching, and replacement, and EKS Auto Mode runs core networking and storage components as built-in functions. You still own application autoscaling settings, certificate setup for custom domains, secret rotation, restore testing, multi-region failover architecture, and cost governance.

Which tools automate patching across AWS and Azure?

AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, Azure Update Manager (which also patches Arc-enabled servers on AWS and GCP), and Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform automate OS patching across AWS and Azure. For Kubernetes nodes, auto-upgrade channels in managed Kubernetes shift node image updates to the provider. None of these tools patch container images or application dependencies, which remain a CI/CD responsibility.

How do I reduce Day 2 work without a platform team?

Move the most time-consuming recurring tasks to the platform. Use managed Kubernetes with auto-upgrade channels or serverless containers, managed databases with built-in backups, and provider-managed certificates, and automate image scanning and rebuilds in CI/CD. A workload platform such as Control Plane also absorbs node patching, cluster upgrades, scaling, failover routing, and security defaults that otherwise need Kubernetes expertise.

What Day 2 tasks does Control Plane take off my team?

Control Plane runs workloads on managed locations in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud with no cluster for your team to operate. Autoscaling with scale to zero, Capacity AI right-sizing within your min and max, automatic TLS certificates, mTLS, a deny-by-default firewall, a tamper-proof audit trail, and geo-routed failover across locations are built in. Your team keeps application updates, image rebuilds, rotation schedules, and replication for stateful data that is not on a replicated template.

Talk to the Control Plane team to see how Day 2 tasks map to your workloads, or sign up free.

title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
description:
arXiv:2611.21946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.

title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.21644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.22485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
description:
arXiv:2611.22244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.22140v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

title: Running Voice Agent Tests Fully Offline With Local Models
description:
Running voice agent tests against cloud APIs means sending your agent configs and test transcripts to a third-party provider. For some teams, such as healthcare, finance, and government, that's not allowed. For everyone else, the per-token cost adds up during development: every test run is a multi-turn conversation plus a judge pass, and you rerun the suite each time you touch a prompt.

Voicetest can run fully offline, with every LLM call going to a model on your own machine. No API keys, no network calls to model providers, and nothing leaves your machine. This post covers why that's now practical, the setup with llama.cpp, how to pick a model for each role, and when to use local versus cloud models.

Why this is practical now

Not long ago, a model that fit on one consumer GPU was a poor stand-in for the hosted models most voice agents run on. That has changed quickly.

Epoch AI's Capabilities Index combines dozens of benchmarks onto one scale. On it, the best open-weight model small enough for one consumer GPU went from 103 (Mistral 7B, September 2023) to 153 (Qwen 3.8 27B, August 2026). That's above GPT-5, which scored 150 when it was released in August 2025.

Local models aren't closing the gap. The frontier keeps moving, and the distance in points is about what it was in 2024. What they do is track the frontier roughly a year behind, and a year-old frontier model is plenty for playing a caller and iterating on prompts. Treat benchmark scores for small models with some care, though: Epoch notes they can be tuned toward benchmarks, so check results on your own test suite before trusting them.

Setup

llama.cpp is the open-source inference engine most local model tools are built on. It ships llama-server, a single binary that downloads a model from Hugging Face and serves it over an OpenAI-compatible API:

brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

Qwen3 models think before they answer by default. --reasoning-budget 0 turns that off. Thinking slows down every turn, and a long think can use up the response budget before any answer comes out, which shows up in voicetest as parse errors and retries.

Voicetest routes model calls through LiteLLM, and LiteLLM's llamafile/ provider talks to an OpenAI-compatible server at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1, which is where llama-server listens. Point all three roles at it:

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
judge = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"

The name after llamafile/ is only a label; the server answers with whatever model it loaded. If the server runs somewhere else, set LLAMAFILE_API_BASE. Then run tests as usual:

voicetest run --agent agents/receptionist.json --tests tests/receptionist.json --all

Picking a model for each role

The three roles don't need the same capability, and it helps to know which one is limiting you.

Simulator. The simulator plays the caller. It follows a persona prompt and moves toward the caller's goal. It's the easiest role, and an 8B model handles it well.

Agent. The agent plays your voice agent. It follows the graph's prompts, keeps track of where it is in the conversation, and chooses transitions. This is the hardest role. Bigger models follow complex graphs more consistently, and a small local model won't behave exactly like the model your production agent runs on. For graphs with real branching, use the strongest model that fits:

llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

Judge. The judge reads each finished transcript and scores it against every metric, explaining its reasoning. An inaccurate judge is worse than a slow one, because it gives you false passes or false alarms. Use the largest model you can run.

One llama-server serves one model, so the simplest setup gives every role the same one, sized for the hardest role you run locally.

To check that everything runs end to end, a tiny model is enough:

llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q8_0 --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0
voicetest smoke-test --model llamafile/qwen3-0.6b

That confirms the pipeline works. It says nothing about whether a prompt change is safe to ship: a model this small will fail plenty of metrics.

Hardware

Memory is the limit. An 8B model at Q4 fits comfortably on a laptop. A 27B model at Q4 needs around 17 GB for its weights, which means a 24 GB GPU or an Apple Silicon Mac with 32 GB or more. Anything much larger needs a workstation.

If you can't run a strong judge locally, there's a practical middle ground: keep the agent and simulator local, and point only the judge at a cloud model:

[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3.8-27b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3.8-27b"
judge = "openai/gpt-4o"

Only judge calls leave your machine, and they contain the simulated transcript and your metric criteria. They don't include your agent's graph or prompts.

The full voice stack, also local

voicetest up starts the services for live audio calls in Docker: a LiveKit server, faster-whisper for speech-to-text, and Kokoro for text-to-speech. With a local model configured, a live call test runs entirely on your machine, through the real audio pipeline, with nothing sent to an outside service.

What you give up

Local runs are slower than hosted inference. Every turn of every conversation waits on your hardware, and the judge pass adds a generation per metric. A suite that finishes in a few minutes against a hosted provider can take much longer locally. That's fine for a suite you run while you work on prompts, and less fine for a CI check on every pull request.

Results are also only as good as the model. A local judge that's much weaker than the model you'd normally use will pass things a stronger judge would fail. Check a sample of local results against a stronger judge before you rely on them.

When to use each

Scenario Recommendation
Iterating on prompts, rerunning tests often Local
Data can't leave your network Local, or local with a self-hosted judge
CI on every pull request Hosted provider, for speed
Final check before deploying Strongest judge you have access to
Limited hardware Hosted provider, or local agent and simulator with a hosted judge

Models can be swapped per role in settings without touching your tests. Iterate locally while you work, then let CI check the same suite against a hosted model before merging.
