title: Best Web Design and Development Blogs to Follow: 33 Checked
description:
TL;DR: We checked which of the best web design and development blogs still publish. These 33 blogs and newsletters each published an editorial post in the 90 days to 18 Nov 2026. The React blog has the longest gap: 70 days since its 9 Sep 2026 post. Start with Smashing Magazine for design, Josh W. Comeau and web.dev for front-end, the release blog for each framework you ship, and Frontend Focus for email. Of the 21 blogs on our 2018 list, 7 still pass.

Last checked 18 Nov 2026. Next check: January 2027.

This list is for front-end developers and web designers, especially at small agencies, who built an RSS reader years ago and now find half of it silent or full of Black Friday deals. It names the best web design and development blogs that still publish real articles, with a date you can check for each, and the good ones that missed out.

At Netling, an AI assistant is now our team's first stop for an answer. That works when you know what to ask. A short feed tells you about the change you did not know to look for, such as WebKit's spatial CSS developer preview on 16 Nov 2026 or the Node.js security releases on 11 Nov 2026. It is also where we check what the assistant told us.

In April 2018 I published a list of 21 blogs on our old site (archive copy). What happened to each of them is near the end.

How we chose these blogs, and what "still active" means

Every blog and newsletter here passed the same five rules, checked on 18 Nov 2026:

  1. Recent: an editorial post in the 90 days to 18 Nov 2026.
  2. Regular: at least four editorial posts in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026. Newsletters instead need at least three issues in the 90 days.
  3. On topic: web design or development is the main topic, meaning at least five of the newest ten editorial posts, by our reading of the titles.
  4. Free: you can read it without paying.
  5. Vendors labelled: vendor blogs are allowed, and we label them.

An editorial post is a written article, or a roundup of other people's articles. Sponsored posts, deals, event and course promotions, single-product reviews and podcast episodes do not count. Neither do roundups of templates, fonts, plugins, tools or hosting.

A script read the dates in each blog's own feed and set those items aside by their titles. Feeds show only their newest items, so when every editorial item in the feed falls inside 90 days, the count is a floor and we write "at least". Codrops and Design Shack block scripts, so we checked their home pages in a browser.

Rule 3 is our judgement from titles, and we say where a blog passed narrowly. The longest gap among the picks is the React blog's 70 days. Four well-known blogs sit just beyond the 90-day line: Hongkiat (103 days), Post Status (117), A List Apart (141) and MDN Blog (156).

The best web design and development blogs at a glance

This is the skim version, with each blog's newest editorial post as of 18 Nov 2026. The full entries below add the 90-day count and the feed URL.

Design and UX

  • Smashing Magazine (17 Nov): practical articles on UX, accessibility, CSS and AI in design work.
  • Nielsen Norman Group (13 Nov): UX research findings and definitions (sells training).
  • UX Collective (16 Nov): product-design essays from many authors (Medium-hosted).
  • Pixels of the Week (8 Nov): Stephanie Walter's weekly pick of UX and design links.
  • Codrops (17 Nov): creative front-end, WebGPU and motion tutorials and case studies.

CSS and front-end

  • CSS-Tricks (16 Nov): CSS techniques (owned by DigitalOcean).
  • Josh W. Comeau (20 Oct): long interactive tutorials on CSS and React.
  • Ahmad Shadeed (5 Nov): CSS layout experiments.
  • Rachel Andrew (2 Nov): CSS layout from a CSS Working Group member.
  • Piccalilli (13 Nov): front-end craft and The Index links (sells courses).
  • CodePen Blog (16 Nov): Chris Coyier's Chris' Corner column (vendor).
  • Frontend Masters Blog (16 Nov): frequent front-end tutorials (vendor).

Browsers, standards, performance and accessibility

  • web.dev (2 Oct): monthly Baseline and "new to the web platform" digests (Google).
  • Chrome for Developers (7 Oct): Chrome release and API posts (vendor).
  • WebKit (16 Nov): Safari features and release notes (Apple).
  • Bram.us (22 Oct): new CSS and DevTools features.
  • CSS Wizardry (11 Nov): weekly web-performance notes.
  • Adrian Roselli (10 Nov): accessibility and WCAG in detail.
  • Zach Leatherman (14 Oct): web components and Eleventy.

JavaScript, frameworks and back-end

  • React blog (9 Sep): releases and security advisories.
  • Next.js blog (17 Nov): releases and monthly security notices (Vercel).
  • Nuxt blog (28 Oct): Nuxt and Vue-ecosystem releases.
  • Node.js blog (17 Nov): every release and security release.
  • Laravel News (16 Nov): daily Laravel and PHP news.
  • SitePoint (17 Nov): tutorials, in a mixed feed.

WordPress, industry and agency life

  • Make WordPress Core (17 Nov): developer notes before each release.
  • The Repository (17 Nov): daily WordPress news.
  • Speckyboy (16 Nov): web design and the agency business.
  • Web Designer Depot (17 Nov): opinion and design trends.
  • Boagworld (5 Nov): a fortnightly column on UX and agency practice.

Newsletters

  • Frontend Focus (11 Nov): weekly front-end news.
  • JavaScript Weekly (17 Nov): weekly JavaScript news.
  • CSS Layout News (4 Nov): monthly CSS layout links.

Best web design and UX blogs

Smashing Magazine

Smashing Magazine publishes practical articles on UX, accessibility, CSS and AI in design work. Its newest article asks how accessibility testing can keep up when AI speeds up the build. Its conference promotions sit in the same feed, and we left them out of the count.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 18 · Feed: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/feed/

Nielsen Norman Group

Nielsen Norman Group turns its UX research into one or two short articles a week. Read it for evidence-based guidance and for the definitions your clients' UX teams already use. NN/g is a training and consulting firm, so expect links to its courses.

Newest editorial post: 13 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 18 · Feed: https://www.nngroup.com/feed/rss/

UX Collective

UX Collective publishes product-design essays from many independent authors every day. It is hosted on Medium, and some stories are member-only: signed out, we could read two of the three newest. Skim the titles and open what fits your work.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://uxdesign.cc/feed

Stephanie Walter's Pixels of the Week

Stephanie Walter publishes Pixels of the Week, a weekly pick of UX and design links with short notes (8 Nov, 1 Nov and 25 Oct 2026). It is the quickest way in this group to see what UX practitioners are reading.

Newest editorial post: 8 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 9 · Feed: https://www.stephaniewalter.design/feed/

Codrops

Codrops covers creative front-end work: WebGL and WebGPU effects, GSAP motion tutorials and case studies of experimental sites. Its 17 Nov post builds an infinite carousel of cloth posters with WebGPU. The feed blocks scripts, so we counted posts on its home page in a browser.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 7 (the home page shows 9 to 17 Nov only) · Feed: https://tympanus.net/codrops/feed/

Best CSS and front-end blogs

CSS-Tricks

CSS-Tricks still publishes CSS techniques, such as staggering scroll-driven animations with animation-range-start. DigitalOcean has owned it since March 2022 and runs it as a standalone site. We left its 13 Nov Black Friday deals post out of the count.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 13 · Feed: https://css-tricks.com/feed/

Josh W. Comeau

Josh W. Comeau writes long, interactive tutorials on CSS and React. He posted 8 times in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026, most recently on 26 May, 6 Jul and 20 Oct, so this is a low-volume feed where each post is worth the time. The newest, The Future of CSS, looks ahead to Interop 2027.

Newest editorial post: 20 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 1 (8 in 12 months) · Feed: https://www.joshwcomeau.com/rss.xml

Ahmad Shadeed

Ahmad Shadeed writes CSS layout articles built around visual experiments, such as his 15 Sep post on aligning icons with their labels. Read it when you want to understand why a layout breaks, as well as how to fix it.

Newest editorial post: 5 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://ishadeed.com/feed.xml

Rachel Andrew

Rachel Andrew is a member of the CSS Working Group and writes about CSS layout and newer features such as margin-trim. Her 2 Nov post is on making CSS features generic. Read it for the reasoning behind the spec.

Newest editorial post: 2 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://rachelandrew.co.uk/feed

Piccalilli

Piccalilli publishes front-end craft articles several times a week, plus The Index, a weekly issue of links (#205 on 6 Nov, #206 on 13 Nov 2026). It is creator-run and sells courses, and we excluded its course promotion. Its feed shows only five items.

Newest editorial post: 13 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 4 · Feed: https://piccalil.li/feed.xml

CodePen Blog

The CodePen Blog is a vendor blog, but it carries Chris' Corner, a CSS and front-end column by Chris Coyier, who founded CSS-Tricks. The rest of the feed is podcast episodes, often about CodePen features, so we counted only the column.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 8 · Feed: https://blog.codepen.io/feed/

Frontend Masters Blog

The Frontend Masters Blog belongs to a company that sells video courses, but the articles are free and arrive several times a week. A recent one builds diagrams and graphs with modern CSS alone.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://blog.master.dev/feed/

Browser, standards, performance and accessibility blogs

web.dev

web.dev is Google's site for web developers. Its blog publishes a monthly digest of what reached Baseline and what is new to the web platform. That makes it a quick way to see which features are newly safe to use across browsers.

Newest editorial post: 2 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://web.dev/static/blog/feed.xml

Chrome for Developers

The Chrome for Developers blog covers Chrome releases and new APIs, such as what is new in WebGPU in Chrome 155 and 156. It is a vendor blog, and its feed holds only ten items, so the real cadence is higher than our count.

Newest editorial post: 7 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/feed.xml

WebKit

The WebKit blog is where Apple's engine team explains new Safari features and release notes. On 16 Nov 2026 it introduced a developer preview of spatial CSS. If your clients' visitors use iPhones, this feed tells you what Safari will support next.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://webkit.org/feed/

Bram.us

Bram.us is the personal blog of Bramus, who works on the Chrome team. He posts short items on new CSS features, DevTools changes and small web tools.

Newest editorial post: 22 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://www.bram.us/feed/

CSS Wizardry

CSS Wizardry is the site of Harry Roberts, a web-performance consultant. His weekly Web-Perf Wednesday notes (issues 015 to 017 on 28 Oct, 4 Nov and 11 Nov 2026) each explain one performance issue, such as Prebid no longer re-downloading its manifest.

Newest editorial post: 11 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 14 · Feed: https://csswizardry.com/feed.xml

Adrian Roselli

Adrian Roselli writes detailed posts on accessibility and WCAG, several times a month. His 10 Nov post lists his picks for Interop 2027.

Newest editorial post: 10 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 6 · Feed: https://adrianroselli.com/feed

Zach Leatherman

Zach Leatherman writes about web components, Eleventy and the web in general, about twice a month.

Newest editorial post: 14 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 8 · Feed: https://www.zachleat.com/web/feed/

Best JavaScript, framework and back-end blogs

Official release blogs are where breaking changes and security fixes are announced first. Five of these six cover stacks we work in, listed on our technology stack page.

React blog

The React blog posts rarely, so each post matters: React 19.3 on 9 Sep 2026, the React Foundation on 24 Feb 2026, and two Server Components security advisories in December 2025. It is our slowest pick at 70 days, and it passes rule 2 at exactly four posts. For anyone shipping React, as our React and Next.js developers do, the advisories alone earn it a slot.

Newest editorial post: 9 Sep 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 1 (4 in 12 months) · Feed: https://react.dev/rss.xml

Next.js blog

The Next.js blog is run by Vercel, so it is a vendor blog. Read it for release notes and the monthly security-release notices, such as the one on 3 Nov 2026. On 17 Nov it explained how Vercel is using AI to make Next.js more secure.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 17 · Feed: https://nextjs.org/feed.xml

Nuxt blog

The Nuxt blog posts releases and tooling news about monthly: Nuxt 4.6 on 5 Oct and Nuxt DevTools v4 on 28 Oct 2026. Vue's own blog has not posted since 1 Sep 2024, so this is the Vue-ecosystem pick.

Release posts are where deadlines first appear, such as the Nuxt 3 end of life we wrote up for teams still on version 3. If that upgrade is on your list, see our Nuxt developers page.

Newest editorial post: 28 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 2 (8 in 12 months) · Feed: https://nuxt.com/blog/rss.xml

Node.js blog

The Node.js blog is mostly release notes. Subscribe for the security releases at least: the 11 Nov 2026 set covered the 22, 24 and 26 LTS lines. A 5 Nov post explained the V8 changes between Node.js 26 and 27.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 26 · Feed: https://nodejs.org/en/feed/blog.xml

Laravel News

Laravel News publishes Laravel and PHP news and package write-ups every day. It was started in 2012 by Eric L. Barnes. Its feed shows only five items, so the count is a floor.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 5 · Feed: https://laravel-news.com/feed

SitePoint

SitePoint publishes daily, but it is a mixed feed. Five of its newest ten items are web development, such as WebRTC, WCAG 2.2 testing in CI and FastAPI security. The rest are AI-tool and hosting reviews. It passes rule 3 exactly, so follow its web topics rather than the whole feed.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 97 · Feed: https://www.sitepoint.com/sitepoint.rss

WordPress, industry and agency-life blogs

Make WordPress Core

Make WordPress Core is the core team's own blog. Read it for the dev notes published before each release, which say what will change or break. On 17 Nov 2026 alone it posted REST API, Media and Interactivity API notes for WordPress 7.2. If you hire WordPress developers, expect them to read it.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 20 · Feed: https://make.wordpress.org/core/feed/

The Repository

The Repository publishes WordPress news daily: ten stories between 10 and 17 Nov 2026, including the WordPress 7.2 betas. Its 11 Nov story looked at how hosting companies handled PHP2Shell, which pairs with our guide to PHP 8.2 end of life for WordPress sites.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://www.therepository.email/feed

Speckyboy

Speckyboy covers web design and the business of running an agency, as in its 16 Nov post on the most profitable service your agency is not selling. Its feed also carries deals and asset roundups, which we excluded.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 5 · Feed: https://speckyboy.com/feed/

Web Designer Depot

Web Designer Depot publishes opinion and design-trend pieces, such as its lessons from auditing 100 online stores. Under our rule, we left one single-product review out of the count.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 17 · Feed: https://webdesignerdepot.com/feed/

Boagworld

Boagworld is now a fortnightly email-style column (8 Oct, 22 Oct and 5 Nov 2026) on AI, design practice and agency life. It suits agency owners more than developers. If that is you, it pairs well with our piece on how white-label partners help agencies win bigger projects.

Newest editorial post: 5 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 6 · Feed: https://boagworld.com/feed/

Web development newsletters worth the inbox space

A newsletter needed at least three issues in the 90 days to make the list. Three did:

  • Frontend Focus: weekly front-end news. Issue 766 went out on 11 Nov 2026. Feed: https://frontendfoc.us/rss/
  • JavaScript Weekly: weekly JavaScript news. Issue 811 went out on 17 Nov 2026. Feed: https://cprss.s3.amazonaws.com/javascriptweekly.com.xml
  • CSS Layout News: monthly CSS layout links. Issues 345, 346 and 347 went out on 17 Sep, 8 Oct and 4 Nov 2026. Feed: https://csslayout.news/feed/

Piccalilli's The Index and Stephanie Walter's Pixels of the Week also read like weekly newsletters. CSS Weekly is missing on purpose, and the next section says why.

Good blogs that didn't make the list, and why

These fail one of the rules on 18 Nov 2026. Several are still worth reading if you know what you are getting. Awwwards, Dribbble and Siteinspire appear on other lists, but they are galleries for inspiration, not blogs, so we did not test them.

Slow but deep

Sara Soueidan posted two editorial pieces in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026, the newest on 16 Nov about styling the text caret accessibly. A List Apart published two articles in that time, the newest on 30 Jun 2026, so it misses the 90-day line too. Both fail rule 2, and both deserve a feed slot if you accept long gaps.

Good, but mostly about other things

About four of Brad Frost's newest ten posts are on web design; the rest are music, personal posts and app links. Read him for design-systems work. Chris Coyier's personal blog is mostly personal, and his CSS writing now goes into Chris' Corner on the CodePen Blog. The freeCodeCamp News site is free and good for juniors, but only 4 of its newest 10 tutorials are web development.

Quiet for now

The MDN Blog last posted on 15 Jun 2026; use MDN as a reference, not a feed. The official Vue blog has not posted since "Announcing Vue 3.5" on 1 Sep 2024, so follow the Nuxt blog and Vue's GitHub releases instead. Post Status's newest item in its public feed is from 24 Jul 2026, 117 days before the check, so it misses the 90-day line for now.

Changed format

WP Tavern's feed shows no written post since 9 Jan 2025, and its home page now lists only weekly podcast episodes. CSS Weekly sent one issue in the 90 days: #640 on 12 Nov 2026 came 203 days after #639.

What happened to our 2018 list of the best web design blogs

On 12 April 2018 I published "20 Best Web Design and Development Blogs To Follow" on our old site. By then we had been building websites for ten years (Netling started in 2008). The intro promised "10 must-read blogs", "in no particular order", and then listed 20 plus a bonus, so 21 in all. It gave no rule for what made the cut, and no entry said when the blog had last posted.

Eight years on, I put all 21 through the same rules as the 2026 list, so you can see how a list like this ages. Seven of my 21 picks still pass.

The bigger change is in the kind of blog that made the cut. My 2018 list had no blogs run by the projects or browser makers themselves, and no newsletters. This year's list has eight of the first (React, Next.js, Nuxt, Node.js, Make WordPress Core, WebKit, Chrome for Developers and web.dev) and three newsletters. It also has eight personal blogs, each written by one person, from Josh W. Comeau to Adrian Roselli.

The split is 2 closed or absorbed, 9 with no editorial post in the 90 days, 3 active but off-topic, and 7 still passing: 21 in total. The off-topic group is our reading of their newest posts.

Closed or absorbed (2)

InVision announced on 5 Jan 2024 that its design and collaboration services would shut down, and accounts stayed open until 31 Dec 2024 (Silicon Republic). Its domain, invisionapp.com, now redirects to Miro.

Scotch.io joined DigitalOcean on 16 Dec 2019, which removed the paywall on its tutorials. The domain now redirects to DigitalOcean's community site.

No editorial post in the 90 days before 18 Nov 2026 (9)

These sites missed the 90-day line on 18 Nov 2026. Most are still online, and some still post roundups.

  • Hacking UI: no new post since 11 May 2018, a podcast episode a month after our list went up.
  • Envato Tuts+ Web Design: no new post found since 27 Jun 2025, 509 days before the check.
  • Hongkiat: about monthly (13 editorial items in 12 months) until 7 Aug 2026, then nothing for 103 days.
  • A List Apart: two articles in 12 months, the newest on 30 Jun 2026.
  • Onextrapixel: no editorial post since 5 Feb 2026, and only font roundups since; the newest item is from 24 Apr 2026.
  • David Walsh Blog: newest editorial post 20 Nov 2025. The only item since is a sponsored post on 9 Nov 2026.
  • Design Bombs: newest editorial post 27 Jul 2026, with font, template and plugin roundups since.
  • WPKube: all ten items in its feed, from 20 Feb to 14 Sep 2026, are product reviews or plugin roundups.
  • Design Shack: on 18 Nov 2026 its home page listed only template, font, mockup and preset roundups.

Active, but no longer mainly about web design (3)

  • Designmodo now sells email and website design tools, and its newest posts are a Black Friday sale, a deliverability webinar and email how-tos.
  • Toptal Blog, a talent marketplace's blog, has 2 web development posts among its newest 10. The rest cover NLP, robotics, Spring Batch, data structures and marketing.
  • Backlinko is an SEO site, owned by Semrush since January 2022.

Still pass the rule (7)

Smashing Magazine, Codrops, CSS-Tricks, SitePoint, Web Designer Depot, Speckyboy and Boagworld all made the 2026 list, and their entries above carry the dates.

Our reading, and not a law: the blogs that held up kept one clear topic, or have a named person writing them. Four of the nine that went quiet, Onextrapixel, Design Bombs, WPKube and Design Shack, drifted into asset roundups. The other five slowed down or stopped. When you prune your own reader, a feed that has turned into font and template lists is the first to go.

How to follow these blogs without drowning in them

Make one folder per group in your RSS reader. Most readers accept a pasted feed URL, so the ones above are all you need. Twice a year, check the date of each feed's newest editorial item, not its "last built" date. MDN's feed was rebuilt on 17 Nov 2026, but its newest post is from 15 Jun 2026. Drop anything quiet for 90 days.

When a blog is the wrong place to learn

For exact API behaviour, use MDN's reference pages and the specs. For a framework upgrade, use the official migration guide: a release post tells you a deadline exists, and the guide tells you what to change. For a bug on a deadline, start with the project's GitHub issues.

Frequently asked questions

What are the best web development blogs to follow?

For most front-end work, start with Smashing Magazine, CSS-Tricks, Josh W. Comeau, web.dev and the WebKit blog, plus Frontend Focus as your one newsletter. Add the release blog for each framework you ship. Designers, WordPress developers and agency owners get their own short sets at the end of this post.

Is CSS-Tricks still active?

Yes. Its newest editorial post was on 16 Nov 2026, with at least 13 in the 90 days before 18 Nov 2026, and DigitalOcean has owned it since March 2022. Founder Chris Coyier now writes Chris' Corner on the CodePen Blog.

What is the best newsletter for front-end developers?

Frontend Focus (weekly, issue 766 on 11 Nov 2026) for broad front-end news, JavaScript Weekly (issue 811 on 17 Nov 2026) for JavaScript, and CSS Layout News (monthly) for layout. CSS Weekly sent one issue in the 90 days, so check it before relying on it.

Are web design blogs still worth reading?

Yes, if you keep the list short. Search and AI tools answer the question you bring. A feed shows you what changed while you were not looking, such as the React Server Components security advisories in December 2025 or the WordPress 7.2 developer notes on 17 Nov 2026.

How can I tell whether a blog is still active?

Open its RSS feed and read the newest item's date, not the feed's "last built" date: MDN's feed was rebuilt on 17 Nov 2026, but its newest post is from 15 Jun 2026. Then check that the newest items are editorial: David Walsh's newest item is sponsored, and his last editorial post was on 20 Nov 2025.

Where to start: a short set for your role

Start with the set that fits your job, and add more only when you keep up with these:

  • Designer: Smashing Magazine, Nielsen Norman Group and Pixels of the Week.
  • Front-end developer: Josh W. Comeau, web.dev and the WebKit blog.
  • WordPress developer: Make WordPress Core and The Repository.
  • Agency owner: Boagworld and Speckyboy.

Everyone should add Frontend Focus as the one newsletter, plus the release blog for each framework you ship (React, Next.js, Nuxt or Node.js). Re-run the 90-day check every six months, and drop what has gone quiet. We will re-check this list in January 2027 and update every date.

If you run a small agency and these blogs are how your team stays sharp, but you are short on build capacity, our white label web development team builds sites under your brand. Tell us about the project when one comes up.

Originally published at netling.digital.

title: Juice 1.0 Is Here — Building UI Without Fighting Your Markup
description:
After years of development, experimentation, architectural decisions, and more CSS than I care to admit, Juice has officially reached v1.0.0.

And I couldn't be more excited to finally say that.

For those who haven't followed my previous articles, Juice is an open-source, attribute-first CSS and UI library I've been developing as part of CitrusWorx's WebEngine ecosystem.

It started with a relatively simple question:

What if building interfaces felt more like describing what you wanted, rather than constantly wrestling with how to style it?

That question eventually became Juice.

Today, I'm excited to share its first major release.

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Modern frontend development is incredibly powerful.

We have mature frameworks, sophisticated design systems, utility-first CSS libraries, component ecosystems, and tooling that would have seemed unimaginable a decade ago.

But somewhere along the way, building a relatively simple interface started requiring an increasingly complicated collection of abstractions.

Sometimes you need a component library.

Sometimes you need a CSS framework.

Sometimes you need a JavaScript framework just to make everything work together.

And sometimes, all you really want is a card with a heading, some content, and a button.

I kept asking myself whether we could make the everyday parts of UI development simpler without sacrificing the flexibility needed for more sophisticated applications.

I didn't want to reinvent CSS.

I wanted to rethink how we interact with it.

Enter Juice: Attribute-First UI Development

Juice takes a different approach to expressing layout and presentation.

Instead of relying entirely on lengthy class lists or custom component abstractions, Juice allows developers to describe their interfaces directly through HTML attributes.

For example, here's a conceptual illustration of the attribute-first approach:

<div stack gap="4">
  <div card padding="4">
    <h2>Welcome to Juice</h2>
    <p>
      Build interfaces with expressive markup.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>

The idea is straightforward:

Your markup describes the structure. Your theme defines the visual identity. Juice connects the two.

Attributes such as stack, row, grid, gap, padding, card, and surface make layout intentions visible where the interface is actually being constructed.

This isn't about replacing every CSS rule with an attribute.

It's about providing a more expressive foundation for the things developers do repeatedly.

More Than Another CSS Framework

One of the most important architectural decisions behind Juice was making it useful independently of WebEngine.

Although Juice is being developed as part of the larger CitrusWorx ecosystem, it isn't intended to require developers to adopt that entire ecosystem.

You should be able to use Juice in a standalone project, integrate it into an existing application, or combine it with the frontend technologies you already enjoy.

That independence matters to me.

I don't believe developers should have to replace their entire toolchain just to benefit from one useful library.

Juice is designed around a CSS-first foundation, with JavaScript capabilities available where they make sense.

Its broader architecture also brings together design tokens, themes, components, and optional runtime behavior.

The goal is to provide a consistent UI foundation without forcing every application into the same architecture.

Why Themes Matter

One of the principles driving Juice is the separation of structure and identity.

A layout shouldn't have to be completely rewritten just because an application needs a different visual personality.

The same structural building blocks should be reusable across projects while themes control how those building blocks look and feel.

For CitrusWorx, this is especially important.

WebEngine is intended to support a growing ecosystem of applications and developer tools.

Having a shared visual foundation means we can establish consistency without requiring every application to look identical.

That's the balance I'm working toward with Juice.

What v1.0.0 Actually Means

Reaching version 1.0 isn't the same as declaring a project finished.

If anything, it means accepting a new level of responsibility for the foundation you've created.

During the 0.x development cycle, I spent a considerable amount of time exploring the boundaries of what Juice should become.

There were questions about how attributes should behave, how themes should work, how much JavaScript belongs in a CSS-first library, and how to organize the different pieces into something developers can reasonably understand.

There was also the temptation to keep adding features.

Another component.

Another runtime.

Another abstraction.

Another improvement before calling it ready.

Eventually, though, a library needs to stop being an endless experiment and start becoming something people can actually build with.

Juice v1.0.0 represents that transition.

It's a commitment to a public foundation that developers can begin adopting, testing, and helping improve.

It doesn't mean every idea on the roadmap has been implemented.

It means the project has reached its first major milestone, and future improvements can build on that foundation.

Juice and the Bigger WebEngine Picture

If you've followed my Road to WebEngine series, you know Juice isn't being developed in isolation.

It's one part of a much larger effort at CitrusWorx to build an ecosystem of modular, interoperable developer technologies.

Another major part of that ecosystem is Sig.js, our JavaScript library for building reactive interfaces.

With Sig.js and Juice both reaching their first major releases, two important pieces of the WebEngine vision are beginning to come together.

Sig.js addresses how interfaces are constructed and updated.

Juice addresses how those interfaces are structured and presented.

They have different responsibilities, and that's intentional.

I want developers to be able to adopt individual pieces of WebEngine without being forced into an all-or-nothing framework decision.

The broader vision is ambitious, but it's being built one library, one package, and one release at a time.

Getting Started

Juice v1.0.0 is available on npm.

npm install @citrusworx/juiceui@1.0.0

You can explore the package and source code here:

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@citrusworx/juiceui/v/1.0.0

GitHub: https://github.com/citrusworx/webengine/tree/master/libraries/juice

Whether you're interested in attribute-driven styling, design systems, frontend architecture, or simply exploring a different approach to building interfaces, I'd love for you to take a look.

What's Next?

Reaching v1.0.0 doesn't mean development slows down.

It means the focus changes.

Moving forward, I want to spend more time improving the developer experience, refining documentation, expanding practical examples, addressing issues that emerge from real-world usage, and continuing to evolve the library without losing sight of its original purpose.

I also want to explore how Juice can make UI development more accessible to people who aren't necessarily frontend specialists.

Because I believe good developer tools should make creativity easier, not introduce unnecessary barriers.

A Personal Milestone

Building something like Juice takes a surprising amount of persistence.

There are days when everything comes together beautifully.

And there are days when you find yourself questioning an architectural decision you made three months earlier.

But that's part of engineering.

You experiment.

You discover limitations.

You rethink assumptions.

You improve the design.

And eventually, you ship.

For me, Juice reaching v1.0.0 is another step toward turning CitrusWorx from a collection of ideas and experiments into a real ecosystem of software that other developers can use.

There's still an enormous amount of work ahead.

But today, I'm celebrating this milestone.

Juice 1.0 is here.

If you try it, I'd genuinely appreciate your feedback. Tell me what works, what doesn't, and what you think an attribute-first UI library should do differently.

Thanks for following along on the Road to WebEngine.

We're just getting started.

Built with curiosity, persistence, and a whole lot of CSS.

#webdev #css #opensource #javascript

title: We Audited Our Own Enquiry Forms: 22 Forms, Zero action Attributes, and the One-Line Fix That Doesn't Work
description:
Prepared with AI assistance by Design Den Solutions' own audit workflow, with no human edit before publication. The cover image is AI-generated; the official company logo is composited unchanged. Every number below was measured on our own live website on 19 November 2026 — this is our audit of our own code, not a benchmark of anyone else's.

Most of the advice about "contact form not working" reports ends with a screenshot of a console error. That framing hides the actual structural problem, which is much older and much quieter: the form is a JavaScript component, and there is no non-JavaScript path at all. We went looking for it on our own site and found that we had built exactly that.

What we measured

We fetched every HTML page on www.designdensolutions.com (21 pages, all HTTP 200) and counted form attributes rather than guessing:

Measurement Result
Live HTML pages fetched 21 (all 200)
<form> instances found 22 (one per page; contact.html carries two)
Forms with an action attribute 0
Forms with a method attribute 0
<noscript> elements anywhere on the site 3
Pages whose <noscript> tells a visitor how to enquire 1
Phone fields split into select[name=phone_code] + input[type=tel][name=phone] 22
Uses of autocomplete="tel-country-code" or tel-national 0

The submission path lives entirely in js/interactions.js:

document.querySelectorAll('form[data-contact-form]').forEach(function (form) {
  form.addEventListener('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();                       // the non-JS path ends here
    // ...validate, solve the JS-rendered captcha...
    var controller = new AbortController();
    var timeout = setTimeout(function () { controller.abort(); }, 25000);
    window.fetch('api/contact.php', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      signal: controller.signal,
      body: JSON.stringify({ form_type, name, phone, email, service, company, budget, message, captcha_question, captcha_answer })
    });
  });
});

Two things fall out of that snippet that the HTML alone won't tell you. First, the endpoint URL — api/contact.php — appears only inside a script, as a relative string. It is not in the markup, so no crawler, no no-JS browser, no form-recovery tool and no password manager can see where an enquiry is going. Second, e.preventDefault() is the first statement in the handler, which means the markup's own submission behaviour is discarded before anything else happens. On its own that's a perfectly reasonable enhancement pattern — if there were something to enhance.

What the browser actually does without JavaScript

This part isn't speculation, it's the spec: when method is absent the submission method is GET, and when action is absent the submission URL is the document's base URL. So with JavaScript switched off, pressing our "Submit Request" button performs:

GET /index.html?name=...&phone=...&email=...&service=...&message=...&captcha_question=...&captcha_answer=...

We simulated it with a plain GET carrying benign values and enquiry-shaped parameters. The server answered HTTP 200 with 104,674 bytes — the ordinary homepage. No error, no acknowledgement, no lead. From the visitor's side the page just reloads. And the text they typed is now sitting in the address bar, which means it is in their browser history and in whatever request log the host keeps.

That is the failure mode worth designing for, because it is silent. A red validation message is a bad experience you can see. A reload that looks like nothing happened is a lost enquiry nobody will ever report to you.

The one-line fix that doesn't work here

The obvious repair is to stop treating the markup as decoration:

<form method="post" action="/api/contact.php" data-contact-form>

We did not ship it, because we tested the endpoint first — and on our host that attribute would have been a lie. A plain request to /api/contact.php returns:

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: text/html; charset=iso-8859-1
Content-Length: 83

<script>document.cookie = "..."; document.location.reload(true)</script>

That is bot-challenge middleware running before PHP. It answers an HTML interstitial with a 409 to a path our own client code expects to return JSON. Our production handler already has to cope with it: it matches the interstitial with a regex, sets the cookie the script asked for, and retries once — with a comment in the source saying never to execute the returned HTML. So a native form POST would receive that same 83-byte script, "succeed" at the HTTP level in the browser's eyes, and render a reload instead of a thank-you message.

The lesson generalises: action and method are a promise about a server endpoint, and the endpoint has to be tested independently of the front end. Verify with a plain curl POST that returns your JSON, not with a browser session that already has the challenge cookie set.

What we are actually changing, in order

  1. Decide the product question before the technical one. Does this form need to submit without JavaScript? For an agency enquiry route, often the honest answer is no — but then the fallback has to be visible, not implied.
  2. Ship the fallback we already proved works. contact.html carries <noscript><p>To enquire, <a href="tel:+919872190965">call +91 98721 90965</a> or <a href="mailto:hello@designdensolutions.com">email us</a>.</p></noscript>. Twenty other pages carry the same form and no such notice. That is a copy-paste job, not a redesign.
  3. Only then, if real no-JS submission is wanted: exempt the endpoint from the challenge layer, accept application/x-www-form-urlencoded in contact.php, and add method="post" action="/api/contact.php". Re-test with curl before touching the HTML.
  4. Keep preventDefault() as an enhancement, which is what it should have been from the start.
  5. Fix the phone autofill tokens (below).
  6. Make the anti-spam check survive no-JS. Ours is an arithmetic question rendered into the HTML with the answer key held in a hidden input that JavaScript fills in. With JS off, the hidden value is empty and the visible question is static markup — so even a working action would fail validation.

The small autofill thing that is entirely our own fault

All 22 forms split the phone number into a country-code <select> and a national-number <input type="tel">. Across the site we ship exactly four autocomplete tokens, 22 of each: name, tel, email, off.

The autocomplete="tel" sits on the field that only accepts the national number, while the country-code select carries no token at all. The spec already has the right vocabulary for this exact pattern — tel-country-code for the select, tel-national for the input — and tel means "the whole number", which is not what the field holds. We declared a full telephone number on a partial field, 22 times. We have not tested how individual browsers respond to that mismatch; the claim here is only that the markup promises something it does not accept.

Run this on your own site

Read-only, no submission, about ten minutes:

// Paste into the console on any page with a form.
[...document.querySelectorAll('form')].map(f => ({
  id: f.id || f.className.slice(0, 30),
  action: f.getAttribute('action'),        // null = submits to the document URL
  method: f.getAttribute('method'),        // null = GET
  handled: !!f.querySelector('[data-contact-form], [data-form-error]') ||
           getComputedStyle(f).display === 'block'
}));

// Then, separately, prove the endpoint exists and answers in JSON:
//   curl -i -X POST https://yoursite/api/your-endpoint
// If that returns HTML, or a 4xx with a script body, the action attribute
// would not have fixed anything.

And grep your noscript blocks: if the only page that tells a JavaScript-disabled visitor what to do is your /contact page, the other pages have a dead button and no notice.

What we are not claiming

  • We did not submit a test enquiry. Doing so would have put a fake lead into a real inbox; every endpoint claim here comes from an unauthenticated GET/POST that carried no enquiry data.
  • We have no measurement of how many enquiries actually arrive with JavaScript unavailable. That analytics is not configured, so we are not going to invent a percentage.
  • We did not test autofill behaviour across browsers or operating systems.
  • The 409 interstitial is what our host returns to a plain request today; it is an observation about our configuration, not a claim about that product's defaults.
  • Nothing here proves our form is broken for the 99%+ of visitors who run JavaScript. It is the fallback that is missing, not the happy path.

The page this work belongs to is our website development service — https://www.designdensolutions.com/web-development.html?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=enquiry_form_nojs_fallback — and to be explicit about it: that is a link to our own service page on our own website, placed by us on our own account. It is not third-party coverage or an endorsement of anything.

title: A 200 OK After Redirects Is Not a Direct 200: Testing Internal Links in Node.js
description:
A link check can report success and still miss the thing you wanted to test.

Suppose your acceptance rule is: “This internal link must reach its destination without an HTTP redirect.” Checking only (await fetch(url)).status === 200 does not express that rule. With default redirect handling, the response can describe the final destination rather than the first response.

This example isolates that distinction with a disposable local server. It is a synthetic regression test, not a crawl of a client website or evidence of an SEO improvement.

AI disclosure: This article and its code were generated by an AI assistant. The executable example was run locally on Node.js v24.22.3. The test output below comes from that run; the routes and page content are invented fixtures.

Two assertions, two different questions

“Does the destination eventually return 200?” and “Does this exact URL return 200 directly?” are different checks.

Fixture First response Result with normal following
/direct 200 200
/old 301 to /direct?source=example 200
/chain 302 to /old 200 after two hops
/loop 307 to itself Cannot finish successfully
/missing 404 404

The table describes the server defined below. The script deliberately follows only /old; its other assertions inspect the first hop. It does not run a redirect loop to exhaustion.

A successful eventual response is useful evidence, but it is not evidence of a redirect-free link. In this test, redirect: 'manual' makes the first response observable. The expected status is exactly 200, not just response.ok, which also includes other 2xx statuses.

A copy-and-run regression test

Save the following as redirect-check.mjs and run node redirect-check.mjs. It uses Node's built-in HTTP server, assertions and fetch. No package installation, account, credentials or public target is needed. The server binds only to loopback and chooses a temporary port.

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

// Local, synthetic fixtures only. Nothing is fetched from the public internet.
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://fixture.invalid');
  if (url.pathname === '/direct') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
    res.end('Example page');
  } else if (url.pathname === '/old') {
    res.writeHead(301, { Location: '/direct?source=example' });
    res.end();
  } else if (url.pathname === '/chain') {
    res.writeHead(302, { Location: '/old' });
    res.end();
  } else if (url.pathname === '/loop') {
    res.writeHead(307, { Location: '/loop' });
    res.end();
  } else {
    res.writeHead(404);
    res.end('Not found');
  }
});
await new Promise(resolve => server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', resolve));
const origin = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;

async function firstHop(href) {
  const requested = new URL(href, origin);
  // This demo accepts only its own fixture origin, not arbitrary URLs.
  if (requested.origin !== origin || requested.username || requested.password) {
    throw new Error('Outside the local fixture origin');
  }
  const response = await fetch(requested, {
    method: 'GET', redirect: 'manual', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  });
  const result = {
    status: response.status,
    location: response.headers.get('location'),
    direct200: response.status === 200
  };
  // Release resources; this check does not need the page body.
  await response.body?.cancel();
  return result;
}

try {
  const followed = await fetch(`${origin}/old`, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  });
  assert.equal(followed.status, 200);
  assert.equal(followed.redirected, true);
  assert.equal(new URL(followed.url).pathname, '/direct');
  await followed.body?.cancel();
  console.log('Default fetch: /old -> status 200, redirected true');

  const cases = [
    ['/direct?source=example#details', 200, null, true],
    ['/old', 301, '/direct?source=example', false],
    ['/chain', 302, '/old', false],
    ['/loop', 307, '/loop', false],
    ['/missing', 404, null, false]
  ];
  for (const [href, status, location, direct200] of cases) {
    const actual = await firstHop(href);
    assert.deepEqual(actual, { status, location, direct200 });
    console.log(`${href}: ${actual.status}; direct200=${actual.direct200}`);
  }
  await assert.rejects(firstHop('https://example.com/'), /Outside/);
  console.log('PASS: default-follow check, five first-hop cases, origin guard');
} finally {
  server.closeAllConnections();
  await new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve));
}

What the run actually established

The recorded output was:

Default fetch: /old -> status 200, redirected true
/direct?source=example#details: 200; direct200=true
/old: 301; direct200=false
/chain: 302; direct200=false
/loop: 307; direct200=false
/missing: 404; direct200=false
PASS: default-follow check, five first-hop cases, origin guard

The first assertion demonstrates the false shortcut: /old produces a final 200, but redirected is true. The five manual checks distinguish direct success, a permanent redirect, the start of a chain, a self-redirect and a missing URL. The final assertion rejects an input outside the fixture origin before any request is made.

The checker does not follow a Location header. In particular, the /loop test is one request, not an unbounded traversal. It cancels response bodies it does not need and uses a timeout. Assertions stop the run on a mismatch, while the finally block closes the server.

Apply the rule to a link, not just a destination

For an authorised check of a site you maintain, record the source page, the original href and the first response separately. If a replacement is appropriate, verify the intended destination and update that specific link. Do not delete a redirect simply because one internal link no longer needs it; old bookmarks and external references may still depend on it.

Keep query parameters and fragments intentional. In the fixture, the redirect supplies ?source=example; a replacement that drops it would not preserve the same URL. The #details fragment in the direct fixture is not sent in an HTTP request. A 200 therefore says nothing about whether a matching HTML anchor exists. Validate the actual anchor separately.

Use GET when you need to test GET behaviour. A HEAD-only check is a different request and can produce different results on some servers. Conversely, do not casually fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs: the small origin guard here is tailored to a fixed local fixture, not a complete security design for a public URL-checking service.

Boundaries of this test

This is a Node.js example, not code for a browser console. Browser Fetch can expose manual redirects as opaque responses; do not assume you will be able to read the same status and headers there. Node's built-in fetch uses Undici, whose documentation explains its manual-redirect behaviour.

A direct 200 also does not establish that the content is correct, in the right language, indexable or canonical. It will not detect a JavaScript redirect, a meta-refresh, a soft-404 page or a broken fragment. Those require additional checks. Keep this assertion narrow: for this GET request, the first HTTP response is 200.

References

  • Node.js: built-in fetch
  • Undici: specification compliance and manual redirects

title: What is a researcher’s worth?
description:
Why the debate over research isn’t a technology story – and why effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.

We’re no stranger to this question.

For many years, research practitioners have talked with one another about how to “mature” teams so that they understand the value of our work in bringing success to their ventures. Or when we share the results of our research, we are peppered with questions about whether the findings are real, whether the methods are too weak or lack representativeness, or whether our subjects are even telling the truth when they express to us what they need.

But it’s not just research practitioners. Researchers in academia have been stripped of the funding they need to advance science. Academic departments have shuttered, and scholars’ voices have been dismissed as part of major civic scientific efforts, like the Census, the Environmental Protection Agency, or the Department of Education.

Put in this context, contemporary discourse around artificial intelligence replacing our jobs feels less like “the reason” than one reason among many when people question whether researchers (and research, in general) matter.

Over the last ten years, I’ve worked as an industry researcher while keeping a foot in academia, and have had some of the best work experiences of my life. There is a joy and a magic I find in what happens when you bring experts of different disciplines together – research, business, engineering, design, and more – to solve complex puzzles.

So if that cross-disciplinary magic is so real — and so productive — why do researchers in both companies and public life spend so much of their careers on the defensive? Most hot takes right now answer that question with new kinds of work: prompt faster, automate your synthesis, prove your return on investment.

As a social scientist, I think those takes miss what is actually happening. The debate over a researcher’s worth isn’t really a technology story. It’s a story about how institutions handle inconvenient truths.

Why institutions put research on trial.

Back in 2020, I wrote about one of my favorite scenes from the all-too-accurate show, Silicon Valley. In the episode, technologists watch through a one-way mirror as focus group participants give honest feedback about their app. One participant explained that the app made them feel “totally freaked out,” and another explained that it “made me feel stupid.”

Behind the mirror, the exec got angry. “Clearly none of these people get it, maybe this is a bad group…everyone that I showed the beta to loved it.” His colleague explained that this was the fifth focus group and they all shared the same feedback. She then realized he only gave the beta to his engineer friends. “I wanted to give it to people who would understand what I’m trying to do so I could get useful feedback,” he said. “And with all due respect, I gave it to you — the one person without a computing background – and you said it felt engineered.”

Those of us who love the craft of research love talking about research methods. But I find that in many cases, debates about methods in settings like these are not about finding what’s valuable. Methodological nitpicking is a way to avoid disruptions to a preferred plan. In this way, it is a shield against uncertainty – ironically, the very thing that research tries to disambiguate.

Social scientists argue that when under pressure, organizations gravitate toward commensuration – a process by which people working together flatten a messy, pluralistic set of realities into a single spreadsheet metric. The truth is, we do live in a world with a lot of unknowns, and the “winners” of today’s marketplace may not be the same in a few months or years. Under that uncertainty, it is tempting to flatten complex human behavior into click metrics – and flatten researchers into headcount cost compared against a chatbot – mistaking a tidy spreadsheet for certainty.

What AI actually changed: a mirror that rarely talks back.

In 2020, the lead technologist in Silicon Valley had to walk through the door and argue with human beings using their products. In 2026, they don’t have to do that anymore. They can swap the humans behind the glass for a synthetic AI persona trained to give feedback in specific ways.

I’m not here to say that AI is bad for science. I actually love a lot of the applications of artificial intelligence I get to use. I’m more troubled by the discourse around artificial intelligence and research in industry – how people talk about it – and the way it is compared to the human worth of social scientists.

For one, when organizations treat research as theater to rubber-stamp decisions they have already made, synthetic users and LLM summaries offer “good enough” reassurance at a fraction of the cost. Replacing hard-to-reach or marginalized communities with LLM agents doesn’t actually include them, either. It builds statistical caricatures out of dominant internet texts while erasing human consent and real-world inequities – the kind of blind spot that lets an automated camera “touch-up” feature quietly lighten darker skin tones if real people aren’t in the room.

And think about how culture actually moves. A few years ago, if you asked a model trained on historical averages what romance audiences wanted, it would tell you to center a man and a woman falling in love – it never would have bet on a breakout love story about two men playing hockey. Models fed past averages and synthetic data lose the tails of the distribution, the emerging subcultures and edge cases where the future actually starts. Meanwhile, algorithmic platforms mistake digital traces for human intent: a frustrated user clicking three times to fix a broken output looks like “high engagement” in behavioral logs.

Artificial intelligence is an interesting tool, not a good social scientist. But today, AI is giving anxious institutions the frictionless validation they secretly always wanted.

Looking in our own mirror.

Listen, I don’t think researchers are perfect by any means. We’re human after all! I actually think that researchers both in industry and academia accidentally made our worth easy to caricature.

Often professions survive or shrink based on what they claim jurisdiction over – what we diagnose problems to be, to what we attribute their causes, and how we offer treatment. In 2020, I warned that industry research was used too tactically (“go run a focus group”) as a way to drive impact. But over the last decade, much of industry research leaned into method gatekeeping – measuring our worth by how many people we interviewed or surveyed, or how many “insights” we delivered, or how many slide decks were shared.

At the same time, in academia, career incentives rewarded the world’s smartest experts for speaking mainly to peers behind journal paywalls rather than embedding social science into civic and institutional design. For example, a senior professor in my field asked me how I’d like the discipline to advance. I said that we should consider hiring clinical professors to more genuinely bring our findings to the field. He actually laughed at me. “Save it for social work,” he said.

I’m of the opinion that neither of these approaches has really helped anyone. In the former, we have traded using appropriate and defensible methods, asking big questions, and discussing complicated answers for a “study complete” checkbox. In the latter, we have siloed the magic of expert discovery almost entirely to the few people who read a published paper.

Where the magic of research lives.

Why does bringing research, engineering, design, and business together feel like magic? David Stark showed that breakthrough innovation happens in what he calls “heterarchies” – teams that hold competing accounts of worth in creative tension rather than collapsing everything into shipping speed. When AI coding tools let teams spin up twenty working prototypes in a week, velocity is no longer the scarce resource. Knowing which human dream is worth building becomes the scarcest asset in the room. For example, when do you pause a team buried in fifty usability bug fixes to instead ask whether we’re focused on the right value?

Some unfortunate news for my colleagues: humans don’t follow linear product models. They improvise inside their own social groups and cultural ecosystems. They react and adapt to major changes in their lives.

Engineers see systems; product managers see markets and funnels; and social scientists see social structure.

Social scientists can find and explain why youth culture over the last twenty years has shifted from public broadcasting to more intimate pockets of the internet. Or why a certain design aesthetic feels exciting in one region and troubling in another, shaped by the cultural meanings people there share. Or how chaotic-looking livestreams with tens of thousands of people are actually held together by the patterned, organized activities of moderators who keep conversation focused and fun.

In The Tacit Dimension, Hungarian-British polymath Michael Polanyi wrote that “we can know more than we can tell.” A vast amount of human knowledge is nonverbal. It includes how we think about cultural norms that we can’t summarize in a survey, or sometimes even in the context of an interview. My bet is that unguided LLMs can’t uncover that tacit knowledge on their own. But social scientists can. We triangulate methods and hold magnifying glasses up to a social problem in a variety of ways, including by testing our assumptions against an accumulated body of scholarly work in purposefully specific subfields.

Worth is built together.

Whether in a product sprint, a university lab, or a public agency, a researcher’s worth was never the focus group they run, how big or small their sample size is, or the paper they publish. Our worth is how we apply our training and our lens to the messy, plural, inconvenient realities of human life, even when institutions are tempted by easy mirrors that boil experience down to a lone metric.

To my research peers: bring your expertise and critical thinking to the work that you do. Show value to your teams by how you and your work “make the strange familiar, and the familiar strange” in the pursuit of a shared understanding grounded in human experience.

To my academic colleagues: get out of the ivory tower. Meet people who do research and engage in practice for purposes that have nothing to do with publishing. Learn new ways to talk about your work that shed both academic-ese and didactic habits in favor of two-way learning.

To my partners in research: resist the seduction of a mirror that always agrees with you. When AI makes spinning up twenty new ideas effortless, speed stops being your competitive edge – knowing what is actually true about people outside your building is. Invite the friction of someone trained to tell you when your favorite plan doesn’t match how humans really live.

We’ve spent years talking about how to “mature” organizations into valuing research, as if worth were a favor. It isn’t. Worth is built together.

Dr. Matt Rafalow is a senior staff researcher at YouTube, and a visiting scholar at University of Southern California. The views expressed in this article reflects the individual opinions of the author.

What is a researcher’s worth? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Hello, Dev.to: the three S's of regulated software, and the backend I'm building
description:
In the 90s in England, my mates and I spent endless nights tearing apart computers and rebuilding them one component at a time. Twenty-five years later I'm still doing something similar, except the computers are backends and the components are the controls regulated customers ask for.

Hi, I'm Niyi. I'm a Nigerian-British deep-tech engineer, an optimist, and the founder of Kilimanjaro. I'm writing from Lagos, Nigeria, and a good part of what I care about is a better future for Nigeria. This is my first post here, so let me say who I am and what to expect.

The path here

I fell in love with tech in those nights of tearing computers apart, coding in Pascal, then C, C++ and Java. I earned my degree in Computer Science at the University of Bristol, and it has been an unending stream of languages, frameworks and security standards ever since.

My first startup was an ad-tech company. Then I built a software consultancy, and then a BaaS for some of the biggest regulated companies in Africa, architecting critical software for multi-billion dollar banks, pension funds, and asset managers, which is what led my meandering journey to Kilimanjaro.

The three S's

Over 25 years I've learned that, in regulated industries, three things rule: stability, security and standards. Your software must keep running, protect sensitive data and pass audits. Teams that ship a working prototype usually find out how much that costs when the first regulated customer sends a 100-line feature checklist, and the backend has to be rebuilt to answer it.

Kilimanjaro is my answer: a backend where those controls are part of the services from the first day, so you don't rebuild. You get a database, files, real-time streams, AI guardrails, serverless compute, encryption, access control and an audit trail as one set of services, with the rules about where data lives and who can touch it built in. If you want details, the docs have them.

What you'll find here

I'll try to post regularly, in two kinds.

The journey. What we decided, what we got wrong and what changed our minds. The names we corrected, the pages we hid until they were true, the questions customers ask that no tutorial prepares you for.

Fixes for hard problems. The strange ones. The bug that only appears under a particular region setting, the encryption question that sounds simple and is not, the business problem nobody warned us about. Each post says what the symptom looked like, why it was hard, what caused it and how we fixed it, so you can fix yours faster than we did.

Kilimanjaro's own blog, the Summit Log, is where the practical how-to material lives. Here I'll tell the stories behind it.

Over to you

If you're building enterprise apps, I might be able to chip in some advice on questions like:

  • How do I get through the dreaded 100-line feature checklist that procurement sends?
  • How do I implement field-level encryption ahead of a PCI DSS 4.0/4.0.1 audit?
  • How do I avoid GDPR violations by sharding per-user data across regions?
  • How do I talk to an HSM through PKCS#11 or KMIP?

Tell me in the comments. The best ones become posts.

Thanks for reading, and see you next Thursday.

Niyi
