title: Hibernate From Scratch: Understanding JPA, Entities, Repositories & Spring Boot
description:
• A beginner-friendly guide to understanding how Java applications communicate with databases using Hibernate and Spring Data JPA.

Introduction

When building a backend application, one of the most important responsibilities is managing data. Applications need to store information, retrieve records, update existing data, and delete records when necessary.

Traditionally, developers used SQL queries and JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) to communicate directly with relational databases.

Although JDBC provides powerful database access, writing SQL queries and manually mapping database records to Java objects can become repetitive, especially in large applications.

This is where JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA come into play.

These technologies simplify database operations by allowing developers to work with Java objects instead of writing SQL queries for every database operation.

In this article, we'll explore these concepts from scratch and understand how they work together in a Spring Boot application.

1. Understanding the Fundamentals

Before writing code, let's understand three important concepts.

What is ORM?

ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapping.

It is a technique that maps Java objects to relational database tables.

For example, imagine an application that manages users.

In Java, we might represent a user using a class:

public class User {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

In a relational database, the same information might be stored in a table:

users

id name email
1 John john@example.com
2 Sarah sarah@example.com

ORM allows us to connect these two representations.

Instead of manually converting database rows into Java objects, an ORM framework handles much of that work.

What is JPA?

JPA stands for Java Persistence API, now officially known as Jakarta Persistence.

JPA is a specification that defines how Java applications should manage relational data.

It provides standard annotations and interfaces for:

  • Mapping Java classes to database tables.
  • Mapping object properties to database columns.
  • Managing entity relationships.
  • Persisting and retrieving data.
  • Managing entity lifecycle operations.

An important thing to understand is that JPA is not an implementation. It defines the rules and standards that persistence providers must follow.

What is Hibernate?

Hibernate is an ORM framework and one of the most widely used implementations of the JPA specification.

It provides the actual functionality behind many JPA operations.

For example, when we use:

userRepository.save(user);

Hibernate can generate the appropriate SQL statement and execute it against the database.

Hibernate handles tasks such as:

  • Generating SQL queries.
  • Mapping database records to Java objects.
  • Managing entity states.
  • Tracking changes to entities.
  • Handling database relationships.
  • Managing persistence contexts.

In simple terms:

  • JPA defines the standard.
  • Hibernate implements the standard.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repository abstractions.

2. How Spring Boot, JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA Work Together

These technologies are often used together in Spring Boot applications.

Let's understand their relationship.

        Spring Boot Application
                 |
                 v
          Spring Data JPA
                 |
                 v
              JPA API
                 |
                 v
             Hibernate
                 |
                 v
           JDBC Driver
                 |
                 v
          Relational Database
          (PostgreSQL / MySQL)

Each layer has a specific responsibility.

Spring Boot

Provides application configuration and integrates the persistence technologies.

Spring Data JPA

Provides repository interfaces and reduces the amount of database-access code developers need to write.

JPA

Defines the persistence standards and annotations.

Hibernate

Implements JPA and performs the actual ORM operations.

JDBC Driver

Allows Java applications to communicate with the database.

Database

Stores the actual application data.

Understanding this architecture makes it easier to identify which technology is responsible for each operation.

3. Setting Up a Spring Boot Project

Let's create a simple Spring Boot application that uses Hibernate and PostgreSQL.

When creating a project using Spring Initializr, include these dependencies:

  • Spring Web
  • Spring Data JPA
  • PostgreSQL Driver
  • Validation

Spring Boot automatically configures Hibernate as the default JPA provider when the JPA starter is included, unless another provider is configured.

A simplified project structure might look like this:

src/main/java/com/example/demo/
│
├── controller/
│   └── UserController.java
│
├── service/
│   └── UserService.java
│
├── repository/
│   └── UserRepository.java
│
├── entity/
│   └── User.java
│
└── DemoApplication.java

Each package has a specific responsibility:

  • entity: Defines database-mapped Java objects.
  • repository: Handles database access.
  • service: Contains business logic.
  • controller: Handles HTTP requests and responses.

This separation makes applications easier to maintain and extend.

4. Understanding Entities in JPA

An entity is a Java class that represents a database table.

Hibernate uses entity metadata to understand how Java objects should be mapped to database records.

Let's create a User entity.

package com.example.demo.entity;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "created_at")
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    public User() {
    }

    // Getters and setters
}

Let's understand the important annotations.

@entity

Marks a Java class as a JPA entity.

Hibernate recognizes this class as something that should be persisted in the database.

@Table

Specifies the database table associated with the entity.

@Table(name = "users")

Without this annotation, JPA derives the table name from the entity name.

@id

Defines the primary key of the entity.

Every entity must have an identifier.

@GeneratedValue

Specifies how the primary key should be generated.

For example:

@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

Common generation strategies include:

  • IDENTITY: Relies on database-generated identity values.
  • SEQUENCE: Uses a database sequence.
  • TABLE: Uses a separate database table to generate identifiers.
  • AUTO: Allows the persistence provider to choose an appropriate strategy.

The best choice depends on the database and application requirements.

@column

Customizes how a Java field maps to a database column.

For example:

@Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
private String email;

This indicates that the column should not accept null values and should contain unique values.

Important: JPA annotations describe mapping and schema-generation metadata. They do not replace proper database constraints and migrations in production applications.

5. Understanding Entity Relationships

Real-world applications rarely contain independent tables.

For example, an e-commerce application might have:

  • Users
  • Orders
  • Products
  • Payments

These tables need relationships to represent how data is connected.

JPA provides four primary relationship annotations.

@OneToOne

Represents a relationship where one record is associated with one other record.

Example: One user has one profile.

@OneToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")
private Profile profile;

@OneToMany

Represents a relationship where one record can be associated with multiple records.

Example: One user can have multiple orders.

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "user")
private List<Order> orders;

@ManyToOne

Represents multiple records associated with one record.

Example: Multiple orders can belong to one user.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "user_id")
private User user;

@ManyToMany

Represents a relationship where multiple records can be associated with multiple other records.

Example: Students can enroll in multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students.

@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(
    name = "student_courses",
    joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
    inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
)
private Set<Course> courses;

Understanding relationships is essential when designing a relational database using JPA.

6. What Are Repositories in Spring Data JPA?

After defining entities, we need a way to perform database operations.

This is where Spring Data JPA repositories become useful.

A repository is an abstraction that provides methods for interacting with the database.

Instead of manually writing SQL queries for basic operations, we can extend an existing Spring Data interface.

Let's create a UserRepository.

package com.example.demo.repository;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

}

That's it!

We haven't written any implementation code.

Spring Data JPA automatically provides the implementation at runtime.

By extending JpaRepository, we get access to several useful methods.

Method Purpose
save() Insert or update an entity
findById() Find an entity by its ID
findAll() Retrieve all entities
existsById() Check whether an entity exists
deleteById() Delete an entity by ID
count() Count available records

For example:

userRepository.findAll();

Retrieves all users.

userRepository.findById(1L);

Retrieves a user with ID 1.

userRepository.deleteById(1L);

Deletes the user with ID 1.

Spring Data JPA generates the required database-access implementation behind these methods.

Custom Query Methods

One of the most useful features of Spring Data JPA is query method derivation.

We can define methods based on the properties of an entity.

For example:

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);

    List<User> findByName(String name);

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
}

Spring Data JPA analyzes these method names and generates the corresponding queries.

We can also write custom JPQL queries using @Query.

@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email")
Optional<User> findUserByEmail(
    @Param("email") String email
);

JPQL operates on entity classes and their properties rather than directly referencing database table and column names.

7. Understanding the Service Layer

In a properly structured Spring Boot application, controllers should not directly contain database operations.

Instead, we introduce a service layer to manage business logic.

Let's create a UserService.

package com.example.demo.service;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.repository.UserRepository;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.List;

@Service
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    public User createUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }

    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userRepository.findAll();
    }
}

Why use a service layer?

The service layer provides a place to implement:

  • Business rules.
  • Validation beyond basic input constraints.
  • Transaction management.
  • Coordination between multiple repositories.
  • Application-specific logic.

For example, before creating a user, we might check whether the email address is already registered.

This keeps the controller focused on handling HTTP requests rather than implementing business rules.

8. Connecting the Application to PostgreSQL

Now we need to configure the database connection.

In Spring Boot, database configuration is commonly defined in:

application.yml

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/demo_db
    username: postgres
    password: your_password
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver

  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    show-sql: true
    properties:
      hibernate:
        format_sql: true

Let's understand the configuration.

datasource.url

Specifies the database connection URL.

username and password

Provide database authentication credentials.

ddl-auto

Controls Hibernate's automatic database schema handling.

Common options include:

Value Description
create Creates the schema and may drop existing tables
create-drop Creates the schema and drops it when the session factory closes
update Attempts to update the schema
validate Checks whether the schema matches the entity mappings
none Disables automatic schema management

For production applications, using validate or none alongside a database migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase is generally a safer approach.

Avoid relying on ddl-auto=update as your production database migration strategy.

9. Understanding the Entity Lifecycle

One of the most important Hibernate concepts is the entity lifecycle.

Hibernate manages entities through different states.

There are four commonly discussed states:

1. Transient

An object is transient when it has been created but is not associated with a persistence context.

User user = new User();
user.setName("John");
user.setEmail("john@example.com");

At this point, the object exists only in application memory.

2. Managed (Persistent)

An entity becomes managed when it is associated with an active persistence context.

For example:

entityManager.persist(user);

Hibernate starts tracking the entity.

Changes made to a managed entity can automatically be synchronized with the database.

3. Detached

An entity becomes detached when it is no longer associated with its persistence context.

For example, after the persistence context is closed, previously managed entities become detached.

Changes to detached objects are not automatically synchronized with the database.

4. Removed

An entity enters the removed state when it is scheduled for deletion.

entityManager.remove(user);

The actual database deletion happens when the persistence context is flushed.

Understanding these states helps explain why Hibernate sometimes executes SQL statements even when we haven't explicitly called a save method.

10. What Is a Persistence Context?

A persistence context is an important part of JPA and Hibernate.

Think of it as an environment that manages entity instances during their lifecycle.

It maintains a collection of managed entities and tracks changes made to them.

For example:

@Transactional
public void updateUser(Long id) {

    User user = userRepository.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow();

    user.setName("Updated Name");
}

Notice something interesting.

We didn't call:

userRepository.save(user);

Yet the updated name can still be persisted.

Why?

Because the entity is managed by the persistence context.

Hibernate detects the changes and synchronizes them with the database during transaction flushing. This mechanism is called dirty checking.

This is one of Hibernate's most powerful features.

11. Understanding Transactions in Spring Boot

A database transaction is a group of operations treated as one logical unit.

Transactions help maintain data consistency.

Spring provides the @Transactional annotation to manage transactions.

Example:

@Transactional
public void transferMoney(
        Long fromAccountId,
        Long toAccountId,
        BigDecimal amount) {

    Account from = accountRepository
        .findById(fromAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    Account to = accountRepository
        .findById(toAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    from.setBalance(from.getBalance().subtract(amount));

    to.setBalance(to.getBalance().add(amount));
}

Both updates should succeed together.

If an applicable unchecked exception occurs, Spring normally rolls back the transaction.

This prevents a situation where money is deducted from one account but not added to the other.

Transactions are particularly important when multiple database operations depend on each other.

12. Understanding Lazy and Eager Loading

When working with entity relationships, Hibernate needs to determine when related data should be retrieved.

JPA provides two common fetching strategies.

Lazy Loading

Related data is retrieved only when it is accessed.

@OneToMany(
    mappedBy = "user",
    fetch = FetchType.LAZY
)
private List<Order> orders;

Eager Loading

Related data is retrieved eagerly as part of loading the entity, although the exact SQL strategy is provider-dependent.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
private User user;

Lazy loading is generally a good default for collections because it avoids unnecessarily loading large amounts of data.

However, it can introduce the N+1 query problem.

For example, retrieving 100 orders and then accessing each order's user might result in one query to retrieve the orders and additional queries to retrieve users.

Possible solutions include:

  • JPQL JOIN FETCH.
  • Entity graphs.
  • DTO projections.
  • Batch fetching.

Understanding fetching strategies is important for building efficient applications.

13. Putting Everything Together: A Simple REST API

Now let's connect everything.

We'll create a REST controller that exposes user-related endpoints.

package com.example.demo.controller;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.service.UserService;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public User createUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        return userService.createUser(user);
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
}

We now have two basic endpoints.

HTTP Method Endpoint Description
POST /api/users Create a user
GET /api/users Retrieve all users

The complete request flow looks like this:

       Client Request
             |
             v
       UserController
             |
             v
        UserService
             |
             v
       UserRepository
             |
             v
          Hibernate
             |
             v
         PostgreSQL

When a client sends a request to create a user:

  1. The controller receives the HTTP request.
  2. The service handles the application logic.
  3. The repository executes the persistence operation.
  4. Hibernate translates the operation into SQL.
  5. The JDBC driver communicates with PostgreSQL.
  6. The database stores the record.
  7. The result is returned through the application layers.

This is the basic architecture behind many Spring Boot applications.

Note: This example demonstrates the persistence flow. A production API should use request/response DTOs, validation, exception handling, and appropriate transaction boundaries rather than exposing JPA entities directly.

14. Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

When starting with Hibernate and Spring Data JPA, there are several common mistakes worth understanding.

1. Confusing JPA with Hibernate

JPA is a specification, while Hibernate is an implementation. They are related but not interchangeable concepts.

2. Using entities directly in REST APIs

Returning entities directly can expose internal database structures and create serialization problems, particularly with bidirectional relationships.

Use DTOs instead.

3. Ignoring entity relationships

Incorrect relationship mappings can cause duplicate records, unexpected SQL queries, or data consistency problems.

4. Using EAGER fetching everywhere

Eager loading can retrieve unnecessary data and negatively affect application performance.

5. Ignoring transactions

Operations involving multiple database changes should have appropriate transaction boundaries.

6. Depending on Hibernate to manage production schemas

Use database migration tools such as Flyway or Liquibase to manage schema changes in a controlled and versioned manner.

Conclusion

Understanding Hibernate, JPA, and Spring Data JPA is an important step toward becoming a capable Spring Boot backend developer.

The key concepts to remember are:

  • ORM connects Java objects with relational database tables.
  • JPA defines the persistence specification.
  • Hibernate implements the JPA specification.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repositories.
  • Entities represent database records.
  • Repositories provide database operations.
  • Services manage business logic.
  • Persistence contexts track managed entities.
  • Transactions help maintain data consistency.
  • Fetching strategies influence database performance.

Rather than memorizing annotations and methods, focus on understanding what happens behind the scenes when an application communicates with a database.

Once you understand how these components work together, building more complex backend systems becomes much easier.

The best way to learn Hibernate is to build something with it. Start with a simple CRUD application, introduce entity relationships, implement transactions, and gradually explore more advanced persistence concepts.

Happy coding! 🚀

title: Bring Live MongoDB Atlas Data Into Microsoft 365 Copilot
description:
The federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas gives organizations a governed way to bring live operational data into the flow of work across Copilot experiences.

To operate efficiently, businesses require timely information about the systems that underpin their organizations. For example, they need to be able to answer questions like: Which incidents are open? Which orders are delayed? What fields and data types are present in the customer collection? The answers they need often live in operational applications built on MongoDB Atlas, while the questions are asked in the productivity tools people use every day.

To help close that gap, MongoDB is excited to introduce a federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas. Now generally available, the connector enables users to ask Microsoft 365 Copilot questions about live data in MongoDB Atlas, bringing operational context into the same experience where people collaborate, analyze information, and make decisions.

The connector surfaces MongoDB Atlas data across Microsoft Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, Researcher in Copilot, Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Word, Excel, and Teams, with additional experiences planned to follow.

Bring operational data into the flow of work

The connector brings MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Copilot through MongoDB’s managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. When a user asks a relevant question, Copilot can query Atlas in real time—instead of relying on a static copy of the data.

This creates a more direct path from a business question to the information needed to answer it, and helps users—who may not have MongoDB expertise—access and analyze live operational data through an AI assistant.

Now, business users can use conversational prompts to:

  • Retrieve live business data without writing database queries.

  • Find and filter customers, transactions, products, orders, content, or operational events.

  • Get quick counts and key performance indicators, such as the number of delayed orders or high-value customers.

  • Summarize and rank data to identify top categories, products, regions, trends, averages, and other business insights.

For example, a user might ask Copilot to summarize the open incidents in an Atlas cluster supporting a payments application, identify delayed orders, or describe the fields and data types in the customer collection for a loyalty service. By industry, a supply chain team can investigate inventory, shipment, and warehouse exceptions. A financial services team can explore customer records, fraud alerts, and transaction investigations. And a retailer can ask questions about orders, loyalty, customer service, and personalization.

The connector can also help power business copilots and agents. Organizations can ground Copilot and other AI assistants in current MongoDB Atlas data for customer service, sales, operations, and decision support, bringing live operational context into the workflows where teams already work.

Connect to live data without migrating or indexing it

Organizations using MongoDB Atlas do not need to migrate their operational data, re-platform their applications, or rebuild their integrations to use the connector.

To do so, an administrator simply approves and enables the connector in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Users then sign in, and their existing Atlas permissions carry through to each query.

MongoDB Atlas remains the system of record. The connector queries Atlas directly rather than indexing a copy of Atlas data into Microsoft 365, so the information returned to users reflects the current state of the underlying application data.

This federated approach helps organizations connect their productivity layer to operational data while keeping that data in the environment where it is managed.

Put governance into every interaction

Making operational data more accessible requires controls that organizations can understand and manage. The connector is designed to support that approach through:

  • Permission-aware access: Each query runs as the signed-in user and honors the permissions already defined in MongoDB Atlas.

  • Administrator control: Admins approve the connector and can manage deployment through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

  • Read-only access: The connector is designed for read-only interaction with Atlas data.

  • Auditability: Administrators can audit connector activity in Microsoft Purview.

  • No separate search index: The connector queries Atlas on demand instead of indexing a copy of Atlas data in Microsoft 365.

Together, these controls give organizations a practical way to make operational information available through Copilot without giving up the governance model around the source data.

A foundation for more productive work

AI-powered productivity depends on access to relevant business context. By connecting Microsoft Copilot and other AI assistants to live MongoDB Atlas data through a federated connection, MongoDB and Microsoft are helping organizations make operational information easier to use without adding a data-movement project or another application to maintain. Users can get answers, summaries, and insights from live data through natural language, while technical teams retain control over the underlying systems and permissions.

For organizations already running MongoDB Atlas on Azure and Microsoft 365 Copilot, the connector provides a way to build on existing investments. Teams can explore high-value operational questions, validate measurable business outcomes, and develop repeatable patterns for bringing current data into everyday decisions.

The result is a simpler path from question to context to action—grounded in the systems organizations already use and governed by the permissions they already have.

title: How I Built a Financial Literacy App with React, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL
description:
Tags (pick these four): react, python, webdev, beginners

Body:

I built Compound, a financial literacy app that teaches things like compound interest, investing basics, and fees through short lessons, quizzes, and calculators. Here's how it's put together and what tripped me up along the way.

What it does

• A lesson path with quizzes that explain why each answer is right
• Calculators for compound interest, DCA, FIRE number, fee impact, mortgage breakdown, inflation hedge, and portfolio building
• Completion certificates
• Family accounts

The stack

• Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel
• Backend: FastAPI + PostgreSQL, deployed on Railway
• Auth: JWT
• Content loading: a protected /admin/seed endpoint that loads the lessons

Three things that tripped me up

  1. "vite: command not found" on Vercel.
    My deploy failed with vite build exited with 127. Exit code 127 means "command not found." My app lives in a frontend/ folder, but Vercel was building from the top of the repo, where there's no package.json, so it never even ran npm install. The fix was one setting: Project Settings → Build and Deployment → Root Directory → frontend.

  2. Keep secrets out of the repo.
    I use .env.example files with placeholder values and keep the real values in my host's environment variables. Before sharing the code, I exported a clean copy with git archive and searched it for .env files, keys, and connection strings. It's a quick check and worth doing every time.

  3. Rotate secrets at the source.
    After my hosting provider disclosed a security incident, I replaced my keys and passwords. The lesson: changing a value in your dashboard isn't enough. Revoke the old key with whoever issued it, or it may still work.

Try it

Live demo: https://compound-frontend-seven.vercel.app

If you'd like the source code to learn from or start your own project, it's available here (one-project license): https://dmlrod.gumroad.com/l/hdcon

What would you add? I'd love to hear what other developers would build into a learning app like this.

title: How Much of SAR Vehicle Recognition Is the Vehicle? Background Shortcuts, Angle Gaps and Partial Libraries on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR
description:
arXiv:2611.21827v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.

title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.22203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.22076v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.

title: Label Created Is Not Shipped: How Fake Tracking Quietly Buys Suppliers Two Weeks
description:
Your dashboard says shipped. The carrier has never seen the parcel.

The customer pastes the tracking number into the carrier's own site, because your store's tracking page has said the same thing for nine days: "Label created." She writes to you — reasonably — that she thinks the number is fake. You write to the supplier. The supplier writes back that the parcel is "in transit, please wait." Three parties, three different stories, and only one verifiable fact: no carrier has ever scanned the box.

This is the most common tracking failure in dropshipping, and it is not always fraud. A tracking number is created when a label is generated, which can happen days before a parcel is packed, handed over, or even exists. USPS says it plainly about its own status: "label created" means a label and a number exist, but the physical parcel has not yet been handed to USPS. The problem starts when that status stops progressing — and when a supplier uses the gap between label and handover to look punctual while nothing has moved.

The four shapes a bad tracking number takes

Not every stuck number is a scam, but stuck numbers fail in recognizable patterns, and a verification framework published this August by LooperBuy for cross-border sellers groups them the same way I now check them:

The number that does not exist. The carrier's official site returns no result at all. This is a fabricated code or a typo that nobody checked — either way, it was pasted into your dashboard without verification.

The label that never becomes a parcel. The number is real and validates everywhere, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. A label was printed, the order was marked shipped, and the box was never dropped off. Some platforms count label creation as shipment, so the supplier gains ten to fifteen extra days before anyone with authority starts asking questions.

The real number going somewhere else. The tracking shows genuine movement — to a different address, a different city, sometimes for a different, older order. Recycled and misdirected numbers are harder to catch than fake ones because every check returns "working." Only the destination gives them away.

The honest delay. A parcel genuinely handed over late, or a carrier that scans late. This happens too, and it is why the response should be an exception process, not an accusation: what matters is how long "label created" sits still, and whether the supplier can produce a handover explanation that matches the carrier's timeline.

Industry trackers note how common the deceptive versions have become: the Better Business Bureau has reported fake-tracking scams up more than 300% since 2020. Your customers read those warnings too. A dead tracking number no longer reads as a delay to them. It reads as a scam with your store's name on it.

Verify tracking like evidence, not like a dashboard field

Step 1: Check the number on the carrier's own site, not an aggregator. Aggregators cache, smooth, and sometimes invent intermediate states. The carrier's native page is the only version that counts in a dispute. DHL's own documentation says shipment events should generally appear within 24–48 hours of a merchant's confirmation — use that window as your escalation threshold for every carrier: label created is acceptable on day one, suspicious on day three, an exception on day five.

Step 2: Record seven facts when the number is issued. Carrier name, service level, tracking ID, dispatch date and timezone, origin country, expected delivery range, and the final-mile carrier if there is a handover. Suppliers provide numbers; almost none provide the context that lets you judge them. Asking for it, every order, changes the conversation when something stalls.

Step 3: Run a first-scan watchdog. The single highest-value check in this whole process is embarrassingly simple: has this parcel received an acceptance or pickup scan within 72 hours of the label? Sort your shipped orders by that one question every morning. Orders failing it go into an exception queue — supplier contacted with the order number and the carrier timeline, customer proactively told there is a delay and what you are doing about it — before the customer discovers it herself.

Step 4: Never reassure a customer with a number you have not opened. "Your parcel is in transit" written over a label-created status is a promise you cannot support. If the carrier shows no acceptance scan, say what is true: the label exists, the carrier has not scanned the parcel yet, you have escalated it, and here is the date by which you will refund or reship if there is still no movement. Specific honesty retains customers that vague reassurance loses.

Step 5: Score suppliers on first-scan time, and act on the score. One slow handover is logistics. A pattern — a supplier whose parcels routinely sit four or five days between label and acceptance — is a business model, and it is being funded by your dispute rate. Track median hours from label to first scan per supplier. It takes one spreadsheet column, and it will change which suppliers you trust with your best sellers faster than any review page will.

This is also a sync problem, not just a supplier problem. In GetDropFlow, the Magento tool I build, tracking numbers sync back to the store order automatically — which is only useful if someone is watching what the tracking does after it arrives. Whatever stack you run, the principle holds: a synced number nobody verifies is just a faster way to publish bad evidence to your own customers.

A concrete example: 60 orders, one quiet supplier

You ship 60 orders in a week through three suppliers. On day four, your first-scan check flags eleven parcels still at label created — all eleven from one supplier, who also supplied fourteen parcels that scanned normally. The supplier replies "warehouse busy, all shipped." The carrier timelines say otherwise for eleven boxes.

Because you caught it on day four instead of day twelve, you have options that still work: you reship the three highest-value orders through a backup supplier, refund two customers who needed the items for a date that has now passed, and tell the other six exactly what is happening with a dated commitment. Total cost: roughly $210 in reshipments and refunds. The alternative timeline — customers discovering dead tracking at day twelve, during the week your dispute window matters most — is the version that ends in chargebacks at several times that cost, plus a supplier problem you find out about from your payment processor.

The takeaway

A tracking number is not proof of shipment. It is a claim, and the carrier's acceptance scan is the proof. Verify numbers on the carrier's own site, escalate anything still at label created after 72 hours, tell customers the specific truth before they go looking, and score your suppliers on the gap between label and first scan. The suppliers who print labels early are buying themselves time with your store's credibility. Stop lending it to them unmonitored.

How many of your currently "shipped" orders have never had a carrier scan? It takes ten minutes to find out, and the number is rarely zero. Tell me what you found in the comments.

— Jinguo, maker of GetDropFlow (https://getdropflow.com)

title: Let your coding agent ask a QA agent: connect TestOptim over MCP with one sign-in
description:
Your coding agent says the change is done. A QA agent can check that. TestOptim runs AI tests on your web app and logs each failure as an issue with steps to reproduce. Its remote MCP server lets an MCP client list your projects, start test runs and read those issues.

Until now you had to create an API key and paste it into the client config. Since Nov 10 you can sign in with OAuth instead. Here is the full flow, step by step.

What we tested

We ran this flow with the MCP Inspector (v2.15.0, MCP protocol 2025-11-25). Other clients that support OAuth sign-in for remote servers use the same flow, but we did not test them for this post.

1. Add the server with only its URL

  • Transport: Streamable HTTP
  • URL: https://api.testoptim.com/api/mcp
  • No Authorization header.

The server answers the first request with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header that points to its OAuth metadata. The client finds the sign-in page from there and registers itself. You do not enter a client ID.

2. Sign in and approve

The client opens TestOptim in your browser. Sign in, then read the consent page. It names the client and lists what it can do:

  • See your projects
  • Start and stop test runs, and read their results
  • Read the issues TestOptim found
  • Start explorations of your app

Select Allow. Only the Owner or an Admin of the organization can approve.

3. The client connects

The browser returns to the client, and the server shows as connected. The client lists 8 tools: list_projects, start_test_run, get_test_run, stop_test_run, list_issues, get_issue, start_exploration and get_exploration.

4. Ask for results

We called three tools:

  1. list_projects returned our 2 projects.
  2. list_issues on one project returned the open issues, with severity and status.
  3. get_issue returned one issue in full: description, 5 steps to reproduce, expected and actual behaviour, the page URL and a screenshot link.

In a coding agent, the same calls look like this: "Run the QA tests on the checkout project and show me the critical issues." The agent calls start_test_run, waits with get_test_run, then reads the results with list_issues and get_issue. A test run uses your plan's test executions, the same as a run started in the app.

5. Remove access when you are done

Each OAuth connection appears in TestOptim under Settings → API keys, named after the client, for example "MCP Inspector (OAuth)". Disconnecting in the client does not remove it. To stop access, revoke it there.

API keys still work

If your client does not support OAuth sign-in, create an API key under Settings → API keys and send it as Authorization: Bearer topt_.... The setup for each client is in the TestOptim MCP README.

TestOptim plans start at $19 a month after a 7-day free trial that needs a card. testoptim.com

title: From GPT-3 to Agents: How AI Rewired Software in Six Years (2020-2026)
description:
If you had told a developer in early 2020 that by the end of 2026 most of their peers would use AI every working day, that software agents would open pull requests, and that a model would be better than a PhD-level human baseline on science questions while still fumbling an analog clock, they would have asked what you were smoking.

Well. It's mid-November 2026.

So let's do something we rarely do in this industry: stop, zoom out, and measure how far AI has actually travelled in six and a half years. Not hype. Numbers, milestones, and one uncomfortable pattern in the data that I think every developer should think about.

And at the end, there's a very concrete story about what all this means for a tool millions of people use, and a deadline that is 15 days away.

First, a correction: AI didn't "arrive" in 2020

Dev.to will eat me alive if I skip this. AI research is decades old. Deep learning broke through in 2012, and the Transformer architecture dropped in 2017.

But 2020 is the year the curve bent for everyone else. GPT-3 showed that if you scale a Transformer far enough, you get something that follows instructions from a handful of examples, with no task-specific training. That one idea (you can "program" a model with text) is the root of almost everything that followed. So I'm using 2020 as year zero of the era we're all living in.

The six-year timeline

Year The moment Why developers cared
2020 GPT-3 arrives (mid-year). AlphaFold 2 dominates the CASP14 protein-folding challenge (late-year). Few-shot prompting is born. And AI cracks a 50-year-old science problem.
2021 DALL·E (Jan). GitHub Copilot technical preview (Jun). For the first time, AI lives inside the editor.
2022 DALL·E 2, open-weights Stable Diffusion, then ChatGPT on Nov 30. Image generation goes open source. ChatGPT turns "AI" into a text box anyone can use; analysts estimated ~100M users within about two months.
2023 GPT-4, Claude, Llama 2 (open weights). Multimodal and long-context models; RAG becomes a default architecture; "prompt engineer" becomes a job title (briefly).
2024 Sora preview. Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry both honour AI-related work. Legitimacy. AI is now science, not just product.
2025 Reasoning models. DeepSeek-R1 open weights (Jan). Terminal and IDE coding agents go mainstream. Models "think" before answering. Costs fall. Developers start delegating, not just autocompleting.
2026 Agents inside everyday workflows. Stanford's AI Index says capability is accelerating, not plateauing. The question changes from "can it do it?" to "can I trust it, and who's accountable?"

What the numbers say

Timelines are fun; surveys are honest. Stack Overflow has been asking developers about AI since 2023, and the trajectory is steep.

Developers using AI tools (Stack Overflow):

2023 2024 2025 2026
44% 62% 79% only ~17% say they don't use AI tools at work

AI agents are the faster story. In the 2025 survey, 31% of respondents used agents. A smaller pulse survey in April 2026 found agent use had almost doubled to 59%, with Claude Code usage among agent users rising from 41% to 55%.

And outside our bubble, Lightcast's read of the Stanford data shows 2.5% of all US job postings now mention AI skills: up 55% in a year and roughly 300% over a decade.

So: massive adoption. Done, right? Not quite.

The uncomfortable pattern: usage up, trust down

Here's the part that doesn't fit the hype narrative.

  • In 2025, 46% of developers said they distrust AI output, versus 33% who trust it. Only 3% said they "highly trust" it.
  • In the 2026 survey, nearly half trust AI output when they can easily verify it. Just 6.6% would trust it with an important decision.
  • The most common frustration in 2025: solutions that are "almost right, but not quite."
  • Governance is lagging: only 24% of respondents said their employer had published approved AI tools or guidance.

I'd argue this is the defining dynamic of 2026: AI has become infrastructure faster than it has become trustworthy. We use it constantly and check it constantly.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index captures the same weirdness from the capability side: models now beat human baselines on PhD-level science questions, yet still fail at tasks like reading an analog clock. Researchers call this jagged intelligence: brilliant peaks, baffling potholes.

My takeaway (opinion, not data): the most valuable developer skill of the next few years isn't prompting. It's verification: writing tests, reading diffs, designing systems where a wrong-but-plausible answer gets caught.

The quiet shift nobody is tweeting about: AI left the data center

In 2020, running a serious neural network meant renting GPUs and calling an API. That model (your data goes up, the answer comes down, and you pay per call) defined the first half of this era.

The second half is different. Thanks to WebAssembly, WebGPU, and runtimes like ONNX Runtime Web, a browser tab can now run real models locally:

import * as ort from "onnxruntime-web";

// Simplified: load a model once, cache it, run inference on-device
const session = await ort.InferenceSession.create("/models/segmenter.onnx", {
  executionProviders: ["wasm"], // or "webgpu" where supported
});

const result = await session.run({ input: imageTensor });
// Nothing was uploaded. No API key. No per-call bill.

Why this matters:

  • Privacy: sensitive data never leaves the device.
  • Cost: inference runs on the user's hardware, so there are no per-image credits.
  • Latency and availability: after the first download there is no round trip, and some tools work offline.
  • Longevity: your tool can't be switched off because someone else's API changed pricing.

That last point just became very real for millions of people.

Case study: the end of an era

For years, remove.bg was the answer to "how do I remove a background?" It popularised one-click AI background removal and was a textbook example of the cloud-API era.

Now its standalone website is closing on December 1, 2026, with the functionality moving into Canva (which has owned it since 2021). Reporting based on remove.bg's own FAQ says the closure is at 9:00 CET, unused pay-as-you-go credits expire, and the self-serve API moves to Leonardo.Ai (also Canva-owned). If you rely on it, export your usage reports and invoices before the cutoff.

There's a lesson here that has nothing to do with any single company: if your workflow depends on someone else's server, it has an expiry date you don't control.

If you're already in the Canva ecosystem, Canva is the official successor and will be fine for you. But if you want something that doesn't ask for an account or a credit card, or send your photos anywhere, read on.

Meet APIC: the on-device approach, in practice

Full disclosure: I built APIC, so weigh my opinion accordingly. But everything below is verifiable in about 60 seconds, which is exactly why I'm comfortable showing it to a room full of skeptical developers.

👉 apic-studio.vercel.app

APIC (Advanced Image Processing Center) is a free, browser-based photo editor where the AI runs on your device. No upload. No credits. No account required to edit or export (there's an optional Google sign-in, nothing more).

Background removal, the remove.bg use case

  • On-device AI cut-out with three model sizes: Light (~5 MB, built for phones), Fast (~44 MB), and Maximum (~176 MB, multi-pass, best on a PC). Models download once and are cached.
  • A Restore / Erase brush to fix hair, fur and awkward edges, plus one-click replacement with white, black or a blurred copy of your photo.
  • Full-resolution output as transparent PNG or WebP.
  • Batch mode: remove backgrounds, resize, compress and convert many images, then download one ZIP.

And because I got tired of juggling ten tabs, it's eleven tools in one

  • Remove Object: paint over a person, sign or blemish; inpainting runs locally (MI-GAN ~28 MB, or LaMa ~208 MB for big, complex fills).
  • AI upscale (2x / 4x) with Real-ESRGAN.
  • Compress to an exact file size ("under 200 KB" for that upload form), resize, and convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, BMP, ICO, PDF and PSD, with HEIC photos accepted as input.
  • Pro colour tools: histogram, RGB curves, HSL mixer, 3-way grading, and 3D LUT (.cube) export for DaVinci Resolve, Premiere and Photoshop.
  • Social presets for 15+ networks with safe-zone guides; Layers with blend modes and PSD import/export; Hide area to blur or pixelate faces, plates and card numbers before you share.
  • A Windows app that runs fully offline, no account needed.

The honest trade-offs (because you'd find them anyway):

  • The first run of any AI tool downloads its model, so it's slower once and fast afterwards.
  • The heaviest models are best on a desktop-class machine. On phones, use Light.
  • It's a browser tool, not a replacement for Photoshop's full ecosystem.
  • I'm one developer shipping this, not a 500-person company. Feedback genuinely shapes the roadmap.

Try it with your hardest photo

Don't test it on a clean studio shot. Take the image remove.bg struggled with (wispy hair, glass, a busy background) and run it through APIC's Remove BG tab on Maximum. Use the Restore brush if needed. If it doesn't hold up, tell me where it failed. If it does, you've just saved yourself a subscription.

Make it your default (it takes 20 seconds)

With 15 days left on the old default, now is the moment to build a new habit:

  1. Open apic-studio.vercel.app and drop in a photo.
  2. Bookmark it and pin the tab, so "remove background" now means one click on your own bookmarks bar.
  3. Send it to the one person in your team, family or client list who still says "just use remove.bg."
  4. Tell me what's missing: a comment below, or find me on GitHub / dev.to. I read everything.

(I also wrote a shorter, practical guide on the remove.bg shutdown specifically: remove.bg Is Shutting Down — Here's a Free, No-Upload Alternative.)

So, how much AI is there in six years?

Started as a research demo behind a waitlist in 2020. By 2026 it's in the editor, the terminal, the job postings, the Nobel Prizes, the survey data, and increasingly, in your browser tab, running on your own hardware.

The next six years won't be about who has the biggest model. They'll be about three questions:

  1. Can I verify it? (trust)
  2. Who controls it? (open weights, on-device, no kill switch)
  3. Does it respect the user? (privacy by architecture, not by policy)

The tools that win on all three won't need a marketing budget. They'll just be the ones people quietly never switch away from.

I'm betting on that. Come try APIC, and tell me where I'm wrong.

Your turn: what was your "oh, this changes everything" AI moment between 2020 and 2026: GPT-3, Copilot, ChatGPT, or something else? Drop it in the comments. 👇

Sources: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 · Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026 coverage · Stanford HAI AI Index 2026 · Lightcast · remove.bg shutdown reporting

title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

title: How to check your Rust port against the Python original (with five real bugs it caught)
description:
You rewrote a Python library in Rust. The benchmarks look great and the test suite is green. One question is left, and it is the one your users care about: does it still do exactly what the old code did?

Your tests can't fully answer that. They check the inputs you thought of. The differences hide in the inputs nobody thought of.

The good news is that a port comes with something most code never has: a complete specification. It's the old code. You don't need to read the Rust or reason about it. Run both versions on the same input and compare what comes back. Repeat until they disagree.

Here is how to do that in practice, and five places it found real bugs.

The idea in one function 

def same(input):
    return python_version(input) == rust_version(input)

Everything else is detail. Where do the inputs come from? How do you compare outputs fairly? What if one side raises and the other doesn't?

Doing it with equiv

I use equiv, an open-source checker written in Rust. It generates inputs and runs each side in its own Python process. It stops at the first input where they disagree. Every run writes a receipt you can re-run byte for byte, which matters when you hand a bug to a maintainer.

Point it at both versions of a function:

equiv review port.py original.py parse str --errors-agree

--errors-agree counts it as agreement when both sides raise, because a port rarely raises the exact same exception class. One side raising while the other returns is still a difference.

If the port is a new release of the same package, give each side its own environment:

equiv review new.py old.py fn str \
  --reference-python old-env/bin/python \
  --candidate-python new-env/bin/python \
  --versions-of yourpackage

Each side reports which version it actually loaded, so you never compare the wrong build by accident.

A note on limits: this is testing, not proof. A clean run means the two versions agreed on every input it tried, and the output says how many. It works on functions that take and return plain Python values.

Five real examples

1. django-rusty-templates: a panic and a wrong count

django-rusty-templates is a Rust implementation of Django's template engine. Compared with Django's own engine across 27 checks:

  • wordwrap panicked on text starting with a non-breaking space.
  • This one is my favourite: 
'a<b'|capfirst|length

(that is, capitalise the string, then count its characters)

Django says 3. The Rust version said 6, because it escaped < to < too early and then counted the extra characters.

Seven differences in all (#587, #593), all fixed in five merged pull requests.

2. LiteLLM: a regression in a release candidate

LiteLLM moved parts of its core to Rust in 1.110. Running the last Python release (1.109.1) against the release candidate, each in its own environment:

  • temperature=1 was suddenly refused for 72 of 405 Claude model names that the previous release accepted (#51394, fixed in #52341).
  • The Rust-backed tokenizer differed from tiktoken on lone surrogates and very large token IDs (#51601, fixed in #51720).

3. sqlfluff: feed it SQL its tests never run

sqlfluff ships a Rust parser next to its Python one, and its CI already compares them on its own fixtures. They agree on all 16,442 statements. The trick was to give each dialect's parser SQL written for other dialects, which CI never does. Three parsers split. In one T-SQL statement, Python read the word day as a date part and Rust read it as a column name (#9095, fixed the next day).

4. ua-parser: three engines, one user agent

uap-python has three interchangeable engines, one of them in Rust. For Applebot's desktop crawler, the Python engine said "Mac" and the Rust engine said "Spider" (#334). The maintainer traced it to one rule and wrote a fix (uap-core#675). Running all three engines over the 17,820 user agents in the project's own tests: 9 disagreements before the fix, none after.

5. dulwich: a panic that except Exception can't catch

dulwich is Git in pure Python with a Rust speed-up for sorting tree entries. With names containing a slash, the Rust comparison stopped being a consistent ordering. Below 21 entries it sorted differently. From 21 entries it panicked, and a PyO3 panic is a BaseException, so ordinary except Exception handling doesn't catch it. The maintainer reproduced it and merged a fix the same day (#2582).

What I'd do if I were porting a library today

  1. Keep the old version runnable until the new one has been compared with it. Once you delete it, you lose your specification.
  2. Test the inputs nobody chose:
    • text that isn't English, including non-breaking spaces;
    • empty values and huge values;
    • inputs from a neighbouring format (another SQL dialect, another user agent family);
    • every input form the API accepts, not just the documented one.
  3. Treat a panic in the port as a bug, even if Python raised too. Python callers can't catch it the normal way.
  4. Decide which side is right before you ship. In the ua-parser case, the Rust engine was the correct one. Either way, your users shouldn't be the ones who find out.

The full write-up, with every issue and pull request linked, is on my site: Running Rust ports against the Python they replace.

If you're porting a library and want a second pair of eyes on it, I'm happy to run it against the original. Say hello in the comments.

title: HandRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Hand Pose Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.22164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.

title: Preserving Visual UI Stability with TypeScript Snapshot Testing in Vue 3: The LegacyCategoryLegend Component
description:
During large-scale frontend modernization efforts, teams frequently convert dozens of components from JavaScript to TypeScript. While stateful components require deep assertions on reactive state, mutations, and API calls, pure static presentation components—such as legends, badges, and informational tooltips—serve a different purpose: preserving visual markup and design token consistency.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3195), I converted the LegacyCategoryLegend component to TypeScript and established an automated snapshot test suite using Vitest.

Here is an architectural look at how lightweight snapshot testing protects visual UI elements during progressive migrations.

1. The Component: Historical Contributor Tier Badges

On the Top Annual Contributors leaderboard, the platform honors historical contribution milestones (prior to the current point-based scoring system).

LegacyCategoryLegend.vue displays color-coded badges mapping to historical recognition tiers:

  • SuperStar (Warning badge): More than 75 merged MRs
  • Star (Info badge): Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  • Enthusiast (Secondary badge): Between 5 and 10 merged MRs 
<!-- LegacyCategoryLegend.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BBadge } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
</script>

<template>
  <div class="text-muted small mt-2">
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="warning">SuperStar</BBadge> More than 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="info">Star</BBadge> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span>
      <BBadge variant="secondary">Enthusiast</BBadge> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
    </span>
  </div>
</template>

Adding <script setup lang="ts"> ensures typed integration with bootstrap-vue-next component exports without any runtime overhead.

2. Fast, Deterministic Snapshot Testing with Vitest

For static presentation components without props or reactive state, writing redundant DOM query assertions for every badge text can be unnecessarily verbose.

Instead, a deterministic snapshot test using shallowMount provides 100% coverage while locking down the exact HTML structure and CSS utility classes:

// LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import LegacyCategoryLegend from './LegacyCategoryLegend.vue';

const createWrapper = () =>
  shallowMount(LegacyCategoryLegend, {
    global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true },
  });

it('matches the snapshot', () => {
  expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});

Why this pattern works well:

  • Instant Regression Detection: Any unintentional change to Bootstrap badge variants (warning, info, secondary), spacing classes (me-3, mt-2), or milestone descriptions is immediately flagged by the Vitest snapshot runner.
  • Stub Slot Rendering: Using global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true } ensures that child slot content (like "SuperStar") is preserved inside <b-badge-stub> rather than discarded.
  • Zero Boilerplate: The spec is concise, clean, and runs in milliseconds.

3. Snapshot Output Verification

When executed, Vitest records the rendered template in __snapshots__/LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts.snap:

// Vitest Snapshot v1
exports[`matches the snapshot 1`] = `
"<div class="text-muted small mt-2">
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="warning">SuperStar</b-badge-stub> More than 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="info">Star</b-badge-stub> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span>
    <b-badge-stub variant="secondary">Enthusiast</b-badge-stub> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
  </span>
</div>"
`;

This guarantees visual and structural stability as the underlying UI library upgrades across minor and major versions.

Key Takeaways

  1. Use Snapshot Tests for Pure Presentational UI: When a component has no internal logic or conditional branching, snapshot testing offers high confidence with minimal test maintenance.
  2. Always Enable renderStubDefaultSlot: In Vue Test Utils, shallow mounting child components can hide slot text unless renderStubDefaultSlot: true is configured.
  3. Every Component Counts: Converting even small UI components to TypeScript ensures the whole codebase maintains 100% type coverage without gaps.

Check out the merged Merge Request on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Contributors MR !3195

Author: Manish Kumar
