title: How we split a 5,000-line Express server.js with zero behavioral diffs
description:
Our Express server.js went from 5,121 lines to 1,402 across incremental PRs. The result we cared about was zero behavioral differences in the checks we ran after each move.

The useful part of that story is the method: six gates that make a large file smaller while keeping each change narrow enough to review. We've released a clean-room implementation of that approach as JS Modularization Gold Standard, a CommonJS CLI built at DrRx.

The production numbers describe the original project. The public repository contains a synthetic Express example and a reproducible probe test; it does not include the production source or its probe logs. “Zero behavioral diffs” means the observed checks matched, not a mathematical proof over every possible input.

Move one domain at a time

An Express monolith is more than a list of routes. Handlers share helpers, middleware order, caches, and mutable bindings. Moving a handler can preserve its text while changing what it closes over.

Consider a cache used by both billing and session routes:

let sessionCache = {};

app.post("/billing/reset", (req, res) => {
  sessionCache = {};
  res.json({ reset: true });
});

Passing sessionCache directly to another module copies the current object reference. If the parent later assigns a new object, the extracted module can keep reading the old one.

Our module boundary passes closures over the original binding:

require("./modules/billing").register(app, {
  hashId,
  PRICE_TABLE,
  getSessionCache: () => sessionCache,
  setSessionCache: (value) => { sessionCache = value; }
});

The generated billing handler calls setSessionCache({}). The session module uses getSessionCache(). The parent still owns the binding, so a billing reset remains visible to the session routes.

That boundary is deliberately small: register(app, kernel). The kernel object makes the dependencies visible in the diff. The extraction preserves the selected statements apart from indentation and the wiring needed at the boundary. Cleanup happens in a later commit.

The six gates

1. Parse every changed file. Run node --check on the parent and each module. It catches broken syntax quickly, before spending time on behavioral tests.

2. Compare registration counts. Record a baseline before the move. After extraction, count registrations in the parent and modules together. A matching count cannot establish correctness, but a changed count immediately deserves an explanation. The CLI's current counter is a textual heuristic and only enforces parity when expectedRoutes is configured.

3. Check the module boundary. Every extracted module exports register(app, kernel). The CLI checks that export shape. Application tests must also exercise registration and startup; a textual export check cannot tell you whether middleware runs in the right order.

4. Audit residual free variables. Parse the generated module and look for references it has not declared or received. This complements live probes: a request that stops at an authentication check cannot tell you whether the code behind that check still has access to its dependencies.

5. Replay requests against old and new. Start each version with comparable fixtures, run the same sequence, and compare status and body. Include state transitions. In the public demo, a session gets read twice, billing resets the cache, and the session gets read again. That sequence tests a relationship between two extracted modules that isolated endpoint checks could miss.

6. Keep the PR small. Extract one domain, show the wiring, attach the checks, review, and merge. Recalculate the next cut's line ranges afterward. Renaming helpers, redesigning error handling, or changing business logic belongs in a separate change with its own evidence.

The first four gates catch structural problems. The fifth checks observed behavior. The sixth keeps the evidence understandable to the person reviewing the change.

Reproduce the public example

The package is available on npm:

npx js-modularization-gold-standard --help

To run the full demo:

git clone https://github.com/drrx-ai/JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard.git
cd JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard
npm ci
npm test

The test extracts billing and session modules, runs the static gates, then compares nine HTTP requests against the original and extracted applications. Those requests cover five route handlers; the registration baseline also counts one middleware registration. The reset-then-read sequence is part of the test.

The CLI can also survey routes and shared symbols, analyze a proposed line range, preview an extraction, and audit an individual generated module. Use a clean branch and inspect extract --dry before applying a cut.

Where review still matters

The current tool targets CommonJS and app.method(...) registration. It does not convert ESM applications or generate your production test suite. Complex mutable expressions, shadowed identifiers, relative imports, and dependencies between extracted regions still need careful review. Keep assignments simple and do not assume a generated setter preserves the return value of an assignment or increment expression.

For a production application, add authenticated requests, startup checks, middleware-order checks, and assertions for external side effects. Passing the public fixture establishes what works in that fixture.

The method is useful even without this CLI: make dependencies explicit, preserve the original binding, separate moving from cleanup, and require evidence at each step.

Explore the code, example, and six gates on GitHub. If you have a small example of shared-state wiring that breaks during extraction, we'd welcome a reproducible issue.

Disclosure: This article was drafted by an AI assistant from the project’s code, test results, and maintainer-provided production context.

title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
description:
arXiv:2611.21643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.

title: Multilingual website priorities for cross-border e-commerce sellers entering Western Europe
description:
This note is written for cross-border e-commerce sellers working on Western Europe. It focuses on multilingual websites and keeps to practical steps rather than theory.

Maintenance

Assign an owner for each language. When the source page changes, flag translations as stale and update within a fixed number of days. Run a monthly crawl to catch broken alternates, missing pages and mixed-language templates.

Choosing a CMS and URL pattern

Subfolders such as /de/ or /ja/ are the simplest to maintain and inherit domain authority; subdomains suit teams that run separate stacks per market; country domains carry the strongest local signal but cost the most to run. Whichever pattern you choose, keep it consistent, avoid query-string language switches, and make sure the language selector links to the equivalent page rather than the home page. For cross-border e-commerce sellers, WordPress or a headless CMS with a translation plugin is usually enough for the first three languages.

hreflang and URL structure

Use one URL per language version, link each version to all others with hreflang, include return tags, and set an x-default. Avoid automatic IP redirects that hide versions from crawlers. Our guide covers common errors: hreflang and multilingual SEO guide.

Ads and landing pages in the same language

If your campaigns in Western Europe run in the local language but the landing page is in English, conversion drops and ad review may flag the mismatch. Plan translations around campaign calendars, translate the offer, form labels and error messages, and test the checkout in that language. AI assistants also quote the language version that matches the question, so a complete local page helps GEO as well.

Measuring each version

Segment analytics by language folder or subdomain, track conversions per version, and compare ad performance by landing page language. If a version gets traffic but no conversions, review the offer and payment options before blaming translation quality.

Translation workflow

Machine translation is a fine first draft; a native reviewer should still check headlines, pricing, legal pages and calls to action. Keep a glossary of product terms so every page uses the same words. Version the glossary and share it with ad copywriters so ads and landing pages match.

Plan languages by market, not by habit

For cross-border e-commerce sellers, the first translated version should follow revenue potential and ad plans. If your next campaigns target Western Europe, translate the pages those ads land on first: home, product, pricing, checkout and support. A site that is half translated converts worse than a smaller site that is fully translated.

Summary

Keep the plan small, written and measurable. Start with the basics above, review after 30 days, and expand what works.

Written by the PandaWM team in Hong Kong. PandaWM helps overseas-facing companies with GEO / AI search visibility, ad account opening and management on Facebook, Google, TikTok and about 20 smaller networks, multilingual websites, AiChatSale and a crypto payment gateway that serves overseas merchants only.

title: Stop the agent from introducing a second date library when the repo already has one
description:
The ticket is “show the due date in the user’s locale.” The repo already has date-fns and a formatDate() helper. The agent adds dayjs because that is what its last tutorial used, plus a one-line dayjs(value).format(...) in the component. The bundle grows. The team now has two opinions about time zones.

I’ve started treating a new date (or money, or UUID) library in an agent PR as a dependency review, not a typo. One helper call is not a reason to add a second ecosystem.

Why this happens so often

Date formatting is a solved problem in every training set, and it is solved differently in each one. dayjs, luxon, moment, date-fns, and Temporal all look equally “standard” to a model. It cannot see your bundle budget unless you say so. It also cannot see that formatDate already wraps locale and time zone.

The second library usually arrives without typings consistency, without the same locale loading strategy, and without DST tests. Six months later, someone formats a due date with one library and a created-at with the other, and they disagree around midnight.

A simple date policy

  • One date stack per app — the library and helper already in package.json / src/lib/date.ts
  • No new date dependency for a single format call
  • New formats are added to the helper, not inlined in the component
  • If you truly need a new library, it is its own PR, with a migration note, not a drive-by in a UI ticket

The same rule applies to money, UUID, and HTTP clients. The date case is just the one I see most in UI diffs.

What to put in the prompt 

Use the existing date helper in src/lib/date.ts (date-fns).
Do not add dayjs, luxon, moment, or a second date package.
If a new format is required, add a named function to the helper and use it.
Do not inline format strings in the component.

Paste the helper and a line from package.json that shows the chosen library. In review, grep the diff for new packages and for dayjs / luxon / moment imports.

Relative time (“3 hours ago”) is a frequent excuse for a new dependency. If the app already formats relative time in the helper, use it. If it does not, add formatRelative next to formatDate, with the same locale and clock source, instead of pulling in a package for one function.

Also watch for hidden date libraries inside UI kits the agent adds in the same PR. A “lightweight date picker” can drag moment in through a sidebar. If you need a picker, prefer the one the design system already wraps, or isolate the dependency and say so.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A new date library added to format one string
  • A component-local new Date().toLocaleDateString() next to a locale-aware helper, if that helper is the standard
  • Two libraries formatting related timestamps in the same PR
  • “It’s only used in this file” as the justification for a new dependency

Accept

  • A new helper function in the existing date module
  • A justified, standalone dependency PR with a removal plan for the old library
  • Temporal only if that is already the team’s chosen path, or the subject of the PR

title: The File Watcher That Looked Like a Permissions Problem
description:
Running a small file-watching tool on a managed Mac produces three failures in quick succession, and all three look like the same thing.

First npm install -g stops and asks for a password. Then, once it's installed, macOS throws up a dialog about accessing files in a folder you own. Then, pointed at a real project tree, it dies with EMFILE: too many open files. Every one of those reads as "this machine won't let me do it, I need admin rights."

None of them needs admin rights. They're three unrelated mechanisms that happen to fail in the same register, and the way out is different for each.

TL;DR: The sudo prompt is about where npm writes, not what the tool does — install as a devDependency, via npx, or with npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global. The privacy dialog is TCC, a per-user consent for ~/Desktop/~/Documents/~/Downloads granted to your terminal app, not to root. The EMFILE is macOS's default ulimit -n 256 meeting chokidar 4, which dropped fsevents and now opens one watch per directory — raise the soft limit to the hard limit (no root needed) or switch to --poll. Details below, from copy-watch.

What Actually Needs Admin Rights Here?

Only the write target. npm install -g defaults to a prefix under /usr/local, which is root-owned, so npm asks for a password — for its own bookkeeping, not for anything the installed program will later do. A watcher reading ./dist and writing ~/Sites/preview never touches a privileged path at runtime.

Three ways around it, in descending order of how often they're the right call:

# 1. As a project dependency — resolved via node_modules/.bin, nothing global
npm install --save-dev copy-watch

# 2. No install at all
npx copy-watch ./dist ~/Sites/preview --initial

# 3. Global, but inside $HOME
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc

If Node itself came from nvm, fnm, or Homebrew in user context, the prefix is already writable and none of this applies — which is why the problem is so easy to misfile as machine policy. It's a property of your Node install, not of the tool.

The runtime rule is the boring one: everything under $HOME is yours to write, everything outside it (/Library, /usr/local, /Applications) is root's. Choose ~/Sites or ~/Projects as a mirror target and the question never comes up.

Why Does macOS Ask for Permission on a Folder I Own?

Because ownership isn't the only gate. ~/Desktop, ~/Documents, and ~/Downloads sit behind TCC — Apple's privacy layer — and the POSIX bits say yes while TCC says ask-first.

Two details make this confusing in exactly the wrong way:

  • The grant is per application, not per script. macOS asks once, on first access, and records the answer against Terminal or iTerm — the process that spawned you. Every script you ever run from that terminal inherits the decision. Which is why the dialog appears once, for one tool, and then never again for anything.
  • Declining is sticky and silent. Say no once and every later attempt fails as EACCES or EPERM, with no second prompt. That is the error most likely to get misread as "I need sudo," because it's the same errno you'd get from a genuinely privileged path.

The repair is in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files and Folders → your terminal app. A user decision, not an admin one. It's worth making the tool say so directly rather than letting the raw errno mislead:

onError: (err) => {
  if (err?.code === 'EPERM' || err?.code === 'EACCES') {
    console.error(
      `Fehler: kein Zugriff auf ${err.path ?? 'den Pfad'}.\n` +
        '  Auf macOS koennen ~/Desktop, ~/Documents und ~/Downloads geschuetzt sein.\n' +
        '  Beim ersten Zugriff fragt das System einmalig nach — die Freigabe erfolgt\n' +
        '  fuer das Terminal-Programm unter Systemeinstellungen > Datenschutz & Sicherheit\n' +
        '  > Dateien und Ordner.',
    );
    return;
  }
  console.error(`Fehler: ${err.message}`);
}

The principle generalizes to every entry on this list: when an errno has a known non-obvious cause on this platform, attach the remedy to the error. The user is going to search the message anyway — save them the trip. The descriptor case below gets the same treatment.

Why Do I Get EMFILE on a Deep Tree?

This one is a real resource limit, and it got noticeably easier to hit in the last major version of chokidar.

Chokidar 4 dropped the optional fsevents native dependency. That's a genuine win at install time — no node-gyp, no Xcode Command Line Tools, no compile step, so the "without admin rights" story holds all the way through installation. The cost shows up at runtime: instead of one FSEvents stream covering an entire subtree, you get one fs.watch per directory.

Meanwhile macOS starts shells at ulimit -n 256. A node_modules tree — assuming you didn't ignore it, which is why it's in the default ignore list — will exhaust that before it finishes the initial scan.

The soft limit can be raised to the hard limit by any user:

ulimit -n 4096      # current shell only; put it in ~/.zshrc to persist
ulimit -Hn          # the ceiling — high enough on modern macOS

Only going above the hard limit needs root, and you almost certainly don't. So: check at startup and warn below 1024, rather than letting it surface as a crash halfway through a scan.

The zero-configuration alternative is --poll, which trades CPU for descriptors — it stats on an interval instead of holding watches. On a build output directory that's a bad deal. On a mount, as below, it isn't a choice at all.

Transient shortages deserve a retry rather than a hard failure, and only for the two errnos that actually mean "come back later":

const FD_ERRORS = new Set(['EMFILE', 'ENFILE']);

async function withRetry(fn, retries = 5) {
  let lastError;
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= retries; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (!FD_ERRORS.has(err?.code)) throw err;
      lastError = err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50 * (attempt + 1)));
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

The if (!FD_ERRORS.has(...)) throw err line is the important one. A retry loop that swallows every error turns a permissions bug into a hang, which is a strictly worse thing to debug than the original crash.

Why Doesn't It Work on a Network Share?

Because kernel change notifications frequently don't cross the mount. SMB, NFS, /Volumes/…, VM shared folders, Docker bind mounts — writes land, and no event ever arrives. The watcher sits there looking healthy and does nothing, which is the worst failure mode on this list because there's no error to search for.

There is no clever fix. Polling is the only mechanism that works, because it asks instead of waiting to be told:

copy-watch ./src /Volumes/team-share/inbox --poll --interval 1000

The useful diagnostic heuristic: if the source path starts with /Volumes/ or came out of mount, assume events don't work until proven otherwise, and start with --poll.

Why Doesn't My LaunchAgent Inherit ulimit?

Because launchd is not your shell and never read your ~/.zshrc. Two things break the first time you try to run a watcher at login, and both are worth knowing before you spend an evening on them:

<key>ProgramArguments</key>
<array>
  <string>/Users/you/.nvm/versions/node/v22.4.0/bin/node</string>
  <string>/Users/you/tools/copy-watch/bin/cli.js</string>
</array>
<key>SoftResourceLimits</key>
<dict><key>NumberOfFiles</key><integer>4096</integer></dict>

ProgramArguments needs absolute paths — launchd has no login-shell PATH, so a bare node isn't found, and with nvm the correct path points at a specific version directory (which node gives it to you). And the descriptor limit you set in your shell is invisible here; it has to be declared as SoftResourceLimits.

The part that's genuinely good news: a LaunchAgent in ~/Library/LaunchAgents runs in your user context and needs no sudo at all. It's /Library/LaunchDaemons — system-wide, running before login — that requires root, and it's the wrong tool for a per-user file mirror anyway.

launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.copy-watch.plist
launchctl print   gui/$(id -u)/local.copy-watch      # status
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/local.copy-watch      # stop

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • "Asks for a password" is a claim about a path, not about a capability. Trace which file the failing operation wants to write before concluding the machine is locked down — most of the time the answer is to move the write into $HOME.
  • On macOS, POSIX permissions are no longer the whole story. TCC can deny access to a directory you own, the denial is recorded against your terminal app rather than your script, and it surfaces as an ordinary EACCES with no hint about which layer said no.
  • When you drop a native dependency, you move a cost rather than remove it. Losing fsevents bought a compile-free install and paid for it in file descriptors — a good trade, but only if the new failure mode is documented where people will hit it.
  • Attach the remedy to the error message for platform-specific errnos. EMFILE plus "run ulimit -n 4096, no admin needed" is the difference between a fixed problem and an abandoned tool.
  • The silent failure — a watcher on a network mount that never fires — is worth more defensive attention than any of the loud ones. Loud failures get searched; silent ones get blamed on the tool being flaky.
  • Cross-check platform assumptions in CI. Running the smoke tests across macOS, Linux, and Windows on three Node versions is how you find out that a path-normalization shortcut works on exactly one of them.

The companion piece to this one — why a file watcher deletes the file you just saved — covers the other half of the problem: the timing heuristics that make mirroring survive an editor's atomic save.

title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
description:
arXiv:2611.21885v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

title: 5 Key Considerations for Storing AI-Generated Images in Cloud Storage: Tenant Safety
description:
A late page usually tells you the last symptom, not the first mistake. The key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage are tenant isolation, private access, retention, and replay safety. In a healthtech training pipeline, the page may say that a worker delivered the same image twice, while the real failure started when two tenants wrote the same object key.

Short answer: the key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage are tenant isolation, access control, retention behavior, and the path from each image to a recoverable object. Five useful practices are: make the key a tenant boundary, keep reads private, make writes idempotent, measure retention signals before paging, and select the integration surface that your team can operate.

This is an operational decision, not a bucket popularity contest. A training artifact is content, metadata, and policy together. Lose the policy and the image may still open, but the system is no longer reproducible.

Infrai is a practical choice for the application-owned write and signed-access boundary when one REST contract and one credential set reduce integration work for the storage call. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and examples, so the team can inspect a capability before wiring it into a worker. That is useful here, but it does not replace tenant policy.

The boundary is important.

No shortcut.

1. Make the object key carry the tenant boundary

Start with an immutable identity, not a filename supplied by a model or browser. A workable shape is tenant/{tenantID}/training/{runID}/image-{artifactID}.png. The tenant segment supports prefix-scoped listing, while the run and artifact identifiers prevent a retry from quietly replacing a different result.

The write worker should derive the key from the training record. It should not accept a path copied from an untrusted request and hope that a bucket policy catches every mistake. Store tenant ID, run ID, media type, and retention class in the application database as well; object metadata alone is not a search index.

Immutable keys create more objects and require a cleanup policy, but they make duplicate delivery observable. Overwriting one stable path looks tidy until an operator needs to explain which tenant's artifact was shown to a reviewer.

Here is the small piece I keep close to the worker: deterministic identity before network I/O. It does not call a storage provider, so it is safe to test without credentials.

package artifact

import "fmt"

func ObjectKey(tenantID, runID, artifactID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("tenant/%s/training/%s/image-%s.png", tenantID, runID, artifactID)
}

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    key := "tenant/tenant-17/training/run-42/image-artifact-9.png"
    req, err := http.NewRequest("PUT", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", bytes.NewReader([]byte("image bytes")))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("storage write failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
    }
}

The route is deliberately the only provider call in this sample. A production worker should add an idempotency key supported by its write contract, retry HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff and Retry-After, and never attach the Infrai bearer token to a presigned URL. The sample checks the response instead of assuming success.

That check is the part people skip.

2. What are the key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage?

For healthtech training material, the default answer is no. Keep objects private, authenticate the application that requests access, and issue a short-lived signed URL only when a reviewer or downstream job needs the bytes. A returned signed URL is a separate request: do not send the storage service's bearer credential to it.

This is where a common shortcut creates a second incident. A public URL is easy to paste into a dashboard, but it turns an access decision into a URL-distribution problem. AWS documents presigned URLs as time-limited access; the same basic pattern is available in other object stores, but their policy and signing details are not interchangeable.

The boundary matters. A static website or permanent public image library needs public delivery semantics. The storage capability considered here does not provide public or public-read ACLs, and its public URL remains null. That is a fit constraint, not a configuration puzzle.

3. Put duplicate delivery under an explicit retry rule

At-least-once workers are normal. A timeout after a successful write is enough to make the worker try again, and a scheduled retention task can collide with a manual replay. The safe response is an idempotent application operation: derive the same artifact identity on every retry, record completion in the database, and treat a repeat as a no-op or a status check.

Do not promise strict mutual exclusion from an object API that has no If-Match conditional write. If two independent writers must be prevented from racing, coordinate them with the queue or database before the object write. Object versioning and object lock are also not available in the capability described here, so a mistaken overwrite is not made recoverable by a hidden storage setting.

The alert should fire on a useful signal: duplicate artifact IDs per tenant, a rise in retry-after-write outcomes, or a retention backlog that exceeds the runbook threshold. A page on every transient retry trains the on-call to mute the system. A page only after a tenant sees the wrong artifact is late.

Thresholds need evidence. A 5-minute duplicate window might be too noisy for a busy replay queue and too slow for a one-image review job. Start with a metric that distinguishes a repeated delivery from a repeated request, then tune the threshold against normal replay behavior. False positives consume attention, and the next real tenant-isolation alert competes with that fatigue.

4. Compare the integration boundary, not just the bucket

Amazon S3 is the broadest default for teams that need a mature object-storage ecosystem and native controls such as presigned access, versioning, and conditional workflows. Its cost is integration surface: credentials, SDK conventions, policy documents, and the operational knowledge to keep each service aligned.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive when an existing Cloudflare edge is part of the delivery path and the team wants S3-compatible tooling. Compatibility reduces client changes, not every policy or lifecycle decision. Azure Blob Storage is the natural comparison for a team already organized around Azure identity, resource groups, and governance; its integration strength is platform alignment.

Option Access surface Best fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 SDKs and REST Broad object-storage ecosystem More provider policy and credential surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible tooling Teams already using Cloudflare delivery Compatibility does not remove lifecycle decisions
Azure Blob Storage Azure SDKs and REST Azure-governed organizations Less compelling without the surrounding Azure platform
Infrai storage One REST API and one key Multi-backend teams reducing integration plumbing No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

This is also where Infrai is not suitable. A static website, permanent public image library, WORM archive, or automatic cross-region recovery plan should use a specialist or an external control plane that supplies those guarantees.

Infrai does not support public ACLs, object versioning, object lock, or automatic cross-region replication. Those limitations are decisive for a public gallery or an immutable archive, even if the REST integration is convenient.

An aggregation layer such as Infrai is useful when the application already needs several backend capabilities and the team values one REST contract over a collection of provider SDKs and keys. Its public discovery surface describes schemas and runnable examples, and its platform convention includes idempotency behavior across many capabilities. The practical benefit is less credential and SDK plumbing; the object still needs a tenant-aware key and a private access policy.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the application-owned write and signed-access boundary when your team wants one key and one REST surface across backend services, and when the storage limits above are acceptable. Choose S3, R2, or Azure Blob instead when you need object versioning, WORM retention, public delivery, provider-specific replication, or a mature migration toolchain as a first-class requirement.

The integration choice should be tested with one useful result. Can a worker create the right tenant-scoped object, record the artifact, issue private access, replay safely, and explain the outcome in a runbook? Count credentials and SDKs, but also count the policy decisions your team must keep synchronized.

5. Instrument retention before it becomes an incident

A retention policy is reproducible only if its inputs are visible. Record the retention class and policy version with the training run. Emit the object key, tenant, action, request ID, and result into application logs without putting sensitive image content in them. Track pending, expired, failed, and replayed operations separately.

The storage boundary has concrete edges: lifecycle rules have a minimum duration of one day, there is no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, metadata is not server-searchable, and there is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration. If a training artifact needs hourly expiry, immutable retention, or a regional recovery plan, put that responsibility in an external control plane or select a specialist that supplies it.

The alert-to-action loop is straightforward. A duplicate-delivery page points to the idempotency record. A retention page points to the policy version and object prefix. A tenant-access page points to the signed-access audit event. The page tells the operator which boundary failed instead of asking them to inspect a bucket by hand.

For a first implementation, keep the write path boring: private object, deterministic key, database record, retry-safe worker, and a signed read. Add multipart handling only when object size requires it, and make abandoned upload cleanup an explicit job because the storage layer does not infer that policy for you.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery documentation and verify the schema before wiring the worker.

Further reading

References:

  • AWS, “Using presigned URLs”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Amazon S3 User Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/
  • Infrai, “Choosing object storage for AI-generated images in a SaaS”: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/best-object-storage-for-ai-generated-images-saas-privat/

title: Centroid Spectral Coupling: Implicit Alignment and Representation Diversity in Self-Supervised Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22158v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims to align augmented views while preserving representation diversity and preventing collapse. Existing non-contrastive methods often address these goals using multiple weighted loss terms. We introduce Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term SSL objective that implicitly couples view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse resistance. CSC constructs centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix. Preserving centroid magnitudes encodes view agreement while encouraging balanced representation energy across spectral directions. We establish an exact decomposition into nonnegative alignment and spectral-imbalance components, characterize the geometry of global optima, and derive finite-loss guarantees for alignment and diversity. We also show that complete constant-output collapse is a strict saddle in normalized representation space. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette show that CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets. A ridge-parameter sensitivity study reveals an empirical alignment--diversity trade-off: increasing $\kappa$ strengthens view alignment but reduces representation effective rank. These results show that a unified spectral objective yields competitive visual representations without explicit contrastive negatives or separately weighted alignment and diversity penalties.

title: Amazon CloudFront Announces WebSocket and gRPC Support for Origin Mutual TLS
description:
Amazon CloudFront (CF) now supports WebSocket and gRPC traffic to application origins in AWS regions, with mutual TLS authentication between CF and the application origin (origin mTLS). Customers can now use TLS certificates to authenticate requests from CloudFront while setting up WebSocket or gRPC connections to their origins. Origin mTLS protects internet facing applications that need persistent, bidirectional or streaming connections, such as chat platforms, collaborative editing tools or live dashboards from unauthenticated requests.

Previously, customers serving WebSocket or gRPC traffic through CloudFront had to use shared secrets or IP allow-lists to identify requests originating from CloudFront. This was operationally complex and did not provide strong authentication. With Origin mTLS, customers can use one TLS based authentication for HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC traffic to an application origin. This works with application origins within AWS such as Application Load Balancer and API Gateway, on-premises origins, and origins hosted outside AWS.

There is no additional charge for origin mTLS, and it is available with pay-as-you-go pricing and in the Business and Premium flat-rate pricing plans. To learn more, visit the CloudFront origin mutual TLS documentation.

title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

title: Preventing Duplicate Contact Names From Silently Corrupting Your Lending Ledger
description:
When building an expense or lending tracker, contact management seems trivial at first glance:

"Just let the user type a name in a text field: 'Rahul'. Save it to SQLite. Done."

In practice, free-form text input without identity modeling quickly degenerates into chaos.

Consider what happens over a year of real-world usage:

  • You lend Rs. 500 to Rahul (your coworker).
  • Three months later, you lend Rs. 2,000 to Rahul (your cousin).
  • Next week, you record a dinner split with Rahul P (the same coworker).

If your app relies on naive string matching or creates unindexed rows for every entry, you face two destructive failure modes:

  1. The Silent Merge: The app assumes every "Rahul" is the same person. Your cousin's loan is merged into your coworker's balance sheet!
  2. The Duplicate Explosion: The app creates three separate cards for "Rahul", "rahul", and "Rahul P.", scattering loan installments across different entries and making it impossible to see total debt in one place.

Here is how FinLedger architected a contact disambiguation engine (PersonDao.kt, LendingDialogs.kt) to eliminate name collisions and duplicate entities.

The Pitfalls of Naive Contact Management 

flowchart TD
    subgraph Failures["The Twin Traps of Free-Form Contact Entry"]
        UserTypes["User Enters Name: 'Rahul'"]

        UserTypes --> Trap1["Failure Mode 1: The Silent Merge
        App matches existing 'Rahul' by string equality.
        Cousin's loan merged into Coworker's record!
        Privacy breach and accounting confusion."]

        UserTypes --> Trap2["Failure Mode 2: Duplicate Explosion
        App creates new entity for every string variance:
        'Rahul', 'rahul ', 'Rahul Patil'.
        Dozens of fragmented cards clutter the UI."]
    end

To build a reliable ledger, an application must decouple identity (who the person actually is) from display labels (what their name looks like on screen).

The FinLedger Architecture: Relational Person Entities

In FinLedger, contacts are first-class domain entities managed by PersonDao.kt, decoupled from individual loan or split records:

flowchart TD
    subgraph PersonArchitecture["Centralized Person Relational Model"]
        Input["User Types Contact Name: 'Rahul'"] --> Normalizer["String Normalizer:
        Trim whitespace, lowercase comparison"]

        Normalizer --> MatchQuery{"Query PersonDao:
        Does an existing contact match
        normalized string 'rahul'?"}

        MatchQuery -->|No Match Found| CreateNew["Create New Person:
        Generate immutable UUID.
        Store name, optional phone & note."]

        MatchQuery -->|Match Found| Disambiguate["Surface Disambiguation Dialog:
        Display matching contacts with metadata:
        - Rahul Patil (Coworker, +91 98XXX)
        - Rahul Verma (Cousin)"]

        Disambiguate --> UserDecision{"User Selects Action"}

        UserDecision -->|Select Existing| BindExisting["Bind to Existing Person ID:
        Aggregates under existing debt history"]

        UserDecision -->|Create Distinct| CreateDistinct["Create New Distinct Person:
        Assign unique UUID. Prompt for nickname/note."]
    end

Let's examine how each safeguard functions in detail:

1. Case-Insensitive String Normalization

Before querying the database, candidate names pass through a strict string sanitizer:

  • Trims leading and trailing whitespace.
  • Collapses multiple internal spaces into a single space.
  • Compares using Unicode-aware case insensitivity (COLLATE NOCASE).

This ensures that typing "Rahul Patil", "rahul patil", or "Rahul Patil " immediately identifies the candidate as the same person rather than spawning three fragmented records.

2. The Interactive Disambiguation Prompt

When you create a loan or split expense and enter a name that matches one or more existing records, FinLedger refuses to make an assumption.

In LendingDialogs.kt, an interactive disambiguation sheet appears:

  • "A contact named 'Rahul' already exists. Is this the same person?"
  • The sheet surfaces the contact's contextual metadata: their phone number suffix, personal note (e.g., "Design Team"), and current outstanding balance.
  • If it is the same person, tapping their card binds the new loan to their existing personId.
  • If it is a different person, tapping "Create as New Person" prompts you to enter a distinguishing note or last name (e.g., "Rahul (Cousin)") and assigns an independent, unique UUID.

3. Immutable Relational Keys (personId)

Every debt record (LendingEntity) and repayment (LendingRepaymentEntity) references the person via an immutable foreign key: personId: String (a UUIDv4).

Because the database relations are bound to the immutable UUID rather than the human-readable string:

  • If you later edit Rahul's display name to "Rahul Patil (Tech Lead)", that edit updates a single row in the persons table.
  • All historical loans, partial repayments, and split expenses across the last three years stay perfectly connected with zero broken references.

Key Takeaway

Contact names in human language are inherently ambiguous; software identifiers must never be.

By establishing a centralized, UUID-driven Person repository with case-insensitive normalization and proactive disambiguation prompts, FinLedger guarantees that doing business with people of the same name never corrupts your financial records.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
description:
arXiv:2611.21920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

title: A job retry should not hide the next job in GitLab CI
description:
A pipeline view should help answer one question quickly: what is still running, waiting, or blocked? In glab ci view, a retry could make that answer incomplete. The retry showed up correctly, but an unrelated item later in the list could disappear. A downstream pipeline trigger could still exist in GitLab while the terminal view gave no sign of it.

This was a rendering bug. The fix does not change which CI jobs run or when a downstream pipeline starts. It changes which entries the CLI keeps when it builds the view.

Three entries are enough to reproduce it

The CLI collects pipeline jobs, then appends downstream pipeline triggers before building the display list. Here is the input order from the regression test, with the downstream entry representing a trigger:

ID  stage   name
 1  test    unit        original attempt
 2  test    unit        retry
 3  deploy  downstream distinct entry

Expected display: unit attempt 2, then downstream (ID 3). The old code returned only unit attempt 2. That is what made the bug easy to miss: the deduplication looked correct if you only checked which retry won.

Where the row went

The old helper did two things. It recorded the last entry for each job key, then used the first repeated key to decide how many output slots to allocate. It assumed duplicates marked the beginning of a retry-only suffix. Here, the second entry repeats test/unit, so the output gets only one slot. The helper fills that slot with attempt 2. It has already seen the downstream entry, but never gives it a slot.

That assumption might hold for one neatly ordered input. It does not hold after the caller appends another stream of entries. The first duplicate tells you that one job was seen before. It tells you nothing about the next entry.

Keep the position and replace the attempt

The proposed fix gives each distinct (stage, name) pair an output index on its first appearance. Every subsequent appearance updates the job at that index. The loop continues through the entire slice, so a new key still receives a new slot after any number of repeats.

input entry       decision                   rows after the step
test/unit #1      append at index 0          [unit #1]
test/unit #2      replace index 0            [unit #2]
deploy/downstream append at index 1          [unit #2, downstream #3]

Using a Go struct as the map key also keeps the two fields separate. The old concatenation made ("ab", "c") and ("a", "bc") both become abc. A struct key distinguishes them without a separator or escaping rule. The scan takes one pass and uses a map entry per distinct key. It preserves the first appearance order and shows the last supplied attempt for each job. This is separate from deciding the configured order of pipeline stages.

The same test failed before and passed after

To isolate the change, the focused test ran against the old helper with only the new test added, then again with the patch:

go test -count=1 -run '^Test_latestJobsKeepsJobsAfterRetry$' ./internal/commands/ci/view
Code under test Observed result
Old helper plus new test Failed. Expected two entries, got one. The missing entry was downstream (ID 3).
Patched helper plus the same test Passed. The test checks that the retry and the downstream entry both survive, in order.

The GitLab merge request includes the patch and the regression test. The full CI-view package tests and the MR pipeline passed. The MR is still open, so this is a proposed fix.

If your own display code collapses repeated events, put an unrelated item immediately after the first duplicate in the test. Then assert the exact output order as well as the winning attempt. That variation catches truncation bugs that a list ending in retries can hide.

AI-assisted writing.

title: In an audit, a green test means the bug is real
description:
An audit report says "this route lets anyone find out which accounts exist". The team reads it, nods and moves on to the next ticket. A test shows the request and the response. Anyone can run it again on their own machine.

TL;DR: in an audit, I write tests that pass as long as the flaw exists. A green test proves the problem, with the exact request and response. Everything runs on an isolated test database, with made-up accounts, never touching production. Once the flaw is fixed, the test is flipped and becomes a regression test. The report keeps its paragraphs for what the tests do not prove.

This article is for developers and leads who order a security audit, or receive one. No security background needed.

The setup: a white-box audit of an API

In September, I ran a white-box audit of an API. Two questions drove the work. Can someone without an account find out who is registered? Can a logged-in user touch another account's data?

The core of the audit was five HTTP tests. An HTTP test sends a real request to the API and checks the response. The five held 21 assertions. An assertion is one precise check, like "the status code is 200".

All five tests were green. That was the bad news.

Here I cover the public routes, the ones that work without an account. The other tests targeted another account's IDs sent in the request body, the topic of a separate article.

An audit test passes when the flaw exists

Usually a green test means the code works. I have written before that a green test only proves what it actually checks. In an audit, I make it check the dangerous behavior on purpose.

Each test describes the flaw as if it were the expected behavior. For example, "with a wrong token, the API returns the profile". If the test passes, the flaw is real. If it fails, the flaw was not reproduced under these conditions. Check the fixtures, configuration and actual response before drawing a conclusion.

That is the big difference with a paragraph. A paragraph can be wrong and nobody notices. A test makes the evidence reproducible. Tests can be wrong too, so review their assertions.

The example: "forgot password" answers 200 or 422

Take the "forgot password" route. You send an email address, and the API sends a link to change the password. Nothing could be more ordinary.

In this API, the response depended on the address. A registered address got a 200 status code, which means "OK". An unknown address got a 422, which means "request rejected".

That difference is enough for account enumeration. Someone tries a list of addresses and keeps the ones that answer 200. They now know who has an account, without any password.

And the route had no explicit rate limit. Nothing slowed down mass attempts.

Here is the audit test, simplified for this article. The API was written in PHP with Laravel, but the idea works in any language.

// Audit test: green means the flaw exists.
public function test_forgot_password_reveals_which_emails_exist(): void
{
    User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(200);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(422);
}

The test creates a fake account, then sends two requests. It passes if the two status codes differ. Green means the flaw exists.

This is not a rare case. In 2026, several CVEs describe exactly the same flaw. Here are two, checked in the official registry.

  • CVE-2026-24468, in the open source project OpenAEV. The /api/reset route answered 400 for an unknown email and 200 for a valid one. It is fixed in version 2.0.13.
  • CVE-2026-58503, in the Frappe web framework. The enumeration went through the reset_password route. It is fixed in versions 15.106.0 and 16.16.0.

Everything happens far from production

An audit must not cause the incident it is looking for. So no test touched production. Not a single request went to it.

The tests ran in a temporary Docker environment. That environment had no access to the outside network. Even a mistake in a test could not reach a real server.

The database was an isolated MySQL test database. The accounts and records were synthetic. Synthetic means made up for the test. No real person is behind them.

During the audit, I did not change the project's code. The proof tests were not added to its repository.

This setup has one more benefit. Anyone on the team can replay the tests, with no production access and no real data.

The report says what the tests do not prove

A test proves one precise thing, and nothing else. The report has to say so. That is where paragraphs really earn their place.

Take the "verify email" route. For an active account, it returned the profile with any non-empty token. That profile also held the account's internal ID.

Combined with "forgot password", this made a chain. You test addresses, then you collect the IDs of the accounts you found. Yet the report states the limit. It works one address at a time, from a guessed list. The audit found no route that hands out every account at once.

The report also splits two lists. On one side, flaws confirmed by a test. On the other, leads seen in the code but not tested. A lead stays a lead until a test confirms it.

Finally, the tests cover the local code, not the deployed application. And the project already had a test checking that one account was denied access to another's data. It passed too. Its green said nothing about the routes my tests targeted.

Once the flaw is fixed, the test flips

The cycle has four steps: reproduce the flaw, fix the code, see the proof fail, then write the protective test.

Green proves the flaw, then the same test keeps it closed. During the audit, the test passes as long as the route answers 200 or 422 depending on the address. After the fix, it expects the same answer for both.

A green audit test is an alarm. It should not stay green. After the fix, it fails, and that is the signal you want.

You then rewrite it the other way around. It becomes a regression test that replays the same request on every code change. For "forgot password", both addresses must receive the expected generic response. Two identical errors are not enough.

// Regression test: green means the flaw stays closed.
public function test_forgot_password_answers_the_same_for_every_email(): void
{
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::fake();
    $user = User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $known = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test']);
    $unknown = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test']);

    // This example's API contract is 200 with this exact generic response.
    $expected = ['message' => 'If the account exists, a reset link will be sent.'];
    $known->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    $unknown->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertSentTo(
        $user, \Illuminate\Auth\Notifications\ResetPassword::class
    );
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertCount(1);
}

This example uses Laravel’s standard notification, intercepted by Notification::fake(). Adapt the status, message and notification to your API. This test does not measure response time. OWASP also asks for a constant response time. Otherwise the delay gives the address away. The rate limit deserves its own test too.

I did this flip on the "verify email" route. After the fix, I added a test that sends a wrong token. It expects a 422 rejection, with no profile data in the response. A second test checks that an unknown account gets the same error.

Why a test beats a paragraph

A report gets read once. A test lives in CI and runs again on every change. It keeps working after the auditor has left.

The test establishes the observed behavior. Severity still depends on the exposed data, required permissions and deployed configuration.

Finally, it sets the expected result without dictating the fix. The team chooses how to fix it. The test only says when it is done.

The checklist

In an audit, every confirmed flaw gets its test. Once the flaw is fixed, that test flips and stays in CI.

  • [ ] Write each suspected flaw as a test that passes if the flaw exists
  • [ ] Run the tests on an isolated test database, never on production
  • [ ] Use only made-up accounts and data
  • [ ] Cut network access from the test environment
  • [ ] Keep flaws confirmed by a test apart from leads seen in the code
  • [ ] Write in the report what each test does not prove
  • [ ] On "forgot password", compare the status code and message for a known and an unknown email
  • [ ] Test response time and rate limiting separately
  • [ ] After the fix, flip each test and keep it in CI

The takeaway

In an audit, green changes meaning. It no longer says "it works". It says "the flaw is here, and here is how to replay it".

Then the same test switches sides. Flipped, it keeps the flaw closed, long after the audit.

Want an audit that delivers proof your team can replay? See my audit and hardening offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Laravel, testing notifications · CVE-2026-24468 (OpenAEV) · OpenAEV, advisory GHSA-v6rg-hf9w-f8ph · CVE-2026-58503 (Frappe) · OWASP, Forgot Password Cheat Sheet · OWASP WSTG, testing for account enumeration · CWE-204, Observable Response Discrepancy

title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks
description:
arXiv:2611.21702v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

title: Understanding AI Computing — Part 3
description:
The Hidden Economics of AI Data Centers

Why the fastest AI chip isn’t necessarily the cheapest — and why utilization matters more than raw computing power.

Understanding AI ComputingImagine spending millions of dollars on the most powerful AI processors available.

You install them in a modern data center, provide enormous amounts of electricity, and connect everything through an ultra-fast network.

Your infrastructure can perform an astonishing number of calculations per second.

But what if much of that computing power remains unused?

The processors still cost money. So do electricity, cooling, networking, and maintenance.

And suddenly, the question is no longer how fast your processors are.

It’s how much useful work they produce for the money you spend.

The Cost of an AI Token

In the previous article, we explored why powerful AI processors can be limited by memory bandwidth rather than computing speed.

That technical limitation has an economic consequence.

When a large language model generates a response, it produces tokens — small units of text.

For an AI service, these tokens represent measurable output.

One useful metric is therefore the cost per million tokens.

Consider a simplified example.

A server costs $10 per hour to operate, including its allocated hardware and infrastructure expenses.

If it produces one million tokens per hour, the cost is $10 per million tokens.

If better optimization doubles its output to two million tokens per hour, the cost falls to $5.

Same hardware. Same operating cost.

Twice the output.

Half the cost per token.

This example is hypothetical, and actual costs depend on the model, workload, and service requirements.

But it illustrates something important.

You don’t necessarily need faster hardware to make AI cheaper. Sometimes you just need to use existing hardware more efficiently.

The Utilization Problem

AI accelerators are expensive, but demand is rarely constant.

During busy periods, servers may operate near their capacity.

At other times, expensive hardware sits idle.

And even when a processor is actively handling requests, its computing units may not be fully utilized.

As discussed in Part 2, memory bandwidth can limit the speed at which a processor performs useful calculations.

Data centers address this partly by processing multiple requests together, a technique called batching.

This improves throughput by allowing the processor to reuse model weights across several calculations.

But there is a trade-off.

Larger batches can increase waiting times, and customers expect their AI assistants to respond quickly.

A service handling interactive conversations must therefore balance efficiency against response time.

A system processing documents overnight can make different choices.

The cheapest way to generate a million tokens is not necessarily the best way to serve a million tokens to customers.

The Real Cost of AI Infrastructure

Electricity attracts considerable attention in discussions about AI data centers.

But it is only one part of the cost.

In a May 2026 analysis, Epoch AI modeled the annualized cost of a hypothetical one-gigawatt AI data center.

Its estimate attributed approximately 60% of total costs to servers, while electricity represented around 7%.

The precise proportions depend on assumptions about hardware prices, electricity costs, financing, and equipment lifetime.

Nevertheless, the example illustrates why energy efficiency alone cannot determine whether an AI processor is economical.

A cheaper or more energy-efficient chip may require additional servers to provide the same service.

Conversely, a more expensive processor may deliver enough additional useful output to justify its price.

Hardware lifetime also matters.

An expensive accelerator does not have to break down to become obsolete.

It only needs to become sufficiently inefficient compared with newer alternatives.

The Cheapest Chip Isn’t Always the Cheapest Solution

Suppose two competing systems can run the same AI model.

One has a lower purchase price and consumes less electricity.

The other costs more but processes substantially more requests while meeting the same response-time requirements.

Which is cheaper?

You cannot answer without considering the complete system.

Hardware, memory, networking, software optimization, operating costs, and actual throughput all influence the result.

That also explains why software matters economically.

Better scheduling, memory management, and optimized computational kernels can increase throughput without replacing the processors.

And it explains why large AI companies invest in specialized hardware and their own software infrastructure.

At enormous scale, even modest improvements in cost per token can translate into substantial savings.

The Real Lesson

The AI industry often measures progress in increasingly impressive numbers of calculations per second.

But customers don’t buy calculations.

They buy useful results.

For an AI service, the important measure is not simply the theoretical performance of its processors, but the cost of delivering the required output at an acceptable speed.

The fastest AI chip is not necessarily the cheapest. The best investment is the system that delivers the required service at the lowest sustainable cost.

And that is the hidden economics of AI data centers.

References & Further Reading

  • Epoch AI — Total Cost of Ownership of a One-Gigawatt AI Data Center
  • NVIDIA — LLM Inference Benchmarking: Fundamental Concepts
  • MLCommons — MLPerf Inference Benchmarks This is Part 3 of Understanding AI Computing, a series exploring the hardware, software, and economics behind modern artificial intelligence.

Next: Part 4 — Apple Metal: A Different Approach to AI Computing.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway

Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems.
