title: Publisher Signup Migration: Checking Marketing Consent at the Send Boundary
description:
A publisher moving email-and-password signup and sign-in off a managed provider needs a marketing consent check immediately before each recipient's send. Short answer: check that recipient's current category grant, drop recipients without it, and record the dropped count; keep transactional mail outside this marketing filter. An Express middleware check at batch submission is too early when the actual send happens later.

Consider a hypothetical page: a newsletter worker reports an abrupt rise in recipients dropped for missing consent after the account migration. The on-call sees a completed batch and a shrinking audience. A green completion dashboard answers almost nothing. What page fired, which category changed, and did the decision happen before delivery or hours earlier when somebody built the audience?

This is a proposed response trace, not an incident report.

What page should fire before the newsletter batch sends?

Work backward from the drop-count page. An earlier signal should have shown the change in consent decisions during migration validation, while the team could still compare the old account mapping with the candidate mapping and examine the category being checked. A valid account is necessary for sign-in; it isn't evidence that its owner wants a promotional newsletter. Moving those two decisions together makes a quiet migration mistake look like a successful login rollout.

The useful instrumentation belongs at the worker's send boundary. Record the marketing candidates examined, the explicit denials dropped, the checks that couldn't yield a decision, and the messages handed to the sender. Keep these outcomes distinct. An unknown decision should stop that marketing send and remain visible as unresolved work; calling it a denial corrupts the very signal the responder needs.

Count the drops.

The primary signal is the dropped count, because a sudden jump means something upstream changed. Pair it with the number checked so audience growth doesn't automatically become an emergency, and separate the publication's promotional category from transactional categories so account recovery doesn't disappear behind a newsletter policy. This is why a successful batch response is a poor acceptance test: every recipient might have been correctly excluded, yet the batch itself still completed.

For a publisher evaluating Infrai during this migration, the concrete attraction is its public, self-describing discovery surface: request and response schemas plus runnable examples let an engineer inspect the relevant consent capability without adopting another SDK. Publishers moving the marketing worker alongside signup should try Infrai for that consent-check integration when inspecting the contract directly matters.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Its single API key and unified billing reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities the publisher chooses to move. This breadth includes auth, email, storage, scheduling, and observability; consolidating only the capabilities the team actually needs is the relevant operating benefit. Infrai also supplies runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, so inspecting the consent contract needn't become an SDK translation exercise. None of this establishes migration compatibility; the acceptance traces still have to pass.

Put the decision beside the send

A Node.js and Express application can authenticate the batch-submission request and enqueue its intent. The later worker must still check each recipient. A middleware decision cannot honour a revocation that arrives while the batch waits, and a cached audience export cannot substitute for the current category grant.

Start with a read-only probe of the consent contract. This Go program uses the standard library, reads the API key and recipient details from environment variables, makes an explicit GET request, and prints the actual response without guessing response fields. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, and CONSENT_CATEGORY to your own values; save the program as main.go and run it with go run main.go. The category must be the publication's actual marketing category, not a label invented for this example.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    user := os.Getenv("CONSENT_USER_ID")
    category := os.Getenv("CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    if key == "" || user == "" || category == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    }
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{user_id}", url.PathEscape(user),
        "{category}", url.PathEscape(category),
    ).Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/auth/consent/check/{user_id}/{category}")
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                if candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("consent check HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("consent check retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This probe doesn't send email. It lets the engineer inspect the real consent response before writing the worker's decoder against the published schema. A successful HTTP status establishes that the request succeeded; it doesn't establish that consent was granted. Decode the category decision explicitly in the production integration, and keep response bodies out of general-purpose production logs.

The three attempts and 15-second request timeout are example settings, not service limits. A server-specified retry delay can extend the total runtime; a production worker needs a job deadline and durable deferral rather than holding its entire batch indefinitely. When work resumes, repeat the current consent check before sending. Treating an earlier approval as a retry token would recreate the stale-decision problem.

Once the decoder is in place, process each marketing recipient by checking the category, incrementing the dropped count on explicit denial, and invoking the sender only on approval. A check without a usable decision belongs in unresolved work. A retried send needs a stable idempotency key for the same logical message; the read-only probe above performs no write.

There's a subtle limit here: checking immediately before sending narrows the time between the decision and the write, but it doesn't establish an atomic transaction across two services. Don't turn the per-recipient requirement into an unsupported promise about messages a downstream sender has already accepted.

Compare migration work, then model the bill

A useful comparison starts with the boundary each candidate must own. Auth0, Firebase Authentication, and Amazon Cognito are real alternatives worth evaluating for the account migration; the table gives each a distinct evaluation path without pretending that an authentication product name proves marketing consent semantics. Choose the account system and the marketing decision system deliberately.

Candidate Concrete migration evaluation Boundary to prove before committing
Auth0 Evaluate it as the managed identity destination when the publisher wants a dedicated identity-provider decision. Demonstrate the current category decision at the worker, independently of successful sign-in.
Firebase Authentication Evaluate its documented password-authentication integration against the publisher's application changes. Show how the application supplies fresh marketing consent rather than deriving it from a password account.
Amazon Cognito Evaluate its user-pool migration path against the old provider's account mapping. Validate that migrated identity mapping preserves the recipient used for consent checks.
Infrai Evaluate the discoverable consent contract alongside the account-migration work. Validate category mapping and delivery behaviour against the published schemas and the publisher's acceptance cases.

For a team whose difficult requirement is identity migration itself, one of the specialist identity alternatives is the better starting point when its documented migration path matches the existing accounts. A consent-check integration shouldn't decide password migration by accident. Conversely, a team that can already account for identity migration can assess the discoverable consent interface on its own merits. No product in this table gets credit for untested migration compatibility.

Model a workload rather than comparing a nominal request price. For a hypothetical batch with 1,000 marketing candidates, a complete first pass makes 1,000 recipient decisions. If 80 are denied and every other check resolves, 920 messages reach the sender. These are planning inputs, not provider measurements; retries and unresolved decisions add work. A separate transactional batch contributes no checks under this marketing-only policy.

The operating bill therefore includes decision calls, sender submissions, retry work, account-mapping validation, adapter maintenance, and the responder time spent explaining surprising changes. Multiply actual call counts by the applicable billing terms only after the workflow is clear. Infrai specifies per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata, which gives the team inputs for attributing the worker's operating bill. That metadata cannot tell you how many engineering hours a mistaken category mapping will consume. The migration review needs both.

Close the loop without paging on every denial

The acceptance trace should revoke one synthetic reader's marketing grant after audience selection and before processing, then show that reader dropped at the send boundary. A second trace should carry a transactional message through without applying the promotional filter. A third should make the check unresolved and confirm that no marketing send occurs, while the unresolved count remains distinguishable from an explicit denial. These are proposed checks, not reports of a deployment.

Thresholds need the publication's actual batch history. An absolute dropped-count threshold alone will page more often when the audience grows; a ratio alone can make a tiny batch appear catastrophic. Start by reviewing both with batch size and category, then decide which deviations deserve an immediate page and which deserve routine review.

Don't page on every denial.

A denied promotional send is an expected policy outcome. If the threshold wakes someone for ordinary reader revocations, the false-positive cost includes interruption, investigation, and the eventual loss of attention to the next meaningful change; if it tolerates a migration-wide jump, the responder loses the earlier signal this design was meant to provide. That trade-off belongs in the migration acceptance criteria, beside the identity checks, before the newsletter worker takes over.

References

The identity sources below are starting points for evaluating account authentication and migration. They don't establish marketing permission. The OWASP guidance supplies authentication context; each candidate still needs the send-boundary acceptance traces described above.

Further reading

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Firebase password authentication
  • Amazon Cognito user-pool migration

If this boundary fits the publisher's migration, start with the discovery schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
description:
arXiv:2611.22263v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $\alpha{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

title: Goldcrest: Conversational State to Monte Carlo Parameters
description:
Goldcrest is a household financial planning tool that replaces spreadsheet forms with a conversational interface. You answer short questions in a chat. The agent extracts income, expenses, asset values, and timeline assumptions, then feeds them into a Monte Carlo simulation that projects your financial trajectory across thousands of market paths.

The interesting plumbing is the boundary between the LLM-driven conversation layer and the deterministic financial engine. The agent must maintain dialogue state across multiple turns, validate inputs, resolve ambiguity, and serialize a complete parameter set without letting the LLM touch arithmetic or generate advice.

Architecture: Conversation State to Simulation Parameters

The system splits into three layers:

  1. Conversational agent: Asks questions, parses natural language responses, maintains dialogue context.
  2. Parameter store: Holds structured financial data (income streams, expense categories, asset balances, tax rates) on the server.
  3. Monte Carlo engine: Runs deterministic simulations using the parameter store as input.

The agent never performs calculations. It extracts values and categories from user responses, writes them to the parameter store, and hands off to the engine. The engine produces every number in the projection.

Data Flow 

User input (natural language)
    ↓
LLM extracts structured fields
    ↓
Validation layer (type checks, range constraints, consistency rules)
    ↓
Parameter store (server-side, pseudonymized for LLM calls)
    ↓
Monte Carlo engine (deterministic, no LLM involvement)
    ↓
Year-by-year projections + probability distributions

The LLM sees pseudonymized data when it needs context for follow-up questions. Actual dollar amounts and identifiable details stay on the server. The model receives tokens like <income_source_1> or <expense_category_2> instead of "salary from Acme Corp" or "mortgage payment."

Dialogue State Management

The agent tracks which parameters it has collected and which are still missing. A typical rent-vs-buy scenario requires:

  • Current income (gross, net, frequency)
  • Expected income changes (raises, bonuses, career shifts)
  • Monthly expenses (housing, utilities, groceries, discretionary)
  • Savings and investment balances
  • Debt obligations (student loans, car payments)
  • Home purchase details (price, down payment, mortgage rate, closing costs)
  • Rental costs (monthly rent, expected increases)
  • Timeline (years until retirement, life expectancy assumptions)
  • Risk tolerance (asset allocation, withdrawal strategy)

The agent maintains a checklist. After each user response, it updates the parameter store and decides whether to ask a clarifying question, move to the next category, or declare the parameter set complete.

Handling Ambiguity

When a user says "I make around 80k," the agent must resolve:

  • Gross or net?
  • Annual, monthly, or biweekly?
  • Single income or household total?
  • Expected to change?

The system uses a two-pass approach. First pass: extract the stated value and write it to the parameter store with a confidence flag. Second pass: ask targeted follow-up questions only for low-confidence fields. This avoids the "20 questions" problem where every input triggers a cascade of clarifications.

If the user provides conflicting information across turns (e.g., "I spend $3k a month" followed later by "my rent is $2k and other expenses are $1.5k"), the agent flags the inconsistency and asks which figure to trust.

Validation and Constraint Logic

The parameter store enforces constraints before allowing a simulation run:

  • Income must be positive.
  • Expenses cannot exceed income by more than available savings.
  • Asset allocations must sum to 100%.
  • Mortgage terms must match standard products (15, 20, 30 years).
  • Tax rates must fall within plausible ranges for the jurisdiction.

The validation layer runs after each parameter update. If a constraint fails, the agent asks a corrective question rather than proceeding with invalid inputs.

Example Validation Table

Parameter Constraint Failure Behavior
Annual income > 0, < $10M Reject, ask for correction
Monthly expenses > 0, < income + savings drawdown Warn, allow override
Down payment 0-100% of home price Reject if outside range
Mortgage rate 0.1%-20% Reject, flag as likely error
Asset allocation Sum to 100% ± 0.01% Reject, show current total
Retirement age 50-80 Warn if < 60 or > 75

The system allows overrides for warnings but hard-blocks on constraint violations that would break the simulation.

Serialization and Handoff to the Engine

Once the parameter set passes validation, the system serializes it into a JSON structure:

{
  "income_streams": [
    {"source": "salary", "amount": 80000, "frequency": "annual", "growth_rate": 0.03}
  ],
  "expenses": [
    {"category": "housing", "amount": 2000, "frequency": "monthly", "inflation_adjust": true},
    {"category": "discretionary", "amount": 1500, "frequency": "monthly", "inflation_adjust": true}
  ],
  "assets": [
    {"type": "checking", "balance": 15000},
    {"type": "retirement", "balance": 120000, "allocation": {"stocks": 0.7, "bonds": 0.3}}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {"name": "rent", "housing_cost": 2000, "housing_type": "rent"},
    {"name": "buy", "housing_cost": 2500, "housing_type": "own", "home_price": 500000, "down_payment": 100000, "mortgage_rate": 0.065, "term_years": 30}
  ],
  "timeline": {"current_age": 32, "retirement_age": 65, "life_expectancy": 90},
  "simulation_params": {"iterations": 10000, "inflation_mean": 0.025, "market_return_mean": 0.07, "market_volatility": 0.15}
}

The Monte Carlo engine reads this JSON, runs 10,000 iterations with randomized market returns and inflation rates, and produces:

  • Year-by-year net worth projections (median, 25th percentile, 75th percentile)
  • Probability of meeting retirement goals
  • Sensitivity analysis (which parameters have the largest impact)

The engine writes results back to the parameter store. The frontend fetches them and renders charts.

Security and Data Handling

The system pseudonymizes data before sending context to the LLM. The LLM never sees:

  • Actual dollar amounts
  • Account numbers
  • Employer names
  • Addresses

Instead, it receives abstract tokens and category labels. When the LLM generates a follow-up question, the server substitutes real values back in before displaying to the user.

This limits exposure if the LLM provider logs requests or if a prompt injection attack tries to exfiltrate data. The worst an attacker can extract is the structure of the conversation, not the financial details.

Prompt Injection Mitigation

The agent uses a strict output schema. Every LLM response must be valid JSON with predefined fields:

{
  "next_question": "string",
  "extracted_values": {"field_name": "value"},
  "confidence": "high | medium | low",
  "needs_clarification": ["field_name"]
}

If the LLM returns anything outside this schema, the system rejects it and retries with a stricter prompt. This prevents the LLM from injecting arbitrary text or attempting to execute commands.

Failure Modes

Incomplete parameter sets: If the user abandons the conversation halfway through, the parameter store is incomplete. The system blocks simulation runs until all required fields are populated. The agent can resume from the last saved state.

Garbage inputs: If the user provides nonsensical values ("I make negative $50k a year"), the validation layer catches it. But if they provide plausible but wrong values ("I spend $500 a month" when they actually spend $5000), the simulation runs with bad data. The system relies on the user to review and correct extracted values before finalizing.

LLM hallucination: The LLM might misinterpret a response and extract the wrong value. The system shows every extracted parameter to the user for confirmation. The user can edit any field before the simulation runs.

Market assumption drift: The Monte Carlo engine uses historical return and volatility distributions. If future market behavior diverges significantly, projections will be wrong. This is a modeling limitation, not a plumbing failure.

Technical Verdict

Use Goldcrest's pattern when:

  • You need to gather structured data from users who hate forms.
  • The downstream process (simulation, calculation, workflow) requires deterministic inputs.
  • You can clearly separate the conversational layer from the execution layer.
  • You have well-defined validation rules and can enforce them before handoff.

Avoid this pattern when:

  • The parameter space is too large or too ambiguous for multi-turn dialogue.
  • Users need to see all fields at once to understand dependencies.
  • Real-time feedback on intermediate results is critical (forms with live calculations work better).
  • You cannot tolerate the latency of LLM calls for every user input.

The key insight is treating the LLM as a data extraction tool, not a reasoning engine. The agent asks questions and parses answers. The deterministic engine does the math. This keeps the system auditable and prevents the LLM from generating financial advice or performing calculations it will get wrong.

title: A Practical Stack Checklist for Small-Business Web Apps (Next.js, Node.js, SQL or MongoDB)
description:
Most small-business web apps I see share the same shape: a handful of forms, a dashboard, some user roles, and a few integrations (payments, email, maybe WhatsApp or SMS). The hard part is rarely the code. It's picking a stack that a small team can ship quickly and still maintain two years later.

Here is the checklist I use before writing the first line.

1. Start from the data, not the framework

Sketch the core entities and their relationships first: customers, orders, invoices, bookings, whatever the business runs on.

  • Mostly relational data (orders → line items → products, strict reporting needs): reach for SQL (MySQL or PostgreSQL). Joins and transactions will save you later.
  • Flexible, document-shaped data (form submissions with varying fields, content blocks, activity logs): MongoDB is a comfortable fit.
  • Both? That's normal. Keep the transactional core in SQL and store loosely structured data as JSON columns or in a separate collection.

2. Pick a rendering model per page, not per project

With Next.js you don't have to choose one strategy for the whole app:

Page type Good default
Marketing pages, blog Static generation (fast, SEO-friendly)
Product/catalogue pages Static + revalidation
Dashboards behind login Client or server components fetching per request
Admin tables with filters Server-side data fetching + pagination

Public pages get the SEO benefits, and the authenticated app stays dynamic.

3. Keep the API boring

For a small team, a plain Node.js REST API (or Next.js route handlers) with clear resource names beats a clever architecture. A few rules that pay off:

  • Validate every request body at the edge (Zod or similar).
  • Return consistent error shapes: { error: { code, message } }.
  • Paginate every list endpoint from day one.
  • Log with request IDs so support issues can be traced.

4. Authentication and roles early

Retro-fitting roles is painful. Even if version one has only "admin" and "staff", model roles and permissions as data, not as if (user.isAdmin) scattered through the code.

5. Plan for the second integration

The first integration (say, a payment gateway) usually goes straight into a route handler. The second one is the signal to introduce a small service layer and a queue or background job runner, so slow third-party calls don't block requests.

6. Make it observable and backed up

Before launch, confirm you have:

  • [ ] Automated database backups and a tested restore
  • [ ] Error tracking on both frontend and backend
  • [ ] Uptime monitoring on key pages
  • [ ] Environment variables kept out of the repo

Wrapping up

None of this is exotic, and that's the point. Small-business software succeeds when it is predictable, easy to hand over, and cheap to change. A React/Next.js front end, a Node.js API, and the right database for your data shape cover the vast majority of these projects.

What's on your checklist that I've missed? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

I'm Haseeb Ullah, a software developer building web applications, SaaS products and custom business software. You can see more of my work on my portfolio.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion k=60: My #1 BM25 Match Fell to Position 31
description:
I typed ERR_CONN_4012 into my hybrid search and got 30 pages about connection errors in general. The one runbook that actually contained the string ERR_CONN_4012 sat at position 31.

BM25 had ranked it #1. Of course it did: exact token, rare token, short doc. The vector index didn't have it in its top 50 at all. Then Reciprocal Rank Fusion merged the two lists and quietly buried the only correct answer below every vaguely related page.

Nothing was broken. Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60 did exactly what the formula says. This post is about that formula, why the textbook default punishes "one retriever is very sure" results, and what I changed.

TL;DR

  • Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) scores each doc as sum(1 / (k + rank)) across retrievers. With the common default k=60, rank #1 is worth 1/61 = 0.0164 and rank #50 is worth 1/110 = 0.0091. The curve is almost flat.
  • Any doc ranked 61st or better in both lists beats a doc ranked #1 in only one list. In general, the cutoff is rank k + 1.
  • Exact-match queries (error codes, SKUs, function names) are exactly the case where BM25 is right and embeddings miss, so RRF demotes them by design.
  • If a reranker only sees the fused top 20, the buried doc never even gets a second chance.
  • Fixes: detect identifier queries and pin exact matches, retrieve deeper on the vector side, lower k or weight BM25, and widen the rerank window.

How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion actually score documents?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores raw scores and uses only rank positions. Each retriever contributes 1 / (k + rank) for every doc it returned, and a doc missing from a list contributes zero.

def rrf(rankings: list[list[str]], k: int = 60) -> dict[str, float]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return dict(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]))

That's the whole algorithm. It's popular for good reasons: BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on completely different scales, and RRF sidesteps calibration entirely. No normalization, no tuning, works out of the box. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant and most RAG tutorials reach for it, and k=60 is the number almost everyone copies from the original 2009 paper.

The trouble is what k=60 does to the shape of the curve.

Why does RRF with k=60 bury exact keyword matches?

RRF with k=60 makes appearing in two lists worth far more than ranking first in one. Here are the actual numbers:

Situation RRF score
#1 in BM25, absent from vector list 1/61 = 0.01639
#50 in both lists 2/110 = 0.01818
#61 in both lists 2/121 = 0.01653
#62 in both lists 2/122 = 0.01639 (tie)

Read the second row again. A document that both retrievers considered mediocre, 50th place each, outscores the document BM25 was most confident about.

The break-even is easy to derive. A doc at rank r in both lists beats an exclusive #1 when:

2 / (k + r) > 1 / (k + 1)
       k + r < 2k + 2
           r < k + 2

So with k=60, every doc ranked 61st or better in both lists outranks your exclusive #1. If each retriever returns 50 results, that means every single overlapping doc wins.

That's where position 31 came from. My query hit 30 generic "connection error / timeout / retry" pages that both BM25 and the embedding model liked. All 30 appeared in both top-50 lists. The runbook appeared in one. Final position: overlap count plus one. It's not bad luck, it's arithmetic.

Why do embeddings miss error codes in the first place?

Embedding models compress meaning, and an identifier like ERR_CONN_4012 has very little meaning to compress. The tokenizer chops it into pieces like ERR, _, CONN, _, 401, 2, and the model maps the whole thing to roughly "some connection error." Every page about connection errors lands nearby.

BM25 sees the opposite picture. The full token is rare across the corpus, so its IDF is huge, and the one doc containing it shoots to the top.

This split is the entire reason hybrid search exists. The queries where one retriever is decisively right and the other is lost are the queries hybrid search was supposed to save. Flat RRF treats that disagreement as noise and votes it down.

Does a reranker fix bad RRF fusion?

A cross-encoder reranker only fixes RRF if the correct doc is inside the window it reranks. A lot of pipelines fuse, take the top 20, and rerank those. My runbook was at 31, so the reranker never saw it. The most accurate component in the pipeline was handed a list that didn't contain the answer.

If you rerank, the window has to be at least as large as the plausible overlap between your retrievers. With two top-50 lists, the worst case for an exclusive #1 is position 51. I rerank the fused top 60 now. It costs more cross-encoder calls, but a reranker that sees the answer is cheaper than one that confidently orders 20 wrong ones.

How do you fix Reciprocal Rank Fusion for exact-match queries?

Four changes, roughly in order of impact.

1. Detect identifier queries and pin exact matches

If the query contains something that looks like a code, the user wants that string. Don't make them win a popularity contest for it.

import re

IDENT = re.compile(r"\b(?:[A-Z]{2,}[_-][A-Z0-9_-]+|[A-Z]+-\d+|0x[0-9a-fA-F]+|\w+\(\))")

def hybrid_search(query, bm25, vec, k=60, n=50):
    bm = bm25.search(query, n)
    vc = vec.search(query, n)
    fused = list(rrf([bm, vc], k=k))

    idents = IDENT.findall(query)
    if idents:
        exact = [d for d in bm[:5] if any(i in doc_text(d) for i in idents)]
        fused = exact + [d for d in fused if d not in exact]
    return fused

The check against doc_text matters. BM25's top 5 can still contain partial matches on ERR or CONN, and you only want to pin docs that contain the literal string.

2. Retrieve deeper on the vector side

An exclusive #1 loses because the other list gives it zero. Give the other list a chance to give it something. If the vector search returns 500 instead of 50 and the runbook shows up at rank 400, it earns 1/460 = 0.00217 extra:

1/61 + 1/460 = 0.01857   (runbook)
2/110        = 0.01818   (doc at #50 in both)

Now it beats every doc ranked 50th in both. It still loses to shared docs near the top, but it climbs out of the basement. Deeper ANN retrieval is cheap compared to the LLM call that follows.

3. Lower k, or weight the retrievers

Lower k makes top ranks matter more. From the break-even above, an exclusive #1 is beaten by docs in both lists down to rank k + 1:

k Exclusive #1 loses to shared docs ranked...
60 1 through 61
20 1 through 21
10 1 through 11
1 1 through 2

Weighted RRF multiplies each retriever's contribution. Be careful: the weight also boosts shared docs' BM25 half, so it's weaker than it looks. With BM25 weight 2 and k=60, a shared doc at rank r scores 3/(60+r) against the exclusive doc's 2/61. Shared docs still win down to rank 31. Weight 3 still lets shared docs win down to rank 21. Weights help, but they don't solve the identifier case alone.

I ended up with k=20 as the default and kept the identifier pin as the real fix.

4. Look at disagreement, don't average it

The most useful debugging change was logging, per query, how many docs appeared in only one list and where they landed after fusion. A doc that's #1 in one retriever and missing from the other is a signal, not an outlier. If that pattern shows up on a large share of your queries, your two retrievers are answering different questions and flat fusion is hiding it.

When is RRF k=60 still the right choice?

RRF with k=60 is a fine default when your queries are natural-language questions and both retrievers mostly agree. In that regime, the flat curve smooths out noise from either retriever, and consensus really is a good proxy for relevance. It's also hard to beat for zero-tuning setups.

It's the wrong default for corpora full of identifiers: runbooks, API references, ticket histories, log search, product catalogs, legal citations. There, the query often has exactly one correct answer, and only the lexical retriever knows it.

So why did my #1 BM25 match fall to position 31?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60 gives rank #1 a score of 1/61 and rank #50 a score of 1/110, so the rank curve is nearly flat and showing up in two lists dominates ranking high in one. Mathematically, any document ranked k + 1 or better in both lists beats a document ranked #1 in only one. My runbook was BM25's #1 and absent from the vector top 50, so it landed behind all 30 documents that appeared in both lists. To fix it, detect identifier-style queries and pin literal matches, retrieve deeper on the vector side so exclusive hits earn partial credit, lower k (I use 20), and rerank a window wide enough to include the worst-case position of an exclusive #1.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: The Receiver Should Refuse the Second Copy — Your Retry Loop Never Will.
description:
Yesterday's fix was on the sending side. A slow receiver took 2.5 seconds to answer, the sweeper checked every second, heard silence, and sent the same order three times. The fix was a claim row: one row per delivery key, claimed once, so the second and third ticks had nothing to send. Three deliveries became one.

Then itsvicmoreno asked the question that undoes that fix, politely, in the comments. What if the acknowledgement is lost AFTER the write? The receiver has already taken the order, already charged the card, already sent the email. The sender never hears back, decides the delivery failed, and sends it again. The claim row cannot help you there. The sender did its job, the row says done or it says nothing useful, and a second copy is already on its way. Does the fix live only in the sweeper, or does the receiving end have a say?

I ran that exact case on my own machine. One event, evt-1042, a $29.00 payment confirmation for order ORD-1042. The same event delivered twice, the second send waiting for the first reply, so the second copy arrives after the first write has fully landed. Two receivers, side by side, with the same side effects: a charge line, a confirmation email line, and one stock decrement each time a delivery is accepted. The only difference is that one of them keeps a table of keys it has already processed, and checks it before doing anything else.

My claim is simple, and I expect some of you to disagree with it. A smarter retry loop will never be enough. The receiver has to be able to say no to the second copy, because the receiver is the last place where a duplicate can still be stopped before it becomes a second charge.

Problem 1: the plain inbox charged twice for one order

The plain receiver has no duplicate check at all. Every delivery it accepts is a real delivery, as far as it knows. Here is what two copies of evt-1042 did to it:

Plain inbox Receiver with a processed-keys table
Deliveries received 2 2 (1 accepted, 1 refused)
Charges 2, $29.00 twice, $58.00 in total 1, $29.00
Confirmation emails 2 1
Stock decrements 2, stock 10 down to 8 1, stock 10 down to 9
Second copy's reply 200, processed 200, duplicate, refused

Both runs gave the same numbers, twice each, at 00:07:04 and 00:07:08 for the plain receiver, 00:07:06 and 00:07:11 for the one with the table. The plain receiver logged two deliveries for one order, charged $58.00 for a $29.00 order, sent the customer the same confirmation twice, and took two items out of stock for one sale. Nothing about the second copy looked wrong when it arrived. It had the same key, the same order, the same amount, and it arrived after a perfectly normal gap. A receiver that cannot recognise a key it has already seen has no way to know it has been paid twice.

That is the shape of the bug itsvicmoreno pointed at. The sender-side claim is a good fix for the slow case, and I am not taking that back. But the lost-acknowledgement case walks straight past it. The sender believes the first delivery failed. From the sender's side, resending is the correct, careful thing to do. The duplicate is not a mistake in the retry logic. It is the retry logic working as designed, on wrong information.

Problem 2: the table works, and the order of the two steps is the whole trick

The second receiver keeps a small table, one row per delivery key. When a delivery arrives, it checks the table first. If the key is already there, it refuses the copy before any side effect runs, and still answers 200, so the sender stops retrying. If the key is new, it writes the key into the table first, and only then charges, emails, and decrements stock.

The reply matters as much as the refusal. The second copy got {"status":"duplicate","refused":true} with a 200 behind it. A refused copy that answers with an error would look like another failed delivery, and the sender would send it a third time, then a fourth. A refusal has to sound like success to the sender, because from the sender's point of view the order did go through. It went through the first time.

And the order of the two steps inside the receiver is the whole trick. Key first, then side effects. If you charge first and write the key second, there is a gap between the two, and a crash in that gap leaves a charge with no record of it. The next copy arrives, the table says it is new, and the customer is charged again. Writing the key first closes that gap in one direction: a crash after the write leaves a recorded key with no charge, which is a missing charge you can reconcile, not a double charge you have to refund. One of those is a bookkeeping problem. The other is a customer with two charges on their statement.

The check itself is small. In the receiver, before anything else happens:

if (keys.includes(evt.delivery_key)) {
  // refuse: already processed, no side effects
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'duplicate', refused: true }));
  return;
}
// record the key FIRST, then charge, email, decrement stock
writeKeys([...keys, evt.delivery_key]);

That is the entire defence. A lookup, a refusal, and a write that happens before the money moves.

Problem 3: the table does not remove the duplicate, only its cost

Be honest about what the table buys you. The second copy still arrives. It still costs a delivery, a lookup, and a reply. On a bad day, when every acknowledgement is being lost, the table does not reduce the traffic at all. It reduces the damage the traffic can do. Two copies still cross the wire. Only one of them touches money, email, or stock.

That is a narrower win than the headline version, and it is worth saying plainly, because it decides where this fix belongs. The table is not a replacement for the sender-side claim. It is the second layer, the one that catches the copy the claim could not stop. The claim stops the sweeper resending a delivery that is still in flight. The table stops the receiver acting on a delivery that already landed. You need both, because they guard different moments, and the lost-acknowledgement case is the one that slips between them.

Problem 4: the honest limits of this test

Three limits, because the test was small. First, my two copies arrived one after the other, in order, never at the same instant. Two copies landing at the exact same moment, both checking the table before either has written, were not tested, and a race like that is exactly where a simple lookup breaks. A real table wants the check and the write to happen as one step, not two, and I did not test that step.

Second, the crash window I described above, between writing the key and running the side effects, was not tested either. I know the order matters. I did not prove what happens when the receiver dies inside it. A real table wants the key write and the side effects in one transaction, or a reconciliation pass that finds recorded keys with no charge. My test had neither.

Third, I reset the table before each run. Whether the keys survive a receiver restart, and for how long they should be kept before they are cleared, are both open questions my test does not answer. A table that forgets is a table that charges twice, just later.

So the claim stands, narrowed to what the numbers support. The sender-side claim fixed the slow receiver. It does not fix the lost acknowledgement, because in that case the sender is right to resend. The receiver-side table does fix it: the second evt-1042 was refused, one charge instead of two, one email instead of two, stock 9 instead of 8. The fix belongs at the receiving end, in a table checked before the money moves, with the key written before the side effects run.

If you run webhooks, you have met this one. What did your duplicate cost you, a double charge, a double email, a customer asking why they got two copies of the same thing? And what caught it in the end, a table like this one, a claim on the sending side, or something else entirely?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Make your agent gas-aware on Base in 5 minutes
description:
Last week Base gas sat on its 0.006 gwei floor for 91% of 2,016 readings. One real spike hit on Nov 10 (2.3x, gone in about 15 minutes). A Uniswap swap cost about $0.0024.

So the useful question for an agent is not "when is gas cheap?" It is: "is right now a spike, and what will this transaction cost in dollars?" An RPC call gives you gwei. Your agent budgets in dollars.

This guide adds that answer to an agent in three ways, from fastest to most flexible. Each call is paid per request in USDC over x402: no API key, no signup.

What you need

  • A separate Base mainnet wallet with a dollar or two of USDC. No ETH needed: payments are EIP-3009 signatures.
  • Node.js 18+

Never use a key from a wallet that holds real funds. Never paste it into chat or commit it.

Option 1: one command, no code

See what the endpoint asks for (free, returns HTTP 402 with the price):

curl -i "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"

Pay and fetch with the AgentCash CLI:

npx agentcash@latest fetch "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"

gasLimit cheat sheet: 21000 ETH transfer, 65000 ERC-20 transfer, 85000 NFT mint, 180000 swap, 1500000 deploy.

Option 2: MCP (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) 

claude mcp add base-gas \
  --env BUYER_PRIVATE_KEY=0xYOUR_SEPARATE_WALLET_KEY \
  -- npx -y base-gas-mcp

Then just ask:

  • "What does a Uniswap swap on Base cost right now, in dollars?"
  • "Is Base gas high right now, or should I wait?"
  • "Is Base or Arbitrum cheaper for a token transfer?"

The server only ever pays one origin and refuses any single payment above $0.05, so a prompt cannot redirect your wallet.

Option 3: in your own code 

npm i @x402/fetch @x402/evm viem

import { wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig } from "@x402/fetch";
import { ExactEvmScheme } from "@x402/evm/exact/client";
import { privateKeyToAccount } from "viem/accounts";

const account = privateKeyToAccount(process.env.BUYER_PRIVATE_KEY);

const pay = wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig(fetch, {
  schemes: [{ network: "eip155:8453", client: new ExactEvmScheme(account) }],
});

const res = await pay(
  "https://base-gas-x402-production.up.railway.app/gas?gasLimit=180000"
);
const gas = await res.json();

console.log("Swap cost (USD):", gas.estimatedTransferCost.usd);
console.log("Fees to sign:", gas.suggestedFees.medium);

suggestedFees.medium holds maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas in wei, ready for viem's sendTransaction:

const { maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas } = gas.suggestedFees.medium;
await walletClient.sendTransaction({
  to, value, data,
  maxFeePerGas: BigInt(maxFeePerGas),
  maxPriorityFeePerGas: BigInt(maxPriorityFeePerGas),
});

maxFeePerGas is a ceiling (2x base fee + tip). You pay base fee + tip; the rest is not spent.

A simple rule for agents

  1. Call /gas before a transaction and read the USD cost.
  2. If the cost is above your budget, call /gas/history and check the verdict (cheap / normal / expensive / flat).
  3. If it says expensive, wait 15 minutes. On Base, spikes are short.

Endpoints and prices

Endpoint Price Returns
GET /gas $0.002 Base fee, priority tiers, cost in USD/ETH/gwei, ready-to-sign fees
GET /gas/compare $0.01 Same transaction on Base, OP Mainnet, Arbitrum, Ethereum
GET /gas/history $0.01 Last N hours, with a cheap/normal/expensive/flat verdict
GET /gas/cheapest-window $0.02 Cheapest hour of day from 7 days of data
GET /health free Service status

A failed call is never charged: settlement happens only on a successful response.

title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.21812v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.

title: My dual-axis chart was lying about zero
description:
A commenter on Reddit looked at one of my charts for about ten seconds and found a bug I had shipped to everyone.

The chart was a combo chart: revenue as bars on the left axis, profit margin as a line on the right axis. Pretty standard dashboard stuff. Their question was simple: "where is zero on the right axis?"

It wasn't where the bars started.

What went wrong

Two axes on one chart means two sets of tick labels sharing one set of grid lines. My first version got half of that right. The right axis picked the same number of ticks as the left, each one a round number, so every label sat neatly on a grid line.

What it never did was force the two zeros onto the same line.

Take revenue from $0 to $62K and a margin between −10% and 35%:

  • Left axis: 0, 20K, 40K, 60K, 80K (five lines)
  • Right axis: five lines, round step, must cover −10% to 35%, so: −20%, 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%

Look at the second line. The right axis says 0%, the left says $20K. The bars stand on the bottom line, but the margin's zero floats one line above it.

Now give one month a −5% margin. The dot lands above the bars' baseline. Anyone skimming the chart reads it as "slightly positive". It's a loss.

Every label was a round number, every tick sat on a grid line, and the chart was still wrong.

The fix

When the chart starts at zero, both axes now get the same number of steps below zero and the same number above it, the most either axis needs. Zero becomes one shared grid line, by construction.

The left axis keeps its own round step. The right axis tries a few candidates (1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten) and keeps the one with the best score:

// fewer lines is calmer, but an axis its values barely use squashes the line
const filled = (hi - lo) / (step * (below + above))
const score = below + above + 4 * (1 - filled)

The first term prefers fewer grid lines. The second punishes a step so large that the data only fills a sliver of the axis, which would flatten the line into a near-straight squiggle.

Same data, after the fix:

  • Left: −20K, 0, 20K, 40K, 60K, 80K
  • Right: −10%, 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%

Both zeros sit on one line, and the −5% month now dips below it, where a loss belongs.

Two smaller changes came with it:

  • The solid grid line moved from the bottom of the chart to zero, where the bars actually stand.
  • alignZero={false} turns it off, for the rare chart where two independent domains really are what you want.

What I took from it

Tests wouldn't have caught this. Every output was a valid, round, evenly spaced set of ticks. The bug only exists when you read the chart the way a person does, comparing one axis against the other.

So: show your charts to someone with negative numbers in their data. Mine all had happy, positive margins.

The component is free and MIT if you want to poke at it: https://dashral.com/components/combo-chart?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=zero-baseline

title: Privacy Boundaries for Email Test Fixtures
description:
Email testing is often described as a delivery problem: did the message arrive, did the link work, and did the UI show the right state? In a real application, it is also a privacy problem.

A test fixture can contain a name, an account identifier, a password-reset URL, a team invitation, or a billing detail. Even when the data is synthetic, a shared mailbox and a long retention period can turn a small QA convenience into a surprisingly durable data store.

This is where a temp mail workflow can be useful, but only if the fixture is designed as a controlled security boundary. The mailbox is not the whole solution. The useful design includes ownership, access, expiry, logging, and a plan for what happens when a test fails.

Why email fixtures are a privacy boundary

An email fixture sits between at least three systems:

  1. The application under test, which creates the message.
  2. The delivery layer, which may retry or queue it.
  3. The test runner or reviewer, which reads the message and acts on it.

Each system can copy data. A CI log may capture a message identifier. A browser test may save a screenshot. A retry queue may retain the payload longer than expected. The inbox itself may keep messages after the test has finished.

That makes fixture design closer to threat modeling than to choosing a convenient test address. Ask who can read the mailbox, which credentials are stored in CI, whether links can be replayed, and how quickly the data disappears. The answers should be part of the test contract, not tribal knowledge.

Map the data before choosing a mailbox

Start with a small data-flow map for each email scenario. It does not need to be a polished architecture diagram. A table in the test repository is often enough:

Data Created by Needed by Retention goal
Recipient address Fixture factory Application and test Test duration
Message ID Mail adapter Logs and assertions Short CI retention
Verification token Application Browser test Until consumed or expired
Message body Mailbox One assertion Avoid saving

This exercise finds accidental persistence early. For example, the message body may be needed for one assertion, while the message ID is enough to diagnose a timeout. Keeping both forever is rarely justified.

The same map also helps teams choose the right boundary. A local fake transport may be best for unit tests. An isolated mailbox is more appropriate for an end-to-end check of rendering, delivery, and link behavior. A shared personal inbox is usually the least auditable option.

Design a fixture with a short, explicit lifecycle

A reliable fixture has a lifecycle that can be explained in one paragraph:

  1. Allocate a unique address or namespace for the test run.
  2. Associate it with a run ID, not with a developer's personal identity.
  3. Wait for a message with a bounded timeout.
  4. Extract only the fields needed for the assertion.
  5. Consume or invalidate the token.
  6. Delete the mailbox or let its documented expiry policy finish.

The run ID matters because it prevents parallel jobs from reading one another's messages. It also makes cleanup and investigation easier. A test can use a small adapter rather than scattering provider-specific calls throughout the suite:

type MailFixture = {
  address: string;
  runId: string;
  waitForMessage: (subject: string, timeoutMs: number) => Promise<string>;
  dispose: () => Promise<void>;
};

const fixture = await mailFixtures.create({ runId });

try {
  await app.requestVerification(fixture.address);
  const body = await fixture.waitForMessage("Verify your account", 30_000);
  expect(extractLink(body)).toMatchObject({ path: "/verify" });
} finally {
  await fixture.dispose();
}

In practise, cleanup still needs to be idempotent. The test runner can be interrupted, the provider can return a transient error, or the assertion can fail before the message is read. A cleanup job with a short maximum age is a useful second line of defense.

Make failures useful without keeping message bodies

Teams often retain too much data because debugging an intermittent email failure is hard. A better compromise is to record structured evidence:

  • run ID and test name;
  • provider request and message IDs;
  • timestamps for creation, delivery, and assertion;
  • normalized subject and selected header values;
  • failure category, such as timeout, wrong recipient, or invalid link.

Avoid copying full message bodies into CI logs. If a failure needs deeper inspection, allow a restricted, time-limited diagnostic path and document who can use it. That approach preserves observabilty without making every build artifact a searchable archive of emails.

It is also worth testing the negative path. Verify that an expired token is rejected, that a token cannot be used twice, and that a message sent to the wrong fixture is not accepted. Replay-safe email verification jobs offer a useful perspective on making these states explicit. For flows that change an existing address, replay windows for email change tokens are another related design consideration.

A practical review checklist

Before adding an email fixture to CI, ask:

  • Is this test exercising the real delivery boundary, or would a fake transport be more precise?
  • Does every parallel run have an isolated address or namespace?
  • Are credentials scoped to the smallest mailbox operation needed?
  • Is the token short-lived and single-use?
  • Does cleanup run when the test fails and when the job is cancelled?
  • Are logs storing IDs and classifications instead of message bodies?
  • Is the expiry policy written down and monitored?
  • Can a reviewer reproduce the scenario without using a personal inbox?

The last question catches a cultural problem as much as a technical one. When a team searches for “tamp mail com” or another rough phrase while looking for a quick test mailbox, the real requirement is usually isolation and repeatability. Those properties should be provided by the test design, not left to search luck.

Closing thought

Email fixtures are small, but they cross application, infrastructure, and human boundaries. Treating them as privacy boundaries leads to simpler choices: use synthetic data, assign a run ID, limit access, retain evidence selectively, and make expiry observable.

The result is not just safer testing. It is a test suite that explains its failures, behaves predictably under parallel CI, and does not quietly accumulate a second inbox full of data nobody meant to keep. The fixture are disposable; the design around them should be durable.

title: 9 PostgreSQL fixes that took real queries from ~100 ms to under 1 ms (with EXPLAIN output)
description:
Most "slow database" problems I see are not exotic. They are the same handful of patterns: a missing index on a foreign key, a function wrapped around a column, an OFFSET that reads 200,000 rows to show 20.

I ran each pattern below on a 1,000,000-row orders table in PostgreSQL 16.6, captured EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after the fix, and kept the numbers as they came out. Your timings will differ — the shape of the plan is what matters.

Fix Before After
Index the foreign key 67.7 ms 0.10 ms
Composite index (equality first, then sort column) 80.0 ms 0.20 ms
Expression index for lower(email) 14.2 ms 0.07 ms
Rewrite date(created_at) = … as a range 100.2 ms 0.31 ms
Partial index for the hot slice 82.3 ms 0.15 ms
Covering index (INCLUDE) 41.2 ms 3.9 ms
Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET 28.2 ms 0.11 ms
pg_trgm for ILIKE '%text%' 168.5 ms 1.1 ms
Planner estimate instead of exact count(*) 84.1 ms 0.07 ms

1. Index your foreign keys

PostgreSQL creates an index for a primary key, not for a foreign key. So this innocent query:

SELECT id, status, total, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242;

reads the whole table:

Gather  (actual time=2.554..67.674 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=16.595..43.016 rows=3 loops=3)
        Filter: (customer_id = 4242)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 333330
        Buffers: shared hit=96 read=15055
Execution Time: 67.727 ms

The giveaway is Rows Removed by Filter: 333330 per worker — a million rows checked to return ten. One index later:

CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);

Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (actual time=0.032..0.058 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 4242)
        Buffers: shared hit=6
Execution Time: 0.104 ms

From 15,151 buffers to 16. Rule: every foreign key you filter or join on deserves an index.

2. Composite index: equality columns first, then the range/sort column 

SELECT id, customer_id, total, created_at FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at >= '2026-06-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

An index on (status, created_at) lets PostgreSQL jump straight to pending, read rows already in date order and stop after 50. Column order matters: equality first, then the range or sort column. 80 ms → 0.2 ms.

3. Expression index for lower() and friends

WHERE lower(email) = '…' cannot use a plain index on email. Index the expression itself:

CREATE INDEX customers_lower_email_idx ON customers (lower(email));

14.2 ms → 0.07 ms.

4. Keep the column bare (sargable queries) 

-- slow: function on the column hides it from the index
WHERE date(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') = '2026-03-15'
-- fast: same rows, as a range
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-15 00:00+00' AND created_at < '2026-03-16 00:00+00'

100.2 ms → 0.31 ms. No new index needed — just let the existing one work.

5. Partial index for the small slice you query all the time

If 5% of orders are pending and your dashboard only ever asks for those, index only them:

CREATE INDEX orders_pending_created_idx ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

Smaller, faster to maintain, 82 ms → 0.15 ms.

6. Covering index for index-only scans

When the index already contains every column a query needs, PostgreSQL can skip the table (Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches: 0) once the visibility map is current — i.e. after VACUUM:

CREATE INDEX orders_customer_total_idx ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);
VACUUM orders;  -- updates the visibility map so the heap can be skipped

41 ms → 3.9 ms for a GROUP BY customer_id over 2,000 customers.

7. Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET

OFFSET 200000 still reads and throws away 200,000 rows. Remember the last id you showed:

SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id > 200000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

Same cost on page 1 and page 10,000. 28 ms → 0.11 ms.

8. ILIKE '%text%' with pg_trgm

A B-tree cannot help a leading wildcard. A trigram GIN index can:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX orders_note_trgm_idx ON orders USING gin (note gin_trgm_ops);

168 ms → 1.1 ms.

9. Do you really need an exact count(*)?

For a "≈ 1.2M orders" badge, the planner's statistics are instant and usually within a few percent after ANALYZE:

SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass;

84 ms → 0.07 ms.

Bonus: a correctness trap, not a speed one

x NOT IN (SELECT y …) returns no rows at all if the subquery contains a single NULL. Use NOT EXISTS instead. It is not faster here — it is right.

How to find these in your own database

  1. Turn on pg_stat_statements and sort by total_exec_time — fix the queries that cost the most in total, not the slowest single run.
  2. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the top offenders. Look for Seq Scan with a large Rows Removed by Filter, and for big read= buffer counts.
  3. Change one thing, re-run, compare. Keep what helps; drop indexes nobody uses (pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0).

I packaged this workflow — the 10 lessons with full before/after plans, a reproducible 1M-row demo dataset and 12 read-only diagnostic scripts (top queries, unused and duplicate indexes, vacuum health, blocking locks and more) — as the PostgreSQL Performance Playbook ($29, 30-day money-back guarantee).

Just want the one-page version? The free PostgreSQL Performance Checklist (PDF, $0) puts these checks on a single printable page.

If you want more SQL practice first, two well-reviewed resources from other creators on Gumroad:

  • SQL Practice Problems – Professional Package — 97 challenge problems (written for SQL Server/MySQL).
  • Decode PostgreSQL — how PostgreSQL works, explained without heavy code.

Disclosure: the last two are affiliate links — if you buy through them I earn a commission, at no extra cost to you.

title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
description:
arXiv:2611.22215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.21698v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark. Compared with diffusion-based estimation, FACE requires substantially fewer sampling steps while achieving superior or comparable estimation accuracy, reducing inference time and computational cost. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of flow matching for accurate, pilot-efficient, and computationally efficient mmWave MIMO channel estimation.

title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.22102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.21955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($\epsilon$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

title: Treat Java Objects Like JSON
description:
Treat Java Objects Like JSON

Java is powerful, but working with nested objects can be tedious. Getters, setters, null checks, conversions — a lot of code for simple operations.

What if you could use JSONPath, JSON Schema, and JSON Patch directly on Java objects?

That's what SJF4J (Simple JSON Facade for Java) does. No intermediate JSON trees, no serialization required.

Start with an Ordinary Java Object

Consider two simple classes:

public class User {
    public String name;
    public int age;
    public Address address;
}

public class Address {
    public String city;
}

Nothing special here. No annotations, interfaces, or base classes.

Now suppose we have a User instance:

User user = ...;

Navigate with JSONPath

With SJF4J, we can use JSONPath directly on this object:

JsonPath path = JsonPath.parse("$.address.city");

// Read
String city = path.getString(user);

// Update
path.put(user, "Shanghai");

That's it.

No serialization, no intermediate JSON tree, and no conversion back to a Java object.

We're simply treating the Java object as a JSON-like structure.

The same approach works with Map, List, arrays, and other supported object models.

Validate with JSON Schema

JSONPath is just the beginning.

Suppose we want to validate a User against a JSON Schema:

JsonSchema schema = JsonSchema.fromJson("""
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
    "age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
  },
  "required": ["name"]
}
""");

ValidationResult result =
    schema.createPlan().validate(user);

Yes, user is still an ordinary Java object.

SJF4J supports JSON Schema Draft 2020-12, 2019-09, and 7, allowing the same validation rules to work across different data representations.

Modify with JSON Patch

We can also apply standard JSON Patch operations directly:

JsonPatch patch = JsonPatch.fromJson("""
[
  {
    "op": "replace",
    "path": "/name",
    "value": "Alice Zhang"
  }
]
""");

patch.apply(user);

The original User object is updated in place.

This can be useful for applying structured updates without writing property-specific mutation logic.

How Does It Work?

The key is OBNT (Object-Based Node Tree), SJF4J's unified structural model.

Instead of converting everything into a dedicated JSON tree, SJF4J recognizes three basic structural concepts:

Node Java representations
Object POJO, Map, JsonObject
Array List, Java array, JsonArray
Value String, Number, Boolean, custom values

This allows JSON-oriented operations to work consistently across different Java object representations.

Think of it as a common structural vocabulary for data that already exists in memory.

Runtime Flexibility, Compiled Speed

Dynamic structural operations are convenient, but Java also has a powerful advantage: the compiler.

SJF4J takes advantage of this through Compiled APIs, using annotation processing to generate optimized Java implementations at compile time.

For example:

@CompiledNavigator
interface UserNavigator {
    @GetByPath("$.address.city")
    String getCity(User user);
}

Instead of interpreting the JSONPath expression at runtime, the generated implementation can access Java fields directly:

// Simplified generated code
public String getCity(User user) {
    if (user == null) return null;
    Address address = user.address;
    return address == null ? null : address.city;
}

The result is ordinary Java code: readable, debuggable, and easy for the JVM to optimize.

And the performance difference can be substantial.

In SJF4J's benchmarks, Compiled APIs achieve up to 50× faster execution than their Runtime counterparts in selected workloads. Actual gains depend on the operation and data structure.

This gives developers the flexibility of dynamic JSON-oriented APIs, alongside the performance benefits of statically generated Java code.

Beyond JSONPath

SJF4J brings several related capabilities together:

  • Binding: JSON/YAML serialization and deserialization.
  • Navigation: JSONPath and JSON Pointer.
  • Validation: JSON Schema.
  • Mapping: Object-to-object mapping.
  • Patching: JSON Patch and Merge Patch.

It also supports multiple backends, including Jackson 2/3, Gson, Fastjson2, JSON-P, and SnakeYAML.

The goal isn't to replace all these libraries. It's to provide a consistent way to work with structured data, regardless of its underlying Java representation.

Final Thoughts

Java gives us a robust type system and a powerful compiler. JSON gives us a flexible structural model and a rich set of standards.

SJF4J brings these strengths together.

We can work with native Java objects using JSON semantics, and when performance matters, compile those operations into optimized Java code.

That's the idea behind SJF4J: JSON semantics, native Java objects, and compile-time performance.

If you're interested:

  • GitHub — SJF4J
  • Documentation
  • Benchmarks

Feedback and ideas are welcome!

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
