title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
description:
arXiv:2611.22075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.

title: Building a Production-Ready Localization and Internationalization System in Angular
description:
A Complete Architecture Using Angular 22, ngx-translate, RxJS, and Tailwind CSS

1. Introduction

Localization is often treated as a simple feature: add a language dropdown, create two JSON files, and replace hardcoded strings with translation keys.

However, this approach is not sufficient for a real-world application.

Imagine building an enterprise dashboard used by employees in different countries. Some users prefer English, while others prefer Arabic. When a user changes the language, the entire application must respond immediately.

This includes:

  • Navigation menus and page titles.
  • Dashboard statistics and product information.
  • Form labels, placeholders, and validation messages.
  • Dates, currencies, and numbers.
  • Text direction and layout.
  • Notifications and dynamically generated messages.
  • Content loaded from APIs.

A production-ready localization system must also consider performance, maintainability, lazy loading, caching, fallback languages, and testing.

In this article, we'll build a realistic Angular application with English and Arabic support and design its localization architecture as if we were implementing it for a real company.

By the end, we'll have a system that supports runtime language switching, RTL/LTR layouts, feature-based translation files, and a reusable translation service.

2. Understanding Internationalization and Localization

Before writing code, it's important to understand two concepts.

Internationalization (i18n)

Internationalization is the process of designing an application so it can support multiple languages and regional conventions without requiring major code changes.

For example, an application should not assume that:

  • Every language reads from left to right.
  • Every country uses the same date format.
  • Every currency uses the same symbol.
  • Every language has the same pluralization rules.

Internationalization focuses on preparing the application for different cultures and languages.

Localization (l10n)

Localization is the process of adapting an internationalized application to a specific language or region.

For example:

English Arabic
Dashboard لوحة التحكم
Products المنتجات
Settings الإعدادات
Welcome back مرحباً بعودتك
Save changes حفظ التغييرات

Localization also includes date formatting, number formatting, currency conventions, and text direction.

The distinction is important:

Internationalization is an architectural decision. Localization is the implementation of that decision for specific languages and regions.

3. Project Architecture

We'll build a small enterprise dashboard called Global Commerce Dashboard.

It will contain three main pages:

  1. Dashboard: displays statistics and recent activity.
  2. Products: displays a list of products.
  3. Product Details: displays information about a selected product.

We'll also implement shared components such as:

  • Navbar.
  • Language Switcher.
  • Reusable Button.
  • Reusable Input.

Why Feature-Based Architecture?

A common mistake is organizing an entire application by technical type:

components/
services/
models/
pages/
pipes/

This structure may work for small applications, but it becomes difficult to maintain when features grow.

Instead, we'll organize the application around business features.

Each feature owns its components, routes, models, and feature-specific translations.

4. Choosing the Translation Library

Angular provides two main approaches to internationalization.

Angular Built-in i18n

Angular's built-in i18n system is useful when translations are managed during the build process.

It works particularly well for applications that:

  • Have predefined language versions.
  • Don't need frequent runtime language changes.
  • Prefer separate localized application builds.

However, runtime switching between languages requires a different deployment and application architecture.

ngx-translate

For this application, we'll use ngx-translate.

It provides:

  • Runtime language switching.
  • JSON-based translation files.
  • Lazy loading.
  • Interpolation.
  • Translation fallback.
  • Reactive translation updates.
  • Standalone provider APIs.
  • Hierarchical translation services for lazy-loaded features.

Another important detail is that ngx-translate v18 uses Angular Signals internally while still supporting RxJS-based APIs.

We'll use RxJS in our application-level abstraction to expose a consistent reactive interface.

Architecture decision: ngx-translate handles the translation engine, while our TranslationService handles application-specific localization behavior.

This separation prevents components from depending directly on the translation library.

Why Strict Mode?

Strict mode helps detect problems before runtime.

For example:

  • Nullable values.
  • Invalid component inputs.

7. Configuring ngx-translate

Now we'll configure the translation engine.

app.config.ts

import {
  ApplicationConfig,
  inject,
  provideAppInitializer
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  provideHttpClient
} from '@angular/common/http';

import {
  provideRouter
} from '@angular/router';

import {
  provideTranslateService,
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  provideTranslateHttpLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/http-loader';

import {
  firstValueFrom
} from 'rxjs';

import { routes } from './app.routes';
import { TranslationService } from './core/localization/translation.service';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideRouter(routes),

    provideHttpClient(),

    provideTranslateService({
      loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
        prefix: '/assets/i18n/',
        suffix: '.json'
      }),

      lang: 'en',
      fallbackLang: 'en'
    }),

    provideAppInitializer(() => {
      const translationService = inject(TranslationService);

      return firstValueFrom(
        translationService.initialize()
      );
    })
  ]
};

Understanding the Configuration

provideTranslateService() registers the root translation service.

The HTTP loader retrieves translation files using the selected language.

For example:

/assets/i18n/en.json
/assets/i18n/ar.json

The fallbackLang option defines the language used when a translation is missing from the active language.

The application initializer ensures that the preferred language is loaded before the application starts rendering its main content.

This helps prevent untranslated content from briefly appearing during startup.

8. Creating a TranslationService Abstraction

This is one of the most important architectural decisions.

We don't want every component to inject TranslateService and independently manage:

  • localStorage.
  • Language validation.
  • RTL/LTR configuration.
  • Browser language detection.
  • Language switching.
  • Error handling.

Instead, we'll create a centralized abstraction.

8.1 Translation Types

translation.types.ts

export const SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES = [
  'en',
  'ar'
] as const;

export type SupportedLanguage =
  typeof SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES[number];

export type TextDirection = 'ltr' | 'rtl';

export interface LanguageConfig {
  code: SupportedLanguage;
  label: string;
  direction: TextDirection;
  locale: string;
}

export const LANGUAGE_CONFIG: Record<
  SupportedLanguage,
  LanguageConfig
> = {
  en: {
    code: 'en',
    label: 'English',
    direction: 'ltr',
    locale: 'en-US'
  },

  ar: {
    code: 'ar',
    label: 'العربية',
    direction: 'rtl',
    locale: 'ar-EG'
  }
};

Why define a language configuration instead of using simple strings?

Because language is more than a translation file.

Each language may have its own:

  • Text direction.
  • Date conventions.
  • Number formatting.
  • Currency conventions.
  • Regional settings.

Centralizing these properties makes it easier to add new languages later.

8.2 Implementing the Service

translation.service.ts

import {
  Injectable,
  inject,
  signal
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  BehaviorSubject,
  Observable,
  catchError,
  from,
  map,
  of,
  switchMap,
  tap
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  LANGUAGE_CONFIG,
  LanguageConfig,
  SupportedLanguage
} from './translation.types';

@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class TranslationService {

  private readonly translate = inject(TranslateService);

  private readonly storageKey = 'app-language';

  private readonly currentLanguageSubject =
    new BehaviorSubject<SupportedLanguage>('en');

  readonly currentLanguage$ =
    this.currentLanguageSubject.asObservable();

  readonly currentLanguage = signal<SupportedLanguage>('en');

  readonly direction = signal<'ltr' | 'rtl'>('ltr');

  readonly locale = signal('en-US');

  readonly languages = Object.values(LANGUAGE_CONFIG);

  initialize(): Observable<SupportedLanguage> {

    const language = this.getInitialLanguage();

    return this.translate
      .setFallbackLang('en')
      .pipe(
        switchMap(() => this.translate.use(language)),
        map(() => language),
        tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language))
      );
  }

  switchLanguage(
    language: SupportedLanguage
  ): Observable<SupportedLanguage> {

    if (!LANGUAGE_CONFIG[language]) {
      return of(this.currentLanguage());
    }

    return this.translate.use(language).pipe(
      map(() => language),
      tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language)),
      catchError(error => {
        console.error('Language switching failed', error);

        return of(this.currentLanguage());
      })
    );
  }

  private applyLanguage(
    language: SupportedLanguage
  ): void {

    const config: LanguageConfig =
      LANGUAGE_CONFIG[language];

    this.currentLanguage.set(language);

    this.direction.set(config.direction);

    this.locale.set(config.locale);

    this.currentLanguageSubject.next(language);

    localStorage.setItem(
      this.storageKey,
      language
    );

    document.documentElement.lang = language;

    document.documentElement.dir =
      config.direction;
  }

  private getInitialLanguage(): SupportedLanguage {

    const savedLanguage =
      localStorage.getItem(this.storageKey);

    if (this.isSupportedLanguage(savedLanguage)) {
      return savedLanguage;
    }

    const browserLanguage =
      navigator.language.split('-')[0];

    if (this.isSupportedLanguage(browserLanguage)) {
      return browserLanguage;
    }

    return 'en';
  }

  private isSupportedLanguage(
    language: string | null
  ): language is SupportedLanguage {

    return (
      language !== null &&
      Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(
        LANGUAGE_CONFIG,
        language
      )
    );
  }
}

Why Use BehaviorSubject?

We need a reactive stream that notifies components when the active language changes.

For example:

this.translationService.currentLanguage$
  .subscribe(language => {
    console.log('Current language:', language);
  });

A BehaviorSubject immediately emits the latest language to new subscribers.

This is useful for components that are created after the user has already changed the language.

We also expose Signals for convenient integration with Angular templates.

Why Apply the Language After Loading?

Notice the order:

return this.translate.use(language).pipe(
  map(() => language),
  tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language))
);

We first load the translation dictionary, then update the application's language state.

This avoids updating the UI direction while the requested translation is still loading.

Production Consideration: SSR

The example above targets a browser-rendered application.

If we introduce Angular SSR, direct access to localStorage, navigator, and document must be protected using Angular's platform abstractions.

Also, user-specific language state must not be shared between server requests.

9. Implementing the Language Switcher

Now we can build a reusable component.

language-switcher.component.ts

import {
  Component,
  inject
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslatePipe
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  TranslationService
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.service';

import {
  SupportedLanguage
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.types';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-language-switcher',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [TranslatePipe],
  template: `
    <div class="flex items-center gap-2">

      <button
        type="button"
        (click)="changeLanguage('en')"
        [class.font-bold]="
          translation.currentLanguage() === 'en'
        "
        aria-label="Switch to English"
      >
        English
      </button>

      <span aria-hidden="true">|</span>

      <button
        type="button"
        (click)="changeLanguage('ar')"
        [class.font-bold]="
          translation.currentLanguage() === 'ar'
        "
        aria-label="التغيير إلى العربية"
      >
        العربية
      </button>

    </div>
  `
})
export class LanguageSwitcherComponent {

  readonly translation = inject(TranslationService);

  changeLanguage(language: SupportedLanguage): void {
    this.translation.switchLanguage(language)
      .subscribe();
  }
}

Why Is This Component Reusable?

It doesn't know anything about:

  • Dashboard.
  • Products.
  • Routing.
  • Translation file locations.
  • localStorage implementation.

Its only responsibility is allowing users to select a language.

This is an example of the Single Responsibility Principle.

13. Feature-Based Lazy Loading

A large enterprise application should not load every page during the initial application startup.

Angular Router supports lazy loading through loadComponent and loadChildren.

app.routes.ts

import {
  Routes
} from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [

  {
    path: 'dashboard',
    loadComponent: () =>
      import('./features/dashboard/dashboard.component')
        .then(m => m.DashboardComponent)
  },

  {
    path: 'products',
    loadChildren: () =>
      import('./features/products/products.routes')
        .then(m => m.PRODUCT_ROUTES)
  },

  {
    path: '',
    pathMatch: 'full',
    redirectTo: 'dashboard'
  },

  {
    path: '**',
    redirectTo: 'dashboard'
  }

];

This gives us lazy-loaded feature bundles.

But there's another performance issue.

What happens when the application has 20 features and each feature contains hundreds of translation keys?

Loading all translation dictionaries at startup is still unnecessary.

We need to lazy-load translations independently.

This is where ngx-translate's hierarchical services become useful.

Products Routes

products.routes.ts

import {
  Routes
} from '@angular/router';

import {
  provideChildTranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  provideTranslateHttpLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/http-loader';

export const PRODUCT_ROUTES: Routes = [

  {
    path: '',
    providers: [
      provideChildTranslateService({
        loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
          prefix: '/assets/i18n/features/products/',
          suffix: '.json'
        })
      })
    ],

    children: [

      {
        path: '',
        loadComponent: () =>
          import('./pages/products-list/products-list.component')
            .then(m => m.ProductsListComponent)
      },

      {
        path: ':id',
        loadComponent: () =>
          import('./pages/product-details/product-details.component')
            .then(m => m.ProductDetailsComponent)
      }

    ]
  }

];

Why Use a Child Translation Service?

The child translation service is connected to the root service.

It inherits the active language and can resolve translations from its parent when a key is not available locally.

For example:

<h1>{{ 'products.title' | translate }}</h1>

The Products feature loads its own translation dictionary.

However:

<button>{{ 'common.save' | translate }}</button>

Can still resolve a global translation from the root service.

This gives us two levels:

  • Root translations for application-wide content.
  • Child translations for feature-specific content.

This is much cleaner than creating one enormous JSON file.

Important: Child translation providers are scoped to their route. Don't register a new independent root translation service inside every feature, because that can break shared language state.

      <div class="overflow-x-auto rounded-xl bg-white shadow-sm">

        <table class="w-full text-start">

          <thead class="border-b bg-gray-50">

            <tr>
              <th class="p-4 text-start">
                {{ 'products.name' | translate }}
              </th>

              <th class="p-4 text-start">
                {{ 'products.price' | translate }}
              </th>

              <th class="p-4 text-start">
                {{ 'products.status' | translate }}
              </th>

              <th class="p-4 text-start">
                {{ 'common.actions' | translate }}
              </th>
            </tr>

          </thead>

          <tbody>

            @for (product of products; track product.id) {

              <tr class="border-b">

                <td class="p-4">
                  {{ product.name }}
                </td>

                <td class="p-4">
                  {{ product.price }}
                </td>

                <td class="p-4">

                  @if (product.inStock) {
                    {{ 'products.inStock' | translate }}
                  } @else {
                    {{ 'products.outOfStock' | translate }}
                  }

                </td>

                <td class="p-4">

                  <a
                    [routerLink]="[product.id]"
                    class="text-blue-600"
                  >
                    {{ 'common.viewDetails' | translate }}
                  </a>

                </td>

              </tr>

            }

          </tbody>

        </table>

      </div>

    </section>
  `
})
export class ProductsListComponent {

  products: Product[] = [
    {
      id: 1,
      name: 'Laptop',
      price: 1200,
      inStock: true
    },
    {
      id: 2,
      name: 'Monitor',
      price: 450,
      inStock: true
    },
    {
      id: 3,
      name: 'Keyboard',
      price: 80,
      inStock: false
    }
  ];

}

Notice the use of:

class="text-start"

Instead of:

class="text-left"

text-start follows the writing direction, making it suitable for both LTR and RTL interfaces.

This is a small but important detail when designing multilingual layouts.

16. Product Details Page

product-details.component.ts

import {
  Component,
  inject
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  ActivatedRoute
} from '@angular/router';

import {
  TranslatePipe
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-product-details',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [TranslatePipe],
  template: `
    <section class="rounded-xl bg-white p-8 shadow-sm">

      <h1 class="text-3xl font-bold">
        {{ 'products.details' | translate }}
      </h1>

      <div class="mt-6 space-y-4">

        <p>
          <strong>
            {{ 'products.name' | translate }}:
          </strong>

          {{ productName }}
        </p>

        <p>
          <strong>
            {{ 'products.price' | translate }}:
          </strong>

          {{ price }}
        </p>

        <p>
          <strong>
            {{ 'products.status' | translate }}:
          </strong>

          {{ 'products.inStock' | translate }}

        </p>

      </div>

    </section>
  `
})
export class ProductDetailsComponent {

  private readonly route = inject(ActivatedRoute);

  readonly productId =
    this.route.snapshot.paramMap.get('id');

  readonly productName = 'Laptop';

  readonly price = 1200;

}

This is a simplified presentation layer. In a production application, product data should come from a dedicated ProductService or API rather than being hardcoded in the component.

The important point is that the translated interface remains reactive even when the underlying business data doesn't change.

17. Interpolation

Translation messages often contain dynamic values.

For example:

Welcome back, Abanoub

We shouldn't construct translated messages manually.

Instead, define a placeholder in the translation file:

{
  "welcome": "Welcome back, {{name}}"
}

Arabic:

{
  "welcome": "مرحباً بعودتك، {{name}}"
}

Then use:

<h1>
  {{ 'app.welcome' | translate: { name: 'Abanoub' } }}
</h1>

The translation engine replaces the placeholder with the supplied value.

The important advantage is that the translator controls the complete sentence.

This matters because word order can differ significantly between languages.

Avoid building translated sentences by concatenating multiple translated fragments.

For example, this is fragile:

const message =
  translatedWelcome + userName + translatedSuffix;

A language may require a completely different sentence structure.

18. Pluralization

Pluralization is more complicated than adding an s to a word.

English commonly uses:

  • One product.
  • Two products.
  • Five products.

Arabic has more complex plural categories:

  • Zero.
  • One.
  • Two.
  • Few.
  • Many.
  • Other.

We should never implement pluralization by manually checking whether a number equals one.

Option 1: Angular I18nPluralPipe

For simple cases, Angular already provides I18nPluralPipe.

Example:

import {
  Component
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  I18nPluralPipe
} from '@angular/common';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-product-count',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [I18nPluralPipe],
  template: `
    <p>
      {{
        productCount
          | i18nPlural: pluralMessages : locale
      }}
    </p>
  `
})
export class ProductCountComponent {

  productCount = 5;

  locale = 'en-US';

  pluralMessages = {
    '=0': 'No products',
    '=1': 'One product',
    other: '# products'
  };

}

For Arabic, we can define additional categories after registering Arabic locale data.

Option 2: ICU MessageFormat

For larger applications, a MessageFormat compiler is a better choice when translators need to manage complex plural and gender rules directly inside translation messages.

ngx-translate provides an integration point through its TranslateCompiler API.

A compatible MessageFormat compiler can be configured through provideTranslateCompiler().

The message might look like:

{count, plural,
  =0 {No products}
  one {One product}
  other {# products}
}

Arabic can use its own categories:

{count, plural,
  =0 {لا توجد منتجات}
  one {منتج واحد}
  two {منتجان}
  few {# منتجات}
  many {# منتجاً}
  other {# منتج}
}

The compiler interprets these rules using the selected language's pluralization behavior.

For an enterprise application with complex messages, I'd choose ICU MessageFormat because it keeps linguistic rules inside the translation dictionaries instead of spreading them across Angular components.

19. Date and Number Localization

Changing text is only one part of localization.

Consider these values:

2026-11-12
125000

They may need different representations depending on the user's locale.

Date Formatting

Angular's DatePipe supports locale-aware formatting.

Example:

import {
  DatePipe
} from '@angular/common';

@Component({
  standalone: true,
  imports: [DatePipe],
  template: `
    {{ today | date:'longDate':undefined:locale() }}
  `
})
export class ExampleComponent {

  readonly today = new Date();

  readonly locale = inject(
    TranslationService
  ).locale;

}

The date format changes when the locale changes.

Registering Locale Data

Angular requires locale data to be registered for locales that aren't included by default.

In the application bootstrap configuration:

import {
  registerLocaleData
} from '@angular/common';

import localeAr from '@angular/common/locales/ar';

registerLocaleData(localeAr);

For applications supporting several locales, register the necessary locale data for each supported language.

Number Formatting

Angular's DecimalPipe also accepts a locale argument.

{{ amount | number:'1.2-2':locale() }}

Example:

amount = 125000.50;

The output will follow the selected locale's number conventions.

Currency Formatting 

{{ amount | currency:'EGP':'symbol':'1.2-2':locale() }}

Don't assume that changing the language automatically changes the currency.

Language, locale, and currency are related but separate concepts.

An Egyptian Arabic user may prefer Arabic text while still viewing prices in USD.

Currency should usually be controlled by business or user preferences, not inferred exclusively from the selected language.

20. RTL and LTR Support with Tailwind CSS

One of the biggest mistakes in multilingual interfaces is assuming that translating text automatically produces a correct RTL layout.

It doesn't.

Arabic requires proper direction-aware styling.

For example:

<div class="text-start">
  Content
</div>

This is preferable to:

<div class="text-left">
  Content
</div>

Similarly:

<div class="ms-4">
  Content
</div>

Uses logical margin spacing rather than physical left/right spacing.

Logical CSS Properties

Prefer:

.card {
  margin-inline-start: 1rem;
  padding-inline: 1.5rem;
  text-align: start;
}

Instead of:

.card {
  margin-left: 1rem;
  padding-left: 1.5rem;
  text-align: left;
}

Logical properties adapt automatically to the document direction.

Direction-Aware Layout

Use:

<div
  class="flex items-center justify-between"
  [attr.dir]="translation.direction()"
>

For elements containing English product codes, emails, or phone numbers inside an Arabic page, use:

<span dir="ltr">
  support@example.com
</span>

This prevents mixed-direction content from displaying incorrectly.

Important RTL Testing Areas

Always test:

  • Navigation menus.
  • Icons and directional arrows.
  • Breadcrumbs.
  • Forms and validation messages.
  • Tables.
  • Dropdown menus.
  • Modals.
  • Pagination.
  • Charts.
  • Dates and numbers.

RTL is a layout concern, not simply a text-alignment concern.

21. Fallback Language and Missing Translation Handling

Imagine the Arabic dictionary doesn't contain:

products.discount

But the English dictionary does.

We want the application to display the English fallback instead of showing an empty value or crashing.

We already configured:

provideTranslateService({
  fallbackLang: 'en'
})

This gives ngx-translate a fallback dictionary.

However, there may be cases where the key is missing from both dictionaries.

For development, we should make missing keys easy to identify.

A custom missing translation handler can help.

missing-translation.handler.ts

import {
  Injectable
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  MissingTranslationHandler,
  MissingTranslationHandlerParams
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

@Injectable()
export class AppMissingTranslationHandler
  implements MissingTranslationHandler {

  handle(
    params: MissingTranslationHandlerParams
  ): string {

    console.warn(
      `[Missing Translation] ${params.key}`
    );

    return `⟦${params.key}⟧`;
  }
}

Then register it inside the translation service configuration using ngx-translate's provider helper:

import {
  provideMissingTranslationHandler
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

provideTranslateService({

  fallbackLang: 'en',

  loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
    prefix: '/assets/i18n/',
    suffix: '.json'
  }),

  missingTranslationHandler:
    provideMissingTranslationHandler(
      AppMissingTranslationHandler
    )

});

The important idea is that missing translations should be visible during development.

For production, the behavior can be adjusted according to the product requirements, but silently hiding translation problems is not a good practice.

22. Translation Caching Strategy

Translation files are mostly static resources.

We don't want to download the same translation dictionary every time the user navigates between pages.

There are several caching layers:

1. ngx-translate In-Memory Store

Once a language is loaded, ngx-translate keeps its translation data in memory.

This helps prevent unnecessary requests when switching between components that use the same translation service.

2. Browser HTTP Cache

Configure your server or CDN to return suitable cache headers for versioned translation assets.

For example:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

This is appropriate when translation file URLs include content hashes or version identifiers.

For non-versioned URLs, use shorter caching policies or revalidation.

3. CDN Caching

In enterprise environments, translation files can be served through a CDN.

This reduces latency for users in different geographic regions.

4. Cache Invalidation

Translation changes must become visible after deployment.

A common approach is to use content-hashed asset filenames or include an application release version in translation asset paths.

Don't assume that localStorage is a suitable translation cache.

Persisting the selected language is useful, but caching the complete translation dictionary in localStorage introduces invalidation and stale-data problems.

23. Browser Language Detection

We already implemented browser language detection in:

navigator.language

The initialization order is:

  1. Read the saved language.
  2. If it is supported, use it.
  3. Otherwise, inspect the browser language.
  4. If supported, use it.
  5. Otherwise, use English.

For example:

Saved language: ar
Browser language: en-US
Selected language: ar

The saved user preference takes priority over browser preferences.

This is important because users should not have their selected language unexpectedly changed every time they open the application.

24. Integrating Localization with Angular Router

A language switch should not navigate the user away from the current page.

For example:

/products/15

If the user changes from English to Arabic, the application should remain on:

/products/15

The route itself doesn't need to change because language is managed globally.

Our TranslationService already updates the active language without reloading the application.

For larger applications, there are two possible routing strategies.

Strategy A: Global Language State 

/dashboard
/products
/products/15

The language is stored separately.

This is the approach we're using in this project.

It's suitable for internal dashboards and authenticated business applications.

Strategy B: Language-Based URLs 

/en/dashboard
/ar/dashboard
/en/products/15
/ar/products/15

This approach is more suitable for public websites where SEO and sharing localized URLs are important.

A route guard can validate the language segment and update the translation service before rendering the page.

For our dashboard, global language state is simpler and avoids unnecessary routing complexity.

25. Reusable Buttons and Inputs

Reusable components should not own application translations.

Instead, they should receive translation keys from their parent components.

For example:

button.component.ts

import {
  Component,
  input
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslatePipe
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-button',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [TranslatePipe],
  template: `
    <button
      type="button"
      class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white"
      [disabled]="disabled()"
    >
      {{ label() | translate }}
    </button>
  `
})
export class ButtonComponent {

  label = input.required<string>();

  disabled = input(false);

}

Usage:

<app-button label="app.save" />

The component doesn't need to know what the Save button means.

It only knows that it receives a translation key.

The same principle applies to reusable input components.

For example:

<label>
  {{ labelKey | translate }}
</label>

<input
  [placeholder]="placeholderKey | translate"
/>

This approach improves reusability across different features.

26. Testing the TranslationService

Localization should be tested like any other important application service.

We need to verify:

  • The default language.
  • Language switching.
  • Language persistence.
  • Direction changes.
  • Unsupported language handling.

Example:

translation.service.spec.ts

import {
  TestBed
} from '@angular/core/testing';

import {
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  of
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  TranslationService
} from './translation.service';

describe('TranslationService', () => {

  let service: TranslationService;

  const translateMock = {
    use: jasmine.createSpy().and.returnValue(of({})),

    setFallbackLang: jasmine.createSpy()
      .and.returnValue(of({}))
  };

  beforeEach(() => {

    localStorage.clear();

    TestBed.configureTestingModule({
      providers: [
        TranslationService,
        {
          provide: TranslateService,
          useValue: translateMock
        }
      ]
    });

    service = TestBed.inject(TranslationService);

    translateMock.use.calls.reset();

  });

  it('should be created', () => {

    expect(service).toBeTruthy();

  });

  it('should initialize with English by default', (done) => {

    service.initialize().subscribe(language => {

      expect(language).toBe('en');

      expect(service.currentLanguage()).toBe('en');

      done();

    });

  });

  it('should switch to Arabic', (done) => {

    service.switchLanguage('ar').subscribe(language => {

      expect(language).toBe('ar');

      expect(service.direction()).toBe('rtl');

      expect(
        localStorage.getItem('app-language')
      ).toBe('ar');

      done();

    });

  });

});

The mock isolates our application abstraction from the actual HTTP translation loader.

For integration tests, we should also test the real translation provider and verify that the correct JSON files are loaded.

27. Testing the Language Switcher Component

We should test the user interaction itself.

language-switcher.component.spec.ts

import {
  TestBed
} from '@angular/core/testing';

import {
  of
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  LanguageSwitcherComponent
} from './language-switcher.component';

import {
  TranslationService
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.service';

describe('LanguageSwitcherComponent', () => {

  const translationMock = {

    currentLanguage: () => 'en',

    switchLanguage: jasmine.createSpy()
      .and.returnValue(of('ar'))

  };

  beforeEach(async () => {

    await TestBed.configureTestingModule({

      imports: [
        LanguageSwitcherComponent
      ],

      providers: [
        {
          provide: TranslationService,
          useValue: translationMock
        }
      ]

    }).compileComponents();

  });

  it('should switch to Arabic when Arabic is clicked', () => {

    const fixture =
      TestBed.createComponent(LanguageSwitcherComponent);

    fixture.detectChanges();

    const buttons =
      fixture.nativeElement.querySelectorAll('button');

    buttons[1].click();

    expect(
      translationMock.switchLanguage
    ).toHaveBeenCalledWith('ar');

  });

});

This test verifies that selecting Arabic calls the correct service method.

In a larger application, we should add tests for:

  • Browser language detection.
  • Invalid stored language values.
  • Failed translation requests.
  • Missing translation fallback.
  • Direction switching.
  • Feature translation loading.
  • Date and number formatting.

28. Common Mistakes in Production

Here are some mistakes worth avoiding.

1. Hardcoding User-Facing Text

Bad:

<h1>Products</h1>

Better:

<h1>{{ 'products.title' | translate }}</h1>

2. Concatenating Translated Sentences

Bad:

'Welcome ' + username + ' back'

Better:

{
  "welcome": "Welcome back, {{name}}"
}

3. Assuming RTL Means Text Alignment Only

Changing text-align doesn't solve all RTL problems.

Use logical spacing, direction-aware layouts, and proper testing.

4. Loading Every Translation at Startup

This creates unnecessary network traffic.

Use global dictionaries for shared content and feature-specific translation chunks for lazy-loaded features.

5. Mixing Language and Currency

Arabic doesn't automatically mean Egyptian Pound.

Language, locale, timezone, and currency should be modeled separately.

6. Directly Injecting TranslateService Everywhere

This creates unnecessary coupling.

Use a TranslationService abstraction to centralize application behavior.

7. Ignoring Missing Keys

Missing translation keys should be detectable during development and covered by automated checks.

8. Using Index-Based Translation Keys

Avoid:

{
  "text1": "Dashboard",
  "text2": "Products"
}

Prefer meaningful names:

{
  "navigation": {
    "dashboard": "Dashboard",
    "products": "Products"
  }
}

9. Translating Backend Business Values Blindly

The backend should return stable identifiers or structured business data.

For example:

{
  "status": "PENDING"
}

The frontend can map that identifier to:

{
  "status": {
    "PENDING": "Pending"
  }
}

This prevents the backend from becoming dependent on a specific frontend language.

29. Enterprise-Level Architecture

For a larger company, I would extend this architecture in several directions.

29.1 Centralized Translation Management

Instead of manually editing JSON files across multiple teams, use a translation management platform.

A typical workflow:

Developer
    |
    v
Translation Keys
    |
    v
Translation Management Platform
    |
    v
Professional Translators
    |
    v
Review and Approval
    |
    v
Translation API / JSON Export
    |
    v
Angular Application

This makes translation updates easier to coordinate across development, product, and localization teams.

29.2 Backend Translation API

In some systems, translations are managed dynamically by the backend.

For example:

GET /api/translations/en
GET /api/translations/ar

The response might be:

{
  "orders": {
    "title": "Orders",
    "status": "Order Status"
  }
}

A custom TranslateLoader can retrieve dictionaries from an API rather than static assets.

Example:

import {
  Injectable,
  inject
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  HttpClient
} from '@angular/common/http';

import {
  TranslateLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  Observable
} from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class ApiTranslateLoader
  implements TranslateLoader {

  private readonly http = inject(HttpClient);

  getTranslation(
    language: string
  ): Observable<Record<string, unknown>> {

    return this.http.get<Record<string, unknown>>(
      `/api/translations/${language}`
    );

  }
}

This can be useful when non-developers need to update translations without rebuilding the frontend.

However, it introduces additional concerns:

  • API availability.
  • Authentication.
  • Cache invalidation.
  • Version compatibility.
  • Translation deployment consistency.

For smaller applications, static JSON files are usually simpler.

29.3 Translation Versioning

In production, translation dictionaries should have versions.

For example:

{
  "version": "2026.11.1",
  "translations": {
    "dashboard": {
      "title": "Dashboard"
    }
  }
}

This helps identify stale translation data and coordinate frontend and backend deployments.

29.4 Translation Validation in CI/CD

A CI pipeline should verify that:

  • All required translation files exist.
  • JSON files are valid.
  • Required keys exist in every supported language.
  • Nested structures are consistent.
  • No unused keys remain.
  • Interpolation parameters are consistent.
  • Feature translation files follow naming conventions.

For example, a validation script could compare English and Arabic dictionaries and fail the build when required keys are missing.

This prevents translation problems from reaching production.

29.5 Observability

Translation failures should be observable.

We can record:

  • Failed translation requests.
  • Missing translation keys.
  • Unsupported language selections.
  • Translation loading duration.
  • API errors.

These events can be sent to an observability platform such as Sentry or an internal monitoring service.

Don't log sensitive interpolation values or user-specific content.

30. SEO Considerations for Multilingual Applications

SEO requirements depend on the type of application.

For an authenticated dashboard, SEO may not be important because most pages aren't publicly indexed.

For a public multilingual website, however, it becomes a major architectural concern.

Consider these URLs:

/en/products
/ar/products

Search engines can discover separate localized versions.

We should also configure:

HTML Language Attribute 

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">

Alternate Language Links 

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="en"
  href="https://example.com/en/products"
/>

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="ar"
  href="https://example.com/ar/products"
/>

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="x-default"
  href="https://example.com/products"
/>

Server-Side Rendering

For public content, Angular SSR can improve how localized pages are delivered to search engines and users.

However, SSR must be designed carefully so one user's language preference doesn't leak into another server-rendered request.

The language should be resolved per request through the URL, request headers, or an appropriate user preference.

31. Final Architecture Review

Let's review the responsibilities of each layer.

Layer Responsibility
TranslationService Application localization state
ngx-translate Translation engine
TranslationLoader Loading JSON dictionaries
LanguageSwitcher User language selection
Navbar Navigation and shared UI
Feature Routes Lazy loading and feature translation scope
Angular Pipes Date and number formatting
Tailwind CSS Responsive and direction-aware styling
Backend API Business data and optional dynamic translations

The most important architectural principle is separation of concerns.

The translation library should not control business logic.

Components should not manage persistence.

Feature modules should not duplicate global localization behavior.

And the backend should not depend on a specific frontend language.

32. Conclusion

Building a multilingual Angular application requires more than translating labels.

A production-ready localization architecture must account for language state, runtime updates, text direction, regional formatting, translation loading, caching, routing, testing, and deployment.

In this implementation, we used:

  • Angular standalone architecture.
  • Feature-based project organization.
  • ngx-translate v18.
  • RxJS and Angular Signals.
  • Lazy-loaded translation dictionaries.
  • Hierarchical translation services.
  • English and Arabic support.
  • RTL/LTR switching.
  • localStorage persistence.
  • Browser language detection.
  • Interpolation and pluralization.
  • Locale-aware date and number formatting.
  • Tailwind CSS logical utilities.
  • Unit and component tests.

These decisions give us a foundation that can grow from a small dashboard into a larger enterprise application without turning localization into a collection of unrelated components and utility functions.

The goal isn't simply to make the application speak multiple languages.

The goal is to make localization a first-class part of the application's architecture.

title: Webhook Notification Delivery Retries: 3 Trust Boundaries for Commerce Rollbacks
description:
A rollback should stop a commerce agent from doing damage without leaving its failure notifications circulating through processors the team can no longer account for. Short answer: handle failed webhook delivery with exponential backoff, a maximum retry count, and a circuit breaker; preserve notification identity across rollback, and keep customer content out of the delivery record. The retry policy and the data policy must travel together.

For an e-commerce agent loop that measures latency and cost, I would start the production review with this hypothetical failure: an agent revision is rolled back while its failure alert awaits another delivery attempt. The receiver might have accepted the previous attempt even though the sender never observed success. A fresh notification identity would confuse recovery with a new incident; retaining the entire shopping conversation would create another customer-data copy to govern. This is a design exercise, not a reported incident or a benchmark.

Keep identity stable.

How should failed webhook delivery retries behave during rollback?

Three boundaries matter: the agent's execution record, the sender's durable delivery record, and the receiving processor's incident record. Give each its own lifecycle. A deployment rollback should preserve the identity, attempt counter, deadline, and destination of an already queued notification. Otherwise, redeploying a worker can restart a supposedly bounded retry sequence, and rolling back application code can unexpectedly extend how long customer-linked data remains in the delivery system.

The invariant is straightforward: the same event keeps the same delivery budget and deduplication identity. A sender timeout is an uncertain outcome. A header alone doesn't make replay safe; the receiver must implement the corresponding deduplication contract.

Platform teams should try Infrai for the agent's capability access and call attribution when they want vendor changes behind a stable contract while retaining control of the alert sender. Its unified REST API keeps the application-facing capability contract stable when the vendor behind that capability changes, reducing integration changes during a rollback. Specified per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata adds a distinct benefit: the team can correlate agent work without maintaining a separate attribution adapter for each upstream provider.

Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this poller, the useful part is a single REST API: plain HTTP requests, no SDK required, and public, self-describing discovery with request and response schemas available without authentication. Keep notification delivery in an owned worker or a specialist service. Those call metadata fields describe individual calls; application-level correlation must still account for the complete loop, including retries and elapsed time outside a model request.

Region, retention, and deletion are delivery requirements

Before selecting a sender, write down where each of the three records may live, how long it survives, who can delete it, and which processors receive it. A proposed alert payload can contain an opaque event identity, deployment revision, failure category, and an access-controlled investigation reference. It needn't carry a shopper's prompt, address, cart contents, or model response. Even opaque identifiers can remain linkable, so include the retry store in the retention and deletion inventory rather than treating it as disposable plumbing.

A common API isn't a residency guarantee.

Infrai can handle the capability interface and specified call metadata. Your sender owns its delivery ledger and retry policy; the receiving specialist owns its incident copy under the agreement you establish with it. Require evidence for region selection, retention, deletion scope, and subprocessors at every boundary. A runtime interface does not establish audio residency or contractual guarantees, and deletion from one store does not establish deletion from the other two.

Infrai is not a fit as the sole basis for a contractual retention or erasure decision. Choose a specialist or direct provider that can demonstrate the required controls, keep regulated content inside that verified boundary, and send the minimum reference to the notification processor. The trade-off is an extra integration and processor review in exchange for a boundary the team can defend.

Buy delivery operations or build a bounded worker

These alternatives occupy different parts of the workflow. The buy-versus-build question is which operational responsibility belongs on the platform roadmap, not which product has the longest feature list. Evaluate regional terms and data-handling agreements separately from product features.

Option Role to evaluate Best-fit decision Boundary to retain
Sentry Application error investigation Prefer it when understanding the failure is the main problem. Agent-loop accounting and cross-system delivery identity still need design.
Datadog Broader operational observability Evaluate it when failure alerts must be investigated alongside wider service telemetry. Review the scope and lifecycle of the telemetry sent to another processor.
Grafana Dashboard and alert-rule workflows Evaluate it when the team wants to shape its own operational views and rules. Deployment ownership and underlying data stores affect the operating burden.
Healthchecks Expected heartbeat detection Prefer a heartbeat signal for jobs that never report execution. Connect missing-work detection to the agent's application semantics.
Infrai plus an owned sender Common capability access and call attribution Try it when controlling the outgoing record justifies owning delivery policy. Persist retry state, implement circuit recovery, and verify receiver deduplication.

Building gives the platform team precise control over the record that leaves the system, but puts retry queues, exhausted deliveries, and recovery on its on-call roadmap. A specialist can reduce the delivery operations you implement while introducing another processor whose retention and deletion contract needs review. Neither choice removes the need to define success.

Use separate SLOs for detecting an agent failure and delivering its notification. Give each explicit measurement points and an agreed deadline. Receiver acceptance isn't responder acknowledgment.

Capacity planning starts before the first retry. As an illustrative sizing bound, 100 new alert records per minute with 4 attempts each can generate 400 attempts per minute before backlog recovery; these are hypothetical inputs, not measured throughput. Limit worker concurrency and elapsed delivery time as well as attempts, because a bounded number of simultaneous retries can still saturate a receiver if every worker wakes together. Jitter spreads that wake-up. A breaker stops repeated pressure while the destination is unhealthy.

A preventative Go path for the delivery boundary

This standalone program reads events for an operator-selected error group and then sends a minimal notification to a separately configured receiver. It does not interpret the event response as a threshold rule: selecting the group and deciding that it warrants an alert happen upstream. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, and WEBHOOK_URL in the environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with Go. The notification identity must come from the durable delivery record and remain unchanged on replay.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryAfter(value string) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 86400 {
            return 24 * time.Hour
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return 0
}

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, target string,
    headers map[string]string, body []byte) error {
    const maxAttempts = 4
    const breakerThreshold = 3
    failures := 0
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, target, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for name, value := range headers {
            req.Header.Set(name, value)
        }
        resp, sendErr := client.Do(req)
        var wait time.Duration
        reason := ""
        if sendErr == nil {
            detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1024))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return nil
            }
            reason = fmt.Sprintf("status %d, response %q, read error %v",
                resp.StatusCode, detail, readErr)
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
                return fmt.Errorf("terminal rejection: %s", reason)
            }
            wait = retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
        } else {
            reason = sendErr.Error()
        }
        failures++
        if failures >= breakerThreshold {
            return fmt.Errorf("circuit open; retain delivery state: %s", reason)
        }
        if attempt+1 == maxAttempts {
            return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted: %s", reason)
        }
        backoff := 250 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<uint(attempt))
        backoff += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(backoff / 2)))
        if wait < backoff {
            wait = backoff
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    group := os.Getenv("ERROR_GROUP_ID")
    id := os.Getenv("NOTIFICATION_ID")
    target := os.Getenv("WEBHOOK_URL")
    if key == "" || group == "" || id == "" || target == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, WEBHOOK_URL")
    }
    destination, err := url.Parse(target)
    if err != nil || destination.Scheme != "https" || destination.Host == "" || destination.User != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("WEBHOOK_URL must be an approved HTTPS receiver without embedded credentials")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    eventsURL := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/events/{error_group_id}",
        "{error_group_id}", url.PathEscape(group), 1)
    if err := send(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, eventsURL,
        map[string]string{"Authorization": "Bearer " + key}, nil); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read selected group: %w", err)
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{
        "event_id": id,
        "category": "agent_failure",
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return send(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, target, map[string]string{
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": id,
    }, payload)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("notification accepted")
}

The webhook payload is an application-owned example, not an Infrai schema. The receiver must explicitly support the chosen Idempotency-Key contract and atomically deduplicate accepted identities with its side effects; adding the header cannot supply that guarantee. The Infrai credential goes only to the API read. Redirects are disabled so an unexpected destination cannot silently become a new processor boundary. Approve the configured receiver before running the program; this is not a URL-validation service.

The 250-millisecond base, 4-attempt ceiling, 3-failure breaker threshold, and 30-second deadline are demonstration parameters. The breaker can stop attempts before the ceiling. Set production values from the receiver contract and your delivery SLO, and treat a Retry-After beyond the remaining deadline as deferred work or an exhausted deadline. The duration parser bounds extremely large numeric values to a day, still well beyond this program's deadline; it does not send early in that case.

This example has a deliberate limitation: the breaker is terminal within one invocation, and retry state is in memory. A production worker needs persisted attempt counts, a shared destination-scoped open state, and a controlled recovery probe before releasing more traffic. Persist the event identity and deadline across rollback too. Restarting this program is not a production recovery policy, and it must not reset the delivery budget.

Keep error details in an operator-restricted channel with its own retention policy. The code surfaces bounded error bodies to aid diagnosis; those bodies can contain sensitive information and should not become the next notification payload.

When retries need a different signal

Repeatedly sending a rejected payload spends the delivery budget on a deterministic mistake. Correct it through a reviewed recovery path. If duplicate notification effects are unacceptable, require receiver deduplication before enabling automatic retries, and make the deduplication window cover the maximum permitted replay horizon.

Silence is separate.

A job that never starts cannot emit its own failure event, so add a heartbeat-oriented signal such as Healthchecks. Prefer Sentry when deeper error investigation is the immediate need, or evaluate Datadog and Grafana when the decision depends on the surrounding telemetry and operational views. A stable backend contract does not replace those specialist decisions.

For rollback acceptance, check that the old notification retains its identity, remaining attempts, delivery deadline, and data-handling restrictions. If the deployment cannot preserve those properties, pause the sender and repair the state transition before replaying queued records.

Sources

References for the delivery semantics, telemetry concepts, and product roles discussed here:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • HTTP semantics and Retry-After
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this capability boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and review the sender and receiver contracts alongside it.

title: Java4Shell pode abrir acesso remoto por falha no decodificador Base64 do Java
description:
Falha no decodificador Base64

A Calif, startup de cibersegurança, anunciou a Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade no decodificador Base64 do Java que pode permitir acesso remoto não autorizado a sistemas internos. Segundo a empresa, o pesquisador Quang Luong identificou a falha com apoio do GPT-6 Cyber, modelo da OpenAI voltado à pesquisa de segurança digital.

A Calif afirma que o Java está presente em sistemas de cerca de 90% das empresas da lista Fortune 500 e é usado em bancos, hospitais, companhias aéreas, empresas de tecnologia e órgãos governamentais.

Como a falha pode ser explorada

O problema ocorre quando o decodificador processa uma sequência malformada: 64 letras A seguidas de um sinal de igual. O comportamento inesperado pode provocar operações indevidas na memória e, em condições normais, encerrar o processo. Os pesquisadores dizem ter usado heap grooming — a organização de dados na memória para influenciar o comportamento do programa — para avançar até um possível acesso não autorizado.

A Calif demonstrou a exploração no Keycloak, sistema de autenticação e gerenciamento de acesso usado por milhares de organizações, entre elas CERN, Hewlett Packard, UnitedHealthcare e NASA. O The New York Times informou ter verificado a descoberta de forma independente e relatou que o teste de demonstração levou menos de uma hora.

Correção e resposta das empresas

A Oracle publicou uma atualização de segurança na terça-feira, 17 de novembro. A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA) recomendou que as organizações instalem a correção imediatamente. Google e Microsoft estavam entre as empresas notificadas durante a divulgação coordenada, que envolveu os países da aliança Five Eyes: Estados Unidos, Canadá, Austrália, Nova Zelândia e Reino Unido.

O Google afirmou que implementou proteções e atualizações em seus serviços após ser informado sobre a falha. Também desenvolveu mecanismos para verificar se ela havia sido explorada e publicou orientações para clientes.

IA e pesquisa de segurança

A Java4Shell é a segunda grande vulnerabilidade que a Calif diz ter identificado com auxílio de modelos da OpenAI nas últimas semanas. No mês anterior, a startup encontrou falhas no PHP. O caso mostra como a IA pode acelerar a busca por vulnerabilidades e a criação de demonstrações de exploração, ajudando equipes de defesa e também podendo reduzir o esforço necessário para ataques.

Thai Duong, diretor-executivo da Calif, afirmou que a exploração não é simples, o que dá tempo para empresas e desenvolvedores instalarem as correções. Ele alertou que sistemas sem atualização nos próximos cinco a dez anos ainda poderão ficar expostos. Na mesma semana, o FBI emitiu um alerta sobre hackers que estariam usando ferramentas autônomas de IA contra órgãos públicos e empresas em diferentes países.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-no-java-pode-permitir-acesso-remoto-a-sistemas-internos/

title: What a short-link redirect costs: about 4 microseconds in Go
description:
A short-link redirect looks like the simplest thing a web service can do: take a slug, return a 301 or 302. It is also the one request every click on every link has to pass through, so we built it as its own service with a written latency budget.

This post walks through that service: the choices we made, the reasons recorded in our ADRs, a few trimmed excerpts from the code, and a benchmark of what one request costs in-process. The benchmark is local and narrow, and we will say exactly how narrow. The conclusion is a little anticlimactic.

Split by latency budget, not by domain

The first decision (ADR-0013) was to divide the system by how fast each part has to be, not by business area. A link service that handled both redirects and link CRUD would share one latency budget between two very different workloads.

So there are three tiers:

  • Hot path: edge-redirect only. Target p50 5 ms and p95 15 ms on a cache hit. Nothing synchronous beyond the cache lookup.
  • Warm path: api-core, analytics-api, billing. User-facing CRUD, ClickHouse queries, payments.
  • Cold path: async workers fed by the event bus, such as click-ingester, notifications and the URL scanner.

The 5 ms figure is a design target recorded in the ADR. It is not a measured production number, and we are not presenting it as one.

The rule this buys is easy to enforce in code review: if it is not a cache lookup, it does not belong in the redirect handler.

Why Go, and why fasthttp

ADR-0002 picks Go for the latency-sensitive services. The reasons are unglamorous: static binaries that deploy trivially, goroutines for concurrency, short and tunable GC pauses, and a team that already knew the language. Rust was considered and set aside because the development cost was not justified at our scale. The ADR names a trigger for revisiting it: if p99 on cache hits exceeds 50 ms sustained at 10K RPS, benchmark Rust for this one service.

ADR-0003 goes one level down and picks fasthttp over net/http for the HTTP layer of this single service. fasthttp pools its request and response objects, which cuts allocation and GC pressure at high request rates. The ADR is honest about the cost: it does not work with the net/http middleware ecosystem, and its ownership rules (you must not hold a RequestCtx after the handler returns) are an easy way to introduce bugs. Every other Go service in the repo stays on net/http and chi.

That ownership rule shows up in the code. When a click is recorded, the handler copies what it needs out of the context before handing work to a goroutine:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
// Snapshot fields before the fasthttp ctx is recycled; the goroutine below
// outlives the request cycle.
fullIP, _ := netip.AddrFromSlice(clientIP(ctx))
acceptLang := string(ctx.Request.Header.Peek("Accept-Language"))
...
h.spawn(func() { h.finishClick(ev, fullIP.Unmap(), acceptLang) })

The lookup: L1, then Redis, then origin

ADR-0004 describes the cache. The source of truth is Postgres behind api-core, and a round trip there on every request would eat the whole budget. So the service asks three places in order.

 client
   |
   v
 Caddy (TLS) --> edge-redirect (Go, fasthttp)
                    |
                    |  1. L1: in-process LRU, TTL in seconds
                    |  2. L2: Redis, longer TTL
                    |  3. origin: api-core (gRPC Resolve, else HTTP)
                    |
                    +--> 301/302 back to the client
                    |
                    +--> goroutine: enrich click, Produce() ---> Redpanda
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                           click-ingester
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                              ClickHouse

The resolver that implements this is short enough to read in one go:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/resolver/resolver.go (trimmed)
func (r *Resolver) resolve(ctx context.Context, host, slug string) (*origin.Link, error) {
    key := cacheKey(host, slug)

    if v, ok := r.l1.Get(key); ok {
        return v, nil
    }
    if v, ok := r.l2.Get(ctx, key); ok {
        r.l1.Set(key, v)
        return v, nil
    }

    link, err := r.origin.Resolve(ctx, host, slug)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    r.l1.Set(key, link)
    r.l2.Set(ctx, key, link)
    return link, nil
}

L1 is hashicorp/golang-lru with expiry. A hit is a map lookup in the same process, with no network at all. The ADR's argument against Redis-only is that every request would pay a network round trip (it estimates 0.5 to 1 ms inside a datacenter) while an in-process hit costs about 50 ns. Redis then absorbs the long tail of less popular slugs so they do not all fall through to origin. The ADR also notes the system degrades sensibly: if Redis is down, L1 still serves recent hits.

The trade-off is that you now have two TTLs, and a short L1 TTL means a deleted link cannot be served forever by one node. That is stated in the LRU's doc comment, and it leads to invalidation.

Cache invalidation

TTLs alone would make edits feel slow. ADR-0004 adds explicit invalidation on link update and delete. What the code does today is this: after every link mutation, api-core deletes the Redis key and publishes the cache key on a Redis pub/sub channel. Each edge process subscribes and evicts its own L1 copy.

// services/edge-redirect/internal/cache/invalidate.go (trimmed)
// api-core already DELs the L2 key; this channel only exists to evict the
// per-process L1 copy so an edit is live in about a second instead of after
// the L1 TTL.
const InvalidateChannel = "elido:link:invalidate"

The subscriber runs in a background goroutine and is never on the request path. If Redis is unavailable, the only consequence is that L1 entries live out their TTL. Note that the ADR text mentions Redpanda for these events; the implementation we read uses Redis pub/sub, and the code is what we describe here.

Clicks: fire and forget

Analytics is the reason a redirect service has side effects at all, and side effects are where latency budgets go to die. The rule from ADR-0013 is that the response never waits for them.

The handler builds a click event from cheap header copies, then starts a goroutine. That goroutine does the expensive parts (IP classification, scanner flagging, truncating the IP, hashing the visitor) and publishes the event to Redpanda, which speaks the Kafka protocol, through a franz-go producer. A separate service, click-ingester, consumes the topic and writes to ClickHouse. The redirect service never talks to ClickHouse.

The consequence is the usual one for this design: a click can be lost if the process dies between the response and the produce call, and we accept that trade for a hot path that has no dependency on the analytics store being up.

What one request costs

Now the numbers. These come from Go's go test -bench . -benchmem on an Apple M3 laptop, run on 2026-11-18. They are in-process handler benchmarks. There is no network, no TLS and no real client, so they measure our code and nothing around it.

Benchmark ns/op B/op allocs/op
Redirect, L1 hit, full request including spawning click work 4032 4680 71
Redirect, L1 hit, request path only 3619 3728 52
Click enrichment (runs off the request path) 911 912 19
Redirect through the CTA overlay page 28781 36526 297
Blocklist check 44 0 0
Query-parameter forwarding (mixed case) 379 192 3

Read the first two rows together: The request path itself is about 3.6 microseconds, and starting the click work adds about 0.4 more. The click enrichment, at roughly 0.9 microseconds, happens after the response is already decided. The blocklist check allocates nothing, which is the kind of result you hope for from a check that runs on every request. The CTA overlay page costs about eight times a plain redirect, since it does more work per request.

The allocation profile

Fifty-two allocations for a redirect is more than a pooled HTTP library might lead you to expect. Profiling the request path shows where they come from:

  • fasthttp header and argument handling, which are the largest allocators.
  • A context.WithTimeout for the origin call, created on every request even when L1 answers and the origin is never called.
  • Client IP parsing with net.ParseIP, done more than once per request.

You can see the second one in the handler:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
resolveCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, h.cfg.OriginTimeout)
defer cancel()
link, err := h.resolver.Resolve(resolveCtx, host, slug)

All three are fixable. Creating the timeout only once the resolver misses L1 is a small change, and parsing the client IP once instead of several times is another.

Why we have not fixed them

At about 3.6 microseconds, the request path uses less than 0.1% of the 5 ms target. If we removed every allocation in the list above and saved, say, a third of that, the user would see no difference. A real redirect spends its time on the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, and the distance between the client and the server. Those are measured in milliseconds, and no amount of work on net.ParseIP changes them.

There is also a cost on the other side of the ledger. Hand-tuning a handler to shave allocations tends to make it harder to read, and this handler already has to deal with passwords, previews, agent-readable JSON responses and warning pages.

So the plan is deliberately boring: keep the benchmarks in the repo so a regression shows up, fix the cheap allocations when we are in that code anyway, and put effort where the time is. We run in production today as a single EU VPS behind Caddy, so network distance is the next thing we would look at, long before another microsecond of Go.

The benchmark does not tell us about p99 under load, GC behavior at sustained throughput, or cache hit rate on real traffic. It tells us our own code is not the problem. That is a narrower claim than "fast", and it is the one we can back up.

What we would repeat

Split services around the budget, because "only cache lookups on the hot path" cannot be enforced inside a shared service. Push slow work behind a queue. Measure in-process, then say what you did not measure.

Elido is a hosted URL shortener built EU-first with custom domains, QR codes and click analytics. The docs are at elido.app/docs.
