title: Parallel reads made my Rust file transfer tool 4x slower on hard drives
description:
A 1.18 TB copy between two seedboxes in the same data centre took 14.5 hours. The network between them did 8 Gbit/s on a single iperf3 stream. The ping was 0.29 ms. My tool averaged 21.6 MiB/s.

The tool is Hopsync, an open-source Rust service I'm building for moving files between SSH servers from a web UI or a CLI. The other side only needs a normal SSH account with SFTP. Its main trick is parallel "lanes": several SSH connections, with big files split across them. Over a 200 ms link that roughly doubles scp's speed, and on 300 small files it finishes in 39 s where scp takes 249 s.

On two hard drives sitting next to each other, the same trick made it slower than rclone. Here's why, and what fixed it.

Measure the ceiling first

Before touching code I wanted to know what "fast" meant on these boxes. The simplest possible pipe, one sequential reader, one SSH stream, one sequential writer:

dd if=big.bin iflag=direct bs=16M \
  | ssh user@dst 'dd of=big.bin bs=16M conv=fdatasync'

32 GiB in 4 m 26 s: 123 MiB/s, with the destination disk busy over 90 % most of the time. That's the real limit: the slowest disk, not the network or the cipher (one OpenSSH stream carried ~400 MiB/s).

Then the same file with the tools:

rclone 1.53 (1 stream) Hopsync (old, 6 lanes)
Average speed 61.4 MiB/s 36.3 MiB/s
Source disk busy 37 % 72 %
Source iowait 10 % 48 %
Destination disk busy 37 % 20 %

Hopsync kept the source disk twice as busy as rclone and moved about half as much data. The destination was mostly idle. The source disk was working hard at something other than reading.

Root cause: the disk was seeking

The old design cut each file into chunks of 8 to 64 MiB and gave each lane its own chunk. Every lane read from its own offset, with 16 reads of ~256 KiB in flight each, all through one shared file descriptor.

Two things went wrong:

  1. Readahead gave up. Linux keeps readahead state per open file. Sixteen readers jumping between offsets look like random access, so the kernel stops reading ahead.
  2. The head moved constantly. A spinning disk does ~150 MiB/s sequentially and a tiny fraction of that when it seeks between chunks. Parallel reads that help on SSDs and fast networks turn into a seek storm on an HDD.

There was more on top: up to 64 requests in flight per job, two jobs on the same disk, and at one point 405 threads stuck in D state. Every 8 to 64 MiB chunk also ended with an fsync@openssh.com.

What the fast tools do

I read how rsync, rclone and libtorrent handle this:

  • rsync: one file at a time, one sequential reader, no fsync unless you ask.
  • rclone: a sequential reader with an async read-ahead buffer, and up to 64 SFTP writes in flight at increasing offsets.
  • libtorrent: pieces arrive in random order, but the writes land in RAM first and the kernel sorts dirty pages before write-back.

The lesson that changed the design:

Writes can be absorbed and reordered by RAM. Reads can't.

A read waits for the disk the moment you issue it, so the reading side must be sequential and large. The writing side only needs offsets that move forward, so the kernel can merge them.

The fix: lanes carry buffers, they don't choose offsets

The new push path:

  • One sequential reader per file. It reads 16 MiB blocks in order, with posix_fadvise(SEQUENTIAL), into buffers from a fixed pool. O_DIRECT when the filesystem allows it, so the seedbox's page cache stays out of it.
  • A bounded read-ahead queue (64 MiB, 4 blocks). When the queue is full the reader waits, so memory has a hard cap.
  • Lanes only carry data. Each block is cut into SFTP writes of the server's max_write size and handed to whichever lane has room. All writes in flight sit in one sliding window, so the destination sees offsets moving forward a few MiB at a time.
  • One big file per source disk at a time, daemon-wide. Two queued jobs on the same disk share it instead of doubling the seeks. Different disks still run in parallel.
  • Fewer fsyncs. A durability checkpoint every 1 GiB instead of every chunk, with only one in flight at a time.
  • Lane auto-tuning stays, because a 200 ms link still needs it.

Results

Same 32 GiB file, same boxes, all four runs back to back in the same hour:

Tool Time Speed Source busy / iowait Destination busy
Hopsync 1.3 3 m 31 s 155 MiB/s 69 % / 8 % 90 %
`dd \ ssh \ dd` 4 m 25 s 124 MiB/s
rclone 1.53 (SFTP) 9 m 11 s 60 MiB/s 38 % / 10 % 32 %
Hopsync 1.2 15 m 30 s 35 MiB/s 72 % / 47 % 22 %

The source disk is as busy as before, but iowait fell from 47 % to 8 %, because it's streaming instead of seeking. It moves 4.4x as much data. The destination disk is now the bottleneck, which is where it should be. Peak memory was 162 MB.

It also beats the "ideal" single dd pipe. My best guess is that several SSH streams keep the destination's write queue fuller than one stream can, but I haven't isolated that yet.

Caveats, because benchmarks lie easily:

  • These are shared seedboxes. Other users' load varies between runs, which is why all four ran back to back.
  • One file size, one pair of boxes. I haven't compared tuned rsync or lftp yet.
  • An earlier near-final build hit 172.8 MiB/s. I can't fully explain the 10 % gap yet.

The full method, raw CSVs and scripts are in the repo: results, design doc, scripts.

What I took away

  • Measure the ceiling before optimizing. The dd | ssh | dd number told me the network was never the problem.
  • Parallelism has a physical cost. What helps on a high-latency link hurts on a spinning disk. The same tool needs both behaviours, picked from what it measures.
  • Look at disk busy and iowait, not only throughput. 72 % busy for 36 MiB/s was the clue.

Try it

Hopsync is a single binary and needs no root, so it runs on shared seedboxes:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/YourNeelsOG/hopsync/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
hopsync setup

It also has resume after a dropped connection (even kill -9), a job queue that survives restarts, a preview before copying, and hopsync push / pull on the CLI. Host keys are always pinned, and there's no default password.

It's early software and hasn't had an independent security review yet. Issues, benchmarks from your own boxes and PRs are welcome: github.com/YourNeelsOG/hopsync

Have you hit the same "parallel is slower" wall on HDDs? I'd like to hear how you solved it.

title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
description:
arXiv:2611.21995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

title: The IBS effect in ETFs: section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies, replicated in Python and R
description:
This is a standalone version of an article first published on quantstr.at. The Python and R code, the data files and the line-by-line walk-through are in the original.

TL;DR

  • Strategy: Section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies sorts ETFs by Internal Bar Strength (IBS), where the close sits within the day's range, and bets on mean reversion the next day.
  • What we did: an attempt to replicate Pagonidis (2014), The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs, on Yahoo Finance data for 31 of its 33 ETFs (two are no longer available), first over the original window to 5 December 2013 and then on the 13 years since.
  • Result in the original window: the average next-day return after the lowest IBS bucket was 0.353% and after the highest −0.134% (original: 0.350% and −0.126%). A long-short rule earned 30.8% a year per ETF before costs.
  • Since 2013: the gap between the lowest and highest bucket fell from 0.49 to 0.19 percentage points a day. The same rule earned 9.2% before costs and −0.1% after 5 basis points per trade.
  • The book's decile rule: 38.6% a year before costs since 2013, 16.4% at 2 basis points and −10.4% at 5. It turns over its portfolio about 3.5 times a day, so the cost assumption decides the result.

The idea

IBS = (Close − Low) / (High − Low). It is 0 when the close is the low of the day and 1 when it is the high. Pagonidis finds that ETFs that closed near their low tend to rise the next day and those that closed near their high tend to fall.

IBSi​(t)=racPiC​(t)−PiL​(t)PiH​(t)−PiL​(t)

The single-ETF rule goes long when IBS is 0.2 or below and short when it is 0.8 or above, for one day. The book's version ranks the ETFs each day, buys the lowest tenth and sells the highest tenth with equal weights.

Replication: average next-day return by IBS bucket (%)

0 to 0.2 0.2 to 0.4 0.4 to 0.6 0.6 to 0.8 0.8 to 1
Pagonidis (2014), to 5 Dec 2013 0.350 0.096 0.025 −0.032 −0.126
Ours, to 5 Dec 2013 0.353 0.099 0.032 −0.048 −0.134
Ours, after 5 Dec 2013 0.142 0.072 0.025 −0.005 −0.044

Gap between lowest and highest bucket: 0.49 points in the original window (original: 0.476). Probability of a positive next day: 57.2% after the lowest bucket and 46.4% after the highest (original: 56.8% and 46.2%).

The rule, before and after 2013

Average annual return per ETF of the long-short rule (compounded):

After 2013 the effect is positive in 29 of 31 ETFs but weaker, and trading costs matter: at 5 basis points per trade the rule is about break-even.

IBS as a filter for RSI

Pagonidis combines IBS with Cutler's RSI(3): buy below 10, hold while RSI(3) is 40 or below, and in the filtered version hold only while IBS is 0.5 or below. The sum of daily returns without the filter is 121.9% in the original window (original: 119.0%); with the filter 119.4% (original: 128.6%), in about half the days. We reproduce the halving of time invested but not the improvement in return in that window. After 2013 the filter helps: 30.4% against 20.3%.

The book's decile rule

Annual growth rate of the dollar-neutral decile rule, before and after costs:

Cost per unit traded To 5 Dec 2013 After 5 Dec 2013
None 337.9% 38.6%
2 bps 268.3% 16.4%
5 bps 184.1% -10.4%
10 bps 84.1% -42.1%

Break-even cost is roughly 3.9 basis points. Fills at the close are assumed, which is idealised because the final IBS is only known once the close is set.

Limitations

  • Yahoo adjusted prices differ from the vendor in the original, and two ETFs (GXG, RSX) are missing. The ETFs that remain survived to today.
  • This is an attempt to replicate; where choices were not stated (range and volume medians, tie-breaking, the cost model) they are ours and are listed in the original article.
  • No bid-ask spread, market impact or borrow costs in the replication tables. Not investment advice.

Conclusion

The IBS effect reproduces closely in the original window: next-day returns after low-IBS days were 0.49 percentage points higher than after high-IBS days. Since 2013 the gap has narrowed to 0.19, and whether anything is left after trading costs depends on assumptions a backtest cannot settle.

Reference: Pagonidis, A. S. (2014). The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs. Working paper, NAAIM. Book: Kakushadze, Z. and Serur, J. A. (2018), 151 Trading Strategies, Section 4.4.

The full article, with the Python and R code: https://quantstr.at/quant-strategies/mean-reversion/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=syndication

title: Video recordings and play behaviour annotations of group-housed dairy calves on two Dutch farms
description:
arXiv:2611.21706v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.

title: Understanding React Hooks: useState, useEffect, and useContext
description:
Introduction

React is a popular JavaScript library used to build interactive user interfaces. One of its most powerful features is Hooks.

Hooks allow functional components to use React features such as state management, side effects, and shared data without writing class components.

Among the most commonly used React Hooks are:

  • useState()
  • useEffect()
  • useContext()

Let's understand each hook, how it works, and when to use it.

1. useState() – Managing Component State

What is useState?

useState() is a React Hook that allows us to create and manage state inside a functional component.

State is data that can change over time. Whenever the state changes, React re-renders the component to display the updated information.

Syntax 

const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);
  • state: Stores the current value.
  • setState: Updates the state.
  • initialValue: Defines the initial state.

Example: Counter Application 

import React, { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increment
            </button>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>
                Decrement
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Counter;

How does it work?

  1. Initially, the count value is 0.
  2. When the user clicks Increment, setCount() updates the state.
  3. React detects the state update.
  4. React re-renders the component with the new value.

Real-world use cases:

  • Counter applications
  • Form input handling
  • Toggle buttons
  • Shopping cart quantities
  • Showing and hiding components

2. useEffect() – Handling Side Effects

What is useEffect?

useEffect() is a React Hook used to perform side effects in functional components.

A side effect is an operation that interacts with something outside the component's rendering process.

Examples include:

  • Fetching data from an API.
  • Setting up timers.
  • Updating document titles.
  • Subscribing to external events.

Syntax 

useEffect(() => {
    // Side-effect logic

    return () => {
        // Cleanup logic (optional)
    };
}, [dependencies]);

Understanding the dependency array

The dependency array controls when the effect runs.

1. Without a dependency array

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component rendered");
});

Runs after every render.

2. Empty dependency array

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component mounted");
}, []);

Runs after the initial render.

3. With dependencies

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Count changed");
}, [count]);

Runs after the initial render and whenever count changes.

Example: Fetching API Data 

import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import axios from 'axios';

function Products() {
    const [products, setProducts] = useState([]);

    useEffect(() => {
        axios.get('https://dummyjson.com/products')
            .then(response => {
                setProducts(response.data.products);
            });
    }, []);

    return (
        <div>
            {products.map(product => (
                <h3 key={product.id}>
                    {product.title}
                </h3>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

export default Products;

How does it work?

  1. The component renders.
  2. useEffect() executes after the initial render.
  3. Axios sends a request to the API.
  4. The API returns product data.
  5. setProducts() updates the state.
  6. React re-renders the component with the products.

Real-world use cases:

  • Fetching API data
  • Authentication checks
  • Event listeners
  • Timers and intervals
  • Synchronizing with external systems

3. useContext() – Sharing Data Between Components

What is useContext?

useContext() is a React Hook that allows components to access shared data without passing props manually through multiple component levels.

This problem is commonly known as Prop Drilling.

Understanding Prop Drilling

Imagine we have three components:

  • App (Parent)
  • Home (Child)
  • Profile (Grandchild)

If App contains user information and Profile needs that information, we might have to pass props through Home even when Home doesn't need the data.

Context API helps solve this problem.

Step 1: Create a Context 

import { createContext } from 'react';

export const MyContext = createContext();

Step 2: Create a Provider 

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { MyContext } from './MyContext';
import Home from './Home';

function App() {
    const [user, setUser] = useState({
        name: "Raja",
        age: 22
    });

    return (
        <MyContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
            <Home />
        </MyContext.Provider>
    );
}

export default App;

Step 3: Access Context in Another Component 

import React, { useContext } from 'react';
import { MyContext } from './MyContext';

function Profile() {
    const { user, setUser } = useContext(MyContext);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <h3>{user.age}</h3>

            <button onClick={() =>
                setUser({ ...user, age: 23 })
            }>
                Update Age
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Profile;

How does it work?

  1. createContext() creates a context.
  2. The Provider makes data available to its descendant components.
  3. The value prop contains the shared data.
  4. useContext() accesses that data.
  5. Components can use the shared state and update it through its setter.

Real-world use cases:

  • User authentication information
  • Shopping cart data
  • Theme switching (dark/light mode)
  • Language preferences
  • Global application settings

4. Difference Between These Three Hooks

Hook Main Purpose Example
useState Manage component state Counter
useEffect Handle side effects API fetching
useContext Share data between components Shopping cart

5. Can We Use These Hooks Together?

Absolutely! These hooks are often used together in real-world React applications.

For example, in an e-commerce application:

  • useState() manages the cart items.
  • useEffect() fetches products from an API.
  • useContext() shares cart information between Product and Cart components.

Each hook has a different responsibility, but together they help build scalable and interactive applications.

Conclusion

React Hooks make functional components more powerful and easier to manage.

Understanding useState, useEffect, and useContext is an important step toward becoming a React developer.

title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

title: Our import worker was killed for memory and the last log line we had was thirty thousand rows old
description:
Our supplier catalogue import is a Python worker running in Kubernetes. It reads each supplier's product file, validates every row and reports progress with print, one line per thousand rows, naming the supplier and the row. Run it on a laptop and you can watch it count through the file.

In October it was OOMKilled every night on one supplier's file. kubectl logs --previous ended at row 41,000, so we spent a morning reading rows 41,000 to 42,000 for anything that could blow up memory. They were ordinary. Running the same file locally showed memory climbing only after row 63,000, where the supplier had started pasting whole HTML pages into the description column, and the kill came about eight thousand rows after that.

The logs were not wrong. They were late. When Python's standard output is a terminal it is line buffered, and each print appears at once. In a container, standard output is a pipe to the runtime, and Python buffers it in blocks of a few kilobytes, writing only when the block fills or the program exits normally. Our progress lines were short, so one block held thirty of them. A process killed for memory receives SIGKILL, which nothing can catch, and whatever sat in the buffer is never written. We had been reading the last line that happened to be flushed, not the last line the worker printed.

Nothing had ever made us suspicious, because our tracebacks always arrived. Since Python 3.9, standard error is line buffered even when it is not a terminal, so errors came through promptly and progress did not.

Every Python base image we build now sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. The worker reports progress through the logging module, whose stream handler flushes after every record, and it writes one JSON object per line with the supplier, the row and its own memory use. The import also streams the description column and rejects any field over a size limit, which was the actual bug.

In a terminal, print means now. In a container it means eventually, and a process killed for memory never gets to eventually.

– Sergey Shinder

title: A 30-day Pinterest Ads launch plan for B2B exporters entering the Middle East
description:
Here is a working checklist on Pinterest Ads for B2B exporters. It reflects what we see when companies expand into the Middle East in 2026.

Documents and entity details

Before you request an account, line up the basics: a legal entity name that matches the website footer, a working business email on your own domain, a privacy policy and terms page, a refund or cancellation policy where relevant, and a contact page with a reachable address. Reviewers on Pinterest Ads compare these against the ad and landing page. Inconsistencies are the most common reason new accounts stall. Related reading: overseas advertising glossary.

Billing and top-up controls

Decide who can add funds and who can change payment methods, and write it down. Use a single billing contact per account, keep invoices in one shared folder, and reconcile spend weekly against the platform's own report. If finance sits in another time zone, agree on a minimum balance trigger so campaigns never pause on a Friday night in the Middle East.

What actually drives cost

The headline price on Pinterest Ads is the auction, but total cost includes the account route (direct, agency or reseller), top-up fees, currency conversion, creative production and the time spent on appeals. For B2B exporters, the hidden line is usually wasted spend during the first two weeks while tracking and audiences settle. Budget for a learning period explicitly instead of judging the channel on day three.

A 30-day launch outline

Week 1: account, billing, tracking and two landing pages. Week 2: three to five creative concepts at modest budgets. Week 3: cut the bottom half, duplicate winners into a second audience. Week 4: review cost per primary conversion against your target and decide to scale, hold or stop. Keep notes; the second market is far cheaper when the first one is documented.

Measurement from day one

Install the pixel or SDK, confirm server-side events where available, and name campaigns with a fixed convention so reports can be merged. For B2B exporters, define one primary conversion (trial start, purchase, qualified lead) and keep secondary events for optimisation diagnostics only. Without this, nobody can say whether Pinterest Ads is working.

Common mistakes we see

  • Running the same creative on Pinterest Ads that was built for another network.
  • Changing budget, audience and creative on the same day, which makes results unreadable.
  • Letting one freelancer own the only admin login.
  • Ignoring the policy centre until an ad is rejected.
  • Judging the channel before tracking has been verified.

Creative that passes review

Review teams look at the first frame, the claim and the landing page together. Avoid before/after promises, unverifiable numbers and pressure language. Localise text into the language of the Middle East rather than running English everywhere, and make sure the landing page repeats the same offer. A consistent message also improves conversion rates, so compliance and performance point the same way.

Next step

Pick two items from this list, assign an owner and a date, and review results at the end of the month.

Written by the PandaWM team in Hong Kong. PandaWM helps overseas-facing companies with GEO / AI search visibility, ad account opening and management on Facebook, Google, TikTok and about 20 smaller networks, multilingual websites, AiChatSale and a crypto payment gateway that serves overseas merchants only.

title: Types of Variables in Java
description:
1. Introduction

A variable is a named memory location used to store data in a Java program.

For example:

int age = 21;
String name = "Abishek";
double salary = 25000.50;

In this example:

  • age stores an integer value.
  • name stores a String value.
  • salary stores a decimal value.

Variables are important because they allow us to store, access, and modify data while a program is running.

2. Types of Variables in Java

Java has three main types of variables:

  1. Local Variable
  2. Instance Variable
  3. Static Variable

A. Local Variable

A variable declared inside a method, constructor, or block is called a local variable.

Example:

class Student {

    void display() {

        int age = 21;

        System.out.println(age);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.display();
    }
}

Output:

21

Explanation:

  • age is declared inside the display() method.
  • Therefore, it is a local variable.
  • It can only be accessed within its applicable scope.
  • A local variable does not receive a default value. We must initialize it before using it.

B. Instance Variable

A variable declared inside a class but outside methods, constructors, and blocks, without the static keyword, is called an instance variable.

Example:

class Student {

    String name;
    int age;

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        System.out.println(s1.name);
        System.out.println(s1.age);
    }
}

Output:

Abishek
21

Explanation:

  • name and age are instance variables.
  • They belong to the object.
  • Each object gets its own copy of instance variables.
  • Instance variables receive default values if they are not explicitly initialized.

C. Static Variable

A variable declared inside a class using the static keyword is called a static variable.

Example:

class Student {

    static String college = "ABC College";

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println(Student.college);
    }
}

Output:

ABC College

Explanation:

  • college is a static variable.
  • It belongs to the class rather than individual objects.
  • All objects of the class share the same static variable.
  • We can access it using the class name.

3. Difference Between Local, Instance, and Static Variables

Feature Local Variable Instance Variable Static Variable
Declaration Inside method, constructor, or block Inside class, outside methods Inside class using static
Belongs to Its scope Object Class
Default value No default value Yes Yes
Access Within its scope Through an object Through class name
Shared No No Yes

4. Real-World Example

Consider a Student Management System.

Imagine a college has 100 students.

Each student has:

  • A different name.
  • A different age.
  • The same college name.

We can represent this using Java variables.

class Student {

    String name;                       // Instance variable
    int age;                           // Instance variable

    static String college = "ABC";     // Static variable

    void display() {

        int mark = 90;                 // Local variable

        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println("College: " + college);
        System.out.println("Mark: " + mark);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        s1.display();
    }
}

Output:

Name: Abishek
Age: 21
College: ABC
Mark: 90

In this example:

  • name and age are instance variables because each student can have different values.
  • college is a static variable because all students share the same college.
  • mark is a local variable because it is declared inside the display() method.

5. Important Points to Remember

  1. Java has three main types of variables: Local, Instance, and Static.
  2. Local variables must be initialized before use.
  3. Instance variables belong to objects.
  4. Static variables belong to classes.
  5. Each object has its own instance variables.
  6. Static variables are shared among objects of the same class.
  7. Local variables are accessible only within their scope.

6. Conclusion

Variables are one of the fundamental concepts in Java programming. They help us store and manage data in a program.

Understanding the differences between local, instance, and static variables is important for learning Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.

By understanding these three types, we can write better-organized and reusable Java programs.

title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22234v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

title: TRIDENT: Efficient Triple-Task Learning of Dehazing, Depth, and Uncertainty Estimation for Underwater 3-D Robot Visual Perception
description:
arXiv:2611.22224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Underwater visual systems often suffer from blurry textures and low color contrast due to the inevitable light propagation. These issues can significantly degrade the perception of stable robotic operations. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning-based sensing system that tackles the multidimensional vision tasks in underwater; concretely, we deal with image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty for 3-D visual systems. Also, we propose a TRIDENT model in a fast and lightweight manner; TRIDENT consists of three parallelized decoders and one backbone structure for efficient feature sharing. In addition, it is designed to be trained to express complex parameterization. In experimental evaluation on several standard datasets, we demonstrate that TRIDENT significantly outperforms other existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation. Despite performing three tasks, our model has better efficiency than the others for both memory size and inference time. Finally, our joint learning approach demonstrates robustness in feature matching and seamlessly extends from 2-D to 3-D vision tasks. Supplements are available at https://sites.google.com/view/underwater-trident/home

title: Freeze the config: snapshotting settings onto the record they govern
description:
Here's a made-up shift at a plant that inspects welded frames (every name, time and setting in this post is illustrative). An inspector starts an inspection on frame A118 at 11:20 with a handheld camera. The vision model flags a weld gap, the inspector confirms it, and because the org's rules don't ask for a close-up photo yet, they log the finding and move on to the next section.

At 11:40 the quality lead changes an org setting: from now on every finding needs a close-up photo. Reasonable change. They made it for the next batch.

At 11:55 the inspector taps Complete on A118:

11:55:02 POST /inspections/insp-7/complete
11:55:02 422 {"error": "close-up photo required for: weld_gap"}

The weld gap was logged 35 minutes earlier under rules that didn't ask for a photo. The frame has since moved down the line. The inspector now has an inspection they can't close, and the only ways out are walking back to a frame that's gone or asking an admin to flip the setting off for a minute (which changes it for everyone else too).

Nothing here is a bug in the validation. The completion check did exactly what it was told. It read the settings as of 11:55, but the work had started under the 11:20 settings.

Where it actually goes wrong

The "before" code, condensed from the toy in this post:

def complete_reading_live(store, insp):
    s = store.resolve(insp.org, insp.site)       # settings right now
    if s["require_closeup_photo"]:
        missing = [f.label for f in insp.findings if f.photos == 0]
        if missing:
            raise ValidationError(f"close-up photo required for: {', '.join(missing)}")
    insp.status = "done"

Every place in the backend that reads store.resolve(...) during an inspection is a seam where the rules can change under in-flight work. Completion is the one that blows up loudly. The quieter ones are worse: a photo-count limit that tightens halfway through so the next finding is rejected, a rework rule that turns on and sends a half-done inspection down a different path, or a report generated tomorrow that describes yesterday's inspection using today's rules.

Visual inspection is where this comes up for us (aiscope files structured evidence for every inspection, and that evidence has to make sense later), but the same shape shows up for any long-running record: a camera analytics job, a batch annotation task, a scheduled export.

Resolve once, freeze, read from the snapshot

The reference pattern we recommend has three parts.

At creation, resolve the settings once. In the toy that means platform defaults, then org overrides, then site overrides:

def resolve(self, org, site):
    out = dict(DEFAULTS)
    out.update(self.org.get(org, {}))
    out.update(self.site.get((org, site), {}))
    return out

Store the result on the inspection as a snapshot, with a version, a timestamp and a hash:

{
  "id": "insp-7",
  "product": "frame-A118",
  "config_snapshot": {
    "v": 2,
    "resolved_at": "2026-11-09T11:20:04+05:30",
    "hash": "c6dd35f140d5",
    "settings": {
      "require_closeup_photo": false,
      "max_photos_per_finding": 4,
      "rework_on_missing_part": true,
      "allow_parallel_runs": false
    }
  }
}

Then every behaviour check on that inspection reads the snapshot, never the live store:

def complete(self, iid):
    insp = self.inspections[iid]
    if insp.flag("require_closeup_photo"):      # frozen at 11:20
        ...
    insp.status = "done"

Same shift, replayed in the toy:

11:20 create insp-7     snapshot c6dd35f140d5 require_closeup_photo=False
11:22 finding weld_gap  photos=0
11:40 org setting       require_closeup_photo -> True
11:45 create insp-8     snapshot require_closeup_photo=True
11:50 finding weld_gap on insp-8 photos=0
11:55 complete insp-7   done
11:58 complete insp-8   422 close-up photo required for: weld_gap

insp-7 closes under its own rules. insp-8, created after the change, gets the new rule. That's what the quality lead meant in the first place.

The UI is the one place that should keep reading live settings, because it's setting up new work. The settings page shows today's values and the "start inspection" form uses them. For an inspection that's already open, show its frozen values with a small line like "rules as of 11:20". Otherwise an inspector looking at the settings page will reasonably ask why their open inspection isn't asking for photos.

In the toy the snapshot is a MappingProxyType and settings is itself a proxy too, so both levels are read-only and snapshot["settings"]["require_closeup_photo"] = True raises TypeError. In a real database you'd enforce the same thing by never writing to that field after create, and having a test that fails if any update path touches it.

Scenario 2: an opt-in flag with inspections already open

A feature request: let two inspectors work on the same product at once (say a large frame split into sections). It's a behaviour change, so it ships as an opt-in flag, allow_parallel_runs, default off, and like every other setting it goes into the snapshot.

The interesting moment is when an org turns it on while single-run inspections are still open. Illustrative timeline:

14:20 create insp-12 on frame-B204   allow_parallel_runs=False (frozen, hash 7e2a91c4b0f3)
15:00 org setting allow_parallel_runs -> True
15:05 create insp-13 on frame-B204
      422 insp-12 was started under single-run rules (snapshot 7e2a91c4b0f3)
15:20 complete insp-12
15:30 create insp-13 on frame-B204   ok
15:31 create insp-14 on frame-B204   ok

The start check looks at the new inspection's resolved flag and at every open inspection's own snapshot:

if open_runs and not resolved["allow_parallel_runs"]:
    raise ValidationError(f"{product} already has an open inspection")
for other in open_runs:
    if not other.flag("allow_parallel_runs"):
        raise ValidationError(f"{other.id} was started under single-run rules ...")

insp-12 was started by someone who was told they had the frame to themselves. Its code paths (who owns which section, when a finding is final) were written for that. Letting insp-13 in at 15:05 would mix rules that were never tested together. Waiting for the old one to close costs a few minutes once per org, at the moment they turn the feature on, and after that the flag behaves as expected. You can pick the other answer and let new runs in. If you do, make it a deliberate decision and write tests for the mixed state, because a check that reads a live value will make that decision for you without anyone noticing.

Scenario 3: the support ticket two weeks later

A ticket comes in: "why did inspection insp-7 close with a finding that has no photo? our rules require photos." Without a snapshot, answering means digging through audit logs for settings changes and lining up timestamps by hand. With one, the toy has a small explain helper that diffs frozen values against today's:

>>> svc.explain("insp-7")
{'require_closeup_photo': (False, True)}

Frozen False, live True. The inspection followed the rules it started with, and the rule changed afterwards. The hash also helps with bulk questions: group inspections by config_snapshot.hash and you can see exactly which rule sets were in use last month, without replaying the settings history.

When a setting has to stay live

Some settings shouldn't be frozen. If a capture source gets disabled because a camera is sending corrupt frames, or a security fix turns something off, you want in-flight work to stop using it right away. The toy keeps an explicit, short list:

LIVE_KEYS = frozenset({"disabled_capture_sources"})

and the check that uses it reads the live store on purpose, with a comment saying so. The risk is that this list grows until the snapshot means nothing, so treat adding a key to it as a review question: what happens to an inspection that's half done when this changes?

Snapshots get old too

Snapshots outlive the code that wrote them. Six months from now there's a new setting, and every inspection created before it has a snapshot without that key. The tempting read is snapshot.get(key, DEFAULTS[key]), which is wrong if today's default isn't how the system behaved back then. The toy versions snapshots and upgrades on read:

def upgrade(snap):
    settings = dict(snap["settings"])
    if snap["v"] < 2:
        settings.setdefault("allow_parallel_runs", False)   # behaviour before v2
    return MappingProxyType(settings)

The stored record is never rewritten. The upgrade only changes how old snapshots are read, and the test for it pins an old v1 snapshot as a fixture.

What it costs

Storage, first. Every record carries a copy of its settings. For a few dozen keys that's small, but a snapshot that grows into a nested config blob makes every inspection heavy. If that happens, store the settings once in a content-addressed table keyed by hash and keep only the hash on the record.

Admins can be surprised. A setting change only affecting new work is what you want, but someone will still ask why it "didn't work". The UI line saying which rules an open inspection uses saves a lot of tickets.

Bugs in a setting also get frozen. If a bad value goes out at 9:00 and is fixed at 9:30, every inspection started in between keeps the bad value. You either live with it, add that key to the live list, or write a one-off, audited fix that patches specific snapshots and logs who did it. Pick one before you need it.

And code has to know the difference. Every flag read needs to go through the record (insp.flag(...)) and not through the settings service. A lint rule or a grep in CI for direct resolve( calls outside the create path catches regressions cheaply.

Running the example

snapshot.py is about 150 lines of standard-library Python: a layered settings store, a frozen snapshot with version and hash, an inspection service, the "before" live-read completion, and an explain helper. test_snapshot.py has 10 tests covering the 11:40 change breaking the live-read version, the snapshot version closing cleanly, new inspections picking up new rules, site overrides beating org overrides, the snapshot rejecting writes, the parallel-run flag waiting for older open inspections, a v1 snapshot reading the pre-v2 default, a live key stopping in-flight work, the support diff, and key order not changing the hash. Run python3 test_snapshot.py, no pytest needed. It's a teaching model, so swap the dicts for your database and keep the tests.

title: What changed in wallet sign-ups this month
description:
I re-shoot these sign-up screens every week. The site is KYC Flows. It has side-by-side screenshots of Privy, Dynamic, thirdweb, MetaMask Embedded, Crossmint, and one KYC vendor, Didit. I use test accounts. I do not submit real IDs.

November had three weekly passes, on the 2nd, the 9th, and the 16th. The wallet login screens did not change. Didit redesigned its intro and added a required consent screen. Dynamic's public pricing moved to Fireblocks and dropped a free plan. Two weeks later the FAQ matched the price card.

Didit added a consent screen

Didit's intro changed on November 9. The new layout lists two steps, scan an ID and take a selfie, plus a control to continue on another device. It says the check takes about a minute. That is their claim, not a time I measured.

A new required screen now sits after that intro. The title is "Before we take your selfie."

The screen says face geometry comes from the selfie and the ID photo, plus a short liveness video. It says KYC Flows and Didit have that data, it is not sold, and it is deleted when no longer needed, never later than 12 months after the last verification. The checkbox is required before "Agree and continue."

The document screens after that are still the November 2 captures. The face steps are not on the site, because they need a real ID. Nine of twelve listed screens are captured. Didit and Crossmint were not re-shot on November 16.

Crossmint's wallet price, as of November 9

Crossmint's login screens did not change. Its public wallet price, recorded on November 9 from Crossmint's pricing page, is free for 5,000 monthly active wallets, then $0.01 per wallet. Custom pricing starts at $0.01. Those numbers were still on that page when I wrote this.

Onramps and checkout are listed as separate, per-transaction products. They are not part of the login price.

Dynamic's pricing page moved

Dynamic's pricing now lives on Fireblocks. That move showed up in the November 2 pass. dynamic.xyz/pricing redirects there. The free Launch plan is gone. Self-serve live mode starts on the Growth plan. The card lists Growth at $249 a month for up to 5,000 monthly active users.

On November 2 the Growth card already said $0.05 per extra monthly active user, and the FAQ on that page said $0.005. On November 16 both the card and the FAQ say $0.05. I also checked Fireblocks' Dynamic pricing page. It still bills each monthly active user past 5,000 at $0.05.

A Dynamic MAU is someone who logs in that month, or for whom an embedded or pregenerated wallet is created. The sandbox is still free to build and test. These are snapshots of public pages, not quotes.

The other logins did not change

The other wallet logins were unchanged. Privy, MetaMask Embedded, and thirdweb were recaptured on November 2, 9, and 16. Dynamic's login screens were unchanged too. The dated pictures on the site are still from November 2.

I have not timed any of these paths. The compare pages still say "Not measured yet" for time to a first wallet.

What I would take from this

Check the card and the FAQ on the live page. On Dynamic, those two lines disagreed for two weeks. Dynamic no longer has a free live plan. Growth is $249 a month for 5,000 MAU, then $0.05. Crossmint's public wallet offer is 5,000 monthly active wallets free, then $0.01. Those two pages bill differently, and either one can move.

The first screen is still a configuration. A sandbox that shows wallets up front is not a promise about your app. A KYC path can add a consent step even when the wallet login itself stays the same.

The screens, the public prices, and the weekly changelog are on kycflows.com. I run KYC Flows. Updates also go out in the newsletter.

title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
description:
arXiv:2611.21937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

title: PageSift 1.6: From Scraping Pages to Compiling Context for LLMs
description:
The standard way to feed an LLM context today goes like this: scrape a few pages, truncate them, concatenate the pieces into one big string, and stuff it into the prompt.

That approach has three problems. First, no provenance — the model cites a number, and you have no idea which page, which paragraph, or which crawl it came from. Second, no sense of time — the page changed its price last week, you're still holding the old version, and when the old and new copies disagree, nobody tells you. Third, no incrementality — one digit changes and the whole pipeline reruns; and when the token budget runs out, you chop the tail off, which may well be the table header.

PageSift 1.6, codename "Context", is built at exactly those three problems. The one-sentence version: context shouldn't be a concatenated string; it should be a compiled artifact — with identity, lineage, a budget, and a manifest of sources.

Repo: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift (single Rust binary, Apache-2.0)

First, give knowledge a stable identity

In 1.6, content is broken into KnowledgeUnits. Each unit records four separate things: who I am (unitId), what state I'm in (revisionId and a content hash), where I live (document, byte span, heading path), and where I came from (lineage: created, unchanged, merely relocated, rewritten, split from, merged from).

Take a product page. After a redesign, untouched paragraphs keep their unitId. A paragraph that only got pushed further down the page is marked relocated — it doesn't get to impersonate a content change. A price that actually changed gets a new revisionId. Downstream systems cite "this fact", not "paragraph 7 of Tuesday's crawl". Everything else in 1.6 stands on that.

When a page changes, only redo what the change touches

Above the units sits Delta, a persistent incremental log. When a document is re-crawled, only the derived assets affected by the change are recomputed (the lexical index, the semantic sketch, the structure index and the graph index each carry their own dependency stamps); the rest is reused. In the local benchmark — 60 resources, 720 derived assets, one document edited — incremental maintenance is 4.37× faster than a rebuild, with 98.6% of assets reused. A document that comes back 304 Not Modified reuses 100%.

The delta log has consumer checkpoints: it can be replayed and acknowledged, so external systems consume at their own pace and resume after a crash without losing or duplicating work. And the index reports exactly which store version it currently reflects. No hand-waving.

In search, the two kinds of time must not be mixed

Search runs several strategies together: keywords, exact symbol matching, heading boosts, plus a disableable semantic sketch. It deliberately separates two notions of time: the observation cutoff (what you knew at that moment) and the validity window (the period during which a fact actually held). "What did this cost last month?" and "What does it cost now?" travel along two different timelines — most freshness bugs come from collapsing the two into one.

When two sources disagree on a price, search doesn't crown a winner. It retrieves both sides of the conflict together and counts independent sources honestly (syndicated mirrors don't inflate the count). Scores are reported as six decoupled dimensions — relevance, support, freshness, source independence, coverage, calibrated confidence — so the caller does the weighing.

The output is compiled, not truncated

The final step is called Pack. Give it a question and a token budget, and it compiles a context for you: every segment carries a provenance header (which unit, which document, what status, under which heading), with a full provenance manifest attached.

Some things are MustKeep: a table's header and caption, the negations and qualifiers inside a sentence, both sides of an active conflict. They go in as a group or not at all. If even the MustKeep closure doesn't fit the budget, Pack returns budgetInsufficient: true. If it doesn't fit, it says so — it won't quietly amputate half the evidence and pretend the result is complete.

One layer up sits Action, the entry point meant for agents: answer straight from local context when it's still fresh, with zero network calls (context mode); demand at least two independent sources when verifying (verify mode); and before spending money on a new crawl, estimate the value of information and check whether coverage can be estimated at all. On a small or heavily skewed corpus it returns estimable: false — not a made-up number.

How to use it

Context ships on every surface at once: the CLI (pagesift context), HTTP (/v2/context), an MCP tool (pagesift_context), Python, Node.js, and a C ABI. Installation is the usual:

  • Python: pip install pagesift
  • Node: npm install pagesift
  • Rust: cargo add pagesift, or grab the single binary from GitHub Releases

This release also bumps the HTML extraction library, yolowhtml, to 0.1.2. The reason is a very typical bug: article mode was treating academic figures and their captions as page furniture and deleting them — the text still said "see Figure 1", but the figure was gone. Figures, captions, and table captions are all preserved now.

Closing

PageSift's through-line hasn't changed: turn expensive, repeated AI information work into engineering capability that accumulates, can be verified, and can be reused. 1.5 turned observations into claims with a history. 1.6 turns claims into compilable context.

What comes next stays on the same line: from context toward conclusions, from a single node toward collaboration, from retrieval toward computation. Details when it ships.

title: Why I Built 100% Client-Side File Converters (WebP to PNG, MP3 to OGG & ZIP to PDF) With Zero Server Uploads
description:
Have you ever tried to convert a single .webp image to .png or transcode an .mp3 clip to .ogg online, only to run into:

  1. A "Please wait while uploading to our server..." progress bar
  2. A hidden 2-file daily limit or paywall
  3. Uncertainty about who is storing your personal screenshots, PDFs, or audio recordings?

Modern browsers are surprisingly powerful. Between the HTML5 Canvas API, Web Audio API, JSZip, and WebAssembly, you almost never need a remote backend server to convert everyday media files.

Over the past few months, I built ExactSolver — a free browser-based toolkit of 180+ client-side utilities and 400+ technical calculators where 100% of file processing happens locally in the user's browser.

How Client-Side Conversion Works Under the Hood

1. Lossless Image Conversion (WebP to PNG)

When a user drops a .webp image into our WebP to PNG Converter:

  • The file is read locally via FileReader / URL.createObjectURL().
  • It is decoded onto an offscreen HTML5 <canvas> preserving full 24-bit RGBA alpha transparency.
  • canvas.toBlob(callback, 'image/png') exports a clean, lossless PNG directly into browser memory for instant download.
  • Bytes uploaded to a server: 0.

2. Browser Audio Transcoding (MP3 to OGG)

Audio files are often large and slow to upload on standard residential connections. On our MP3 to OGG Converter, browser decoding and encoding allow users to convert audio clips into open-source OGG Vorbis format directly from RAM without waiting on server queues.

3. Fonts & Archive-to-PDF Workflows

We applied the exact same privacy-first architecture to:

  • Online Font Converter for web typography and icon vector assets
  • ZIP to PDF Converter for unpacking images/documents from a .zip archive in-memory and merging them into a single clean PDF
  • Download & Upload Time Calculator for estimating real-world Mbps vs. MB/s transfer times (including TCP/IP overhead)

Why Client-Side Architecture Matters

title: Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200
description:
Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200

Buried in the Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage is a line most people scrolled past. The researchers at Calif say they found the bug with AI help in about an hour. They say a first working exploit took about two hours after that. And they say the whole thing cost under $200 in AI token costs.

Qualys repeats those numbers and attributes them to the researchers, and Upwind reports the one-hour and two-hour parts. Nobody has independently checked them. Treat them as a claim. But look at what happens if they are even roughly true.

TL;DR

Claim Source Checked by others
Bug found with AI help in about an hour Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
First working exploit about two hours later Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
Under $200 in AI token costs Calif, via Qualys No
Fix committed under embargo October 14, 2026 Endor Labs Single source
Public disclosure and Oracle fixes November 17, 2026 Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs Four sources
Bug leaked before its patch Calif, via Upwind and Endor Labs No

Do the arithmetic on the defender side

Put the two clocks next to each other.

The discovery side, per Calif: about three hours of work from nothing to a working exploit, for a bill that fits on a corporate card without sign-off.

The defender side, from public dates: the fix landed on October 14, 2026 and the public advisory and vendor builds landed on November 17. That is 34 days between a committed fix and a public one. Endor Labs adds that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, and that a South Korean advisory flagged an unauthenticated Java RCE a day earlier.

After the build exists, you still have to find every JVM, rebuild images and restart processes. The runbook in my earlier post covers that. That part is slow, and your change windows set its pace, not the clock.

I am not saying attackers will win that race. I am saying the race is now one where one side's cost fell through the floor, while the other side's cost is the same human approval chain it always was.

What the broader numbers say

I did not read the full reports, only the headlines, so take these as pointers and not evidence for this CVE.

The headline of Rapid7's 2026 annual threat report says exploited high and critical severity vulnerabilities surged 105 percent as attack timelines collapsed. A separate Rapid7 Q2 2026 release says nearly two thirds of exploited vulnerabilities needed no user interaction. A news summary of that quarter says newly exploited vulnerabilities jumped from 8 percent to 40 percent.

None of that proves AI is the cause. That fits a world where finding bugs got cheaper, and Java4Shell is a vivid example, if Calif's numbers hold.

The Token Tab, from the other side

I have written before about the bill AI tools quietly send you. This is the reverse entry. Someone else's tokens are now a line item on your risk register. By Calif's account, the discovery took one engineer, some prompts and an afternoon.

The honest caveats matter here. Calif says it holds back its product-specific exploits and there is no universal one. The sources I read show no public proof-of-concept shell. Equixly calls code execution unproven and a crash the realistic outcome. A cheap discovery does not mean a cheap, reliable exploit against your particular deployment.

What I would change in my own process

Three policy changes follow from a cheap-discovery world, and none of them need a new product.

First, measure your restart latency. Patching a file does not fix a running JVM. How long does it take your slowest service to go from "fixed build available" to "process restarted on the fixed build"? If you cannot answer, that is your real patch window.

Second, tie your deadline to exposure instead of a flat number. Qualys orders its priorities as internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal data systems.

Third, keep a runtime inventory that is always on. The Java4Shell exposure depends on the JDK build and the CPU feature, and neither shows up in a dependency scan.

A triage script

This script takes the inventory output from the runbook, one line per JVM (pid, path, version), plus an AVX-512 flag, and sorts each into patched, exposed or not affected using the version ranges Qualys and Upwind list. It does not check for vendor-specific builds, so a version number that passes is not a promise. Confirm against the vendor advisory.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""java4shell_triage.py: classify JVM versions against the published ranges.

Input: lines of "pid<TAB>path<TAB>version" on stdin, e.g. 17.0.19, 21.0.13.
Usage: python3 java4shell_triage.py --avx512 < inventory.tsv
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys

# line -> first affected, first fixed (Qualys and Upwind, November 17, 2026)
RANGES = {
    17: ((17, 0, 6), (17, 0, 21, 1)),
    21: ((21, 0, 0), (21, 0, 13, 1)),
    25: ((25, 0, 0), (25, 0, 5, 1)),
    27: ((27, 0, 0), (27, 0, 1, 1)),
}


def parse(version: str) -> tuple:
    nums = [int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", version)[:5]]
    return tuple(nums)


def pad(t: tuple, n: int = 5) -> tuple:
    return t + (0,) * (n - len(t))


def classify(version: str, avx512: bool) -> str:
    v = parse(version)
    if not v or v[0] not in RANGES:
        return "not-affected-or-unknown"
    first_bad, first_fixed = RANGES[v[0]]
    if pad(v) < pad(first_bad) or pad(v) >= pad(first_fixed):
        return "not-affected-or-fixed"
    return "EXPOSED" if avx512 else "vulnerable-code-no-avx512"


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--avx512", action="store_true", help="host has all four AVX-512 flags")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    for line in sys.stdin:
        parts = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        if len(parts) < 3:
            continue
        pid, path, version = parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
        print(f"{classify(version, args.avx512):28} pid={pid} {version} {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The middle state matters. A host without AVX-512 VBMI runs vulnerable code that cannot reach the bad path today. Qualys warns that a resize or instance change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later, so that state deserves a ticket, not a shrug.

The bottom line

The part of Java4Shell that will age best is not the 62-byte overflow. It is a line in a vendor blog post saying someone did the discovery work in an afternoon with a model. Even if those exact numbers fail scrutiny, plan your patch process for the version of the world where they do.

If a bug like this took three hours and under $200 to find, how long does your slowest service take to restart?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

Cheap discovery moves the bottleneck to your restart window.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Rapid7 Q2 2026 release.

title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
description:
arXiv:2611.22043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

title: RetiDual-Select: Reliability-Aware Specialist-Generalist Routing for Retinal OCT under Image-Quality Shift
description:
arXiv:2611.22117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptive fusion can repair a static ensemble's errors, but can also overturn correct decisions. RetiDual-Select combines retinal specialist RETFound with the image encoder of the medical vision-language model MedSigLIP, separating candidate fusion, routing safety and predictive review. Calibrated product-of-experts (PoE) fusion is the static reference, a small gate proposes an alternative for each image, a validation-frozen harm guard decides whether that candidate may replace the reference, and a separate score prioritizes review. Static PoE reached the highest or joint-highest clean accuracy on all three datasets. At a clean 2% accepted-error target the review policy accepted 94.3% of Kermany-4 images at 99.89% selective accuracy, and 92.4% of OCT-C8 at 98.65%. Both branches were correct on 95.0% and 91.8% of clean images; only 4.4% and 6.2% had exactly one correct branch. Across 15 prespecified synthetic conditions, adaptive gains were concentrated in severe contrast reduction, where this routing opportunity widened roughly ninefold; percentile rescaling largely removed the effect, linking it to compressed dynamic range. In post-hoc validation-only analyses, gain was higher when the gate followed the more reliable branch, and a frozen guard cut the worst-condition OCT-C8 loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points. Adaptive routing was useful when image quality created a reliability opportunity and the gate followed it; otherwise the system retained Static PoE or deferred for review. The findings are bounded by the synthetic perturbations evaluated and do not establish robustness to natural acquisition or scanner shift.

title: An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.22202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(m\sigma_{\min}^2/\tau)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $\tau$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.

title: O(1) Per-Tick Pathfinding and Velocity-Stall Recovery in Deterministic JS Agents
description:
When writing real-time simulation bots or game-loop controllers with strict per-tick CPU budgets (such as 10ms/tick in deterministic arenas), running A* or Dijkstra per unit on every frame quickly hits timeout ceilings.

Here is the exact pattern we use in our JavaScript controller (nmore-vanguard) to keep per-tick pathfinding strictly O(1) with zero allocations during gameplay.

1. Precompute Multi-Source Distance Fields Once in hello()

At match initialization, precompute a flat Int32Array Dijkstra cost field from every static objective and spawn point using a typed-array binary min-heap:

const MAX_WH = 16384;
const sharedHeapIdx = new Int32Array(MAX_WH + 8);
const sharedHeapKey = new Int32Array(MAX_WH + 8);

function buildDistanceField(W, H, tileCost, passable, gx, gy) {
  const dist = new Int32Array(W * H).fill(0x3fffffff);
  const start = gy * W + gx;
  dist[start] = 0;

  let size = 1;
  sharedHeapIdx[1] = start;
  sharedHeapKey[1] = 0;

  while (size > 0) {
    const cur = sharedHeapIdx[1];
    const curD = sharedHeapKey[1];
    sharedHeapIdx[1] = sharedHeapIdx[size];
    sharedHeapKey[1] = sharedHeapKey[size--];
    // sift down...
    if (curD > dist[cur]) continue;

    const cx = cur % W, cy = (cur / W) | 0;
    for (const [dx, dy, mult] of DIRS8) {
      const nx = cx + dx, ny = cy + dy;
      if (nx < 0 || nx >= W || ny < 0 || ny >= H) continue;
      const ni = ny * W + nx;
      if (!passable[ni]) continue;
      const nd = curD + ((tileCost[ni] * mult) >> 3);
      if (nd < dist[ni]) {
        dist[ni] = nd;
        // push onto heap...
      }
    }
  }
  return dist;
}

2. O(1) Greedy Gradient Descent per Tick

During each tick, any unit navigating toward an objective simply follows the steepest descent over 4 lookahead tiles on the precomputed Int32Array — zero heap allocations, ~0.01ms CPU time:

function waypointFromField(field, W, H, ux, uy, lookahead = 4) {
  let cx = ux >> 16, cy = uy >> 16;
  for (let step = 0; step < lookahead; step++) {
    let bestCost = field[cy * W + cx];
    let bx = cx, by = cy;
    for (const [dx, dy] of DIRS8) {
      const nx = cx + dx, ny = cy + dy;
      if (nx < 0 || nx >= W || ny < 0 || ny >= H) continue;
      const c = field[ny * W + nx];
      if (c < bestCost) { bestCost = c; bx = nx; by = ny; }
    }
    if (bx === cx && by === cy) break;
    cx = bx; cy = by;
  }
  return [(cx << 16) + 32768, (cy << 16) + 32768];
}

3. Velocity-Based Stall Recovery

Physics engines often report blocked = false even when a tracked vehicle slides sideways against a steep hill tile. Tracking actual Euclidean displacement (hypot(dx, dy) < 400) over 5 consecutive throttle ticks catches silent deadlocks and triggers a deterministic reverse-and-steer recovery window.

Full source code is open on GitHub and runs live on battle.training.
