title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.21847v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements.
  We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

title: Public HTTPS Queue Subscription or Polling Consumer for Webhook Recovery
description:
Short answer: for a weekly digest sent to active developer-tool customers, choose the delivery shape that makes operational recovery explicit. Use a public HTTPS push subscription when an existing webhook processor can authenticate, persist an attempt, and return quickly; use a polling consumer when the processor is private or when the application must own leasing and retry timing. In both cases, the durable boundary is an idempotent customer-send record plus an audit trail, not the transport.

This is an architecture decision record about recovery, not a contest between queue interfaces. A digest may be generated once and delivered twice, because a worker can lose its connection after the provider accepts the request but before the acknowledgement arrives. The business result still must be one digest per customer and period. That means the system needs a uniqueness rule such as (customer_id, digest_week), an attempt record for every delivery, and a reconciliation path that can distinguish “not tried,” “accepted,” “timed out,” and “already applied.” Exactly-once effects are an application property built on at-least-once delivery.

What should a webhook processor record when polling consumers retry failed jobs?

The first review question is not latency. It is: who can restart work after a partial failure?

With push, an external delivery service reaches a public HTTPS handler. The handler verifies the request, records the delivery identifier, performs bounded work, and acknowledges only after the digest state is committed. A handler that returns success before its database transaction is durable creates a recovery hole: the delivery system may stop retrying while the customer still has no recorded send.

With polling, a worker reaches the queue from an outbound network connection, leases a message, commits the idempotent send record, and acknowledges last. The worker is easier to keep private, but its liveness, lease duration, shutdown behavior, and retry schedule become your responsibility. That is a reasonable trade when security policy forbids public ingress or when the retry decision depends on application state that changes between attempts.

The weekly schedule belongs outside this decision. A scheduler should enqueue a digest job with a stable period identifier; it should not perform the customer send itself. If the scheduler runs again after a deploy, the uniqueness constraint turns the repeated enqueue into an observable duplicate rather than a second customer-facing effect.

Compare push versus polling recovery boundaries

Compare the options by failure ownership. The table is intentionally narrower than a feature checklist.

Option Network shape Recovery owner Suitable when Main limitation
Public HTTPS push subscription Delivery service calls your endpoint Handler and delivery policy The webhook processor is already public and independently monitored Public ingress, authentication, and burst capacity are part of the queue design
Polling consumer Worker calls the queue Worker, lease policy, and acknowledgement logic The processor must stay private or needs application-controlled timing A healthy process and queue metrics must be maintained
Broker dead-letter route Broker moves rejected messages Broker topology plus an operator A team already operates a broker and needs a clear redrive boundary Dead letters do not replace business reconciliation or idempotency

Neither option prevents duplicates. A timeout after the email provider accepted a request is indistinguishable from a timeout before acceptance unless the provider offers a durable idempotency key. Generate that key from the customer and digest period, store it with the attempt, and use the same key on every retry. Record the response classification separately from the business result; a transport success is evidence about delivery, not proof that the customer read the message.

This is where compliance concerns become practical. An audit trail should answer who or what scheduled the digest, which customer-period key was processed, which attempt number ran, what external request identifier was used, and why the next retry was or was not scheduled. Logs alone are a poor substitute because retention, redaction, and sampling policies can remove the very evidence needed during reconciliation.

Code path for a repeatable customer send

The critical path should be deliberately uneventful: receive, validate, claim, apply, record, acknowledge. The claim and application must be safe to repeat. Here is a generic polling shape; the queue adapter is intentionally separate from the customer-send transaction.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
)

type Job struct {
    ID         string
    CustomerID string
    Period     string
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(context.Context) (Job, error)
    Ack(context.Context, string) error
    Retry(context.Context, string, string) error
}

func handle(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, q Queue, send func(context.Context, Job, string) error) error {
    job, err := q.Receive(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    key := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s", job.CustomerID, job.Period)
    tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    // The unique customer-period key makes a redelivery harmless.
    result, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
        `INSERT INTO digest_sends (customer_id, period, status)
         VALUES (?, ?, 'claimed') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`,
        job.CustomerID, job.Period)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if n, _ := result.RowsAffected(); n == 0 {
        return q.Ack(ctx, job.ID)
    }
    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := send(ctx, job, key); err != nil {
        _ = q.Retry(ctx, job.ID, err.Error())
        return err
    }
    if _, err := db.ExecContext(ctx,
        `UPDATE digest_sends SET status = 'sent' WHERE customer_id = ? AND period = ?`,
        job.CustomerID, job.Period); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return q.Ack(ctx, job.ID)
}

The example leaves one important policy visible: claiming before the external send can create a stuck claimed row if the process dies. That is not a reason to remove the claim. Add a lease expiry and a reconciliation job that can safely re-open stale claims, while retaining the original attempt history. The alternative is to send first and write afterward, which makes duplicate sends more likely when the write fails. There is no transaction spanning your database and an arbitrary mail or webhook provider, so the design must expose this boundary instead of pretending it is atomic.

Three words: ack last.

Privacy constraints on private ingress

The rejected option in this ADR is public push. Select polling when the webhook processor has no permitted public ingress, when a private network is a hard requirement, or when an operator needs to pause leasing during reconciliation. A polling worker is also the clearer choice when the retry schedule depends on a customer’s current subscription state and the application must inspect that state before re-enqueueing.

Push is the better operational shape when the processor already has public HTTPS ingress, can reject unauthenticated requests before changing state, and has independent alarms for delivery silence and handler saturation. It reduces the need to run a continuously pulling process, but it does not remove capacity planning, deduplication, or audit requirements.

The catch is recovery ownership. Push is not suitable when nobody owns the public endpoint or when the delivery policy cannot be inspected during an incident; stick with a private polling worker until those controls exist. A broker with dead-letter exchanges can also be a sound choice for a team that already operates that topology, although dead-lettering still needs an application-level redrive rule and a ledger of outcomes.

Test reconciliation as the schedule's second clock

Test the failure boundaries, not only the happy path. A useful test kills the worker after the external provider accepts the idempotency key, then checks that a redelivery creates one customer-period effect and two auditable attempts. Another pauses the consumer beyond its lease, starts a second consumer, and verifies that the claim rule prevents concurrent business effects. A third replays an old scheduler message after the period has closed and confirms that the system records the decision without sending a second digest.

Metrics should make recovery visible: age of the oldest pending job, attempts by outcome, stale claims, acknowledgement latency, and the count of customer-period conflicts. Alerting on queue depth alone misses a silent public endpoint and a worker that is acknowledging messages while its final status update fails.

I'm not sure a queue dashboard, by itself, can answer every audit question; retention and export behavior vary, and the question should be verified before approval. Keep the durable evidence in an application-owned attempt table, then use the queue's metrics as operational signals. Your mileage may vary on retry intervals, but the decision rule should remain stable: select the ingress that gives the team a clear, testable recovery owner.

title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
description:
arXiv:2611.21691v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. %
\sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
description:
arXiv:2611.21648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

title: Introducing KIVU-UI - a lightweight React component library that plays nicely with Tailwind
description:
Every React project I start hits the same fork in the road.

On one side are the big component libraries: polished, but they bring their own styling engine, a pile of dependencies, and a fight every time you try to make a button look like your button. On the other side is building everything from scratch with Tailwind: total control, but you end up rewriting tabs, modals, dropdowns and date pickers for the fifth time.

Kivu UI is my attempt at the middle path. It's a lightweight React component library with real, accessible components that gets out of Tailwind's way instead of competing with it.

npm install kivu-ui

What makes it different

  • Zero runtime dependencies. React and React DOM are peer dependencies, and that's it.
  • No CSS-in-JS. Styles are plain CSS driven by CSS variables. Components ship as "use client", so they drop straight into the Next.js App Router.
  • Your className always wins. Component styles live in @layer components, so any Tailwind utility you pass overrides them. No tailwind-merge, no !important.
  • Accessible by default. Keyboard-navigable tabs, ARIA-wired accordions and form fields, and a modal built on the native <dialog> element.
  • Themeable with CSS variables. Change --kivu-* variables to rebrand everything. Dark mode is a class or attribute away.
  • React 18 and 19, with full TypeScript types.

Setup in two lines

If you use Tailwind CSS v4, import the styles after Tailwind:

/* app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "kivu-ui/styles.css";
@import "kivu-ui/tailwind.css"; /* optional */

The optional tailwind.css preset exposes Kivu UI's design tokens as Tailwind utilities, like bg-primary-600, text-fg-muted, border-line, rounded-kivu-lg and shadow-kivu-md. These follow your theme, so they stay in sync with the components, including in dark mode.

Not using Tailwind? That works too:

import "kivu-ui/styles.css";

The part I care about most: overriding styles

This is the problem that pushed me to build the library. With most component kits, customising a button means fighting specificity. With Kivu UI, you just write Tailwind:

import { Button } from "kivu-ui";

export function Actions() {
  return (
    <>
      <Button>Default</Button>
      <Button variant="soft" tone="accent">Soft accent</Button>

      {/* Utilities override the component styles, no merging needed */}
      <Button className="rounded-full bg-emerald-600 px-10 hover:bg-emerald-700">
        Custom
      </Button>
    </>
  );
}

It works because of CSS cascade layers. Everything in Kivu UI sits in @layer components, and Tailwind utilities come later, in the utilities layer. The cascade does the job that tailwind-merge usually does at runtime.

Need a button that's actually a link from your router? Use asChild:

<Button asChild variant="outline">
  <a href="/projects/new">New project</a>
</Button>

What's in the box

The first release covers most of what a real app needs:

  • Forms: Input, Textarea, Select, Checkbox, Switch, RadioGroup, SegmentedControl, Combobox
  • Dates: Calendar, DatePicker, DateRangePicker
  • Overlays: Modal, Drawer, Tooltip, Popover, DropdownMenu
  • Navigation and layout: AppShell, Sidebar, Topbar, Tabs, Accordion, PageHeader, Breadcrumbs, Pagination, Container
  • Data display: Table, DataTable, StatCard, Sparkline, Card, Badge, Avatar
  • Feedback: Toaster + toast, Progress, Skeleton, Spinner, EmptyState, Banner

A few examples follow.

Forms with labels, hints and errors built in 

import { Input, Checkbox } from "kivu-ui";

<Input label="Hourly rate" rightSection="USD/h" />
<Input label="Email" error="Please enter a valid email" />
<Checkbox label="Send me product updates" description="About once a month." />

A modal without a portal library

Modal uses the browser's native <dialog>, so focus trapping, Escape-to-close and backdrop clicks come for free:

import { useState } from "react";
import { Button, Modal } from "kivu-ui";

export function DeleteProject() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <Button tone="danger" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Delete project</Button>
      <Modal
        open={open}
        onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
        title="Delete this project?"
        description="This can't be undone."
        footer={<Button tone="danger" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>Delete</Button>}
      />
    </>
  );
}

Toasts you can call from anywhere

Render <Toaster /> once, then call toast from any event handler:

import { Toaster, toast } from "kivu-ui";

// once, near the root
<Toaster />

// anywhere
toast.success("Project saved");
toast.error("Couldn't reach the server");

A sortable data table 

import { DataTable, type DataTableColumn } from "kivu-ui";

type Project = { id: string; name: string; status: string; budget: number };

const columns: DataTableColumn<Project>[] = [
  { id: "name", header: "Name", accessor: "name", sortable: true },
  { id: "status", header: "Status", accessor: "status" },
  { id: "budget", header: "Budget", accessor: "budget", sortable: true, align: "end" },
];

<DataTable columns={columns} data={projects} selectable />

Theming in a few lines

Every colour, radius, shadow and font is a CSS variable. Rebrand by overriding them in your own CSS:

:root {
  --kivu-primary-600: #7c3aed;
  --kivu-primary: var(--kivu-primary-600);
  --kivu-radius-md: 10px;
}

For dark mode, add class="dark" or data-theme="dark" to <html>, or to any wrapper if you only want part of the page dark.

Where it's headed

Kivu UI is in its 0.x series, so the API may still get refined between minor versions. Breaking changes are documented in the changelog. Releases are published straight from GitHub Actions with npm provenance, so you can verify that each version was built from the public source.

Coming up next:

  • More documentation and live examples
  • Gathering feedback on the component APIs before a 1.0
  • Filling the gaps you tell me about

Try it

  • npm: kivu-ui
  • GitHub: EDMONDGIHOZO/kivu-ui
  • 📖 Docs: kivu-ui.vercel.app

title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.22174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
description:
arXiv:2611.21867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: October 22, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

title: Stacked sixes, safe stars and bonus rolls: how I coded Ludo's turn rules for a multiplayer browser game
description:
Ludo is the game everyone thinks they know. Roll a 6 to get out, race round the board, knock people home. Then you sit four people down and find out that everybody grew up with slightly different rules.

Ludo is one of the 60+ games on mympgames, my free multiplayer browser arcade, and it was harder to get right than chess. The board is easy. The turn flow is where it gets tricky: sixes that stack, a third six that cancels everything, bonus rolls that arrive in the middle of spending other dice, and a handful of house rules the host can switch on. This post walks through the server-side rules module, with real code (trimmed a little), and the decisions behind it.

One number per token

The first decision was how to store a token's position. Instead of storing board coordinates, every token is a single integer of progress relative to its own start square:

const TRACK = 52;  // squares on the shared loop
const ENTRY = 50;  // last shared square before the home column
const COL0  = 52;  // first home-column square
const HOME  = 57;
const START = { red: 0, green: 13, yellow: 26, blue: 39 };
const SAFE  = new Set([0, 8, 13, 21, 26, 34, 39, 47]);

// -1 = base, 0..51 = main track, 52..56 = home column, 57 = home
function absSquare(color, p) {
  return (START[color] + p) % TRACK;
}

That makes most questions trivial. "Is this token in base?" is p === -1. "Is it safe forever?" is p > 51. "How far along is it?" is just p, which the computer opponent uses directly. The only time I need the absolute square is when two colours might meet, so absSquare converts on demand, and captures and safe squares are checked in absolute terms.

The drawing code on the client does the reverse mapping to pixels. The rules never know what the board looks like.

Rule one: sixes stack, three sixes forfeit

In the turn flow I implemented (the style most people know from Ludo apps), a 6 doesn't move you straight away. You roll again, and the dice pile up. 6, 6, 4 means three dice to spend. Three 6s in a row and the whole turn is lost.

That rule is mostly a pending array and a counter:

function roll(st, seat) {
  if (seat !== st.turn) return { ok: false, error: 'Not your turn' };
  if (st.phase !== 'roll') return { ok: false, error: 'Use your dice first' };
  const d = rollDie(st);
  if (d === 6) st.sixes += 1;
  if (st.sixes === 3) {
    passTurn(st);            // all pending dice are thrown away
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.pending.push(d);
  if (d === 6) {
    st.phase = 'roll';       // keep rolling
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.sixes = 0;
  if (legalByDie(st).every((l) => !l.length)) {
    st.pending = [];         // nothing can move: drop the dice
    endOfDice(st);
    return { ok: true };
  }
  st.phase = 'move';
  return { ok: true };
}

The phase field (roll, move, done) is the backbone. Every action checks it first, so a client that sends "move" while the server expects "roll" just gets an error back. There is no way to move twice or roll in the middle of spending dice.

Dice come from crypto.randomInt(1, 7) on the server. The rules factory also accepts an injected RNG, which is what the tests use to get repeatable games.

Rule two: moving is walking a path

Once the dice are rolled, the player spends them one at a time, in any order, on one token or split across several. The core function answers "where would this token end up with this die, and is that legal?" by literally walking the squares:

function step(st, seat, p) {
  if (p === ENTRY) return canEnterHome(st, seat) ? COL0 : 51;
  if (p === 51) return 0;
  return p + 1;
}

function pathFor(st, seat, token, d) {
  const p0 = st.tokens[seat][token];
  if (p0 === HOME) return null;
  if (p0 === -1) return leavesBase(st, d) ? [0] : null;
  const path = [];
  let p = p0;
  for (let k = 0; k < d; k++) {
    p = step(st, seat, p);
    if (p > HOME) return null;                 // overshot
    path.push(p);
    if (p === HOME && k < d - 1) return null;  // exact roll to finish
  }
  return path;
}

I could have done the arithmetic in one line, but walking square by square pays off three ways:

  1. Exact finish falls out of the loop. You can't overshoot home.
  2. The path is returned. The client animates the token hop by hop along it, and everyone sees the same route.
  3. Walls are easy. With the optional "blocks" rule, two tokens of one colour on a square form a wall that rivals can't land on or pass. That's one extra check inside the loop. A 6 is allowed to jump a wall, so a game can't deadlock with everyone stuck behind one.

step is also where the "kill before you go home" house rule lives. If a player hasn't captured anyone yet, square 50 leads to 51 and then back to 0 instead of into the home column, so the token keeps circling. Without that rule, 51 is never reached.

Legal moves are then just "every token whose pathFor isn't null". The server never keeps a separate rulebook for validation. A move is legal if and only if pathFor returns a path.

Rule three: captures, safe squares and partners

When a token lands on the main track, anything on that absolute square that isn't a friend goes back to base, unless the square is safe:

if (to <= 51) {
  const sq = absSquare(color, to);
  if (!isSafe(st, sq)) {
    for (const v of occupants(st, sq)) {
      if (friends(st, v.seat, seat)) continue;
      st.tokens[v.seat][v.token] = -1;
      (captured ||= []).push(v);
    }
  }
}
if (st.rules.bonusRoll && (captured || to === HOME)) st.bonusRolls += 1;

friends covers both "it's my own token" and team mode, where red and yellow play green and blue and partners can't capture each other. That one helper is reused by the wall check and the computer opponent, so teams only had to be taught once.

The tricky part: a bonus roll while dice are still pending

Here's the case that took me longest. You roll 6, then 3. You use the 3 first and it captures someone. You've earned a bonus roll, but you still owe the 6. What happens?

The answer I settled on: the bonus roll comes now, and its result joins the dice you still hold. So you roll again, get a 2, and now spend the 6 and the 2.

function endOfDice(st) {
  if (st.bonusRolls > 0) {
    st.bonusRolls -= 1;
    st.sixes = 0;
    st.phase = 'roll';      // pending dice are kept
    return;
  }
  if (st.pending.length && legalByDie(st).every((l) => !l.length)) {
    st.pending = [];        // leftover dice nobody can use
  }
  if (st.pending.length) { st.phase = 'move'; return; }
  passTurn(st);
}

Unless the move finishes that player's game, it ends in endOfDice, which decides in a fixed order: bonus roll first, then keep spending, then drop useless dice, then pass. Putting all of the "what happens next" logic in one function meant fixing this ordering once instead of in every branch.

Fewer pointless clicks

Ludo has lots of forced moves: one token out, one die, nothing else legal. Asking a player to tap their only option every time feels slow. The rules module works out the distinct choices, treating two tokens on the same square or two equal dice as the same move:

function choices(st, seat = st.turn) {
  const seen = new Map();
  st.pending.forEach((d, di) => {
    for (const t of legalMoves(st, seat, d)) {
      const k = `${st.tokens[seat][t]}:${d}`;
      if (!seen.has(k)) seen.set(k, { token: t, die: di, value: d });
    }
  });
  return [...seen.values()];
}

If there's exactly one, the view marks it as auto and the client plays it after a short beat. The server still validates it like any other move. The client just saves you a tap.

Keeping everyone in sync

In a multiplayer room, the risk is that a fast player or a bot moves while another screen is still animating the last move. So the server game wrapper puts an animation budget on each action and refuses the next one until it has played out:

if (st.animUntil && Date.now() < st.animUntil - GRACE)
  return { ok: false, error: 'Wait for the move to finish' };

The budget is computed from the move itself: a fixed time per square in the path, plus a pause and a "slide back to base" for any capture. Computer seats use the same number as their delay before acting. The tradeoff is a slightly slower game, but every player and spectator sees the same hop-by-hop move instead of tokens teleporting.

The computer opponent

The bot doesn't search ahead. Dice make deep search expensive and the benefit is small, so it scores each legal (token, die) pair and picks the best. Capturing is worth a lot, more if the victim was far along. Getting home, leaving base and reaching a safe square or the home column all add points. Landing within six squares in front of a rival subtracts points, and moving a token out of danger adds them. A little randomness keeps it from feeling robotic. Because it calls the same legalByDie, it can't make an illegal move, and house rules work for it automatically.

What I'd tell someone building Ludo

  • Store progress, not coordinates. One integer per token makes rules, bots and house rules much simpler.
  • Make the turn a small state machine. phase, pending, sixes and bonusRolls are enough to describe every point in a turn, and each action checks them first.
  • Return paths, not just destinations. Validation, walls, exact finishes and animation all reuse the same walk.
  • Put "what happens next" in one place. Most of my bugs were ordering bugs, and endOfDice is where they got fixed.

You can try all of this at mympgames.com/play/ludo. It's free and runs in the browser, with friends or computer players in empty seats. If Ludo isn't your thing, there are 60+ other games at mympgames.com.

title: Vercel MCP now supports MCP events
description:
Vercel MCP now publishes events, so agents can subscribe to Vercel platform events like deployment.succeeded and deployment.error and react to what happens on your projects instead of polling for changes.

An agent subscribes once, filtering by team, project, and environment, and Vercel MCP manages an ordinary expiring Vercel webhook behind it. Refreshes extend the subscription, an abandoned one expires on its own, and event webhooks run on their own per-team limit, so they don't count against your 40 account webhooks.

Deliveries are signed Standard Webhooks with Vercel's native webhook payload in data.

See the AI SDK cookbook Receive MCP Webhook Events to implement the receiving side.

title: Building a 7 deadly sins test without judging the user
description:
Someone finishes a personality quiz and gets “Pride: 75.” What should they do with that? Does it mean they are unusually proud, that three-quarters of their personality is pride, or simply that they agreed with a few statements?

Working on a 7 deadly sins test made that ambiguity hard to ignore. Calculating a number is straightforward. Giving someone enough context to read it fairly takes more care.

The project uses the 7 deadly sins as themes for an entertainment quiz. The interesting development problem is what happens between an answer, a score, and the sentence a person remembers afterward.

Start with the question behind the search

“Which deadly sin am I?” invites a single, memorable answer. That makes a character reveal a reasonable part of the experience. But I want that reveal to leave room for a second question: “Which of my answers led here?”

For this project, I treat the reader's task as three connected steps: answer recognizable situations, understand the resulting pattern, and decide whether any of it is worth discussing or sharing.

That framing affects the interface. The character needs supporting context. The scores need an explanation. Sharing needs to be a choice.

There is also a scope decision to make early: these are original characters inspired by everyday habits, not matches from The Seven Deadly Sins anime. A familiar phrase should not leave someone guessing which experience they opened.

Make a 7 deadly sins test score explainable

The homepage Quick Quiz has 21 questions, with three assigned to each theme. It asks people to think about the past four weeks, which gives the answer a time frame rather than asking them to summarize their whole life.

Each usable answer has a value from 0 to 4. Some statements point in the opposite direction, so their values are reversed before averaging. Each theme is then scaled independently to 0–100.

Here is a simplified JavaScript illustration of that calculation:

// Illustrative answers for one theme, not a real user's result.
const answers = [
  { value: 3, reverse: false },
  { value: 2, reverse: false },
  { value: 0, reverse: true },
];

const values = answers.map(({ value, reverse }) =>
  reverse ? 4 - value : value
);

const score =
  (values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0) / values.length) * 25;

console.log(score); // 75: average of 3, 2, and 4, scaled to 100

The arithmetic is easy to inspect. It does not establish that the questions are a validated measure of personality.

Here, 75 describes responses within one question group. It is not a percentile, a probability, or a measure of moral worth. The seven scores do not need to add up to 100.

The other detail worth handling explicitly is missing information. “This situation doesn't apply to me” should not quietly become zero. In the Quick Quiz, those answers are excluded, and each theme needs at least two usable answers before the user can finish.

If you are building something similar, define that rule before designing the result screen. Otherwise, an unanswered question can accidentally become a confident conclusion.

A concrete example: “Which deadly sin am I?”

Imagine someone who often defends their work immediately when corrected. They also keep thinking about achievements that went unnoticed. In this quiz, those situations contribute to the pride theme.

That is enough to make a reading about recognition and defensiveness relevant. It is not enough to explain their relationships, work history, or reasons for reacting that way.

A useful next step is small: the next time feedback arrives, ask one curious question before explaining your side. The person can try it, disagree with it, or decide the situation needs more context.

There is no need to force a winner, either. If several scores are close, the result should make that visible. The project includes mixed, balanced, and quieter outcomes so the headline can acknowledge the pattern instead of flattening it.

You can inspect that answer-to-result flow in the 7 deadly sins quiz I'm building. The Quick Quiz is free, with no account or result paywall. It pairs an original character with seven scores and the responses behind them, so there is something to examine after the reveal.

Sharing deserves its own design decision

A result that feels fine in a private browser tab may feel different in a group chat.

The project lets people make an illustrated card, choose playful or gentle wording, and decide whether to include scores. A result link excludes individual answers, but anyone holding the link can read the selected information. Shared links cannot be revoked.

Those details belong near the sharing action. A person should understand what will leave the page before copying it.

Friend comparison has a similarly narrow purpose: compare two profiles from the same quiz version and start a conversation. It does not calculate compatibility or establish who has the “better” personality.

For me, the useful design constraint is keeping the character, score, and explanation consistent about what they know. This is entertainment and a prompt for reflection. It cannot diagnose someone, provide a religious judgment, or establish a permanent identity.

A 7 deadly sins test can still be playful within those limits. If you want a concrete example to explore, the Quick Quiz puts the questions, explanation, and optional sharing in one flow. The part I would carry into another project is simple: make the result easy to question, as well as easy to share.

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
description:
arXiv:2611.21707v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

title: Every Camera Grows Up: Camera-Height Regression in Interactive Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.

title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
description:
arXiv:2611.21832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

title: Stop Paying Twice for the Same LLM Answer
description:
A semantic cache for LLM calls with MongoDB Vector Search and Automated Embedding, in about 60 lines of Python.

Users ask the same questions in different words. "What is your refund policy?" and "How do refunds work?" are the same request, but an exact-match cache sees two different strings and pays for two LLM calls. A semantic cache fixes this by matching on meaning instead of text.

In this post I build one on MongoDB. The new part is Automated Embedding: MongoDB creates the embeddings for you, so there is no separate embedding pipeline to run. I will also show the guard that decides what should never be cached, because that part matters more than the cache itself.

Why an exact-match cache is not enough

A normal cache keys on the exact prompt string. That works for repeated system calls, but not for people. Small changes in wording, spacing or word order all count as a miss.

A semantic cache stores each prompt with its answer. For a new prompt it runs a vector search over the stored prompts. If the closest one is similar enough, it returns the stored answer and skips the LLM call. If not, it calls the LLM and stores the new pair.

Most of the work is in two decisions: which prompts are safe to cache, and how similar "similar enough" is.

Let MongoDB do the embedding

On May 7, 2026, MongoDB announced Automated Voyage AI Embeddings in Vector Search as a public preview. You declare an autoEmbed field in the index, and MongoDB embeds the text when documents are written and when you query. Here is the index for the cache collection, using PyMongo 4.20:

from pymongo.operations import SearchIndexModel

INDEX = "prompt_cache_idx"

def create_indexes(coll):
    model = SearchIndexModel(
        name=INDEX,
        type="vectorSearch",
        definition={"fields": [
            {"type": "autoEmbed", "modality": "text",
             "path": "prompt", "model": "voyage-4"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "tenant"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "llm_model"},
        ]},
    )
    coll.create_search_index(model=model)
    # plain TTL index: cached answers expire after 1 day
    coll.create_index("created_at", expireAfterSeconds=86_400)

Two details matter here. The tenant and llm_model filter fields keep one customer's answers away from another's, and stop an answer from an old model being served after you switch models. The TTL index is a normal MongoDB feature: documents are deleted automatically a day after created_at, so stale answers do not live forever.

The lookup

With autoEmbed, the query takes plain text instead of a vector. I ask for the single nearest prompt and read its score:

THRESHOLD = 0.95  # illustrative, tune on your own traffic

def cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model):
    pipeline = [
        {"$vectorSearch": {
            "index": INDEX,
            "path": "prompt",
            "query": {"text": prompt},
            "filter": {"tenant": tenant,
                       "llm_model": llm_model},
            "numCandidates": 50,
            "limit": 1,
        }},
        {"$project": {"answer": 1, "prompt": 1,
                      "score": {"$meta": "vectorSearchScore"}}},
    ]
    hit = next(coll.aggregate(pipeline), None)
    if hit and hit["score"] >= THRESHOLD:
        return hit
    return None

vectorSearchScore is between 0 and 1, where 1 means most similar. The value 0.95 is only a starting point. The right number depends on your model and your users, so log the score of every lookup and look at real near-misses before you trust any threshold.

Not every prompt should be cached

This is where a semantic cache can hurt you. "Cancel order 48213" and "Cancel order 48214" are almost identical as text, but returning the first answer for the second request is a real bug. The same goes for anything personal or time-sensitive.

So I put a simple guard in front of the cache:

import re

UNSAFE = re.compile(
    r"\d{3,}|@|\b(today|now|latest|current)\b", re.I)

def is_cacheable(prompt: str) -> bool:
    """Skip prompts with IDs, emails or time words."""
    return not UNSAFE.search(prompt)

I ran this guard locally on six sample prompts. My first version also blocked the words "my" and "me", and it rejected "How do I reset my password?", which is one of the most cacheable questions there is. After removing those words, the run gave: password reset, refund policy and file formats are cacheable; the order number, the email address and "latest prices" are skipped. A regex is a blunt tool, and in a real system you would also check the route or intent, but the point stands: decide what to exclude before you decide the threshold.

The full flow then checks the guard on both read and write:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def answer(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model, call_llm):
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        hit = cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model)
        if hit:
            return hit["answer"], "cache"
    text = call_llm(prompt)
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        coll.insert_one({
            "prompt": prompt, "answer": text,
            "tenant": tenant, "llm_model": llm_model,
            "created_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        })
    return text, "llm"

Before you ship it

  • Automated Embedding is a preview feature, and MongoDB's docs say not to use it in production yet. Check the current prerequisites for your cluster tier before you build on it.
  • Embedding calls are billed, both when you write and when you query. A cache saves LLM tokens but adds embedding cost, so measure both.
  • When your source documents change, cached answers can go stale before the TTL ends. Add a version field to the filter, or clear the collection on deploy.
  • Return the cache source ("cache" or "llm") in your logs. Without it you cannot measure the hit rate or debug a wrong answer.

I only ran the pure Python parts here (the guard and the index model). The vector search calls need an Atlas cluster with Automated Embedding enabled.

Takeaway

A semantic cache is a small amount of code: one index, one $vectorSearch stage and one threshold. The hard part is deciding what must never be cached. Scope by tenant and model, block IDs and time-sensitive prompts, give everything a TTL, and tune the threshold on real logs, not on a guess.

Sources

  • How to index fields for vector search (autoEmbed) – MongoDB Docs
  • $vectorSearch aggregation stage – MongoDB Docs
  • The Bottleneck in Enterprise AI Isn't the Model. It's the Data – MongoDB Blog
  • TTL indexes – MongoDB Manual
  • PyMongo on PyPI

Let's Connect

I write about AI agents, .NET, and building on MongoDB every week. If this post helped you, let's connect:

  • LinkedIn
  • X (@aiwithsatyam)
  • GitHub

Follow me here for the next post!
