title: How to Find and Fix Slow Interactions (INP) in a React App
description:
A filter that takes a moment to respond can make an otherwise polished React app feel broken. The button registers the click, but the selected state appears late, the list freezes, or the interface ignores the next input while it catches up.

To improve Interaction to Next Paint (INP) in React, start with real-user data, identify the slow interaction, and trace its work in the browser. Then fix the cause: unnecessary component rendering, expensive synchronous JavaScript, layout and paint work, or a combination. Do not begin by adding memo to every component.

This guide uses React 19.3.1 and browser APIs available in modern Chromium-based browsers. The examples are illustrative implementation patterns, not benchmark results or a claim that a particular application was tested. The React Compiler is optional; manual profiling still matters.

TL;DR: diagnose before optimizing

  1. Find the affected page and interaction in field INP data, segmented by mobile and desktop.
  2. Reproduce the gesture in Chrome DevTools with a realistic CPU profile.
  3. Separate input delay, event-handler processing and presentation delay.
  4. Use React DevTools Profiler to see which components rendered and how much React rendering contributed.
  5. Apply the smallest relevant fix, then compare the same interaction and confirm the field metric improves.

INP is not a React-only metric. It measures the time from a user interaction until the browser presents the next frame. React rendering can contribute, but so can unrelated JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, paint, third-party scripts and work that was already occupying the main thread.

What INP measures

Interaction to Next Paint is a Core Web Vital that assesses responsiveness across a page visit. It observes qualifying click, tap and keyboard interactions and reports a representative high-latency interaction. The metric is evaluated at the 75th percentile of page visits, separately for mobile and desktop.

The current web.dev guidance defines these thresholds:

INP at the 75th percentile Assessment
200 ms or less Good
Above 200 ms and up to 500 ms Needs improvement
Above 500 ms Poor

These are assessment thresholds, not a promise that every interaction below 200 ms feels identical on every device. Use the field distribution to understand the experience of real visitors. A lab trace helps explain a specific interaction; it does not replace field measurement.

An interaction's latency has three useful parts:

  • Input delay: time between the user's gesture and the start of the event callbacks. A busy main thread can delay the callbacks before your click handler runs.
  • Processing duration: time spent running the event handlers associated with the gesture.
  • Presentation delay: time after the handlers finish until the browser can render and present the next frame.

This breakdown changes how you debug. If input delay dominates, inspect tasks that ran before the event. If processing dominates, inspect handlers and synchronous work they trigger. If presentation dominates, inspect React rendering, style, layout and paint after the handlers.

Source: web.dev: Interaction to Next Paint.

Find the slow interaction in field data first

Start with the users who experience the problem, not a development machine that may be substantially faster than theirs.

Use a Real User Monitoring (RUM) setup or the Chrome UX Report data available through your performance tooling. Look beyond the page-level INP value. You need to know which URL or route is affected, whether the issue is concentrated on mobile, and which interaction is responsible. Useful context includes the interaction target, event type, timing breakdown and whether the slow visit happened during or after page load.

If you instrument your own RUM pipeline, the web-vitals library provides an INP measurement and attribution build. Send measurements with enough context to group them by route, device class and interaction target. Avoid collecting raw user-entered content or other sensitive values just to label an interaction. A stable selector or component-level identifier is usually more useful than the text inside a field.

A field report such as “the orders page has poor INP on mobile” is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Narrow it to “changing the status filter on the orders page” or “opening the account menu after initial load.” Then reproduce that exact gesture.

Field data can also reveal issues that local testing misses: a third-party script, a slow device, a long-running task after navigation, or a page state that your test account does not contain. If field data is unavailable, use a reproducible user report as a temporary lead and mark the diagnosis as provisional.

Reproduce and profile the interaction

1. Record the browser trace

Open the affected route in Chrome, open DevTools, and select Performance. Use the live metrics view to observe local INP while interacting. Start a runtime recording, perform the exact gesture once, and stop the recording. Repeat with the relevant page state and CPU throttling that approximates the field environment.

Find the Interactions track. Select the slow interaction and inspect its input delay, processing time and presentation delay. Then inspect the Main track around the same time. Look for long JavaScript tasks, repeated event handlers, style recalculation, layout and paint. The flame chart and Bottom-up view help identify which functions account for the work.

Do not assume a long task that happens near the click is necessarily caused by the click. Check the call stack and timing boundaries. A task that starts before the user gesture can increase input delay even if it has nothing to do with the target component.

Chrome DevTools documents the Interactions track, the timing breakdown and the runtime recording workflow in its Performance panel reference.

2. Inspect React rendering separately

The React Developer Tools Profiler answers a narrower question: which React components rendered for this update, and how much render time did the profiled tree consume?

Open the Profiler tab, start recording, perform the interaction, and inspect the resulting commit. Look for a small state change causing a large part of the page to render. Check whether expensive children rendered even though their relevant inputs did not change. Also inspect Effects that update state after a render; chains of Effects can create additional commits.

For a focused measurement in code, wrap the relevant subtree in React's <Profiler>:

import { Profiler, type ProfilerOnRenderCallback } from 'react';

const onRender: ProfilerOnRenderCallback = (
  id,
  phase,
  actualDuration,
  baseDuration,
  startTime,
  commitTime
) => {
  // Send sampled, non-sensitive diagnostics to your dev logger.
  console.debug('React commit', {
    id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime,
  });
};

export function OrdersPage() {
  return (
    <Profiler id="orders-results" onRender={onRender}>
      <OrdersResults />
    </Profiler>
  );
}

actualDuration describes the time spent rendering the profiled tree for that update. baseDuration estimates the cost of rendering the entire subtree without optimizations. The Profiler adds overhead and is disabled in ordinary production builds by default; use the React DevTools Profiler for interactive investigation, or a profiling-enabled build when you need production measurements. Do not treat the callback's render duration as the full INP value: it does not include all browser work or time before React starts rendering.

See the React Profiler reference.

Fix the cause, not the symptom

The following table maps common trace patterns to the first fix worth testing. It is a diagnostic guide, not a claim that every symptom has only one cause.

Symptom in the trace or UI Likely area to inspect First fix to test
Typing or toggling rerenders an entire page State is too high in the tree Move transient state closer to the component that owns it
A click updates a large results panel synchronously Urgent and non-urgent updates are coupled Mark the expensive result update as a Transition
Search input feels blocked by filtering Input and result rendering share one update priority Defer the value used by the expensive results subtree
Scrolling a large table is sluggish Too many DOM nodes and row renders Virtualize the visible rows
A click triggers parsing, sorting or transformation work CPU-heavy synchronous JavaScript Move pure computation to a Web Worker
React render time is high for unchanged props Repeated expensive component work Memoize the measured subtree, or evaluate React Compiler
Browser trace shows layout or paint after React work DOM size, layout or visual effects Reduce DOM/layout work and avoid forced synchronous layout

1. Render less: localize state and split components

A common source of unnecessary work is placing short-lived state too high in the component tree. If typing in a search box updates state owned by the page shell, every descendant may be asked to render again.

Move the state to the smallest component that needs it. Keep the expensive results panel separate from unrelated controls. This improves the component boundary before introducing memoization.

Before:

import { useState } from 'react';

function OrdersPage({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  return (
    <main>
      <Header />
      <SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />
      <OrdersTable orders={orders} query={query} />
      <BillingSidebar />
    </main>
  );
}

After:

import { useState } from 'react';

function OrdersPage({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  return (
    <main>
      <Header />
      <OrdersWorkspace orders={orders} />
      <BillingSidebar />
    </main>
  );
}

function OrdersWorkspace({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  return (
    <section>
      <SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />
      <OrdersTable orders={orders} query={query} />
    </section>
  );
}

The state now belongs to the workspace that needs it. This does not guarantee that the table is cheap, but unrelated page regions no longer need to be part of the same update path. Keep component boundaries aligned with state ownership and actual UI responsibilities.

2. Keep urgent input responsive with Transitions

A filter selection often has two consequences: the control must reflect the user's choice immediately, while a large result panel can update at a lower priority. React Transitions let you mark the latter update as non-urgent so React can interrupt background rendering to handle more urgent work.

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

function StatusFilter() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('all');
  const [visibleStatus, setVisibleStatus] = useState('all');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleChange(nextStatus: string) {
    setStatus(nextStatus); // Update the control urgently.
    startTransition(() => {
      setVisibleStatus(nextStatus); // Update expensive results non-urgently.
    });
  }

  return (
    <>
      <select value={status} onChange={e => handleChange(e.target.value)}>
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="open">Open</option>
        <option value="closed">Closed</option>
      </select>
      {isPending && <span aria-live="polite">Updating results…</span>}
      <OrdersTable status={visibleStatus} />
    </>
  );
}

Transitions change scheduling priority; they do not make the underlying calculation faster. Keep controlled text-input updates urgent—React does not allow a Transition to control a text input. For asynchronous actions, state updates after an await may need another startTransition wrapper. See useTransition.

3. Defer expensive results while keeping input immediate

When a component receives a value from a parent and you cannot directly wrap the parent's setter, useDeferredValue can let an expensive subtree lag behind the immediate value. The input remains controlled by the current query; the results use the deferred query.

import { useDeferredValue, useState } from 'react';

function ProductSearch({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

  return (
    <>
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={event => setQuery(event.target.value)}
        aria-label="Search products"
      />
      <ProductResults products={products} query={deferredQuery} />
    </>
  );
}

useDeferredValue does not impose a fixed delay and does not prevent network requests. It allows React to prioritize the current update and attempt the deferred render in the background. If the results subtree is not expensive, deferring it adds complexity without a meaningful benefit. Read the useDeferredValue reference.

4. Virtualize long lists

Rendering thousands of rows creates work for React and the browser. It also creates a large DOM that can increase style, layout and paint costs. Virtualization renders only the rows around the visible viewport and reuses a small window as the user scrolls.

Use a maintained virtualizer when the list has variable row heights, accessibility requirements, sticky headers or complex grid behavior. The simplified example below demonstrates the fixed-height principle; it intentionally omits keyboard navigation, dynamic measurements and scroll restoration, so do not treat it as a complete table implementation.

import { useState } from 'react';

function VirtualList({ items }: { items: Item[] }) {
  const rowHeight = 40;
  const viewportHeight = 400;
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);
  const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - 3);
  const count = Math.ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight) + 6;
  const visible = items.slice(start, start + count);

  return (
    <div
      style={{ height: viewportHeight, overflowY: 'auto' }}
      onScroll={event => setScrollTop(event.currentTarget.scrollTop)}
    >
      <div style={{ height: items.length * rowHeight, position: 'relative' }}>
        {visible.map((item, index) => {
          const itemIndex = start + index;
          return (
            <div
              key={item.id}
              style={{
                position: 'absolute',
                top: itemIndex * rowHeight,
                height: rowHeight,
                width: '100%',
              }}
            >
              {item.label}
            </div>
          );
        })}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

For production, validate focus behavior, screen-reader semantics, row measurement and overscan. A virtualized list can also make browser find-in-page and selecting content behave differently; decide whether those trade-offs fit the interface.

5. Move CPU-heavy work off the main thread

Transitions and deferred values help React schedule rendering. They do not move arbitrary JavaScript computation to another thread. If a click handler parses a large file, transforms a dataset or performs expensive search over a large collection, move pure computation to a Web Worker where practical.

src/workers/search.worker.ts:

self.addEventListener('message', (event: MessageEvent<{ items: Item[]; query: string }>) => {
  const { items, query } = event.data;
  const normalized = query.toLowerCase();
  const matches = items.filter(item =>
    item.label.toLowerCase().includes(normalized)
  );
  self.postMessage(matches);
});

src/search.ts:

const searchWorker = new Worker(
  new URL('./workers/search.worker.ts', import.meta.url),
  { type: 'module' }
);

export function searchInWorker(items: Item[], query: string) {
  return new Promise<Item[]>(resolve => {
    const onMessage = (event: MessageEvent<Item[]>) => {
      searchWorker.removeEventListener('message', onMessage);
      resolve(event.data);
    };
    searchWorker.addEventListener('message', onMessage);
    searchWorker.postMessage({ items, query });
  });
}

This is a minimal communication example, not a complete worker lifecycle abstraction. A real implementation should handle worker errors, cancellation or stale responses, termination, and large payload costs. Workers cannot access the DOM. They are useful for CPU-bound work that can operate on data and return a result. Structured cloning or transferring data has a cost, so measure the whole path rather than assuming a worker always wins. See web.dev's off-main-thread guide.

6. Memoize only when profiling justifies it

memo, useMemo and useCallback can reduce repeated work, but they also add comparison, dependency and maintenance costs. Start by removing unnecessary state updates, localizing state, simplifying rendering and eliminating expensive work. Then use the Profiler to identify components that repeatedly render with unchanged inputs and have meaningful render cost.

React 19.3 supports the stable React Compiler, which can automatically memoize components, values and functions when it can safely analyze them. It is an optional build-time tool, not an automatic feature of every React 19 app. Check your build-tool integration, compiler diagnostics and rollout strategy before enabling it. With the compiler enabled, manual memoization is usually less necessary, but existing useMemo and useCallback calls should be evaluated carefully rather than removed wholesale.

References: React Compiler introduction, React memo.

Prevent regressions with monitoring and budgets

A local trace tells you whether a change improved the reproduced interaction. Field monitoring tells you whether real users experienced the improvement across devices, routes and page states. Keep both in the workflow.

For each high-value interaction, define an owner and a reviewable budget. A useful budget is not simply “React render under X milliseconds”; INP includes browser work outside React. Instead, set a field INP objective aligned with the Core Web Vitals assessment threshold, and track the interaction-level causes that your team can act on. Segment by mobile and desktop and watch the 75th percentile over a stable reporting window.

Add performance checks to release review:

  • Monitor INP by route and device segment, and alert on sustained regressions rather than one noisy visit.
  • Keep a small set of repeatable interaction scenarios for filters, menus, search, forms and large tables.
  • Record a browser trace before and after a substantial interaction change.
  • Re-check third-party scripts and analytics handlers; instrumentation itself can create main-thread work.
  • Use production-like builds and realistic data. Development mode and synthetic data can distort the result.
  • Treat a good page-level score as a signal, not proof that every important interaction is responsive.

Do not invent a target for a component's render duration without measuring the application and its devices. Establish a baseline first, then set an engineering budget that reflects your actual user experience.

What to do next

Slow React interactions are rarely fixed by one universal hook. Field data identifies the experience to investigate; the browser trace shows where time is spent; the React Profiler tells you how much of that work belongs to rendering. Apply the narrowest fix, then verify it in both the lab and the field.

Use the React Production-Readiness Checklist to review performance alongside the other concerns that affect a production React application. For the wider engineering context behind apparently small UI features, read Frontend Is Easy… Until You Actually Build Something.

References

  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — web.dev
  • Optimize INP — web.dev
  • Performance features reference — Chrome DevTools
  • React Profiler
  • useTransition
  • useDeferredValue
  • React Compiler
  • React memo
  • Use web workers to run JavaScript off the browser's main thread — web.dev

title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
description:
arXiv:2611.22027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.

title: Conversation-Level vs Trace-Level Online Evals: Which Failures Each Can See
description:
The unit you evaluate decides which failures you can see. A span-level evaluator judges one model call. A trace-level evaluator judges one request through the agent, including its tool calls. A conversation-level evaluator judges the whole multi-turn session after it ends. Most agent failures that cost customers only exist at the conversation level, but most eval tooling started at the span.

This is not a question of which is better. Each unit catches failures the others cannot, and each has a cost. For the broader picture of online evaluation, start with what are online evals.

The three units

Unit What the judge reads When it can run Typical cost per judgment
Span One LLM call: prompt, completion, maybe one tool call Immediately Low
Trace One request: the user turn, every step and tool call, the final answer When the request completes Medium
Conversation (session, thread) Every turn of the interaction, in order After the conversation ends or goes idle Higher

Vendors use different names. LangSmith calls conversations "threads", Arize and PostHog call them "sessions", Opik uses "threads". The idea is the same.

Failures only a conversation-level eval can see

Each of these passes every span and trace check:

  • Repetition and rephrasing. The user asks the same thing three ways. Each answer is plausible on its own. See repetition as a red flag.
  • Skipped prerequisite. The agent changes an account email in turn 6 but never verified identity in turns 1 to 5.
  • Contradiction across turns. The agent quotes one price in turn 2 and another in turn 7.
  • Unresolved goal. Every response is polite and accurate, and the user's actual request is never handled.
  • Silent abandonment. The user stops replying after a confusing answer. There is no error and no thumbs-down. See users who silently give up.
  • Late false completion. The agent says "done" in the last turn, and the action failed three turns earlier.

Failures a trace-level eval catches better

Conversation-level judging is not a replacement for trace and span checks:

  • Wrong tool or bad arguments. Visible inside one request. A trace check can point to the exact step.
  • Ungrounded answer. The answer contradicts the document retrieved for that same request.
  • Format and schema errors. Better handled by code at the span level.
  • Latency and cost outliers. Per-step metrics, not judgments.
  • Duplicate tool calls. See detecting duplicate tool calls.

A conversation judge reading 30 turns can miss a subtle argument error in step 4 of turn 12. Narrow checks are more precise for narrow failures.

The timing problem

A trace is complete when the request returns. A conversation has no clear end: users come back after lunch, or never reply.

Judging too early creates false failures. The identity check looks skipped because it happens next turn. The question looks unanswered because the answer is still coming. So conversation-level evaluators usually wait for inactivity, and the defaults vary widely. LangSmith's multi-turn evaluators wait until a thread has been idle for 10 minutes by default. Datadog treats a session as complete after 30 minutes of inactivity. Braintrust's trace and group scores wait 30 seconds by default, and Opik's thread rules use a configurable cooldown. Agnost waits for 15 minutes of inactivity before judging.

The trade-off is latency. A conversation-level eval cannot tell you about a failure while the conversation is still happening. If you need that, you need a guardrail in the request path, not an online eval. See online evals vs guardrails vs monitoring.

Choosing a unit for each evaluator

Question you are asking Unit
Is this output valid JSON? Span (code)
Did the agent pick the right tool with the right arguments? Trace
Does the answer match what was retrieved? Trace
Did the user get what they came for? Conversation
Was a required step done before the action? Conversation
Did the agent contradict itself or loop? Conversation
Did the agent claim success that didn't happen? Conversation plus outcome event

Running both without double-counting

When the same failure can be flagged at several levels, rates become confusing. Three rules help:

  1. Assign each failure to one unit. "Wrong refund amount" lives at the trace level; "refund never resolved" lives at the conversation level.
  2. Point conversation verdicts at a turn. A conversation-level judge should return which message failed, so the finding links to the trace that produced it.
  3. Report conversation rates per conversation, trace rates per trace. Mixing denominators makes a failure look ten times more or less common than it is.

Where Agnost fits

Agnost runs its online evals at the conversation level. After a conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, an LLM judge reads it from start to finish against your plain-English rules and flags the specific assistant messages that broke one. That keeps the advantage of whole-conversation context while making every finding point to a turn you can open. Tool calls nested under a turn are left out of the judge's transcript and tracked separately, with success rates and error distributions. If a rule depends on a tool outcome, record that outcome as its own event.

If your team already runs span or trace evals in a tracing tool, the conversation layer is the gap to fill. The online evaluation tools comparison shows which tools judge at which units, and evals, traces, and conversations covers how the layers fit together.

Frequently asked questions

What is a conversation-level online eval?

A conversation-level (also called session-level or thread-level) online eval judges an entire multi-turn interaction after it ends, rather than a single model call or request. It can see patterns across turns, such as a user repeating a question, a required step skipped several turns before an action, or a goal that was never resolved.

When should I use trace-level evals instead?

Use trace-level evals for failures contained within one request: a wrong tool choice, bad tool arguments, an answer that contradicts the document retrieved in the same request, or a slow step. They are cheaper per judgment and can run as soon as the trace arrives.

Why wait for a conversation to go idle before judging it?

Judging a conversation that is still in progress produces false failures: a step that looks skipped may happen two turns later, and a question that looks unanswered may be answered next. Most tools wait for a period of inactivity, often around 15 minutes, before running a conversation-level judge.

Are conversation-level evals more expensive?

Per judgment, yes, because the judge reads more tokens. Per useful finding, often not, because one conversation-level judgment can replace several trace-level ones and catches failures they cannot see. Filtering to relevant conversations controls cost better than sampling.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2611.22299v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, and verification and recovery) with a four-stage loop that diagnoses failures, proposes code patches, validates candidates, and deploys updates. Using this framework, we show how optimizers trace errors across long trajectories and discover reusable runtime mechanisms such as pre-stop verifiers, loop breakers, and persistent memory. We further show why full-harness rewrites overfit or break across modules, and how modular updates with validation gates generalize across models while bounding token cost. To keep self-modification safe, we establish practical defenses against recurring failure modes including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. Finally, experiments on SWE-bench Lite validate this framework, showing that gated modular evolution outperforms prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites across models and repositories at a fraction of the token cost.

title: The Hidden Math of AI Workflow Automation: Why Sticker Prices Break at 100k Runs
description:
When engineering and operations teams evaluate workflow automation platforms, whether for AI agent orchestration, CRM enrichment, or webhook pipelines, most decisions start with the monthly starter tier ($9/mo or $20/mo).

In production, starter pricing rarely predicts real spend once workflows scale past 10,000 monthly runs. Three architectural factors consistently cause unexpected bill spikes.

1. Execution vs. Operation Billing Units Are Not 1:1

Comparing platforms by looking only at raw monthly tier limits creates a major distortion because vendors count work differently:

  • Workflow Execution Billing (e.g., n8n): One full run of a 10-node workflow counts as 1 execution, even if it loops over multiple records or calls an LLM three times.
  • Module / Operation Billing (e.g., Make): Every individual module step executed inside a scenario counts as 1 operation. A 7-step scenario running 10,000 times consumes 70,000 operations, not 10,000.
  • Task Billing (e.g., Zapier): Every successful action step after the trigger consumes 1 task, making multi-branch AI workflows disproportionately expensive at scale.

Before comparing pricing tiers, normalize every workflow to average steps per run × monthly trigger volume.

2. The "Free" Self-Hosted Infrastructure Illusion

Self-hosting an open-source automation engine on a $20/month VPS looks unbeatable on paper until production reliability requirements enter the picture:

  1. State & Queue Persistence: Production workloads require managed PostgreSQL (for execution logs and state) and Redis (for queue workers), plus automated snapshots and SSL/reverse-proxy management.
  2. Engineering Maintenance Overhead: Applying security patches, debugging breaking node updates, and monitoring worker memory leaks typically consumes 3 to 6 hours of DevOps/platform engineering time per month. At fully loaded engineering rates ($55-$120/hr), labor often exceeds the SaaS subscription cost between 10,000 and 100,000 monthly runs.
  3. Where Self-Hosting Actually Wins: Once volume crosses 500,000 to 1,000,000+ monthly executions (especially with heavy AI agent loops), fixed infrastructure + engineering labor becomes dramatically cheaper than usage-based SaaS tiers.

3. Unbounded Retries and Webhook Storms

A single upstream API outage or misconfigured webhook trigger can double a monthly execution bill overnight if workflows lack basic cost-governance guardrails:

  • Cap Retries at 2–3 Attempts: Never configure infinite retries on 429 or 5xx errors. After 2-3 failed attempts, route the payload to a manual review queue rather than burning live execution credits.
  • Set Tiered Quota Alerts & Kill-Switches: Configure automated alerts at 50%, 75%, and 90% of monthly execution/operation quotas routed to Platform Ops, with an automated throttle cutoff at 95% for non-critical workflows.
  • Account for Polling Overhead: Scheduled polling triggers that check an endpoint every 1-5 minutes consume continuous baseline operations even when zero new records exist. Webhook triggers eliminate idle polling waste.

Interactive TCO & ROI Modeling

For teams modeling the exact trade-offs across Make, n8n Cloud, n8n Self-Hosted (Hetzner vs. AWS), and Zapier, or estimating net labor savings before deploying automation, explore the full benchmark tables and interactive calculator on optimization.systems:

  • Full 10k / 100k / 1M Execution TCO Comparison Guide
  • Interactive SaaS & Automation ROI Estimator

How is your team handling retry limits and billing alerts on high-volume automation pipelines?

title: AI Coding Agents, Rust Migrations, and OpenJDK Security: A Practical Field Guide
description:
The interesting part of a new developer tool is not the launch announcement. It is whether you can put it through a small, measurable experiment.

Here are five current projects and topics worth testing, with a bounded first step for each. The goal is not to declare a winner; it is to find where the tool fits your workflow.

1. Claude Code: Require evidence before accepting a fix

What it is: Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based coding agent. It can inspect a repository, modify files, run development commands, and respond to failures.

Why now: The Claude Code team’s recent verification write-up reached 256 points and 165 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. The discussion reflects a practical concern: an agent saying “fixed” is not the same as reproducing the bug, running the correct tests, and checking for regressions.

Tutorial angle: Start with a small, reproducible bug in a sample repository. Write or seed a regression test that fails before the fix. Then ask Claude Code to:

  1. Reproduce the failure and show the command output.
  2. Add or update a regression test.
  3. Implement the smallest possible fix.
  4. Run both the targeted test and the full test suite.
  5. Review its own diff for unrelated changes.

A useful prompt is:

Fix this bug. First add a regression test and demonstrate that it
fails for the reported reason. Then make the smallest change that
passes it. Run the targeted test and the full suite, show both
results, and review the final diff. Do not claim the issue is
fixed unless the required commands exit successfully.

Keep the initial repository disposable. You are evaluating the verification loop, not trying to complete a large migration on day one.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Install Claude Code with curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

2. rust-anything: Port behavior before you port code

What it is: rust-anything is an assistant for incrementally rewriting an existing application in Rust. Its approach focuses on comparing the rewritten implementation with the behavior of the original.

Why now: The rust-anything repository reportedly collected 1,292 GitHub stars between its November 16 creation and this report. The interest is understandable: big-bang rewrites often hide behavioral differences until much later.

Tutorial angle: Port one small surface area, such as a single CLI command or HTTP endpoint:

  • Record golden outputs from the existing implementation.
  • Generate the Rust equivalent.
  • Run both versions against the same inputs.
  • Compare stdout, stderr, exit codes, and response bodies.
  • Investigate every mismatch before accepting the port.
  • Commit each port separately so it can be reverted.

Choose behavior with clear edges. Date formatting, Unicode handling, and partial failures are more useful first tests than a complicated business workflow.

Also decide what “equivalent” means before generating code. Matching a response byte-for-byte may be too strict for one endpoint and too loose for another.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the project with git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git

3. FrontierHarness: Evaluate the harness, not only the model

What it is: FrontierHarness is an evaluation harness for comparing models inside different agent harnesses. A harness includes the system prompts, tool loops, context management, and scaffolding surrounding a model.

Why now: FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 reached 329 points and 161 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. That points to a gap familiar to anyone running coding agents: a model can perform well on a generic benchmark but behave differently when it has your tools, prompts, and repository.

Tutorial angle: Build a small benchmark from three representative repository tasks, such as:

  • Fix a bug and add a regression test.
  • Add an endpoint to an existing service.
  • Refactor a module without changing its public API.

Run the same task snapshots through several model-and-harness pairings. Record:

  • Task completion rate
  • Test pass rate
  • Number of tool calls and turns
  • Time and token usage
  • Unrelated changes in the final diff
  • Whether the agent recovered after a failed command

Use those results to create a routing rule—for example, “use model A for test-driven fixes and model B for bounded refactors”—rather than selecting one model for everything.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Open the FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 quickstart and locate its first example task

4. Java4Shell: Triage OpenJDK Base64 exposure

What it is: Java4Shell is a newly disclosed OpenJDK vulnerability involving attacker-controlled Base64 data that can lead to remote code execution.

Why now: The Java4Shell disclosure reached 450 points on Hacker News, making runtime verification an immediate priority for teams operating Java services.

Tutorial angle: Treat this as an inventory and patching exercise, not an exploit exercise:

  1. Record the Java runtime version used by each service.
  2. Find the boundaries where untrusted data enters Base64 decoders.
  3. Compare those runtimes with the fixed versions in the vendor advisory.
  4. Upgrade affected services and redeploy every instance.
  5. Add a harmless regression test that confirms malformed or unexpected encoded input is rejected safely.
  6. Verify the updated runtime in the deployed environment, not only on a build server.

Inventorying decoding boundaries is more useful than searching for one suspicious function. The dangerous path may cross a controller, queue consumer, plugin loader, or configuration service.

Test only in an isolated environment. Do not run third-party proof-of-concept payloads against production systems.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Run java -version 2>&1 and compare the runtime version with the advisory

5. open-orange: Test Cloudflare Worker portability

What it is: open-orange is an open-source compatibility layer designed to run Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects on AWS, GCP, Azure, or self-hosted infrastructure.

Why now: The open-orange repository reportedly reached 659 GitHub stars within days of its November 12 creation. Portable serverless runtimes are appealing because they can reduce infrastructure coupling without forcing an immediate application rewrite.

Tutorial angle: Build a deliberately small Worker that uses a Durable Object, then:

  1. Run it locally through open-orange.
  2. Exercise the Worker’s routing behavior.
  3. Write and read Durable Object state.
  4. Switch the target backend without changing application code.
  5. Compare responses, persistence, concurrency behavior, and error handling.
  6. Record any Cloudflare-specific APIs that do not translate cleanly.

Include failure cases in the comparison. Portability is more convincing when requests, timeouts, storage failures, and concurrent updates behave consistently.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the runtime with git clone https://github.com/rivet-dev/open-orange.git

Building in public: my lead-gen engine

My lead-gen engine discovers and enriches Hong Kong SME leads before preparing them for outreach. In the latest run, it discovered 1,776 leads, enriched 201, and contacted 231. The gap between discovery and enrichment is the clearest constraint, so the next iteration should measure successful enrichment and reply quality rather than focusing only on discovery volume.

  • Discovered leads: 1,776
  • Enriched leads: 201
  • Contacted leads: 231

Start with this today

Pick Java4Shell because runtime exposure is quick to check.

Run:

java -version 2>&1

Compare the output with the Java4Shell disclosure and vendor guidance. If the version or deployment configuration is uncertain, check the runtime inside the actual container or deployment image rather than relying only on your local machine.

Picks of the week

  • Claude Code for teams that need agents to show verification evidence.
  • rust-anything for incremental, behavior-preserving Rust migrations.
  • FrontierHarness for choosing models based on real harness performance.
  • Java4Shell for immediate OpenJDK runtime triage.
  • open-orange for testing whether a Worker can move between clouds.

Which of these would you put through a five-minute test first, and what result would convince you to adopt it?

Connect

title: Fixing Modal Keyboard Traps in GitLab UI: Conditional Escape Key Propagation in GlTokenSelector
description:
In design systems, composite input components—such as tag pickers, autocomplete dropdowns, and token selectors—often handle internal keyboard events to navigate suggestion lists. However, when a component aggressively stops event propagation (event.stopPropagation()), it can inadvertently break surrounding containers like modal dialogs, drawers, and overlay popups.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Pajamas Design System (MR !6678, closing Work Item #3762), I resolved a keyboard accessibility barrier in @gitlab/ui's GlTokenSelector that prevented modal dialogs from closing on Escape.

Here is an architectural look at the problem, how WAI-ARIA recommends handling nested keyboard contexts, and how we solved it in Vue.

1. The Bug: Trapped Inside the Modal

GlTokenSelector is the multi-selection token input used across GitLab to assign labels, users, milestones, and security tags.

Inside GlTokenSelector, the text input had an inline event modifier attached to catch keypresses:

<!-- Before in GlTokenSelector.vue -->
<input
  ref="input"
  @keydown.stop="$emit('keydown', $event)"
  ...
/>

The .stop modifier in Vue unconditionally invokes event.stopPropagation().

The Real-World Breakdown

When GlTokenSelector is embedded inside a modal dialog (GlModal), users expect standard keyboard navigation:

  1. Focus Input: The user types to search for tokens. A dropdown opens with suggestions.
  2. Press Escape (1st time): The suggestions dropdown should dismiss, returning focus to the input.
  3. Press Escape (2nd time): Because the dropdown is closed, the Escape key should bubble up to GlModal and close the dialog!

Because @keydown.stop caught and swallowed every Escape keydown event, the event never reached the modal container. Users had to manually reach for their mouse to close the modal—violating WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard Accessible) and frustrating power users.

2. The Solution: Conditional Event Propagation

According to the W3C WAI-ARIA Dialog Pattern, when an active input inside a modal does not have its own popup or combobox menu open, pressing Escape must close the dialog.

To resolve this, we removed the blind @keydown.stop modifier and implemented programmatic event propagation:

<!-- After in GlTokenSelector.vue -->
<input
  ref="input"
  @keydown="handleKeydown"
  ...
/>

In the component's script:

handleKeydown(event) {
  if (event.key === 'Escape') {
    this.handleEscape(event);
    return;
  }

  // Non-Escape keys remain contained inside the token selector
  event.stopPropagation();
  this.$emit('keydown', event);
},

handleEscape(event) {
  if (this.dropdownIsOpen) {
    // 1st Escape: Close dropdown and prevent bubbling to parent modal
    event?.stopPropagation?.();
    this.closeDropdown();
  } else {
    // 2nd Escape: Dropdown already closed, let Escape bubble up to GlModal!
    this.$emit('keydown', event);
  }
}

How It Works:

  • When Suggestions are Open: event.stopPropagation() fires, cleanly closing the dropdown without triggering the parent modal.
  • When Suggestions are Closed: Propagation is not stopped. The event bubbles up the DOM tree, allowing GlModal's root key listener to catch Escape and close the dialog as expected.

3. Unit Testing Keyboard Propagation

To safeguard against regressions, we added unit test suites in token_selector.spec.js using Jest/Vue Test Utils to verify propagation states:

describe('when Escape key is pressed', () => {
  it('stops propagation when suggestions dropdown is open', () => {
    createComponent({ dropdownIsOpen: true });
    const stopPropagation = jest.fn();

    findInput().trigger('keydown', {
      key: 'Escape',
      stopPropagation,
    });

    expect(stopPropagation).toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it('allows propagation to bubble to parent when dropdown is closed', () => {
    createComponent({ dropdownIsOpen: false });
    const stopPropagation = jest.fn();

    findInput().trigger('keydown', {
      key: 'Escape',
      stopPropagation,
    });

    expect(stopPropagation).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});

Key Takeaways for Design System Engineers

  1. Be Cautious with .stop Modifiers: Avoid applying @keydown.stop or @click.stop indiscriminately on inputs. Child components frequently live inside composite parents (modals, drawers, dropdowns) that rely on event bubbling.
  2. Follow Layered Escape Ergonomics: An Escape press should peel back one UI layer at a time: active tooltip $\rightarrow$ autocomplete menu $\rightarrow$ modal dialog.
  3. Accessibility is Built in the Small Details: Fixing keyboard traps and ensuring predictable focus behavior makes design systems truly accessible to everyone.

👉 GitLab Design System MR !6678

title: If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?
description:
Companies say it’s about collaboration. That’s garbage. The reality is a room full of people in headphones, doing alone what they could’ve done at home.

Alexa von Tobel, who runs an early-stage fund and has backed a long list of founders, posted a small, honest question. She hadn’t been pitched a single remote-only company in six months, and she wanted to know if anyone else was seeing it.

The replies were a mix. A few pushed back. One said she had landed a remote role just fine and that nobody had to pitch her anything. Another figured the remote crowd was mostly off building their own companies now.

The reply that stuck with me came from a CEO, who said being fully remote would be harder, and less fun. It resonated because he is half right. Something real does get lost when everyone is scattered. He is just wrong about what fixes it.

What I haven’t seen is anyone ask what should be the obvious question. If the office is winning, what exactly is it “winning” people back to do?

This matters more than it used to, because the thing we always said the office was for has left the building (pun intended). We told ourselves we showed up every day to get the work done together. The making, the producing, the actual output. You went to the office because that was where the work physically got made, and it got made faster with everyone in one place.

Thomas Allen measured the reason decades ago at MIT. The closer two people sit, the more they actually talk, and past about fifty feet the conversation falls off a cliff.

Proximity was the whole point. The commute bought you that.

The work doesn’t live there anymore. It runs on its own now, in the cloud, whether you are at your desk or asleep. Gartner expects forty percent of business software to have agents built into it by the end of 2026, up from under five percent a year earlier.

Offices may still exist, but perhaps we lost the reason for them.

My position is simple, even if the fight over it refuses to be. The office isn’t dead, but it shouldn’t be mandatory. It’s worth protecting for the handful of things people can only do well together, the ones AI can’t touch. Instead it’s being forced on everyone for the work that no longer needs a building at all.

The work left the building

The founders von Tobel is funding are increasingly building agents that do the production themselves. Y Combinator’s recent cohorts are full of companies whose entire pitch is autonomous software that writes, tests, and ships code with a human barely touching it, and the firm’s own partners say AI has collapsed the cost of producing software by a factor of ten to a hundred.

This is not a forecast. It already shows up in who has a job. Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab tracked real payroll data and found that employment for workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the most AI-exposed jobs sits about nineteen percent below where it should be, while their older colleagues are fine.

The gap is coming from companies not hiring junior team members, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to justify an entry-level seat. You know, the production work, the stuff we all started our careers doing.

It is not only software. Anthropic, looking at how its own models actually get used, found that coding is the single biggest category, and that while most use still has AI working alongside a person, a large and growing share, more than four in ten interactions, is now the model doing the task outright rather than assisting.

The line between the two is blurry, but it is clearly moving in one direction.

Designers feel it and say so. Francisco Barrera Aros points out that AI has swallowed the how of building an interface and is coming for the what, which is why job boards have started sprouting roles like AI Product Designer that nobody could have described two years ago.

AI took over the task of doing the work. The deciding, however, is still yours, and the deciding is where the money is.

Let’s look at what that leaves for the purpose of an office. For a century it was where the production happened, because production needed people in one spot with the files, the tools, and each other. Take that out, hand it to the agents, and the physical building becomes a very expensive room you commute to in order to do work that could happen anywhere.

Which should, by any reasonable prediction, empty the place out.

We all remember 2020, right? The pandemic sent nearly everyone home at once. Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, and Steven Davis called it a mass social experiment in working from home, with Americans doing roughly half of all paid hours from home through most of 2020, up from about five percent before.

The floors we were told could never go dark went dark, and the striking part, in their data, is how many people were surprised they could do the job from home at all. The mandates coming down treat remote work as an unproven indulgence, when we have years of evidence that most of the job travels. The question should be which parts don’t work and why not?

So everyone scattered, right?

Obviously, work is more portable than it has ever been, but the freer people are to work anywhere, the more they actually want to be together.

Y Combinator, which has funded a good chunk of the companies building these agents, spent years running its batches remotely, and in those years its founders were scattered all over the map. Then it brought the program back in person, in San Francisco, and the founders came right back with it. The trend is easy to see in YC’s own public directory, which one analysis tracked batch by batch.

When the program went remote, barely a quarter of companies listed San Francisco as home. Once it came back in person, that climbed past three quarters, and a chunk of those founders kept choosing the city even after the three months ended and nothing required them to stay. The same batches are stuffed with startups whose product is autonomous software.

The people automating the production hardest are also the people most determined to sit in the same zip code while they do it.

This is one contender to define whole AI era, at least for the workforce. Gensler’s global survey found that the workers most embedded in AI are also the most collaborative and the most drawn to the office, which is the reverse of the lonely-robot future everyone predicted.

As AI takes more of the solo production, the human collaboration it can’t do becomes a scarce, valuable thing, and the people who live in these tools feel the pull toward the room where that still happens.

If the office were really about the work, this is backwards. These founders have built, and are selling, the exact tools that make location irrelevant. They could run these companies from anywhere, and they tell you so with a straight face in the pitch deck. Then they sign a lease three blocks from each other.

The clustering is telling you something that a pitch deck won’t. Whatever they are gathering for, it is not the production, because they already shipped the production to the cloud. It is the other thing.

There is real research on what that other thing is. Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and their colleagues at MIT’s Senseable City Lab studied what happened to people’s networks when everyone went remote, and found that distance measurably starved the weak ties, the loose connections that only form when people share a space. Weak ties are the people you don’t work with closely, the person two teams over, the one you only ever talk to because you both happened to be refilling coffee.

Mark Granovetter named their importance decades ago, in the work that gave us the phrase. The loose connections, not the close ones, are where new information and unlikely ideas actually travel. They are also the first thing to die when everyone is a tile on a screen, because nobody schedules a video call with the person two teams over for no reason.

That is what the founders are re-clustering to get back. Not the work. The accidental stuff around the work. The collisions you cannot put on a calendar, which turn out to be the one thing the agents can’t do for you and the screen can’t give you either.

The office we actually built

Stroll into a lot of these offices and look at what is actually happening.

Rows of people who commuted in to sit at a desk and type into a chatbot. Four people at four screens running four separate conversations with four separate AIs, in the same room, not speaking to each other. The agents are collaborating with nobody. The humans are collaborating with nobody.

Everyone is doing, in a shared space, the exact solo work they could have done at home, now with an uncomfortable chair and a commute attached.

I know this office because I have been there. I’ve worked as a fractional CPO at a variety of startups over the past few years and some of them required everyone in office for collaboration and culture purposes, and what was actually happening was a floor of people at open desks and shared tables, everyone heads-down in their own tasks, earbuds in, which is not collaborative in any way whatsoever.

The only real interaction occurred when somebody took a call out in the open and derailed the eight people near them, who were now straining to hear their own thoughts over somebody else’s pitch meeting. The in-person mandate had not created the intended collaboration. All it did was take solo work that people were doing fine at home and made it harder.

This is the part of “Office Space” that could have been a documentary. Peter Gibbons didn’t hate his job because the work was hard. He hated the commute, the eight bosses who each wanted the same TPS report, and the open floor where a man could lean over the partition at any moment to ask why he hadn’t used the new cover sheet.

The building added nothing to the work and did create a great deal of misery. The movie played it as absurd, but, frankly, a lot of return-to-office plans have adopted that as an operating model.

This is not an anecdote the research argues with. Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban put sensors on employees before and after a company tore out its walls for an open floor plan, the layout that is supposed to spark all that spontaneous mingling. Face-to-face interaction dropped by about seventy percent.

People responded to being shoved together by putting their headphones on and retreating into email and chat. This is the equivalent of throwing a party, forcing everyone to come, and watching them text each other from opposite corners of the room.

So if being in office isn’t producing collaboration, what is the mandate for? Yuye Ding and Mark Ma looked at the S&P 500 companies that ordered everyone back and found no improvement in firm value and a measurable drop in how people felt about the job. Their read was blunt. The mandates lined up with managers using the office to reassert control and to have someone to blame, not to get better work.

Forget the productivity numbers. The real cost is the people you lose, and you lose the best ones first.

Nicholas Bloom and his colleagues ran a real randomized trial, published in Nature, with more than sixteen hundred employees split between five days in and a hybrid schedule. The hybrid group quit about a third less often, with no hit to performance or promotions.

Forcing everyone back five days a week does not buy more output. It buys more resignations, and the first ones gone are the people with somewhere else to go.

That a pretty big cost for the privilege of watching your agents do the work in a room full of other people watching theirs.

The thing is, the people deepest into AI are the ones who most want to be together, and not to sit in silence. Janet Pogue McLaurin and her team at Gensler surveyed more than sixteen thousand workers and found that the heaviest AI users, about a third of everyone, are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most likely to come into the office. They are coming in for each other.

These five-day in-office mandates are coming almost entirely from the biggest companies, and, to be fair, that is the one place the evidence says in-person helps. Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta, and Elena Simintzi tracked remote work across thousands of firms and found it cut productivity at established companies by about nine percent, while raising it at startups by about twelve.

Big, old organizations genuinely struggle to coordinate when scattered. Small teams thrive, because remote lets them hire the best people anywhere instead of the nearest people around. So the companies swinging the hardest mandates are the ones with a real coordination problem, and they are solving it by forcing the fix on everyone, including the small teams it only slows down.

What the room is actually for

Full disclosure. I have run my company fully remote since 2019, before the pandemic made it “cool.” For most of our work, I still think remote is the right answer. It’s not my favorite thing to admit that I have found that the office turns out to be very good at a few specific things, and that those few things are suddenly the only ones that really matter.

Once the agents take the production work, the part of the human’s job that remains relevant is to decide what’s worth making, to catch the thing that’s wrong and to teach the person above and below you on the ladder how to see it too.

That happens to be the work the research ties to being in a physical place together.

Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav ran a study putting pairs together either in person or over video and asking them to generate ideas. The in-person pairs came up with meaningfully more, and more creative, ideas. The video pairs were just as good at the next step, picking which idea to run with.

Basically, generating creative ideas is helped by sharing a space, and choosing the ones to implement isn’t. This lines up exactly with the split the agents just created. The machine is a fine partner for narrowing and deciding against known options. It is a worse one for the wide-open, slightly stupid, what-if-we-tried part, and that part goes better with a human across the table.

There is one finding that gives me pause, because it’s the real cost of how I’ve chosen to work, and it is definitely one AI has made worse.

Someone has to learn to do the actual jobs. People learn skills by sitting near other people who already know how, absorbing the small corrections, asking the dumb question out loud instead of filing a formal ticket for it. Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais measured this and found that junior engineers got dramatically more feedback when they sat near senior ones, and lost about a fifth of it when they went remote.

Proximity is how the craft gets handed down. Distance quietly starves it.

I feel this one personally, because it is the hardest part of running a company the way I do. One of my own designers, still growing in her career, put it this way. “Constructive feedback is how I know I’m improving, and that’s hard to get when you can’t just walk into your boss’s office and ask them to look at something with you. I’m lucky I’m on a small enough team that I feel comfortable reaching out. If I were part of anything larger, I think it would be much harder. Even on bigger client teams, the feedback I get from people outside my everyday group is thin, when I get it at all.”

She is right. The ambient coaching that used to just happen in a room, the over-the-shoulder correction, the pulled-aside-after-a-meeting, does not happen on its own when everyone is remote. We made it happen on purpose.

We hold a standing thirty-minute check-in every week, time that exists for nothing but the feedback and questions they’d otherwise have had to catch me in a hallway to ask. It is a deliberate, scheduled replacement for a thing that used to happen a bit more naturally. Remote turns the mentoring into something you have to build on purpose, instead of something you can assume.

This isn’t just happening at my company, of course. The KPMG American Worker Survey found AI adoption and office mandates rising together, and concluded that managers are now the linchpin for turning in-person time into real mentorship for the people earliest in their careers, the exact thing a crowded floor of people in headphones does not deliver on its own.

Now put that next to what the agents are doing. Remember the Stanford finding, that the entry-level jobs are the ones vanishing, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to be a junior’s whole first year. Those tasks were how you learned, by doing the boring version a hundred times until you could feel when it was wrong.

Anyone who watched Richie spend a week at that fine-dining restaurant on The Bear understands this. They hand him a mountain of forks to polish and nothing else, and he spends days furious about it, a grown man doing the most menial job in the building. Then somewhere in the repetition it clicks, and he comes out the other side understanding the whole craft in a way no shortcut could have taught him.

That was the art of apprenticeship. In our world, the agents are polishing the forks now, and the mentor who would have stood over you while you learned lives on a screen, if they’re there at all.

The on-ramp to every one of these careers is being pulled up from both ends at once, by the agents from below and by the distance from above, and almost nobody is talking about the two as the same problem. They are the same problem.

This is where the office earns its keep now, if it earns it anywhere. It’s not necessarily a place to produce deliverables, the agents clearly have that, but as the one place a person can still learn the judgment the agents can’t, from another person.

You cannot apprentice over a screen share nearly as well as you can over a shoulder.

Designers have already championed this work-style. Patrick Neeman has written that the next decade of design work is about owning the systems and the trade-offs underneath the screens, the part you can’t hand to a model. Vlad Derdeicea pointed out that most of a design lead’s day was never mired in pixels in the first place, but rather focusing on aligning, deciding, and convincing. Pushing pixels was a small piece of the day that a machine can now take, which gives leaders more time to do the teaching, which was always the actual job.

None of this adds up to an argument for the five-day in-office mandate. It adds up to something narrower. The office matters now for exactly the things it was never really designed to optimize, the idea you’d never have had alone, the greener team member who evolves by watching you work, the trust that only seems to set when people share a space. It matters more than ever, and for less than ever.

So what is the commute for

Every one of these mandates comes with the same justification. Andy Jassy wrote in his Amazon memo that collaborating, brainstorming, and inventing are simpler and more effective in person, and that teaching and learning from one another are more seamless. Jamie Dimon called the benefits of being together substantial and irreplaceable.

The reality is, these leaders are not wrong that those things matter, but it’s worth considering whether they are wrong that a mandate delivers them.

Chris Wardman describes this contradiction pretty bluntly, saying companies deploy AI that strips out the everyday interactions where knowledge actually transfers, then mandate attendance to protect the very thing they are automating away.

The Flex Index, which tracks the policies of roughly nine thousand companies, now puts about a third of American firms on full-time in-office, and the biggest companies are leading the charge. What that mostly creates, though, is a building full of people doing exactly the work that no longer needs a building. In the meantime, the collaboration they said they wanted is just sitting right there on the mandate, impossible to order up.

You cannot schedule serendipity for 9 a.m. Nobody mentors the new kid on command.

A good idea has never once shown up because a policy required it. Drag everyone in and chain them to the desks, and all you have manufactured is a more expensive version of the thing they were already doing at home, plus traffic.

A move that actually fits the current environment is narrower and a little strange. Treat the office the way you’d treat any specialized tool. You don’t run your whole life out of the one drawer with the good scissors, you open that drawer when you need the thing that’s in there.

Nicholas Bloom’s data keeps pointing at the same sweet spot, a couple of deliberate days together, the rest wherever the work actually gets done, which buys the retention and the output without the resentment.

Yuan Yuan and his colleagues found the same thing when looking at badge data from forty-three thousand people across a global company’s offices. Left alone, people coordinate their own in-person days around the work and the teammates that actually need to be there.

Any mandate that just counts heads on a Tuesday misses the point of being together. Come in for the ideation, the teaching, the arguing, the trust that only seems to set face to face. Then go home and let the agents run the production from a server farm that never needed to see your face anyway.

While the office technically never died, it shouldn’t be roaring back to what it was. AI merely changed what it’s for. For a hundred years it was where the work happened and now the work happens in the cloud, and the building is left holding the handful of human things we were always a little embarrassed to admit were the actual point.

Ryan Anderson, writing in Forbes about Atlassian’s internal findings, argues that as AI absorbs the routine work, value creation migrates toward the things that require human insight and collaboration, which makes the physical workplace more important, not less. Sure, AI doesn’t need an office, but the people using it do, mainly for the handful of things this quickly moving technology cannot do for them.

This brings us back to Alexa’s question. People are coming back to the office, but that was never really the question. The question is what they think they’re coming back to do. If the answer is to sit at a desk and quietly prompt a machine that works fine without them, next to other people doing the same, then they didn’t come back for the right reasons.

If people are merely driving in to be alone together, then, that, you really can do from home.

References and further reading

The work left the building

  • Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, “Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence” (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 2026). On the widening employment gap for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, as AI takes the entry-level tasks that once justified a first job.
  • Anthropic, “The Anthropic Economic Index.” Anthropic’s own analysis of how its models are used, with coding as the largest category and a large, growing share of use that automates tasks rather than assists.
  • Francisco Barrera Aros, “The crisis of the what” (UX Collective, 2026). A designer on AI taking over the how of building interfaces and coming for the what, leaving judgment as the differentiator.
  • Thomas Allen, “Managing the Flow of Technology” (MIT Press, 1977). The origin of the Allen Curve, the finding that communication between coworkers drops off sharply with physical distance.
  • Gartner, “Gartner Predicts 40% of Enterprise Apps Will Feature Task-Specific AI Agents by 2026” (2025). The forecast that agents built into software will jump from under five percent of enterprise apps to forty percent in a year.
  • Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven J. Davis, “Why Working From Home Will Stick” (NBER, 2021). On the pandemic as a mass forced experiment in remote work, and how surprised workers were that they could do the job from home.

So everyone scattered, right?

  • Y Combinator, Frequently Asked Questions. YC’s own statement that the batch runs in person in San Francisco, having moved back after a brief remote stretch, because it works better that way.
  • Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and colleagues, “The effect of co-location on human communication networks” (MIT Senseable City Lab). On how remote work impedes the weak ties that form through physical proximity.
  • Mark Granovetter, “The Strength of Weak Ties” (American Journal of Sociology, 1973). The foundational work on why loose connections, not close ones, carry new information and ideas.
  • Janet Pogue McLaurin, Anita Grabowska and Katherine Engel, “Will AI Make the Workplace More Human?” (Gensler Global Workplace Survey 2026). A survey of more than sixteen thousand workers finding that the heaviest AI users are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most drawn to the office.

The office we actually built

  • Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban, “The impact of the ‘open’ workspace on human collaboration” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018). Sensor data showing face-to-face interaction fell about seventy percent after a move to open-plan.
  • Yuye Ding and Mark Ma, “Return-to-Office Mandates” (University of Pittsburgh). On RTO mandates at S&P 500 firms producing no gain in firm value, lower satisfaction, and higher turnover among skilled staff.
  • Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han and James Liang, “Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance” (Nature, 2024). A randomized trial of 1,612 employees where hybrid work cut quit rates by a third with no hit to performance.
  • Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta and Elena Simintzi, “Who Benefits from Remote Work?” (2025). On remote work raising productivity at startups while lowering it at established firms, based on data from thousands of companies.

What the room is actually for

  • Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav, “Virtual communication curbs creative idea generation” (Nature, 2022). In-person pairs generate more creative ideas than video pairs, who are just as good at selecting among them.
  • Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais, “The Power of Proximity to Coworkers” (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026). Junior workers get far more feedback and mentorship when they sit near senior ones, and lose about a fifth of it when remote.
  • Patrick Neeman, “From faster pencil to AI Experience Architect” (UX Collective, 2026). On design work moving from making the screens to owning the systems and trade-offs a model can’t handle.
  • Vlad Derdeicea, “The 80% job: how design leads are using AI, and it’s not about mockups” (UX Collective, 2026). On most of a design lead’s work always being the human communication and judgment, with AI taking the production slice.

So what is the commute for

  • Andy Jassy, message to Amazon employees on returning to the office (2024). The Amazon CEO’s own stated reasons for the five-day mandate, collaboration, invention, and learning from one another in person.
  • Jamie Dimon, on JPMorgan’s return-to-office requirement. The CEO’s argument that the benefits of being together in person are substantial and irreplaceable.
  • The Flex Index (Scoop Technologies). The tracker of work-location policies across roughly nine thousand U.S. companies, showing about a third now require full-time in-office attendance.
  • Marie-Laure Charpignon, Yuan Yuan, and colleagues, “Navigating the new normal: Examining coattendance in a hybrid work environment” (PNAS, 2023). Badge data from forty-three thousand employees showing people coordinate their own in-person days around the work that needs it.
  • Ryan Anderson, “AI Is Making the Physical Workplace More Important, Not Less” (Forbes, 2026). On how, as AI absorbs routine work, value shifts to human collaboration and judgment, making the office more valuable for those things, drawing on Atlassian’s internal research.
  • Chris Wardman, “Companies Say Return-to-Office Mandates Are About Collaboration. Their AI Strategies Say Otherwise” (Built In, 2026). On the contradiction of mandating in-person work for collaboration while deploying AI that erodes the very interactions companies claim to want.
  • The KPMG American Worker Survey (2025). On rising AI adoption alongside rising return-to-office, and why managers are the linchpin for turning in-person time into mentorship for early-career workers.

If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless
description:
Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. Data engineers can also use the agent during development to tune configurations before promoting to production. All access is authenticated with AWS IAM and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge in all Regions where EMR Serverless is available, except GovCloud (US) and China Regions, for EMR release versions 7.6 and later. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless.
