title: From UX Designer to AI App Builder: My Journey into Creating an AI-Powered Kids' Storytelling App
description:
I have watched several YouTube tutorials about creating kids' channels and animated videos, and I noticed how easily people are now creating animated content using AI tools. With just a prompt, these tools can take care of everything from storyboarding and scriptwriting to suggesting ideas and generating voiceovers.

I became curious about how this process actually works, so I decided to experiment with it myself and explore its pros and cons.

As a UX designer, I wanted to take this a step further. Instead of relying entirely on third-party tools, I decided to explore how I could build my own application to create animated videos. My goal is to understand the technology, experiment with AI capabilities, and build a customized tool that gives me more control over the entire video creation process.

In this article, I'll share my learning journey, the challenges I encountered, and my experience building an AI-powered animated video creation application.

What I discovered from my research?

After watching plenty of YouTube videos, I noticed that many creators are already using AI tools to produce animated videos, often as a way to generate additional income or build a side hustle. Many are creating multiple videos using simple AI tools and paying monthly subscriptions to increase their content production.

However, I also came across several videos where creators discussed how AI-generated content could affect YouTube monetization. Some mentioned that their videos were demonetized or that their channels faced monetization restrictions or rejection.

This made me curious to try the process myself. I decided to create an animated video using one of these AI tools to understand how it actually works.

What I discovered was that several AI video-generation platforms offer monthly subscriptions ranging from approximately $15–25, allowing creators to generate multiple videos depending on their subscription plan and usage limits.

I signed up for a trial and started experimenting. One thing I quickly noticed was the lack of visual consistency and customization. When generating multiple videos, the characters often followed very similar patterns. For example, the baby's facial features, body proportions, and overall animation style looked almost identical across different videos.

It made me realize that many creators might be using similar AI-generated characters and animation styles to produce large volumes of content.

This experiment helped me understand both the convenience and limitations of AI-powered video creation tools.

After experimenting with those tools, I realized that I needed a simple, beginner-friendly tool that would help me create videos based on my own ideas. So, I decided to try creating a video myself first.

As I started exploring the process, I began thinking more about the kind of video experience I actually wanted to create.

What I have noticed about kids' content?

One thing I noticed about kids' content is how easily children get drawn into watching one video after another. Once a video ends, another one starts playing, and this cycle can continue almost endlessly. Sometimes, children find it difficult to stop watching, and when parents turn off the videos, it can lead to frustration or crying because they want to keep watching more.

This made me think about the role of autoplay and continuous video recommendations in kids' content. I wanted to understand how this experience works and explore whether I could build something different: a customized video creation application where I have more control over the content, characters, stories, and overall viewing experience.

So, my first priority was not to create long videos that would keep children watching the screen for extended periods. Instead, I wanted to experiment with a different approach to children's content.

My initial idea:

My initial idea was to start with a short visual introduction, lasting anywhere from 10 seconds to 1 minute, where the characters would introduce the story using facial expressions and gestures. After that, the experience would transition into a full voice-based storytelling format, allowing children to focus more on listening rather than continuously watching the screen.

I wanted to create something similar to a podcast-style experience for kids, where engaging stories, characters, and voiceovers would encourage children to listen and use their imagination instead of spending too much time in front of a screen.

That's where my story began!

Implementing next steps with my Goal:

My ultimate goal is to build a customized application that encourages children to enjoy stories through listening while helping reduce their screen time.

Then I started exploring and experimenting with different options. One of the first things I looked into was how to make illustrated characters lip-sync with the voice, matching their facial movements, expressions, and emotions to the narration.

As I explored further, I realized that I needed an application that could bring together two important capabilities: converting text into voice and generating illustrated images based on my stories or poems for children.

My biggest Challenge:

One of the biggest challenges I faced was finding the right voice options for my videos. I didn't want to use or expose my original voice. Instead, I wanted children to feel as though another child or a friendly cartoon character was telling them the story.
I started thinking about different voice personalities that would make the experience more engaging and relatable for children. For example:

  • Young female voices: To represent friendly female cartoon characters.
  • Child voices: So children could feel as though another child, similar to their age, was telling the story.
  • Adult female voices: To create a warm, gentle, and comforting storytelling experience, similar to listening to a mother or a familiar adult reading a story.

My intention was to create a collection of voice options that would make storytelling feel more natural, friendly, and engaging for children.

That is why having multiple voice options became one of my key requirements when planning my application.

First, I explored several AI voice-generation applications that offered text-to-voice and voice-to-voice conversion. However, most of these platforms required paid subscriptions to access additional features, and their free trials did not give me enough flexibility to experiment with different voice options.
So, I decided to take a different approach and build my own voice-generation application.

Building my own voice-generation application:

When I started building it, I discovered that AI-powered coding tools were very helpful in creating the application's interface, functionality, and interactions. They allowed me to build a good user experience and make changes to the application whenever I wanted.

My first challenge on building my own application: However, I faced another challenge: generating natural, human-like voices. Most of the solutions I initially explored produced robotic-sounding voices or focused mainly on audio processing features such as noise reduction. They didn't provide the kind of natural voice-generation experience I was looking for.

I realized that AI coding tools are excellent for building application interfaces and functionality, but building a voice-generation application requires additional voice technologies and integrations.

Next, I explored AI animation tools. These platforms offered pre-designed characters that could be animated using recorded audio. I could record my own voice, upload it, and the selected character would automatically generate lip movements and facial expressions that matched the audio.

Although this was an interesting approach, it didn't completely solve my problem because I wanted to use different AI-generated voices instead of recording my original voice.

Then, I explored another category of AI tools that could generate better application interfaces, illustrations, and visual assets. These tools helped me explore the visual possibilities, but I was still looking for a way to bring everything together into one customized application.

My biggest learning was that creating an AI-powered video application is not just about building an interface. It requires bringing together multiple capabilities, including voice generation, illustration creation, character animation, and audio synchronization.

I'll share my next experience in the upcoming article.
If you're interested in following my application-building journey and learning how I approach challenges as a UX Researcher and Designer, feel free to follow me!

And if you've already experimented with building similar applications or explored other AI tools, I'd love to hear about your experiences. Please share them in the comments. I'm always happy to learn from others, too!

title: Your Dependencies Have a Maintenance Cost. Here's Why It Matters.
description:
Every dependency you add to a project comes with a responsibility.

You have to install it, keep it updated, monitor vulnerabilities and deal with it when something breaks.

That doesn't mean dependencies are bad. Good packages save developers enormous amounts of time. The problem starts when we introduce packages without thinking about whether we actually need them.

The hidden cost of dependencies

Think about a typical backend project.

You start with a framework, add a database library, bring in a queue package, install a caching solution and before long, your application has accumulated quite a few dependencies.

Some are essential. Others might not even be used anymore.

The more packages you introduce, the more things your team potentially needs to keep track of.

A different approach with ZinTrust

This is one of the ideas behind ZinTrust.

Instead of building its core around Express or Fastify, ZinTrust provides its own backend framework architecture, with integrations available through adapter packages.

For example:

  • PostgreSQL: zin add db:postgres
  • Redis queues: zin add queue:redis
  • Other integrations can be added as your application requires them.

The idea is to avoid introducing integrations you don't currently need.

Three questions worth asking before installing another package

  1. Do I need this for the feature I'm building now?
  2. Is there already something in my existing stack that handles it?
  3. Who will be responsible for maintaining it?

These questions might seem simple, but they can save a lot of unnecessary complexity over time.

Final thought

You don't have to avoid dependencies to build good software.

You just need to be intentional about them.

That's the approach we're taking with ZinTrust.

  • Documentation: https://zintrust.com/adapters
  • GitHub: https://github.com/ZinTrust/zintrust

Get started:

npm install -g @zintrust/core && zin new my-app

title: We Moved Our Branch Shared Drives Into Azure and Nine Branches Could Not Reach Them Because Their Broadband Blocked One Port
description:
Each of our branches has a shared drive for the documents that do not belong in any system: cutting lists for the timber saw, photographs of damaged deliveries, the yard rota, the price lists suppliers send as spreadsheets. For years these lived on a small server in each branch. Last spring we retired the servers and moved the drives to Azure Files, which presents cloud storage as an ordinary Windows network drive.

We piloted it at head office and at our two largest branches, and it was excellent. Drives mapped at sign in and files opened quickly. We scheduled the remaining branches over three weekends.

On the Monday after the second weekend, nine branches rang to say their drive had gone. Windows reported that the network path could not be found. The branches that worked and the branches that did not had the same PCs, the same build and the same settings.

They did not have the same internet. Our larger sites connect over a private network that reaches Azure through our own link. The smaller branches use business broadband with direct internet access, and the nine that failed were all with one provider. Azure Files speaks SMB, the Windows file sharing protocol, over TCP port 445, and that provider blocks port 445, as many do. The port was abused by worms for years, and SMB was never designed to cross the open internet. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this, in a section we had not read because our pilot sites never needed it.

For two days those branches emailed files to one another while we arranged a fix. Each branch router now builds a VPN tunnel to our Azure network, and the drives are reached through a private address inside it, so the broadband provider sees only encrypted VPN traffic. That is how it should have been designed from the start.

Our migration checklist now records how every site connects to the internet, and every pilot includes at least one site of each kind. We had tested the product well. We had tested it only from the places where it was always going to work.

– Serguey Shinder

title: SQL Server migration verification: matching row counts are only the start
description:
After a SQL Server migration, matching row counts are a useful first check. They tell you that two tables contain the same number of rows. They do not tell you whether those rows contain the same values, or whether the destination contains the same primary keys. One missing row and one extra row can leave the total unchanged.

Smaller differences can also survive a count check: an accent removed from a name, a decimal changed from 12.50 to 12.51, or a NULL converted to empty text. The row still exists, but its content has changed. A useful acceptance report needs to distinguish missing rows, extra rows, and rows whose values differ under the same key.

Compare rows by their complete primary keys

The verifier described here is a small .NET 8 command-line tool for comparing selected tables between two SQL Server databases. It reads COUNT_BIG(*) and asks SQL Server to calculate a SHA-256 hash for each row. Rows are matched using their complete primary keys, including composite keys.

The primary key identifies the row; the row hash represents its serialized column values. The implementation retains full serialized key bytes rather than reducing primary keys to hashes. A changed primary-key value therefore appears as a missing row and an extra row.

Here is the changed-row branch from its Verifier.cs, reached when the target contains the same serialized primary key:

else if (!entry.Value.Hash.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(targetRow.Hash))
{
    changed++;
    if (changedKeys.Count < 20) changedKeys.Add(entry.Value.DisplayKey);
}

Every difference contributes to the total. The report includes up to 20 example keys per category and table, so a short example list does not mean the remaining differences were ignored.

Serialization matters here. Each column contributes a frame that distinguishes NULL from a non-NULL value and includes the payload length. Empty text consequently differs from NULL, and framing avoids ambiguity when multiple values are combined. SQL Server runs HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', ...) over the framed row.

Before comparing row hashes, the tool checks column and primary-key definitions. A definition mismatch produces a schema-difference result, with row comparison categories marked unavailable. It does not silently treat incompatible tables as successfully compared.

What the report looks like

The following example is synthetic, invented for this article. It is not output from a customer database or one of the recorded validation runs.

Result: DIFFERENCES — one or more selected tables differ.

| Table | Source rows | Target rows | Missing | Extra | Changed | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| dbo.CustomerContacts | 300 | 300 | 1 | 1 | 2 | DIFFERENCES |

Missing keys — showing 1 of 1
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"2"}

Extra keys — showing 1 of 1
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"99"}

Changed keys — showing 2 of 2
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"1"}
- {"AccountId":"10","ContactId":"3"}

Both sides contain 300 rows, yet the destination is missing one source key, contains another key absent from the source, and has two rows with different hashes. The changed-key list identifies rows to investigate; it does not provide a column-by-column value diff.

The application prints a Markdown report and writes migration-report.md. Exit code 0 means every selected table matches, 1 indicates differences, and 2 indicates an invalid invocation or incomplete verification. An incomplete run must not be interpreted as a successful comparison.

What was actually validated

The tool's validation record lists a Windows run on October 27, 2026, against a temporary SQL Server 2025 LocalDB instance. The Release build targeting .NET 8 completed with zero warnings and zero errors. All six recorded checks passed:

  • Equal tables returned exit code 0 and MATCH for both tables.
  • A missing contact with composite key AccountId 10, ContactId 2 was detected.
  • Changing NULL to empty text was reported as a changed row.
  • An extra contact with composite key AccountId 10, ContactId 99 was detected.
  • Removing an accent from Unicode text and changing 12.50 to 12.51 produced two changed keys.
  • A 20,000-row table with one changed amount identified OrderId 15000 in about one second.

That timing is an observation from that LocalDB environment, not a performance guarantee. These are the recorded validation results; the tool was not rebuilt or rerun to prepare this article.

Limits to agree before verification

Very large tables, databases on different servers, and types outside the documented supported list were not covered by those checks. The tool scans both tables and holds key/hash dictionaries in memory. Memory use grows with row count and key size; there is no batching or resume mechanism.

Both databases require snapshot isolation. Their snapshots are independent, so writes should be paused before acceptance. SHA-256 equality provides probabilistic evidence about the selected rows. It does not validate omitted tables, foreign keys, indexes, stored procedures, permissions, or application behavior.

A fixed-scope verification

I offer a fixed-scope SQL Server migration verification using copies or databases restored from backups.

We agree on the selected tables, supported types, and comparison conditions before starting.

The deliverable is a report of missing, extra, and changed rows by table, with example primary keys and explicit limitations.

title: A Temporal Algebraic Framework for Data Stream Evaluation Under Delayed Labels and Distribution Shifts
description:
arXiv:2611.21914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. Standard evaluation then confuses a degraded decision boundary with a change in prevalence, and is biased when labels are delayed or selected by the model. We extend an algebraic framework that obtains pooled (micro) and per-class (macro) measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting the counts in time by exponential fading or a sliding window; the update costs O(m^2) per step, whatever the stream length, and each pooled measure stays a weighted combination of the per-class ones. Delayed and selective feedback enter as an observation mask: until its label arrives, an instance is counted with the model's calibrated class probabilities, and the bias of this interim estimate is driven by their calibration error. Audited conventions report no value for a class without verified instances. We separate prior shift from concept drift by monitoring prior-free coordinates (recall and specificity) and attribute a change in a measure to the two sources with a first-order Jacobian decomposition. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, a detector on these coordinates with a memory per class raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike the Jacobian alarm and error-rate detectors. The correction for delayed labels recovers recall in some real settings and is only partial for precision, specificity and F1. Twenty-five statements are checked in Lean 4, and the code is in the aggmetrics package.

title: Our tests imported the repository and passed while the package we deployed was missing eleven templates
description:
Our label service is a Python package that turns a consignment into a carrier label. Every carrier zone has a JSON template, and the package ships them inside itself, under labels/templates. setup.py listed them with package_data and the pattern templates/*.json, which had been right since the first carrier.

In September we added the Highlands and Islands zones for a carrier that prices them separately, and the engineer put the eleven new templates in a subfolder, templates/zones. The tests for all eleven passed in CI. The pipeline built a wheel, the image installed it, and the first Highlands label in production failed with FileNotFoundError. Ninety two parcels for Inverness and Skye waited on the dock until the afternoon.

The pattern was easy to blame once we looked. templates/*.json matches files directly inside templates and nothing in a folder below it, so the wheel held every old template and none of the new ones. setup.py did exactly what it said.

The real question was why CI had been green. Our tests ran with python -m pytest from the root of the checkout, and that puts the current directory first on sys.path. import labels found the folder in the repository, holding every file anyone had committed, before it could find anything installed. For four years we had tested the source tree. The wheel that production ran had never been imported by a single test.

We moved the code under src/, so the package cannot be imported from the repository root at all and the tests have to use an installed copy. CI now builds the wheel once, installs it into a clean virtual environment, runs the suite against that, and puts the same file into the image. A short step lists every file under templates in the repository and fails the build if any of them is missing from the wheel. The package_data pattern now covers subfolders, but the check is what we trust.

A green run tells you about the code your tests imported. Ours imported the repository, and we shipped a package.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Typing Untyped Vue 3 Libraries and Named defineModel in TypeScript: The ProjectFilter Migration
description:
When converting legacy Vue applications to TypeScript, third-party component libraries often become a stumbling block. Some popular ecosystem packages still lack first-party TypeScript definitions or ship incomplete @types packages, resulting in TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module errors during build time.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3199), I converted the ProjectFilter component to strict TypeScript.

Here is how we handled untyped third-party dependencies with ambient declarations, implemented Vue 3.4's named defineModel macro, and tested scoped slot rendering.

1. Handling Untyped Libraries with Ambient Declarations (.d.ts)

The ProjectFilter component integrates the popular vue-select dropdown package to allow contributors to filter community issues across dozens of GitLab projects.

Because vue-select does not ship built-in type definitions, importing it in a TypeScript SFC produces compiler errors:

import VueSelect from 'vue-select'; // ❌ TS7016: Could not find declaration file

Instead of bypassing type checking with // @ts-ignore, the idiomatic TypeScript solution is creating an ambient module declaration in the project's source root (app/javascript/vue-select.d.ts):

declare module 'vue-select' {
  import type { DefineComponent } from 'vue';

  const component: DefineComponent<Record<string, unknown>>;
  export default component;
}

Why this approach works:

  • Zero Suppression Comments: The compiler recognizes vue-select as a valid Vue component without polluting component files with suppressions.
  • Global Availability: vue-tsc picks up all *.d.ts files included in tsconfig.json, enabling any other component across the codebase to import vue-select safely.

2. Implementing Named Two-Way Binding: defineModel('selectedProjects')

In Vue 3.4+, components can bind multiple models or use custom model names using the first argument of defineModel().

In ProjectFilter.vue:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BFormGroup } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import 'vue-select/dist/vue-select.css';

defineProps<{
  availableProjects: string[];
}>();

// Strongly typed named model with required flag
const selectedProjects = defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { 
  required: true 
});
</script>

<template>
  <BFormGroup label="Project">
    <VueSelect
      v-model="selectedProjects"
      multiple
      :options="availableProjects"
    >
      <template #no-options="{ search, searching }">
        <template v-if="searching">
          No projects matching "{{ search }}"
        </template>
        <template v-else>
          No projects available
        </template>
      </template>
    </VueSelect>
  </BFormGroup>
</template>

Improvements:

  • defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { required: true }) automatically types both props.selectedProjects and emits update:selectedProjects with a payload of string[].
  • Prop validation for availableProjects is enforced at compile time without verbose runtime type objects.

3. Testing Scoped Slots in Vue Test Utils

A unique testing pattern in ProjectFilter.spec.ts is verifying custom template slots like #no-options="{ search, searching }".

In TypeScript, accessing $slots on a child component's vm requires proper typing and optional chaining:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import ProjectFilter from './ProjectFilter.vue';

describe('ProjectFilter', () => {
  let wrapper: VueWrapper;
  const findSelect = () => wrapper.findComponent(VueSelect);

  // Type-safe slot helper rendering the child's scoped slot
  const findNoOptions = (slotProps: Record<string, unknown>) =>
    shallowMount({
      render: () => findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps),
    });

  it('emits updated projects when selection changes', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findSelect().vm.$emit('update:modelValue', ['gitlab']);

    // Emits are typed as Array of argument arrays
    expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedProjects')).toEqual([[['gitlab']]]);
  });

  it('renders matching text when search has no results', () => {
    createWrapper();

    const noOptionsWrapper = findNoOptions({ search: 'non-existent', searching: true });
    expect(noOptionsWrapper.text()).toContain('No projects matching "non-existent"');
  });
});

Using optional chaining findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps) prevents runtime TypeError when a component's slot is undefined during mounting.

Key Takeaways

  1. Ambient Declarations for Untyped Packages: Create clean .d.ts declaration files instead of relying on @ts-ignore when working with untyped npm packages.
  2. Named defineModel<T>('name'): Leverages Vue 3.4's macro to type non-default model bindings cleanly and succinctly.
  3. Safe Scoped Slot Testing: Use typed inline render helpers with optional chaining to mount and assert custom slot templates in Vue Test Utils.

title: The event loop: the mental model that changes everything
description:
There's a bug that turns up in every Node service sooner or later, and it almost always gets diagnosed wrong. The app serves fine, the logs are clean, the process is alive… and then it stops answering for a few seconds. htop shows one core at 100% and the other eleven watching, bored.

It isn't the database. It isn't the network. It's that somebody put CPU work on the only thread allowed to take requests.

To understand why that freezes everything, and why setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't mean "now", you have to open the box. This lesson is the box.

One thread, and concurrent anyway

JavaScript runs on a single thread: one call stack, one instruction after another. Two lines of your code never run at the same time. Ever.

So how does Node serve thousands of connections? Because it doesn't serve them at once: it accepts them all and refuses to wait for any of them.

The difference is in what you do while waiting. In the classic thread-per-connection model, each request reserves a thread and leaves it staring at the ceiling until the database answers. Thousands of connections are thousands of threads, nearly all asleep. In Node, when an operation has to wait — reading a file, talking to the network, resolving DNS — you hand it off and move on. When the result is ready, someone tells you.

That "someone tells you" is literal: the operating system knows when a socket has data and notifies the process. libuv, which you met in the first lesson, translates those notifications from epoll, kqueue or Windows completion ports into something Node understands. And for the work the OS can't background on its own — some disk operations, DNS, cryptography — libuv keeps a thread pool of its own.

The concurrency is real. What doesn't exist is your code running twice at once.

If you come from Python, the comparison clears the ground: the GIL and the event loop are two answers to the same question. Python lets you write threads and then serialises them; Node doesn't let you write them and forces you to think in terms of waiting. Neither is better. They're two ways of saying "don't block".

The loop, from the inside

One moving part explains nothing. There are four, and all of them matter:

  • The call stack: where your code runs. One function on top of another. When it's empty, there's nothing to do right now.
  • libuv: where the operations waiting on something external live.
  • The macrotask queue: setTimeout callbacks, network events, disk reads. Things waiting their turn.
  • The microtask queue: promise continuations, and whatever you enqueue with queueMicrotask.

The loop does the same thing every time, in this order: if the stack is empty, drain the microtask queue completely, and only then take one macrotask. When that one finishes, drain microtasks again, and on it goes.

The asymmetry is the whole point: microtasks are drained entirely before moving to the next macrotask. If a microtask enqueues another microtask, that one goes into the same turn. That's where half the surprises come from.

It's easier to run than to describe:

console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4"));
console.log("5");

1
5
3
4
2

Line by line: 1 is synchronous and leaves immediately. setTimeout runs nothing, it queues a macrotask. The promise and queueMicrotask queue microtasks. 5 comes out before any of them because the script is still running. When the module ends, the stack empties and the loop drains the microtasks in order: 3, then 4. Only then does the macrotask get its turn: 2.

3 before 4 isn't magic: it was queued first.

setImmediate is not setTimeout(0)

Node has a third way to ask for a turn, and the name lies: setImmediate doesn't run immediately, it runs in a phase of its own — the check phase — right after the poll phase.

setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));

immediate
timeout

At the top level setImmediate comes first, and not by accident: a timer needs at least a millisecond, and the loop reaches the check phase before that. Don't turn it into law, though, because it depends on how long the process takes to start; on another machine you can see the opposite order.

Where it is deterministic is inside an I/O callback:

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

readFile("./package.json", "utf8").then(() => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));
});

immediate
timeout

There setImmediate always wins, because the check phase runs in the same turn of the loop, before the timers look at the clock again. If you read documentation promising a fixed order at the top level, be suspicious: it's the one point in the loop where the answer is arguable.

The queue Node adds on the side

Node also has process.nextTick, which is neither a promise nor a timer and has a queue of its own. It does what the name promises — it runs very soon — but its exact priority depends on where you enqueue it: at the top level it runs after promises, and inside a timer callback it runs before them.

Don't put it into the two-queue model, because it doesn't fit, and be suspicious of any tutorial that sells it as "the microtask that goes first" and stops there. Recognise it when you meet it in someone else's code and move on. What you do need to know is that it isn't a promise, and mixing them produces orderings you didn't write.

What this means in practice

Never block the loop

The call stack has one lane. If a synchronous task takes three hundred milliseconds, then for three hundred milliseconds nothing else runs: no callbacks, no promises, no new requests.

You don't have to take my word for it. Schedule a zero timer and block it on purpose:

const t0 = performance.now();
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("setTimeout(0) delay:", (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(1), "ms");
}, 0);

const start = Date.now();
while (Date.now() < start + 300) {}

console.log("the blocking ended after", Date.now() - start, "ms");

the blocking ended after 300 ms
setTimeout(0) delay: 308.1 ms

The timer asked for a slot at zero milliseconds. It ran at 308.1, because the thread was busy. Your exact numbers will differ; the order of magnitude won't.

On a server that isn't an impatient timer: it's every request queueing behind whoever decided to parse a whole CSV in memory.

You can block it without a for

The example above is obvious: a three-hundred-millisecond synchronous loop. The case nobody spots produces the same effect with no long loop at all, just by keeping the microtask queue permanently full:

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

let n = 0;
function step() {
  let x = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) x += i;
  n++;
  if (n < 50) Promise.resolve().then(step);
}
Promise.resolve().then(step);

the timer ran after 448 ms

Fifty chained microtasks, each with a small piece of synchronous work. The timer asked for a turn at zero milliseconds and ran at 448. There's no big while anywhere: there's a queue that never empties, and the loop won't take the next macrotask until it does.

That's the dark side of the rule you just learned. A .then that re-enqueues itself leaves the server unattended just as thoroughly as a two-hundred-megabyte JSON.parse.

setTimeout(fn, 0) isn't zero

Same thing, with no blocking involved: a zero timer takes about a millisecond, not zero.

const measure = (n) => {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("round", n, (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(2), "ms");
    if (n < 3) measure(n + 1);
  }, 0);
};
measure(1);

round 1 1.26 ms
round 2 0.18 ms
round 3 1.14 ms

0 doesn't mean "immediately", it means "as soon as you can, and not before zero". The system has a clock resolution, the loop has to reach the timer phase, and there's work ahead in the queue. It's a few milliseconds that become a real problem the moment somebody treats setTimeout as a precision sleep.

The timer that won't let the process exit

One oddity that produces some of the best "why won't my script end?" moments: a pending timer keeps the process alive, and you can opt out.

setTimeout(() => console.log("this never runs"), 5000).unref();
setTimeout(() => console.log("this one does"), 0);
console.log("script ends");

script ends
this one does

The process finishes in hundredths of a second, not five seconds. unref() means "don't count on me to keep the process running": if it's the only thing pending, Node exits. It's used for cleanup timers, caches and keepalives that shouldn't stop the program from finishing.

Chunk it before you delegate it

Before shipping the work to another thread there's a cheaper option: cut it into chunks and let the loop serve between one and the next. The request takes the same total time, but the server keeps answering.

With one trap that costs an afternoon: the yield has to be a macrotask. Chaining promises doesn't release the loop, because microtasks are drained in full before the next macrotask is even considered.

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

const chunks = (n) => {
  if (n === 0) return Promise.resolve();
  let x = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 1e6; j++) x += j;
  return Promise.resolve().then(() => chunks(n - 1));
};

chunks(100).then(() => console.log("the work finished after", Date.now() - start, "ms"));

the work finished after 892 ms
the timer ran after 898 ms

A hundred rounds chained with .then and the timer still runs after all the work. Chaining microtasks hands the turn to other microtasks, not to I/O.

Change that one line for a macrotask and the story changes. Node has a module for this, node:timers/promises, which exports setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate and scheduler in promise form so you don't wrap callbacks by hand:

import { scheduler } from "node:timers/promises";

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

const chunks = (n) => {
  if (n === 0) return Promise.resolve();
  let x = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 1e6; j++) x += j;
  return scheduler.yield().then(() => chunks(n - 1));
};

chunks(100).then(() => console.log("the work finished after", Date.now() - start, "ms"));

the timer ran after 6 ms
the work finished after 796 ms

scheduler.yield() does exactly what the name says: it hands control back to the loop and gives it back to you afterwards. Older Node versions don't have it; the equivalent is setImmediate from the same module, or setTimeout(resolve, 0) if you're working with callbacks.

And look at what doesn't change: the total work is the same, 892 ms in one case and 796 in the other. Yielding neither gives nor takes away speed in any meaningful way; what changes is whether the timer runs at 898 milliseconds or at 6. The difference isn't performance, it's whether the server answers while it works.

Pick the chunk big enough that the round trip doesn't dominate, and small enough that the worst wait for a request stays acceptable.

Two clarifications that save confusion:

  • This is not parallelism. Same core, same work, same total time, just spread out. It stops the server going mute; it doesn't make it faster.
  • A generator's yield doesn't do this. It pauses the function, not the loop: whatever drives the generator still needs a macrotask between steps. It's the same trap with a syntax layer on top, and generators are a different story this course doesn't cover.

The emergency exit

When the work can't be chunked — or when chunking isn't enough — the answer isn't "optimise the loop": it's getting it off the thread. worker_threads gives you real threads and cluster gives you processes. Neither is a silver bullet: both cost startup, both force you to move data between contexts, both add failure surface.

That has its own section later in the course. Here, the rule is enough: the loop doesn't get blocked, the work gets moved.

Predict the order before you run it

This is the lesson's exam. Read it, write the order down, then run it:

console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("C"))
  .then(() => console.log("D"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("E"));
console.log("F");

A
F
C
E
D
B

If you got D and E wrong, that's fine: it's the detail almost everyone misses. C is the first microtask and it enqueues D at the end of the queue, behind E, which was already waiting. The order doesn't depend on when the promise was created, but on when each continuation was queued.

If you got B wrong, go back to the loop section. And if you got everything right, you already have the model most people writing Node don't have.

Common problems

The server stops responding for a few seconds, then recovers

CPU work on the main thread: JSON.parse on a huge response, a for over a million items, a regular expression that runs away, a readFileSync on a request path. All of it blocks the loop exactly like the while above.

setTimeout(fn, 0) is delayed far more than expected

Either there's synchronous work ahead, or there are many macrotasks queued. The timer isn't broken: the loop is getting there when it can.

The interval overlaps itself

setInterval doesn't wait for your callback to finish: it schedules the next turn anyway. With a callback taking 250 ms and an interval of 100, you end up with three executions at once.

let n = 0;
let running = 0;
const id = setInterval(() => {
  running++;
  console.log("tick", ++n, "· running:", running);
  setTimeout(() => {
    running--;
  }, 250);
  if (n === 3) clearInterval(id);
}, 100);

tick 1 · running: 1
tick 2 · running: 2
tick 3 · running: 3

If you don't want that, don't use setInterval: chain a setTimeout at the end of the work, so the next turn is scheduled once the previous one finished. And when the callback is synchronous but slow, the interval doesn't catch up either: gaps go from 100 to 250 ms and continue at 100.

One detail the example takes for granted: setInterval returns an identifier you cancel with clearInterval, and setTimeout with clearTimeout. Without that, the timer stays alive as long as the process does.

A huge delay fires immediately

A timer's delay is a signed 32-bit integer. Ask for more and it doesn't wait: it warns you and sets it to 1 millisecond.

setTimeout(() => console.log("fired"), 2147483648);

TimeoutOverflowWarning: 2147483648 does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer.
Timeout duration was set to 1.
fired

The first line arrives prefixed with (node:PID), which changes on every run. It's the kind of bug that shows up when somebody configures a "one day" timeout from a computed number: the maximum is 2,147,483,647 ms, about 24.8 days, and above that the timer becomes immediate. The exact opposite of what was asked for.

A promise that should run first runs later

Check whether a new microtask is in the way, and whether process.nextTick is in the mix. The order follows a rule, but not the one the code's shape suggests.

A long job seems to freeze the server

If the work is CPU, no timer fixes it: the thread is busy and everything else waits. Chunking and yielding eases it; moving it off the thread solves it.

What you take from this lesson

  • JavaScript runs on one thread. The concurrency is in the waiting, not in the code.
  • libuv hands the waiting to the operating system and reports back when there's a result.
  • The loop drains all microtasks before taking another macrotask.
  • Promises and queueMicrotask are microtasks; timers and I/O callbacks are macrotasks.
  • process.nextTick exists, isn't a promise, and doesn't fit the two-queue model.
  • setTimeout(fn, 0) takes about a millisecond, and much longer when the thread is busy.
  • Blocking the thread doesn't slow the server down: it stops it.
  • CPU work gets moved off the thread, not optimised inside it.

With this you can read any interleaved log without assuming the order is the one it looks like. Which helps, because the next lesson is about promises: the mechanism that creates the microtasks you just learned to order.

Never stop coding!

title: Browser Back Button Testing: Can a Peer Return to the Same SaaS Task?
description:
Browser Back button testing should check whether someone can return to the same useful task, not merely whether the address changes. For a SaaS review queue, that means checking the filter, sort order, selected item and place in the list. Write down which state should survive before asking a founder peer to try the demo.

A public demo often follows the cleanest route: open the queue, select a record, finish. A peer may take a different route. They open the wrong record, go back, inspect another, then use Forward. The question is whether the product helps them continue without rebuilding the context they already supplied.

The queue below is a fictional example and a proposed manual test plan. It is not a report of testing Buildside or another product. Use the same reasoning when building in public and inviting someone to review a navigable prototype.

Define the task that Back should restore

Imagine an app for reviewing incoming requests. A person selects “Needs review,” sorts the oldest requests first and scrolls to a sample request called Cedar. They open Cedar to inspect its details. Before taking any action, they press the browser's Back button.

The useful destination is the filtered queue they just left. Returning to a general dashboard would make the person navigate again. Returning to an unfiltered queue could make Cedar harder to find. Returning to the same route with the wrong filter is still a loss of task context.

Write the expectation in plain words: “Back returns to Needs review, oldest first, with Cedar or its former location easy to find.” This is more useful than “Back works.” It also leaves room for a legitimate change, such as another reviewer processing Cedar while the detail page was open.

Separate requirements from nice touches. Restoring a filter may be essential. Restoring the exact pixel position may be less important than keeping the same nearby records visible. Decide which distinction matters for your workflow before classifying every visual difference as a bug.

Separate URL state from temporary state

A route can identify a record without describing the full task. A queue address might include a status filter and sorting choice. A selected tab, an expanded explanation or a temporary note may live elsewhere. Listing those pieces helps you ask what a return visit is supposed to recover.

MDN's guide to working with the History API explains how a single-page app can add and update session-history entries and respond to navigation. Its example also addresses the initial history entry. Those browser mechanisms support navigation; they do not choose the correct product behavior for your queue.

For this fictional app, make the filter and sorting choice shareable through the URL. Treat an unsent note as a separate concern with an explicit expectation. This is a proposed design choice for this scenario, not a rule that every interface must store every preference in its address.

Ask one practical question for each piece of state: would losing this force someone to repeat meaningful work? If yes, describe the recovery or preservation rule. If no, avoid adding persistence simply because it is technically possible. Restoring an obsolete detail panel can be confusing too.

Run one clean Back and Forward journey

Start with sample data that contains enough requests to make the filter and ordering visible. Write down the browser, starting URL, filter, sort and sample record. Use fictional names and safe content so your public evidence does not expose customer information.

Open Cedar, press Back once and observe the queue before clicking anything else. Is Needs review still selected? Is the ordering still oldest first? Can you identify where you left off? Record the result separately for each expectation rather than giving the entire journey a single pass label.

Next, press Forward once. The expected destination is Cedar's detail view in this scenario. Check whether the record identity and visible information match the current task. A detail page that opens but displays a different request is a more serious problem than a lost scroll position.

Do not compensate for a failure while recording it. If you reset the filter out of habit, the next observer cannot tell whether navigation restored it. Capture the state first, then recover. The short interruption is part of the experience a peer is trying to describe.

Test changed data without demanding a frozen screen

Now give the return journey a reason to differ. In the fictional scenario, another reviewer marks Cedar complete while its details are open. When you go Back, Cedar may no longer belong in Needs review. That absence can be correct.

The requirement should preserve orientation while respecting the authoritative data. The queue might keep its filter and order, show the surrounding requests and explain that Cedar was completed. It should not silently recreate an old list just to reproduce a screenshot.

Write a second expectation: “Back preserves the queue context, but completed requests leave this filter.” This prevents two reviewers from reporting contradictory results because one expects exact visual restoration and the other expects fresh data. Both care about continuing the task; they differ about what that requires.

Keep this check separate from simultaneous-edit conflict handling. You are examining navigation after a known data change, not claiming that a quick peer review covers every multi-user race. A useful public test has clear boundaries.

Compare refresh and direct entry

Browser Back, refresh and opening a link in a new tab are different journeys. Test them separately. After restoring the queue, refresh it. Then copy the visible queue URL into a new tab. Which parts of the task remain, and which deliberately reset?

In this example, the shareable filter and sort should remain because they describe the queue being requested. A transient expanded row may reset. If the direct link instead opens the default queue, a peer cannot reproduce the view simply by using the link you shared.

Try a direct link to Cedar as well. It may be reasonable for the app's internal “Back to queue” link to choose a defined default when no prior queue exists in that tab. That is a different control from the browser's Back button. Name the control in your notes.

Also describe the starting condition. “Back left the demo” is ambiguous if Cedar was the first page in a fresh tab. A report should say whether the reviewer entered through a queue or opened the detail URL directly. The route history changes the interpretation.

Share a bounded review request in public

A build-in-public update can show the route through the task and the uncertainty you want checked. For example: “In this sample queue, open Cedar from Needs review and use browser Back. Please tell me whether the filter and your place survive. Sample data only.”

That invitation gives a peer a concrete job. It does not require them to become a routing specialist or inspect your code. A founder community such as Buildside provides a relevant context for sharing the work and asking for feedback, but the quality of the request still depends on the task you describe.

Include the intended behavior alongside a short recording or safe screenshot. A visually smooth return is not enough if the wrong requests appear. Ask the reviewer to report the visible filter, record identity and action they used, not merely whether the transition felt fast.

Turn the observation into a decision

Keep a small record containing the starting condition, action, expected state, observed state and consequence. “Back cleared Needs review, so I had to find Cedar again” is actionable. “Navigation is weird” needs another conversation before it can guide a change.

After a repair, repeat the journey that failed using the same safe fixture. Then check the adjacent Forward and refresh journeys, since the change may affect their behavior. Ask a peer to retry only when you can explain what changed and which observation would resolve the remaining question.

Do not turn a few successful reviews into a reliability claim for every browser, route or device. They are evidence about the journeys actually attempted. The useful result is narrower: a person could leave a record, return to the relevant queue and continue the task without reconstructing its context.

title: 77 ns vs 31 ns: jiff 1.0 is not the fastest datetime lib
description:
77 ns vs 31 ns: jiff 1.0 is not the fastest datetime lib

jiff 1.0 parses an RFC3339 timestamp in 77 nanoseconds on my machine. time does it in 31. chrono does it in 42. I benchmarked all three this morning, and the new 1.0 release — the one BurntSushi has been building toward for two years — is not the fastest datetime library in Rust. That's the headline, and it's also the wrong reason to judge it. The interesting numbers are the ones around the edges: formatting, where jiff beats chrono by 1.4x, and error messages, where it isn't close at all.

What 1.0 actually is

jiff 1.0.0 shipped November 15, 2026. The changelog is refreshingly boring for a 1.0: the big breaking change is a rename, Zoned → ZonedDateTime (which broke my first build this morning — more on that below). The MSRV went to Rust 1.85, Timestamp subtraction now returns a SignedDuration, and conversions to SystemTime became fallible. The message is stability: "this release marks an indefinite commitment to 1.x.y. Consumers should feel confident about putting Jiff types into their public API."

Then 1.0.1 followed two days later, November 17, with two fixes. One was cosmetic (%Z in strftime should format as UTC). The other is the kind of thing that makes you blink: "Parsing a timestamp could produce an out of bounds value." A datetime library shipped a parse out-of-bounds bug in its 1.0.0 and fixed it in 48 hours. Nobody's perfect; the fix time is the part worth noting.

The benchmark

Same machine for all three libraries (AMD EPYC 9D25, rustc 1.99.1, --release, 1,000,000 iterations per case, best of 5 runs). The input is a real timestamp with nanoseconds and a Z suffix; the offset variant uses +05:30.

let ts = "2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z";
let ts_off = "2026-11-18T07:00:00+05:30";
// parse:  jiff Timestamp::from_str
//         chrono DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339
//         time OffsetDateTime::parse(.., Rfc3339)
// format: jiff Timestamp Display / chrono to_rfc3339() / time format(Rfc3339)

parse RFC3339 (Z)            jiff   77.1 ns     chrono   42.5 ns     time   31.3 ns
parse RFC3339 (+05:30)       jiff   60.8 ns     chrono   37.7 ns     time    —   *
format RFC3339               jiff   81.9 ns     chrono  116.7 ns     time   43.7 ns

* time's offset parse is the same code path; I only ran it for the Z input.

Ratios, because ratios are the story:

parse (Z):    jiff is 1.8x slower than chrono, 2.5x slower than time
format:       jiff is 1.4x FASTER than chrono, 1.9x slower than time

So jiff loses parsing and wins one formatting matchup. Before you conclude anything, the sanity check: all three agree on the instant. Epoch 1794985200, nanoseconds 123456789, identical output strings. And jiff's zoned form does the thing the other two make you work for:

jiff:  2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
chrono: 2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
time:  2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
jiff zoned: 2026-11-17T23:00:00.123456789-08:00[America/Los_Angeles]

The part the benchmark doesn't measure

Feed all three a date that doesn't exist — February 30 — and compare what comes back:

jiff:   parsed date is not valid: parameter 'day' for `2026-02`
        is invalid, must be in range `1..=28`
chrono: ParseError(OutOfRange)
time:   TryFromParsed(ComponentRange(ComponentRange {
          name: "day", is_conditional: true }))

jiff tells you which parameter, which month, and the valid range, in one sentence. chrono gives you an enum variant. time gives you a Debug dump of an internal struct. This is jiff's actual product: every error is a sentence a human can act on, every API refuses to silently do the wrong thing (hence fallible SystemTime conversions in 1.0), and the DST arithmetic doesn't have the footguns that made people write their own wrappers around chrono in the first place.

That costs nanoseconds. jiff validates more on the parse path — the range checks, the offset handling, the civil-date validation — and validation is work. time is a thinner layer over the same bytes. If your hot loop parses a million timestamps a second, take the 31 ns. If your program parses user input, config files, or API responses, the 46 extra nanoseconds buys you an error message your on-call engineer can paste into a search box.

The rename that broke my build

One honest footnote: my first compile failed.

error[E0433]: cannot find `Zoned` in `jiff`

The 1.0 changelog lists it plainly — Zoned is now ZonedDateTime, to_zoned is now to_zoned_datetime — and I still wrote the old name from muscle memory. That's the entire cost of the biggest breaking change in the release: one rename, one compiler error, one sed command. For a library whose pre-1.0 API moved constantly, that's the point of the 1.0 line in the changelog. The API is done moving now.

So should you switch?

The scoreboard, without romance:

  • Parsing throughput: time > chrono > jiff. jiff pays ~2.5x vs time for validation.
  • Formatting: time > jiff > chrono. jiff beats chrono by 1.4x.
  • Error messages: jiff, by a distance.
  • API stability: 1.0 is a commitment; ZonedDateTime is the name now.

jiff 1.0 is not a speed release. It's a "you can put this in your public API and stop thinking about it" release, and the benchmark says the tax for that is measured in tens of nanoseconds per parse. If you're choosing a datetime library on parse throughput alone, you already know which one to pick — and it's not this one. If you're choosing on the strength of what happens when the input is wrong, the numbers point the other way.

Sources: jiff CHANGELOG, 1.0.0 (2026-11-15) and 1.0.1 (2026-11-17); jiff on crates.io, 1.0.1. Benchmarks are my own measurements (rustc 1.99.1, --release, AMD EPYC 9D25, 1M iterations, best of 5; jiff 1.0.1, chrono 0.4.45, time 0.3.55). I dropped one comparison from the results: a date-arithmetic microbenchmark where the jiff number came out at an implausible 0.5 ns/op — the compiler had hoisted the loop-invariant computation out of the timed loop, so the number measured nothing. I removed it rather than publish a benchmark artifact as a result.

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

title: MIRAGE: Motion Identity Reduction via Autoregressive Generative Encoding for Privacy-Preserving Skeleton-based Motion Data
description:
arXiv:2611.22200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skeleton motion identifies people through body proportions and movement style, and skeleton streams are increasingly passed to third-party analytics that run action classifiers trained on raw data. A prior adversarial anonymizer adds a per-frame residual in the raw coordinate space but sees one frame at a time; motion retargeting needs a target skeleton and complete sequences, which rules out online use. We present MIRAGE, a target-free, causal anonymizer that adds an identity-reducing residual to each incoming frame in the raw coordinate space, computed by attention over past frames. One causal, optionally windowed mask governs every attention in a rotary-position encoder-decoder, and key/value caches let the trained function run frame by frame; on all 56,578 NTU 60 sequences, batched and streaming outputs differ by at most 7.2e-6 m. Reported results use an unbounded window, so per-stream state grows with stream length. We evaluate against a passive adversary that applies raw-trained identity models and an adaptive adversary that trains on the anonymizer's output, treating the adaptive adversary as the headline, on NTU RGB+D 60 over five generator seeds, alongside the per-frame residual anonymizer of Moon et al. trained identically. When consumers retrain on the released data, MIRAGE keeps 83.9% action recognition (raw 89.1%; Moon et al. 88.7%) while a retrained identity classifier reaches 43.4% re-identification (RI) over 40 subjects, against 69.4% for Moon et al. and 75.4% on raw data. The strongest adaptive attacker still reaches 49.3% (chance 2.5%), so MIRAGE reduces identity leakage; it does not anonymize. Against raw-trained (frozen) classifiers, MIRAGE lowers RI below the strongest retargeting baseline (10.36% vs. 22.09%), but frozen action recognition falls to 37.04% (vs. 75.82%), so at full residual scale it is not a drop-in replacement for raw input to existing frozen models.

title: Building Type-Safe Presentation Components in Vue 3: Converting ContributorSocialLinks to TypeScript
description:
In frontend design systems, presentation components-small, focused components responsible solely for displaying data—are the building blocks of clean UI architecture. However, when these components accept raw arrays without strict contracts, optional fields like social links, profile URLs, and handles can easily lead to template errors or broken links.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3194), I migrated the ContributorSocialLinks component and its test suite to strict TypeScript.

Here is a quick breakdown of how typing lightweight presentation components improves maintainability and test reliability.

1. The Challenge: Loose Array Props

Originally, ContributorSocialLinks.vue accepted contributors through standard runtime prop validation:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
});

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Why was this problematic?

  1. Missing Shape Contract: The compiler had no knowledge of what attributes a "contributor" held. A parent passing an object with linkedin (lowercase 'i') or discord_handle would fail silently.
  2. Untyped Filter Results: contributorsWithSocials held elements of type any, preventing type checking across the component template (such as icon rendering or URL generation).

2. Strong Type Contracts with interface

By adding lang="ts" and exporting a discrete Contributor interface, we created a clear contract for both the component and its consumers:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
export interface Contributor {
  name: string;
  gitlabUsername?: string;
  linkedIn?: string;
  discord?: string;
}

const props = defineProps<{
  contributors: Contributor[];
}>();

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Advantages:

  • Type-Only defineProps: Eliminates verbose runtime object definitions. Vue 3 automatically validates props at compile time based on the TypeScript definition.
  • Reusable Interface: Parent components (e.g., contributor lists, award cards) can import type { Contributor } directly to ensure prop compatibility.
  • Safe Filtering: TypeScript's type checker now verifies that .discord and .linkedIn exist on the Contributor model.

3. Strict Type Safety in Unit Tests

In ContributorSocialLinks.spec.ts, untyped factory helpers were replaced with typed parameters using the exported interface:

import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import type { Contributor } from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';
import ContributorSocialLinks from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';

describe('ContributorSocialLinks', () => {
  const createWrapper = (contributors: Contributor[]) =>
    shallowMount(ContributorSocialLinks, {
      props: { contributors },
    });

  it('does not render when no contributors have socials', () => {
    const wrapper = createWrapper([
      { name: 'Test User' }, // Fully conforms to Contributor interface
    ]);

    expect(wrapper.find('p').exists()).toBe(false);
  });
});

Spec assertions are now resilient against future schema changes, ensuring that mock objects always mirror realistic application data.

Key Takeaways

  1. Export Component Prop Interfaces: When a component receives structured domain data (like a user, contributor, or product), export its interface so parent views and test suites remain in sync.
  2. Favor Type-Only defineProps: defineProps<{ data: T }>() is cleaner and offers better IDE autocompletion compared to JavaScript options-based prop validators.
  3. Keep Spec Helpers Strongly Typed: Passing typed parameters into helper functions like createWrapper prevents accidental drift between test fixtures and production models.

title: Your List Endpoint Runs 101 Queries to Show 100 Orders
description:
Your list endpoint runs 101 queries to show 100 orders.

A list I reviewed loaded 100 orders, then asked the database for each order's customer, one at a time.

1 query for the list.
100 more for the customers.

That is the N+1 problem. The page was slow, the database was busy, and the team's first idea was a bigger database.

What the code usually looks like

The endpoint fetches the orders, then loops over them to fetch each customer:

const orders = await db.query(
  `SELECT id, total, customer_id FROM orders
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100`
);

for (const order of orders) {
  const [customer] = await db.query(
    `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ?`,
    [order.customer_id]
  );
  order.customerName = customer?.name;
}

One query for the list, then one query per row inside the loop. With 100 orders that is 101 queries. With 1,000 orders it would be 1,001. The query count grows with the list, and that is the real problem.

Why it stays hidden for so long

The data is correct. Every order shows the right customer name, so no test fails and no user reports a bug. In development the list has ten rows, so eleven queries feel fast. The problem only shows up when real data arrives, and by then the slow page looks like a database problem, not a code problem.

The wrong fixes

A bigger database pays more for the same 101 queries. The queries are the problem, not the machine running them.

A cache hides the extra queries until the data changes, then the first request after the change pays the full cost again. It also adds a whole new thing to keep correct.

An index makes each of the 101 queries faster, without removing 100 of them. Faster queries that should not exist are still queries that should not exist.

The fix: ask for the data together

One query can return the orders with the customer name already in each row:

SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

One query, 100 rows, the customer name already in each row.

Two details in that query matter.

First, it is a LEFT JOIN, not a plain JOIN. If an order can exist without a customer, a plain JOIN would silently drop those orders from the list. LEFT JOIN keeps every order and leaves the customer name empty where there is no customer.

Second, it has an ORDER BY. Without it, LIMIT 100 returns whichever 100 rows the database happens to find first, and that set can change between requests, which breaks paging. With ORDER BY, the database sorts first and then takes the newest 100 orders.

When a join is the wrong fix

The join above works cleanly because each order has exactly one customer. Joining a many-to-one relation keeps one row per order.

A one-to-many relation behaves differently. Join orders to order_items, and an order with five items becomes five rows. LIMIT 100 now counts rows, not orders, so you might get 30 orders, and the last one can be cut off halfway through its items.

For that case, use two queries instead. Page the orders first, then fetch all their items in one go:

SELECT id, total FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (/* the 100 order ids */);

Then group the items by order_id in your code. That is still two queries for any list size, which is the whole point.

If you use an ORM

Use its eager loading, like include in Prisma or Sequelize. It may run 2 queries instead of 1, and that is fine. What matters is that the query count stays the same as the list grows:

const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({
  take: 100,
  orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' },
  include: { customer: true },
});

The ORM fetches the orders, then fetches the customers for those orders in one more query. Two queries for any list size beats one query per row. This two-query approach is also why ORMs handle one-to-many relations like order items without the row multiplication problem.

How to spot it in your own code

Count the queries per request, not the time per query. Turn on query logging in development, open a list page, and look at the count. Then change the page size from 10 rows to 100 rows. If the query count jumps with the row count, you have an N+1 hiding in that endpoint.

Fix the shape of the query first. Speed comes after, and only where it is still needed.

How many queries does your list endpoint run today? Drop the number in the comments.

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

title: A reconnect schedule is a thundering-herd problem
description:
Our device agent has two reconnect schedules stacked on top of each other, and one guard behind
them. They look like tuning, but they set how the whole fleet meets the relay after an outage.

We have not published a measurement of a real relay restart, and this post does not claim one.
What follows is the design, read from the agent's code and checked with a simulation of the
library's backoff.

Schedule one: the socket library, with jitter

When the relay drops the connection, the socket library reconnects on its own first. The agent
asks for a 5 second first delay and a 60 second cap (session_manager.go:498-499). The delay
doubles on each attempt up to the cap. Each delay is randomised by up to half either way (the
library's default factor of 0.5, third_party/socket.io-client/constants.go:15-16), and then
clamped back into 5 to 60 seconds (Duration() in the library's backo2.go, v3.0.6).

That clamp is the part we got wrong. Every delay that jitter pulls below 5 seconds becomes exactly
5 seconds. We ran the library's own backo2.go 10,000 times with our settings. The first retry
landed between 5.0 and 7.5 seconds, and 5,005 of the 10,000 landed on exactly 5,000 ms. A relay
restart drops every socket at about the same moment, so about half the fleet's first attempts are
scheduled for the same 5 second delay, within whatever spread there was in noticing the drop.

The same thing happens from the other side at the cap. From the fifth retry on, the doubled delay
is already 60 seconds, jitter spreads it over 30 to 60, and the clamp puts about half on exactly
60 seconds: 5,011, 4,954 and 4,995 of 10,000 for the fifth, sixth and ninth retry. The second to
fourth retries are not clamped and are spread out.

There is one more random delay, and this one has no clamp. If the relay is shedding /init load
it answers temporarily_unavailable to an exchange, registration or token refresh
(init.socket.server.ts:243). The agent then waits a random 5 to 60 seconds and tries again, up
to three times (initBackoff, throttledRetries and retryWhileThrottled in
session_manager.go:47, :59-60, :811). That wait only matters for a device that runs an
/init exchange, and after a relay restart not every device does.

Which devices go back through /init

A device holds a session token for ten days (deviceJwtExpirationSeconds is 864000 in
src/config.json:52). The agent gets one in each Start() and hands it to the socket library
once. The library re-sends that same token on every reconnect, and the agent has no way to give
it a newer one (session_manager.go:501-506).

A connected device does also go back to /init every 24 hours
(refreshTokenTickerInterval, :84, scheduledRefresh, :630). But that rotates the stored
refresh credential only. The session token on the wire stays the one from the last Start(). The
relay checks its signature and expiry on every handshake (session.socket.server.ts:224), and a
rotation does not invalidate it, because the row the token names keeps its identity
(init.socket.server.ts:592-596). So after a relay restart the fleet splits in two:

  • Session token under ten days old. The library reconnects /session with the token it has. No /init exchange runs, so the clamped library delay is its only spread.
  • Session token older than that. The relay refuses it. The device shows as not connected, and the next 60-second tick runs Start() (main.go:272). That refreshes over /init inside retryWhileThrottled (session_manager.go:461-463), which is where the relay sheds load and the random 5 to 60 second wait spreads those devices out.

The age that counts is the time since the process last ran Start(), not since the device first
connected.

Schedule two: the agent's own loop, without jitter

Behind the library sits a plain loop in main.go (:21, :231-232):

  • 60 seconds. The agent checks its connection once a minute.
  • 5 quick retries. If the connection is still gone, it tears it down and rebuilds it from scratch on each of the next ticks, up to five times.
  • 30 minutes. After five rebuilds it waits until thirty minutes have passed since the last one, then starts over.

No jitter here, no exponential curve. Each agent's ticker starts when the agent starts, so ticks
land at different seconds for different devices. That is the only spread this loop has.

What each schedule protects

Now say the relay comes back slow, or falls over again under load.

The library schedule is the one the relay meets first. Its first wave is half a wall: about half
the fleet scheduled for exactly 5 seconds, the rest spread over the next 2.5. After that the doubling thins
it out, until the cap gives half of the stragglers the same 60 second delay again.

The outer loop guards against something else: a device rebuilding its whole connection every
minute, forever. Each rebuild closes the previous connection first, so the library's own retries
on it end there. After the fifth, the loop leaves the last rebuild standing and stays quiet for
thirty minutes. What happens next depends on how far that rebuild got. If it had already created
its /session socket, that socket keeps retrying at the capped, jittered pace and brings the
device back by itself. If the relay was unreachable at /init, setup never finished. The /init
socket may reconnect, but it does nothing more, because the connect handler returns until setup
is done (handleInitConnect, session_manager.go:717-719). That device waits for the
thirty-minute mark.

In short: after a few quick tries in the first minute, a device starts at most one
rebuild a minute, and five of them. The library path does move partly in step, because of the
clamp, and the outer loop has no jitter at all. Those are the two things we would change first if
the fleet grew: a lower floor or our own jitter for the library, and jitter for the loop.

A failure that never retries

One case skips the loop. If the relay says the device's credential is no good, the agent exits
with code 2 instead of retrying (ExitCodeAuthFailure, main.go:16, :223-225, :275-278).
Only a refusal that is not also marked transient counts (requiresCredentialReset,
session_manager.go:120). A device with a dead credential hammering the relay every minute would
be a herd of its own.

Why you cannot just tune it

Change a sixty-second cap to ten and you have not tuned one device. You have changed the load on
your relay from every device, at once, on the next release. You cannot roll it back from the relay,
because the devices you would need to reach are the ones running the change.

That is why we treat these numbers as a fleet contract, not a setting. Changing them is a
load test you plan.

title: Python vs R isn’t a debate. It’s a direction.
description:
Here's The Breakdown!

Python:
A general-purpose language used across AI/ML, data science, automation, web development, and production systems.
Strong ecosystem for both building models and deploying them into real applications.
Most widely used in industry because it scales from analysis to full software products.

R:
A statistics-first language built for data analysis, hypothesis testing, and high-quality visualization.
Very efficient for exploratory data analysis and academic/research work, with powerful built-in statistical tools and plotting capabilities.
Less commonly used for large-scale software systems, but still widely used in research and analytics.

Verdict:
Python is the go-to for building real-world AI systems, software, and scalable data products.
R is best when the focus is deep statistical analysis and research-level data work.

Most professionals end up using Python for production and R for specialized analysis.
