title: Saga in microservices: orchestration or choreography?
description:
Most of you have probably heard of the Saga pattern in microservice architectures. It helps coordinate a business process that spans multiple services and cannot be handled by a single transaction.

Each participant in a Saga commits a local change. If a later step fails, the system runs compensating actions to bring the process back to an acceptable state. But who should manage the sequence of steps: the services themselves, or a dedicated coordinator?

Orchestration or choreography?

With choreography, services react to one another’s events, and there is no central coordinator. With orchestration, a dedicated coordinator defines the order of actions, tracks the process state, and decides what to do when something fails.

The choice depends on the complexity of the business process and the level of control it requires. Let’s compare both approaches using the same example.

Example: placing an order

Choreography: services react to events

Consider an order workflow. The Order service publishes an OrderPlaced event. The Inventory service checks availability and attempts to reserve the items. It then publishes either StockReserved or StockUnavailable.

After receiving StockReserved, the Payment service processes the payment and publishes either PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed. Once payment succeeds, the Shipping service creates a shipment.

No single service owns the entire workflow: each participant reacts to the events it needs. The services remain independent, but the order’s state is spread across their handlers. When something goes wrong, understanding what happened may require tracing a chain of events across several services.

For example, if payment fails, the Inventory service needs to receive a failure event and release the reservation. If a shipment cannot be created after payment succeeds, the system needs a recovery step: retry, cancel the payment, or route the order for manual handling.

Choreography is easy to follow while the process is short and reactions are simple. As branches and recovery paths accumulate, it becomes harder to understand.

Orchestration: one component coordinates the steps

An Order Saga can manage the workflow instead:

  1. Ask the Inventory service to reserve the items.
  2. Start payment after the reservation is confirmed.
  3. Request shipment creation after payment succeeds.
  4. If payment fails, ask Inventory to release the reservation.
  5. If shipment creation fails, retry or run the agreed recovery flow.

The orchestrator tracks the order’s state and decides what to do when a step fails or times out. The process is easier to observe, but the coordinator itself must be operated and maintained. Its role is to manage the sequence of steps, not to take business logic or data ownership away from the services.

How to choose

Choreography Orchestration
Process Short and mostly linear Long-running or branching
Process state Reconstructed from events Tracked by the coordinator
Failure handling Distributed across participants Defined in the workflow logic
Main cost Harder to trace as the process grows An additional component to operate

If the steps are simple and services can react to events independently, choreography may be enough. If the team needs to track the state of each order, handle timeouts, and manage several failure paths, orchestration gives the process an explicit owner.

One thing remains true in either approach: compensation is not a transaction rollback. Releasing reserved stock or cancelling a payment is a new action, and that action can fail too. Handlers need to be idempotent; retries, timeouts, stuck orders, and manual recovery should be planned for in advance.

title: Claude 5 vs GPT-6: Which AI Model Should You Choose in 2026?
description:
The Claude-versus-GPT question has moved on from Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4 Turbo. The current Tokuse catalog offers the Claude 5 family (claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5) and OpenAI's GPT-6 family (gpt-6-sol, gpt-6.1-sol) through the same platform. Model IDs, limits, and rates change often, so this guide focuses on the routing decision instead of quoting numbers that will be stale by the next release.

Try Tokuse: Create a free account and send your first request through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Short answer: There is no universal winner. Start with claude-sonnet-5 as the balanced default for coding, analysis, and agent workflows. Escalate to claude-opus-5 for the hardest reasoning and long-horizon tasks. Test gpt-6.1-sol on the same evaluation set when you need an OpenAI-family route, a second opinion, or a fallback. Then route by task and verify the current rates on the Tokuse pricing page.

What changed since the GPT-4 era

  • Model IDs are versioned. Use the exact IDs from the live catalog. Old aliases such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4 Turbo no longer describe the current lineup.
  • The API surface is shared. Claude 5 models on Tokuse support both OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. GPT-6 models are available through the OpenAI-compatible API.
  • Capabilities are not inherited. Context limits, output limits, modalities, and tool behavior belong to each model. Check them in the catalog rather than assuming they carry over from an older generation.
  • Sticker price is a poor decision variable. Input/output mix, caching, retries, and fallbacks change the real bill. Compare cost per successful task.

Quick comparison

claude-sonnet-5 claude-opus-5 gpt-6.1-sol
Position in the Tokuse catalog Balanced Claude 5 model for coding, analysis, and versatile agent workflows Flagship Claude 5 model for the most demanding reasoning, coding, and long-horizon agent tasks The 6.1 release in the GPT-6 Sol line for OpenAI-compatible workloads
Good starting point for Coding agents, code review, analysis, support, general automation Complex refactors, difficult debugging, long-running agent loops Teams standardized on OpenAI APIs, cross-checks, and fallback routes
API protocols on Tokuse OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic-compatible OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic-compatible OpenAI-compatible
Rates and limits Check the live pricing page Check the live pricing page Check the live pricing page

This table describes positioning and integration shape, not measured performance. It is not a benchmark.

Coding and agent workflows

claude-sonnet-5 is the natural default for coding agents, review passes, and multi-step tool use. It is positioned as the balanced Claude 5 tier, which makes it a reasonable first route for most production traffic.

Use claude-opus-5 as an escalation tier. Route a task there when Sonnet 5 fails your quality gate: ambiguous debugging, large refactors, architecture decisions, or agent loops that need to hold a plan for a long time. Escalation keeps the expensive tier tied to work that actually needs it.

gpt-6.1-sol belongs in the same evaluation. Its value is not that it wins every task by default; it is that it gives you an OpenAI-family route with the same request shape as the rest of your GPT integrations. If gpt-6-sol is already pinned in production, compare gpt-6.1-sol against it on a holdout set before changing the alias.

Writing and document analysis

Long-form writing and document analysis reward consistent instruction following and careful revision. Run the same brief through Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and GPT-6.1-sol. Score tone, structure, factual constraints, and edit distance. The model that needs the fewest human edits is often the cheaper one in practice, even when its token rate is higher.

Do not choose a writing model from a single sample. A small test set is enough to disqualify a route, not enough to promote one.

Reasoning and long tasks

Opus 5 is the right place to test the hardest reasoning and long-horizon agent work in the Claude line. The practical pattern is to keep it behind a quality gate, not in the default path.

For GPT-6, test both gpt-6-sol and gpt-6.1-sol before standardizing on one. Point releases can change behavior, and the only reliable check is your own task set. If the two models are indistinguishable on your evaluations, choose the route that is easier to operate and confirm the rate on the pricing page.

Why this article does not quote prices

Tokuse rates depend on the model, the access group, the input/output mix, cache behavior, and retries. They also change. Quoting a per-million-token number here would be misleading within weeks.

Instead, measure:

  • Tokens consumed per successful task
  • Retry and fallback rate
  • Cache hit rate
  • Human review time per accepted output

Then compare the total cost of the workflow, not the headline rate. A cheaper model that needs repeated attempts can lose to a more expensive model that succeeds once.

Always confirm current rates on the Tokuse pricing page.

A practical routing policy

  1. Start with claude-sonnet-5 for coding, analysis, support, and routine agent steps.
  2. Sample real traffic through gpt-6.1-sol as a parallel candidate. Keep gpt-6-sol as a regression comparison if it is already in use.
  3. Escalate only the failing slices to claude-opus-5.
  4. Re-run the evaluation when you change a model ID, prompt template, or tool schema.
  5. Re-check limits and rates before launch. The catalog is the source of truth.

One endpoint, two protocols

All four models are available through the Tokuse OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://tokuse.com/v1. Claude models can also be called through the Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages endpoint.

  • Chat Completions guide
  • Anthropic Messages guide
  • Practical guide to cutting AI API costs

Avoid model lock-in

Keep model IDs in configuration, not scattered through application code. An OpenAI-compatible gateway lets the application keep one client while you change the model alias, add a fallback route, or run a second model in shadow mode. Claude's Anthropic-compatible endpoint is there when you need the native message format, but it should not force a second integration if the OpenAI shape is enough.

Bottom line

Choose Claude 5 when you want a balanced default and a clear escalation path: claude-sonnet-5 for most work, claude-opus-5 for the hardest tasks. Keep GPT-6 in the evaluation, especially when you need an OpenAI-family route or a fallback. The final decision should come from task-level evaluation and the live rates on tokuse.com/pricing.

Last updated November 2026. Model IDs, limits, and prices change; verify them on the Tokuse pricing page before production use.

title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark
description:
arXiv:2611.21823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

title: Which Platform Gives the Best Visibility and Control Over Cloud Instances, Containers, and VMs? (2026): A See-Versus-Act Matrix by Workload Type
description:
No single tool gives both full visibility and full control over cloud instances, containers, and VMs on every cloud, so the best choice depends on whether you need to see workloads or act on them. Observability platforms such as Datadog and Dynatrace see the most, control platforms such as HPE Morpheus Enterprise and Azure Arc offer the broadest ongoing lifecycle control, and platforms that also run the workloads, such as Control Plane, give both for the workloads they run.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Seeing a workload and acting on it are different jobs, and the right platform depends on which job you need for cloud instances, containers, and VMs.

  • Hyperscaler tools such as AWS Systems Manager, Azure Arc, and Google Cloud’s fleet tools go deepest in their own cloud and reach other environments through agents, connectors, or attached Kubernetes clusters.
  • Azure Arc and HPE Morpheus Enterprise offer the broadest lifecycle control across environments, while Datadog and Dynatrace see nearly everything and act only through workflow automations that call other tools’ APIs.
  • Red Hat OpenShift with OpenShift Virtualization and SUSE Rancher with Harvester manage containers and VMs together on Kubernetes through KubeVirt.
  • Control Plane fits teams that want to run containers across AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and on-premises locations, and VMs on Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s) locations, without having to operate Kubernetes clusters, with visibility and control built in.

Which platform offers the best visibility and control over cloud compute instances, containers, and virtual machines?

The answer depends on which workload types you run, how many clouds and on-premises environments you span, and whether you need to see, act, or both.

Platform Category Cloud instances Containers VMs (on premises / hypervisor) Clouds and environments What it does not cover
AWS Systems Manager + CloudWatch Hyperscaler native See and act (patching, inventory, automation) See (ECS and EKS metrics and logs) See and act on hybrid-activated servers AWS; Azure and Google Cloud VMs through Cloud Connector; on-premises servers and other clouds through hybrid activations No container orchestration actions; Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and other machines outside Azure and GCP need a manual agent install and hybrid activation
Azure Arc + Azure Monitor Hyperscaler native, multi-cloud control See and act (Arc-enabled servers on AWS, GCP, other clouds, and on premises) See and act (Arc-enabled Kubernetes on any conformant cluster) See and act (Arc-enabled VMware vSphere and SCVMM) Azure, AWS, GCP, other clouds through the agent, on premises, VMware, SCVMM Automatic onboarding covers AWS and GCP (preview) only, so Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VMs need a manual agent install; container runtime protection outside Azure needs Defender for Cloud
Google Cloud (Compute Engine, GKE, Google Cloud Observability) Hyperscaler native See and act (Compute Engine) See and act (GKE, plus fleet management of attached EKS, AKS, and on-premises clusters) See and act (Google Cloud VMware Engine for vSphere VMs) GCP; Kubernetes clusters on AWS, Azure, and on premises through fleets Reach outside GCP is Kubernetes only, with no control of other clouds’ instances
HPE Morpheus Enterprise Cloud management platform See and act (provision, resize, decommission across clouds) See and act (Kubernetes cluster provisioning and container management) See and act (VMware, Hyper-V, Nutanix, SCVMM lifecycle) AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle Cloud, VMware, Hyper-V, Nutanix, bare metal No deep observability; relies on integrations for metrics and traces
VMware Cloud Foundation (vCenter, VCF Operations) Virtualization platform No lifecycle control of public cloud instances See and act (vSphere Kubernetes Service clusters on VCF) See and act (full VM lifecycle on vSphere) VMware on premises and VCF-based hyperscaler services (Amazon EVS, Azure VMware Solution, Google Cloud VMware Engine) No management of native public cloud instances
Red Hat OpenShift + OpenShift Virtualization Kubernetes platform No See and act (container orchestration, monitoring, policies) See and act (KubeVirt VMs alongside containers) On premises, AWS, Azure, GCP, IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure No management of cloud instances outside its clusters
SUSE Rancher + Harvester Kubernetes platform No See and act (multi-cluster container management) See and act (Harvester VMs integrated in Rancher) Containers on premises, AWS, Azure, and GCP; Harvester VMs on on-premises bare metal No management of cloud instances outside its clusters
Datadog Observability See (infrastructure monitoring, cloud integrations) See (container and Kubernetes monitoring, APM) See (agent-based VM monitoring) AWS, Azure, GCP, on premises, any host the agent supports No native provisioning, patching, or orchestration; actions run through Workflow Automation calls to cloud APIs
Dynatrace Observability See (full-stack monitoring, cloud integrations) See (Kubernetes and container monitoring, root-cause analysis) See (agent-based VM and host monitoring) AWS, Azure, GCP, on premises, any host OneAgent supports No native provisioning or patching; remediation runs through Workflows connectors (Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, Ansible)
IBM Turbonomic Resource optimization See and act (resize, scale, suspend, start, delete unused volumes) See and act (container resource resizing) See and act (resize, move, suspend VMs on vSphere, Hyper-V, Nutanix) AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, VMware, Hyper-V, Nutanix, Kubernetes, OpenShift Does not deploy new workloads from templates; actions are limited to optimization
Terraform / OpenTofu Infrastructure as code Act (provision, modify, destroy across clouds) Act (provision Kubernetes resources and container services) Act (provision VMs on vSphere, Hyper-V, and clouds) Any environment with a provider No runtime metrics, logs, or traces; visibility is limited to declared state and drift detection
Control Plane Production workload platform (containers and VMs) See and act on Managed Kubernetes worker nodes, which Control Plane provisions and autoscales on supported providers; does not manage standalone instances See and act (runs containers on AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and MK8s locations, with built-in logs, metrics, traces, and cost view) See and act (VM workloads through the KubeVirt add-on on MK8s locations with KVM-capable nodes) AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, on premises through MK8s or BYOK Instances, VMs, or clusters not connected to Control Plane

Hyperscaler stacks give the deepest integration in their own cloud. AWS Systems Manager reaches Azure and Google Cloud VMs through Cloud Connector and on-premises or other-cloud servers through hybrid activations, Azure Arc brings servers, Kubernetes clusters, and vSphere and SCVMM VMs into Azure’s management plane, and Google Cloud reaches outside GCP only for Kubernetes clusters, through fleets and GKE attached clusters.

Observability platforms cast the widest net for visibility. Datadog and Dynatrace collect metrics, traces, logs, and cost data from instances, containers, and VMs everywhere, and their workflow features can trigger scripted fixes, but they do not manage workload lifecycle. IBM Turbonomic sits between observability and control. It sees resource use and executes resizing, placement, suspend, and capacity actions, though it does not deploy new workloads.

Infrastructure-as-code tools such as Terraform and OpenTofu act broadly, provisioning and changing resources across clouds, but they track only declared state and drift, with no runtime monitoring. Platforms that run workloads directly, such as Control Plane, see and change those workloads through the same API.

What do visibility and control mean for each workload type?

Each workload type needs different things to see and do, and tools fall short in predictable places.

Workload type Visibility you need Control you need Where tools usually fall short
Cloud instances (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure VMs) Inventory, configuration state, patch status, cost attribution, security posture, performance metrics Provisioning, patching, resizing, stopping, tagging, access management Hyperscaler consoles show other clouds’ instances only after agent or connector onboarding
Containers on managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) Pod and node health, resource use, network topology, image vulnerabilities, deployment status Scaling replicas, rolling updates, admission policies, RBAC, network policies Observability tools see containers but cannot enforce policies; Kubernetes dashboards show state but lack cost attribution
Containers on serverless container services (Cloud Run, Fargate, Azure Container Apps) Request metrics, latency, error rates, cold starts, cost per request or per vCPU-second Deployment, revision management, concurrency limits, IAM bindings Little access to underlying infrastructure metrics; scaling behavior is opaque; control does not carry across clouds
VMs on vSphere, Hyper-V, or KVM Guest OS health, hypervisor metrics, storage IOPS, snapshot state, license compliance Provisioning, live migration, snapshots, patching, decommissioning Cloud-native tools reach on-premises hypervisors only through agents or connectors; VM platforms often lack container awareness
VMs on Kubernetes (KubeVirt) VM health as a Kubernetes resource, node resource pressure, storage provisioning status VM lifecycle through Kubernetes APIs, live migration, resource limits, scheduling affinity Observability tools without a KubeVirt integration treat VMs as pods; Kubernetes dashboards may not surface VM-specific metrics
Bare-metal servers Hardware health, firmware versions, IPMI or BMC status, power state Firmware updates, BIOS configuration, OS provisioning, power cycling Most cloud management tools assume a hypervisor or container runtime; bare-metal visibility needs dedicated agents or out-of-band management

Which platform fits which situation?

Choosing a platform starts with your current environment, team, and main workload types.

Situation Start with Why What you still need
One cloud, mostly instances Your hyperscaler’s native tools (Systems Manager, Azure Monitor, Google Cloud Observability) Deepest integration, lowest setup effort, no extra licensing A cross-cloud observability tool if you add a second cloud; an IaC tool for repeatable provisioning
Azure-heavy with on-premises servers Azure Arc + Azure Monitor Arc-enabled servers extend Azure management to on premises and other clouds; Arc-enabled VMware vSphere manages existing VMs A configuration management tool for complex OS fleets; a container security platform if you run Kubernetes
VMware estate moving to containers VMware Cloud Foundation with vSphere Kubernetes Service, or HPE Morpheus Enterprise VCF manages existing VMs while vSphere Kubernetes Service adds Kubernetes; Morpheus manages VMs and containers across clouds An observability platform for application metrics and traces; a FinOps tool for cost attribution
Kubernetes everywhere, some VMs OpenShift with OpenShift Virtualization, or Rancher with Harvester Both run containers and VMs on Kubernetes through KubeVirt A cloud management platform for non-Kubernetes instances; an observability stack if built-in monitoring falls short
Many clouds, need one dashboard Datadog or Dynatrace for visibility; HPE Morpheus or Azure Arc for control Observability platforms see across every cloud; Morpheus and Arc act across clouds and on premises An IaC tool for provisioning; a policy engine for governance; a FinOps platform for cost optimization
Teams that want production containers and VMs with built-in visibility and control, without having to operate Kubernetes clusters Control Plane Runs containers natively on four clouds and VM workloads on MK8s locations, with observability, cost, and changes through one API A hyperscaler tool or cloud management platform for resources not connected to Control Plane

How do you combine tools without overlap?

Combining tools works when each one has a clear job, because overlap means two tools acting on the same resource, conflicting inventories, or duplicated cost data.

  • Designate one inventory source of truth. If you use Azure Arc, let Arc’s resource graph be the canonical list of servers and clusters; if you use Datadog, let its infrastructure map be the canonical view.
  • Assign one place to act per workload type. Instances go to Systems Manager or Morpheus, containers to your Kubernetes or workload platform, and VMs to vCenter, Morpheus, or your Kubernetes-based VM tool.
  • Enforce a tagging standard across clouds. Tags drive cost allocation, access policies, and automation scope, and a tag that exists in AWS but not in Azure breaks cross-cloud cost and access reports.
  • Keep one audit store. Forward CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, and platform audit logs into one searchable store so every change to a workload lands in one place, and standardize governance across dozens of cloud accounts so the trail stays consistent.
  • Split actions by lifecycle phase. If Terraform provisions a VM and Morpheus also changes its configuration, one will overwrite the other, so let the IaC tool create and destroy resources, let the operations tool patch and resize them, and run drift detection to catch crossover.

The 10 best multi-cloud management platforms compares the wider landscape.

How does Control Plane give visibility and control over containers and VMs?

Control Plane runs workloads across clouds and on-premises locations, so the same platform that runs them shows and changes them, and Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

For containers, Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and on Kubernetes clusters you already operate through BYOK or on clusters Control Plane provisions through MK8s. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations, and a workload runs in every location of its GVC, active-active across regions and clouds.

For VMs, Control Plane runs VM workloads through the KubeVirt add-on on MK8s locations with KVM-capable nodes, either bare metal or nested-virtualization instances. On MK8s locations, Control Plane also provisions and autoscales the worker nodes, so the instances under your workloads are visible and managed too.

Logs and metrics are collected automatically and explored in a built-in Grafana, and traces use Control Plane’s OpenTelemetry tracing provider once a sampling rate is set. The console’s Cost & Usage view shows spend per org and per resource with a projected total, and a tamper-proof audit trail records every platform action, showing who changed what across the org. A single view of cost and security across multiple clouds covers how to join this with data from other tools.

The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API. The MCP server lets AI assistants deploy, diagnose, scale, and roll back workloads, and access is controlled through Control Plane policies. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane’s scope ends at what it runs, so instances, VMs, or clusters not connected to Control Plane stay with a hyperscaler tool or a cloud management platform such as Azure Arc or HPE Morpheus Enterprise, and teams evaluating hybrid cloud platforms or Kubernetes management platforms often pair one of those with Control Plane.

FAQ

Short answers on visibility and control over instances, containers, and VMs.

Which platform offers the best visibility and control over cloud compute instances containers and virtual machines?

No single platform is best at both across all three workload types on every cloud. For visibility, Datadog and Dynatrace cover instances, containers, and VMs across all major clouds. For lifecycle control, Azure Arc and HPE Morpheus Enterprise reach the most environments. For teams that run containers and VMs on one platform, Control Plane provides both for the workloads it runs on AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and on-premises locations.

What is the difference between cloud visibility and cloud control?

Visibility means seeing what exists and how it performs, including inventory, health, metrics, cost, and security posture. Control means acting on workloads by provisioning, scaling, patching, stopping, migrating, and enforcing policy. Observability tools see broadly and execute changes only through workflow automations, while orchestration platforms execute changes but may not see resources outside their own scope.

Can one tool manage both containers and virtual machines?

Yes. Red Hat OpenShift with OpenShift Virtualization and SUSE Rancher with Harvester use KubeVirt to run VMs as Kubernetes resources alongside containers, HPE Morpheus Enterprise manages both across clouds, and Control Plane runs containers and VM workloads under the same API.

Is Azure Arc good for managing AWS and on-premises servers?

Yes, especially when Azure is your governance center. Arc-enabled servers bring AWS instances, GCP instances, other clouds’ machines, and on-premises servers into Azure for inventory, policy, monitoring, and patching. Arc-enabled Kubernetes projects any conformant cluster into Azure, and Arc-enabled VMware vSphere and SCVMM manage on-premises VMs through the Azure portal.

Does Datadog let you control infrastructure?

Partly. Datadog is primarily an observability platform. Its Workflow Automation and App Builder can trigger actions such as starting, stopping, or rebooting EC2 and Azure VMs and scaling Auto Scaling Groups, but it does not provision infrastructure, patch operating systems, or orchestrate containers. Teams pair it with Terraform for provisioning, Systems Manager for patching, or a Kubernetes platform for orchestration.

Can Kubernetes run virtual machines?

Yes, through KubeVirt, an open-source project that runs VMs alongside containers on Kubernetes. OpenShift Virtualization is Red Hat’s supported implementation, Harvester is SUSE’s, and Control Plane uses KubeVirt to run VM workloads on its Managed Kubernetes locations.

What is the best single pane of glass for multi-cloud compute?

For visibility, Datadog and Dynatrace come closest, covering instances, containers, and VMs through agents and cloud integrations. For control, HPE Morpheus Enterprise and Azure Arc offer the broadest reach for provisioning and lifecycle management. No tool gives complete visibility and control for every workload type on every cloud, so most teams combine an observability platform with a control platform.

How does Control Plane manage containers and VMs?

Control Plane runs containers as serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads on its managed AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions or on your own Kubernetes clusters, and runs VM workloads on its Managed Kubernetes locations. Logs, metrics, traces, cost, and the audit trail are built in, and every change goes through one Control Plane API.

Do I need separate tools for visibility and control?

In most cases, yes. Observability platforms collect and correlate data across environments and act only through automations, while orchestration and management platforms execute changes but have narrower cross-environment visibility. The cleanest setup assigns one inventory source of truth, one place to act per workload type, and a shared tagging standard.

title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
description:
arXiv:2611.21696v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network. Although established in fine-tuning pretrained models, its effects in vision networks trained from scratch are commonly assessed by training each candidate recipe. We show that, in this setting, the rate-related component of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computable directly from its multiplier profile. Across matched-control comparisons, changes in test accuracy closely track changes in training loss (r = -0.996), which supports an optimization-progress explanation of the short-budget rate effect. Increasing the untuned base learning rate tenfold shifts the rate-matched contrast upward in all six tested architectures (p = 0.016) and increases the number of architectures in which a published discriminative schedule, excluded from model fitting, outperforms the uniform control from two to five of six (p = 0.031). Within the evaluated strategy space, a parameter-weighted power mean with exponent 0.35 (95% confidence interval [0.20, 0.50]) accounts for 42.6% of within-architecture variance, compared with 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training improves the selected candidate's mean percentile rank from the 26th to the 10th and reduces its mean accuracy shortfall relative to the best candidate from 3.70 to 1.12 points. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget increases; relative to tuned baselines, the overall strategy effect falls within the prespecified practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures. A separate grouping-related contrast can persist at long budgets, although its direction and magnitude depend on the architecture.

title: Amazon RDS now supports fast storage volume initialization
description:
Amazon RDS now initializes storage volumes faster when you perform a point-in-time restore (PITR), create a read replica, or convert a Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ. Each of these operations creates storage volumes from a snapshot, and the data blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 before you can access them. With fast storage volume initialization, you get a fully performant DB instance in a predictable amount of time.

Previously, the initialization rate varied with your workload and with which blocks were accessed. As there was no dedicated bandwidth, so you could see increased I/O latency and had no way to tell when an instance would reach full performance. Now, each database instance is initialized at up to 4 TiB per hour, across every gp3 and io2 storage volume attached to the instance. If concurrent initialization across your account exceeds the available bandwidth, the remaining blocks initialize on a best-effort basis, so initialization is never slower than today. Your DB instance stays available and usable while initialization runs.

Fast storage volume initialization is enabled by default and no action is required. To follow progress, use the StorageOperationStatus and StorageOperationPercentProgress fields in the Amazon RDS console, the DescribeDBInstances API, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs.

This capability is available at no additional cost for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, RDS for Db2, RDS for Microsoft SQL Server, and RDS for Oracle, in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Amazon RDS storage in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

title: Five Tailwind breakpoints ship in our CSS, two of them do all the work, and one changes nothing at all
description:
Responsive design is usually discussed as a design decision and shipped as a pile of sm: and lg: prefixes nobody audits afterwards. I wanted the audit: how many media queries does our stylesheet contain, how many of them ever fire on a real page, and how much changes when they do.

The subject is Nakodo, 76 public pages served by Next 16, styled with Tailwind v4, 154,378 bytes of CSS in two files.

Every media query in the stylesheet

Pulling the CSS and brace-matching each @media gives 41 top-level blocks (one more is nested inside another) holding 22,155 bytes, which is 14.4% of the stylesheet:

Condition Blocks Rules Bytes
(min-width:40rem) = sm, 640px 3 138 7,755
(min-width:64rem) = lg, 1024px 2 55 3,128
(min-width:48rem) = md, 768px 2 27 1,352
(min-width:80rem) = xl, 1280px 2 5 174
(min-width:96rem) = 2xl, 1536px 1 1 27
(min-width:420px) 1 1 74
(min-width:360px) 1 1 48
not all and (min-width:40rem) = max-sm 1 4 137
not all and (min-width:64rem) = max-lg 1 1 29
(hover:hover) 8 49 4,492
(prefers-reduced-motion:no-preference) 10 45 4,130
(prefers-reduced-motion:reduce) 3 4 310
(forced-colors:active) 6 6 499

Two things stand out before any page is loaded. The sm blocks are 45 times the size of the xl blocks, and the entire 2xl breakpoint is this:

@media (min-width:96rem){.container{max-width:96rem}}

.container has zero uses in 69,066 lines of application code. A media query ships for a screen size we never designed for, carrying a rule for a class we never use.

Every responsive prefix in the source 

sm:        367 uses in 72 files
lg:        135 uses in 25 files
md:         50 uses in 23 files
xl:          5 uses in  3 files
2xl:         0 uses in  0 files
max-sm:      4 uses in  1 file
max-lg:      1 use  in  1 file
min-[420px]: 2 uses in  2 files
min-[360px]: 1 use  in  1 file

Five of those 5 xl: uses: two xl:table-cell and one xl:block plus xl:ml-0 in the results table behind the login, and one xl:grid-cols-5 in the marketing footer. That last one is the only xl: utility that reaches a public page, and it is there once per page, 76 times in total:

<nav aria-label="Footer" className="grid grid-cols-2 gap-x-8 gap-y-8 sm:grid-cols-3 xl:grid-cols-5">

Counting prefixes in the delivered HTML of all 76 pages:

Prefix Uses Pages carrying it Distinct utilities
hover: 5,143 76 10
sm: 1,795 76 48
lg: 802 76 25
md: 347 76 9
motion-reduce: 339 66 2
group-hover: 319 70 1
min-[360px]: 76 76 1
xl: 76 76 1
2xl: 0 0 0

The nine distinct md: utilities across the whole public site are md:block, md:flex, md:gap-8, md:grid-cols-2, md:grid-cols-3, md:hidden, md:order-none, md:table and md:text-sm. That is the complete vocabulary of our 768px breakpoint.

Which widths actually change a page

Class counts are not behaviour. The test that matters is: render the same page at one pixel either side of each boundary and count the elements whose layout-relevant computed styles differ. I drove Chrome through the DevTools protocol, setting the viewport with Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride before each load, and compared display, flex-direction, text-align, order, position, visibility, font-size and the number of grid columns for every element in the body.

page                                    elements  359/360  419/420  639/640  767/768  1023/1024  1279/1280  1535/1536
/pricing                                     978        0        0        3       12          5          1          0
/glossary                                    721        0        0        2        8          3          1          0
/guides/how-to-find-youtube-influencers      856        0        0        7        8          3          1          0
/for/agencies                                739        0        0        3        8          3          1          0

Including padding and gap changes adds about four more elements at 640 per page. Nothing else moves.

So on a typical public page of this site, out of 700 to 1,000 elements:

  • 640px restyles two to seven elements. One of them is always the footer nav going from two columns to three.
  • 768px restyles eight to twelve, almost all of them display: a mobile block becoming a table cell, a hidden element appearing.
  • 1024px restyles three to five.
  • 1280px restyles exactly one element on every page, and it is the footer nav again, going from three columns to five. Measured in the browser: 232px 232px 232px becomes 126.398px 126.398px 126.398px 126.398px 126.406px.
  • 1536px restyles nothing. The media query fires (matchMedia("(min-width:96rem)").matches flips to true at exactly 1536), and because the only rule inside it targets an unused class, the page height is identical: 5,208px either side on the home page, 7,068px on the glossary.

That last line is the measurement I wanted. A week ago I checked that our pages render identically at 1280px and at 4K and concluded the design simply stops caring above a certain width. Now I know the mechanism: it stops caring at 1,280px, where one footer gains two columns, and the breakpoint above that is a no-op shipped by the framework's default theme.

The two custom boundaries never fire on a public page at all. min-[420px]:grid-cols-4 is on a stats row behind the login, and min-[360px]:inline-flex is one header button:

<Button asChild className="hidden min-[360px]:inline-flex">

That button is hidden below 360px because it was the one thing that would not fit when I checked the site at 320px. A one-pixel audit found it; a one-rule media query fixed it.

What I take from this

The honest summary is that this site has two breakpoints, not five. 640px handles phone-to-tablet, 768px handles the few places where a table replaces a stack, 1024px handles the sidebar layouts, and the top two exist because they came with the toolkit.

Three changes, in order of how much they are worth:

  1. Delete nothing. The 27 bytes of the 2xl block and the 174 of xl are not a performance problem, and container may be used later. Saying "we audited this and it is fine" is a legitimate outcome, and the audit took an hour.
  2. The nine md: utilities are a vocabulary small enough to write down, so write it down. A responsive scale nobody can recite is a scale nobody can use consistently, and ours fits in one line of a design note.
  3. The footer is the only element on the public site that responds to the top two breakpoints. If I ever want to prove that a layout change is design rather than habit, that is the element to start from.

You can reproduce the whole thing from outside: load the pricing page, the glossary or any guide at 1279px and 1280px, and watch the footer columns. Everything above the footer will be byte-for-byte the same.

title: Java String.format() Cheat Sheet: %s, %d, %.2f, Flags and Locale
description:
On a laptop with German regional settings, String.format("%.2f", 0.5) returns "0,50" instead of "0.50" — and the very next Double.parseDouble(...) fails with NumberFormatException: For input string: "0,50". Surprises like this disappear once you understand how string formatting in Java actually works.

String formatting in Java means building a string from a template in which format specifiers (%d, %s, %.2f and others) are replaced with argument values. Formatted output is produced by String.format(), String.formatted() (Java 15+), System.out.printf() and the java.util.Formatter class, which powers all of them. You can format numbers, strings, characters, dates and times.

String.format(), printf() and formatted(): which one to use

If you need the result as a string, use String.format() or "template".formatted(); if you want to print it right away, use System.out.printf(); if the text is assembled in several steps or written to a file, use the Formatter class. All of them understand exactly the same template syntax.

Method What it returns Since When to use it
String.format(template, args...) A new string Java 5 You need the formatted string itself (Java's sprintf)
"template".formatted(args...) A new string Java 15 Same as above, but shorter; great with text blocks
System.out.printf(...), System.out.format(...) The same PrintStream; prints to the console Java 5 Formatted console output
PrintWriter.printf(...) The same PrintWriter; writes to a stream Java 5 Writing to a file or a network stream
new Formatter(...).format(...) The same Formatter; accumulates the result Java 5 Building text from several calls, writing to an Appendable or a file

System.out is a static field of type PrintStream, which is why it has the printf() and format() methods. They are two names for the same method: printf() exists to make C programmers feel at home. Unlike print() and println(), which print a single value as is, printf() takes a template plus any number of arguments. Under the hood, every method in the table uses Formatter.

Throughout this lesson, the output in comments is shown for Locale.US. With a locale such as German or French, you will see a comma instead of the decimal point (details in the Locale section).

public class PrintfExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("Formatted string: %.2f%n", 1000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.format("%s, next year you will be %d%n", "John", 23);

        String str = String.format("Price: $%.2f", 99.5);
        System.out.println(str);

        String greeting = "Hello, %s! You have %d new messages.".formatted("Anna", 5);
        System.out.println(greeting);
    }
}
// Output:
// Formatted string: 333.33
// John, next year you will be 23
// Price: $99.50
// Hello, Anna! You have 5 new messages.

The formatted() method shines with text blocks (Java 15+): you write the template as is, without concatenation or \n.

String json = """
        {"name": "%s", "age": %d}
        """.formatted("Anna", 30);
System.out.print(json);
// Output: {"name": "Anna", "age": 30}

Format specifier syntax

A format specifier is a part of the template that starts with % and describes how to print the next argument. Its general form is %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion; only the % sign and the conversion character are required, everything else is optional.

%[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion
Part What it sets Example
argument_index$ Argument number (starting at 1), followed by $ %2$s — the second argument
flags Alignment, sign, leading zeros, grouping separators %-10s, %,d, %+d
width Minimum field width in characters %8d
.precision Digits after the decimal point for numbers; maximum length for strings %.2f, %.3s
conversion Conversion type (required) d, s, f, x

The argument index lets you reuse one value several times or change the order of arguments. The %<s form means "the same argument as the previous specifier":

public class ArgumentIndexExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("Hello %1$s!%n%1$s, how are you?%n"
                        + "Welcome to the site %2$s%n",
                "John", "www.site.com");
        System.out.printf("%d in hexadecimal: %<x%n", 255);
    }
}
// Output:
// Hello John!
// John, how are you?
// Welcome to the site www.site.com
// 255 in hexadecimal: ff

Java format specifiers: table

The conversion character defines how the argument is interpreted: %d is an integer, %f a floating-point number, %s a string, %c a character, %b a boolean. The argument type must match the specifier, otherwise you get an IllegalFormatConversionException at runtime.

Specifier What it prints Example Result
%d Decimal integer (int, long, BigInteger…) format("%d", 42) 42
%s / %S String representation (toString()) format("%S", "java") JAVA
%f Floating-point number in decimal notation, 6 digits after the point by default format("%f", 3.14159) 3.141590
%e / %E Floating-point number in scientific notation format("%e", 12345.678) 1.234568e+04
%g / %G Floating-point number: scientific notation if, after rounding, the value is less than 10^-4 or at least 10^precision, otherwise decimal. Precision = total number of significant digits (6 by default) format("%g", 12345.678) format("%g", 0.00001234) 12345.7 1.23400e-05
%a / %A Floating-point number in hexadecimal notation format("%a", 1.0) 0x1.0p0
%x / %X Integer in hexadecimal format("%X", 255) FF
%o Integer in octal format("%o", 8) 10
%c / %C Character (char or an int code point) format("%c", 65) A
%b / %B Boolean: false for null, the value itself for a Boolean, true for any other object format("%b", null) false
%h / %H The argument's hash code in hexadecimal format("%h", "hi") d01
%t / %T Date and time (with a suffix: %tY, %tF…) format("%tY", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 16)) 2026
%n The platform-specific line separator format("a%nb") a and b on separate lines
%% A literal % sign format("%d%%", 50) 50%

Uppercase variants (%S, %X, %E, %G, %A, %B, %H, %C, %T) work like their lowercase counterparts but convert the result to upper case: %x gives ff, %X gives FF; %b gives true, %B gives TRUE. There are no uppercase forms of %d, %f and %o.

What does this code print?

System.out.printf("%b %b %b%n", "false", null, 0);

Answer: true false true. The string "false" is not a Boolean but an ordinary non-null object, so %b turns it into true. The number 0 also gives true: in Java, unlike C, zero does not mean "false". Only null becomes false.

Width and precision

Width (%10s) sets the minimum number of characters in a field: a shorter value is padded with spaces on the left, or on the right with the - flag. Precision (%.2f) sets the number of digits after the decimal point for floating-point numbers, rounding with HALF_UP; for strings (%.3s) it sets the maximum length, and the rest is cut off.

public class WidthPrecisionExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double x = 1000.0 / 3.0;
        System.out.println("Unformatted: " + x);
        System.out.printf("[%.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%8.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%-8.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%10s][%-10s]%n", "Java", "Java");
        System.out.printf("[%.3s]%n", "Formatter");
        System.out.printf("[%3s]%n", "Formatter");
    }
}
// Output:
// Unformatted: 333.3333333333333
// [333.33]
// [  333.33]
// [333.33  ]
// [      Java][Java      ]
// [For]
// [Formatter]

The last line shows a non-obvious detail: width is a minimum, not a maximum. A longer value is printed in full, and your columns drift apart. To truncate a string you need precision: %-10.10s always prints exactly 10 characters.

Width and alignment are what you need to print a table in the console:

public class TableExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8s%n", "Item", "Price");
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8.2f%n", "Bread", 45.5);
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8.2f%n", "Coffee", 89.9);
    }
}
// Output:
// Item         Price
// Bread        45.50
// Coffee       89.90

Formatting float and double with %f

The %f, %e and %g specifiers accept float, double, their wrappers and BigDecimal; there is no separate specifier for float and no %lf for double. Integer specifiers never convert floating-point values: %d with a float argument throws IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Float.

float price = 19.99f;
double discount = 12.5;
System.out.println(String.format("%.2f", price));
System.out.println(String.format("%.1f%%", discount));
System.out.println(String.format("%08.3f", -3.14159));
// Output:
// 19.99
// 12.5%
// -003.142

Format flags

Flags go right after % (or after the argument index) and control alignment, the sign of a number, leading zeros and grouping separators. Several flags can be combined: %,(.2f prints a negative number in parentheses and with grouping separators.

Flag What it does Example Result
- Left-justify (requires a width) format("[%-5d]", 42) [42 ]
0 Pad with zeros instead of spaces (numbers only, requires a width) format("%05d", 42) 00042
+ Always print the sign format("%+d", 42) +42
space Put a space before positive numbers (to line them up with negative ones) format("[% d]", 42) [ 42]
, Locale-specific grouping separators format("%,d", 1234567) 1,234,567
( Enclose negative numbers in parentheses format("%(d", -42) (42)
# Alternate form: 0x prefix for %x, 0 for %o format("%#x", 255) 0xff 
public class FlagsExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%,.2f%n", 10000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.printf("%,(.2f%n", -10000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.printf("%09.2f%n", 10000.0 / 3.0);
    }
}
// Output:
// 3,333.33
// (3,333.33)
// 003333.33

Incompatible flags throw an exception: + together with a space, or - together with 0, gives IllegalFormatFlagsException, and - or 0 without a width gives MissingFormatWidthException.

The Formatter class

The java.util.Formatter class is the engine behind formatted output in Java: String.format() and printf() create one internally. You use Formatter directly when the text is built from several format() calls or when the result should go straight into a StringBuilder, a file or a stream.

The format() method of Formatter converts its arguments according to the template and appends the result to the accumulated text, which you get back with toString(). A minimal Java Formatter example:

import java.util.Formatter;

public class FormatterExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Formatter formatter = new Formatter();
        formatter.format("This %s is about %n%S %c", "book", "java", '8');
        System.out.println(formatter);
    }
}
// Output:
// This book is about
// JAVA 8

The Formatter(Appendable, Locale) constructor writes directly into a StringBuilder and sets the locale at the same time. Formatter implements Closeable, so when it writes to a file, close it with try-with-resources. All constructors and conversions are listed in the official Formatter Javadoc.

import java.util.Formatter;
import java.util.Locale;

public class FormatterBuilderExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        Formatter formatter = new Formatter(sb, Locale.US);
        formatter.format("%-8s%6.2f%n", "Tea", 3.5);
        formatter.format("%-8s%6.2f%n", "Coffee", 12.0);
        System.out.print(sb);
    }
}
// Output:
// Tea       3.50
// Coffee   12.00

Locale: dot or comma

Number and date formatting depends on the locale: without an explicit Locale, String.format() and printf() use the system default (Locale.getDefault(Locale.Category.FORMAT)). In German and French the decimal separator is a comma, and the grouping separator is a dot or a space, so the same program prints different strings on different machines.

import java.util.Locale;

public class LocaleExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double price = 1234.567;

        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.US, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.FRANCE, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%.2f", 0.5));
    }
}
// Output:
// 1,234.57
// 1.234,57
// 1 234,57
// 1234.57
// 0,50

The French line looks like it contains an ordinary space, but it does not: since Java 13 (CLDR locale data) the French grouping separator is the narrow no-break space U+202F, and older JDKs used the no-break space U+00A0. A test such as assertEquals("1 234,57", result) typed with a regular space fails, and so does parsing that string back with code that expects plain spaces.

format() and printf() have an overload that takes a Locale as the first parameter. formatted() has no such overload — it always uses the default locale. The new Locale("de", "DE") constructor is deprecated since Java 19; use the constants (Locale.GERMANY), Locale.forLanguageTag("de-DE") or Locale.of("de", "DE") (Java 19+) instead.

Rule of thumb. For data that another program will read (CSV, JSON, SQL, logs that get parsed), pass Locale.ROOT or Locale.US explicitly. Rely on the default locale only for text that a human reads.

Formatting dates and times

The %t specifier (or %T for upper case) with a suffix prints part of a date or time: %tY is the year, %tm the month, %td the day, %tB the month name, %tH:%tM hours and minutes, %tF the ISO date. The argument can be a LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Date, Calendar or long.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Locale;

public class DateFormatExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 16);
        System.out.println(String.format("%tF", date));
        System.out.println(String.format("%1$tm/%1$td/%1$tY", date));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.US, "%1$tB %1$te, %1$tY", date));
    }
}
// Output:
// 2026-10-16
// 10/16/2026
// October 16, 2026

Note the %1$: without the index, every %t specifier expects its own argument, and the template "%tm/%td/%tY" with a single date throws MissingFormatArgumentException. For complex date patterns, modern code usually reaches for java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.

Common mistakes and the exceptions they throw

The compiler does not check format strings: mistakes surface only at runtime as unchecked exceptions, subclasses of IllegalFormatException (which extends IllegalArgumentException). Here are the most frequent cases and how to fix them:

Code What happens How to fix it
format("%d", 3.5) IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double Use %f for floating-point values or cast with (int)
format("%s and %s", "A") MissingFormatArgumentException: Format specifier '%s' Pass all arguments or reuse one with %1$s
format("%-05d", 7) IllegalFormatFlagsException: Flags = '-0' Pick one flag: %-5d or %05d
format("%i", 7) (a habit from C) UnknownFormatConversionException: Conversion = 'i' Java prints integers only with %d
format("Save 50%") UnknownFormatConversionException: Conversion = '%' Escape the percent sign: 50%%
format("%s", "a", "b") No exception, output a — the extra argument is silently ignored Match the number of specifiers and arguments (IDEs highlight this)
format("%d", (Integer) null) No exception, output null Check the value for null beforehand

%n or \n? Use %n in templates: it inserts the line separator of the current OS (\r\n on Windows, \n on Linux and macOS). \n always produces a single LF character — correct only when a file format or protocol requires exactly that.

DecimalFormat and MessageFormat

Besides String.format(), the java.text package offers two formatting classes: DecimalFormat formats a number by a pattern such as #,##0.00, and MessageFormat inserts arguments by number in curly braces {0}, {1} — the approach used in UI localization bundles.

import java.text.DecimalFormat;
import java.text.DecimalFormatSymbols;
import java.text.MessageFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

public class TextFormatExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DecimalFormat df = new DecimalFormat("#,##0.00",
                DecimalFormatSymbols.getInstance(Locale.US));
        System.out.println(df.format(1234567.891));

        System.out.println(MessageFormat.format("File {0} contains {1} lines", "data.txt", 1500));
        System.out.println(MessageFormat.format("File {0} contains {1,number,#} lines", "data.txt", 1500));
    }
}
// Output:
// 1,234,567.89
// File data.txt contains 1,500 lines
// File data.txt contains 1500 lines

A MessageFormat quirk: numbers in {1} are formatted with the locale's grouping separators, so 1500 becomes 1,500. The {1,number,#} format prints the number without separators. Another one: a single quote in a MessageFormat pattern is an escape character, so an apostrophe has to be doubled — "Don''t" prints Don't.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a sprintf equivalent in Java?

Yes: String.format() (or "template".formatted() in Java 15+) returns the formatted string, and System.out.printf() corresponds to C's printf. The syntax is similar but not identical: there is no %i or %u, %n is the line separator, and %b accepts any object. More in the section Common mistakes and the exceptions they throw.

Does Java have f-strings or string interpolation?

No. Java has no equivalent of Python's f-strings: you cannot write variable names inside a string literal. String Templates (STR."Hello \{name}") appeared as a preview feature in JDK 21 (JEP 430) and JDK 22 (JEP 459), but they were removed in JDK 23 and are not part of the language. The closest options are "Hello, %s!".formatted(name), String.format() or plain concatenation "Hello, " + name + "!".

What is the difference between printf() and println()?

println() prints a single value and always adds a line break. printf() takes a template and any number of arguments, but adds no line break on its own — you have to put %n into the template.

Which is faster: String.format() or concatenation with +?

Concatenation is noticeably faster: every String.format() call parses the template and creates a Formatter. In loops and hot code, build strings with + or a StringBuilder, and keep String.format() for places where readability and alignment matter. All concatenation options are compared in Java String Concatenation.

How do I keep two decimal places without rounding?

%.2f always rounds with HALF_UP: String.format("%.2f", 1.999) gives 2.00. To drop the extra digits instead, use BigDecimal: new BigDecimal("1.999").setScale(2, RoundingMode.DOWN) returns 1.99.

This article was originally published on ExamClouds, part of a free Java Core course with lessons, practice tasks and quizzes.
