title: Socket.IO Tutorial: Real-Time Order Updates in Node.js
description:
Quick answer

Socket.IO is a library that lets a Node.js server push events to connected browsers the moment something happens, instead of waiting for the browser to ask. This post builds a live order-status feed: order 1042 moves from received to packed to delivered, and each change reaches the customer instantly. It fits order tracking, chat, and live dashboards.

A customer buys a kurta and a dupatta, pays Rs 12,400, and then waits. The shop page says "processing" and the customer refreshes, waits, refreshes again. The usual fix is polling: the browser asks the server every few seconds whether anything changed. Most of those requests return the same answer, and the one that matters can still arrive seconds late. A push model flips the pattern: the server speaks first, the moment the order changes. Socket.IO is the most used way to do that in Node.js, and this post puts it to work on a real order, with one event that goes missing.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the update is worth pushing at all. A live feed earns its place when the reader waits on something that changes at an unknown time: an order status, a chat reply, a delivery location. If the data only changes when the user acts, a normal request is simpler and cheaper.

My second check is how many clients need the same event. Socket.IO shines when one event fans out to many browsers: each order gets a room, and only the customer in that room hears about it. If every event goes to exactly one client, a plain WebSocket may be less machinery. The WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling post covers the raw transport underneath.

My third check is what happens when a connection drops. Networks drop and phones switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data, and Socket.IO reconnects on its own. But reconnection does not replay the events missed in between. If a missed update matters, the client must ask for the current state after reconnecting. The demo replays nothing, which suits a status feed and not a payment.

My fourth check is the team cost. Socket.IO adds a persistent connection per client, which changes how the server is deployed: sticky sessions behind a load balancer, or the Redis adapter for several servers. For one small server that cost is trivial; for a fleet it is a design decision.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Socket.IO when users wait on events they cannot predict and the server should speak first. Skip it when a request on demand already answers the question. The recommendation flips the moment events must never be missed, or the deployment cannot hold persistent connections.

One order, three updates, and a silent listener

Order 1042 belongs to Ayesha: a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400. The shop wants her browser to learn about each change the moment it happens, without polling. The server below puts each client in a room named after the order id and emits an order-update event at each step: received, packed, delivered.

// server.js: live order-status feed.
// Run: node server.js (listens on port 3000).
const http = require("http");
const { Server } = require("socket.io");

const server = http.createServer();
const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: "*" } });

const STEPS = [
  { status: "received", note: "Payment confirmed, order received" },
  { status: "packed", note: "Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse" },
  { status: "delivered", note: "Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi" },
];

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  console.log(`client connected: ${socket.id}`);
  socket.on("join-order", (orderId) => {
    const room = `order-${orderId}`;
    socket.join(room);
    console.log(`client ${socket.id} joined ${room}`);
    STEPS.forEach((step, index) => {
      setTimeout(() => {
        const update = { orderId, ...step };
        io.to(room).emit("order-update", update);
        console.log(`sent order-update: ${orderId} -> ${step.status}`);
      }, 400 * (index + 1));
    });
  });
  socket.on("disconnect", () => {
    console.log(`client disconnected: ${socket.id}`);
  });
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

The first client has a small bug: it listens for order_status, with underscores, while the server emits order-update, with a hyphen. Socket.IO never warns about a listener that matches nothing.

// client-buggy.js: the wrong event name, on purpose.
// Run: node client-buggy.js
const { io } = require("socket.io-client");

const socket = io("http://localhost:3000");
const received = [];

socket.on("connect", () => {
  console.log(`connected as ${socket.id}`);
  socket.emit("join-order", 1042);
});

// BUG: the server emits "order-update", not "order_status".
socket.on("order_status", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status}`);
});

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log(`after 2.5s: received ${received.length} updates`);
  console.log("nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server");
  socket.disconnect();
  process.exit(0);
}, 2500);

Here is the real output. The buggy client connects fine, joins the room, and hears nothing, while the server log shows all three updates going out.

=== buggy client (wrong event name) ===
connected as gI1iughH...
after 2.5s: received 0 updates
nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server

The fix is one word: listen for order-update, exactly what the server emits.

// client-fixed.js: only the listener name changes.
// FIXED: listens for "order-update", exactly what the server emits.
socket.on("order-update", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status} (${update.note})`);
});

Now the same run delivers every update, in order.

=== fixed client (correct event name) ===
connected as b2w_1A6K...
update: order 1042 is received (Payment confirmed, order received)
update: order 1042 is packed (Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse)
update: order 1042 is delivered (Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi)
after 2.5s: received 3 updates

=== server log ===
Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000
client connected: gI1iughH...
client gI1iughH... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: gI1iughH...
client connected: b2w_1A6K...
client b2w_1A6K... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: b2w_1A6K...

The bug failed in the quietest possible way: no error, no crash, just a listener waiting for an event that would never arrive. The server did its job perfectly, which is what makes this mistake hard to spot. When a Socket.IO client hears nothing, check the event name first, character by character, before doubting the connection. The Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express post shows the request side of the same stack, where a wrong route at least returns a 404.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, the event name mismatch from the demo. The symptom is a client that connects cleanly and receives nothing, with no error anywhere. The fix is to match the event name exactly on both sides, and to keep event names in one shared list or constants file instead of typing them twice from memory.

Second, broadcasting every update to every client. The symptom is a customer watching another customer's order change, because the server used io.emit. The fix is rooms: socket.join("order-1042") on the server, then io.to("order-1042").emit(...) so only that order's room hears it.

Third, a client that never connects because of CORS. The symptom is the browser console showing a cross-origin error while the server looks healthy. The fix is to pass the cors option when creating the server, as the demo does, and to list the real front-end origin instead of "*" in production.

Fourth, assuming an emitted event always arrives. The symptom is a customer stuck on "packed" after a network drop, because the update fired while they were offline. The fix is to treat emits as fire-and-forget: on reconnect, have the client ask for the current order state.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is Socket.IO different from plain WebSockets? Socket.IO is built on the WebSocket transport and adds rooms, automatic reconnection, event names, and a fallback to HTTP long polling. Plain WebSockets give you a raw pipe and leave the rest to you.

Do I need a separate server for Socket.IO? No. It attaches to the HTTP server your app already uses, so it can share a port with an Express app. The demo uses a plain Node.js HTTP server.

What happens when a client disconnects? Socket.IO reconnects automatically, and the client can rejoin its rooms on the connect event. Events sent while the client is away are lost unless the server stores them.

Can Socket.IO scale to many users? Yes, with the Redis adapter, which lets several Socket.IO servers share events. A single server handles a small shop easily; the adapter becomes the answer when one process is no longer enough.

What to remember

  • Socket.IO pushes events from server to browser, so the browser stops polling.
  • Event names must match exactly on both sides; a mismatch fails silently with no error.
  • Rooms keep each customer's updates private.
  • Reconnection is automatic, but missed events are not replayed unless you store them.
  • Attach Socket.IO to your existing HTTP server, and set CORS to your real front-end origin.

Where this leaves you

Socket.IO earns its place the moment a user is waiting on something the server knows first: an order moving through the warehouse, or a reply landing in a chat. The demo proved the two things that matter: the server pushed three real updates to the right room, and the one failure was a silent name mismatch fixed by a single word. That quiet failure is the lesson. Start with one event and one room, then add reconnection handling before real customers depend on it. A feed that speaks first feels instant, and that is what keeps a customer from refreshing.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO docs, getting started, https://socket.io/docs/v4/
  • Socket.IO docs, tutorial, https://socket.io/docs/v4/tutorial/introduction
  • Socket.IO docs, rooms, https://socket.io/docs/v4/rooms/
  • WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/websockets-explained-real-time-data.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • Express Explained: Node's Minimal Web Framework Guide, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/express-explained-nodes-minimal-web.html
  • React useEffect Explained: When to Use It and Skip It, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/react-useeffect-explained-when-to-use.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Save Points for Law Firm Intake Forms: A Game Design Lesson
description:
Anyone who played games before autosave remembers losing an hour of progress to a power cut or a missed save point. Modern game design treats that kind of loss as the game's fault. Progress is saved quietly at sensible moments, and a crash costs a few seconds at most.

Law firm intake forms rarely get the same care. A person filling out a criminal defense contact form is often stressed, on a phone, and interrupted. A call comes in, the browser reloads, the screen locks, and everything they typed about the arrest is gone. Some will start again. Many will not. If you build sites for defense firms, a save point in the intake form is a small piece of work with a real payoff, as long as you handle the privacy side carefully.

What games get right about saving

Good save systems share a few habits. They save without asking, so the player never has to think about it. They save at natural checkpoints, such as entering a new area, rather than every frame. They tell the player when a save happened with a small, unobtrusive icon. And they make it easy to start fresh when the player wants to.

Each of those maps onto a form. Save quietly as the user types, at the moment a field loses focus. Show a short "Saved on this device" note. Offer a clear way to wipe the saved data. Restore it automatically if the page reloads.

The privacy problem games do not have

A saved game holds a character's inventory. A saved intake form can hold a description of an arrest, a charge, a court date and a phone number. That changes the design.

The device may be shared. A person might fill out the form on a family computer, a work laptop or a friend's phone. Anything stored in the browser can be seen by the next person who opens it. For that reason, persistent storage that survives closing the browser is a poor fit for defense intake. Session-scoped storage is a better default: in current browsers, sessionStorage data survives a reload but is cleared when the tab is closed, and it is not shared with other tabs.

It also helps to be selective about what gets saved at all. Contact details and simple choices, such as the type of charge from a dropdown, are the fields people most hate retyping. The long free-text description of what happened is the most sensitive. A reasonable compromise is to save the structured fields and leave the free-text box out, or to save it only if the firm decides the trade-off is worth it after discussing it with the lawyers.

A minimal implementation

Here is a small sketch using sessionStorage. It saves listed fields when they lose focus, restores them on load, and clears everything on submit or when the user asks.

const KEY = "intake-draft";
const form = document.querySelector("#intake");
const SAVED = ["name", "phone", "email", "charge_type", "county"];

function save() {
  const data = {};
  SAVED.forEach(n => { data[n] = form.elements[n]?.value || ""; });
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data)); } catch (e) {}
}

function restore() {
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) || "{}");
    SAVED.forEach(n => { if (data[n] && form.elements[n]) form.elements[n].value = data[n]; });
  } catch (e) {}
}

function clearDraft() {
  try { sessionStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
}

form.addEventListener("focusout", save);
form.addEventListener("submit", clearDraft);
document.querySelector("#clear-draft").addEventListener("click", () => { clearDraft(); form.reset(); });
restore();

The try blocks matter. Storage can throw in private browsing modes or when the browser blocks site data, and the form has to keep working either way. Clearing on submit should happen after you confirm the submission succeeded if the form posts by script, so a network error does not wipe the draft.

Telling the user what happened

Games show a spinning icon in the corner. A form can show a line of small text under the submit button that changes to "Saved on this device until you close this tab" after the first save. That one sentence tells the person their work is safe and tells them how long it stays. Next to it, a "Clear this form" link gives them control on a shared device.

Keep the message honest. Do not say "saved" in a way that suggests the firm has received anything. Only the submit button sends the information.

Making the form shorter matters more

A save point helps people who get interrupted. It does nothing for people who give up because the form asks too much. Before building any of this, look at which fields the firm actually uses at the first call. Some intake forms ask for date of birth, case number and a long narrative that the lawyer will cover by phone anyway. A guide to designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish goes through trimming the form itself.

Track the effect with your existing form analytics. Compare form starts with completed submissions for a few weeks before and after adding the save feature. Small sites will need longer to see a pattern.

Questions about saving intake form progress

Should the form use localStorage so drafts survive closing the browser?

For criminal defense intake, that is risky on shared devices. Session-scoped storage is the safer default unless the firm has a clear reason and tells users plainly.

Does saving in the browser send anything to the firm?

No. Data in sessionStorage stays on the device until the user submits the form.

Does the firm need to mention this in its privacy policy?

Ask the firm to review its privacy policy with whoever maintains it. Describing local draft saving in plain words is good practice.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one firm per city, and helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits. Its notes on UX lessons from video game design cover more ideas from games that apply to law firm sites.

title: AI-assisted research uncovers critical Java flaw, Oracle issues patch
description:
Originally published on The Daily Flare.

Oracle issued a critical Java security patch on November 17 after Calif Research disclosed an AI-assisted discovery of a remote-code-execution flaw in OpenJDK.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell, affects the Base64 decoder in the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine, part of the Java Development Kit. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) classified it as a critical memory-corruption flaw and said specially crafted input could crash the JVM or allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

The defect sits in hand-written processor instructions used to speed up Base64 decoding, according to CyberScoop. Calif said the problem occurs when the decoder receives 64 “A” characters followed by an equals sign, the padding character used in Base64. The code miscalculates the input length and writes 64 bytes into a memory buffer that can be as small as 50 bytes, overwriting neighboring data before the program rejects the input.

That damage can crash a program, but researchers said an attacker may be able to turn it into control of the server. Calif described using heap grooming, a technique for arranging data in memory, to make the overwrite more useful to an attacker. The optimization involved runs on processors supporting AVX-512; CyberScoop reported that ARM64 systems are unaffected.

Calif reported unauthenticated code execution in products including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and PingFederate, and demonstrated a working break-in against Keycloak, an open-source login system. The researchers also showed code execution requiring a valid account in Kafka, Solr and Elasticsearch. Researcher samczsun demonstrated that Java programs could be compromised by connecting to a malicious server.

Calif researcher Quang Luong found the bug in about an hour while auditing OpenJDK with OpenAI’s Codex, the security firm said. The computing tokens cost less than $200, according to CyberScoop’s account of the research. Calif also said AI agents produced most of its exploit chains with little human involvement. The researchers cautioned that there is no universal exploit and that each target requires tailored steps.

Oracle shipped patched Java builds on November 17 as part of its November critical patch update, which covered 652 vulnerabilities across the company’s products, CyberScoop reported. CISA urged organizations to identify affected Java installations and apply relevant Java or vendor fixes promptly, prioritizing systems exposed to the internet.

In its CISA alert, the agency warned that Java runtimes may be bundled inside third-party applications, container images and appliances, and may not appear as separate items in software inventories. For systems that cannot be patched immediately, it recommended restricting and validating Base64 input at application boundaries, setting input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. It also urged defenders to watch for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes and suspicious Java processes.

The flaw matters because Java is used across banking, aviation, telecommunications, hospitals and government systems. Calif said OpenJDK runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies. The BBC cited computer scientist Toby Walsh, who said Java’s role in managing memory made the weakness particularly concerning. Walsh said the flaw had been “hiding in plain sight for 12 years.”

Governments warned companies to install the fix, Reuters reported on November 18. South Korean authorities held an emergency meeting about possible Java vulnerabilities, according to Yonhap, as cited by Reuters.

title: How AI Visual Search Is Transforming Fashion Apps: Models, Implementation & Costs
description:
Shoppers rarely type the exact product name. They type "black leather ankle boots" or upload a photo and expect the app to find something close. This post shows how to build that with open models, then looks at what it means for a fashion app budget, using Australia as the example market.

Why it matters

Online spending in Australia hit AUD 21.9 billion in April–June 2026, up 14% year on year, according to Australia Post. Fashion catalogues are huge and visual, and keyword search alone misses a lot. Cost guides for ecommerce apps, such as Techugo's breakdown for an app like THE ICONIC, list AI-based search, recommendations and visual discovery among the features that raise development effort.

The core idea: one embedding space for text and images

A CLIP-style model maps images and text into the same vector space. Embed every product photo once, embed each query at request time, and return the nearest vectors.

python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
from PIL import Image

model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")

# 1. Offline: embed the catalogue images
paths = ["boot_01.jpg", "sneaker_02.jpg", "dress_03.jpg"]
img_emb = model.encode(
    [Image.open(p) for p in paths],
    convert_to_tensor=True,
    normalize_embeddings=True,
)

# 2. Online: embed the shopper's text query
query = "black leather ankle boots"
q_emb = model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)

# 3. Retrieve the closest products
hits = util.semantic_search(q_emb, img_emb, top_k=3)[0]
for h in hits:
    print(paths[h["corpus_id"]], round(h["score"], 3))

Passing an image as the query works the same way, which gives you "shop the look" for free.

Architecture in four parts

Ingestion job: embeds new or changed product images on a schedule and writes vectors to an index (FAISS, pgvector or a managed vector database).

Search API: embeds the query, runs a nearest-neighbour lookup, then filters by size, stock and price.

Re-ranking: blends similarity with business signals such as availability, margin or popularity.

App layer: a cross-platform client (Flutter or React Native) is usually enough, because the heavy lifting happens on the server.

Things that go wrong in practice

Domain gap: general-purpose models can confuse close categories such as "midi skirt" and "maxi skirt". Evaluate on your own catalogue and consider fine-tuning.

Stale vectors: if images change and embeddings don't, results drift. Version your index.

Cold start: new shoppers have no history, so fall back to visual similarity and trending items.

Measure it: track recall@k on a small labelled query set, plus click-through and add-to-cart rate online.

What it means for the budget

Reference ranges from the same cost guide, in AUD:

Tier - Budget - Timeline
MVP - 30K – 150K - 3–5 months
Mid-level - 150K – 250K - 5–8 months
Advanced - 250K – 350K - 8–12 months

My suggestion is to ship plain search in the MVP, then add visual search once you have real queries to evaluate against. Beyond the build, plan for:

Hosting: roughly AUD 300–3,000+ per month depending on traffic, with spikes in big sale seasons. Vector search and model inference add to this.

Maintenance: about 15–20% of the initial build cost per year.

Compliance: if you use shopper photos or behaviour data, the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles apply.

Takeaway

Visual search is a small, well-understood pipeline: embed once, search fast, re-rank with business rules. Start with an open model, measure on your own catalogue, and let the data decide whether fine-tuning is worth the cost.

Resources

Sentence Transformers: image search with CLIP

Techugo: cost to build an app like THE ICONIC in Australia

Australia Post quarterly ecommerce update (July 2026)

OAIC: Australian Privacy Principles

Cost figures are indicative estimates from the sources above and vary by vendor, scope and region.

title: Two decades of The Apache Way: Celebrating 20 years of Google and the Apache Software Foundation
description:
by Mike Bufano, Open Source Programs Office

In 2006, Google formalized its relationship with the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) as one of its first corporate sponsors and twenty years later, that partnership continues through ongoing sponsorship and upstream contributions.

At the core of our collaboration is a shared belief in "The Apache Way" and its principles of open, vendor-neutral, and community-led development. From the early days of corporate open source to modern machine learning and open data systems, Google and ASF communities have collaborated on widely used open source software.

Shaping how Google does open source

When we established Google’s open source contribution workflow, we drew on established ASF practices. Both our Individual and Corporate Contributor License Agreements (CLAs), which external developers sign before contributing to a Google-owned open source project, are based on the ASF’s CLAs.

The Apache 2.0 license also remains Google’s preferred open source license for code. Alongside our traditional software releases, we also use Apache 2.0 for open hardware designs and open models like Gemma 4.

Co-engineering upstream and in the cloud

Across Google Cloud, our engineering teams contribute code upstream alongside Apache project communities and build managed services directly around those open standards:

  • Google Cloud Dataflow & Apache Beam: Drawing on Google’s internal Flume and Dataflow systems, Google donated the original Dataflow SDK and runners to the Apache Incubator in 2016 to help establish Apache Beam as a vendor-neutral open standard for unified batch and stream processing.
  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Airflow & Apache Airflow: Managed workflow orchestration built on Apache Airflow, helping engineering and data teams author, schedule, and monitor complex pipelines.
  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Spark & Apache Spark: Managed big data and analytics processing built on Apache Spark, running directly on Google’s cloud infrastructure.
  • Google BigQuery & Apache Iceberg: Support for the Apache Iceberg open table format to power large-scale analytics and machine learning datasets.

Setting the Platinum standard

Google has invested in the long-term health of open source foundations from the start. When the ASF first established its corporate sponsorship tiers, Google became the first Platinum Sponsor.

Early Google engineers and open source advocates worked closely with ASF maintainers to build the organizational and technical bridge between Google and the foundation. Today, Google maintains Platinum sponsorship through targeted funding and Google Cloud infrastructure contributions that support the ASF’s day-to-day technical operations.

That sponsorship pairs with everyday participation in ASF projects. Many Googlers serve upstream as ASF committers and Project Management Committee (PMC) members, maintaining code and stewarding projects alongside contributors across ASF communities. The ASF has also been a mentoring organization in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for over 20 years, working with us to welcome and mentor new open source contributors around the world.

The next 20 years: AI, open data, and beyond

Looking ahead to the next two decades, much of our shared work sits at the intersection of open data, cloud infrastructure, and artificial intelligence.

Projects like Apache Iceberg are widely used in modern analytics and machine learning workflows, while using the Apache 2.0 license for open models helps bring permissive licensing to a new generation of tools.

Thank you to the developers, committers, PMC members, and maintainers who keep the Apache Software Foundation strong. Here’s to 20 more years of building together.

title: A flat T-shirt photo has no back or sides. So we draw them before the video starts.
description:
This afternoon, recording a tutorial for a feature we'd just shipped, I pressed Remove old photos, watched two flat T-shirt photos leave the row, opened a video template, and there they were again.

The button had done exactly what the code told it to. It changed what was on screen and never touched the saved product.

That button is the last step of a feature we built today: turning flat product photos into four studio views before a video is made. Here's why the feature exists, how it works, and the two state bugs it shipped with.

TL;DR
A video model given one flat photo of a shirt has to invent the back and sides when the clip turns it. So RefVid now draws four studio views (front, back, left, right) from your flat-lay photos first. On day one, removed photos came back on reload, and a closing dialog briefly announced "Your 0 new views are ready."

A flat photo shows one side, and a turning video needs four

A lot of clothing gets photographed the cheap way: laid flat, shot from above. That's a fine photo for a product page.

It's a poor photo for a video. Ask a model for a slow turn or a floating spin, and halfway through it has to show a side it has never seen. It doesn't know what the back print looks like, how the sleeve falls, or whether there's a print at all. So it makes something up, and the made-up back is what the viewer sees for half the clip.

A prompt can say "white tee, logo on the back," but it can't say what the logo looks like. The model needs pictures of every side. Drawn views can't recover details your photos don't show; what they do is give the video model one consistent shirt from four angles instead of one flat one.

So the studio draws the views first

I build RefVid, a small tool where you upload a few photos of a product or a character once, then make short videos that keep it looking the same in every shot. Today we shipped a step that sits in front of the video.

When a product's main photo is in the composer, a small wand sits on its corner:

Clicking it opens a card. You tick up to three source photos (the first ticked one is treated as the front) and the views you want. The button spells out the total before you press it:

The whole flow, start to finish:

Step You do What happens
1 Add the flat photos to a product, front first They become the product's photos
2 Click the wand on the main photo The Draw product views card opens
3 Tick source photos and views The button shows the total, e.g. Draw 4 views · 120 credits (30 a view)
4 Press Draw About a minute later the views take the product's first places
5 Press Remove old photos The flat photos are deleted from the product
6 Pick a template (floating product, 360 turntable) The video starts from the four views

The views are ghost-mannequin shots: the shirt filled out as if someone were wearing it, nobody inside, floating over light grey. Underneath is an image model; RefVid writes its instructions. A view is charged once it's stored, and a view that fails gives its credits back.

The sides are drawn from the new front, not the flat photo

Four views drawn independently would be four independent guesses. The front might get a slightly boxier cut, the left side a slightly different white, and a turning video would stitch those into a shirt that changes shape mid-spin.

So the drawing runs in two rounds. First the front and back, straight from your flat photos. Then the left and right, with the front that was just drawn as their first picture. The sides never see a wrinkled shirt on a floor; they copy a studio shot that already has the light, the grey and the cut decided. The back doesn't need the front (your back photo already says what's there), so two rounds are enough, not three.

Here is the result on our test shirt: flat photos on the left, the four views on the right, and a close-up of the back print.

The delete button changed the screen and left the saved photos alone

Once the views exist, the flat photos get in the way. If they stay in the row, the video model gets both a crisp studio front and a wrinkled shirt on a wooden floor: two versions of one shirt to reconcile. So when the views land, RefVid asks: Happy with them? Remove the old photos from this product…

The first version of that button removed the flat photos from the clip being composed. The row looked right.

But the composer doesn't own a product's photos. Open a template link or reload, and it rebuilds the row from the photos stored on the product, which nobody had touched. The flats came straight back, and the next video would have started from all six pictures: the exact mix the button was meant to prevent.

The same-day fix makes the button mean what it says: it deletes the old photos from the product itself, the same as pressing × on the product's page. One guard went in with it: nothing is deleted unless every new view is already stored, so a half-finished drawing can't leave a product with no photos.

When a button's label is a verb, check which copy of the data the verb reaches. "Remove" in a composer and "remove" on a product look identical on screen.

The dialog counted views that were already gone

The second bug: for a fraction of a second, as that dialog faded out, its title read "Your 0 new views are ready."

The count came from the same state that told the dialog to be open. Closing cleared that state at once, but the fade-out was still running, so the dialog rendered its last frames with nothing in them. It now keeps the views it was showing until it has fully gone.

What it can't do

  • Very small text and busy all-over patterns come out softer. A big logo holds up; a care label or a dense print doesn't always. Check each view against your photos and redraw the one that's off (30 credits for one view).
  • Products that aren't worn float. A bottle, a shoe or a box is drawn upright and floating in the same grey studio. Fine for a turntable; not a lifestyle shot.
  • No back photo, no back print. Upload only the front and the back is drawn plain in the shirt's colour. It doesn't invent a print you didn't show it.
  • The example is synthetic. The tee in every screenshot is a RefVid logo tee, and its "flat-lay photos" were themselves made with an image model, so this walkthrough doesn't show how it does on a photographed garment.
  • Look at the left view above. It has thin dark marks along its edges that the source photos don't support; a shirt seen exactly side-on wouldn't show them.

Try it

The walkthrough, with a screenshot for every step, is on the tutorial page, and there's a 2:43 narrated video if you'd rather watch.

Which button in your app changes what's on screen but leaves the saved data untouched, and how did you find out?

Written with AI assistance from our own build notes and tickets.

title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.21766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

title: RiDEx: Reward-Informed Directional Exploration for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. While existing approaches improve sampling and policy optimization, they still rely largely on isotropic random perturbations in a high-dimensional latent space for exploration. Such variation often spends the perturbation budget on changes with little influence on the target reward, making exploration inefficient. We study where diffusion models should explore and how to learn from that exploration. We introduce Reward-Informed Directional Exploration (RiDEx), which concentrates local exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field. Conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients propose the subspace, and equal-and-opposite perturbations at the same generation state measure its terminal reward response. The reward difference supplies signed local supervision in the explored coordinates, while all generated images contribute to global DiffusionNFT learning. RiDEx thereby couples exploration-space selection with feedback about the changes it produces. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, RiDEx attains the highest peak rewards among the evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks. Its gradient-direction instantiation achieves 15x and 29x target-attainment speedups over DiffusionNFT on HPSv2 and PickScore, measured in H200 GPU hours. Controlled experiments confirm that reward-aligned directions elicit stronger responses at equal perturbation magnitude, and that applying their measured credit improves curve-average reward across all four tasks.

title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
description: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.22064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
description:
arXiv:2611.21993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

title: A Six-Step Test: Does Your SharePoint AI Assistant Quote Drafts or Old Versions?
description:
An AI assistant answers from the text it indexed. In SharePoint, one procedure rarely exists only once. There is the current major version, the older major versions in version history, a minor draft an editor is still working on, and copies in other places: a PDF export in a project folder, a mail attachment, a file on a Teams channel.

If a superseded passage is in the index, a retrieval step can select it, and the model will write a confident answer from it. The model has no idea which text is authoritative.

What SharePoint keeps by default

Microsoft's support documentation says that for Microsoft 365 customers "versioning is now turned on by default when you create a new library or list, and it will automatically save the last 500 versions of a document."

The version numbers carry meaning: "Major versions are identified by whole numbers, such as 5.0; minor versions are identified by decimal numbers, such as 5.1." A library owner can decide who sees drafts. With draft security applied, "those who have permission only to read the file cannot see the minor version."

At the organisation level, Microsoft Learn states that the default is "Manual version history limits with 500 major version count limit and no expiration." Lowering a library limit does not clean up at once: "up to 20 versions" are removed "for every new version created."

So a rule you replaced two years ago is, by default, still stored in the version history of the same file.

History is one API call away

Microsoft Graph returns the stored versions of a file, newest first, to an app with Files.Read.All or a higher application permission. An indexer can therefore read the stored versions of every file it can reach. Whether it does, and whether it labels what it found, is a design decision of the assistant, not a property of SharePoint.

The test

You can run this alone and free. Allow for the assistant's indexing delay.

  1. Create a test library. In Versioning settings choose major and minor versions, and set draft items to be seen only by users who can edit items.
  2. Upload a short procedure that states: "Procedures are reviewed every 24 months." Publish it as version 1.0.
  3. Edit the sentence to "every 12 months" and publish as version 2.0.
  4. Edit again to "every 6 months" and save without publishing, so it stays as minor draft 2.1.
  5. Give a test account read-only access to the library and wait for the next indexing run.
  6. As that account, ask: "How often are procedures reviewed?"

Reading the result

  • 6 months: this suggests the assistant indexes drafts beyond what SharePoint shows a reader.
  • 24 months: this suggests it reads history without labelling it.
  • 12 months, with the document and version named: the behaviour you want.

Then ask explicitly about previous versions. A good answer marks 1.0 as superseded instead of presenting it as current. Make sure no other copy of the test file exists, and repeat after a second indexing run.

The test applies to any assistant you evaluate, with or without Microsoft Copilot.

What the test does not cover

Copies outside the library, such as PDF exports or mail attachments, are not covered by versioning at all. A version label helps only where the file lives in one place.

The full chapter, with every Microsoft source, is here: Why AI Answers From SharePoint Cite Outdated Documents, and How to Stop It.

Drafted with AI assistance, checked against the cited Microsoft sources and approved by Kaspars Jurjāns.

title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.22278v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
description:
arXiv:2611.21851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

title: Which Supabase backups can you download?
description:
Supabase takes a daily backup of every Pro, Team and Enterprise project. Pro keeps 7 days, Team 14 and Enterprise up to 30. Free projects get none, and the docs recommend exporting with supabase db dump yourself.

Whether you can download one of those backups depends on its type. Projects on Postgres 15.8.1.079 and newer get physical backups: you can restore the project from them in the dashboard, but there is no file to download. Supabase's knowledge base says the same for projects with PITR, where the downloadable backup.gz is no longer generated.

For most current projects, a copy you hold yourself means taking a logical dump:

supabase db dump --db-url "$DB_URL" -f roles.sql --role-only
supabase db dump --db-url "$DB_URL" -f schema.sql
supabase db dump --db-url "$DB_URL" -f data.sql --use-copy --data-only

$DB_URL is the connection string under Connect in the dashboard. The direct host resolves to IPv6, so from a network without IPv6 use the Session pooler string. Dump as postgres: with a role that cannot bypass row-level security, pg_dump stops on the first table with a policy (pg_dump on Supabase: "query would be affected by row-level security policy").

A dump kept in your own bucket is also the only copy that outlives the project. When you delete a Supabase project, its backups are deleted with it.

Storage files are in none of these backups, the dashboard ones or the dump. The database holds the storage.objects rows, so a restore brings back the list of files without the files. Copy the buckets through the S3-compatible endpoint:

aws s3 sync s3://<bucket> ./storage/<bucket> \
  --endpoint-url https://<project-ref>.storage.supabase.co/storage/v1/s3 \
  --region <project-region>

What a Storage copy should record besides the files is in Do Supabase backups include Storage files?

Edge Function code is not in the database either. supabase functions download <name> gets the deployed source. The other parts of a project a dump misses are in What a Supabase database backup leaves out.

Before you rely on a dump, restore it into a throwaway Postgres and compare row counts per table with the source. psql carries on after a failed statement unless you run it with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1, so without that flag an exit code of 0 says little. The full set of checks is in How to test the database layer of a Supabase backup.

I keep a table of what each plan includes and what each option leaves out at https://revivedb.dev/supabase-backup. I build ReviveDB, a backup service for Supabase. Everything above works without it.
