title: Building a fast Telegram inline bot: what actually matters
description:
Every inline Telegram bot lives or dies by two things: relevance and latency. There is no onboarding, no menu, no conversation — a user types @yourbot query in any chat, a panel appears above the keyboard, and they tap a result.

I built an image search bot (@repinlybot) and this post is about the Telegram side of it: how inline mode works, which parameters actually change behaviour, and

Enabling inline mode

In BotFather:

/setinline
Choose a bot: @yourbot
Prompt: Search images…

The prompt is the placeholder users see. Keep it short and make it obvious what they can type.

The update flow 

User types "@yourbot cats"
        |
        v
Telegram --inline_query--> your backend
        <--answerInlineQuery-- your backend
        |
        v
Panel with results -> tap -> content sent to the chat

Two update types matter:

  • inline_query — the user typed or changed the query.
  • chosen_inline_result — the user picked a result. This is your conversion event.

chosen_inline_result is only delivered if you enable it in BotFather (/setinlinefeedback). It is off by default, and without it you have no idea whether anyone actually uses your results.

Answering a query

A minimal handler:

bot.on('inline_query', async (ctx) => {
  const query = ctx.inlineQuery.query.trim();
  const offset = Number(ctx.inlineQuery.offset || 0);

  if (query.length < 2) {
    return ctx.answerInlineQuery([], {
      switch_pm_text: 'Type a search query',
      switch_pm_parameter: 'empty',
      cache_time: 0,
    });
  }

  const page = await search(query, offset, 24);

  await ctx.answerInlineQuery(
    page.items.map(toResult),
    {
      cache_time: 300,
      is_personal: false,
      next_offset: page.hasMore ? String(offset + 24) : '',
    }
  );
});

Four parameters do most of the work.

cache_time

How long Telegram caches the answer for the same query. For image search, 300 seconds is reasonable. But for short or empty queries use 0 — otherwise a user who fixes a typo still sees the cached "nothing found" result.

is_personal

Set true if results depend on the user (history, saved items, language). Otherwise Telegram may serve one user's cached results to another. For a public image search, false is correct.

next_offset

Pagination. Telegram calls you again with this offset when the user scrolls. Return an empty string when there is nothing more. If you always return empty, users see one page and think that is all.

switch_pm_text / switch_pm_parameter

Renders a button that opens a private chat with the bot. Use it for empty states instead of leaving a blank panel.

Result types: URL vs cached file

For photos you have two options:

// 1. Let Telegram fetch and cache the file
{
  type: 'photo',
  id: String(item.id),
  photo_url: item.fullUrl,
  thumbnail_url: item.thumbUrl,
  photo_width: item.width,
  photo_height: item.height,
  title: item.title,
  description: item.author,
}

// 2. Send a file Telegram already has
{
  type: 'photo',
  id: String(item.id),
  photo_file_id: item.fileId,
  title: item.title,
}

The second one is effectively instant, but file_id is only valid for your bot. The pattern that works well:

  1. Return photo_url the first time.
  2. On chosen_inline_result, look up the item by result_id.
  3. Store the file_id that Telegram assigned to the file.
  4. On subsequent queries, return photo_file_id.

This avoids re-downloading the same image on every search.

The 500 ms budget

If the panel takes a second to appear, users describe the bot as slow or broken. Everything else is secondary.

What helped:

Small thumbnails. The panel is a grid. Serving 1000 px images there is the fastest way to make it feel sluggish. 200–300 px on the long edge is enough.

Query normalization and cache. " Scandinavian Bedroom " and "scandinavian bedroom" should hit the same cache entry.

Skip the origin for short queries. You cannot stop Telegram from sending an inline_query on every keystroke, but you can avoid hitting the backend: check the cache first, and skip search under 2 characters.

Paginate, do not dump. 20–30 results per page. More results means a bigger response and a slower panel.

Images that Telegram cannot fetch

A direct image URL is not always fetchable. Some CDNs require a Referer, block unknown user agents, or return HTML instead of an image. Telegram then silently drops the thumbnail.

The fix is an image proxy or CDN you control:

Telegram -> your proxy -> origin
              |
              +- cache: 300 px thumb + original on demand

This also gives you resizing, format normalization, and the ability to swap the origin later without touching the bot. Budget for it: it is the least glamorous part and the one that decides whether half your results render at all.

Metrics that matter

  • Queries — how many times the bot is invoked.
  • Answers — how many inline_query calls got a non-empty result.
  • Choices — how many chosen_inline_result events.
  • Choice rate = choices / answers.

If the choice rate is low, the problem is relevance. If the answer rate is low, the problem is coverage or normalization. Neither is fixed by adding features.

Also log queries with zero results. It is the cheapest product research you will ever do.

Lessons

  1. Latency is the feature. A relevant result that arrives in 2 seconds loses to a good result in 300 ms.
  2. Handle the empty state. A blank panel reads as "the bot is dead".
  3. Cache the file, not just the search. file_id reuse is a free speedup.
  4. Treat mobile networks as the default. Thumbnails, not originals.
  5. Enable chosen_inline_result early. Otherwise you are flying blind.

Try it

@repinlybot — inline image search for Telegram chats.

If you are building an inline bot, the two areas worth over-investing in are thumbnails and the query cache. Everything else is comparatively straightforward.

title: Easy Setup for Cloud Infrastructure Orchestration Across AWS and Azure (2026): What Each Tool Needs Before Your First Deploy
description:
The tools with the simplest installation and setup for cloud infrastructure orchestration across AWS and Azure are the single-binary IaC CLIs Terraform and OpenTofu, the Pulumi CLI (plus your language runtime), agentless Ansible, and hosted run platforms such as HCP Terraform, Spacelift, and env zero (formerly env0) that can manage state and runners for you. The setup they share is cloud identity: an AWS IAM role, an Azure service principal or managed identity, and OIDC federation so CI holds no long-lived keys, plus a remote state backend with locking when you run Terraform or OpenTofu yourself. Platforms such as Control Plane go a step further for workloads by deploying to AWS and Azure locations from a single definition without you building a cluster or connecting a cloud account in either cloud.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

The tools with the simplest setup for orchestration across AWS and Azure are Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Ansible, and hosted IaC platforms like HCP Terraform, Spacelift, and env zero.

  • Install is the easy part. Terraform and OpenTofu are single binaries, Pulumi adds a language runtime, and Ansible is a pip package. That step takes minutes.
  • Identity, CI, and state are the real setup. You configure an AWS IAM role, an Azure service principal or managed identity, and a CI runner or hosted execution environment, plus a remote state backend with locking when you run Terraform or OpenTofu yourself.
  • Use OIDC federation so CI holds no long-lived keys. AWS IAM identity providers and Azure federated identity credentials let GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and other runners assume cloud roles without stored secrets.
  • Provisioning tools and workload platforms solve different problems. IaC tools provision cloud resources, and workload platforms deploy and run applications. Teams running applications on both clouds typically use both.
  • Hosted runners remove state and runner setup. HCP Terraform, Spacelift, and env zero can manage state storage and execution for you, but you still configure cloud credentials.
  • Native tools mean two toolchains. CloudFormation covers AWS and Bicep covers Azure, with separate template languages and pipelines.
  • Where Control Plane fits. Control Plane deploys and runs workloads, including open-source databases from its Template Catalog, on AWS and Azure locations from one definition, with no cloud account to connect for its managed locations. Its Terraform and Pulumi providers let it work alongside the IaC you use for VPCs and account-level cloud resources.

Which tools provide an easy installation and setup process for cloud infrastructure orchestration across AWS and Azure?

Most tools in this space install in minutes, Crossplane excepted because it needs a Kubernetes cluster, and the real setup is everything each tool needs before the first change lands on both AWS and Azure.

Tool Install State or backend you set up AWS credentials Azure credentials Runs from What you operate afterward
Terraform (CLI) Single binary download or package manager Local state file by default; for teams, an S3 bucket with use_lockfile or Azure Blob with lease locking that you create and configure IAM role or IAM user; an IAM OIDC identity provider for CI Service principal or managed identity; a federated identity credential for CI Laptop, any CI runner State backend, CI runner, provider upgrades, module maintenance
OpenTofu Single binary download or package manager; a largely compatible fork of Terraform 1.5 Same as Terraform: S3 with use_lockfile or Azure Blob with lease locking Same as Terraform Same as Terraform Laptop, any CI runner Same as Terraform
Pulumi CLI install via package manager plus a language runtime (Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, or Java) Pulumi Cloud by default (sign up, then authenticate CI with an access token or Pulumi OIDC), or a self-managed S3, Azure Blob, or local backend IAM role or IAM user; OIDC for CI through Pulumi ESC or Pulumi Deployments, or your CI’s own OIDC trust Service principal or managed identity; a federated identity credential for CI Laptop, any CI runner, Pulumi Deployments Provider upgrades and program maintenance; with a self-managed backend, also the state backend and CI runner
Ansible pip install ansible, which bundles the amazon.aws and azure.azcollection collections; then install their Python SDK dependencies (boto3 and the azcollection requirements file) No state file; inventory files or dynamic inventory IAM role or IAM user; aws configure sso or environment variables Service principal; az login or environment variables Laptop, any CI runner (agentless, over SSH, WinRM, or cloud APIs) Inventory, playbooks, collection upgrades, CI runner
Crossplane A Kubernetes cluster first; then the Crossplane Helm chart and service-scoped providers such as provider-aws-s3 and provider-azure-storage, which pull in provider-family-aws and provider-family-azure The Kubernetes API server (etcd) holds desired state; you operate the cluster IAM role; a ProviderConfig using IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, or a Secret with access keys Service principal or managed identity; a ProviderConfig using a Secret or managed identity Kubernetes cluster (self-managed, EKS, or AKS) Kubernetes cluster, Crossplane and provider upgrades, ProviderConfig objects
HCP Terraform Sign up; optionally install the Terraform CLI locally Managed by HCP Terraform (no bucket to create) Dynamic provider credentials through an OIDC trust between HCP Terraform and AWS IAM Dynamic provider credentials through an OIDC trust between HCP Terraform and Microsoft Entra ID HCP Terraform hosted runners Provider upgrades, modules, workspace configuration
Spacelift Sign up; connect your VCS repository Managed by Spacelift (a per-stack option) or your own backend Cloud integration: an IAM role whose trust policy uses Spacelift’s external ID Cloud integration: create it in Spacelift, admin-consent its Entra application in your tenant, then assign that enterprise application an RBAC role Spacelift hosted runners or self-hosted workers Provider upgrades, stack configuration
env zero (formerly env0) Sign up; connect your VCS repository Managed by env zero when its remote backend is enabled, or your own backend OIDC: an IAM OIDC provider trusting env zero, then an IAM role OIDC: a federated identity credential on an Entra app registration, then an RBAC role assignment env zero hosted runners or self-hosted agents Provider upgrades, template maintenance
AWS CloudFormation + Azure Bicep AWS CLI for CloudFormation; Azure CLI for Bicep (the Azure CLI installs the Bicep CLI automatically on first use) CloudFormation stacks in AWS; Bicep deployments tracked by Azure Resource Manager IAM role or IAM user with CloudFormation permissions Service principal or managed identity with an RBAC role scoped to the target resource groups AWS Console or CLI and Azure portal or CLI, or two CI pipelines Two template languages, two pipelines, CloudFormation drift detection on AWS and what-if previews on Azure
Control Plane Control Plane’s cpln CLI or the Control Plane console Managed by the Control Plane API None to deploy to Control Plane-managed AWS locations; to let workloads call your own AWS services, connect an AWS cloud account (an IAM role Control Plane can assume) for Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) None to deploy to Control Plane-managed Azure locations; to let workloads call your own Azure services, connect an Azure cloud account (a service principal (the Azure SDK method), or Control Plane’s Azure Function App connector) for UCI Control Plane console, cpln CLI, Terraform or Pulumi provider, or the Control Plane MCP server, all through the Control Plane API Workload definitions and Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) configuration; Control Plane runs autoscaling, observability, and security

Every IaC tool needs cloud credentials configured in both AWS and Azure. The differentiator is whether you also manage state storage, a CI runner, and a Kubernetes cluster yourself. Hosted platforms absorb the state and runner burden, and workload platforms absorb the workload runtime burden.

What setup does every tool need on AWS and Azure?

Every IaC tool needs a deployment identity in each cloud, an OIDC trust for each CI system or hosted platform, and, when you run the tool yourself, a state backend.

Step AWS Azure Why it matters
Identity the tool runs as IAM role (preferred) or IAM user Service principal or user-assigned managed identity Every API call is authenticated as this identity; a role avoids long-lived access keys
Short-lived CI credentials via OIDC An IAM OIDC identity provider for your CI system (for example, GitHub Actions), then an IAM role whose trust policy pins the token audience to sts.amazonaws.com and the subject to a specific repository and branch or environment A federated identity credential on an Entra ID app registration or user-assigned managed identity, matched to your CI system’s issuer and subject No stored cloud keys in CI secrets; tokens are short-lived and scoped to each pipeline run
Least-privilege scope IAM policies split into a read-only plan role and an apply role scoped to the services your templates manage RBAC role assignment at the subscription or resource group scope; Contributor cannot create role assignments, so templates that manage RBAC need Role Based Access Control Administrator at a narrow scope Limits accidental or malicious changes to resources outside the deployment scope
Local developer login aws configure sso, then aws sso login az login (browser flow or device code) Developers authenticate without long-lived credentials on their laptops
State storage and locking S3 bucket with versioning, default encryption, blocked public access, and use_lockfile (Terraform has deprecated the DynamoDB lock table in favor of use_lockfile) Azure Storage account with a Blob container; lease-based locking is built in Prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state; versioning enables rollback
Audit trail AWS CloudTrail records management (control-plane) API calls by the deployment identity; create a trail to keep them past 90 days, and data events need extra configuration Azure Activity Log records control-plane operations on resources in the subscription; export it to keep entries past 90 days Links infrastructure changes to identities and timestamps

Identities and state backends are set up once per cloud account, and each new CI system or hosted platform adds its own OIDC trust and role. State files can contain secrets, so treat the backend as sensitive. Secrets management best practices covers storing and rotating the credentials this setup creates.

What does each kind of tool leave you to run after setup?

Setup is a one-time cost, and each kind of tool leaves different work with your team afterward.

Tool type Setup covers Still yours after setup
IaC CLIs (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi) Infrastructure definition, plan, and apply; providers for AWS and Azure resources State backend availability and backups, CI runner, provider and module upgrades, drift detection, secret injection, policy enforcement, cost controls
Hosted IaC run platforms (HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env zero) Everything the CLI covers plus managed state, locking, hosted runs, VCS integration, policy checks, and cost estimation Cloud credential rotation (unless you use OIDC), provider and module upgrades, workspace or stack configuration, approval workflows
Configuration management (Ansible) VM and service configuration, application deployment, ad hoc tasks across AWS and Azure targets Inventory accuracy, playbooks and collections, CI runner, SSH key or WinRM credentials; with no state file, drift shows only when playbooks rerun in check mode
Kubernetes-based reconcilers (Crossplane) Continuous reconciliation of declared infrastructure, drift correction, composition abstractions Kubernetes cluster operations (upgrades, scaling, etcd backups), Crossplane and provider upgrades, ProviderConfig management, debugging reconciliation failures
Cloud management platforms (HPE Morpheus Enterprise, CloudBolt) A portal for provisioning, governance, cost management, and self-service catalogs across clouds The platform or SaaS subscription, integrations, catalog curation, user and role management
Native tools (CloudFormation, Bicep) Deep integration with each cloud’s API and resource model Two toolchains, two template languages, two CI pipelines, no shared state or abstraction across clouds
Workload platforms (Control Plane) Workload deployment across AWS and Azure locations from one definition, autoscaling, observability, security, open-source databases from Control Plane’s Template Catalog, and UCI access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived keys in code Workload definitions and GVC configuration; IaC for cloud resources such as VPCs, provider database services, and account-level IAM

The top infrastructure as code tools guide covers each IaC engine in more depth.

How do you choose the easiest tool for your team?

The easiest tool depends on your team’s size, skills, and what you are deploying.

  • One engineer with a laptop who needs AWS and Azure resources: start with Terraform or OpenTofu. A single binary, a low-cost S3 or Azure Blob backend, and aws sso login and az login get you running with few moving parts.
  • A team using GitHub Actions that wants managed state and policy checks: HCP Terraform, Spacelift, or env zero remove the state backend and runner burden. All three support OIDC federation with AWS and Azure, so the pipeline stores no cloud keys.
  • A platform team already running Kubernetes : Crossplane declares AWS and Azure resources as Kubernetes custom resources and reconciles them continuously. The trade-off is operating the cluster and Crossplane controllers.
  • An ops team that configures VMs and middleware : Ansible is agentless, connects over SSH or WinRM, and has mature amazon.aws and azure.azcollection collections. Pair it with an IaC tool for provisioning.
  • A team that wants to deploy workloads to both clouds without building clusters : a workload platform deploys to multiple clouds from a single definition and needs no per-cloud cluster or credentials to start.

The best tools for deploying applications across AWS, GCP, and Azure compares deployment tools more broadly, and teams with many cloud accounts can standardize governance across dozens of cloud accounts.

How does Control Plane simplify setup across AWS and Azure?

Control Plane deploys and runs production workloads across clouds, and its setup centers on those workloads.

Setup starts with the Control Plane console or the cpln CLI, both of which work against the Control Plane API. You create a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) and add AWS and Azure locations to it. A workload deployed to that GVC runs in every location you selected, so one workload definition deploys to both clouds. You do not build or operate a Kubernetes cluster in either cloud for Control Plane-managed locations, and deploying there needs no AWS or Azure account connection.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. You connect a cloud account only when workloads need your own cloud services: an IAM role on AWS, a service account on GCP, or a service principal or Control Plane’s Function App connector on Azure. UCI then issues short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime.

The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API. Teams that already use Terraform or Pulumi can keep those tools for the cloud resources around their workloads and use the Control Plane providers for the workload layer. Control Plane can also export its configuration as Terraform.

Clusters you already run can join a GVC through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own servers can join through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), including on premises.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane runs workloads, including open-source databases such as PostgreSQL and Redis from Control Plane’s Template Catalog. Cloud resources such as VPCs, provider database services like Amazon RDS or Azure SQL, and account-level IAM policies stay in Terraform or Pulumi. Multi-cloud management platforms in 2026 compares platforms that manage workloads across clouds.

FAQ

Short answers on setting up infrastructure orchestration across AWS and Azure.

Which tools provide an easy installation and setup process for cloud infrastructure orchestration across AWS and Azure?

Terraform and OpenTofu install as single binaries, Pulumi as a CLI plus a language runtime, and Ansible via pip. Hosted run platforms such as HCP Terraform, Spacelift, and env zero simplify setup further by managing state and execution. All of them still need an AWS IAM role and an Azure service principal or managed identity, ideally with OIDC federation so CI holds no long-lived keys; self-run Terraform and OpenTofu also need a remote state backend with locking. Workload platforms such as Control Plane deploy applications to AWS and Azure from one definition, with no cluster to build and no cloud account needed for Control Plane-managed locations.

Is Terraform or Pulumi easier to set up for AWS and Azure?

Pulumi is slightly faster to start because Pulumi Cloud is its default state backend, while Terraform defaults to a local state file and needs a remote backend or HCP Terraform configured explicitly for team use. Cloud credential setup is nearly identical, and both support OIDC federation so CI stores no cloud keys. The choice usually comes down to HCL (Terraform) or general-purpose languages (Pulumi).

Do I need separate tools for AWS and Azure?

No, if you use a multi-cloud IaC engine like Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi, each of which has providers for both clouds. A single engine still uses separate AWS and Azure resource definitions, but keeps one language, workflow, and state format. With cloud-native tools you maintain CloudFormation templates for AWS and Bicep templates for Azure.

How do I connect GitHub Actions to AWS and Azure without storing keys?

Use OIDC federation in both clouds. In AWS, create an IAM OIDC identity provider with the issuer token.actions.githubusercontent.com and audience sts.amazonaws.com, then an IAM role whose trust policy restricts assumption to your repository and branch or environment. In Azure, create a federated identity credential on an Entra ID app registration or user-assigned managed identity with the GitHub Actions issuer and subject. Grant the workflow id-token: write permission, then use the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials and azure/login actions. No access keys or client secrets are stored in the repository.

Where should Terraform state live for a multi-cloud setup?

In one remote backend you can lock and secure, or one backend per cloud. A common pattern is an S3 bucket with use_lockfile for AWS-targeted configurations and an Azure Storage account with Blob lease locking for Azure-targeted configurations. The requirements are encryption at rest, versioning for rollback, access limited to the deployment identity, and locking to prevent concurrent applies.

Is OpenTofu a drop-in replacement for Terraform?

Mostly yes for configurations written for Terraform 1.5 and earlier, since OpenTofu forked from that release and keeps the same language, state format, and providers. You switch by replacing terraform with tofu in local and CI scripts. Configurations that use features added in later Terraform releases, or the cloud block for HCP Terraform, need review against OpenTofu’s migration guide. S3 with use_lockfile and Azure Blob lease locking work the same way.

Is Ansible good for multi-cloud orchestration?

Yes, for configuring VMs, deploying applications, and running ad hoc tasks across AWS and Azure with the amazon.aws and azure.azcollection collections. It is agentless and connects over SSH or WinRM. Ansible keeps no state file, so detecting drift means rerunning playbooks in check mode. Ansible is commonly paired with an IaC tool that provisions the infrastructure it configures.

How does Control Plane deploy to AWS and Azure?

Through a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) with AWS and Azure locations. A workload deployed to that GVC runs in every selected location from one workload definition. Control Plane-managed compute runs in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions, and deploying there needs no AWS or Azure account connection and no Kubernetes cluster to build or operate. Teams that use Terraform or Pulumi manage the GVC and workloads through the Control Plane providers.

What is the difference between provisioning infrastructure and deploying workloads?

Provisioning creates cloud resources like VPCs, subnets, databases, IAM roles, and storage accounts, which IaC tools like Terraform, OpenTofu, and Pulumi handle. Deploying workloads runs your application code on compute in one or more clouds, with autoscaling, observability, and networking included, which is the layer workload platforms like Control Plane cover. Multi-cloud teams commonly use both.

Talk to the Control Plane team to see workload deployment across AWS and Azure from one definition, or sign up free to try it yourself.

title: Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026: what to do
description:
Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at its v4 cutover on November 16, 2026. Existing trace-level evaluators keep producing scores until then and stop after it. The replacement is an observation-level evaluator, usually pointed at the root observation of each trace. If you rely on trace-level evaluators, upgrade your SDK, run the in-app upgrade, and compare old and new scores side by side before the 16th. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date.

We make Agnost AI, which judges whole conversations rather than single traces. For many teams the right answer is to stay on Langfuse and migrate, and this page says so. Every Langfuse claim below comes from Langfuse's own docs, checked on 2026-11-12. For background, see what online evals are.

What is changing

Langfuse v4 moves to an observations-first data model: "One denormalized observations table replaces read-time joins between traces and observations." Evaluators move with it.

  • What is deprecated. "Trace-level evaluators are built on the old trace-centric data model and are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4."
  • When. "Langfuse Cloud becomes v4-only on November 16, 2026." On that date, legacy v3 APIs, features, and ingestion are removed.
  • What happens to existing evaluators. On Cloud, they "keep running until the v4 cutover" and then "stop producing results." Historical results stay accessible.
  • What replaces them. "Observation-level evaluators are the recommended target for live production data." LLM-as-a-judge can now run on observations or on experiments.
  • Self-hosted. There is no forced cutover, and v3 gets security patches through January 2027. On self-hosted v4, trace-level evaluators stop once you run in events_only mode, so Langfuse says to migrate evaluators as the last step before switching.
  • Sessions. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions, as Langfuse does not inherently know when a session has concluded." Multi-span evaluation is planned on the new model but not described as available.

Option A: stay on Langfuse and move to observation-level evaluators

This is the right path if your trace-level evaluators judged one request: a single answer, a retrieval plus a response, one agent run. The steps from Langfuse's migration guide:

  1. Upgrade the SDK or ingestion path. Python SDK v4.7.0 or later, JS/TS SDK v5.4.0 or later, or direct OpenTelemetry ingestion with the header x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4.
  2. Keep trace input and output for now. After the upgrade, trace input and output are no longer written automatically. If your old evaluators read them, keep calling set_current_trace_io() (Python) or setActiveTraceIO() (JS/TS) until the new evaluators are validated. These methods are removed in Python SDK v5 and JS/TS SDK v6.
  3. Run the upgrade in Langfuse. Open Evaluation in the app. On Cloud, the Halo assistant handles minor changes. Self-hosted deployments use the coding-assistant path.
  4. Check the target and variable mapping. If every variable came from the trace, target the observation that holds the same values, often the root. If values are split across observations, write them to the root or to a dedicated evaluation observation, or pass trace fields down with propagate_attributes(). Remapped evaluators default to the filter isRootObservation = true.
  5. Check the score count. A trace-level evaluator wrote one score per trace. An observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, so a trace with three matches gets three scores. Narrow the filter to one observation if dashboards or alerts assume one score per trace.
  6. Run old and new side by side, then switch. Compare scores on the same traffic and deactivate the trace-level evaluator when they agree. To revert, deactivate the new evaluator and reactivate the old one.

Do this before November 16. After the cutover there is no old evaluator left to compare against, and any alert built on those scores goes quiet.

If your evaluator judged a conversation. Some teams used trace-level evaluators to judge multi-turn behavior, because the trace carried the chat history. Langfuse's guide to evaluating sessions suggests writing the complete history onto the root observation or the LLM call that receives it, then evaluating that. To avoid judging every turn, tag the final trace (for example conversation_end) and filter on the tag. This works, but your application has to decide when a conversation has ended. The alternative is to compute session scores in your own job and send them with only a sessionId.

Option B: evaluate whole conversations instead

Some failures only exist across turns: the user repeats a request three times, the agent skips an identity check two turns before a refund, or it claims a task is done when no tool call succeeded. One observation cannot show these. Conversation-level vs trace-level online evals lists which failures need which unit.

Agnost AI is built for this unit. You write rules in plain English, and an LLM judges each conversation against them after it has been idle for 15 minutes, in batches rather than in real time. What it does and does not do:

  • Verdicts are pass or fail per assistant message. There are no numeric scores, and the judge's reasoning is not stored.
  • Judging reads the conversation. Tool and sub-agent spans are excluded from the judge's input.
  • No sampling. Every conversation is judged, up to your plan's event limit (Free 1,000, Starter 10,000, Pro 1,000,000 events a month).
  • Backfill. Adding or editing a rule scores your last 1,000 conversations, so you see examples before trusting the rate.
  • Alerts go to Slack or email. There are no webhooks and no CI integration.
  • A fired alert can start Auto Improve, which opens a pull request for your team to review.

Agnost AI accepts OpenTelemetry, so it can read the same spans you send to Langfuse. Keep Langfuse for tracing, prompts, datasets, and observation-level evaluators, and add Agnost AI as a second span processor for conversation rules. Agnost AI vs Langfuse shows the setup, and Agnost AI vs Langfuse vs Arize compares how each catches quality failures.

Option C: other tools with conversation-level online evals

If you are moving off Langfuse anyway, these tools document live evaluation above a single span. Each summary comes from the vendor's docs, checked on 2026-11-12.

  • LangSmith. Multi-turn online evaluators run "once per completed thread, not once per trace." A thread counts as complete after an idle period: 10 minutes by default, 2 minutes minimum. The judge can see all messages or the full trajectory with tool calls. Sampling and filters are supported. Limits: traces must carry a messages list, only runs from the past 7 days count, at most 500 threads per execution, and 10 multi-turn evaluators per workspace.
  • Braintrust. Online scoring runs at span, trace, or group scope. Trace scope waits for an idle timeout (30 seconds by default), and its LLM judges can reference a {{thread}} variable. Group scope scores related traces together, up to 64 traces over a 24-hour interval by default.
  • Arize AX. Session-scoped evaluation tasks can run continuously, with a one-time backfill and sampling per session. Results are written to the root span of the session's first trace. Open-source Phoenix runs session evaluation as code: pull spans, group by session, run judges, and log session annotations yourself.
  • Opik. Online evaluation rules run at trace, thread, or span scope. Thread rules wait for a 15-minute cooldown by default and include templates for task completion, coherence, and user frustration. Rules only score data logged after you create them, unless you run them manually on older items. Opik is open source and its Pro Cloud plan is $19 a month.

Which to choose

If your situation is… Choose
Your evaluators judge one request or one agent run Stay on Langfuse; migrate to observation-level evaluators
You self-host Langfuse and are not on events_only yet Stay on Langfuse; migrate before switching modes
You need multi-turn judging and can mark the last turn yourself Stay on Langfuse; put the history on the root observation and filter on a tag
You want plain-language rules over every whole conversation, with alerts and PRs, next to Langfuse Agnost AI alongside Langfuse
You are on LangChain or LangGraph and want thread-level judges LangSmith
You want open-source thread rules with a frustration template Opik
You already use Arize and want session-scoped tasks Arize AX

For a broader comparison, see Langfuse alternatives for user and conversation analytics and the best online evaluation tools for AI agents.

Frequently asked questions

Are Langfuse trace-level evaluators deprecated?

Yes. Langfuse's docs say trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4. On Langfuse Cloud they keep running until the v4 cutover on November 16, 2026, and stop producing results after it. Self-hosted deployments have no forced date; there, trace-level evaluators stop once you switch Langfuse v4 to events_only mode.

What replaces trace-level evaluators in Langfuse?

Observation-level evaluators. You point the evaluator at one observation, usually the root observation that already holds the trace's input and output, and map its variables from that observation. Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps, and the Evaluation page in the app offers an upgrade path. Note that an observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, not one per trace.

Will my existing Langfuse evaluators keep running after November 16?

Not on Langfuse Cloud. Existing trace-level evaluators keep running until the cutover, then stop producing results. Historical scores stay accessible. You can run old and new evaluators side by side before the date and deactivate the trace-level one once the new one matches.

Can Langfuse evaluate a whole conversation or session?

Not with a built-in live evaluator. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators cannot be applied directly to sessions because it does not know when a session has ended. Its suggested workarounds are to write the full conversation history onto one observation and evaluate that, often only on a tagged final turn, or to add session scores yourself through the SDK, API, or annotation queues.

What is the best Langfuse alternative for evals?

For most teams, staying on Langfuse and moving to observation-level evaluators is the cheapest path. If you need live evaluation of whole multi-turn conversations, LangSmith has multi-turn online evaluators, Opik and Arize AX have thread- or session-scoped online rules, and Agnost AI judges every conversation against plain-language rules. Agnost AI can run next to Langfuse on the same OpenTelemetry data, so you do not have to replace it.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: Autoscaling Adds Waiters, Not Ovens. Here's What Actually Breaks at 10x Load
description:
A signed enterprise deal or a viral campaign puts the same pressure on a platform: 10x the normal traffic, arriving faster than anyone budgeted for. The instinct is to trust autoscaling to absorb it, and autoscaling does its job exactly as designed. The problem is what it was designed to scale. It adds more stateless application instances, which were already the most elastic part of the system, and does nothing for the database connection pool, the cache origin, or the shared job queue underneath them. Manoj Yerrasani, VP of Global Platform Engineering at NBCUniversal, put it plainly after operating at Super Bowl scale: "auto-scaling is a lie." More app servers just means more processes competing for the same fixed set of database connections, and that competition is where the outage actually starts.

Four questions that predict where a platform breaks first

The Load Shape Audit is four diagnostic questions, not a tool you install:

  • Request shape: how many backend calls does a single user action trigger? A page load that fans out to six API endpoints multiplies your real request volume by six before traffic even grows.
  • Data shape: how many different access patterns are competing on one database? Write-heavy configuration writes and read-heavy analytics queries fighting over the same connection pool degrade both.
  • Tenant shape: does one large tenant's workload saturate a shared resource, connection pool, job queue, cache, search index, and degrade service for every smaller tenant on the same infrastructure?
  • Failure shape: when something has to give, is there a predetermined priority order, or does the system degrade randomly?

Signal 3 is the one most platforms discover the hard way. Neon's production analysis and the AWS whitepaper on SaaS tenant isolation both document the same pattern: one noisy tenant degrading everyone sharing its infrastructure.

The pattern that fixes the most common request-shape failure

When a cache misses under load, the naive implementation lets every concurrent request for that same uncached key hit the database independently, ten simultaneous cache misses become ten identical queries. The fix is request collapse, also called singleflight: the first request triggers the real query, and every other request for the same key waits on that one result instead of firing its own.

const inFlight = new Map();

async function getWithSingleflight(key, fetchFn) {
  if (inFlight.has(key)) {
    return inFlight.get(key); // piggyback on the request already running
  }
  const promise = fetchFn()
    .finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
  inFlight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}

That's a handful of lines, and it turns a thundering herd of duplicate queries into one query with N waiters. It's also exactly the kind of fix that autoscaling can't provide, because the problem was never a shortage of application instances.

Isolating the noisy neighbor, in order of cost

Tenant-shape problems get fixed in escalating stages, and jumping straight to the most expensive one wastes engineering time you don't have during an incident:

  • Row-level isolation at the database layer. PostgreSQL row-level security enforces tenant boundaries in the database itself, not in application code that a future developer might bypass.
  • Per-tenant connection pools and job queue lanes. A large tenant gets its own lane instead of competing with everyone else for the same shared pool.
  • Full tenant silo. Dedicated infrastructure per tenant, the most expensive option, reserved for the tenants whose load actually justifies it.

What this looked like on a real platform

Brocoders rebuilt Adact's platform on Node.js and Nest.js with a split database layer, PostgreSQL for write-heavy campaign configuration, MongoDB for read-heavy analytics, so the two access patterns stopped fighting over the same connection pool. Server-side rendering behind CloudFront collapsed what had been multiple API calls per page load into a single request. That architecture held through a campaign that generated 18,000 leads in 10 days and sustained over 2 million requests at peak across more than 3 million visitors in six months, without the app-server layer being the thing that mattered most. We run full-stack delivery with our own DevOps, no outsourced infra, so the team building the feature is the same team that has to answer when a connection pool saturates at 2am.

Pre-launch checklist before you trust autoscaling with a 10x event

  • Run expected load in staging at least twice before launch, not once, and not in production.
  • Freeze configuration changes the week of launch. Ben Maurer's 2015 analysis of Facebook outages found human error during change windows was a leading cause, not raw traffic.
  • Map every shared resource: connection pools, caches, job queues, search indexes, and who else is competing for each one.
  • Write explicit traffic-tier priorities before you need them: what's protected (checkout, auth), what degrades gracefully (recommendations), what gets dropped with a message.
  • Set numeric thresholds for architectural work, not vibes: "at X concurrent users the read path splits, at Y tenants we move to per-tenant pools."
  • Don't build the full silo model preemptively. Every extra service boundary adds deployment surface and on-call pages before the load that justifies it arrives.

If you're staring down a 10x traffic event and want a second technical opinion on which layer actually breaks first, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.

title: 5 Database Performance Checks for Mining IT Teams
description:
Our Mining database performance checklist
Enterprise applications, asset management platforms and reporting tools depend on databases that remain available and responsive. A slow application may be caused by inefficient queries, storage contention, missing maintenance or infrastructure capacity rather than an issue in the application itself.
For mining businesses operating across sites and offices, the following checks help IT teams prioritise database reliability.
1. Check query and workload performance
Review slow-running queries, execution plans, locking, wait events and changes in peak usage. Establish a performance baseline for each critical workload and identify whether recent changes have increased response times.
Ask: Can we identify the queries responsible for the largest performance impact?
2. Review capacity and resource contention
Assess CPU, memory, storage latency, disk utilisation and database growth. Check that capacity forecasts reflect seasonal processing, reporting and planned application changes. Cloud database sizing should be reviewed alongside cost.
Ask: Do we know when our critical environments will reach capacity thresholds?
3. Verify backup and restore capability
Successful backup jobs do not prove that recovery will meet business requirements. Test restores, confirm recovery point and recovery time objectives, and verify dependencies such as encryption keys, configuration and connectivity.
Ask: When was the last successful recovery test, and what did it prove?
4. Review patching, versions and privileged access
Identify unsupported database versions, delayed security patches, unnecessary privileges and configuration drift. Plan upgrades around application compatibility, maintenance windows and rollback procedures.
Ask: Which databases present the greatest security or support risk today?
5. Confirm proactive monitoring and ownership
Ensure alert thresholds reflect business-critical services, not just server availability. Document who receives alerts, who investigates them and how incidents escalate outside business hours.
Ask: Would our team detect degradation before users report it?
What to do next
Record each check as Pass, Needs attention or Not assessed. Prioritise systems by business criticality and assign an owner and target date to each finding. title: Redict Is Deprecated: How to Migrate to Valkey When It Rejects Your dump.rdb
description:
Redict is deprecated. The announcement went up on November 17, 2026, and it says Redict 7.3.6 is the final release. That release from October 2025 patched CVE-2025-49844 and three other CVEs. Nobody will patch the next one.

If you run Redict, or you package it for a distro, you have to move. The announcement makes migrating to Valkey sound like a config rename. For at least one person in the Lobsters thread it wasn't: Valkey refused the existing dump.rdb, and the reason is a single integer in a header file. I'll go through why that happens and the one config line that should get you past it. Then come three migration paths (RDB copy, replication, Docker Compose) and what I'd do if you'd rather go back to Redis 8.

Why the Redict project gave up

Redict forked Redis OSS 7.2.4 in March 2024 under LGPL-3.0. The bet was that a copyleft fork would protect the community from the next licence rug-pull. The announcement admits the bet lost on two fronts. Valkey got the momentum, and Redis went back to an OSI licence when Redis 8 added AGPLv3 next to RSALv2 and SSPLv1 in May 2025.

The author, Drew DeVault, recommends Valkey and specifically advises against going back to Redis. The argument is that Redis still requires a contributor licence agreement, and a CLA is what makes a relicence possible in the first place. One commenter in the Lobsters thread credited antirez for the return to open source and hoped Redis had learned from its mistakes, but admitted to being pessimistic. The company already relicensed once, in March 2024, and it still holds a CLA that lets it do it again. For me that's reason enough to stay off Redis.

Valkey vs Redis 8 vs staying on Redict

Redict 7.3.6 Valkey 9.1 Redis 8.x
Licence LGPL-3.0 BSD-3-Clause AGPLv3 / RSALv2 / SSPLv1 (your pick)
Governance Independent fork, now deprecated Linux Foundation Redis Ltd., CLA required
Security fixes None after 7.3.6 3 years per minor (policy) Ongoing (8.4.2 was a security release)
Managed hosting Effectively none ElastiCache, Memorystore, Aiven, DigitalOcean Redis Cloud
Loads a Redict RDB Yes With rdb-version-check relaxed (see below) Not a supported path

The managed-hosting row decides it for a lot of teams. When AWS launched ElastiCache for Valkey it priced it 33% below the other engines on serverless and 20% below on node-based clusters, and existing reserved-node discounts carry over. Valkey 9.1 shipped in May 2026 with automatic TLS certificate reloading and database-level ACLs.

There's one case where I'd pick Redis 8: if you want the bundled query engine, JSON and time series modules, and AGPL is fine for your use.

Why a plain container swap to Valkey fails: RDB version 12

The announcement's container advice is to "pull the valkey container instead". In the Lobsters thread, legoktm reports that this failed for them because "the RDB formats were incompatible". Because they only used Redict as a cache, they deleted the dump and moved on.

The cause is in the headers. Redict's src/rdb.h has carried #define RDB_VERSION 12 since the 7.3.0 tag. Valkey's src/rdb.h says:

RDB 11 is the last open-source Redis RDB version, used by Valkey 7.x and 8.x.
RDB 12-79 are reserved for Redis non-compatible RDB formats

Valkey 9 numbers its own format 80 and up. When a stock Valkey sees version 12, it treats the file as foreign and refuses it. Valkey's own migration guide only promises compatibility with Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier, and a Redict dump isn't one of those.

The escape hatch is a config flag. Valkey 8.1 added rdb-version-check (#1604), and #2543, merged for 9.0, extended relaxed mode to foreign formats. In relaxed mode Valkey loads only the types and opcodes it understands and errors out on anything else. Redict 7.3.0's rdb.h defines the same object types (0 through 21) and opcodes that Valkey 9.0 reads, including the cluster-only SLOT_INFO opcode, so a Redict dump shouldn't contain anything relaxed mode has to reject. Per the shipped valkey.conf, the setting "also applies to replication and the RESTORE command", so it covers all three migration paths below. The default is strict.

I haven't seen anyone publicly confirm a full Redict-to-Valkey load in relaxed mode yet, so do it on a copy first.

Step 0: find out what you actually have 

redict-cli INFO server | grep -E 'redict_version|redis_version'
redict-cli INFO keyspace
redict-cli CONFIG GET dir
redict-cli CONFIG GET dbfilename
redict-cli CONFIG GET appendonly

Write down the key counts from INFO keyspace, because you'll compare them at the end. If the instance is a pure cache and you can survive a cold start, skip all of this: stop Redict, start Valkey on an empty data dir, and you're done. That's what legoktm did.

Path 1: RDB copy (short downtime, simplest)

Stop the writers first, then take a fresh snapshot:

redict-cli SAVE
cp /var/lib/redict/dump.rdb /var/backups/redict-dump.rdb

Move the config over, as the announcement suggests (/etc/redict.conf to /etc/valkey.conf), and add the line from the section above. Stop Redict, then copy the dump into Valkey's data dir (paths vary by distro, so check what CONFIG GET dir told you):

cp /var/lib/redict/dump.rdb /var/lib/valkey/dump.rdb
chown valkey:valkey /var/lib/valkey/dump.rdb

The config:

# valkey.conf
dir /var/lib/valkey
dbfilename dump.rdb
rdb-version-check relaxed
appendonly no

Leave appendonly no for the first start. The Valkey migration doc warns that with AOF enabled, the copied RDB won't be imported. Start Valkey and check:

valkey-cli INFO keyspace
valkey-cli INFO server | grep -E 'server_name|valkey_version'

Valkey still reports redis_version:7.2.4 for client compatibility, so check valkey_version to see what's really running. When the key counts match, run valkey-cli BGSAVE so the data is rewritten in Valkey's own format. If you use AOF, turn it on at runtime with valkey-cli CONFIG SET appendonly yes, which builds the AOF from the data already in memory. Flipping it to yes in the file and restarting can bring Valkey up from an empty AOF instead of your RDB. Run valkey-cli CONFIG REWRITE so appendonly yes is saved to valkey.conf, then edit the file to set rdb-version-check back to strict. That takes effect on the next restart.

Path 2: replication cutover (near-zero downtime)

Run Valkey next to Redict, with rdb-version-check relaxed in its config (plus masterauth if Redict has a password), and point it at Redict:

valkey-cli REPLICAOF redict-host 6379
valkey-cli INFO replication   # wait for master_link_status:up

Once the replica has caught up, pause writes in the app, check that master_repl_offset matches on both sides, and promote:

valkey-cli REPLICAOF NO ONE

Point the clients at Valkey and resume. The write pause only has to cover the offset check and the client switch. The Valkey docs warn that writes which reach the old primary during the switch can be lost, so don't skip the pause.

Path 3: the Docker Compose swap 

services:
  cache:
    # was: registry.redict.io/redict:7.3.6
    image: valkey/valkey:9.1
    command: ["valkey-server", "/usr/local/etc/valkey/valkey.conf"]
    volumes:
      - ./valkey.conf:/usr/local/etc/valkey/valkey.conf:ro
      - cache-data:/data
volumes:
  cache-data:

Keep the same named volume and the dump comes along. Make sure dir in the config matches the mount path and that valkey.conf has rdb-version-check relaxed for the first boot. Run docker compose exec cache valkey-cli INFO keyspace before you let traffic back in. If you don't add the flag, you get exactly what legoktm hit.

Going back to Redis 8 instead

Redis 8.2's rdb.h also says RDB_VERSION 12. That looks convenient, but the two version 12s were defined independently, and Redict's own compatibility page says switching back from Redict to Redis is not supported. I wouldn't trust a raw file copy here. Use a client-level copy (RIOT or RedisShake, both listed in Valkey's migration doc) against a staging Redis 8 first, then compare key counts. You'll also need to rename redict-cli to redis-cli in your scripts and swap the systemd units back.

The checklist

  • INFO keyspace counts recorded before you start
  • Backup copy of dump.rdb kept outside the data dir
  • rdb-version-check relaxed for the first load only, then back to strict
  • AOF off on first boot, then enabled with CONFIG SET appendonly yes once the data is loaded
  • Scripts updated for valkey-cli (although redis-cli still works against Valkey)
  • Distro packagers: ship a redict to valkey transition package so people get the upgrade instead of quietly running an unpatched server

I'm moving everything to Valkey, and the CLA is the reason I'm not considering Redis. If you think that's the wrong call, I'd like to hear the argument. What are you running in production now: Valkey, Redis 8, or something else like DragonflyDB or KeyDB? And did your Redict data survive the move?

Sources

  • Redict is deprecated and the Lobsters discussion
  • Redict 7.3.6 release notes
  • Redict compatibility with Redis
  • Redict rdb.h at 7.3.0, Valkey rdb.h, Redis 8.2 rdb.h
  • Valkey migration guide and valkey.conf (9.0)
  • Valkey PR #2543: relaxed RDB check for foreign formats
  • Valkey release and support policy
  • Valkey 9.1 release post
  • Redis: now available under AGPLv3 and antirez: Redis is open source again
  • Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey announcement

title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.
