title: Why I Rewrote type-tune from TypeScript to Rust 🦀
description:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript and gambas, not crabs! 🦐

And yet, somehow, I ended up building a tool in Rust. 🙀🦀

Recently, I released a new open-source CLI tool called type-tune.

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…
View on GitHub

type-tune finds shared TypeScript types and helps move them to a better place without manually updating imports, dependencies, and barrel exports.

But why is a TypeScript tool created by a TypeScript lover written in Rust? 🤔

🐈 It All Started with TypeScript

Naturally, the original implementation of type-tune was written in TypeScript.

It was already complete by September, with nearly 20,000 lines of TypeScript, including tests, comments, and blank lines.

Around that time, I happened to watch this video by DHH.

I didn't agree with everything, but I particularly liked the idea of taking advantage of this era to pursue things that genuinely excite us.

Of course, outside of personal projects, I don't think we can simply hand everything over to AI. Someone still needs to understand and maintain the software.

But while watching the video, a simple thought crossed my mind.

If it's possible to go from Rails to Rust, why not TypeScript to Rust? 🦀

🦀 From TypeScript to Rust

I already had a working implementation, design documents, tests, and well-defined TypeScript types.

For example, translating a data model like this:

type CandidateKind = "typeAlias" | "interface";

type Candidate = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  kind: CandidateKind;
  referrers: string[];
};

Into something like this:

enum CandidateKind {
    TypeAlias,
    Interface,
}

struct Candidate {
    id: String,
    name: String,
    kind: CandidateKind,
    referrers: Vec<String>,
}

Of course, migrating the entire application involved much more than translating type definitions.

But having an existing design and implementation made it much easier.

With the help of AI, I completed the migration in less than a month while working on it as a side project.

The results were satisfying 😻

  • Better execution performance.
  • Native binary distribution.
  • No Rust development environment required for npm users.

You can still install type-tune like any other familiar TypeScript development tool.

pnpm add -D type-tune

The npm launcher requires Node.js 22+, but the core implementation runs as a native binary.

So far, so good!

Except for one little problem. 😿

🙀 type-tune Got Faster. Its Developer Got Slower.

I barely knew Rust. 😹

I'm comfortable reviewing AI-generated TypeScript code, but with Rust, I'm still learning the fundamentals.

For example, consider ownership and borrowing.

In TypeScript, this is perfectly fine:

function printName(name: string) {
  console.log(name);
}

const name = "OrderSummary";

printName(name);
console.log(name); // OK

However, a similar implementation in Rust doesn't compile.

fn print_name(name: String) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(name);
    println!("{}", name); // Error: value borrowed after move
}

The ownership of name is transferred to print_name.

One way to fix this is to borrow the value instead.

fn print_name(name: &str) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(&name);
    println!("{}", name); // OK
}

Another option is to clone the value.

print_name(name.clone());
println!("{}", name); // OK

Both solutions compile, but cloning unnecessarily can introduce additional allocations.

So when AI generates a .clone(), I need to understand whether it's actually necessary or whether borrowing would be more appropriate.

The same applies to visibility boundaries.

For example, making an internal helper public might solve an accessibility issue:

pub fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

But if the function is only used within the same crate, exposing it publicly may be unnecessary.

pub(crate) fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

And if it's only used within its own module, it can remain private.

fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

The compiler accepts all three declarations, but each represents a different architectural decision.

I'm also still learning when macros are appropriate and when ordinary functions are sufficient.

AI can generate code that compiles, but I still need to understand whether its design choices are appropriate.

In TypeScript, I can make these decisions relatively quickly. In Rust, I often need to stop and learn something before continuing my review.

AI can generate Rust code much faster than I can understand it.

I wanted to accelerate the development of my side project, but I introduced a new bottleneck.

Myself.

What a wonderful optimization! 😹

🎨 Creating Without Learning

Of course, I could just vibe code.

I could keep pressing Enter whenever AI asks for approval and probably release features faster.

But for me, creating something without learning anything is just another task.

And I believe that if I keep doing nothing but those tasks, I'll gradually lose my ability to create.

I enjoy using AI to learn unfamiliar concepts and explore new approaches.

But I don't want to spend my time simply producing things without understanding them.

I don't want to become a very expensive Enter key. 😹

Do I regret choosing Rust?

Not at all!

It was a valuable experience, and I'm grateful that we live in a time when we can challenge ourselves like this so easily.

Now, let's talk about what I actually built!

🛠️ The Design Behind type-tune

One architectural decision remained unchanged throughout the migration.

Scan / Plan / Apply

Consider a typical TypeScript project.

src/
├── features/
│   ├── orders/
│   │   └── order-page.ts
│   ├── dashboard/
│   │   └── dashboard.ts
│   └── reports/
│       └── reports.ts

Initially, a type belongs to the orders feature.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

But as the application grows, other features start importing it.

// features/dashboard/dashboard.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function calculateRevenue(orders: OrderSummary[]) {
  return orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.total, 0);
}

// features/reports/reports.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function createReport(order: OrderSummary) {
  return `${order.id}: ${order.total}`;
}

The type is still useful, but its original location may no longer be appropriate.

Tools like Knip help us remove unused code.

type-tune tackles a different problem: reorganizing types that are still in use.

🔍 1. Scan 

pnpm exec type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

type-tune analyzes exported type aliases, interfaces, references, and relevant dependencies to identify potential extraction candidates.

No source code is modified.

📋 2. Plan

Finding a type that can be moved doesn't necessarily mean it should be moved.

That's why type-tune generates a reviewable plan.

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --out .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

It generates two files:

  • plan.json — Candidate metadata and validation information.
  • plan.md — A human-readable, editable plan.

Every candidate is ignored by default.

Here's a simplified example of plan.md:

- [ignore] <candidate-id> `OrderSummary`
  - kind: `typeAlias`
  - from: `src/features/orders/order-page.ts`
  - to: `src/features/orders/types/order.ts`

You can approve the candidate and customize its destination.

- [ignore] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
+ [apply] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
    - kind: typeAlias
    - from: src/features/orders/order-page.ts
-   - to: src/features/orders/types/order.ts
+   - to: src/domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

Perhaps it belongs in a shared directory, a domain-specific module, or exactly where it is now.

That's an architectural decision.

You decide what moves and where.

🚚 3. Apply

Preview the selected changes:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md \
  --dry-run

Then apply them:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

The resulting project structure:

src/
├── domains/
│   └── orders/
│       └── types/
│           └── order-summary.ts  ← Moved!
└── features/
    ├── orders/
    │   └── order-page.ts
    ├── dashboard/
    │   └── dashboard.ts
    └── reports/
        └── reports.ts

The type now lives in its new home.

// domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

Supported imports are updated automatically.

- import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";
+ import type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

And the original module retains a compatibility re-export.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

type-tune also validates the rewrite using the TypeScript compiler and rolls back changes if normal validation fails.

You should still review the resulting diff and run your project-specific tests and builds.

🧩 Automate the Work, Not the Decisions

Why separate Scan, Plan, and Apply?

Because discovering opportunities, making architectural decisions, and executing changes are different responsibilities.

type-tune even supports optional AI-assisted review:

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --ai-review \
  --ai-dry-run

AI can provide additional review notes, but it doesn't control the source code rewrite. The command above previews the AI review request without contacting a provider.

Interestingly, this is also how I want to work with AI in my own development.

Automate the tedious work without taking architectural decisions away from developers.

That's the philosophy behind type-tune.

💚 Give Your TypeScript Types a Better Home!

You can start by simply scanning your project.

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

No need to move anything yet. Just see what you find! 😸

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…


View on GitHub


type-tune-docs.vercel.app

Feedback, ideas, issues, and contributions are always welcome!

And if you're a Rust developer, please teach this poor TypeScript cat how to become a competent crab. 😹🦀

Small. Simple. Useful. Built Together!

Thank you for reading! 🙌💚

title: Unsupervised Multi-modal Medical Image Registration via Invertible Translation
description:
arXiv:2611.22152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In medical imaging, the alignment of multi-modal images plays a critical role in providing comprehensive information for image-guided therapies. Despite its importance, multi-modal image registration poses significant challenges due to the complex and often unknown spatial relationships between different image modalities. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised translation-based multi-modal registration method, termed Invertible Neural Network-based Registration (INNReg). INNReg consists of an image-to-image translation network that converts multi-modal images into mono-modal counterparts and a registration network that uses the translated mono-modal images to align the multi-modal images. Specifically, to ensure the preservation of geometric consistency after image translation, we introduce an Invertible Neural Network (INN) that leverages a dynamic depthwise convolution-based local attention mechanism. Additionally, we design a novel barrier loss function based on Normalized Mutual Information to impose constraints on the registration network, which enhances the registration accuracy. The superior performance of INNReg is demonstrated through experiments on two public multi-modal medical image datasets, including MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT pairs. The code is available at https://github.com/MeggieGuo/INNReg

title: Animated candlestick chart in React for a shadcn dashboard
description:
I needed a candlestick card for a shadcn dashboard. Here is what I ended up doing, and when a real trading library is the better call.

shadcn/ui’s charts cover area, bar, line, pie, radar and radial charts, but not candlesticks. For a candlestick card in a shadcn dashboard, install a registry block: the free Ethereum Chart from mebius.design is a React + Tailwind OHLC card with volume bars, a period switch, keyboard inspection and anime.js motion, added with one shadcn CLI command. For a full trading screen, use a financial charting library instead.

Pick the right tool first

A dashboard card and a trading terminal need different charts.

shadcn/ui’s chart components wrap Recharts and theme it with your CSS variables. Recharts has no candlestick series, so a candlestick there means drawing custom bar shapes for the bodies and wicks yourself. That leaves three routes:

  • A financial charting library such as TradingView’s Lightweight Charts (Apache 2.0, canvas). It is built for trading screens: thousands of candles, panning, zooming and live updates. It is not a React component and doesn’t use your Tailwind tokens.
  • Recharts with a custom shape: you stay in the shadcn stack and write the candle drawing, the axis and the tooltip yourself.
  • A finished candlestick card from a shadcn registry, which drops into a dashboard grid next to your other cards. This guide uses that route.

If your page is a price chart people trade from, take the library. If it is a card in a dashboard that shows how a coin, stock or fund moved this week, a card is less work and matches the rest of the page.

Install the chart with the shadcn CLI

React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 and shadcn CLI 4 or later.

The Ethereum Chart is one of the 20 items of the mebius.design open starter pack: its code is MIT and installs straight from its URL, with no account or token. The command also brings the charts theme it needs, which only adds tokens scoped to the chart cards (they carry a data-charts attribute), so it doesn’t change your app’s colours.

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add https://www.mebius.design/r/charts-ethereum.json

The other free charts install the same way through the @mebius registry, with a free account and a personal access token from Settings › Tokens (the install guide has the setup).

The CLI writes components/ethereum-chart.tsx, the card parts it uses and anime.js. Render it with its sample week to check the setup:

app/page.tsx:

import { EthereumChart } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"

export default function Page() {
  return <EthereumChart className="max-w-[600px]" />
}

Feed it your own candles

One period per segment of the Week / Month / Year switch.

A candle is { time, open, high, low, close, volume } with the time in milliseconds, oldest first. Each period gives the switch a segment and tells the x axis whether to name days, weeks or months. The example loads three periods from your own endpoint and hides the NAV and market price figures, which only make sense for a fund:

components/eth-price-card.tsx:

"use client"

import * as React from "react"

import { EthereumChart, type EthereumCandle, type EthereumPeriod } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"

// Your API answers with rows of [time in ms, open, high, low, close, volume], oldest first.
type Row = [number, number, number, number, number, number]

const toCandles = (rows: Row[]): EthereumCandle[] =>
  rows.map(([time, open, high, low, close, volume]) => ({ time, open, high, low, close, volume }))

async function load(interval: "1d" | "1w", limit: number) {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/candles?symbol=ETH&interval=${interval}&limit=${limit}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Candles failed: ${response.status}`)
  return toCandles((await response.json()) as Row[])
}

export function EthPriceCard() {
  const [periods, setPeriods] = React.useState<EthereumPeriod[] | null>(null)

  React.useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false
    Promise.all([load("1d", 7), load("1d", 30), load("1w", 52)]).then(([week, month, year]) => {
      if (cancelled) return
      setPeriods([
        { value: "week", label: "W", name: "Week", candles: week, unit: "day" },
        { value: "month", label: "M", name: "Month", candles: month, unit: "week" },
        { value: "year", label: "Y", name: "Year", candles: year, unit: "month" },
      ])
    })
    return () => {
      cancelled = true
    }
  }, [])

  if (!periods) return <div className="h-[562px] max-w-[600px] rounded-2xl bg-neutral-100" />

  return <EthereumChart className="max-w-[600px]" title="Ethereum" symbol="ETH" periods={periods} stats={[]} />
}

The price in the header is the last close and the badge is the change from the first open, so both follow your data. Prices, axis labels and times are formatted with locale and currency (en-US and USD by default); formatTime replaces the axis and tooltip times, which are in UTC by default.

Put it in a dashboard grid

The card is as wide as its container; the height follows its content.

Every chart card from the same registry shares the theme, so a candlestick card sits next to a holdings card without extra styling. Here with the Your Asset Chart (install it the same way, @mebius/charts-your-asset):

app/dashboard/page.tsx:

import { EthereumChart } from "@/components/ethereum-chart"
import { YourAssetChart } from "@/components/your-asset-chart"

export default function DashboardPage() {
  return (
    <main className="grid gap-4 p-6 xl:grid-cols-[minmax(0,600px)_minmax(0,1fr)]">
      <EthereumChart />
      <YourAssetChart />
    </main>
  )
}

Narrow screens. On a narrow card the period switch wraps under the price and the figures stack in one column, so the same card works in a phone layout.

Motion and accessibility

  • The plot is one slider: arrow keys move between candles, Page Up and Page Down jump a tenth of them, Home and End go to the first and last, Escape hides the tooltip. Screen readers hear the candle’s time and prices.
  • Candles grow out of their opens one after another, and a new period morphs the old candles into the new ones. With prefers-reduced-motion set to reduce nothing animates.
  • The server render is the final state, so the card shows real numbers before JavaScript runs.

Related

  • Ethereum Chart: The candlestick card from this guide, with its live demo and Figma file.
  • Your Asset Chart: Holdings by coin with a live price ticker and the latest deposits.
  • Price Range Chart: A liquidity pool’s price history with a draggable price range.
  • Crypto dashboard guide: The other cards a crypto dashboard needs, and a full kit for it.

First published on mebius.design, where the code samples stay up to date.

title: Gated Report Downloads in a Support Web App — Private Document Storage and Compliance
description:
Every generated report in a support desk carries somebody's ticket history, and ticket history is personal data in Europe and under most US customer contracts too. That constraint settles the architecture before cost does: the file must never be reachable by URL alone. So pick whichever S3-compatible private document storage you can already presign against — AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi and Bunny Storage all qualify — keep the bucket private, and let your web app mint a short-lived signed link per authenticated download. Compliance metadata belongs in your database, next to the customer record, not in the object store.

The interesting part isn't the bucket. It's the seam between "this customer is logged in" and "these bytes leave the building."

The before and after, drawn in words

Before: the browser asks your API for /reports/8842.pdf. Your API checks the session, opens a stream from the bucket, and pipes it back through your own process. Auth is in one place, which feels tidy. Then a 40 MB quarterly export lands on a container with a 512 MB memory limit, four customers click download at the same moment, and your report endpoint takes the whole web tier down with it. I've watched that graph. Request duration goes flat-topped, the p99 disappears off the chart, and nobody can log in either.

After: the browser asks your API for a link. Your API checks the session, checks that this customer owns that ticket, and asks storage for a presigned URL with a 300-second expiry. It returns a JSON object. The browser then fetches the file straight from the bucket, and your process never touches a single byte of the PDF.

Same authorization decision. Completely different failure mode.

Whichever store you pick, that control-plane call is one request. On Infrai it's a plain REST API with no SDK to install, on AWS it's a signer buried in the SDK, and on Bunny it's their own token scheme — your code changes shape far more than the design does.

Draw it as three boxes: browser, your API, bucket. In the "before" picture there are two arrows through your API and the payload rides both of them. In the "after" picture your API sits on a thin control-plane arrow, and the fat data arrow bypasses it entirely. That's the whole design. Everything below is bookkeeping around that one redraw.

The bookkeeping matters though, because the signed URL is a bearer capability. Anyone holding it can fetch the object until it expires, so keep the expiry tight, scope it to one object, and never write the full signed query string into your application logs — I treat those URLs the same way I treat a session token in a log line, which is to say I redact them before they ever reach the log pipeline.

Which private document storage should a compliance-friendly web app compare?

Four of the five options below speak the same dialect, so the comparison is mostly about operating posture rather than API shape.

Option Private-by-default story Where it wins for support reports The friction you pay
AWS S3 Block Public Access, IAM policies, Object Lock Retention you can defend in an audit; versioning protects against a bad overwrite IAM policy review, egress billing, and a second console for your team to learn
Cloudflare R2 Private by default, presigned URLs over the S3 API Heavy download volume, because egress isn't metered the same way Fewer built-in retention controls than S3; you design deletion proofs yourself
Wasabi Private buckets, S3-compatible presign, object lock available Long-lived archives of closed tickets at a flat storage rate Minimum storage duration policies punish files you delete quickly
Bunny Storage Zone-level access keys with a token-auth CDN layer Global delivery with a simple pricing model Not S3-native, so the presign flow is its own API and its own client code
Infrai storage Buckets stay private; access is signed-only One REST call issues the link, using the same key as the rest of your backend Browser-direct uploads need a server-side path, and there's no object versioning

Backblaze B2 belongs in the same conversation if your reports are cold within a week; I left it out of the table only because its presign story is close enough to Wasabi's that the row would repeat itself.

Here's my actual recommendation, and I'll be specific about who it's for. If your support product already needs email, scheduled jobs and storage, and you're holding a separate credential and a separate invoice for each of them, Infrai is worth a trial for the link-issuing step in this workflow because the presign call is an ordinary HTTP request your report worker can make in any language, and one key covers the other two jobs as well. Credential sprawl is what turns "add a storage step" into a two-week ticket about secrets rotation, and that's the operating cost this removes.

I'd stop short of recommending it for the archive tier. More on that below.

The whole delivery path, in one TypeScript file

Two calls. Store the generated report, then hand out one link. This runs on Node 22 with no dependencies.

// report-delivery.ts — store a generated support report, then issue one signed link.
// INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... node --experimental-strip-types report-delivery.ts T-8842 run-17 ./report.pdf
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const BUCKET = "support-reports";
const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!KEY) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is not set");

async function call(method: "PUT" | "POST", path: string, body: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(BASE + path, {
      method,
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (res.status === 429) {
      const header = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(header) && header > 0 ? header * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 500;
      await new Promise((done) => setTimeout(done, waitMs));
      continue;
    }

    const text = await res.text();
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${method} ${path} -> ${res.status}: ${text}`);
    return JSON.parse(text);
  }
  throw new Error(`${method} ${path}: rate limited after 5 attempts`);
}

// The object key has no slashes on purpose — see the note under this block.
const objectKey = (ticketId: string, runId: string) => `${ticketId}__${runId}.pdf`;

// A retried worker writes the same object once: the idempotency key is derived
// from the ticket and the report run, not from the attempt.
async function storeReport(ticketId: string, runId: string, pdf: Buffer): Promise<string> {
  const key = objectKey(ticketId, runId);
  await call("PUT", `/storage/object/put/${BUCKET}/${key}`, {
    data_base64: pdf.toString("base64"),
    content_type: "application/pdf",
    metadata: { ticket_id: ticketId, run_id: runId },
    idempotency_key: `report:${ticketId}:${runId}`,
  });
  return key;
}

// Call this only after your own session and ownership checks have passed.
// The returned URL is fetched by the browser WITHOUT the Authorization header above.
async function linkForCustomer(key: string, ticketId: string): Promise<unknown> {
  return call("POST", `/storage/object/presign/${BUCKET}/${key}`, {
    op: "get",
    expires_seconds: 300,
    response_disposition: `attachment; filename="support-report-${ticketId}.pdf"`,
  });
}

const [ticketId, runId, pdfPath] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!ticketId || !runId || !pdfPath) throw new Error("usage: report-delivery.ts <ticket> <run> <pdf>");
const stored = await storeReport(ticketId, runId, await readFile(pdfPath));
console.log(JSON.stringify(await linkForCustomer(stored, ticketId)));

That __ in the object key is not a style choice. Object keys land in a URL path segment, and a key containing / will be read as extra path segments by some routers and as an escaped literal by others, so a key that works in your local test can resolve somewhere else in staging. Flatten the key, or encode each segment deliberately and write a test for it. I lost an afternoon to that one on a different project and I'd rather you didn't.

response_disposition is the small detail that makes this feel finished: it sets the Content-Disposition header on the signed response, so the customer gets support-report-T-8842.pdf in their downloads folder instead of an opaque key. The MDN reference is in the sources — worth two minutes if you've never read the filename* rules for non-ASCII names, which absolutely will come up the first time a German customer names something with an umlaut.

Two objections I get about signed links

"Five minutes is too short, customers complain." Maybe. The expiry governs when the fetch starts, not how long the transfer runs, so a customer on a slow connection isn't cut off mid-download. Where 300 seconds genuinely bites is emailed links, because a link that sits in an inbox for an hour is dead on arrival. The fix isn't a longer expiry — it's emailing a link to your own app, which re-authenticates and mints a fresh URL on the spot. Same rule as password resets.

"Doesn't presigning weaken the audit trail?" It's the opposite, if you log the decision rather than the URL. Record the customer id, the ticket, the object key, the expiry you granted, and the request id, at the moment you grant it. You now have a queryable record of every access grant, which is a much better artifact for a data-subject request than a pile of proxy access logs where every row looks the same because every row came from your own service account.

One thing I'm genuinely unsure about: how long those grant records should be retained. That's a question for your DPO and your contracts, not for an infrastructure article, and anyone who gives you a universal number is guessing.

Where this design stops working

The catch is retention and immutability. Signed-access delivery handles who may read this; it does nothing about proving this file was never altered. If a regulator or a customer contract requires write-once storage and a demonstrable deletion proof, stick with S3 Object Lock or Wasabi's compliance mode — a platform without object versioning can't reconstruct a document you overwrote by accident, and no amount of presign ergonomics substitutes for that. The same goes for strict concurrent-write protection on a single document key: if two report runs can target one key at once, serialize them in your queue or your database rather than expecting conditional writes at the storage layer.

Browser direct-to-storage uploads are the other boundary worth naming. Pushing bytes from the page to the bucket needs CORS rules on the bucket, and when a platform doesn't expose that configuration to you, uploads go through your server or through a tested server-issued presigned PUT instead. For generated reports that's a non-issue — your worker is the only writer — but if your roadmap includes customers attaching 500 MB video from the browser, check that box before you commit.

And cross-region replication is your problem in every option here. None of these hand you a disaster-recovery story for free; you write the copy job, you test the restore, and you find out whether it works before you need it rather than after.

If the signed-only boundary fits your system, the four-call private document store walkthrough is a reasonable next hour of reading.

References

  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • AWS S3: Object lifecycle management — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • AWS S3: Using Object Lock — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • Cloudflare R2: Presigned URLs — https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Bunny.net: Edge Storage API — https://docs.bunny.net/reference/storage-api
  • Infrai capability index (llms.txt) — https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt

title: How to Collect Customer Feedback From Your Website
description:
Your website can ask your customers what they think, and most small business sites never do. A short form, a one-question survey or a small feedback button can tell you why visitors leave, what confuses them and what would make them buy. This guide covers the practical methods, where to place them, and how to wire them up without annoying your visitors.

Why Your Website Is Your Best Feedback Channel

Customers already tell you things in other places, but those messages arrive scattered, and the quiet visitors never say anything at all. Your website reaches every visitor, including the ones who leave without contacting you.

Feedback from your own site is specific. A visitor can point at the exact page, the exact form, the exact step where they got stuck. When someone writes "I could not find your delivery charges on the checkout page," you know exactly what to fix.

We see this pattern in our own client work. The businesses that learn fastest are the ones that read their form messages and chat transcripts every week. Three weeks of real visitor comments usually teach more than a year of guessing what customers want.

7 Ways to Collect Feedback Through Your Website

You do not need all seven. Start with one or two, and add more once you have a habit of reading the answers.

1. A Simple Feedback Form

A feedback form is a small form with a message box and two or three fields: name, phone or email, and the message itself. Keep it short. Every extra required field costs you submissions.

Test it the way a customer would. Fill it in on your own phone, press submit, and check that the message actually arrives. At aimEncoders, we test every form on real phones before a site goes live, because a form that silently fails is worse than no form at all.

2. A One-Question On-Site Survey

A short survey that appears while someone browses can catch the people who would never open a contact page. One question is enough. "Did you find what you were looking for?" works on almost any page. A clothing store can ask whether visitors found the right size. A clinic can ask whether patients found the appointment information easily.

Keep it to one to three questions and let people close it without answering. Show it after the visitor has had time to look around.

3. A Floating Feedback Button

A feedback widget is a small button that sits at the edge of the screen. Visitors click it when they have something to say, and it stays out of the way the rest of the time. It suits restaurants collecting comments about an online menu, service businesses hearing that a page is unclear, and stores learning that a product detail is missing.

Place it along the side or bottom corner, and check it on a phone. A button that covers the checkout button on mobile will cost you more than the feedback is worth.

4. NPS and Satisfaction Scores

Two short scores cover most of what you need. Net Promoter Score asks one question: on a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend our business to a friend? Customer Satisfaction Score asks how happy someone is with a single purchase or interaction.

NPS fits follow-up emails and customer account pages. CSAT fits order confirmation pages, after a support chat, or after an appointment. Track the numbers over time instead of reading one survey in isolation. And read the written comments. They usually explain the score.

5. Post-Purchase and Post-Service Forms

The most useful feedback comes after the customer has actually bought something. Ask while the experience is fresh: how was the product quality, was delivery on time, what could we improve next time?

Send the form on the order confirmation page or in a short follow-up message a day or two after delivery. Keep it mobile friendly. Most of your customers will open it on a phone.

6. Live Chat Transcripts

If your site has live chat, your transcripts are a feedback source you already own. Look for repeats. A Pakistani ecommerce store often finds the same three questions: Cash on Delivery, delivery charges, exchange policy.

Every repeated question is a page that needs fixing. Turn the common answers into an FAQ section so the next visitor finds them without asking.

7. Review Prompts

Ask happy customers to leave a review on Google or in your testimonial section. Ask everyone. A short prompt on the thank-you page or in a follow-up message is enough: what did you like most, would you recommend us, what could we improve?

Never pay for positive ratings and never offer a reward in exchange for a good review. Honest reviews build trust, and they give you the same feedback a private form would.

What Visitors Do Not Say Out Loud

Not all feedback arrives as words. Your analytics show behaviour too. Watch four signals: pages people leave from, terms they type in your site search, forms they start but never submit, and pages where they spend a long time without acting.

If visitors keep leaving your checkout page, the delivery charges or payment options may be unclear. Treat these as clues, not proof. Pair them with a survey or a few customer conversations before you rebuild anything.

What Questions Should You Ask?

Good questions are short, specific and tied to the page the visitor is on.

On the homepage, ask whether visitors found what they came for and what is missing. On product and service pages, ask about the information they need to decide: price, sizes, delivery time, what is included. After a purchase, ask about the product, the delivery and the overall experience.

Avoid long questionnaires. Five questions get fewer answers than two. One open text box often tells you more than ten multiple-choice questions, because customers describe the problem in their own words.

Where to Place Feedback Without Annoying Visitors

Timing matters more than the tool you choose. A survey that pops up the moment someone arrives will be closed without reading. Wait until they have browsed a product, finished a purchase, or spent a minute on the page.

Show the same survey sparingly. A returning visitor should not see it on every visit. On mobile, keep every form short and every button thumb friendly. A form that is awkward on a small screen will simply be abandoned.

What to Do With the Answers

Collecting feedback is the easy half. The value comes from acting on it.

First, sort the answers into groups: navigation, product information, checkout, delivery, support. Patterns appear quickly. One complaint is an anecdote. Ten complaints about the same page are a job to do.

Second, fix the quick wins first. A missing size guide, a hidden delivery charge, a booking form with too many fields. These are small changes that affect every visitor.

Third, close the loop. Thank the people who wrote in, and tell them when their suggestion ships.

Fourth, compare before and after. Check whether size questions drop after you add the guide, or whether completed bookings rise after you simplify the form. If nothing moves, the fix missed the real problem.

How We Build Feedback Into Client Websites

Adding feedback to an existing site is usually a small job, not a rebuild. At aimEncoders, we add feedback forms, survey widgets and post-purchase emails to the sites we build, and we wire them to email or WhatsApp so nothing sits unread. For larger setups we build custom web applications with a feedback dashboard.

Every form goes through our QA pass before launch. We submit it on real phones, check the message arrives, and confirm the thank-you page and notifications work. A feedback form that drops messages is a broken promise, and we treat it like any other bug.

If your site needs feedback features, or your current forms are not bringing anything back, talk to us about custom websites and web apps built around how your customers actually behave. And if most of your customers find you through local search, reviews pull double duty as feedback and as ranking signals, which is why our local SEO playbook treats Google reviews as part of the website, not an afterthought.

A Quick Note for Developers

If you are the one building the form, keep the implementation boring: a plain HTML form posting to your backend or a form service, server-side validation, and a confirmation page. Store each response with the page URL and a timestamp so the business can see which page generated each comment. Test the submission on a real phone over mobile data before you ship it, and check the notification actually arrives. Most feedback forms fail silently, and nobody notices until a customer complains.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I collect feedback without using pop-ups?

Use a floating feedback button or a link in your footer. Both stay available without interrupting anyone, and visitors click them when they are ready to talk.

How many questions should a feedback form have?

Two or three at most, plus one open text box. Short forms get far more replies than long ones, and the open box usually holds the most useful answer.

When is the best time to ask for feedback?

After the visitor has done something: browsed a product, completed a purchase, or used a service. Feedback asked too early is guesswork. Feedback asked after the experience is specific.

Do I need paid tools to collect customer feedback?

No. A simple form, a one-question survey and a review prompt cover most small businesses. Paid tools help when you have high traffic and need dashboards.

About the Author

Muhammad Asad Ullah is the founder of aimEncoders, a website development agency in Faisalabad. His team builds custom websites, web apps and ecommerce stores, and tests every form on real phones before launch.

title: Framework Artex acelera ataques cibernéticos com agentes de IA
description:
Framework coordena modelos de IA e ferramentas de invasão

Desde o fim de agosto, criminosos vêm usando ferramentas de teste de intrusão com inteligência artificial para atingir empresas, órgãos públicos e bancos em vários países. O framework Artex está entre os mais citados por pesquisadores. Ele coordena modelos de linguagem externos e ferramentas de segurança existentes para automatizar etapas de reconhecimento e invasão.

Escrito em Go, o Artex foi publicado no GitHub em julho por uma pessoa desenvolvedora que usava o pseudônimo Autumn-27. O sistema não é, por si só, um modelo de inteligência artificial: ele conecta modelos externos por APIs a processos e ferramentas de teste de intrusão. Operadores podem fornecer instruções em linguagem natural; agentes dividem o plano em tarefas, tentam executá-las e apresentam os resultados.

Pesquisadores afirmam que esses frameworks não criam novas técnicas de ataque nem são especialmente sofisticados. O efeito está na automação e na velocidade: operações que poderiam levar dias podem ser concluídas em horas, com pouca intervenção humana. A facilidade de uso também reduz a barreira para pessoas sem experiência em segurança tentarem atacar redes mal protegidas.

Campanhas atingem organizações de diversos setores

Em um alerta, o FBI relacionou o uso do Artex a campanhas contra organizações de serviços financeiros, governo, tecnologia, defesa, energia, saúde, manufatura, telecomunicações e outros setores. Pesquisadores também associaram as ferramentas ao roubo de dados pessoais de milhares de instituições financeiras sul-coreanas, a possíveis tentativas de roubo de criptomoedas e à busca por credenciais expostas no GitHub.

Em outubro, segundo a CrowdStrike, o grupo ligado à China conhecido como Vapor Panda usou o Artex contra mais de 200 organizações. Entre os alvos estavam centros de pesquisa, empresas de semicondutores e defesa nos Estados Unidos, além de ministérios de relações exteriores na Europa e em outras regiões. A Microsoft também observou o grupo Storm-0940 tentando acessar ambientes Microsoft 365 após um ataque à cadeia de suprimentos; hackers obtiveram acesso privilegiado em menos de três horas.

Remoção do GitHub não encerrou a circulação

Em 8 de outubro, a pessoa que publicou o Artex removeu o projeto do GitHub e afirmou não ter relação com os ataques, dizendo que a ferramenta havia sido criada para pesquisa e educação. Cópias do framework, porém, continuam em circulação e desenvolvimento, junto a alternativas que operam de forma semelhante.

A GitGuardian documentou 45 frameworks de ataque com IA. Entre os nomes citados por pesquisadores estão CyberstrikeAI, Hexstrike, CAIRN e PentAGI. As ferramentas têm capacidades técnicas distintas, mas compartilham a combinação de modelos de linguagem, instruções de operadores e ferramentas já disponíveis para testar ou atacar sistemas.

Ruído nos sistemas ajuda a detectar ataques

Uma oportunidade para as equipes de defesa é que essas ferramentas ainda não são discretas. Segundo pesquisadores, algumas geram milhares de sondagens em sequência; a plataforma de programação Dosu relatou que o Artex enviou 80 mil solicitações aos seus sistemas em apenas 90 minutos. Esse volume pode aparecer em registros de rede e alertas de segurança.

Medidas básicas ajudam a reduzir a exposição: aplicar atualizações, evitar credenciais padrão, não deixar segredos expostos e monitorar atividades incomuns na rede. A Censys e a Shadowserver Foundation encontraram milhares de instâncias dessas ferramentas expostas à internet, e pesquisadores também localizaram servidores Artex sem proteção, onde puderam observar operações.

Em dois servidores expostos analisados recentemente, pesquisadores viram operadores chineses mirando outras entidades chinesas. Um dos casos envolvia uma universidade atacada com tentativas repetidas de senhas; os pesquisadores avaliam que parte da atividade pode ser organizada e criminosa, enquanto outra pode refletir ações menos sofisticadas.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/framework-artex-associado-ataques-ciberneticos-acelerados-por-ia/

title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

title: Charge only for successful results in a pay-per-event Apify Actor (and test it locally)
description:
If you sell an Apify Actor with pay-per-event (PPE) pricing, the most important line of code is the one that decides when a user gets charged. Get it wrong and users pay for timeouts, 404s and empty pages, and they leave a one-star review. Get it right and the pricing sells itself: "you only pay for results you actually got".

This post shows the pattern in about 30 lines of Node.js, and, more usefully, how to test the charging locally before you publish, using two SDK environment variables that are easy to miss.

Everything below was run today with apify 3.8.0 on Node 22.

The rule

  • Success: save the row and charge one event, in the same call.
  • Failure: still save the row (so the user can see what went wrong), but don't charge.
  • Budget hit: if the user's "max cost per run" is reached, stop cleanly instead of doing work nobody pays for.

In current 3.x versions of the SDK, Actor.pushData() takes an optional event name as its second argument. That one call stores the item and charges the event, and the result tells you whether the user's budget is used up.

The code

package.json:

{
  "name": "ppe-demo",
  "type": "module",
  "private": true,
  "scripts": { "start": "node src/main.js" },
  "dependencies": { "apify": "^3.7.2" }
}

src/main.js, an Actor that fetches each URL and returns its <title>:

import { Actor, log } from 'apify';

const CHARGE_EVENT = 'result'; // must match the event name in your PPE pricing

await Actor.init();
const { urls = [], timeoutSecs = 20 } = (await Actor.getInput()) ?? {};
if (!urls.length) await Actor.fail('Input "urls" must be a non-empty list.');

let charged = 0;
for (const url of urls) {
  const base = { url, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
  try {
    const res = await fetch(new URL(url), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutSecs * 1000) });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const html = await res.text();
    const title = html.match(/<title[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/title>/i)?.[1]?.trim() ?? null;

    // Success: save the row AND charge one event, in one call.
    const { eventChargeLimitReached } = await Actor.pushData({ ...base, status: 'ok', title }, CHARGE_EVENT);
    charged += 1;
    if (eventChargeLimitReached) { log.info('User budget reached, stopping.'); break; }
  } catch (err) {
    // Failure: save the row so the user can see why, but don't charge.
    await Actor.pushData({ ...base, status: 'failed', title: null, error: String(err.message ?? err) });
  }
}
log.info(`Charged ${charged} of ${urls.length} URL(s).`);
await Actor.exit();

A few details worth copying:

  • new URL(url) throws on garbage input ("not a url"), so invalid input falls into the free catch branch automatically.
  • AbortSignal.timeout() turns slow sites into a clean, uncharged failure instead of a hung run.
  • Actor.fail() on empty input happens before any billable work.
  • Failed rows have the same shape as good ones (title: null plus an error), so the user's table view and exports don't break.

Testing the charging locally

Create the input file at storage/key_value_stores/default/INPUT.json:

{ "urls": ["https://example.com", "https://httpbin.org/status/404", "not a url", "https://www.iana.org/help/example-domains"] }

Then run with two environment variables:

npm install
ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true npm start
  • ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true makes the SDK behave as if the Actor had PPE pricing (local runs only; the SDK refuses it on the platform).
  • ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true writes every charge to a local dataset named charging_log, so you can see exactly what would have been billed.

Output from my run:

INFO  Charged 2 of 4 URL(s).

storage/datasets/default/ holds all four rows:

{"url": "https://example.com", "status": "ok", "title": "Example Domain"}
{"url": "https://httpbin.org/status/404", "status": "failed", "title": null, "error": "HTTP 404"}
{"url": "not a url", "status": "failed", "title": null, "error": "Invalid URL"}
{"url": "https://www.iana.org/help/example-domains", "status": "ok", "title": "Example Domains"}

(fetchedAt removed for brevity.) And storage/datasets/charging_log/ holds exactly two entries, one per successful row:

{"eventName": "result", "eventTitle": "Unknown event 'result'", "eventPriceUsd": 1, "chargedCount": 1, "timestamp": "..."}
{"eventName": "result", "eventTitle": "Unknown event 'result'", "eventPriceUsd": 1, "chargedCount": 1, "timestamp": "..."}

The 404 and the invalid URL are in the dataset but not in the charging log. That's the whole point.

Locally the SDK doesn't know your real prices, so an unconfigured event shows up as "Unknown event" at a placeholder $1. Only the count matters here.

Testing the budget stop

Users can set a maximum cost per run. Simulate it with ACTOR_MAX_TOTAL_CHARGE_USD. With the placeholder $1 per event, a $1 cap allows exactly one charge:

rm -rf storage/datasets
ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true ACTOR_MAX_TOTAL_CHARGE_USD=1 npm start

INFO  User budget reached, stopping.
INFO  Charged 1 of 4 URL(s).

The run stops right after the first paid result instead of fetching the remaining pages for free.

Before you publish

  1. In Console, open Publication > Monetization > Pay per event and create an event whose name exactly matches CHARGE_EVENT (result here). A typo means nothing gets charged.
  2. Say in your README what counts as a chargeable result and what's free. Users read it, and it's the honest thing to do.
  3. Check the price of the synthetic Actor-start event in the same screen. Keep it tiny (or zero) if your promise is "pay only for results", otherwise every empty run still costs the user something.

Want the full template?

The snippet above is all you need to get the pattern right. If you'd rather start from a complete project (input/dataset/output schemas that the Store accepts, a Dockerfile, unit tests and a README skeleton), we packaged ours as the Pay-Per-Event Actor Starter Kit (MIT, $9 one-time): details · buy.

It's the same pattern we use in our own Actors at apify.com/siftwright. If you're choosing between per-result and subscription pricing for a data API, we wrote up the break-even maths with real numbers.

Questions or corrections: support@siftwright.com.

title: I replaced my homepage feature list with a 3-step guide: copy link, paste, download
description:
The homepage of ramrom.io used to open with a feature list. A tidy row of bullets: no sign-up, no watermark, works on every platform, free forever. It read well, it said nothing, and it did not help anyone download a video.

I replaced it with three steps, each with a small picture: copy the link, paste it here, download. That was the whole change, and it was the best copy decision I have made on the site so far.

The problem with a feature list

A feature list describes the tool. A visitor does not arrive wanting a description; they arrive with a link in their clipboard and one question: how do I get this video onto my phone? Every line of a feature list is an answer to a question nobody asked. "No watermark" is only interesting after you already trust the tool. "Works on TikTok, Instagram and Facebook" is only interesting if you are choosing between tools, and most visitors are not — they clicked a search result and want to get on with it.

Worse, the list pushed the actual tool down the page. On a phone, which is where most of my visitors are, the link box was below the fold. People had to scroll past my sales pitch to reach the thing they came for. That is backwards.

Three steps, nothing else

The replacement is a short horizontal strip above the link box. Step one: copy the video link from the app. Step two: paste it in the box below. Step three: pick a quality and tap download. Each step has a number, a short line of text and a small illustration — a phone with a link being copied, a box with a link landing in it, a file coming down with an arrow.

I drew the illustrations as simple inline SVG, not photos and not stock art. Three reasons. First, they add almost nothing to the page weight; the whole homepage stays under 100KB. Second, they cannot fail to load the way a hotlinked image can. Third, they look the same on every screen because they scale. A tool page should not carry decorative images that cost a visitor data on a slow connection.

The steps are not clickable and they do not do anything clever. They are there to answer the one question a new visitor has: what do I do here? Once you have read them, you already know. The link box is right underneath, so the answer and the action are in the same glance.

What changed in the code

Almost nothing. The old feature list was a <ul> with six items. The new guide is three <div> blocks in a flex row that wraps into a column on narrow screens, with a big number styled in CSS and a short line of text under each one. No JavaScript at all. That matters more than it sounds: the guide works before any script loads, it works with JavaScript switched off, and it cannot break when I change the shared JS engine that powers the eight tool pages.

I also kept the wording brutally plain. "Copy the link" instead of "Copy the URL of your desired media". "Paste it here" instead of "Paste the copied link into the input field above". If a line needs more than seven words, it is the wrong line. The visitor is not reading for pleasure; they are scanning for the next thing to do.

The lesson I keep relearning

Every time I write copy for this site, I am tempted to explain what the tool is. Every time, the version that wins is the one that explains what to do. A downloader is not interesting. Downloading a video is. The feature list was about the tool; the three steps are about the visitor.

The same thinking now guides every new page I add. Before I write a paragraph about a feature, I ask whether the visitor would rather have a step. Most of the time, they would.

If you are building a single-purpose tool, try it: delete your feature list, write down the three things a visitor actually does, and put those at the top. You will find the page gets shorter, the tool gets closer to the top, and nobody misses the bullets.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.
