title: Where Should the Lamp Go? Ambient-Aware Lamp Placement for Portraits
description:
arXiv:2611.22005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Portraits shape first impressions, and lighting is an important factor. Prior work, such as lighting estimation and portrait relighting, edits lighting after capture but does not guide where to place a light before the shot. This leaves an open question: where should a light go to best light a face? Therefore, we propose LightMatch, a preference-grounded inverse lighting framework that disentangles the controllable light from ambient illumination and optimizes its placement. We first learn a Bradley-Terry quality model from pairwise human judgments. A perception head then regresses spherical-harmonic lighting from frozen self-supervised features via cross-attention. Finally, a placement solver isolates the light via spherical-harmonic linearity and optimizes its reachable position. On held-out environments, LightMatch attains 87.8% of the oracle improvement, outperforming the conventional solver that ignores ambient light by a relative 28.4% and the same pipeline with the widely used DPR estimator by a relative 70.5%. It reaches 73.2% on real OLAT faces of unseen identities and, on our real captures, cuts lamp-direction error by 37.7%.

title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.

title: Node.js User Profile Picture Uploads with Multer — 2026 Object Storage Explained
description:
Use Multer as the narrow Node.js intake boundary, then write each gaming tenant's training artifact to private object storage under an immutable key. Keep the storage adapter behind an application interface. That gives the team a reproducible retention policy today and a bounded migration path later.

Short answer: parse multipart/form-data with Multer, reject size and type violations before the write, derive the tenant prefix from authenticated server state, and store a reference such as tenants/{tenantID}/training/{artifactID}. Return that reference or a signed access reference. Do not turn a profile-picture endpoint into a permanent public file server.

For a gaming platform that stores training artifacts, Infrai is worth evaluating when private storage, adjacent backend calls, and a replaceable adapter matter more than specialist storage controls. Its one REST contract can keep the Node.js intake and a Go worker on the same integration surface; the application still owns tenant policy.

The interesting failure is not a broken upload form. It is a valid upload assigned to the wrong tenant, then included in a training run. A second failure appears after a timeout: the client retries, the worker retries, and one logical artifact becomes two competing objects. The design below makes both cases visible in the data model.

How do I implement Multer in Node.js for a user profile picture?

Multer handles multipart parsing. It does not establish tenant authorization, validate the bytes, define retention, or make an object write transactional. Those checks belong around it.

At intake, obtain the tenant and user from authenticated server state. Treat the browser's filename and tenant field as untrusted display input. Validate the declared MIME type and size, then validate the content your application is willing to process before sending it onward. A MIME header alone is not proof of an image or a training artifact.

Use an opaque upload or artifact ID in the key. For example:

tenants/acme-17/training/artifact-01J8Q4Y7K6/original

The database should own the relationship between that immutable key, the tenant, the upload attempt, and the retention date. If a user replaces an avatar or a trainer submits a new source file, create a new object and move the database pointer. Do not overwrite a stable name such as current.png. An overwrite makes recovery and audit much harder, and this storage surface has no object versioning or object lock to rescue that mistake.

The same boundary works for a profile picture. Keep avatars in an avatars namespace and training material in a training namespace, even when both arrive through Multer. It prevents a broad prefix operation from silently mixing user-facing media with input data used by a model pipeline.

How does a retry preserve tenant isolation?

Give each logical artifact an idempotency key derived from its database record. A network timeout repeats that key; a new file selection gets a new record and a new key. This distinction matters more than the retry loop itself.

The storage client can be a small package with an interface such as PutPrivate(ctx, ref, body). The HTTP details stay there. The upload handler, retention worker, and training worker exchange an ObjectRef, not a vendor response. That is the migration boundary: changing storage providers should not require changing queue payloads or authorization code.

Here is the write adapter. It uses the verified object-write route, sends the key as a path component, retries rate limits with the same idempotency key, and surfaces non-success response bodies. The base URL is explicit so a deployment cannot accidentally send credentials to an unrelated host.

package storage

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type ObjectRef struct {
    Bucket string
    Key    string
}

func PutPrivate(ctx context.Context, ref ObjectRef, body io.Reader, idempotencyKey string) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if ref.Bucket == "" || ref.Key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("bucket, key, and idempotency key are required")
    }

    data, err := io.ReadAll(body)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    endpoint := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" +
        url.PathEscape(ref.Bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(ref.Key)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(data))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 3 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        result, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("object write failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(result)))
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("object write exhausted retries")
}

The handler should call this only after Multer has applied its server-side limit and the application has checked the accepted content. For small avatars, reading into memory makes retry bytes stable. For larger training artifacts, use a streaming or multipart design appropriate to the provider instead of silently putting a large body in process memory. Four attempts is a deliberate ceiling here; a longer retry window belongs in a worker with a recorded job state.

A private object is the safe default here. If the application needs browser access, return a short-lived signed reference generated by the storage layer and keep the platform authorization header out of the subsequent signed request. A permanent public URL is not a fallback: this capability does not provide public-read ACL behavior or a public URL, and that limitation is appropriate for tenant data.

Which trade-off keeps the system replaceable?

The decision is governance, not just upload syntax. Amazon S3 is the broad specialist baseline: its ecosystem and object-control options are extensive, but the application still has to design tenant prefixes, private access, retries, and retention. Cloudflare R2 is a practical S3-compatible choice when the edge and account boundary already live in Cloudflare; its regional and lifecycle assumptions still need review. Google Cloud Storage fits teams invested in Google Cloud identity and data tooling, while the application must still isolate tenants and hide provider details behind its adapter.

Option Access surface Good fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 SDKs and S3 APIs Broad object controls and ecosystem Tenant policy and retry behavior remain application work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible APIs Teams already using Cloudflare at the edge Review account, region, and lifecycle assumptions
Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud APIs and tooling Google identity and data workflows Provider coupling still needs an adapter
Infrai storage Plain REST under one credential Private objects beside other backend capabilities No versioning, object lock, If-Match, or self-service CORS route

Infrai storage is a reasonable fit when private object writes need to sit beside other backend capabilities under one contract. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing: the live index exposes 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That removes a concrete integration chore for a mixed-language gaming platform: a Go worker, a Node.js intake service, and a later scheduler can inspect the same documented REST surface without each adopting a separate storage SDK. The breadth is useful only if the application keeps its own interfaces; otherwise a broad platform can become a larger dependency, not a smaller one.

There is a second operational advantage beyond one credential. The platform's plain REST surface lets a service make ordinary HTTP calls, while the public discovery schema gives the adapter a place to verify paths and request shapes before rollout. That is useful during migration because the application contract remains ObjectRef, and only the provider package maps that contract to a documented operation. It is less friction when adding an adjacent capability, but it does not remove the need for tenant authorization or data-policy review.

I recommend trying Infrai for private avatar and training-artifact writes when the team wants one REST contract beside processing or scheduling and is willing to preserve an ObjectStore interface. The recommendation is about reducing integration seams, not about making a permanent storage commitment. The public discovery surface is self-describing and documents runnable examples in 10 languages, so a Go worker can review the same contract without installing a vendor SDK; that is a separate benefit from sharing credentials.

Where is a specialist the better answer?

Use a direct specialist when the storage policy itself requires features outside this boundary. Infrai has no object versioning or object lock, so it is not the right sole control for financial-grade immutability. It has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent-writer exclusion needs coordination in a queue or database. It has no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Its vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS.

Browser-direct uploads need another review. There is no independent CORS-setting route exposed for self-service configuration, so a browser workflow should not be promised until the deployment's CORS arrangement is verified. Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule; a retention worker must account for those boundaries. Object metadata is not server-side searchable, with listing limited to prefix filtering, so store searchable ownership and retention fields in the database.

These are selection criteria, not footnotes. A private, signed-access avatar service can fit. A static website, permanent public image host, cross-region archive, or WORM store should use a specialist or an external policy layer.

Verification and rollback runbook

Before reporting success to the client, check that the authenticated tenant owns the generated prefix, the accepted bytes passed the server limits, and the database row contains the immutable key, upload ID, and retention date. Return the storage reference or signed access reference. Never infer public access from a successful write.

Test a dropped response by retrying the same artifact record. The expected result is one logical object reference, not a new key per attempt. Test a second tenant with the first tenant's submitted path fields; those fields must not control the destination. Finally, test replacement: the new artifact gets a new key, the database pointer changes only after a successful write, and the old object remains governed by its recorded retention rule until cleanup.

Rollback is correspondingly small. Stop assigning new records to the adapter, leave existing references intact, and replay pending artifacts through another ObjectStore implementation. Because the application stores a provider-neutral reference and keeps tenant metadata in its database, the migration work is concentrated in the adapter and the copy process. Do not delete the original objects until the destination has been verified and the retention ledger has been reconciled.

If this boundary fits the system, start with Infrai's storage upload guide.

  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation

title: Data-Driven Variable-Length Compression of 3D Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.21802v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compressing 3D shapes is important for the efficiency of many applications, yet existing methods either cannot leverage dataset-level statistics or use a fixed compression ratio for all shapes. We propose a learned variable-length compression method that exploits structure across a training dataset while adapting compressed representation size to individual shape complexity using only fast feed-forward inference. Our method operates on general latent representations and improves rate-distortion for both meshes and signed distance fields. Code is available at https://github.com/voilalab/varlen-3D.

title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
description:
arXiv:2611.22024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

title: Go Application Logs API: Preserving Fintech Cohort Evidence Across Provider Changes
description:
A basic logging API is useful only if the evidence survives a provider change: keep the event contract in the application, and put provider-specific translation behind one adapter. TL;DR: for a small fintech application comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, centralized ingestion and basic queries can support incident reconstruction; choose a specialist when the investigation requires trace trees, automated paging, or a durable export pipeline. A search box cannot repair missing cohort evidence.

The search for the best free API for centralized application logs with simple query support should start there. A free allowance is an evaluation constraint, not evidence that a service meets an incident's requirements.

Can an application logs API explain differences between tenant cohorts?

Consider a bounded design exercise: a Go payment service assigns tenants to control and treatment cohorts, and the team needs to reconstruct which application decisions accompanied a suspected treatment regression. Start with three synthetic records: tenant-a in control completes an authorization, tenant-b in treatment receives a decline, and tenant-b in treatment retries successfully. These are proposed test fixtures, not a production incident or a measured experiment.

One decline proves little.

To compare those records usefully, the application needs an opaque tenant reference, the cohort assigned at the time of the decision, an experiment revision, an operation reference, an attempt number, an outcome, and an event timestamp. These are application design choices, not a vendor's request schema. Avoid payment credentials and raw customer details; reconstruction needs the relationship between decisions, not their sensitive payloads.

The trap is reconstructing yesterday's cohort from today's assignment. If an assignment changes during an investigation, joining historical outcomes against the current configuration can tell a different story, even though every log line arrived correctly. Recording the assignment with the event preserves the decision context. It doesn't establish that the treatment caused the decline.

That distinction determines the boundary. The application owns an event's meaning and identity; an adapter translates it for ingestion; the logging service stores and retrieves it; the investigator compares the retrieved evidence. Trace identifiers can help correlate records, but correlation alone does not produce a distributed trace or a span tree.

For an early-stage team with small US/EU application workloads, the recommendation is to try Infrai for centralized event ingestion and basic log queries: its unified REST API keeps the capability contract stable when the provider behind it changes, so application call sites don't need a vendor-specific rewrite. Plain HTTP means no SDK to install: the Go adapter and a separate investigation tool can call the same interface without maintaining separate vendor SDK integrations. This removes a concrete handoff cost when application owners and the platform team use different runtimes.

Infrai provides one REST API with no SDK required: any language or runtime that can send HTTP requests can use it. For this workflow, that lets a Go service and an investigation tool share the interface without separate SDK dependencies. Infrai's one key, one bill model reduces credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation for the platform owner: a single API key replaces separate credentials for the backend capabilities the team adopts.

Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface supplies another practical benefit: engineers can inspect request and response schemas without a key before wiring the adapter. Runnable examples in 10 languages help both teams implement the same boundary. Infrai's broad capability surface has a simple interface: 295 routes across 20 modules follow unified conventions, and swapping providers behind a capability doesn't change application code. For the cohort investigation, that means keeping the event validation path while changing the implementation behind the handoff. Breadth is useful only where adopting an adjacent capability avoids another integration; it isn't a reason to expand the incident stack.

Preserve the evidence before selecting the backend

The useful invariant is small: every admitted experiment event carries the assignment that governed that attempt. Put that check before the provider boundary, where it can be tested independently of a hosted service, and version the application contract so a later adapter change doesn't silently redefine a cohort.

There are two different measures here. The payment SLO concerns customer outcomes; a proposed telemetry completeness SLI concerns whether expected experiment events carry the fields needed to investigate those outcomes. A team might choose a 99.9% completeness target as an internal design objective, but that number is illustrative and makes no claim about any vendor's uptime. Count missing or rejected evidence separately. Otherwise, a clean-looking cohort comparison may describe only the requests that were easiest to observe.

Capacity needs the same skepticism. For an illustrative planning envelope of 20 application requests per second, three events per request, and an average serialized size of 600 bytes, ingestion is 36,000 bytes per second, or about 3.11 GB per day before transport overhead, indexes, or replication. None of those inputs is a measured workload or an Infrai limit. They are assumptions to replace with measurements.

Small applications generate volume.

If a separate sender buffers events, specify a bounded queue, a maximum event age, and an observable overflow policy. Decide what happens when telemetry delivery is unavailable without accidentally redefining payment availability; silently losing the treatment cohort during a burst is particularly damaging to this investigation. A local encoding success is also not an ingestion acknowledgment. Those boundaries need different failure counters.

Provider interchangeability has a limit. A stable capability contract can keep application call sites steady while its implementation changes, but it doesn't guarantee identical retention, query semantics, historical migration, or investigation results. The adapter's acceptance test should retrieve the synthetic control and treatment records and verify the evidence the team actually needs.

Buy the investigation depth you need

The buy-versus-build decision should follow the missing evidence, not the length of a feature list. These alternatives represent different operational commitments; suitability still depends on an acceptance test against the team's data and deployment requirements.

Option What the team buys or builds Incident-reconstruction trade-off
Infrai Use a common REST capability for centralized ingestion and basic queries; build the application's evidence contract and adapter. Fits a small workload with straightforward lookup needs. Choose a specialist for advanced distributed tracing or log export.
Grafana Loki Adopt a logging stack organized around labels and LogQL; decide who operates it. A candidate when label selection and log-query workflows fit the platform. Owning the deployment means owning capacity and on-call work.
Elasticsearch Build or adopt an indexed search workflow around its query interface. Consider it when richer search requirements justify an indexing and operations decision; test mappings and queries against the cohort fixtures.
Better Stack Evaluate managed logging as an alternative to operating the backend yourself. A candidate when reducing backend operations drives the purchase. Validate ingestion, retrieval, retention, and incident workflow before committing.

These are real alternatives, not interchangeable adapters by default. Loki's label model and Elasticsearch's indexed search model make different demands on the representation of evidence. Better Stack belongs in the managed-service evaluation. An HTTP interface alone doesn't erase those differences.

Infrai's scope here remains centralized ingestion and basic filtering. Build the choice around that scope. For paging rules and notification delivery, use a dedicated alerting system; for missed scheduled work, evaluate a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks. An investigator who needs source-map resolution, crash symbolication, or session replay should evaluate a specialist for those artifacts.

Retention policy, selective user-data deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions need a separate acceptance decision. Don't assume the basic logging boundary supplies those workflows, or treat an application log store as the sole compliance archive. Similarly, capture experiment assignments in the event itself rather than relying on a flag service to supply a historical change audit, evaluation statistics, or dependency history.

The recommendation becomes narrower, and more useful: buy a basic log capability when the question is which recorded application decisions differed between cohorts; buy deeper observability or a separate evidence system when the question requires artifacts outside those records.

A Go check at the query boundary

The preventative path has two acceptance checks: verify the event's decision context before ingestion, then verify retrieval through the selected adapter. For the three synthetic fixtures, reject a missing cohort or experiment revision before emitting a record. During retrieval, distinguish the two attempts for the same operation rather than counting the successful retry as an independent payment.

The following standalone program checks the HTTP side of retrieval. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with Go. It uses only the standard library, sends an explicit GET, checks status, and bounds both retries and response size. It prints the returned response without assuming a response schema or adding filter parameters.

This is the query-boundary check; the application still owns the cohort comparison.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 90 {
            return 91 * time.Second
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        delay := time.Until(date)
        if delay < 0 {
            return 0
        }
        return delay
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (1<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 1<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("response exceeds local 1 MiB limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("query returned HTTP %d: %s",
                resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The retry budget is deliberately finite. If Retry-After exceeds the overall waiting budget, the context expires and ends the operation rather than retrying before the server's requested delay. This read-only example needs no write deduplication; a production sender should separately verify the ingest contract's idempotency behavior before enabling write retries.

An HTTP success establishes that a response arrived. It does not establish cohort completeness. Retrieve the fixtures through the chosen contract, check their experiment revisions and attempt identities, and keep the payment SLO separate from the evidence SLI. If the investigation needs end-to-end span timing or a compliance archive, select that capability explicitly instead of stretching a basic log query into a promise it cannot support.

Sources

References for the logging concepts and the alternatives in the buy-versus-build decision:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Elasticsearch documentation
  • Better Stack logging documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the request contracts and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation, then use the same cohort fixtures to evaluate the alternatives.

title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control
description:
arXiv:2611.21865v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. Instruction-driven editing pipelines often leave such user-intent underspecified, while inpainting editors condition generation on explicitly defined edit support but not on the spatial assignment of individual edit concepts. PromptPack addresses both limitations by equipping diffusion editors with two explicit 'Edit Guides': an edit-role partition that labels each pixel as 'Keep,' 'Permit,' or 'Modify' to specify where edits may occur, and a regional-prompt assignment that maps spatial regions to text prompts to specify which concepts apply where. These guides may be manually specified or, for source-object edits, automatically derived from a text-grounded SAM 3 mask. Without retraining, PromptPack injects independently embedded regional prompts into the editor's fixed-length text sequence and uses the Edit Guides to spatially mask attention, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. We integrate PromptPack into FlowEdit FLUX, FlowEdit SD3, and FLUX Kontext and demonstrate improved requested-concept placement and protected-content preservation across all three integrations on PIE-Bench++. In a pairwise user study, PromptPack achieves an 87% preference rate over FlowEdit FLUX, establishing PromptPack as a practical, training-free interface for intent-aligned diffusion editing.

title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
description:
arXiv:2611.21825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.

title: VK 广告代理户还是自开户：App 开发团队怎么选
description:
以下是关于VK 广告的一份工作清单，来自 2026 年我们协助App 开发团队拓展西欧时的观察。

为什么VK 广告要单独规划

很多团队把 Meta 或 Google 的做法直接复制到新平台，VK 广告往往不吃这一套。受众意图、素材形式、审核规则都不同，出错的代价通常是账户被封而不是效果差一点。App 开发团队进入西欧之前，先为每个平台写一页计划：谁负责账户、用什么付款方式、哪些落地页已经过审、达到什么数据才加预算。

充值与付款权限管理

明确谁能充值、谁能改付款方式，并写成制度。每个账户只设一个账单联系人，发票统一存放，每周用平台报表对账。如果财务在其他时区，约定一个余额预警线，避免周五晚上在西欧因余额不足停投。

能过审的素材

审核会同时看首帧、卖点和落地页。避免前后对比、无法证明的数字和催促性用语，文字本地化成西欧的语言，落地页重复同一个优惠。信息一致既能过审，也能提升转化。

开户前要备齐的资料

主体名称要和网站页脚一致，准备自有域名的企业邮箱、隐私政策、服务条款、退款政策和可联系的联系页面。VK 广告的审核会把这些信息和广告、落地页放在一起比对，不一致是新账户卡审最常见的原因。延伸阅读：广告平台开户费用对比。

常见错误

  • 把别的平台素材原样搬到VK 广告。
  • 同一天同时改预算、受众和素材，结果无法解读。
  • 唯一的管理员账号握在一个外包手里。
  • 广告被拒之前从不看政策中心。
  • 追踪还没验证就判断渠道好坏。

第一天就把数据打通

安装像素或 SDK，能做服务端事件就做，广告系列命名统一规则，方便合并报表。App 开发团队应只定义一个主转化（试用、购买或有效线索），其他事件只做诊断用，否则没人说得清VK 广告到底有没有效果。

30 天上线节奏

第 1 周：账户、付款、追踪和两个落地页；第 2 周：3–5 个素材方向小预算测试；第 3 周：砍掉后一半，把赢家复制到第二个受众；第 4 周：对照目标看主转化成本，决定加量、维持或停止。把过程记下来，第二个市场会便宜很多。

要点

这些事都不复杂，但必须按顺序做：先事实和追踪，再放量。

作者：熊猫出海 PandaWM（香港团队）。业务包括 GEO/AI 搜索优化、Facebook/Google/TikTok 及约 20 个小众平台广告开户与代投、多语言网站、AiChatSale，以及只服务海外商户的加密支付网关。

title: Why I Chose Node.js Caching for SaaS Export Signed URLs: Rate-Limit Control
description:
Short answer: For a Node.js SaaS export pipeline, cache still-valid signed URLs, persist the export job and object key, and use exponential backoff with idempotent retries around presign calls; object storage should deliver the bytes directly.

File exports are a storage problem and a request-shaping problem. A presign endpoint should not run on every export-page refresh. My default is to persist the export job and object key, cache one still-valid signed URL for a short window, then retry with exponential backoff when the presign call is rate-limited.

That is the whole fix in one sentence. Keep the app in charge of access decisions; let storage deliver the finished object.

Infrai is one option for that presign boundary, using one key and one bill across backend capabilities while its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas with runnable examples, so wiring the capability does not require learning a new SDK first.

What changes between a refresh storm and a controlled download?

Picture the request path as a small diagram in words: browser asks for an export, API checks the export record, API reuses a cached URL or signs once, and the browser downloads directly from the bucket. In the failure mode, every refresh repeats the signing step, several workers retry immediately, and the rate limiter sees a burst for the same object.

I once debugged a similar shape with a counter rather than a dashboard: 12 refreshes in a minute became 12 signing calls for one key. The useful number was not download bandwidth. It was duplicate presign work. A short cache window and a stable export record removed that multiplication.

The record needs an application-owned idempotency key, such as accountId:exportId. Store the object key, job state, and the signed URL expiration timestamp. If a user requests the same export again, return the existing job while it is valid. If the URL is near expiry, sign a replacement once and update the record under a database lock or queue. In a busy SaaS tenant, that coordination also has to cover a worker finishing at the same moment that a browser refresh arrives: the winner writes the URL and expiry, while the loser rereads the record instead of issuing a second presign call. This is where a tiny mutex or transactional compare-and-set earns its keep, because retrying a duplicate signing request can make a rate-limit incident look like a storage outage even when downloads themselves are healthy.

The catch is that access control and delivery simplicity pull in different directions. A long-lived public URL is easy to share, but this storage setup does not provide a public-read ACL or a permanent public URL. Keep the link private and short-lived when the export contains account data.

How should Node.js handle presign rate limits, caching, and retries?

Here is a minimal TypeScript sketch. It uses one storage route, an explicit method, bearer authentication, a client idempotency key, and Retry-After when the service supplies it. The response body is checked instead of assuming a 200.

type PresignResult = { url: string; expires_at?: string };

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function presign(bucket: string, key: string, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<PresignResult> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({}),
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return (await response.json()) as PresignResult;

    const body = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 4) {
      throw new Error(`presign failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

In production, put the result in Redis or your database with an expiry comfortably before the signed URL expires. Add a per-export mutex so two concurrent requests do not both discover a cache miss and sign twice. The retry loop is for transient pressure, not a substitute for that coordination.

Do not use the trial balance for persistent writes; the storage facts mark that balance as restricted. Also watch the bucket rather than guessing. Export files accumulate quietly, and lifecycle cleanup has a one-day minimum expiration, so hourly cleanup is not an option here.

Which storage choice fits a private export pipeline?

The table is intentionally about boundaries, not a winner badge. Verify current regional, retention, and deletion terms with the provider before committing regulated data.

Option Strength in this workflow Boundary to check
Amazon S3 Mature object storage and presigned-download pattern You own policy, region selection, lifecycle rules, and the number of SDKs and credentials in the app
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage option for teams already using Cloudflare Confirm the regions, retention controls, and egress assumptions that fit your users
Azure Blob Storage Natural fit when the rest of the SaaS runs on Azure identity and regions Confirm equivalent signed-link, deletion, and processor-contract details
Infrai storage One REST API with a public discovery surface and runnable examples, so a Node.js service can inspect a capability before wiring it No public URLs, object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or self-service CORS route; lifecycle expiry is at least one day

I recommend trying Infrai for the presign step when your team values a self-describing API and wants one authenticated surface across backend capabilities. Discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, and the same key and conventions can reduce integration bookkeeping around the export service. That does not move your processor boundary: the object still lives with the selected storage vendor, and your legal and regional requirements remain yours to verify.

Stick with direct S3, R2, or Blob APIs when you need provider-specific replication, WORM-style retention, public hosting, or browser upload CORS that you must configure yourself. This gateway is not suitable when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable through versioning or when an hourly lifecycle policy is mandatory. Your mileage may vary by jurisdiction; I am not sure a generic API layer can satisfy a contract that names a particular processor or region, so get that answer in writing.

What should you measure after the fix?

Start with four counters: presign requests, 429 responses, cache-hit rate, and exports requested per job id. Add object count and bucket usage so cleanup is visible. A healthy trace should show many page views leading to one presign call, followed by direct downloads.

When a job is complete, retain its object key and status long enough for the product policy, then delete the object and record together. The storage lifecycle route can help with the retention floor, but application deletion is still the clear path for an account-erasure request. Keep logs free of signed URLs; log the export id, key hash, status, latency, and request id instead.

The practical rule is simple: cache the permissioned link, not the permission decision. Re-check ownership in your API, reuse the signed URL only inside its validity window, and make retries boring.

Further reading

  • Capability index
  • Storage discovery example
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • AWS EFS managed file system
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob shared access signatures
  • Node.js fetch API

For the storage presign schema and a runnable starting point, see the storage capability index.

title: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB
description:
Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

  • Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.

  • Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.

  • Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

Why do sessions need a database?

Say a team deploys its Strands agent as an AWS Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation runs in a disposable environment (i.e., a scratchpad for the agent). There may be no local disk, and no guarantee that the next invocation lands on the same instance, so the state tied to one process is invisible to the next.

With this integration, every agent session is saved in MongoDB. Each invocation loads the session by its ID and carries on, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. Long-term memories the agent saves to MongoDBMemoryStore persist beyond the session, so they’re available the next time that user returns.

Figure 1. Stateless agent architecture keeps state out of the agent process.

Two Lambda instances serve consecutive turns of the same session. Both read and write the session via MongoDBStorage and long-term memory via MongoDBMemoryStore, so neither depends on the other's local state. That matters most for enterprises with many teams running Strands agents across different machines. They get one MongoDB-backed foundation for agent state and memory, instead of building and maintaining separate systems to store and retrieve sessions and memory.

What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

  • Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place.

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

  • No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op. For example, if the agent extracts "Prefers metric units and a 24-hour clock" a second time, the store keeps the copy it already has, with its original timestamp and expiry. This means that, as a developer, you don’t need to write your own deduplication logic, and your memory store stays clean, regardless of how often the agent re-extracts the same fact.

  • Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata. This isolation is enforced by the package, not by the server, so where a tenant boundary is also a compliance boundary, give each tenant its own database or collection, with credentials restricted to it, and MongoDB enforces the boundary itself.

  • Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

How it works

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

As you can see above, the query and the stored fact share no words, but the store still finds it. This path needs an Atlas cluster with an embedding model registered. If you already produce your own embeddings, the store can index and query them instead; the README covers the additional code required.

Figure 2. Without an embedding pipeline, memory is just text in and text out. Atlas generates and stores the embeddings and embeds each query before running $vectorSearch.

store.add() writes plain text and returns. Atlas embeds it in the background, and embeds each search query the same way before running $vectorSearch. Bringing your own embedding model is optional.

Sessions and memory together: One connection config serves both. Hand them to the agent and let the SDK wire them up:

The storage= parameter makes MongoDB the default backend for five SDK subsystems, including sessions, context offloading, and transcripts. The SDK's SnapshotSessionManager saves the conversation under its session ID, and any agent built with that ID restores it. MemoryManager gives the model a tool to search memory and, with add_tool_config=True, one to save to it. There's no MongoDB-specific session class to learn.

Figure 3. After a Strands agent is wired to MongoDB, it can save and restore conversations and search long-term memory without any MongoDB-specific session code.

Three agent parameters do the wiring. storage= points the SDK's storage subsystems at MongoDBStorage, session_manager= saves and restores the conversation by session ID, and memory_manager= gives the model search and save tools backed by MongoDBMemoryStore.

Get started today!

strands-mongodb requires Python 3.10 or later and strands-agents 1.54.0 or later. MongoDBStorage works on any MongoDB deployment; memory search with Automated Embedding needs MongoDB Atlas. Install it with the following commands:

Moving from the mongodb_memory tool or a community MongoDB package? MIGRATION has the field mapping and a copy script.

Explore the source, open issues, or contribute on GitHub. 

The README covers connection options, the full configuration reference, and index privileges.

  • Strands memory overview

  • Strands storage documentation

  • Strands session management documentation

title: ORA-04068 After a Deploy: The Retry Works. The Package State Is Gone.
description:
The release went fine. Every script ran, every package compiled, the smoke test passed. A minute later the application log fills with this:

ORA-04068: existing state of packages has been discarded
ORA-04061: existing state of package body "APP.PRICING" has been invalidated
ORA-04065: not executed, altered or dropped package body "APP.PRICING"

Then it stops. A few dozen errors, one per connection, and nothing after. Someone opens an incident, someone else suggests rolling back, and by the time anyone looks, the errors are gone.

The package isn't broken. It holds state, the deploy threw that state away, and Oracle told each session about it the first time it came back. The error is the visible part. The quieter part is that the retry works with the state reset, and not only for the package you deployed.

This post covers what the error means, which packages and which changes raise it (two of them look harmless), what a connection pool sees, and how to deploy PL/SQL without it. It ends with a lab that proves each step on Oracle Database Free 26ai.

What the error means

Each session that uses a package gets its own copy of the package's variables: its package state. A counter, a cached config row, a flag set at login, a lookup table loaded once. Oracle's PL/SQL Language Reference calls a package stateful if it declares at least one variable, constant or cursor, and stateless otherwise. That state lives for the whole session.

Except when the package body is recompiled. A deploy (CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY), an explicit ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE, or an automatic recompile after something the package depends on changed. The state in every session was built by the old code, so it can't be kept. The next time a session calls the package, Oracle discards that state and raises ORA-04068. The two errors under it say which package, and why.

In the lab, a session called a package with one variable, a call counter, twice: 1, 2. The deploy replaced the package body. The session's next call failed with exactly the three errors above. The call after that worked, ran the new code, and returned 1. The counter started again from its initial value.

Two things the error does not do, both checked in the lab:

  • It doesn't roll back the session's transaction. The session had an uncommitted insert before the deploy. It was still there after the error.
  • It doesn't come back. It's raised once per session per recompile. The next call re-creates the package state from scratch and runs.

It's the state, not the change

Whether a deploy raises ORA-04068 doesn't depend on how big the change is. It depends on whether the package holds state when it's recompiled. In the lab, a session used each package, one change was deployed, and the session called the package again:

Package Change deployed Next call
no package variables new body no error, new code at once
no package variables new spec (a function added) and body no error, new code at once
only a literal constant (c_rate CONSTANT NUMBER := 5) new body no error, new code at once
a constant set at load (c_loaded CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE) new body ORA-04068
one variable ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE BODY, no code change ORA-04068
a %ROWTYPE variable on ORDERS ALTER TABLE orders ADD a column ORA-04068
a variable, but the code names its columns the same ADD column no error

Three of these surprise people.

A constant isn't always a constant. Oracle treats a package as stateless if its state can't change for the life of a session, which is the case when every item is a compile-time constant. A literal is one. SYSDATE isn't: its value is set when the session first uses the package. So c_loaded CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE makes the package stateful, and the deploy that changed nothing else raised ORA-04068.

A recompile with no change is enough. ALTER PACKAGE pricing COMPILE BODY, with the exact same code, raised it. So does any script that recompiles invalid objects after a release, for every stateful package it touches.

DDL on a table can do it, with no PL/SQL deploy at all. A package body with a variable declared as orders%ROWTYPE depends on the table's column list. ALTER TABLE orders ADD a column invalidated it, and the next call raised ORA-04068. A package that used the same table but named its columns stayed VALID and didn't raise it. So the ADD COLUMN that waited politely for its lock can still throw errors at the application once it runs.

The other direction also held. A package with no variables switched to the new code silently, even when its spec changed. In a hand run, a standalone function that called that package was invalidated by the spec change, recompiled itself on its next call, and also raised nothing.

It resets packages the release didn't touch

The documentation has one more sentence that's easy to read past: all of a session's package states can be lost if any of its instantiated packages is invalidated and revalidated.

The lab tested it. A session used two packages, PRICING and AUDIT_CTX, each with its own counter. The release recompiled only AUDIT_CTX.

PRICING   (not redeployed): 1, 2, 3        then, after AUDIT_CTX's error: 1
AUDIT_CTX (recompiled):     1, ORA-04068, 1

PRICING kept counting until the session called AUDIT_CTX and got ORA-04068. After that, PRICING was back to 1 too. Its code hadn't changed and nobody had deployed it, but its state was gone. (In a hand run, recompiling a package without variables didn't do this: the session's other packages kept their state.)

So "we only changed one package" doesn't limit the damage. Any session that hits ORA-04068 for any package starts again with every package's state at its initial value. If one of them caches a user's permissions, a tenant ID or a feature flag, the retry that "fixed" the error runs with the defaults.

A recompile of a stateful package doesn't fail the deploy. It fails the next call in every session that had used the package, once, and that session's retry starts with every package's state at its initial value. Packages without state, SERIALLY_REUSABLE packages and edition-based redefinition avoid the error.

What a connection pool sees

A connection pool turns one recompile into a burst. Each pooled connection is a session, so each one that had used the package raises ORA-04068 once.

The lab opened 8 sessions; 6 of them called the package, 2 didn't. After one deploy, every session called it twice:

first round after the deploy:  6 of 8 calls failed with ORA-04068
second round:                  0 of 8

The 2 sessions that had never used the package got the new code with no error. The 6 that had used it failed once each, even though the call they made after the deploy only read a version string and never touched the variable. What's discarded is the session's copy of the package, not one variable.

That's the shape to recognize in a log: a burst right after a deploy, about one error per connection, then nothing. A pool of 200 connections gives you up to 200 errors and 200 resets of the package state. Unless your code retries, each of those errors is a failed user request.

Find the stateful packages before you deploy

There's no column in the data dictionary that says "this package is stateful", but PL/Scope can tell you. Compile with identifier collection on, then list the declarations at package level:

ALTER SESSION SET plscope_settings = 'IDENTIFIERS:ALL';
ALTER PACKAGE pricing COMPILE;          -- for each package you want to check

SELECT object_name, object_type, name, type
FROM   user_identifiers
WHERE  object_type IN ('PACKAGE', 'PACKAGE BODY')
AND    usage = 'DECLARATION'
AND    type IN ('VARIABLE', 'CONSTANT', 'CURSOR')
AND    usage_context_id = 1               -- declared at package level, not inside a subprogram
ORDER  BY object_name, object_type;

In a hand run on 26ai it listed the counter variable, a package-level cursor, and both constants. It didn't list the packages without package-level declarations. Check the CONSTANT rows by eye: a literal (:= 5) is stateless, anything else (:= SYSDATE, a function call) isn't. Note that ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE is itself a recompile, so run this on a test database, not under a live application.

Deploy without it

There are four ways to deal with it. They're not equal.

1. Keep state out of packages. A package without variables has nothing to discard. In the lab it took the new code with no error every time, spec change included. If a value must survive across calls, keep it somewhere a recompile doesn't touch: a table, or an application context (SYS_CONTEXT), which belongs to the session rather than to a package. In a hand run, a tenant ID set in an application context was still there after ORA-04068 had reset the package counter in the same session. This is the real fix, and it means changing the code.

2. Retry once in the application. The second call works, so catching ORA-04068 and retrying the call makes the burst invisible to users. It's cheap, and many teams do it. But the retry runs with every package's state reset, including packages the deploy didn't touch. Only retry if the code re-creates any state it needs, for example by re-running its login initialization.

3. PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE. A serially reusable package keeps its state only for the duration of one server call. In the lab, the deploy raised no error and the very next call ran the new code. The cost is in the name: the counter was 1 on every call, before and after the deploy, because nothing survives between calls. And a serially reusable package can't be called from SQL at all: SELECT pricing.version FROM dual failed with ORA-06534: Cannot access Serially Reusable package. It suits packages that only use their variables within one call. It isn't a switch you can turn on for a package that relies on its state.

4. Edition-based redefinition (EBR). Editions let two versions of the same package exist at once. Each session sees the version in its own edition. The release is compiled in a new edition while running sessions keep using the old one:

-- once, as a DBA: enable editions for the schema owner (this can't be undone)
ALTER USER app ENABLE EDITIONS;

-- per release
CREATE EDITION rel2;
GRANT USE ON EDITION rel2 TO app;

-- the deploy, in a session switched to the new edition
ALTER SESSION SET EDITION = rel2;
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pricing AS ... END;

-- when you're ready for new connections to get the release
ALTER DATABASE DEFAULT EDITION = rel2;

In the lab, a session in the old edition (ORA$BASE) called the package before and after the new body was compiled in REL2: 1, 2, 3. No error, no reset, still the old code. A new session also got the old code until ALTER DATABASE DEFAULT EDITION = REL2; after that, new sessions got the new code. A connection pool moves to the release as its connections are replaced, and none of them sees ORA-04068 on the way.

EBR is in every edition of the database, Free included. The catch is preparation: ENABLE EDITIONS is one-way, and tables aren't editioned, so changes to table structure need editioning views and crossedition triggers to fully avoid downtime. For PL/SQL-only releases, it does exactly what this error needs.

Prove it

The lab runs Oracle Database Free in a container. Each "user" session is a SQL*Plus session that calls the package, waits for the deploy, then calls it again:

drill    case                                                 result
error    package body replaced under a live session           ORA-04068 / 04061 / 04065 once; the retry works,
                                                              counter back to 1; uncommitted insert kept
collat   only AUDIT_CTX recompiled, session also uses PRICING PRICING reset to 1 too, after AUDIT_CTX's error
which    no variables (new body; new spec)                    no error, new code
         a literal constant                                   no error, new code
         CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE                             ORA-04068
         ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE BODY, no code change       ORA-04068
         %ROWTYPE variable, then ALTER TABLE ... ADD          ORA-04068 (named columns: no error)
pool     8 sessions, 6 had used it, one deploy                6 errors, then 0
serial   PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE                             no error, new code at once; counter always 1;
                                                              ORA-06534 from SQL
edition  new body compiled in edition REL2                    live session: no error, 1, 2, 3 on the old code;
                                                              new sessions: new code after the default switch

Don't take my word for it — run it. The package-state lab asserts every row: the three-error stack and the counter starting again at 1 after the retry, with the uncommitted insert still there; the untouched package reset by another package's error; which packages and changes raise it and which don't; exactly 6 errors from the 6 pooled sessions that had used the package and none on the second round; the serially reusable package's missing error, missing state and ORA-06534; and the live session in the old edition counting on with no error. If any of that doesn't reproduce, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

What teams get wrong

  • Rolling back a good release. The burst looks like a broken deploy. It's one error per connection, and it's over by the time anyone looks. Rolling back is another recompile, and another burst.
  • Assuming the retry is clean. It runs, but with every package's state reset, including packages the release didn't touch.
  • Thinking CONSTANT means stateless. Only compile-time constants do. := SYSDATE makes the package stateful.
  • Recompiling "just to be safe". A no-change COMPILE BODY raises it for every session that had used the package.
  • Forgetting that table DDL recompiles PL/SQL. An ADD column under a %ROWTYPE package variable raises it, with no PL/SQL in the release.
  • Adding SERIALLY_REUSABLE to make the error go away. It does, along with the state, and SQL can no longer call the package.

Frequently asked questions

What does ORA-04068 existing state of packages has been discarded mean?

A session had used a PL/SQL package that holds state (package-level variables, cursors, or constants that aren't compile-time constants), and the package body was recompiled since: by a deploy, an ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE, or an automatic recompile after a dependency changed. Oracle can't keep state built by the old code, so on the session's next call it discards the state and raises ORA-04068, with ORA-04061 and ORA-04065 naming the package. The next call re-creates the state from scratch and works.

Why does ORA-04068 go away when I run the call again?

Because the error is raised once per session per recompile. The failing call discards the session's package state; the next call re-instantiates the package with its initial values and runs the new code. In the companion lab the retry worked every time, but a counter the session had built up was back to 1. Any value the package had cached for the session is gone.

How do I prevent ORA-04068 after deploying a PL/SQL package?

Keep state out of packages you redeploy (a package with no variables, or only literal constants, switched to new code with no error in the companion lab), retry the call once in the application if your code can re-create the state it needs, use PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE for packages that only need state within one call, or deploy with edition-based redefinition so running sessions keep the old version. In the lab, a session in the old edition saw no error and kept its state while the new code was compiled in a new edition.

Can ORA-04068 happen for a package I didn't change?

Yes, in two ways. A package is recompiled automatically when something it depends on changes: in the companion lab, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN invalidated a package with a %ROWTYPE variable on that table, and the next call raised ORA-04068. And once a session gets ORA-04068 for any package, it loses the state of all its packages: in the lab, a package the release never touched was reset to its initial value after another package's error.

Does PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE fix ORA-04068?

It avoids it: in the companion lab, a serially reusable package raised no error after its body was replaced, and the next call ran the new code. But its state lasts only for one server call, so a counter was 1 on every call, and it can't be called from SQL: a SELECT that called it failed with ORA-06534. Use it for packages that don't rely on state between calls.

Does a package constant cause ORA-04068?

Only if it isn't a compile-time constant. Oracle treats a package whose items are all compile-time constants as stateless, and a literal (CONSTANT NUMBER := 5) is one: in the companion lab that package switched to new code with no error. A constant set from SYSDATE or a function call gets its value at run time, so the package is stateful, and in the lab it raised ORA-04068 after a deploy.

ORA-04068 after a deploy isn't a failed release. It's every session that had used a stateful package finding out that its state is gone, once, and starting again with all of its package state at the initial values. Know which of your packages hold state, keep it out of the ones you redeploy, and when you can't, compile the release in a new edition so the live sessions never notice. Then prove it with the package-state lab, where one deploy fails 6 of 8 pooled connections once and resets a package nobody deployed.

Originally published at uptimearchitect.com.

title: My keyword filter read "tomografia computadorizada" as a computer purchase
description:
I follow the small municipalities around my region in Brazil. Everything they buy is published as a text description in a national procurement API, and a share of those purchases is IT work I can bid on: maintenance contracts, network cabling, software licenses, toner, a hosted portal. The API has no full text search worth using, so I wrote a filter over the object description. Last run made 424 requests across four procurement modalities, found 165 objects containing an IT term, and marked 12 of them as billable under the MEI occupations I hold today.

The filter is a keyword classifier. It has two ways to be wrong, and they cost very different things. A false positive costs me a minute of reading. A false negative costs the opportunity and leaves no trace in the run. Everything below came from a real object that fooled it.

Accents first, because the source is Portuguese

Object descriptions arrive in uppercase, with and without accents, and often carry a platform prefix like [Portal de Compras Publicas] -. Both get normalized before any matching:

def sem_acento(txt):
    n = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', txt or '')
    return ''.join(c for c in n if not unicodedata.combining(c)).lower()

def limpa_objeto(txt):
    """Remove prefixos de plataforma tipo '[Portal de Compras Publicas] - '."""
    t = re.sub(r'^\s*\[[^\]]{0,60}\]\s*-?\s*', '', (txt or '').strip())
    return re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', t).strip()

NFKD decomposition plus a filter on combining characters turns Manutenção into manutencao. Without it, half my keyword list never matches, and the failure is invisible because a filter that finds nothing looks like a quiet week.

Short terms need a word boundary

Seventy-four terms make up the strong list. Most are long enough that a plain substring test is correct: computador should match computadores, and that inflection is the normal case in Portuguese. Short terms behave differently, because they live inside other words.

    for termo in FORTES:
        if len(termo) <= 3:
            if re.search(r'\b' + re.escape(termo) + r'\b', t):
                achados.append(termo)
        elif termo in t:
            achados.append(termo)

One term in the list is short enough to need it: ti. A plain substring test on those two letters fires on licitacao, noticia and importante, which appear in most of a procurement feed. Everything longer stays on the substring test, rack included, because computador has to match computadores and that inflection is the rule rather than the exception.

Ambiguous words need a companion in the same sentence

Four terms are real IT vocabulary and also everyday Portuguese: servidor (server, or civil servant), suporte tecnico (IT support, or support for anything), cartucho (printer cartridge, or respirator cartridge), licenca (software license, or a professional registration fee). Those four never classify an object on their own:

    if all(a in TERMOS_FRACOS for a in achados):
        if not any(c in t for c in COMPANHIA_IT):
            return achados, 'termo ambiguo sem companhia de TI'

The companion list has 53 entries, from impressora to cabeamento. The rule was added after a measurement on 19/10/2026 over 173 findings: without it, 15 objects entered by mistake, among them medical expert examinations, uniforms, a marmitex lunch contract, a water cooler, an LED panel rental, and two consultancy contracts in social assistance and public transparency. No legitimate object was lost by adding it.

That measurement is the reason I trust the rule. Fifteen wrong entries in 173 was enough to act on, and losing no legitimate object is what made the rule safe to keep.

The reject list is a log with dates

Eighty-three entries exist to kill a match even when a strong term is present. Each one came from a specific sentence:

  • tomografia computadorizada matched computador.
  • filmes radiologicos para impressora de imagens medicas matched impressora.
  • leite integral UHT para pacientes, acompanhantes e servidores da Fundacao matched servidor.
  • independente de transcricao is boilerplate at the end of a metalwork contract and matched transcricao.
  • licenca anual de Anotacao de Responsabilidade Tecnica matched licenca.
  • linha fixa for a telephone line matched telephony, which is not an occupation of mine.

The comments in the file carry the date of the scan that produced each group. That turns the reject list into a record of what the source actually contains, and the next person editing it can see why a line exists instead of deleting it as noise.

One reject entry nearly killed a real opportunity

Civil servants are everywhere in this feed. A notice for a basic computing course aimed at municipal employees is a legitimate purchase I can invoice, and it contains the word servidor in its most common sense. The reject rule therefore has an exception:

    for r in RUIDO:
        if r in t:
            if r in RUIDO_SERVIDOR and any(f in t for f in SERVICO_DE_MEI):
                continue
            return achados, r

If the noise belongs to the group about people, and the same object also matches a service I actually sell, the object survives. Without those two lists, curso de informatica para os servidores municipais would be dropped by my own filter, silently, and it is one of the few things I can invoice.

The tests are a list of inputs that must be rejected

The test file holds 15 positive cases and 24 negative ones, and it fails the run when any of them misses. A negative case passes when the classifier finds no term at all, or when it finds terms and returns a reason to discard:

for nome, txt in negativo:
    a, m = v.classifica(txt)
    ok = (not a) or bool(m)
    falhas += 0 if ok else 1

The negative list is the valuable half, because I wrote it by pasting objects that had already fooled the filter. AQUISICAO DE FILMES RADIOLOGICOS DRY FILM PARA IMPRESSORA DE IMAGENS MEDICAS is in there. So is a car rental that mentions computer maintenance, and a school lunch contract that mentions IT equipment.

One case checks the reason, not the outcome. A bank accreditation notice matches digitacao and would be labeled with my data entry occupation. The correct behavior is a discard by a specific noise entry, so the assertion names the entry:

achados, ruido = v.classifica(txt_banco)
ok = bool(achados) and ruido in ('instituicoes financeiras', 'arrecadacao de tributos',
                                 'documento de arrecadacao municipal')

Written as "no profile, therefore fine", that test would pass for any future reason, including a rule that drops legitimate notices. The same notice, from Senador Modestino, had already been published as billable before the fix.

Recall fails without a message

On 16/11/2026 a Diamantina notice for aquisicao de computadores was marked as outside my MEI, which was wrong, since buying computers falls under a commerce occupation I can use. The fix added four phrases that name the purchase explicitly: aquisicao de computadores, fornecimento de computadores, aquisicao de microcomputadores, aquisicao de computadores e perifericos.

I did not add computador alone to that list, even though it would have caught the case. It would also match spare parts, maintenance and rental, and those are different occupations. The narrower fix costs a future miss and keeps the report honest.

That is the asymmetry I plan around. Precision errors show up in the output and get fixed in a minute. Recall errors do not show up at all, which is why the report is read every week instead of trusted. The test suite catches what I thought of. Reading the notices catches what I did not.

Today the filter has 74 strong terms, 53 companion terms and 83 noise entries. Run against the current snapshot of 164 objects, none of them would be dropped by the rules as they stand, and the control suite finishes with zero failures. None of that says the next municipality uses a phrase I have not seen.

Se você mantém algum filtro de palavra-chave em cima de texto de terceiro, comenta qual foi o primeiro falso positivo que te obrigou a escrever um teste. Eu respondo em português aqui embaixo.
