title: What's inside one AI data answer, and how to build a 'show your work' panel for it
description:
"Revenue is up 18%." Is it? An AI answer about your data that arrives as one sentence gives the reader nothing to check, so they either trust it blindly or come and ask you.

A good answer has parts. This post takes one real response apart and builds the small panel that shows each part in the right place.

The parts

Here is a real answer from FactQL's public sample data, to the question "Who are our top 5 customers by total spend?":

Part Field Where it goes
The answer in words explanation On top, always visible
The rows it came from data.columns, data.rows A table under the answer
The query that ran sql Folded away, one click to open
Where the numbers came from lineage.text A small line, when present

The order is the point: answer first for people in a hurry, rows for people who want to check, the query for the one person who needs it.

The code

Two functions. toView shapes the response and has no DOM in it, so you can unit-test it. renderAnswer draws.

// Turn a raw answer into exactly what the panel shows. No DOM here, so it is easy to test.
export function toView(a, maxRows = 10) {
  const table = a.data ?? {};                       // rows live under "data"
  const columns = table.columns ?? [];
  const rows = (table.rows ?? []).map((row) =>
    row.map((v) => (typeof v === "number" && !Number.isInteger(v) ? Number(v.toFixed(2)) : v)));
  return {
    ok: a.result === "success",
    answer: a.explanation ?? "No answer.",
    columns,
    rows: rows.slice(0, maxRows),
    hiddenRows: Math.max(0, rows.length - maxRows),
    query: a.sql ?? null,                           // folded away by default
    source: a.lineage?.text ?? null,                // "where the numbers came from", when present
  };
}

// The panel itself: answer on top, rows under it, the query behind a click.
export function renderAnswer(a, el) {
  const v = toView(a);
  const add = (tag, text, parent = el) => { const n = document.createElement(tag); n.textContent = text; parent.append(n); return n; };
  el.textContent = "";
  add("p", v.answer);
  if (v.rows.length) {
    const t = add("table", ""), head = add("tr", "", t);
    v.columns.forEach((c) => add("th", c, head));
    v.rows.forEach((row) => { const tr = add("tr", "", t); row.forEach((cell) => add("td", String(cell), tr)); });
    if (v.hiddenRows) add("p", `…and ${v.hiddenRows} more rows`);
  }
  if (v.source) add("p", v.source);
  if (v.query) { const d = add("details", ""); add("summary", "The query that ran", d); add("pre", v.query, d); }
}

Testing the shaping

I ran toView in Node against the real response (18 Nov 2026), with maxRows set to 3:

{
  ok: true,
  answer: 'Your top 5 customers by total spend are Karl Seal, Tim Cary, Russell Brinson, Harry Arce and Daisy Bates. ...',
  columns: [ 'customer_id', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'total_spend' ],
  rows: [ [ 526, 'KARL', 'SEAL', 358.12 ], [ 468, 'TIM', 'CARY', 344.06 ], [ 380, 'RUSSELL', 'BRINSON', 324.04 ] ],
  hiddenRows: 2,
  query: 'SELECT ...',
  source: null
}

Five small decisions, and why

  1. Round floats for display. The raw value was 358.1200000000005. Nobody wants that in a table.
  2. Cap the rows and say how many are hidden. A table of 4,000 rows is not "showing your work".
  3. Use textContent, never innerHTML. Cell values are data. Treat them as text.
  4. Treat optional parts as optional. In my test lineage came back null, so the panel shows that line only when it exists.
  5. Fold the query. Most readers never open it. The ones who do are the ones who would otherwise message you.

When there's no data answer

The second test case is a response with no rows. toView returns the sentence and empty arrays, and the panel shows just the sentence. No empty table, no broken layout.

What do your users ask for first when they doubt a number: the rows, or the query?

title: How I set up a JSON mock server for a frontend team in an afternoon
description:
Last spring our frontend team had a sprint planned around a new orders dashboard. The designs were done, the tickets were groomed, and the backend was nowhere close. The API contract existed as a shared doc with three open comments on it. Four frontend devs were about to spend two weeks building against TODO and hard-coded arrays.

I'd seen that movie before. Everyone writes their own fake data inside components, nobody's fake data matches anyone else's, and the week the real API lands you spend two days ripping out mocks and finding out the date format was different all along.

So I blocked off an afternoon and gave the team a shared mock server instead. Here's exactly what I did, what worked, and the one thing I'd do differently.

Start from the contract, not from the UI

The temptation is to look at the Figma file and invent data that makes the screens look good. Don't. Open the API contract (or whatever the backend team has written down, even a Slack thread) and copy the field names exactly. If they say created_at in snake case, your fake data says created_at in snake case, even if it annoys you.

I asked the backend lead for fifteen minutes and we agreed on three endpoints:

  • GET /orders returning a list
  • GET /orders/:id returning one order with line items
  • PATCH /orders/:id to update status

That was enough to unblock the whole dashboard.

The JSON file

I used json-server because it takes a single file and gives you REST routes for free. Install it as a dev dependency so it's pinned with the project:

npm install --save-dev json-server

Then a mock/db.json at the repo root:

{
  "orders": [
    {
      "id": 1001,
      "status": "pending",
      "customer_name": "Test Customer A",
      "total_cents": 4599,
      "currency": "USD",
      "created_at": "2026-03-02T09:14:00Z",
      "items": [
        { "sku": "SKU-RED-01", "qty": 2, "price_cents": 1500 },
        { "sku": "SKU-BLU-07", "qty": 1, "price_cents": 1599 }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": 1002,
      "status": "shipped",
      "customer_name": "Test Customer B",
      "total_cents": 0,
      "currency": "USD",
      "created_at": "2026-03-01T22:40:00Z",
      "items": []
    }
  ]
}

Notice order 1002. Zero total, empty items. I put that in on purpose. Mock data that only has happy, fully populated records trains your UI to break on the first weird row in production.

Add a script:

"scripts": {
  "mock": "json-server --watch mock/db.json --port 4000"
}

Run npm run mock and you've got GET /orders, GET /orders/1001, PATCH /orders/1001 and friends, all backed by a file you can commit.

Point the app at it with one variable

The frontend already read its API base URL from an env var. I added a .env.mock:

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000

and a script dev:mock that loaded it. That's the whole switch. No if (isMock) branches in components, no special fetch wrapper. When the real API shows up, you change the URL and nothing else.

Fake the slow and the broken too

Real APIs are slow sometimes and fail sometimes. A json mock server that always answers in 2ms hides every loading-state bug you have. json-server takes a --delay flag, so I added a second script:

"mock:slow": "json-server --watch mock/db.json --port 4000 --delay 1500"

For errors I wrote a tiny middleware file that returns a 500 whenever a request has ?fail=1 on it. Twelve lines. It caught two missing error states in the first week, which paid for the whole afternoon.

What I got wrong

I let the mock data drift. By week two people had added fields to db.json that weren't in the contract because "the UI needed it." Some of those were reasonable asks, but they never made it back to the backend team. When the real API landed, three fields we'd been rendering didn't exist.

The fix is boring. Any change to db.json goes in its own PR, and the backend lead is a required reviewer on that path. Mock data is a contract, and contracts need two signatures.

There's a deeper issue too, and it's the reason I don't think hand-written mocks should live forever. A file you wrote by hand only knows what you thought the API would do. Once a real backend exists, it's worth looking at approaches that capture real responses and replay them, so your fakes are grounded in actual traffic. If you want the bigger picture on how a json mock server fits next to recorded mocks and other options, that write-up covers the trade-offs well.

My opinion: keep it dumb

People asked if we should add GraphQL, auth simulation, random data generators, the works. I said no. The value of this setup was that anyone on the team could open one JSON file and understand what the "API" would return. The moment your mock needs its own documentation, it's become a second backend that nobody owns.

Faker-style random data is the one I'd push back on hardest. Random names are fine, but random structure makes bugs unreproducible. If a teammate says "the table breaks on order 1002," everyone should see the same order 1002.

How the sprint actually went

The frontend shipped the dashboard against the mock in nine working days. The real API landed on day eleven. Switching over took about half a day, most of it spent on those three drifted fields I mentioned. Not zero, but a lot better than four devs idling for a week.

A practical tip before you try this

Put the mock server in the repo, not on someone's laptop or a shared box. When it's a committed file plus an npm script, new hires get it on day one, CI can run against it, and nobody has to ask "is the mock up?" ever again.

What's the weirdest record you keep in your mock data on purpose?

title: ARG-Avatar: Animation-Rendering Guidance for Efficient Feedforward Avatar Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.22207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.

title: Edtech Video Generation: Expiring Capabilities Before Offering Classroom Media Options
description:
Short answer: Read video generation capabilities at startup, constrain the options offered by your application, and refresh that snapshot on an expiry. For an edtech workflow that compresses classroom images before serving them and generates promotional video from approved material, keep moderation approval as a separate publication requirement. A supported generation option doesn't establish that the content is appropriate for students.

Start there.

The recommendation has two parts because the evidence answers two different questions: capability discovery tells the application what it can offer, while an application-owned review decision determines what it should publish. Compression belongs downstream of that decision in this proposed workflow. Smaller files are useful; they're poor evidence of moderation coverage.

What page fired when the form offered an unsupported option?

That's the first question in the postmortem, even for a hypothetical incident. A dashboard showing successful requests cannot establish that the form offered valid choices, and a generation completion counter cannot establish that the source image passed the school's review policy. Define the signal around the violated promise: the application accepted a choice outside its current capability snapshot, or publication proceeded without approval for that asset revision.

Those are different pages.

Consider a proposed test fixture with 3 classroom images: a worksheet screenshot, a student photograph, and a teacher-approved illustration. These are synthetic test cases, not observations from a production deployment. Each needs an independent review outcome before the serving pipeline compresses it; a file-format decision says nothing about whether the student photograph has the required approval. If a crop or replacement changes what the image depicts, require a new review decision under the application's policy instead of copying an old approval merely because the filename stayed the same.

The capability cache has a separate trap. A form opened before a refresh can submit after the available choices have changed. Validate again when accepting the submission. The browser's dropdown is a convenience, not the enforcement point.

For an existing Node.js Express application, populate application state before enabling the form, render from the current snapshot, and validate submitted choices at the request boundary. The operational example below uses Go; it doesn't assume an undocumented video response schema.

How should we check video generation capabilities before offering classroom options?

Choose an expiry as an application policy, then record when the snapshot was fetched and when it becomes unusable. A proposed starting value is 5 minutes, subject to review against the workflow's tolerance for stale options; that number isn't a provider guarantee. Refresh periodically and replace the snapshot only after the response has passed application schema checks. Avoid overwriting a usable snapshot with an empty value just because a refresh attempt failed.

Once the expiry passes, stop accepting new generation choices until a validated snapshot is available. Existing approved images can follow their own serving policy. This trades some availability of new work for a clear promise about the options the form accepts, which is easier to defend than silently trusting an indefinitely old list.

Keep the moderation record attached to the asset revision and policy revision, and keep the capability snapshot revision attached to the generation submission. These are proposed application records, not vendor response fields. They let a reviewer distinguish an unsupported choice from a missing content approval without guessing from a chart.

Infrai fits teams that want a plain REST API without installing an SDK, with one key and one bill for the account-usage and email handoff. That means the statement worker can fetch usage and send the prepared report without managing separate credentials for those calls. Its self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas, which help validate that boundary. The combined approach has a trade-off: one vendor to trust and one outage surface.

It doesn't replace the school's moderation policy.

Compare the boundary each tool actually owns

Moderation coverage means being able to explain which assets were reviewed, under which policy, and what happens to unreviewed revisions. Evaluate Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit as alternative media-stack candidates against those same acceptance questions: where does review run, how is its decision bound to the exact compressed output, and can publication be blocked? These are evaluation requirements, not claims that the three products have identical moderation features.

The surrounding statement workflow has another set of alternatives. Keep their roles explicit.

Option Role in the alternative stack Boundary to keep explicit
Stripe metering Usage metering component Metering evidence is separate from the content approval record.
Puppeteer Application-controlled PDF rendering component A rendered statement doesn't validate generation choices or approve images.
Amazon SES Email delivery component Sending a statement doesn't establish that its underlying usage and review records agree.

The Stripe metering + Puppeteer + SES version involves 2 service account setups, Stripe and AWS, with separate credential sets; Puppeteer is a software dependency rather than a third hosted-service signup. The application needs glue to collect usage, render the statement, associate it with the correct recipient, and handle delivery retries. This separation is a reasonable choice when the team wants independent ownership of those stages, and an existing deployment may already have most of that work in place.

A combined API is attractive when credential and schema consistency are the maintenance burden. A separate stack is preferable when independent control of metering, rendering, and delivery matters more. Neither arrangement proves that the school's moderation requirements have been met. Use MDN's image format guide for format decisions after review, and retain separate evidence for content approval.

Implement the usage-to-email handoff without inventing a PDF contract

The operational seam needs a working check too. This example fetches account usage and inserts its JSON representation into an application-prepared email batch payload, using the same key and base URL for both calls. Statement layout stays in the application: PDF rendering can remain an application step, while this example sends a textual usage statement. No PDF API contract is assumed.

Save this as main.go. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and MEDIA_API_BASE_URL to your deployment's credentials and versioned API base URL. Set EMAIL_BATCH_TEMPLATE to the path of a complete email batch request constructed against the published request schema, with the literal string {{USAGE_JSON}} inside its message text. These names and the marker are local application conventions. Set STATEMENT_ID to a stable identifier for the recipient batch and reporting period; reuse it when retrying the same statement, and change it for a different statement. Run with go run main.go.

The template requirement matters. Recipient and message fields aren't guessed here, and encoding/json escapes the inserted usage as JSON string data. Validate the completed payload against the published schema before scheduling the workflow.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing environment variable: " + name) }
    return value
}

func call(method, route string, body []byte, statementID string) ([]byte, error) {
    base := strings.TrimRight(required("MEDIA_API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+route, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        if body != nil { req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json") }
        if statementID != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", statementID) }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 { return data, nil }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            delay = time.Until(deadline)
            if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func insert(value any, usage string) any {
    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        return strings.ReplaceAll(v, "{{USAGE_JSON}}", usage)
    case []any:
        for i := range v { v[i] = insert(v[i], usage) }
    case map[string]any:
        for key := range v { v[key] = insert(v[key], usage) }
    }
    return value
}

func run() error {
    usage, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/account/usage", nil, "")
    if err != nil { return err }
    if !json.Valid(usage) { return fmt.Errorf("usage response is not JSON") }
    template, err := os.ReadFile(required("EMAIL_BATCH_TEMPLATE"))
    if err != nil { return err }
    if !bytes.Contains(template, []byte("{{USAGE_JSON}}")) {
        return fmt.Errorf("template is missing the usage marker")
    }
    var payload any
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(template))
    decoder.UseNumber()
    if err := decoder.Decode(&payload); err != nil { return err }
    body, err := json.Marshal(insert(payload, string(usage)))
    if err != nil { return err }
    _, err = call(http.MethodPost, "/email/batch/send", body, required("STATEMENT_ID"))
    return err
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("Statement request accepted.")
}

A successful response establishes request acceptance, not final email delivery. The retry loop handles rate limiting with a bounded budget and honors Retry-After; the write carries a stable idempotency key. Maintain a durable application send ledger for reruns beyond the platform's default 24-hour deduplication window. Keep account information and raw error bodies inside access-controlled operational tooling.

This example checks the account-to-email seam. It isn't a capability parser or a moderation classifier. Each needs its own acceptance evidence.

Verify the gates, then roll back the affected stage

Before enabling the form, test a fresh snapshot, an expired snapshot, and a submission from a form opened before refresh. Only choices accepted by current application validation should start new generation work. Add a changed-image fixture to ensure that approval for the old revision cannot authorize publication of its replacement. These tests exercise the promises that matter to the person carrying the pager.

Test the statement handoff separately with a controlled recipient and a stable statement identifier. Confirm that usage reaches the prepared message, a rate-limit response produces a delayed retry, and retrying the same write doesn't create a second logical statement. Reconcile request acceptance with delivery evidence before marking the statement delivered.

For rollback, disable new generation submissions if capability freshness cannot be established, retain the last validated snapshot for diagnosis, and keep unapproved assets out of publication. If compression changes an approved asset's rendering, return serving to the previous approved artifact while reviewing the new output. If statement delivery is affected, stop that sender and retain its ledger so a restart can distinguish unfinished work from completed sends.

Page on the broken promise. A green dashboard can wait.

References

  • MDN, Image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Formats/Image_types
  • Stripe, Usage-based billing: https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based
  • Puppeteer documentation: https://pptr.dev/
  • Amazon SES developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • Cloudinary documentation: https://cloudinary.com/documentation
  • imgix documentation: https://docs.imgix.com/
  • ImageKit documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs

title: Cloudflare Turns a Spending Cap Into a Runtime Decision
description:
TL;DR

  • Spend Management is a billing control in Cloudflare that sets a dollar limit on usage-based products and pauses the product when the limit is reached; it entered Beta on 13 November 2026 for pay-as-you-go accounts, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.
  • The configuration is small: a spending limit, a recipient email and one or more alert thresholds, set in the dashboard under Manage Account, Billing, Spend limits, or through the REST API and the cf CLI with a spend policy that carries threshold_cents and an action of usage_block.
  • Cloudflare built the control on a two-stage metering pipeline: parsers bucket raw events into one-minute windows, a second service merges those partial aggregates over five-minute windows, and the consolidated data is archived before the Usage Engine reads it.
  • The Usage Engine partitions processing by account, keeping each account's usage and subscription state together with local state and a durable write-ahead log, so pricing runs in parallel across accounts and survives a failed processor.
  • The Rating Engine combines usage records, subscription information and pricing rules, holds usage as pending when subscription data arrives late, applies included allowances and prices accumulated usage.
  • Enforcement travels through Quicksilver, Cloudflare's internal key-value store for global replication: the runtime picks the cap up on its periodic refresh and rejects capped invocations from local state, which keeps rating out of the request path.
  • A pause stops the invocations that incur cost. In Workers, Cron Triggers and Queue consumers stop. Static assets remain available. The block clears when the limit is raised, the policy is disabled or the next billing cycle starts.

Cloudflare's own screenshot of the Workers configuration: block usage at the limit, a 10 dollar cap, a recipient address and two alert thresholds. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

What Spend Management turns on in the dashboard

The launch post opens with the demand behind the feature: spend controls had been the most requested item from developers on the platform, and Cloudflare counts more than 10 million developers building on it. Usage notifications and budget alerts already existed for paid plans, and the billing documentation describes them as emails sent when account-wide usage-based spend crosses a dollar threshold. The new part is a limit that stops the product.

The configuration sits behind that sentence. A pay-as-you-go account enables controls on a product, sets a spending limit, names a recipient for notifications and picks one or more alert thresholds. The API call in the post carries the same fields as JSON: a name, a product identifier, an enabled flag, threshold_cents set to 10000, an action of usage_block and a notification address. The cf CLI exposes the same objects with list, create, get, update, delete and two audit commands.

Cloudflare's usage-based billing documentation lists the supported products, the included allowances and the notification options behind Spend Management. Source: developers.cloudflare.com/billing/understand/usage-based-billing, retrieved 15 November 2026.

One detail in the post is easy to miss and matters at month end: the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, so a subscription that starts on 10 October gives a cycle from 10 October to 10 November. A team that sets a cap mid-cycle is measuring against a billing window that has already begun.

Two metering stages aggregate usage close to the source

Every invocation produces measurements, and the post names them: requests, CPU time, execution duration or storage operations, depending on the product. Shipping that volume intact to a rating engine would not scale, so Cloudflare aggregates close to the source in two stages.

The first stage runs next to parsing. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements and combines matching ones into buckets that typically cover one minute, and the post is candid that several records can still describe the same account and time window. The second stage is a separate service that merges those partial aggregates with the same grouping rules over windows that typically cover five minutes, then archives the consolidated result as a durable dataset for analytics and reconciliation.

Cloudflare's diagram of the metering pipeline: parse, one-minute buckets, a merge over five-minute windows, then the Usage Engine and Rating Engine. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

The ordering is the interesting engineering decision. Volume falls before the expensive systems see it, so the Usage Engine and the Rating Engine only handle accumulated usage. For an operator reading this from outside, the lesson transfers to any internal metering work: the cost of a billing pipeline is dominated by the volume carried forward at raw resolution.

The Usage Engine keeps each account in one partition

The Usage Engine turns aggregated measurements into usage records, the standardized shape that carries an account identifier, a usage window, a usage metric, a measured quantity and the relevant product dimensions. Its other job is to map each product-specific meter onto the standardized usage metrics that the billing system supports.

Cloudflare's flow for one capped billable event: usage reports, the Usage Engine, the Rating Engine, policy evaluation, notifications, and the cap propagated to every node. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

Cloudflare partitions that processing by account, so an account's usage and subscription information meet in the same place and its accumulated usage plus included allowances can be maintained without coordinating with other pricing processors on every update. Each partition holds local state for fast access and a durable write-ahead log on disk, which the post credits with four properties: less cross-partition coordination, consistent pricing, parallel processing and recoverability after a failure.

The Rating Engine prices accumulated usage against allowances

The Rating Engine answers one question: given what the account has consumed, its subscription and its pricing, how much has it spent so far. It brings together usage records, subscription information and pricing rules covering rates, included allowances and billing rounding.

Cloudflare's pause notification: Workers reached a 10 dollar limit, the block is dated, and the notice states what a pause means. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

Usage and subscription data arrive as independent streams, so the two streams carry no ordering guarantee. The post describes the consequence directly: when usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, the engine retains it as pending and revisits it after the subscription information arrives, which tolerates a delayed webhook while retaining that usage for later pricing. The engine also applies the included allowance before pricing any excess, and it prices accumulated usage, with rounding applied to the total.

Two outputs follow. Policy evaluation decides whether a warning or blocking threshold has been reached, and reporting pushes estimated charges to the dashboard and sends the email alerts.

Enforcement runs on local state that Quicksilver propagates

Cloudflare's audit log for spend policies, listing the change, the member and the new limit. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

The rating engine stays out of the request path. When a policy blocks, the policy service sends the cap to the runtime configuration service and to Quicksilver, the internal key-value store Cloudflare built for fast global replication and low-latency access, and the cap propagates to all nodes asynchronously. Each runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.

The post states the property that makes this work: enforcement uses local state, so a request never waits on the Rating Engine. The architectural point for anyone designing a similar control is the split between where the decision is computed and where it is applied. The trade-off is a cap with a distributed enforcement delay: after policy evaluation, asynchronous propagation and periodic refresh leave an interval in which some runtimes may still accept billable invocations, so the configured amount cannot guarantee the final spend.

Runtime effects of the pause

A cap that lands rejects new invocations of the product, with one qualification the post states plainly: Cloudflare pauses the customer-code invocations that incur cost. In Workers, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations stop. Static assets continue to be served.

Netics visual, 15 November 2026: the five stages a capped invocation passes through, as the post describes them.

That behaviour decides how a cap should be sized. A site whose traffic is mostly cached assets keeps answering requests. Scheduled jobs and queue consumers behind background work stop. An operator planning a cap around a public launch should expect the visible page to remain available. Asynchronous work accumulates unprocessed until the limit is raised, the policy is disabled or the next cycle begins.

The dashboard adds two facts an operator needs for the same discussion. Costs for each supported product appear in near real time, under 10 minutes, and an audit log records who changed a limit and when a cap was reached. Both feed the same operational question: how much spend can accumulate between the moment a threshold trips and the moment the block is picked up across the network.

Cloudflare is explicit that this is a first step. More products will follow, the team wants the gap between measurement and enforcement down toward a minute, and the post describes a future where calls are tagged so spend can be attributed to an application or an agentic task and paused across products. For now the control covers Workers and Durable Objects, and the cloud infrastructure and cost control work that teams already run at the account level gains a runtime counterpart.

Netics visual, 15 November 2026: what the pause covers in Workers, and how the block clears.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications
description:
Introducing Xanout: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications

I've been working on Xanout, a lightweight, TypeScript-first server router designed to make backend development simpler and more flexible.

The idea behind Xanout is straightforward: provide developers with a clean routing system built around web standards without introducing unnecessary complexity.

What is Xanout?

Xanout is a server-side routing library for building HTTP applications and backend services.

It provides a simple foundation for handling HTTP requests, defining routes, and organizing server-side application logic.

What can you build with Xanout?

Xanout can be used as a foundation for building:

  • REST APIs — Create structured APIs for web and mobile applications.
  • Authentication systems — Implement login, registration, authorization, and session-based authentication.
  • Backend services — Build application backends and business logic.
  • API gateways — Organize and manage HTTP endpoints.
  • Microservices — Develop lightweight HTTP-based services.
  • Middleware-driven applications — Handle authentication, logging, validation, error handling, and request processing.

Why Xanout?

Some of the ideas behind the project:

  • TypeScript-first development.
  • Lightweight routing architecture.
  • Web-standard APIs and interfaces.
  • Flexible middleware handling.
  • Simple and developer-friendly API design.

I want developers to focus on building their applications rather than dealing with unnecessary framework complexity.

Project Links

  • Website & Documentation: https://xanout.devnax.com/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/devnax/xanout

What's Next?

Xanout is still evolving. I'm working on improving its architecture, developer experience, and overall capabilities.

If you're interested in TypeScript, backend development, or open-source projects, I'd appreciate your feedback.

Feel free to explore the project, share your thoughts, or contribute.

Thanks for reading!

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: Rethinking Perceptual Similarity for Remote Sensing: Multi-Layer Attention Scoring and Human Preference Benchmarking
description:
arXiv:2611.21816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Perceptual similarity metrics for natural images transfer poorly to remote sensing (RS), where severe geospatial and semantic failures can remain visually plausible while still being decisively wrong for downstream use. To address this, we develop a novel human-aligned perceptual quality metric for generated RS imagery and evaluate it across several generation tasks. We first conduct a controlled perturbation study where we progressively increase the severity of common synthetic perturbations. Using the layer-wise Aligned Attention Score (AAS) responses in RemoteCLIP, we find that different RS artifacts are best captured at different depths. Based on these findings, we introduce Remote Sensing Perceptual Distance (RSPD), a pairwise metric that averages seven independently calibrated layer distances without tuning on human-preference labels. To evaluate our metric on realistic RS generation tasks, we construct a blind, reference-conditioned two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) benchmark with five 300-triplet subsets spanning synthetic artifacts, airborne and spaceborne super-resolution, SAR-to-optical translation, and timeseries controls. We also construct a 300-triplet ordered misregistration benchmark with deterministic labels. Using the same RemoteCLIP checkpoint, RSPD substantially outperforms simple cosine distance with the final global embedding and is competitive with the strongest generic baselines across the realistic RS generation tasks.

title: Regularized Score Centering
description:
arXiv:2611.21791v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21882v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.

title: Vork Research Preview Targets Agent-Written 3D and VFX
description:
Vork is available as a source-available, free research preview of a headless 3D and VFX engine built for AI agents. An agent can define an entire scene in code—including shaders, materials, cameras and physics—render it on the GPU, inspect the output and revise the code without operating an editor. Developers can write ordinary scene JSON directly or generate it through Python and TypeScript SDKs, giving agent workflows a documented rendering interface rather than a graphical control path. The project describes these capabilities in its repository.

Code is the control surface

The project says its core API fits in about 2,500 tokens. Vork is written in Rust and Slang, renders through Vulkan and Metal on Linux, Windows and macOS, and exposes public hooks that can change camera rays, material response, light propagation and film response without modifying the renderer itself. Those hooks and implementation details are documented in the README.

A local workflow starts with vork init, which creates a project containing a renderable JSON scene; initialization flags can also provide editable TypeScript or Python scene files. Render quality is configured separately from scene content: std/previs is intended for iteration, std/draft uses scene-ray lighting, std/final is the default delivery profile, and std/path enables path transport. The repository documents the commands and the distinct purposes of these profiles.

Scene authoring and command-line help do not require a GPU. Rendering requires Apple Silicon or an NVIDIA or AMD GPU with Vulkan ray-query support, while the project also offers remote rendering through vork cloud. By default, the renderer combines raster visibility with hardware ray-traced lighting; a path tracer is available separately. Vork’s hardware requirements and rendering modes are listed by the project.

Benchmark caveats limit the comparison

Vork reports that its million-bird demonstration rendered 192 frames at 1080p in 97 seconds on one NVIDIA L4. It projects that Blender EEVEE would take 13–18 minutes at the same sample count, and separately reports timings 1.1–2.3 times faster than EEVEE for default stills and movies and about 8–11 times faster for the bird flock. These are Vork’s published measurements and projections.

The project explicitly calls these results timings rather than equal-quality speedups. Its draft and final measurements used four and eight samples respectively with OIDN on an NVIDIA L4, while the Blender 5.2.1 results were retained baselines rather than fresh runs and used different settings. Driver caches and clocks were not controlled; Vork’s movie times include startup and scene loading, while Blender’s exclude those stages after a still-image prime. The benchmark notes disclose these methodological differences.

Visual review also found softer edges, grainier defocus, wall mottling and changes to sparse or spectral highlights at the tested budgets. Nineteen earlier comparisons failed the experiment’s declared no-worse FLIP condition, and that quality experiment was not repeated for the reported build. The project includes both findings among its benchmark qualifications.

Analysis: Programmability shifts the verification burden

Analysis: Vork’s more consequential proposition is its interface design, not the headline speed range. A compact scene API and programmable GPU hooks give an agent direct control over rendering behavior instead of asking it to manipulate an editor. That could make custom effects and simulations easier to express as code, but it also expands the scene-specific programs that a team must inspect, test and reproduce. The project’s small API, editor-free workflow and public program hooks support this interpretation.

The unresolved trade-off is control versus verification. Vork’s documentation warns that increasing samples cannot restore transport omitted by a render profile and recommends inspecting path-rendered output when necessary. It also says its furnace tests, analytic oracles and render tests can catch errors but do not guarantee that every scene is physically exact. Teams evaluating the preview therefore still need shot-specific visual checks; the published timing comparison cannot settle whether its faster profiles preserve the properties a particular production requires. Those rendering and validation limits are stated in the project documentation.

title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. title: I taught a music transformer to play jazz with me in real time
description:
duetto is a jazz partner for a MIDI keyboard. You pick a tune, and a pretrained transformer plays it with you in real time as a trio (solo, chords and walking bass), comping while you play and soloing when you rest.

This is the model alone on Autumn Leaves at 160 bpm:

Code: github.com/RiccardoCataldi/duetto

No model was trained or fine-tuned for this. Everything below is about inference: how to take a general-purpose symbolic music model and constrain its decoding until it behaves like a jazz trio that follows a chart and listens to you.

1. The model and its tokens

duetto uses the Anticipatory Music Transformer (AMT, Thickstun et al.), a decoder-only transformer trained on the Lakh MIDI dataset.

AMT encodes music as a flat sequence of events, each made of three tokens:

token meaning resolution
time absolute onset 10 ms ticks
duration how long the note lasts 10 ms ticks
note instrument × pitch one token per (GM program, MIDI pitch)

The instrument is part of the note token (NOTE_OFFSET + program * MAX_PITCH + pitch). That has two useful consequences:

  1. A duo is just one sequence. The player's notes are written into the context as one instrument, the model's as others. The model continues the sequence; it doesn't need to know which notes are "yours".
  2. Each voice can be a different instrument in the context. duetto's bass is written as General MIDI program 32 (acoustic bass), because that is how bass lines are labelled in Lakh MIDI, so the notes it writes under that label move like a bass line. What you actually hear is decided later by the synthesizer.

Out of the box, AMT continues a sequence plausibly, in pop-MIDI style. It has no notion of a chart, a beat grid, chord-scale relationships or jazz phrasing, and it often doubles notes, since Lakh MIDI files are full of duplicated tracks. Everything that follows is about adding those constraints.

2. Constrained decoding, one slot at a time

Each event is sampled as three separate steps, and each step gets its own logit mask before nucleus sampling:

for slot in range(3):            # time, duration, note
    logits = self._logits()      # one forward pass, with KV cache
    mask = torch.full_like(logits, -float('inf'))
    ...                          # open only what is allowed in this slot
    token = sample(nucleus(logits + mask, top_p))
    self.seq.append(token)

Time slot: when may each voice play?
Every voice has a window of allowed onsets, built as a mask over ticks:

  • not earlier than now + 150 ms, to cover sampling and network latency;
  • not inside a phrase-ending breath for the solo;
  • for the walking bass, only on the next beat: the mask opens a single tick;
  • for comping under a solo, only inside the slot where the next chord stab falls;
  • snapped to the subdivision chosen for the next two bars (eighths, triplets, sixteenths), and never faster than can be articulated at the tune's tempo.

The time mask is the union of all the voices' windows. Which voice actually plays is decided in the next slots.

Duration slot.
Comped chords are short, or held for one to three beats in a ballad. A solo note is at least a detached eighth. A quoted phrase keeps its original durations, or slightly shorter.

Note slot: which voice, which pitch?
Given the sampled onset, only the voices whose window contains that tick are opened, each limited to its own register. On top of the mask, duetto adds biases, not hard constraints:

bias effect
chord tones of the current bar +1 logit
tensions (9, 11/#11, 13) +1 logit
out-of-scale notes for the chord pushed down
third or seventh on the beat a chord starts (guide tones) pushed up
a chromatic approach off the beat allowed, then the target chord tone gets +6
keys near the player's hands while they play −2, so it stays out of the way
notes already sounding, or a run about to repeat a third time masked

The distinction between masks and biases is the core design choice. Masks encode things that are wrong (playing the bass off the beat, doubling a note). Biases encode things that are idiomatic (guide tones, chord tones). The model still chooses among the idiomatic options, which keeps the output varied in a way purely rule-based generation is not.

3. Real time: a one-second lookahead with rollback

The music can't wait for the model, and the model can't know what you'll play next. duetto handles this with a sliding buffer:

  • The server keeps about one second of music sampled ahead of the current time, and streams it to the client as timestamped note messages.
  • When you play, your note is appended to the context and the server sends a cut <onset> message: everything it had planned after that point is discarded on both sides and resampled, now conditioned on what you played. A commit window (500 ms by default) keeps the near future fixed unless your note contradicts it, so the accompaniment doesn't stutter at every key you press.
  • Rollback is cheap because the KV cache is cropped rather than rebuilt: unwinding n events removes 3n positions from the cache, and only the new tokens are fed again.
  • When the context fills up, or absolute time approaches the model's maximum, the last ~20 s of events are kept and re-timed to start at 0, the way the training sequences start, and the cache is rebuilt once.

One less obvious issue: AMT reads a long silence as "this is a sparse piece" and tends to stop playing altogether. duetto caps the silence the model may leave, and after it, forces a note from the solo voice.

Measured latency per note (one event, three tokens): ~12 ms with AMT-medium and ~18 ms with AMT-large on an RTX 3080 Ti; ~90 ms with AMT-large on a Jetson Orin Nano. The model runs on a GPU host behind a small line-based TCP protocol, while the laptop handles MIDI input, FluidSynth and a live piano roll. It also runs on a single machine (CUDA, Apple Silicon or CPU).

4. A jazz vocabulary from the Weimar Jazz Database

Chord tones and a beat grid produce correct output, but not idiomatic output. For that, duetto uses the Weimar Jazz Database (WJD), a corpus of hand-transcribed solos by jazz soloists, in two ways.

Statistics. Note choice per chord type and melodic interval transitions in bebop lines are extracted from WJD and added as biases: which notes soloists play over a dominant, which intervals follow which.

Licks. The solos are cut into phrases of one to four bars, at the boundaries where the soloist started and ended a phrase (including the pickup notes before the bar line). Each phrase is stored key-independently and indexed by the chord progression underneath it. While soloing, duetto can look up a phrase that was played over the same changes as the next bars of the tune, transpose it and quote it.

Quoting is also done through the masks: for each event of the lick, the time mask opens exactly one tick and the note mask exactly one pitch. The model still runs a forward pass on every quoted note, so its context stays consistent, and when the quote ends it continues from a line that sounds like its own.

On top of that:

  • Development. A quoted phrase can be repeated as is, displaced by a beat, cut to its first half, or inverted, the way soloists develop a motif.
  • Connections. Between two licks it inserts a short pickup: a scale walk, a chromatic approach or an enclosure of the next phrase's first note.
  • Tempo filter. Licks whose note rate would be unplayable at the current tempo are excluded.
  • Your licks. Phrases you play over the tune are indexed the same way, so it can quote them back.
  • Arc. Density, register and subdivision follow a curve over each chorus, peaking about three quarters through.

5. Voicings and bass, partly rule-based

Not everything goes through the model's preferences.

  • Comping is biased toward four-note rootless voicings, choosing the inversion closest to the previous one (minimal voice movement). While the player is playing, it reduces them to shells (third and seventh).
  • Walking bass gets a note on every beat from the time mask. The pitch is biased toward the root when a bar or a chord begins, toward a semitone from the next root on the beat before a chord change, and mostly stepwise in between.
  • Bossa uses a fixed rhythmic figure (root and fifth with ties, anticipating the next bar's root).
  • Ballads plan each solo phrase in advance: a target note (a third, seventh or tension of the chord where the phrase ends) is chosen first, a rhythm is borrowed from a WJD phrase, and the pitches are biased toward the target.

6. Charts

A tune is a plain-text chart: title, key, tempo, chords bar by bar, and an optional melody that the solo can paraphrase.

title: Autumn Leaves
key: G minor
bpm: 120
Cm7 | F7 | Bbmaj7 | Ebmaj7 | Am7b5 | D7 | Gm6 | % |
> Eb5:4 | -:1 F4:1 G4:1 A4:1 | D5:2 D5:2 | ...

The chord symbols are parsed into root, quality and scale, and these feed the masks and biases above. Style (swing, bossa, even eighths, ballad), part (comp, solo, duet) and around a dozen "character" controls (density, harmony, groove, vocabulary...) adjust the same parameters live.

What I'd take away

  • A pretrained general model plus constrained decoding gets surprisingly far in a domain it wasn't trained for, without any fine-tuning data.
  • Separate hard constraints (masks) from stylistic preferences (biases). Masks keep the output valid, biases make it idiomatic, and the model supplies the variation.
  • For real-time generation, sample ahead and roll back with KV-cache cropping, rather than generating on demand.
  • A small annotated corpus (WJD) is more useful as retrievable material and statistics than as training data.

The code is open source under a noncommercial license: github.com/RiccardoCataldi/duetto. If you play, I'd like to hear what it gets wrong musically. If you work on generative models, feedback on the decoding approach is welcome too.

title: What Are Online Evals? Online vs Offline Evaluation for AI Agents
description:
Online evals are evaluations that run on an AI agent's real production traffic. Instead of feeding the agent a prepared test set, an evaluator (an LLM judge, a code check, or a user signal) scores the conversations, traces, or tool calls that real users already produced. Offline evals tell you whether a change is safe to ship. Online evals tell you whether the shipped agent is working.

The term comes from machine learning, where "offline" evaluation uses a held-out dataset and "online" evaluation measures a model while it serves traffic. For LLM agents, the split matters more than it did for classic models. An agent's inputs are open-ended, its tools change state in other systems, and its failures are often fluent and polite. A test set can only contain the failures someone already imagined.

Online vs offline evals at a glance

Offline evals Online evals
Input A fixed dataset of prepared cases Real production conversations, traces, or spans
When it runs Before release, usually in CI or an experiment After the interaction, continuously
Ground truth Expected answers, references, or a rubric Usually none; a judge, a rule, or an outcome signal
Main question Did this change make known cases worse? What is going wrong for real users right now?
Catches Regressions on known cases Unknown failure modes, drift, new user goals
Misses Anything not in the dataset Nothing until it happens at least once
Cost driver Dataset size times the number of runs Traffic volume times judge cost, reduced by sampling
Output A pass rate or score comparison between versions Rates over time, flagged examples, alerts

Neither column replaces the other. The useful pattern, covered below, is a loop in which online evals find failures and those failures become offline test cases.

What an online eval is made of

Every online eval has the same five parts, whatever tool runs it.

  1. A unit. What gets judged: a single LLM call (span), one request through the agent (trace), or a whole multi-turn conversation (session or thread). The unit decides which failures are even visible. A span-level judge cannot see that the user asked the same question four times. Read conversation-level vs trace-level online evals for how to choose.
  2. A trigger. When the judgment runs. Span and trace evals can run as soon as the data arrives. Conversation evals usually wait until the conversation has gone quiet, because judging a half-finished conversation produces false failures.
  3. An evaluator. The thing that decides. An LLM judge reading a rubric, deterministic code (schema validation, regex, a tool-result comparison), or a signal from the user or a downstream system, such as a thumbs-down, a refund request, or a support ticket.
  4. A population. Which traffic is judged: everything, a sample, or a filtered slice such as one agent, one customer tier, or conversations that used a refund tool.
  5. An action. What happens with the result: a dashboard rate, a review queue, an alert, a new regression test, or a code change.

Teams that skip part 5 end up with a dashboard of scores nobody acts on. The setup guide walks through each part with defaults.

What online evals catch that offline evals miss

Offline evals are strongest on known behavior: the canonical refund question, the formatting contract, the tool the agent must call. Production adds the cases nobody wrote down.

  • New user goals. People ask an onboarding agent about billing, or ask a coding agent to explain a stack trace it never saw. No test case exists because nobody predicted the request.
  • Silent wrong answers. The agent states a 30-day return window after retrieving a 14-day policy. Nothing errors. See how to catch wrong answers that don't show up as errors.
  • False success. The agent says the cancellation is done, but no cancellation call succeeded. See detecting when an agent claims success without acting.
  • Multi-turn friction. Each reply is reasonable in isolation, but the user rephrases four times and leaves. Only a conversation-level evaluator sees the pattern.
  • Drift. A model update, a prompt edit, or a changed upstream API slowly shifts behavior. Offline evals pass because the dataset did not change. See agent drift in production.

The 12 production failures your evals will never catch lists more. Read that title as "your offline evals": every item on it is a job for an online eval.

What online evals cannot do

Online evals have limits worth stating plainly.

  • They are retrospective. A failure has to happen before it can be scored. If a failure must never reach a user, it needs a guardrail or a code check in the request path, not an online eval. See online evals vs guardrails vs monitoring.
  • They inherit the evidence you send. A judge cannot verify a refund it cannot see. If the tool result or the system-of-record outcome is not captured, the evaluator can only judge what the agent said.
  • Judges make mistakes. An LLM judge needs a labeled sample before its rate is trustworthy. See how to calibrate an LLM judge.
  • They cost money at scale. Judging every conversation with a strong model adds up. See what LLM-as-a-judge costs in production.

The loop: online failures become offline tests

The two kinds of eval are most useful when connected.

  1. An online eval flags a pattern in production, for example the agent confirming refunds before the refund tool succeeds.
  2. Someone reviews the flagged examples and confirms the failure is real.
  3. A fix is proposed and reviewed: a prompt change, a tool contract, a code check.
  4. Representative failing examples, plus healthy controls, become offline regression cases. Turn production failures into regression tests covers how to do this without replaying real side effects.
  5. After the fix ships, the same online eval measures whether the failure rate actually fell.

Step 5 is the one most teams skip, and it is the one that tells you whether the fix worked. What to do when an online eval fails covers the whole path from flag to verified fix.

How Agnost AI runs online evals

Agnost is built around the online half of this loop, for conversational agents.

  • Rules in plain English. You write the behavior you expect, such as "state the cancellation policy before completing a cancellation". Each rule is an evaluator. How to define agent failures in natural language covers how to write rules a judge can apply consistently.
  • Whole-conversation judgment. Once a conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, an LLM judge reads it end to end against your active rules and flags the specific assistant messages that broke one. Conversations are processed in batches, so this is a review layer, not a real-time filter.
  • No sampling knob. Every analyzed conversation is judged, up to your plan's monthly event limit. When you add or edit a rule, Agnost also scores your most recent 1,000 conversations so the rule starts with a baseline.
  • Intents alongside rules. The same judge labels what users were trying to do, so a violation rate can be read per user goal.
  • Alerts and fixes. A rule's violation count can trigger a Slack or email alert. A fired alert can start Auto Improve, which opens a pull request for your team to review and re-checks the alert about an hour after the change merges.

What Agnost does not do is also worth knowing. Verdicts are pass/fail flags with the evidence message, not graded scores. There is no CI gate, and violations are a classified finding, not enforcement. Teams that need dataset experiments or a CI eval step often run Agnost alongside an offline eval tool; if Braintrust is on your shortlist for that job, Braintrust alternatives for AI agent evaluation compares it with the other options. The online evaluation tools comparison shows where each product fits, and the Violations guide covers setup.

Where to start

If you run no online evals today, start small:

  1. Pick one failure that would cost you a customer, such as a false completion, a skipped identity check, or a wrong policy answer.
  2. Write it as a single, narrow rule with clear evidence.
  3. Run it over a week of production conversations and read 20 flagged and 20 unflagged examples.
  4. Fix the rule wording until you agree with the judge, then set an alert threshold.

One trusted evaluator that someone acts on is worth more than twenty scores on a dashboard. For the difference between the evaluation layers in more depth, read evals, traces, and conversations: what each one catches.

Frequently asked questions

What are online evals?

Online evals are evaluations that run on an AI system's real production traffic instead of a prepared test set. An evaluator, usually an LLM judge, a code check, or a user signal, scores live conversations, traces, or spans after they happen, so the team can see how the agent behaves with real users and real tools.

What is the difference between online and offline evals?

Offline evals run a fixed dataset through the agent before a change ships and compare the results with expected answers or a rubric. Online evals score production traffic after it happens. Offline evals answer whether a change is safe to release; online evals answer whether the released agent is actually working for users.

Do online evals replace offline evals?

No. Offline evals catch regressions on known cases before release. Online evals find the failures nobody wrote a test for. The useful loop turns online-eval failures into new offline test cases, so the same failure is caught before the next release.

Are online evals the same as guardrails?

No. A guardrail runs inline and can block or rewrite a response before the user sees it, so it must be fast and cheap. An online eval runs after the interaction and only observes, so it can use a slower, more careful judge and look at the whole conversation.

Should online evals score every conversation or a sample?

Score everything for rare, high-severity failures and when volume is low enough to afford it. Sample when the judge is expensive and the failure is common enough that a sample still finds it. Whatever you choose, record the denominator so a rate can be interpreted.

How does Agnost AI run online evals?

You write rules in plain English, such as 'confirm identity before sharing account details'. Agnost's LLM judge checks every analyzed production conversation against those rules once the conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, flags the assistant messages that broke a rule, reports violation counts, and can alert Slack or email when a threshold is crossed. An alert can also open a pull request that is re-checked after merge.

title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
description:
arXiv:2611.22238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
description:
arXiv:2611.22227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.
