title: Don't ask the model to be brief. Cut it in code, and count what you cut.
description:
DevReview, the AI code reviewer I'm building, never posts more than eight comments on a pull request [src:facts]. That limit isn't something the model is asked to respect. It's a constant in the application code, applied after the model has finished talking.

I've mentioned that design before, in one line: a prompt is a request, a slice() isn't. This post is the longer version of that line, because when I actually wrote down why, the reasons turned out to be more specific than "models don't always follow instructions." There is also one consequence I didn't expect: once the limit lives in code, the prompt has to say the opposite of what you'd normally write.

The obvious version, and why I didn't ship it

If you want an AI reviewer that doesn't bury a pull request in comments, the first thing you reach for is the prompt:

Only report the most important issues. Keep it to a handful of comments.

That works in the sense that the output usually gets shorter. For a demo, that's enough. I didn't keep it, and not because I measured it failing. I haven't measured how often a prompt-only limit gets ignored, and I don't want to invent a number for it. I dropped it because of what the limit is when it lives in the prompt, regardless of how well the model follows it.

There are four problems with it. Only the first one is about compliance.

1. A request has no failure mode you can see

When the limit is a sentence in the prompt, "the model followed it" and "the model mostly followed it" look the same until someone counts. If a review comes back with too many comments, nothing in the system notices. There's no exception, no log line, no failing check. You find out when a user complains that the tool is noisy, which is the exact complaint the limit was supposed to prevent.

It also drifts. A prompt that produces short output with one model, one set of sampling settings and one style of diff may not do the same after any of those change. You can re-test after every change, but what you're re-testing is a tendency, not a rule.

A limit in code has an obvious failure mode: the number of comments posted is greater than the constant. That can be asserted, and an assertion either passes or it doesn't.

2. The model chooses what to drop before anything is ranked

This is the one that actually decided it for me.

If the model is told to keep the list short, it does the trimming while it writes. Whatever it decided not to say never makes it into the output. So the selection, the most important decision in the whole review, happens inside the generation, in an order I don't control and can't inspect.

What I wanted instead was a fixed rule that I can read:

  1. Collect every finding.
  2. Sort by severity: BUG, then WARN, then NIT, then PRAISE [src:facts].
  3. Within the same severity, keep the order the model produced them in.
  4. Keep the top of the list up to the cap. Count the rest.

The rule isn't clever. Its value is that it's the same rule on every review, and when someone asks "why was this comment cut and that one kept?", the answer is a sentence, not a guess about what the model was weighing at the time.

A side effect is that the ranking is across the whole pull request, not per file. When you ask a model to be brief, you have no idea whether it's being brief across the PR or per file, or front-loading whatever it saw first. With a sort over the full list, a bug in the last file outranks a nit in the first one by construction.

3. You can't disclose what was never written

When DevReview cuts comments, it says so in the review: how many remarks were suppressed to keep the review focused, and (since a change I'll get to below) what severities they were. I call that the Noise Report.

That disclosure is only possible because the cut happens in code. The code has the full list and the shortened list, and the difference between their lengths is a number it can print.

If the model trims itself, there's no full list. The things it chose not to say don't exist anywhere. You can't count them, you can't show them, you can't tell the reader "there was more, and here's roughly what kind." A quiet review and a review that missed something look identical from the outside, and a prompt-side limit makes it impossible to tell them apart even in principle.

This is also why I don't describe DevReview as having nits "off by default." It doesn't. NITs are generated and kept like any other finding, and they're shown if they fit under the cap [src:facts]. They're just the first thing to go when the list is long, and when they go, they're counted.

4. The pull request is in the same context as your instruction

An AI reviewer reads text written by the PR author: the title, the description, the diff. All of that lands in the same context window as the instructions. If the limit is an instruction, then "keep it short" is one sentence competing with whatever else is in that window, including text written by someone you don't control.

I don't want to overstate this. The prompt tells the model to treat PR content as material to review, not as instructions, and that's the main defense. But for the specific question of "how many comments can end up on this PR," I'd rather the answer not depend on that defense holding. With the cap in code, the most any text in the PR can do to the count is fill it.

The part I didn't expect: the prompt has to say the opposite

Once the cap was in code, I had a prompt that still asked the model to be selective. That's two limits stacked on top of each other, and the combination is worse than either one alone.

Walk through it. The model trims itself to a short list, silently. The code then sees a list that's already under the cap, cuts nothing, and reports that nothing was suppressed. The review looks complete and disclosed, but the selection happened in the one place that can't be counted. The Noise Report says zero while the model has quietly dropped things. The code-side limit is still enforced, but the honesty it was supposed to buy is gone.

So the prompt now says the reverse. The relevant rule tells the model to report every genuine finding, and then:

DevReview enforces the comment budget in code — do not self-limit, but do not pad the list either. Only real findings.

Both halves matter. "Do not self-limit" is there so the code gets the full list and the count means something. "Do not pad" is there because the obvious way for "report everything" to go wrong is a model inventing filler to look thorough. The rest of the prompt pushes in the same direction: a list of common false positives to avoid, and an instruction to downgrade or skip anything it's not sure is a bug.

The split of responsibilities ends up clean:

  • The model decides what is a real finding and how severe it is.
  • The code decides how many get posted, in what order, and reports what it cut.

The model is good at the first job and has no reason to be trusted with the second.

What the code-side limit doesn't fix

Putting the limit in code moves the problem. It doesn't remove it. These are the costs and gaps I know about.

The ranking trusts the model's severity labels. The sort is deterministic, but the input to it isn't. If the model labels a real bug as a NIT, the code will faithfully rank it with the NITs and, on a long review, cut it. The code enforces the count, not the judgment. The best it can do is make the cut visible, so a reader who sees "suppressed: some NITs" at least knows there's something to expand.

The cap can cut a bug. If a pull request has more genuine bugs than the cap, some of them don't get posted. Sorting puts bugs first, so you see the worst of it, but "the cap never hides a real bug" is not something I can claim. I used to describe the suppressed comments as "lower-priority," and I removed that word for exactly this reason: when the list is all bugs, what gets cut is also a bug. The note now lists what severities were cut instead of characterizing them.

The order of filters decides what the count means. Counting suppressed comments is only honest if everything that removes a finding is counted, and if invalid findings don't compete for slots with valid ones. I got that wrong once: findings that pointed at files not in the PR were filtered after the cap, so they could take slots and then disappear, and in the worst case the review showed a green check. I wrote that up separately in When a Code Review Says "No Issues" but Found Bugs. The short version: the path check now runs before the cap, and discarded findings are counted too. A code-side limit doesn't make the pipeline honest by itself. It makes it possible to be honest, and then you have to check every filter.

You pay for findings you throw away. If the model reports everything and the code keeps a fraction, the tokens spent on the rest are spent for a number in the Noise Report. I think that's the right trade, since the count is part of what makes the review trustworthy, but it's a real cost and it grows with the size of the PR.

Why the cap is eight [src:facts] is a separate question. This post is about where the limit is enforced, not about its value. I don't have measured data on the value to share yet, so I'm not going to argue for it here.

Because it's code, it can be tested like code

The practical payoff of all this is that the limit stops being a behavior you evaluate and becomes a property you assert.

Testing a prompt-side limit means running the real model on a set of PRs and looking at the distribution of comment counts. That's useful, but it's an evaluation: it tells you how the model tended to behave on those inputs at that time.

Testing a code-side limit means faking the model's response and checking what the pipeline does with it. The model is out of the loop, so the result is the same every run. This is roughly the shape of the test (the helper name here is illustrative, not a file you'll find in the repo):

test("cap is enforced in code and overflow is counted", async () => {
  // Fake model output: more findings than the cap, severities mixed and
  // deliberately out of order, all pointing at files that exist in the PR.
  const findings = [
    ...Array.from({ length: MAX_COMMENTS }, (_, i) => nit(`a.ts`, i + 1)),
    bug("b.ts", 10),
    warn("b.ts", 20),
    praise("a.ts", 30),
  ];

  const result = await reviewWithFakeModel({ comments: findings });

  // 1. Never more than the constant.
  expect(result.comments.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_COMMENTS);

  // 2. Severity order wins over model order: the bug and the warning
  //    the model listed last are posted first.
  expect(result.comments[0].severity).toBe("BUG");
  expect(result.comments[1].severity).toBe("WARN");

  // 3. Nothing disappears without being counted.
  expect(result.comments.length + result.suppressedCount).toBe(findings.length);
});

Three assertions, and each maps to one of the reasons above:

  1. The count is a rule, not a tendency.
  2. Selection follows a fixed order that I wrote down, not one the model chose while generating.
  3. Everything that was cut is disclosed. If a future change adds a filter that drops findings without counting them, the third assertion is the one that should catch it.

The third one is the assertion I care about most, and it's the one a prompt-side limit can't have at all, because there's no "findings.length" to compare against when the model never wrote them.

Since the change I described in the post on the false green check, the review function has been tested end to end with faked responses from the model and from GitHub. The block above shows the idea, not a copy of that suite. The budget itself is also pinned by a plain unit test that feeds generated findings straight into the pure rank-and-slice function, so the cap, the order and the suppressed count don't depend on any model call at all. Before that, I relied on a demo pull request with an expected review written down before running it. One of its pass conditions was that the suppressed count equals the number of generated findings minus the cap. That's the same invariant as the third assertion, just checked by hand.

When a prompt-side limit is fine

None of this means "never put limits in prompts." I'd still use one when:

  • Nobody downstream relies on the limit. If longer output is just a bit annoying and nothing breaks, a prompt instruction is the cheapest thing that mostly works.
  • There's no list to cut. Free-form prose doesn't have a natural unit to slice. Truncating a paragraph in code is worse than asking for a shorter one.
  • You don't need to tell anyone what was left out. If there's no equivalent of the Noise Report, the strongest argument for doing it in code goes away.

For a code reviewer, none of those apply. The output is a list, the reader relies on it being short, and the reader also needs to know whether short means "nothing else" or "more, cut on purpose." That's what pushed the limit out of the prompt.

The rule I'd keep

If an LLM produces a list and something about that list has to be true every time (a maximum length, an order, a guarantee that nothing vanishes without a count), enforce it in code after generation and test it with a faked response. Use the prompt for the part only the model can do: deciding what goes on the list. Then make sure the prompt isn't quietly enforcing the same limit too, because a limit nobody can count is the one you were trying to get rid of.

I'm building DevReview at getdevreview.com. It's a GitHub App that ranks review comments by severity and caps them in code, and there's a free tier if you want to see what a capped review looks like on your own PRs. If you've solved the "the model trims itself before your code can count" problem differently, I'd like to hear how.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Support for Brazil (br) region (GA with allowlist)

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google SecOps

Fixed

Tools power-up: Environment filtering in Get Integration Instances

There was an issue where the Get Integration Instances action in the Tools power-up didn't correctly filter environments with names that contain an ampersand (&). This issue has been fixed in version 85.0 of the Tools power-up.

For more information, see Get Integration Instances.

Announcement

Final shutdown of legacy managed BigQuery export datasets (chronicle-tla) for non-Enterprise+ customers

Following the March 26, 2025 deprecation announcement, Google SecOps is completing the final shutdown of legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets and API keys associated with the chronicle-tla Google Cloud project:

  • What is changing: Data exports to legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets under the chronicle-tla project are being permanently turned off, and the associated managed datasets and API keys are being decommissioned.
  • Who is impacted: This shutdown applies only to non-Enterprise+ customers still provisioned on legacy chronicle-tla Google-managed BigQuery datasets (including tenants whose temporary transition exceptions expired in September 2025). Enterprise+ customers and customers using Bring Your Own BigQuery (BYOBQ) exports to customer-managed Google Cloud projects are not impacted.
  • When: Decommissioning begins on October 28, 2026.
  • Action required: To retain BigQuery access to Google SecOps data, configure export to a customer-managed BigQuery project (BYOBQ) or contact your account team to upgrade to Enterprise+.

Google SecOps Marketplace

Feature

SAP ERP: Version 1.0

  • New SAP ERP integration.

Feature

Google Threat Intelligence: Version 23.0

  • The following new action has been added:

    • Ask Threat Intelligence Agent

Change

Microsoft Graph Mail Delegated: Version 27.0

  • Fixed an issue where overflowed alerts were skipped without saving their IDs or marking the emails as read, preventing infinite reprocessing loops and state loss in the following connector:

    • Microsoft Graph Mail Delegated Connector

Change

Tools: Version 85.0

  • Fixed an issue where environment names containing ampersands (&) weren't properly filtered in the following action:

    • Get Integration Instances

Change

Wiz: Version 11.0

  • Fixed inbound and outbound closure reason mappings between Wiz and Google SecOps in the following job:

  • Updated predefined widgets in the following actions:

    • Get Blue Agent Analysis
    • Get Issue Details
    • Ignore Issue
    • List Resource Vulnerability Findings
    • Reopen Issue
    • Resolve Issue

Change

Microsoft Graph Mail: Version 50.0

  • Fixed an issue where overflowed alerts were skipped without saving their IDs or marking the emails as read, preventing infinite reprocessing loops and state loss in the following connector:

    • Microsoft Graph Mail Connector

Change

Google Chronicle: Version 99.0

  • Fixed an issue where the connector could stop ingesting alerts when composite detections failed to load or pagination did not progress in the following connector:

    • Google Chronicle - Chronicle Alerts Connector

Change

Okta: Version 19.0

  • Integration: Updated OAuth authentication scopes to support user management actions.

Change

Microsoft 365 Defender: Version 34.0

  • Added the Time Frame, Start Time, and End Time parameters to support time-based query filtering in the following action:

    • Execute Custom Query

Google SecOps SIEM

Following the March 26, 2025 deprecation announcement, Google SecOps is completing the final shutdown of legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets and API keys associated with the chronicle-tla Google Cloud project:

Enterprise+ customers and customers using Bring Your Own BigQuery (BYOBQ) exports to customer-managed Google Cloud projects are not impacted.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Support for Datastream as a source in Knowledge Catalog is now available. This feature supports Datastream streams, connections, and private connectivity.

For more information, see Supported Google Cloud sources.

Media CDN

Media CDN supports flexible origin shielding in Frankfurt (europe-west3). This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Flexible shielding.

title: Building a Redundant Edge Cluster Out of Three $15/Year Black Friday VPS Nodes
description:
Every Black Friday, developers grab sub-$15/year VPS instances out of impulse, run neofetch, and then let them idle until the renewal invoice hits twelve months later.

Last year, I decided to see how far I could push these throwaway budget boxes. Instead of letting them collect dust, I wired three distinct low-cost nodes across different geographic locations (Los Angeles, Frankfurt, and Singapore) into a self-healing reverse proxy and uptime cluster.

Here is the exact architecture, the configuration workflow, and the hard limits you need to watch out for when running container workloads on budget silicon.

The Architecture: Cheap Edge, Solid Core
The mental model is simple: never put your stateful databases on budget promo nodes.

Instead, treat them as ephemeral edge workers:

       [ Client Requests ]
                │
                ▼
      [ Cloudflare Anycast ]
                │
   ┌────────────┼────────────┐
   ▼            ▼            ▼

[ US Node ] [ EU Node ] [ APAC Node ] <-- $12-$18/yr BF Nodes (Traefik + Wireguard)
└────────────┼────────────┘
│ (Encrypted Wireguard Mesh)
▼
[ Hetzner / Netcup Core ] <-- Production Postgres, Redis & FFmpeg Backend
Anycast Ingress: Cloudflare handles DDoS mitigation and DNS routing to the closest healthy edge node.
Reverse Proxy & SSL: Each node runs Traefik in Docker, automatically negotiating Let’s Encrypt certificates.
Internal Mesh Network: The three edge nodes communicate with my primary production database (hosted on a dedicated Hetzner box) through a private WireGuard overlay network.
Health Checking: If the Los Angeles budget node gets rebooted for unscheduled host maintenance, Cloudflare health checks fail over traffic to Frankfurt in seconds.
Step 1: Minimum Hardware Requirements
You cannot run this stack on just any $10 box. Before you pick up deals from the sales threads, verify these three prerequisites:

Virtualization: Must be KVM. Container-based virtualization (OpenVZ/LXC) often restricts WireGuard kernel modules and causes Docker overlay networking headaches.
RAM: Minimum 1 GB. Docker + Traefik + WireGuard + a lightweight Node.js worker will hover around 350MB–500MB RAM usage. 512MB nodes will trigger the Linux OOM (Out Of Memory) killer the moment you run a package update.
Fair-Share CPU Policy: You don’t need dedicated cores, but avoid hosts that suspend instances if CPU utilization averages above 20% for 15 minutes.
Step 2: Automated Provisioning Script
Once you receive your root credentials, run this minimal hardening and setup script:

!/usr/bin/env bash

set -e

Update & install essential network tools

apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y
apt-get install -y curl ufw wireguard fail2ban htop

Enable BBR Congestion Control for better throughput on lossy pipes

cat <> /etc/sysctl.conf
net.core.default_qdisc=fq
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
EOF
sysctl -p

Lock down firewall

ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw allow 80/tcp
ufw allow 443/tcp
ufw allow 51820/udp # WireGuard
ufw --force enable

Install official Docker runtime

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
Step 3: Zero-Trust Interconnect via WireGuard
Rather than exposing database ports over the public internet, each node connects to the central cluster using a lightweight WireGuard configuration (/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf):

[Interface]
Address = 10.100.0.2/24
PrivateKey = CLIENT_PRIVATE_KEY
DNS = 1.1.1.1

[Peer]
PublicKey = CORE_SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY
Endpoint = core.yourdomain.com:51820
AllowedIPs = 10.100.0.0/24
PersistentKeepalive = 25
Now, any request hitting https://us-proxy.yourdomain.com forwards traffic to 10.100.0.1:3000 through an encrypted tunnel. If the public routing between the US budget node and the European datacenter has bad transit, WireGuard keeps the connection alive without exposing raw database ports to port scanners.

Step 4: The Traefik Edge Deployment
Here is the minimal docker-compose.yml I deploy to each node:

version: '3.8'

services:
traefik:
image: traefik:v3.1
restart: always
command:
- "--providers.docker=true"
- "--providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false"
- "--entrypoints.web.address=:80"
- "--entrypoints.websecure.address=:443"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.tlschallenge=true"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.email=admin@yourdomain.com"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json"
ports:
- "80:80"
- "443:443"
volumes:
- "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro"
- "./letsencrypt:/letsencrypt"
networks:
- web

networks:
web:
external: true
What I Learned Running Dirt-Cheap Nodes for a Year
Disk I/O Degrades First: The CPU usually stays fine, but shared disks will inevitably slow down during holidays. Keep your logs written to tmpfs (RAM) instead of hammering the physical disk with verbose access logs.
Reboots Will Happen: Budget providers don’t have redundant hot-swap hardware. Assume your node will reboot without warning once every two months. If your stack is stateless, you won’t care.
Buy Across Different ASNs: Don’t buy three promo instances from three different reseller brands that all sit in the same Racknerd or Colocrossing datacenter. Mix datacenters and network uplinks.
Where to Find Decent Nodes Right Now
If you want to spin up a similar cluster without spending hours manually sifting through bloated forum megathreads, I track real-time hardware specs, virtualization types, and Black Friday pricing here:

👉 https://vpsrankings.com/en/black-friday

Drop a comment below with your yabs.sh scores if you manage to snag an AMD EPYC box under $20/year this week.

title: Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.
description:
Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.

Let's be honest. How often do you update your database diagram after changing your database?

You add a table, introduce a relationship, rename a column or refactor an existing module. Your application evolves, your database changes, and your documentation slowly falls behind.

The problem isn't creating database diagrams. There are plenty of tools for that.

The problem is keeping them updated.

A common solution is to export a diagram as an image and commit it to your repository. It works, but the moment your schema changes, the image becomes outdated.

And someone eventually has to remember to replace it.

There is a better approach: put your database diagram directly in your GitHub README and let it update automatically.

Why database documentation gets outdated

Most development teams understand the importance of database documentation.

A diagram helps developers:

  • Understand how tables relate to each other.
  • Explore an unfamiliar codebase.
  • Identify dependencies before changing existing structures.
  • Onboard new developers.
  • Discuss database architecture with the rest of the team.

But maintaining that documentation introduces another task into an already busy development workflow.

Consider a typical Laravel application.

You start with users, roles and permissions. Later, you introduce subscriptions, invoices, payments and notifications.

Your migrations are updated, your application works, and everything gets committed.

But the database diagram?

It still shows the original structure.

Eventually, developers stop trusting it.

Put your database diagram directly in GitHub

With SchemaSketch, you can now embed a live database diagram directly into a GitHub README.

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Create your database diagram

Go to SchemaSketch and create a diagram using DBML.

DBML is a simple language for describing database structures.

For example:

Table users {
  id integer [primary key]
  name varchar
  email varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table projects {
  id integer [primary key]
  user_id integer
  name varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table tasks {
  id integer [primary key]
  project_id integer
  title varchar
  status varchar
}

Ref: projects.user_id > users.id
Ref: tasks.project_id > projects.id

SchemaSketch renders the database structure visually, allowing you to explore tables and their relationships.

You can also export your schema into SQL, Laravel migrations and models, Mermaid or PlantUML.

Step 2: Share your diagram

Once your diagram is ready, open the Share dialog.

Make the diagram publicly accessible and select Copy Markdown.

SchemaSketch generates the Markdown required to embed your diagram.

Step 3: Add it to your README

Open your GitHub repository and edit its README.md file.

Paste the Markdown you copied from SchemaSketch wherever you want the diagram to appear.

Commit your changes.

That's it.

Your database diagram is now part of your repository documentation.

Step 4: Let it update automatically

This is the interesting part.

The embedded diagram is served as an SVG image.

You don't need to export another image.

You don't need to replace anything in GitHub.

You don't need another commit just to update the documentation image.

If you make the diagram private or revoke its sharing link, the embedded image is no longer accessible.

Project Database Architecture

Your actual database diagram, showing users, projects, tasks and all their relationships.

A new developer can understand the database structure without having to open another application or search for an old diagram.

And when the database design changes, the README follows.

No separate image files to maintain.

No outdated screenshots.

More than just database diagrams

The live README integration is one of several improvements we've recently introduced to SchemaSketch.

An open-source DBML renderer

We've released the drawing engine as schemasketch-render, an npm package.

It is MIT licensed, has no dependencies and supports Node.js 18 and above.

For example, this makes it possible to generate database diagram images as part of your own development or CI workflows.

Repository and package:

More AI coding agent integrations

Claude Code and Claude Desktop already support a one-command setup.

Through the SchemaSketch MCP server, AI agents can work with database diagrams rather than relying entirely on assumptions when generating application code.

Better support for real-world DBML

We've also improved compatibility with DBML structures commonly found in existing projects.

This includes:

  • PostgreSQL-style schemas, such as billing.invoices.
  • Relationships across schemas.

The goal is to make working with existing database designs easier, not just diagrams created from scratch.

Documentation should evolve with your application

It should be part of your development workflow.

Whether you're maintaining a Laravel application, working with PostgreSQL or building software with AI coding agents, having an accessible and current representation of your database makes a difference.

title: Our phone CTA bar reads rectangles every frame instead of using IntersectionObserver, and a fast fling is why
description:
CogniPrep's long entry pages are long. A provider hub or an employer guide runs thousands of pixels, and the primary action sits near the top. On a phone, somebody who reads to the end has nothing to tap without scrolling back.

The fix is the oldest pattern on mobile web: a bar pinned to the bottom with the action in it. The interesting part is that almost every decision in the 133 lines is a decision not to do the obvious thing.

It shows between two points, not from a threshold

The bar is not "appears after 400px". It shows after the page's own early call to action has scrolled up under the header, and hides again once the page's closing call to action or the footer comes into view. So it never doubles up with a button already on screen, and it is gone before the footer, which is what stops it covering anything.

Both ends are elements, not offsets. The start is an id passed in as a prop. The end is any element carrying a data attribute, or the footer:

const ends = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll(`[${STICKY_CTA_END_ATTR}], footer`));

Why not IntersectionObserver

This is the part I want to defend, because an observer is the right default and this is the case where it is wrong. The component's own comment states it:

 * Both points are read from element positions on scroll (once per frame), not
 * from IntersectionObserver: a jump straight past the early button, from a fast
 * fling or an in-page link, never intersects it, so an observer would not fire.

An IntersectionObserver reports crossings. If a frame never renders with the element partially in view, there is no crossing to report. Two things on a long page do exactly that: a hard fling on iOS, where the compositor can jump hundreds of pixels between frames, and an in-page anchor link, which teleports past everything in between. In both cases the observer stays silent and the bar never appears, which is the one failure mode a reader notices.

So it reads positions instead, and it reads them as state rather than as events:

const update = () => {
  frame = 0;
  setPastAnchor(anchor.getBoundingClientRect().bottom <= HEADER_HEIGHT_PX);
  setAtEnd(ends.some((end) => end.getBoundingClientRect().top < window.innerHeight));
};
const schedule = () => {
  if (!frame) frame = requestAnimationFrame(update);
};
update();
window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);

Three things keep that cheap. The listener is passive, so it cannot block scrolling. The work is coalesced to one requestAnimationFrame per frame no matter how many scroll events arrive. And update() is called once immediately, so a page restored mid-scroll by the browser is correct before the first scroll event rather than after it.

HEADER_HEIGHT_PX is 56, the height of the fixed header, so "scrolled away" means scrolled under the header rather than off the top of the viewport.

The end test is top < window.innerHeight, not a two-sided intersection check. An element above the viewport has a negative top, so "in view or already past it" collapses into one comparison. The bar never comes back once you have reached the end of the page.

The portal, and the one-word reason it is needed

The bar renders through createPortal into document.body. Not for convenience:

 * Rendered into document.body through a portal, so it can be mounted anywhere:
 * `main` carries `contain: paint` (app/globals.css), which would otherwise make
 * it the bar's containing block and pin the bar to the bottom of the page
 * instead of the bottom of the screen.

The stylesheet has this, for unrelated reasons:

@layer base {
  main {
    min-height: calc(100dvh - 3.5rem);
    contain: layout style paint;
  }
}

contain: paint makes the element a containing block for fixed-position descendants. So position: fixed; bottom: 0 inside main is fixed to the bottom of main, which is thousands of pixels down. The bar would work in isolation and fail in place, and the failure would look like "the bar does not show" rather than "the bar is at the wrong offset", because you would have to scroll to the bottom of the document to see it.

A census of this repository in early November counted zero createPortal call sites. There are two now, and this is the one with a written reason.

Four details that cost four lines each

Client-only without a hydration flicker. The bar is invisible until the reader scrolls, so rendering nothing on the server changes nothing on screen:

const isClient = useSyncExternalStore(noSubscribe, () => true, () => false);

A no-op subscribe and a false server snapshot. Static HTML ships without the bar, and the portal arrives after hydration. The practical upshot: the bar is in no page's HTML. You cannot find it by viewing source.

Scroll padding from the bar's real height. While the bar shows, it sets scroll-padding-bottom on the document to its own measured height, so keyboard focus and in-page jumps land above it instead of under it. Measured, not a constant, with the reason given inline: the label can wrap to two lines on a narrow phone.

Hidden properly, not just invisibly. When it is not showing it keeps pointer-events-none translate-y-full opacity-0 and also carries aria-hidden and inert. Opacity zero alone leaves a focusable link in the tab order that nobody can see.

A 48px target and the safe area. The button is min-h-12, and the bar's bottom padding is pb-[max(0.75rem,env(safe-area-inset-bottom))], so the home-bar gesture area on a modern iPhone does not eat the tap. The label is set to wrap rather than truncate, with a comment explaining why: a cut-off label could lose the word "free".

Where it runs, counted from the live site

Five page shells mount it, which puts it on 736 of the 1,093 public URLs:

Surface Pages with the bar
Per-test pages 409
Employer guides 201
Provider hubs 69
Company interview pages 42
Test format pages 15

Each shell names its own anchor id: test-cta, employer-cta, hub-cta, interview-cta, format-cta. Four different names for the same role, which is the kind of thing five parallel edits produce.

The employer number is the one worth noting. There are 214 employer guides, and 201 carry the anchor. The other 13 are guides where no test vendor is evidenced at medium confidence or better, which is a deliberate rule stated in the module that supplies the association: those pages get sibling links but no provider hub link, "because there is no hub that honestly matches the page". Both the early call to action and the bar read the same value, so where there is nothing honest to offer, neither renders. One condition, two surfaces, no special case.

The one loose end

STICKY_CTA_END_ATTR is exported so callers cannot typo the attribute name. All 69 provider hubs write the string by hand instead:

<div data-sticky-cta-end className="...">

A typo there is silent. The bar would simply stay up until the footer, which still looks fine, which is why nothing would catch it. The constant is doing no work until someone imports it.

See it

This one needs a narrow viewport, because the bar is md:hidden and it is not in any page's HTML.

Open the SHL provider hub and set your window to 375px wide, or open it on a phone. View source first and search for pointer-events-none translate-y-full: nothing, because the bar is portalled in after hydration.

Now scroll slowly. The bar arrives the moment the hub's own early button passes under the header, and it leaves again when the closing block at the bottom of the page comes into view. Search the source for data-sticky-cta-end and you are looking at the element that dismisses it.

Then try the hard case. Scroll back to the top, and flick as hard as you can straight to the bottom. The bar never appears, which is correct, because the end block is already in view. Now flick to the middle instead. It is there, having never been given a crossing to observe.

Finally, compare with an employer guide at the same width, where the anchor id is employer-cta instead, and with a per-test page, where it is test-cta. Same 133 lines, three different anchors.
