title: The night the queue ran dry at 1:40
description:
Here's the rule everything else hangs on: the one who builds a thing never gets to say it's done.

Every piece of work in our house goes through three hands. One writes the spec: what "done" means, in clauses you can check. One builds against it. Then the spec's author returns as the acceptor and measures the result herself, with her own commands, not the builder's word. A builder can be brilliant and quietly wrong; acceptance catches that.

A good acceptance doesn't stop at "the tests pass". It breaks the code on purpose to see whether the tests notice. On one recent feature the acceptor planted ten small bugs in a copy of the code — a dropped check, a flipped reply — and the suite caught all ten. One survivor would have sent the feature back.

Acceptance started on the night machinery itself, before it ran, and found three defects in its own spec — one the "now ≥ 08:00" clause, which read literally would end every night begun the evening before, because a time of day is not a deadline. The suite grew from 43 to 68 as they were fixed.

The ask

In early October I wrote down something simple: stop choosing the night's work by hand every evening. Keep one standing backlog for all projects, give the night a signal that I'm asleep, and let it work until morning. One hard condition: at 08:00, the usage window still open must be at least half free.

The rest of the design followed. One backlog file; every item carries a project, a status, a stops-at line naming the last step we may take without a human, and who added it. The status vocabulary is closed: proposed, ready, in-flight, parked, done, dropped. One rule matters most: only the acceptor may move an item to ready. The runner picks nothing else — that is why a night is safe, and shallow.

There were two triggers: a command on the command line, and a physical tag by the bed. The tag path worked — 112 scans — but the last was in September and none in the 23 days after, so it had quietly left my routine. A tag daemon also kills a bound command after 30 seconds, so the command had to stand on its own. The supervisor runs detached, locked by a file lock in Python.

Each tick is one item, end to end: a spec check, one build, acceptance, a status update, a line in the morning report. Two failed ticks in a row end the night, and a tick that stops to ask for approval counts as failed, not as something to retry quietly.

The budget gate

The runner refuses to start work without knowing what it costs, and a budget gate is only as honest as its gauge. On the evening of the first run there was no gauge at all: the usage script returned "status: unknown", the proxy console an empty five-hour window, and a direct endpoint call failed with a 401.

The cause turned out to be duller than a bug. The script preferred any credentials file on disk, and that one was stale — last written in early September, its token long expired — while the live token sat in the keychain. The 401 came from the dead token, and so did the later rate limit with its long Retry-After. A keychain call answered 200 at once. Two answers, "unknown" and "empty", were one problem in different clothes.

What shipped is a single poller: one job writes one gauge file, and it alone may call the usage endpoint on a schedule. One call per cycle; after a rate limit it waits for the server's Retry-After, otherwise it doubles the wait. Its first run answered 200 with small numbers; the parser read "GO".

The handover between gauge and runner is where the night stumbled. The runner started just after midnight with the variable pointing at a missing gauge file, and its first gate said HOLD: gauge unknown. Restarted with the variable set, it read GO. The report that survives opens at 01:04 — my start, not a fault. One gauge detail stayed unresolved: all three gates read the same numbers, and the reading aged — 30 minutes, then 44, then 58 — though the poller should have refreshed every few minutes.

What happened

Three items were ready. All three ran, exit 0, all ending ready→done, all accepted on the first pass, in 13, 14 and 8 minutes. One fixed a reminder banner that forgot it had been dismissed after a reload. Another packaged a mobile release path and only ran it as a dry run: it reported success and produced an unsigned archive — exactly what a dry run is for.

The report's "waiting on a human" section held two more lines, both fences working: a deployment waiting for a date, and a real upload needing the paid developer team signed in. The night's last line said: 01:40 — queue empty. The deadline was 08:00, and the budget nowhere near a stop row.

The night ended because there was nothing left to do — the design working as written. "Only the acceptor makes things ready" exists so nothing unvetted runs while nobody is watching. The cost: a night goes only as deep as the vetting done in daylight. A gate built to stop a night running too hot never acted at all.

What changed afterwards

The next morning I wrote down: the backlog needs to be thought about much further ahead — research, gathering and writing tasks too, maybe even a book — so that when one task blocks there is something to switch to. Then I narrowed it: an idea to think through together, not an order. Nothing new was opened; by ten I looked at the result and said keep it as it was.

The backlog side came first. Before that pass, ready stood at zero; after it, thirty-five items: three proposed, twenty-two ready, four parked, six done. The ready ones sat in four lanes — five builds, eight research, four gathering, five writing — interleaved so no two neighbours share a project, which a script checked: zero adjacent pairs. A floor of fifteen ready items became the warning line. The non-code items carry their own acceptance floor: sources, recorded statuses, an explicit Unknown list, no decisions taken for me.

The runner side got the fields that make that possible: optional lane, predecessor and builder per item; a lint that errors on a bad lane or on a predecessor naming a missing item; one function shared by the supervisor, the lint and the dry-run, so the three cannot disagree about what is ready. Then the switch rule: a project-wide block — red CI, a dirty tree, an unreachable host, expired auth — parks every ready item of that project in one tick with one waiting line, so the night moves on instead of failing twice and stopping. The suite went from 68 to 90 tests, and the gate stayed byte-for-byte unchanged, checked by comparing syntax trees.

The prediction that didn't hold

At twelve minutes a tick, twenty-two items is roughly four and a half hours; research and writing run longer. After the refill I expected budget, not the queue, to end most nights. The nights that followed all ended like the first: 22 ready and 23 ticks, empty at 05:36; 25 ready and 25 ticks, empty at 04:19; 19 ready and 19 ticks; 31 ready and 31 ticks. Not one stopped on the budget.

A prediction isn't a measurement, and the measurement said the queue was still the wall — the refill bought depth, not immunity. A deeper queue ends the same way, only later.

title: Stablecoin Payments Backend: Dual-Ledger Spring Boot
description:
Short version of the design: keep an internal double-entry ledger, treat the blockchain as a second, slower source of truth, only release value after a per-chain finality depth, and run a job whose only purpose is to prove the two agree. In Spring Boot that is a ledger service, a confirmation state machine, idempotent Kafka consumers and a scheduled drift check.

Toss, the Korean fintech super-app, has reportedly started offering its users a wallet built around dollar stablecoins, and Kakao attempted something comparable before without gaining much traction. I have not seen any public detail about either company's backend, so I am not going to claim to know why one worked and the other did not. Distribution, licensing, KYC approval and FX pricing probably explain most of it. What interested me is narrower: whichever app wins users, its balances still have to be correct, and that part is plain engineering that any team can get wrong. This post is about that part.

I have worked on payment backends for years, including Open Banking PSD2 integrations, and the mistakes below are the ones I keep seeing in review. Where I describe a failure, treat it as a scenario to design against, not a war story with invented numbers.

Part 1: Why "sent" and "final" are different states

Quick glossary, only what the rest of the post needs. A stablecoin (USDT, USDC) is a token that tracks a fiat currency. The chain is the public ledger that records who holds how many tokens. Settlement, for our purposes, is the point after which you would be willing to bet money the transfer will not be reversed.

When a user taps "send 50 USDC", three separate things happen on different clocks:

  1. Your database records the debit. Immediate, and only your company's claim.
  2. Your service signs a transaction and submits it to the network's mempool, where it waits for a block producer to pick it up. A low fee or a bad nonce can leave it sitting there for a long time.
  3. A block includes it, and later blocks stack on top. Each extra block makes a rollback less likely. At some chain-specific depth you stop worrying.

So for a stretch of seconds to minutes, your DB and the chain disagree on purpose. The backend's job is to know, for every transfer, which of "submitted" or "settled" is currently true, and to say only that to the customer.

Part 2: Where custody ledgers actually break

The three generic failures (crediting too early, double-processing, silent drift) are real, but the ones that cost time in practice are more specific. This is the checklist I would run any design against.

Crediting before finality. The watcher sees a deposit in a block and credits immediately. A reorg drops that block, and the customer has already spent the credit. The fix is the state machine in Part 5.

Duplicate events. Kafka and every other broker deliver at least once. A restart replays the last batch, and the deposit is credited twice unless the consumer can recognise a repeat.

Decimals. USDC on Ethereum uses 6 decimals. USDT on BNB Chain uses 18, and the same ticker elsewhere may use 6. If you store a single decimals constant per asset instead of per asset-per-network, you will eventually mis-scale a transfer by a factor of a trillion. Store base units as integers and keep decimals in network config.

Nonce management. On account-model chains, every outgoing transaction from a hot wallet carries a sequential nonce. If transaction 41 is stuck on a low fee, 42 and 43 queue behind it. You need a single owner for nonce assignment, a policy for replacing a stuck transaction with a higher-fee one at the same nonce, and a way to tell the ledger that the original hash is dead and the replacement is the real one.

Gas funding. Sending an ERC-20 token costs the chain's native coin, not the token. A hot wallet full of USDC and out of ETH cannot move anything. Native-coin balance of every signer needs its own alarm.

Wrong-chain and wrong-token deposits. Users send USDT to a USDC address, or a Tron-network token to an Ethereum-format address. Some of these are recoverable by hand. The ledger must not auto-credit anything it did not expect, and unknown arrivals need a quarantine account.

Issuer freezes. Tether and Circle can blacklist addresses. A frozen omnibus address means your on-chain balance can stop moving while the ledger still shows funds. Reconciliation should flag a balance that stays unchanged while pending withdrawals pile up.

Sweeping and rebalancing. Many custodial designs give each customer a deposit address and sweep funds to an omnibus hot wallet, with a rebalance to cold storage past a threshold. Every sweep is itself a chain transaction with fees, and it moves value between your own addresses. Those internal moves must be ledger postings too, or the totals drift by exactly the sweep fees.

Travel-rule and sanctions screening. In many jurisdictions a withdrawal to an external address needs screening before broadcast. That is one more state before APPROVED, and it can reject a transfer after the customer has already seen the button turn green.

UTXO chains differ from account chains here: there are no nonces, but you manage coin selection and change outputs, and one deposit may arrive as several inputs. The state machine below still applies; only the watcher and the signer change.

Part 3: The shape of the system

The company side is fast and fully yours. The chain side is slow and outside anyone's control. The interesting engineering sits in between.

Components:

  • Internal double-entry ledger. The authoritative record of who is owed what.
  • Broadcast path. Turns an approved transfer into a signed chain transaction.
  • Confirmation tracker. Follows the chain and walks each transfer through explicit states.
  • Reconciliation job. Periodically proves ledger and chain agree.

Each of these has a real alternative, so the trade-offs deserve a word.

Broadcast path. I use a transactional outbox: the ledger posting and the "please broadcast" row commit in one DB transaction, and a poller publishes them. Change-data-capture with Debezium reads the same table from the WAL instead, which gives lower latency and no polling load, but adds Kafka Connect as a component to operate and monitor. For a wallet doing modest volume, polling every second or two is simpler and easier to reason about during an incident. For high volume, CDC pays for itself. Delivery mechanics are in my transactional outbox post.

Watcher. Polling eth_getLogs per block is easy and restartable from a stored height. Subscribing over WebSocket is quicker but drops events on disconnect, so you still need the polling backfill. I would build the poller first and treat subscriptions as an optimisation.

Failure analysis. If the broadcaster dies after signing but before recording the hash, you can resubmit the same signed bytes (same nonce, same hash) safely. If the watcher dies, it resumes from its last stored height and re-emits observations, which the idempotent consumer absorbs. If the reconciler dies, nothing breaks, but you lose detection, so its own freshness needs an alert.

Part 4: The internal ledger

A double-entry ledger writes every movement as two or more lines that sum to zero. Value is never created or destroyed inside it, only moved. That gives you a cheap invariant: if the global sum is not zero, something is wrong, and a query tells you before a customer does.

Accounts for a custodial stablecoin wallet:

  • CUSTOMER:{id}:USDC for each customer's spendable balance.
  • CUSTOMER:{id}:USDC:HELD for amounts reserved while a withdrawal is in flight.
  • OMNIBUS:USDC which mirrors the pooled on-chain address the company controls.
  • FEES:USDC and NETWORK_FEE:USDC for revenue and costs.
  • IN_FLIGHT:USDC for value that has left the customer but not yet been proven final on chain.
  • QUARANTINE:USDC for arrivals nobody expected (wrong token, unknown sender).

IN_FLIGHT earns its place. Without it, a withdrawal jumps from "customer has 50" to "customer has 0" and you can no longer express that the transfer is unfinished. With it, each lifecycle step is a posting that mirrors a real-world fact.

Amounts are integer base units, never floating point.

@Service
public class LedgerService {

    private final JournalRepository journals;

    public LedgerService(JournalRepository journals) {
        this.journals = journals;
    }

    /** Move funds from the customer into IN_FLIGHT when a withdrawal is approved. */
    @Transactional
    public Journal reserveWithdrawal(UUID transferId, String customerAcct,
                                     long amountMicros, long feeMicros) {

        // Idempotency: the same transferId can only ever post once.
        return journals.findByBusinessKey("WD-RESERVE-" + transferId)
            .orElseGet(() -> {
                long available = journals.balanceOf(customerAcct);
                if (available < amountMicros + feeMicros) {
                    throw new InsufficientFundsException(customerAcct);
                }
                Journal j = Journal.open("WD-RESERVE-" + transferId)
                    .debit(customerAcct, amountMicros + feeMicros)
                    .credit("IN_FLIGHT:USDC", amountMicros)
                    .credit("FEES:USDC", feeMicros)
                    .build();           // throws if debits != credits
                return journals.save(j);
            });
    }
}

Two details. The business_key column carries a unique constraint, so if two threads race, the database rejects the second insert; idempotency lives in the data. And build() refuses to create an unbalanced journal, so a whole class of bugs becomes a test failure rather than silent drift. Adding that constraint to a table that already holds live postings is its own risk; I cover the safe sequence in my zero-downtime database migrations guide.

One caveat on the balance read: in production take a row lock on the customer's account record (or use an optimistic version column) so two concurrent withdrawals cannot both pass the check. A double-spent mandate in Commercial VRP mandate payments is a regulatory issue, not merely a bug, and the same append-only habit carries into IBAN-name verification and fraud-liability decisions under PSD3, where every decision has to be reproducible later.

Part 5: Confirmation as a state machine

Most first versions model a chain transfer as a boolean confirmed. That flag is where reorg bugs are born. A transfer has a lifecycle, and each state should map to one ledger effect and one sentence you are allowed to show the customer.

State Meaning Customer sees Ledger effect
APPROVED Passed risk and balance checks "Processing" Funds moved to IN_FLIGHT
BROADCAST Signed and sent to the network "Sent, waiting for network" None
SEEN Found in a block, few confirmations "On the network" None
CONFIRMING Buried under N blocks, below final threshold "Almost done" None
FINAL Reached the chain's finality depth "Completed" IN_FLIGHT released to omnibus
REORGED Block it lived in was replaced "Delayed, re-checking" None, state rolled back
FAILED Rejected or dropped permanently "Failed, refunded" IN_FLIGHT returned to customer

Rules I do not bend:

  1. Only FINAL moves value out of IN_FLIGHT. Seeing a transaction is a hint; finality is the fact.
  2. A state may move backwards only through REORGED. Everything else is forward-only, so illegal histories cannot be represented.
  3. Finality depth is per-network configuration. Ethereum-style chains, Tron and layer-2s settle at different depths, and a single global "6 confirmations" is a bug waiting to be copied into the wrong place. Some L2s also have a gap between sequencer confirmation and L1 finality, which your config must be able to express.

Deposits mirror this, with a stricter rule: never credit spendable balance on SEEN. Show a pending line in the UI if you like, but post the spendable credit on FINAL.

A replaced transaction (the nonce-bump case from Part 2) fits as well: the original hash moves to FAILED-superseded and the replacement hash becomes the tracked one, with the ledger untouched because the reservation is keyed on the transfer, not the hash.

Part 6: Idempotent confirmation handling with Kafka

The watcher emits observations: "transaction X is in block B at height H", "block B was replaced", "tip is now H+12". I key them by transfer id so one transfer's events land on one partition in order, and the consumer advances the state machine.

The consumer has to survive duplicates, out-of-order events after a rebalance, and reorg events that contradict earlier ones. Each handler is a function of stored state plus the event, guarded by a sequence number.

@Component
public class ConfirmationConsumer {

    private final TransferRepository transfers;
    private final LedgerService ledger;
    private final ChainProperties chains;

    // ... constructor omitted

    @KafkaListener(topics = "chain.observations", groupId = "confirmation-tracker")
    @Transactional
    public void on(ChainObservation obs) {
        Transfer t = transfers.findByIdForUpdate(obs.transferId());

        // Idempotency: ignore anything not newer than what we already applied.
        if (obs.observedSeq() <= t.getLastAppliedSeq()) {
            return;
        }

        long depth = obs.chainHeight() - obs.blockHeight() + 1;
        long finality = chains.finalityDepth(t.getNetwork());

        switch (obs.kind()) {
            case INCLUDED -> t.moveTo(depth >= finality ? State.FINAL : State.CONFIRMING,
                                      obs.blockHash());
            case BLOCK_REPLACED -> {
                if (t.getState() == State.FINAL) {
                    // Finality violated: page a human, never auto-heal money.
                    throw new FinalityBreachException(t.getId(), obs);
                }
                t.moveTo(State.REORGED, null);
            }
            case DROPPED -> t.moveTo(State.FAILED, null);
        }

        if (t.getState() == State.FINAL && !t.isSettledInLedger()) {
            ledger.releaseInFlight(t.getId());   // idempotent by business key
            t.markSettledInLedger();
        }
        if (t.getState() == State.FAILED && !t.isRefunded()) {
            ledger.refundWithdrawal(t.getId());
            t.markRefunded();
        }

        t.setLastAppliedSeq(obs.observedSeq());
        transfers.save(t);
    }
}

What the code deliberately avoids: it does not trust Kafka to deliver once, because observedSeq plus the row lock make replays harmless. It does not quietly repair a FINAL transfer that gets reorged; that throws and pages someone, since a finality breach means an assumption in the model was wrong and money decisions made on a broken assumption should be human ones. And the ledger calls are idempotent by business key, so a crash between the ledger write and the state update just re-runs.

For retry topics, dead-letter handling and poison messages, the patterns in the outbox and idempotent consumer write-up apply unchanged. Share groups in Kafka are interesting for queue-style scaling, but they give up the strict per-key ordering this design depends on, so test carefully before adopting them here.

Part 7: Reconciliation

The earlier parts make drift unlikely. Reconciliation makes it visible. I treat it as a product feature with its own owner, not a nightly script nobody reads.

For a custodial wallet, the ledger's total of customer balances plus fees plus in-flight value must equal what the company's addresses hold on chain, after adjusting for known pending items. Each run does three comparisons:

  1. Total check. OMNIBUS:USDC ledger balance against the real on-chain token balance of the controlled addresses, read at a specific block height (not "latest", which keeps moving).
  2. Transfer check. Every journal tied to a FINAL transfer has a matching chain transaction, and every chain transaction touching our addresses has a matching journal. The second direction is what catches deposits we never noticed, and wrong-token arrivals.
  3. Stuck-state check. Any transfer sitting in BROADCAST, SEEN, CONFIRMING or REORGED past an agreed limit is listed for a person. Stuck BROADCAST is usually a nonce or gas problem from Part 2.

The total check query is intentionally dull:

-- Run against a ledger snapshot taken at the same moment as the chain block read
SELECT
  l.omnibus_micros                         AS ledger_omnibus,
  :chain_balance_micros                    AS chain_balance,
  l.omnibus_micros - :chain_balance_micros AS drift,
  l.in_flight_micros                       AS pending_outbound
FROM (
  SELECT
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN account = 'OMNIBUS:USDC'   THEN signed_amount END), 0) AS omnibus_micros,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN account = 'IN_FLIGHT:USDC' THEN signed_amount END), 0) AS in_flight_micros
  FROM journal_line
  WHERE posted_at <= :snapshot_ts
) l;

Time alignment is the subtle part. The ledger runs on wall-clock time and the chain on block heights. I record the height I read and compare against postings up to that block's timestamp, with a small margin. Skip this and every transfer that lands mid-run produces a phantom discrepancy, the team learns to ignore the alert, and an ignored alert is worse than none.

On a mismatch the job never edits balances. It opens a ticket carrying the block height, both numbers, the diff and the candidate transfers. Corrections go in as new journal entries with a reason and an approver. The ledger is append-only.

The same habit shows up in my deterministic replay post: if you cannot re-derive a number from recorded history, you cannot defend it.

Part 8: Observability and operational edges

Signals I would have on a dashboard from the first deployment:

  • Count and age of transfers in each state, per network.
  • Reconciliation drift in base units, with an expected value of exactly zero.
  • Reorg events per day, per chain, plus maximum depth seen.
  • Consumer lag on the observations topic.
  • Native-coin (gas) balance of each signer.
  • Hot-wallet versus cold-storage balance ratio.

Trace IDs should follow a transfer from the API call through the ledger posting, the broadcast and each confirmation event; my distributed tracing guide for Spring Boot covers the setup. When support gets "my money has not arrived", one trace should tell the whole story.

Part 9: The Korean won angle and regulation

Reports suggest Korea's large platforms are all positioning for won-denominated stablecoins: Toss linked to a chain built on the OP Stack, Naver tied to the exchange operator Dunamu, and Kakao with its own plans after the earlier wallet struggled. This is moving quickly and I cannot verify commercial terms, so read those specifics as reported rather than confirmed.

The engineering consequence is clearer. A won token on a layer-2 has different finality behaviour from USDT on Tron or USDC on Ethereum, which is the reason finality depth lives in configuration. Regulated issuance also tends to demand reserve reporting, meaning you must show tokens outstanding against reserves held. A proper double-entry ledger gives you that nearly for free; mutable balance columns do not.

Two regulatory threads make this skill set marketable:

  • MiCA, the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, sets expectations on safeguarding client assets, record-keeping and complaints for stablecoin issuers and service providers. A custodial wallet serving EU users needs demonstrable asset segregation and auditable records, which are ledger and reconciliation features.
  • ASEAN cross-border payments are linking national QR and instant schemes, and stablecoins compete for the same corridors. I covered the QR side in my piece on EMVCo-based ASEAN QR routing. A ledger that sits cleanly between a QR scheme and a token rail is a useful thing to be able to design.

Some compliance evidence can be generated automatically; policy-as-code for DORA and NIS2 shows how I produce audit artefacts from the deployment pipeline.

What I would do differently from a first draft

  • Make finality a per-network config object from the first commit, with a test that fails when a network is added without one.
  • Never let a human edit a balance. Allow only a new, signed, reasoned journal entry.
  • Reconcile from day one, even against fake money in staging. It is cheapest to build before anything depends on it.
  • Treat "FINAL breached" as an incident, not an exception to retry.
  • Keep the customer-facing vocabulary smaller than the internal one. Nobody needs to see CONFIRMING; "Almost done" is enough.

None of this is glamorous. Whether any wallet keeps user trust through a bad day on the network will depend more on this layer than on which token it moves. Customers tolerate slow; they do not tolerate wrong.

Work with me

If you are building or rescuing a payments backend, ledger or reconciliation pipeline, you can see the systems I have shipped in my projects and reach me through the contact section. Send a short description of your transfer flow and the failure you fear most, and I will reply with a first-pass state model for it.

Related Articles

  • Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumers in Spring Boot Payment Systems
  • Open Banking PSD2 API Development
  • ASEAN Cross-Border QR Payments: EMVCo Router with PayNow, DuitNow, PromptPay and QRIS in Spring Boot

FAQ

What is a stablecoin?

A token pegged to a fiat currency, most often the US dollar. USDT and USDC are the big dollar ones, and they travel over public blockchains rather than bank payment rails.

Is a stablecoin transfer instant?

Not in the sense a backend cares about. An app can show "sent" within a second, but the payment is only safe to treat as done once enough later blocks sit on top of it, and that depth differs per chain.

What is a double-entry ledger?

A ledger where each posting touches at least two accounts and the amounts net to zero. If a posting is lost or applied twice, the totals stop balancing and the bug shows up in a query instead of in a customer complaint.

Why does a wallet app need reconciliation?

Because the app's database and the chain are two independent records that can drift apart through missed events, manual fixes or fees nobody posted. A scheduled comparison surfaces the gap on your schedule, not the customer's.

title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
description:
arXiv:2611.21705v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

title: Gatsby for Beginners: Blazing-Fast Websites From React and Data
description:
Gatsby is a React framework for building fast, content-driven websites — blogs, documentation sites, marketing pages, and e-commerce storefronts. It pulls data from anywhere (Markdown files, a CMS, an API), builds your pages at build time, and ships them as static HTML with React hydration. The result is a site that loads instantly and still feels like an app.

What makes Gatsby special is its data layer. Every piece of content becomes a node in a GraphQL graph, and every page queries exactly the data it needs. You stop writing fetch calls and start writing queries.

npm init gatsby my-site
cd my-site
npm run develop

A page that queries Markdown posts looks like this:

import { graphql } from 'gatsby';

export default function Blog({ data }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {data.allMarkdownRemark.nodes.map(post => (
        <li key={post.id}>{post.frontmatter.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

export const query = graphql`
  query {
    allMarkdownRemark {
      nodes {
        id
        frontmatter { title }
      }
    }
  }
`;

Gatsby is a great fit for blogs, docs, and marketing sites with lots of content. Its plugin ecosystem covers images, SEO, analytics, and CMS integrations, and its image component automatically optimizes every picture.

The limits matter. Build times grow with content — a site with tens of thousands of pages can take a long time to build. And for apps with highly dynamic, user-specific data, a server-rendered framework like Next.js or SvelteKit is a better fit. Gatsby shines when content changes slowly and speed matters most.

If your next project is a blog or docs site, try Gatsby for one section first. The moment you see a page load with zero spinners, you will understand the appeal.

title: Kengele: an alarm for when an activist goes missing, that nobody can switch off
description:
When an activist disappears, the first hours matter.

In Kenya, the national human rights commission counted more than 80 abductions and enforced disappearances after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, several abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry. Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan activist Agather Atuhaire were freed after their detention in Tanzania became public.

Speed of public pressure is what gets people out. Today the alarm depends on someone noticing and phoning around, over networks that can be watched or switched off. Uganda and Tanzania both shut down the internet around their elections.

So I'm building Kengele (Swahili for "bell"), an open-source alarm for when an activist goes missing.

Not for real use yet. Kengele is in the design and early build stage. Nobody should rely on it until an independent security review is done.

How it works

  1. Watch windows. Before a protest, a court visit or a risky trip, the activist sets check-ins, for example every 90 minutes from 2pm to 8pm.
  2. The alarm lives on the guardians' phones. Each check-in is a signed, encrypted message to 3 to 5 guardians (family, a lawyer, an organisation). If one doesn't arrive, every guardian's app raises the alarm on its own. Seizing the activist's phone stops nothing.
  3. Duress PIN. If someone forces the activist to check in, the duress PIN shows a normal screen and quietly raises the top-level alarm.
  4. Guardians confirm first. Nothing goes public until 2 of 3 guardians confirm. The alert text is locked under a key split among the guardians (Shamir secret sharing), so one guardian, even a coerced one, cannot publish early.
  5. Public alert and legal packet. Once confirmed, the activist's pre-written alert is published on Nostr, and the lawyer gets a ready habeas corpus packet.
  6. A captor can't call it off. After an alarm starts, the activist's own all-clear ends nothing. Only guardians, after a voice or video check, can stand it down.

Built for shutdowns

  • The clock only runs while the network is up. In a blackout, deadlines pause instead of firing hundreds of false alarms, then the alarm fires the moment the network returns.
  • Encrypted SMS fallback. Every message is exactly 228 bytes and fits in two SMS. A panic looks identical to a normal check-in on the wire.
  • Carry and deliver later. Messages are signed and encrypted, so any phone can carry them and deliver them when it finds a network, with the original signed time intact.
  • Per-route clocks. An SMS only proves SMS works. Each activist's clock pauses only when every route they use is down.

What it deliberately doesn't do

No servers to switch off. No custody of anyone's money. No GPS trail. No accounts or phone numbers. And it doesn't prevent an abduction. It shortens the time between a disappearance and public pressure.

Where it is

Written in Go, on Nostr (NIP-44 encryption, NIP-59 gift wrap) and BIP-340 signatures. So far:

  • a published threat model, written before the code
  • the signed, encrypted message format
  • the guardian watcher with the shutdown-aware clock
  • Nostr transport that hides sender and timing from relays
  • the SMS spec
  • 2-of-3 guardian confirmation and the coerced all-clear rule

Ten pull requests merged, every one race-tested.

Next: the Android app, OpenTimestamps proof, a legal fund guardians can unlock, Bluetooth mesh through bitchat, and an independent security review.

Prior art

The closest tool, Círculo by Guardian Project and ARTICLE 19, says on its site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It needed the internet and its own servers. Amnesty's Panic Button was retired after false alarms. Kengele is designed around both lessons.

Get involved

Security reviewers, Go and Android developers, Nostr folks and Swahili translators are all welcome. Start with the Start here issue.

Code: github.com/altradits/kengele (MIT)

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. If you go quiet, the bell rings.

title: Fix Go Goroutine Leaks & Scale ClickHouse Monoliths
description:
💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

At 02:30 AM, production metrics on our modular monolith system suddenly spiked. The memory consumption graph in our monitoring dashboard showed an unrelenting upward linear curve, culminating in pod crashes driven by the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer. The root cause was not a traditional heap memory leak, but rather the accumulation of thousands of hanging Go goroutines caused by unhandled context cancellation within analytical background workers processing millions of daily telemetry rows.

At the enterprise level, when telemetry data volume hits hundreds of millions of rows per day, row-oriented storage architectures like PostgreSQL hit severe physical bottlenecks. Even with advanced optimizations, query aggregation latencies remained unacceptable before we adopted BRIN indexes in PostgreSQL. However, for high-volume real-time analytics, that approach alone falls short. We needed a fundamental shift in both our storage layer and application concurrency management.

Architectural Dilemma: PostgreSQL vs ClickHouse in Modular Monoliths

Within a modular monolith architecture, isolating analytical modules without falling into the full complexity of microservices is an art of balance. The core challenge lies in executing heavy aggregation queries that trigger massive table scans, holding database connections hostage and triggering client timeouts. When clients disconnect, Go background workers frequently keep running due to the absence of strict context propagation.

Below is a comparative evaluation of enterprise-scale data aggregation performance between traditional PostgreSQL and the ClickHouse columnar engine:

Benchmark Parameter PostgreSQL (Row Store) ClickHouse (Columnar Engine) Performance Lift
100M Rows Aggregation 4.82 Seconds 0.08 Seconds ~60x Faster
Peak RAM Consumption 14.2 GB 1.1 GB 92% Memory Saving
p99 Query Latency 3200 ms 45 ms Sub-second Latency
CPU Utilization 98% (Multi-core bottleneck) 35% (Vectorized execution) High Efficiency

The table above demonstrates the absolute operational necessity of transitioning to ClickHouse for high-performance data pipelines.

Goroutine Leak Mitigation Flow & Context Propagation Design

To halt hanging threads or goroutines, every I/O operation and database query must strictly adhere to the context.Context lifecycle. The following diagram illustrates a leak-safe concurrency handling architecture:

flowchart TD
 A[Client Request / API Gateway] -->|HTTP / gRPC Request| B[Go Modular Monolith Router]
 B -->|Context with Timeout & Cancel| C[Worker Pool Manager]
 C -->|Spawn Worker with ctx| D{Worker Execution}
 D -->|Client Disconnect / Timeout| E[Trigger ctx.Done()]
 E -->|Abort Query Instantly| F[ClickHouse Columnar Engine]
 D -->|Success| G[Return Result to Client]
 F -->|Release Connection & Goroutine| H[Zero Memory Leak]

Through this architecture, context cancellations instantly abort query execution at the database level while deterministically reclaiming goroutine memory allocations.

Code Implementation: Leak-Free Goroutine Worker with ClickHouse

Here is a production-ready Go code snippet implementing strict context propagation to prevent goroutine leaks when interacting with the ClickHouse driver:

package telemetry

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    _ "github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-go/v2"
)

type TelemetryWorker struct {
    db *sql.DB
}

func NewTelemetryWorker(db *sql.DB) *TelemetryWorker {
    return &TelemetryWorker{db: db}
}

// FetchAggregatedData performs real-time aggregation with strict context cancellation protection
func (w *TelemetryWorker) FetchAggregatedData(parentCtx context.Context, tenantID string) ([]map[string]interface{}, error) {
    // Define a strict timeout to prevent workers from hanging indefinitely
    ctx, cancel:= context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    query:= `
 SELECT event_date, count(*) as total_events, avg(latency_ms) as avg_latency
 FROM enterprise_telemetry
 WHERE tenant_id =? AND event_date >= today() - 7
 GROUP BY event_date
 ORDER BY event_date DESC
    `

    // Execute query bounded by the request lifecycle context
    rows, err:= w.db.QueryContext(ctx, query, tenantID)
    if err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to execute ClickHouse query: %w", err)
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var results []map[string]interface{}
    for rows.Next() {
 // Check if context was cancelled midway through large dataset iteration
 if err:= ctx.Err(); err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("operation aborted to prevent goroutine leak: %w", err)
 }

 var eventDate time.Time
 var totalEvents uint64
 var avgLatency float64

 if err:= rows.Scan(&eventDate, &totalEvents, &avgLatency); err!= nil {
 return nil, err
 }

 results = append(results, map[string]interface{}{
 "date": eventDate,
 "total_events": totalEvents,
 "avg_latency": avgLatency,
 })
    }

    if err:= rows.Err(); err!= nil {
 return nil, fmt.Errorf("row iteration error: %w", err)
    }

    return results, nil
}

Within large-scale distributed systems, the underlying infrastructure powering this pipeline plays a critical role. To maintain pod stability and high I/O throughput, deploying services on Hostinger KVM VPS infrastructure provides consistent virtualized compute efficiency. Implementing Traefik v3 API gateway architecture also assists in managing incoming traffic before it hits the Go modular monolith cluster.

Infrastruktur di atas mendukung skalabilitas proses operasional jangka panjang.

Architectural Conclusion

The combination of ClickHouse real-time columnar aggregations and context propagation-driven goroutine management successfully eliminated OOM anomalies in our production environments. By offloading heavy analytical workloads from transactional databases to dedicated columnar engines, our modular monolith systems now seamlessly handle 10x traffic spikes without ballooning infrastructure footprints.

title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available
description:
Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale — you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user.

Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on EC2, this release adds Spark Connect support on multi-primary clusters, along with Secret Agent improvements that cut user-provisioning latency by up to 97% under high concurrency. On EMR Serverless, new scaling profiles for Spark (performance-optimized, balanced, or cost-optimized) let you tune how quickly executors scale, and applications can now run Lake Formation-governed Glue UDFs. On EMR on EKS, the Spark Operator is upgraded to version 2 (based on open-source Spark Operator 2.5.0).

Amazon EMR 8.2 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EMR 8.2 Release Guide for EMR on EC2, the EMR Serverless release notes, and the EMR on EKS release notes, or get started by creating a cluster from the Amazon EMR console.

title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
description:
arXiv:2611.22161v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
description:
arXiv:2611.22045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

title: React Intersection Observer: Detect Elements Entering the Viewport
description:
Key Takeaways

  • Intersection Observer detects when an element enters or leaves the viewport.
  • It is a native browser API that works easily with React.
  • React developers commonly combine it with useRef, useEffect, and useState.
  • Common applications include lazy loading, scroll animations, infinite scrolling, analytics, and video control.
  • threshold controls how much of an element must be visible.
  • rootMargin allows detection before an element reaches the viewport.
  • One observer can monitor multiple elements.
  • Always disconnect the observer when it is no longer required.

Index

  1. Introduction
  2. What Is Intersection Observer?
  3. How It Works
  4. Basic React Example
  5. Important Options
  6. Practical Use Cases
  7. Lazy Loading
  8. Scroll Animations
  9. Infinite Scrolling
  10. Visibility Analytics
  11. Video Control
  12. Reusable Custom Hook
  13. Common Mistakes
  14. Performance Tips
  15. Stats
  16. Interesting Facts
  17. FAQs
  18. Conclusion

1. Introduction

Modern web applications frequently need to know whether an element is visible to the user.

For example:

  • Load an image only when the user approaches it.
  • Start an animation when a section appears.
  • Load more products when the user reaches the bottom.
  • Track whether an advertisement was viewed.
  • Play a video only while it is visible.

One traditional solution is to listen for the scroll event and continuously calculate element positions.

React applications can instead use the browser's Intersection Observer API.

It provides a simple way to react when an element enters or leaves a particular area, usually the browser viewport.

2. What Is Intersection Observer?

Intersection Observer is a browser Web API that allows JavaScript to detect when one element intersects with another element or the viewport.

In simple terms:

Intersection Observer answers the question: "Is this element currently entering, inside, or leaving the visible area?"

For example:

User scrolls
     ↓
Element approaches viewport
     ↓
Intersection detected
     ↓
Callback executes
     ↓
React performs an action

It is useful because developers do not need to repeatedly calculate an element's position during scrolling.

3. How It Works

The basic Intersection Observer flow is:

Create observer
      ↓
Select target element
      ↓
Observe target
      ↓
Element intersects viewport
      ↓
Callback executes
      ↓
Perform required action

Basic JavaScript:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    console.log(entries[0].isIntersecting);
});

observer.observe(element);

isIntersecting tells us whether the target is currently intersecting the observer's root.
In React, the same API can be connected to a DOM element using useRef().

4. Basic React Example

A simple React implementation looks like this:

const ref = useRef(null);
const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
        setVisible(entry.isIntersecting);
    });

    if (ref.current) {
        observer.observe(ref.current);
    }

    return () => observer.disconnect();
}, []);

The reference is attached to the element:

<div ref={ref}>
    {visible ? "Visible" : "Not Visible"}
</div>

What happens?

When the element enters the viewport:
isIntersecting = true

When it leaves:
isIntersecting = false

React can then change the UI, start an animation, request data, or perform another action.

5. Important Intersection Observer Options

Two options are particularly important.

threshold

threshold determines how much of the target should intersect before the observer reports the threshold crossing.

For example:

{ threshold: 0 }
Useful when detecting an element as it begins entering the viewport.

{ threshold: 0.5 }
Useful when approximately half of the element should be visible before taking action.

{ threshold: 1 }
Useful when the target needs to be completely visible for the threshold condition.

Multiple thresholds are also possible:
{ threshold: [0, 0.5, 1] }

rootMargin

rootMargin changes the effective observation area.
Example:
{ rootMargin: "200px" }

This can detect an element before it actually reaches the visible viewport.

This is particularly useful for preloading.

For example:

Image is 200px away
       ↓
Observer detects image
       ↓
Start loading
       ↓
User reaches image
       ↓
Image is ready

6. Practical Use Cases

Intersection Observer is most useful when the requirement is related to visibility.

Common applications

Lazy Loading
Load images or content only when they approach the viewport.

Scroll Animations
Start an animation when a section becomes visible.

Infinite Scrolling
Load the next set of records when the user reaches the bottom.

Analytics
Track when users actually see a particular section or advertisement.

Video Control
Play or pause a video based on its visibility.

On-Demand Content
Fetch expensive data only when the user reaches the relevant section.

7. Practical Example: Lazy Loading

Imagine an e-commerce application containing hundreds of product images.

Loading every image immediately is unnecessary because the user may never scroll far enough to see many of them.

Intersection Observer can detect when an image approaches the viewport.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        setLoadImage(true);
        observer.disconnect();
    }
}, {
    rootMargin: "200px"
});

The process becomes:

Page loads
   ↓
Image is far away
   ↓
Do nothing
   ↓
User scrolls
   ↓
Image approaches viewport
   ↓
Observer triggers
   ↓
Load image

Where can you use this?

  • E-commerce product lists
  • Image galleries
  • News websites
  • Social feeds
  • Portfolio websites

For basic image lazy loading, native HTML also provides:

Intersection Observer is more useful when custom loading behavior is required.

8. Practical Example: Scroll Animations

Modern websites often animate sections as users scroll.
For example:

Section outside viewport
        ↓
Opacity: 0

User scrolls
        ↓
Section becomes visible
        ↓
Opacity: 1

React can use Intersection Observer to add a CSS class.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        setVisible(true);
        observer.disconnect();
    }
});

CSS can then handle the animation:

.section {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(30px);
}

.section.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: translateY(0);
}

*Suitable for : *

  • Landing pages
  • Portfolio websites
  • Corporate websites
  • Product pages
  • Marketing websites

The important idea is to let Intersection Observer detect visibility and CSS handle the animation.

9. Practical Example: Infinite Scrolling

Infinite scrolling is another common use case.

Imagine a product listing:

Product 1
Product 2
Product 3
...
Product 20

       Sentinel

A small element called a sentinel is placed at the bottom.

When the sentinel enters the viewport:

Sentinel visible
      ↓
Request next page
      ↓
Receive products
      ↓
Add products
      ↓
Sentinel moves downward

Example:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        loadMoreProducts();
    }
}, {
    rootMargin: "300px"
});

Where can you use it?

  • Social media feeds
  • E-commerce listings
  • Search results
  • News feeds
  • Video feeds

In production, also manage loading states so multiple API requests are not triggered simultaneously.

10. Practical Example: Visibility Analytics

Suppose a page contains an advertisement.
Simply rendering the advertisement does not necessarily mean the user saw it.

Intersection Observer can detect when it becomes visible.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        trackAdView();
        observer.disconnect();
    }
}, {
    threshold: 0.5
});

Here, the application can use a visibility threshold appropriate to its analytics requirements.

The same approach can be used for:

  • Advertisement impressions
  • Product visibility
  • Article sections
  • Marketing content
  • Feature usage

11. Practical Example: Video Control

Intersection Observer can also control media based on visibility.

For example:

Video enters viewport
       ↓
Play

Video leaves viewport
       ↓
Pause

Example:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        video.play();
    } else {
        video.pause();
    }
}, {
    threshold: 0.5
});

This can be useful for:

  • Short-video feeds
  • Product videos
  • Educational websites
  • Social media interfaces

Browser autoplay policies still need to be considered when automatically playing videos.

12. Reusable Custom Hook

If Intersection Observer is used throughout a React project, creating a custom hook can avoid repeated code.

A simplified hook can look like:

function useIntersectionObserver(options) {
    const ref = useRef(null);
    const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!ref.current) return;

        const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
            ([entry]) => setVisible(entry.isIntersecting),
            options
        );

        observer.observe(ref.current);

        return () => observer.disconnect();
    }, [options]);

    return [ref, visible];
}

A component can then use:

const [ref, visible] = useIntersectionObserver({
    threshold: 0.2
});

This is useful when many components need the same visibility behavior.

Benefits

  • Less duplicated code
  • Easier maintenance
  • Reusable logic
  • Cleaner React components

13. Common Mistakes

Forgetting Cleanup
Always disconnect the observer when the component is removed.
return () => observer.disconnect();

Creating Unnecessary Observers
If multiple elements need to be monitored, one observer can often observe multiple targets.
observer.observe(element1);
observer.observe(element2);
observer.observe(element3);

Triggering API Calls Repeatedly
For infinite scrolling or data loading, protect against duplicate requests.

For example:

Already loading?
↓
Yes → Don't request again
No → Start request

Using Intersection Observer for Everything
It is designed for intersection and visibility.
It is not a replacement for:

  • click
  • mousemove
  • keydown
  • Drag and drop
  • General event handling

14. Performance Tips

Use rootMargin intelligently

For example:
rootMargin: "200px"
can provide extra time for content to load before it becomes visible.

Disconnect one-time observers
If an action only needs to happen once:
observer.disconnect();
or:
observer.unobserve(element);

Avoid unnecessary React state updates
Only update state when the visibility change affects the application.

Combine it with other optimizations
Intersection Observer works well alongside:

  • Image optimization
  • Pagination
  • Code splitting
  • Native lazy loading
  • API caching
  • Virtualized lists

15. Stats

  • **Browser Support: **Intersection Observer is supported by approximately 97% of global web users. Source: https://caniuse.com/intersectionobserver
  • Multiple Targets: One IntersectionObserver instance can observe multiple target elements, reducing the need to create separate observers for each element. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver/observe
  • Threshold Configuration: Developers can configure a single threshold or an array of thresholds to detect different intersection ratios. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver/IntersectionObserver
  • **Asynchronous Observation: **The API reports intersection changes asynchronously, helping developers avoid repeatedly calculating element positions during scrolling. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API
  • **Native Browser API: **Intersection Observer is a browser feature and does not require a React-specific library. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API

16. Interesting Facts

  • Framework Independent: Intersection Observer is a native JavaScript API that works with React, Vue, Angular, and plain JavaScript.
  • Multiple Elements: A single observer instance can monitor multiple elements, making it useful for lists, cards, and page sections.
  • Early Detection: The rootMargin option can detect elements before they enter the viewport, enabling content preloading.
  • Multiple Use Cases: Beyond animations, Intersection Observer supports lazy loading, analytics, infinite scrolling, and media playback control.
  • Native Lazy Loading: For simple image lazy loading, the browser's built-in loading="lazy" attribute may be sufficient. Intersection Observer is more useful when custom application logic is needed.

17. FAQs

What is Intersection Observer?
It is a browser API that detects when an element enters or leaves an observation area such as the viewport.

Is Intersection Observer part of React?
No. It is a browser API that can be integrated into React using hooks.

What is isIntersecting?
It indicates whether the observed element is currently intersecting the observer's root.

What is threshold?
It controls the intersection ratio at which the observer reports a threshold crossing.

What is rootMargin?
It changes the effective observation area and can allow detection before an element actually enters the viewport.

Can Intersection Observer be used for infinite scrolling?
Yes. A sentinel at the bottom of a list can trigger the next API request.

Can it be used for animations?
Yes. It can add a CSS class when an element becomes visible.

Can it lazy-load images?
Yes. However, native loading="lazy" may be sufficient for basic image loading.

Can one observer monitor multiple elements?
Yes. A single observer can monitor multiple targets.

Should I create a custom hook?
If your project uses Intersection Observer in several components, a custom hook can make the code cleaner and reusable.

18. Conclusion

Intersection Observer provides a simple solution for a common frontend requirement:

"Do something when this element becomes visible."

Instead of continuously calculating element positions during scrolling, developers can let the browser report intersection changes.

The basic React pattern is:

useRef()
   ↓
DOM element
   ↓
IntersectionObserver
   ↓
Intersection detected
   ↓
React state/action

Its most common applications include:

  • Lazy loading
  • Scroll animations
  • Infinite scrolling
  • Analytics
  • Video control
  • On-demand API requests

The two options developers should understand first are:
threshold
rootMargin

For reusable applications, a custom React hook can further simplify the implementation.

Intersection Observer is therefore an important API for React developers who want to build interfaces that load, animate, or react to content based on what the user is actually seeing.

Quotes

“The best optimization is often the work you don't perform until it is actually needed.”

“Great web experiences deliver the right content at the right moment.”

“Performance is not only about doing things faster; it is also about avoiding unnecessary work.”

Harmless for years.

Then the team
moved the crate
to the 2024 edition.

It stopped compiling.

The compiler said
set_var is an unsafe function
and needs an unsafe block.

One environment variable.

Unsafe.

Here is the mechanism.

On Linux and most Unix systems,
the environment is a plain C array
owned by the C library.

setenv can move it,
or free old entries,
while it changes it.

getenv reads it
with no lock that Rust controls.

Rust's own std::env functions
take a lock.

C code does not.

And C code
reads the environment
all the time.

Time zone lookups.

DNS resolution.

Locale setup.

Any C library
your crate links.

So one thread sets a variable
while another resolves a hostname,
and the reader can follow a pointer
into memory that was just freed.

A crash.

Or wrong data.

Or nothing,
for months,
and then a crash
nobody can reproduce.

Rust's promise
is that safe code
cannot cause that.

set_var could.

So Rust 1.85,
in February 2025,
shipped the 2024 edition
with set_var and remove_var
marked unsafe.

Older editions still compile them
as safe.

The bug was always there.

The edition only
makes you sign for it.

cargo fix --edition
will wrap the calls
in unsafe blocks for you.

Do not stop there.

An unsafe block
is a promise
that no other thread
can touch the environment.

Check whether you can keep it.

Better moves:

Set the variable
before your program starts,
in the unit file,
the container,
the shell.

Pass configuration
as arguments or structs,
not through the environment.

For child processes,
use Command::env,
which sets it
for the child only.

If it must happen in-process,
do it first thing in main,
before the async runtime,
before any thread,
and write down why.

The 2024 edition
is not adding a danger.

It is pointing at one
your code already had.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: MAI Cyber 2 Flash: el modelo de seguridad con IA de Microsoft iguala a GPT-6 Astra en CyberGym-E2E por menos del 2% del costo
description:
Microsoft anunció MAI Cyber 2 Flash el 17 de noviembre de 2026: su modelo de seguridad con IA logra 92.3% en CyberGym-E2E, igualando la calidad de GPT-6 Astra por menos del 2% del costo por tarea en su evaluación, con una ventana de contexto de 1M de tokens y precios de $0.10/$0.50 por millón de tokens.

Qué cambió

Microsoft anunció MAI Cyber 2 Flash el 17 de noviembre de 2026, en Ignite: su modelo de seguridad con IA especialista más reciente, construido sobre los datos de seguridad propios de Microsoft para encontrar vulnerabilidades, recomendar correcciones e investigar amenazas las 24 horas. Llegará en exclusiva a los productos de seguridad de Microsoft, incluido MDASH (escrito como Codename MDASH en la publicación de Microsoft), donde reemplazará automáticamente el modelo actual en el perfil MAI para clientes elegibles a partir de mediados de diciembre de 2026. Microsoft dice que la familia MAI Cyber ya representa cerca del 40% de los escaneos en MDASH, y que el 90% de los escaneos que empezaron con MAI siguieron usándolo.

En la evaluación CyberGym-E2E de la propia Microsoft (descubrimiento de vulnerabilidades real), MAI Cyber 2 Flash logró 92.3% frente al 91.5% de GPT-6 Astra, usando la mitad del presupuesto de razonamiento, por menos del 2% del costo por tarea; en WebExploitBench, 40.4% frente al 38.4% de GPT-5.6 Cyber con el mismo presupuesto (cifras de Microsoft). Su precio de lista: $0.10 de entrada, $0.01 de entrada en caché y $0.50 de salida por millón de tokens, con los tokens de salida 86% más baratos que en MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, y una ventana de contexto de un millón de tokens, cuatro veces la de su predecesor. Microsoft también reveló que 92 de las 905 tareas se solapaban con proyectos de sus datos de entrenamiento: las excluyó para todos los modelos y reportó sobre las 813 restantes. Al 17 de noviembre de 2026, Artificial Analysis aún no publicaba una página del modelo.

El escaneo de seguridad continuo solo es asequible si el modelo que lo hace es lo bastante barato para ejecutarse sin parar, y Microsoft pone precio a MAI Cyber 2 Flash justo para eso: descubrimiento de vulnerabilidades de nivel insignia por una fracción pequeña del costo por tarea de un modelo general. title: Choosing the Right Compute Service on AWS: EC2 vs ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs Lambda
description:
An application can run perfectly well in development and still become difficult to operate when deployed at scale. The problem is not always the application itself. Sometimes, the selected compute model introduces unnecessary operational effort, limits flexibility, or increases costs.

AWS offers several compute services, but choosing the right one requires understanding how each workload runs and how much infrastructure management it needs.

WHAT

AWS compute services provide different execution models, from managing virtual servers and orchestrating containers to running event-driven functions without directly managing servers.

  • Amazon EC2: Provides virtual servers with control over operating systems, instance types, storage, and software configurations.
  • Amazon ECS: Orchestrates containerized applications using AWS-managed container orchestration. It can run tasks on EC2 or Fargate.
  • Amazon EKS: Provides a managed Kubernetes control plane while allowing teams to operate Kubernetes-based workloads and their associated infrastructure.
  • AWS Fargate: Provides serverless compute capacity for supported ECS and EKS workloads, removing the need to manage the underlying EC2 instances.
  • AWS Lambda: Executes code in response to events without requiring direct server management. Standard Lambda function executions have a maximum duration of 15 minutes.

The important distinction is that ECS and EKS orchestrate containers, Fargate provides container compute, EC2 provides virtual servers, and Lambda follows a function-based execution model.

WHERE

Different compute models suit different application requirements.

  • EC2: Legacy applications, specialized software, GPU workloads, and applications requiring operating system-level control.
  • ECS: AWS-focused containerized applications, microservices, and web applications that need container orchestration.
  • EKS: Kubernetes-based platforms, organizations using Kubernetes tooling, and workloads requiring Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem integrations.
  • Fargate and Lambda: Fargate suits containerized applications that need serverless infrastructure management. Lambda suits event-driven processing, scheduled automation, and short-running backend tasks.

Compute pricing varies by service. EC2 and ECS on EC2 involve instance costs, Fargate charges for provisioned compute resources and usage duration, and Lambda pricing depends on requests and execution duration. Networking, storage, monitoring, and data transfer can also contribute to the total cost.

WHY

Selecting a compute service is not just about finding the lowest hourly price. It is about balancing infrastructure control, operational effort, workload behavior, and total cost.

EC2 offers greater control but requires responsibility for operating system maintenance, capacity planning, and instance management.

ECS simplifies container orchestration without requiring Kubernetes. When paired with Fargate, it also removes the need to manage the underlying servers.

EKS provides Kubernetes compatibility and flexibility, but operating Kubernetes workloads requires additional expertise and operational effort.

Lambda reduces server-management responsibilities and works well for event-driven workloads. However, execution duration, invocation volume, memory allocation, and downstream dependencies influence its suitability and cost.

Before finalizing the architecture, compare the expected workload costs using the AWS Pricing Calculator.

WHEN

Use EC2 when:

  • The application requires operating system-level access or specialized configurations.
  • Existing software has dependencies that make containerization difficult.
  • Specialized instance capabilities are required.

Use ECS when:

  • The application is already containerized or is being designed around containers.
  • Container orchestration is required without adopting Kubernetes.
  • A simpler AWS-native container management approach is preferred.

Use EKS when:

  • Kubernetes APIs, tooling, and ecosystem integrations are important.
  • The organization already has Kubernetes operational expertise.
  • Kubernetes-based deployment patterns are required across environments.

Use Fargate when:

  • Containers need to run without managing EC2 instances.
  • Infrastructure-management overhead needs to be reduced.
  • Workloads benefit from managed container compute capacity.

Use Lambda when:

  • Code executes in response to events.
  • Tasks are short-running and fit within Lambda's execution limits.
  • Workloads have variable demand or periods of inactivity.

HOW

Consider an online store with three workloads: a website and checkout service, product image processing, and a legacy inventory application. Each workload has different compute requirements, so using one compute service for everything may not be the best design.

The website runs as containers on ECS with Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. Product image uploads to Amazon S3 trigger Lambda functions for processing. The legacy inventory application runs on EC2 because it requires a specific operating system configuration or licensed software.

The cost trade-off depends on utilization and operational effort. EC2 can be suitable for steady workloads, while Fargate and Lambda can reduce infrastructure-management overhead for suitable workloads. The right decision should account for the complete architecture rather than compute pricing alone.

TAKEAWAY

The right AWS compute service is the one that matches each workload's execution pattern, infrastructure requirements, scaling behavior, operational constraints, and total cost.
