title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.21651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

title: RDS Extended Support Charges on the AWS Bill? A MySQL 8.0 or PostgreSQL 13 Database Passed Its End of Standard Support
description:
As of November 18, 2026, this post sums up the official pages linked here.

The problem

Your Amazon RDS line on the AWS bill went up this month. Nobody changed an instance size, added storage or bought anything new. The database runs the same version as last month. The new cost is RDS Extended Support.

This can catch many teams this year. RDS for MySQL 8.0 reached its RDS end of standard support on July 31, 2026. RDS for PostgreSQL 13 reached it on February 28, 2026. In this post we show what the charge is and why it started without anyone clicking anything. We also show how to find the databases behind it and stop it safely.

Root cause: an old major version keeps running, for a fee

Here is how AWS describes it. Extended Support "allows you to continue running a database on a major engine version" past its RDS end of standard support date. AWS charges extra for this. (RDS Extended Support)

Charges start "the day after the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

For the two versions most teams ask about, AWS's own calendars show:

Version RDS end of standard support Extended Support year 1 pricing starts Year 3 pricing starts RDS end of Extended Support
RDS for MySQL 8.0 31 July 2026 1 August 2026 1 August 2028 31 July 2029
RDS for PostgreSQL 13 28 February 2026 1 March 2026 1 March 2028 28 February 2029

(Sources: MySQL on Amazon RDS versions and Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. MySQL 5.7, PostgreSQL 11 and PostgreSQL 12 are already past their end of standard support too; see the same pages.)

The MySQL page also notes that "MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 are now only available under RDS Extended Support."

Why nobody "turned it on"

Enrollment is the default in many setups:

  • With the AWS CLI or RDS API, if you "don't specify the RDS Extended Support setting, Amazon RDS defaults to enabling RDS Extended Support." AWS adds that the same default applies when you automate with CloudFormation or other services. It keeps the database available past the end of standard support. In the console, the setting "isn't selected by default." (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • When an enrolled database reaches the date, RDS enrolls it automatically. AWS says this "doesn't change the database engine and doesn't impact the uptime or performance of your DB instance." (RDS Extended Support)

So the database keeps working exactly as before. The only thing that changes is the bill.

How the charge is priced

For provisioned RDS for MySQL instances, AWS says "RDS Extended Support is priced per vCPU per hour." The price also depends "on the AWS Region and calendar date." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)

The pricing pages give these examples:

  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2026. Starting March 1, 2026, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)
  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 on a db.r5.large in US East (N. Virginia) in the first year: "$0.200 per hour, or 2 vCPUs x $0.100 per vCPU-hr." (same page)
  • RDS for PostgreSQL 12 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2025 to February 28, 2027. Starting March 1, 2027, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing)

These are AWS's worked examples, not the rate for every version and Region. Read the pricing page for your engine, version and Region before you estimate a bill. The formula AWS gives is simple: number of vCPUs x the hourly rate for your Region and pricing year, for every hour the instance runs.

Five details make the bill bigger than people expect. All five come from the FAQ on the MySQL and PostgreSQL pricing pages and the charges page:

  1. Multi-AZ standbys pay too. With one standby, you are charged "on both your primary and standby instances." With two readable standbys, on the primary and both standbys.
  2. Read replicas pay too, if they run a major version past its end of standard support.
  3. Reserved Instances do not help. "RDS Extended Support charges are independent of instance charges. Therefore, Reserved Instance discounts are not applicable to RDS Extended Support charges."
  4. A restore can start a new charge. Snapshots themselves are not charged. But restoring a DB snapshot "to a new DB instance after end of standard support" is charged "RDS Extended Support pricing for that instance." The same applies if you create a new instance on that version.
  5. The price goes up in year 3. The first two years use the year 1 and 2 rate. Year 3 pricing starts "on the first day of the third year."

Step 1: find the databases behind the charge

List every DB instance with its engine, version and enrollment:

aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,Engine,EngineVersion,DBInstanceClass,MultiAZ,EngineLifecycleSupport]' \
  --output table

AWS says that if Extended Support is available for a database, the response includes EngineLifecycleSupport. The value open-source-rds-extended-support means the database is enrolled. The value open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled means enrollment was turned off. (Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support)

Enrollment alone is not a charge. AWS notes that "Charges for RDS Extended Support only start when your DB engine version has reached the RDS end of standard support." So the list you care about is: enrolled and on a major version whose end of standard support has passed. For Aurora clusters and Multi-AZ DB clusters, run describe-db-clusters as well, because the setting lives at the cluster level.

In the console, the Databases page has an RDS Extended Support column. If you do not see it, AWS says to turn it on under the Preferences icon. (same page)

The command lists one Region at a time, so run it in every Region you use (add --region).

Step 2: check the dates for each version

You can read the support dates from the CLI instead of a web page:

aws rds describe-db-major-engine-versions \
  --engine mysql \
  --major-engine-version 8.0

AWS says the response includes SupportedEngineLifecycles, with a start and end date for standard support (open-source-rds-standard-support) and for Extended Support (open-source-rds-extended-support). This works for the open source engines (MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL), not the commercial ones. (Viewing support dates, describe-db-major-engine-versions)

Use --engine postgres for PostgreSQL.

Step 3: stop the charge the right way

AWS lists two things that stop the charge. One is upgrading "to an engine version that's covered under standard support." The other is deleting "the database that's running a major version past the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

Option A: plan and test a major version upgrade (the usual fix)

Upgrade to a major version with a long standard support window, not just the next one. AWS warns that "The charges will restart if your target engine version enters RDS Extended Support in the future." (same page) Two examples from the calendars:

  • MySQL: 8.4 has RDS end of standard support on 31 July 2029.
  • PostgreSQL: 14 reaches its RDS end of standard support on 28 February 2027, only a few months away. PostgreSQL 16 runs to 28 February 2029, and 17 to 28 February 2030.

For RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and Aurora MySQL, AWS says you can use Blue/Green Deployments to move off an Extended Support version. This works as long as Blue/Green supports your engine, Region and version. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

If you upgrade in place, know what the command does. The CLI reference covers --engine-version. It says: "Changing this parameter results in an outage and the change is applied during the next maintenance window unless the ApplyImmediately parameter is enabled." A major upgrade with a non-default parameter group needs a parameter group from the new version's family. You must also set --allow-major-version-upgrade. (modify-db-instance) Test on a restored copy first. That copy is charged Extended Support while it runs on the old version.

Option B: delete what nobody uses

Old read replicas, a forgotten test database, a copy restored "just to check something." Each one is charged on its own. If it is not needed, take a final snapshot and delete it. Snapshots are not charged Extended Support. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

Be careful with "just turn it off"

You can change enrollment at any time with the EngineLifecycleSupport setting. In the CLI, that's --engine-lifecycle-support open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled. But AWS warns about disabling it on a database "that is already past its standard support end date." In that case, "the instance or cluster automatically upgrades to the next supported major version." (RDS Extended Support)

That is a major version upgrade you did not test, and if the database is in production, it happens to production. Use this only after the application has been tested on the new version.

Step 4: stop new charges from appearing

  • Set the option on purpose in code. Because the CLI and API default to enrollment, add --engine-lifecycle-support (or EngineLifecycleSupport) to your create and restore scripts so the choice is visible. AWS notes that if you set open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled and the end of standard support has passed, creating the instance "will always fail." That is a useful guard against new databases on old versions. (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • Put the next dates on the calendar. PostgreSQL 14 (28 February 2027) is the next big one for many teams. Run the Step 1 command a few months ahead of each date.

When it still goes wrong

  • The charge came back after an upgrade. You upgraded to a version that later reached its own end of standard support. AWS's example: a PostgreSQL 11 database upgraded to 12 on April 30, 2024 was charged again from March 1, 2025. (RDS Extended Support charges)
  • The bill is bigger than one instance should cost. Count the standbys and read replicas. Each is charged.
  • You bought Reserved Instances and the line is still there. RI discounts do not apply to this charge.
  • Extended Support has an end too. AWS says it is available "for up to 3 years past the RDS end of standard support date." After that, RDS "will automatically upgrade your major engine version." (RDS Extended Support)

What to check first

  1. Which DB instances and clusters are on MySQL 5.7, MySQL 8.0, PostgreSQL 11, 12 or 13, and are they enrolled?
  2. How many vCPUs does each have, counting standbys and read replicas?
  3. Which ones can be deleted, and which need an upgrade plan?
  4. Is the target version far enough from its own end of standard support?
  5. Do your create and restore scripts set --engine-lifecycle-support on purpose?

Docs checked (November 18, 2026)

  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support with Amazon RDS (what it is, automatic enrollment, changing enrollment, forced upgrade when disabled past the date, up to 3 years)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support charges (start date, standbys, what stops the charge, charges restarting, the PostgreSQL 11 example)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Creating a DB instance or a Multi-AZ DB cluster with RDS Extended Support (CLI and API default to enrollment, console does not, disabled option makes creation fail past the date)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support (EngineLifecycleSupport values, console column, enrollment vs charges)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing support dates for engine versions and AWS CLI describe-db-major-engine-versions (SupportedEngineLifecycles)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, MySQL on Amazon RDS versions (MySQL 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4 dates)
  • Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Release Notes, Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL 13, 14, 16 and 17 dates)
  • AWS CLI, modify-db-instance (--engine-lifecycle-support values, --engine-version outage note, --allow-major-version-upgrade)
  • Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing (per vCPU-hour pricing, the Ohio and N. Virginia examples, Multi-AZ, read replicas, Reserved Instances, snapshots and restores, Blue/Green)

If AWS changes a date or price after we publish this, tell us at info@cloudskillconsulting.com and we'll update the post.

CloudSkill Consulting LLC helps teams with fixed-fee cloud projects, FinOps reviews and IT staffing. Learn more at cloudskillconsulting.com.

title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.22296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

title: How Many Persistent Features Does a Biometric Need? A Law Linking Equal Error Rate to Feature Count and Persistence
description:
arXiv:2611.21973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A biometric designer controls the number of features and their temporal persistence. Earlier empirical work linked the equal error rate (EER) to persistence and to the required number of features by straight lines. We derive the law behind these regularities. For $N$ independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation $\rho$, scored by cosine similarity, Fisher's $z$-transform turns the genuine and impostor scores into two normals, giving $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{atanh}\rho)$ and, inversely, $N=(2q/\operatorname{atanh}\rho)^2$ with $q=\Phi^{-1}(1-\mathrm{EER})$; intercorrelated features enter through an effective count $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The central extension lets persistence vary across comparisons with spread $\tau$ on Fisher's scale: $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-m/(\sqrt{\tau^2+v}+\sqrt{v}))$ with $v=1/(N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2)$, which for a normal spread has a floor $\Phi(-m/\tau)$ that no number of features can lower. With no fitted parameter the simple law reproduces published simulations and the EER-ICC line, and predicts the KCC-EER relation of eye-movement embeddings on GazeBase ($R^2=0.88$), though less well on GazeBaseVR ($0.63$). Read from the genuine and impostor scores, the general form matches the EER of eye movements, keystroke dynamics, the ECG and face embeddings over 101 conditions with $R^2=0.98$ and a median error of $0.6$ points, against $0.87$ and $1.9$ points for the simple law. The 61 eye-movement, keystroke and ECG conditions check consistency on the same scores; the 40 face conditions use held-out subjects, with the same accuracy. The product $\tau\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2}$ gives a design rule: adding or decorrelating features pays fully while it is well below one and little once it exceeds about three, where only higher or more uniform persistence helps.

title: CorrectCast: Selective Multimodal Context for Scale-Aware Residual Correction in Precipitation Nowcasting
description:
arXiv:2611.22178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.

title: How I Built a Sub-Second Next.js 14 Web App with Turnkey Local SEO on Cloudflare Workers
description:
When building websites for local businesses, traditional platforms like WordPress often suffer from bloated plugins, 4-second load times, and poormobile PageSpeed scores.

For my recent project—**Sravya Tech Rentals** (a camera rental business in Banglore)—I wanted to prove that modern full-stack web engineering can radically outperform standard website builders.

### The Stack:
- **Framework:** Next.js 14 (App Router)
- **Styling:** Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui primitives
- **Deployment:** Cloudflare Workers Edge Network (sub-second response worldwide)

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
description:
arXiv:2611.21964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
description:
arXiv:2611.22189v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In computational pathology, high-magnification whole-slide image analysis preserves tissue detail but requires encoding many patches, whereas lower magnification reduces computation by covering a higher field of view per patch while sacrificing detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation matches features that often encode detail unreachable by low-magnification input, sometimes requiring slide-level labels that limit scalability. To address those issues, we introduce Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation (SRED), which transfers regional event occurrences that encode reachable high-level interactions between details without slide-level labels. We use a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to learn an event dictionary from 20x teacher features. Logical OR pooling records whether each event is detected in any spatially aligned patch, retaining both localized and shared evidence within the corresponding 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional targets without slide-level labels. Visual analysis identifies dictionary components responsive to recognizable histological patterns, supporting target interpretation. Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification and grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts. Runtime matches native 5x, with an average 11.58x speedup over 20x.

title: Flutter Animations: From Implicit to Explicit, and When to Use Each
description:
Series 6 — Part 1 of 1

Flutter Animations: From Implicit to Explicit, and When to Use Each

A standalone guide on mastering Flutter's animation primitives

Animations had been on my backlog for weeks. Everything I built was functional but static. My mentor suggested I dedicate time specifically to the Flutter animation system — not just using packages, but understanding how the underlying primitives work.

I spent two days reading the Flutter animation docs and implementing a series of examples that moved from the simplest implicit animations up to AnimationController with custom curves and sequences.

Implicit animations: the easy starting point

Flutter's implicit animation widgets handle the AnimationController lifecycle for you. AnimatedContainer is the classic example — change any property (color, size, padding) and Flutter will tween between the old and new values over a specified duration:

AnimatedContainer(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  curve: Curves.easeInOut,
  width: _expanded ? 200 : 100,
  color: _expanded ? Colors.blue : Colors.grey,
)

Other useful implicit widgets:

  • AnimatedOpacity (fade in/out)
  • AnimatedPadding
  • AnimatedDefaultTextStyle
  • AnimatedPositioned inside a Stack

These cover most UI transitions without any manual controller management.

Explicit animations with AnimationController

When you need full control — custom sequences, interruption handling, or value-driven animations — you move to explicit animations with AnimationController:

class _MyWidgetState extends State<MyWidget> with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _controller;
  late final Animation<double> _opacity;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller = AnimationController(
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 500),
      vsync: this,
    );
    _opacity = Tween<double>(begin: 0, end: 1).animate(
      CurvedAnimation(parent: _controller, curve: Curves.easeIn),
    );
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }
}

The vsync: this mixin (SingleTickerProviderStateMixin) ties the animation to the widget's frame callback, preventing off-screen animations from consuming resources.

Fixing bugs in the implementation

  • Missed First Frame: I hit a bug where the animation was completing but the widget was not rebuilding. The cause: I was calling setState() inside the animation listener, but the listener was added after _controller.forward() — so the first frame was missed. The fix was to add the listener before calling forward().
  • Controller in ViewModel anti-pattern: I also saw a common mistake when integrating animations into an MVVM app: putting AnimationController inside a ViewModel. This does not work because AnimationController requires a TickerProvider (a vsync), which is a widget concern. AnimationController belongs in a State class, not a ViewModel.

What I learned

  • Start simple: Start with implicit animations (AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity) — they cover most use cases.
  • Control with explicit: Use explicit AnimationController when you need sequencing, interruption, or programmatic control.
  • Lifecycle cleanup: Always dispose AnimationController in dispose() — skipping this leaks memory.
  • MVVM boundary: AnimationController belongs in State, not ViewModel — it requires a TickerProvider.
  • Listener order: Add animation listeners before calling forward() or reverse() to catch the first frame.

title: Adiós Notion: Datalaria Pulse o la Gestión Editorial desde Git
description:
Publicado originalmente en Datalaria.

Durante años, los equipos de ingeniería y creadores técnicos que publicamos en arquitecturas estáticas (Jamstack, Hugo, Astro, Next.js o MkDocs) hemos convivido con una contradicción flagrante: gestionamos el código fuente con el máximo rigor de la integración continua, pero administramos la estrategia editorial con herramientas desconectadas del repositorio.

En el papel, el flujo parecía inmejorable. Creas una base de datos relacional en Notion o una tabla en Airtable, diseñas un tablero Kanban con columnas cromáticas (Idea, Borrador, En Revisión, Programado, Publicado), configuras vistas de calendario y añades propiedades para el recuento de palabras, las categorías SEO y los enlaces bilingües.

Sin embargo, a medida que el blog escala y supera el umbral de los 50 o 100 artículos técnicos, se manifiesta de forma inevitable la patología de la doble entrada: la realidad del repositorio Git y la ficción de la base de datos externa divergen irremediablemente.

🗺️ Hoja de Ruta de la Serie Datalaria Pulse

Para entender cómo encaja cada pieza del rompecabezas de Content Ops as Code, esta serie se compone de 5 entregas estructuradas:

  1. 🟢 Parte 1 (Este artículo): Adiós Notion: Datalaria Pulse o la Gestión Editorial que se Escribe Sola desde Git
  2. ⚪ Parte 2 (Dom 22/11): Del Front Matter al Índice: Pydantic v2, Paridad Bilingüe y Automatización con CI/CD
  3. ⚪ Parte 3 (Mié 25/11): Tabla Ejecutiva, Tablero Kanban y Calendario Mensual en React 19 sobre un Índice Estático
  4. ⚪ Parte 4 (Dom 29/11): Google Analytics 4 y Search Console Automatizados: Cómo Medir el ROI Orgánico de Cada Post, App y Kit
  5. ⚪ Parte 5 (Mié 02/12): Gestión Editorial para Equipos de Documentación, SEO y Marketing: de Notion a Excel en 5 minutos y Fábrica con IA

0. Objetivos de la Fase y de este Artículo: Hacia la Gobernanza Editorial Autónoma

Esta entrega marca el pistoletazo de salida de Datalaria Pulse, dedicado por entero a resolver de raíz la gobernanza de activos editoriales técnicos mediante nuestro sistema operativo propio:

Objetivos Estratégicos:

  1. Erradicar la Doble Entrada Administrativa: Eliminar para siempre la necesidad de mantener sincronizadas manualmente bases de datos externas (Notion, Airtable, Trello) frente al repositorio Git.
  2. Implantar la Filosofía Content Ops as Code: Tratar los artículos Markdown y sus metadatos YAML con las mismas disciplinas de la ingeniería de software: validación por esquemas estrictos (Pydantic v2), paridad bilingüe determinista y compilación automatizada en CI/CD.
  3. Monetización y Modelo Dual-Mode: Poner a disposición de la comunidad dos modalidades operativas:
    • Datalaria Pulse Kit (Standalone): Paquete comercial descargable con Plantilla Maestra Excel 2016/365, conector Power Query M, migrador en 5 minutos de Notion y escáner universal CLI sin dependencias externas.
    • Datalaria Pulse Pro (Cloud Multi-Tenant): Arquitectura colaborativa sobre Supabase PostgreSQL con autenticación, sincronización en tiempo real Web ↔ Localhost y espacio de trabajo privado por usuario.

Objetivos Específicos de este Artículo 1:

  • Demostrar el coste oculto y los fallos estructurales de la gestión editorial manual en proyectos basados en Git.
  • Formalizar el Principio de Invarianza y la arquitectura de 4 capas de Datalaria Pulse.
  • Presentar la suite de visualizaciones ejecutivas (Dashboard Analytics, Tabla interactiva, Tablero Kanban de 5 columnas, Calendario mensual y Diagnóstico de Salud).
  • Facilitar el acceso inmediato al Sandbox interactivo y a la descarga del Kit de recursos.

1. Conexión con el Ecosistema Datalaria: De LifeOps a la Toma de Decisiones

Datalaria Pulse no es una herramienta aislada; es la culminación de los principios de ingeniería, arquitectura de datos y rigor analítico desarrollados a lo largo de nuestras publicaciones y aplicaciones anteriores:

  1. La Filosofía de Plataforma de LifeOps: En nuestra plataforma integral LifeOps demostramos cómo estructurar un sistema operativo personal y profesional combinando una SPA reactiva con persistencia serverless en Supabase. Pulse adopta ese mismo patrón de diseño modular, trasladándolo de la gestión de hábitos y tareas personales al gobierno corporativo de contenidos técnicos.
  2. Erradicación del Sesgo HiPPO en la Suite de Toma de Decisiones: En nuestra guía sobre priorización cuantitativa (DAR, RICE y Business Case) demostramos que el juicio directivo fracasa cuando se basa en intuiciones no parametrizadas. En Pulse aplicamos esa misma disciplina matemática a la redacción: sustituimos las opiniones subjetivas sobre qué publicar mediante un algoritmo de scoring SEO determinista (0 a 100) y métricas relativas objetivas de tráfico orgánico (Google Analytics 4 relativizado a base 100).
  3. Higiene de Datos y Pipelines en Ingeniería S&OP: Al igual que en la cadena de suministro filtramos el ruido del ERP antes de entrenar modelos probabilísticos de demanda, en Pulse limpiamos el contenido léxico (extrayendo código fuente y metadatos) para medir la profundidad real del conocimiento transferido.
  4. Gobernanza bajo Spec-Driven Development (SDD): Siguiendo las directrices de nuestra constitución técnica y el flujo de Agentes de IA Operativa, Pulse garantiza que ningún activo se publica si no cumple las invariantes de paridad lingüística (INV-PULSE-1..5) auditadas por scripts reproducibles.

2. La Falacia de la Doble Entrada: El Abismo entre Notion y Git

Cualquier profesional que haya intentado mantener un calendario editorial en Notion en paralelo a un repositorio en GitHub conoce este ciclo de degradación:

  1. La Divergencia de Títulos y Slugs: Decides ajustar el título de un artículo en el front matter de Markdown para optimizar el Click-Through Rate (CTR) en Google o renombras la carpeta para mejorar el slug SEO. En Git haces git commit -m "seo: refine slug" y lo despliegas en segundos. Notion nunca se entera. Tres semanas después, la tarjeta en Notion apunta a un enlace roto o conserva un título arcaico.
  2. La Mentira de las Fechas de Publicación: Retrasas una publicación dos semanas en el front matter (date: 2026-11-20) porque un análisis cuantitativo requiere revisión adicional. En el repositorio el post queda programado de forma estricta. Pero en Notion la tarjeta sigue marcada como publicada el día 5. El calendario ejecutivo que revisa la dirección ya no coincide con la producción real.
  3. La Ceguera de la Paridad Bilingüe: Si publicas en español y en inglés, mantener la trazabilidad manual de qué traducciones están pendientes, cuáles quedaron desactualizadas tras un cambio técnico y cuáles tienen paridad completa exige un esfuerzo administrativo insostenible. El resultado habitual son artículos huérfanos y enlaces cruzados rotos.
  4. La Deuda Administrativa (Toil): El autor técnico termina dedicando el 20% de su tiempo productivo a tareas burocráticas de actualización manual de tarjetas en lugar de redactar contenido de alto valor o programar algoritmos.

En la ingeniería de software moderna resolvimos este problema hace décadas bajo el paradigma Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) y Configuration as Code (Kubernetes): la infraestructura no se administra rellenando formularios en portales web; se declara en código auditable y versionado.

¿Por qué no aplicar exactamente el mismo principio a la gestión de contenidos técnicos? Así nace la filosofía Content Ops as Code.

3. El Principio de Invarianza: Content Ops as Code

El principio fundamental de Content Ops as Code es categórico:

Invariante Central: En un blog o documentación técnica, los ficheros Markdown y sus cabeceras Front Matter en Git son la Única Fuente de Verdad (Single Source of Truth). Ninguna base de datos externa tiene autoridad sobre el estado de un contenido.

Bajo este modelo, la gestión editorial deja de ser una tarea manual reactiva y se transforma en un proceso de compilación determinista:

Dimensión Gestión Tradicional (Notion / Airtable) Content Ops as Code (Datalaria Pulse)
Fuente de Verdad Base de datos SaaS cerrada y externa. Ficheros .md y .yaml en el repositorio Git.
Sincronización Manual (propensa al olvido y al error humano). Instantánea y automática con cada git commit.
Paridad de Idiomas Checklist manual en casillas de verificación. Detección algorítmica de timestamps y emparejamiento.
Auditoría SEO Estimaciones estáticas rellenadas a mano. Calificación determinista en tiempo de build (0-100).
Métricas de Rendimiento Desconectadas o exportadas manualmente en CSV. Ingesta directa de GA4/GSC relativizada a base 100.
Coste de Licencias \$10-\$25/usuario/mes en plataformas SaaS. Coste cero de infraestructura (ficheros estáticos / Git).

4. La Arquitectura de Datalaria Pulse

Para materializar esta filosofía en el ecosistema Datalaria, hemos construido y puesto en producción Datalaria Pulse: un motor integral que lee directamente nuestro árbol de contenidos y genera un panel ejecutivo en tiempo real.

4.1. Extracción y Validación Determinista con Pydantic v2

En lugar de depender de scripts frágiles de expresiones regulares, Pulse implementa contratos formales de datos con Pydantic v2. Cada artículo es parseado extrayendo:

  • Título y descripción en ambos idiomas.
  • Fecha de publicación formal y timestamp de última modificación física según el log de Git (git log -1 --format=%cI).
  • Conteo real de palabras mediante limpieza léxica (eliminando bloques de código fuente, shortcodes de Hugo como app-ref o mermaid, y etiquetas HTML).
  • Taxonomía estricta validada contra esquemas de categorías oficiales.

4.2. Gobernanza de Paridad Bilingüe

Pulse compara de forma determinista la versión en español con su réplica en inglés evaluando cinco estados posibles:

  1. complete: Ambos artículos existen y han sido sincronizados dentro de una ventana de tolerancia temporal.
  2. missing_en: El artículo existe en español pero carece de traducción al inglés.
  3. missing_es: Existe en inglés pero falta la versión en español.
  4. outdated_en: La versión en español ha recibido actualizaciones sustanciales en Git posteriores a la traducción inglesa.
  5. outdated_es: La versión en inglés fue actualizada sin propagar los cambios a español.

4.3. Invariantes de Seguridad y Privacidad (Dogfooding Seguro)

Para poder publicar la aplicación en abierto sin comprometer información sensible del negocio, diseñamos las invariantes formales INV-PULSE-1 e INV-PULSE-2:

  • INV-PULSE-1 (Aislamiento de Activos Privados): Ninguna idea en estado borrador privado o anotación interna puede filtrarse al fichero público.
  • INV-PULSE-2 (Relativización Matemática): Las páginas vistas absolutas y los ingresos de Google Analytics 4 nunca se exponen al navegador; se normalizan a un índice base 100 respecto a la mediana del blog y percentiles estadísticos (0% a 100%).

5. Datalaria Pulse en Acción: La Suite de Visualizaciones

El resultado visible de este pipeline es una aplicación web reactiva construida en React 19 + TypeScript, compilada estáticamente dentro del portal Hugo y disponible tanto en modo sandbox sin registro como en modo colaborativo con sincronización en la nube.

🚀 App Oficial en Datalaria: Datalaria Pulse — Probar Demo en Vivo

La plataforma articula 5 vistas complementarias:

  1. Dashboard Analytics & KPIs: Muestra métricas macro del ecosistema (183 activos gobernados: 118 artículos bilingües, 47 lanzamientos y versiones SemVer de aplicaciones 🚀 APP / ⚡ APP vX.Y y 18 ediciones de Kits B2B 📦 KIT bajo las invariantes INV-PULSE-1..8, con 100% de paridad bilingüe), profundidad léxica acumulada (~215.000 palabras técnicas indexadas), tiempo de lectura total (~18,5 horas) y valoración económica del patrimonio de contenidos.
  2. Tabla Ejecutiva con Filtros Interactivos: Búsqueda en tiempo real por título, filtro tipo píldora por estado (Publicado, Programado, Borrador), ordenación multidireccional por fecha o score SEO, y paginación rápida (10, 25 o 50 registros).
  3. Tablero Kanban de 5 Columnas: Flujo visual estilo Notion (Idea ➔ Borrador ➔ En Revisión ➔ Programado ➔ Publicado) con conteo dinámico de tarjetas y tarjetas interactivas que abren el modal de detalle editorial.
  4. Calendario Mensual Notion: Proyección cuadrangular de 35 casillas por mes con navegación cronológica, destacando los lanzamientos programados para los próximos trimestres.
  5. Salud Editorial & ROI: Auditoría de enlaces internos, alertas de artículos desactualizados y seguimiento de paridad lingüística.

6. Hoja de Ruta de la Serie Editorial

Este artículo inaugura una serie técnica de 5 entregas donde desgranaremos paso a paso cada componente de la arquitectura:

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them

Understanding ACH Return Codes: A Developer's Guide

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A transaction you thought was settled comes back rejected, and you need to know why and what to do next. The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) publishes a standardized set of return codes—R01 through R85—that tell you exactly what went wrong. This article breaks down the most common ones and how to handle them in code.

The Big Three: R01, R03, and R10

R01: Insufficient Funds

What it means: The recipient's account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit. This is the most common return code.

When it fires: 1–2 business days after the ACH debit is initiated, during the bank's settlement window.

How to handle it:

  • Log the return with timestamp and amount.
  • Mark the payout as "returned" in your database, not "failed"—there's a difference.
  • Notify the recipient (usually via email or in-app).
  • Offer retry options: wait 3–5 business days and retry, or switch to a different payout rail (e.g., Visa Direct for faster settlement). 
async function handleR01Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);

  payout.status = 'returned';
  payout.returnCode = 'R01';
  payout.returnedAt = new Date();
  payout.retryCount = (payout.retryCount || 0) + 1;

  if (payout.retryCount <= 2) {
    // Schedule retry in 5 business days
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5));
    await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
      subject: 'Payout returned — will retry',
      message: `Your $${payout.amount} payout was returned due to insufficient funds. We'll retry on ${addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5).toDateString()}.`
    });
  } else {
    // Max retries exceeded; escalate
    payout.status = 'manual_review';
    await notifySupport(payout);
  }

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
}

R03: No Account / Account Closed

What it means: The account number or routing number is invalid, or the account has been closed.

When it fires: 1 business day after initiation (banks catch this quickly).

How to handle it:

  • This is a permanent failure. Do not retry.
  • Flag the recipient's bank details as invalid.
  • Require the user to update their account information before attempting another payout.
  • Consider blocking future payouts to that account until verified. 
async function handleR03Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);
  const recipient = await db.recipients.findById(payout.recipientId);

  payout.status = 'failed';
  payout.returnCode = 'R03';

  // Mark bank account as invalid
  recipient.bankAccount.status = 'invalid';
  recipient.bankAccount.invalidReason = 'No account or account closed';
  recipient.bankAccount.requiresUpdate = true;

  await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
    subject: 'Bank account information is invalid',
    message: 'The account you provided does not exist or is closed. Please update your bank details.'
  });

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
  await db.recipients.save(recipient);
}

R10: Unauthorized / Unauthorized Debit

What it means: The account holder did not authorize this debit, or the authorization is outside the agreement terms.

When it fires: Up to 60 days after the original debit (this is a consumer dispute).

How to handle it:

  • Investigate immediately. This may indicate fraud or a customer complaint.
  • Halt further payouts to that recipient until resolved.
  • Contact the customer to verify legitimacy.
  • If legitimate, you may need to resubmit with corrected authorization.

title: A server that almost never says no
description:
Most servers are taught to say no. Bad request? 400. Unknown shape? 422. You're strict, you're correct, and somewhere a client fixes its bug and tries again.

vitals-receiver almost never says no, because for this server "no" means "delete this forever". This post is the long version: how it's put together, why each piece is shaped the way it is, and the things that went wrong on the way to the public repo. There's real code below, copied from the repo with comments trimmed.

What it is

It's a small self-hosted receiver for Apple Health exports. An iPhone app of mine (not public yet) sends batches of HealthKit samples over the home network. The receiver stores them in SQLite, outside the repo, and serves two pages on the machine itself: a fitness page with activity rings, the week and a card per metric, and an ops page that tells you whether the pipe is still alive.

It's TypeScript on Node 22, with Fastify, better-sqlite3 and zod. MIT-licensed. You can try it without a phone:

npm ci && npm run demo

That seeds a synthetic store from a fixed seed in the system temp directory and serves it. npm run demo -- --groups=sleep shows one metric group, --groups= shows the empty state. Ctrl-C stops it cleanly. Every number you'll see there is generated. No real reading has ever been in the repo.

The one rule

The phone never reads our response body. What it does next depends only on the status code:

  • No answer, 408, 425, 429, any 5xx: the batch stays in an outbox on the device and is retried under the same exportId and batchSequence, backing off from 15 minutes to an hour, for up to seven days.
  • 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, a bare 413, any 3xx: the batch is dropped the moment we answer. Nothing on the phone ever tries it again.

So on this endpoint a 4xx isn't feedback. It's a delete button, and the server is the one pressing it. Everything else in the design follows from that.

Two doors, never connected

One process, two Fastify instances, one store:

const ingest = buildIngestServer({ config, store, token, log });
const read = buildReadServer({ store, config });

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await ingest.listen({ host: config.ingestHost, port: config.ingestPort });
  await read.listen({ host: config.readHost, port: config.readPort });

Look at the arguments. The ingest door gets token. The read door doesn't, and that's on purpose. Ingest faces the LAN, accepts POST, and checks the phone's credential. The read door is bound to loopback, serves the pages, and has no way to reach the credential, because it was never handed one. It can't leak what it never holds.

The split exists so two credentials never meet. If you put a reverse proxy with its own login in front of the dashboard, the proxy only ever points at the read door. Then the proxy password can't be replayed into ingest, and the phone's token can't read the data back. The README is blunt about it: the day you route a proxy to ingest is the day both separations stop being true.

The read door also enforces "read-only" in code instead of just promising it:

  app.addHook("onRequest", async (req, reply) => {
    if (req.method !== "GET" && req.method !== "HEAD") {
      void reply.header("allow", "GET, HEAD");
      await reply.code(405).send({ ok: false, error: "read-only listener: GET and HEAD only" });
      return reply;
    }
    return undefined;
  });

The ingest door mirrors it: any non-POST gets a 404 that says "this port accepts POST only", and that request still gets a row in the delivery log.

The token

The credential is 32 random bytes, hex, written to a file with mode 600. npm run token:mint makes it and never prints the value. The server re-reads the file only when its mtime changes, so rotating the token needs no restart. If there's no token at startup, the server refuses to start: a LAN-facing listener with no credential is worse than no listener.

The comparison:

export function tokenMatches(expected: string | null, provided: unknown): boolean {
  if (expected === null || expected.length === 0) return false;
  const candidate = Array.isArray(provided) ? provided[0] : provided;
  if (typeof candidate !== "string" || candidate.length === 0) return false;
  const a = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(expected).digest();
  const b = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(candidate).digest();
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

timingSafeEqual throws if the two buffers differ in length, and a length check before it would itself leak the length. Hashing both sides first gives two 32-byte digests every time. The comparison is constant-time and the length can't be measured either.

The ingest path, step by step

The handler is a short ladder. Every rung that would normally be a 4xx is a 200 here.

First, Fastify's body parsing goes away. If the framework parses JSON, a broken body becomes Fastify's 400 before our code ever sees it, and the batch is lost. So the body is taken as a raw string, whatever the Content-Type says:

  app.removeAllContentTypeParsers();
  app.addContentTypeParser("*", { parseAs: "string" }, (_req, body, done) => done(null, body));

Then:

  1. Credential. A wrong or missing one gets a 401. This is one of the two errors the server allows itself, because it's a configuration mistake the owner has to see. That batch is lost, and the README says so in bold.
  2. JSON. Bytes we can't parse are still health data. They go to quarantine and the phone gets a 200.
  3. Schema version. The wire contract says "reject unknown versions". We don't. 
    let parsed: unknown;
    try {
      parsed = JSON.parse(ctx.raw);
    } catch (err) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unparseable-json", err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err));
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }

    const version = (parsed as { schemaVersion?: unknown } | null)?.schemaVersion;
    if (version !== SCHEMA_VERSION) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unknown-schema-version", `schemaVersion=${JSON.stringify(version)}`);
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }
  1. Envelope shape. zod, with loose objects everywhere, because the contract only ever adds fields within version 1. A mismatch goes to quarantine with every zod issue written into detail.
  2. Probe. The app's "test connection" button sends connectivityTest: true with no samples. That gets a delivery row and nothing else. A probe that somehow carries samples is treated as an export. We never throw samples away over a flag.
  3. Samples, one at a time. The envelope's samples is typed unknown[] on purpose, and each sample is validated on its own. One malformed sample goes to quarantine instead of costing the 999 good ones beside it.

The only other error is 413, for a body over 2 MB. The phone caps a batch well under that, so if it ever fires, the fix is to raise the cap, not to shrug. And there's a 500 for real bugs. It's survivable because the phone retries a 5xx, but its body isn't kept, so the README calls it "a defect, not weather".

The store

Five tables in one SQLite file, WAL mode, migrations tracked by user_version:

  • samples: one row per HealthKit sample, keyed on its uuid, with the original JSON kept in raw.
  • runs and batches: one row per export run and per batch. Run aggregates are recomputed from batches on every ingest, so a re-delivered batch can't inflate them.
  • deliveries: every request that reached us, including the refused ones.
  • quarantine: the bytes we couldn't turn into samples. 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS quarantine (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  received_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  remote_addr TEXT,
  reason      TEXT NOT NULL,
  detail      TEXT,
  headers     TEXT NOT NULL,
  body        TEXT NOT NULL,
  bytes       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  delivery_id INTEGER
);

The headers are stored minus the credential. The token appears nowhere in the database file. That was checked against the real database file of a running server, not by reading the code.

deliveries is the table I'd keep if I could keep only one. The sender can't hear us, so this is the only place our side of every conversation is written down: status, bytes, how many samples were stored, how many were duplicates, how many were rejected, and how long it took.

The pages

/ is the fitness page: three rings, a Monday-first week strip, a card per metric with data. It has no scripts and no images, plus a CSP that allows exactly one same-origin stylesheet. /pipe is the ops page: the delivery log, export runs with their real span, how fresh each data type is, and quarantine. /api/summary and /api/fitness serve the same models as JSON, through the same code path, so the page and anything reading it can't drift apart.

/healthz answers 200 or 503, and it's the one read route that writes. It upserts a probe row into the store, so dbWritable is proven on every call instead of assumed. It also reports startedAt, and I'll come back to why.

What went wrong

The rule above sounds tidy. Getting the code to actually keep it took longer. These are the real problems, in the order we hit them.

1. The receiver was counting wrong, quietly. The first store reported stored: N for every sample it was handed, whether it already had it or not. Its upsert on uuid let a re-delivered batch rewrite the provenance of rows that were already correct. Worse, HealthKit was observed re-minting the uuid for identical heart-rate content, about 12 rows per real reading. The fix: insert-once, plus a partial unique index for that one type only.

ON CONFLICT(uuid) DO NOTHING
ON CONFLICT(content_id) WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate' DO NOTHING

Why only that type? For the other types the content id collides by design. In one measurement, 720 real samples carried 195 distinct ids, and a global unique index would have kept 195 and thrown away 525. Stored, duplicate and rejected also became three separate counters. Before, "we already had it" and "we couldn't store it" were the same number, and they need opposite reactions.

2. The test suite was testing the calendar. Two days later, npm test gave 102 pass and 9 fail on a commit that had been green. The day before, the same command on the same commit gave 104 and 7. Nothing had changed but the date. The unit tests pinned a clock, but the HTTP server read the wall clock, so pages built from fixtures dated on the 19th correctly reported "these numbers are from the 19th, not today". The product was honest and the tests were wrong. The fix makes the clock a dependency:

  now?: () => Date;

  const now = deps.now ?? (() => new Date());

It's a function, not a Date: a server that outlives its requests would otherwise freeze "today" at boot. It's optional, so production passes nothing and doesn't notice the seam. The comment in the repo says it better than I can: a suite that reads the wall clock is a suite that tests the calendar, and the calendar always wins eventually.

3. Half the delivery log was crying wolf. The ops page flagged "run metadata drift" whenever a batch disagreed with its run's first batch on generatedAt or the time window. But for one export mode, the window is each batch's own bracket and differs by design. The real store showed 201 of 420 deliveries carrying a false drift note. The fix compares only what the contract says is identical across a run, and keeps the run's window as the real extent of its batches. Before that, /pipe showed a one-hour window for a run that actually spanned 190 hours.

4. An invariant with nothing behind it. The fitness model has a rule: today is partial, always, and never counts toward an average. It was enforced in four places, and only one of them, steps, was tested. For each of the other three, the reviewer flipped partial: day === today to partial: false and the suite still passed, 123 of 123. So each site got a test that fails if you flip it. The repo also had no CI at all. Now it has a workflow that runs typecheck and the suite on every push and pull request.

5. The founding rule was written wrong. The first commit said the phone "never retries", so any non-2xx at all was data loss. Reading the app's source showed otherwise. It retries no answer, 429 and 5xx from an outbox for seven days, and drops only the permanent codes. That changes the meaning of a 500 from "lost" to "retried". Four stale comments had to be rewritten, and a README truth pass checked every claim against the code. A good rule with a wrong reason is a bug waiting for someone to "simplify" it.

6. A silent day had two possible meanings. Some days had zero deliveries. Was the receiver down, or did the phone just not send? The store couldn't say, because it only records what arrives. The fix was one log line and one field:

  return `vitals: started ${new Date(startedAt).toISOString()} commit ${rev}`;

The same instant shows up as startedAt on /healthz. With it, a gap reads as a receiver gap (started after it) or a phone gap (up the whole time). The investigation that prompted it found the phone silent in all three gaps, except one 63-minute slice when the machine was simply powered off. A small silence:check script, meant to run hourly, asks /healthz from the outside and speaks only when the phone has gone quiet.

7. Shutdown that wouldn't shut down. The first shutdown closed both servers, checkpointed the WAL and exited. A probe showed the hole: a request that had sent headers and 11 of its 500 body bytes, then SIGTERM, and the process was still alive more than 25 seconds later. Even a finished request held it open, because its keep-alive socket wasn't idle when close() ran, and Node's default keep-alive is 72 seconds. Now the drain is capped at 10 seconds by default (VITALS_DRAIN_CAP_SECONDS). Because every store write is synchronous inside one transaction, a request cut by the cap is cut before its handler runs, so there's nothing half-written to roll back.

Where it is now

The first version landed in one day, in five slices, with 42 tests. A two-line mutation (dropping uuid normalisation, conflating claimed with stored counts) made two of them fail, so we knew the suite bites. By the time it went public it had a README written for strangers, a vendored copy of the payload contract so the fixture checks run on a clean clone, an identity scrub and an MIT licence. That was 126 tests. At the last count it was 216, all green, with typecheck in CI.

It's a monitor with a store attached, not an analytics product. If you need a boring, honest pipe from your phone to your own disk, and you'd rather it keep the weird bytes than refuse them, take it. The code is public on GitHub under the MIT licence.

title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires.
  In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

title: AI 工具公司进入拉美的Naver 广告 30 天上线计划
description:
经常有客户问我们Naver 广告该从哪里开始。下面是我们给AI 工具公司的精简版，适用于拉美市场。

开户前要备齐的资料

主体名称要和网站页脚一致，准备自有域名的企业邮箱、隐私政策、服务条款、退款政策和可联系的联系页面。Naver 广告的审核会把这些信息和广告、落地页放在一起比对，不一致是新账户卡审最常见的原因。延伸阅读：广告平台开户费用对比。

费用到底由什么决定

Naver 广告的竞价只是表面成本，总成本还包括开户渠道（直开、代理或二级代理）、充值手续费、汇率差、素材制作以及申诉耗费的时间。对AI 工具公司来说，最容易被忽略的是前两周学习期的浪费，应该把学习期预算单独列出来，而不是第三天就下结论。

为什么Naver 广告要单独规划

很多团队把 Meta 或 Google 的做法直接复制到新平台，Naver 广告往往不吃这一套。受众意图、素材形式、审核规则都不同，出错的代价通常是账户被封而不是效果差一点。AI 工具公司进入拉美之前，先为每个平台写一页计划：谁负责账户、用什么付款方式、哪些落地页已经过审、达到什么数据才加预算。

常见错误

  • 把别的平台素材原样搬到Naver 广告。
  • 同一天同时改预算、受众和素材，结果无法解读。
  • 唯一的管理员账号握在一个外包手里。
  • 广告被拒之前从不看政策中心。
  • 追踪还没验证就判断渠道好坏。

30 天上线节奏

第 1 周：账户、付款、追踪和两个落地页；第 2 周：3–5 个素材方向小预算测试；第 3 周：砍掉后一半，把赢家复制到第二个受众；第 4 周：对照目标看主转化成本，决定加量、维持或停止。把过程记下来，第二个市场会便宜很多。

第一天就把数据打通

安装像素或 SDK，能做服务端事件就做，广告系列命名统一规则，方便合并报表。AI 工具公司应只定义一个主转化（试用、购买或有效线索），其他事件只做诊断用，否则没人说得清Naver 广告到底有没有效果。

能过审的素材

审核会同时看首帧、卖点和落地页。避免前后对比、无法证明的数字和催促性用语，文字本地化成拉美的语言，落地页重复同一个优惠。信息一致既能过审，也能提升转化。

下一步

从清单里挑两项，指定负责人和日期，月底复盘结果。

作者：熊猫出海 PandaWM（香港团队）。业务包括 GEO/AI 搜索优化、Facebook/Google/TikTok 及约 20 个小众平台广告开户与代投、多语言网站、AiChatSale，以及只服务海外商户的加密支付网关。

title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.22382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

title: CEVA: Complementary Evidence Verification via Frame-Level Reorganization for Short-Video Fake News Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.22141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.

title: Beyond Appearance: Where Forest Visual Place Recognition Actually Fails
description:
arXiv:2611.21996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

title: Learning Optimal Transport Plans Via Autoregressive Token Regression
description:
arXiv:2611.22218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for finding the minimum cost coupling between probability distributions. Classical solvers remain the gold standard for this task. At the same time, OT is an ideal testbed for studying whether learning-based amortized models can internalize the structure of OT type problems. Here, ground-truth solutions are available and marginal constraints are explicitly defined. Also, exact discrete solutions have well-characterized sparsity. We describe ToR-OT, a transformer-based model that learns to predict discrete OT plans through autoregressive token regression. We reframe OT into a structured sequence generation task. ToR-OT decodes sparse transport plans as sequences instead of solving an optimization task at test time. We focus on three properties: (a) Zero-shot generalization: pretraining on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances allows a single model to generalize to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics without retraining, (b) Sparse primal decoding: by exploiting the inherent sparsity in exact discrete OT solutions, the decoder predicts only nonzero entries (avoids dense coupling outputs), (c) Amortized inference: on low-dimensional discrete problems, ToR-OT gives accurate approximate plans and compares favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines. Overall, ToR-OT is not yet a replacement for classical solvers, but a step toward understanding how autoregressive transformers can learn structure of constrained optimization problems like OT.

title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.21917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.

title: How to train a quadruped robot to walk with reinforcement learning on one GPU
description:
Teaching a four-legged robot to walk is the "hello world" of robot reinforcement learning: thousands of copies of the robot try to follow velocity commands in parallel, and PPO turns their attempts into a walking policy. This walkthrough sets up a Unitree Go2 velocity task with Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning built on MuJoCo Warp and Newton, and shows the one command that trains it.

pip install alloy-engine gymnasium

1. Build the environment and step it 

import numpy as np
from alloy.envs.loco import go2_velocity

env = go2_velocity(num_envs=2, device="cpu")
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
print(env.obs_groups, {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in obs.items()})
for _ in range(10):
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(np.zeros((2, 12), np.float32))   # zeros hold the stand
print(tuple(reward.shape), env.xp.to_numpy(env.state["base.height"]).round(2))
env.close()

('policy', 'critic') {'policy': (2, 55), 'critic': (2, 79)}
(2,) [0.27 0.27]

The environment returns two observation groups: 55 numbers for the policy (what a real robot could measure) and 79 for the critic (the same plus values only a simulator knows, which helps training). The action is 12 joint targets; zeros hold the standing pose, with the base 0.27 m above the ground. The first build compiles kernels, so it takes a few minutes on a CPU.

2. Train on a GPU with one command 

pip install "alloy-engine[envs]" rsl-rl-lib
python -m alloy.envs.loco.train --num-envs 4096 --iterations 400 --out runs/go2

This trains PPO with rsl_rl across 4,096 parallel Go2 worlds on one NVIDIA GPU, prints a line every 25 iterations and saves the checkpoint as runs/go2/model_last.pt. Add --terrain rough to train on rough tiles instead of flat ground.

Alloy also ships wrappers for Stable-Baselines3 and skrl; the RL guide covers them.

Keep in mind

  • The policy walks blind: it has no height scan, and there are no stairs or gaps.
  • There is no actuator model, and no policy trained this way has been run on a real robot yet.
  • Training in practice needs a GPU. The docs keep the full list of limits.

Links

  • Docs page this is based on: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/how-to/quadruped-rl/
  • Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16312

title: Why Do Users Abandon Chatbot Conversations?
description:
Most businesses add a chatbot with a simple goal: answer questions faster and take some load off the support team. Then they open the analytics and find something awkward. A big share of people start a conversation and leave after two or three messages, without getting what they came for.
That drop-off is rarely random. People walk away from chatbots for fairly consistent reasons, and most of them are fixable. Here are the ones we see most often.

The bot doesn't understand the question

This is the big one. Someone types a plain sentence, and the bot replies with something that has nothing to do with it. One bad answer is forgivable. Two in a row and the person is gone, usually for good.
The cause is often that the bot was trained on how the company talks about its products, not on how customers talk. People write in half sentences, use slang, make typos and ask three things at once. If the bot only handles tidy questions, it will fail on real ones.

Endless loops with no way out

We have all been there. You pick an option, the bot offers the same menu again, you try another, and you land back where you started. When there is no visible way to reach a human, frustration builds quickly.

A good chatbot knows its limits. After a failed attempt or two it should hand over to a person, or at least say honestly that it can't help with this one. Hiding the escape route doesn't keep users, it just makes them leave angry.

Too many questions before any help

Some bots ask for a name, an email address, an order number and a reason for contact before answering anything. For someone who just wants to know a delivery date, that feels like paperwork.

Ask only for what you actually need, and ask at the moment it becomes necessary. If the bot can answer a general question without personal details, let it.

Long, stiff replies

Walls of text don't work in a chat window, especially on a phone. Neither does a response that reads like a legal notice. People expect short messages that sound like a person wrote them.

Breaking an answer into small pieces, using plain words and offering a clear next step makes a noticeable difference. A reply that ends with a useful button or a direct question keeps the conversation moving.

Slow or unreliable responses

A chatbot exists to save time. If replies take several seconds, or the widget freezes on mobile, the whole point is lost. Performance problems are easy to overlook during testing on a fast office connection, but real users are often on weaker networks and smaller screens.

Pretending to be human

People don't mind talking to a bot. What bothers them is being misled. When a bot hides what it is, then fails to act like a person, trust drops fast. Being upfront about what it can help with sets the right expectations and usually leads to better conversations.

The chat window itself is badly designed

A lot of abandonment has nothing to do with the bot's brain. Tiny buttons, a window that covers the content people are trying to read, awkward input fields and unclear options all push users away before the conversation gets going. This is where UI and UX design matters as much as the underlying technology. A chatbot should feel like part of the product, not a pop-up stuck on top of it.

Nobody improves it after launch

Many chatbots are built once and then left alone. But customer questions change, products change and new problems appear. Reading the conversations where people dropped off is one of the most useful things a team can do. You will quickly see the questions the bot can't answer and the points where people give up.

If you want to see how chatbots are being used across different sectors, take a look at the chatbot and AI industry page. And for teams planning to build or rebuild one, our design and development expertise shows how we approach the work from interface to engineering.

What to take away

Users don't leave chatbots because they hate automation. They leave because the experience wasted their time. Understand real questions, keep replies short, offer a way to reach a person, design the interface with care, and keep tuning it over time. Do that and the conversations people finish will start to outnumber the ones they abandon.

What made you close a chatbot window last time? Share it in the comments.

title: FrameSeg3D: Learned Local Frames for Segmenting Small Parts on High-Resolution 3D Scans
description:
arXiv:2611.22124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans, such as nails on hand scans and teeth on intraoral scans, poses three challenges: 1) each part covers a tiny fraction of the scan, 2) its boundary is only a subtle change of height and curvature, and 3) it faces its own direction. Existing methods fall into two groups, and both fall short. The first group processes the whole scan at once and sees each part too coarsely. Point and mesh networks must shrink the scan to fit in memory, so a small part keeps only a few of its points. Multi-view methods render images of the whole object, so each part fills only a few pixels and a tilted part is seen from the side. The second group first finds each part and then segments it up close. But these methods find the parts with knowledge about one kind of part, for example the shape of the dental arch for teeth. Such knowledge does not carry over to other kinds of parts. We find that accuracy is limited by how a part is seen, from which direction and at what scale, not by how many points land on it. We therefore present FrameSeg3D. It first predicts a local frame for every part, its center and the direction it faces, from a low-resolution view of the whole scan. It then segments the part in views around its frame normal at the scanner's resolution, so covering the whole scan no longer costs resolution. Because every part arrives centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale, one segmentation network can serve different kinds of parts and learn from few labeled masks. We test FrameSeg3D on two kinds of parts, nails and teeth. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5), with the most accurate tooth boundaries (boundary IoU 70.5).
