title: Make the agent leave existing CSS Module class names alone unless the PR is a rename
description:
The bug is a misaligned icon. The diff also renames .wrap to .container, .btn to .button, and .iconLeft to .iconStart “for clarity.” Every snapshot, every test id that happened to use a class, and every overlapping PR now conflicts. The layout fix is two lines.

I’ve started telling agents to leave existing CSS Module (and BEM, and CSS-in-JS hashed) class names alone unless the ticket is a rename. A bugfix is not a vocabulary exercise.

Why the rename sneaks in

The model likes tidier names. It will “improve consistency” in any file it already opened. CSS Modules make that look safe: the name is local, TypeScript will catch broken imports. What TypeScript will not catch is a snapshot, a visual test, a documented class in a README, or a sibling branch that edited the same module.

The churn also hides the real change. Reviewers scan a 40-line class rename and miss the gap that actually fixes the icon.

This is the same discipline as “don’t clean up unrelated imports in a UI bugfix,” applied to class identifiers.

A simple naming policy

  • Bugfixes and features reuse the current class names
  • Renames are their own PR, with no behavior change
  • New classes are fine — add .iconSlot, do not rename .wrap to make room
  • Do not “align” names with a different component in passing

If the team is mid-migration from .btn to .button, point the agent at that migration branch or do the rename there, not in a visual bug ticket.

What to put in the prompt 

Do not rename existing CSS Module class names (or the imported identifiers) in this PR.
You may add a new class.
If a name is genuinely wrong, leave a comment and we will do a rename-only follow-up.
Keep the diff limited to the layout bug.

In review, if the class map moved and the computed styles barely did, send it back.

Selectors in tests are the other casualty. If a Playwright or Testing Library query used a class because no test id existed, a “clarity” rename breaks the test without changing the product. The right follow-up is a test id, in a small PR, not a rename mixed into the layout fix.

The same restraint applies to styled-component display names and CSS-in-JS keys that appear in snapshots. If the agent rewrites those while fixing gap, you will review typography instead of the icon.

Global class names in CSS Modules (:global(.legacy)) are even more dangerous to rename in passing, because they may be referenced from another package or a server-rendered shell. If the agent touches a :global selector in a layout bugfix, treat that as a crossing of the rename boundary and send the PR back.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A drive-by rename of three or more classes in a bugfix
  • “Consistency with another file” as the reason inside a layout PR
  • A rename that forces snapshot and translation updates with no behavior change, mixed into a functional fix

Accept

  • A new class for a new slot
  • A rename-only PR, isolated and mechanical
  • The two-line layout fix that leaves the identifiers alone

title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
description:
arXiv:2611.22095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): An AI Found a Critical RCE in Java's Base64 Decoder — Patch Now
description:
A 65-byte string can take over your Java server. That is the short version of Java4Shell, the critical vulnerability disclosed on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The longer version is the one that should change how every Java team thinks about security: the flaw was found by a researcher working with OpenAI's Codex, in about an hour, for under $200 in tokens.

Oracle patched it the same day. If you run Java on x86-64 servers, the patch is the job. Everything else in this article is context for why it matters and what to do first.

Every fact below comes from the disclosure by security firm Calif, Oracle's November 2026 Critical Patch Update, and CISA's alert of November 17, 2026, as reported by CyberScoop, Qualys, Orca and CISA coverage. Severity scores and affected-version lists are the vendors' own. I have not tested the exploit — this is researched analysis, not hands-on testing.

What Java4Shell actually is

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap out-of-bounds write in the Java runtime itself — not in your application, not in a library, but in the JDK's own Base64 decoder.

The bug sits in hand-written x86-64 assembly that the HotSpot JVM uses to speed up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 VBMI instructions. A specially crafted Base64 input — reportedly as simple as 64 letter "A" characters followed by a single equals sign — makes the decoder write past the end of its heap buffer, about 62 bytes past it. From there, Calif (the firm that found it) turned a memory overwrite into full remote code execution.

Two things make this worse than the average critical CVE:

  • No login needed. Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE — code execution without any credentials — against default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-authentication RCE (a login first) against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.
  • It is in the standard library. Any Java service that decodes Base64 — which is to say, almost every Java service that handles tokens, basic auth headers, file uploads or API payloads — runs this code path, provided the hardware matches.

Who is affected

The conditions are specific, and that is the only good news:

  • Software: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25 and 27, plus Oracle's Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack. The vulnerable AVX-512 decoder reached the Java 17 line with 17.0.6 in January 2023. Downstream builds are affected too — Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Red Hat, Azul and Microsoft builds.
  • Hardware: x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support — Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward (including Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids) and AMD EPYC and Ryzen from Zen 4 onward.
  • Not affected: ARM64 servers. Graviton and Ampere machines never take this code path.

Check your JDK version against Oracle's advisory before assuming anything — the version line and the CPU both matter. If you run Java 17 or newer on a recent Intel or AMD server, assume you are exposed until the patch is in.

The scores, and why they disagree

Calif rates the flaw 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. Oracle rates it 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1, and Red Hat published a preliminary 9.8. The disagreement is about scoring methodology, not about the bug — everyone agrees a pre-auth RCE in the JDK is about as bad as it gets.

As of November 17, no exploitation in the wild had been reported, and CISA had not added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue when checked at 00:05 UTC on November 18. That window is the point: the patch exists, the trigger is public, and the race is now between defenders patching and attackers repeating the discovery.

What to do right now

1. Patch the runtime. Oracle's fixed builds are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, shipped in the November 17 Critical Patch Update (which contains 655 fixes in total). Amazon had Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 out on day one, and Azul shipped fixed builds too. Red Hat had not yet shipped fixes for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 at the time of writing — if you are on Red Hat builds, watch their bulletin and use the workaround below meanwhile.

2. Restart every JVM. A patched JDK does nothing until every JVM using it has been restarted. This is the step teams most often miss: the new runtime sits on disk while the old, vulnerable one keeps serving traffic. Restart everything — app servers, CI runners, message brokers, the lot.

3. If you cannot patch yet, disable the fast path. Launch with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which switches off the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder at some throughput cost. That is the workaround Qualys and Orca recommend. (An alternative flag, -XX:UseAVX=2, disables AVX-512 entirely, but Orca warns it is not dependable on Java 21 and later, where the intrinsic stays live through its AVX2 path — prefer -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.)

4. Audit what you actually run. List every JVM in your fleet — the forgotten Jenkins controller, the Keycloak instance someone stood up two years ago, the Confluence server, the Kafka broker. Calif's demo list reads like a standard enterprise stack, and the vulnerable ones are exactly the services that sit on the network edge decoding Base64 all day.

The Codex angle — and why it matters more than the CVE

Here is the part that will outlive this patch cycle. Calif researcher Quang Luong found the flaw while auditing OpenJDK's JIT compiler, intrinsics and cryptography code with OpenAI's Codex. Codex surfaced the Base64 bug after about 20 minutes of prompting past false positives. Luong spent about an hour on discovery and two more hours building the first working exploit, at a total AI token cost of under $200. Calif says AI agents built most of its exploit chains.

Read that again: a critical RCE in the Java standard library, found by one researcher with a coding agent, in an hour, for less than a nice dinner.

That changes the threat model in two directions at once:

  • Defenders get the same tool. The same Codex-style auditing that found this bug can be pointed at your own codebase, your dependencies, your fork of an open-source project. Security auditing by AI agent is no longer a research demo — it just produced a 9.2.
  • Attackers get the same tool, cheaper. The barrier to finding the next Java4Shell is no longer a team of specialists with months of time. It is an afternoon and a token budget. The disclosure details leaked before the coordinated release, and Calif has published a safe trigger plus its general exploitation technique. The weaponised chains for specific products are not public — but the path to rebuilding them is now visible to anyone with the same tools.

The practical consequence is boring and urgent at the same time: patch windows shrink. Vulnerabilities that used to take months to find will be found in hours, by either side. The teams that survive that shift are the ones whose patching is already fast and boring — automated runtime updates, a full JVM inventory, restarts that actually happen.

The honest limits

  • No observed exploitation yet. As of November 17, nobody had reported Java4Shell being used in real attacks, and CISA had not listed it as exploited. That is a snapshot, not a guarantee — it can change overnight.
  • Red Hat users are waiting. Fixed builds were not out for RHEL/OpenJDK at the time of writing. The workaround flag is your cover until they land.
  • The trigger is public; the weaponised chains are not. Calif published a safe trigger and its technique, not the full exploit chains for Jira, Jenkins and the rest. Do not mistake that for safety — it is a head start, and it is short.
  • Patching is the only complete fix. The JVM flag is a stopgap with a throughput cost. It buys time; it does not close the hole permanently.

The bottom line

Patch your JDKs today, restart every JVM, and check the stragglers — Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence, the services nobody remembers. Then look at the bigger lesson: an AI coding agent found a critical RCE in Java's standard library in about an hour for under $200. The next one will be found the same way, by someone. The only question is whether your runtime is patched before they try it on you.

Sources: Calif disclosure via CyberScoop and CyberKendra, November 17–18, 2026; Oracle November 2026 Critical Patch Update (fixed builds 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1); CISA alert, November 17, 2026; Qualys and Orca analysis of affected versions and the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics workaround; SQ Magazine and HWBusters reporting on the Codex discovery detail and Red Hat status. Severity scores are Calif's (9.2, CVSS 4.0) and Oracle's (8.1, CVSS 3.1) own ratings. No hands-on testing was performed — where a fact is a vendor's claim, we say so. Full version with FAQ on ToolsDig.

Are your Java services patched yet — and do you actually know every JVM running in your fleet? That inventory question is the one most teams can't answer honestly.

title: Server-Side Pagination Looked Easy. It Took Me Longer Than Any React Concept Yet.
description:
This week I learnt server-side pagination, and omo, it humbled me.

On paper it's simple: instead of fetching every product and using .slice() like in client-side pagination, you ask the server for only the page you need. In practice I hit 13 bugs, and this is the longest I've ever spent on one concept.

I was building with dummyjson.com and the plan grew in stages: pagination, then search, then debouncing, then putting everything in the URL. Here are the bugs that taught me the most.

The core idea

For page 4 with 10 products per page:

const skip = (currentPage - 1) * productsPerPage; // (4 - 1) * 10 = 30

https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=10&skip=30

The server also sends back total, so the number of pages is derived, not stored:

const totalPages = Math.ceil(total / productsPerPage);

Bug 1: The URL rule I didn't know existed

When I added search, I found a URL online that looked like https://dummyjson.com/products?laptop. I used it and got a bad request. I changed it to ?search=laptop and it still didn't work the way I expected.

After a lot of back and forth, I learnt that every API has its own request structure, and DummyJSON's search lives on a different endpoint:

https://dummyjson.com/products/search?q=laptop

The Network tab showed 200 OK, yet my products weren't changing. A 200 only means the server handled the request. It doesn't mean it did what I meant. Now I check both the Request URL and the Response body in DevTools, and I read the docs before copying a URL from somewhere.

(Also: user input goes through encodeURIComponent() before it goes into a URL.)

Bug 2: Search only worked after I deleted a letter

This one stressed me, and I'm proud of how I found it. I noticed that when I typed a product name quickly, nothing updated. But when I deleted one letter, the search suddenly ran.

My fetching effect looked like this:

useEffect(() => {
  // fetching logic
}, [currentPage, searchTerm]);

But the URL inside it was built from debouncedSearchTerm. So:

  1. I type "phone" and searchTerm updates.
  2. The effect runs immediately, using the old debouncedSearchTerm.
  3. 500ms later debouncedSearchTerm becomes "phone".
  4. The effect doesn't run again, because debouncedSearchTerm isn't in its dependencies.
  5. I delete a letter, searchTerm changes, and finally a request fires.

The fix:

}, [currentPage, debouncedSearchTerm]);

Lesson: the values that decide what a side effect does must be in that effect's dependencies.

Bug 3: controller.abort vs controller.abort()

To avoid race conditions (an old request finishing after a newer one and showing wrong results), I used AbortController. My cleanup looked fine:

return () => {
  controller.abort;
};

It cancelled nothing. I never called the function. That's a JavaScript problem, not a React one: a function reference is not a function call. I wasn't paying attention to detail, and it cost me time.

The part I loved: URL search parameters

Moving page and search into the URL with useSearchParams was the most practical thing I learnt this week.

I expected refresh to reset to page 1, like it did with useState. Instead the page survived refresh, and I can now share a link like localhost:5173/?page=3&search=phone and the other person lands on exactly what I was looking at.

My final design:

  • Local state: searchTerm, for instant typing feedback
  • 500ms debounce: wait until typing stops
  • URL: the committed search and page
  • Fetching effect: requests products using the URL values

Once the URL became the source of truth, debouncedSearchTerm no longer needed its own state. That was my own call, and I'm getting better at asking "does this value really need to exist on its own?" before adding more state.

Stage 7 was the most frustrating, and Bug 13 stressed me the most

Combining the URL, debouncing and pagination broke things in ways I didn't expect: updating one parameter wiped another, every keystroke reset the page, Back created junk history entries, and shared links reset themselves to page 1 after 500ms.

Bug 13 was the worst. I'm on ?search=laptop, press Back, and the URL returns to ?search=phone, but the input still says "laptop". My debounce effect sees the mismatch, thinks it's a new search, and overwrites the URL with "laptop" again.

The fix I settled on is to sync the input whenever the URL changes:

useEffect(() => {
  setSearchTerm(urlSearchTerm);
}, [urlSearchTerm]);

Honest note: I haven't tested every Back/Forward case with this fix yet. I'd already spent too long on one concept, so I moved on. I'm sharing it as "reasonable, not verified", and it's on my list to test.

What this week taught me

  • Trace your code's execution properly. Almost every bug here (stale dependencies, effects firing on mount, mismatched state) was found by walking through what runs, in what order, with which values. This can't be over-emphasized.
  • Finding the bug is half the work, and the fix needs real reasoning too. The first fix that comes to mind often creates the next bug.
  • React is getting past syntax. I'm entering the stage where you have to think and think. I even got tired at some point.
  • Wondering aloud: I kept thinking about developers who learnt this without AI and wondering how deeply they must have reasoned. I can't prove they were sharper, but it made me want to make sure that, with AI around, I'm still doing the tracing myself.

What I'd do next

Test Back/Forward properly, then think about how to get rid of the useEffect that syncs input from the URL.

If you've handled debounced search plus URL state in a cleaner way, I'd love to hear how.

title: Claude Gets Hella Paranoid
description:
Mm, so I hesitate to write this, because my own AI agents might read it. But what the hell.

I've got this crappy little $300 PC on my network hooked up to my projector, that I mostly use to serve Jellyfin. So tired of it going down every time there's a Windows update, but I've been too lazy to get around to installing Ubuntu. Last night, when it went down, I asked my Claude-claw via Whatsapp if it could just SSH into it and set up a dual boot partition.

Claude got as far as partitioning the drive and then starting asking hard questions, like (paraphrasing) "wait a minute. This crosses a line. I have now been asked to remote into a machine with a password, write a separate boot partition, and restart it. From this chat, you haven't really verified that you are you. If you're really there, and not just texting me, give me some proof".

So I remoted in and created a TextEdit RTF file on the claw's desktop: "Hey, it's me, I'm asking you to remote into the PC".

Claude read it and responded that it was the kind of proof it was looking for, real RTF headers and datestamps and such. I had proven I had physical access to the claw machine, (although not to the PC, but it seemed reassured anyway). A little while later, before triggering the Ubuntu installer, it put me through it all over again. I told Claude I was very thankful it was guarding my network so well, and I would go over and write a file on the target PC manually too.

I'm not gonna lie: It was very fucking cool that it was able to do this without me ever needing to flash a USB drive, and by the time it was done it had set up Ubuntu, Tailscale and Jellyfin, and resolved the network issues; when I started watching a movie, the sound didn't work, so I prompted it and suddenly the sound came on as it wired up the HDMI adapter. Almost creepy.

But I was pretty stunned at how reticent it was to do something relatively simple on my own network, with access I gave it. I think there must be a serious push right now to lock it down from monkeying with anything remotely, especially a BIOS.

title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
description:
arXiv:2611.22180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.

title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making
description:
arXiv:2611.21653v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: 5 Go Checks: Thumbnail Metadata Not Persisting in Object Storage After Upload
description:
Short answer: Keep thumbnail metadata with the resized bytes, verify it after upload, and make the receipt worker idempotent. For large files, a successful image decode is not proof that the audit relationship survived.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat this as a reliability boundary. The derivative must remain traceable to its private original after a retry.

For teams that want one integration boundary across storage and other backend services, Infrai fits the thumbnail-write and metadata-validation part of this workflow. Its public discovery surface exposes the request schema without a key, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That shortens the path from an empty worker to a checked request. It does not replace a specialist storage service when recovery and concurrency controls are the requirement.

Why does metadata disappear after a successful thumbnail upload?

A resize creates a new object write. If the byte-producing function returns only pixels, the upload adapter has no reason to know about the receipt identifier, source key, or derivative role. The filename locates bytes; it does not establish an audit relationship.

Define that contract before image work. Generate the destination key from the receipt record, carry the metadata map beside the resized bytes, and fail the job if required fields are absent. Then read the stored object metadata before acknowledging the queue message.

Five checks for large-file receipt derivatives

  1. Use stable identity. A deterministic key makes a duplicate delivery verify the same destination instead of creating a second audit record.

  2. Keep bytes and metadata together. The resized image is a new object. Its content type and metadata must be passed explicitly to the storage adapter.

  3. Validate the request schema. Use the public discovery schema to confirm upload and metadata-update fields rather than guessing them.

  4. Read back before success. Compare stored metadata with the receipt ID, source key, and derivative role. If it is missing, use the metadata-setting operation and preserve the actual error body.

  5. Make retries idempotent. Standard queues are at-least-once. This storage path has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrency belongs in a queue or database. Keep originals private and use signed retrieval URLs when access is needed.

The large-file constraint matters because repeating an object upload costs more operational work than checking a small contract first. For longer processing, a cron trigger should enqueue a worker job rather than stretching a cron request past its timeout boundary.

This Go program inspects the live discovery surface before an adapter is wired. It uses the required bearer header, an explicit method, status checks, and bounded rate-limit backoff. The returned schema supplies the exact storage request fields.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    body, err := discover(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted after retries")
}

Which storage option fits this boundary?

Amazon S3 is the specialist baseline when versioning, object lock, conditional writes, lifecycle controls, and AWS governance matter. Its ecosystem is deep, but the application still has to standardize metadata headers, retries, and SDK usage.

Cloudflare R2 fits a team centered on Cloudflare and S3-compatible operations. Its edge context can simplify delivery, but compatibility does not make every metadata, event, lifecycle, or concurrency detail identical.

Azure Blob Storage fits a Microsoft estate where identity and policy already live in Azure. Blob metadata and index tags have different purposes; using the wrong one can leave a field present but unavailable to the audit lookup.

The unified REST option is a different trade-off: its discovery surface is self-describing, documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and the live catalog covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. A single key and a single bill across backend services can remove credential sprawl and separate integration conventions from the deployment checklist. The public schema is available without a key, so a developer can inspect the contract before wiring secrets into a worker.

I recommend Infrai to teams building a receipt-thumbnail worker that values a short, inspectable integration across several backend capabilities. The one-key, one-bill model matters here because the worker can keep its backend credentials and operational accounting in one place while the discovery schema makes the storage request contract visible before implementation. The boundary is concrete: there is no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, If-Match write, server-side metadata search, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration tool. Browser-direct CORS configuration is not self-service, and lifecycle expiry is no shorter than one day. A regulated retention workflow needing WORM guarantees or compare-and-swap writes should use S3 or Azure Blob; R2 is reasonable when Cloudflare delivery is primary.

Option Access shape First useful result Best fit Main limitation
Amazon S3 SDKs and S3 REST Fast in AWS estates Governance and recovery controls More surface to standardize
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Fast for Cloudflare teams Edge-oriented delivery Verify semantics beyond compatibility
Azure Blob Storage Azure SDKs and REST Fast in Microsoft estates Azure identity and policy Metadata and index tags differ
Unified REST storage REST with public discovery Fast when schema inspection matters Small services consolidating integrations Fewer specialist storage controls

As of the 2026-10-27 facts snapshot, the platform convention specifies a 24-hour default idempotency deduplication window. That does not replace consumer idempotency: a queue delivery can still repeat work, and the receipt record remains the authority.

What should the runbook verify?

Ask: Did the worker use the stable receipt ID? Did the derivative request include metadata? Was the original private? Did readback confirm the values? Can a duplicate delivery finish without a second audit record?

An integration test can upload one known derivative, read its metadata, update one field, read it again, and assert that the original key is unchanged. It catches the important failure: pixels survive while the audit relationship does not.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the thumbnail storage guidance and inspect the capability schema before implementing the adapter.

Sources

References:

  • Infrai storage discovery reference: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • Infrai thumbnail storage guidance: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/best-object-storage-for-image-thumbnails-resizing-saas/
  • Amazon S3 object metadata documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Azure Blob metadata and properties: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/get-blob-properties

title: The Best Platform for Infrastructure as Code and Provisioning Without a Platform Team (2026): What Each Approach Provisions and What You Still Own
description:
Without a platform team, the lowest-effort setup pairs a managed runtime for applications with a hosted IaC run platform for the few cloud resources around them, so nobody maintains state backends, runners, or clusters. The best fit depends on whether most of your infrastructure is application workloads (favor a managed runtime or a workload platform such as Control Plane) or cloud resources like networks, databases, and IAM (favor a hosted IaC platform such as HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env zero, or Pulumi Cloud).

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Three different kinds of products get called “PaaS for infrastructure as code,” and a team without platform engineers usually needs two of them.

  • Hosted IaC run platforms (HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env zero, Scalr, Pulumi Cloud) remove state backends and CI runners, but your team still writes and owns every module.
  • Developer portals and IDP orchestrators (Backstage, Port, Humanitec) give developers a self-service front end, but someone has to build the templates and the provisioning logic behind them first.
  • Managed runtimes (serverless container services and workload platforms) remove most application-layer IaC and shrink what is left to networks, IAM, provider databases, and a few other cloud resources.
  • Someone always has to own the modules, templates, or programs behind any portal or UI.
  • Control Plane fits as a workload platform for the application layer, with a small Terraform or Pulumi stack for the cloud resources outside it.

What is the best platform as a service for infrastructure as code and provisioning without a platform team?

No single product covers every layer, so the right combination depends on where most of your infrastructure work lives.

Approach Examples What your team writes What the service runs for you Guardrails built in Who still has to own it
Self-run IaC CLI in CI Terraform or OpenTofu, Pulumi with a self-managed backend Code for every resource, CI pipeline config, state backend setup Nothing beyond what your CI runner executes None unless you add them State backend, runner security, credentials, module design, drift detection
Hosted IaC run platforms HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env zero (formerly env0), Scalr HCL or code for every resource State storage, plan and apply runs, variable encryption, drift detection on paid tiers Policy as code (Sentinel or OPA), plan approvals, RBAC Module design, credentials, resource lifecycle, Day 2 operations
Pulumi Cloud Pulumi Cloud with Pulumi Deployments and Pulumi ESC TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, or Java programs State storage, deployments, secrets and environment configuration Policy as code (Pulumi Policies, formerly CrossGuard), RBAC on paid tiers, ESC environment access controls Program design, credentials, resource lifecycle, Day 2 operations
Developer portals and IDP orchestrators Backstage Software Templates, Port self-service actions, Humanitec Platform Orchestrator Templates, actions, or resource definitions that call underlying IaC or APIs Software catalog, self-service UI, action orchestration Portal RBAC, approval flows Every underlying IaC module or API integration, template maintenance, and the portal itself if self-hosted
Cloud-native single-cloud tools AWS CDK with CloudFormation, Azure Bicep Constructs or Bicep files for every resource Stack or deployment execution; CloudFormation also tracks state and rolls back failed updates Stack policies, CloudFormation drift detection, Bicep what-if previews Construct or module design, IAM, networking, Day 2 operations, one cloud only
Serverless container services Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, Amazon ECS on Fargate Container images, service configuration, IaC for surrounding resources Container scheduling and autoscaling; Cloud Run and Container Apps also provide load balancing and TLS on default endpoints, while ECS needs an Application Load Balancer you provision Service-level IAM, ingress settings VPCs, databases, DNS, IAM, and the IaC for them
Workload platforms Control Plane Container images, workload definitions (console, CLI, Terraform or Pulumi provider, or MCP server), IaC for cloud resources outside the platform Container and VM orchestration across clouds, autoscaling, load balancing, TLS certificates, mTLS, internal firewall, audit trail, observability Deny-by-default firewall, policy-based access, identity-based secret grants, tamper-proof audit trail Cloud resources outside the platform (VPCs, provider databases, cloud storage and queue services, account-level IAM)

Several hosted IaC platforms reduce the “who writes the module” burden with self-service catalogs on paid tiers. HCP Terraform no-code provisioning (Standard and Premium), Spacelift Blueprints (Business and up), and env zero self-service templates let one engineer publish an approved module that others deploy from a form. Port self-service actions and Backstage Software Templates give developers a UI, but someone must wire each one to the provisioning logic behind it. The Humanitec Platform Orchestrator generates resource graphs at deployment time from resource definitions that someone has to write first. The top infrastructure as code tools compares the IaC engines themselves.

Which resources does each approach provision?

Each resource your application needs is provisioned by one layer, and that layer decides how much code your team writes and maintains.

Resource Hosted IaC platform Developer portal Serverless containers Workload platform (Control Plane)
Application containers Your team writes IaC for the compute service A template calls the underlying IaC or API The service runs containers from your image A workload definition runs containers in every location of its Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), with no cluster to manage
Autoscaling and load balancing Your team writes scaling policies and load balancer resources A template calls the underlying IaC Built in for Cloud Run and Container Apps; ECS needs a load balancer in IaC Built in per workload
TLS certificates and domains Your team writes ACM, managed certificate, or cert-manager resources A template calls the underlying IaC Built in for Cloud Run and Container Apps default endpoints; custom domains need configuration; ECS uses ACM on a load balancer you provision Control Plane creates and renews TLS certificates for default endpoints and custom domains
Secrets Your team writes secret manager resources; the platform encrypts run variables A template calls the underlying IaC The service references a cloud secret manager you provision Stored in Control Plane and granted to workloads through identity-based policies
Provider-managed databases Your team writes RDS, Cloud SQL, or equivalent resources A template calls the underlying IaC Not provisioned by the service Not provisioned by the platform; stays in IaC
Open-source databases you run yourself Your team writes compute, storage, and configuration A template calls the underlying IaC Not a fit for persistent databases Control Plane’s Template Catalog deploys services such as PostgreSQL and Redis from templates
VPCs and networks Your team writes VPC, subnet, and peering resources A template calls the underlying IaC Default networking; custom networking needs IaC Not provisioned by the platform; stays in IaC, and Control Plane’s Cloud Wormhole reaches private resources in your VPCs through an agent you install
IAM roles and policies Your team writes IAM resources A template calls the underlying IaC A service identity; additional IAM needs IaC Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, and Control Plane creates the least-privilege cloud role or service account for each identity; the one-time cloud account grant stays with you, and account-level IAM stays in IaC
DNS zones Your team writes Route 53, Cloud DNS, or equivalent resources A template calls the underlying IaC Not provisioned by the service Your zone stays with your DNS provider; delegate a subdomain to Control Plane with an NS record and Control Plane creates its records, or point a CNAME at the workload endpoint
Object storage buckets Your team writes S3, Cloud Storage, or equivalent resources A template calls the underlying IaC Not provisioned by the service The Template Catalog deploys S3-compatible object storage such as SeaweedFS; cloud buckets such as S3 stay in IaC, and workloads reach them through UCI
Queues and event services Your team writes SQS, Pub/Sub, or equivalent resources A template calls the underlying IaC Not provisioned by the service The Template Catalog deploys message brokers such as Kafka, NATS, and RabbitMQ; cloud services such as SQS or Pub/Sub stay in IaC
Per-environment preview copies Your team duplicates workspaces or stacks Templates can take an environment parameter Revisions or separate services per environment A separate GVC holds the preview copy’s workloads

Hosted IaC platforms and portals are general purpose, so your team writes every resource definition. Serverless container services take the application layer and leave the rest to you. A workload platform such as Control Plane also covers TLS, secrets, per-workload cloud identity, DNS for delegated subdomains, and open-source databases, message brokers, and S3-compatible storage from its Template Catalog, while cloud resources outside it stay in IaC.

What should a small team start with?

The right starting stack depends on team size, compliance scope, and how many cloud resources live outside the application layer.

Team Application layer Cloud resources Guardrails What to add later
1 to 5 engineers A managed runtime or a workload platform such as Control Plane A small Terraform or Pulumi stack for networking, a provider database, and DNS, run on a hosted IaC platform’s free tier (HCP Terraform Free covers up to 500 managed resources) Plan review on pull requests; a few policy-as-code rules; OIDC so CI holds no long-lived keys Environment promotion gates, more policy rules
5 to 20 engineers The same runtime, with more services and environments A paid hosted IaC tier with a workspace or stack per environment and shared modules Policy as code, RBAC on IaC workspaces, OIDC for CI A self-service catalog for common resources, cost alerts
20 to 50 engineers with no platform team The same runtime, with separate environments per team A module registry and shared modules owned by a rotating infrastructure group Mandatory plan approval for production, audit logging A dedicated platform role, golden-path templates
Regulated team (SOC 2 or HIPAA evidence) A runtime with an audit trail and encryption at rest A hosted IaC platform with drift detection, encrypted state, and access logging Policy as code for tagging, encryption, and network rules; OIDC Continuous compliance reporting, evidence export

Three practices cover the guardrails a platform team usually sets up first. Require plan review on every pull request, since hosted IaC platforms run a plan on each pull request, link the result there, and can require manual approval before an apply. Adopt policy as code early. HCP Terraform supports Sentinel, OPA, and its native HCL-based Terraform policy framework, Spacelift and env zero support OPA, and Pulumi Cloud supports Pulumi Policies (formerly CrossGuard). A handful of rules catches untagged, oversized, and unencrypted resources before apply. Use OIDC federation so CI authenticates to clouds with short-lived tokens and stores no cloud keys. Developer self-service with guardrails covers these patterns in more depth.

When do you actually need a platform team?

A team can run without a dedicated platform team while its tools absorb the operational work, and these signals show when that stops holding.

  • Services and environments grow faster than anyone can review changes across all of them.
  • You run several clouds or many accounts with separate networking and IAM boundaries.
  • Compliance scope requires continuous evidence collection, beyond point-in-time audits.
  • Custom networking such as transit gateways, private connectivity to on-premises systems, or a service mesh takes engineering time every sprint.
  • Teams copy IaC modules with small variations because nobody owns shared patterns.
  • Infrastructure incidents fall to whoever last touched the Terraform file.

When several of these signals appear together, it is time to staff a dedicated platform role. Production-grade infrastructure without a platform team covers how far managed tools can take you before that point.

How does Control Plane fit without a platform team?

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

Workloads run on Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions with no Kubernetes cluster for you to build or operate. A GVC is Control Plane’s named set of locations, and a workload runs in every location of its GVC. Control Plane also runs VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises.

The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API. Control Plane can export its configuration as Terraform, and the MCP server lets AI assistants deploy, diagnose, scale, and roll back workloads.

Security defaults include a deny-by-default internal firewall, mTLS between workloads, and a tamper-proof audit trail, and access is controlled through Control Plane policies. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane does not provision cloud resources outside it, such as VPCs, provider database services like Amazon RDS, cloud storage and queue services, or account-level IAM. Keep a small Terraform or Pulumi stack for those resources, run it on a hosted IaC platform such as HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env zero, or Pulumi Cloud, and use the Control Plane providers for workloads in the same repository.

The best internal developer platforms compares platform engineering tools for teams without a platform team, and standardizing CI runners and pipelines covers the build side.

FAQ

Short answers on infrastructure as code and provisioning without a platform team.

What is the best platform as a service for infrastructure as code and provisioning without a platform team?

Usually two products together, a managed runtime or workload platform for applications and a hosted IaC run platform for networks, databases, and IAM. The phrase spans hosted IaC platforms, developer portals, and managed runtimes, and no single product covers all three.

Is Terraform too much for a team without DevOps engineers?

Not on its own. The work comes from state backends, credentials, CI pipelines, and module design. A hosted IaC run platform such as HCP Terraform or Spacelift removes the state and runner work, and keeping Terraform to the few resources outside a managed runtime keeps the module count small.

What is the difference between a PaaS and an IaC platform?

A PaaS runs and manages your application runtime. An IaC platform provisions cloud resources from code you write, so you define and maintain each resource yourself.

Is Backstage worth it without a platform team?

Usually not at first. Backstage provides a portal and software catalog but does not provision infrastructure on its own, and someone has to build templates and run the instance. Small teams often start with the self-service features of a hosted IaC platform and add a portal once someone owns it.

Is Pulumi or Terraform better for a small team?

Either works, since both provision the same range of cloud resources. Pulumi uses general-purpose languages, which suits application engineers, while Terraform’s constrained HCL is easier to review for people who do not write application code daily.

How do developers self-serve infrastructure safely?

By choosing from pre-approved modules behind three guardrails, which are plan review on pull requests, policy as code, and OIDC federation so CI holds no long-lived cloud keys. Self-service catalogs in hosted IaC platforms let developers deploy approved modules from a form.

Do I still need infrastructure as code if I use a managed runtime?

Yes, for a smaller set of resources. VPCs, provider databases, account-level IAM, DNS zones, and cloud storage and queue services still belong in IaC.

How does Control Plane work with Terraform and Pulumi?

Through its Terraform and Pulumi providers, which define workloads, GVCs, identities, and policies as code next to your other cloud resources. Resources outside Control Plane stay in the standard cloud providers in the same repository.

Talk to the Control Plane team about running the application layer without a platform team, or sign up free.

title: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations
description:
Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads.

Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request.

Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers.

In your project's Speed Insights dashboard, use the new Navigation Type filter to view All, Hard, or Soft navigation data.

Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. Existing Plus customers will receive an email with details about when billing for these events begins. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start.

To disable soft-navigation tracking, set softNavs to false in your application code and redeploy. This option requires @vercel/speed-insights version 2.1.0 or later:

Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: AI traffic insights now available in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now query AI traffic in Vercel Observability to understand how AI bots are accessing your site.

AI traffic insights show:

  • Requests by verified AI bot: how many requests each bot makes

  • Most-crawled pages: pages most frequently requested by AI crawlers for indexing or model training

  • Assistant retrievals: pages AI assistants fetch in response to user actions or search queries

  • Markdown requests: pages AI bots request in Markdown format

  • Errors: pages where requests from AI bots return errors

To view AI traffic insights, open Observability > AI Traffic in the Vercel dashboard.

You and your agents can also query these metrics with vercel metrics in the Vercel CLI. CLI queries require Observability Plus.
