title: tx-explainer: اقرأ معاملة Solana بلغة بسيطة
description:
العثور على معاملة (transaction) في Solana سهل، لكن قراءتها صعبة. المستكشف (explorer) يعطيك توقيعًا (signature)، وقائمة من مفاتيح الحسابات، وتعليمات (instructions) بياناتها سلسلة من البايتات. لتعرف ما الذي حدث فعلًا، عليك أن تتذكر أن أول بايت في تعليمة Token هو وسم (tag)، وأن المبالغ أعداد صحيحة بترتيب little-endian وبلا فاصلة عشرية، وأن برنامج Anchor يخفي اسم التعليمة خلف discriminator من 8 بايتات.

tx-explainer يقوم بهذه القراءة مكانك. تعطيه توقيعًا، أو بايتات المعاملة الخام، أو ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا في ملف، فيطبع ما فعلته كل تعليمة في جمل بسيطة، ثم الرسوم، ووحدات الحساب (compute units)، وتغيّرات الأرصدة.

هو أداة فك ترميز للقراءة فقط: لا يوقّع ولا يرسل أي شيء أبدًا. والـ README صريح في حدوده: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني (not audited)، وهو موجّه أولًا إلى devnet وtestnet وlocalnet، والنص المبسّط اجتهاد قدر الإمكان ولا يغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج.

ماذا يقدّم

هذا ناتج الأداة على معاملة حقيقية من devnet موجودة ضمن ملفات الاختبار:

$ tx-explainer --file test/fixtures/devnet-memo.json
Transaction 5zhK…  [legacy]
Status: succeeded
Fee: 0.0000155 SOL (of which priority ≈ 0.0000105 SOL)
Compute units: 26,021 of 70,000 requested

What happened:
  1. [Compute Budget] Set compute unit limit to 70,000
  2. [Compute Budget] Set priority fee to 150,000 micro-lamports per compute unit
  3. [Associated Token Account] Create (if missing) the associated token account Expy…TCA6 for wallet 6a1w…BNqd and mint 4wMp…jY4y, paid by 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer)
  4. [SPL Token] Transfer 1,236.871165 tokens of mint 4wMp…jY4y from 55Xo…AmDQ to Expy…TCA6 (authority 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer))
  5. [Memo] Memo: "helm-payout-v1:…"

Token balance changes:
  55Xo…AmDQ (owner 2VyJ…TeEs): -1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y
  Expy…TCA6 (owner 6a1w…BNqd): +1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y

البرامج المدمجة. الأداة تعرف البرامج التي تظهر في أغلب المعاملات:

  • System: التعليمات CreateAccount وAssign وTransfer وCreateAccountWithSeed، وعمليات الـ nonce، وAllocate وTransferWithSeed.
  • SPL Token وToken-2022: تهيئة الـ mint والحسابات، وTransfer وTransferChecked، وApprove وRevoke وSetAuthority وMintTo وBurn وCloseAccount وFreeze وThaw وSyncNative وغيرها. أما تعليمات امتدادات Token-2022 فتُذكر برقمها فقط.
  • Associated Token Account: التعليمات Create وCreateIdempotent وRecoverNested.
  • Compute Budget: التعليمات SetComputeUnitLimit وSetComputeUnitPrice وRequestHeapFrame وSetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit.
  • Memo (الإصداران v1 وv2)، ويُعرض كنص UTF-8.

أي برنامج Anchor عبر الـ IDL. مرّر ملف IDL الخاص بالبرنامج بالخيار --idl (صيغة Anchor 0.30 وما بعدها)، فتعرض الأداة اسم التعليمة، والوسائط بعد فك ترميز Borsh (structs وenums وvec وoption والمصفوفات)، وأسماء الحسابات، وأسماء الأخطاء المخصّصة إن فشلت المعاملة.

بيانات الـ RPC الوصفية (metadata). عندما يأتي الإدخال من getTransaction، يضمّ الناتج أيضًا الحالة (مع أسماء أخطاء Anchor)، والرسوم، وتقديرًا لرسوم الأولوية (priority fee) يساوي حد وحدات الحساب × سعر الوحدة، ووحدات الحساب المستهلكة، والتعليمات الداخلية (CPIs)، وتغيّرات رصيد SOL، وتغيّرات أرصدة التوكنات بالخانات العشرية الصحيحة.

رسائل legacy وv0. الصيغتان مدعومتان. عناوين جداول البحث (address lookup tables) تُحلّ من meta.loadedAddresses. وفي الإدخال الخام، حيث لا توجد هذه البيانات، تُعرض بالشكل table[index].

ثلاث طرق للتشغيل. نفس منطق فك الترميز متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI)، وكمكتبة TypeScript، وكواجهة ويب صغيرة تعمل كليًا داخل المتصفح وتتصل مباشرة بالـ RPC العام للشبكة المختارة. يضع الـ README رابطًا لنسخة تجريبية حية من هذه الواجهة: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/tx-explainer/.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع ثم ابنِه:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer
cd tx-explainer
pnpm install
pnpm build

ثم شغّل الـ CLI من مجلد المشروع:

node dist/cli.js <signature> --cluster devnet           # fetch via getTransaction
node dist/cli.js <signature> --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899
node dist/cli.js --raw <base64-or-base58 tx bytes>      # offline, no metadata
node dist/cli.js --file saved-getTransaction.json --idl target/idl/my_program.json
node dist/cli.js ... --json                             # machine-readable
node dist/cli.js serve --port 8787                      # web UI on 127.0.0.1

الشكلان الأولان يجلبان المعاملة من شبكة أو من الـ validator المحلي. الخيار --raw يعمل بلا اتصال على بايتات بصيغة base64 أو base58. والخيار --file يقرأ ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا، وهذا مفيد في تقارير الأخطاء والاختبارات. أما --json فيعطي نفس الشرح كبيانات منظّمة يستطيع سكربت أن يقرأها.

وكمكتبة، ثلاث دوال تغطي الحالة الشائعة:

import { explain, render, fetchTransaction } from "tx-explainer";
const e = explain({ rpc: await fetchTransaction(sig, "https://api.devnet.solana.com") }, { idls: [myIdl] });
console.log(render(e));

الدالة fetchTransaction تجلب المعاملة، وexplain تبني الشرح المنظّم، وrender تحوّله إلى النص الذي رأيته في الأعلى.

كيف يعمل من الداخل

يصف الـ README أربع وحدات صغيرة، ومعرفة هذا التقسيم تفيدك إن أردت إضافة decoder جديد:

  1. الملف message.ts يحلّل صيغة الإرسال (wire format) يدويًا: أطوال compact-u16، والتواقيع، وترويسة الرسالة، ومفاتيح الحسابات، والتعليمات المجمّعة، وجداول البحث في v0. ثم يستنتج من الترويسة إن كان كل مفتاح موقّعًا (signer) أو قابلًا للكتابة (writable).
  2. الملف programs.ts فيه decoder صغير لكل برنامج مدمج. كل واحد يقرأ وسم التعليمة (u32 في System وu8 في Token) وحقولها بواسطة Reader يعمل بترتيب little-endian.
  3. الملف anchor.ts يقارن أول 8 بايتات من بيانات التعليمة مع الـ discriminator لكل تعليمة في الـ IDL، ثم يفك ترميز الوسائط بـ Borsh انطلاقًا من شجرة الأنواع في الـ IDL.
  4. الملف explain.ts يجمع كل ذلك مع بيانات الـ RPC: أرصدة التوكنات تعطي الـ mint وعدد الخانات العشرية، والتعليمات الداخلية تعطي الـ CPIs، والأرصدة قبل وبعد تعطي الفروقات.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق، والناتج اجتهاد. الجمل وسيلة مساعدة لقراءة المعاملة. لا تغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج، ولا ينبغي أن تبني عليها وحدها قرارًا يخص أموالًا حقيقية.
  • امتدادات Token-2022 تُعرض برقمها فقط. رسوم التحويل، والتحويلات السرّية، وباقي تعليمات الامتدادات لا تُحوَّل إلى جمل.
  • بعض البرامج يُذكر اسمها فقط. تعليمات Stake وVote وAddress Lookup Table والـ loader تُعرَّف بالاسم دون فك ترميزها.
  • رسوم الأولوية تقديرية. تُحسب بالصيغة ceil(limit × price / 1e6). وإن لم تحدّد المعاملة حدًّا، تفترض الأداة القيمة الافتراضية: 200 ألف وحدة حساب لكل تعليمة.
  • الإدخال الخام بلا بيانات وصفية. مع --raw لا توجد حالة ولا رسوم ولا تغيّرات أرصدة ولا تعليمات داخلية، لأن هذه المعلومات تأتي من الـ RPC وليس من بايتات المعاملة.
  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
description:
arXiv:2611.22009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

title: How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)
description:
How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)

Most Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage on day one was either "your servers are on fire" or "it only crashes the JVM." Both skip the mechanism, and the mechanism tells you who is at risk. This post walks through why the bug exists, what the sources actually established, and what a defender can watch for.

I have not reproduced the bug. Everything below comes from public write-ups by Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys and Calif, and I flag where they disagree.

TL;DR

Claim Status
Heap write past the output array on x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI Reproduced by Endor Labs (under an emulator) and Upwind (on real hardware)
JVM crash from a remote request Consistent across sources
Pre-auth RCE in named products Claimed by Calif, no public proof-of-concept
Attacker-controlled write contents Not supported, the written bytes are constant
Exploited in the wild None reported, not in CISA KEV as of November 17

Why an intrinsic exists at all

HotSpot ships a pure-Java Base64 decoder. When the JIT sees that decoder running hot, it can replace the Java loop with an intrinsic, a hand-written assembly stub for the target CPU. On x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, the stub decodes wide blocks at once.

Equixly makes two points that matter for exposure. The intrinsic replaces the Java code only after the JIT compiles the decoder, which on a busy server happens within seconds. And the vector path only engages above a length threshold. Endor Labs gives the threshold as 31 bytes on Java 21, 25 and 27, and 128 bytes on Java 17.

That is why the shortest triggers differ by version. 65 characters is enough on 21, 25 and 27. 17 needs 129.

The tail bug

The block loop handles most of the input. The last characters, including padding, go through a tail routine. Per Upwind, a malformed string ending in a stray = makes the tail calculate a negative output length. A small write becomes a full 64-byte write, 62 bytes beyond the end of the output array. Endor Labs measured 62 bytes for a single = tail and 63 for ==.

Two properties follow from the measurements.

First, the overflow content is fixed. Endor Labs says the bytes stay the same regardless of the input data. An attacker controls the length of the input and the heap layout around the destination array, not the bytes that get written.

Second, Java still rejects the input afterwards with an IllegalArgumentException. The exception is a useful tell, as the detection section below shows, but it fires after the damage.

Upwind also ran 300,000 well-formed inputs and saw no overflow, so ordinary traffic is not at risk. The trigger is a malformed string.

What the fix looks like

Endor Labs reports the fix as JDK-8393212, "Base64 optimization improvements," a four-line change that adds a guard before the size computation and routes short padded tails to the scalar path. Engineers committed it under embargo on October 14, 2026. Endor Labs also notes that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, while Oracle's builds had shipped.

The vulnerable code arrived in 17.0.6 in January 2023 through a backport from JDK 18, and Equixly flags the 17.0.6 starting point as its own inference from backport history.

From crash to code execution

The crash path is simple. If the 62 stray bytes land on a live object, they overwrite its header, and the usual result is a SIGSEGV inside garbage collection, per Endor Labs. Equixly warns the crash log will not mention Base64, because the garbage collector reads the damaged object later.

Calif claims much more, in five stages.

Stage Claimed step
1 Corrupt an array length
2 Corrupt a second array to leak heap contents, which Calif calls JavaBleed
3 Repair object headers so the JVM keeps running
4 Groom the heap remotely so the overflow lands on a chosen object
5 Write into the JVM code cache

Endor Labs marks every one of these as Calif's claim. Calif says there is no universal exploit, and that each target needs its own decoder route, writable buffer, readable feedback channel and heap layout. The sources I read do not discuss address space randomization at all, so I will not call it a barrier or a bypass.

This is why your exposure depends on the application and not just the JVM. A service that decodes attacker data with Base64.getDecoder() on a hot path, and reflects some of the result, has the shape Calif describes. A service that never decodes attacker input is a crash risk at worst. Whether HTTP Basic or JWT parsing in a given product qualifies is an open question in the sources, so I treat it as unknown.

What does not reach the bug

Per the write-ups, these cases never reach the bug.

  • The MIME decoder takes the scalar path.
  • Third-party Base64 libraries that do not call java.util.Base64 do not reach the intrinsic.
  • ARM64 hosts, including Graviton, Ampere and Apple silicon, have no such stub. Equixly ran 794 crafted inputs on Temurin 17.0.21 for arm64 and saw no stray writes.
  • x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI, such as Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake and AMD before Zen 4.

One discrepancy to know about: Equixly requires AVX-512 BW as well as VBMI, while Cyber Security News names only VBMI. Qualys lists four CPU flags (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2) and says all four must appear.

Detection engineering

You cannot detect this with a dependency scan, since the flaw is in the runtime. You detect it at the edge, in the logs and on the host.

Edge rules

The malformed shape is checkable without decoding. Padded Base64 has a length divisible by 4, so a token ending in = or == with a length that is not a multiple of 4 fails on sight. Upwind's heuristic adds a size floor of 32 characters. Endor Labs suggests 65 as the lower bound when you run mixed Java versions. Equixly offers this rule for the Authorization header.

^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$

I have not tested it. Run it in log-only mode against production traffic first, because a wrong rule that blocks real logins is its own outage.

Application logs

Every trigger throws after the write. A burst of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in a request handler, clustered by source address, is the signal Endor Labs recommends. Paced or fragmented Base64 traffic at a high rate from one source fits the same pattern, since heap grooming needs repeated attempts.

Host signals

  • New hs_err_pid*.log files with a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine and a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame
  • Repeated JVM restarts of one service
  • Java processes that spawn a shell or open new outbound connections
  • Oversized or binary-looking responses from endpoints that echo decoded input, which would match the leak stage Calif describes 
# Recent JVM crash logs and their crash lines
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

A crash log alone is not evidence of an attack. JVMs crash for plenty of other reasons. A cluster of crashes that line up with decode-heavy requests from one source is.

Where the sources disagree

I kept a list while reading, and you should keep your own.

  • Oracle's status. Equixly wrote that the fix was still pending. Qualys, Upwind and Cyber Security News say Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17.
  • Severity. Qualys attributes the 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) to the researchers, Equixly to South Korea's NCSC, and nobody has published a vector string. Cyber Security News calls the 8.1 (CVSS 3.1) the OpenJDK advisory score, and Equixly says Oracle has not said which of its November flaws carries that score.
  • Java 8. Qualys and Cyber Security News list Oracle's 8u511b33-perf Performance Pack as affected. The same sources call standard Java 8 not affected.
  • The CVE mapping. Endor Labs marks the mapping from this bug to CVE-2026-114938 as not confirmed, because it could not retrieve the OpenJDK advisory. Check the CVE record yourself before you cite it in a ticket.

The bottom line

The mechanism is narrow: one assembly tail, one hardware feature, one malformed input shape. The reach is wide, because it sits in the runtime that bundled products carry. The honest status on November 17 is a proven crash, a claimed code execution chain and a patch that exists.

If you only do one thing, put a malformed-padding check in front of your Base64 decoding paths and an alert on the exception, then patch on your normal fast track. If a public exploit lands next week, you will already be watching the right signal.

What would you want your WAF to tell you about a bug class it cannot see inside the runtime?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

A bug in the runtime is a bug in everything that runs on it.

Sources: Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys, Cyber Security News, Calif.

title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
description:
arXiv:2611.21878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

title: Anker SOLIX and Shopify: Putting Portable Power Conditions Near the Purchase
description:
Cover: archived official product-page screenshot; capture date not independently confirmed.

A portable-power storefront can attract visitors from multiple markets, while an individual product may be intended for a narrower one. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus US page places a North American power-standard notice near the purchase information. Its FAQ also separates different input and output scenarios. These are observations of the US page on 17 November 2026; stock and content may change.

Make the qualifier part of the choice

Regional information is more useful when customers see it while considering the option, rather than after checkout. Keep the actual region, model and relevant requirements alongside the relevant product description. A country selector alone cannot decide whether equipment is suitable for an installation.

The page's FAQ distinguishes several ways the unit can be connected and which outputs are usable in each case. That is a meaningful content-design lesson: one headline number cannot represent every configuration. A merchant should refer users to the applicable official instructions, not reproduce a simplified table as a substitute for them.

The source article also questions how a fragmented site might affect discovery. That is a hypothesis to investigate with crawl data and analytics; the visible pages do not establish an SEO loss or a percentage of affected users.

Turn six operating cases into a navigable explanation

The FAQ on the reviewed page lists six input conditions and identifies usable and non-usable outputs for each. For example, its fourth condition describes a unit connected to a 120 V wall outlet without a generator and lists the L14-30R output as unavailable under that condition. This is a manufacturer-specific statement for the named model and setup, not a general electrical rule.

As a design exercise, a merchant could move a concise link to relevant setup information closer to the purchase choice, then let readers inspect the full FAQ. A selector would need a maintained, reviewed source for every state and a clear escalation path for unanswered questions. The text-only sample below deliberately does not implement that selector or advise on wiring.

Treat version and fulfillment information as data, not decoration

The page compares F3800 Plus and F3800 and includes firmware-specific information for a solar-input specification. A comparison should bind any value to its model, firmware and source date, rather than promoting the largest number to an unconditional headline. This creates work for content owners: when a firmware revision or manual changes, they need to know which entries to review.

The original analysis asks whether delivery and site architecture create friction. Test those questions directly: can a customer find shipping options for their address, and can they navigate between the appropriate brand pages? A visible domain boundary alone does not prove an SEO penalty, and an absent service option in one view does not establish that no such option exists elsewhere.

A small information module for Shopify

The example uses custom.purchase_guide on a product to reference a metaobject containing region_notes, setup_notes and requirements_notes. The merchant creates and verifies the fields. This simply displays explanatory text. It does not select a market, check electrical conditions or calculate eligibility.

{%- comment -%}
  Information display example; not production-ready.
  Display merchant-verified text only. This does not determine compatibility,
  electrical safety, medical suitability, inventory, delivery, or runtime.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign guide = product.metafields.custom.purchase_guide.value -%}
{%- if guide != blank -%}
  {%- assign region_notes = guide.region_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign setup_notes = guide.setup_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign requirements_notes = guide.requirements_notes.value -%}
  {%- if region_notes != blank or setup_notes != blank or requirements_notes != blank -%}
<section class="purchase-guide" aria-label="Product information">
  <h2>{{ product.title | escape }}</h2>
  {%- if region_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Region</h3>
    <p>{{ region_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if setup_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Setup</h3>
    <p>{{ setup_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if requirements_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Use and installation conditions</h3>
    <p>{{ requirements_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
</section>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Validate the decision flow

Test whether a visitor can find the region notice before selecting a configuration; then verify that each installation statement is connected to an exact model and manufacturer source. If a page changes, remove or revise the associated copy rather than treating an old screenshot as current. For electrical design, consult the manufacturer and a qualified professional.

Source: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus US page.

title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
description:
arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.21975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

title: Docusaurus for Beginners: Turn Markdown Into a Beautiful Documentation Site
description:
Docusaurus is Meta's open-source tool for building documentation websites, and it is the default choice for an enormous number of open-source projects. You write Markdown, and Docusaurus turns it into a fast, searchable, versioned docs site with navigation, dark mode, and a blog — all with almost no configuration.

The reason so many projects use it is simple: docs live next to the code, in Markdown, and the site builds itself. You do not design a docs site; you write docs, and Docusaurus handles the rest.

npx create-docusaurus@latest my-docs classic
cd my-docs
npm start

A doc page is just Markdown with front matter:

---
title: "Getting Started"
sidebar_position: 1
---

# Getting Started

Install the package, then run the command below.


bash
npm install my-package

Docusaurus is a great fit for project documentation, API guides, tutorials, and any site where content is mostly Markdown. Versioning lets you keep docs for v1 and v2 side by side, and the built-in search works without a server.

The limits are narrow. Docusaurus is a docs site generator, not a general app framework — if you need custom interactivity everywhere, you will fight it. Heavy customization of the theme takes real React work. And for a simple blog, a lighter tool may be enough.

But if you maintain an open-source project or a product with real documentation, start with Docusaurus. Your users will thank you, and your docs will finally stay up to date.

title: Your AI agent copied the web page onto iOS. Start from the platform.
description:
Say you already have a web tool at example.com for logging a site visit, and you ask your AI agent for the iOS screen. The reply is the web page, transplanted: a left sidebar, hover-only extra actions, and a floating button copied from another platform. On a phone held in one hand, the sidebar is gone, and so are the actions that lived on hover.

The agent copied a familiar surface onto the wrong platform.

This is a fictional illustration of how Design Decision Method handles platform guidance, not a case study or a measured result. The product details below are invented for the example.

Start from the platform you are actually building

The live docs already put the device in establish context. When choosing a visual system, they say to keep a system the project already has, and when it has none, to select from the platform. For other web work, the fallback is Material 3. Borrow an interaction pattern when it solves the task. Do not copy another organization's branding.

The docs are plain that this is not a ranking: the procedure routes work across Material 3, platform guidelines, and a project's own rules, among other sources, and does not rank those sources or copy their branding.

What the live introduction does not spell out is how that choice changes on iOS versus Android versus the web. That detail lives in the agent procedure.

What the procedure actually selects

If a suitable existing system, brand, or platform direction is already in place, the procedure says to retain and extend it. A new iOS screen is not automatic permission to invent a second identity.

When there is no existing system, the procedure gives conditional rows, not a favourite:

  • For a native Apple interface, use Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and system controls for the supported OS and SDK. Do not mandate the newest material or an OS upgrade.
  • For Android or Compose, use Material 3, and only use Expressive options where the brief or project calls for them and the installed library supports them.
  • For other web or cross-platform work, Material 3 is the fallback, with implementation support checked.

The routing guidance is just as direct for a native mobile screen: use the platform's guidance for navigation and controls. Avoid mimicking one platform's material on another.

A short note for the example.com iOS screen might look like this:

Platform: A native iOS screen, not a wrapped copy of the website.
Keep: The product's existing brand colour roles, if they already exist.
Follow the platform: System navigation and controls for the supported OS and SDK. Every action that existed on the web stays reachable without hover.
Do not copy: The web sidebar, hover-only overflow, or a floating action pattern brought over from another platform.
Do not add: A new visual material the brief did not ask for, or a required OS upgrade.

Choose the visual system still starts with what the project already has. Platform selection is the next question: which conventions this surface should actually follow.

Brand can travel. Chrome often should not.

Choosing the visual system is separate from borrowing an interaction pattern. The procedure's visual-system reference adds a practical split: native platform conventions can coexist with brand typography and imagery when behaviour stays coherent. The site-visit log can keep its colours. It should not keep a sidebar that iOS does not use, or actions that disappear without a pointer.

The same split runs the other way. A later Android screen should not be dressed in iOS chrome to look "consistent." A web page should not assume a gesture that only exists on a phone. Rebuild the pattern in the target stack — meaning, behaviour, focus, and feedback — instead of pasting another platform's markup.

Structure each view already asks the agent to adapt the layout to the device without dropping a capability the task needs. Hover-only actions on an iOS screen fail that test.

Keep it proportional

Name the platform, keep a suitable existing brand, and write down the conventions you will not transplant. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. It does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee a better native screen. What it gives you is a place to catch a copied surface before it ships on the wrong platform.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Read the DDM docs
  • Visual-system adoption checks
  • Repository README and install notes

title: Bridging Instant Payment Switches (ISO 20022 / Real-Time Rails) and Core Banking Mainframes (COBOL COMP-3)
description:
High-throughput domestic instant payment switches — from UPI and IMPS in India to Pix in Brazil, SEPA Instant in Europe, and FedNow in the United States — settle front-end ISO 20022 messages in milliseconds. Yet behind the API gateway, the authoritative system of record in Tier-1 banks frequently remains an IBM Z mainframe executing CICS, Db2, and COBOL COMP-3 packed-decimal batch and online ledgers.

When Global Capability Centers (GCCs) and core-banking modernization squads attempt to strangle or bridge these estates using naive LLM code translation, two silent failure modes appear immediately:

  1. IEEE-754 Binary Float Drift on COMP-3 Nibbles: A COBOL PIC S9(13)V99 COMP-3 field packs two decimal digits per byte with a trailing sign nibble (0xC positive, 0xD negative, 0xF unsigned). Mapping packed decimals into binary floats introduces sub-paisa / sub-cent rounding drift across millions of daily clearing legs.
  2. Dual-Write Timeout Ambiguity Between Instant Switches and CICS: When an ISO 20022 pacs.008 credit transfer times out at 1,500 ms while a CICS LUW (SYNCPOINT) commits downstream, naive retry loops double-post the ledger unless bounded by deterministic idempotency keys and outbox reconciliation.

Reference Blueprint: Deterministic ISO 20022 to COMP-3 Airlock 

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN

def unpack_comp3(buf: bytes, scale: int) -> Decimal:
    digits = "".join(f"{b >> 4}{b & 0x0F}" for b in buf[:-1])
    high, sign = buf[-1] >> 4, buf[-1] & 0x0F  # <1>
    raw = Decimal(f"{digits}{high}").scaleb(-scale)  # <2>
    if sign not in (0x0C, 0x0D, 0x0F):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid COMP-3 sign: {hex(sign)}")
    signed = -raw if sign == 0x0D else raw
    quantum = Decimal(10) ** -scale
    return signed.quantize(quantum, rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)  # <3>
Annotation Architectural Description
<1> Sign-Nibble Isolation: Extracts the high-order final digit and EBCDIC sign nibble (0x0C/0x0D/0x0F) without intermediate float casting.
<2> Exact Base-10 Scaling: Applies Decimal.scaleb(-scale) to honour implied V99 copybook decimal alignment deterministically.
<3> Banker Rounding Invariant: Enforces ROUND_HALF_EVEN quantization prior to ledger comparison or Z3 equivalence verification.

Six Exit Gates for Core-Banking & GCC Modernization Teams

  • SMF-Weighted GraphRAG Lineage: Rank live CICS transaction hot-paths from production SMF Type 110 telemetry before slicing a single COBOL paragraph.
  • OIDC-to-RACF Identity Airlocks: Map cloud OIDC JWTs to RACF IDIDMAP / PassTickets so zero-trust audit trails remain unbroken.
  • Z3 Concolic Equivalence Proofs: Prove mathematically that refactored Java/Go/Rust services produce identical outputs across every boundary condition.
  • 30-Day Shadow Dual-Run Parity: Reconcile full billing-cycle clearing files bit-for-bit before retiring LPAR MSU capacity.

Open-Access Workbench & Worldwide Editions

  • Interactive Browser Lab (COMP-3 Hex Decoder & 4HRA MSU-to-Cloud TCO Estimator): digbijoylabs.github.io/iron-silicon-bridge
  • Open-Access Working Paper (CERN Zenodo DOI): doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24243905
  • Full 259-Page Engineering Handbook (The Iron–Silicon Bridge by Jay Thorne):
    • Canonical Architecture Overview
    • Amazon India Edition (INR) · Worldwide 13-Country Storefronts & 10-Language Hub

title: The path to AI FDE #17: Lists and dictionaries: holding many values
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Yesterday you wrapped code in functions. Today you learn to hold many values at once, instead of one variable per value.

Python has two containers you’ll use every day. A list keeps things in order, like a numbered queue. A dictionary keeps things by name, like a form with labelled boxes. Put them together, a list of dictionaries, and you get the exact shape of most data that AI tools send and receive. By the end you’ll have a small script that sums up a made-up playlist.

Part A · Lists

1. A list keeps items in order, and counts from 0. Make a list with square brackets and commas. Save this as lists.py in your sandbox folder:

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[2])
print(fruits[-1])
print(len(fruits))

Run it with python3 lists.py (Windows: python lists.py):

apple
cherry
cherry
3

Each item has a position number called an index, and Python starts counting at 0. So fruits[0] is the first item and fruits[2] is the third. A negative index counts from the end: fruits[-1] is always the last item. len() tells you how many items there are.

Because counting starts at 0, the last index is one less than the length. Ask for fruits[3] and you get:

IndexError: list index out of range

That “one too far” slip is called an off-by-one error. It’s the most common list mistake there is.

2. Add, count, slice and sort. Lists can grow and change. Try this:

scores = [7, 3, 9]
scores.append(5)
print(scores)
print(len(scores))
print(scores[1:3])
print(scores[:2])
print(sorted(scores))
print(scores)
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)

[7, 3, 9, 5]
4
[3, 9]
[7, 3]
[3, 5, 7, 9]
[7, 3, 9, 5]
[9, 7, 5, 3]

Line by line:

  • .append(5) adds one item to the end.
  • Slicing, scores[1:3], gives a new list from index 1 up to but not including index 3. Leave out the first number and it starts at the beginning, so scores[:2] is the first two items.
  • sorted(scores) gives back a new sorted list and leaves the original alone, which is why the next line still prints [7, 3, 9, 5].
  • .sort() sorts the list itself. reverse=True (a keyword argument, from yesterday) sorts from biggest to smallest.

One trap: .sort() changes the list and returns None. So result = scores.sort() leaves result as None. If you want a sorted copy, use sorted().

Part B · Dictionaries and friends

3. A dictionary stores values under names, called keys. Use curly braces, with a key, a colon, and a value for each entry:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book["title"])
book["pages"] = 320
book["year"] = 2020
print(book)
print(len(book))

Moon Garden
{'title': 'Moon Garden', 'author': 'A. Rao', 'year': 2020, 'pages': 320}
4

You look a value up by its key, not by position: book["title"]. Assigning to a new key, book["pages"] = 320, adds an entry. Assigning to a key that already exists replaces its value, because each key appears only once. And the dictionary remembers the order you added the keys.

Ask for a key that isn’t there and Python stops with:

KeyError: 'rating'

A list is for “the third one”. A dictionary is for “the one called title”.

4. Read safely with .get(), and loop with .items(). When a key might be missing, use .get() instead of square brackets:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book.get("rating"))
print(book.get("rating", "no rating yet"))
print("year" in book)
for key, value in book.items():
    print(key, "->", value)

None
no rating yet
True
title -> Moon Garden
author -> A. Rao
year -> 2019

.get("rating") gives None for a missing key instead of crashing, and .get("rating", "no rating yet") gives the fallback you choose. in checks whether a key exists. .items() hands you each key and value as a pair, so a for loop can unpack both at once.

A simple rule: use square brackets when the key must be there (a crash tells you something is wrong), and .get() when it might be missing.

5. Tuples are fixed, and sets drop duplicates. Two more containers, each with one special trick:

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
tags = {"sci-fi", "classic", "sci-fi"}
print(len(tags))
print("classic" in tags)
print(sorted(set(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])))

3 4
2
True
['a', 'b', 'c']

A tuple uses round brackets. It’s like a list you can’t change after it’s made, which suits values that belong together, such as a point’s x and y. x, y = point unpacks it into two names. Try point[0] = 10 and you get TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.

A set uses curly braces without colons. It keeps each value only once, so the repeated “sci-fi” counts once and len(tags) is 2. That makes sets great for “which different values are there?” Sets have no order, so there’s no tags[0]; use sorted() when you want to show them in order. One gotcha: {} on its own makes an empty dictionary, so an empty set is set().

6. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON. Put dictionaries inside a list and you can hold a whole table of records:

import json

books = [
    {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019},
    {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023},
]
print(books[1]["title"])
for b in books:
    print(b["title"], b["year"])
print(json.dumps(books))

Paper Boats
Moon Garden 2019
Paper Boats 2023
[{"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}, {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023}]

Read books[1]["title"] from left to right: position 1 in the list, then the key “title” in that dictionary. The for loop visits each record in turn.

The last line uses Python’s built-in json module (you’ll learn how import works in issue #20). json.dumps() turns the data into JSON text, the format web APIs, and the AI tools later in this series, send and receive. It looks almost the same as Python. The differences: JSON always uses double quotes, True becomes true, and None becomes null. Tomorrow you’ll read and write JSON files.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create playlist.py, a made-up playlist as a list of dictionaries: 
playlist = [
    {"title": "Morning Run", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 4},
    {"title": "Rainy Bus", "artist": "Paper Cups", "minutes": 6},
    {"title": "Late Tea", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 3},
]

total = 0
titles = []
artists = set()
for song in playlist:
    total = total + song["minutes"]
    titles.append(song["title"])
    artists.add(song["artist"])

print("Songs:", len(playlist))
print("Total minutes:", total)
print(sorted(titles))
print(len(artists), "artists")
print(playlist[0].get("year", "unknown"))
  1. Run python3 playlist.py. You should see: 
Songs: 3
Total minutes: 13
['Late Tea', 'Morning Run', 'Rainy Bus']
2 artists
unknown

“The Toys” appears twice, but the set keeps it once, so there are 2 artists. None of the songs has a "year" key, so .get() gives the fallback.

  1. Change the last line to print(playlist[0]["year"]). Read the last line of the error: KeyError: 'year'. Change it back.
  2. Add print(playlist[3]). You get IndexError: list index out of range: three songs means indexes 0, 1 and 2. Remove the line.
  3. Find the longest song with a loop. Start with longest = playlist[0], then for each song, if song["minutes"] > longest["minutes"], set longest = song. Print longest["title"]. You should get Rainy Bus.

Check your understanding: (a) In ["a", "b", "c"], what’s the index of "c"? (b) What’s the difference between book["rating"] and book.get("rating") when there’s no rating? (c) What does sorted() do that .sort() doesn’t?

Answer: (a) 2, because counting starts at 0 (or -1, counting from the end). (b) Square brackets raise KeyError; .get() returns None (or the fallback you give it). (c) sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone; .sort() changes the list itself and returns None.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Off-by-one: using len(x) as an index. The last item is x[len(x) - 1], or just x[-1].
  • Expecting a slice to include the end: x[1:3] stops before index 3.
  • KeyError from square brackets on a key that might be missing. Use .get(), or check with in first.
  • Writing x = x.sort(), which leaves x as None.
  • Writing {} for an empty set. That’s an empty dictionary; use set().

Takeaway

A list keeps items in order and counts from 0. .append(), len(), slicing and sorted() cover most of what you’ll do with one. A dictionary stores values under unique keys: square brackets when the key must exist, .get() when it might not, .items() to loop. Tuples are fixed and sets keep each value once. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Almost every AI tool I’ll call takes a list of dictionaries in and hands a dictionary back, so reading data[0]["text"] without thinking is a skill worth drilling now. Tomorrow: strings, files and JSON, so that data can come from a file and go back to one.

Over to you: think of something you track, such as books, runs or recipes. Reply with one record as a Python dictionary, like {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}.

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “An Informal Introduction to Python”, Lists (indexing from 0, negative indexes, slicing, len(), .append()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists
  2. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, More on Lists (.append(), .sort(), list methods). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#more-on-lists
  3. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Tuples and Sequences (tuples, unpacking) and Sets (duplicates removed, set() for an empty set). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#tuples-and-sequences
  4. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Dictionaries (keys are unique, insertion order, in, KeyError) and Looping Techniques (.items()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#dictionaries
  5. Python docs, “Built-in Types”, dict.get (returns the default, or None, for a missing key). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict.get
  6. Python HOWTO, “Sorting Techniques” (sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; reverse=True). https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html
  7. Python docs, “json” (json.dumps(), and how Python types map to JSON). https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (IndexError, KeyError, TypeError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up (the books, songs and artists are invented) and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

title: A Polite Reply Is Not Work Done: Five Jobs a Chatbot Leaves Undone
description:
A customer got a polite apology from the chatbot — and nothing else. The refund never moved, the booking never changed. The reply was fast, friendly, and correct in every word. It was also the end of the job, as far as the chatbot was concerned. The customer was still waiting, and the business did not know it, because a reply had been sent and the thread looked finished.

This article was drafted with AI assistance. It is written in plain English for people who run businesses, not for people who build software, and it makes no claim about any particular product. It is about the question this morning's post asked — when did a polite reply leave the real job undone? — and it works through five jobs a chatbot leaves undone, using the tools people already use, so you can check my working and tell me where I got it wrong.

The difference is one word: done

A chatbot's job ends when it has answered. An agent's job ends when the work is done — or when a human has said no. That sounds like a small difference. In a normal day it is the whole difference, because most of the work a small business does after a customer writes in is not answering. It is moving money, moving dates, moving orders, and chasing the people who went quiet.

Here are five jobs, numbered, each one with the tools people already use. Each one starts with a polite reply. Each one ends with the job still waiting.

1. The refund that never moved

A customer writes on WhatsApp: the order arrived damaged, can I have my money back? The chatbot apologises, explains the returns policy, and offers a form. The customer fills in the form. Nothing else happens. The refund is a job in the bank account or in Stripe — someone has to look at the order, check the amount, and press the button. The chatbot cannot press it, and nobody told a person that a form had been filled in.

The tools are ordinary: WhatsApp for the message, Gmail for the form, Stripe or the bank for the money, a spreadsheet for the record. Each one does its part. The gap is between them — the message arrived in one place, the money lives in another, and nobody owns the step in between.

2. The booking that never changed

A customer books for Thursday at 4pm, then writes to move it to Friday at 10am. The chatbot says "Of course, I have noted your request" — and nothing is noted anywhere that matters. Thursday 4pm stays booked in Google Calendar, Friday 10am stays free, and the slot that could have gone to the next person waiting sits empty twice over: once when the customer does not come on Thursday, once when nobody offers the freed time to anyone else.

The booking page, Calendly, does its part well — the customer picks a slot themselves. But a booking page cannot handle the customer who wants something the page does not offer, and it cannot hear a change that arrives as a message. The change lives in the message thread. The diary lives in the calendar. The owner is the only bridge between them, and the owner is busy.

3. The invoice nobody chased

An invoice is fourteen days overdue. The chatbot can write a beautiful reminder — "We hope you are well, a gentle reminder that invoice 1042 is now due" — and it can write it in seconds. But a reminder that is written and never sent chases nobody. The invoice sits in the spreadsheet, the customer's email sits in Gmail, and the polite draft sits in a chat window that closed when the owner got distracted.

This is the job with no deadline on it, so it never gets done. It is also the job that would tell the owner the most: which customers pay late every time, which ones pay when asked once, and which ones have quietly stopped paying at all. A reply is not a chase. A chase ends with money in the account or a decision to stop supplying — and a chatbot does neither.

4. The follow-up that never happened

A customer asked a question on Tuesday, got a polite answer, and never bought anything. Or a customer booked, did not show up, and nobody asked why. The follow-up is the job that has no owner and no deadline, so it waits forever — and it is the job that would tell the business the most about where it leaks.

The tools make it worse, not better. WhatsApp keeps the whole conversation in one thread, which is where the customer actually is — but a message thread is not a list, and a question buried under forty other messages is a question lost. The chatbot answered the question. Nobody answered the silence that followed it.

5. The wrong order that stayed wrong

The wrong item arrived. The customer writes in, the chatbot apologises, explains how returns work, and the customer is told someone will be in touch. Nobody is in touch, because "someone will be in touch" is not a job assigned to anyone. The replacement is never arranged, the courier is never booked, the wrong item sits in the customer's hallway, and the customer tells the next person they know that this business does not fix its mistakes.

The fix is four small jobs — check the order, arrange the replacement, book the collection, tell the customer when it is coming — and each one is a step in a different tool. The chatbot did the first step, the polite one, and the other four waited for a person who never got the message.

What a workforce does with the reply

This is the kind of work an AI workforce is for — not the clever part, the ordinary part. The reply is written, and then the work behind it is done too: the refund is drafted with the amount checked against the order, the booking change is drafted against the free slots, the reminder is drafted with the invoice number and the amount in it, the follow-up is drafted for the customer who went quiet, the replacement is drafted with the courier booked. And nothing is sent before you have seen it. You read the draft, you fix a line if it needs fixing, you say yes — and the customer hears from you the same day, not the next week.

The relief is not that a machine answered faster. It is that the answer stopped being the end of the job. You still decide what counts as a refund, what counts as a change, and what counts as a chase. You still approve every word that leaves. The difference is that the moving, the checking, and the chasing are done before you sit down, so the minutes you have are spent deciding — not digging through messages to find out what was never done.

Which job goes first

The refund goes first, because money is moving and a person is deciding right now. A customer who asked for their money back and heard nothing by the end of the day is a customer who is already telling someone else. The booking change goes next, because a freed slot has a value that drops to nothing the moment the hour passes. The invoice chase follows — it is the easiest of the five to get right, because it is the same message every time, with the facts changed. The replacement and the follow-up come after, because they need a judgement call: which item to send, what to say to the person who never showed.

That order is my answer. It is also a guess, and it is the part I most want corrected.

The short version

A polite reply is not work done. A chatbot's job ends when it has answered; the five jobs behind the answer — the refund, the booking change, the invoice chase, the follow-up, the replacement — still wait for a person. The tools most businesses use each do one part well; the gap is between them, and the owner is the glue. Let a workforce do the work behind the reply, draft it all, and keep the sending in your hands: you pick the order, you approve every word, and the polite apology stops being the last thing the customer ever hears.

So — when did a polite reply leave the real job undone in your business? Which of these five would you hand over first, and which would you never hand over? Tell me in the comments. I would rather be corrected than agreed with.

title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Wheelchair Configuration Classification in Accessible Automated Vehicle Applications
description:
arXiv:2611.21945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Making automated vehicles accessible requires consideration of vulnerable road users, including wheelchair users. To offer a more tailored experience that supports independence for this group, vehicle design needs to accommodate the wide range of wheelchair configurations. However, wheelchairs are individualized, varying in frame geometry, propulsion, and visual appearance. Moreover, occupants or accessories may obscure visual cues. Existing mobility-aid datasets only label the presence of a wheelchair, rather than describing its specific configuration. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (WCID), comprising 467 face-blurred images across 192 capture groups solely for evaluation. Each image is annotated with (i) a two-class label of manual or powered, (ii) a chair subtype, (iii) occupancy, viewpoint, setting, lighting, occlusion, propulsion, and control, with a 273-image validation split and 194-image test split. Three convolutional neural network backbones and a frozen vision-language probe are trained on an external image dataset and evaluated on WCID to measure cross-dataset generalization, while also testing robustness using Gaussian blur. Convolutional models do well on clean images, but performance drops under strong blur, leaving a gap before deployment. Code, split assignments, labels, trained weights, and the face-blurred images is available at: https://github.com/Mi3-Lab/MAID

title: BLUETTI and Shopify: Making Portable Power Compatibility Easier to Understand
description:
Cover: archived official product-page screenshot; capture date not independently confirmed.

On the BLUETTI AC200L US page, a note about connecting a B210 battery names the required cable and links to it. That is an instructive piece of information architecture: a constraint and a relevant next step are placed close together instead of making the shopper reconstruct the relationship from separate product pages.

The same page listed AC200L as discontinued when reviewed on 17 November 2026. This is a historical interface analysis, not an offer or a claim about present availability. The manufacturer's wording must be checked again before any use. No claim is made about the site's private implementation or Shopify plan.

Distinguish a useful pointer from a safety verdict

A cable link answers “where is the item mentioned in this note?” It does not prove that a complete installation is appropriate. A customer still needs the model-specific connection instructions, current regional documentation and any other relevant conditions. Likewise, comparing a single voltage value in JavaScript is not a full electrical safety check: component ratings, current, temperature, connection method and installation context may matter.

The original analysis identified a risk in burying accessory requirements. The concrete observation above is narrower: for this page and the reviewed connection note, the cable was linked. A redesign should preserve and clarify such a link rather than incorrectly claim it is absent.

Explain a system without turning a diagram into a verdict

The AC200L page discusses an RV use case with a TT-30 connection and a separately sold D40 regulator. It also presents bundles with different abbreviated accessory names. For a first-time visitor, an explanation of what each component does, whether it is included and which documents govern its use may be more useful than an unexplained bundle suffix. That is a proposed improvement, not a measured customer-service outcome.

Separating package content from compatibility is especially valuable for expandable systems. A content model might record the base product, optional battery, relevant cable and a source document as separate entries; an editor then confirms the relationship for the specific version and region. The small snippet below shows text fields only, not this complete relationship model.

The source article also discusses purchasing quantities and split shipments. Those claims need current account- and market-specific evidence before they are used as facts. A reusable design principle is still available: show any verified quantity conditions or separate-shipment information next to the offer, with an explicit source and review date. Never fabricate a delivery promise or a discount tier to fill an empty field.

Data model for a store's verified guidance

Keep bundle contents, related accessories and compatibility conditions as distinct fields. Associate each statement with the exact configuration and maintain a documented source and review date in the content workflow. Do not expose a “safe” label merely because a required field is present.

The Liquid sample below renders a product metafield custom.purchase_guide referencing a metaobject with the plain-text fields package_notes, accessory_notes and compatibility_notes. The snippet intentionally renders text only; a production accessory link needs a separately validated resource field and proper link behavior.

{%- comment -%}
  Information display example; not production-ready.
  Display merchant-verified text only. This does not determine compatibility,
  electrical safety, medical suitability, inventory, delivery, or runtime.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign guide = product.metafields.custom.purchase_guide.value -%}
{%- if guide != blank -%}
  {%- assign package_notes = guide.package_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign accessory_notes = guide.accessory_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign compatibility_notes = guide.compatibility_notes.value -%}
  {%- if package_notes != blank or accessory_notes != blank or compatibility_notes != blank -%}
<section class="purchase-guide" aria-label="Product information">
  <h2>{{ product.title | escape }}</h2>
  {%- if package_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>What is included</h3>
    <p>{{ package_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if accessory_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Related accessories</h3>
    <p>{{ accessory_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if compatibility_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Applicable conditions</h3>
    <p>{{ compatibility_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
</section>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Editorial test

Ask a reviewer to identify which cable is required for a named connection, where the source is, and whether the store actually offers it. Then test an unavailable or discontinued option and confirm that the interface does not suggest that it is currently purchasable. This exercise tests understanding of the page, not physical compatibility.

Source: BLUETTI AC200L US page; page content and availability can change.

title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
description:
arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

title: GridDriver: On-Board BEV-Based Language Planning and Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.21924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
