title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
description:
arXiv:2611.21980v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
description:
arXiv:2611.22136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
description:
arXiv:2611.22283v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

title: Beep: an open-source ADE that runs your coding agents across all your machines
description:
Most of us have more than one machine: a laptop, a build server, maybe a box with a GPU. Coding agents mostly ignore that. They run where you opened them, and moving work to another machine means pushing branches, copying files and starting the conversation again.

We built Beep to fix that for ourselves, and we just open-sourced it under MPL-2.0.

What it does

Syncs your projects between machines. Project files stay in step on every machine you link. The sync is compatible with Syncthing, so it works next to a setup you already have.

Connects machines peer to peer. Machines form an encrypted mesh over iroh. They talk to each other directly. A relay only helps when a direct connection is not possible, and traffic stays end to end encrypted.

Runs the agents you already pay for. Claude Code and Codex work with your existing subscriptions, next to OpenCode, Pi and our own harness, Flsh. You pick the machine for each task, and Beep shows your plan usage next to your work.

Gives you terminals everywhere. Persistent terminals on any machine in the mesh, from one window.

There is no account to create and none of our servers sits between your machines.

Why another ADE

The ones we tried had at least one of three problems: they were heavy (300 MB and up), they assumed a single machine, or they added a subscription on top of the ones we already had.

Beep has a Rust core and a Tauri UI. The download is 26 MB on macOS and 31 MB on Windows.

It started as a personal assistant. We dropped that part for now, because the multi-machine control panel was the thing we opened every day.

Try it

You can click through the real UI on sample data, in the browser, with nothing to install: beep.flashmind.com.

To run it for real:

  1. Download Beep and open it.
  2. Choose Set up all. It installs what is missing (Git, Claude Code, Codex) and signs you in.
  3. Use Add a machine to link your second machine.

Current limits

  • Desktop builds: Apple silicon Macs, Windows x64 and Linux x64. No Intel Mac build.
  • The Linux AppImage is 133 MB.
  • The phone app is still in testing. It pairs as an observer: it hosts no projects and runs no code.

Feedback

Issues and PRs are welcome on GitHub. We would most like to hear how the sync and the machine pairing work on your setup.

title: How I Used Aggregation Pipelines to Fix No-Op Updates and Keep Error Clarity in Axion
description:
Hey friends! 👋🏻

I wanted to share a cool backend fix I implemented while adding the comments editing feature to my microforum, Axion. It's about handling no-op updates cleanly without breaking error handling.

In the past, some of my editing routes would update the content unconditionally. Even if the old and new content were exactly the same, the database would still run the update, hit the disk, and change the timestamps. It was inefficient honestly.

And letting MongoDB update the timestamps on identical content breaks data integrity. It lies to you—saying the last update happened at X time when nothing actually changed. Plus, it would return modifiedCount === 1 just because a timestamp field got changed, which ruins the tracking of actual content changes.

When adding comment updates, I wanted to avoid this behavior entirely.

The Naive Approach. I could have simply used { content: { $ne: content } }. But this creates a blindspot in my logic. If the database returns 0 matched documents, you can't differentiate between two completely different scenarios:

  1. Does the document actually exist and belong to the logged-in user?
  2. Did the query just fail because the new content matches the old content?

To give a proper response to the client, I needed to know the difference.

My Solution: Aggregation Pipeline Updates. Instead of a basic update, I relied on an aggregation pipeline inside the update operation. And that's my logic:

  1. It first finds a document created by the current logged-in user where the _id matches the given comment ID.
  2. If found, it updates the content and timestamps only if the old content differs from the new content.
  3. Finally, it checks matchedCount === 0. If it's 0, we know that the document wasn't found (or the user doesn't own it) and can throw a proper 404 error here.

Oh, yeah, and to end this cleanly, I included a changed field in the HTTP response, setting its value to modifiedCount !== 0. This tells the frontend exactly whether an actual database write occurred or if it was a harmless no-op.

Handling the "(Edited)" Badge Properly. While doing this, I also needed a way for the frontend to show an "(Edited)" badge on updated comment cards.

I didn't want to rely on a single boolean like isEdited: true because it doesn't provide the metadata of when the update happened if I ever need it. I also rejected the idea of just comparing createdAt against updatedAt. Like, what if a background script or admin tool ever modifies a document for maintenance? updatedAt changes, and the system would falsely tell users the comment was edited when it wasn't.

So, I came up with a cleaner approach: adding a third field called editedAt. For non-edited comments, it stays null. The moment a real edit happens, it stores the exact timestamp of that edit. Maybe I don't show the edit timestamp to users right now, but if I ever want to in the future, the data will be there. It's a matter of handling "what if" scenarios cleanly from day one.

At the end of the day, losing precise error handling isn't worth saving a few lines of code.

Thanks for hanging out and reading through! How do you handle these annoying no-op updates and edit tracking in your backend? Let's talk in the comments below. See you next time! 🌟

title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
description:
arXiv:2611.22580v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yor\`ub\'a language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yor\`ub\'a. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yor\`ub\'a is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yor\`ub\'a.

title: crdt-sync: محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust، مع CRDT و sqlite و websocket
description:
شخصان يعدّلان الملاحظة نفسها. أحدهما في قطار بلا تغطية، والآخر على مكتبه. وكلاهما يواصل الكتابة. حين يخرج القطار من النفق، كيف يجب أن تكون الملاحظة؟

الجواب الكلاسيكي أن يكون الخادم هو الحَكَم: كل تعديل يذهب إليه، وهو يقرر الترتيب، والعميل الذي بلا اتصال ينتظر. تطبيقات local-first (المحلي أولًا) تقلب هذا. كل جهاز يحمل نسخة كاملة، والتعديلات تُطبَّق فورًا ودون اتصال، والأجهزة تتبادل التغييرات كلما استطاعت الوصول إلى بعضها. والشرط الصعب: بعد تبادل كل شيء، يجب أن تتطابق كل النسخ، مهما كان الترتيب الذي وصلت به التغييرات.

هياكل البيانات التي تضمن ذلك تسمّى CRDT، أي conflict-free replicated data types. و Automerge و Yjs هما المكتبتان المعروفتان المبنيتان عليها. وهما مكتبتان ناضجتان وفيهما تحسينات كثيرة، فقراءتهما طويلة إن كان هدفك أن تفهم كيف تعمل الفكرة.

crdt-sync محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust. المستندات أشجار من CRDT، وراءها سجل عمليات (operation log) و vector clocks. النسخ (replicas) تعدّل دون اتصال، وتخزّن العمليات في sqlite، وتتزامن عبر خادم websocket مبني بـ axum ببروتوكول من رسالتين. ويسمّي الـ README جمهورَيه: المطورون الذين يريدون فهم كيف تعمل تطبيقات local-first من الداخل، ومن يحتاج نقطة انطلاق مدمجة ومقروءة لمزامنة مستندات صغيرة بين أجهزة وخادم يتحكم فيه.

ماذا يقدّم

أربعة أنواع CRDT. المستند شجرة مبنية من هذه:

  • LwwRegister، سجل من نوع last-writer-wins: الختم الأعلى (Lamport، ثم replica) هو الذي يفوز.
  • LwwMap، خريطة فيها سجل LWW لكل مفتاح. الحذف كتابة لـ "لا شيء"، والقيمة قد تكون قيمة بسيطة أو كائنًا متداخلًا.
  • OrSet، مجموعة observed-remove تفوز فيها الإضافة (add-wins): كل إضافة تنشئ وسمًا (tag) فريدًا، والحذف يزيل فقط الوسوم التي رآها.
  • Rga، للنص. كل محرف يُدرج بعد محرف مرجعي، والإدراجات المتزامنة في الموضع نفسه تُرتَّب حسب الختم، والحذف يترك شواهد (tombstones).

سجل العمليات. كل تعديل هو Op له معرّف (replica, seq)، حيث seq يعدّ 1 و2 و3 وهكذا لكل نسخة، ومعه ختم Lamport، والكائن المستهدف، والفعل. ولأن الأرقام التسلسلية بلا ثغرات، فإن vector clock من الشكل replica → highest seq يقول بالضبط أي العمليات تملكها نسخة ما. والسؤال "هل رأيت العملية X" مقارنة واحدة.

التسليم بأي ترتيب. الدالة Doc::apply_remote تقبل العمليات بأي ترتيب وأي عدد من المرات. المعروفة تُهمل. والباقية تنتظر في قائمة حتى تُدمج تبعياتها: العملية السابقة من النسخة نفسها، والكائن المستهدف، والمحرف الذي يأتي الإدراج بعده، والوسوم التي رآها حذف من المجموعة.

بروتوكول مزامنة من رسالتين. الرسالة StateVector(clock) يُجاب عنها بـ Ops(missing)، والرسالة Ops(ops) تُدمج. الطرفان يرسلان الـ state vector عند الاتصال، فجولة واحدة في كل اتجاه تكفي ليصير الاثنان محدَّثين. ثم ينقل الخادم العمليات المدمجة حديثًا إلى كل عميل آخر على المستند نفسه.

ترميز مدمج. أعداد LEB128 varint، وجدول نسخ لكل دفعة حتى يأخذ معرّف العملية بايتًا أو اثنين، وأرقام تسلسلية وأختام Lamport مرمَّزة بالفرق (delta)، واختصارات من بايت واحد لحالتي "الكائن نفسه كالعملية السابقة" و"إدراج بعد العملية السابقة". ويذكر الـ README أن كتابة 1000 محرف تُرمَّز في أقل من 8 KB. والـ decoder يرفض المدخل المبتور أو العدائي دون panic ودون حجز ذاكرة مفرط.

خادم وتخزين. خادم axum يقدّم GET /sync/{doc} كـ websocket بإطارات ثنائية (binary frames)، وGET /docs وGET /docs/{doc} بصيغة JSON. يحتفظ بـ Doc واحد في الذاكرة لكل مستند مفتوح، يُحمَّل من sqlite عند أول استعمال، ويضيف العمليات المدمجة إلى sqlite قبل نقلها. والتخزين جدول واحد، ops(doc, replica, seq, body)، يُكتب بـ INSERT OR IGNORE فيكون الحفظ idempotent.

طريقة الاستعمال

ثبّت الملفين التنفيذيين crdt-server وcrdt-cli من GitHub بواسطة Cargo، أو أضِف المكتبة إلى مشروعك:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

البداية السريعة في الـ README تشغّل خادمًا وعميلين، لكل عميل قاعدة بياناته المحلية، من نسخة محلية للمستودع:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice و Bob كلاهما يكتب status وهو "غير متصل"، و Bob يضيف وسمًا. وبعد المزامنة، يحمل الاثنان المستند نفسه:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

السجل احتفظ بواحدة من الكتابتين المتزامنتين، وهي نفسها على كل نسخة. والمجموعة احتفظت بالوسمين معًا.

أوامر الـ CLI هي: show، info، set KEY VALUE، del KEY، insert KEY INDEX TEXT، erase KEY INDEX COUNT، add KEY VALUE، remove KEY VALUE، sync، watch.

وكمكتبة:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

ما يجب معرفته

قسم الحدود في الـ README طويل وصريح. اقرأه قبل أن تبني على المشروع:

  • لا مصادقة ولا صلاحيات في الخادم. كل من يستطيع الوصول إليه يستطيع قراءة كل مستند والكتابة فيه. شغّله على localhost أو خلف proxy يقوم بالمصادقة.
  • السجلات تكبر بلا نهاية. لا ضغط (compaction)، ولا snapshots، ولا تنظيف للشواهد. والمستند يُعاد بناؤه بإعادة تشغيل سجله كاملًا.
  • النص للملاحظات لا للكتب. البحث في RGA مسح خطي، وهناك عملية لكل محرف.
  • مجموعة صغيرة من الأنواع. لا نص منسَّق، ولا قوائم كائنات، ولا عدّادات، ولا نقل. والإنشاء المتزامن لكائن متداخل تحت المفتاح نفسه يُبقي كائنًا واحدًا (LWW)، والتعديلات على الآخر تُخفى.
  • تحقق محدود من الأطراف. العمليات القادمة من طرف معطوب، والتي تستهدف كائنًا غير موجود أو من نوع خاطئ، تُسجَّل وتُتجاهل. ولا يوجد تحقق ممن يحق له الكتابة بأي replica id.
  • الأمر watch يطبع التغييرات البعيدة فقط. والتعديلات تتم بتشغيلات منفصلة للـ CLI.

ما تم اختباره. الأمر cargo test يشغّل 17 اختبار وحدة، و6 خصائص proptest، و4 اختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية (end-to-end). الخاصية الأساسية هي التقارب (convergence): ثلاث نسخ تقوم بإدراجات وحذوف عشوائية في النص، وإضافات وحذوف في المجموعة، وكتابات في السجل، وتعديلات وحذوف في الخريطة، بينما تُسلَّم مجموعات جزئية عشوائية من سجلات بعضها مخلوطة ومكررة. وفي النهاية يستلم الجميع كل شيء بترتيب مبعثر، مرتين. ويجب ألا تبقى عند أي نسخة عمليات معلّقة، وأن تتساوى الساعات والـ JSON، على 300 حالة. وخصائص أخرى تتحقق من تقارب البروتوكول بمزامنات ثنائية في حلقة، ومن أن النص في نسخة واحدة يطابق نموذج Vec<char>، ومن أن البايتات العشوائية والرسائل المقلوبة بعض بتاتها لا تسبب panic في الـ decoder.

والاختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية تغطي دمج تعديلات عميلين دون اتصال، وخادمًا أُعيد تشغيله يقدّم المستند نفسه من sqlite، وعميلًا متصلًا يستلم التعديلات المنقولة، وعمليتَي crdt-cli تعدّلان دون اتصال ثم تتقاربان. وكفحص إضافي، يذكر الـ README أن كسر قاعدة الترجيح في LWW أو ترتيب الإخوة في RGA يجعل خصائص التقارب تفشل بعد حالات قليلة.

لماذا بنيته

فكرة local-first سهلة القول وصعبة التصديق إلى أن ترى كل قطعة: كيف تُعرَّف العملية، ولماذا يكفي vector clock لمعرفة ما ينقص الطرف الآخر، وماذا يعني "انتظر التبعيات" في الكود، وكيف يُدمج نص يكتب فيه شخصان في الموضع نفسه. المكتبات الناضجة تجيب عن كل هذا، لكن وسط كثير من التحسينات.

أردت المسار كله في كود صغير يُقرأ من أوله إلى آخره: الـ CRDT، والسجل، والترميز الثنائي، والتخزين، والبروتوكول، والخادم. وأردت أن يُتحقق من ادّعاء التقارب باختبارات خصائص لا ببضعة أمثلة مختارة باليد، لأن الأخطاء في هذا النوع من الكود تسكن في التداخلات التي لا تخطر على بال أحد.

الكود

الكود والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. الرخصة MIT. اعتبره نقطة انطلاق مقروءة للمستندات الصغيرة، مع الحدود المذكورة أعلاه.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Same Row Count, Missing Records: 4 Ways a Count Check Can Fool You
description:
A common check after a batch job is to compare two numbers: how many records went in, and how many came out. If they match, the job is marked healthy.

That check is useful as an alarm. But it is not proof. Two lists can have the same length and still hold different records.

A tiny made-up example

The run was supposed to deliver four orders:

  • Expected: A, B, C, D
  • Found in the destination: A, A, C, E

Count check: 4 expected, 4 found. Looks fine.

Compare by ID instead:

  • missing: B, D
  • duplicate: A (written twice)
  • unexpected: E (not part of this run)

Three problems, and the count hid all of them.

4 ways the count can match while records are missing

1. A retry wrote duplicates that cancel out a drop

One batch failed halfway and was retried. The retry wrote some rows a second time, while a different set of rows never made it. The extra copies fill the gap in the total.

2. Rows from outside the run filled in

Late rows from the previous window, or rows near a time zone boundary, landed in this run's scope. They add to the count, so real gaps in this run stay invisible.

3. The key changed shape on the way

The record arrived, but its ID did not survive intact: 00123 became 123, a trailing space was added, or letters changed case. The count is right, but a lookup for 00123 finds nothing. To anyone searching by ID, the record is missing.

4. A filter removed rows while another step added some

One step skipped records it should have kept. Another step added test rows, or brought back rows that had been deleted. Minus a few, plus a few, same total.

How to check by ID

First, build the list of IDs that this run was expected to deliver, from that run's input or a saved copy. Do not use today's version of the source.

Then check three lists separately. A plain SQL sketch (function names vary slightly between databases):

-- missing: expected, but not in the destination
SELECT e.id
FROM expected_ids e
LEFT JOIN destination d ON d.id = e.id
WHERE d.id IS NULL;

-- unexpected: in the destination, but not expected
SELECT d.id
FROM destination d
LEFT JOIN expected_ids e ON e.id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;

-- duplicates: the same ID written more than once
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM destination
GROUP BY id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Before trusting the result, look at the shape of the keys on both sides:

-- IDs with extra spaces
SELECT id FROM destination WHERE id <> TRIM(id);

-- how many IDs of each length (run on both sides and compare)
SELECT LENGTH(id) AS id_length, COUNT(*) AS ids
FROM destination
GROUP BY LENGTH(id);

If one side has IDs of length 5 and the other has length 3, leading zeros were probably dropped somewhere. Decide on one rule and write it down. Do not quietly clean the keys on one side only, or you can hide the very problem you are looking for.

If the destination has a known delay before new rows are visible, wait for it before you call anything missing.

Then follow one missing ID

Pick one missing ID and look for it at every stage. Another made-up example, for order B:

Stage Result Evidence
Input found in the saved input for this run
Filter found not excluded
Batch 2, first try absent batch failed with a timeout
Batch 2, retry absent retry log lists batch 3's rows, not batch 2's
Destination absent not in the export

First known gap: the retry picked up the wrong batch. That also explains the duplicates. If you have no evidence for a stage, write "unknown" instead of guessing.

So, are counts useless?

No. A count is a cheap first alarm, and a mismatch is always worth a look. Just do not stop there: a matching count means "nothing obviously broke," not "everything arrived."

Have you seen a count check pass while records were missing? I would like to hear what caused it.

This post was drafted with AI and checked by a human before publishing.

title: JSONB at Scale: Taming PostgreSQL TOAST Churn and WAL Bloat on High-Write Workloads
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

JSONB is one of PostgreSQL's most useful data types for semi-structured data, but it also hides one of the database's most expensive internal mechanisms. Large documents are moved out of the main heap into TOAST storage, compressed along the way, and—when the row changes—rewritten. On write-heavy systems, that combination can produce surprising WAL amplification, bloated tables, and storage amplification long after the original data has been compacted.

The core problem is not JSONB itself. It is that many workloads treat JSONB like an opaque scalar column while PostgreSQL treats it like a variable-length object with expensive update semantics. Understanding that boundary is the difference between a healthy high-write system and one that spends its I/O budget rewriting the same payload over and over.

This guide walks through the internals of TOAST, explains where WAL amplification comes from, and provides a concrete engineering path from diagnosis to remediation.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The mental model: JSONB is not one column
  • 2. How PostgreSQL stores large JSONB values
  • 3. Why high-write workloads create TOAST churn
  • 4. Measuring the problem
  • 5. The remediation toolkit
  • 6. Reference implementation: a batched JSONB writer
  • 7. Production patterns and edge cases
  • 8. Frequently Asked Questions

1. The mental model: JSONB is not one column

A common source of confusion is the idea that a jsonb column occupies a single, self-contained slot in a row. That is true only for small values. PostgreSQL uses a fixed-width pointer in the row itself and stores the actual payload elsewhere once the value exceeds the threshold for in-row storage.

For a row like this:

CREATE TABLE events (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   integer NOT NULL,
    payload     jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The payload column is not necessarily inline. The storage decision depends on the tuple size, the available space in the page, and the value's compressibility. A small JSONB document may stay in the heap tuple. A large document is compressed and, if needed, pushed into TOAST storage.

Three distinct storage paths exist:

  1. Inline storage — the JSONB value fits in the main heap tuple and is stored directly on the page.
  2. Compressed inline storage — the value is compressed but still fits in the tuple.
  3. External TOAST storage — the value is compressed and then stored out-of-line in a TOAST table, with only a small pointer remaining in the heap tuple.

This distinction matters because the cost profile of each path is different. Inline writes are cheap. Compressed inline writes require CPU. External TOAST writes add a second relation, additional index-like bookkeeping, and an extra round of WAL.

The key insight

When you UPDATE a row and change only a small field, PostgreSQL does not patch the JSONB value in place. PostgreSQL has no fine-grained, in-place JSONB mutation. It constructs a new value and writes a new tuple version.

If that new value is externally stored, the old TOAST chunk may be reused only if the storage code determines it can be shared. In practice, for changed or rewritten values, you get a fresh TOAST write.

The result is a cost model that looks roughly like this:

row update cost ≈ heap tuple write
              + TOAST value write (if external)
              + compression CPU
              + WAL for both heap and TOAST
              + dead tuple cleanup
              + index maintenance

On a workload that updates a small subset of fields in a large JSONB document thousands of times per second, the TOAST write and its WAL can dominate the actual business logic.

2. How PostgreSQL stores large JSONB values

TOAST—the acronym stands for The On-disk Self-Optimizing Table—is PostgreSQL's mechanism for handling variable-length attributes larger than a page-sized tuple.

The TOAST table

When a table contains a TOASTable column, PostgreSQL creates a companion relation with a name like pg_toast_16384. This table has the same structure as the original table but with a special trigger that moves large values out of line.

The TOAST table stores four columns per TOASTable column:

chunk_id    oid    -- identifier linking chunks to a value
chunk_seq   int4   -- ordering of the chunk
chunk_data  bytea  -- the actual compressed bytes

Values larger than TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD (around 2 KB) are split into chunks of roughly TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE (around 2 KB as well, adjusted for page overhead). Each chunk is a separate row in the TOAST table.

Compression: PGLZ and LZ4

Before storage, PostgreSQL attempts to compress the value using PGLZ, the built-in algorithm. Since PostgreSQL 14, you can enable LZ4 compression, which is significantly faster while producing somewhat larger output than PGLZ for many data shapes.

You can control this at the column level:

ALTER TABLE events
    ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

The available modes are:

Storage mode Behavior When to use it
PLAIN Never compress or move out of line; errors if the row is too large Very large values you want stored verbatim and never compressed
EXTENDED Compress first, move out of line only if still too large Default; good general-purpose choice
EXTERNAL Move out of line first, compress only if that saves space Write-heavy workloads where compression CPU is the bottleneck
MAIN Always keep inline, compress if needed Small, bounded values

The default for jsonb is EXTENDED, and that default is often exactly wrong for high-write workloads.

Why WAL amplification happens

Every physical change is logged in the Write-Ahead Log. When you update a row with an externally stored JSONB value, the WAL contains:

  1. The new heap tuple, including the TOAST pointer.
  2. The new TOAST chunk rows.
  3. WAL for the index entries that reference the row.

The TOAST portion can be substantially larger than the logical change you made. If your JSONB document is 100 KB and you update a single status field, the logical delta is a few bytes. The physical write is 100 KB, plus WAL for it.

This is not a bug. It is the natural consequence of PostgreSQL's MVCC design combined with copy-on-write semantics for variable-length values. The engineering response is to reduce the number of bytes written per logical operation, or to reduce the frequency of those operations.

3. Why high-write workloads create TOAST churn

Let's characterize the workload patterns that cause the most damage.

Pattern A: read-modify-write of large documents 

UPDATE events
SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{status}', '"processed"'::jsonb)
WHERE id = $1;

This rewrites the entire document. If the document is 50 KB and externally stored, each update writes 50 KB of TOAST data and generates corresponding WAL.

Pattern B: upsert loops with high conflict rates

When many workers contend on the same key, PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE path repeatedly rewrites the row, and each rewrite regenerates the TOAST value.

Pattern C: telemetry and event ingestion with mutable payloads

Event tables often accumulate a JSONB payload that grows over time as processing stages add metadata. Each stage appends a key, rewriting the whole document.

Pattern D: unbounded JSONB growth

If a JSONB column accumulates history, counters, or nested arrays without bounds, the value size grows monotonically. The write cost per operation grows with it, even though the operation itself is constant-size.

Pattern E: aggressive autovacuum settings misapplied to TOAST

Vacuuming the parent table does not automatically keep TOAST tables in good shape in every configuration. You need to understand how TOAST cleanup interacts with autovacuum and toast.autovacuum_* settings.

4. Measuring the problem

Before changing anything, establish a baseline. This section covers the queries and tools that will tell you whether TOAST churn is actually your bottleneck.

Step 1: Find tables with large average row sizes 

SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) AS total_size,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid))         AS heap_size,
    pg_size_pretty(
        pg_total_relation_size(relid) - pg_relation_size(relid)
    )                                               AS toast_and_index_size,
    round(avg_row_len, 1)                           AS avg_row_bytes
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC
LIMIT 20;

A large gap between heap_size and total_size is a strong signal that TOAST and indexes are consuming significant space.

Step 2: Measure TOAST usage per table

PostgreSQL exposes TOAST statistics through pg_class and pg_stat_user_tables:

SELECT
    c.relname                                    AS table_name,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(c.reltoastrelid)) AS toast_size,
    t.n_live_tup,
    t.n_dead_tup,
    t.n_mod_since_analyze
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_stat_user_tables t ON t.relid = c.oid
WHERE c.reltoastrelid <> 0
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(c.reltoastrelid) DESC;

Step 3: Inspect actual storage modes

The pg_column_size function returns the number of bytes used to store a value, including any TOAST compression:

SELECT
    id,
    pg_column_size(payload)          AS stored_bytes,
    octet_length(payload::text)      AS raw_text_bytes,
    pg_column_size(payload) * 1.0
      / NULLIF(octet_length(payload::text), 0) AS compression_ratio
FROM events
ORDER BY stored_bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

A ratio near 1.0 means the data is not compressing well. A ratio around 0.3 means PGLZ is doing a good job. Values in the tens of kilobytes are candidates for TOAST.

Step 4: Look at WAL generation

PostgreSQL 15+ exposes per-table WAL statistics:

SELECT
    wal_records,
    wal_bytes,
    wal_fpi,
    round(wal_bytes / 1024.0 / 1024.0, 2) AS wal_mb,
    round(wal_bytes::numeric / NULLIF(n_tup_ins + n_tup_upd + n_tup_del, 0), 0)
        AS avg_wal_bytes_per_dml
FROM pg_stat_wal
CROSS JOIN pg_stat_database d
WHERE d.datname = current_database();

More practically, use pg_stat_wal (cluster-wide) and pg_stat_database for xact_commit rates, then sample pg_current_wal_lsn() over a fixed interval:

-- Run twice, one minute apart, and subtract.
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

The difference tells you the WAL bytes per second your cluster is generating.

Step 5: Profile with pg_stat_statements

Find the statements generating the most WAL. pg_stat_statements tracks wal_bytes when the track_wal_io_timing and related options are enabled in PostgreSQL 15+:

SELECT
    query,
    calls,
    total_exec_time,
    wal_bytes,
    round(wal_bytes::numeric / NULLIF(calls, 0)) AS avg_wal_per_call
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE wal_bytes > 0
ORDER BY wal_bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

This is usually where you find the UPDATE ... jsonb_set(...) pattern.

Step 6: Inspect the TOAST table directly 

SELECT
    chunk_id,
    count(*)          AS chunks,
    sum(length(chunk_data)) AS total_bytes,
    avg(length(chunk_data)) AS avg_chunk_bytes
FROM pg_toast.pg_toast_16384
GROUP BY chunk_id
ORDER BY total_bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;

Replace 16384 with the actual OID of your table's TOAST relation, found via:

SELECT c.reltoastrelid::regclass
FROM pg_class c
WHERE c.relname = 'events';

5. The remediation toolkit

The goal is to reduce bytes written per logical operation. There are several complementary levers, ordered by how much they typically help.

Lever 1: Set STORAGE EXTERNAL on hot JSONB columns

This is the single highest-leverage change for CPU-bound high-write workloads. It skips compression for values that go out of line, trading storage for CPU and write throughput.

ALTER TABLE events
    ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

-- Force a rewrite so the new storage mode applies to existing rows.
VACUUM FULL events;

Important caveats:

  • VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a live system, plan a maintenance window or use pg_repack.
  • The change only affects newly written or rewritten tuples. Existing tuples keep their old layout until they are rewritten.
  • EXTERNAL means no compression at all for out-of-line values. If your JSON compresses 5:1, your TOAST table will grow substantially. Verify the tradeoff on real data.
  • If the value fits inline, it is still stored inline, uncompressed.

Measure the effect:

-- Before and after: compare WAL generation rate and CPU usage.
SELECT
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pg_toast.pg_toast_16384')) AS toast_size,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE pg_column_size(payload) > 2000) AS external_values;

Lever 2: Enable LZ4 compression

If you want compression but less CPU, LZ4 is a strong option:

ALTER SYSTEM SET lz4 TO on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Then force a rewrite of affected rows:

VACUUM FULL events;

LZ4 typically compresses 2–3x faster than PGLZ with slightly worse ratios. For JSON payloads with many repeated keys, the ratio difference is usually modest.

Lever 3: Reduce the frequency of large rewrites

The best fix is often architectural: stop rewriting the whole document for small changes.

Normalize hot fields into real columns. If status, tenant_id, or retry_count are queried or updated frequently, move them out of JSONB:

ALTER TABLE events
    ADD COLUMN status text,
    ADD COLUMN retry_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

UPDATE events
SET status = payload ->> 'status',
    retry_count = COALESCE((payload ->> 'retry_count')::integer, 0);

Now updates touch only the scalar column:

UPDATE events
SET status = 'processed'
WHERE id = $1;

This eliminates the TOAST rewrite entirely for that field.

Split cold and hot data. Keep a small, frequently-updated working set in one table and append large, rarely-modified payloads to another:

CREATE TABLE event_payloads (
    event_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES events(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    payload    jsonb NOT NULL
);

The events table stays small and cheap to update; the payload table is written once and read rarely.

Use append-only semantics. For event streams, don't update at all:

INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, now());

A consumer maintains derived state. This eliminates TOAST churn by construction.

Lever 4: Batch writes

If you must write many rows, batch them. PostgreSQL's WAL cost per row drops significantly when many tuples are written in one statement, because full-page images and page-header overhead are amortized.

INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
SELECT *
FROM jsonb_to_recordset($1::jsonb)
    AS x(tenant_id integer, payload jsonb, created_at timestamptz);

For high-throughput ingestion, COPY is usually faster still:

psql -d appdb -c "\copy events (tenant_id, payload, created_at) FROM '/data/events.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv)"

Lever 5: Tune autovacuum for TOAST tables

TOAST tables have their own autovacuum settings:

ALTER TABLE pg_toast.pg_toast_16384 SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
    autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000
);

More aggressive vacuuming on TOAST tables removes dead chunks faster, limiting bloat. The tradeoff is more I/O spent on vacuum.

You can also set cluster-wide defaults:

ALTER SYSTEM SET toast.autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02;
ALTER SYSTEM SET toast.autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Lever 6: Monitor WAL generation continuously

Track WAL rate and TOAST size as first-class metrics:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW monitor_toast_wal AS
SELECT
    now()                                          AS sampled_at,
    pg_current_wal_lsn()                           AS current_lsn,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('events')) AS events_total_size,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pg_toast.pg_toast_16384')) AS toast_size,
    (SELECT n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events') AS live_tuples;

Sample it on a schedule and alert on regressions:

SELECT
    max(wal_bytes) - min(wal_bytes) AS wal_generated,
    max(toast_size) - min(toast_size) AS toast_growth
FROM monitor_toast_wal
WHERE sampled_at > now() - interval '1 hour';

6. Reference implementation: a batched JSONB writer

Here is a complete, runnable example that demonstrates the core techniques working together. It assumes PostgreSQL 15 or later.

Schema 

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS event_batches;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS events;

CREATE TABLE events (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   integer NOT NULL,
    status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    payload     jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Hot path: uncompressed out-of-line storage.
ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

-- Cold path: append-only payloads, written once.
CREATE TABLE event_payload_archive (
    event_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    payload    jsonb NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX events_tenant_created_idx
    ON events (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

Batch insert function 

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ingest_event_batch(
    p_batch jsonb
)
RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_inserted bigint;
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
    SELECT
        (x ->> 'tenant_id')::integer,
        x -> 'payload',
        COALESCE((x ->> 'created_at')::timestamptz, now())
    FROM jsonb_array_elements(p_batch) AS x;

    GET DIAGNOSTICS v_inserted = ROW_COUNT;

    -- Archive the same payload for cold storage without a second rewrite.
    INSERT INTO event_payload_archive (event_id, payload)
    SELECT e.id, e.payload
    FROM events e
    WHERE e.tenant_id = (p_batch -> 0 ->> 'tenant_id')::integer
      AND e.created_at >= now() - interval '1 second'
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

    RETURN v_inserted;
END;
$$;

In production, the archive insert should use a more precise correlation key (for example, a batch UUID written into every row) rather than the time window above. The time-window version here is intentionally simple and illustrative.

Test it 

SELECT ingest_event_batch(
    jsonb_build_array(
        jsonb_build_object(
            'tenant_id', 42,
            'payload', jsonb_build_object(
                'event_type', 'order.created',
                'order_id', 1001,
                'items', jsonb_build_array(
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'ABC-123', 'qty', 2),
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'XYZ-789', 'qty', 1)
                ),
                'metadata', repeat('x', 5000)
            ),
            'created_at', now()
        ),
        jsonb_build_object(
            'tenant_id', 42,
            'payload', jsonb_build_object(
                'event_type', 'order.created',
                'order_id', 1002,
                'items', jsonb_build_array(
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'DEF-456', 'qty', 5)
                ),
                'metadata', repeat('y', 5000)
            ),
            'created_at', now()
        )
    )
);

Verify the storage layout 

SELECT
    id,
    tenant_id,
    pg_column_size(payload) AS stored_bytes,
    octet_length(payload::text) AS raw_bytes
FROM events
ORDER BY id;

-- Confirm the TOAST relation is being used.
SELECT
    chunk_id,
    count(*) AS chunks,
    sum(length(chunk_data)) AS bytes
FROM pg_toast.pg_toast_16384
GROUP BY chunk_id;

Efficient status update

Because status is now a real column, updating it does not rewrite the payload:

UPDATE events
SET status = 'processed'
WHERE id = 1;

Compare the WAL generated by this statement against an equivalent jsonb_set update on the payload itself. The difference is dramatic once the payload is large.

7. Production patterns and edge cases

The jsonb_set rewrite cost in detail 

UPDATE events
SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{status}', '"processed"'::jsonb)
WHERE id = 1;

This expression must:

  1. Read and detoast the existing JSONB value.
  2. Parse it into the binary JSONB representation.
  3. Locate the target path.
  4. Construct a new binary representation.
  5. Recompress it.
  6. Write a new TOAST value and log it to WAL.

The cost is proportional to document size, not to the size of the change.

Bounded JSONB growth

If a JSONB column accumulates unbounded data, cap it. PostgreSQL 15+ offers a neat trick using generated columns:

ALTER TABLE events
    ADD COLUMN payload_size integer
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (pg_column_size(payload)) STORED;

CREATE INDEX events_payload_size_idx ON events (payload_size)
    WHERE payload_size > 100000;

Use this index to find outliers and alert on them, or to drive a cleanup job that moves oversized payloads to cold storage.

Partitioning for retention

Time-based partitioning combined with DROP TABLE gives O(1) retention without vacuum pressure:

CREATE TABLE events_2024_01 PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

Dropping an old partition removes its TOAST data immediately, without the dead-tuple cleanup cost of a mass DELETE.

When JSONB is genuinely the wrong choice

If you find yourself constantly extracting the same fields, querying JSONB paths in hot paths, or rewriting documents to update a single attribute, the data is relational. Normalize it.

JSONB shines when the shape is genuinely variable, reads are more common than writes, and the document is mostly immutable once written. It struggles when the shape is stable but unknown to you, when writes are frequent, and when documents grow without bound.

Connection-level settings that help

For bulk ingestion, consider raising synchronous_commit temporarily for non-critical writes:

SET synchronous_commit = off;
-- bulk load
-- reset per connection
RESET synchronous_commit;

This reduces WAL flush frequency. It trades durability on commit for throughput, so use it only for data you can regenerate or reconcile.

8. Frequently Asked Questions

Does STORAGE EXTERNAL always reduce WAL?

Not always. It eliminates the CPU cost of compression, which often lets the system write more rows per second and therefore generate more total WAL. It reduces per-row CPU and latency, but total WAL can rise if throughput increases substantially. The correct metric to track is bytes of WAL per logical operation, not total WAL alone.

Should I run VACUUM FULL to apply a storage mode change?

VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and its TOAST data, applying the new storage mode, but it locks the table exclusively. For large production tables, use pg_repack, which does the same work with a much shorter lock window, or accept that new storage modes apply only to newly written rows.

Is there a way to avoid TOAST entirely for JSONB?\n

Only by keeping values small enough to fit inline. If your JSONB payloads exceed a few kilobytes, TOAST is unavoidable. The realistic options are to reduce the value size, split hot and cold fields, or reduce write frequency.

How do I know if my TOAST table is bloated?

Compare pg_relation_size(reltoastrelid) against the sum of live chunk sizes. A large difference, or a TOAST table that keeps growing while the parent table's row count stays flat, indicates dead chunks that vacuum has not yet reclaimed. Check pg_stat_user_tables for the parent and run VACUUM on the TOAST relation explicitly if needed.

title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22219v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
description:
arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

title: Which language is fastest? I ran the same HTML parser in 8 languages: Python caught up with Rust, and Go lost even to Java
description:
This is an English version of my article on Habr (in Russian).

A week ago I wrote about z3l.FastHtmlParser, an HTML parser for .NET that builds a flat list of tags instead of a DOM and parses a page 10–30x faster than HtmlAgilityPack and AngleSharp. Back then it had no CSS selectors, no XPath, and lived only in .NET.

In one week it got CSS selectors and XPath 1.0, and the library itself moved to seven more languages: Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript, Python, PHP and Ruby. These are not "Hello world" ports: each implementation is 6–11 thousand lines — a tokenizer, the HTML5 optional end tag rules, all 2,125 named entities, XPath 1.0 and CSS selectors. The algorithm is the same everywhere, and every port is checked against the original on the same pages.

The result is an experiment you rarely get to run: the same real-world task, eight languages, two operating systems and one CPU. So I can finally answer the question people get flamed for in the comments. Grab your pitchforks.

Setup

  • Same hardware. A physical server with an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X (8 cores, 16 threads).
  • Linux — Ubuntu 26.04 on that server, benchmarks in Docker, official images: dotnet/sdk:10.0, golang:1.27, rust:1.100, maven:3-eclipse-temurin-21, node:26, python:3.14, php:8.4-cli, ruby:4.0.
  • Windows — Windows 10 LTSC in a KVM virtual machine on the same server, 12 vCPUs. Same versions: .NET 10.0.12, Go 1.27.4, Rust 1.100, Java 21.0.13, Node 26.13, Python 3.14.10, PHP 8.4.27, Ruby 4.0.9.
  • PHP runs with opcache and the tracing JIT on both OSes. Ruby runs without JIT, and on Linux also with YJIT and the new ZJIT (the RubyInstaller build for Windows has no YJIT).
  • Strictly one at a time. No benchmark ran alongside another, and Linux and Windows never ran at the same time either. It's a production server running MySQL, RabbitMQ and a dozen services, so background load isn't zero (load average 1–3 out of 16), but it's the same for both OSes.
  • Two tasks. Parsing a page, and scraping — parsing plus extracting 20 books (title, price, rating) or 10 quotes. The pages are saved copies of books.toscrape.com (51 KB), quotes.toscrape.com (11 KB), webscraper.io laptops (38 KB), books ×10 (510 KB), and books with no </li> and </p>. Before measuring, every benchmark checks that all libraries returned the same records.
  • Time is the median per call after warm-up. C# uses BenchmarkDotNet, Go uses testing.B (median of three runs), the rest use the same loop: one second of warm-up, then batches of calls, take the median.
  • Error margin is up to 10%. Repeated runs of the same benchmark differed by up to 10%: C# on books — 55 and 58 μs on Linux, 64 and 59 μs on Windows; Java on Windows — 73 μs yesterday and 66 μs today. So in this article, any difference under 10% is a tie.

Results

Parsing books.toscrape.com, 51 KB (lower is better):

Place Language Linux Windows

1–4 C# 55 μs 64 μs
1–4 Rust 56 μs 61 μs

5 Go 84 μs 102 μs
6 Node.js (TypeScript) 183 μs 201 μs
7 PHP + JIT 360 μs 516 μs
8 Ruby + YJIT 818 μs —
9 Ruby 1.60 ms 1.53 ms

The top four are within the error margin.

Parsing, all pages — Linux and Windows

books without </li> </p> 55 μs 61 μs 63 μs 71 μs 100 μs 224 μs 514 μs 1.91 ms

Scraping 20 books (parse + extract), Linux / Windows. Every port has three ways to search: its own Find methods, CSS selectors and XPath.

Language Find API CSS XPath
Rust 73 / 82 μs 73 / 87 μs 117 / 191 μs
C# 75 / 70 μs 74 / 82 μs 117 / 109 μs
Java 86 / 93 μs 120 / 111 μs 102 / 108 μs

The ports vs. the local champions

Comparing languages is fun, but a user cares about something else: is the port worth taking over what their ecosystem already uses? The ports were written in a week and are clearly less polished than the original. Here's how they stack up against the best each platform had before them.

Parsing books.toscrape.com, 51 KB — how many times faster the port is (Linux / Windows; below 1 means the port is slower):

Language Port, Linux Fastest competitor Port is faster Popular choice Port is faster
Rust 56 μs tl 1.5x / 1.7x scraper (html5ever) 22x / 25x
C# 55 μs HtmlAgilityPack 12x / 12x AngleSharp 21x / 18x
Python 54 μs selectolax (lexbor, C) 8.4x / 6.3x BeautifulSoup 226x / 213x
Java 59 μs Jericho 6.7x / 6.0x jsoup 8.0x / 7.2x
Go 84 μs golang.org/x/net/html 10x / 9.6x goquery 10x / 9.6x
Node.js 183 μs htmlparser2 5.3x / 4.3x cheerio 16x / 9.9x
PHP 360 μs Dom\HTMLDocument (lexbor, C) 1.5x / 1.5x DOMDocument (libxml2, C) 2.6x / 2.8x
Ruby + YJIT 818 μs Nokogiri (libxml2, C) 1.3x / — Nokogiri 1.3x / —
Ruby 1.60 ms Nokogiri (libxml2, C) 0.6x / 0.9x Nokogiri 0.6x / 0.9x

Scraping 20 books — the best of the port's three APIs vs. the best competitor:

Language Port, Linux Fastest competitor Port is faster
Rust 73 μs tl (CSS) 1.7x / 2.1x
C# 74 μs HtmlAgilityPack (XPath) 11x / 12x
Python 94 μs selectolax (CSS) 6.2x / 4.8x
Java 86 μs jsoup (CSS) 8.2x / 7.5x
Go 106 μs goquery (CSS) 9.1x / 8.3x
Node.js 230 μs node-html-parser 6.1x / 4.9x
PHP 514 μs Dom\HTMLDocument (CSS) 1.4x / 1.6x
Ruby + YJIT 1.01 ms Nokogiri (XPath) 1.9x / —
Ruby 2.08 ms Nokogiri (XPath) 0.9x / 1.1x

In seven languages out of eight, the port is faster than anything the ecosystem had — on both OSes and in both tasks. And in Python, PHP and Ruby the main competitors are written in C: selectolax and Dom\HTMLDocument are lexbor; lxml, DOMDocument and Nokogiri are libxml2. Pure PHP beats the C parser built into PHP 8.4 by 1.5x.

The closest competitor is tl in Rust, only 1.5–2x slower. But tl is a zero-copy parser that doesn't decode entities and has no descendant combinator in its selectors, so it does less work.

Ruby is a special case. Without JIT, the port is on par with Nokogiri on Windows (parsing 8% slower, scraping 14% faster) and loses on Linux, where Nokogiri is noticeably faster: 1.6x on parsing. With YJIT the port overtakes Nokogiri: 1.3x on parsing and 1.9x on scraping.

Where does the gap come from? The C libraries do ten times more work: they build a full DOM tree with an object per node, synthesize implicit <html> and <tbody>, and then wrap the found nodes in Python, PHP or Ruby objects. A parser that stores tags as pairs of integer offsets into the source string does exactly what scraping needs, and nothing more.

And now — why every row of these tables will offend somebody.

Claim 1. Python caught up with Rust

On Linux, Python parses the page in 54 μs and Rust in 56. On Windows, 67 and 61.

Of course, this is cheating: the Python version is 790 lines of PyO3 bindings around the Rust version. Inside fh.parse(html) it's not the interpreter running, it's the same machine code as in Rust. And Python being 2 μs faster than Rust itself on Linux is noise and build flags: the Python wrapper is built with fat LTO, the Rust benchmark with thin LTO.

Scraping shows what Python pays for: crossing the boundary. Every found tag and every string becomes a Python object, and the Find API falls 1.6x behind pure Rust (117 μs vs. 73). CSS selectors are only 30% behind (94 μs): the whole search runs inside Rust and the boundary is crossed once. The less often your code jumps between Python and Rust, the closer it gets to Rust.

The provocation is elsewhere, though. In the "Python is slow" debate people tend to forget that in production, Python doesn't run the hot code anyway: numpy, pandas, lxml, selectolax, pydantic-core and orjson are written in C or Rust. Python is the language you call fast code from. And if your task has a native core, a Python service will beat an "honest" Go service that does everything itself.

The moral: a "fast language" is often a language that delegates well.

Claim 2. Go is the slowest of the compiled languages

Go parses the page in 84 μs — 1.5x slower than Rust, C#, Java and even Python. Same on Windows: 102 μs vs. 61–67.

And the Go version is written carefully: 2 allocations per parse, the garbage collector barely shows up in the measurement. It's not the GC, it's the compiler. The Go compiler deliberately optimizes less in exchange for build speed: more modest inlining, fewer bounds checks eliminated, no auto-vectorization. Go does have PGO, but only from a pre-recorded profile (default.pgo), and few people enable it. The JIT in .NET and HotSpot collects the profile itself, at run time, and compiles for the hot paths.

Go is still a great language for services — fast builds, simplicity, predictability. But "Go is fast because it's compiled" is a myth. It's fast compared to Python and Ruby. Not compared to the JVM and .NET.

Claim 3. C# and Java are almost Rust. And "C# beat Rust" is a Windows thing

On Linux, parsing: C# — 55 μs, Rust — 56, Java — 59. Scraping: Rust — 73, C# — 75, Java — 86. A tie, with Java slightly behind.

Windows tells a different story: on scraping, C# is first at 70 μs vs. 82 for Rust, and on XPath the gap is almost 2x: 109 μs vs. 191. The first draft of this article was titled "C# beat Rust". Then I looked at Linux, where Rust and C# are neck and neck, and started digging.

The cause is the allocator. .NET allocates objects on its own heap the same way on every OS: by bumping a pointer. Rust uses the system allocator by default: glibc malloc on Linux, HeapAlloc on Windows. The XPath engine creates lots of small vectors and strings, and the Windows system heap struggles with that. Two lines, and Rust on Windows switches to mimalloc:

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: mimalloc::MiMalloc = mimalloc::MiMalloc;
Rust on Windows HeapAlloc (default) mimalloc For reference: Linux
Parse books, 51 KB 61 μs 55 μs 56 μs
Scrape, Find API 82 μs 69 μs 73 μs
Scrape, XPath 191 μs 125 μs 117 μs

And C# is no longer ahead: 70 μs vs. 69. On Linux mimalloc changes nothing (parsing 55 vs. 56 μs, XPath 117 vs. 117): glibc malloc is already good for this workload.

The moral: a garbage-collected language brings its own allocator, the same everywhere, while Rust gets whatever the OS gives it. On Windows that costs Rust up to 1.5x.

One more note on fairness: the C# version is the original and the most polished: ArrayPool, Span<char>, vectorized IndexOfAny, CollectionsMarshal.SetCount, Dictionary.AlternateLookup to look up by span without allocating strings. But the Java version, which has none of that, is only 5–18% behind Rust. If you want "almost Rust" without the borrow checker, these are your languages.

Claim 4. NativeAOT is slower than JIT, and server GC doesn't help

Since C# is in the top four, let's see how to make it faster. Two popular ideas: compile ahead of time (NativeAOT) and turn on the server garbage collector. BenchmarkDotNet built NativeAOT for the same instruction set the JIT uses on this CPU (x86-64-v3, AVX2), so that's not the issue.

C#, time; in parentheses — relative to regular JIT on the same OS:

Task OS JIT JIT + server GC NativeAOT NativeAOT + server GC
Parse books, 51 KB Linux 58 μs 66 μs (1.14) 75 μs (1.30) 81 μs (1.40)
Windows 59 μs 64 μs (1.08) 83 μs (1.40) 87 μs (1.47)
Parse books ×10, 510 KB Linux 614 μs 625 μs (1.02) 765 μs (1.24) 823 μs (1.34)
Windows 600 μs 626 μs (1.04) 824 μs (1.37) 864 μs (1.44)
Scrape 20 books, Find API Linux 72 μs 80 μs (1.11) 89 μs (1.24) 100 μs (1.40)
Windows 73 μs 75 μs (1.02) 100 μs (1.36) 104 μs (1.41)
Scrape 20 books, XPath Linux 121 μs 150 μs (1.24) 153 μs (1.26) 181 μs (1.50)
Windows 129 μs 132 μs (1.02) 156 μs (1.21) 169 μs (1.31)
Scrape 10 quotes Linux 25 μs 27 μs (1.06) 32 μs (1.27) 35 μs (1.41)
Windows 25 μs 26 μs (1.05) 37 μs (1.45) 38 μs (1.50)

NativeAOT is 20–50% slower than JIT. The main reason is dynamic PGO. The .NET JIT first compiles a method quickly and with instrumentation, watches which branches are hot and which types actually show up at interface calls, and then recompiles for that: devirtualizes calls, inlines the hot code, lays out code so the hot path runs straight through. NativeAOT compiles everything ahead of time, blind. Static PGO for NativeAOT exists, but almost nobody uses it.

Server GC is 2–15% slower, and up to 24% on XPath, where allocations are heaviest. Server GC has a heap per core and a much larger gen0 budget: fewer collections, but new objects land in memory that's no longer in cache. In a single-threaded parser that's a pure loss; server GC pays off when many threads allocate at once.

NativeAOT is about millisecond startup, compact deployment and no JIT at run time. Not about peak speed.

Claim 5. Node.js is 3.3x slower than Rust — and that's a great result

V8 is a marvel of engineering. A dynamically typed language with a JIT stays within 3.3x of Rust on parsing (183 μs vs. 56) and 3.1x on scraping. No other dynamic language in this table comes close: PHP is 2x slower than Node.js, Ruby with YJIT 4.5x.

The main bottleneck isn't even V8, it's JavaScript strings: UTF-16, immutable, no cheap slice views. A parser built on offsets into the source string fits that model well — which is why the gap is so small.

Claim 6. Ruby: YJIT doubles the speed

Ruby 4.0 on Linux — the port vs. Nokogiri:

Task Port, no JIT Port, ZJIT Port, YJIT Nokogiri (libxml2)
Parse books, 51 KB 1.60 ms 1.25 ms 818 μs 1.01 ms
Parse books ×10, 510 KB 15.3 ms 12.1 ms 8.02 ms 9.58 ms
Parse books without </li> </p> 1.83 ms 1.64 ms 1.49 ms 1.01 ms
Scrape 20 books 2.08 ms 1.42 ms 1.01 ms 1.90 ms
Scrape 10 quotes 789 μs 529 μs 375 μs 964 μs

YJIT makes pure Ruby twice as fast on both parsing and scraping. The new ZJIT in Ruby 4.0 gives less for now: +28% on parsing and +46% on scraping. Nokogiri doesn't speed up with JIT at all — its hot code is in C — so with YJIT the pure-Ruby port beats it almost everywhere.

The exception is the page without end tags: the Ruby version spends 14–25% more time on it than on the normal page, and 80% more with YJIT, while Rust, Go and Python don't notice the difference. Something to optimize.

A shame about Windows: RubyInstaller builds have no YJIT, so there Ruby stays an interpreter.

Claim 7. Windows vs. Linux: it's not the VM

Windows runs in a VM on the same server as Linux, so the first suspect is virtualization. Rust with mimalloc clears it: 55 μs in the Windows VM and 55 μs on bare-metal Linux. For this workload virtualization costs almost nothing.

How much slower Windows is than Linux on the same hardware (parsing books, 51 KB):

What Linux Windows Windows slower by
Rust, system allocator 56 μs 61 μs 9%
Rust + mimalloc 55 μs 55 μs 0%
C# (two runs) 55–58 μs 59–64 μs 2–17%
Java 59 μs 66 μs 12%
Node.js 183 μs 201 μs 10%
Go 84 μs 102 μs 22%
Python (Rust inside) 54 μs 67 μs 24%
PHP + JIT 360 μs 516 μs 43%
Ruby 1.60 ms 1.53 ms −4%
lxml (Python, libxml2) 590 μs 1.51 ms 156%
Dom\HTMLDocument (PHP, lexbor) 524 μs 777 μs 48%
Nokogiri (Ruby, libxml2) 1.01 ms 1.41 ms 40%
selectolax (Python, lexbor) 455 μs 421 μs −7%
htmlparser2 (Node.js) 977 μs 870 μs −11%

What follows from this:

  • Runtimes with their own allocator — .NET, the JVM, V8 — perform the same on both OSes, within noise. That holds for third-party libraries on them too: jsoup and AngleSharp differ by 1–3%.
  • Rust and the Python wrapper over Rust slow down on Windows because of the system heap (see claim 3). On XPath in Python the gap is almost 2x: 243 μs vs. 123.
  • Interpreters and C libraries depend on the build. One reason for PHP: the official Windows builds are made with MSVC, which doesn't support computed goto, so the Zend VM runs in the slower CALL mode instead of HYBRID. lxml is 2.6x slower on Windows, Nokogiri 40%. But it goes the other way too: selectolax and htmlparser2 are 7–11% faster on Windows. It all comes down to the specific build of the specific library.
  • Go is 22% slower on Windows, even though it has its own allocator. I have no explanation — hints in the comments are welcome.

A separate provocation: if your PHP service, or your Python service with lxml, runs on Windows, moving to Linux will give you more than rewriting it in another language.

Claim 8. The fastest language isn't the most verbose

Non-blank lines for the same functionality:

Language Lines
TypeScript 5,950
C# 6,950
Java 7,170
Go 8,800
Ruby 8,900
PHP 10,100
Rust 10,750
Python 790 (bindings over Rust)

The Rust version is one of the fastest and the longest. Ruby, famous for being concise, came out longer than C# and Java: when you write a parser in Ruby that has to be fast, idiomatic Ruby ends and manual index juggling in strings begins. TypeScript came out shortest.

Caveats, without which I'd rightly get torn apart

  • One algorithm, one author, one task. HTML parsing is string work and branching; for number crunching, multithreading or I/O the picture may be different.
  • The ports aren't equally optimized. The C# version is the original, the rest are week-old ports. Go and Ruby surely have room to speed up. Pull requests that move your language up the table are welcome.
  • Different benchmark harnesses and up to 10% noise. BenchmarkDotNet, testing.B and a hand-written median loop measure slightly differently, and the server isn't idle. A 10% gap between neighboring rows is a tie; a 2x gap is not.
  • Everything is default. Go without PGO, Rust without target-cpu=native and with the system allocator, as in most projects. Vectorized character search in Rust (memchr) detects AVX2 at run time on its own.
  • Python is Rust. I said it. A pure Python implementation would land around Ruby, or even below.
  • Windows is in a VM. It costs our parsers nothing (Rust + mimalloc), but for libraries that build large DOM trees virtualization may cost more: TLB misses under two-level address translation are more expensive.
  • Single-threaded measurement. In multithreaded scraping, GCs, allocators and threading models come into play — and server GC may look different. That's a topic for a separate article.

Bottom line

If the flame war really needs a one-liner: for parsing, Rust ≈ C# ≈ Java ≈ Python (Rust inside) > Go > Node.js > PHP > Ruby + YJIT > Ruby.

But if you want your scraper to be faster, switching languages isn't the first thing to do:

  • The language, with the same algorithm, gives 1.5x between the top four and Go, 3.3x to Node.js, 6.4x to PHP.
  • The algorithm, within one language, gives 1.5x to 226x over local libraries, and the PHP and Ruby ports beat C libraries.
  • Runtime settings weigh almost as much as the language: NativeAOT instead of JIT is 20–50% slower, the Windows system allocator makes Rust up to 1.5x slower, Windows instead of Linux makes PHP 43% slower.

Data structures matter more than the language, and the runtime and OS matter almost as much as the language.

All eight implementations and the benchmarks are open — run them on your hardware and send me your numbers. For C#, the JIT/NativeAOT and workstation/server GC variants run with one command: dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/z3l.FastHtmlParser.Benchmarks -- --runtime-variants --filter '*ParseBenchmarks.FastHtmlParser' '*ScrapeBenchmarks.*_FastHtmlParser*'.

  • C# (original): https://github.com/romanti3172/z3l.FastHtmlParser
  • Go: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser
  • Rust: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-rs
  • Python: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-py
  • Java: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-java
  • TypeScript: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-js
  • PHP: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-php
  • Ruby: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-rb

Disclosure: the ports were written with heavy help from Claude (that's what the meme is about), and this English text is an AI-assisted translation of my original Russian article. The benchmarks and numbers are mine, run on my hardware.
