title: Higher-Order Interaction Reconstruction via Integral Physics-Informed Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.21935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing higher-order interactions is a fundamental challenge in complex networked systems, with applications in ecological, social, and biological networks. This inverse problem is inherently difficult due to the combinatorial complexity of higher-order structures, the strong nonlinearity of the underlying dynamics, and the prevalence of noisy and sparse observations. In this article, we propose a novel integral physics-informed neural network (IntegralPINN) framework for higher-order interaction reconstruction. Instead of { penalizing derivative-based physics residuals,} we adopt an integral formulation over temporal intervals, which naturally suppresses high-frequency noise and mitigates derivative-induced instability. We further introduce a continuous parameterization of interaction tensors, enabling tractable identification of higher-order structures via gradient-based optimization. We provide theoretical analysis establishing a noise-robust error bound that is independent of derivative amplification when the integration window satisfies an excitation condition. Extensive experiments on ecological dynamics, social contagion, and neuronal synchronization systems demonstrate that IntegralPINN achieves accurate and robust reconstruction under noisy and sparse observations, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Java4Shell: AI Found a Critical Java Flaw in About an Hour — Here's What to Patch
description:
Java4Shell: AI Found a Critical Java Flaw in About an Hour — Here's What to Patch

By Shakeel Ahmed — AI Growth Lab

A critical vulnerability in Java's core libraries was found by an AI-assisted researcher in about an hour, weaponized into a working exploit in about two more hours, and patched by Oracle the same day it was disclosed. The flaw, nicknamed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), is a memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder — and if you run Java 17 or newer on modern Intel or AMD servers, you should patch now. CISA has already issued an alert urging immediate patching, and there is no exploitation in the wild reported yet — which means the window to fix this before attackers catch up is still open, but it will not stay open long.

What Is Java4Shell?

Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, the code behind java.util.Base64.Decoder — one of the most widely used utilities in the entire Java ecosystem. Almost every Java application that handles tokens, certificates, file uploads, API payloads, or serialized data touches Base64 somewhere, which is what makes this flaw so dangerous despite its narrow trigger.

The bug lives in the HotSpot JVM's AVX-512 VBMI intrinsic, in a function called generate_base64_decodeBlock. When the JVM runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI support, it uses a hand-optimized, hardware-accelerated path to decode Base64 data. That fast path contains a memory-corruption flaw: specially crafted Base64 input can write past the end of a heap buffer. A heap out-of-bounds write is one of the most serious classes of memory bugs, because it can corrupt adjacent data structures — and, in the hands of a skilled attacker, turn into arbitrary code execution inside the JVM process.

Security firm Calif, which disclosed the flaw on November 17, 2026, rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 — critical. Oracle, which released patches in its November Critical Patch Update the same day, rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity. The gap between the two scores is a judgment call about how hard the bug is to exploit reliably. Calif's own demonstrations suggest the difficulty is lower than Oracle's score implies: the firm demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the default configurations of Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, and PingFederate, and post-authentication remote code execution on Gerrit, Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, Solr, and Spinnaker. "Pre-auth" matters enormously — it means an attacker needs no account, no login, and no credentials. Any internet-reachable instance of those products running an unpatched JVM was, in principle, remotely exploitable.

Who Is Affected?

The exposure is broad but specific, and that specificity is good news for triage:

  • Affected versions: Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, including Java 21, 25, and 27. If you run Java 17, 21, 25, or 27, assume you are affected until you verify your patch level.
  • Affected hardware: Only x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI instructions — Intel Xeon processors from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids, and AMD EPYC processors based on Zen 4 and later. The bug is in the AVX-512 accelerated code path, so machines without that instruction set never take the vulnerable path.
  • Not affected: ARM64 systems. If your fleet runs on ARM — including AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, or Ampere — the vulnerable intrinsic does not exist on your platform.
  • Affected products: Any Java application that decodes Base64 on a vulnerable JVM and CPU combination. The headline demonstrations cover Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, PingFederate, Gerrit, Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, Solr, and Spinnaker — but those are demonstrations, not an exhaustive list. Any enterprise Java application that accepts Base64 input from untrusted sources is potentially in scope.

Note the version floor: 17.0.6. If you are still running Java 8 or 11 in production — and plenty of enterprises are — this particular flaw does not apply to you, because the vulnerable AVX-512 intrinsic was introduced later. That is not a reason to stay on an old version, but it does mean your patching priority for this CVE is lower than for teams on Java 17 and above.

The AI Angle: Found in an Hour, Exploited in Two More

The most talked-about part of Java4Shell is not the bug itself — it is how it was found. Researcher Quang Luong used OpenAI's Codex with GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model tuned for security research, to find the flaw in approximately one hour and build a first working exploit in about two more hours. Total token cost: under $200.

That timeline should change how every engineering team thinks about vulnerability research. A task that once required days or weeks of expert manual code auditing — reading thousands of lines of JVM intrinsic code, reasoning about vectorized memory operations, and constructing a proof of concept — was compressed into a single afternoon by one researcher working with a model. Calif describes the approach as the "centaur hacker": human plus model, each doing what it does best. The human directs, hypothesizes, and validates; the model reads code at inhuman scale, spots the anomaly, and iterates on exploit variants far faster than a person typing alone.

Wiz's Atlas AI system independently produced a proof of concept within about two hours and confirmed remote code execution on Jira, Confluence, and Jenkins — a second data point that this was not a one-off fluke. Two separate AI systems, two working exploits, same afternoon.

The defensive implication is double-edged. On one hand, AI-assisted research finds real bugs faster, which means vendors and the open-source community can fix more flaws before attackers find them. On the other hand, the same capability is available to attackers. The window between disclosure and mass exploitation is shrinking. A vulnerability that took weeks to weaponize in 2020 can be weaponized in hours in 2026. Patching speed is no longer a nice-to-have — it is the primary defense.

Calif is acting responsibly with the disclosure: the firm is withholding product-specific exploits and has published only a safe reproducer, giving defenders time to patch. But the technical details of the bug are public, and the reproducer alone gives skilled attackers most of what they need. The clock is running.

There is also an uncomfortable footnote. The flaw reportedly leaked before the patch was ready — South Korea's National Cyber Security Center issued an advisory on November 16, a day before the coordinated disclosure. Leaks compress the patching window further and are a reminder that coordinated disclosure timelines are fragile.

How to Patch Java4Shell Right Now

Patching is straightforward, and Oracle's November Critical Patch Update contains the fix. Here is the order of operations:

1. Find every vulnerable JVM

Inventory your Java runtimes before you patch anything. Check every server, container image, CI runner, and developer machine:

java -version

Then check whether the underlying CPU exposes AVX-512 VBMI:

grep -o avx512_vbmi /proc/cpuinfo | head -1

If the CPU flag is absent, that host is not exposed to this flaw through the accelerated path. If it is present and the JVM is unpatched Java 17.0.6 or later, that host is in scope. Pay special attention to container images — a base image with an old JDK can silently ship the vulnerable runtime into dozens of services, and container rebuilds are where patches most often get missed.

2. Apply Oracle's November Critical Patch Update

Upgrade to the patched OpenJDK release for your Java version — Java 17, 21, 25, or 27. If you use a distribution build (Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat's build), apply the equivalent patched release from your vendor; all major distributors shipped fixes alongside Oracle's update. Rebuild and redeploy container images, and restart every JVM process — a patched JDK on disk does nothing for a JVM that is still running the old code in memory.

3. If you cannot patch immediately, use the JVM flag

Qualys notes that a single JVM flag can close the exposure where patching must wait. The flag disables the vulnerable AVX-512 accelerated Base64 path, forcing the JVM to fall back to the safe software decoder. There is a small performance cost — Base64 decoding gets slower — but for most applications it is negligible compared to the risk of remote code execution. Apply the flag as a temporary mitigation on every exposed service, then patch properly as soon as your change window allows. Do not treat the flag as a permanent fix: it is a tourniquet, not a cure.

4. Prioritize internet-facing services first

Patch in this order: internet-facing Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak, Artifactory, and PingFederate instances first, then internal instances of the same products, then everything else running Java 17+. Calif demonstrated pre-auth RCE on the first group in default configurations — those are the systems an internet-wide scan will find first. If you run any of those products, check your vendor's advisory as well; several have issued their own guidance on top of Oracle's patch.

5. Verify the fix

After patching, confirm the running JVM is actually the patched build — java -version on the live process or container, not just the installed package. If you applied the mitigation flag instead, confirm it is present in the process's JVM arguments. Then watch for follow-up advisories: researchers are actively probing related code paths, and Calif has a track record here — the firm previously found PHP2Shell in October 2026 and a vulnerability nicknamed Squidbleed. Related flaws in adjacent code have a habit of surfacing after a big disclosure.

Why This One Matters More Than the Average CVE

Enterprise Java has had critical vulnerabilities before — Log4Shell in 2021 is the obvious comparison — but Java4Shell is different in two ways. First, the bug is in the JVM itself, not in a library you can upgrade independently. Every Java application on an affected runtime shares the exposure, which makes the blast radius unusually wide and the fix unusually centralized: one JDK upgrade closes it everywhere. Second, the discovery story is a preview of the new normal. AI-assisted vulnerability research is no longer a lab curiosity. It found a critical flaw in one of the most audited codebases in the world, in an hour, for less than $200.

That changes the economics of both offense and defense. For defenders, the lesson is to invest in patch velocity: automated JDK upgrades, container rebuild pipelines, and runtime inventories that can answer "where are we running Java 17+ on AVX-512?" in minutes, not days. For the industry, the lesson is that the most heavily reviewed code still hides critical bugs — and the tools that find them are now cheap enough for anyone to run.

No exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 17, according to VulnCheck and Sophos. That is the best news in this story, and it is also temporary. Patch now, while the window is still open.

title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.22151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

End-user safety identifier labels for abuse monitoring

End-user safety_identifier request labels are available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) and Veo (predictLongRunning) API calls. API resellers and multi-tenant apps can pass an anonymized per-user ID in labels to attribute policy violations to individual end users. Targeted attribution helps prevent enforcement actions across an entire Google Cloud project.

For formatting requirements and code samples, see Pass an end-user safety identifier in API calls.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Carbon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-carbon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Govern agents on any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster with Agent Gateway for cross-cloud (Limited Preview)

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available in Limited Preview. It extends Agent Platform governance to agents that run on Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes clusters outside of Google Cloud, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Red Hat OpenShift, and bare-metal clusters. Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

For more information, see Set up Agent Gateway for cross-cloud.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.1100-gke.125 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.1100-gke.125 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.12-gke.500.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.
  • Upgraded Container-Optimized OS (COS) to milestone 121 (cos-121-18867-652-7), which removes the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs.
  • Updated the Ubuntu 22.04 node and admin workstation base image to ubuntu-gke-op-2204-1-33-v20261024 to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) root CAs (USN-8944-1).

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a user cluster left an orphaned k8s-health-check-reader-binding-<cluster-namespace> ClusterRoleBinding on the admin cluster. Health check permissions now use a namespaced RoleBinding, and legacy ClusterRoleBinding objects are automatically cleaned up.
  • Fixed an issue where adding IP addresses to an existing MetalLB address pool of an advanced user cluster left the cluster stuck in the UPDATING state. The update is now rejected during validation; to add IP addresses, add a new address pool instead.
  • Fixed an issue where preflight checks erroneously required the control plane VIP (loadBalancer.vips.controlPlaneVIP) to be in the control plane node subnet when the control plane load balancer mode is set to manual.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.12-gke.500.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a user cluster left an orphaned k8s-health-check-reader-binding-<cluster-namespace> ClusterRoleBinding on the admin cluster. Health check permissions now use a namespaced RoleBinding, and legacy ClusterRoleBinding objects are automatically cleaned up.
  • Fixed a race condition where bmctl check cluster --snapshot could fail with a panic: send on closed channel error when taking Node Agent snapshots.
  • Fixed an issue where removing a node from a cluster left behind its local PersistentVolume resources instead of garbage collecting them. This fix applies to Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal local PersistentVolume resources created after upgrading to 1.34.1100-gke.125; existing orphaned PersistentVolume resources must be deleted manually.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where resetting or removing a control plane node could remove the wrong etcd or etcd-events member if another control plane node's IP address shared the same prefix (for example, 10.201.0.2 and 10.201.0.26), causing the affected node to become NotReady and stalling cluster upgrades.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.

Feature

Capacity buffers, including active and standby capacity buffers, are generally available for GKE Standard and Autopilot clusters running version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 or later. Capacity buffers let you pre-provision and optionally suspend standby compute capacity using the CapacityBuffer custom resource (autoscaling.x-k8s.io/v1beta1) to accelerate workload scaling and mitigate capacity constraints. To get started, see About capacity buffers.

The latest version in the Regular channel is Looker 26.20.

title: Google showed an AI Overview on all 40 email-marketing searches. YouTube was its top source
description:
If you market an email tool, assume your buyers will see Google's AI Overview before your ranking. It appeared on all 40 US searches in this test, covering how-to questions, best-of lists and brand comparisons. The source it cited most often was YouTube, in 31 of the 40 Overviews. YouTube ranked among the regular results on only 4 of the 40 pages. Of the domains cited in an Overview, only 62 of 283 also appeared in the regular results on the same page.

What the Overviews cited

I ran 40 email-marketing searches through automatic/google-search-results-scraper on November 18, 2026 UTC, in English with the country set to us. Each search read one results page. The Actor reports the Overview's status and its cited links on that page. All 40 rows came back present. The 40 Overviews held 308 cited links from 139 distinct domains. One Overview, for "best email service provider for developers", had no cited links.

Domain Overviews citing it Cited links Pages where it ranked in regular results
youtube.com 31 49 4
reddit.com 24 24 16
zapier.com 13 13 3
mailchimp.com 11 14 4
campaignmonitor.com 7 7 4

Domains are hostnames without www., so help.klaviyo.com counts separately from klaviyo.com. Regular results are the page's organic list, with roughly 7 to 10 links per page. Some Overviews cited several YouTube videos, giving 49 YouTube links across 31 Overviews. Reddit was closer to its regular ranking. It ranked among the regular results on 16 pages and was cited in 24 Overviews.

Does the type of search matter?

I wrote 14 how-to questions, 13 best-of or tool searches and 13 searches that name a brand. The full list is in the snapshot.

Search type Searches With an Overview Citing YouTube Citing Reddit
Question or how-to 14 14 12 8
Best-of or tool search 13 13 9 8
Brand, pricing or comparison 13 13 10 8

Questions leaned most on video. Brand searches still sent readers toward the brands. In all 12 brand searches that named a vendor, the Overview cited at least one named vendor's own site. "Mailchimp pricing", "sendgrid vs mailgun" and "brevo review" were among them. I counted twilio.com as SendGrid's site. I left out "substack alternatives" because it asks for rivals.

For an email product, I'd put a short video and an honest Reddit answer on my content list next to the blog post. On these pages, they were the two most-cited sources. Keep your own pricing and comparison pages current, too, because Overviews for brand searches cited them.

Limits

This is a single collection from one country, in English, without a signed-in Google account. AI Overviews change between runs and between users, so repeat the searches before relying on one count. I chose the 40 searches. They indicate patterns for this niche and do not measure all of Google. The regular results include a YouTube link only when Google ranks it among the organic links. A separate row of videos elsewhere on the page might not be counted. Nine organic links could not be resolved, and the script skips them. The first run reached its 300-second limit after 18 searches. I split the remaining 22 into two more runs with the same country and language. Every search has exactly one results page in the snapshot.

Reproduce the tables

Download the captured analysis fields as overviews.json. The snapshot preserves the returned order. It keeps the cited and organic URLs and omits answer text. Save the code as overviews.py and run python3 overviews.py overviews.json.

import json
import sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse

runs = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text())["runs"]
pages = [page for run in runs for page in run["items"]]
order = runs[0]["input"]["queries"]  # all 40; runs 2 and 3 finish the rest
groups = {"Question or how-to": order[:14], "Best-of or tool search": order[14:27],
          "Brand, pricing or comparison": order[27:]}

def domain(url):
    return (urlparse(url).hostname or "").removeprefix("www.") if url else None

by_term = {page["term"]: page for page in pages}
assert sorted(by_term) == sorted(order)
present = [p for p in pages if p["aiOverviewStatus"] == "present"]
print("Searches", len(pages), "with an AI Overview", len(present))

cited_in = Counter()
links = Counter()
for page in present:
    domains = [domain(url) for url in page["aiOverviewSources"]]
    links.update(domains)
    cited_in.update(set(domains))
print("Cited links", sum(links.values()), "distinct domains", len(links))
print("Overviews with no cited links", sum(not p["aiOverviewSources"] for p in present))

def in_organic(page, site):
    return site in {domain(url) for url in page["organicUrls"]}

for site, overviews in cited_in.most_common(5):
    organic = sum(in_organic(page, site) for page in pages)
    print(f"{site}: cited in {overviews} overviews ({links[site]} links), "
          f"organic results on {organic} pages")

for name, terms in groups.items():
    group = [by_term[t] for t in terms]
    print(name, len(group),
          "overviews", sum(p["aiOverviewStatus"] == "present" for p in group),
          "youtube", sum("youtube.com" in map(domain, p["aiOverviewSources"]) for p in group),
          "reddit", sum("reddit.com" in map(domain, p["aiOverviewSources"]) for p in group))

pairs = shared = 0
for page in present:
    cited = {domain(url) for url in page["aiOverviewSources"]}
    organic = {domain(url) for url in page["organicUrls"] if url}
    pairs += len(cited)
    shared += len(cited & organic)
print(f"Cited domains also in the same page's organic results: {shared} of {pairs}")

vendors = {"mailchimp": {"mailchimp.com"}, "klaviyo": {"klaviyo.com", "help.klaviyo.com"},
           "beehiiv": {"beehiiv.com"}, "substack": {"substack.com"}, "kit": {"kit.com"},
           "sendgrid": {"sendgrid.com", "twilio.com"}, "mailgun": {"mailgun.com"},
           "brevo": {"brevo.com"}, "mailerlite": {"mailerlite.com"},
           "activecampaign": {"activecampaign.com"}, "hubspot": {"hubspot.com"},
           "postmark": {"postmarkapp.com"}, "constant contact": {"constantcontact.com"}}
named = own_site = 0
for term in groups["Brand, pricing or comparison"]:
    if term.endswith("alternatives"):
        continue  # names one brand but asks for its rivals
    sites = set().union(*(v for k, v in vendors.items() if f" {k} " in f" {term} "))
    named += 1
    own_site += bool(sites & {domain(u) for u in by_term[term]["aiOverviewSources"]})
print(f"Brand searches citing a named vendor's own site: {own_site} of {named}")

To run a fresh check in your own niche, put your searches in queries and use the saved first input object as the body for POST https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/automatic~google-search-results-scraper/runs?maxTotalChargeUsd=0.15&timeout=600 with an Apify bearer token. When the run finishes, read defaultDatasetId from the run record, then fetch GET https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/{datasetId}/items?format=json. Each row's aiOverview has status, text and sources. Use the 600-second timeout above for 40 searches, or split them across runs as I did.

On November 18, 2026 UTC, the run records listed customer prices of $0.0015 per results page and $0.005 per GB of memory per run start. At the default 2 GB, that's $0.01 per start. The Actor's README says the page price becomes $0.002 on November 23, 2026. At the November 18 prices, these three runs would have cost a customer about $0.09 for 40 pages. On the publisher account, they used $0.067 of platform usage.

Searches Run ID Dataset ID Result

19–29 aTFyGo3gFj0xJvd5s W9QPJVBfhOlMcJcbz 11 pages
30–40 5wsKVXR4phhWe6THj SDdG5aZ6jvzBTgyJb 11 pages

title: Building Type-Safe Multi-Facet Search in Vue 3: Converting LanguageFilter to TypeScript
description:
In community-driven open-source portals like GitLab, developers explore issues based on their technical skills—whether they write Go, Ruby, Vue/TypeScript, or Python. Providing clean, multi-select search facets allows contributors to filter hundreds of opportunities down to the exact technologies they care about.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3198), I converted the LanguageFilter component and its test suite to strict TypeScript.

Here is a look at building type-safe multi-select filters in Vue 3, managing two-way array state, and ensuring robust test coverage.

1. Multi-Select State: Moving Beyond Primitive Models

Single-value inputs (like text boxes or radio buttons) usually bind to string or number. However, multi-select facet filters manage dynamic string arrays (string[]).

Previously, LanguageFilter.vue used generic runtime options:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
defineProps({
  availableLanguages: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
});

const selectedLanguages = defineModel('selectedLanguages', {
  type: Array,
  required: true,
});
</script>

While this validated that the prop was an Array, it did not enforce the element type of the array. Passing an array of numbers, objects, or null values would satisfy runtime validation but cause rendering glitches in the dropdown chips.

2. Compile-Time Type Safety with Vue 3.4 Macros

By converting to <script setup lang="ts">, we typed both the available options and the reactive selection collection:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BFormGroup } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import 'vue-select/dist/vue-select.css';

// Strictly typed array of language names (e.g. ['Ruby', 'Go', 'Vue'])
defineProps<{
  availableLanguages: string[];
}>();

// Strongly typed two-way model binding
const selectedLanguages = defineModel<string[]>('selectedLanguages', {
  required: true,
});
</script>

<template>
  <BFormGroup label="Language">
    <VueSelect
      v-model="selectedLanguages"
      multiple
      :options="availableLanguages"
    >
      <template #no-options="{ search, searching }">
        <template v-if="searching">
          No issues in {{ search }}
        </template>
        <template v-else>
          No languages available
        </template>
      </template>
    </VueSelect>
  </BFormGroup>
</template>

Key Benefits:

  • Element-Level Type Safety: Both availableLanguages and selectedLanguages are guaranteed to be string[]. The compiler flags any attempt to push non-string entities.
  • Named Two-Way Model: defineModel<string[]>('selectedLanguages', { required: true }) creates a contract where the parent must bind v-model:selectedLanguages, automatically typing the event payload for update:selectedLanguages.

3. Strict Event and Slot Testing with Vitest

In LanguageFilter.spec.ts, we eliminated loose typing in test helpers and refined emitted event assertions:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import LanguageFilter from './LanguageFilter.vue';

describe('LanguageFilter', () => {
  const defaultProps = {
    availableLanguages: ['Ruby', 'Go'],
    selectedLanguages: [],
  };

  let wrapper: VueWrapper;
  const createWrapper = (props = {}) =>
    wrapper = shallowMount(LanguageFilter, {
      props: { ...defaultProps, ...props },
      global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true },
    });

  const findSelect = () => wrapper.findComponent(VueSelect);

  // Safe helper to render the child component's custom no-options slot
  const findNoOptions = (slotProps: Record<string, unknown>) =>
    shallowMount({
      render: () => findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps),
    });

  it('emits updated language selection when an option is picked', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findSelect().vm.$emit('update:modelValue', ['Ruby']);

    // Checking exact emit structure: [[['Ruby']]]
    expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')).toEqual([[['Ruby']]]);
  });

  it('renders helpful message when searched language has no issues', () => {
    createWrapper();

    const noOptionsWrapper = findNoOptions({ search: 'Haskell', searching: true });
    expect(noOptionsWrapper.text()).toContain('No issues in Haskell');
  });
});

Notice the event assertion:

expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')).toEqual([[['Ruby']]]);

Rather than asserting wrapper.emitted('update:selectedLanguages')[0], matching the entire emitted event array verifies both the payload and the exact call count in a single check.

Key Takeaways

  1. Type Array Elements, Not Just Array: In TypeScript SFCs, always specify string[] or T[] rather than generic Array to prevent bad data downstream.
  2. Harmonize Filter Facet APIs: Keeping filter components uniform (LanguageFilter, ProjectFilter) with consistent named models (selectedLanguages, selectedProjects) makes parent filter bars clean and modular.
  3. Full Event Array Assertions: In Vue Test Utils, asserting against the entire emitted event array (expect(wrapper.emitted('event')).toEqual([[payload]])) guards against unexpected duplicate emissions.

title: AWS Lambda adds support for GPU instances on Lambda Managed Instances
description:
AWS Lambda now supports GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances using EC2 G-series instances. You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads including AI inference, media processing, 3D rendering, scientific computing, and financial simulations on Lambda without managing GPU drivers, frameworks, or scaling. Lambda runs multiple invocations concurrently in each execution environment and scales responsively based on GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency to keep your GPUs busy and reduce costs. GPU-accelerated functions integrate with the same 200+ AWS event sources as other Event Functions, so you can add GPU compute as another step in your serverless application.

Running GPU workloads today requires customers to provision hardware, manage driver and framework dependencies, and build custom scaling and capacity management. With this launch, you can go from code to a running GPU workload in minutes. Lambda provides GPU base images preconfigured with frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch. You can run workloads with large artifacts using container images and NVMe ephemeral storage of up to 32 GB each. To reduce startup time, Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading and streaming artifacts directly from Amazon S3. For resilience, you can select G-series instance types from multiple generations in the allowed instance types for your capacity provider. Lambda provisions instances from the newest generation that meets your function requirements and falls back to older generations when capacity is unavailable.

GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances and EC2 G-series instances are available. You can configure GPU-accelerated functions using the AWS Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use this feature through coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex by installing the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. You pay the EC2 On-Demand price (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply) for your instance, plus a 9.75% Lambda management fee and $0.20 per million requests. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda Pricing.

title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.22262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
description:
arXiv:2611.22069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

title: How we read Korea's crypto licence register, and why the file fights back
description:
In Korea a crypto business may serve customers only on a report that the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (KoFIU) has accepted, renewed every three years. KoFIU publishes the list of those businesses, but not as an API: it is an Excel file attached to a notice on its board, and the link to that file changes on every page load.

We read it every day for X-RAY, and today we are publishing the reader as open source: github.com/xrayme1337/kofiu-vasp-register.

Three things make the file hard to read:

  1. The download works only inside the session that listed the notice. The file id is minted per request and tied to a cookie, so the reader lists the board, keeps the cookies and downloads in the same session.
  2. The header is not fixed. Some months it is one row, some months two, with group cells such as a renewal heading above its date. The reader maps a column only by its whole label and fails loudly on a label it does not know, instead of guessing.
  3. The file carries personal data next to company data: the representative's name and the office address. The reader never reads those columns, and masks phone numbers and e-mail addresses in anything it logs.

What it returns per provider: the service and legal name, the business registration number (with its check digit verified), the businesses it may run (buying and selling, exchange, transfer, custody, brokerage), and the dates of acceptance, renewal and any cancellation. A provider that leaves the file is reported as having left it, never as revoked: the file does not say why.

The data is public under Korea's Public Data Act; credit KoFIU (kofiu.go.kr) where you show it.

If you would rather not run a scraper, X-RAY serves the whole register, with each provider tied to its company, to AI agents over MCP: x-ray.me/registers/korea-vasps.

title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
description:
arXiv:2611.21978v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
description:
arXiv:2611.21923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.21983v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

title: What are the best Shadeform alternatives for buying GPU time?
description:
Shadeform is good at one job: finding a GPU virtual machine across 30+ clouds and launching it from one account, so the right alternative depends on whether you also want someone to finish the run for you. Nodus takes the job itself, runs it on the cheapest capacity that will finish it, and restores its checkpoint if a machine is lost, at $2.60 per NVIDIA H100 SXM hour on the Nodus pricing page.

SkyPilot is the open-source choice for your own cloud accounts, Vast.ai has some of the lowest H100 sticker prices, and Runpod suits per-second container pods. We build Nodus, so read with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own docs or pricing page, and every sum is written out.

What does Shadeform actually do for you?

Shadeform is a broker for VMs, not a job runner. Its docs describe a cloud GPU marketplace where you compare availability, price and specs across 30+ providers, then launch through one console, REST API, shade CLI or MCP server. Each instance is a plain VM you SSH into, with an optional startup script, container and persistent volume.

The pricing model is simple. Shadeform's FAQ says it charges the same rate as going direct to the provider, with no extra fee, and passes your payment through. By default it launches into its own account with each provider (Shade Cloud), so you never sign up with them. You can also link your own provider account to spend existing credits or a negotiated rate.

The same FAQ is clear about the limits. Shadeform inherits each provider's SLA, and its Docker launch option starts a container on your VM rather than running a serverless one. On spot instances, a reclaimed machine is terminated, and the guide asks you to checkpoint to a volume, make jobs resumable, and poll and relaunch yourself.

Which Shadeform alternative fits which buyer?

Pick by who handles the run after launch. Shadeform and Vast.ai hand you a machine. SkyPilot and Nodus take a job and keep it going.

Option What you buy Who restarts a lost run H100 price signal Good fit
Shadeform VMs from 30+ clouds, one bill You, from your own checkpoints Single H100 listings $1.66 to $5.99, average $3.47 Finding the cheapest live VM across clouds
Nodus Jobs, Workspaces, Sandboxes, Functions Nodus, from the last committed checkpoint H100 SXM $2.60 Runs that should finish without babysitting
SkyPilot Open-source scheduler over your accounts SkyPilot managed jobs Whatever your clouds charge Teams with several cloud accounts and credits
Vast.ai Marketplace GPU instances You H100 SXM from $1.70, median $1.73 Lowest sticker price, flexible hosts
Runpod Per-second container pods You H100 SXM $4.39 Secure, from $2.69 Community Containers on one provider

Sources: Shadeform H100 directory and FAQ, Nodus pricing and attempts and recovery, SkyPilot managed jobs, Vast.ai pricing, Runpod pricing. Prices checked November 18, 2026.

One caveat on the Shadeform row. Its cheapest single-H100 listing is a PCIe VM, while the Nodus rate is for the H100 SXM, so the cards are close but not identical. Shadeform's directory also changes as providers come and go, and its own cheapest-GPU guide shows that the lowest listed price is not always available.


Shadeform's spread is the story: its listings run from below Nodus to more than twice the Nodus rate.

Is Nodus cheaper than Shadeform for an 80-hour H100 run?

Nodus is cheaper than the average Shadeform H100 listing and dearer than the cheapest one. Take a fine-tune that needs one H100 for 80 hours, priced at each listed rate.

Option Rate per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours
Shadeform, lowest listing $1.66 $132.80
Vast.ai H100 SXM median $1.73 $138.40
Nodus H100 SXM $2.60 $208.00
Runpod Community, from $2.69 $215.20
Shadeform, average listing $3.47 $277.60
Runpod Secure $4.39 $351.20
Shadeform, highest listing $5.99 $479.20

Each row is the rate times 80: for example $2.60 x 80 = $208.00 and $3.47 x 80 = $277.60. Against the average Shadeform listing, Nodus saves $69.60 on this run. Against the cheapest listing, Nodus costs $75.20 more, if that listing is live when you need it and the run never loses its machine.


At list prices the cheapest VM wins a clean run; the average Shadeform listing costs 33% more than Nodus.

How much rework can a cheaper listing absorb before Nodus wins?

The cheapest rate only stays cheapest while the run goes cleanly. When a VM is lost and your scripts restart from scratch, you pay again for the hours you redo. That gives a simple break-even rule we use when pricing runs:

A listing at price p beats Nodus only if p x (1 + r) is below $2.60, where r is the share of the run you expect to redo.

Solving for r gives the rework each Shadeform price tier can absorb. These assume the Nodus run redoes nothing, which is close to true for a checkpointed Job that loses only the minutes since its last checkpoint.

  • $1.66 listing: 2.60 / 1.66 = 1.566, so it stays cheaper until you redo 56.6% of the run.
  • $1.99 listing: 2.60 / 1.99 = 1.307, so the limit is 30.7%.
  • $2.48 listing: 2.60 / 2.48 = 1.048, so the limit is 4.8%.
  • $2.50 listing: 2.60 / 2.50 = 1.040, so the limit is 4.0%.

On the 80-hour run, 4.0% is 3.2 hours. Losing one machine late in the run without a good resume path wipes out the saving from a $2.50 listing. The $1.66 listing has far more room, which is why it is a fair pick for short, restartable work.


Below about $2 a GPU-hour, a listing can survive real rework; near $2.50, one bad restart erases the gap.

What happens on Nodus when a machine is lost mid-run?

Nodus starts a new attempt somewhere else and restores your files. Its attempts and recovery page describes the sequence. On a reclaim notice, Nodus asks your program for an urgent checkpoint while it prepares a replacement, which starts only once the old machine is provably gone. A machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and is declared lost after 60 seconds on shared capacity.

The contract is files, not memory. Your program writes weights, optimizer state and its step counter to /nodus/state, and the checkpoint guide shows the Job spec defaults:

recovery:
  continuity: Checkpointed      # restore the latest checkpoint into each new attempt
  checkpoint:
    paths: [/nodus/state]       # up to 64 absolute paths, all saved in one checkpoint

That is the work Shadeform's spot guide leaves to you: the polling, the relaunch and the restore. For a wider view of the same pattern across providers, see how GPU capacity failover works.

Where is Shadeform the better choice?

Shadeform is the better choice when you want a VM, not a managed run. If your team lives in SSH, tmux and its own scripts, a plain machine with no new job format is the shortest path. Shadeform gets you one from many providers without opening many accounts.

It also wins on price discovery. One API call sorted by price across 30+ clouds is hard to beat for finding the cheapest live H100, and its lowest listing in this check, $1.66, is below the Nodus rate. Short jobs that restart cleanly can bank that difference.

Three more cases favour it. You can link your own provider accounts and launch into them to spend existing credits. Shadeform offers reserved contracts, with a 12-month minimum term on its pricing page. And if you already use SkyPilot, Shadeform has a SkyPilot guide that adds its catalog as one more cloud.

Are SkyPilot, Vast.ai and Runpod better fits for some teams?

Yes, each one fits a narrower buyer than Shadeform or Nodus.

SkyPilot is the closest to Nodus in spirit. It is open source under Apache 2.0 and runs jobs on Kubernetes, Slurm, reserved GPUs or 20+ clouds that you hold accounts with. Its managed jobs recover from preemptions, node crashes and GPU errors, and your job can reload its latest checkpoint. You run the software and keep the provider bills.

Vast.ai is the sticker-price option. Its pricing page lists the H100 SXM from $1.70 per hour, with a 30-day median of $1.73. Like a Shadeform VM, you handle restarts yourself. Our Vast.ai alternatives post goes deeper.

Runpod fits teams that want per-second container pods on one provider. Its pricing page lists the H100 SXM at $4.39 per hour on Secure Cloud and from $2.69 on Community Cloud. See our Runpod alternatives guide for the trade-offs.

Can you connect a Shadeform account to Nodus?

No. Nodus's cloud accounts docs list AWS, GCP, Azure and a set of API-key clouds such as Lambda, Nebius and Runpod, and Shadeform is not among them. If you hold credits with one of the listed clouds, you can connect that account directly and have Nodus spend those credits before Nodus capacity (Beta).

How do you move a Shadeform workflow to Nodus?

Keep your training script and point its saves at /nodus/state. Then submit it as a Job from the project directory, with a dry run first. The commands come from the install and quickstart pages:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus run --name finetune --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 25 --timeout 8h --dry-run -- python train.py

The dry run uploads the directory and shows the estimate without starting anything. Remove --dry-run to submit. --max-cost sets a hard dollar limit for the Job, and nodus describe job/finetune shows its attempts, placement and cost. Your SSH key, startup script and polling loop go away; the state directory replaces them.

If you want to compare GPU types before committing, a Sweep runs the same Job across several GPUs and reports the cheapest and fastest cell. Our post on running one training job across several GPU clouds covers the wider design.

FAQ

Does Shadeform have more GPUs than going to a provider directly?

No. Its FAQ says it taps each provider's on-demand pool, so what you see on Shadeform is what you would see at the provider. What it adds is one search, one account and one bill across them.

Does Nodus work the same way as Shadeform?

No. Shadeform lists VMs for you to launch and manage, while Nodus runs the work itself. You submit a Job, Function or TrainingJob, Nodus picks the capacity, and recovery and billing are per run.

Do Shadeform spot instances resume automatically?

No. Its spot guide says a reclaimed instance is terminated and marked preempted, and billing stops. Restarting it, on spot or on-demand, is up to your own polling and relaunch code.

Can an AI agent buy GPU time through Shadeform or Nodus?

Both have a hosted MCP server. Shadeform's lets Claude Code, Cursor or Codex find and manage instances. The Nodus server creates resources only after an accepted dry run and runs under the person's own projects and spending limits.

Which data centers do Shadeform GPUs run in?

Shadeform's FAQ says it guarantees all GPUs are in Tier 3 or Tier 4 data centers. Machine SLAs are the underlying provider's, which Shadeform shares on request.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: I Built an AI Loop That Finds "Lost My Work" Bugs and Fixes Them Until the Test Passes
description:
We've all done it. You fill in a long sign-up form, a job application, or a checkout, press Back or Refresh, and everything you typed is gone. These "lost my work" bugs are everywhere, and unit tests rarely catch them because they only show up in a real browser.

For the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI, I built StillHere: a loop that catches these bugs in a real browser and keeps fixing them until the test passes.

What it does

StillHere runs a closed loop:

  1. Find it. Kane CLI drives a real Chrome session through a journey described in plain English: fill in a checkout, open another page, press Back, press Refresh, and check the cart, details, and current step are still there.
  2. Fix it. If anything is wiped, Kane's failure report becomes a repair prompt for the Codex coding agent, which fixes the app without weakening the test.
  3. Prove it. The exact same Kane objective re-runs, unchanged, until it passes.

It works for any form or multi-step flow via --objective, not just checkout.

How I built it

Node.js with no dependencies. StillHere calls Kane CLI with --agent, parses its NDJSON result, writes a failure report with evidence and screenshots, and pipes a repair prompt to codex exec. A sample shop with a real Back/Refresh bug is included, and npm run demo:loop resets the bug so you always see fail, fix, pass. Built solo with Codex.

What Kane caught

In the recorded run, pressing "Back to checkout" wiped the order: the cart, the customer's details, and the review step were all gone. Codex fixed it by saving state in sessionStorage plus browser history and restoring it on load and Back. Kane then passed through both Back and Refresh. The test was never changed to make it pass.

Challenges

Chrome crashed when launched from a sandbox, so Kane runs from a normal terminal. Long Kane runs timed out, so the default timeout became 300 seconds. I also made sure a run with no final Kane result counts as incomplete, not as a failure for the agent to "fix."

What I learned

Verifying in a real browser catches bugs a mock never would, and keeping the test fixed is what makes an AI fix trustworthy.

What's next

A GitHub Action that runs the loop on every pull request, plus ready-made objectives for sign-up, login, and multi-step forms.

Try it

  • Code and setup: https://github.com/Mzee04/stillhere
  • Demo: https://youtu.be/4R3yvR5oKvg

title: Swagger UI is from 2011. It’s Time to Upgrade to Scalar.
description:
You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe APIs, and everything working perfectly.

Then someone opens your /docs endpoint.

And there it is. The same old Swagger UI.

Don't get me wrong. Swagger UI is great and has served developers for years. But API documentation can look and feel much better.

That's where Scalar comes in.

What Is Scalar?

Scalar is an open-source API documentation tool that gives your OpenAPI documentation a cleaner, more modern interface.

Think of it as Swagger UI, but with a better developer experience.

Here's what makes it interesting:

  • Modern UI: Clean layout, dark mode, and customizable themes.
  • Built-in API client: Test endpoints directly without switching to Postman.
  • Code snippets: Generate request examples in JavaScript, Python, Go, and more.
  • Authentication: Support for Bearer tokens, API keys, and other OpenAPI security schemes.
  • OpenAPI support: Works with your existing OpenAPI specifications.

And the best part?

You don't need to change your backend or rewrite your API schemas.

Swagger UI vs. Scalar

Here's a quick comparison:

Feature Swagger UI Scalar
UI Design Traditional accordion layout Modern, clean interface
Dark Mode Requires customization Built-in
API Testing Basic Try it out Integrated API client
Code Snippets Configurable request snippets Multiple languages and clients
Authentication Bearer, API keys, OAuth2 Bearer, API keys, OAuth2
Search Endpoint filtering Integrated reference search
Customization CSS and configuration Built-in themes and configuration
OpenAPI 3.1 Supported Supported
Open Source Yes Yes

Both tools do the job, but Scalar focuses more on the overall developer experience, especially when exploring and testing APIs.

How Easy Is It to Integrate?

If you're using Fastify with @fastify/swagger already configured, it's just a few lines.

Install Scalar:

npm install @scalar/fastify-api-reference

Register it in your Fastify application:

await fastify.register(
  import('@scalar/fastify-api-reference'),
  {
    routePrefix: '/docs',
    configuration: {
      theme: 'purple',
    },
  }
);

Now open:

http://localhost:3000/docs

That's it. Your existing OpenAPI specification now has a modern documentation interface.

Scalar also supports NestJS, Express, Next.js, and other frameworks.

Should You Replace Swagger UI?

Not necessarily.

Swagger UI is still actively maintained and supports OpenAPI 3.1, authentication, and interactive requests.

Scalar simply offers a different, more polished experience for exploring and testing APIs.

If you're happy with Swagger UI, there's no reason to rush.

But if you want better-looking, developer-friendly API documentation without much effort, Scalar is definitely worth trying.

Final Thoughts

We spend hours improving our backend architecture, performance, and code quality.

Why not give the same attention to our API documentation?

A great API deserves a great developer experience.

Give Scalar a try on your next project.

title: In a Chat Message, the Formatting Is Part of the Data
description:
A lot of my work runs through one Slack channel. I post numbered requests, REQ-141, REQ-142 and so on, and a browser agent picks them up, does the work, and answers in the thread. A small script posts a weekly request of its own every Monday, and before posting it works out the next free number by reading the channel history.

On Monday the script posted REQ-143. There was already a REQ-143. I had posted it myself at one in the morning.

The underscore is a word character

The numbering code was one line:

nums = [int(n) for m in history for n in re.findall(r"\bREQ-(\d{3})\b", m["text"])]

That looks right. \b is a word boundary, so it stops XREQ-143 from matching, and the trailing \b stops it from reading the first three digits of REQ-1430.

But the requests I post go through a connector that writes my titles in italics, and Slack stores italics as underscores. My request's text began:

_REQ-143: Go ahead with part B now_

A word boundary is the point between a word character and a non-word character. In regex, word characters are letters, digits and the underscore. So between _ and R there is no boundary. Both sides count as "word". \bREQ never matched, my request was invisible to the counter, and the script happily took 143 again.

To the parser, the markup isn't around the message. It is the message.

I had been thinking of _..._ as "how it looks". The regex was reading what was actually stored, and what was stored was an underscore glued to the front of the thing I was searching for.

The fix keeps the guard I actually needed, digits after the number, and drops the one that assumed clean text before it:

re.findall(r"REQ-(\d{3})(?!\d)", text)

I tested it against the shapes that really occur in the channel, not the one I'd imagined:

>>> re.findall(r"REQ-(\d{3})(?!\d)", "_REQ-143: x *REQ-142* REQ-1234")
['143', '142']

Italic, bold and plain all match, and a four-digit number doesn't produce a false 123.

The language tag that ate a line

The same day, a request listed fifteen properties in a code block, so the agent would see a clean list:

```1. First property (city)
2. Second property
...
```

The agent answered items 2 to 15. I resent the missing one as part of the next request, formatted the same way. It went missing again.

Text on the same line as an opening triple backtick isn't content. It's the language tag, the thing that tells the renderer to highlight python or js. My first item had been sent as a language called 1. First property (city), which the renderer treated as metadata and quietly didn't show. Nothing errored. The list simply started at 2.

The fix is a newline after the opening fence, every time:

```
1. First property (city)
2. Second property
```

The same mistake twice

Both bugs came from writing for the renderer and forgetting that something else reads the source. I wrote italics so a title would look like a title. I put a list on the fence line so the message would look compact. In both cases the thing reading the text downstream, a regex in one, a markdown parser in the other, saw characters I'd stopped noticing.

What I do now:

  • Match against the stored form, not the displayed one. If a channel stores formatting as characters (_, *, ~, backticks), assume any line you parse may be wrapped in them. Don't lean on \b beside text that might start with an underscore.
  • Test parsers with real messages from the channel. My regex test strings were all clean, plain-text REQ-142. The channel has never contained a clean one.
  • Put a newline after every opening code fence in anything a machine will read. The first line belongs to the tag.

Neither bug was clever. Both sat in the gap between what a message looks like and what it contains.

title: Temporal Pseudo-RGB Encoding for Label-Free Detection of VEEV Infection in Human Brain Endothelial Cells
description:
arXiv:2611.21892v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Label-free detection of viral infection is central to antiviral screening and pathogen surveillance. Most deep-learning methods analyze individual frames and do not model temporal progression. We evaluate temporal pseudo-RGB encoding, which stacks three time-offset brightfield frames ($t{-}6$ h, $t{-}3$ h, $t$) as the red, green, and blue channels of a single image so that morphological change becomes color and an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural network (CNN) can be trained on infection trajectories without architectural modification. In human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMVEC) infected with Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) TC-83, a multi-task network predicts infected-versus-mock status and time post-infection in one forward pass. Across three experimental runs under leave-one-row-out cross-validation, with all 36 wells scored out of fold, the encoding reaches 91.6% accuracy against 87.4% for the single-frame model (paired difference $+4.2$ percentage points, 95% CI $[+2.5, +6.1]$; sign-flip $p = 3\times10^{-5}$; well-level inference, conditional on three runs). At the late-phase endpoint (40-48 h), where floating cells and debris can make conventional brightfield images difficult to interpret, the advantage widens to $+23.9$ points (95% CI $[+19.2, +28.9]$). Time post-infection is recovered on the fixed row split with MAE = 1.31 h ($R^2 = 0.975$). Among the temporal models tested the encoding has the highest mean accuracy, at a fraction of the cost of the recurrent and 3D convolutional alternatives, though only its margin over the single-frame model is resolved; the tested ViT-B/16 backbone showed no corresponding gain, so the finding is limited to convolutional backbones and this virus-cell system.

title: URL-Synchronized Pagination in Vue 3: Typing RoutePagination and Testing External Behavior
description:
In data-heavy dashboards, tables, and issue trackers, pagination should always synchronize with the browser's URL query parameters. Storing the active page number in ?page=X enables users to share direct links, bookmark filtered views, and use browser back/forward buttons seamlessly.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3200), I migrated the shared RoutePagination component and its unit test suite to TypeScript.

Beyond adding type annotations, this migration provided an opportunity to modernize the component's two-way binding using Vue 3.4's defineModel() macro and refactor the test suite from inspecting internal component state to asserting user-facing behavior.

1. Modernizing Two-Way Binding with defineModel<number>()

Previously, RoutePagination.vue relied on runtime prop definitions and untyped model declarations:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  totalRows: { type: Number, required: true },
  perPage: { type: Number, required: true },
});

const currentPage = defineModel({ required: false, type: Number });
const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage) => {
  router.push({ query: { ...route.query, page: newPage } });
};
</script>

The TypeScript Refactoring

In the migrated version, we introduced compile-time type declarations and handled asynchronous router promises cleanly:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import { onMounted } from 'vue';
import { useRoute, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { numberParam } from '~/common/QueryParams';

const props = defineProps<{
  totalRows: number;
  perPage: number;
}>();

// Strongly typed two-way v-model binding
const currentPage = defineModel<number>();

const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage: number | string) => {
  const query = route.query;
  // Explicitly void floating navigation promise
  void router.push({ query: { ...query, page: newPage } });
};

onMounted(() => {
  const page = numberParam(route.query.page) || 1;
  currentPage.value = page;
});
</script>

Key Technical Details:

  • defineModel<number>(): Replaces manual modelValue prop and update:modelValue emit declarations with Vue 3.4's type-safe macro.
  • Handling Floating Promises (void router.push): Calling asynchronous routing methods without await can trigger @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises. Adding void explicitly marks the promise as intentionally unawaited in event callbacks.

2. Refactoring Specs: Testing External Contracts, Not Internal State

In older specs, unit tests frequently inspected component internals using wrapper.vm:

// ❌ Old Anti-Pattern: Checking private component internals
expect(wrapper.vm.currentPage).toBe(2);

While wrapper.vm works in JavaScript, relying on it creates fragile tests that break whenever internal variable names change. It also creates typing friction in TypeScript because wrapper.vm is not strictly typed unless heavily annotated.

The Modernized Spec

In RoutePagination.spec.ts, we refactored assertions to observe what the user and parent components actually observe:

  1. Child Props: Verifying what the underlying <BPagination> component receives.
  2. Emitted Events: Verifying what update:modelValue emits to the parent.
  3. URL State: Verifying what router.currentRoute.value.query reflects. 
import { flushPromises, mount, type VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import type { Router } from 'vue-router';
import { createTestRouter } from '~/spec/testHelpers';
import RoutePagination from './RoutePagination.vue';

const defaultProps = { totalRows: 10, perPage: 5 };

let router: Router;
let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = mount(RoutePagination, {
    props: { ...defaultProps, ...props },
    global: { plugins: [router] },
  });
};

const findBPagination = () => wrapper.findComponent(BPagination);
const findPage2Button = () => findBPagination().find('button[aria-posinset="2"]');

beforeEach(async () => {
  router = await createTestRouter('/leaderboard');
});

describe('changing page', () => {
  it('updates route and emits current page', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findPage2Button().trigger('click');
    await flushPromises();

    // Asserting actual URL query change
    expect(router.currentRoute.value.query).toStrictEqual({ page: '2' });

    // Asserting child UI received modelValue update
    expect(findBPagination().props('modelValue')).toBe(2);
  });
});

Key Takeaways

  1. Use defineModel<T>(): Simplifies component code by replacing separate prop/emit definitions with a single typed reactive reference.
  2. Handle Router Promises: Use void router.push(...) in event handlers where awaiting the navigation is unnecessary.
  3. Test the Black Box: Test emitted events and child component props rather than private wrapper.vm properties. Tests will be sturdier and easier to type.

Check out the merged Merge Request on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Contributors MR !3200
