title: EcoFlow, Jackery, BLUETTI and Anker SOLIX: Shopify Lessons From Four Portable Power Stores
description:
Cover: EcoFlow official US page, captured 17 November 2026; the article compares four storefronts.

A comparison of storefronts is most useful when the rows describe the same type of decision. These four portable-power pages illustrate different ways to help shoppers navigate information. The following is a US-site observation reviewed on 17 November 2026, not a product-performance ranking, a conversion study, or a claim that every brand uses a particular Shopify plan.

Four observable patterns

  1. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: product details, service information and configuration choices appear along the purchase journey. The page also qualifies a central-air-conditioning example with a laboratory condition.
  2. Jackery HomePower: the navigation offers routes by product type and by scenario, including home-backup solution levels.
  3. BLUETTI AC200L: a note on a particular battery connection links to its required cable. The reviewed main option was discontinued; this is historical analysis, not an availability claim.
  4. Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus: a North American power-standard notice is visible near the purchase area and the FAQ distinguishes operating conditions.

Each observation comes from a different page and model. Do not combine their electrical specifications into one fictitious product or compare prices from different regions and dates as if they were simultaneous offers.

Compare purchase journeys without inventing outcomes

Use the same sequence for each site: how a visitor enters the catalog, how the page identifies the specific offer, how conditions are attached to a claim, and how the next relevant step is presented. EcoFlow's scene-based charging explanation, Jackery's category and scenario navigation, BLUETTI's named accessory link and Anker SOLIX's operating-condition FAQ are different kinds of evidence; they should not be scored as if they measured the same thing.

The original article contrasts independent stores with marketplaces and asks whether detailed guidance gives the brand a reason for a customer to stay. That is a useful research question. Page content alone cannot establish that shoppers will not return to a marketplace, that a design reduces returns, or that one brand has the highest conversion rate. A merchant could evaluate those hypotheses with task testing and appropriately collected first-party data.

For a fair editorial comparison, retain source URL, market, date, page type, model and the precise observation for each cell. Pricing, stock and offers should be compared only after aligning market and time; if the required evidence is missing, leave the comparison out. Treat AI-search visibility as a separate experiment, not a guaranteed result of adding markup.

Define the comparison dimension first

For a content team, two reasonable dimensions are the entry path and the way qualifying conditions are presented. A row about “entry path” should contain an observation of the same kind for each site; a row about “conditions” should describe each site's handling of conditions. These are design observations, not proof of customer behavior. If an observation cannot be confirmed for one brand, omit the row until the evidence is complete rather than inventing a value.

The code below displays two editorial comparison rows from a custom.store_comparison page metafield referencing a metaobject. It requires four entries for each row, escaping text rather than mixing live products' attributes. It does not fetch competitor pages or validate that entered observations are true.

{%- comment -%}
  Storefront information architecture comparison; illustrative only.
  Do not infer product performance, electrical safety, or business results.
  Only use verified observations; do not supply invented defaults.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign comparison = page.metafields.custom.store_comparison.value -%}
{%- if comparison != blank -%}
  {%- assign ecoflow_entry = comparison.ecoflow_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign jackery_entry = comparison.jackery_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign bluetti_entry = comparison.bluetti_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign anker_entry = comparison.anker_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign ecoflow_condition = comparison.ecoflow_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign jackery_condition = comparison.jackery_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign bluetti_condition = comparison.bluetti_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign anker_condition = comparison.anker_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign entry_complete = false -%}
  {%- assign condition_complete = false -%}
  {%- if ecoflow_entry != blank and jackery_entry != blank and bluetti_entry != blank and anker_entry != blank -%}{%- assign entry_complete = true -%}{%- endif -%}
  {%- if ecoflow_condition != blank and jackery_condition != blank and bluetti_condition != blank and anker_condition != blank -%}{%- assign condition_complete = true -%}{%- endif -%}
  {%- if entry_complete or condition_complete -%}
<table class="store-comparison">
  <caption>Storefront information architecture comparison</caption>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">Dimension</th><th scope="col">EcoFlow</th><th scope="col">Jackery</th><th scope="col">BLUETTI</th><th scope="col">Anker SOLIX</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    {%- if entry_complete %}
    <tr><th scope="row">Entry path</th><td>{{ ecoflow_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ jackery_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ bluetti_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ anker_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td></tr>
    {%- endif %}
    {%- if condition_complete %}
    <tr><th scope="row">Applicable conditions</th><td>{{ ecoflow_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ jackery_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ bluetti_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ anker_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td></tr>
    {%- endif %}
  </tbody>
</table>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Testing and editorial review

The table hides an incomplete row rather than presenting a four-way comparison with a missing value. Verify all four combinations of missing and present rows, and test long labels on narrow screens. A production implementation should also provide responsive table behavior and preserve the relationship between column and row headers. Re-check each source before use; these pages may change independently. A poster-style comparison, if used, should reflect each site's observed visual identity and be reviewed for factual and typographic accuracy.

title: Giga Energy Secures $1 Billion AI Cloud Deal for 60 MW Data Center in Hunting County, Texas
description:
U.S.-based AI data center developer Giga Energy has signed a 10-year, USD 1 billion lease with an unnamed AI cloud provider for Project Clay, a 60 MW GigaBase AI data center campus in Hunt County, Texas.

Giga broke ground on the project in July and will develop, own, and operate the campus, which the customer will use for AI computing capacity. The site is slated to be ready for service in spring 2027.

*GigaBase Targets Faster Data Center Deployment
*
Alongside the lease announcement, Giga officially unveiled GigaBase, its data center system engineered to tackle lengthy construction timelines, heavy water consumption, and strain on local utilities.

As part of its expansion into Data Center Projects in the US, the company says Project Clay will be completed in under eight months, less than half the time of traditional builds.

Power Strategy Taps Underutilized Capacity
A cornerstone of the project is an investment in new electrical infrastructure that draws on underutilized capacity from dedicated power infrastructure in the county.

The design ensures the campus does not pull from distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses.

Giga positioned the project against the priorities laid out by Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has called for data centers to pay for their own power, deploy water-efficient cooling technologies, prevent infrastructure costs from shifting onto residents, and ensure communities benefit from growth.

This is exactly the kind of AI infrastructure Texas needs," said Brent Whitehead, president and co-founder at Giga Energy.

"Communities shouldn't have to choose between economic growth and protecting local resources. We've engineered our GigaBase system and development approach so they don't have to."

Cooling System Runs Independently of Local Water
Project Clay replaces open-loop evaporative cooling with a fully closed-loop system that operates independently of local water supplies, whether municipal or groundwater, to cool its IT equipment.

According to the company, the facility consumes no water for compute operations.
The only local water use will come from sinks and employee bathrooms, comparable to a small business office and on par with the annual usage of two homes. Giga frames this approach as aligning with Texas' growing emphasis on water-efficient data center development in drought-prone regions.

Jobs and Tax Revenue Head to Hunt County

The roughly 30-acre campus will serve hyperscale and AI cloud customers while, according to Giga, generating lasting economic value for the county.

The build phase is expected to create approximately 300 construction jobs, with 24 permanent full-time positions carrying estimated annual salaries of USD 116,000 to USD 180,000.

The project is also projected to generate millions in new recurring annual tax revenue that the company says can help fund local schools, infrastructure, emergency services, and other essential public needs.
"We believe AI infrastructure should leave a community stronger than it found it. That means creating high-paying jobs, expanding the local tax base, and making long-term investments that benefit residents for decades," said Whitehead.

"Hunt County is gaining an economic engine that will support schools, public services, and future growth for generations."

*Off-Site Manufacturing Drives the Schedule
*
At the heart of the GigaBase system is a factory-first construction model in which much of the facility is manufactured off-site before final assembly in the community.

Giga says this approach significantly shortens construction schedules, reduces truck traffic, minimizes disruption to local roads and housing, and allows communities to realize economic benefits sooner.
The company describes the resulting campus as faster to build, lighter on local infrastructure, and purpose-built to be a long-term community partner.

Giga has previously promoted the concept under the banner "shovel-ready to rack-ready in 9 months" when introducing the GigaBase system.

Company Background and the Deal's Significance

Giga Energy is a U.S.-based manufacturer, developer, and operator of modular AI data centers, actively contributing to the growth of data center projects and infrastructure development in the US.

The company operates factories in Long Beach and Houston, has delivered more than 7 GW of electrical infrastructure, and has more than 258.5 MW of critical IT capacity completed and under development.

The 10-year, USD 1 billion lease represents a significant commercial milestone for the young company as it scales its modular approach. The customer, an AI cloud provider, has not been publicly named.

With demand for AI infrastructure accelerating across the United States, Giga leaders say the next generation of data centers must do more than power technology and must also earn the trust of the communities where they are built.

The company frames Project Clay as that philosophy in practice, pairing large-scale computing capacity with measures intended to avoid burdening existing residents and utilities.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Skin-Tone Color Casts in Ultra-Lightweight Photo Retouching Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.22106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Color casts are expected to come from the scene or camera, and a retouching model removes them. We report a case where the model leaves one: an ultra-lightweight retouching network renders human skin greener than the original because it under-restores the skin chroma that a degradation removes and, even on clean inputs, adds a small hue shift of its own. A common paired-data-free recipe, synthetic self-supervision (degrade high-quality images, learn to restore them), silently produces this cast while whole-frame PSNR/SSIM stay essentially unchanged. In a representative 6,825-parameter histogram-conditioned network, the cast appears in 52 of 70 portraits under a ground-truth-anchored, white-balance-free protocol. Both a histogram-conditioned and a CNN-conditioned network develop the cast under synthetic self-supervision, yet both are near-neutral in-domain when trained on MIT-Adobe FiveK expert pairs. Image-level objectives miss it: a global-mean green loss worsens the cast (52/70 to 57/70). With zero added parameters, our per-pixel, skin-masked, asymmetric green-excess loss reduces the cast to 1/70 across stratified skin tones (68.1% to 2.2% over the 70,000-image FFHQ corpus; 64.4% to 0.8% on held-out CelebA-HQ photos). In-domain FiveK PSNR/SSIM are unchanged (+0.13 dB, +0.004), at the cost of a small whole-frame CIEDE2000 increase (8.77 to 9.69) and a magenta over-correction where skin is nearly neutral (skin Delta a* -1.5 to +4.4 and CIEDE2000 5.6 to 6.4 on clean inputs): the loss targets the signed green-magenta axis, not total skin-color fidelity. The same loss suppresses the cast across three ultra-light architectures. A whole-frame green metric correlates with skin-region CIEDE2000 at the method level (Spearman rho = 0.89). The final network exports to a 35 KB TFLite model.

title: Physical UX in Angular, from CSS springs to easter eggs on a CV site
description:
A CV site is a strange thing to over-engineer. Most visitors stay for under a minute. That is exactly why I spent so much time on how mine moves: in a short visit, the feel of the interface is part of the message. A button that gives under your finger and springs back, or a menu selection that glides instead of flickering, says "someone cared" faster than any paragraph.

My thesis: an interface should behave like a small physical world with one set of rules. One material, one gravity, one press, one spring. Those rules should be written down as tokens, checked by the build, and switched off as a set when the user asks for less motion.

This is how I did that on my CV site (live, source), a prerendered Angular 22 app with signals and no zone.js. It covers what research and platform guidelines say, what I took from them, where I deviated, the easter eggs I added on purpose, and the bugs that taught me the most.

TL;DR

  • One material. Every duration, curve, radius and state colour is a CSS custom property. A Node script fails the build when a component uses a raw number of milliseconds or a hand-mixed hover colour.
  • Springs without JavaScript. A damped spring is sampled into a CSS linear() easing. A little bounce for small things, a no-overshoot variant meant for size and layout, no bounce at all on exits.
  • Feedback timing follows the research. A press responds within 80 ms, tooltips wait 400 ms and then "warm up", exits are shorter than entrances, and a navigation jump glides once instead of hopping through every section.
  • Scroll-driven choreography in CSS. animation-timeline: view() with the easing inside the keyframe. One scroll-derived number, --p, drives three elements of the header hand-over.
  • Reduced motion removes movement as a set, because every movement duration token goes to zero. The figure, the confetti and the pointer effects are not mounted at all.
  • The easter eggs are deliberate. They form a discoverable second layer: never required, hidden from assistive tech, off under reduced motion, no data collected. The reasoning draws on the peak–end rule. It is design intent, not a measured result.
  • The engineering keeps it sustainable. Pure TypeScript logic at 100 % coverage, a thin rendering layer, 220 unit and 114 end-to-end tests, axe, a strict CSP with build-time script hashes, and a Lighthouse gate.

1. One material: tokens, and a build that enforces them

The first decision was to think in kinds of motion rather than milliseconds: a press, a short state change, a medium move, a ring spreading out, something big arriving, a playful flourish. Each kind gets one token:

// app/src/styles/_tokens.scss (trimmed)
// Spring: stiffness 220, damping 22, mass 1 (about 3 % overshoot), sampled for linear().
--ease-spring: linear(0, 0.049, 0.164, 0.308, 0.458, 0.597, 0.717, 0.815, 0.891, 0.947,
  0.985, 1.009, 1.023, 1.03, 1.031, 1.029, 1.025, 1.02, 1.016, 1.012, 1.008, 1.005, 1.003, 1.001, 1);
--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);    /* entering */
--ease-in: cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15);    /* leaving: the exit is quicker than the entrance */
--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);     /* a move across the screen, and loops */
--ease-spring-smooth: linear(0, 0.079, 0.236, /* … */ 0.998, 1); /* no overshoot: size, layout, big surfaces */
--dur-tap: 80ms;    /* a press goes in within a tenth of a second */
--dur-fade: 200ms;  /* opacity and colour only */
--press-scale: 0.96;
--tip-delay: 400ms;
--dur-press: 150ms;
--dur-short: 250ms;
--dur-med: 400ms;
--dur-ring: 600ms;
--dur-long: 700ms;
--dur-play: 900ms;

The curves are borrowed. --ease-in-out is Material 3's emphasized cubic-bezier(.2, 0, 0, 1) and --ease-in is its emphasized accelerate (.3, 0, .8, .15), from the material-web motion tokens. The durations sit on Material's 50 ms grid but use fewer steps: six are easy to choose between, sixteen are not.

Tokens only help if they are used, so scripts/check-design.mjs fails the build when:

  1. a corner radius above 6 px is not a token (or a full round),
  2. a transition duration is a number rather than a --dur-* token,
  3. an animation under one second is not a token (long and endless ones are allowed),
  4. a hover, pressed, selected or current state is painted with an on-the-spot color-mix() instead of a --tint-* token.

The transition rule is the interesting one. It has to tell a duration apart from a delay:

// app/scripts/check-design.mjs (trimmed)
for (const m of text.matchAll(/(?<![\w-])transition:\s*([^;}]*)/g)) {
  // each property's first time is its duration (a second one is a delay): it must be a token, not a number
  for (const item of m[1].split(/,(?![^(]*\))/)) {
    const first = item.match(/(\d*\.?\d+m?s)|var\(--(?:dur|lag|lead)[^)]*\)|calc\([^)]*\)/);
    if (first?.[1]) at(m.index, 'duration', `"transition: ${item.trim().slice(0, 60)}" … use a --dur-* token`);
  }
}

left var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms passes (the 90 ms is a delay) and opacity 200ms ease fails. It is a regex linter, not a CSS parser, and it has still caught me several times.

2. The physics

Springs in CSS with linear()

linear() takes a list of progress points and connects them with straight segments. MDN points out that with enough points it approximates any curve, and the values may go above 1, which is all an overshoot needs. I simulated a damped spring once (stiffness 220, damping 22, mass 1) and pasted 25 samples into the token.

The numbers behind it: the damping ratio is ζ = 22 / (2·√220) ≈ 0.74, and the overshoot of an underdamped spring with that ratio is about e^(−ζπ/√(1−ζ²)) ≈ 3 %. You can read that off the curve, which peaks at 1.031.

Is 3 % right? Apple's WWDC23 session Animate with springs describes a spring by duration (pacing) and bounce. Bounce 0 is the default ("a great general purpose spring"), around 15 % "doesn't feel very bouncy yet" but brisker, 30 % gives "noticeable bounciness", and above about 0.4 "may feel too exaggerated for a UI element". Apple's bounce is not my damping ratio, so I don't claim an exact mapping. My spring is gentle and reserved for small things: a press releasing, a chip label flipping, the menu pill, a commit dot growing. Anything that changes size or layout should get --ease-spring-smooth (no overshoot) or an ease-out, because bouncing layout makes text wobble. That is Apple's zero-bounce default where it matters.

linear() is a shape, not a time, so the duration is chosen per use: 250 ms for a press release, 400 ms for the menu pill. Pacing first, then bounce, as the talk suggests.

What CSS springs cannot do is keep velocity. Apple notes that a retargeted spring "uses the velocity it had when it was retargeted". A reversed CSS transition starts again from rest. That is acceptable for a menu pill, and it is one reason the figure in section 5 lives in TypeScript.

Press: in within 80 ms, out with a spring

NN/g's response-time limits (going back to Miller 1968 and Card et al. 1991) say that 0.1 s is "about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously". NN/g's animation and attention article applies the same number to feedback: the effect "must begin within 0.1 seconds of the initial user action". So the press goes in within --dur-tap (80 ms) with an ease-out, and goes back over 250 ms with the spring:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
.chip, .btn {
  transition: scale var(--dur-short) var(--ease-spring),
    background-color var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out), box-shadow var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out);
}
.chip:active, .btn:active {
  scale: var(--press-scale);
  transition-duration: var(--dur-tap);
  transition-timing-function: var(--ease-out);
}

The trick is that the transition declared on the state you are going to wins. Going into :active, the 80 ms ease-out applies. Leaving it, the base rule's 250 ms spring applies. One property, two different physics, no script.

On iOS Safari none of this showed up at first. WebKit bug 138816, filed in 2014, documents that :active on touch only applies when the page has a touch event listener. The fix is one passive no-op listener in home.ts, with a comment explaining why it is there.

Exits are shorter than entrances

NN/g's animation duration guidance says most UI motion belongs in 100–500 ms, that entrances "usually need a subtly longer duration" than exits, that ease-out suits things arriving and ease-in things leaving, and that "completely linear motion looks weird". The role cards in the Experience section follow it with the native ::details-content pseudo-element and interpolate-size:

// app/src/app/sections/experience.ts (styles, trimmed)
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  details { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }
  details::details-content {            /* the state it goes to when closing */
    block-size: 0; opacity: 0; overflow: clip;
    transition: block-size var(--dur-short) var(--ease-in), opacity var(--dur-press) var(--ease-in),
      content-visibility var(--dur-short) allow-discrete;
  }
  details[open]::details-content {      /* the state it goes to when opening */
    block-size: auto; opacity: 1;
    transition: block-size var(--dur-med) var(--ease-spring), opacity var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out) 50ms,
      content-visibility var(--dur-med) allow-discrete;
  }
}

Opening takes 400 ms with the spring and a text fade that starts 50 ms late. Closing takes 250 ms with ease-in and no spring. content-visibility … allow-discrete keeps the content painted while it collapses (the MDN ::details-content page shows the same pattern). Browsers without these features simply open the card at once, which is a fine fallback.

Tooltips: a delay, then a warm-up

A tooltip that appears the instant the pointer crosses it turns a row of icons into flicker. NN/g's mega-menu guidance uses a 0.5 s rest before showing hover content. PatternFly defaults to a 300 ms entry delay. I picked 400 ms (--tip-delay). Keyboard focus shows the tip at once, because NN/g's tooltip guidelines warn that hover-only tooltips are inaccessible.

The delay becomes annoying once the reader is looking for tooltips, for example when running along the menu. So core/tips.ts adds a warm-up: once a tip has really been shown (it listens for the animationstart of tip-in), leaving it puts html.tips-warm on the page for 300 ms, and in that window the CSS sets animation-delay: 0s. Escape sets html.tips-off until the pointer or the focus moves. The script only toggles classes. The timing stays in CSS.

A selection pill that travels, stretches and waits

The desktop menu has one selection pill. It is a real element positioned with CSS anchor positioning on whichever link currently holds anchor-name: --nav-target. When the anchor changes, left and right transition. To make it feel like something with mass, the leading edge moves fast with an ease-out and the trailing edge follows with the spring, so the pill stretches in the direction of travel:

// app/src/app/shell/header.ts (styles, trimmed)
.links { --lead: calc(var(--dur-short) * 0.75); --lag: var(--dur-med); }
.links[data-dir='right'] .sel {
  transition: left var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms, right var(--lead) var(--ease-out) 90ms, …;
}
.links[data-dir='left'] .sel {
  transition: left var(--lead) var(--ease-out) 90ms, right var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms, …;
}
@media (hover: hover) {
  .links:has(a:hover) a[aria-current]:not(:hover) { anchor-name: none; }
  .links a:hover { anchor-name: --nav-target; }
  .links:has(a:hover) .sel { transition-delay: 0s; }
}

The 90 ms delay is a small piece of hover intent. It applies only on the way back to the current item, so a pointer that crosses the menu's edge for a moment does not send the pill away and back. Following the pointer is immediate. The only script involved sets data-dir.

A navigation jump glides once

Clicking "Contact" in the menu smooth-scrolls past four sections. In the first version the active-section tracker named each of them in turn, and the pill hopped across the whole menu. Accurate, and wrong. holdActive(id) in core/active.ts now names the destination at once and ignores everything in between until scrollend fires, or after 1.2 s if the page didn't have to scroll. The smooth scroll itself is scroll-behavior: smooth in CSS, which reduced motion turns off. No script animates a scroll.

Scroll-driven reveals, with the easing inside the keyframe

Section content settles in as it enters the viewport, using animation-timeline: view(). No IntersectionObserver and no script:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .reveal { animation: reveal linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: entry 0% entry 40%; }
  }
}
@keyframes reveal {
  from { transform: translateY(18px); animation-timing-function: var(--ease-out); }
  to { transform: none; }
}

On a scroll timeline the animation's own linear is correct, since the element should track the scroll 1:1. But a linear ramp stops dead at the end of its range. An ease-out on the keyframe (it applies from that keyframe to the next) lets the element settle while still being driven by the scroll. It is transform-only, so a contrast audit never catches faded text mid-reveal.

One scroll number, three elements

As you scroll past the hero, the large portrait drains from the top, the header's avatar slot fills from the bottom like a progress bar, and the name is written out beside it. An earlier version flew a cloned image across the page, which meant layout reads every frame, a duplicate image and z-index fights with the glass header. The current version computes one number and lets CSS do the rest:

// app/src/app/shell/avatar-dock.ts (trimmed)
const distance = img.getBoundingClientRect().bottom + window.scrollY - slot.getBoundingClientRect().bottom;
const raw = distance > 0 ? clamp01(window.scrollY / distance) : 1;
const p = reduce.matches ? (raw >= 1 ? 1 : 0) : raw;
box?.style.setProperty('--p', p.toFixed(3));   // the hero portrait
brand.style.setProperty('--p', p.toFixed(3));  // the header avatar and the name

.portrait img { clip-path: inset(calc(var(--p, 0) * 100%) 0 0 0 round var(--radius)); }      /* drains */
.fill        { clip-path: inset(calc((1 - var(--p, 0)) * 100%) 0 0 0); }                     /* fills */
.mark        { --edge: calc(var(--p, 0) * 140%);                                              /* is written */
               mask-image: linear-gradient(90deg, #000 calc(var(--edge) - 40%), transparent var(--edge)); }

It runs backwards when you scroll back up. The header image reuses the hero's currentSrc (no second request), nothing reads layout at scrollY === 0, and under reduced motion p simply jumps from 0 to 1.

Time-based easing, not per-frame easing

The animated background draws contour lines with marching squares on a canvas. They drift with the scroll and bend around the pointer. Its first version eased with per-frame factors, t += (goal - t) * 0.12. On a 120 Hz display that runs twice as often and settles twice as fast. The fix is exponential easing with time constants:

// app/src/app/shell/backdrop.ts
const dt = Math.min(100, stamp ? now - stamp : 16.7);
stamp = now;
const ease = (ms: number): number => 1 - Math.exp(-dt / ms);
t += (g.t - t) * ease(130);   // 0.12 per frame at 60 Hz ≈ a 130 ms time constant
bump = { x: bump.x + (aim.x - bump.x) * ease(85), y: …, k: bump.k + (aim.k - bump.k) * ease(200) };

The constants come from the old factors (−16.7 / ln(1 − 0.12) ≈ 130 ms), so 60 Hz looks exactly as before. And the loop stops once everything has settled.

3. What the research says, and what I did with it

Most of these are guidelines or conventions, not controlled studies. The table says which is which.

iOS :active needs a touch listener WebKit bug 138816 (bug report) One passive no-op touchstart home.ts

Where I deviated:

  • I use bounce at all. Apple's default is zero. I use a little, on small, user-initiated things, where it reads as "this object has mass". I would not defend it on anything big.
  • Some motion is longer than 500 ms. --dur-ring (600), --dur-long (700) and --dur-play (900) exceed NN/g's range. They are used for one-off flourishes, never for something the user waits on.
  • I have no user research of my own. Everything above was verified by tests and by watching. Nothing was measured with real users.

4. Reduced motion, done as a set

Because every movement uses a token, reduced motion is mostly one rule:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  :root { --dur-tap: 0s; --dur-press: 0s; --dur-short: 0s; --dur-med: 0s; --dur-ring: 0s; --dur-long: 0s; --dur-play: 0s; }
  .chip:active, .btn:active { scale: none; }
  ::view-transition-group(*), ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) { animation: none !important; }
}

Everything that uses a duration token becomes instant. States still change and nothing is left half-animated. On top of that:

  • Scroll-driven reveals sit inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, so they never apply.
  • scroll-behavior goes back to auto, so menu jumps are instant.
  • The figure, the confetti, the pointer-lit surfaces and the portrait tilt are not started. Each checks matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and returns before attaching anything.
  • The background contour lines are drawn once and stay still. An end-to-end test scrolls and moves the mouse, then compares a checksum of the canvas pixels before and after.

The intent is to remove movement and keep fades: A List Apart treats "non-moving properties, like opacity, color, and blurs" as unlikely to cause trouble, and a fade still tells the user what changed. To be honest about the current state, the --dur-fade token that reduced motion leaves alone is not used by any component yet, so most fades become instant too (see the limits).

For WCAG 2.2.2, the only thing that moves on its own for more than five seconds is the aurora behind the hero. It pauses when the hero leaves the screen, runs two alternations (drift 70s … 2 alternate) and then rests, and it is off under reduced motion. WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) is covered because all interaction-triggered motion goes through the same query.

5. Gamification as a deliberate technique

The site has a second layer that you don't need and might not find. It exists on purpose.

The mechanics:

  • The figure. A small Prince of Persia-style stick figure sits at the end of the soft-skills row. Rest the mouse on a tile and it pulls itself up and runs after the pointer: it jumps gaps, grabs and climbs ledges, drops down, and climbs a web line to tiles far above. Leave past the end of the row and it runs off the cliff. In about a quarter of falls it shoots a web line and swings back. Otherwise a small cross rises over a patch of swamp in the footer, on the side it fell from. On touch screens, taps act as the pointer.
  • The scratch card. The hero portrait has a coin cursor. Drag over it and the photo scratches off to reveal one of ten prizes per language (never the same twice in a row): familiar scams that give themselves away, plus a copy-address button. Clear about two fifths (a quarter on touch) and the rest falls away in confetti. The card stays for five seconds with a countdown line, and then the photo heals.
  • Shift ×3. A photo scene, then a "stats sheet" that reads the page's own numbers live from the browser's Performance APIs: requests, third-party requests, cookies, storage keys, bytes, LCP, CLS, plus the release, test counts and coverage written at build time. The easter egg is also evidence.
  • The career graph. Experience drawn as a contribution graph (one square per year per skill family) that you scrub with a pointer or a finger.
  • The header hand-over from section 2.

The intent, and what it is based on:

  • A peak and a clean ending. The peak–end rule (NN/g, based on Kahneman and Fredrickson's research) says that people judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and by its end. So there is one peak that is the visitor's own doing (scratching, or watching the figure fall) and a quiet, slightly funny ending: the footer, where the visitor's own play is still visible as crosses in the swamp.
  • A discoverable second layer. The coin cursor, a console line (stat → shift shift shift), the figure waiting on the end of the row. Hints, not instructions. I don't cite a curiosity study here because I didn't verify one I'd stand behind. This is design intent.
  • Variation. Injected randomness varies the figure's jumps and rescues, and the prize changes, so a second go isn't a replay.
  • Craft affects perceived quality. The aesthetic-usability effect (Kurosu & Kashimura, 1995) says people judge attractive products as easier to use. That is a reason to care about polish, and a warning that polish can hide problems. Hence the gates in section 6.

The guardrails, which matter more than the mechanics:

  • Never required, never in the way. All of the content is readable without touching any of it. The figure has pointer-events: none and never takes a click. The scratch card's prize is inert and aria-hidden until it has been won. Then it becomes a role="status" region.
  • Hidden from assistive tech. The figure, the graveyard, the confetti canvas and the career-graph drawing are aria-hidden. The roles list under the graph remains the readable source.
  • Off under reduced motion. The figure is not mounted, there is no confetti, and the hero tilt is off.
  • Keyboard-safe. Shift ×3 (within 700 ms) ignores held-key repeat and resets on any other key, so typing capital letters never triggers it. Escape always leaves the scene.
  • No data collected. The graveyard lives in a signal for the lifetime of the page and nowhere else. There are no analytics. The stats sheet counts third-party requests and shows "0".
  • It costs nothing up front. The figure is behind @defer (on viewport(row); prefetch on idle), and the scene, the sheet and the command palette are @defer blocks rendered only when opened (angular.dev on @defer).

What I can't claim: that any of this improves retention or recall. I have no analytics by choice and no study of my own. It is designed against recognised principles and checked for harm (accessibility, performance, privacy). Whether it works is anecdotal.

6. The engineering that keeps it sustainable

A pure logic layer and a thin renderer

core/buddy.ts (about 1,200 lines) is pure TypeScript with no DOM. Geometry and pointer go in, and a View comes out: position, facing, nine joint angles, spin, web line. Inside: a hip under one gravity (1200 px/s², about four times "real" for a 57 px figure, as old games did), two-bone inverse kinematics to planted feet, ballistic jump planning, ledge hangs with a damped sway, pull-ups, a web swing, sitting and falling. Randomness is injected (new Buddy(random = Math.random)).

sections/buddy.ts (about 260 lines) renders it as an inline SVG with nine <g> joints, setting style.rotate each frame. It is DOM rather than canvas because it must go behind or in front of real tiles that tilt on hover, inherit currentColor in both themes, and be clipped by the tile it hides behind.

Because the logic is pure, the tests check physics, not snapshots. The spec rebuilds the drawn figure with forward kinematics, independently of the IK, and asserts properties:

// app/src/app/core/buddy.spec.ts (trimmed)
it('never slides a foot that is on the ground, and never puts one into it', () => {
  const views = sprint();
  let planted = 0;
  for (let i = 1; i < views.length; i++) {
    const [a, c] = [feet(views[i - 1]!), feet(views[i]!)];
    for (const k of [0, 1]) {
      expect(c[k]!.y).toBeLessThan(LONG.fixed + 1e-6);
      if (Math.abs(a[k]!.y - LONG.fixed) < 1e-6 && Math.abs(c[k]!.y - LONG.fixed) < 1e-6) {
        planted++;
        expect(Math.abs(c[k]!.x - a[k]!.x)).toBeLessThan(1e-6);
      }
    }
  }
  expect(planted).toBeGreaterThan(100);
});

Other tests check that jumps follow a parabola of the one gravity, that joints move smoothly through every change of state (bounded second differences), and that the web rescue follows random(). The same split holds for core/contours.ts (marching squares), core/scratch.ts, graph/*, content/* and search/search.ts. Components are covered end to end instead.

Gates

npm run verify runs strict type-checking, ESLint, unit tests (220, with 100 % statement/branch/function/line coverage of the logic layer), a 7:1 contrast check, the design check, the build, a privacy check, a check that docs/ matches the committed sources, Playwright (114 tests, including axe over WCAG 2.2 AA tags, reduced-motion emulation and CSP-violation listeners) and Lighthouse on both pages, mobile and desktop. Accessibility, best practices and SEO must be exactly 100. Performance has a floor of 95 because it is a noisy lab metric. Desktop scores 100. Mobile simulation has ranged from the high 80s to the high 90s on my machine, so a mobile miss gets re-run and investigated.

Static, hydrated, almost silent

  • SSG + hydration. Both language pages are prerendered (RenderMode.Prerender) and hydrated with provideClientHydration(withEventReplay()). There is no router in the browser: the language switch is a signal plus history.pushState. There is no zone.js in the dependencies. The one place that needs an immediate render calls appRef.tick() explicitly.
  • Lazy work. @defer for the figure and the overlays, and content-visibility: auto on three below-the-fold sections. The built main bundle in docs/ is about 381 kB before compression, under a budget that warns at 400 kB and fails at 450 kB.
  • A strict CSP as a meta tag (GitHub Pages can't send headers). scripts/csp.mjs hashes every inline script in the prerendered HTML at build time and writes script-src 'self' 'sha256-…', with object-src 'none', base-uri 'self' and form-action 'none'. Styles keep 'unsafe-inline' because the prerendered HTML carries style attributes. That is a known compromise.
  • One documented outside request. connect-src allows exactly https://dev.to/api/articles. The research block fetches my article list when it comes within 300 px of the viewport, with credentials: 'omit', referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer', an 8-second AbortController timeout, a loader and an error notice. A failure keeps the list fetched at build time, so the section is never empty.

7. Five bugs worth sharing

1. The spring that never ran. The new role-card spring looked exactly like the old ease-out. Further down the same stylesheet sat an older disclosure block with the same selectors and an ease-out transition. Same specificity, later in the source, so it won silently. Fix: delete it and keep one owner per selector. Lesson: when a motion change "does nothing", search for the selector before tuning numbers.

2. Two @keyframes reveal. I found this one while writing the article. _layout.scss defines reveal as a fade-and-rise for section headings, and _motion.scss defines reveal as a transform-only rise. Both land in one global CSS file, and keyframes don't cascade: "the last one encountered by the parser is used". So the headings never fade. That is the safer outcome for contrast audits, but by luck, not design. Fix: distinct names, and a design-check rule against duplicate @keyframes. Lesson: animation names are global.

3. The language switch that vibrated. The switch ran inside a View Transition (a root cross-fade), and the changed texts had their own entrance animation. They played back to back and the page shuddered. Fix: no View Transition here. Render synchronously, then restart one class on the live DOM:

// app/src/app/core/lang.ts
private settle(): void {
  const root = this.doc.documentElement;
  root.classList.remove('swap');
  void root.offsetWidth;          // a layout in between, so every switch plays from the start
  root.classList.add('swap');
  clearTimeout(this.swapTimer);
  this.swapTimer = setTimeout(() => root.classList.remove('swap'), 600);
}

Lesson: a View Transition is a choreography of its own. Don't stack another on it. (The theme switch keeps one, a circle growing from the button, since nothing else animates there.)

4. CLS 0.123 in the hero. On desktop the text is vertically centred next to the portrait. Until the image arrived, the portrait's box had no height, the row was only as tall as the text, and then the text jumped down. Fix: reserve the row from the first frame with grid-template-rows: minmax(min(20rem, 38vw), auto). CLS went to 0 in a throttled local simulation. Lesson: width/height on the <img> doesn't help when the container's size depends on it.

5. content-visibility versus the target-size audit. I put content-visibility: auto on every below-the-fold section. Lighthouse then reported buttons in Projects and About as "obscured", measured against cards of a section that was still a placeholder. Fix: keep it on Experience, Skills and Contact only, with a comment saying why. Lesson: optimisations that change geometry can confuse geometry-based audits.

Bonus: the 120 Hz per-frame easing bug from section 2. A constant like 0.12 in an animation loop usually means it is there.

8. What I would do differently, and the limits

  • The spring is bouncy on tall cards. About 3 % overshoot is pleasant on a 44 px button and visible on a 500 px role card (around 15 px). The cards should use --ease-spring-smooth for block-size and keep the bouncy spring for small things, which is the rule I wrote down myself.
  • "Keep the fades" is not fully implemented. --dur-fade exists and is not used. Under reduced motion most fades become instant too. The right fix is to move opacity and colour transitions onto --dur-fade and let the check enforce it.
  • Exits are inconsistent. The command palette has a spring entrance and no exit animation: it just disappears. The role cards get exits right, but the palette does not.
  • CSS springs don't carry velocity. Interrupt the pill mid-flight and it starts again from rest. For real interruptible motion you need script, as the figure does.
  • The evidence for the gamification is intent, not measurement. I chose not to track visitors, so I can't tell you whether anyone remembers the swamp.
  • The design check is a regex. It is cheap and useful but blind to some patterns (it missed the duplicate keyframes).
  • Mobile Lighthouse performance is noisy enough that a hard 100 would be a flaky gate. I keep the floor and investigate misses.

9. A checklist you can copy

  • [ ] Durations and curves are tokens, organised by kind of motion, not by number.
  • [ ] The build fails on a raw duration, a raw radius or a hand-mixed state colour.
  • [ ] Press feedback starts within 100 ms. Release can be slower and springier.
  • [ ] Exits are shorter than entrances and use ease-in. Entrances use ease-out. Nothing linear except scroll-linked motion.
  • [ ] Springs: bounce only on small things, none on layout or size changes.
  • [ ] Tooltips wait (300–500 ms) on hover, appear instantly on focus, warm up after the first one, and close on Escape.
  • [ ] A programmatic scroll names its destination once and doesn't report every section it passes.
  • [ ] Scroll-driven animations: linear on the timeline, easing on the keyframe, transform-only where contrast matters.
  • [ ] One scroll-derived custom property can drive several elements. Avoid flying clones.
  • [ ] Any rAF easing uses 1 - Math.exp(-dt / tau), not a per-frame factor.
  • [ ] Reduced motion zeroes the movement tokens and doesn't mount decorative motion.
  • [ ] Nothing moves on its own for more than five seconds without a way to stop it.
  • [ ] iOS: a passive touchstart listener so :active works.
  • [ ] Easter eggs: never required, aria-hidden, off under reduced motion, no data collected, lazy-loaded.
  • [ ] Animation names are global, so search for duplicate @keyframes.

The site is at er2es.github.io and all of the code above is in github.com/er2es/er2es.github.io (MIT). Try resting the mouse on the soft-skills row, scratching the portrait, or pressing Shift three times. If you find a motion bug, I'd like to hear about it.

title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
description:
arXiv:2611.22252v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis.
  Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only.
  Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings.
  Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types.
  Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

title: How I made a phone animation go from ~35 fps to ~140 fps: draw once, then only move it
description:
I build InviteMeOut, an app for invitations and small-business pages that open with an animation: a wax seal that breaks, curtains that part, a towel that wipes dust off a car. The opening is the first thing a guest sees, so it has to be smooth on a three-year-old phone, not just on my laptop.

One of them wasn't. Here's what was wrong and the rules I follow now.

The slow version

The opening for a car-detailing business page wipes a layer of dust off the screen with a towel. The first version did it the "obvious" way:

  • a full-screen SVG mask that grew as the towel moved,
  • feGaussianBlur and feTurbulence filters for soft, dusty edges,
  • the towel itself as a filtered SVG, animated with SMIL,
  • a scale on the whole layer, and a backdrop-filter: blur() pill floating on top.

In Chrome's phone emulation it ran at about 35 fps. On a real phone it was worse. Every frame the browser had to re-run the filters over the whole screen, re-rasterize the mask, and re-blur whatever sat under the pill.

The fast version

Same look, different work per frame:

  1. The dust is a <canvas> drawn once. Each frame only erases the new strip the towel just covered, using globalCompositeOperation = "destination-out". Nothing is redrawn from scratch.
  2. The towel is rendered once and only moved, with transform: translate3d(...). The GPU moves a texture it already has.
  3. Sheen, glints and dust puffs are transform + opacity only. These two properties can be animated without layout or repaint.
  4. The backdrop-filter element is removed before the animation starts. A blur over something that changes every frame is one of the most expensive things you can ask a phone to do.
  5. Sizes are in px, not SVG viewBox units, so the same towel looks the same on a narrow phone and a wide one.

Result in the same emulation: about 140 fps, and smooth on real phones.

The rules I use for every opening now

  • Draw heavy textures once (a canvas or a static image), then never redraw them.
  • Animate only transform and opacity.
  • No animated masks, filters or background-position.
  • No backdrop-filter over anything that moves.
  • Measure before calling it done. I use a tiny requestAnimationFrame logger that records frame times in phone view: 
const times = [];
let last = performance.now();
function tick(now) {
  times.push(now - last);
  last = now;
  if (times.length < 300) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  else {
    const avg = times.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / times.length;
    console.log("avg fps:", Math.round(1000 / avg), "worst frame ms:", Math.max(...times).toFixed(1));
  }
}
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

One more thing: sound needs a tap

Phones won't play audio until the user touches the page. Instead of fighting that, the tap that breaks the seal (or starts the wipe) is the same gesture that starts the music. It feels intentional, and it's the only reliable way.

If you want to see the openings in action, they're at invitemeout.app. Free on the web and on the iPhone. I'm building it solo, so feedback on what stutters on your phone is very welcome.

title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2611.21969v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.

title: Oggi guidate per loro. Domani guideranno senza di voi.
description:
Come algoritmi, piattaforme digitali e robotaxi stanno cambiando il controllo economico del trasporto professionale.

C'è una domanda che dovrebbe interessare ogni tassista, conducente NCC, sviluppatore di piattaforme di mobilità e imprenditore del trasporto.

Che cosa succede quando il software che oggi vi procura lavoro diventa anche il sistema che può sostituirvi?

Non è più una domanda fantascientifica.

Per anni abbiamo raccontato le piattaforme di ride-hailing come un'innovazione capace di mettere in contatto passeggeri e autisti. Un'applicazione, un algoritmo di assegnazione, un sistema di pagamento e una commissione.

Un modello apparentemente semplice.

Ma dietro quell'interfaccia esiste un'architettura economica molto più importante: quella che determina chi controlla la domanda, i prezzi e la relazione con il cliente.

1. Il vero potere non è possedere le automobili

Una piattaforma può organizzare milioni di spostamenti senza possedere ogni automobile e senza assumere direttamente ogni conducente.

Il suo vantaggio competitivo è un altro: controlla il punto di accesso del passeggero al servizio.

Chi possiede l'interfaccia attraverso cui il cliente prenota può influenzare:

  • Quali offerte vengono visualizzate.
  • Come vengono calcolati e presentati i prezzi.
  • Quale conducente riceve una determinata richiesta.
  • Quali informazioni restano disponibili all'autista.
  • Se il cliente ritornerà direttamente dal professionista o dalla piattaforma.

Naturalmente, i modelli differiscono tra operatori e mercati. Non tutte le piattaforme determinano il prezzo nello stesso modo.

Ma il principio economico resta:

Chi controlla la domanda possiede un potere negoziale enorme su chi fornisce il servizio.

2. Dall'algoritmo di assegnazione all'automazione del conducente

Tecnicamente, una piattaforma di mobilità dispone già di alcuni componenti fondamentali per gestire un servizio automatizzato:

  • Un sistema per acquisire richieste di trasporto.
  • Un motore di pricing e assegnazione.
  • Un'infrastruttura per localizzazione e instradamento.
  • Un sistema di pagamento e gestione dell'esperienza del cliente.
  • Una base di utenti abituati a prenotare attraverso la stessa applicazione.

Nel ride-hailing tradizionale, il servizio fisico è fornito da un conducente.

In uno scenario robotaxi, parte di quel lavoro viene affidata a un veicolo autonomo, mentre restano necessari gestione della flotta, manutenzione, assistenza, supervisione e altre attività operative.

Il cambiamento più significativo è che l'interfaccia del passeggero può rimanere esattamente la stessa.

Il cliente apre l'applicazione, indica la destinazione, visualizza un prezzo e prenota.

Quello che cambia è chi, o che cosa, esegue la corsa.

3. I miliardi investiti non sono un'ipotesi

Il 19 marzo 2026 Uber e Rivian hanno annunciato una partnership che prevede investimenti potenziali fino a 1,25 miliardi di dollari entro il 2031, subordinati al raggiungimento di obiettivi tecnologici.

Il programma iniziale riguarda 10.000 robotaxi Rivian R2, con un'opzione per arrivare complessivamente a 50.000 veicoli.

I primi impieghi commerciali sono pianificati dal 2028.

Non significa che 50.000 veicoli siano già operativi.

Significa che esiste un progetto industriale formalizzato, accompagnato da impegni economici e obiettivi di distribuzione.

In Europa il processo è già cominciato.

Nell'agosto 2026 Uber, Pony.ai e Verne hanno avviato un servizio di corse autonome prenotabili tramite Uber a Zagabria. Nella fase iniziale è previsto un operatore di sicurezza a bordo.

La direzione degli investimenti è chiara, anche se la velocità della transizione resta incerta.

4. Il rischio più grande è perdere il cliente prima del lavoro

Immaginiamo un tassista con vent'anni di esperienza.

Conosce la città, ha una licenza, sostiene i costi del veicolo, paga assicurazioni e manutenzione.

Ma i passeggeri prenotano quasi esclusivamente attraverso una piattaforma.

Se domani cambia l'offerta disponibile sull'applicazione, quanti di quei passeggeri continueranno a cercare proprio lui?

Il problema è che il professionista può conservare la propria autorizzazione senza conservare il rapporto commerciale con il cliente.

Le leggi disciplinano il trasporto, le autorizzazioni, la sicurezza e le condizioni di esercizio.

Non garantiscono che un cliente rimanga fedele a un determinato conducente.

È questo il rischio strategico che il settore dovrebbe affrontare oggi.

5. Non tutte le piattaforme devono diventare operatori di robotaxi perché il rischio esista

Uber, Bolt, Lyft, FREE NOW e gli altri operatori non hanno strategie identiche.

Sarebbe scorretto sostenere che tutti abbiano gli stessi investimenti, gli stessi progetti o le stesse condizioni operative.

Il punto è più generale.

Un mercato nel quale il passeggero appartiene commercialmente alla piattaforma rende il fornitore fisico del servizio più facilmente sostituibile.

Oggi quel fornitore è un tassista, un conducente NCC o una flotta.

Domani, nei mercati dove tecnologia e normative lo permetteranno, potrà essere anche un veicolo autonomo.

6. Come dovrebbe essere progettata una piattaforma alternativa

La tecnologia non è necessariamente il nemico del professionista.

Un sistema moderno può gestire richieste, pagamenti, disponibilità, localizzazione, tariffe e dispatching senza sottrarre all'operatore ogni decisione economica.

Per realizzare un modello di questo tipo servono alcuni principi architetturali.

Autonomia tariffaria

Il conducente deve poter definire le condizioni economiche del proprio servizio nei limiti delle disposizioni applicabili.

Trasparenza degli algoritmi

Prima di accettare una corsa, il professionista dovrebbe conoscere il compenso previsto e le commissioni.

Continuità del rapporto commerciale

Le centrali e gli operatori devono poter mantenere e gestire i rapporti con i clienti che acquisiscono, nel rispetto della normativa sui dati personali.

Interoperabilità

Un professionista non dovrebbe dipendere tecnicamente da un unico intermediario per svolgere ogni attività.

Tecnologia al servizio dell'operatore

Il software dovrebbe ridurre i costi e aumentare l'efficienza, non necessariamente imporre le condizioni economiche.

7. La scelta che abbiamo fatto con UrbanGo

Abbiamo sviluppato UrbanGo partendo da un principio diverso.

Il professionista imposta le proprie tariffe, nel rispetto delle normative locali.

Quando opera attraverso una centrale, questa può applicare il proprio listino alle corse che gestisce, e l'autista conosce le condizioni prima di accettare.

Anche UrbanGo applica una commissione.

La differenza che vogliamo costruire non è l'assenza di costi, ma la trasparenza e la possibilità per gli operatori di governare le proprie condizioni economiche.

Non crediamo che il progresso tecnologico debba essere fermato.

Crediamo però che sia necessario distinguere tra digitalizzare un settore e trasferirne il controllo economico a pochi intermediari.

Conclusione: chi controllerà il prossimo mercato?

I robotaxi continueranno a evolversi.

Alcuni arriveranno sul mercato, altri progetti incontreranno ostacoli tecnologici, economici o normativi.

Ma per i professionisti del trasporto esiste una decisione che non può aspettare il 2030.

Continuare a utilizzare la tecnologia come strumento della propria impresa, oppure lasciare che sia la piattaforma a determinare il futuro della propria impresa.

Il vero tema non è soltanto chi guiderà l'automobile.
È chi controllerà la relazione commerciale quando il passeggero salirà a bordo.

UrbanGo, app per autisti

Fonti

  • Uber e Rivian, comunicato ufficiale del 19 marzo 2026.
  • Uber, Pony.ai e Verne, lancio del servizio a Zagabria, 19 agosto 2026.
  • Uber e Pony.ai, partnership europea del 13 agosto 2026.
  • UrbanGo, pagine App autisti, Prezzi e Termini del servizio.

Articolo di opinione e analisi industriale. Le strategie e gli investimenti citati non devono essere attribuiti indistintamente a tutte le piattaforme nominate.

title: Designing an RF switch matrix for automated test
description:
A switch matrix looks like a simple box: N inputs, M outputs, and a controller. In practice most of the engineering effort goes into three decisions that are hard to change later — port topology, isolation budget, and control architecture. This note walks through the trade-offs that show up when specifying matrices for semiconductor ATE, satellite payload test benches and EMC labs.

Start from the measurement, not the port count

The first question is not "how many ports" but "what gets measured through the path". A matrix that routes a vector network analyzer to 24 devices under test has different requirements from one that switches a spectrum analyzer between eight antenna feeds.

Two numbers drive everything:

  • Insertion loss budget. Every switch in the path adds loss, and that loss changes the calibration reference. A 4x24 matrix built from cascaded SP6T switches can easily put 1.5 dB between instrument and DUT if the topology is careless.
  • Isolation requirement. Cascaded switches multiply isolation, but only if unused ports are terminated. An open port reflects energy back into the matrix and it shows up as crosstalk on the measured port.

The second point is the one that bites most often. A matrix built from 80 dB switches can measure 60 dB of isolation if a single unused port is left open. Terminating every unused port in 50 ohms is not a refinement, it is part of the specification, which is why the load's return loss and power rating matter as much as the switch.

Reflective or absorptive switching

Mechanical coaxial switches are usually reflective: when a port is deselected the signal bounces back. In a well-terminated matrix that is acceptable, and it keeps cost and insertion loss low.

PIN diode switches come in both flavours. The absorptive version terminates the off port internally so the source always sees a matched load. For receive chains with low noise amplifiers, or any path where a reflection can stress a sensitive front end, absorptive is the safer default. The price is a little more insertion loss and a little more bias current.

Waveguide paths above 26 GHz change the calculus again. Waveguide switches are reflective by construction, and the flange interface matters more than the switch itself: a WR28 switch mounted on a mismatched flange will show worse return loss than the datasheet suggests.

Control architecture, the part everyone underestimates

A matrix is only as good as its driver. Three decisions determine whether the system is pleasant to work with:

  1. Switching element choice. Mechanical switches give low loss and high isolation but switch in milliseconds. When the sequence needs microsecond transitions, the matrix wants PIN diodes on the fast paths and mechanical switches elsewhere, in a hybrid arrangement.
  2. Logic level and latching. TTL inputs can be driven straight from a tester's digital IO. 28 V control is common in industrial and military racks. Latching elements hold state with power removed, failsafe elements return to a defined port. Choosing the wrong one shows up as intermittent path errors months later.
  3. State readback. Without readback the controller cannot tell "commanded" from "actually switched". A matrix that reports its true position saves hours of debugging when a sequence fails at 3 a.m.

Termination, cooling and the boring details

High port count matrices concentrate power. Absorptive switches and terminations dissipate what the DUT reflects, and a rack of 24 ports can turn a few watts of reflected power into a thermal problem. Finned coaxial loads and terminations exist for exactly this reason.

The mechanical details matter as well: connector grade (2.92 mm versus 2.4 mm versus 1.85 mm), torque consistency across operators, and whether the matrix is serviceable when one switch fails. A matrix designed as one sealed unit becomes scrap when a single port dies.

A short specification checklist

  • Port count and topology, with the full path loss budget written down
  • Isolation target, and the termination plan for unused ports
  • Switching speed per path, and whether hybrid mechanical/PIN is needed
  • Control logic, latching behaviour and state readback
  • Connector types and grades, matched across the whole path
  • Worst case power dissipation and the cooling path

Most of these are cheap to get right at design time and expensive to fix once the rack is built. If you are specifying a matrix for a new test bench, the numbers worth arguing about are loss, isolation and termination. The rest follows.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.
