title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
description:
arXiv:2611.22000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.

title: Protección y Recuperación de Datos NoSQL: Backups Automatizados con MongoDB Atlas, GitHub Actions y Render Copiar
description:
Introducción

En el desarrollo de sistemas informáticos, almacenar información correctamente es fundamental. Sin embargo, existe un aspecto igual de importante que muchas veces pasa desapercibido: ¿qué sucede cuando los datos se pierden, se eliminan accidentalmente o la base de datos presenta un problema?

Una aplicación puede funcionar perfectamente y, aun así, estar expuesta a pérdidas de información si no dispone de una estrategia adecuada de respaldo y recuperación.

Como parte del curso de Base de Datos II de la Universidad Privada de Tacna, desarrollamos en equipo una aplicación web que utiliza MongoDB Atlas como base de datos NoSQL y que incorpora mecanismos automatizados para generar, verificar y recuperar copias de seguridad.

Para completar la solución, integramos GitHub Actions como herramienta de automatización y Render como plataforma de despliegue.

En este artículo presentaré cómo organizamos nuestra solución, las tecnologías utilizadas, el funcionamiento de los respaldos y los aprendizajes obtenidos durante su implementación.

Enlaces del proyecto

  • Repositorio público: https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy
  • Aplicación desplegada: https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com
  • Base de datos: MongoDB Atlas.
  • Automatización: GitHub Actions.
  • Despliegue: Render.

1. La importancia de proteger los datos en una aplicación NoSQL

Cuando una aplicación utiliza una base de datos alojada en la nube, es posible pensar que la información está completamente protegida gracias a la infraestructura del proveedor.

Sin embargo, disponer de un sistema de replicación no significa necesariamente contar con una copia de seguridad independiente.

Por ejemplo, si un administrador elimina accidentalmente los documentos de una colección, esa operación puede propagarse a las réplicas de la base de datos.

Por esta razón, es necesario implementar mecanismos que permitan recuperar información almacenada en un momento anterior.

Durante nuestro proyecto trabajamos con tres conceptos fundamentales:

Respaldo (Backup): consiste en generar una copia de los datos que pueda utilizarse posteriormente.

Restauración (Restore): permite recuperar la información desde un respaldo previamente generado.

Recuperación ante desastres: comprende los procedimientos necesarios para restablecer la información y los servicios después de un incidente.

Nuestro objetivo fue integrar estos mecanismos en una aplicación funcional y demostrar que es posible automatizar procesos de recuperación utilizando herramientas de desarrollo modernas.

2. Descripción de la aplicación desarrollada

Para implementar y demostrar nuestra estrategia construimos una aplicación web que representa una pequeña tienda.

El sistema utiliza Node.js y Express para gestionar las solicitudes HTTP y MongoDB Atlas como servicio de almacenamiento documental.

La aplicación permite registrar productos, consultar sus datos, eliminarlos y administrar determinados procesos de respaldo.

Principales funcionalidades

  • Registro de productos con nombre, precio y cantidad disponible.
  • Visualización de los productos almacenados.
  • Eliminación de registros.
  • Comunicación con MongoDB Atlas.
  • Generación de respaldos desde una interfaz administrativa.
  • Consulta de información sobre los respaldos generados.
  • Verificación del estado de conexión con la base de datos.

Para el manejo de los respaldos, la aplicación incorpora operaciones protegidas mediante un token de administrador, evitando que cualquier solicitud pueda acceder directamente a esas funciones.

La interfaz web sirve como demostración práctica del funcionamiento de la base de datos y de los procedimientos de protección implementados.

3. Tecnologías y arquitectura del sistema

Seleccionamos un conjunto de tecnologías que nos permitiera integrar desarrollo web, almacenamiento NoSQL, automatización y despliegue continuo.

Tecnología Función
MongoDB Atlas Almacenamiento de documentos NoSQL
Node.js Ejecución del código JavaScript del servidor
Express Desarrollo de la API web
Docker Empaquetado de la aplicación
GitHub Control de versiones
GitHub Actions Pruebas, backups y automatización
Render Publicación de la aplicación
OpenSSL Cifrado de los archivos de respaldo

¿Cómo se relacionan estos componentes?

Cuando un usuario accede a la aplicación, Render entrega la interfaz y ejecuta el servidor Express.

El servidor establece una conexión con MongoDB Atlas para realizar operaciones sobre las colecciones.

De manera independiente, GitHub Actions ejecuta procesos programados para generar respaldos, probar su restauración y almacenar los archivos resultantes como artefactos.

Esta separación es importante porque la aplicación y el sistema de respaldos no dependen del mismo proceso de ejecución.

Además, utilizamos Docker para facilitar la configuración y reproducción del entorno de desarrollo.

4. Diseño de nuestra estrategia de respaldo

Uno de los primeros pasos fue establecer qué características debía cumplir el mecanismo de protección.

Decidimos implementar un sistema de respaldo lógico automatizado, en el que los documentos de MongoDB se exportan a archivos que pueden almacenarse y recuperarse posteriormente.

Esta decisión estuvo relacionada con el uso del clúster gratuito M0 de MongoDB Atlas, que no proporciona las mismas funciones de backup administrado disponibles en determinadas modalidades de pago.

Objetivos de recuperación

Para organizar nuestra estrategia consideramos dos indicadores:

RPO (Recovery Point Objective):

Representa la cantidad máxima de datos recientes que estamos dispuestos a perder ante un incidente.

Establecimos como objetivo un RPO de 24 horas, mediante la programación de un respaldo diario.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective):

Representa el tiempo máximo esperado para recuperar el servicio después de una interrupción.

Nuestro objetivo de diseño fue realizar una recuperación en menos de cinco minutos para el conjunto reducido de datos de demostración.

Estos valores representan metas del proyecto. Su cumplimiento real depende de factores como la ejecución del respaldo, la disponibilidad de los archivos y el tiempo efectivo de restauración.

Aplicación del principio 3-2-1

También tomamos como referencia la conocida estrategia 3-2-1, que propone mantener varias copias de los datos, utilizar medios de almacenamiento diferentes y conservar al menos una copia fuera del entorno principal.

En nuestra solución, la información original reside en MongoDB Atlas, mientras que los respaldos automatizados se almacenan como artefactos de GitHub Actions.

Estos artefactos también pueden descargarse y conservarse en otro almacenamiento para completar una estrategia con una tercera copia independiente.

De esta manera, evitamos depender exclusivamente del proveedor que aloja la base de datos.

5. Implementación del respaldo lógico

El componente principal de la estrategia se encuentra en el archivo:

src/backup-lib.js

Este módulo contiene la lógica utilizada para crear respaldos, restaurar documentos, calcular verificaciones de integridad y administrar la retención.

¿Por qué utilizamos Extended JSON?

MongoDB trabaja con tipos BSON que no siempre pueden conservarse correctamente utilizando una conversión tradicional a JSON.

Por ejemplo, existen tipos como:

  • ObjectId: identificadores de documentos.
  • Date: valores de fecha.
  • Decimal128: números decimales de alta precisión.

Para preservar estos tipos utilizamos Extended JSON (EJSON) en su representación canónica.

Un fragmento del código implementado es:

async function* lineas() {
  for await (const doc of cursor) {
    documentos++;
    yield EJSON.stringify(doc, {
      relaxed: false
    }) + '\n';
  }
}

Este procedimiento recorre los documentos de una colección y los transforma a EJSON.

Posteriormente, la información se comprime utilizando gzip:

await pipeline(
  Readable.from(lineas()),
  zlib.createGzip(),
  fs.createWriteStream(archivo)
);

El resultado es un archivo comprimido con extensión .jsonl.gz por cada colección.

Esta implementación permite procesar los documentos mediante flujos de datos, evitando cargar toda la colección simultáneamente en memoria.

6. Integridad de los archivos y metadatos

Crear archivos de respaldo no es suficiente. También necesitamos comprobar que la información pueda recuperarse correctamente.

Para solucionar este problema, implementamos verificaciones mediante SHA-256, un algoritmo criptográfico que permite calcular una huella digital de los archivos.

Cada respaldo incorpora un archivo llamado:

metadata.json

Este archivo registra información como la identificación del respaldo, el nombre de la base de datos, las colecciones exportadas, la cantidad de documentos, los índices y sus respectivos checksums.

¿Para qué sirve el checksum?

Supongamos que un archivo de respaldo se modifica accidentalmente o sufre una corrupción durante su almacenamiento.

Cuando intentamos restaurarlo, el sistema vuelve a calcular su hash SHA-256 y lo compara con el valor registrado originalmente.

Si ambos valores son diferentes, el archivo se considera alterado y se rechaza la restauración.

Un fragmento utilizado en nuestro proyecto es:

const actual = await sha256(
  path.join(dirBackup, info.archivo)
);

if (actual !== info.sha256) {
  throw new Error(
    `Checksum inválido en la colección "${nombre}"`
  );
}

Una característica importante es que esta verificación se realiza antes de iniciar la modificación de los documentos de destino.

Así reducimos el riesgo de utilizar respaldos dañados durante un proceso de recuperación.

7. Proceso de restauración de MongoDB

Una parte esencial del proyecto fue implementar el procedimiento inverso: recuperar los documentos almacenados en un respaldo.

Para ello desarrollamos el script:

scripts/restore.js

Este componente utiliza las funciones de restauración disponibles en nuestra biblioteca.

Etapas de recuperación

Primera etapa: validación del respaldo

Se comprueba la existencia de los archivos y se verifican sus checksums SHA-256.

Segunda etapa: lectura de documentos

Los archivos comprimidos se descomprimen y los documentos EJSON se convierten nuevamente a sus tipos correspondientes.

Tercera etapa: inserción de registros

La restauración organiza los documentos en lotes de hasta 1000 registros para insertarlos en MongoDB.

Cuarta etapa: recuperación de índices

Se recrean los índices registrados en los metadatos, conservando estructuras importantes para las consultas.

Quinta etapa: verificación final

Se compara el número de documentos restaurados con el número registrado durante el respaldo.

De esta manera, el procedimiento no termina únicamente después de insertar información, sino que incorpora una validación adicional.

Importante: la restauración predeterminada elimina los documentos existentes en las colecciones incluidas en el respaldo antes de volver a insertarlos. Por ello, debe ejecutarse sobre una base de datos de prueba o bajo un procedimiento de recuperación previamente autorizado.

8. Pruebas automatizadas del sistema

Para demostrar que los respaldos funcionan, incorporamos pruebas automatizadas utilizando las herramientas de Node.js.

Estas pruebas se encuentran en:

test/backup.test.js

Una de las pruebas genera una colección de 2501 documentos, incluyendo valores especiales de MongoDB.

Después crea un respaldo, elimina la colección de prueba y ejecuta la restauración.

Finalmente, verifica que se hayan recuperado correctamente los documentos, sus tipos y el índice configurado.

También incorporamos otras pruebas para comprobar:

  • Que la política de retención conserve únicamente la cantidad de respaldos configurada.
  • Que un archivo modificado sea rechazado por una verificación SHA-256 incorrecta.
  • Que los registros recuperados mantengan los tipos de datos originales.

El comando para ejecutar estas pruebas es:

npm test

Estas verificaciones son importantes porque permiten identificar errores en el proceso de recuperación antes de utilizar el sistema con información relevante.

Una de nuestras principales conclusiones técnicas fue que un respaldo es realmente útil cuando se ha comprobado que puede restaurarse.

9. Automatización de backups mediante GitHub Actions

Una vez implementado el sistema de respaldo, el siguiente objetivo fue evitar que su ejecución dependiera de una persona.

Para ello configuramos GitHub Actions mediante el archivo:

.github/workflows/backup.yml

Este workflow utiliza una programación automática:

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 5 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

La expresión cron programa el respaldo diariamente a las 05:00 UTC, equivalente a las 00:00 en Perú.

También incorporamos workflow_dispatch, que permite iniciar manualmente el proceso desde GitHub.

¿Qué hace el workflow?

El flujo realiza las siguientes actividades:

  1. Descarga el código desde el repositorio.
  2. Prepara Node.js e instala las dependencias.
  3. Se conecta a MongoDB Atlas y genera el respaldo lógico.
  4. Restaura el respaldo en una instancia temporal de MongoDB para verificarlo.
  5. Prepara un archivo comprimido y aplica cifrado AES-256 cuando está configurada la contraseña de respaldo.
  6. Publica el archivo como artefacto de GitHub Actions, con una retención configurada de 30 días.

La conexión a MongoDB Atlas utiliza credenciales almacenadas en GitHub Secrets.

Para el cifrado se utiliza el secreto BACKUP_PASSPHRASE.

En la configuración actual, el workflow permite continuar sin cifrar si ese secreto no está definido y genera una advertencia. Para un entorno de producción sería recomendable exigir obligatoriamente su configuración y detener la publicación cuando falte.

Esta automatización representa una mejora importante respecto a generar respaldos manualmente, porque permite incorporar el procedimiento a una rutina programada y verificable.

10. Integración continua y despliegue en Render

Además de los respaldos, desarrollamos un segundo workflow encargado de realizar pruebas y automatizar la publicación de la aplicación.

Este archivo se encuentra en:

.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

El proceso comienza cuando se realizan cambios en el repositorio.

Funcionamiento del pipeline

1. Validación del código

GitHub Actions prepara un entorno de ejecución y ejecuta las pruebas automatizadas contra un servicio temporal de MongoDB.

2. Construcción con Docker

Cuando las pruebas finalizan satisfactoriamente, se construye una imagen Docker como comprobación de que la aplicación puede empaquetarse correctamente.

3. Despliegue automatizado

Si el cambio corresponde a la rama principal, GitHub Actions utiliza el deploy hook de Render para solicitar una nueva publicación.

4. Verificación del servicio

El pipeline consulta el endpoint:

/health

Este endpoint permite verificar que el servidor responda y pueda establecer comunicación con MongoDB.

Gracias a este procedimiento, la publicación está vinculada al resultado de las pruebas.

Aplicación desplegada

Nuestra aplicación utiliza MongoDB Atlas como servicio de base de datos y Render para ejecutar el servidor Node.js.

Se puede acceder desde:

https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com

La configuración de infraestructura de Render se encuentra declarada en render.yaml, lo que facilita reproducir la configuración del servicio.

11. Cómo ejecutar el proyecto localmente

El repositorio incluye un entorno configurado con Docker Compose.

Para obtener el proyecto se puede utilizar:

git clone https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy.git

cd NoSQL-Backup-Strategy

Posteriormente, se inicia la aplicación y la base de datos local:

docker compose up -d --build

Para cargar los datos de demostración:

docker compose exec app node scripts/seed.js

El sistema incorpora cinco productos de ejemplo, como una laptop, un monitor y accesorios informáticos, además de registros de clientes.

Después podemos ingresar a:

http://localhost:3000

Para comprobar el funcionamiento de las pruebas automatizadas dentro del contenedor:

docker compose exec app npm test

También es posible generar un respaldo manual:

docker compose exec app npm run backup

Y restaurarlo en una base de datos local independiente, evitando modificar los registros originales:

docker compose exec -e DB_NAME=tienda_restaurada app npm run restore

Estos comandos permiten explorar el funcionamiento del proyecto y comprender el ciclo de respaldo y recuperación utilizando un entorno de desarrollo aislado.

12. Resultados y aprendizajes obtenidos

El desarrollo de esta solución nos permitió integrar diferentes conocimientos del curso de Base de Datos II.

Entre los principales resultados alcanzados destacan:

  • Implementación de una aplicación web conectada a MongoDB Atlas.
  • Desarrollo de mecanismos de respaldo lógico de documentos NoSQL.
  • Conservación de tipos BSON utilizando EJSON.
  • Compresión de respaldos y verificación mediante SHA-256.
  • Recuperación de documentos e índices.
  • Pruebas automatizadas para validar integridad y restauración.
  • Configuración de procesos programados mediante GitHub Actions.
  • Integración de Docker y despliegue automatizado en Render.

Uno de los aprendizajes más importantes fue comprender que la protección de datos no consiste únicamente en guardar archivos.

Es necesario considerar la frecuencia de los respaldos, la seguridad de las credenciales, la integridad de la información y los procedimientos que se seguirán ante una pérdida de datos.

También identificamos oportunidades de mejora, como incorporar alertas ante fallos de ejecución, exigir siempre el cifrado y almacenar copias adicionales en servicios independientes.

Para escenarios de mayor escala también sería necesario evaluar mecanismos de respaldo que proporcionen garantías de consistencia durante escrituras concurrentes y opciones de recuperación a un punto específico en el tiempo.

13. Conclusiones

El desarrollo de este proyecto nos permitió comprender la importancia de implementar estrategias de respaldo y recuperación para bases de datos NoSQL alojadas en la nube.

En primer lugar, comprobamos que MongoDB Atlas puede integrarse con aplicaciones web desarrolladas mediante Node.js y Express, ofreciendo una plataforma adecuada para gestionar información documental.

En segundo lugar, la implementación de respaldos mediante EJSON, compresión gzip y verificaciones SHA-256 nos permitió conocer diferentes mecanismos que contribuyen a preservar la información y detectar posibles alteraciones.

Finalmente, la incorporación de GitHub Actions y Render demostró cómo las prácticas de automatización pueden aplicarse tanto a la publicación de aplicaciones como a los procedimientos de protección de datos.

La experiencia nos ayudó a fortalecer nuestros conocimientos sobre bases de datos NoSQL, desarrollo web, integración continua, despliegue automatizado y recuperación ante fallos.

El principal aprendizaje es que una estrategia de backup no debe limitarse a generar copias, sino que también debe garantizar procedimientos verificables para recuperar la información cuando sea necesario.

Referencias y documentación

Para comprender las tecnologías utilizadas, pueden consultarse las siguientes fuentes oficiales:

  • MongoDB Documentation — Bases de datos, BSON, respaldos y restauración.
  • GitHub Actions Documentation — Automatización de workflows y ejecución programada.
  • Render Documentation — Despliegue de servicios web y configuración de infraestructura.
  • Node.js Documentation — Desarrollo de aplicaciones y procesamiento de archivos.

Créditos del proyecto

Artículo elaborado por: Ana Cecilia Esteban Ramos.

Proyecto desarrollado en equipo por:

  • Ana Cecilia Esteban Ramos.
  • Saúl José Alvarado Urbano.

Curso: Base de Datos II.

Institución: Universidad Privada de Tacna.

Repositorio del proyecto: https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy

Aplicación desplegada: https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com

Este proyecto fue desarrollado como una experiencia práctica para aplicar conceptos de bases de datos NoSQL, estrategias de respaldo, restauración y automatización de servicios en la nube.

¡Gracias por leer! Espero que nuestra experiencia resulte útil para estudiantes y desarrolladores interesados en implementar mecanismos de protección y recuperación de datos mediante tecnologías modernas.

title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
description: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

  • Unified 1,048,576-token limit and long decodes: Supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response).   • Capabilities, consumption options, and endpoints: Supports the GenerateContent API, the Interactions API, the OpenAI compatibility Chat Completions API, function calling, code execution, computer use, URL context, Grounding with Google Search, Google Maps, Enterprise Web Grounding, Parallel and Exa Web Search, Agentic video understanding, Standard PayGo with Usage Tiers, Priority PayGo, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput (685 tokens per second per GSU) on the global endpoint and in the us and eu multi-regions.

Change

In GKE version 1.35.1-gke.1516000 or later, GKE Dataplane V2 clusters use a unified cilium-cni configuration instead of a chained CNI setup. With this change, Cilium configures the Pod default gateway by using its node-local virtual router interface (cilium_host), which has the statically assigned link-local IP address 169.254.4.6.

As a result, node-local kubelet health checks (kube-probe for liveness, readiness, and startup probes) and NodeLocal DNSCache traffic now originate from 169.254.4.6 instead of the .1 address of the node's Pod CIDR range (for example, 10.x.x.1).

If your workloads only accept traffic from specific IP address ranges, for example through application-level IP allowlists or web server ACLs, allow traffic from 169.254.4.6/32 before you upgrade. Otherwise, health checks for these workloads might fail.

For more information, see Using GKE Dataplane V2.

Clusters that run GKE version 1.39 and later don't support Policy Controller. This feature is available in Preview.

title: Next.js 15 & React 19 Production Patterns: Avoiding Client Bundle Bloat with Server Actions
description:
One of the most common mistakes AI assistants make in Next.js 15 App Router projects is slapping 'use client' at the top of page-level components.

Here is the clean boundary pattern to enforce in your codebase:

Keep 'use client' at the Leaves

Only interactive buttons, inputs, and stateful widgets need client hydration. Data fetching, permission checks, and database queries belong strictly in Server Components.

Structured Server Action Responses

Avoid throwing raw exceptions from Server Actions—return predictable discriminated results instead:

'use server'

import { z } from 'zod'

const CreateItemSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(2).max(100),
})

export async function createItemAction(formData: FormData) {
  const parsed = CreateItemSchema.safeParse({ title: formData.get('title') })
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { success: false as const, error: 'Invalid title input.' }
  }
  // Persist to DB inside authenticated context...
  return { success: true as const, data: parsed.data }
}

Pair With Strict Linting Rules

When your .cursorrules explicitly dictates Zod boundary parsing and Server-Component-first layout trees, Cursor generates clean Next.js 15 PRs on the first pass.

title: BATMoS: Budget-Aware Guidance Allocation for Efficient Video Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2611.22028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.

title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22094v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

title: Refresh token rotation in Express + TypeScript, explained (with a free boilerplate)
description:
Most Express auth tutorials stop at "sign a JWT, put it in a header, done." That works until you need to log someone out, or until a token leaks. Then you discover a JWT can't be revoked.

In this post I'll walk through the pattern I use instead: short-lived access tokens + rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection. All the code comes from an open-source starter I published, linked at the end.

The problem with long-lived JWTs

A JWT is valid until it expires. The server doesn't keep a list of them, which is the whole point: no database lookup per request.

That also means:

  • You can't log a user out of other devices.
  • If a token is stolen, the attacker keeps access until it expires.
  • Making it expire in 15 minutes fixes that, but now users log in every 15 minutes.

The fix: two tokens with two jobs

Access token Refresh token
Format JWT Random opaque string
Lifetime 15 minutes 30 days
Stored on server No Yes, hashed
Sent on Every API request Only to /auth/refresh
Revocable No (but expires fast) Yes

The access token keeps requests fast. The refresh token is the revocable part, so it lives in the database.

Why hash it? Same reason you hash passwords: if your database leaks, the attacker shouldn't get working sessions.

import { createHash, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

export const randomToken = (bytes = 48) => randomBytes(bytes).toString("base64url");
export const sha256 = (v: string) => createHash("sha256").update(v).digest("hex");

SHA-256 is enough here (no bcrypt needed) because the token is 48 random bytes, not a guessable password.

Rotation: every refresh issues a new token

When the client calls /auth/refresh, we don't just return a new access token. We also revoke the refresh token it used and return a new one.

Every login starts a family (a random id). All tokens rotated from that login share it:

await refreshTokens.create({
  userId: user.id,
  tokenHash: sha256(refreshToken),
  family,              // same for the whole login session
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
});

Reuse detection: the part most tutorials skip

Here's the trick. After rotation, the old token is revoked. A legitimate client never sends a revoked token again, because it already has the new one.

So if a revoked token shows up, someone copied it. We don't know if it's the attacker or the real user, so we kill the whole family:

async refresh(refreshToken: string) {
  const record = await this.refreshTokens.findByHash(sha256(refreshToken));
  if (!record) throw AppError.unauthorized("Invalid refresh token");

  if (record.revokedAt) {
    // Replay of an already-rotated token: assume theft.
    await this.refreshTokens.revokeFamily(record.family);
    throw AppError.unauthorized("Refresh token reuse detected; session revoked");
  }
  if (record.expiresAt.getTime() <= Date.now()) {
    throw AppError.unauthorized("Refresh token expired");
  }

  const user = await this.users.findById(record.userId);
  if (!user) throw AppError.unauthorized("Invalid refresh token");

  await this.refreshTokens.revoke(record.id);
  return this.issueTokens(user, record.family); // new access + new refresh
}

Both the attacker and the user get logged out of that session. The user logs in again; the attacker can't.

Logout becomes trivial

  • Logout: revoke the family of the refresh token.
  • Logout everywhere: revoke every token for the user.
  • Password change: revoke everything (whoever had the old password loses access).

Testing it without a database

The service only talks to a RefreshTokenRepository interface. In production it's MongoDB; in tests it's a Map. That makes the security tests fast and readable:

it("detects refresh token reuse and revokes the whole session", async () => {
  const { refreshToken: stolen } = await registerUser();
  const rotated = (await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: stolen })).body.refreshToken;

  // Attacker replays the old token -> rejected, and the session is killed.
  await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: stolen }).expect(401);
  // The legitimate user's newer token no longer works either.
  await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: rotated }).expect(401);
});

The whole suite (17 tests) runs in about a second.

Two more details worth copying

Don't leak which emails exist. Return the same error for "wrong password" and "no such user", and compare against a dummy bcrypt hash when the user doesn't exist so the response time is the same.

Let MongoDB clean up for you. A TTL index on expiresAt deletes expired tokens automatically:

expiresAt: { type: Date, required: true, expires: 0 }

Get the full code

Everything above (plus roles, Zod validation, error handling, Docker and the tests) is in a free, MIT-licensed starter:

👉 github.com/baivoo28/express-saas-starter

Clone it, set one env var, run npm run dev. If you find something to improve in the auth flow, issues and PRs are welcome. A ⭐ helps other people find it.

description:

title: Edge-Adaptive Hiera-Seg Model for Building-Integrated Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.21680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Building integrated photovoltaic power forecasting is challenging because facade orientation, rooftop geometry, nearby buildings, vegetation, cloud movement, module temperature, inverter status and edge device reliability jointly affect power generation. This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short term BIPV power forecasting with multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion. RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance measurements, module temperature, facade orientation, rooftop masks, shading labels, sky condition, historical power and edge device state are aligned into synchronous forecasting windows. HieraSeg extracts hierarchical regions from facade, rooftop, sky, shadow and background images, while the edge-adaptive module changes feature weights under missing frames, latency shifts and local shading changes. The segmentation branch identifies occluded module areas and separates facade, rooftop, sky and background evidence before the forecasting head estimates future BIPV output. Experiments are designed on a simulated multibuilding BIPV dataset with unseen building and unseen orientation tests. The model reports predicted power, confidence interval, dominant evidence, occlusion contribution, orientation contribution and energy-management review priority. This output is intended to show whether the forecast is driven by irradiance change, visible shading, orientation response, stale edge information or recent power history. The framework supports local forecasting at edge controllers with limited communication delay and computing resources, linking visual occlusion, irradiance dynamics and power history to traceable forecasting results for building energy management, microgrid scheduling and BIPV operation planning.

title: 96 rows out of 47,114: when 92% of your joins return nothing and 97% of the rest return the wrong match
description:
A join returns rows. That is all it promises. It does not promise the rows mean anything.

We learned this the expensive way. A league dashboard was reading 46 competitions. The database holds 751 for the same predictions. Nobody had changed a query; nobody had deleted a row. The join had been succeeding for months — returning thousands of rows, every one attached to the wrong match.

This is the audit, run against production: ai_predictions (47,209 rows, 47,114 graded), matches (85,580) and nami_matches (89,601). The lesson is narrower than "test your joins": row counts cannot validate a join, and the only thing that can is a semantic assertion on the payload.

The join everyone writes

ai_predictions has a column named match_id. matches has a primary key named id. The query writes itself:

SELECT m.competition_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled
GROUP BY 1;

It runs in under a second. It returns 46 rows. It is wrong.

The first warning sign is parent coverage, which nobody computes because the query already returned data:

SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled)                            AS settled,
  COUNT(*)                                                                       AS joined_by_id,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled), 2) AS pct
FROM ai_predictions p JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled;

settled  joined_by_id  pct
  47114          3736  7.93

92.07% of graded predictions have no parent in matches. On a foreign key that is a catastrophe. Here it produced silence, because a join returning some rows looks like one that works.

The resolved rows are worse than the missing ones

The 7.93% that resolved are not correct. They are collisions — two unrelated integer sequences that happen to overlap. Three independent checks prove it, and any one alone would have caught it.

Check 1 — the scores disagree. A prediction stores the final score it was graded against; so does the match row. If the join is real they must match.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS comparable,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.match_home_score = m.home_score
                          AND p.match_away_score = m.away_score) AS agree,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.match_home_score = m.home_score
                          AND p.match_away_score = m.away_score) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled AND p.match_home_score IS NOT NULL AND m.home_score IS NOT NULL;

comparable  agree  pct
      3581     96  2.68

97.32% of resolved rows hang off a match with a different final score. The same check against the correct key returns 99.77% — coming up.

Check 2 — the calendar disagrees. Compare the day the prediction was written with the day the joined match kicked off:

|created_at - kickoff|    rows
0 days                       0
1-3 days                     6
4-30 days                2,479
31-180 days              1,251

Zero same-day. Six within three days. 3,730 rows point at a match that had already been played — sometimes weeks before the prediction existed.

Check 3 — the labels disagree. Join both tables to the same 3,736 predictions and compare competition IDs: 3,736 of 3,736 disagree, 100%. And the true competitions behind those rows number just 4 — four real competitions scattered across 46 invented ones.

That is the failure mode: a broken join does not produce empty output. It produces plausible, confidently wrong output, and the error is concentrated rather than random.

Why nothing stopped it: three ID spaces, zero foreign keys

The schema holds more than one identity per match, and every one is a bare integer:

matches.id                 811  ..  92,780         (dense, curated)
matches.nami_id        4,336,437 .. 4,670,168      (vendor natural key)
nami_matches.nami_id   4,336,437 .. 4,670,170
nami_matches.id              3 .. 25,340,015       (sparse surrogate)
ai_predictions.match_id  3,974 .. 24,360,892

The ranges overlap, which is why the collision rate is 7.9% instead of 0%. The column type cannot tell the spaces apart, and neither can the planner. The constraint that would have failed loudly is missing:

SELECT conname, conrelid::regclass AS tbl, confrelid::regclass AS ref
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE contype = 'f' AND conrelid::regclass::text IN ('ai_predictions','matches');

matches_competition_id_fkey  matches  competitions
matches_home_team_id_fkey    matches  teams
matches_away_team_id_fkey    matches  teams

matches has three outbound foreign keys. ai_predictions has none — its match_id, model_id and user_id are unconstrained integers, each a join waiting to mis-resolve.

The key that is actually correct

ai_predictions.match_id references nami_matches.id, the sparse surrogate of the raw feed. Not matches.id, not matches.nami_id. Same query, different target:

WITH joined AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.created_at, n.match_time,
         p.match_home_score AS p_home, p.match_away_score AS p_away,
         n.home_score_regular AS n_home, n.away_score_regular AS n_away
  FROM ai_predictions p
  LEFT JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                        AS settled,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE match_time IS NULL)                      AS no_parent,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at > match_time)                 AS written_after_kickoff,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL
                          AND (p_home <> n_home OR p_away <> n_away))  AS score_mismatch,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL
                          AND p_home = n_home AND p_away = n_away)
             / COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL), 2) AS score_agreement_pct
FROM joined;

settled  no_parent  written_after_kickoff  score_mismatch  score_agreement_pct
  47114          0                     81             106                99.77

100% parent coverage, zero orphans, scores agreeing on 46,680 of 46,786 comparable rows. The league dimension goes from 46 competitions to 751 and from 3,736 rows to 47,114 — a 12.6× larger evidence base, obtained by changing one identifier in an ON clause.

The residual deserves naming rather than rounding: 81 rows written after kickoff and 106 score disagreements (0.23%). Those are real defects, not join errors. A working key does not mean a clean table; it means the defects are visible at the right grain instead of laundered into wrong-parent rows.

The missing bridge

matches remains worth keeping — curated competition and team foreign keys, lottery classification, scheduling metadata. It is just reachable by four hops, not one, since matches.nami_id resolves against nami_matches.nami_id for 85,314 of 85,580 rows (99.69%):

ai_predictions.match_id -> nami_matches.id -> nami_matches.nami_id
                        -> matches.nami_id -> matches.id

The fix: make the join assert on its own payload

A foreign key on nami_matches.id prevents future orphans, and we added one. But it would not have caught this bug: match_id values inside matches.id's range are valid children of matches.id, because they happen to be. Referential integrity was never violated. Semantics were.

So the durable fix is a validated view that carries the assertion inside it:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_predictions_graded AS
SELECT p.id AS prediction_id, p.model_id, p.created_at,
       p.prediction_direction, p.hit, p.hit_1x2,
       n.id AS nami_match_id, n.competition_id, n.match_time,
       n.home_score_regular, n.away_score_regular,
       (p.match_home_score = n.home_score_regular
        AND p.match_away_score = n.away_score_regular) AS score_consistent,
       (p.created_at <= n.match_time)                  AS written_before_kickoff
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled
  AND p.match_home_score IS NOT NULL
  AND n.home_score_regular IS NOT NULL;

Consumers read the view, not the table. The two booleans then become a contract test that fails the build instead of the dashboard:

import psycopg2

DSN = "postgresql://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"
SQL = """
WITH t AS (
  SELECT p.created_at, p.match_home_score AS p_home, p.match_away_score AS p_away,
         n.match_time, n.home_score_regular AS n_home, n.away_score_regular AS n_away
  FROM ai_predictions p LEFT JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled)
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NULL),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at > match_time),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p_home = n_home AND p_away = n_away),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL)
FROM t
"""

def test_join_integrity():
    with psycopg2.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SET statement_timeout = '120s'")
        cur.execute(SQL)
        n, orphans, late, agree, comparable = cur.fetchone()
    assert round(100.0 * (n - orphans) / n, 2) >= 100.0, f"orphans={orphans}/{n}"
    assert round(100.0 * agree / comparable, 2) >= 99.5, "score disagreement too high"
    assert late <= 200, f"late-written rows={late} exceed known defect class"

Against the old join target the first assertion fails by 92 points. Against the correct one it passes with 0 orphans, 99.77% agreement and 81 late rows — three numbers a reviewer can argue with.

What the wrong join cost

naive matches.id correct nami_matches.id
rows reached 3,736 47,114
competitions 46 751
score agreement 2.68% 99.77%
orphans unmeasurable 0
rows both joinable and semantically true 96 46,680

96 of 47,114. 0.20%. That is the end-to-end correctness of the join as written; every per-league rate built on it was a statistic about collisions.

The generalisable part is that join success rate is a vanity metric: it measures whether two integer domains intersect, which in any schema with more than one surrogate key they always will. The only metric that means something is semantic agreement on a field both sides independently observed — here the final score, plus the calendar. Two checks, a few lines of SQL, available the whole time.

For every join in your reporting layer, name the field that would have to agree if the join were real. If you cannot name one, you do not have a join. You have a Cartesian product with good manners.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
description:
arXiv:2611.22050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

title: Django annotate() vs aggregate(): Performance Traps and Fixes
description:
aggregate() and annotate() both push calculations into the database, but they answer different questions.

The difference

aggregate() annotate()
Returns A dictionary, one row A queryset, one row per object
Chainable No Yes
Typical use Totals, dashboards Per-row values, filter/order by computed data 
from django.db.models import Count, Sum, Avg

# aggregate: one summary
Order.objects.filter(status="paid").aggregate(
    revenue=Sum("total"), average=Avg("total"), orders=Count("id")
)

# annotate: one value per customer
Customer.objects.annotate(order_count=Count("orders"), total_spent=Sum("orders__total"))

Replace loops and N+1 

# Slow
total = sum(o.total for o in Order.objects.filter(status="paid"))

# Fast
total = Order.objects.filter(status="paid").aggregate(t=Sum("total"))["t"]

Trap 1: join inflation (silent wrong numbers) 

Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders"),
    item_count=Count("orders__items"),
)

Two aggregates across different multi-valued relations multiply rows. Fixes:

# distinct=True for counts
Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders", distinct=True),
    item_count=Count("orders__items"),
)

Or use a Subquery for one of them:

from django.db.models import Subquery, OuterRef, Count, IntegerField
from django.db.models.functions import Coalesce

item_counts = (
    OrderItem.objects
    .filter(order__customer=OuterRef("pk"))
    .order_by()
    .values("order__customer")
    .annotate(c=Count("id"))
    .values("c")
)

customers = Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders"),
    item_count=Coalesce(Subquery(item_counts, output_field=IntegerField()), 0),
)

Don't use distinct=True with Sum or Avg: it de-duplicates values, not rows.

Trap 2: one query per number 

from django.db.models import Q

Order.objects.aggregate(
    paid=Count("id", filter=Q(status="paid")),
    refunded=Count("id", filter=Q(status="refunded")),
    revenue=Sum("total", filter=Q(status="paid")),
)

One scan, three answers.

Trap 3: group by with default ordering 

Order.objects.order_by().values("status").annotate(n=Count("id"))

values() before annotate() groups by those fields. A default Meta.ordering leaks into GROUP BY unless you clear it.

Trap 4: annotating just to filter 

Customer.objects.alias(order_count=Count("orders")).filter(order_count__gt=10)

alias() (Django 3.2+) computes the value without selecting it. Also filter on plain columns before annotating so fewer rows get grouped.

Trap 5: counts used as existence checks 

from django.db.models import Exists, OuterRef

Customer.objects.filter(Exists(Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk"))))

Big tables

  • Index filter columns and check qs.explain(analyze=True)
  • Cache totals that can be slightly stale
  • Use summary tables or materialized views for heavy reports
  • Count without annotations when you can, since .count() on an annotated queryset may wrap it in a subquery

Full guide

The complete post covers aggregating over annotations, a decision guide, a checklist, and an FAQ:

👉 https://blog.reiteachaigean.com/blog/django-orm-annotate-vs-aggregate-performance

Related reads:

  • select_related vs prefetch_related: Practical Examples

  • How to Fix Slow Django Admin Pages

title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
description:
arXiv:2611.21639v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.

title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.22103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

title: Checking an uploaded resume PDF before anyone reads it
description:
If your job board, career-services portal or review queue accepts resume PDFs, about 30 lines of Node.js can flag files with little extractable text, or with nothing that looks like an email address or phone number. Parsers work from the text they can pull out of the file, and that text can be missing things the page shows.

The failure that convinced me to check for this comes from a ReadableResume parsing test where a sample resume had its name and contact details in a Google Docs text box. Google Docs exported the box as a picture. The page looked complete, but the PDF's text had no name, email or phone, and the open-source parser in the test took the first heading, "EDUCATION", as the person's name. It got 34 of 46 fields right.

The check

This uses pdf.js in Node to pull the text out the way a parser would start, then runs three checks: fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters, no email match and no phone match.

// check-resume.mjs — usage: node check-resume.mjs resume.pdf
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { getDocument } from "pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs";

const EMAIL = /[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+(\.[\w-]+)+/;
const PHONE = /\+?\d[\d\s().-]{7,}\d/;

async function checkResume(path) {
  const data = new Uint8Array(await readFile(path));
  const pdf = await getDocument({ data }).promise;
  const pages = [];
  for (let number = 1; number <= pdf.numPages; number++) {
    const page = await pdf.getPage(number);
    const content = await page.getTextContent();
    // Rebuild lines from text items; hasEOL marks the end of a line in pdf.js
    let text = "";
    for (const item of content.items) text += item.str + (item.hasEOL ? "\n" : "");
    pages.push(text);
  }
  const text = pages.join("\n");
  const firstLine = text.split("\n").map((line) => line.trim()).find(Boolean) ?? "";
  const problems = [];
  if (text.replace(/\s/g, "").length < 200) problems.push("fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters: possibly a scan or an image saved as PDF");
  if (!EMAIL.test(text)) problems.push("no text matched the email pattern");
  if (!PHONE.test(text)) problems.push("no text matched the phone pattern");
  return { pages: pdf.numPages, characters: text.length, firstLine, problems };
}

console.log(await checkResume(process.argv[2]));

I ran it on a one-page sample resume exported from Google Docs, then on the same file after turning it into an image-only PDF with ImageMagick (magick -density 150 sample.pdf scanned.pdf), which is roughly what a scan or a "print to image" gives you:

$ node check-resume.mjs sample.pdf
{ pages: 1, characters: 1494, firstLine: 'Grace Liu', problems: [] }

$ node check-resume.mjs scanned.pdf
{
  pages: 1,
  characters: 0,
  firstLine: '',
  problems: [
    'fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters: possibly a scan or an image saved as PDF',
    'no text matched the email pattern',
    'no text matched the phone pattern'
  ]
}

Both files look the same on screen. The script pulled 1,494 characters from the original and none from the image-only copy.

What to do with the result

  • No text at all. Ask for a fresh export from the original document instead of rejecting the upload outright. A scan or an image saved as PDF has no text until something runs OCR on it.
  • No email or phone match. Paste the PDF's text into a plain editor and look for the contact details. If they're missing there but visible on the page, in a text box or an image, ask the person to move them into the body of the document and export again.
  • Show the first line the script extracted. "Your PDF's text starts with 'EDUCATION'" lets the uploader compare it with the page and see whether their name made it into the text.

What this doesn't catch

A PDF can pass all three checks and still read badly. The script can't tell whether the words come out in the right order, whether a two-column layout mixed lines together, or whether a job's dates wrapped onto a second line in a narrow table column. That last one cost 6 fields in the same test: the parser read the year on the second line as the company. To check by hand, paste the text into a plain editor and read it top to bottom, checking that each job's dates still sit with the right entry; this guide on what to look for in the pasted text goes through the other cases. A free ATS resume checker shows what the same open-source parser put in each field and every line of text it read from the first three pages of a PDF; the file stays in your browser.

The phone pattern is loose on purpose so it accepts numbers with country codes, and it's too loose in one way: it also matches a date range like 2023 - 2024, so this check can miss a missing phone number. The parser in that test only recognised US-style numbers.

A form for review requests

If you review resumes by hand, ask people to upload the PDF or Word file they plan to submit. A resume review request template on Tally collects that file along with the role they're applying for, their career stage and when they need feedback. The job posting link is optional.

I work on ReadableResume, which ran the parsing test and makes the checker mentioned above.
