title: Integrating Multi-Modal LLMs into Governed BPMN Pipelines
description:
Customer Onboarding and Know Your Customer (KYC) compliance represent one of the most operationally friction-heavy domains in enterprise banking. Processing a single retail or corporate onboarding application requires verifying heterogeneous, unstructured visual documents: government-issued passports, national identity cards, utility bills for proof of address, tax identity certificates, and corporate articles of incorporation.

Traditionally, banking systems addressed document processing using one of two unsatisfactory approaches:

  1. Legacy OCR Systems: Brittle, template-based Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines that require rigid pixel-coordinate mapping. Minor layout shifts, scans with poor lighting, or folded document corners cause extraction pipelines to fail, sending up to 40% of documents to manual data-entry queues.
  2. Unconstrained AI Scripts: Standalone Python/AI scripts that send documents to Large Language Models (LLMs) and execute database writes directly. While highly flexible, unconstrained AI scripts lack operational governance, process visibility, regulatory audit trails, and stateful human escalation paths.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms resolve this dilemma by constructing Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipelines. By embedding Multi-Modal LLMs (capable of simultaneous vision and textual inference) directly inside Flowable BPMN 2.0 process engines, document intelligence is treated as a stateful, auditable step within a enterprise-grade business workflow.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Mapping & Document Extraction Taxonomy

Within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) alignment, onboarding document processing is divided across isolated service domains. Multi-modal vision models extract facts, while BPMN gateways enforce compliance state transitions.

BIAN Service Domain Document Category Multi-Modal Inspection Scope Extracted Fact Payload Flowable Gateway Rule Fallback Target
Identity Verification Government Passport / ID Photo validity, MRZ text parsing, hologram/tamper check ID Number, Full Name, DOB, Expiry Date Confidence score ≥0.92 AND Expiry > Today KYC Analyst User Task
Party Data Management Utility Bill / Bank Statement Address layout validation, issuing authority verification Resident Address, Issue Date, Account Holder Name Issue Date ≤90 Days AND Name Match Compliance Review Task
Customer Onboarding Articles of Incorporation Corporate entity structure, beneficial ownership parsing UBO Names, Registration Number, Tax ID All UBOs Identified AND Sanction Checked Senior Underwriter Task
Credit Assessment Tax Return / Financials Income table extraction, auditor seal verification Gross Annual Income, Net Tax Paid, Audit Status Income ≥ Min Loan Qualification Threshold Credit Exception Task

Mathematical Model: Multi-Modal KYC Confidence & Risk Scoring

To prevent flawed AI extractions from silently propagating into core customer databases, a multi-modal extraction step evaluates a composite Document Confidence Index Ckyc-total​ :

Ckyc-total​=wvision​⋅Cvision-quality​+wmrz​⋅Cmrz-match​+wfield​⋅Cfield-extract​

Where:

  • Cvision-quality​ is the multi-modal model's visual assessment of document integrity (detecting blur, glare, edge truncation, and digital manipulation).
  • Cmrz-match​ is a deterministic checksum algorithm evaluating Machine Readable Zone (MRZ) characters against extracted visual text fields.
  • Cfield-extract​ is the average log-probability confidence score across extracted key-value fields.
  • wvision​,wmrz​,wfield​ are normalized weighting factors such that ∑w=1.0 .

If Ckyc-total​<Θauto-approve​ (typically set to 0.92), the BPMN engine routes the extracted payload alongside visual bounding-box metadata directly to a human compliance officer for visual verification.

Architecture Topology: Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipeline

The architecture strictly isolates Stateless Multi-Modal AI Inference from Stateful Workflow Management (Flowable) and Core Customer Persistence.

                   GOVERNED MULTI-MODAL BPMN PIPELINE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | FLOWABLE BPMN 2.0 PROCESS ENGINE                                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Start Onboarding ] ───► [ ServiceTask: MultiModalKycDelegate ]               |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |                            Calls Vision Inference API                           |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |  [ ExclusiveGateway: Evaluate Confidence & Compliance Rules ]                   |
  +-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------+
                                              |
            ┌─────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┐
            | Confidence >= 0.92 & Valid                                        | Confidence < 0.92 OR Expired
            v                                                                   v
  +-----------------------------------+                               +-----------------------------------+
  | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |                               | FLOWABLE HUMAN KANBAN TASK        |
  |                                   |                               |                                   |
  | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |                               | 1. Render Side-by-Side Image UI   |
  | [ Persist Verified Data ]         |                               | 2. Highlight Extracted Fields     |
  +-----------------------------------+                               | 3. Await Human Review Sign-Off    |
                                                                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                                                                                        |
                                                                               Human Officer Approves
                                                                                        |
                                                                                        v
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+
                                                                      | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |
                                                                      | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+

Technical Implementation: Flowable BPMN 2.0 & Multi-Modal Java Delegate

1. Flowable Process Definition (kyc-onboarding-process.bpmn20.xml)

This BPMN 2.0 XML definition orchestrates document extraction via a custom Java Delegate, evaluates extraction confidence via an exclusive gateway, and routes to a human user task if validation criteria are unmet.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<definitions xmlns="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL"
             xmlns:flowable="http://flowable.org/bpmn"
             targetNamespace="BIAN/CustomerOnboarding">

  <process id="kycMultiModalOnboarding" name="Multi-Modal KYC Onboarding" isExecutable="true">

    <startEvent id="startEvent" name="Onboarding Document Uploaded" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="startEvent" targetRef="extractDocumentTask" />

    <!-- Service Task executing Multi-Modal Vision AI Extraction -->
    <serviceTask id="extractDocumentTask" 
                 name="Extract ID Document via Multi-Modal AI" 
                 flowable:class="com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate.MultiModalKycDelegate" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="extractDocumentTask" targetRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" />

    <!-- Exclusive Gateway evaluating Confidence & Expiry Boundaries -->
    <exclusiveGateway id="evaluateConfidenceGateway" name="Confidence & Validity Check" />

    <!-- Path 1: Automated Approval (High Confidence & Valid Document) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore >= 0.92 && !isDocumentExpired && isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Path 2: Human Compliance Escalation (Low Confidence or Data Anomaly) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="humanReviewUserTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore < 0.92 || isDocumentExpired || !isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Human Task for Manual Compliance Review -->
    <userTask id="humanReviewUserTask" 
              name="Human KYC Compliance Review" 
              flowable:candidateGroups="kyc_compliance_officers">
      <documentation>
        Review document extraction anomaly for Application: ${applicationId}. 
        Confidence Score: ${kycConfidenceScore}. Reason: ${extractionFailureReason}
      </documentation>
    </userTask>

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="humanReviewUserTask" targetRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" />

    <exclusiveGateway id="checkHumanDecisionGateway" name="Human Decision?" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'APPROVED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="rejectApplicationEnd">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'REJECTED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <serviceTask id="createPartyAccountTask" 
                 name="Persist Party Record in Core Database" 
                 flowable:delegateExpression="${createPartyRecordDelegate}" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="createPartyAccountTask" targetRef="onboardingApprovedEnd" />

    <endEvent id="onboardingApprovedEnd" name="Onboarding Approved" />
    <endEvent id="rejectApplicationEnd" name="Onboarding Rejected" />

  </process>
</definitions>

2. Multi-Modal Vision Java Delegate Implementation (Java 21)

This Java Delegate transmits document image bytes to a multi-modal vision endpoint using Structured JSON Schema Outputs. It parses the response, computes checksum validations, and sets execution variables in Flowable's memory context.

package com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.DelegateExecution;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.JavaDelegate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.Base64;

@Component
public class MultiModalKycDelegate implements JavaDelegate {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public void execute(DelegateExecution execution) {
        String applicationId = (String) execution.getVariable("applicationId");
        byte[] documentImageBytes = (byte[]) execution.getVariable("documentImageBytes");

        System.out.println("Executing Multi-Modal Vision Extraction for Application: " + applicationId);

        try {
            // 1. Convert Document Bytes to Base64 Data URI
            String base64Image = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(documentImageBytes);

            // 2. Construct Multi-Modal Prompt with Structured Schema Response Format
            String requestPayload = buildVisionApiPayload(base64Image);

            // 3. Invoke Multi-Modal Vision API Endpoint (Internal Enterprise Gateway)
            HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(requestPayload))
                    .build();

            HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

            // 4. Parse Extracted Facts & Confidence Metrics
            JsonNode resultNode = objectMapper.readTree(response.body());
            String rawJsonContent = resultNode.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
            JsonNode extractedFields = objectMapper.readTree(rawJsonContent);

            String idNumber = extractedFields.path("idNumber").asText();
            String fullName = extractedFields.path("fullName").asText();
            String expirationDateStr = extractedFields.path("expirationDate").asText();
            String mrzCode = extractedFields.path("mrzCode").asText();
            double confidenceScore = extractedFields.path("overallConfidenceScore").asDouble();

            // 5. Evaluate Deterministic Business Logic Rules
            LocalDate expirationDate = LocalDate.parse(expirationDateStr, DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
            boolean isExpired = expirationDate.isBefore(LocalDate.now());
            boolean isMrzValid = validateMrzChecksum(idNumber, mrzCode);

            // 6. Set Flowable Execution Variables for Gateway Evaluation
            execution.setVariable("extractedIdNumber", idNumber);
            execution.setVariable("extractedFullName", fullName);
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", confidenceScore);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", isExpired);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", isMrzValid);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", 
                    isExpired ? "DOCUMENT_EXPIRED" : (!isMrzValid ? "MRZ_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH" : "NONE"));

        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("Multi-Modal Extraction Failed: " + e.getMessage());
            // Fallback: Force flow to Human Review Task by setting low confidence
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", 0.0);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", true);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", false);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", "VISION_API_EXECUTION_FAILURE");
        }
    }

    private String buildVisionApiPayload(String base64Image) {
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
              "messages": [
                {
                  "role": "user",
                  "content": [
                    {"type": "text", "text": "Extract passport data matching JSON schema: idNumber, fullName, expirationDate (YYYY-MM-DD), mrzCode, overallConfidenceScore."},
                    {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,%s"}}
                  ]
                }
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(base64Image);
    }

    private boolean validateMrzChecksum(String idNumber, String mrzCode) {
        // Deterministic check: Verify MRZ line 2 contains exact ID number string
        return mrzCode != null && !mrzCode.isEmpty() && mrzCode.contains(idNumber);
    }
}

Regulatory Auditability, Bounded Autonomy, and Privacy

Deploying AI document processing under financial regulatory frameworks (such as EBA ICT guidelines, OCC Bulletins, and GDPR) mandates strict auditability and data governance:

1. Side-by-Side Visual Review Interface

When an application routes to the humanReviewUserTask, the Flowable operational UI renders the raw document image alongside the extracted fields. Extracted text is highlighted with bounding-box coordinates returned by the vision model, allowing human compliance officers to verify facts in seconds.

+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
| DOCUMENT SOURCE IMAGE (PASSPORT)   | EXTRACTED FACTS & CONFIDENCE METRICS|
|                                    |                                    |
| [ PHOTO ]  P<GBRSMITH<<JOHN<<<<<<  | Full Name:   John Smith  [99.8%]   |
|            1234567897GBR8501010... | ID Number:   123456789  [99.5%]   |
|                                    | Exp. Date:   2028-05-12 [98.1%]   |
| [!] MRZ Checksum Passed            | Overall Confidence: 99.1% (PASSED)  |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

2. Immutable Audit Snapshot Logging

AI extractions must never overwrite historical compliance logs. For every document processed, the pipeline persists an immutable JSON audit snapshot to the central compliance data lake (Elasticsearch / S3 WORM storage), linking the raw document SHA-256 hash to the Flowable ProcessInstanceId:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-KYC-2026-881204",
  "flowableProcessInstanceId": "PROC-901283",
  "bianDomain": "IdentityVerification",
  "documentHash": "sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "aiModelId": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
  "extractedPayload": {
    "idNumber": "123456789",
    "fullName": "John Smith",
    "expirationDate": "2028-05-12",
    "mrzChecksumPassed": true
  },
  "confidenceScore": 0.991,
  "gatewayOutcome": "AUTOMATED_APPROVAL",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:45:00Z"
}

3. Zero Data Retention at LLM Inference Layer

To comply with GDPR and local data residency laws, calls to third-party or internal multi-modal LLM gateways must use Zero Data Retention (ZDR) endpoints. Document image payloads are processed in-memory during inference and immediately purged from model memory without training log retention.

Embedding Multi-Modal LLM vision intelligence directly into Flowable BPMN pipelines solves the dual challenge of manual KYC bottlenecks and unconstrained AI risk. By relegating multi-modal vision models to structured fact extraction and leveraging BPMN exclusive gateways for rule evaluation and human escalation, modern core banking architectures achieve high operational throughput, sub-second onboarding execution, and complete regulatory compliance across all BIAN service domains.

title: How I Built VeloGrad (v1.1.0-beta): A C++20, Rust, and CUDA Deep Learning Engine from Scratch
description:
​

IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN / VeloGrad

Bare-metal, native-first deep learning & autoregressive inference engine in C++20, Rust, CUDA & Python.

VeloGrad (Beta)

VeloGrad is a bare-metal, native-first, pure-compiled deep learning and autoregressive inference engine engineered from scratch in C++20, Rust, CUDA, and Python by Ayushman Singh Rathore.

It eliminates Python runtime overhead, framework memory bloat, and garbage collection pauses by introducing an aligned static arena memory architecture, ahead-of-time (AOT) fused compute kernels, an empirical ~66.7% KV-cache and activation VRAM reduction engine, enterprise ZeRO-3 / FSDP distributed scaling with CPU/NVMe offload, and a natural-language autonomous training orchestrator (velograd.instruct).

Important

Public Beta Notice (v1.1.0-beta)

VeloGrad v1.1.0-beta is now in public beta.
All core compute kernels, hardware-fused operators, universal frontier model architectures (from 100M edge models up to 1T+ parameter MoE networks), Paged KV-cache VRAM reduction, ZeRO-3 FSDP parameter sharding, and natural-language autonomous training directives (velograd.instruct) have been verified with complete zero-defect automated test and benchmark suites. Community testing, empirical benchmarks, and feedback are…



View on GitHub




​Hey DEV community! My name is Ayushman Singh Rathore, and I’ve been building VeloGrad—an open-source tensor, autograd, and distributed training framework written in C++20, Rust, and CUDA with Python bindings.

​Today I’m releasing v1.1.0-beta into Public Beta. Before diving into the architecture, I want to share an honest builder lesson from v1.0.0 that completely changed how I ship code.

​The v1.0 Wake-Up Call: Auditing AI-Generated Scaffolding

​When I first pushed v1.0.0, I leaned too heavily on an AI coding agent to draft the initial scaffolding and README.md. Right after publishing, I audited the repository line by line and realized the agent had hallucinated benchmark claims and left broken Python bindings and stubbed functions.

​Instead of leaving an unverified repo up, I pulled back, stripped out every unverified claim, added a clear Public Beta status, and spent days rewriting, compiling, and testing the actual systems code so that every single line in the README is backed by real, executable code.

​What’s Inside VeloGrad v1.1.0-beta

​VeloGrad is designed to strip away Python dispatch overhead and GPU memory fragmentation during model training and fine-tuning by keeping the memory arena, autograd tape, and fused kernels inside a tight native runtime—while automatically falling back to AVX2/NEON SIMD kernels on CPU-only Linux, macOS, and Windows machines.

​1. Fused Forward & Backward Kernels (CUDA + SIMD Fallback)

​Instead of launching separate memory-bound kernels for every operation, VeloGrad fuses common transformer primitives into single passes:

​Fused GEMM + Bias + Activation (Forward & Backward)

​Fused RMSNorm + Residual Add

​Fused RoPE + Tiled Flash-Style Self-Attention

​Single-Pass Fused Cross-Entropy Loss (computes log-softmax and gradients without materializing massive [batch, seq, vocab] logit tensors in VRAM)

​Fused Multi-Tensor AdamW

​2. Static Arena Allocation & ~66.7% KV/VRAM Compression

​Dynamic allocations (cudaMalloc) during training loops cause fragmentation and latency spikes. VeloGrad pre-allocates a deterministic static memory arena and pairs block-quantized Paged KV-Cache with activation checkpointing (recompute_backward), cutting KV-cache and activation VRAM overhead by up to ~66.7% compared to unquantized baselines.

​3. ZeRO-3 Sharding + CPU Parameter Offloading

​To let developers train and fine-tune larger models on consumer GPUs without hitting OOM walls, VeloGrad implements ZeRO-3 (FSDP) parameter sharding and CPU parameter offloading over NCCL (with a cross-platform TCP/Ring fallback when NCCL isn't present), supporting SafeTensors and GGUF weights across Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, and Mistral model families.

​4. Natural-Language Training Orchestration (velograd.instruct)

​Alongside standard Python Tensor and nn.Module APIs, v1.1.0-beta introduces velograd.instruct, which auto-detects your local GPU/CPU topology and maps plain-English training directives directly into a configured sharding and training pipeline:

import velograd

Auto-detects available GPUs/RAM, loads weights, and configures sharding + VRAM compression

velograd.instruct(
"Fine-tune Llama-3.2-3B on local_dataset.jsonl with ZeRO-3 offloading and 66.7% KV compression"
)
How to Test v1.1.0-beta on Your Machine
​If you want to compile it and run the reproducible PyTorch comparison and VRAM profiling scripts on your own GPU or CPU laptop:
git clone https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad.git
cd VeloGrad
pip install -e .

Run the verification suite and benchmarks

pytest
python benchmarks/bench_vs_pytorch.py
python benchmarks/profile_vram.py
What’s Next & Call for Beta Testers
​Because this is a Public Beta, real-world hardware diversity is what matters most right now. If you test VeloGrad on NVIDIA RTX cards, multi-GPU workstations, Apple Silicon, or Windows/Linux CPUs, please open an issue on GitHub with your build logs or benchmark numbers!
​Repository: https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad

title: Every Heist Needs a Mastermind. So Does Your Backend.
description:
Every app you use runs a small heist behind the scenes.

Say you order a pair of shoes. One part of the system checks that the shoes are in stock. Another takes your payment. A third ships the box. Each one is a service, a small program with one job. Think of them as a crew: the inside guy, the safecracker and the driver.

Now picture that crew with no plan. They just message each other and hope it works out. The stock check says yes, the payment is still pending, and the driver leaves anyway. Nobody notices anything went wrong until the customer calls asking about an order they were never charged for, or one that never showed up.

Every heist needs a mastermind. In software, that’s called an orchestrator.

The orchestrator holds the plan and tells each service when to move. The driver doesn’t leave until the payment clears. If the payment fails, it tries again. If it still fails, the shoes go back on the shelf so you don’t end up shipping something nobody paid for. And every move is written down, so when something goes wrong, you can see exactly what happened and when.

That’s orchestration. It isn’t about making each service smarter. It’s about having one place that knows the whole plan.

Unmeshed is the orchestrator for your backend. If your services are talking to each other and hoping for the best, take a look at how it works:
Unmeshed Workflows

title: How to Turn One Photo Into a 12-Second AI Birthday Video (Candles, Zodiac Props, and Audio)
description:
AI birthday video generator from a single photo: they pop champagne on a park bench, blow out a Scorpio cake, or light a crown cake at the car window. Most people only think of a birthday clip five hours before midnight, which leaves zero time for a group shoot or an editing timeline. Turning one photo into a full 12-second birthday scene in your browser—with no slideshow, no timeline, and no subscription—is the shortest way to get a real celebration clip ready before the clock hits twelve.

Putting someone inside a 12-second birthday scene from one camera-roll photo comes down to three details: what kind of photo keeps their face intact, which prompt lines control the cake number and star sign, and how to add the birthday song after downloading the vertical MP4.

1. Pick one unobstructed photo, not a collage

Single-photo video models keep identity steady when the input shows one face clearly in even lighting:

  • Front or slight three-quarter angle: Sunglasses, heavy bangs over one eye, or side profiles force the model to guess the hidden half of the face when the head turns toward the cake.
  • Keep hands and props away from the chin: A drink held in front of the mouth during the source shot often melts into the candle-blowing motion.
  • Cropping: Waist-up or chest-up shots give the scene room for a seated park bench, a table with a layered cake, or a car window frame without squeezing the subject into a corner.

For pets—especially dogs in party hats or gift boxes—the same rule applies: look for clear markings on the coat and ears in bright daylight rather than a dim indoor blur. That is the exact setup behind the happy birthday dog video templates.

2. Edit the three variables before pressing generate

Every preset scene on AI Birthday Video Generator lets you rewrite the prompt before generating a 12-second 720p vertical (9:16) clip on Seedance 2 Mini:

  1. Age or candle number: Swap the number on the candle (28, 30, 50) explicitly in the prompt so the closeup matches the year.
  2. Star sign & table props: Change Scorpio cake and the black scorpion prop to match their sign, or switch to a crown cake and warm car-window framing.
  3. On-screen birthday text: If you want their first name or a short line written right on a sign, frosting, or black-and-white freeze frame, use the happy birthday AI templates built around readable in-frame lettering.

Note on the reference frames above: those frames come from creator posts on Instagram (@prachikarkun) and TikTok (@kidsaroundtheworldmimo) showing the visual look—they were not generated on our site.

3. Export and drop the birthday song in your posting app

The generated 9:16 MP4 finishes with its own party sound effects (cork pop, ambient chatter, celebratory beat) and no watermark, without locking a copyrighted song into the video file. Once you save the clip:

  • Instagram Stories / Reels & TikTok: Upload the 9:16 MP4 directly and pick the birthday song from the app audio library before posting at midnight.
  • Family WhatsApp or iMessage: Send the clip as-is—vertical 720p fills the phone screen immediately on tap.

Pricing and guarantees

AI Birthday Video Generator runs on a one-time pay-per-clip model with no subscription: $4.99 for your first clip (on accounts that have never paid), then $9.99 per single clip, or $19.99 for a 3-clip pack and $29.99 for a 5-clip pack. Unused clips stay on your balance, and any run that fails returns to your balance automatically.

If you were making a 12-second birthday clip tonight for a friend or family member, which detail matters most to lock down first—the exact age on the candles, their zodiac table props, or their name written across the cake?

title: Best Static Website Hosting Services in 2026
description:
TL;DR

  • Use Render Static Sites when your frontend runs alongside a backend API, background workers, or a database on the same platform.
  • Pick Netlify when your team relies on shareable preview links for every pull request before merging.
  • Choose Vercel when your team already builds with Next.js and exports a static site.
  • Before committing, check three deal-breakers that vary by host: commercial plan rules, whether hitting a cap pauses your live site, and SPA deep-link rewrites.

Shipping a static site like a React, Vue, or docs build sounds routine on paper. You run a build, get a folder of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, and upload them. In practice, picking the wrong host creates real headaches.

Once your site leaves localhost, you still have to connect your Git repo for auto-deploys, configure HTTPS on a custom domain, and add rewrite rules so refreshing /account/settings does not return a 404. You also need to watch the bill: does every pull-request preview eat into your monthly quota, and will one busy project pause every other site on the team?

A small frontend team should not face server-style surprises just to publish static files. Below, I compare nine static hosts, explain which workflow each fits best, break down pricing traps, and share a pre-launch checklist before you switch DNS.

Static site hosting comparison at a glance

Static hosting serves prebuilt HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets for docs sites and single-page apps (SPAs). If a request needs server-side rendering or backend code execution, you need an application service alongside static hosting. Inspect your build output directory to be sure.

Managed hosts serve files over a content delivery network (CDN) and handle TLS certificates automatically. This table compares managed Git and CLI workflows from provider docs.

Product and plan Git deploys, previews, and build limits Custom domains, HTTPS, and routing Pricing and usage limits
Render Static Sites Git deploys, PR previews Managed SSL, root/www redirect, rewrites Render pricing, plan bandwidth and build allowances
Netlify (Credit plans) Git deploys, PR previews Custom domains, HTTPS Shared team credits, exhaustion can pause all team sites
Vercel (Hobby) Git deploys, previews (100/day) Domains, HTTPS Personal use only, commercial sites need paid plans
Cloudflare Pages (Free) Git deploys, previews (500/mo, 1 concurrent, 20-min max) 100 domains/project, 2,000 static / 100 dynamic _redirects Free build limits, 25 MiB max per file
DigitalOcean App Platform Repo deploys, 1-hour build max Domains, HTTPS, routing varies by setup 3 free static apps, bandwidth billing applies
AWS Amplify Hosting Managed Git deploys, previews Custom domains, SSL Separate build, storage, bandwidth billing, account-dependent free tier
Azure Static Web Apps Repo deploys, staging Managed SSL, config routing No bandwidth overage on Free, per-preview and total storage caps
Firebase Hosting CLI deploys, preview links Domains, SSL, config rules Project storage and bandwidth, Spark limits can stop serving
GitHub Pages Repo publishing, workflow build rates Custom domains, HTTPS No free hosting for commercial SaaS or e-commerce

Watch the difference between build concurrency (how many builds run at once), build duration (how long one build can run), and deploy frequency (daily or monthly caps). A high monthly cap still leaves your team waiting if concurrency is capped at one.

Which static website host fits your site?

Render Static Sites for a frontend alongside application services

I pick Render when a static frontend belongs to an app that also needs an API, background workers, or a database. Its dedicated static site service serves files over a CDN without an application server, while Render web services and Render Postgres share the same dashboard. One platform means one set of permissions, deploys, and bills.

When moving a domain over, Render automatically pairs your root domain and www subdomain with a main-domain redirect (custom domains), and supports redirect and rewrite rules for SPAs. Check Render pricing for current plan allowances before locking in your team setup.

Netlify for pull-request preview workflows

I look at Netlify when reviewing live preview links on every pull request is central to how a team works. The key billing rule to watch on Netlify is the difference between preview builds and production deploys.

Under Netlify's credit-based pricing plans, creating a Deploy Preview uses 0 credits (though visitors loading that preview still count toward web requests and bandwidth), while successful production deploys consume credits. Read the credit rules carefully. Because running out of shared team credits can pause all projects, including live production sites, a shared team budget is an uptime risk as well as a billing concern.

Vercel for Next.js frontend workflows

I shortlist Vercel when a team is already built around Next.js and wants tight frontend preview links. Remember that static hosting only covers prebuilt HTML, CSS, and JS files. If your Next.js app needs server-side rendering, middleware, or API routes, check Vercel's compute pricing and limits separately.

Vercel Hobby limits you to 100 deployments per day and is strictly for personal, non-commercial use. Company or client sites need a paid plan, so check Vercel pricing for per-seat fees and included usage before building a team budget around the starter tier.

Cloudflare Pages for Git-based publishing within file limits

Cloudflare Pages works well when your repo uses standard Git deploys and your output fits its limits. Keep Cloudflare Pages separate from Workers Static Assets: Cloudflare publishes a Pages-to-Workers migration guide, so check current guidance before starting a new project.

On the Free plan, Cloudflare allows 500 builds per month, one concurrent build, a 20-minute build timeout, and a 25 MiB max size per file. That per-file cap matters most if your site serves large downloads or videos. Also check _redirects limits (2,000 static and 100 dynamic rules) and test what happens to your live site if a build fails or hits a quota.

DigitalOcean App Platform for small static-only apps

I consider DigitalOcean App Platform when a team already runs servers on DigitalOcean and wants to group a few small static sites in one place. DigitalOcean advertises three free static-only apps on its App Platform pricing page. Because one app can hold multiple components, check the billing docs to see how components are counted and when adding a backend service moves you off the free static tier.

Routing also takes a bit of checking. DigitalOcean's limits and URL-routing guide behave differently depending on the rule type, so verify your exact domain redirects, path redirects, and SPA fallback rules before moving DNS.

AWS Amplify Hosting for managed publishing with pay-as-you-go billing

AWS Amplify Hosting fits teams already on AWS who want Git-connected deploys without wiring up an S3 bucket and CloudFront distribution by hand. AWS's static website guide keeps those two paths separate.

Amplify's pricing page charges separately for build minutes, stored files, and bandwidth served. A busy docs repo and an asset-heavy download site therefore hit completely different parts of the bill. Before relying on a free tier, check whether your AWS account is still eligible for its introductory free offer.

Azure Static Web Apps for Azure-centered teams

Azure Static Web Apps makes sense for teams already anchored in Azure who want built-in staging environments for pull-request reviews. Watch the storage limits: Azure's quotas docs cap storage both per environment and across all environments combined, which limits how many open PR previews you can keep around.

Free plans do not allow paid bandwidth overages, and the plans and quotas pages list slightly different custom-domain counts for Standard, so confirm the exact limit in your subscription. Use the configuration guide to set SPA fallback routes and excluded paths.

Firebase Hosting for Firebase-centered teams

Firebase Hosting works cleanly for static sites and SPAs whose teams already use the Firebase CLI and preview links. Its hosting configuration keeps redirects, rewrites, and headers in firebase.json alongside your code, so teammates can review routing changes right in Git.

Keep Firebase Hosting separate from Firebase App Hosting. Firebase's product comparison reserves App Hosting for server-rendered apps. Before choosing Spark or Blaze, review storage, bandwidth, and limit rules, because hitting Spark limits can take the site offline and Blaze usage is shared across your Firebase project.

GitHub Pages for eligible project and documentation sites

GitHub Pages is a natural fit for open-source project sites and repository docs. Read GitHub's intended-use policy before assuming it covers company sites: it forbids free hosting for online businesses, e-commerce sites, and commercial SaaS, even though organization docs may qualify.

Check deep-link routing early too. Generated docs sites with an HTML file per page work out of the box, while React or Vue SPAs break when someone refreshes a sub-page unless a rewrite rule serves index.html.

What your team actually pays

Static hosting bills vary by deploy frequency and asset size. A docs site that deploys twenty times a day burns build minutes and deploy credits while barely touching bandwidth. A marketing site with large videos or downloads barely touches build limits while burning through bandwidth and request caps.

Check pricing for Render, Netlify, Vercel, DigitalOcean, or AWS Amplify, and add up six cost items:

  1. Plan base fee and per-seat charges
  2. Build minutes and extra concurrent builds
  3. Production-deploy credits
  4. Outbound bandwidth and request volume
  5. Storage for production and open preview builds
  6. Hosting-related DNS or domain fees (separate from domain registration)

Also check how a provider handles hitting a cap, through alerts, spending limits, automatic top-ups, overage fees, or hard pauses. Confirm whether a limit stops only new deploys or takes your live site offline too, especially when projects share one team budget.

Choose the host and verify it before switching DNS

Pick the provider whose deploy flow, plan rules, and limit behavior match your team, then test four things on a staging URL before updating production DNS:

  1. Confirm your build finishes inside the timeout and PR previews update on new commits.
  2. Refresh a nested SPA route like /account/settings directly, and check that a missing file like /assets/missing.js returns a real 404 instead of index.html.
  3. Verify SSL certificates issue cleanly and www redirects to your root domain (or vice versa) in one hop.
  4. Push a broken build on a test branch to confirm your last working deploy stays live and can roll back fast.

If your static site is the frontend for an app that also needs an API, background workers, or a PostgreSQL database, start with Render Static Sites so you can deploy frontend and backend services from the same workspace without splitting bills and permissions across providers.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best hosting service for static websites?

The best choice depends on your stack and workflow. Pick Netlify for shareable PR preview links, Vercel for Next.js static exports, and Render Static Sites when your frontend runs alongside backend APIs and databases. Verify commercial rules, routing support, and cap behavior.

Can I host a commercial static website for free?

Yes, if the provider's terms allow business use and your traffic stays within free limits. Check Vercel's fair-use rules and GitHub Pages' restrictions on commercial SaaS and online businesses before deploying company sites there.

Does a React or Next.js app count as a static website?

Yes, if your build outputs plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files without server-side rendering or middleware. Client-side routing works on static hosts, though refreshing nested URLs usually requires an SPA rewrite rule.

Can a static website use a database?

Yes. Static hosting only covers frontend file delivery. Your browser app can read and write dynamic data through a secured backend API, such as pairing Render Static Sites with a Render web service and Render Postgres in one workspace.

Can I move hosts without changing my domain?

Yes. Keep your domain at your registrar and point DNS records to the new host. The files are portable, so focus on translating redirect rules, SPA fallbacks, and cache headers, then test the preview URL and SSL certificate before updating DNS.

title: HTTP 100 Continue Expectation Header: When Clients Pause Before Sending Body
description:
Originally published on Code Beneath.

The HTTP 100 Continue Expect header is a mechanism that lets a client pause before sending a request body and wait for server permission. When a client sends Expect: 100-continue in the headers, it holds back the message body and waits for the server to respond with status code 100 (Continue) or reject the request outright. Many developers ignore this header entirely, leading to timeout hangs, wasted bandwidth on large uploads, or confused clients. Understanding the HTTP 100 continue expect header example implementation patterns is essential for building robust APIs that handle large payloads, file uploads, and resource-constrained scenarios efficiently.

Why Clients Send the Expect Header

Before uploading a 500 MB file or posting a large JSON body, a client may want to check: will the server accept this request at all? Perhaps the authentication token is invalid, the resource does not exist, or the content type is wrong. Without the Expect header, the client would waste time and bandwidth sending the entire body, only to receive a 401 or 400 response from the server.

With Expect: 100-continue, the flow is different. The client sends headers and waits. The server reads the headers, validates them, and either says "100 Continue, send the body" or "417 Expectation Failed" or rejects with another 4xx status. Only if the server says 100 do you transmit the body.

This is especially useful in handling HTTP requests where you need to validate early and avoid expensive resource allocation. A multi-part file upload endpoint can reject bad requests before the kernel buffers megabytes of data.

The Protocol Flow

The sequence goes like this:

  1. Client sends request line, all headers (including Expect: 100-continue), and waits without sending the body.
  2. Server reads the request headers, validates them (auth, content-type, size limits), and either sends 100 Continue or sends a final response like 417 Expectation Failed or 401 Unauthorized.
  3. If server sends 100, client sends the request body.
  4. Server reads the body, processes it, and sends the final response (200, 201, etc.).
  5. If server sends a final response (not 100), client stops and does not send the body.

Most clients set a timeout on the wait for 100 Continue, often 1 second or configurable. If the server does not respond within that window, the client may assume the server does not understand the header and send the body anyway.

Go Server: Accepting and Rejecting 100-Continue

Here is a complete, runnable Go server that demonstrates proper handling. The http.Server in Go does not automatically handle the Expect header, so you must do it manually. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
)

func uploadHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Check for Expect: 100-continue
    if r.Header.Get("Expect") == "100-continue" {
        // Validate headers before reading body
        contentLength := r.ContentLength
        maxSize := int64(10 * 1024 * 1024) // 10 MB limit

        if contentLength < 0 {
            // Content-Length not provided or chunked
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusLengthRequired)
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "Content-Length required\n")
            return
        }

        if contentLength > maxSize {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "File too large: %d > %d\n", contentLength, maxSize)
            return
        }

        // All checks passed, tell client to send the body
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue)
        // Important: flush the response to ensure client receives 100
        if f, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok {
            f.Flush()
        }
    }

    // Now read the body (after sending 100 or skipping this logic entirely if no Expect)
    body, err := io.ReadAll(r.Body)
    if err != nil {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest)
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "Failed to read body: %v\n", err)
        return
    }
    defer r.Body.Close()

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    fmt.Fprintf(w, `{"uploaded": %d, "status": "success"}`+"\n", len(body))
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/upload", uploadHandler)
    log.Println("Server listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Key points in this Go server:

  • We check the Expect header after the headers are parsed.
  • We validate Content-Length and other constraints before signaling 100.
  • We call w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue) to send 100.
  • We call Flush() to ensure the response is sent immediately, not buffered.
  • We then proceed to read the body with io.ReadAll(r.Body).
  • If validation fails, we send a final error status (417, 413, etc.) and do not send 100; the body is never read.

Python Server: Same Pattern with Flask

Here is the equivalent in Python with Flask. Flask does not automatically handle 100-continue either, but we can intercept the request before the WSGI server reads the body. 

from flask import Flask, request, Response
import sys

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def handle_expect_continue():
    """
    Intercept requests with Expect: 100-continue before WSGI reads the body.
    This runs before the route handler is called.
    """
    if request.headers.get("Expect") == "100-continue":
        # Validate headers
        content_length = request.content_length
        max_size = 10 * 1024 * 1024  # 10 MB

        if content_length is None:
            # No Content-Length header; reject
            return "Content-Length required\n", 411

        if content_length < 0:
            return "Invalid Content-Length\n", 400

        if content_length > max_size:
            return f"File too large: {content_length} > {max_size}\n", 413

        # All checks passed; send 100 Continue
        # We write directly to the WSGI input stream's underlying socket
        sys.stdout.flush()
        # In production, use the WSGI environ to access wsgi.input
        # and write to the client socket directly.
        # For now, we rely on the Flask test client or a proper WSGI server
        # to handle this. A real implementation requires gunicorn/uWSGI
        # middleware or a custom WSGI wrapper.

@app.route("/upload", methods=["POST"])
def upload():
    """
    Handle file upload. By the time this route is called,
    the client has already received 100 (or not).
    """
    if request.content_length is None:
        return "Content-Length required\n", 411

    data = request.get_data()
    return {
        "uploaded": len(data),
        "status": "success"
    }, 200

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # For testing with built-in server (not production-grade)
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8080, debug=False)

Flask's built-in development server does not handle Expect properly because it is single-threaded and does not separate header parsing from body reading. In production, use Gunicorn, uWSGI, or another WSGI server that lets you inject middleware to send 100 Continue at the socket level before the WSGI app reads the body. The pattern is to write the HTTP response "HTTP/1.1 100 Continue\r\n\r\n" directly to the client socket.

Python WSGI Middleware for 100-Continue

Here is a production-ready WSGI middleware that wraps any Flask or other WSGI app and handles 100-continue correctly by writing to the environ: 

import sys
import io

class Expect100ContinueMiddleware:
    """
    WSGI middleware that sends 100 Continue when appropriate.
    """
    def __init__(self, app, max_size=10*1024*1024):
        self.app = app
        self.max_size = max_size

    def __call__(self, environ, start_response):
        """
        Called by the WSGI server for each request.
        """
        expect = environ.get("HTTP_EXPECT", "").lower()

        if expect == "100-continue":
            content_length_str = environ.get("CONTENT_LENGTH", "")

            # Validate before reading body
            if not content_length_str:
                # Send 411 Length Required
                start_response("411 Length Required", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Content-Length required\n"]

            try:
                content_length = int(content_length_str)
            except ValueError:
                start_response("400 Bad Request", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Invalid Content-Length\n"]

            if content_length < 0:
                start_response("400 Bad Request", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [b"Negative Content-Length\n"]

            if content_length > self.max_size:
                start_response("413 Payload Too Large", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
                return [f"File too large: {content_length} > {self.max_size}\n".encode()]

            # Send 100 Continue to the client
            wsgi_input = environ["wsgi.input"]
            if hasattr(wsgi_input, "_sock"):
                # Direct socket access (not always available)
                try:
                    wsgi_input._sock.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 100 Continue\r\n\r\n")
                except Exception:
                    pass  # Ignore if socket not available

        # Call the wrapped WSGI app
        return self.app(environ, start_response)


# Example usage with Flask
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/upload", methods=["POST"])
def upload():
    return {"status": "success"}, 200

# Wrap the Flask app with the middleware
app.wsgi_app = Expect100ContinueMiddleware(app.wsgi_app)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Use a proper WSGI server: gunicorn -w 1 app:app
    app.run(port=8080)

This middleware validates headers before the WSGI app reads the body, and conditionally sends 100 Continue.

Go Client: Sending Expect: 100-Continue

Now let us write a client that actually sends the Expect header and handles the response properly: 

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

func uploadWithExpect(serverURL string, data []byte) error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
    }

    body := bytes.NewReader(data)
    req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", serverURL, body)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to create request: %w", err)
    }

    // Set the Expect header to signal the server
    req.Header.Set("Expect", "100-continue")
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")

    // Important: explicitly set Content-Length so the server knows size before body arrives
    req.ContentLength = int64(len(data))

    log.Printf("Sending request with Expect: 100-continue, body size: %d bytes\n", len(data))

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("request failed: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    // Read the final response body
    respBody, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to read response: %w", err)
    }

    log.Printf("Server responded with status: %d\n", resp.StatusCode)
    log.Printf("Response body: %s\n", string(respBody))

    if resp.StatusCode >= 400 {
        return fmt.Errorf("server rejected request: %d", resp.StatusCode)
    }

    return nil
}

func main() {
    // Test data: 5 MB
    testData := bytes.Repeat([]byte("x"), 5*1024*1024)

    err := uploadWithExpect("http://localhost:8080/upload", testData)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Upload failed: %v\n", err)
    }

    log.Println("Upload succeeded")
}

Key points in the client:

  • We set Expect: 100-continue in the headers.
  • We set Content-Length explicitly so the server knows the body size.
  • We call client.Do(req), which handles the 100 Continue protocol automatically in Go: it waits for the 100 response before sending the body, or if it gets a final status, it stops.
  • The Go HTTP client has a default timeout of about 1 second for waiting on 100 Continue; if it does not arrive, it sends the body anyway.

Python Client: Sending Expect Header

In Python, the standard library urllib does not support 100 Continue well, but the requests library has better support: 

import requests
import io

def upload_with_expect(server_url, data):
    """
    Upload data using Expect: 100-continue.
    The requests library handles the protocol automatically.
    """
    headers = {
        "Expect": "100-continue",
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
    }

    # Create a BytesIO object to send as body
    body = io.BytesIO(data)

    print(f"Sending {len(data)} bytes with Expect: 100-continue")

    try:
        # requests automatically handles 100 Continue if present
        resp = requests.post(
            server_url,
            data=body,
            headers=headers,
            timeout=10,
        )

        print(f"Server responded: {resp.status_code}")
        print(f"Response: {resp.text}")

        if resp.status_code >= 400:
            raise Exception(f"Server error: {resp.status_code}")

        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Upload failed: {e}")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_data = b"x" * (5 * 1024 * 1024)  # 5 MB
    success = upload_with_expect("http://localhost:8080/upload", test_data)
    if success:
        print("Upload succeeded")

Comparison: When to Use Expect: 100-Continue

Scenario Use Expect: 100-continue? Reason
Large file uploads (100 MB+) Yes Avoid wasting bandwidth if server rejects early (auth, quota, format).
REST API with small JSON payloads (<100 KB) No Latency cost (extra round trip) outweighs benefit. Just send it.
WebRTC or streaming over UDP/QUIC N/A Not applicable; these protocols do not use HTTP semantics.
Resumable uploads with chunking Yes Server can reject at chunk boundaries or validate chunk signatures early.
gRPC or Protocol Buffers No gRPC has its own flow control and backpressure mechanisms; Expect not used.
Slow network, high payload latency Yes Server can reject before kilobytes arrive; saves time and data.

Common Mistakes

Not Flushing the 100 Response

If the server sends w.WriteHeader(http.StatusContinue) but does not call Flush(), the response may be buffered. The client waits forever (until timeout) for the 100 response, then sends the body anyway. Always flush after writing the 100 status.

Sending 100 After Reading Headers Incompletely

If you send 100 Continue and then discover a validation error, you cannot send another status code. The connection is locked into sending the body. Always validate all headers first (Content-Length, Content-Type, auth, etc.) before sending 100.

Client Not Setting Content-Length

If the client sends Expect: 100-continue without Content-Length, the server cannot validate the payload size upfront. Many servers will reject this or ignore the Expect header. Always pair Expect with an explicit Content-Length.

Ignoring the Header Entirely

Some servers read the entire request body without checking for Expect. This breaks the protocol: the client is waiting for 100, the server is reading the body, and they deadlock. Go and Python HTTP libraries handle this internally, but custom socket code must respect the header.

Timing Diagram

Client                                    Server
  |                                          |
  | POST /upload HTTP/1.1                   |
  | Expect: 100-continue                    |
  | Content-Length: 5000000                 |
  | (no body yet)                           |
  |---------------------------------------->|
  |                                    [parse headers]
  |                                    [validate size, auth, etc.]
  |                                    [all OK]
  |                                   
  | HTTP/1.1 100 Continue                   |
  |<----------------------------------------|
  |                                          |
  | [5MB body]                              |
  |---------------------------------------->|
  |                                   [read body]
  |                                   [process]
  |                                          |
  | HTTP/1.1 200 OK                         |
  | Content-Type: application/json          |
  | {"uploaded": 5000000, "status": ...}   |
  |<----------------------------------------|
  |                                          |

Measuring the Impact

To see real timing differences, use curl with the -w flag to measure handshake time vs. upload time: 

#!/bin/bash

# Generate a 10 MB test file
dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=10 of=testfile.bin 2>/dev/null

echo "=== Upload WITH Expect: 100-continue ==="
time curl -X POST \
  -H "Expect: 100-continue" \
  --data-binary @testfile.bin \
  -w "\nConnect: %{time_connect}s, Time-to-first: %{time_starttransfer}s, Total: %{time_total}s\n" \
  http://localhost:8080/upload

echo ""
echo "=== Upload WITHOUT Expect header ==="
time curl -X POST \
  --data-binary @testfile.bin \
  -w "\nConnect: %{time_connect}s, Time-to-first: %{time_starttransfer}s, Total: %{time_total}s\n" \
  http://localhost:8080/upload

On a good network with a responsive server, the difference is small. But if the server rejects the request (e.g., 401), the Expect version saves the time it would take to send the body.

FAQ

Does HTTP/2 support Expect: 100-continue?

HTTP/2 deprecates the Expect header in favor of its own flow control mechanisms. HTTP/2 uses SETTINGS frames and WINDOW_UPDATE to signal backpressure. However, if your HTTP/2 implementation maps it to HTTP/1.1 at the boundary, the header still works.

What if the server never sends 100 or a final status?

The client will wait for a configured timeout (usually 1-2 seconds) and then send the body anyway. This is a safety mechanism to handle servers that do not understand Expect. After the timeout, the client assumes it is safe to proceed.

Can I send 100-continue for GET requests?

Technically yes, but it makes no sense. GET requests do not have a body, so there is nothing to pause on. The server will likely ignore the header. Use Expect only with POST, PUT, or PATCH.

Should I always send Expect when uploading files?

Only for large files or when early validation is critical. For small uploads (under 1 MB), the latency of the extra round trip often outweighs the savings. Measure your use case.

How does Expect interact with Content-Encoding?

Expect is about request headers and size validation. Content-Encoding (gzip, deflate, etc.) happens after validation. The Content-Length in the Expect header validation should be the encoded size that actually goes on the wire.

What status codes reject Expect: 100-continue?

Common rejections: 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 413 Payload Too Large, 417 Expectation Failed. Any status code other than 100 or 1xx tells the client to stop sending the body.

Does nginx support Expect: 100-continue?

Yes. Nginx respects the Expect header by default. If you send Expect: 100-continue, nginx will read your headers, validate them against its proxy settings, and either send 100 or reject before the body is buffered. This is one reason nginx is efficient for file uploads.

title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
description:
arXiv:2611.21645v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.

title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
description:
arXiv:2611.21804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.
