title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2611.22120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

title: GeoBIM for an Airport: Keeping BIM, GIS, and the Tunnel in One Coordinate System
description:
Most coordination failures I have seen on airport work were not geometry failures. They were unit failures. One team exports feet, another exports meters, and the tunnel arrives 3.28 times too long. The model still looks convincing, which is what makes it dangerous.
The project was HNTB's airport redevelopment: a terminal expansion, new boarding bridges, adjusted stand positions, and a deep tunnel beneath the apron. My work sat between the BIM team and the GIS team. I wrote the transforms, ran the checks, and kept the merge log. That space between the two teams is the GeoBIM gap.

Two origins, one model

BIM models usually start at a local origin near the building. GIS data arrives in a projected coordinate system, often a state plane zone or a UTM zone. Neither is wrong. They are just different answers to the question of where zero is. Before any merge, we picked one projected system, documented the EPSG code, and defined the vertical datum. Everything else converted into that frame. We called it the project frame. It had a name, a number, and a keeper.
The rule was simple: if a file did not state its coordinate system, it did not enter the merge. No exceptions for small layers. Small layers are how a fence ends up in the river. We also kept a short manifest for each layer: source, date, units, owner. It fit on one screen and answered most questions before they became meetings.

The transform in code

The conversion itself is short. The care is in the details around it.
Two things bite here. Axis order is one; some libraries expect latitude before longitude, and some expect the reverse, so we always use always_xy and test with a known point. Units are the other; a State Plane system may be in survey feet while the design is in meters. The vertical datum is a third. A model can be perfect in plan and eleven inches off in elevation.

Three checks before the first merge

We ran three checks in Python before anyone looked at the model. First, control points: eight survey monuments, each within two centimeters. Second, a bounding box sanity check: does the terminal sit inside the airport fence, and does the fence sit inside the county? Third, a vertical check against two known benchmarks. If any check failed, the merge stopped. We logged the results next to the file name, so the next person could see what had been verified. The control points were not evenly spread, which made the far taxiway the real test.
The checks caught more than bad data. They caught bad habits. A vendor once shipped a model that had been rotated ninety degrees to fit a drawing sheet. The bounding box did not notice. The control points did.

Where GeoBIM paid for itself

The tunnel was the reason. It carried the baggage system, a corridor for passengers, and a utility bank, and each had a clearance envelope. In a federated model, we could cut a section anywhere along its 900 feet and see all three at once. A clash detection pass found a duct bank intruding into the passenger envelope. Moving it in the model cost an afternoon. Moving it after the tunnel lining was poured would have cost a season.

Generated massing has a place

When we needed options, not answers, I used GenAnywhere. I selected the apron area on the map, generated a massing model, and dropped it into the same coordinate system. It gave us a believable mesh in minutes, at a level of detail that was honest about what it was. We used it to kill weak layouts before they earned a survey. It does not carry systems, and it should not. A massing study that pretends to be a design is worse than a sketch. The massing model inherits the coordinate system of the selection, not of the CAD file, which is one less thing to convert.

The rule I keep

Put the coordinate system in the file name and the document header. If two people on the same project cannot answer where the origin is, stop and fix that before modeling anything else. Interoperability starts with a number everyone agrees on. Everything after that is just geometry. A number everyone agrees on is cheaper than a meeting about a number.

title: idl-codegen: عميلان بأنواع محددة لـ TypeScript و Dart من Anchor IDL
description:
برنامج Anchor يصف نفسه في ملف IDL: تعليماته (instructions)، وحساباته، وأنواعه، وأحداثه، وأخطاؤه، وبذور (seeds) عناوين الـ PDA. جهة البرنامج تولّدها لك macros الخاصة بـ Anchor. أما جهة العميل (client) فمنها يبدأ العمل اليدوي. على أحدهم أن يكتب الدالة التي تحوّل الوسائط بترميز Borsh، وتضع أمامها الـ discriminator المكوّن من 8 بايتات، وترتّب الحسابات بالترتيب الصحيح مع أعلام signer وwritable الصحيحة، وتشتق عناوين الـ PDA من نفس البذور التي يستعملها البرنامج.

كتابة ذلك مرة واحدة أمر مقبول. لكن كتابته مرتين، بـ TypeScript لتطبيق الويب وبـ Dart لتطبيق Flutter، تعني نسختين يجب أن تبقيا متطابقتين مع البرنامج ومع بعضهما. وبايت واحد خاطئ في إحداهما يعطي معاملة تفشل على السلسلة برسالة خطأ لا تشرح الكثير.

idl-codegen يقرأ ملف Anchor IDL (مواصفة 0.30 وما بعدها) ويكتب العميلين معًا. والـ README يبدأ بتحذير يجب ذكره هنا أيضًا: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني. العملاء المولَّدون يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون ترميز الحسابات، ولا يوقّعون ولا يرسلون شيئًا. راجع الكود المولَّد مقابل برنامجك قبل استعماله مع أموال حقيقية، وجرّب على devnet أولًا.

ماذا يقدّم

أمر واحد ينتج مجموعتين من الملفات:

  • TypeScript: الملفان <name>.ts وborsh.ts، ويعتمدان على @solana/web3.js v1.
  • Dart: الملفان <name>.dart وborsh.dart، ويعتمدان على package:crypto، وهما موجّهان لتطبيقات Flutter.

كل عميل يحتوي نفس المكوّنات.

معرّف البرنامج. الثابت PROGRAM_ID في TypeScript و<name>ProgramId في Dart.

الأنواع. في TypeScript تحصل على interfaces، وعلى الـ enums في شكل اتحادات { kind: ... }، وعلى دوال encodeX / decodeX. وفي Dart تحصل على أصناف (classes) فيها encode وstatic decode. الـ enums التي بلا بيانات تصبح enum عادية في Dart، والتي تحمل بيانات تصبح أصنافًا من نوع sealed.

بناء التعليمات. الدالة createXInstruction(accounts, args) تُرجع TransactionInstruction في TypeScript. ونسخة Dart تأخذ وسائط مسمّاة وتُرجع Instruction. الحسابات التي لها address ثابت في الـ IDL، مثل System Program، تأخذه كقيمة افتراضية. والحسابات الاختيارية تأخذ معرّف البرنامج كقيمة افتراضية، وهذا عُرف Anchor للتعبير عن "None".

فك ترميز الحسابات. الدالة decodeXAccount(data) تتحقق من الـ discriminator قبل الفك، وفي TypeScript توجد أيضًا isXAccount.

الأحداث (events). الدالة decodeXEvent(data) في اللغتين.

دوال PDA. الدالة findXPda(...seeds) تُولَّد من pda.seeds في الـ IDL: البذور الثابتة، وبذور الحسابات، وبذور الوسائط، وحالات seeds::program مثل حسابات التوكن المرتبطة (ATA). وعميل Dart يأتي بدالة findProgramAddress خاصة به.

الأخطاء والثوابت. في TypeScript: ERRORS و<Name>Error.fromCode(). وفي Dart: <name>Errors و<Name>Exception.fromCode(). ومعها قيم #[constant] المعرّفة في البرنامج.

تحويل الأنواع يتبع نفس الفكرة في الجهتين: u64 وi64 وu128 وi128 تصبح bigint / BigInt؛ والأعداد الصحيحة الأصغر تصبح number / int؛ وpubkey يصبح PublicKey / Pubkey؛ وbytes يصبح Uint8Array / Uint8List؛ وOption<T> يصبح T | null / T?. أما tuple structs وtuple variants فتصبح values: [...] في TypeScript وfield0, field1 في Dart.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع وشغّل المولّد من مجلد المشروع:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen
cd idl-codegen
pnpm install
pnpm gen target/idl/my_program.json --ts app/src/generated --dart mobile/lib/generated
# or after `pnpm build`:  node dist/cli.js <idl.json> --ts <dir> --dart <dir>

الوسيط الأول هو ملف الـ IDL الذي كتبه anchor build. والخياران --ts و--dart هما مجلدا الإخراج. كود TypeScript المولَّد يحتاج @solana/web3.js v1 في تطبيقك، وكود Dart المولَّد يحتاج package:crypto.

ثم في تطبيق الويب:

import { createIncrementInstruction, findCounterPda } from "./generated/counter_todo.js";
const [counter] = findCounterPda(wallet.publicKey);
const ix = createIncrementInstruction({ authority: wallet.publicKey, counter }, { by: 1n });

ونفس النداء في تطبيق Flutter:

import 'generated/counter_todo.dart';
final (counter, _) = findCounterPda(authority: me);
final ix = createIncrementInstruction(authority: me, counter: counter, by: BigInt.one);

المقطعان يشتقان نفس الـ PDA ويبنيان نفس بايتات التعليمة. التوقيع والإرسال يبقيان في كودك أنت، بالمحفظة وطبقة الـ RPC التي يستعملها تطبيقك أصلًا.

كيف اختُبر

الكود المولَّد لا ينفع إلا إذا وثقت في البايتات، ولهذا يدور أغلب قسم الاختبارات في الـ README حول هذه النقطة.

  • اختبارات golden. كل IDL في test/fixtures/ يُولَّد ثم يُقارن بايتًا ببايت مع test/golden/. الملفات هي counter_todo وescrow، وهما IDL حقيقيان من مشاريع Anchor مجاورة، وkitchen_sink المكتوب يدويًا ليغطي كل الأنواع: مجموعات حسابات متداخلة، وحسابات اختيارية، وenums تحمل بيانات، وtuple structs، وu128/i128، وf64، ومصفوفات ثابتة الطول، وseeds::program.
  • مترجمات صارمة. كود TypeScript المولَّد يمرّ من tsc --strict، وكود Dart المولَّد يمرّ من dart analyze --fatal-infos. ويُتجاوز فحص Dart إن لم يكن dart موجودًا في الـ PATH.
  • السلوك. دوال PDA تطابق PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync، بما فيها عناوين ATA. بيانات التعليمة هي الـ discriminator متبوعًا بوسائط Borsh. والحسابات تمرّ بدورة encode ثم decode وتعود كما كانت، مع التحقق من الـ discriminator.
  • بين اللغتين. برنامج Dart في test/golden/dart/bin/check.dart يبني نفس التعليمات وعناوين PDA وبايتات الحسابات، والاختبار يتحقق من أن ناتجه يطابق عميل TypeScript بايتًا ببايت.

هذا الفحص الأخير كشف خطأً حقيقيًا. على Dart 3.9 VM كانت الدالة BigInt.modPow تُرجع نتائج خاطئة لبعض المدخلات ذات 255 بت، فتعطّل فحص وقوع النقطة على منحنى ed25519 الذي تعتمد عليه findProgramAddress. لذلك يستعمل كود Dart المولَّد الآن خوارزمية square-and-multiply خاصة به.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق. العملاء يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون البيانات فقط، لكن تعليمة خاطئة قد تحرّك أموالًا بعد أن توقّعها. قارن الناتج مع برنامجك وجرّبه على devnet أولًا.
  • الأنواع العامة (generics) مرفوضة. الـ IDL الذي يستعمل generics لا يُولَّد منه شيء.
  • بعض بذور PDA تصبح بايتات خام. البذور التي تقرأ بيانات حساب (path: "list.next_id") أو حقلًا من وسيط من نوع struct تتحول إلى وسيط bytes خام. وإن كانت تعليمة أخرى تشتق نفس الحساب من وسيط بسيط، يستعمل المولّد ذلك الشكل الأبسط.
  • coption لم يُختبر مع برنامج حقيقي. هو مدعوم في الترميز وفك الترميز، لا أكثر.
  • ملفات IDL القديمة تحتاج تحويلًا. ملفات IDL السابقة لـ Anchor 0.30 يجب تحويلها أولًا بالأمر anchor idl convert.
  • web3.js v1. ناتج TypeScript موجّه إلى @solana/web3.js v1.

لماذا بنيته

المشكلة هي التكرار. ملف الـ IDL يحتوي أصلًا كل ما يحتاجه العميل: أنواع الوسائط، وترتيب الحسابات، والـ discriminators، والبذور، ورموز الأخطاء. كتابة العميل يدويًا تعني نسخ هذه المعلومات إلى كود، ثم نسخها مرة ثانية عندما يوجد تطبيق موبايل بـ Dart بجانب تطبيق ويب بـ TypeScript. بعدها يجب تكرار كل تغيير في البرنامج في مكانين، ولا شيء ينبّهك عندما يتأخر أحدهما عن الآخر.

توليد العميلين من نفس الـ IDL يلغي خطوة النسخ، ويجعل اختبار أحد الناتجين مقابل الآخر ممكنًا. إذا أنتج عميل TypeScript وعميل Dart نفس البايتات لنفس المدخلات، ووافق عميل TypeScript مكتبة @solana/web3.js في عناوين PDA، يضيق المجال كثيرًا أمام اختلاف صامت. وخطأ BigInt.modPow مثال جيد على قيمة هذه المقارنة: لا شيء في كود Dart كان يبدو خاطئًا، ولم تكشفه إلا مقارنة البايتات.

الكود

المولّد، وملفات الاختبار، وملفات golden، والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Ask the agent for a reduced-motion path when it adds an animation
description:
The agent adds a delightful entrance: a 400ms slide plus a fade, triggered whenever the drawer opens. It looks polished in the default OS setting. On a machine with “reduce motion” enabled, the drawer still slides, because nobody asked the model to read prefers-reduced-motion.

I’ve started requiring a reduced-motion note in any agent PR that adds an animation, transition, or view transition. The note can be “wrapped in the existing motion-safe utility” or “this one is a 150ms opacity fade, which we allow.” Silence is not a plan.

Why this gets dropped

The happy path is what the prompt described: “animate the panel in.” Tutorials still lead with @keyframes and transition: all. prefers-reduced-motion is a second paragraph the model will skip unless you make it a gate.

The cost is not theoretical. Vestibular-sensitive users, people who enabled the OS setting, and anyone in a reduced-motion CI story will all see the same motion you thought was optional decoration.

You do not have to delete every animation. You do have to define the reduced path: usually cut transform/layout motion, keep a short opacity fade if the team allows it, or jump to the end state.

A simple motion policy

  • Any new animation ships a reduced-motion path in the same PR
  • Prefer the existing helper — motion-safe:, @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce), or the design-system motion mixin
  • No transition: all
  • State, not only CSS — if you use a JS animation library, it must honor the same media query or the platform matchMedia

If the team already wrote a reduced-motion article or a token scale, point the agent at that file instead of restating the CSS.

What to put in the prompt 

If you add a transition, animation, or view transition, include a prefers-reduced-motion path in the same PR.
Use the existing motion helper in src/styles/motion.css.
Do not use transition: all.
In the PR body, say what still moves (if anything) when reduced motion is on.

Add a Storybook or Playwright case with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce if you already test other a11y states there. A screenshot of the default theme is not coverage.

View Transitions and shared-element animations are included. If the agent adds document.startViewTransition or a view-transition-name, the reduced-motion path should skip the transition or fall back to a plain swap. The CSS View Transitions API does not make the OS setting optional.

Carousel autoplay, skeleton shimmer, and infinite logo marquees are also motion. If marketing wants them on by default, they still need a stop when the user asked for less movement. “It is decorative” is an argument for honoring the setting, not for ignoring it.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A new transform animation with no reduced-motion branch
  • transition: all 300ms
  • A JS animate() call that ignores the media query
  • “It’s a short animation, so it’s fine” with no policy citation

Accept

  • An existing motion-safe / motion-reduce utility applied correctly
  • An instant end-state (or a short opacity-only fade, if your scale allows it) under reduced motion
  • A PR note that names the helper and the reduced behavior

title: A Go web service on a free container tier: a 15 MB image and tens of megabytes of RAM
description:
TL;DR: A net/http service with a health endpoint, graceful shutdown and the port read from the environment, built by a two-stage Dockerfile into a 7 MB binary and an image around 15 MB. What it uses at runtime on 512 MB and a quarter of a CPU, how to add a database without adding bloat, how to embed static files in the binary, and what sleep looks like in the logs.

If a free container tier was designed for one language, it was Go. A Go web service compiles to a single static binary, starts in milliseconds and idles in a few tens of megabytes, so 512 MB and a quarter of a CPU is not a constraint, it is a surplus. This guide builds a small HTTP service the way it should be built for a container: a two-stage Dockerfile, a tiny image, a health endpoint, graceful shutdown, and the port read from the environment.

The service

Standard library only. net/http is enough for most services and it keeps the binary small. Go 1.22 and later route by method and path pattern, so no router package is needed for this:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    port := os.Getenv("PORT")
    if port == "" {
        port = "8080"
    }

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /health", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
        w.Write([]byte("ok"))
    })
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /api/time", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"now": time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)})
    })

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:              ":" + port,
        Handler:           mux,
        ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }

    go func() {
        log.Printf("listening on :%s", port)
        if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && err != http.ErrServerClosed {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
    }()

    stop := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    signal.Notify(stop, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
    <-stop

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    log.Println("shutting down")
    srv.Shutdown(ctx)
}

Three things in there earn their keep on a container host. PORT from the environment, so the platform decides the port.

ReadHeaderTimeout, so a slow client cannot hold a connection open forever on a small instance. And the SIGTERM handler: when a container is stopped, or a free container goes to sleep after 15 minutes without traffic, the runtime sends SIGTERM first; a server that shuts down cleanly finishes in-flight requests instead of dropping them.

The Dockerfile 

FROM golang:1-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum* ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates && adduser -D -u 10001 app
USER app
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
  • golang:1-alpine tracks the current Go 1.x release, so the tag does not go stale. Pin golang:1.27-alpine if you want reproducible builds.
  • CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a static binary; -s -w strips symbols and debug info. The service above builds to roughly 7 MB.
  • The final image is Alpine plus certificates plus the binary: about 15 MB. scratch would be smaller still, but Alpine gives you a shell for debugging and the CA bundle for outbound HTTPS.
  • Running as a non-root user costs nothing and is the first thing a security scan looks for.

If you deploy without a Dockerfile, SnapDeploy generates one when it sees go.mod: a two-stage build with CGO_ENABLED=0 onto an Alpine runtime, much like the above. The generated builder uses a Go 1.21 image; if your go.mod declares a newer Go, the toolchain directive downloads it during the build. For control over the version, keep your own Dockerfile.

What it uses at runtime

Measured on the service above: about 10 MB of resident memory idle, under 30 MB while handling a few hundred requests a second, and start-up in well under a second. Against a 512 MB container that leaves room for in-memory caches, a SQLite file for read-mostly data, or an embedded queue, none of which a Node or JVM service could afford in the same box. Wake-up on the free tier is about 60 seconds, but almost all of that is the platform starting the container; the Go process itself is ready as soon as it is scheduled.

If you want to see the numbers yourself, GODEBUG=gctrace=1 prints heap sizes at each collection, and /proc/self/status inside the container shows VmRSS.

Deploying

  1. Push the repository to GitHub with the Dockerfile.
  2. In SnapDeploy, Containers → Deploy from GitHub → choose the repository. Confirm the port (8080 here).
  3. Deploy. Go builds are quick; the first build is a few minutes because the base images are pulled and modules downloaded, later builds reuse the cached module layer.
  4. Hit /health on the containers.snapdeploy.app URL, then /api/time.

When Go still needs more than the free tier

  • It has to answer at any hour. Free containers sleep after 15 minutes without traffic. Always-On Small is $12/month for the same 512 MB; a Go service rarely needs the 2 GB Medium.
  • It needs a database that persists. The container filesystem is ephemeral, so the SQLite trick above is for caches and read-only data. PostgreSQL Mini is $29/month; a $1 DB Sprint Pack gives you 12 hours of it to test against.
  • It needs a custom domain. Always-On again; free containers live on containers.snapdeploy.app.

Adding a database without adding bloat

The one dependency most services need is a database driver. With pgx the binary grows by a few megabytes and the service still idles well under 30 MB. Read the connection string from DATABASE_URL, which a SnapDeploy add-on injects and every other provider gives you to paste, and keep the pool small: a free container will never need more than a handful of connections, and a PostgreSQL Mini allows 50 in total.

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
cfg.MaxConns = 4
pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)

Make the health handler run pool.Ping(ctx) with a one-second timeout. When the container wakes after sleeping, the first request will re-establish the pool; a ping with a timeout turns a hung database into a clear 503 instead of a slow page.

Static files inside the binary

If the service also serves a small front end, the embed package puts the files into the executable, so the image stays one binary and there is nothing to copy or mount:

//go:embed static/*
var static embed.FS

mux.Handle("GET /", http.FileServerFS(static))

Go 1.22 added http.FileServerFS; on older versions use http.FileServer(http.FS(static)). Either way the files are read from memory, which is the fastest static file server you will run on a quarter of a CPU.

What sleep looks like in the logs

Because the service handles SIGTERM, a container going to sleep after 15 quiet minutes leaves a clean trail: shutting down, then the process exits with code 0. A service that ignores the signal is killed after the platform's stop timeout and exits with code 137, which looks like a crash in the logs and drops any request that was in flight. Ten lines of shutdown code are the difference between "sleeps politely" and "keeps dying every night" when you read the runtime log a week later.

Free tier: 4 containers, 512 MB and 0.25 vCPU each, 100 container-hours a month, 10 deploys a day, no card. Details on the free tier docs page; the Docker hosting page covers what happens when you bring your own image instead of a repository.

Multi-Region DR on AWS/Azure/GCP: What RTO/RPO Tiers Actually Cost in India (2026)
description:
If you've only ever tested failover in a staging environment, here's the gap between the demo and production reality: picking an RTO number is really picking an architecture, and the architecture is really picking a cost.

There are four patterns worth knowing cold. Backup-and-restore is cross-region snapshots plus a runbook — cheap (+10–20% over single-region spend), slow (4–24hr RTO). Pilot-light keeps a synced database and pre-wired networking in region two with compute scaled to near-zero — a solid middle ground (+20–40%, 1–4hr RTO). Warm-standby runs a genuinely live, scaled-down stack in region two continuously — this is where most production systems should land (+40–70%, 15–60min RTO). Active-active runs full capacity in both regions simultaneously behind a load balancer, with real-time bidirectional replication — expensive (+80–150%+) but near-zero RTO. Treat those percentages as planning ranges, not quotes: your real premium depends on how much of the stack you replicate, how you size the standby, and how chatty your data layer is.

Three things that bite engineers who haven't built this before: cross-region egress isn't free (₹1.5–2.5/GB between India regions adds up fast on a chatty database), reserved-capacity discounts (25–70% off on-demand) materially change which tier is affordable, and nobody budgets for the quarterly failover drill that actually proves the DR plan works instead of just existing on a diagram.

If you're building on India infrastructure specifically: AWS's Mumbai (ap-south-1) + Hyderabad (ap-south-2) pair, Azure's Central India + South India pair, and GCP's asia-south1 + asia-south2 pair are the natural defaults — not just for latency, but because RBI's payment-data localisation rule means DR copies of payment data can't legally live offshore anyway.

We wrote up the full RTO/RPO cost breakdown, including an INR pricing table by business size, here: Multi-Region Cloud Architecture & Disaster Recovery Cost for Indian Businesses in 2026.

title: Why We Built 100 Mobile-First Interactive Wedding Websites Instead of WhatsApp PDFs
description:
For years, digital wedding invitations have been stuck in an awkward middle ground: heavy multi-page PDF documents or 30-second video clips sent as WhatsApp attachments.

From a UI/UX standpoint, PDFs are inherently flawed for smartphones:

They are designed for print dimensions, forcing users into constant pinch-to-zoom gestures.
Venue addresses are static text—guests can't tap them to open turn-by-turn GPS navigation.
File sizes of 10MB to 15MB cause friction and data consumption on mobile networks.

At Wedding Blues, we engineered an entirely new paradigm: bespoke, interactive 9:16 mobile-first wedding websites.

Here is a breakdown of the architectural and UX principles behind our collection of 100 interactive wedding experiences.

1. Native 9:16 Mobile-First Viewport

Over 98% of digital wedding invitations are opened on smartphones. Rather than retrofitting desktop layouts or landscape cards, our suites are built strictly in a vertical 9:16 aspect ratio.

  • Ergonomic alignment: Text and typography are calibrated for natural handheld reading distance without zooming.

  • Smooth vertical scrolling: Feels like a high-end mobile editorial rather than an administrative document.

  • Cross-platform responsiveness: Optimized for iOS Safari and Android Chrome viewports.

2. Tactile Kinetic Web Animations

Traditional wedding invitations carry deep emotional weight because of the physical unboxing ritual: breaking a wax seal and unfolding the envelope.

We translated that ritual to the web:

  • Tap-to-Open Wax Seal: Guests tap the screen to trigger an animated envelope opening sequence with realistic seal parting physics and ceremonial background audio.

  • Palace Jharokha Reveals: Architectural teak doors and royal arches that part smoothly to reveal the ceremony schedule.

3. Integrated Guest Utility Layers

Static cards only communicate dates; interactive web invites act as an active event concierge:

  • One-Tap GPS Navigation: Every listed ceremony (Mehendi, Sangeet, Haldi, Vivah, Reception) has turn-by-turn navigation buttons opening Google Maps or Apple Maps directly.
  • Smart Calendar Syncing: Guests tap an "Add to Calendar" button to sync the auspicious Muhurat into Google Calendar or Apple Calendar.
  • Frictionless WhatsApp RSVP: One-touch RSVP confirmation buttons route guest headcounts directly to the hosts.

4. Live Dual-Language Regional Switching
In multicultural Indian weddings, family elders often prefer reading traditional shlokas, blessings, and lineage in their mother tongue (Hindi or Gujarati), while younger friends and global guests prefer English.

Instead of distributing two separate sets of PDFs, we implemented a live regional language switcher. A floating control toggle allows guests to instantly swap the entire invitation between English, Hindi, and Gujarati with zero page reloads.

Conclusion

_As web technologies advance, digital invitations are evolving from flat files into rich, interactive micro-applications that honor heritage while delivering modern mobile convenience.

To test live interactive 9:16 smartphone concepts, animated wax-seal suites, and live phone previews, visit Wedding Blues._

title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

title: Why Punitive Streaks Make Users Quit—And What I Built Instead for a Step Tracker
description:
Traditional habit and fitness apps love strict daily streaks. On paper, the psychology makes sense: once someone hits a 25-day streak, loss aversion keeps them coming back every single day so they don't break the chain.

Until life happens.

Someone gets sick, travels across time zones, or misses a single day of walking—and watches a 40-day streak reset to zero. In behavioral psychology, that triggers the "what-the-hell effect": once the streak is broken, the user feels like they've already failed, closes the app, and never opens it again.

Designing a Non-Punitive Care Loop
While building Fitness Quest, I wanted walking to feel rewarding without turning a missed day into a guilt trip. Instead of a binary streak counter that resets to zero, daily steps translate into cumulative care progress for virtual pet companions (Lumi and Luna).

Here is how the loop differs from standard streak trackers:

Progress pauses instead of resetting: If you skip a walk or take a rest day, your pet doesn't get sick, lose health, or die. Your progress simply waits until your next walk.

Micro-wins over rigid thresholds: Even a short 10-minute walk contributes visible care progress rather than failing an arbitrary 10,000-step daily quota.

Emotional attachment without anxiety: Users open the app to check on their companion rather than to avoid a red warning notification.

What This Taught Me About Consumer Utility UX
Most developer-built productivity and health tools over-index on strict metrics—red charts, broken chains, and aggressive push notifications. Designing around forgiveness instead of punishment lowers daily pressure, which paradoxically makes people stick with the habit longer.

Have you ever abandoned an app specifically because you broke a long streak? What retention mechanics actually keep you coming back without feeling forced?

title: Two Counterexamples for e-means
description:
arXiv:2611.22065v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) combines exponential averaging and cluster revival. We give two counterexamples to its published recipe with higher final loss than standard k-means (Lloyd, 1982) from identical initial centers. Mass-based revival can destroy a global optimum and make the ratio of expected losses unbounded even with k-means++ seeding.

title: AI couldn't see the bug. Working examples from Clay UI changed that
description:
Originally published on LinkedIn.

I wanted readers to turn the pages of The Art of AI like a real book. On my laptop the animation looked right. On my phone, parts of the page flashed black.

Several attempts to fix it with Claude Opus 5.5 failed. Working examples found through Clay UI pointed to a better approach, which we proved in an Android emulator and checked on my phone. Opus built the first working prototype, and Fable 5.2 settled it and brought it to the version that is live today.

This article is about how we got from plausible fixes to a page turn that works, and what made the difference.

A book that should turn like paper

The Art of AI is an illustrated book of short reflections on artificial intelligence, published as a website. I prepared the code for the page turn myself, so that a page lifts at the corner, curls softly and settles on the next one. When it broke on my phone, I asked Claude Opus 5.5 to help me fix it.

What I saw on the phone

During a turn, parts of the page went black. Often the whole lower half vanished behind a straight edge under the illustration, and sometimes stripes ran across the paper. A few frames later the page was fine again, so it looked like a flicker. On a computer none of this happened.

This is a screenshot I took on my phone in the middle of a turn. The text is cut off and the left half of the page is simply missing.

Why the AI kept failing

The AI failed several times before it got anywhere. Its first report said: "I couldn't find a single flash frame." It had checked in a desktop browser set to a phone's screen size. That copies the size of a phone, but not its small graphics memory, and that is where the fault lived. Reading the code did not reveal the cause.

My own assumption didn't help. I said it had not flickered before, but the older version broke the same way in an Android emulator. There was no recent change to blame.

The older version in the Android emulator. Stripes and broken paper run across both pages, with the same library and the same pages as before.

The emulator gave shaky answers too: the same unchanged build broke in 17%, 27% and 53% of frames on three runs. So the AI guessed and tested one suspect after another, from shadows and the paper texture to the illustrations and browser hints. None of them fixed it.

Frames from one emulator recording of the live site. Black lower halves, half-drawn pages and stripes appear in different frames of the same turns.

The way out: working examples from Clay UI

The AI failed again and again; the way out came from the patterns in Clay UI, which is open source on GitHub. Clay UI searches catalogs of ready-made interface components and downloads their source code. For a page-flip book it found two working examples: page-flip from Kokonut UI and book-flip from Avara.

What Clay UI does, in under 40 seconds of clay: proven components from real libraries, shaped to your style. Watch the film.

They paid off first on the buttons. Ours switched off during every turn and faded to 42% opacity. Kokonut keeps its buttons on and ignores extra clicks in code, and we did the same.

The controls frame by frame during page turns. In the left column, before the fix, Previous and Next fade out on every turn.

On the pages, the examples changed the question. It stopped being "what is wrong with my page" and became "what do working page turns do differently". In plain words: my version made the phone redraw the whole page again and again during a turn. The working examples draw the page once and then only move that finished image.

For developers: Avara turns a page with a 3D rotation, which the graphics chip can apply to an already painted layer. My library cut the page to a new shape in every frame, so the browser had to repaint it 60 times a second. With a paper texture and a large illustration on every page, the phone ran out of graphics memory, and each missing tile showed as black.

A quick copy of Avara's approach, with rigid pages, removed the black halves, but the page turned like a board. I wanted the soft curl. The patterns gave us the direction; proving it and building it were still ahead.

The key: patterns plus emulation and tests

The patterns inspired a much stricter process. Opus 5.5 limited Chrome's graphics memory in the emulator to 96 MB, a deliberately low setting that imitates a phone under pressure. From then on the bug appeared every time, just as on my phone. Then it ran a control: the same library with plain pages, under the same limit, turned 65 frames without a broken one.

The control run: the same library with plain pages, recorded frame by frame. Every turn draws cleanly.

So in this test the library alone held up. The difference was my heavy pages, painted again in every frame. A memory reading showed that my page held 118 MB of graphics memory even at rest.

The drawing below shows the difference in what the phone has to do in every frame of a turn.

The tests also showed why guessing never worked. Removing one ingredient made the page lighter, but it was still painted again in every frame.

Fable 5.2 settles it

Opus 5.5, guided by the Clay UI patterns, found the direction and built a first prototype: the turn drawn from finished pictures of the pages. In the emulator, under the same low memory limit, we checked 949 animation frames in a row and found no broken one. Fable 5.2 settled the matter and brought it to the version that is live today.

Fable measured the graphics memory and wrote its own page-curl engine on a canvas, a drawing surface inside the browser. A script photographs each of the 86 pages in a fixed phone layout. During a turn the canvas finds the fold line, keeps the front of the page flat and mirrors the back of the paper over the fold, so nothing on the page is painted again. When I opened it on my phone, I wrote back: "It looks very good, I can't see anything breaking."

The comparison below comes from the emulator with the 96 MB limit. The top two rows are the old version and the bottom two the canvas version, turning the same pages.

The last details

The first version showed a picture of the page during a turn and switched back to live text when the turn ended. Every small difference between the two showed as a jump. Fable 5.2 fixed them one by one:

  • The chapter 9 title sat on three lines during a turn and on two after it. The line breaks are now recorded with the pictures and forced on the live page.
  • After each turn the text got a little thinner and the illustration twitched. The pictures had been taken on a Mac, which draws text bolder than a phone. They are now taken without that, and the picture stays on screen after the turn too, so there is no switch to see.
  • A zoomed illustration jumped at the end of closing. It now lands on the picture's exact spot, with matching corners and shadow.
  • A page now has to finish turning before the next turn can start.

What made the difference

On its own, AI kept failing on this. Working patterns from Clay UI showed what good page turns do differently, and a detailed process of emulation and tests turned that idea into proof. Opus 5.5 found the direction with them, and Fable 5.2 finished the job. The Clay UI source is on GitHub.

The last part was mine. Our automated checks missed a title that changes lines and text that gets a little thinner. I caught them by reading my own book on my own phone. You can turn its pages at theartofai.behavio.one.

About the author: Marcin Tabędzki, author of The Art of AI, builds Clay UI and AI tools at Behavio One. Find me on LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/marcin-tabedzki

title: Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals
description:
arXiv:2611.21655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.

title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
description:
arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

title: The path to AI FDE #16: Functions: reusable pieces of logic
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Last week your code learned to decide and repeat. Today you learn to name a piece of code and reuse it, so you write it once and call it whenever you need it.

That named piece of code is a function. You’ve already used other people’s functions: print(), len(), type(). Today you write your own. By the end you’ll have a small script that shares pizzas fairly between friends, built from two tiny functions.

Part A · Building a function

1. def defines a function; calling it runs it. Save this as greet.py in your sandbox folder:

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Asha")
greet("Ben")

Run it with python3 greet.py (Windows: python greet.py):

Hello, Asha
Hello, Ben

The first two lines are the definition. def starts it, greet is the function’s name, (name) lists its inputs, and the line ends with a colon. The indented lines under it are the function’s body, just like the blocks in last week’s if and for.

Defining a function doesn’t run it. Python just remembers it under the name greet. The body runs only when you call the function: its name followed by brackets, greet("Asha"). Two calls, two greetings. Python reads your file from top to bottom, so put the def above the first line that calls it.

2. Parameters are the input slots; arguments are the values you put in them. A function can take more than one input:

def area(width, height):
    print(width * height)

area(3, 4)
area(10, 2)

12
20

width and height are the parameters: the names in the definition. 3 and 4 are the arguments: the values you pass when you call it. Python matches them in order, so the first argument goes into the first parameter. Inside the body, width is 3 and height is 4.

Leave one out, with area(3), and Python stops with:

TypeError: area() missing 1 required positional argument: 'height'

The message names the slot you left empty. People mix up the two words all the time, and it rarely matters, but now you know which is which.

3. return sends a result back. Without it, you get None. Our area prints the answer, but the rest of your program can’t use it. Change print to return:

def area(width, height):
    return width * height

total = area(3, 4) + area(10, 2)
print(total)

32

return hands a value back to the line that called the function. You can picture area(3, 4) being replaced by 12, so the line becomes total = 12 + 20. That’s the difference: print shows a value to a human; return gives it to your code.

Forget return, and the function still runs but hands back None (Python’s “no value here” from issue #14):

def double(n):
    n * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)

None

The function worked out 10 and then threw it away. return also ends the function immediately: any lines after it in the same block never run.

Part B · Functions that are easy to use

4. Defaults and keyword arguments let callers skip or name inputs. Give a parameter a default value with = in the definition, and callers can leave it out:

def make_tea(cups, sugar=1, milk=True):
    return f"{cups} cup(s), {sugar} sugar, milk: {milk}"

print(make_tea(2))
print(make_tea(2, sugar=0))
print(make_tea(milk=False, cups=1))

2 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: True
2 cup(s), 0 sugar, milk: True
1 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: False

The first call uses both defaults. The second passes a keyword argument, sugar=0, which sets that one input by name. The third names every input, so the order no longer matters. Names make calls easier to read too: make_tea(2, sugar=0) says more than make_tea(2, 0). One rule: arguments without names come first. make_tea(sugar=0, 2) gives SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument. Later in the series you’ll see the same shape in AI code, such as a function that splits text with a default size=500.

The one trap: never use a list as a default. The default is created once, when Python reads the def, and then shared by every call:

def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item("apple"))
print(add_item("pear"))

['apple']
['apple', 'pear']

The second call “remembers” the apple. (append adds an item to the end of a list; lists get their own issue tomorrow.) The fix is to default to None and make a fresh list inside:

def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

Now the two calls print ['apple'] and ['pear'].

5. Scope: names made inside a function exist only inside it. Each call gets its own private workspace. Names created there disappear when the function ends:

def bake():
    dough = 200
    print("inside:", dough)

bake()
print(dough)

inside: 200
NameError: name 'dough' is not defined

(Python prints a few more lines above the NameError, called a traceback. You’ll learn to read those in issue #19.) The part of a program where a name exists is its scope. dough is a local name: it belongs to bake.

The other direction is softer: a function can read a name defined outside it. With greeting = "Hi" at the top of the file, a function can use greeting. But if a function assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local for the whole function. So this fails:

count = 0

def bump():
    count = count + 1

bump()

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

The clean habit: pass values in as arguments and return results out.

def bump(n):
    return n + 1

count = 0
count = bump(count)
count = bump(count)
print(count)

This prints 2. (Python has a global keyword that lets a function change an outside name. You’ll rarely need it; passing in and returning out is easier to follow.)

6. Give each function one job, and a name that says what it is. Small functions are easier to read, test and reuse. Here, one function does the maths and another builds the sentence:

def to_fahrenheit(c):
    """Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit."""
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

def describe(c):
    f = to_fahrenheit(c)
    return f"{c}°C is {f}°F"

print(describe(100))
print(describe(-40))
print(to_fahrenheit(0) == 32)

100°C is 212.0°F
-40°C is -40.0°F
True

Three habits are packed in here:

  • One job each. to_fahrenheit only converts. describe only words the answer, and it reuses to_fahrenheit instead of repeating the formula.
  • A quick check. to_fahrenheit(0) == 32 prints True, so you know the maths is right. Because the function returns a value instead of printing it, it’s easy to test. That’s where proper tests (lesson 4.6) start.
  • A docstring. The string in triple quotes on the first line of the body says what the function does. Many editors show it when you hover over the name.

Give functions names that say what they do, in snake_case, the Python style guide’s choice for function names: to_fahrenheit, make_tea, add_item. If you can’t name a function without using “and”, it’s probably doing two jobs.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create pizza.py, for sharing made-up pizzas between friends: 
def slices_each(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many whole slices each person gets."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) // people

def leftover(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many slices are left after a fair share."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) % people

print(slices_each(3, 5), leftover(3, 5))
print(slices_each(2, 4, per_pizza=6), leftover(2, 4, per_pizza=6))
print(slices_each(people=7, pizzas=1))
  1. Run python3 pizza.py. You should see: 
4 4
3 0
1

Three pizzas of 8 slices is 24; shared by 5, that’s 4 each with 4 left over. (// and % are whole-number division and remainder, from issue #14.)

  1. Delete the word return in slices_each (keep the maths) and run it again. The first number on each line becomes None. Put it back.
  2. Add print(slices_each(3, 0)) at the end. Read the last line of the error: ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero. You can’t share between nobody. (Handling errors like this properly is issue #19.) Remove the line.
  3. Write a third function, pizzas_needed(people, slices_each=3, per_pizza=8), that returns how many pizzas to order. Hint: -(-a // b) rounds a division up. With 10 people, it should return 4.

Check your understanding: (a) In def area(width, height):, are width and height parameters or arguments? (b) What does a function return if it has no return line? (c) Why did the second add_item("pear") call also show the apple?

Answer: (a) Parameters: the names in the definition. The values you pass in a call are the arguments. (b) None. (c) A list default is created once, when the def runs, and every call shares it. Use None as the default and make a new list inside.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Forgetting return, then wondering why the result is None.
  • Printing inside a function when the caller needs the value. Return it, and print outside.
  • Defining a function and never calling it (no brackets, no run).
  • Using a list or dictionary as a default (def f(x=[])). It’s shared between calls.
  • Trying to change an outside variable from inside a function. Pass it in and return the new value.

Takeaway

def names a block of code, and calling it runs it. Parameters are the input slots, and arguments are the values you put in. return hands a result back; without it you get None. Defaults and keyword arguments make calls short and clear. Names made inside a function stay inside. Keep each function to one job.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Every AI app I build later is a stack of small functions: one to load text, one to call a model, one to check the answer. Tomorrow: lists and dictionaries, the two containers that hold almost all the data you’ll touch.

Over to you: what’s a task you’d turn into a function? Reply with its name and its inputs, like make_tea(cups, sugar=1).

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, Defining Functions (def, the body is indented, a function without return returns None; docstrings). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions
  2. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, More on Defining Functions (default argument values, “the default value is evaluated only once”, keyword arguments, positional arguments before keyword arguments). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#more-on-defining-functions
  3. Python glossary, “parameter” and “argument” (the difference between the two). https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-parameter
  4. Python reference, “Execution model”, Naming and binding (a name assigned inside a function is local to it). https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding
  5. Python FAQ, “Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError when the variable has a value?” and “Why are default values shared between objects?”. https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-am-i-getting-an-unboundlocalerror-when-the-variable-has-a-value
  6. PEP 8, “Style Guide for Python Code” (function names are lowercase, with words separated by underscores). https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#function-and-variable-names
  7. PEP 257, “Docstring Conventions” (what a docstring is; triple double quotes). https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (TypeError, NameError, UnboundLocalError, ZeroDivisionError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

Free: the 5-page roadmap from Novice to AI FDE.

If this was useful, subscribe to The Path to AI FDE for the next issue.

title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.22038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).

title: A test run that can hang forever is broken
description:
This one covers November 10 to 17. It was a week about tests that finish: my workflow kit moved onto Node's own test runner and learned to end a run that has stopped doing anything. The rest went into a new engine for my awesome lists, a deploy fix in my framework, and how my machines upgrade Node.

A hung npm test is not a slow one

workkit is my workflow kit for Claude Code: GitHub issues as the work list, labels as the pipeline, hooks that enforce the rules. Agents run most of my test suites now, usually in the background. A suite that waits on a socket that never closes does not fail. It just sits there, and so does the agent waiting on it.

Version 0.94 puts every root npm test and every workkit prove under a supervisor. It checks the run every five minutes (tests.check changes that), and each check asks two questions. Was the run's log written since the last check? Did any of its processes use the processor? Processor time counts as work once it reaches 1 percent of one core over the check.

The verdicts are simple:

  • Output or work: alive. Nothing happens.
  • Neither, two checks in a row: frozen. The evidence goes in the log, one line per process, then the run is ended with exit code 124.
  • No output for six checks, but working: a look. The run keeps going, and the call attached to it prints the evidence and exits 125.

A busy run is never ended, however long it takes. A frozen one ends with a line that says why:

detach: no output and no processor use for <N> minutes, so the run was ended (exit 124)

Inside a run there is a second bound. The runner ends a suite file's whole process group after 600 seconds (TEST_DEADLINE=<seconds> sets another) and reports one timed-out failure, so one stuck file costs a line in the report instead of the whole run.

Why it matters: "it's still running" used to be a guess. Now it is a measurement, and the two exit codes tell an agent whether to wait or to go look.

The runner is Node's now

The other half of the week was the runner itself. Since version 0.95, a workkit suite is plain node:test: describe, test, the usual hooks, and an expect with Jest's matchers, exported from workkit-core/test. Any suite runs alone with node <file>. The kit's own case engine, with its group, assertEq and selfRun, is gone.

Removing an API means migrating everyone on it, so the release shipped workkit convert. It rewrites an old-shape suite in place and maps each statement one for one: group('x') becomes describe('x', ...), assertEq(actual, wanted) becomes expect(actual).toBe(wanted). It only rewrites a file it fully understands. Cases made in a loop, a whole-file skip or a setup line between cases leave the file byte for byte, with one line saying where and why:

converted <path> (<n> cases)
left <path>:<line> <why>

A file already on Node's functions is left alone, so a second run changes nothing. My own machine-setup repo moved over the same week.

The next release built on that base: --filter=<text> runs only the cases whose full name, describe path included, holds the text, and a bare run at a monorepo root also runs each workspace member's own npm test.

Why it matters: Node's runner is the one every JavaScript developer can already read. The kit stops maintaining a test framework and keeps only the parts that are its job: finding suites, bounding them, and recording proof.

24 copies of the same bots, now one engine

I maintain 24 public awesome lists. Each one had its own copy of the same three jobs: a pull request check that judges a new entry, a weekly sweep for dead links and archived repos, and a daily sync of the shared text. Each copy had its own scripts and tests. A fix meant 24 commits.

awesome-kit is new this week, and it holds that code once. A list now carries three short workflow files, each calling the kit's composite action with one command:

jobs:
  sweep:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: ianwieds/awesome-kit@v2
        with:
          command: sweep

GitHub fetches the kit at the tag the list names, so a kit release reaches every list without a commit to any of them. Moving a list onto it deleted 1,628 lines from each one, about 39,000 lines across all 24.

The 2.0 release added awesome-kit setup. Run in a fresh repo, it scaffolds every missing file a list needs, writes the three workflows, runs sync, and sets the repo's description and topics through gh. It never overwrites a file the list owns, and since 2.0.1 it fails before any write when the config names a different repo than origin.

Two details I like. The pull request check runs on pull_request_target, so it can comment on a fork's PR, but it checks out only the base branch and reads the head README as data, never code. And the daily job keeps one empty commit on a maintenance branch, so GitHub never pauses the Monday sweep after 60 quiet days.

Why it matters: a new list starts with one command, and a fix reaches every list at its next run.

Deploys that stop growing the repo

omega is my framework for shipping a website, backend, desktop app and browser extension from one project. Each deploy pushes a snapshot to a deploy ref, and every snapshot chained on the one before, so the mirror grew by a full copy per deploy.

A change now on main (not in a release yet) re-roots that chain on GitHub's side before each deploy. Through the git data API, the deploy ref's tip becomes a parentless copy of its own tree, the push waits until the ref reads that root, and the new snapshot chains on it. The ref then holds one root, the latest snapshot, and any admin publish since. Nothing older.

Why it matters: a deploy mirror should cost the same on deploy 500 as on deploy 5.

Node upgrades that cannot strand a terminal

One private story, from the scripts that set up my machines. They used to move the default Node to the newest release as soon as it installed. If a global package then failed to install, every new terminal opened on a Node with missing tools.

Now a new release becomes the default only once its global packages are in. A failed install leaves new terminals on the release that worked. Globals install only when missing or behind, so the package firewall I route npm through keeps its 133 MB binary between runs.

Why it matters: an upgrade is stage first, then flip the pointer. Flip it first and a half-finished upgrade is the default.

Next week I want the supervisor's two exit codes wired into how my agents react to a stuck run. What does your test runner do when a test never returns? Comments are open.

title: The Comparison Surface a Multi-Model Song Generator Has to Expose
description:
If you ship a generative feature with more than one model behind it, the hard interface problem is not "can we call an API." It is whether a user can tell what was held constant and what was allowed to change.

I am writing this as an interface-level design memo, not as a source-code review and not as a listening test. I have not inspected private architecture, latency budgets, or training data. The questions below can be asked of any public song-generation UI, including one that offers a single model with multiple takes. They become urgent as soon as a product asks a person to choose among models.

The job is comparability, not novelty

A multi-model music UI fails in a particular way. The user writes a prompt, picks a familiar model, gets a finished-sounding track, and then tries a second model with a slightly different prompt because the first take "wasn't quite right." At that point the product has not provided a comparison. It has provided two unrelated experiments.

That is a UX issue before it is a model-quality issue. If prompt text, lyrics, duration, vocal setting, and output intent can drift between runs without being visible, the interface is training people to confuse taste with noise.

A useful test is simple: can a careful user answer, after two runs, "these two files were produced from the same brief"? If the answer is "I think so," the comparison surface is too weak.

Questions to ask of the public UI

The following questions do not require access to internals. They only require a page that is honest about state.

Prompt identity. Is the exact prompt still visible after a run, and can it be reused without retyping? If the product shows sample songs with their prompts, can those prompts be inspected before they are reused? A prompt that disappears into a history card with no copy path will not survive a fair comparison.

Lyrics path. Are "describe a song and let the system write words," "paste my lyrics and sing them as written," and "instrumental, no vocal" first-class paths, or are they hidden in the same box? If section tags such as [Verse] and [Chorus] matter, does the UI explain them before the user spends a run? A comparison that silently lets one model invent lyrics while another is bound to a pasted chorus is not a model comparison.

Model metadata before spend. Can the user see, before confirming a run, the model name, how many takes come back, whether length is user-set or automatic, and how credits will be charged? A selector that only shows brand names forces people to learn those differences from a FAQ, or from regret.

Voice and language controls. Are male, female, automatic, and instrumental choices visible as controls, not only as adjectives inside the prompt? If the product claims multilingual singing, is the language an explicit setting or an implied side effect of the lyric text?

Comparison without losing context. After two or more takes exist, can they be played in one context with the shared prompt still on screen? A library of isolated tracks is not the same as a comparison surface.

Export and rights as product states. Are download formats and commercial-use conditions visible as plan or asset states, or only as marketing language? A user who cannot tell whether a file is for personal use or whether a commercial license applies is being asked to decide after the fact.

If you are building a similar system, write these questions into a test plan. Click through the UI as if you were trying to keep a brief constant, and note every place the interface makes that discipline harder.

A public example of a comparison surface

Public homepage view of the five-model comparison (Suno, Mureka, ElevenLabs, Lyria, MiniMax). Verified official screenshot, not a personal test result.

SongMaker is a useful public example because it sells the comparison as the product idea, not as an advanced setting. The homepage describes an AI song maker that runs Suno, Mureka, ElevenLabs, Lyria, and MiniMax in one place, and tells you to try one prompt on every model and keep the song you like best. That is a workflow promise, not a quality benchmark.

The public AI Song Generator page is more concrete about the surface itself. It shows sample tracks that reveal the prompt on hover, so a style can be inspected before it is reused. It separates a prompt-based path from a Custom mode in which you paste lyrics, mark sections with tags, and optionally set length. It lists five models with published run rules: Suno at five credits per run, two songs, length up to six minutes; Mureka from five credits per run, two takes; ElevenLabs at twelve credits per minute, length up to five minutes, described as instrumental; Lyria at six credits per run, one song, singing pasted lyrics in Custom mode; MiniMax at twelve credits per run, and it can write lyrics if the box is left empty. Vocal controls are presented as male, female, auto, or instrumental. Downloads are listed as MP3, WAV, or FLAC, and the FAQ states that a commercial license is included with annual plans, while free and monthly plans are for personal use.

Those published differences are the metadata a comparison surface should expose before spend. They also show why a naive A/B is easy to get wrong. If you paste lyrics for Lyria and leave the lyrics empty for MiniMax, you are no longer testing the same brief. If you judge ElevenLabs against Suno without noticing that the official description frames ElevenLabs as an instrumental, length-controlled option, you are comparing different jobs.

I am not inferring how the models are orchestrated or billed internally, and I am not ranking how they sound. I am only pointing at visible interface facts that make a fair comparison possible.

A compact test matrix

If you are specifying a similar UI, a first test matrix can stay this small:

Requirement What to verify in the UI Easy failure
Prompt invariance Same text is replayable across models Prompt edited accidentally between runs
Lyrics binding Custom lyrics stay identical, or both runs are set to generate words One run invents a chorus, the other sings a pasted one
Pre-spend metadata Takes, length control, and credit cost visible before confirm User learns the cost only from a receipt
Job control Instrumental or vocal is an explicit state Mix compared against a sung track by accident
License state Personal use vs commercial license is visible before distribution User assumes every paid file is cleared for commercial use

A team can add latency, error recovery, and accessibility later. If this matrix fails, richer engineering will not save the comparison.

Limits that belong in the same memo

Published credit examples go out of date, and they should be re-checked on the live page before anyone treats them as a specification. A start with ten free credits, as the topic page describes, is enough to think about the workflow; it is not evidence about output quality. License text should be read in its precise form: annual plans include a commercial license; free and monthly plans are described as personal use. Downstream platforms such as YouTube and Spotify have their own rules for AI-generated music.

Do not pretend a public marketing page is a system design document. Use it as a set of visible states and as a reminder of what users will try to compare. If your own product offers more than one model, the work is to make that comparison honest: same brief, visible differences, and no silent change in the job the model was asked to do.

title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
description:
arXiv:2611.22514v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

title: Our Clean Up Merged Two Builders Who Shared a Yard and Put the Son on Stop for His Father's Debts
description:
Last year we ran a project to remove duplicate customer accounts. Over twenty years our branches had opened new accounts for customers they could not find quickly on the screen, and about six thousand accounts looked like the same customer twice. Duplicates do real harm, from split credit limits to statements showing half the balance.

A data quality tool scored pairs of accounts on name, address, phone number and email, and merged any pair that scored above a threshold. We checked a sample of a few hundred by hand, found the matches convincing, and let it merge four thousand two hundred accounts over a weekend.

Three weeks later a groundworker rang our credit controller, furious. His account was on stop, and the statement explaining why listed invoices he had never seen. His father runs a building firm from the same yard on the edge of a village. They share a surname, an address and an office phone, and the father's account was overdue. The tool had seen two accounts with nearly the same name at the same address and made them one, and our credit rules had done the rest.

When we looked properly, a hundred and thirty eight merges had joined different businesses: fathers and sons, brothers, and firms renting units on the same industrial estate whose addresses differed only by a unit number the tool treated as noise. Unpicking them was far harder than merging had been. Every invoice, payment and credit note had to be returned to the right customer by branch staff who knew them.

A duplicate is an inconvenience you can live with. A wrong merge is a mistake that spreads through every record attached to it. We had treated the threshold as a measure of how alike two accounts looked, when the question that mattered was whether they were the same business.

Merges are now proposals. Limited companies are merged only when their registration numbers match. Sole traders and partnerships are proposed to the branch that opened the accounts, and someone there confirms each one. Every merge keeps the original accounts so it can be reversed, and the tool is tested on samples drawn from shared addresses, which is where its mistakes live.

Two records that look alike are a question for someone who knows the customers, not an answer.

– Serguey Shinder
