title: NonoDB in practice #1: expiring invite tokens without Redis or cron
description:
Every small product eventually grows the same little subsystem: one-time
invite links.

A teammate clicks "Invite", we generate a token, send a URL, and the link must
work exactly once and stop working after seven days. It also has to be
auditable — "who invited whom, and when was the link used?" — because support
will ask.

The classic stack for this is three moving parts:

  1. Redis with SETEX invite:<token> 604800 <payload> for the expiry.
  2. Postgres for the durable invite record and the audit trail.
  3. A cron job that deletes stale rows so the table does not grow forever.

That is a cache, a database, and a scheduler for a feature that stores maybe a
few thousand rows. On a 1 GB VM it is also three more things that can page you
at 2 a.m.

This post rebuilds the feature with one process: NonoDB, a single Rust
daemon that owns LMDB files and speaks HTTP/JSON. The whole thing fits in the
same mental model as SQLite, but with document semantics, TTL, and per-document
history built in.

The requirements, written down

Before choosing anything, I wrote the actual contract:

  • A token is a random 32-byte value, stored hashed.
  • Default lifetime: 7 days.
  • Some invites are shorter — a support re-invite should die after 1 hour.
  • A token can be consumed at most once, even if two requests race.
  • Consuming a token must be atomic with marking it used.
  • We keep the invite record for audit, but not forever.
  • The whole service must run on a 1 vCPU / 1 GB VM next to the app.

The important line is number four. Expiry is not authorization. A TTL is a
garbage collector, not a lock. If two requests arrive at the same time, "is it
expired?" followed by "mark it used" is a race unless the check and the write
happen in one transaction.

Run the daemon

NonoDB publishes Linux amd64/arm64 images. Pin an exact version in
production; latest should be a deliberate choice, not an accident.

export NONODB_AUTH_FILE="$PWD/nonodb-auth.json"
nonodb-cli auth init
export TOKEN=$(nonodb-cli auth token create admin)

docker volume create nonodb-data
docker run -d --name nonodb \
  -e NONODB_AUTH_FILE=/etc/nonodb/auth.json \
  -e NONODB_TCP=0.0.0.0:7878 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7878:7878 \
  --group-add "$(id -g)" \
  -v "$NONODB_AUTH_FILE:/etc/nonodb/auth.json:ro" \
  -v nonodb-data:/var/lib/nonodb \
  ghcr.io/essmos/nonodb:0.26.0

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7878/healthz

The daemon runs as an unprivileged user. TCP requires the auth registry; the
Unix socket is the trusted local channel. For a single-host app, mounting the
socket into the app container is even simpler, and there is no bearer token to
rotate.

Create the collection once

NonoDB collections can carry a default TTL and a history retention setting.
Both are opt-in.

from nonodb import NonoDB

db = NonoDB(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:7878", token=TOKEN)
invites = db.collection("invites")

db.create_collection(
    "invites",
    ttl_seconds=7 * 24 * 3600,   # default: 7 days
    ttl_purge_history=False,     # keep revisions for audit
)
db.set_collection_history("invites", 20)

Two details matter here:

  • The collection default applies to documents inserted after it is set. It does not rewrite existing documents.
  • ttl_purge_history=False means an expiry leaves a delete tombstone in history instead of erasing the revisions. For an audit trail, that is what we want, at the cost of some disk.

There is no cron entry and no cleanup container.

Insert an invite with a per-document override

The default is seven days, but the support workflow needs one hour. The reserved
top-level _ttl field overrides the collection default for that document:

import hashlib
import secrets
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

def bson_date(value: datetime) -> dict:
    """Wrap an instant in MongoDB Extended JSON for the HTTP API."""
    return {"$date": value.isoformat()}

def create_invite(team_id: str, email: str, ttl_seconds: int = 7 * 24 * 3600):
    raw = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    token_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    invites.insert({
        "_id": token_hash,          # lookup by hash, never store the raw token
        "team_id": team_id,
        "email": email.lower(),
        "used": False,
        "created_by": "dashboard",
        "expires_at": bson_date(now + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)),
        "_ttl": ttl_seconds,        # cleanup window, not the auth check
    })
    return raw

# Support re-invite: valid for one hour.
raw_token = create_invite("team_42", "new@example.com", ttl_seconds=3600)

_ttl is metadata: it is stored outside the document and is not returned by
reads. An update that does not mention _ttl preserves the current expiry, so
"resend invite" can extend or shorten the window explicitly:

def extend_invite(token_hash: str, ttl_seconds: int = 7 * 24 * 3600):
    new_deadline = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)
    invites.update(
        {"_id": token_hash},
        {"$set": {"_ttl": ttl_seconds, "expires_at": bson_date(new_deadline)}},
    )

Consume the invite exactly once

This is where the Redis-plus-Postgres version needed a transaction or a Lua
script. In NonoDB, find_and_modify selects one document, applies the update,
and returns the image — all inside the single writer transaction.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def consume_invite(raw_token: str) -> dict | None:
    token_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw_token.encode()).hexdigest()
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    old = invites.find_and_modify(
        {"_id": token_hash, "used": False, "expires_at": {"$gt": bson_date(now)}},
        {"$set": {"used": True, "used_at": bson_date(now)}},
        new=False,
        projection={"_id": 1, "team_id": 1, "email": 1, "used": 1},
    )
    return old   # None means: unknown, already used, expired, or swept

Two concurrent requests cannot both receive the invite. The second one matches
nothing, because the first transaction already set used: true. There is no
read-modify-write gap in application code, and no distributed lock.

The Python client passes the Extended JSON object through unchanged. Over raw
HTTP, NonoDB also accepts numeric milliseconds and RFC 3339 strings with Z or
a numeric offset; naive local times are rejected as ambiguous.

TTL is cleanup, not the security boundary

This deserves its own section because it is the most common design mistake with
any TTL feature, including Redis.

NonoDB TTL is eventual. A document stays readable until the background
maintenance worker sweeps it, normally within a few seconds of expiry. That is
perfect for garbage collection and terrible as the only check for "is this link
still valid?"

So the application contract has two checks, and the find_and_modify filter
above already carries both:

  1. used == false — enforced atomically by the write transaction.
  2. expires_at > now — the hard deadline, independent of cleanup timing.

The TTL setting exists so that the collection does not grow forever, and so that
support does not see year-old invites in the GUI. It is not SETNX.

If a document somehow survives long past its deadline, the expires_at filter
still rejects it. TTL remains the janitor, not the bouncer.

The audit trail is already there

Because history is enabled on the collection, the insert and the consume are
recorded as revisions in the same LMDB transaction as the current document.
There is no second write path to forget.

revisions = invites.history(token_hash, limit=10, include_docs=True)
for rev in revisions:
    print(rev["rev"], rev["op"], rev["at"], rev.get("doc", {}).get("used"))

rev is a global monotonic revision ID. For one document, revisions are ordered
but not necessarily consecutive — another document's write can take a number in
between. get_version(token_hash, rev) returns one exact revision, or None if
retention has pruned it.

The retention setting caps revisions per document at 20. For invites that is
plenty: created, maybe extended once, consumed, expired.

A real audit export can then be a single aggregation over the collection or a
batch of reads, without joining two databases.

What about the "expired invites" dashboard?

Support wants a count of live invites per team. With a secondary index on
team_id this is a normal indexed query:

invites.create_index(field="team_id")

live = invites.count({"team_id": team_id, "used": False})

count({}) is O(1) in NonoDB; filtered counts use the index when the filter
matches it. For a grouped report:

list(invites.aggregate([
    {"$match": {"used": False}},
    {"$group": {"_id": "$team_id", "live": {"$sum": 1}}},
    {"$sort": {"live": -1}},
    {"$limit": 20},
]))

No separate analytics store, no nightly rollup.

What this costs

The feature now has:

  • one daemon,
  • one data volume,
  • one collection with a TTL default and history retention,
  • no cache server,
  • no cron job,
  • no cleanup Lambda.

On a small VM the idle daemon is in the single-digit-megabyte range, which is
the main reason I reached for it instead of adding another service. Backups are
a single LMDB directory, and the daemon supports native or restic backups with
encryption if the data ever leaves the box.

When I would not do this

Honesty is useful in a tutorial:

  • If the app already runs Postgres and the team knows it well, a partial unique index plus a scheduled DELETE is a perfectly good solution. NonoDB wins when you do not want to operate a second database server.
  • If you need cross-collection transactions across many entities, a relational database with real foreign keys is still the safer default.
  • If the token volume is in the tens of millions per day, measure first. NonoDB serializes writes through one writer thread, which is ideal for this workload but not a horizontally sharded write firehose.

For the actual shape of this problem — a few thousand short-lived records, one
small VM, one process, atomic consumption, and an audit trail — one binary is
easier to reason about than three services.

Try it 

docker run --rm -it \
  -e NONODB_AUTH_FILE=/etc/nonodb/auth.json \
  -e NONODB_TCP=0.0.0.0:7878 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7878:7878 \
  -v "$PWD/nonodb-auth.json:/etc/nonodb/auth.json:ro" \
  -v nonodb-data:/var/lib/nonodb \
  ghcr.io/essmos/nonodb:0.26.0

The full API surface used here — create_collection, _ttl, find_and_modify,
history, aggregate — is in the NonoDB docs. If you want the next article in
this series, it will take the same daemon and build a job queue with leases and
retries, again without Redis.

NonoDB is MIT-licensed. I am writing this series while exploring it; the
examples above are run against the 0.26 release.

title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
description:
arXiv:2611.21622v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts.
Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors.
Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%).
Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.

title: Next.js Server Actions: Swallowed Redirects and Body Limits
description:
Server Actions fail in three quiet ways, and none of them throws where the bug actually is.

Symptom. Three failures appear after moving a form to Server Actions. The action validates, redirect("/dashboard") runs, the browser stays on the form. Or every upload over a megabyte dies with 413 Request Entity Too Large / Body exceeded 1mb limit. Or useActionState never updates — the action throws, and all the user sees is a generic An error occurred in the Server Components render with a digest instead of your message.

Cause. redirect() and notFound() do not return; they throw a framework-controlled exception that unwinds the render. A try/catch around the call swallows it, and the action completes normally. Separately, Server Actions deserialise their arguments server-side through a body parser with a fixed size limit, and anything thrown inside an action is serialised across the network boundary — an Error instance, a class instance, or a Date in useActionState state cannot make that trip and is replaced with a digest.

Fix. Call redirect() after the try/catch block or rethrow it with isRedirectError/unstable_rethrow; raise serverActions.bodySizeLimit and validate size before upload; and return plain serialisable objects from actions — { ok: false, fieldErrors } — never caught Error objects.

How an action crosses the boundary

An action is a POST to the current route, RSC-encoded, awaited by the client, whose return value must be serialisable through the same encoding. That single sentence explains all three failures.

// app/actions.ts
"use server";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

export async function createPost(prevState: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const title = String(formData.get("title") ?? "");

  try {
    if (!title) throw new Error("Title is required");
    await db.post.create({ data: { title } });
  } catch (error) {
    return { ok: false, message: (error as Error).message }; // never rethrow
  }

  redirect("/posts");   // OUTSIDE the try: redirect throws by design
}

Reproduce the swallowed redirect with the snippet above minus the comment: move redirect() inside try and the form posts, the row is created, and nothing navigates, because the catch block returns a state object instead. The same mistake removes the navigation from notFound() and from unauthorized().

Next.js 15 and 16 ship a size limit of 1 MB per action body. It applies to the whole multipart payload, so a 900 KB image plus form fields can exceed it.

// next.config.ts — Next.js 15+ top-level key; Next 14 used experimental
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "4mb" },
};

// client: check before the request, so the user gets a real message
const MAX = 4 * 1024 * 1024;
if (file.size > MAX) return { ok: false, message: "File must be under 4 MB" };

A proxy in front of the app has its own limit. Vercel caps request bodies at 4.5 MB for serverless functions, so raising bodySizeLimit past that changes nothing; uploads that large belong in a direct-to-storage signed URL.

Version and boundary reference

Boundary What crosses it Fails when Fix
Client → action arguments FormData, serialisable values File outside FormData, class instances pass FormData, or a base64 string
Action → client return plain object, string, number, array Error, Date, Map, class return { error: string }
Action → framework thrown control-flow errors caught in try/catch isRedirectError / unstable_rethrow
Body parser whole multipart payload over bodySizeLimit raise limit or upload directly
Next.js version Redirect error helper Size limit location
13.4–13.5 isRedirectError in next/dist/client/components/redirect not configurable
14.x isRedirectError (unstable path) experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit
15.x unstable_rethrow added serverActions.bodySizeLimit
16.x unstable_rethrow stable behaviour serverActions.bodySizeLimit

Edge cases and the fixes that work

1. Rethrowing the redirect instead of restructuring

When the redirect genuinely belongs inside the guarded block, the framework's own predicate is the correct escape hatch:

import { isRedirectError } from "next/dist/client/components/redirect-error";

try {
  await save(formData);
  redirect("/done");
} catch (error) {
  if (isRedirectError(error)) throw error;   // let the framework unwind
  return { ok: false, message: "Save failed" };
}

That import path is internal and moves between minors. unstable_rethrow(error) from next/navigation is the documented wrapper and covers redirect, not-found, and forbidden in one call.

2. useActionState and non-serialisable state

useActionState keeps the action's return value in React state, which means it is sent through the RSC payload on every update. An Error instance, new Map(), or a Date cannot be encoded and throws Only plain objects, and a few built-ins, can be passed to Client Components from Server Components.

type State = { ok: boolean; message: string; fieldErrors?: Record<string, string> };

export async function updateProfile(_prev: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const parsed = schema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, message: "Check the form", fieldErrors: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors };
  }
  await db.profile.update(parsed.data);
  return { ok: true, message: "Saved" };   // plain object, no Date
}

Convert timestamps to ISO strings at the boundary. Error digests exist on purpose: in production an uncaught action error is redacted so an internal stack trace never reaches the browser, which is exactly why a catch that returns error.message must first convert the error into your own string.

3. The 413 that is not the action's limit

Body exceeded 1mb limit comes from the action parser; 413 Request Entity Too Large with no Next.js log line comes from the platform. Check both before changing config:

# platform limit, not framework limit
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST https://app.example.com/api/upload \
  -F "file=@big.zip"

If the plain route returns 413 while a small action works, the reverse proxy is the limit. For Vercel, request.body above 4.5 MB cannot be raised by configuration at all.

4. revalidatePath order relative to the redirect

Data cache invalidation belongs before the redirect, because the redirect ends the action.

await db.post.update({ where: { id }, data });
revalidatePath("/posts");
revalidateTag("posts");
redirect(`/posts/${id}`);   // last statement, never followed by more work

redirect() returning a typed never means code after it is unreachable and tsc will flag it. That is a feature: use it to prove the action cannot continue after navigation.

5. Actions called outside a form

<form action={}> passes FormData automatically; a startTransition call does not. Passing an object works, but passing a File directly does not — only FormData carries binary through the action encoding.

"use client";
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => publish(post.id))} disabled={isPending}>
  Publish
</button>

6. Error boundaries do not catch action errors in production

An error.tsx boundary catches render errors, and an uncaught action error arrives as a redacted digest that error.tsx never sees unless the client rethrows it. Handle expected failure inside the action and return state; reserve throwing for genuinely broken invariants, where a digest and a server log are the right outcome.

Common mistakes and version gotchas

  • redirect() inside try/catch — swallowed. Move it out or rethrow with unstable_rethrow.
  • redirect() in a setTimeout or after await past the response — the action has returned, so the navigation is lost.
  • Returning Error from an action — not serialisable; return a string or a plain object.
  • useActionState action that does not take (prevState, formData) — React passes the previous state as the first argument and the signature mismatch shows as formData.get is not a function.
  • bodySizeLimit under experimental on Next.js 15+ — ignored, and the 1 MB default stays.
  • revalidatePath after redirect — unreachable; invalidate first.
  • Actions used as event handlers directly — onClick={myAction} posts nothing; wrap in startTransition or use a form.

Related tools. Paste a failed payload and inspect it with the JSON formatter, test a multipart request without the app in the way using cURL to code, and compare the action's serialised state between the versions in a text diff.

title: What gets rebuilt in a hundred merged changes
description:
Every design system has a gap between what it offers and what gets written. You can argue about that gap in the abstract for a long time. I wanted to look at it in real code, change by change, so I took a popular open-source document-sharing product and replayed its last hundred merged changes against the components and tokens it has today.

This is what I found, how I checked it, and why the product stays anonymous.

The method

The idea is simple. Take a repository's recent history and, for each merged change, ask one question: did this change add something the codebase already had?

For each change, the check looks only at the lines that change added, not the whole file it touched. It compares them with the components and design tokens the repository declares. Two kinds of finding count.

  • Hand-built UI where a component already existed: a button element styled by hand where the codebase has Button, a pulsing grey block where it has a skeleton loader component.
  • A raw value exactly equal to a token or scale step that already existed: a pixel size that is a step on the spacing scale, a colour that is the value of a declared colour token.

One rule matters more than the rest. A finding of hand-built UI is kept only if the component already existed when the change was made. Building a button by hand before anyone had written Button is not a mistake. It is how components start.

The replay runs on a temporary copy of each commit and never touches the working repository. Nothing is uploaded, and no AI model is involved in the check itself.

What it found

Of the last hundred merged changes, all but a handful touched the product's UI source.

  • 4 of them added hand-built UI where the codebase already had the component. The most common case by far was a hand-built loading placeholder where the skeleton loader component existed. Raw buttons and inputs, and a new toggle built from scratch where a Toggle component already existed, made up the rest.
  • 9 of them wrote a raw value exactly equal to an existing token or scale step: white and near-black colours that were already tokens, pixel sizes that were already steps on the scale, z-index values that matched a declared layer.

The check also turned up values that matched nothing: widths, font sizes and radii that sat between two steps of the scale. Those are a different kind of finding. They are not a bypass, because there was no token to bypass. They are a question for the team: is this a new step, or a value that should round to an existing one?

There were contrast findings too, text colours on backgrounds below the WCAG contrast minimum. I am leaving those aside here. They are worth fixing, but they are not about reuse.

How I checked it

A count like this is only worth publishing if each finding holds up. So every finding in this note was checked by hand against the source: the line the change added, the component or token it was compared with, and whether that component existed at the time.

It is the step I will not skip. A check that names a pattern can be wrong, and the cost of a wrong claim about someone else's code is much higher than the cost of a missing one.

I have replayed other products the same way. Their notes have not yet been read by hand, so I am not quoting their numbers. What I can say is that the results varied a lot between products, which is itself useful: this is not a fixed rate of sloppiness. It depends on how visible the components are and how a team works.

Why the product is anonymous

The product is open source, the history is public, and anyone could run the same replay. I still will not name it, for three reasons.

  • These findings describe how code gets written under time pressure, by people and, more and more, by coding agents. They are not a verdict on the team, and a name invites that reading.
  • A wrong claim with a company's name on it is the real risk, to them and to me. Anonymising by default removes it.
  • If a team wants to see the full note about their own code, the right way is to offer it through their public channels, and let them decide what happens next.

So I describe the findings in plain words and never paste their code.

What it says about agents

None of these changes is labelled as written by an agent, and I make no claim that they were. What links them to agents is the shape of the mistake.

In an October benchmark of Saer, Codex hand-built UI the codebase already had a component for in 22 runs without access to the design system, and in 5 with it, out of the same number of runs on each side. The patterns were the same ones this replay found: loading placeholders, buttons, inputs and empty states built fresh beside the component that already existed.

An agent writes from what it can see. A person in a hurry does the same. As more changes are written with agents, the number of chances to rebuild something goes up, and so does the value of a check that asks the reuse question on every change.

What I take from it

  • Replay history before you argue about drift. A hundred real changes say more than any amount of opinion.
  • Judge only the lines a change adds, and only against components that existed when it was made.
  • Read every finding by hand before you publish a count.
  • Keep values that match nothing apart from values that bypass a token.
  • Describe the pattern, not the team.

The replay is part of Saer, the tool I am building to keep coding agents on the design system a codebase already has. You can request early access at saer.app.

title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
description:
arXiv:2611.22240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

title: Captors can force the PIN. They still can't switch the alarm off.
description:
The short version, for everyone: Kengele is a free safety alarm for activists. If captors force an activist to unlock their phone and say "I'm safe", the alarm now keeps ringing. Only 2 of the activist's 3 trusted contacts can switch it off, and only after seeing or hearing them on a call. The rest of this post shows exactly how, with code you can run yourself.

Kengele is an open-source alarm for activists in East Africa. Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia: "if you go quiet, the bell rings."

Why it exists

  • Amnesty International counts over 83 enforced disappearances around Kenya's 2024 and 2025 Gen Z protests.
  • When someone disappears, how fast the public finds out often decides how fast they are released. Today that depends on someone noticing and phoning around.
  • The closest tool for human rights defenders, Círculo, says on its own site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It depended on one organisation's servers.

How it works, in plain words

  1. Before a risky event, the activist sets a time window, for example "2pm to 8pm, check in every 90 minutes".
  2. They check in from their phone. Each check-in goes to 3 to 5 guardians: family, a lawyer, a trusted organisation.
  3. If a check-in doesn't arrive, each guardian's phone raises the alarm on its own. There is no central server, so there is nothing to shut down or seize.

For developers: check-ins are signed, encrypted Nostr events (NIP-17/44/59) sent over public relays. The watcher logic runs on each guardian's device.

The problem this update fixes

Kengele already had a duress PIN: a second PIN that unlocks to a normal-looking screen but quietly raises the alarm. But a captor can force someone to give their real PIN and send "I'm safe". Before this change, that was enough to end the alarm.

The new rule (PR #31)

Once an alarm has gone off (a missed check-in, a panic button or a duress PIN):

Who says "safe" What happens
The activist alone Guardians see "the activist says they are safe". The alarm keeps ringing.
The activist + 1 guardian Not enough. The activist's word never counts towards the vote.
2 of 3 guardians The alarm stands down.

Each guardian also has to speak to the activist by voice or video before their "safe" can be sent. The app enforces this. It isn't just a guideline.

And the activist's "I'm safe" never delays a public alert. If guardians are already confirming the alarm, their confirmations keep counting.

Proof

Without reading code: every change is public. Open pull request #31 to see what changed, when, and the written reasoning. The cover image shows the project's automatic checks (tests) running. Each PASS means the rule held.

For developers: the guardian's all-clear is built by GuardianAllClearEvent, which returns ErrNotVerified unless it receives a record of a voice or video call (body.go#L128-L140). The record stays on the guardian's device and is never sent.

The core test (confirm_test.go#L328):

func TestActivistAllClearAloneEndsNothing(t *testing.T) {
    // After a panic, captors force the activist to unlock with the real
    // PIN and send an all-clear. The alarm must stay, and the release must
    // still happen when a second guardian confirms.
    ...
    o = expect(t, None)(f.clearFrom(t, tl, f.activist.priv, 1, t0, t0))
    if !o.ActivistSaysSafe || o.By != NotCleared || tl.Epoch() != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("activist all-clear ended the alarm: %+v epoch=%d", o, tl.Epoch())
    }
    ...
    // The pending confirmation survived, and the second one releases.
    expect(t, Release)(f.confirm(t, tl, 2, 1, t0.Add(time.Minute), t0.Add(time.Minute)))
}

Run it yourself (needs Go 1.24 or newer):

git clone https://github.com/altradits/kengele
cd kengele
go test -race -v -run 'AllClear|PlusOne|Coerced' ./internal/confirm

Our run (Go 1.26.5, commit 00783f7):

--- PASS: TestSingleCoercedGuardianCannotPublish (0.16s)
--- PASS: TestActivistAllClearAloneEndsNothing (0.09s)
--- PASS: TestActivistPlusOneGuardianIsNotEnough (0.07s)
--- PASS: TestGuardianAllClearNeedsVerification (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestAllClearByTwoGuardians (0.07s)
--- PASS: TestAllClearRaces (0.27s)
--- PASS: TestConcurrentActivistAllClearAndConfirms (0.14s)
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/confirm   2.142s

What it still can't stop

Being honest about the limits matters more than the feature (threat model §4.5):

  • Captors can pressure the activist during the video call too. Pick guardians who know the activist well, and agree a spoken code word in advance.
  • If 2 of 3 guardians are compromised, they can switch the alarm off. That's the trade-off by design, so pick guardians who don't live, work or get arrested together.

Status and how to help

Kengele is still being designed and is not for real use until an independent security review is published.

  • No coding needed: digital-security reviewers, Swahili translators, and anyone who works with activists and can tell us what we're missing.
  • Developers: Go, Android/Kotlin, Nostr, Bitcoin (miniscript, OpenTimestamps).

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: Which Companies Use AWS? Real-World Examples Across Industries
description:
A beginner-friendly look at well-known companies that run on AWS, grouped by industry, and why they chose it.

tags: aws, cloud, beginners, devops

vishalcloudjourney

When I started learning AWS, one question kept coming back to me: is anyone actually using this at scale, or is it just a certification topic?

The answer is that AWS runs a huge share of the internet, from streaming and banking to space agencies and healthcare. In this post I've grouped well-known companies by industry and noted what they use AWS for.

1. Streaming and Entertainment

  • Netflix runs its streaming platform, recommendation engine and data analytics on AWS (EC2, S3, DynamoDB).
  • Disney+ uses AWS for video delivery and scaling during big launches.
  • Twitch uses AWS for live video and chat at global scale.
  • Epic Games hosts the backend for Fortnite and its game services on AWS.
  • Formula 1 uses AWS for race data analytics and machine learning insights.

2. E-commerce, Travel and Social Platforms

  • Airbnb runs its booking and search platform on AWS (EC2, S3, RDS).
  • Expedia Group moved a large part of its travel platform to AWS.
  • Pinterest uses AWS for content storage and recommendation systems.
  • Reddit uses AWS for hosting and media delivery.
  • Slack relies on AWS for messaging infrastructure at scale.
  • Lyft runs its ride-sharing platform on AWS.

3. Banking, Fintech and Finance

  • Capital One went "all in" on AWS and shut down its own data centers.
  • Goldman Sachs uses AWS for data and analytics workloads.
  • Nasdaq uses AWS for market data and cloud-based trading infrastructure.
  • Coinbase runs its crypto exchange platform on AWS.
  • Intuit (TurboTax, QuickBooks) uses AWS for its financial software products.

4. Healthcare and Pharma

  • Pfizer uses AWS for research and data processing.
  • Moderna used AWS for drug discovery and data analysis.
  • Johnson & Johnson uses AWS for cloud and analytics workloads.
  • Philips uses AWS for its HealthSuite digital health platform.

5. Automotive and Manufacturing

  • BMW Group uses AWS for its connected car and data platform.
  • Toyota uses AWS for connected vehicle and mobility services.
  • Siemens uses AWS for industrial IoT workloads.
  • GE uses AWS for industrial and digital services.

6. Technology and Software

  • Adobe runs parts of Creative Cloud and its marketing products on AWS.
  • Samsung uses AWS for services supporting its devices and apps.
  • Zillow runs its real estate data platform on AWS.

7. Government and Science

  • NASA / NASA JPL uses AWS to store, process and share space mission and image data.
  • Public sector bodies use AWS through dedicated regions, including AWS GovCloud (US).

Why Do These Companies Choose AWS?

  1. Scalability: capacity grows with demand, like a show launch or a big sale.
  2. Global reach: many Regions and Availability Zones put apps close to users.
  3. Pay-as-you-go pricing: no need to buy hardware up front.
  4. Breadth of services: compute, storage, databases, AI/ML, analytics and security in one place.
  5. Security and compliance: support for many industry standards.

What This Means for Beginners Like Me

Seeing these names made the learning feel more real. The same services I practice with, such as EC2, S3, IAM, VPC and RDS, are the building blocks behind apps used by millions of people. If you're starting your AWS journey, you are learning skills the industry actually uses.

Note: Companies change their cloud setups over time, and many use multi-cloud. For the latest details, check the AWS Customer Success Stories page.

  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.

title: Keep CSS scroll snap targets visible below a fixed header
description:
A scroll-snap layout can select the correct section and still feel broken: the section heading lands beneath a fixed header. The snap rule is not necessarily wrong. The scrolling container simply has no knowledge that part of the visible area is occupied by persistent chrome.

The implementation decision is to reserve that shared space on the scroll container with scroll-padding-top, using the fixed header’s height. This changes the container’s effective snapport: when a section snaps to start, the browser treats the area below the header as the useful top edge. The section can retain its existing scroll-snap-align: start, and the container can retain mandatory vertical snapping.

That separation matters. Child alignment describes where a target aligns; scroll padding describes the usable viewing region in which it should become visible. Adding spacing to every section may appear to work, but it changes content geometry and repeats a viewport-level concern in each target. For a header shared by all targets, the scroller owns the offset.

The expected result is that later snapped headings appear below the fixed header without weakening snap strictness or moving heading content inside each section. A useful verification checks the geometric relationship, not only a scroll offset: after snapping, the heading’s top edge should be at or below the header’s bottom edge. It should also confirm that the original snap type and child alignment remain in place.

There is an important boundary case. The first target begins at scroll position zero, so a top padding offset cannot create negative scroll space above it. It may still sit beneath a fixed header. If targets need different individual offsets rather than one shared overlay allowance, child-level scroll-margin is the more appropriate tool. And if the interaction requires arbitrary pixel-perfect positioning rather than navigation through snap targets, reconsider whether scroll snap fits the interaction.

Working example 

export function snapFixture({ scrollPadding = false } = {}) {
  const paddingRule = scrollPadding ? 'scroll-padding-top: 50px;' : '';

  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <style>
    * { box-sizing: border-box; }
    html, body { margin: 0; height: 100%; overflow: hidden; }
    #scroller {
      height: 300px;
      width: 320px;
      overflow-y: auto;
      scroll-snap-type: y mandatory;
      ${paddingRule}
      border: 1px solid #345;
    }
    #fixed-header {
      position: fixed;
      top: 0;
      left: 0;
      z-index: 1;
      width: 320px;
      height: 50px;
      padding: 14px 12px;
      background: #172554;
      color: white;
      font: 16px sans-serif;
    }
    section {
      height: 300px;
      scroll-snap-align: start;
      padding: 0 12px;
      font: 16px sans-serif;
    }
    section:nth-child(odd) { background: #dbeafe; }
    section:nth-child(even) { background: #dcfce7; }
    h2 { margin: 0; padding-top: 0; line-height: 50px; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <header id="fixed-header">Fixed header (50px)</header>
  <main id="scroller" tabindex="0" aria-label="Snapped sections">
    <section id="first"><h2>First section</h2></section>
    <section id="second"><h2>Second section</h2></section>
    <section id="third"><h2>Third section</h2></section>
  </main>
  <script>
    window.snapToSection = function snapToSection(name) {
      const section = document.getElementById(name);
      const scroller = document.getElementById('scroller');
      if (!section || !['first', 'second', 'third'].includes(name)) {
        throw new RangeError('Unknown snap target: ' + name);
      }

      // offsetTop includes the scroller border, while snapping is calculated from
      // its scrollable padding edge. Account for both that border and the
      // container-owned scroll padding before stopping short of the snap point.
      const scrollPaddingTop = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(scroller).scrollPaddingTop) || 0;
      const targetTop = section.offsetTop - scroller.offsetTop - scroller.clientTop - scrollPaddingTop;

      // Stop slightly before the adjusted target so mandatory snapping chooses
      // the container's actual snap point rather than relying on border offsets.
      scroller.scrollTo({ top: targetTop - 12 });
    };
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/scroll-snap-fixed-header-scroll-padding

title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
description:
arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

title: AVIF vs WebP vs JPEG in 2026: one photo, same width, real bytes
description:
This is a web performance benchmark of image formats. AVIF came out 51% smaller than JPEG on our test photo at the same 1920 px width. WebP came out 39% smaller. Support is no longer the excuse: 95.35% of users can see AVIF.

We took one 9.8 MB camera photo (4964 × 2782), resized it to 1920 × 1076, and encoded it with the same engine at Auto quality:

Format Bytes vs JPEG
JPEG q85 183.7 KB +31%
JPEG Auto 140.3 KB base
WebP Auto 85.5 KB −39%
AVIF Auto 69.3 KB −51%

Yet almost nobody ships it

The 2025 Web Almanac found only 0.7% of LCP images in AVIF. WebP support sits at 96.74%, AVIF at 95.35% (caniuse, August 2026 data). The gap between "supported" and "shipped" is mostly build tooling.

Three things that trip people up

  1. Quality numbers don't transfer. AVIF q80 is not JPEG q80. On one test image AVIF q80 weighed 159.5 KB, while JPEG q80 weighed 82.1 KB. Tune each format on its own scale.
  2. <picture> order matters. The browser takes the first type it supports, not the smallest file. Put AVIF first.
  3. Measure decode on a cheap phone. We measured bytes, not decode time. AVIF decode costs more CPU, and that lands in LCP's render delay.

The setup we ship 

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="hero-800.avif 800w, hero-1920.avif 1920w" sizes="100vw">
  <source type="image/webp" srcset="hero-800.webp 800w, hero-1920.webp 1920w" sizes="100vw">
  <img src="hero-1920.jpg" width="1920" height="1076" alt="..." fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

Are you serving AVIF in production yet? If not, what's blocking you: encode time, CDN, or the CMS?

Method and the full comparison: https://blinkimg.com/blog/avif-vs-webp-vs-jpeg?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=avif-webp-jpeg

title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
description:
arXiv:2611.21974v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.21846v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.

title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
description:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (https://maritime.sh). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.

Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY

There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:

You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.

It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.

We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:

1. Agent lifecycle management.

There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.

2. Custom environments.

Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.

3. Cost optimization.

If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.

So what did we build differently?

We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.

We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.

As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.

Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.

We want your feedback.

If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.

Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?

Happy to answer any questions in the comments.

https://maritime.sh

title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

title: Go Storage API: Malformed Object Responses While Uploading Resized Images — Audit Recovery
description:
A malformed upload response should page the thumbnail worker only after the client has proved that the response is unusable. The least complex recovery path is to validate status and body shape, retry only an idempotent write, and preserve the original receipt separately from every resized derivative.

TL;DR: treat a resized receipt as a derived object, never as the audit copy. Record request IDs and response headers before retrying. Use bounded backoff for transient failures, but send a permanently malformed response to a quarantine queue after the retry budget is spent. For a marketplace, retention and deletion rules matter more than a short upload example.

The page that fires after the thumbnail upload

The alert arrives from the image worker, not checkout. A receipt has already been accepted, the worker has decoded a thumbnail, and the PUT for receipts/tenant-42/order-91827/thumb-320.webp returns a status that does not match the body the client expects. The on-call sees thumbnail_upload_invalid_response, a request ID if the service supplied one, and the object key. They should not see a second thumbnail because a blind retry happened to succeed.

The first action is to freeze the original receipt's deletion timer and inspect request and response logs. Was the request sent to the intended bucket and key? Was the body resized bytes rather than a base64 wrapper? Did the service return JSON when the client expected an object envelope, or did a proxy return HTML? A malformed reply can indicate a service problem or a wrongly formatted client request; the response alone does not identify which.

The signal that should have fired earlier is a client-side response validator. A 2xx status is necessary, but it is not proof that the client received usable data. Log status, content type, byte count, request ID, and a bounded hash of the response body. Do not log receipt contents. Alert on a sustained rate or queue-age breach, not one malformed response during a deploy. A noisy page trains the team to ignore the signal needed for recovery.

Keep it boring.

For this narrow workflow, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants one key and one bill across backend services, while keeping receipt objects private or signed-only. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. The limitation is important: it is not the right sole control for immutable financial records.

What should the upload retry prove?

A retry is safe only when repeating the write cannot create an ambiguous audit state. Give the derived thumbnail a deterministic key based on receipt identifier, transform version, and dimensions. If a worker receives the job twice, both attempts target the same derived object rather than timestamped copies.

The original receipt needs a separate application-database record: object key, content digest, tenant, order identifier, received time, and retention deadline. Storage metadata is not a search index. Keep audit-query fields in the database and use storage for bytes.

This is the small part of a Go client I want beside the worker. It calls Infrai's public storage capability discovery endpoint and validates the response before the worker relies on the documented presign contract. The actual object write remains private or signed-only; this sample does not turn the receipt into a public URL.

package uploadcheck

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func InspectStorageCapability() error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("build upload request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send upload request: %w", err)
    }
    return ValidateUploadResponse(resp)
}

func ValidateUploadResponse(resp *http.Response) error {
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read upload response: %w", err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, summarize(body))
    }
    if len(bytes.TrimSpace(body)) == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned an empty body")
    }
    var value any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &value); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned malformed JSON: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func summarize(body []byte) string {
    body = bytes.TrimSpace(body)
    if len(body) > 256 {
        body = body[:256]
    }
    return string(body)
}

The validator confirms transport status and JSON syntax; it does not invent response fields. Use the documented response schema for stricter checks. For a retryable error, use exponential backoff and honor Retry-After. Cap attempts and total time. For a non-retryable 4xx response or a body that fails validation repeatedly, record the failure durably and quarantine the job. A queue message is acknowledged only after the derivative is confirmed or the failure is recorded.

When the endpoint supports an idempotency key, derive it from the receipt ID and transform version and send that same key on every retry. A 429 is a scheduling signal, not permission to tight-loop.

The route is deliberately shown once. A returned presigned URL is a separate request: use it without the Infrai authorization header. Do not turn this sample into a public-read or static-site-hosting pattern.

Is the original receipt actually protected from deletion?

A successful thumbnail write does not prove that the original is safe, and a successful retry does not repair an accidentally overwritten audit object. Name the policies separately: derivative cleanup and original retention.

Use private or signed-only access for the original. Avoid public-read patterns and permanent public URLs for receipts containing customer and seller information. A storage service with no object versioning or object lock cannot provide recovery from accidental overwrite or a financial-grade WORM requirement by itself. Put that requirement in an external retention system, database-coordinated workflow, or storage product whose documented controls meet it.

If strict concurrent writes are required, an API without If-Match support needs queue or database coordination. Deterministic naming prevents many duplicate writes; it does not create compare-and-swap. Lifecycle expiration with a one-day minimum cannot express hourly cleanup for temporary resize artifacts. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup plan when automatic abort rules are unavailable.

Before deleting an original, check the database retention deadline and any open audit case. A cleanup job should be idempotent: deleting an already absent derivative is a successful end state, while deleting the original before the retention decision is a policy failure.

Why did the storage object API return a malformed response?

The useful comparison is the coordination required when the response is malformed and the receipt must remain available for audit.

Option Useful recovery characteristic Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Mature multipart-upload workflow and broad ecosystem for retries, lifecycle, and integrity checks Versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle, and permissions still need deliberate configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible operations can fit an existing worker Verify exact consistency, lifecycle, event, and retention behavior
Google Cloud Storage Strong Google Cloud identity, logging, and retention integration Teams outside that platform may carry more IAM coupling
Infrai storage One REST API and one key can reduce backend credential and integration sprawl; public discovery documents schemas and examples No versioning or object lock, no If-Match, and no public-read ACL

Infrai is a reasonable option for private receipt derivatives when one key and one bill across backend services, plus application-managed retention, fit the workflow. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. The recommendation is narrow: marketplace teams should try it for coordinated private uploads when they can keep the audit record and retention decision outside object storage.

S3 is the better fit when Object Lock or a deep multipart ecosystem is the deciding control. R2 deserves direct evaluation for an S3-shaped application. GCS is stronger when Google Cloud identity and retention are already the operating baseline. None removes response validation.

Recovery runbook for the next malformed response

Capture request ID, status, content type, response size, object key, transform version, and attempt number. Compare the request log with expected content type and byte count. Look for an HTML or proxy-generated body, truncation, incorrect key encoding, or a client format the endpoint does not accept.

Then check: original exists; retention deadline is intact; derivative key is deterministic; last attempt is recorded; retry budget remains. Retry only after the write can be repeated safely. If validation fails again, quarantine the job with its diagnostic envelope and keep the original available.

The false-positive cost is concrete: every unnecessary page interrupts an operator, and every automatic retry adds load while obscuring the first failure. The opposite mistake is worse. Treating any 2xx as success can advance the queue and leave the system to discover the missing thumbnail much later.

The rule is short: validate before acknowledge, make derived writes repeatable, and make retention independent from thumbnail success.

That is the whole point.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage thumbnail guide and verify the response contract in your worker before enabling cleanup.

Further reading

  • Amazon S3 Multipart Upload overview
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Google Cloud Storage retention policies
  • Infrai storage guidance for image thumbnails

References

title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
description:
arXiv:2611.21998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
