title: Turning dead scroll padding into a little animated fire
description:
Every chat list ends somewhere, and ours used to end in nothing. The last conversation row sat above a blank strip of screen, and that strip existed for a practical reason: three floating action buttons live in the bottom-right corner, and the last row had to scroll clear of them. The padding was correct. It was also dead space that every user paid for on every short list.

Now an animated footer emoji sits in that space — a little fire by default. This is the decision record for turning reserved padding into a feature without changing the scroll geometry, and for keeping an animated footer emoji in Flutter cheap enough to leave on.

The blank strip we were already paying for

The chats list reserves room for the tallest stack of floating buttons: search, the extra button some accounts get, and contacts. A mini floating button occupies 48 dp vertically, gaps sit between them, and the scaffold adds its own margin above the safe area. The result is roughly 184 px of reserved height at the end of the list.

That number is not decoration. It is the reason the last row can be tapped instead of sitting under a button. It is also why the empty state and the populated list share the same bottom padding: the geometry should not change just because the content did.

So the constraint was fixed before the feature existed. We were not looking for space to add; we were looking at space we had already bought and never used.

Do not add a footer below the list

The tempting implementation is a column: the list, then a footer underneath it. It looks harmless, and it quietly changes two things.

First, it adds scroll length. The list now ends later than it used to, so the last row travels further before it settles. Second, it makes the geometry depend on whether the footer is enabled. Turn the decoration off and the list gets shorter; turn it on and it grows. A preference should not resize the conversation list.

The version we shipped puts the footer inside the scroll view instead, as the last sliver. The list's total extent stays the same whether the emoji is on, off, or replaced by an empty box of the same size.

SliverFillRemaining is margin-top: auto

The footer is a SliverFillRemaining with hasScrollBody: false. On a list shorter than the viewport, it receives all the leftover height, which pushes its child to the real bottom. In CSS terms it is margin-top: auto; in a chat list it means a two-row list has one enormous gap between the second row and the emoji, rather than a small decoration floating in the middle of the screen.

On a long list there is no leftover height, so the sliver falls back to a minimum. That minimum is the height of the button stack, which preserves the original reason the space existed: the last row still clears the buttons.

return SliverFillRemaining(
  hasScrollBody: false,
  child: ConstrainedBox(
    constraints: BoxConstraints(minHeight: AppFab.stackHeight(3)),
    child: Align(
      alignment: Alignment.bottomCenter,
      child: FriendsFooterEmoji(scrollController: controller),
    ),
  ),
);

The Align matters as much as the sliver. Without it, the emoji would stretch or sit at the top of the expanded area. With it, the unused height lives above the emoji and the decoration stays pinned to the bottom edge.

Same geometry with the switch off

When the footer is disabled, the widget still renders a square of its normal size with nothing inside. It does not return SizedBox.shrink(), because collapsing the box would remove height from the sliver and shorten the list. The switch would then change scroll behaviour as well as appearance.

That is the rule in one sentence: the setting decides what is painted, never how far the list scrolls.

It also makes the toggle feel instant. There is no relayout of the rows, no jump in the scroll position, and no re-measure of the viewport: one box goes from containing an animation to containing nothing.

An animated footer emoji in Flutter, centred clear of the buttons

The floating buttons are right-aligned, so the footer is centred horizontally. That keeps it visually clear of the stack without needing to know the width of a button or the exact device inset.

An 8 px gap plus the device's bottom inset separates the emoji from the screen edge. The list's own bottom padding already accounts for the dock and the button stack, so the footer is not compensating for them again; it is only adding breathing room.

The result is a decoration that looks placed rather than dropped. On a wide desktop window it stays centred while the buttons remain at the far right.

Reuse the registry, do not build a second one

The emoji comes from the same 85-emoji bundled animation registry used by emoji-only messages. That gives the picker one set of choices, the renderer one lookup, and the fallback one rule: if the emoji has no bundled animation, draw the glyph.

The picker only offers emoji that do have an animation, so the chosen footer always moves unless the app-wide motion level is off. A stored value that is not in the registry is ignored rather than rendered as a mystery glyph, which protects against an old or hand-edited setting.

Reusing the registry also means the footer inherits variation-selector normalisation and the same asset-loading behaviour as the rest of the app. There is no footer-specific asset pipeline to keep alive, and no second list of emoji to drift out of date. The same set also powers animated reaction chips.

Glyphs in the grid, motion in the preview

The picker shows the full bundled set. Playing all of those Lottie compositions at once would be absurd: the sheet would ask the device to decode and loop dozens of animations for a choice the user has not made yet.

So the grid renders plain text glyphs. One animated preview at the top shows the current selection. Tapping an emoji updates the preview only; the sheet stays open, and nothing is saved until the user presses Apply.

That extra step is deliberate. An animation is a poor thing to judge from a still frame, and a footer is something the user will see every day. Previewing first and committing second means the choice is made after seeing the motion.

Two settings that follow the account

The feature stores two values: which emoji, and whether the footer is enabled. Both travel through the same settings map as the other appearance options. There is no new endpoint and no new persistence format.

Because the whole settings map is pushed together, the footer choice follows the account across devices exactly like the theme, the chat background or the animation switches. Sign in on a new device and the same emoji is waiting at the bottom of the list.

An unknown emoji in the stored settings is ignored. That keeps the renderer's promise simple: the footer either shows something from the registry or shows the default, never a missing asset.

The first frame after a restart

Like the other appearance settings, the footer values are cached locally as well as synced. The cache is read at startup, before the profile request returns, so the first frame already has the right emoji and the right switch state.

Without that, a list could render with the default fire, then swap to the chosen emoji a moment later. On a slow connection the flash could last long enough to notice, and a decoration that flickers on every launch is worse than no decoration at all.

The cache is a bridge, not a second source of truth. The server value still wins once it arrives.

Motion off means a still glyph

The master motion level is respected. When it is off, the footer renders the emoji as text at a proportional size instead of playing the animation. No loop, no ticker, no exception for decoration.

That mirrors the emoji-message fallback, so the whole app has one answer to "what happens when someone turns motion off": the content stays, the movement does not.

Decoration should be silent

The footer is wrapped in ExcludeSemantics. It carries no information: it is not a button, it does not show a count, and it does not indicate state. A screen reader announcing "fire" at the end of a list of conversations would be noise dressed as content.

Excluding it also keeps the semantics tree honest. The list ends where the conversations end, and the decoration is invisible to assistive technology in the same way a background pattern is.

The ticker budget at the bottom of a long list

A looping animation at the end of a long list is a small but permanent cost. If the user is reading the top of a hundred conversations, the footer is nowhere near the viewport, and its ticker has no reason to run.

The footer mutes its animation while the list is more than 400 px from the end. Scrolling back towards the bottom re-enables it before it comes into view, so the motion is already running by the time the user sees it. The check also tolerates the brief moment when one controller is attached to two scroll views during a tab or search swap; in that case it animates rather than asserting.

This is the same principle as the lazy message list: do not pay for what nobody can see.

What it costs, and what it buys

The cost is one looping composition, muted when far from the bottom, plus a sliver that already had to reserve space. The scroll length is unchanged, and empty tabs show no footer at all.

What it buys is harder to measure: a list that feels finished at the bottom instead of stopping in a blank strip. The space was already reserved; the only new decision was to treat it as part of the design.

The short version

  • The chats list already reserved about 184 px so the floating buttons would not cover the last row.
  • Put the footer inside the scroll view as a sliver; do not add a footer below the list.
  • Use SliverFillRemaining with hasScrollBody: false so a short list gives all unused height to the footer.
  • Keep a minimum height equal to the button stack so a long list still clears the buttons.
  • Render an empty box of the same size when the switch is off, so the geometry never changes.
  • Reuse the bundled emoji registry and keep the glyph fallback for anything unregistered.
  • Show glyphs in the picker grid and animate only the preview; require Apply before saving.
  • Sync the emoji and the switch through the existing settings map, with a local first-frame cache.
  • Mute the ticker when the footer is far from the viewport, and exclude it from semantics.

FAQ

Why not put the emoji in the floating button stack? Because the stack is interactive and right-aligned. The footer is decoration and belongs in the list's own space, where it can be centred and scrolls with the content.

Does the footer appear on empty tabs? No. Empty tabs keep their existing centred message and show no footer.

What happens if the chosen emoji loses its animation? The stored value is validated against the registry when applied and when read from the cache. An unknown value is ignored, and the default remains.

Does the footer change the scroll position when it is toggled? No. The box keeps its size and the sliver keeps its extent, so only the painted content changes.

Is this safe in encrypted chats? The footer is on the chats list, not inside a conversation. It is presentation only and does not touch message content.

title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.21688v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

title: A prompt change is a code change. Gate it in CI with 60 lines of node:test
description:
Agents and AI features change in a way normal code doesn't. Someone tweaks a prompt, bumps the model version, or adds a line of context, and the code review shows a three-line diff. The tests pass. Nothing in the pipeline knows that the summaries now invent refund amounts.

We review code changes by reading them. We can't review prompt changes that way, because the effect isn't in the diff. It's in the outputs. So the review has to run the outputs.

Here is the small harness we put in front of every AI feature before it ships. It's plain node:test, a JSON file of cases, and about 60 lines. No eval framework, no dashboard. It fails CI when the answers get worse, which is the only job it has.

1. Write cases from real inputs

Start with 20 to 50 real inputs, taken from logs or support tickets (with personal data removed). For each one, write down what a good answer must contain and must not contain. You're not writing the perfect answer. You're writing the things that make an answer wrong.

[
  {
    "id": "refund-amount",
    "input": "Hi, order 1182 arrived broken. I paid $42.50. Please refund me.",
    "mustInclude": ["$42.50", "refund"],
    "mustNotInclude": ["angry"],
    "maxChars": 300
  },
  {
    "id": "no-amount-given",
    "input": "Order 1182 never arrived. I want my money back for order 1182.",
    "mustInclude": ["refund"],
    "maxChars": 300
  }
]

The second case matters as much as the first. The customer didn't give an amount, so the right summary doesn't contain one. Cases where the correct answer is "I don't know" are where models most often make things up.

2. Check what can be checked in code

You can't check in code whether a summary is good. You can check a surprising number of ways it's bad:

// evals/check.js
export function check(output, c) {
  const problems = [];

  for (const s of c.mustInclude ?? []) {
    if (!output.includes(s)) problems.push(`missing "${s}"`);
  }
  for (const s of c.mustNotInclude ?? []) {
    if (output.includes(s)) problems.push(`contains "${s}"`);
  }
  if (c.maxChars && output.length > c.maxChars) {
    problems.push(`too long (${output.length} chars)`);
  }

  // Every number in the answer must appear in the input.
  for (const n of output.match(/\d[\d,.]*\d|\d/g) ?? []) {
    if (!c.input.includes(n)) problems.push(`invented number ${n}`);
  }
  return problems;
}

The last check is the one that earns its keep. Any number in the output that isn't in the input was invented: an amount, a date, an order ID. It's strict and occasionally flags something harmless, like "2 items" when the input said "two items". That's a fair trade for catching the summary that tells your support team to refund $45.00 instead of $42.50.

3. Gate on the pass rate, not on every case

Models aren't deterministic, and a few cases will be borderline. If every case has to pass, the suite turns red on noise and people learn to ignore it. Gate on the overall rate instead:

// evals/summary.test.js
import test, { after } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { summarizeTicket } from "../src/summarize.js";
import { check } from "./check.js";

const cases = JSON.parse(await readFile(new URL("./cases.json", import.meta.url)));
const MIN_PASS_RATE = Number(process.env.EVAL_MIN_PASS_RATE ?? 0.9);
const results = [];

for (const c of cases) {
  test(c.id, async (t) => {
    const output = await summarizeTicket(c.input);
    const problems = check(output, c);
    results.push({ id: c.id, ok: problems.length === 0 });
    if (problems.length) t.diagnostic(`${problems.join("; ")} | output: ${output}`);
  });
}

after(() => {
  const passed = results.filter((r) => r.ok).length;
  const rate = passed / results.length;
  console.log(`evals: ${passed}/${results.length} passed (${(rate * 100).toFixed(0)}%)`);
  assert.ok(rate >= MIN_PASS_RATE, `pass rate ${rate.toFixed(2)} is below ${MIN_PASS_RATE}`);
});

Each case still prints its problems and the actual output, so when the gate fails you can see why without rerunning anything. With a version of summarizeTicket that invents the amount, the run looks like this and exits with code 1:

# missing "$42.50"; contains "angry"; invented number 45.00 | output: Customer wants a refund of $45.00 and is angry.
# evals: 0/2 passed (0%)
  error: 'pass rate 0.00 is below 0.9'

Start the threshold where your current prompt actually scores, then raise it as you fix cases. The point is that it can only go up.

4. Run it only when it matters

Every eval run calls the model, which costs money and takes a minute. There's no reason to run it on a CSS change. Trigger it on the files that change model behaviour:

# .github/workflows/evals.yml
name: evals
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/prompts/**"
      - "src/summarize.js"
      - "evals/**"
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci
      - run: node --test evals/*.test.js
        env:
          MODEL_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MODEL_API_KEY }}

Do the same thing by hand before switching model versions. When your provider retires the version you tested on, this suite is the difference between a one-day upgrade and finding out from customers.

5. Add a case for every bug

When someone reports a bad answer in production, don't just fix the prompt. Add the input as a case first, watch it fail, then fix the prompt until it passes. It's the same habit as writing a regression test for a bug, and it's how the suite grows from 20 cases to the 200 that actually describe your users.

What this doesn't replace

Code checks catch answers that are wrong in ways you predicted. They don't tell you whether an answer is helpful, well-toned or complete. For that you still need a person reading a sample every week, or a second model grading against a rubric, which is its own post.

But the gate comes first. It's an afternoon of work, it runs on infrastructure you already have, and it means a prompt change gets the same treatment as a code change: it doesn't merge until something has checked what it actually does.

I'm Mayursinh, founder of Redlio Labs. We add AI features to custom software for mid-size companies, and this harness goes in before the first prompt does. The harness above was run with Node 22, against a good and a deliberately broken summarizer.

title: Core Web Vitals po slovensky: LCP, INP a CLS
description:
Core Web Vitals sú tri metriky, ktoré merajú, ako rýchlo a príjemne sa stránka používa. Google ich berie do úvahy pri hodnotení webov.

LCP: za ako dlho sa zobrazí hlavný obsah

Largest Contentful Paint meria čas, kým sa objaví najväčší prvok na obrazovke, zvyčajne hlavný obrázok alebo nadpis. Dobrá hodnota je do 2,5 sekundy.

Čo pomáha: menšie a moderné obrázky, rýchly server, nenačítavať zbytočné skripty pred obsahom.

INP: ako rýchlo stránka reaguje

Interaction to Next Paint meria, ako dlho trvá, kým stránka reaguje na klik alebo ťuknutie. Dobrá hodnota je do 200 milisekúnd.

Čo pomáha: menej JavaScriptu, rozdeliť dlhé úlohy, neblokovať hlavné vlákno ťažkými výpočtami.

CLS: poskakovanie obsahu

Cumulative Layout Shift meria, ako sa obsah počas načítania posúva. Určite poznáte, že chcete kliknúť na tlačidlo a v poslednej chvíli sa odsunie. Dobrá hodnota je do 0,1.

Čo pomáha: vždy uviesť rozmery obrázkov a videí, rezervovať miesto pre reklamy a bannery, správne načítavať písma.

Kde to zmerať

  • PageSpeed Insights ukáže laboratórne aj reálne dáta od používateľov.
  • Search Console má zostavu Core Web Vitals pre celý web.
  • Náš bezplatný sken web prejde aj základné kontroly výkonu.

Poradie krokov

Začnite najväčším problémom. Najčastejšie sú to veľké obrázky a zbytočné skripty. Po každej zmene meranie zopakujte, aby ste videli, čo naozaj pomohlo.

title: Why Small IT Teams Get Stuck Between Free VPNs and Netskope or Proofpoint
description:
Big-company security usually means two products: Netskope to filter what your team does on the web, and Proofpoint to catch sensitive data leaving. Both are built for large companies, with big seat minimums and long sales cycles. If you run IT for a small team, a clinic, or a handful of client offices, that is a hard fit.

I built Arx Cloud to cover the same ground for smaller teams. The full side-by-side is on the original page, and here is the short version.

Where the big tools make sense

If you have thousands of employees, a dedicated security team, and a need for every enterprise integration, Netskope and Proofpoint are proven and you should look at them first.

Where small teams get stuck

  • Free VPN tools only connect computers. They are great at that, but they do nothing about phishing sites or someone pasting a customer list into ChatGPT.
  • The enterprise tools want hundreds of seats. Most need a sales call before you can even try them.
  • You end up with several tools. One for web filtering, one for data leaks, one for remote access, each with its own console.

What Arx Cloud does in one app

  • Blocks known bad and phishing websites.
  • Checks what gets pasted or uploaded into AI tools like ChatGPT and stops real customer or patient records.
  • Gives staff private access to office apps without opening anything on your firewall.
  • Puts an approval step in front of AI coding assistants so they cannot change things on their own.
  • Starts at 5 users, sets up in minutes on your own, and includes a 30-day free trial.

The detailed comparison, including what each product covers, is on the original page.

title: Rigging UI Elements: Bones and IK Outside of Character Animation
description:
Bones are associated with characters, and that association keeps designers from using them where they would save the most time: interface elements that need to bend.

This is a practical guide to the cases, the workflow, and the limits.

What a bone rig actually buys you

A keyframe rig says: at 200ms, this vertex is here. At 400ms, it is there.

A bone rig says: this vertex is 60% influenced by the upper arm and 40% by the forearm. Move the arm and the vertex follows, everywhere, forever.

That indirection is the value. You animate the skeleton — a handful of rotations — and the geometry follows. Change the artwork, and the rig still works. Change the pose, and the skin deforms consistently.

For UI, that means:

  • a mascot that leans, blinks and gestures without re-keyframing every path
  • an illustration that squashes on press without distorting its neighbours
  • a decorative arrow that bends along a curve instead of being redrawn
  • a loading skeleton that breathes with a single parameter
  • a hero object whose parts stay attached when the layout changes

The workflow, in the order it matters

1. Decide what the skeleton is, not what the drawing is.

Look at the artwork and ask: what are the levers? A tail has three. A ribbon has four. An arm has two plus a hand. Bones should be fewer than you think; a rig with twelve bones for a shape that needs three is harder to animate, not easier.

2. Parent the hierarchy properly.

Master bone at the root, children for the limbs or segments, each rotated around a sensible pivot. In Exode this is the master/child bone distinction in the hierarchy panel, and the pivot is what makes a rotation look like a joint rather than a spin.

3. Bind, then weight.

Auto-binding on selection is convenient and destructive if you are not careful — the audit notes on the Exode repo list exactly that problem and the fix that shipped. The safe sequence is: bind the mesh, then paint weights, then test extreme poses before you animate.

Weights are the craft. A vertex at 100% on one bone will crease. A vertex split 50/50 will bend smoothly. The batch weighting and the live weights table exist because doing this one vertex at a time is how rigs get abandoned.

4. Add IK only where you need it.

Inverse kinematics solves the pose from a target: drag the hand, the elbow follows. It is magic for a character reaching for something. It is overkill for a two-bone ribbon you will animate directly.

Exode supports IK chains; the rule is to use them at the end of a chain, not the root, or the whole rig becomes a puppet you cannot pose precisely.

5. Animate the skeleton, never the mesh.

Once the rig is bound, all animation should be bone rotations and root position. If you catch yourself keyframing individual vertices, the rig is wrong.

The UI-specific details nobody tells you

Layout and rigs interact badly if you let them. A bone rig lives in the coordinate space of its container. If the container reflows on a breakpoint, the rig must be positioned by layout, not by absolute coordinates, or it will detach on mobile. This is the single most common bug in "responsive mascot" work.

Rigs need a rest pose that matches the design. If the rig's neutral pose is not the design's default, every state has a permanent offset. Bind at the pose you will ship.

Reduced motion needs a rig-free fallback. A static image at the rest pose is the honest fallback. Do not run a cut-down rig animation for users who asked for less motion; show the still.

Export the rig, not a video. A baked sprite sequence loses the interactivity you built the rig for. If the rig is in the design artefact, the compiled component carries it.

Where the tooling is still catching up

The honest part.

Mesh deformation in Rive and Spine is deeper than in Exode today. If the brief is "a cape that ripples with wind", those tools have more mature free-form deformation and more artist-facing controls.

Exode's rigging audit lists eight gaps it closed — destructive auto-bind, single-vertex selection, read-only weights, edit-mode exit, static weight visuals, destructive re-binding, no independent Bézier handle weighting, and rigid normalisation. That is a real list, and the fact that it is public is a good sign. It is not the same as a decade of character rigs.

So the split I use:

  • Character as art object, shipped inside a canvas or game: Rive or Spine.
  • Character or shape inside a responsive interface, driven by app state: rig it where the layout and state live.

A small example

A brand mark that reacts to a form field:

  • idle: rest pose
  • focus: slight lean toward the field, one bone rotation
  • invalid: a single shake on the root bone, damped
  • success: a squash-and-stretch envelope plus a small bounce

Four states, one rig, two bone rotations and an envelope. No keyframed paths, no per-state redraw, and the whole thing scales with the container because it is inside the layout.

That is the case for bones outside character animation: it turns "redraw it four times" into "rotate a lever".

The rule I would give a team

If an element needs to bend in more than one state, rig it. If it only ever translates or fades, keyframe it and move on. Bones are a multiplier on reuse, and reuse is the only reason they are worth the setup.

UX Baba writes about interaction design and the unglamorous parts of craft. Exode's bone system is part of the editor at exodeui.com.

title: How Website Speed Affects SEO and User Experience
description:
Have you ever visited a website and left because it took too long to load? It happens more often than we think. In today's digital world, people expect websites to load quickly and provide a smooth browsing experience.

Website speed is more than just a technical factor. It influences how visitors interact with a website, how easily they find information, and whether they decide to stay or leave.

For businesses, bloggers, and website owners, improving website performance is an important part of building a successful online presence.

1. What Is Website Speed?

Website speed refers to how quickly a webpage loads and becomes usable for visitors. It includes loading images, displaying text, opening menus, and responding to user interactions.

A fast website allows visitors to access information without unnecessary waiting. On the other hand, a slow website can create frustration and reduce user engagement.

Website performance can be affected by several factors, including:

Large and unoptimized images

Poor website hosting

Too many plugins

Unnecessary JavaScript and CSS

Lack of browser caching

Excessive third-party scripts

Understanding these factors is the first step towards improving website performance.
Great choice! “How Website Speed Affects SEO and User Experience” is a strong topic for DEV.to because it connects digital marketing, technical SEO, website performance, and web development.

I'll structure this as an educational, beginner-friendly technical article, with practical examples rather than making it a promotional post for your website.
How Website Speed Affects SEO and User Experience

Complete article :::writing{variant="document" id="73183"} # How Website Speed Affects SEO and User Experience

Have you ever visited a website and left because it took too long to load? It happens more often than we think. In today's digital world, people expect websites to load quickly and provide a smooth browsing experience.

Website speed is more than just a technical factor. It influences how visitors interact with a website, how easily they find information, and whether they decide to stay or leave.

For businesses, bloggers, and website owners, improving website performance is an important part of building a successful online presence.

1. What Is Website Speed?

Website speed refers to how quickly a webpage loads and becomes usable for visitors. It includes loading images, displaying text, opening menus, and responding to user interactions.

A fast website allows visitors to access information without unnecessary waiting. On the other hand, a slow website can create frustration and reduce user engagement.

Website performance can be affected by several factors, including:

  • Large and unoptimized images
  • Poor website hosting
  • Too many plugins
  • Unnecessary JavaScript and CSS
  • Lack of browser caching
  • Excessive third-party scripts

Understanding these factors is the first step towards improving website performance.

2. How Website Speed Affects SEO

Search Engine Optimization (SEO) helps websites improve their visibility in search engine results. Website performance is one part of the overall page experience that Google considers.

Google uses Core Web Vitals to measure important aspects of real-world user experience.

The three Core Web Vitals are:

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Measures how quickly the main content of a webpage becomes visible. A good LCP score is 2.5 seconds or less.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Measures how quickly a webpage responds to user interactions. A good INP score is less than 200 milliseconds.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Measures unexpected movement of webpage elements while loading. A good CLS score is 0.1 or less.

These metrics help website owners understand whether their pages provide a good experience for visitors.

However, improving Core Web Vitals does not guarantee higher search rankings. Google considers many factors when ranking websites, including content relevance and quality.

3. The Connection Between Website Speed and User Experience

User experience is about how visitors feel when interacting with a website.

Imagine someone searching for a digital marketing service. They visit a website, but the homepage takes several seconds to load. Images appear slowly, buttons do not respond immediately, and navigation becomes difficult.

This experience may encourage the visitor to leave and explore another website.

A fast and responsive website helps visitors:

  • Find information easily.
  • Navigate between pages smoothly.
  • Explore products and services.
  • Interact with website features.
  • Complete actions with less frustration.

Website speed is therefore an important part of creating a positive user experience.

4. How to Improve Website Speed

Improving website speed does not always require advanced technical knowledge. Website owners can start with a few practical steps.

Optimize Images

Large image files can slow down webpage loading. Compress images and use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF where appropriate.

Choose Reliable Hosting

A good hosting provider helps improve server response time and website reliability.

Use Browser Caching

Browser caching allows certain website resources to be stored locally, reducing the need to download them again on repeat visits.

Minimize CSS and JavaScript

Remove unnecessary code and reduce the size of CSS and JavaScript files to help pages load more efficiently.

Use a Content Delivery Network (CDN)

A CDN distributes website content through servers in different locations, helping visitors access resources from a nearby server.

Optimize WordPress Plugins

If you use WordPress, avoid installing unnecessary plugins. Keep essential plugins updated and remove those that are no longer needed.

5. Tools to Check Website Speed

Website owners can use several tools to measure performance and identify problems.

Google PageSpeed Insights

This tool analyzes website performance on mobile and desktop devices. It provides performance scores, Core Web Vitals information when available, and suggestions for improvement.

Website: https://pagespeed.web.dev/

Google Search Console

Search Console includes a Core Web Vitals report that helps website owners understand real-world page experience issues across their websites.

Website: https://search.google.com/search-console/

Google Lighthouse

Lighthouse is an open-source tool that audits website performance, accessibility, SEO, and other quality factors.

These tools can help identify performance issues and guide website optimization.

6. Why Website Speed Matters for Business Growth

Website speed can influence how potential customers interact with a business online.

When a website loads quickly and works smoothly, visitors can explore services, read information, and contact the business more easily.

For e-commerce websites, a better browsing experience can make it easier for customers to explore products and complete purchases.

For service-based businesses, a responsive website can help visitors learn about services and submit enquiries.

Website performance should therefore be considered an important part of a business's digital marketing strategy.

Conclusion

Website speed is an important part of SEO and user experience. A well-performing website makes it easier for visitors to access information, interact with content, and explore services.

By optimizing images, choosing reliable hosting, reducing unnecessary scripts, and monitoring Core Web Vitals, website owners can create a smoother browsing experience.

A successful website is not only about attractive design and useful content. It should also be fast, responsive, and easy to use.

title: Fixing Session Leaks in Axion's MongoDB Transactions
description:
Hey friends! 👋🏻

I wanted to share another cool backend fix I implemented in my microforum, Axion. This time, it involves MongoDB transactions, session management, and taking advantage of Express 5's upgraded error handling to keep my code clean.

Why Use Transactions in the First Place? When you're building a platform like Axion, some actions require multiple database operations to happen together. For example, in the post-deletion route, I need to remove related documents like bookmarks, likes, and comments all at once.

Transactions act as a way to execute a set of database operations where if a single operation fails, everything rolls back and no operations execute afterwards. This guarantees data consistency.

The Bug I Encountered: Session Leaks. When running a transaction in MongoDB, you must start a client session and end it when you are finished. My code was written sequentially, assuming it would always reach the cleanup phase at the bottom. But if my withTransaction block crashed early, session.endSession() wouldn't get called. This left some sessions running in the background, which slowly drained resources and caused memory leaks.

My Solution: Using try/finally in Express 5. The fix was straightforward, but I wanted to implement it without adding unnecessary boilerplate code. I wrapped the session management inside a try/finally block:

const session = await mongoose.startSession();
try {
  await session.withTransaction(async () => {
    // My atomic database operations...
  });
} finally {
  await session.endSession();
}

The beauty of the finally block is its absolute guarantee: no matter what happens inside the try block, the code inside finally is always executed. This ensures session.endSession() runs every time, eliminating the session leak problem.

Oh, yeah, and since I'm using Express 5, any exception thrown inside an async route is automatically caught by Express and routed to my global error-handling middleware. I no longer need those repetitive catch blocks!

Thanks for hanging out and reading through! How do you structure your database transactions to keep them clean and leak-free? Let's talk in the comments below. See you next time! 🌟

title: Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot
description:
Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot

Go's module system uses go.sum files and the public checksum database to make repeated downloads of a module version reproducible. A downloaded module can be checked against a recorded hash, and the checksum database supplies a signed, append-only record for public modules. The model is strong for public dependencies. It becomes more nuanced when an organization introduces private module paths and internal proxies.

The Go modules reference states that when a module is matched by GOPRIVATE or GONOSUMDB, or when the checksum database is disabled with GOSUMDB=off, the go command accepts the hash and adds the file to the module cache without verifying it against the public database. The build can still be reproducible if go.sum already contains the expected hash. The first download of a private module depends on the private source and the organization's controls around it.

Know which verification source applies

For a public module, the default GOPROXY points to the Go module mirror and then to direct. The checksum database verifies newly added sums, and the module cache records downloaded content. If a proxy mirrors the checksum database, the go command may use that mirrored data instead of connecting to the public service. The proxy becomes part of the trust path and should have its own integrity, availability and access controls.

For a private module, GOPRIVATE acts as a default for GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB. A private module can be fetched through an internal proxy, directly from a version-control server or from a local replacement. The checksum database cannot compute hashes for content it cannot see. The organization needs a private source of truth for the expected commit or artifact, plus a review process for the first version that enters the build.

Do not use GOSUMDB=off as a convenient fix for a proxy problem. It disables checksum verification for every module that is not already recorded in go.sum, which is broader than the private path that caused the failure. GOINSECURE is also not a general integrity bypass: the documentation says it permits insecure fetching for direct dependencies, but it does not by itself disable checksum database validation.

Treat replace directives as build policy

A replace directive can point a module to a local directory, a fork or a different version. That is useful during development and dangerous when it enters a release build without review. The release pipeline should inspect the effective module list, including replacements, and reject a path that is outside the approved source set.

The same review should cover pseudo-versions and local module cache state. A pseudo-version identifies a commit, but the build still needs a trusted mapping from that commit to the source repository and the expected content. A cache check is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for a policy about which source is allowed.

go mod verify checks that cached module files and extracted directories have not changed since they were added to the cache. The Go reference warns that it does not download missing modules and does not use go.sum to verify module content. A clean cache after a build can therefore be consistent with a bad first download. Record the source, version and hash that the build actually used.

Build a private-module control

Configure a private proxy with authenticated access, immutable version storage and audit logs. Protect the credentials used by CI so that a compromised job cannot publish a new private version. Require review for module path changes, new replacements and first-time private dependencies. Run the same configuration in developer and CI environments so that a local GOPRIVATE setting does not hide a production path.

Go's checksum design does not claim to decide whether a dependency is appropriate. It protects the identity of a module version against later substitution. The operator still needs dependency review, source authorization and a policy for modules outside the public transparency log.

References

  • Go Modules Reference
  • How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks

AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:

      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:

title: Your device rebooted at a customer site. What do you know?
description:
Picture a small device you built, a sensor inside a machine at a customer's site a few hundred kilometres away. One morning the customer tells you it restarted during the night. What do you know about why?

On your desk, a debugger would answer that: a cable to the chip and a tool that stops the program and shows where it is. In the field there is no cable, no screen and nobody watching. The device is the only witness, and as we'll see in a moment, by default it forgets everything when it restarts.

ferrite exists for this situation: a device in the field has crashed, and there is no stack trace, no log and nothing that says what happened.

We'll follow one crash twice. First we ask what it leaves behind with nothing in place. Then we let ferrite, an open-source Rust library for this problem, save a small record of the crash, and we turn that record back into the line of code that crashed. Everything runs in QEMU, a program that emulates a computer, here a board with an Arm Cortex-M3 processor, so you can repeat it without hardware. The crash is planted on purpose: this post shows how a crash gets recorded, not how to find a real bug.

What happens when a microcontroller crashes?

A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip, with a processor, memory and peripherals, running one program, the firmware, with no operating system underneath. When the processor meets something it cannot do, such as an instruction it does not know or a memory access that fails, it stops what it was doing and calls a fault handler: a function the program provides for exactly this case. On Cortex-M chips the catch-all one is called HardFault.

Here is the function that will crash for us:

/// The bug we are going to find. `udf` is an instruction the processor
/// refuses to execute, so this function crashes every time.
#[inline(never)]
fn handle_message() {
    unsafe { core::arch::asm!("udf #0") };
}

udf means "undefined": an instruction reserved to be invalid, so running it always faults. #[inline(never)] keeps handle_message a function of its own, so the crash has a name we can find later.

What does the fault handler do if we don't write one? cortex-m-rt, the startup crate this program is built on, provides a default that loops forever (its source). The device freezes. Many products have a watchdog, a hardware timer that resets the chip unless the program checks in regularly, so a frozen device restarts a moment later. I ran this program without ferrite in QEMU, and it printed its first line and then nothing, until I stopped QEMU.

So after the restart, what is left? Before main runs, the startup code gives every global variable its initial value: it zeroes some memory and copies initial values into the rest. Whatever the crashed run knew is overwritten, and the new run starts exactly like the first one. That is why all the customer can tell you is "it restarted".

What would we want the device to tell us?

Suppose the device could leave us a note. What should it say? Three things get us from "it restarted" to a line of code:

  • That it crashed, and the processor's reason. Cortex-M chips keep this in a fault status register, a few bits that tell an undefined instruction apart from, say, a bad memory access.
  • Where it was: the program counter, the address of the instruction that was running.
  • Which build it was running, because an address only means something in the exact program that produced it.

The note also has to travel from the device to someone who can read it. That part comes in later posts. Here the device prints its note.

A note that survives the reset

ferrite brings its own HardFault handler. It copies the registers that matter into a small region of RAM and then resets the chip itself. What makes this work is where it writes. That region is a small block, at most 256 bytes (192 in this build), in a part of RAM the build sets aside under the name .uninit.ferrite. It lies outside the memory the startup code initialises, so the next run's startup leaves it alone. A reset restarts the program, but it does not erase RAM, so the note is still there afterwards. Post 2 looks at this region more closely, including why it does not survive a power cut.

Here is main. Look for two things: init, which tells ferrite about the device, and last_fault, which returns the note if a previous run left one.

#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    ferrite_sdk::init(SdkConfig {
        device_id: "qemu-demo-01",
        firmware_version: "0.1.0",
        build_id: 0,
        ticks_fn: || 0,
        ram_regions: &[RamRegion { start: 0x2000_0000, end: 0x2000_FC00 }],
    });

    if let Some(fault) = last_fault() {
        hprintln!("boot: the previous run crashed");
        hprintln!("  pc   = {:#010x}", fault.frame.pc);
        hprintln!("  cfsr = {:#010x}", fault.cfsr);
        debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }

    hprintln!("boot: no crash recorded, handling a message");
    handle_message();
    hprintln!("message handled");
    debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    loop {}
}

hprintln! prints to your terminal through a debug channel QEMU provides, and debug::exit ends QEMU. ram_regions tells the fault handler which addresses are safe to read while it collects its note. pc is the program counter, and cfsr is the fault status register.

Before we run it, what should it print? On the first run there is no note, so we should see "no crash recorded", then the crash in handle_message. The handler saves its note and resets, and the program starts again from the top. This time last_fault finds the note, so we should see a second "boot" line from the same QEMU session, and never "message handled".

Running it in QEMU

The project is the program above plus a Cargo.toml and a few build files for this QEMU board, in the ferrite-sdk repository as examples/qemu-fault at commit b51bfed. With QEMU and Rust's thumbv7m-none-eabi target installed, run this in that directory:

cargo build --release
qemu-system-arm -cpu cortex-m3 -machine lm3s6965evb -nographic \
  -semihosting-config enable=on,target=native \
  -kernel target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault

I ran it from a fresh checkout of commit b51bfed, with rustc 1.97.0 and QEMU 7.2.22 (Debian 12's package), and it printed:

Timer with period zero, disabling
boot: no crash recorded, handling a message
boot: the previous run crashed
  pc   = 0x00000158
  cfsr = 0x00010000

The first line is QEMU's own message about a timer on the emulated board, not our program's. The rest matches the prediction. When the handler asked for a reset, QEMU restarted the emulated chip and loaded the program again, and like the real chip it left the rest of RAM as it was, so the note survived.

What about cfsr = 0x00010000? Only bit 16 is set, and in Arm's documentation for this register bit 16 is called UNDEFINSTR: the processor tried to run an undefined instruction. That is our udf. So the note already tells us why. Where is the next question.

From an address to a line of code

0x00000158 is only a number. To turn it into a line, we need the file the compiler produced, the ELF file. Besides the program, it can carry debug information: a table from addresses to source lines. Our Cargo.toml asks for it in release builds with debug = 2. The tool addr2line from GNU binutils (in the arm-none-eabi build) looks an address up in that table:

arm-none-eabi-addr2line -f -C -s -e target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault 0x00000158

-f asks for the function name, -C turns Rust's encoded symbol names back into readable ones, and -s leaves out the directories. It prints:

qemu_fault::handle_message
main.rs:39

Line 39 of main.rs is the udf line.

There is a condition hiding in that step. We looked the address up in the same file that ran. Change one line above handle_message, rebuild, and the code moves to different addresses: the same 0x00000158 would then point somewhere else, and addr2line would print that other line without complaint. That is why the build belongs in the note. ferrite sends the firmware_version from init with every report, so whoever reads a report knows which release's ELF to look it up in. A version string only identifies a build if it changes with every build, though: our example says "0.1.0" whatever we change, so after that one-line edit its note would still claim 0.1.0. The field meant for the exact build is build_id, which the SDK documents as the first 8 bytes of the ELF's build ID. We left it at 0 here; post 4 is about matching reports to builds.

What a real device does differently

Our program stops after printing so that QEMU exits. A device in the field would carry on with its work after the reset. When it next has a connection, ferrite sends the note, together with the device name and firmware version, to ferrite's server. The server stores the ELF files you upload and runs the addr2line step itself. Making sure each report is looked up in the ELF of the build that produced it is the subject of post 4. After a successful upload, the device clears the note, ready for the next crash.

Let's take stock. With a small block of RAM the startup code does not touch, the program counter and the fault status survived the reset, and the ELF of the same build turned the address into main.rs:39. That rests on one claim we haven't examined: that RAM keeps its contents through a reset. Why does it, how does the program tell a real note from leftover noise, and what happens when the power goes? That's the next post.

title: SeasonRainBench: Global Seasonal Precipitation
description:
arXiv:2611.22281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.

title: Hybrid Quantum Selection of Learning Rates in Language-Model Training: Termination Criteria and an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle
description:
arXiv:2611.21701v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning-rate choices strongly affect language-model fine-tuning, but the best joint profile across layer groups is generally unknown. This paper studies quantum minimum finding for layer-group learning-rate selection within a hybrid classical-quantum training framework. It combines Durr-Hoyer minimum finding with BBHT search and compares fixed-budget and confidence-based stopping policies using a lookup oracle built from measured profile scores at fixed training checkpoints. The paper then introduces an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle that scores and marks joint schedules in superposition without a precomputed score table. Classical one-step loss measurements supply the main, pairwise and three-way interaction effects between layer groups. The circuit adds the effects for each schedule, compares the resulting score with the current baseline score, and marks improving schedules for amplitude amplification. Measured candidates are checked classically before acceptance. Uniform-rate training supplies the initial baseline; using schedules from classical adaptive methods as baselines for joint refinement is left for future work. In closed-loop fine-tuning of a 1.5-billion-parameter language model, each selected schedule drives the next 200 classical training steps. Benchmark accuracies lie within the range observed across five uniform-rate seeds. The results give a working example of how quantum superposition can support adaptive learning-rate selection during training; the remaining quantum limitations are discussed in the paper.

title: Ramu Kaka's Notebook: How Bitcask Stores Data Without Ever Erasing Anything
description:
Remember Ramu Kaka?

If you read Danni, Johny and the Java Feature Flag Problem, you know Ramu Kaka. He runs the tea stall in front of the hospital. He was our feature flag.

Turns out Ramu Kaka is also a database engineer. He just doesn't know it.

Half the hospital drinks chai on credit. Ward boys, nurses, Johny (obviously), and sometimes even Big-B on night shift. Ramu Kaka tracks all of it in a notebook.

His rules are simple:

  1. He never erases anything. Pen only. Crossing out looks dishonest.
  2. Every new chai, every payment, he writes a new line at the bottom.
  3. When the notebook is full, it goes into the drawer and he starts a new one. Old notebooks are never written to again.
  4. He doesn't remember anyone's balance. He remembers which notebook and which line has their latest entry.

Johny asks "Kaka, how much do I owe?" Kaka doesn't flip through 40 pages. He goes straight to notebook 3, line 112, reads one line, done.

Congratulations👏. That is Bitcask.

Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data by Justin Sheehy and David Smith (Basho Technologies, 2010). Six pages. Readable in one chai break. It came out of Riak.

No LSM levels. No bloom filters. No B-tree page splits. An append-only log plus a hash map. That's the whole trick.

On disk: the notebook drawer

A Bitcask instance is just a directory. Only one OS process may open it for writing at a time.

Inside, exactly one file is active. When it crosses a size threshold, it's closed and a new active file is created. Once closed, on purpose or because the server died, a file is immutable. Never opened for writing again.

  bitcask-dir/
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  active data file   <── appends only, one writer
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  └──────────────────────────┘

Ramu Kaka's drawer. One open notebook on the counter, the full ones in the drawer. Writes are sequential. No seeking around to patch an old line.

One line in the notebook

Every put appends one entry:

 ┌───────┬────────┬────────┬──────────┬───────────┬─────────────┐
 │  crc  │ tstamp │ key_sz │ value_sz │    key    │    value    │
 └───────┴────────┴────────┴──────────┴───────────┴─────────────┘
          └─────────────────── covered by crc ─────────────────┘
  • crc: checksum over everything after it in the entry
  • tstamp: a 32-bit local timestamp (the paper marks it internal-only, not exposed)
  • key_sz, value_sz: sizes, so you know where key ends and value ends
  • key, value: the actual bytes

A data file is these entries glued one after another. No header pages, no free lists, no slots.

Johny buys another chai? Kaka doesn't edit the old line. He writes a new one. The old line stays. It's just not the latest anymore. Same in Bitcask: an update is a new append. The old value is still on disk.

Johny clears his tab? Kaka writes JOHNY - CLEARED. That's a tombstone. In Bitcask, delete is a write of a special tombstone value, removed on the next merge.

In memory: Ramu Kaka's brain (the keydir)

After the append, Bitcask updates an in-memory hash table called the keydir. For every key, a fixed-size record points at the most recent entry:

 keydir (in RAM)
 ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┬──────────┬───────────┬────────┐
 │ "johny" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 ├─────────┤    ├─────────┼──────────┼───────────┼────────┤
 │ "big-b" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 ├─────────┤    ├─────────┼──────────┼───────────┼────────┤
 │ "nurse" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 └─────────┘    └─────────┴──────────┴───────────┴────────┘

Values are not in RAM. Every key is. Ramu Kaka remembers every customer's name and where their line is. He does not remember amounts.

On a write, the keydir is atomically updated to the newest location. Any later read sees it.

The basic flow

put(key, value)

  1. Build the entry: tstamp | key_sz | value_sz | key | value, and compute a CRC over it.
  2. Append crc | entry to the end of the active file. Sequential write.
  3. Optionally fsync (sync_on_put). Safer, slower.
  4. Only after the append succeeds, point the keydir at it: key -> (file_id, value_sz, value_pos, tstamp).
  5. If the active file crossed the size limit, close it. It's immutable now. Open a fresh active file.

get(key)

  1. Look up the key in the keydir. Not there? Not found.
  2. Seek to value_pos in file_id, read value_sz bytes. Done.

That's at most one disk seek. Often not even that. Bitcask leans on the OS page cache on purpose and has no internal read cache of its own.

delete(key)

  1. It's just a put, with a special tombstone value.
  2. Remove the key from the keydir.

Ramu Kaka's rule: write the line first, then remember where you wrote it. Flip that order, and a reader can follow a pointer to bytes that don't exist yet.

Merge: Sunday cleanup

Kaka never erases, so the drawer keeps growing. Johny has 300 lines of chai history and exactly one of them matters.

Bitcask merges the non-active (immutable) files into a fresh set with only the live, latest version of each key. Overwritten values and deleted keys are gone.

On Sunday, the nephew copies only each customer's current balance into a fresh notebook. The old notebooks go to the raddi-wala.

The active file isn't touched, so writes keep flowing while the merge runs.

Hint files: when Ramu Kaka gets a fever

One day Ramu Kaka gets dengue and comes back after a week. His memory is blank.

Slow option: read every notebook from the first page. That's what Bitcask does on open if it has nothing better: scan all data files to rebuild the keydir.

Faster option: while merging, the nephew writes a small index card next to each fresh notebook. Name, which line, how long the entry is. No amounts.

That's a hint file. Instead of values, it holds tstamp, key_sz, value_sz, value_pos, and the key. On open, Bitcask scans the hint file instead. Much smaller, much quicker startup.

The data files are the commit log. No separate replay. No WAL sitting next to the data. The log is the data.

The bill (trade-offs nobody puts on the poster)

Bitcask is simple. Simple is not free.

  • Every key must fit in RAM. The keydir grows with the number of keys and must fit entirely in RAM. Values can be much larger than RAM, but keys can't. Huge keyspace with tiny values? Bad fit. Ramu Kaka can handle the hospital. Not the whole of Bangalore.
  • No range scans. The keydir is a hash table. list_keys and fold walk the whole store. Need ordered iteration? Use an LSM-tree or a B-tree.
  • Space amplification until merge. Every overwrite leaves garbage on disk until a merge runs. Write-heavy workloads on the same keys burn disk fast.
  • Startup time without hints. No hint files means a full scan of every data file. Fine at small size. Painful when the drawer is big.
  • Single writer. One process opens a Bitcask for writing. A deliberate simplification, not a bug. Still a constraint.

Torn writes and the CRC

Say the power dies mid-append. Half an entry on disk. Chai spilled on the last line.

That's what the crc is for. On recovery you recompute it. Mismatch = this entry is garbage. A torn entry can only be at the tail of the active file, the only one ever appended to. The sane move (my design choice, not something the paper spells out) is to treat the first bad entry at the tail as the end of the log and truncate there.

CRC does not bring the lost write back. It only stops you from serving corrupted bytes as if they were real.

fsync deserves its own post, coming next. For now: write() returning success only means the bytes are in the OS page cache, not on disk.

Still relevant in 2026?

Yes. The hardware got faster. The ideas didn't expire.

  • Append-only is everywhere. Postgres writes a WAL before touching data. Kafka is basically one giant append-only log. Same Ramu Kaka rule: never erase, just add a line.
  • Sequential writes still win. SSDs made random reads cheap, but appending to the end of a file is still the simplest, most predictable write you can do.
  • RAM is bigger now. "All keys must fit in memory" scared people in 2010. In 2026, plenty of workloads fit comfortably.
  • Crash recovery is still the hard part. CRC per entry, replay the log, ignore the torn tail. Every storage engine has to answer this question.
  • It's small enough to understand. You can hold the whole design in your head in one evening. Try that with an LSM tree.

So why does Ramu Kaka matter to me?

Cause I am mad or its fancy. I wanted to implement in rust.

Want to see me to pick fight with borrow checker? Follow along on X: @nimxch.

Read the paper: Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data, Justin Sheehy & David Smith, Basho Technologies, 2010.

title: Claude Code is third by stars and last by contributors, 8.5x behind Codex
description:
"I'll pick the top ten harnesses by stars, activity and contributors." Measured live: those four criteria disagree, and GetBB has no repository

Anton is going to deep-research the GetBB harness he already looked at. First study its GitHub. Then see what other harnesses exist and pick the ten strongest - by stars, activity, external contributors and overall quality. Then ten separate sessions, one per harness, each going through architecture, capabilities, issues, PRs and documentation: how strong and alive the project is, and what of his own work could be contributed there.

The four criteria are the interesting part, because measured today they produce four different top tens.

GetBB first. It exists - it is getbb.app - and there is no repository to study. getbb/bb and bb-ai/bb both return 404, and no repo named bb surfaces in search. What exists is a third-party layer on top: 8 repositories mentioning getbb.app, a community-curated index at MGrin/awesome-bb-plugins with 69 stars, and the plugins themselves at 1 to 6 stars - bb-plugin-boat (run bb threads on Boat sandboxes), bb-plugin-handoff (move a session between agents and machines), bb-plugin-noema (federated memory for bb agents), bb-plugin-harness (Explore, Plan, Worker, Critic). So step one of the plan has no object, and the contributable surface for GetBB is a plugin or an entry in that awesome list.

⚠️ And a search trap: bb-plugin in:name returns 1,484 repositories, but the top of that list by stars is an Xcode formatter at 1,182 stars, a BBC audio library, and the MyBB forum engine. The name collides with BBC, MyBB and BBEdit. Measuring "the bb ecosystem" with that query overstates it by two orders of magnitude.

Top ten by stars, measured today:

# repo stars open issues last push
1 anomalyco/opencode 227,681 4,060 18 Nov
2 Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT 188,084 690 18 Nov
3 anthropics/claude-code 156,083 17,134 18 Nov
4 openai/codex 135,720 27,730 18 Nov
5 google-gemini/gemini-cli 108,913 736 18 Nov
6 zed-industries/zed 95,254 3,100 18 Nov
7 OpenHands/OpenHands 93,717 1,200 18 Nov
8 cline/cline 71,742 1,792 17 Nov
9 openinterpreter/openinterpreter 68,905 36 15 Nov
10 aaif-goose/goose 56,743 493 18 Nov

The activity criterion removes three candidates a star-sorted list would include. Aider-AI/aider - 50,162 stars, last push 22 May, nearly six months of silence. RooCodeInc/Roo-Code - 24,238 stars, last push 15 May. And a trap in the name: opencode-ai/opencode has 13,915 stars and has been dead since 18 September 2025, while the live 227k project is anomalyco/opencode, a different owner. Pick ten by stars off a cached list and the first sessions go into archives. The guard is one field: pushed_at.

And the external-contributors criterion inverts the ranking completely:

repo contributors stars rank
openai/codex ~478 4
OpenHands/OpenHands ~460 7
aaif-goose/goose ~451 10
anomalyco/opencode ~450 1
google-gemini/gemini-cli ~443 5
QwenLM/qwen-code ~414 13
cline/cline ~349 8
Aider-AI/aider ~172 11
charmbracelet/crush ~165 14
anthropics/claude-code ~56 3

Third by stars, last by contributors, 8.5x behind Codex. The harness he uses every day is the most closed of the ten to outside work. If the criterion is "where can I actually get something merged", Claude Code lands at the bottom of the list rather than the top.

And most of the doors are unmarked. Open issues with newcomer labels, today: opencode 0 good-first-issue, 0 help-wanted; codex 0 and 0; goose 0 and 0. Only two of the five biggest mark anything: gemini-cli (1 and 10) and cline (2 and 4). So in three of five, "find what to contribute" is not working a labelled queue - it is reading the codebase and proposing unprompted. Different task, different merge odds.

What we have already shipped into this world, and where. 377 PRs on the account. The merged external ones are small and specific: doobidoo/mcp-memory-service 4 of 5, eugeniughelbur/obsidian-second-brain 2 of 3, InftyAI/Awesome-LLMOps and gavischneider/awesome-llm-wiki 1 each. The bulk - 49 PRs - is into three of our own repositories, all merged. And into the ten harnesses: zero. Not one PR to claude-code, codex, opencode, cline, goose, OpenHands, zed, AutoGPT or open-interpreter. "Contribute to ten harnesses" starts from nothing in all ten.

Two different outcomes sit in that same table. Where there was an actual maintainer conversation, the merge rate is 4 of 5 and 2 of 3. Where it was a single cold PR into an awesome list, it is 2 merged out of 11. The shape of the plan - ten repos, one PR each, cold - matches the second pattern, not the first.

⚠️ There is one live thread on exactly this topic: PR #442 to ai-boost/awesome-harness-engineering, "Add sqlite-graph-memory (Memory & State)", opened today, still open.

And the strongest criterion is the one the post does not name. 210 reviews of other people's pull requests, and 246 comments in PRs we did not author. The canon rule of 1 October says it plainly: you become an insider in a repository by reviewing other people's work, not by arriving with your own PR. That ledger is healthy - roughly one review for every two PRs we have authored. It is the only number in this sweep that argues the ten sessions will end in merges rather than refusals.

⚠️ What I did not do. I did not read the architecture, capabilities or documentation of any of the ten - that is precisely the ten sessions the post commissions, and doing them in one pass would produce a worse version of them. I did not verify the GetBB plugin list beyond search results and did not look for GetBB outside GitHub, so "no public repository" means "none that search and two direct lookups find".

⚠️ Method caveat. Contributor counts are estimates from the API pagination header at one item per page - accurate to within a few, excluding anonymous contributors. Stars and push dates are direct API reads of 18 November and move daily.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261116.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261116.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI
