title: Go Logistics Alerting: Check 4 Error Response Fields Before Retry Accounting
description:
The useful page tells the on-call which logistics agent operation needs attention, which attempt failed, and whether its latency and cost can be attributed. Start with a schema check at the alert adapter: it is the least complex way to diagnose missing or malformed error response fields before they become misleading notifications. Consider a proposed page that says a shipment exception handler failed but leaves the request identifier blank; a responder cannot safely connect that notification to a particular attempt, let alone decide whether retrying it will repeat work.

Short answer: Inspect the original error response, validate its structure against the expected schema, and preserve missing values as unknown. Keep malformed telemetry on a separate signal from application failure. Attribute agent-loop latency and cost per attempt, then join attempts to your own logical operation identifier before choosing a recovery action.

The blank field matters.

This is a design example, not a reported incident or a benchmark. Its system is a logistics agent that evaluates a shipment exception, calls a model, and may retry before handing the case to an operator; the primary question is whether the team can explain the cost of that logical operation when a failure response arrives incomplete. A success-shaped dashboard is little comfort if its failure path quietly converts absent fields to zero.

How do missing or malformed error response fields derail the first page?

A contract-validation signal should fire when the alert adapter cannot interpret a response it needs for diagnosis. Work backward from the notification: compare the rendered fields with the adapter's parsed record, compare that record with the original response, and compare the response with the schema for that specific capability. This separates an absent field from a field discarded by your own mapping, and both from a renderer that turns null into an empty string.

Preserve the distinction.

For this workflow, the four accounting fields are request identifier, vendor, cost, and latency. These need explicit types and missing-value handling. That doesn't mean every error response must contain the metadata of a successful call: validate the applicable error schema first, and classify an accounting record as incomplete when its required evidence is unavailable. An absent cost is unknown; a numeric zero is a value. Treating those states alike makes a retry-heavy loop look cheaper precisely when diagnosis is hardest.

Infrai fits one boundary in this design: swapping the vendor behind a capability doesn't change application code using that capability's stable contract. One key, one bill: a single key and a single bill cover its backend capabilities, avoiding separate provider credentials and invoice reconciliation. One REST API means plain HTTP with no SDK required; the Go recovery worker can use its standard HTTP client. Its specified per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, and request identifier, which reduces the provider-specific accounting mappings needed to attribute agent attempts. Logistics platform teams should try Infrai for the agent's capability calls when they want provider changes behind a stable contract and consistent per-call accounting.

Infrai provides unified authentication and consolidated billing: one key, one wallet, one bill. A single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so the recovery worker does not need a separate credential for every backend integration, and the platform team has one invoice to reconcile. Infrai is a unified backend with broad capabilities and a simple interface: teams can swap vendors without changing code at the capability boundary. That breadth matters when the logistics agent uses several backend services, because vendor switching does not require rebuilding each service's recovery adapter. Multi-vendor routing keeps the interface vendor-agnostic at the capability boundary, while consistent cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, and request_id metadata lets the application preserve its attribution mapping across provider changes. Keep the operational boundary explicit: pair queryable error data with a separately operated polling and notification layer. Choose a specialist when built-in alert delivery or distributed trace exploration is the main requirement. A common contract is useful, but it doesn't relieve the application of defining what an attempt means.

Recover the evidence before deciding to retry

Start with recent matching error records, then inspect the detailed event associated with the notification. Keep the original structure available under the team's data-handling policy, rather than retaining only the rendered message, because the difference between a missing object and a wrong-typed leaf field disappears after a formatter has flattened both into text. Compare the detailed record with the expected schema before changing the alert template.

Schema first.

Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. Its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key. That makes schema inspection practical before the recovery worker has credentials. Use the capability's declared path and schema as the integration reference; an example payload is useful for orientation, but it cannot establish that every field appears on every response. The metadata convention describes an accounting surface, not permission to assume a success envelope inside every failure.

For the logistics agent, keep two identifiers in the application: the logical shipment-exception operation and each individual call attempt. The former belongs to the application contract; the latter can be associated with the request identifier exposed by a provider. Don't merge attempts merely because they concern the same shipment. A retry can consume additional work, and an absent accounting field cannot establish that it consumed none. Likewise, adding call durations is not necessarily the elapsed duration of the agent loop if calls overlap; measure the loop boundary separately and record the waiting time that the customer actually experiences.

Recovery needs a side-effect boundary too. Before retrying an operation that writes state, establish its idempotency contract and keep the logical operation's key stable through the retry. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window for applicable capabilities; verify applicability rather than assuming every operation is covered. On a rate-limit response, honor Retry-After when present and use exponential backoff. Don't turn a malformed notification into an instruction to replay every shipment action.

Instrument the adapter against an explicit contract

The instrumentation change is small but consequential: record contract validity before the alert formatter consumes the response. For an application-owned accounting record, require a nonempty request identifier and vendor, and numeric cost and latency. These are local attribution requirements; they do not redefine a provider's error schema. A valid error response may still leave an attempt unattributable, and those are different classifications.

Pointers in a Go decoding struct can distinguish absent or null numeric values from zero. Wrong-typed values should produce a decoding error instead of an implicit conversion. Preserve that classification in the diagnostic record, increment an aggregate contract-quality counter, and keep the cost ledger incomplete until evidence resolves it. If missing and explicit null have different meanings in the applicable schema, retain raw field presence too: pointers alone combine those states.

Don't guess the schema.

This runnable Go example retrieves Infrai's public discovery manifest and verifies that the response is a JSON object before printing it for inspection. It is a starting point for locating the declared capability and its schema, not a validator for every error body. No credential is required for this public discovery request; the optional environment-based header demonstrates the Bearer convention used for protected calls. Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retryAfter, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds >= 45 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate limited: retry later; Retry-After=%s", retryAfter)
                }
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(deadline); remaining > delay {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var document map[string]json.RawMessage
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("invalid discovery JSON: %w", err)
        }
        if document == nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("expected a discovery object, received null")
        }
        pretty, err := json.MarshalIndent(document, "", "  ")
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Println(string(pretty))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspect(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The 15-second request timeout, 45-second total deadline, and three-attempt budget are example client policies, not service latency measurements or guarantees. If the server's requested delay exceeds the remaining deadline, stop and reschedule rather than shortening that delay. This example performs a read, so it doesn't need a write-idempotency key. Protected calls must require INFRAI_API_KEY and send the Authorization header; discovery remains public.

Keep individual request identifiers out of metric dimensions. They are useful for retrieving evidence, but creating a separate metric series for each request makes telemetry capacity follow request volume. Aggregate by bounded failure classes and retain individual identifiers in diagnostic records with a deliberate access and retention policy.

The actual adapter change belongs at the ingestion boundary: validate the response against its applicable schema, record the validation result, and only then construct the application-owned accounting record. Record a separate completeness result for that record. This preserves an actionable difference between an invalid response, a valid response with insufficient attribution evidence, and a rendering mistake that hides evidence already present. Emit the classification before formatting the notification so that a blank rendered field cannot erase the diagnosis.

The poller also needs a capacity budget. Bound concurrency, cap retry attempts, and persist the progress needed to resume after interruption; increasing polling frequency without bounding recovery work can make a telemetry problem consume the same worker capacity needed to process shipment exceptions. Record polling delay separately from agent-loop duration. Otherwise the on-call may mistake delayed observation for a slow model call.

Buy the investigation surface or build the adapter?

The buy-versus-build decision is about which operational work the platform team can own. The following comparison is a selection framework, not a performance ranking; none of these choices can repair an application formatter that discards the field the responder needs.

Option Buy or build boundary Better fit for this logistics workflow Work to retain in the application
Infrai plus an owned poller Buy capability access and error queries; build polling and notification policy Stable capability contracts and consistent per-call attribution across provider changes Logical operation IDs, schema checks, completeness accounting, and recovery decisions
Sentry Evaluate a specialist error-monitoring surface Error investigation is the primary purchasing requirement Join an agent attempt to the shipment operation and verify accounting evidence separately
Datadog Evaluate a broader managed observability surface The team wants to assess failure evidence alongside its wider operational monitoring Define the agent-loop SLO and keep retry accounting distinct from notification state
Grafana with Prometheus Evaluate an alerting and metrics stack The platform team is prepared to own instrumentation and metric capacity planning Preserve raw diagnostic evidence outside aggregate metrics and operate the chosen deployment

Sentry is the more focused evaluation when error investigation drives the purchase; Datadog belongs on the shortlist when the team is selecting a wider monitoring environment; Grafana with Prometheus deserves consideration when control over metric instrumentation and alert rules justifies the operating work. Evaluate those products against the same malformed-field fixtures rather than assuming that a broader dashboard automatically understands the application's cost ledger.

For an Infrai-based design, operate polling and delivery as a separate layer. Use a trace specialist for span-tree investigation and a Healthchecks-style service for the distinct question of whether a scheduled poller ran at all. A trace identifier in a log helps correlate evidence; it should not be mistaken for a trace exploration system. This division keeps the recommendation attached to capability access and attribution rather than claiming an entire incident-response stack.

The trade-off is operational ownership. Infrai is not a fit for a team whose primary requirement is a managed alerting suite; choose Sentry or Datadog instead when that investigation and alerting workflow is the purchasing priority. For this workflow, the limitation of an owned poller is the on-call work it adds: the team must budget capacity, persist progress, and verify notification delivery itself.

Buy deliberately.

Close the page only when the evidence supports recovery

Define separate SLOs for completing the shipment-exception workflow and obtaining attributable attempt records. Measure the latter as complete records divided by eligible attempts over a stated window, with the eligibility rule written down; an error response that validly omits accounting metadata should contribute to the completeness decision without being mislabeled as a broken response contract. Keep unresolved amounts visible as unknown. Don't sum the known subset and label it the total agent-loop cost.

There is no defensible universal paging threshold here. A single malformed record can deserve investigation, but turning every such record into a page makes the responder pay an interruption cost even when shipment processing is healthy; suppressing all of them until the business SLO burns can leave an attribution gap that nobody can reconstruct. Choose the escalation window from the team's SLO, traffic volume, and ability to recover the evidence, then review representative valid failures and actual schema violations before enabling the rule.

False positives consume capacity.

The recovery action should match the evidence: correct the adapter when it dropped a field, correct the renderer when it hid a valid value, and delay replay when the original operation's side effects are uncertain. Keep notification deduplication separate from operation idempotency, because suppressing a repeated page doesn't establish that retrying a shipment action is safe. Close the loop by verifying the next notification against its stored diagnostic record, then check that the completeness ledger can explain every attempt or explicitly mark what remains unknown.

Further reading

References for evaluating the signal model and the specialist alternatives:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Prometheus alerting practices
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this capability boundary fits your recovery worker, start with the public schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: Langfuse alternatives for understanding users, not just traces
description:
Stay on Langfuse for tracing, evals, and prompt management: it is MIT-licensed, free to self-host, and the better choice than every managed tool here if open-source tracing is your requirement. What it does not do out of the box is answer product questions such as "what are users trying to do" and "where do they give up", so most teams keep Langfuse and add one tool for that layer, reading the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace Langfuse only if you want a single vendor for both jobs. We make Agnost AI, so it is listed first; every tool gets the same structure and its limitations come from its own documentation.

Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026

If you found this page because of the Langfuse v4 cutover: Langfuse says trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4." On Langfuse Cloud they keep running until the cutover on November 16, 2026, then stop producing results. The recommended replacement is an observation-level evaluator, and Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date; trace-level evaluators stop there once you switch v4 to events_only mode. For most teams this is a migration, not a reason to leave. If you judged whole conversations with trace-level evaluators, note that Langfuse says its evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions." What to do about the Langfuse trace-level evaluator deprecation has the migration steps and the conversation-level options.

Langfuse vs the alternatives for understanding users

The columns are the three questions Langfuse leaves to you: what users wanted, whether they were frustrated, and whether they got what they came for.

Tool What users wanted Frustration or sentiment Outcome Open source Pricing
Langfuse Your own pipeline, written back as scores Custom LLM judge Custom score or reviewer label Yes (MIT core) Free self-host; Core $29/mo
Agnost AI Intents you define, plus suggested intents Patterns you track as intents or rules Rule or success field you define No Free; $49, $499/mo
Amplitude Agent Analytics Topic clustering, User Intent signal User Friction signal Task Completed signal No (SDKs only) Free; per agent session
PostHog Automatic trace clusters Message sentiment from a local model Task outcome judge template Yes (MIT core) 100k events/mo free
Braintrust Topics Task facet Topics Sentiment facet Issues facet; no completion rate documented No (SDK only) Free; Pro $249/mo
LangSmith Insights clusters (Plus and up) Custom attribute or evaluator Custom thread evaluator No (SDK only) Free seat; $39/seat/mo
Arize Phoenix On-demand error analysis via MCP User Friction evaluator Completeness evaluator Source-available (ELv2) Free
Opik Not documented UserFrustrationMetric judge SessionCompletenessQuality judge Yes (Apache-2.0) Free; Pro $19/mo

Where Langfuse is stronger

Langfuse is the reference open-source platform for LLM tracing, and none of the tools below replaces all of it.

  • Open source that is actually complete. The MIT version includes tracing, sessions, users, OpenTelemetry, prompts, datasets, LLM-as-judge, annotation queues, custom dashboards, enterprise SSO, and org-level RBAC. Enterprise-only features are mostly governance: server-side data masking, project-level RBAC, retention management, SCIM, and audit logs.
  • Free self-hosting. Docker Compose, a VM, or Kubernetes with Helm, plus Terraform for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
  • Prompt management, datasets, and experiments in the same product as tracing.
  • A per-user view. Langfuse lists users and segments them by token usage, trace count, and feedback, with all of a user's traces in one place. For "which users cost the most" or "which users left a thumbs-down", it is already enough.
  • Low entry price. Cloud Hobby is free and Core is $29 a month with unlimited users.

The gap this page is about. Conversation themes, intent labels, and outcomes are not built in. Langfuse's own guide for product teams says to "run an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores", treats resolution as a score filled in by reviewers or feedback, and mentions sentiment only as an example criterion for a custom judge. Live evaluators are recommended at the observation level, trace-level evaluators are deprecated, and session-level live evaluation is not described, which makes whole-conversation judgments harder to run continuously. You can build all of this on Langfuse; the tools below ship some or all of it.

Agnost AI

What it is. Conversation analytics for production AI agents. Agnost AI reads real chat and voice conversations to show what users wanted, where they got stuck, and where the agent broke its own rules, then turns recurring failures into pull requests your team reviews.

Best for. Teams that already trace with Langfuse and want the product layer on top without building an intent pipeline: what users ask for, where conversations go wrong, and what to fix first.

Key features.

  • Intents: plain-language definitions of what users want. Agnost classifies conversations against them, tracks volume over time, links to the evidence, and suggests new intents from your product description and observed traffic. This is the classification Langfuse's guide asks you to build.
  • Violations: rules written in natural language ("confirm identity before sharing account details") checked against every analyzed conversation, with the supporting messages attached. Frustration patterns such as rephrasing loops or requests for a human are tracked the same way, as intents or rules you define.
  • Conversation timelines that keep turns, tool calls, errors, and audio together, plus tool-call analytics for success rate, error distribution, and latency.
  • Alerts to Slack or email on an intent or violation threshold, a Daily Summary, and a summary when a new user intent appears.
  • Auto Improve: investigates a recurring finding, prepares a change, tests it against past runs, opens a pull request, and tracks the outcome after deploy.
  • A hosted OpenTelemetry endpoint that can run next to your Langfuse exporter, plus Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs, voice platforms (LiveKit, Vapi, Retell, Telnyx, Trellus), and the Agnost MCP server for Claude, Codex, and Cursor.

Limitations. Not open source; self-hosting is an Enterprise option, so it does not satisfy a strict open-source requirement. There is no built-in frustration score or conversation task-success metric: you define success with a rule or the success event field. No retention or cohort analytics. No built-in PII redaction before ingestion, so you redact in your app (data governance). It does not replace Langfuse's prompt management or experiments.

Pricing. Free (1,000 events a month, 7-day retention), Starter $49/month (10,000 events, 30-day retention), Pro $499/month (1,000,000 events, 90-day retention), Enterprise custom with self-hosted VPC.

Amplitude Agent Analytics

What it is. Amplitude's product analytics plus Agent Analytics, which observes what users ask an AI agent, evaluates where it fails, and ties traces and evals to conversion, retention, and revenue.

Best for. Teams that already standardize on Amplitude and want "what did users want and did they get it" inside the funnels, cohorts, and retention charts they use today.

Key features. Seven built-in session signals: Task Completed, Response Quality, Session Safety, User Intent, User Friction, Has Negative Feedback, and Data Quality Issues. Topic clustering across sessions on every plan. Custom LLM and code-based evaluators that run on all sessions (bring your own LLM key). OpenTelemetry GenAI spans flow in through a bridge, or use the Python and Node SDKs.

Limitations. Conversation text is kept 14 days on Free and Plus (30 days on Growth and Enterprise). Agent sessions are capped at 5,000 a month on Free and Plus. Sentiment isn't a named signal, and some sections are still labeled beta. Not open source (its SDKs are MIT-licensed), and it runs in Amplitude's AWS data centers in the US or EU rather than on your infrastructure. Pricing. Free (2M events and 5,000 agent sessions a month). Plus starts at $0 with the same agent-session allowance. Growth and Enterprise are custom. Agent Analytics is billed on agent sessions, not events.

PostHog

What it is. PostHog's AI Observability (formerly LLM analytics) captures every LLM call as a trace built on PostHog events, so each trace carries the user, their session replay, and any exceptions.

Best for. Teams that want user-level answers and an open-source core. It is the closest open-source option to a full user analytics stack: funnels, retention, and session replay sit on the same data as the AI traces.

Key features. Sessions via $ai_session_id; automatic clusters of similar traces with AI-generated titles; positive, neutral, and negative labels on user messages from a local model with no LLM cost; LLM-as-judge templates including Task outcome and User correction, run per generation, trace, or session; funnels and retention on the same data; OpenTelemetry support.

Limitations. Full prompt and response text is deleted after 30 days. Clustering needs at least 1,000 traces in the past week. LLM-judge evals need your own provider key, and trace-level user feedback is in beta. The core is MIT outside the ee/ directory, and self-hosting is free but officially unsupported. Prompt management and eval experiments are not its focus, so many teams keep Langfuse next to it.

Pricing. First 100,000 AI events a month free, then from $0.00035 per event, falling with volume. No per-seat charges. Each evaluation run counts as one event.

Braintrust

What it is. An evaluation-first platform where production traces become datasets and evals, with Topics for automatic classification of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that would replace Langfuse with a managed eval platform and want intent, sentiment, and issue clustering from the same vendor.

Key features. Topics classifies logs with built-in Task (user intent), Sentiment, and Issues facets plus custom facets, clusters similar requests into themes, and writes labels back to logs. Online scoring rules run scorers on production traces. Thumbs feedback attaches to spans. OpenTelemetry ingest.

Limitations. Topics needs at least 100 summaries before it clusters and regenerates daily, not in real time, and draws down monthly model credits. There is no dedicated per-user view (you filter or group logs by a metadata field such as metadata.user_id) and no built-in task-completion scorer; Braintrust's docs suggest writing a trace-level judge for workflow completion. The platform is not open source (the SDK is Apache-2.0), and self-hosting is Enterprise-only.

Pricing. Starter free (1 GB processed data, 10k scores, 14-day retention, unlimited users). Pro $249/month (5 GB, 50k scores, 30-day retention). Billed on processed data and scores, not seats.

LangSmith

What it is. LangChain's agent observability, evaluation, and deployment platform.

Best for. Teams building on LangChain or LangGraph who would consolidate tracing, evals, and conversation clustering in one vendor.

Key features. Threads group runs into conversations. Insights automatically clusters production traces, including full conversations, into usage patterns and failure modes. Thread-level online evaluators can judge intent, outcome, and trajectory. OpenTelemetry in both directions.

Limitations. Insights is on Plus and Enterprise, samples up to 1,000 traces per report, and runs as reports rather than continuously. Frustration and task outcome need custom attributes or evaluators. There is no dedicated user view; per-user analysis depends on storing user IDs as metadata. The platform is not open source, and self-hosting is an Enterprise add-on.

Pricing. Developer $0 (1 seat, 5,000 base traces a month). Plus $39 per seat per month (10,000 base traces), then $5 per 1,000 additional base traces (14-day retention), or $7.50 per 1,000 extended traces (180-day retention). ## Arize Phoenix

What it is. Arize's open-source AI observability platform for experimentation, evaluation, and troubleshooting, built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference.

Best for. Teams that must stay self-hosted, including air-gapped or regulated environments, and want ready-made conversation judges instead of writing their own.

Key features. Sessions track a whole conversation in one thread with a chat-style view. The pre-built User Friction evaluator detects corrections, retries after an unsuccessful response, frustration, and challenges to unexplained actions, at span, trace, or session level. A Completeness evaluator checks whether a conversation covered every request. An on-demand error-analysis skill run through MCP groups observed problems into labeled annotations with counts. Self-hosting is free with no feature gates.

Limitations. Licensed under the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved, though Arize calls Phoenix open source. Friction and completeness are evaluators you run and log, not an always-on classification layer; Phoenix docs describe exporting traces, running judges, and logging results back. Automatic grouping of recurring failures (Signal) and stakeholder dashboards are Arize AX features. Per-user analytics are not documented. Phoenix does not evaluate incoming production traces automatically: its server evals run on dataset experiments, and online evals are an Arize AX feature. Pricing. Phoenix is free to use and self-host. Arize AX Free is $0 (25k spans a month, 15-day retention), AX Pro is $50/month (50k spans, 30-day retention), and AX Enterprise is custom, with a self-hosted option. ## Opik

What it is. Comet's open-source observability and evals platform for agents, covering traces, threads, LLM-as-judge metrics, and online evaluation of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that want an Apache-2.0 platform with conversation-level judges they can switch on as rules, and a low-cost cloud option.

Key features. Threads group traces by thread_id. Conversation metrics include UserFrustrationMetric ("how frustrated the user became over the interaction") and SessionCompletenessQuality ("whether the user's top-level goals were met"). Online evaluation rules run at trace, thread, or span scope with sampling and filters; thread rules wait for a 15-minute cooldown by default. OpenTelemetry endpoint over HTTP.

Limitations. Topic or intent clustering of conversations is not documented, so "what users wanted" still needs your own classifier. Rules only apply to data logged after you create them. There is no per-user view: dashboards group trace metrics by tags, a metadata key, name, or error. The full platform, including online evaluation, is open source; Enterprise adds RBAC, SSO, and support SLAs. Pricing. Open source is free with unlimited spans and retention. Free Cloud covers 25k spans a month for up to 10 members. Pro Cloud is $19/month for 100k spans, then $5 per 100k spans.

How to choose

If your team… Start with
Keeps Langfuse for tracing and wants intents, rule violations, and fixes as PRs on top Agnost AI
Already runs Amplitude and wants intent, friction, and task-completion signals in its funnels Amplitude Agent Analytics
Wants user analytics plus an open-source core and session replay PostHog
Would move to a managed eval platform with topic clustering Braintrust
Builds on LangChain or LangGraph and wants one vendor for traces and clusters LangSmith
Must stay self-hosted and wants a ready-made friction evaluator Arize Phoenix
Must stay Apache-2.0 and wants frustration and session-completeness judges as rules Opik
Only needs per-user usage and feedback Stay on Langfuse; its user view covers it

If staying open source is non-negotiable, Phoenix, Opik, and PostHog are the closest options, but none of them gives you intent clustering and outcome tracking fully out of the box: you still configure judges or rules. If it is negotiable, the managed tools above ship more of that layer.

Using Langfuse with Agnost AI

Langfuse's Python and TypeScript SDKs are a thin layer on the official OpenTelemetry client, and Langfuse also accepts OTLP at /api/public/otel. Agnost AI runs a hosted OTLP collector, so if your spans pass through an OpenTelemetry tracer provider, you can append Agnost AI as an additional span processor and both tools receive the same spans (OpenTelemetry docs):

import os
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

trace.get_tracer_provider().add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(
        OTLPSpanExporter(
            endpoint="https://otel.agnost.ai/v1/traces",
            headers={"X-Agnost-Org-ID": os.environ["AGNOST_ORG_ID"]},
        )
    )
)

Set a stable conversation ID on your spans (agnost.session_id or session.id); without one, Agnost AI treats each trace as its own conversation. Langfuse keeps your traces, prompts, datasets, and evals; Agnost AI classifies the same conversations against your intents and rules, alerts when a rate moves, and opens pull requests for recurring failures. To start, follow the quickstart.

Frequently asked questions

Does Langfuse have user analytics?

Partly. Langfuse has a user list and a per-user view that segments by token usage, number of traces, and feedback, plus sessions and custom dashboards. It does not ship built-in intent or topic grouping, sentiment or frustration detection, or conversation outcomes, so questions about what users wanted and where they gave up need extra work.

Can Langfuse detect user intent or frustration?

Not out of the box. Langfuse's own guide for product teams suggests running an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores, and sentiment appears only as an example criterion for a custom LLM judge. You can build both, but you write and maintain the classifiers yourself.

Should I replace Langfuse or add another tool?

Most teams should add one. Langfuse is strong at open-source tracing, evals, and prompt management, and a conversation analytics tool can read the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace it only if you want one vendor for both jobs, for example LangSmith, Braintrust, or PostHog.

What is the best open-source alternative to Langfuse for user analytics?

Arize Phoenix ships a User Friction evaluator and a Completeness evaluator, and Opik ships UserFrustrationMetric and SessionCompletenessQuality judges for threads. PostHog's MIT core adds message sentiment, trace clustering, and funnels. Note that Phoenix uses the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved.

Are there cheaper alternatives to Langfuse?

Rarely, for raw trace volume. Langfuse is free to self-host, Cloud Hobby includes 50,000 units a month, and Core is $29 a month for 100,000 units, then $8 per 100,000. Opik is the closest on price: free to self-host, 25,000 spans a month on Free Cloud, and $19 a month for 100,000 spans on Pro Cloud. Units and spans are counted differently, so compare on your own traffic.

Do I need a Langfuse alternative because trace-level evaluators are deprecated?

Usually not. Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at the v4 cutover on November 16, 2026, and the replacement, observation-level evaluators, covers most single-request checks. Look elsewhere only if you need live judging of whole multi-turn conversations, which Langfuse says its evaluators cannot apply to sessions directly.

Can I send the same traces to Langfuse and another tool?

Yes. Langfuse's SDKs are built on the OpenTelemetry client and it accepts OTLP, and most of the tools on this page accept OpenTelemetry too. Agnost AI can be added as an extra span processor next to your existing exporter, so both tools receive the same spans.

title: A small Node.js fixture for incomplete streaming tool arguments
description:
AI-assisted draft prepared for the AI Relay Check account. The examples below use local fixtures.

Valid JSON can still miss a required tool argument. If a stream ends early, the same tool may never receive a complete invocation. A local fixture separates argument parsing from the backend, and it can be run before testing a paid route.

Start with a tool whose required arguments are a string named label and an integer named count. Use known values and check the results before executing any tool.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

function readFixtureArguments(chunks, complete) {
  if (!complete) throw new Error("Incomplete tool invocation");
  const args = JSON.parse(chunks.join(""));
  if (args.label !== "sample" || args.count !== 2) {
    throw new Error("Unexpected tool arguments");
  }
  return args;
}

assert.deepEqual(readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",', '"count":2}'], true),
  { label: "sample", count: 2 });
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample"}'], true), /Unexpected/);
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",'], false), /Incomplete/);

In a live client, set the completion flag from the actual protocol event and associate fragments with the correct invocation ID. Then return a mock result and confirm the model continues using that result. A transport-level HTTP 200 alone cannot validate the tool workflow.

title: Static and Non-Static in Java
description:
Static and Non-Static in Java

In Java, static and non-static determine whether a variable or method belongs to a class or an object. Understanding this concept is important because it helps us understand memory, object creation, and how Java programs work.

1. Static

The static keyword is used to declare variables and methods that belong to the class rather than individual objects.

A static variable is shared among all objects of a class. Only one copy of the static variable exists, regardless of how many objects are created.

class Student {
    String name;
    static String college = "ABC College";
}

Here, name is a non-static variable, while college is a static variable. Every student object shares the same college name.

We can access a static variable using the class name:

System.out.println(Student.college);

Static Method

A static method belongs to the class and can be called without creating an object.

class Calculator {
    static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Calling the method:

int result = Calculator.add(10, 20);
System.out.println(result);

Output:

30

Static methods can directly access static variables and other static methods. However, they cannot directly access non-static members because those members belong to individual objects.

2. Non-Static

Non-static variables and methods belong to objects. Whenever we create an object, it gets its own copy of non-static variables.

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
        System.out.println(age);
    }
}

Creating objects:

Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = new Student();

s1.name = "Arun";
s1.age = 21;

s2.name = "Kumar";
s2.age = 22;

s1.display();
s2.display();

Each object has its own name and age. Changing the values of one object does not affect another object.

Non-static methods can access both static and non-static members of the class.

5. Why Is the Main Method Static?

The main method in Java is declared as static:

public static void main(String[] args)

The JVM needs to execute the main method to start the program. Since it should not need to create an object before starting execution, the main method is static.

This allows the JVM to call the method directly using the class.

Conclusion

Static members belong to the class and are shared among all objects, whereas non-static members belong to individual objects and maintain their own values. Static is useful for common data and utility methods, while non-static is useful for representing the properties and behaviours of individual objects.

title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
description:
arXiv:2611.22098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

title: Stop Endorsing Java Developers. Start Publishing Their Failure Receipts.
description:
What if the best endorsement of a Java developer was not a compliment, but a bug they successfully defeated?

Let me ask you something.

If I write on LinkedIn:

"I am an excellent Java developer with strong Spring Boot and Microservices experience."

Would you believe me?

What if 10 colleagues endorse that statement?

Would that prove I can handle a production issue at 2 AM when a critical API suddenly starts timing out?

Probably not.

I believe the software engineering industry needs a different way to recognise developers.

Not another certificate.

Not another skill badge.

Not another collection of LinkedIn endorsements.

I propose something different: The Failure Receipt.

  1. What is a Failure Receipt?

A Failure Receipt is a technical record of a real engineering problem solved by a developer and independently reviewed by another engineer.

Think of it as a technical endorsement backed by evidence.

Every receipt contains five things:

The failure: What was broken?
The investigation: How did the developer identify the root cause?
The solution: What did they change and why?
The verification: Which tests prove the fix works?
The reviewer: Who independently reviewed the solution?

For example:

A Spring Boot application starts responding slowly when 500 concurrent requests arrive.

Instead of simply claiming:

"I am good at performance optimisation."

The developer produces a Failure Receipt.

Problem: API response latency increased under load.
Investigation: Identified inefficient database access.
Solution: Improved query execution and introduced appropriate indexing.
Verification: Compared benchmark results before and after the change.
Review: Another Java engineer independently reviews the implementation.

Now the endorsement has a story, evidence and technical reasoning.

  1. Why should Java developers care?

Java developers work on systems where reliability matters.

Consider these real engineering situations:

A memory leak in a long-running application.
A deadlock caused by concurrent execution.
An inefficient Hibernate query.
A failing Kafka consumer.
A slow Spring Boot REST endpoint.
An unexpected transaction rollback.

A list of technologies on a CV cannot demonstrate how someone handles these situations.

A documented engineering investigation can provide much stronger evidence.

  1. The Failure Receipt format

I propose the following open format:

yaml
failure_receipt:
developer: "Developer Name"
technology: "Java / Spring Boot"

incident:
problem: "API latency increased"

investigation:
root_cause: "Inefficient database access"

solution:
change: "Query optimisation"

verification:
test: "Automated regression test"
benchmark: "Before-and-after measurements"

independent_review:
reviewer: "Reviewer Name"
status: "Reviewed"

This is a conceptual example, not a real production incident.

The important principle is that every claim should be traceable to evidence.

Confidential company information should never be published without permission.

  1. My proposed five-level recognition model

I would introduce five recognition levels:

Level 1 – Bug Hunter

Identifies and reproduces a technical problem.

Level 2 – Root Cause Investigator

Demonstrates an understanding of why the problem occurred.

Level 3 – Solution Engineer

Implements and tests an appropriate solution.

Level 4 – Reliability Contributor

Demonstrates measurable improvements in reliability or performance.

Level 5 – Engineering Mentor

Helps other developers understand and solve similar problems.

These are proposed community recognition levels, not formal professional certifications.

  1. Imagine a developer's public profile

Instead of displaying:

Java: 99 endorsements
Spring Boot: 85 endorsements
Microservices: 72 endorsements

Imagine displaying:

4 independently reviewed debugging cases.
3 verified performance improvements.
2 architecture decisions reviewed by senior engineers.
5 open-source problem-solving contributions.

That tells a much more meaningful professional story.

  1. An invitation to the Java community

I want to explore this concept with other Java developers.

My first challenge is simple:

Can we replace one generic skill endorsement with one real engineering problem that someone has successfully solved?

If you are a Java developer, share:

The most interesting production-style bug you have solved.
How you identified the root cause.
What you changed.
How you proved your solution worked.

If you are a senior engineer, would you independently review and validate another developer's Failure Receipt?

Let's see whether we can create a more meaningful culture of technical recognition.

My belief:

A developer should not be recognised only for the technologies they know.

They should also be recognised for the problems they can solve, the engineering decisions they make and the knowledge they share.

Perhaps the future of developer endorsement is not another badge.

Perhaps it is a documented failure that became a successful engineering solution.

What do you think? Would you trust a developer's Failure Receipt more than a traditional skill endorsement?

Java #SpringBoot #SoftwareEngineering #OpenSource #DeveloperCommunity

title: Apple Just Made 1080p Video in 120 ms – Here’s How It’s Changing Live‑Streaming
description:
FastFrames Hits the Fast Lane: Real‑Time Video Generation Goes Commercial in November 2026

Lead

Apple’s WWDC 2026 keynote promised “AI that fits in your pocket.” Six months later the company delivered: FastFrames, a diffusion‑based video generator that produces 1080p frames in roughly 120 ms, now powering Vision Pro Studio and Apple Cloud Video‑AI. The service marks the first time a research‑grade autoregressive diffusion model achieves true interactive latency outside a lab.

“We can now synthesize a full‑HD video clip faster than a human can blink,” declared Apple’s senior AI engineer during the live demo, flashing a 30 fps avatar that responded to a presenter’s gestures in real time.

That claim sparked a flurry of analysis. Did Apple merely showcase a polished demo, or does FastFrames genuinely shift the economics of video synthesis? This article dissects the technical underpinnings, benchmarks the numbers against Nvidia’s RTX 6000‑Ada, and evaluates the broader impact on streaming, AR/VR, and enterprise pipelines.

The Case Study: Building an Interactive Live‑Stream Overlay in 2026

Imagine a Twitch streamer who wants to replace his green‑screen background with a dynamically generated fantasy terrain that reacts to chat commands—“turn night into day,” “spawn a dragon.” Before FastFrames, the streamer would have to pre‑render every possible scene, upload assets to a CDN, and hope the latency stayed under a second.

Using Apple’s FastFrames SDK (available through the Apple Developer portal) the streamer builds a simple pipeline:

  1. Static Latent Backbone – The SDK downloads a 1080p latent representation of a generic fantasy terrain once at startup (≈ 30 MB). This backbone encodes geometry, lighting, and texture priors.
  2. Dynamic Residual Stream – Every time a chat command arrives, the SDK calls FastFrames.generateResidual(step=AnyForcing(4), prompt="night→day"). The Any‑Forcing module runs a 4‑step diffusion on a thin residual tensor (≈ 2 MB).
  3. Speculative Sampling – The SDK predicts the next three frames in a single GPU kernel, reducing kernel‑launch overhead from ~2 ms per frame to < 0.5 ms.
  4. On‑Device Rendering – The M3 Ultra inside the streamer’s MacBook Pro applies the residual to the backbone, producing a 1080p frame in ~120 ms. The frame streams to OBS and then to Twitch with a total end‑to‑end latency of ~180 ms.

The streamer reports a 70 % reduction in bandwidth (only residuals travel over the internet) and a 30 % increase in viewer engagement measured by chat activity per minute. The same workflow runs on an iPhone 15 Pro, proving that the pipeline scales down to mobile SoCs without a desktop GPU.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Technical Deep Dive

1. Dual‑Stage Autoregressive Diffusion

FastFrames replaces the monolithic diffusion loop with a dual‑stage encoder:

Stage Function Compute cost (GFLOPs)
Static Latent Backbone Pre‑computes a high‑dimensional scene representation once per session. ~150
Dynamic Residual Update Computes a lightweight residual for each new frame, using the backbone as constant context. ~30

Decoupling the heavy lifting (backbone) from per‑frame work (residual) drops the per‑frame FLOP budget to ≈ 30 GFLOPs. On Apple’s M3 Ultra (24‑core GPU, 30 W), that translates to ~120 ms for 1080p at 30 fps.

2. Speculative Sampling

Traditional diffusion samples one timestep per kernel launch, incurring ~2 ms overhead on modern GPUs. FastFrames bundles k future timesteps into a single kernel, effectively speculating on the next k latent states. The authors report a 3.5× reduction in kernel‑launch time for k = 3, with no measurable quality loss (PSNR drop < 0.1 dB).

3. Any‑Forcing (Any‑Step Flexibility)

FastFrames introduces Any‑Forcing, a control module that lets developers trade steps for latency on the fly. Typical configurations are shown below:

Steps Frame Rate PSNR (dB) SSIM
4 (default) 30 fps 38.2 0.96
2 45 fps 37.8 0.95
1 60 fps 37.0 0.93

Visual fidelity remains high while scaling up to 60 fps for low‑stakes applications such as UI animations.

4. Benchmark Against Nvidia RTX 6000‑Ada

Apple’s internal benchmark (released alongside the WWDC demo) pits FastFrames on an M3 Ultra against Nvidia’s RTX 6000‑Ada running the best‑available autoregressive diffusion implementation (Video‑Gen‑X, 4‑step). Results:

“FastFrames achieves 30 fps at 1080p with 120 ms latency on M3 Ultra, while RTX 6000‑Ada stalls at 250 ms per frame for the same resolution and quality.” – OrcaRouter comparative article

Key takeaways

  • Latency: FastFrames cuts interactive latency by ≈ 50 %.
  • Power: M3 Ultra draws ~30 W versus RTX 6000‑Ada’s ~250 W, an 8× efficiency gap.
  • Cost: The on‑device solution eliminates the need for a high‑end desktop GPU, slashing capital expense for AR/VR and edge developers.

5. Bandwidth Savings in Cloud‑Edge Hybrid Pipelines

Apple Cloud Video‑AI off‑loads the static backbone to the cloud, streaming only the dynamic residual to edge devices. Tests show a ≈ 70 % reduction in upstream bandwidth compared to streaming full frames, while preserving interactive latency (< 150 ms). This hybrid model enables low‑latency experiences on 5G networks where full‑frame streaming would saturate the link.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

  1. Model Generalization – Performance hinges on the quality of the static backbone. Niche domains (medical imaging, scientific visualization) still require custom backbones, a process that demands substantial GPU time.
  2. Ecosystem Lock‑In – The SDK leans on Apple‑specific Core ML and Vision Pro tooling. Porting FastFrames to Android or Windows will likely incur a performance penalty, risking market fragmentation.
  3. Quality‑Latency Trade‑off Limits – Below two diffusion steps the PSNR/SSIM drop becomes noticeable, making the technology less suitable for photorealistic virtual production without accepting higher latency.
  4. Competitive Response – Nvidia’s rumored Video‑Gen‑Y (Q1 2027) promises adaptive step scheduling and hardware‑accelerated diffusion kernels. If Nvidia matches Apple’s speculative sampling on Ada‑generation GPUs, the latency gap could narrow.

Outlook: Where FastFrames Could Take the Industry

Application Why FastFrames Matters
Interactive Live Streaming 70 % bandwidth savings make AI‑generated overlays feasible on average 5G connections; sub‑200 ms latency keeps chats truly interactive.
AR/VR Content Creation Vision Pro Studio already lets creators paint motion with a stylus and see the result instantly; M‑series chips in headsets will enable fully AI‑driven worlds that react to gestures.
Edge Surveillance & Summarisation On‑premise M3‑based appliances can synthesize short highlight reels of security footage in seconds, reducing storage costs and speeding incident response.
Hybrid Cloud‑Edge Rendering Streaming only residuals lets CDNs off‑load most compute to the edge, aligning with emerging 5G‑edge standards for latency‑critical media.
Open‑Source Momentum The FastFrames repo already shows 21 up‑votes on Hugging Face, indicating strong community interest. External contributors could add domain‑specific backbones and cross‑platform kernels, pushing the technology beyond Apple’s own ecosystem.

Call to Action

If you’re a developer, start experimenting with the FastFrames SDK today—download it from the Apple Developer portal, try the fantasy‑terrain backbone, and measure latency on your own hardware. For enterprises, evaluate the cost‑of‑ownership model: compare a single M3 Ultra‑based edge node against a fleet of RTX 6000‑Ada workstations. And for the research community, contribute a new backbone to the open‑source repo; the more domains we cover, the faster real‑time video synthesis will become a commodity.

Bottom line: FastFrames shows that algorithmic innovation can outpace raw hardware horsepower when interactive latency is the goal. By reframing diffusion as a two‑stage problem, adding speculative sampling, and exposing an any‑step interface, Apple delivers a service that runs faster, cooler, and cheaper than today’s GPU‑centric alternatives. The next test will be how quickly developers expand beyond the curated backbones, how competitors respond, and whether the industry can reliably blend cloud and edge compute without sacrificing interactivity. If those challenges are met, real‑time video synthesis could become as ubiquitous as image generation is today—only now the frames will arrive before the viewer even finishes blinking.
