title: Self-hosting an LLM server on a GPU SageMaker Code Editor space with Kronk
description:
Some teams do not want prompts or models to leave hardware they control. This post walks through running Kronk, an open-source Go model server built on llama.cpp, on a GPU instance behind Amazon SageMaker Studio's Code Editor, with an install that survives restarts and no public endpoint.

What we built

  • A SageMaker Studio domain in VPC-only mode, with subnets that reach the internet through a NAT gateway.
  • A Code Editor space on ml.g5.2xlarge (one NVIDIA A10G, 24 GB) with a 100 GB EBS volume.
  • A lifecycle configuration (LCC) that installs Kronk once, repairs CUDA library paths, and starts the server on every app start.
  • Access to the API and the admin UI through an SSM tunnel. Nothing is exposed on the network.

Kronk serves OpenAI-compatible chat, embeddings and reranking endpoints, plus an Anthropic-compatible Messages API and a browser admin UI. By default it listens on 127.0.0.1:11435.

Why Code Editor

Code Editor is a VS Code-based IDE, so writing and running non-Python code in it (here a Go server and a Go client) feels like working on a local machine, with a terminal and an EBS-backed home directory. We did not try a JupyterLab space, which also has a terminal and exposes ports through /jupyterlab/default/proxy/<port>/. The trade-off for Code Editor is in the networking section below.

The lifecycle configuration

An LCC for a Studio app must finish within five minutes, and a download plus library install can take longer. The pattern that works is an LCC that does almost nothing: it writes a launcher script to EBS and runs it with nohup in the background. The launcher is idempotent, so it installs only on the first start.

The version below is the one that ended up working:

#!/bin/bash
# CodeEditor LCC: persist the Kronk model server. Returns fast; heavy work runs under nohup.
set -u
KDIR=/home/sagemaker-user/kronk-bin
mkdir -p "$KDIR"

cat > "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh" <<'EOS'
#!/bin/bash
# Idempotent and instance-agnostic: installs Kronk once (on EBS), makes sure the CUDA backend's
# shared libraries resolve, then (re)starts the server detached on loopback.
set -u
KDIR=/home/sagemaker-user/kronk-bin
KVER=1.33.2
LOG="$KDIR/start.log"
EXTRA="$KDIR/cuda-libs"          # pip-installed CUDA libs live on EBS (installed once)
exec >> "$LOG" 2>&1
echo "=== $(date -u) start-kronk begin ==="

unset HTTP_PROXY HTTPS_PROXY http_proxy https_proxy
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1 no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1
export KRONK_BASE_PATH=/home/sagemaker-user/.kronk
export KRONK_WEB_API_HOST=127.0.0.1:11435   # loopback only; reach it via the CE proxy
export PATH="$KDIR:$PATH"

HAS_GPU=0
if nvidia-smi -L; then HAS_GPU=1; else echo "no NVIDIA GPU detected -> cpu"; fi

curl -sS -m 15 -o /dev/null -w "github reachability http=%{http_code}\n" https://github.com || echo "WARN: github unreachable"

if [ ! -x "$KDIR/kronk" ]; then
  echo "Installing kronk v$KVER"
  curl -fsSL --retry 3 --connect-timeout 20 -o "$KDIR/kronk.tgz" \
    "https://github.com/ardanlabs/kronk/releases/download/v${KVER}/kronk_${KVER}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" || { echo "download failed"; exit 1; }
  tar -xzf "$KDIR/kronk.tgz" -C "$KDIR"
  f=$(find "$KDIR" -type f -name kronk -perm -u+x | head -1)
  [ -n "$f" ] && [ "$f" != "$KDIR/kronk" ] && mv "$f" "$KDIR/kronk"
  chmod +x "$KDIR/kronk"; rm -f "$KDIR/kronk.tgz"
fi
"$KDIR/kronk" --version || true

if [ "$HAS_GPU" = 1 ]; then export KRONK_PROCESSOR=cuda; else export KRONK_PROCESSOR=cpu; fi
"$KDIR/kronk" libs --local || echo "WARN: libs install failed"

# --- Make the CUDA backend's dependencies resolve (generic across images/instances) ---
if [ "$HAS_GPU" = 1 ]; then
  CUDA_SO=$(find "$KRONK_BASE_PATH/libraries" -name 'libggml-cuda.so' 2>/dev/null | head -1)
  if [ -n "$CUDA_SO" ]; then
    missing() { LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}" ldd "$CUDA_SO" 2>/dev/null | awk '/not found/{print $1}'; }
    add_libdirs() {  # add every dir that holds libcublas* to LD_LIBRARY_PATH
      for d in $(find /usr/local/cuda* /opt/conda "$EXTRA" -name 'libcublas*.so*' 2>/dev/null | xargs -r -n1 dirname | sort -u); do
        case ":${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}:" in *":$d:"*) ;; *) export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$d:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}";; esac
      done
    }
    add_libdirs
    M=$(missing)
    if [ -n "$M" ]; then
      echo "CUDA backend still missing: $M -> installing via pip into $EXTRA"
      MAJOR=$(echo "$M" | grep -o 'so\.[0-9]*' | head -1 | cut -d. -f2)
      case "$MAJOR" in 12) PKGS="nvidia-cublas-cu12";; *) PKGS="nvidia-cublas nvidia-cublas-cu${MAJOR:-13}";; esac
      mkdir -p "$EXTRA"
      for p in $PKGS; do
        python3 -m pip install --quiet --target "$EXTRA" "$p" && { echo "pip installed $p"; add_libdirs; [ -z "$(missing)" ] && break; } || echo "pip $p failed"
      done
      M=$(missing)
    fi
    if [ -z "$M" ]; then echo "CUDA deps OK; LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"; else echo "WARN: unresolved CUDA deps: $M (Kronk will fall back to CPU)"; fi
  else
    echo "WARN: libggml-cuda.so not found under $KRONK_BASE_PATH/libraries"
  fi
fi

# Env file so interactive shells (kronk CLI, tests) match the server
cat > "$KDIR/env.sh" <<EOF
export PATH="$KDIR:\$PATH"
export KRONK_BASE_PATH=$KRONK_BASE_PATH
export KRONK_PROCESSOR=$KRONK_PROCESSOR
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
EOF

"$KDIR/kronk" server stop || true
"$KDIR/kronk" server start --detach
sleep 8
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "health http=%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/models || true
grep -o '"gpu-count":[0-9]*' "$KRONK_BASE_PATH/kronk.log" | tail -1
echo "=== $(date -u) start-kronk done ==="
EOS
chmod +x "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh"

# Fire and forget so the LCC finishes well under the 5-minute limit
nohup "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh" > "$KDIR/nohup.out" 2>&1 &
disown
echo "kronk launcher started in background"
exit 0

Things to note:

  • Kronk and its models live under /home/sagemaker-user, on EBS, so the 640 MB model and the 217 MB CUDA library bundle are downloaded once.
  • The version is pinned (1.33.2). The project releases often.
  • The server binds to loopback. The UI and API are reached through the tunnel described below.

Problems we hit

1. A dead proxy. An older LCC in the domain set HTTP_PROXY to a proxy host that no longer existed, so the first install failed after a 137-second timeout. Checking the route tables showed the subnets already had 0.0.0.0/0 through a NAT gateway, so the proxy was not needed. Lesson: do not copy proxy settings from old LCCs without checking that the proxy exists.

2. The default Code Editor image was not allowed. The domain's default Code Editor image was a custom one that the user profile could not launch (not present in list of custom images). Setting the first-party sagemaker-distribution-gpu image on the space and the app fixed it.

3. The LCC must be allowed on the user profile. CreateApp rejects an LCC that is not in the user profile's (or domain's) LifecycleConfigArns. Updating a profile replaces the whole list, so read the existing settings first.

4. It ran on the CPU. The first chat worked, but nvidia-smi showed 0 MiB used and the reply came back at 18.9 tokens per second. The Kronk log said "gpu-count":0 and memory-topology: cpu-only. ldd on libggml-cuda.so showed libcublas.so.13 => not found: the driver was fine, but the linker could not find the cuBLAS library the CUDA backend needs. The libraries were present under /opt/conda, just not on the search path. The launcher now reads ldd, adds the directories that contain libcublas*, falls back to pip install --target if they are missing, and logs what it decided. After that the log showed "gpu-count":1 and the same request ran at about 352 tokens per second (346 in the admin chat).

To confirm the fix, open System > Running in the admin UI after a request. With the model on the GPU, the resource budget shows CUDA0 with the model's 4.44 GiB reserved there and only about 158 MiB in system RAM. In the CPU run, the same plan was cpu-only, with the memory charged to system RAM.

One caveat: the admin Info page still prints a warning that "ggml enumerated no GPU device". We believe that is the page's own probe running without the library path that the launcher sets for the server, but we did not confirm it. The speed (about 350 tok/s against 19), the Running page and the server log all agree on the GPU.

5. Code Editor has no /proxy/<port>/ path. In JupyterLab you can open a local server at /jupyterlab/default/proxy/<port>/. Code Editor in the new Studio does not offer that, and we got Unsupported URL path. The answer was remote access.

Reaching the UI without exposing anything

Enable RemoteAccess on the space (this requires recreating the app), make sure the execution role can start SSM sessions, and add an SSH entry on your laptop that uses the AWS-provided sagemaker_connect helper. Then forward the port:

ssh -L 11435:127.0.0.1:11435 <your-space-host-alias>

and open http://localhost:11435.

If you prefer a GUI, desktop VS Code with the AWS Toolkit can connect to the same space over SSM. In the AWS Explorer, open SageMaker AI, then Studio, find the running space, and click the remote-access icon next to it.

The Ports panel then forwards 11435 for you, and you can browse the Kronk files on EBS (kronk-bin, .kronk) next to a terminal on the GPU instance.

You also need the Session Manager plugin and credentials that allow sagemaker:StartSession. One caution: if your connect helper script runs with set -x, it prints the SSM stream URL and session token to the terminal. Remove the -x.

Calling it from Go

The server speaks the OpenAI chat-completions format, so a client needs only the standard library. This one does the same thing as the curl command and prints the speed numbers that Kronk returns in usage:

// Minimal client for a Kronk model server (OpenAI-compatible chat completions).
// Does the same thing as:
//
//  curl http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/chat/completions \
//    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
//    -d '{"model":"unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}]}'
//
// Run on the instance (VS Code remote window) or on your laptop through the
// SSM tunnel (ssh -L 11435:127.0.0.1:11435 <host>); both reach http://127.0.0.1:11435.
package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type message struct {
    Role    string `json:"role"`
    Content string `json:"content"`
}

type request struct {
    Model     string    `json:"model"`
    Messages  []message `json:"messages"`
    MaxTokens int       `json:"max_tokens,omitempty"`
}

type response struct {
    Choices []struct {
        Message struct {
            Content          string `json:"content"`
            ReasoningContent string `json:"reasoning_content"`
        } `json:"message"`
        FinishReason string `json:"finish_reason"`
    } `json:"choices"`
    Usage struct {
        PromptTokens     int     `json:"prompt_tokens"`
        CompletionTokens int     `json:"completion_tokens"`
        TotalTokens      int     `json:"total_tokens"`
        TokensPerSecond  float64 `json:"tokens_per_second"`
        TTFTMillis       float64 `json:"time_to_first_token_ms"`
    } `json:"usage"`
    Error any `json:"error"`
}

func main() {
    baseURL := flag.String("url", envOr("KRONK_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:11435"), "Kronk base URL")
    model := flag.String("model", "unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0", "model ID exactly as listed by /v1/models")
    prompt := flag.String("prompt", "Say hi", "user prompt")
    maxTokens := flag.Int("max-tokens", 0, "max completion tokens (0 = server default)")
    showReasoning := flag.Bool("reasoning", false, "also print reasoning_content")
    flag.Parse()

    body, err := json.Marshal(request{
        Model:     *model,
        Messages:  []message{{Role: "user", Content: *prompt}},
        MaxTokens: *maxTokens,
    })
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, strings.TrimRight(*baseURL, "/")+"/v1/chat/completions", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    // Only needed if you later enable authorization on the server.
    if key := os.Getenv("KRONK_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Minute}
    start := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    raw, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(raw))))
    }

    var out response
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &out); err != nil {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w\n%s", err, raw))
    }
    if len(out.Choices) == 0 {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("no choices in response: %s", raw))
    }

    c := out.Choices[0]
    if *showReasoning && c.Message.ReasoningContent != "" {
        fmt.Printf("[reasoning]\n%s\n\n", strings.TrimSpace(c.Message.ReasoningContent))
    }
    fmt.Println(strings.TrimSpace(c.Message.Content))
    fmt.Printf("\n-- finish=%s prompt=%d completion=%d tok/s=%.1f ttft=%.0fms wall=%s\n",
        c.FinishReason, out.Usage.PromptTokens, out.Usage.CompletionTokens,
        out.Usage.TokensPerSecond, out.Usage.TTFTMillis, time.Since(start).Round(time.Millisecond))
}

func envOr(k, def string) string {
    if v := os.Getenv(k); v != "" {
        return v
    }
    return def
}

func fatal(err error) {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "error:", err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run it from your laptop through the tunnel, or on the instance itself. The SageMaker Distribution image does not include Go, so install it under your home directory, which lives on the EBS volume and survives restarts:

cd ~
curl -fsSLO https://go.dev/dl/go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/go-sdk && tar -xzf go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz -C ~/go-sdk --strip-components=1
rm go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
echo 'export PATH=$HOME/go-sdk/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc
go version

Then:

go run main.go -prompt "Say hi" -reasoning

Use the model ID exactly as /v1/models lists it. Kronk rejects bare names.

What the UI shows

The admin UI covers model management (including pulling from Hugging Face), a VRAM calculator, a chat playground, running models and slots, and the library bundles for the llama.cpp, whisper.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp runtimes.

Security notes

  • The admin page shows a banner: "running unsecured on all ports without an admin password." The server was started with open authorization, and only the loopback interface and the SSM tunnel stand between it and anyone else. For anything beyond a single-user test, set an admin password and enable authorization, as described in Kronk's security documentation, before binding it to any other interface.
  • Keep the instance in private subnets. The setup above never needs an inbound rule.
  • Model downloads from Hugging Face need no token for public repos such as the Qwen3 GGUF build we used. Gated repos do.

Results

CPU fallback GPU (A10G)
Model Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0
Decode speed 18.9 tok/s about 346-360 tok/s (curl, admin chat, Go client)
Time to first token n/a about 65 ms cold, about 7 ms warm

A 0.6B model is a smoke test, not a benchmark. With roughly 20 GB of usable VRAM, a 14B model at Q8 or a 30B-class mixture-of-experts model at Q4 is the realistic next step. Context length and slot count drive the KV cache size, so tune context-window and nseq-max in model_config.yaml.

Trade-offs

llama.cpp is built for low to moderate concurrency. For many simultaneous users, a server such as vLLM usually has higher throughput on the same GPU. For private, single-team inference with a simple operational story, Kronk was easy to run.

Cleanup

The GPU instance bills while the app runs. Stop the app when you are done (an idle timeout helps), then delete the app, the space and the LCC.

title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
description:
arXiv:2611.22210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

title: ExplicitIR: Explicit Spatial Policy Fields for All-in-One Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.22222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images blindly from inputs with various degradation types and levels using a single model. However, the adaptation policy in most existing methods remains implicitly encoded in feature representations, leaving the restoration decision neither explicitly represented nor independently controllable. Since real-world degradations vary spatially, applying uniform updates across the entire image leads to over-smoothing of clean areas and under-correction of localized degradations. To address these limitations, we present ExplicitIR, which represents the restoration policy as two explicit per-pixel fields: Budget, which determines where and how strongly to update, and Style, which selects between narrow and wide context windows. Specifically, ExplicitIR incorporates a Spatial Policy Estimator (SPE) to predict these fields, explicitly representing the restoration policy and capturing spatially-varying degradations, which are then applied by Policy-Adaptive Decoder Blocks (PADB) through adaptive fusion of narrow- and wide-window responses, enabling independent control and precise local modulation. This design enables spatially-adaptive restoration in a single forward pass, without requiring task labels, prompts, or test-time degradation estimators. Extensive experiments on three-task and five-task benchmarks demonstrate that ExplicitIR achieves performance competitive with the strongest all-in-one baselines.

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

title: Aligning Vue 3 Components with OpenAPI Types: Converting CurrentYearTable to TypeScript
description:
In full-stack web applications, frontend models can easily drift out of sync with backend APIs when types are manually redefined or left untyped. By integrating OpenAPI schema generators into the build pipeline, client applications can consume authoritative backend models directly in their Vue components.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3218, closing Issue #868), I converted the CurrentYearTable leaderboard component to TypeScript.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we typed props using generated OpenAPI contracts, applied the withDefaults macro, and constructed tests using model factories.

1. The Challenge: Generic Array Props

In the original implementation, CurrentYearTable.vue received leaderboard records using generic JavaScript options:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
import { computed } from 'vue';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
  fromDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
  toDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

While functional, type: Array gave zero insight into what properties a contributor record contained (such as user handles, merged MR counts, or bonus points). If the backend API renamed or removed a property, the frontend would fail silently at runtime.

2. Deriving Prop Types from OpenAPI Specs

Rather than hand-crafting a duplicate Contributor interface that could drift over time, the project generates TypeScript contracts directly from openapi.yaml.

In CurrentYearTable.vue, we imported GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse and indexed its records:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse } from '~/api/generated';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = withDefaults(defineProps<{
  contributors: GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'];
  fromDate?: string;
  toDate?: string;
}>(), {
  fromDate: '',
  toDate: '',
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

<template>
  <ContributorsTable
    :contributors="contributors"
    :filter-data="filterData"
  />
</template>

Why this is a best practice:

  1. Single Source of Truth: The TypeScript type GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'] is generated directly from the backend Rails API definition. If an API contract changes, vue-tsc immediately flags any breaking changes across all views.
  2. withDefaults Macro: Provides idiomatic default values for optional string props (fromDate?: string, toDate?: string) without runtime object overhead.

3. Writing Resilient Specs with Model Factories (ADR 005)

Per the project's architectural guidelines (ADR 005: Model Factories in Specs), test fixtures should not be hard-coded object literals with incomplete shapes. Instead, tests use factory functions that populate complete, valid schema defaults.

In CurrentYearTable.spec.ts:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';
import { createLeaderboardContributor } from '~/spec/factories/leaderboard';
import CurrentYearTable from './CurrentYearTable.vue';

// Factory generates a valid, complete OpenAPI leaderboard record
const mockContributor = createLeaderboardContributor();

let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = shallowMount(CurrentYearTable, {
    props: {
      contributors: [mockContributor],
      ...props,
    },
  });
};

const findContributorsTable = () => wrapper.findComponent(ContributorsTable);

it('renders ContributorsTable with contributors and default filterData', () => {
  createWrapper();

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('contributors')).toEqual([mockContributor]);
  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '',
    toDate: '',
  });
});

it('renders ContributorsTable with custom fromDate and toDate in filterData', () => {
  createWrapper({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });
});

Using createLeaderboardContributor() ensures that our test mocks strictly adhere to the OpenAPI schema without breaking when new fields are introduced.

Key Takeaways

  1. Leverage Generated API Types: Import types directly from OpenAPI or GraphQL code-generators (Response['key']) to eliminate manual duplication and catch breaking API updates.
  2. Use withDefaults(defineProps<{ ... }>(), { ... }): The standard Vue 3 pattern for combining compile-time type definitions with default prop values.
  3. Adopt Model Factories in Tests: Test helpers like createLeaderboardContributor() ensure test mocks always reflect production API contracts.

Check out the merged Merge Request on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Contributors MR !3218

Author: Manish Kumar

GitLab: @manishpatel00

title: crdt-sync: a small local-first sync engine in Rust, with CRDTs, sqlite and websockets
description:
Two people edit the same note. One is on a train with no signal, the other at a desk. Both keep typing. When the train leaves the tunnel, what should the note look like?

The classic answer is to make the server the judge: every edit goes to it, it decides the order, and a client without a connection waits. Local-first apps turn this around. Each device holds a full copy, edits apply immediately and offline, and devices exchange changes whenever they can reach each other. The hard requirement is that after exchanging everything, all copies are identical, no matter in which order the changes arrived.

Data structures with that guarantee are called CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types. Automerge and Yjs are the well-known libraries built on them. They are mature, optimized libraries, which makes them a long read if your goal is to learn how the idea works.

crdt-sync is a small local-first sync engine in Rust. Documents are trees of CRDTs, backed by an operation log and vector clocks. Replicas edit offline, store operations in sqlite, and sync through an axum websocket server with a two-message protocol. The README names its two audiences: developers who want to understand how local-first apps work underneath, and those who need a compact, readable starting point for syncing small documents between devices and a server they control.

What it does

Four CRDT types. A document is a tree built from these:

  • LwwRegister, a last-writer-wins register: the highest (Lamport, replica) stamp wins.
  • LwwMap, a map with an LWW register per key. A delete is a write of "nothing", and a value can be a scalar or a nested object.
  • OrSet, an observed-remove set with add-wins behaviour: each add makes a unique tag, and a remove deletes only the tags it observed.
  • Rga, text. Each character is inserted after a reference character, concurrent inserts at the same spot are ordered by stamp, and deletes leave tombstones.

An operation log. Every edit is an Op with an id (replica, seq), where seq counts 1, 2, 3 and so on per replica, plus a Lamport timestamp, a target object and an action. Because sequence numbers have no gaps, a vector clock replica → highest seq says exactly which operations a replica has. "Have I seen op X" is one comparison.

Delivery in any order. Doc::apply_remote accepts operations in any order, any number of times. Known ones are dropped. The rest wait in a pending list until their dependencies are integrated: the previous op of the same replica, the object they target, the character an insert goes after, and the tags a set-remove observed.

A two-message sync protocol. StateVector(clock) is answered with Ops(missing), and Ops(ops) is integrated. Both ends send their state vector on connect, so one round trip each way brings both up to date. The server then relays newly integrated operations to every other client on the same document.

A compact encoding. LEB128 varints, a per-batch replica table so op ids take one or two bytes, delta-coded sequence numbers and Lamport times, and one-byte shortcuts for "same object as the previous op" and "insert after the previous op". The README states that typing 1000 characters encodes to under 8 KB. The decoder rejects truncated or hostile input without panicking or over-allocating.

A server and storage. The axum server exposes GET /sync/{doc} as a websocket with binary frames, plus GET /docs and GET /docs/{doc} as JSON. It keeps one in-memory Doc per open document, loaded from sqlite on first use, and appends integrated ops to sqlite before relaying them. Storage is one table, ops(doc, replica, seq, body), written with INSERT OR IGNORE so saving is idempotent.

How to use it

Install the two binaries, crdt-server and crdt-cli, from GitHub with Cargo, or add the library to a project:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

The README's quick start runs a server and two clients, each with its own local database, from a clone of the repository:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice and Bob both set status while "offline", and Bob adds a tag. After syncing, both hold the same document:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

The register kept one of the two concurrent writes, the same one on every replica. The set kept both tags.

The CLI commands are show, info, set KEY VALUE, del KEY, insert KEY INDEX TEXT, erase KEY INDEX COUNT, add KEY VALUE, remove KEY VALUE, sync and watch.

As a library:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

Things to know

The README's limitations section is long and plain. Read it before you build on this:

  • No authentication or authorization on the server. Anyone who can reach it can read and write every document. Run it on localhost or behind an authenticating proxy.
  • Logs grow forever. There is no compaction, no snapshots and no tombstone garbage collection. A document is rebuilt by replaying its whole log.
  • Text is for notes, not books. RGA lookups are linear scans, and there is one op per character.
  • A small set of types. No rich text, lists of objects, counters or moves. Concurrent creation of a nested object under the same key keeps one object (LWW), and edits made to the other are hidden.
  • Limited peer validation. Ops from a buggy peer that target a missing object or the wrong kind are logged and ignored. There is no check of who may write which replica id.
  • watch only prints remote changes. Edits are made with separate CLI invocations.

What is tested. cargo test runs 17 unit tests, 6 proptest properties and 4 end-to-end tests. The main property is convergence: three replicas perform random text inserts and deletes, set adds and removes, register writes and map sets and deletes, while random subsets of each other's logs are delivered shuffled and duplicated. In the end everyone receives everything in a scrambled order, twice. All replicas must have no pending ops, equal clocks and equal JSON, over 300 cases. Other properties check protocol convergence over pairwise syncs in a ring, that single-replica text matches a Vec<char> model, and that random bytes and bit-flipped messages never panic the decoder.

The end-to-end tests cover offline edits from two clients merging, a restarted server serving the same document from sqlite, a live client receiving relayed edits, and two crdt-cli processes that edit offline and converge. As a sanity check, the README notes that breaking the LWW tie-break or the RGA sibling ordering makes the convergence properties fail within a few cases.

Why I built it

The idea behind local-first is easy to state and hard to trust until you have seen every piece: how an operation is identified, why a vector clock is enough to know what a peer is missing, what "wait for dependencies" means in code, and how text can merge when two people type at the same position. The mature libraries answer all of this, but inside a lot of optimization.

I wanted the whole path in one small codebase that can be read end to end: the CRDTs, the log, the binary encoding, the storage, the protocol and a server. And I wanted the convergence claim to be checked by property tests and not by a few hand-picked examples, because the bugs in this kind of code live in the interleavings nobody thinks of.

Get the code

The source and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. It is MIT licensed. Treat it as a readable starting point for small documents, with the limits listed above.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Our label service logged every carrier rejection for three weeks and the reason was always [Object]
description:
Our label service is a Node.js application that books parcels with four carriers. When a carrier refuses a booking, the service catches the error from the HTTP client and logs it with one line we had written years earlier: console.error('carrier rejected label', err.response.data). A counter of rejections per carrier feeds a dashboard, and that counter is what started this.

In September rejections from one carrier rose from a handful a day to about two hundred, all on its Saturday service. Each morning the on-call engineer opened the logs, found the rejections, and read this:

carrier rejected label { fault: { errors: [ [Object] ] } }

The carrier's actual reason was inside that [Object]. Node formats objects passed to console.log and console.error with util.inspect, and its default depth is two. The response body was the top level, fault was one level down, errors was two, and each error object sat at the third level, so it was printed as a placeholder. The line looked like a log of the failure. It was a log of the shape of the failure.

Because the line said nothing, the rejections were filed as the carrier being unreliable, and the parcels were rebooked by hand on the weekday service. That went on for three weeks. Then someone replayed one booking with curl and read the full body: the carrier had withdrawn Saturday delivery for a list of rural postcodes and published the change in a partner bulletin nobody on our side received. Our own code had been told which field and why, every time.

The service now logs through pino, which writes one JSON object per line and serialises the whole response body, with a size cap rather than a depth limit. The carrier's error code is a label on the rejection counter, so the dashboard shows the reason instead of only the volume, and a new code appearing for the first time raises a ticket. We also searched every service for console calls that log an object, and found nineteen.

A log line that names the failure without its reason feels complete when you read it. It is the most expensive kind, because it stops people looking.

– Sergey Shinder

title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.22039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.

title: Fan-Out Shipment Updates in Node.js: Retry Backoff for Delayed Messages
description:
A shipment update sent to thousands of game players is not one job. It is a set of independently failing deliveries, and that distinction changes the retry design.

Short answer: persist one delivery intent per subscriber and channel, schedule retryable failures as delayed queue messages with capped exponential backoff and full jitter, and make the delivery effect idempotent. Acknowledge only after the next state is durable; route exhausted or permanent failures to a dead-letter state.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied to an at-least-once transport. A queue can redeliver. The application must make redelivery harmless.

What does a shipment fan-out need to preserve?

Consider shipment SHIP-4821 for a newly purchased game item. The update goes to a player inbox, mobile push, a guild feed, and an analytics consumer. Each subscriber has a separate latency budget and failure mode. If all recipients share one message, one slow push provider controls the fate of the whole batch, while reconciliation cannot explain which recipient was actually delivered.

The durable unit should be a delivery intent identified by (shipment_id, subscriber_id, channel). Store its status, attempt count, next due time, last failure classification, and an idempotency key in a database. Keep the shipment event immutable. The delivery row describes what the system intended and what happened; the queue schedules work but should not become the system of record.

The invariants are more important than the delay curve:

  • A subscriber receives at most one business effect for one shipment and channel, even after redelivery.
  • Every retry has a durable due time and a finite attempt budget.
  • A transient failure can be retried without holding unrelated subscribers.
  • A permanent failure remains inspectable instead of consuming infinite capacity.
  • Acknowledgement follows durable business state.

The uncomfortable boundary is the external call followed by the local commit. If a push provider accepts the request and the worker exits before recording success, the next attempt must reuse the same provider-facing idempotency key or query the provider. If the database commits but acknowledgement is lost, redelivery is expected; a unique delivery key turns the second application into a no-op. Those are ordinary states in an at-least-once design, not exotic edge cases.

How should failed jobs use exponential backoff in a delayed queue?

Treat backoff as load shaping. For attempt n, calculate upper = min(cap, base * 2^n) and choose a random delay from zero through upper. Full jitter keeps a shared outage from waking every worker at the same instant. The cap prevents an old shipment from acquiring an unbounded tail, while the attempt budget defines when the system stops trying.

Classification comes before scheduling. A timeout, temporary network failure, or rate limit is usually retryable. An invalid player identifier, revoked consent, or permanently rejected payload should go straight to a dead-letter state. Record the classification with the retry decision; a count without a reason is poor evidence during reconciliation.

The reader may implement the worker in Node.js, but the critical transition below is Go so the state changes are explicit and dependency-free. Scheduler stands for the queue adapter. Its contract is deliberately generic, which keeps the retry policy independent of a commercial client library.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "math/rand"
    "time"
)

type Delivery struct {
    ShipmentID  string
    Subscriber  string
    Channel     string
    Attempt     int
    MaxAttempts int
}

type Scheduler interface {
    Publish(ctx context.Context, queue string, body Delivery, delay time.Duration, key string) error
}

func fullJitter(attempt, base, capSeconds int, r *rand.Rand) time.Duration {
    upper := base
    for i := 0; i < attempt && upper < capSeconds; i++ {
        upper *= 2
    }
    if upper > capSeconds {
        upper = capSeconds
    }
    return time.Duration(r.Intn(upper+1)) * time.Second
}

func scheduleRetry(ctx context.Context, q Scheduler, d Delivery, r *rand.Rand) error {
    d.Attempt++
    key := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%s", d.ShipmentID, d.Subscriber, d.Channel)
    if d.Attempt >= d.MaxAttempts {
        return q.Publish(ctx, "shipment-dead-letter", d, 0, key)
    }
    wait := fullJitter(d.Attempt, 5, 3600, r)
    return q.Publish(ctx, "shipment-delivery", d, wait, key)
}

The key is stable for the logical delivery, not freshly generated for each attempt. The queue adapter may receive the same publish request again after a worker restart; its idempotency behavior, or an outbox publisher in front of it, must prevent duplicate scheduling from becoming duplicate business effects.

Do not sleep inside the worker for the whole delay. A short local retry can be reasonable within a request deadline, but a delayed queue message makes pending work visible and lets the worker process other deliveries. That difference matters during a deploy, when in-memory timers disappear or compete with shutdown.

Which retry boundary is easiest to reconcile?

There are several valid boundaries, and they should not be confused:

Boundary Useful for Main limitation
In-worker timer A short operation inside one request budget Uses a worker slot and is fragile across restart
Delayed queue message An independent, reconstructible delivery attempt Requires duplicate handling and attempt metadata
Database due-time scan Long schedules driven by business state Requires polling, leases, and lock discipline
Workflow history Multi-step work with timers and compensation More operational state than one delivery needs

The practical choice is determined by the failure you need to explain. If the question is “why has this player not received the shipment?”, a delivery table with an audit trail is more useful than a queue dashboard. If the question is “which independent attempt should run next?”, a delayed message is a good scheduling boundary. If several steps must agree before the process advances, a workflow record is a better model.

A transactional outbox is useful when writing the delivery row and publishing its first message must be coordinated. Commit the business change and an outbox row together; a publisher can retry the outbox operation using the same logical key. This still does not make the external provider call magically atomic with the database. It makes the recovery evidence durable.

How do Node.js workers prove that retries are safe?

Observability should show more than queue depth. Track ready messages, delayed messages, oldest delivery age, retry counts by failure class, dead-letter growth, and shipment-to-acknowledgement latency. Segment those measures by channel so a mobile provider's rate limit does not hide a healthy in-game inbox consumer.

Each state change should record the shipment ID, subscriber ID, channel, attempt, idempotency key, classification, chosen delay, worker version, and timestamps. Logs are not enough: retention, sampling, and concurrent retries can erase the causal sequence needed for an audit trail.

Test the gaps deliberately: provider acceptance followed by a worker crash, duplicate delivery after a committed transaction, a rate limit with and without a retry hint, malformed payloads, clock skew near a due time, and dead-letter replay. Property tests can assert that the delay never exceeds its cap and that one delivery key cannot produce two successful business transitions.

Three words: make it replayable.

I am not sure one backoff curve can suit a provider with second-scale recovery and another with hour-scale recovery; your mileage will vary with provider behavior and the business deadline. The invariant is stable even when the curve changes: no unbounded retries, no early acknowledgement, and no delivery effect without an auditable idempotency decision.

When are delayed messages the wrong choice?

Delayed delivery fits when each attempt is independent, the payload can be rebuilt, and the deadline fits the queue's retention and delay limits. It is not suitable when the operation needs a long queryable schedule, human approval, compensation across several systems, or coordinated progress among many steps. Persist the workflow state and choose a scheduler or workflow engine whose history matches that business process.

There is a second trade-off. A high-value shipment may justify an outbox, reconciliation job, and manual review even when the queue supports delayed delivery. A low-value cosmetic notification may accept a shorter retention period and a smaller retry budget. The right abstraction follows the consequence of duplication and loss, not the convenience of the queue API.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies

title: Cheapest Cloud Hosting Platforms in 2026: Compare the Full Cost
description:
TL;DR

  • There's no universal cheapest cloud hosting platform in 2026. Start with a managed platform like Render or Northflank if you want infrastructure handled for you, and use unmanaged VMs like DigitalOcean Droplets only when your team wants to take on the extra server and database upkeep.
  • Think in terms of total cost of operation (TCO) rather than headline instance prices. Add up compute, databases, storage, backups, transfer, workspace fees, builds, and observability on the provider bill, then account for your team's ongoing engineering time alongside it.
  • Vercel, Supabase, and Neon cover different parts of an application stack, so their subscriptions aren't equivalent hosting quotes.
  • Model the same workload and recovery requirements before comparing bills. Scale-to-zero can reduce idle compute charges without eliminating storage or other costs.
  • Choose a full-stack managed platform like Render when you want persistent web services, background workers, and managed PostgreSQL in one place, with Git deployments, automatic SSL, and private networking built in.

You have an application ready to ship, several pricing tabs open, and plans that seem to describe entirely different products.

Look closely at what each tab actually gives you. One quotes a blank virtual machine where you install and maintain everything yourself. Another covers frontend hosting and serverless functions without a database, and a third prices standalone Postgres with nowhere to run your backend API. Comparing their starting prices side by side is misleading because most of them leave half your architecture off the quote.

Before I commit to a hosting setup, I want clear answers on four points:

  • What happens to the database
  • How much data you can afford to lose
  • Who restores it
  • Whether the advertised transfer allowance covers responses to your customers

We'll examine what a complete cloud hosting bill includes, compare affordable cloud hosting options by what they provide, model comparable small application workloads, and estimate engineering time instead of treating it as free.

What a complete cloud hosting bill includes

I separate the provider's invoice from the estimated economic value of the team's work. Both matter, and mixing them hides where your money and engineering hours actually go.

Full-cost equation

Provider bill =
  application compute + database compute + persistent storage
  + backups + network transfer + platform and team fees
  + applicable builds and observability

Estimated recurring full cost =
  provider bill + estimated recurring engineering labor

Providers meter compute either through continuously allocated instances (billed while provisioned, including idle periods) or through usage metrics such as requests, CPU seconds, and active memory. Many platforms combine a base workspace or plan fee with usage allowances and per-unit overages.

Internet egress is data leaving a provider's network for the public internet. Map public client responses, application-to-database queries, and cross-region or cross-provider traffic separately, and include dedicated IPv4 addresses, NAT gateways, or load balancers whenever your topology requires them. Render's billing guide shows how network topology changes those lines.

Hold region, currency, traffic, compute sizing, database capacity, availability, and recovery targets constant across every quote. Matching RAM labels alone doesn't guarantee equivalent performance.

Recovery also carries distinct price tags. Your recovery-point objective (RPO) sets how much recent data you can afford to lose, recovery-time objective (RTO) sets how fast service must return, and retention sets how far back recovery history goes. Scheduled backups store recovery copies, point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores to a specific moment within your retention window, and high availability runs redundant standby infrastructure for automated failover. As Render's database pricing guide details, dropping a resilience feature you actually need creates an illusion of savings rather than an equivalent quote.

Compare affordable cloud hosting options by what they provide

Affordable cloud hosting falls into three operating models: full-stack managed platforms, self-managed servers (with optional deployment tooling), and specialist services that only run one layer of your app. For most product teams without dedicated infrastructure staff, a full-stack managed platform hits the practical TCO sweet spot because one platform handles your web services, background jobs, database, TLS, and internal networking on a single bill.

Option Stack coverage and billing model What your team still owns Best fit
Render Full-stack managed platform for web services, background workers, cron jobs, static sites, managed Postgres (with PITR included on paid plans), and Key Value over a free private network. Predictable instance tiers plus workspace plan and overages Application code, instance sizing, schema migrations, and restore validation Default choice when you want your entire app and database stack managed in one place
Northflank Managed container services, jobs, and database add-ons on Northflank Cloud or your own cloud VPC, metered per second across vCPU, memory, disk, and egress Application operation, container/cluster configuration, and BYOC cloud account management Teams wanting granular container controls or bring-your-own-cloud deployments
DigitalOcean Droplets Unmanaged Linux VMs where you can run apps and self-hosted PostgreSQL, billed by VM size plus optional backup, volume, and transfer add-ons OS patching, firewalls, TLS, deploy pipelines, database administration, and recovery Teams with existing Linux and database ops automation
Coolify Open-source deployment control plane (self-hosted free or Coolify Cloud subscription) layered onto VMs you rent separately Underlying workload servers, host security, OS updates, and application database backups Developers who want Heroku-style Git deploys on their own cheap VPS hardware
Vercel Frontend CDN delivery and serverless function execution, billed by plan, team seats, and metered usage Pairing an external database and separate host for persistent workers or long-running backends Frontend-heavy Next.js apps whose backend fits serverless execution
Supabase Managed Postgres bundled with Auth, Storage, Realtime, and Edge Functions, billed by org plan plus per-project compute, storage, and add-ons (such as PITR) Hosting custom persistent APIs, frontends, and background workers elsewhere Apps built directly around Supabase's bundled Postgres and auth primitives
Neon Serverless Postgres with scale-to-zero, branching, and backend primitives, metered by compute unit-hours and stored data Hosting your web frontend, persistent API servers, and background workers elsewhere Variable or multi-tenant Postgres workloads paired with a separate app host

Looking at the shortlist through a TCO lens exposes two common traps. Going down-market to raw Droplets or Coolify lowers the monthly server line, although you still pay for workload VMs and inherit every OS patch, firewall rule, and database restore yourself (Coolify Cloud only backs up its control plane, and even within DigitalOcean, Droplets, App Platform, and Managed Databases are separate products). Going sideways into specialist tools splits your architecture across vendors: Supabase notes its custom-domain feature isn't meant for frontend hosting via Edge Functions, and neither Neon nor Vercel gives you persistent background workers and managed Postgres under one roof.

That's why I lean toward a unified platform like Render as the starting baseline for a typical SaaS or API team. Checking Render's documentation and workspace plans, you get Git or Docker deploys, automatic SSL, private networking, and managed Postgres without assembling glue between three billing dashboards, whereas Northflank makes sense if you specifically need BYOC cluster workflows.

Model comparable small application workloads

A grounded cloud hosting cost comparison starts from fixed workload inputs. Take a small always-on production stack in US East billed monthly in USD: one web API with roughly 1 vCPU and 1 to 2 GB RAM, one PostgreSQL database with 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, and 10 GB of stored data plus disk headroom, 10 GB of monthly public API responses, and a 7-day recovery window targeting a 24-hour RPO and RTO without multi-node high availability.

Rather than building seven repetitive spreadsheets, let's model the two archetypes at opposite ends of the ownership spectrum: Render for a unified full-stack managed platform, and DigitalOcean Droplets for raw self-managed VMs. Every other option maps onto or between those two baselines. Northflank follows a similar managed-platform structure with container metering, Coolify layers a control plane onto that same VM bill, and Vercel, Supabase, or Neon each require a second vendor to cover both the persistent API and Postgres.

On Render, you price a fixed monthly web service tier for the API alongside a separate managed Render Postgres compute tier and expandable per-GB database storage. That quote already bundles Git or Docker deployments, zero-downtime rollbacks, automatic TLS, health checks, and built-in log retention, with monthly build-pipeline minutes and team controls governed by your workspace plan.

Recovery and networking widen that functional gap. Paid Render Postgres plans include continuous point-in-time recovery and logical exports without a separate backup-retention surcharge, and internal API-to-database queries in the same workspace and region travel free over Render's private network. On DigitalOcean Droplets, you rent two Linux VMs (colocating the API and Postgres on one machine saves an instance fee at the cost of shared resource contention and a single failure domain). Enabling DigitalOcean's paid Droplet backup add-on only captures VM-level disk snapshots, so meeting a real PostgreSQL recovery target still requires wiring up logical dumps or WAL archiving to separate object storage yourself.

On raw server invoices alone, two unmanaged Droplets will normally price out lower than a managed web-plus-database stack on Render, and Droplets bundle generous outbound transfer pools with no workspace fee. What that lower invoice leaves off the page is everything around the VMs: CI build runners, reverse proxies, TLS renewal, VPC firewall rules, monitoring, and tested database restores all become infrastructure your team has to assemble and maintain.

Two common variations change these baselines predictably:

  • Scale-to-zero databases such as Neon suspend compute after idle periods (five minutes by default on Free and Launch), cutting idle compute spend while retained storage stays billable. Splitting your frontend and backend across Vercel plus Supabase or Neon adds separate plan floors, cross-provider database traffic, and combined wake-up latency on cold requests.
  • Adding a background worker or cron job introduces its own compute line, and upgrading from backups to automated failover adds standby database nodes, such as a matching standby on Render Postgres or DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL. Avoid substituting a stripped-down tier like DigitalOcean App Platform's development database, which omits default backups.

Estimate engineering time instead of treating it as free

Even on a managed platform, your team retains real operational work. The table below models illustrative monthly hours for a small production service so labor stays visible alongside the provider invoice. Swap in your own hours and loaded engineering rate.

Task Management boundary Managed hours Self-managed hours
Patching Provider base infrastructure where covered, team application dependencies 0.25 1
Infrastructure changes Provider mechanisms, team configuration 0.25 0.5
Database maintenance Provider service maintenance where covered, team schema and queries 0.25 0.5
Backup verification Team verifies usable recovery 0.5 0.75
Monitoring Team owns application health 0.5 0.5
Deployment debugging Team 0.5 0.5
Incident allowance Shared according to failure 0.75 1.25
Total hypothetical hours 3 5

At an illustrative $100 per engineering hour, recurring operations represent $300 per month on a managed platform versus $500 per month self-managed. Strong existing Terraform/Ansible automation and Linux expertise might pull self-managed upkeep down to 2 hours ($200/month), whereas a product-focused startup without dedicated ops engineers will feel every hour pulled away from shipping features.

Track one-time setup (say, 4 hours managed vs. 8 hours self-managed) and future migration effort separately rather than folding them into monthly run rate or pretending they cost zero.

Weigh the tradeoffs across simplicity, cost, and scale

Start by ruling out any setup that misses a non-negotiable requirement on availability, recovery window, region, or compliance. Skipping database recovery to shave a few dollars off a quote creates risk rather than savings.

From the viable options left, match the operating model to what your team actually optimizes for. Choose a full-stack managed platform like Render when operational simplicity and shipping speed come first across your web services, workers, networking, and managed Postgres, or pick Northflank when you need granular container controls or bring-your-own-cloud VPC deployments. Run DigitalOcean Droplets (with or without Coolify) when minimizing the raw server bill matters most and your team already maintains Linux and backup automation, and pair Vercel with Neon or Supabase when your architecture centers on serverless frontends or scale-to-zero branching databases.

Whichever path fits your team, pressure-test the one variable most likely to swing your bill, whether that's outbound egress, database growth, or maintenance hours, and run a real restore drill before production cutover.

Conclusion

Chasing the lowest sticker price on a pricing page rarely produces the lowest total cost of operation. Once you include database recovery, outbound transfer, and the engineering hours spent keeping servers healthy, the real question is which operational tradeoffs fit your team.

For most product teams without dedicated infrastructure staff, starting on a full-stack managed platform like Render is the practical default. Running web services, background workers, private networking, and managed Postgres in one place eliminates both DIY server maintenance and the billing sprawl of stitching separate frontend and database vendors together.

Self-managed VMs and specialist serverless stacks still earn their keep when you already have mature ops automation or strictly spiky workloads. Keep the provider invoice, recurring engineering hours, and recovery plan visible side by side, and choose the stack built for the team you actually have.

Frequently asked questions

What is the cheapest cloud hosting platform?

There's no universally cheapest cloud hosting platform. Look at total cost of operation (TCO) rather than headline server rates by adding up application and database compute, storage, backups, network transfer, and workspace fees on the provider bill, then accounting for ongoing engineering labor alongside it. For most product teams without dedicated ops staff, a full-stack managed platform like Render avoids both DIY server upkeep and multi-vendor billing sprawl.

Is a VPS cheaper than a managed cloud platform?

A VPS can have a lower infrastructure invoice than a managed cloud platform, but that doesn't establish a lower full cost. Include database protection, storage, network charges, and the time needed to maintain and recover the stack. Existing server expertise and automation can substantially reduce the incremental work for your team.

Does a platform subscription include compute and a database?

A platform subscription may include compute or database usage, but coverage varies by plan. Check workspace or seat charges separately from application resources, database resources, and included usage. For example, Render prices its managed PostgreSQL separately from application services, so a workspace plan alone isn't a complete application-and-database quote.

Can free cloud hosting support a production application?

Free cloud hosting can support a production application if its terms and capabilities meet that application's requirements. Check commercial eligibility, uptime behavior, resource limits, data persistence, recovery, and support before relying on a free tier. Keep promotional credits out of the recurring baseline, or show separately when they expire.

Can Supabase or Neon replace an application host?

Supabase and Neon pair PostgreSQL with backend primitives such as authentication, data APIs, and serverless functions, although neither subscription replaces a host for persistent custom web servers or background workers. Unless your entire backend fits inside their functions, you either pair them with a separate application host or run your web services, workers, and managed Postgres together on a full-stack platform like Render.

title: How to catch an expiring or broken SSL certificate before your visitors do
description:
Many TLS certificates now live 90 days, and the maximum lifetime for all public certificates is dropping in steps (200 days since March 2026, 47 days by 2029). Auto-renewal handles most of it, until a DNS change, a moved server or a forgotten subdomain breaks the renewal and nobody notices until visitors see a browser warning.

Here is what to check, how to do it for free with tools you already have, and how to run the same checks on a long list of domains.

The four problems to look for

1. Expiry. The certificate is past its end date, or will be soon. You want a warning weeks ahead, not on the day.

2. Wrong name. The certificate is valid but does not cover the name the visitor typed. Typical after a migration: example.com is covered, www.example.com or shop.example.com is not.

3. Broken chain. The server does not send its intermediate certificate. Desktop browsers often repair this on their own, so the site "works for me", while API clients, payment callbacks and bots fail.

4. Self-signed or private CA. Fine on an internal tool, a problem on anything public.

Option A: openssl for one host

openssl is installed on most Linux and macOS machines and ships with Git for Windows:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -enddate -ext subjectAltName

This prints who the certificate is for, who issued it, its end date and every name it covers. -servername matters: without it, a server hosting several sites may hand you the wrong certificate. To check the chain, look for Verify return code: 0 (ok) in the output of the first command alone.

Option B: a short Python script for a list

Python's standard library can do a strict check, the same way an API client would, with no extra package:

import socket, ssl
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def check(host, port=443, warn_days=30):
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()  # verifies the chain and the hostname
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=10) as sock:
            with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host) as tls:
                cert = tls.getpeercert()
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        return f"BAD {host}: {e.verify_message}"
    except OSError as e:
        return f"ERR {host}: {e}"
    end = datetime.fromtimestamp(ssl.cert_time_to_seconds(cert["notAfter"]), timezone.utc)
    days = (end - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).days
    return f"{'OK ' if days > warn_days else 'BAD'} {host}: {days} days left"

for line in open("domains.txt", encoding="utf-8"):
    if line.strip():
        print(check(line.strip()))

Expired certificates, wrong names, self-signed certificates and missing intermediates all end up in the BAD branch with the reason. One limit: when verification fails, Python does not give you the certificate, so you see why it failed but not its dates or names. For that, fall back to the openssl command above. Run the script daily from cron or a scheduled task and you have a basic monitor.

Option C: a hosted checker for bulk jobs

Disclosure: this one is ours. We publish SSL Certificate Checker on Apify. You paste a list of domains, host:port pairs or full URLs, and it does one TLS handshake per host, up to 100 in parallel. Unlike the script above, it still reads and reports the certificate when it is not trusted.

from apify_client import ApifyClient  # pip install apify-client

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("extas_corp/ssl-certificate-checker").call(
    run_input={"domains": ["example.com", "smtp.example.com:465"], "warnDays": 21})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if not item["ok"]:
        print(item["host"], item.get("daysLeft"), item["warnings"], item["error"])

A certificate served for the wrong host comes back like this (shortened):

{
  "host": "wrong.host.badssl.com",
  "ok": false,
  "trusted": false,
  "trustError": "Hostname mismatch, certificate is not valid for 'wrong.host.badssl.com'.",
  "subject": "*.badssl.com",
  "daysLeft": 45
}

Each row also has the issuer, validFrom / validTo, all alternative names, a wildcard flag, the TLS version and cipher. ok is true only when the certificate is trusted, not expired and not expiring within warnDays. DNS, connection and timeout errors are reported on their row and do not stop the run.

It is free during launch: you only pay Apify's own platform usage, which the free monthly credit covers for normal use. Limits: it is not a full TLS security scan (no cipher enumeration, no vulnerability tests), revocation is not checked, STARTTLS ports such as SMTP 587 are not supported, and a CDN may serve a different certificate in another region than the one the check runs from.

What to put on the list

  • Every hostname, not only the main domain: www, apex, api, mail, old marketing subdomains.
  • Mail and other TLS services on their own ports (465, 993).
  • The vendors you depend on: an expired certificate on a payment or webhook endpoint breaks your site too.

Run it daily, alert only on BAD, and the next expiry becomes a ticket instead of an outage.

title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
description:
arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
description:
arXiv:2611.21907v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
description:
arXiv:2611.22499v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model.
  Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant.
  The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.

title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
description:
arXiv:2611.21952v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.
