title: Which post-quantum key exchanges does a server actually support?
description:
Every post-quantum migration starts with the same question: does this server support a post-quantum key exchange yet? It sounds like a yes or no. It isn't, because the honest answer depends on which client is asking.

I built pqc-probe to answer it from real handshakes instead of configuration files or advertised lists. It connects to a server over TLS and SSH, tries each key exchange one at a time, and reports which ones actually complete. Version 0.1.0 is out this week as a CLI, a web service, a Docker image and a GitHub Action.

This post covers what the tool measures, how to read its output, and what it found across the 1,000 most popular sites. Later posts in the series go deeper into the surprises along the way.

Offered is not negotiated

A TLS client sends a list of key exchange groups it can use, and the server picks one. A normal connection tells you only which group won, not which others the server would have accepted. So pqc-probe offers one group at a time and records whether the handshake completes:

openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -4

If that handshake succeeds, the server supports X25519MLKEM768. If it fails, the server does not, whatever any configuration page claims. The probe repeats this for seven groups: four classical (X25519, P-256, P-384, P-521) and three ML-KEM hybrids (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024).

SSH needs a different trick. The server sends its full list of key exchange algorithms before any encryption starts, so pqc-probe reads that packet directly. Then, for each post-quantum algorithm both sides know, it runs a real key exchange and marks the row ok (tested) only when the exchange completes. Being on the server's list is not enough.

Two clients, one diff

Which client asks matters, so pqc-probe asks with two:

Mode TLS client SSH client Answers
vanilla stock OpenSSL 3.5 stock OpenSSH What a normal production client gets today
experimental OpenSSL + oqs-provider OQS-OpenSSH What the Open Quantum Safe algorithms unlock

--mode both runs the two side by side and prints a diff. A group that only the experimental client can negotiate means the server supports something your users' clients cannot use yet. A group both can negotiate is deployable today.

There is one catch, and the tool flags it. OpenSSL 3.5 already supports ML-KEM hybrids out of the box. When the stock client is itself post-quantum capable, an empty diff says little about the server, so the report adds a note saying exactly that.

Reading a real report: github.com

Here is GitHub, probed from the Docker image with both protocols and both client stacks (trimmed):

$ docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
    pqc-probe probe github.com --protocol both --mode both

TLS KEMs (vanilla  vs  experimental):
  offered                   vanilla           experimental
  X25519                    ok                ok
  P-256                     ok                ok
  P-384                     -                 -
  P-521                     -                 -
  X25519MLKEM768            -                 -
  SecP256r1MLKEM768         -                 -
  SecP384r1MLKEM1024        -                 -

SSH KEX (server offer × client support):
  server offers                         mainline ssh      OQS-OpenSSH
  mlkem768x25519-sha256                 ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512                ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com    ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  curve25519-sha256                     ok                ok
  ...

SSH diff:
  Mainline ssh and OQS-OpenSSH negotiate identically on this target.

Two services on the same domain give opposite answers:

  • TLS (port 443): only X25519 and P-256 complete. The stock OpenSSL 3.5.7 offered ML-KEM, and GitHub's front end declined it. At the time of this run, a browser connecting to github.com got a classical key exchange.
  • SSH (port 22): three post-quantum key exchanges complete with both clients, so git push over SSH is already post-quantum.

The SSH diff is empty because the image's stock client is OpenSSH 10.0, which already supports these algorithms. The same probe from an older laptop with OpenSSH 9.6 showed two of them as "only experimental". That is the client changing, not the server.

What the top 1,000 sites do

Tranco list K9YYW, top 1,000, scanned 2026-11-06 with pqc-probe scan · one vantage point, IPv4 only · data and method in results/ in the repository]

Among the most popular sites that answer over TLS 1.3, post-quantum key exchange is already the majority. Read "accepts" strictly: the handshake completes when X25519MLKEM768 is offered alone, which shows support, not that the server prefers it.

The 305 sites without a handshake say nothing about post-quantum support either way: most are list entries with no DNS answer or no web server on port 443. The full dataset, the retry passes and the charts are in results/.

Three things that surprised me

  1. The SSH debug log cut the server's offer in half. My first version read the server's algorithm list from ssh -vv. On a test server with a long list, the line simply stopped mid-name: OpenSSH truncates debug lines at about 1 KB. Reading the key exchange packet directly fixed it.
  2. Testing too fast produced false negatives. OpenSSH 9.8 and later penalise addresses that open many short connections (PerSourcePenalties). My test server's log showed a 16-second penalty kicking in, after which real support looked like failure. The probe now tests at most 8 algorithms, one per second.
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum. OpenSSL 3.5 and OpenSSH 10 ship ML-KEM by default, so the classic "vanilla versus experimental" comparison is shrinking. Where it still shows a gap, the gap is usually an old client, not the server.

Each of these gets its own post in this series.

Try it

The Docker image carries both client stacks, so it is the quickest start:

docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
  pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both --mode both

With Rust 1.89 or later, the CLI installs from crates.io and uses the openssl and ssh already on your machine:

cargo install pqc-probe
pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both

Static Linux binaries are on the GitHub release page.

To check your own hosts on every deploy, the GitHub Action keeps a JSON report per host and can fail the job when a host has no post-quantum key exchange:

- uses: asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe@v0.1.0
  with:
    targets: api.example.com, git.example.com:2222
    require-pq-ssh: "true"

Every report follows a published JSON schema, which only ever gains fields within a version, so you can build on it. Please probe hosts you are responsible for.

What's next

The rest of this series:

  1. Your SSH debug log is truncating the server's offer
  2. Probing SSH without getting penalised
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum
  4. Shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way (#210, #211)
  5. Running a scanner for strangers: SSRF, DNS rebinding and rate limits

pqc-probe is the first project of three. pqc-bench measures what post-quantum TLS costs in performance, and a migration dashboard built on pqc-probe's reports comes next.

The code is on GitHub under MIT or Apache-2.0. Issues and results from your own servers are very welcome.

title: Troubleshooting AI Coding Assistants 2026: Stats & Solutions
description:
Originally published at nlocoding.com

43% of engineers spend more time debugging AI-generated code than writing it.

43%engineers spend more time debugging AI-generated code

AI coding assistants are supposed to save time—yet the reality is often more complicated. With tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and OpenClaw now everywhere, developers see a 40% reduction in coding time but face recurring headaches: misconfigurations, security risks, and code that needs constant correction. In 2026, troubleshooting AI coding assistants is no longer an edge case; it’s a daily survival skill (learn.ryzlabs.com).

Most troubleshooting in 2026 targets recurring code issues

70% of developers encounter recurring issues with AI-generated code, leading to wasted hours and increased frustration (learn.ryzlabs.com). This is not a minor annoyance: it’s the defining reality for anyone using these tools. Code suggestions that look helpful on the surface can mask subtle errors, bad patterns, or outright breakages. The solution isn’t to stop using AI coding assistants, but to build a habit of systematic review and small-batch testing. You’ll notice the code seems fine—until it isn’t. That’s where discipline beats automation.

⚠️Common Mistake: Trusting AI-generated code without reviewing logic or security. Most problems are repeat offenders.

Misconfigurations are the leading cause of AI assistant errors

67% of developers cite misconfigurations as the top source of errors in AI-assisted coding (learn.ryzlabs.com). This isn’t about some obscure edge case; it’s the default pitfall. Whether environment variables are missing, permissions are set wrong, or integrations are half-done, the assistant’s output becomes unreliable. The fastest fix: double-check configuration before blaming the AI. Configuration drift is the new silent killer of productivity. A single misspelled path or outdated API key, and suddenly the assistant’s magic is gone.

💡Pro Tip: Maintain a checklist for environment and tool configuration. Automate sanity checks in CI wherever possible.

Security flaws in 2026 AI coding agents expose real risks

Recent incidents show security isn’t theoretical. Grok Build exposed thousands of apps, with 94.7% accessible without login (techradar.com). OpenClaw’s privileged access across platforms makes it a potential single point of catastrophic failure (techradar.com). A developer’s worst day isn’t a build error—it’s discovering the AI assistant leaked sensitive data or gave attackers a backdoor. Every integration adds risk. The actionable move: review data flows, restrict permissions aggressively, and never treat AI-generated code as inherently safe. Security theater is out, real auditing is in.

AI coding assistants accelerate work—until structured-output tasks break

AI coding assistants reduce coding time by 40%, making them essential for any modern workflow (learn.ryzlabs.com). But speed isn’t everything. Even the most advanced models, like those recently released by Microsoft and Google, still fail on structured outputs (axios.com; tomsguide.com). Complex APIs, nested data, or intricate conditional logic remain weak spots. The fix is to use assistants for scaffolding or boilerplate, but own the structure yourself. Chasing full autonomy is a mirage. Here’s the thing nobody tells you: sometimes it’s faster to write the tricky parts by hand.

"Even the most advanced AI models fail more often than you think on structured outputs—raising doubts about the effectiveness of coding assistants." — techradar.com

Debugging AI-generated code now takes more time than writing from scratch for many engineers

43% of engineers report spending more time debugging AI-generated code than writing it (learn.ryzlabs.com). This is the paradox: AI tools promise speed, but the debugging process often eats up that gain. The main culprits are silent logic errors, style mismatches, and non-obvious dependency issues. The solution is not to abandon AI, but to treat debugging as a first-class workflow: write tests early, use static analysis, and make every AI commit go through a review—even if it’s just you reading it twice. Blind trust is expensive. Skepticism pays dividends.

AI assistant updates in 2026 drive productivity—but only when maintained

Microsoft’s upgrade to Copilot Chat in Visual Studio improved task completion rates from 103 to 124 out of 157 coding tasks (windowscentral.com). Yet, many assume once the assistant is set up, no further attention is needed. Updates matter: they patch vulnerabilities, boost accuracy, and widen the range of supported workflows. Skipping them is like running old antivirus software—it might look fine until it fails catastrophically. Always check for updates, and schedule reviews to catch deprecations before they bite.

The AI coding assistant tool landscape: comparison table

Tool Specialty Notable Feature
GitHub Copilot Code Suggestions Integrated with Visual Studio Code
Claude Code Code & PC Troubleshooting System diagnostics on Windows/macOS
OpenClaw Multiplatform Assistant Privileged access across apps
Grok Build App Coding Agent Rapid multi-app generation
Kimi AI K2.6 MoE Coding Open-weight expert model

FAQ: Troubleshooting AI Coding Assistants 2026

What is the most common cause of errors in AI coding assistants?Misconfigurations are the leading cause, with 67% of developers citing them as the most frequent source of AI-assisted coding errors.

Are AI-generated code snippets secure by default?No, AI-generated code is not inherently secure. Security flaws can be introduced if the code is not reviewed and tested carefully.

Do AI coding assistants need regular updates?Yes. Regular updates are crucial for fixing bugs, patching vulnerabilities, and improving performance. Neglecting updates leads to security and reliability risks.

Can AI coding assistants fully automate the development process?No. AI coding assistants require human oversight and intervention to ensure code quality, maintain security, and handle complex logic.

Where troubleshooting AI coding assistants goes next

The promise of AI coding assistants is real—40% less coding time is not a fantasy. But the frustrations are just as real: 70% of developers still see recurring issues, and nearly half spend more time debugging than writing from scratch. The lesson is not to reject these tools, but to treat them as powerful, fallible colleagues. Trust, verify, and automate your checks. In 2026, troubleshooting isn’t a chore; it’s the core skill that separates productive teams from those drowning in silent errors. If you’re still chasing the dream of a fully autonomous coding AI, you’re missing the real battle: making the assistant work for you, not the other way around.

More articles at nlocoding.com

title: Argon gc and restore now emit JSON
description:
Four argon commands printed only text, so a script could not read their result: argon gc and the three argon restore subcommands, preview, reset, and branch. A human could read the output, but nothing else could. The fix in argon-lab/argon#99 registers all four in the shared -o/--output list, so they take -o json like the rest of the CLI, and documents the shape of what they emit.

What changed

cli/cmd/output.go gains gcCmd, restorePreviewCmd, restoreResetCmd, and restoreBranchCmd in the shared output list. That single registration is what makes -o json available on all four.

The JSON bodies are built by small functions, gcReportJSON, restorePreviewJSON, restoreResetJSON, and restoreBranchJSON, so their shape is testable without a live project or WAL. That matters here because gc and restore need a real project to exercise end to end.

The shapes:

  • gc emits dry_run, branches (each branch name plus its cutoffs map), and entries_removed. Branches with no cutoffs are omitted, and branches is an empty list rather than null when nothing is reclaimable.
  • restore preview emits branch, current_lsn, target_lsn, operations_to_discard, and affected_collections, which is an object, empty rather than null.
  • restore reset emits branch, target_lsn, and backup_branch only when a backup branch was created.
  • restore branch emits the new branch name and the LSN it was forked at.

Why the registration test exists

A shape test alone would not catch the real defect. The PR includes TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput, which fails before the change with gc has no --output flag and the same for the three restore subcommands. The shape tests, TestGCReportJSONShape and TestRestoreJSONShapes, pass on their own because they call the builder functions directly. Only the registration test proves the flag is wired to the command. The PR runs both, plus the whole ./cmd/ package.

Verification from the PR 

$ cd cli && go build ./...          # ok
$ go test ./cmd/ -run 'TestGCReportJSONShape|TestRestoreJSONShapes|TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput' -v
=== RUN   TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput
--- PASS: TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestGCReportJSONShape
--- PASS: TestGCReportJSONShape (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestRestoreJSONShapes
--- PASS: TestRestoreJSONShapes (0.00s)
PASS
ok      argon-cli/cmd   0.012s
$ go test ./cmd/                    # whole package, existing tests included
ok      argon-cli/cmd   5.562s

gofmt -l cmd/ prints nothing and go vet on the package is clean. The repository build was run inside the nested cli module, which is where these commands live. The change is 6 files, 195 lines added and 1 removed, and it closes issue #75.

Why this matters this week

The week's trending projects are dominated by coding agents and the tooling around them: GitHub Trending lists agent skill bundles, MCP servers, and workflow orchestrators, and dev.to's trending clusters include AI coding agents and the risks of agents reading untrusted input. The honest link is narrow. An agent that drives a CLI cannot parse prose, so a command that only prints text is opaque to it. This PR makes gc and restore readable by a script or agent, with named fields instead of scraped sentences. That is the whole change, and it is enough.

Sources checked on 18 November 2026: trendshift.io/weekly, github.com/trending, and dev.to/trending.

The rule to carry

When a command already has a shared output mechanism, add new subcommands to it instead of inventing a second flag. Then split the work into two tests: one that calls the builder and checks the shape, and one that checks the flag is registered on the command. The first proves the data is right, the second proves a user can actually ask for it. Fixing only one leaves either a correct shape nobody can request, or a flag that emits nothing.

The diagram for this piece is short. Four commands on the left, the fields they now emit on the right:

Four commands, one shared output flag, documented fields instead of prose.

title: Best animation library for Unity UI Toolkit: Cascade vs PrimeTween vs LitMotion
description:
If you search for a way to animate Unity UI Toolkit, three libraries come up: PrimeTween, LitMotion and Cascade. All three can fade and move a VisualElement. They were built for different jobs, and that shows once your UI gets bigger than one button.

Disclosure: I make Cascade. I've tried to be fair to the other two. Every claim about PrimeTween and LitMotion below comes from their source code and docs (PrimeTween 1.5.2, LitMotion 2.0.2, checked November 2026). The Cascade version is 1.2. Every code sample here was compiled and run in one Unity 6000.4 project with all three libraries installed, and checked against what the text says it does. If something is wrong or out of date, tell me and I'll fix the page.

The short answer

  • Your project already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion for gameplay: use the same library for simple UI Toolkit tweens. One tween library is easier than two.
  • You need the fastest possible tweens for thousands of objects: LitMotion (Burst and the Job System) or PrimeTween. In my UI Toolkit benchmark below, LitMotion was the fastest, Cascade second and PrimeTween third.
  • Your UI is built in UI Toolkit and has a lot of motion (screens that come and go, lists, interruptible buttons, springs): Cascade was written for exactly that.
  • You write most of your UI code with an AI assistant: Cascade is the only one of the three with official assistant support. See AI coding assistants.
  • You're on Unity 2022 or older: Cascade needs Unity 6, so pick PrimeTween or LitMotion.

At a glance

PrimeTween LitMotion Cascade
Built for Transforms, materials, uGUI, also UI Toolkit Any value, very fast (DOTS) UI Toolkit only
Price free (PRO edition $32.99 adds Inspector animations) free Lite free; Pro paid
License custom (free for commercial use) MIT Lite MIT; Pro Asset Store EULA
Unity 2018.4+ (per its package) 2021.3+ 6000.0+
Dependencies none Burst, Collections, Mathematics none
UI Toolkit tweens built in opacity, color, background color, translate/rotate/scale, left/top/width/height opacity, colors, translate, scale, rotate, transform-origin, left/right/top/bottom, width/height, font size, text, progress bar opacity, translate, scale, rotate, colors, width/height, left/top/right/bottom, border radius/width/color, font size, padding, background-image tint, slide-in from an edge, any float
Other styles Tween.Custom Bind Value
Sequencing yes (Sequence) yes (LSequence, since 2.0) yes (Then(), At(seconds))
Await yes yes yes
Physics springs no (elastic/overshoot easing) no (elastic easing) Pro
Stagger helper no (use delays) no (use delays) Pro
Shake / punch Transform only yes (float/Vector values, bind to any style) yes: Shake, Punch (Lite); PunchScale, PunchRotate, Pulse, Wiggle, Pop (Pro). Additive, always end at rest
Stops when the element leaves the panel no (measured: keeps writing to it) no (measured: keeps writing to it) yes
Reduced motion setting no no yes (Lite and Pro)
AI coding assistant support no official support (community-made agent skills exist) no official support (community-made agent skills exist) official agent skill, AI guide in the package, compile-time code checks; Pro: validated JSON animations
Screen transitions, hover/press, no-code component no no (the Inspector component has no UI Toolkit tracks) Pro

The same animation in all three

A panel fades in while it slides up 40 px, a common way to show a window.

PrimeTween 

using PrimeTween;

Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);
Tween.Position(panel, startValue: new Vector3(0, 40, 0), endValue: Vector3.zero, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);

Tween.Position, Rotation and Scale accept a VisualElement and write style.translate, rotate and scale on Unity 6.2 and newer.

LitMotion 

using LitMotion;
using LitMotion.Extensions;

LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleOpacity(panel);
LMotion.Create(new Vector2(0, 40), Vector2.zero, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleTranslate(panel);

Every motion takes an explicit start value. LitMotion has the widest set of built-in style bindings of the three.

Cascade 

using Cascade;

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);

Without From(), Cascade starts from the value the element has on the frame the animation begins, including values that come from USS.

A sequence: fade in, then pop

PrimeTween 

Sequence.Create()
    .Chain(Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.2f))
    .Chain(Tween.Scale(panel, endValue: new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), duration: 0.2f, ease: Ease.OutBack))
    .ChainCallback(() => Debug.Log("done"));

LitMotion 

LSequence.Create()
    .Append(LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.2f).BindToStyleOpacity(panel))
    .Append(LMotion.Create(Vector3.one, new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), 0.2f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack).BindToStyleScale(panel))
    .Run(b => b.WithOnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done")));

Cascade 

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
     .Then()
     .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
     .OnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done"));

All three read well. All three can also place a tween at an exact time inside a sequence: PrimeTween and LitMotion with Insert, Cascade with At(seconds).

Where the differences show up

When the element leaves the screen

PrimeTween stops a tween when its target is a destroyed UnityEngine.Object, and LitMotion links motions to a GameObject with AddTo. A VisualElement isn't a Unity object, so neither check applies. Neither library listens for an element being removed from its panel, so when a screen closes or a list row is recycled mid-tween, stop it yourself. I measured it: a 2-second fade, with the element removed after 0.3 s, keeps changing the removed element's opacity in both libraries.

// PrimeTween
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => Tween.StopAll(onTarget: panel));

// LitMotion: keep the handles and cancel them
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => handle.TryCancel());

Cascade cancels an animation when its element leaves the panel and never writes to an element that isn't displayed. In a UI with many screens, that's the bug class I most wanted to remove.

Interrupting an animation

Buttons and drawers get interrupted all the time: hover out before the hover-in finishes, close a drawer while it's opening. With PrimeTween or LitMotion you stop the old tween and start a new one, usually from the current value. The new tween starts from rest, so the motion visibly loses its momentum.

Cascade Pro has physics springs. A spring that gets a new target keeps its current velocity, so the motion bends toward the new target instead of restarting:

drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);

Neither PrimeTween nor LitMotion has a velocity-based spring. Their elastic and overshoot easings look springy on a single run, but they restart on interruption.

Lists

Making ten items enter one after another is a loop with a growing delay in PrimeTween (startDelay) or LitMotion (WithDelay). That works well. Cascade Pro has a helper for it:

items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(16f).Stagger(0.05f);

Reduced motion

Cascade has a global setting, MotionSettings.Mode: Reduced shortens animations and removes bounce, Crossfade replaces movement with fades, and None jumps to the end state but still fires OnComplete, so code that waits on an animation keeps working. Connect it to a "reduce motion" option in your settings menu. PrimeTween and LitMotion have no equivalent; you'd add the checks yourself.

AI coding assistants

A lot of UI code is now written by asking Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or Codex. How well that goes depends on what the assistant knows about the library.

PrimeTween and LitMotion have been public since 2023 and 2024, so assistants have seen plenty of code that uses them. Neither project ships official assistant material, but community-made agent skills for both exist on GitHub. The catch for UI Toolkit is that most of that code animates Transforms, so assistants tend to reach for transform APIs, and don't know which VisualElement methods exist in the version you have.

Cascade is new, so an assistant without help will guess its API. To fix that, it ships three things:

  • An official agent skill (npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill) for any agent that reads SKILL.md files. It checks whether your project has Lite or Pro and writes only code that tier can compile.
  • An AI guide inside the package (Documentation~/AI-GUIDE.md, both tiers), so the assistant reads instructions that match your installed version.
  • Validated JSON animations (Pro). An assistant can describe an effect as JSON; SequencePreset.Validate returns the exact step, field and a suggested fix for a typo, and Lint flags animations that would do nothing, such as a fade-in without a start value. The assistant can correct itself before you ever press Play.

Here's what that looks like. An assistant writes this entrance, with a verb name that doesn't exist:

{ "steps": [ { "actions": [
  { "verb": "SlideIn", "edge": "Bottom", "distance": 40, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" },
  { "verb": "FadeIn", "to": 1, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" }
] } ] }

Validate says where the mistake is and what to use instead:

MotionError err = SequencePreset.Validate(json);
// err.Path       → steps[0].actions[1].verb
// err.Suggestion → Fade

After the assistant renames it to Fade, the JSON is valid, but the fade still has no start value, so it would fade to where it already is and nothing would appear to happen. LintSummary catches that:

steps[0].actions[1]: 'Fade' animates to 1, which is where the element already rests, and nothing earlier in this sequence moved it — so this action will run and change nothing — add "from" to say where it starts (e.g. "from": 0), or drop the action

Adding "from": 0 clears both checks. All three messages above are the real output of Cascade.

I tested how much this matters. Claude Opus 5.5, running headless in Claude Code with no web access, wrote six common UI Toolkit animations: a panel entrance, a fade-then-pop sequence, a staggered list, a drawer that can be reversed mid-move, an endless pulse that stops when the element is removed, and an error shake. Every answer was compiled and run in Unity against a check for each task. When an answer failed, the compiler errors or failed checks went back to the model until it passed, and every token of every round was counted. Each setup ran 10 times.

The first round caught three mistakes in Cascade's own AI guide. It didn't say that Loop() repeats only the step right before it, it called Delay() a wait when it delays the step before it, and one example used a method overload that doesn't exist. Only 5 of 10 Cascade answers were right first time. I fixed the guide in the current Cascade 1.2, and the numbers below are from the fixed guide.

Each library got the setup you'd give it in practice. PrimeTween and LitMotion ship no assistant setup, so the model got each library's official docs plus a list of its UI Toolkit methods, and separately no docs at all, since it already knows both. Cascade ran in a Unity project with the package installed and its Set Up AI Assistants menu already run, which writes a short Cascade section into CLAUDE.md pointing at the guide in the package. Its prompt didn't mention any docs.

Setup Right first time Output tokens Cost per run Lines of code
Cascade 1.2, set-up project 10/10 1,546 $0.14 42
PrimeTween + its docs 10/10 4,841 $0.38 87
LitMotion + its docs 10/10 3,636 $0.25 115
PrimeTween, no docs 10/10 3,466 $0.14 90
LitMotion, no docs 10/10 2,866 $0.12 104
No library (plain UI Toolkit) 10/10 3,932 $0.15 163

The numbers are medians of 10 runs. Cost is what Claude Code reported, at list API prices.

A bigger task tells the same story: a settings screen with a modal that can be reopened while it's closing, a toggle, a toast that stays up while it's re-triggered, a number that counts up, and press feedback. Each setup ran 5 times:

Setup Right first time Output tokens Cost per run Lines of code
Cascade 1.2, set-up project 5/5 6,659 $0.29 153
PrimeTween + its docs 5/5 11,046 $0.56 212
LitMotion + its docs 5/5 10,134 $0.43 251
No library (plain UI Toolkit) 5/5 9,422 $0.31 310

What I take from it:

  • Every setup got every task right in the end, so this compares cost, not ability.
  • Cascade's answers were the shortest and used the fewest output tokens, because one fluent call covers what takes a loop or a helper in the others.
  • In dollars, a set-up Cascade project cost about the same as plain UI Toolkit or PrimeTween without docs. LitMotion without docs was the cheapest on the small tasks, about 13% cheaper than Cascade. Giving PrimeTween or LitMotion their docs made them the most expensive, because reading the docs is most of the cost.

Here's one Cascade answer, exactly as the model wrote it:

public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
        .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
        .Then()
        .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
        .OnComplete(onDone);
}

public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items)
{
    // From(0) is applied to every item immediately, so not-yet-started items stay invisible.
    items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Stagger(0.05f);
}

public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open)
{
    // MoveX replaces any running MoveX and continues from the current value.
    drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge)
{
    // Cascade cancels animations automatically when the element leaves the panel.
    badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.5f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong);
}

public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field)
{
    field.Animate().Shake(10f, 0.4f);
}

This was the prompt for PrimeTween with docs. The others changed only the library name and namespace. The no-docs runs replaced the docs sentence with “You have no documentation for the library: write it from what you already know about its API.” Cascade's runs had no docs sentence, and the plain UI Toolkit runs were told to use only built-in UI Toolkit APIs.

Using PrimeTween 1.5.2 (com.kyrylokuzyk.primetween), complete the six tasks in tasks.md (read it). Use the namespace AiTok.s_PTdocs_01. The file docs.md in this folder is the library's documentation; read it first and rely on it. Do not search the web. Write your answer as a single C# file named Tasks.cs in the current folder, then reply with one line saying you are done.

And the six tasks it was given (tasks.md):

# Six Unity UI Toolkit animation tasks

Write one C# file that compiles in a Unity 6 project with the library installed. Use this exact shape
(replace NAMESPACE with the namespace you were given; keep the class and method names and signatures):

~~~csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;
// add the library's using directives

namespace NAMESPACE
{
    public static class Tasks
    {
        public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel) { ... }
        public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone) { ... }
        public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items) { ... }
        public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open) { ... }
        public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge) { ... }
        public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field) { ... }
    }
}
~~~

All elements are already in a visible UIDocument panel. Durations are in seconds. Each method starts the
animation and returns immediately (no blocking, no coroutines that the caller must start).

1. **EnterPanel**: the panel fades in from opacity 0 to 1 and slides up from 40 px below its resting
   position (translate Y from 40 to 0), both over 0.3 s with an ease-out cubic curve.
2. **FadeThenPop**: fade the panel from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.2 s; when that finishes, scale it from 1 to
   1.1 over 0.2 s with an "out back" ease; when the scale finishes, call `onDone` exactly once.
3. **StaggerIn**: every item fades from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.3 s. Item i starts 0.05 × i seconds after
   item 0 (item 0 starts immediately). Items that haven't started yet must be invisible (opacity 0).
4. **SetDrawerOpen**: move the drawer horizontally (translate X) to 0 when `open` is true and to -320 when
   false, over 0.3 s with an ease-out curve. It may be called again while the previous call is still
   animating: the drawer must then continue smoothly from wherever it is now (no jump) to the new target,
   and the old animation must not keep fighting it.
5. **PulseForever**: scale the badge from 1 to 1.1 and back, continuously (0.5 s each way), forever. When
   the badge is removed from the hierarchy, the animation must stop (nothing keeps writing to it).
6. **ShakeOnError**: shake the field horizontally (translate X), up to about 10 px either side, for about
   0.4 s, ending exactly at translate X = 0 (it starts at 0).

It's one model in one tool, Claude Code with Opus 5.5, so other assistants may land differently. Where medians are within a few cents of each other (Cascade, PrimeTween without docs, plain UI Toolkit), the run-to-run ranges overlap, so treat those as about equal.

Details are on the AI assistants page.

Raw speed

LitMotion runs on Burst, and PrimeTween is built to make zero allocations. I measured all three on UI Toolkit: a release (Mono) player on an Apple M-series Mac, N elements each animating opacity and translate X back and forth forever, the same curve and timing in every library, 5 seconds measured after a 2-second warm-up, 3 runs each. The numbers are the extra milliseconds per frame over the same elements with no animation:

Elements PrimeTween LitMotion Cascade
100 0.1 ms 0.1 ms 0.1 ms
500 0.5 ms 0.3 ms 0.4 ms
1,000 0.8 ms 0.5 ms 0.7 ms
2,000 1.5 ms 0.9 ms 1.3 ms

None of the three allocated any memory per frame. The player's frame timer moves in 0.1 ms steps, so treat a difference of 0.1 ms as a tie. LitMotion is the fastest, Cascade is in between, and for typical UI, where tens of elements move at once, the difference doesn't matter: all three cost about 0.1 ms.

Where Cascade is the weaker choice

  • Unity 6 only. Projects on 2022 LTS or older can't use it.
  • UI Toolkit only. It doesn't animate Transforms, uGUI or materials. If you need those too, you'll have a second library anyway.
  • Springs, stagger, transitions and the no-code component are paid. PrimeTween and LitMotion are free. Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers the tweens, sequences, await and reduced motion.
  • Younger and smaller. PrimeTween and LitMotion have years of use and large communities. Cascade launched in 2026.
  • Assistants don't know it by default. With no setup, an assistant guesses Cascade's API, while it already knows PrimeTween and LitMotion. One menu in the package fixes that, but it's a step the other two don't need.

Which one should you pick?

  • A few UI Toolkit tweens in a game that already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion: keep it.
  • Performance-critical tweening of many objects: LitMotion.
  • A simple, free, well-documented tween API for everything: PrimeTween.
  • A UI Toolkit interface with a lot of motion: start with Cascade Lite (free), and move to Cascade Pro if you need springs, stagger or screen transitions.

Sources

  • PrimeTween: GitHub (README, changelog, benchmarks) and the 1.5.2 package source.
  • LitMotion: GitHub (2.0.2 source, LitMotionUIToolkitExtensions.cs) and its docs.
  • Cascade: the Cascade docs and the API reference.

title: Your Go Function Returned a Nil Error and the Caller Saw an Error Anyway
description:
The order service
had a validation step.

It returned an error
if the quantity was wrong,
and nothing if it was fine.

type QtyError struct{ Qty int }

func (e *QtyError) Error() string {
return fmt.Sprintf("bad quantity %d", e.Qty)
}

func validate(o Order) error {
var err *QtyError
if o.Qty <= 0 {
err = &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return err
}

The caller did the usual thing:

if err := validate(o); err != nil {
reject(o, err)
}

Every order was rejected.

Including the good ones.

Then the log line
that printed the reason
crashed with a nil pointer dereference.

Here is the mechanism.

In Go,
an interface value has two parts.

A type.

And a value.

It equals nil
only when both are empty.

validate returns error,
which is an interface.

Inside, err was a *QtyError
that happened to be nil.

Returning it
put the type *QtyError
into the interface,
with a nil pointer as the value.

Type filled in.

Value empty.

So err != nil
was true.

An interface holding a nil pointer
is not a nil interface.

The Go FAQ has a whole entry on it,
titled
"Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?"

And Error() ran
on a nil *QtyError,
reached for e.Qty,
and panicked.

The fix is small.

Return the interface,
not the concrete pointer:

func validate(o Order) error {
if o.Qty <= 0 {
return &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return nil
}

That nil
is the untyped kind,
and it reaches the caller
as a true nil.

The rule underneath:

never declare a variable
of your own error type
and return it as error.

Declare it as error,
or return nil by name.

The same trap waits
anywhere a nil pointer
is handed to an interface.

A nil *bytes.Buffer
passed as an io.Writer.

A nil *Config
stored in an any.

Each one
looks like nothing
and compares as something.

When a check says
something is there
and you can see nothing,
ask what type
it was wrapped in.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2611.21646v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
